targets.success_criterion: At least 1 PAIR of eBL fragments meeting ALL of: (a) at verification time both public records have joins == [], no corpus-chapter manuscript link (checked against the manuscripts lists of all chapters via /api/texts), no reference, uncuratedReference or note naming a composition, and genre absent or 'OTHER:Uncertain'; (b) neither fragment aligns to any eBL chapter or Oracc edition under the ebl-fragment-identification thresholds (otherwise it belongs to that target); (c) the unidentified set searched is defined by a published deterministic rule and its museum-number list is frozen (hash) before alignment; after normalising readings to sign names (the public 'signs' field), the two fragments share an alignment of at least 2 consecutive lines or at least 12 consecutive signs with at most 10% mismatches; (d) the alignment score has p < 1e-4 against a null that aligns the fragment to all other fragments of the frozen set with line order shuffled, Bonferroni-corrected over all pairs tested; (e) the shared text is not a formula recurring in at least 5 unrelated compositions (omen protases, incantation refrains, lexical entries, colophons, year names), verified by corpus-wide counting over the eBL corpus and Oracc; (f) the pair is not in the top 10 returned for either fragment by eBL's public ngram-matcher library (TF-IDF overlap strategy, default n-values) when the verifier runs it over the same frozen set; (g) the two museum numbers are not the same physical tablet (different collection or non-adjoining provenance, and no published direct join recorded). Claim as 'candidate indirect join'; CONFIRMED only when the eBL team or an Assyriologist accepts it. Records (a) and the library run (f) are re-executed live immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: A pair meeting (a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (g) that DOES appear in the public ngram-matcher top 10 for one fragment but is recorded nowhere in either eBL record (no join, chapter link, reference, uncuratedReference or note) and not in the publications the records cite.
A cluster of at least 3 unidentified fragments that pairwise meet (a)-(g) and whose union, aligned, yields a composite of at least 5 consecutive lines with each line attested on at least 2 fragments.

targets.verification_method: The verifier fetches both fragment records via the public eBL API (timestamp recorded), checks joins/genres/references/uncuratedReferences/notes and the chapter manuscript lists, recomputes the alignment with independent code on the public sign-name field, re-runs the shuffled-line null over the frozen set (hash checked), pip-installs the public ngram-matcher library and runs it for both fragments over the same set, checks formulaicity against the eBL corpus and Oracc, and confirms the fragments are not a recorded direct join. Throttled API fetching of a 1,000-2,000 fragment set plus alignment fits in under an hour on a 10-core Mac.
angles: Pull the unidentified set via the query endpoint (throttled), normalise readings to sign names, index sign 4-grams with inverted lists and only align pairs sharing 2+ rare 4-grams (rare = document frequency < 20).
Weight shared n-grams by inverse corpus frequency so that lexical-list and omen formulae do not dominate (the eBL matcher's TF-IDF variant is the baseline to beat).
Use physical metadata (collection, script, period, dimensions) only as a tie-breaker, never as evidence; Kuyunjik (K., Sm., Rm., DT) fragments are the densest source of duplicates.
Build the shuffled-line null once per fragment and reuse it across all its pair tests; report Bonferroni over the number of pairs actually scored.
Cluster pairwise hits into connected components to attempt the p2 multi-fragment composite.
pitfalls: Formulaic genres (Summa alu protases, Maqlu refrains, Hh lexical entries, Ur III year names, colophons) produce long shared sign runs that are NOT shared compositions; enforce (e) by corpus-wide counting.
Two museum numbers can be the same tablet (direct join already published but unrecorded in eBL, or re-numbered); check cited publications and the eBL 'joins' field live.
Sign-reading normalisation errors (homophone indices, broken-sign brackets, x signs) can both create and hide matches; use sign names and treat damaged signs as wildcards with a penalty.
Some records have restricted authorizedScopes; use only public data, throttle requests and respect eBL terms of use.
The in-platform matcher endpoint (/api/fragments/{id}/match) is not public (403); only the open-source ngram-matcher library run on public API data counts as the baseline gate.

The public 'signs' field encodes editorial restorations (bracketed text in the record's ATF) exactly like attested signs, so a shared run can be an editor's restoration matched against itself. Derive attested positions from each record's text tokens (the enclosureType field marks BROKEN_AWAY parts) and count only runs attested on both fragments. Found 2026-10-16: re-aligning 1,109 raw-sign overlaps on attested signs kept 123, and the strongest raw hit (VAT.18937 | VAT.25937, 71 shared signs) had 42 restored signs on one side.

'Genre absent' in eBL mostly means uncurated, and the uncurated set is dominated by administrative and legal records. Identifying labels live in references[].notes (e.g. 'Income of barley') and in 'dossiers' (e.g. 'Babylon N1'), not in 'notes' or 'genres'; read those fields for clause (a), and treat any archive edition as a fail. Of 808 records of candidate pairs checked on 2026-10-16, only 37 were clean on all fields.

Clause (d) as written (p < 1e-4 after Bonferroni over all pairs tested, by line-shuffled simulation) cannot be reached by simulation: with thousands of pairs the level is below 1e-8 and a pooled null of 10^4-10^5 shuffles floors at about 1e-4. State a reachable level or accept a pre-registered parametric (Gumbel) tail; 'beats every control' remains checkable.

angles: Hybridise rather than replace: use the learned model only to reweight the thermodynamic model's base-pair probabilities, so the worst case degrades to RNAstructure instead of to 0.12.
Cross-domain import (domain generalisation in vision): train with family labels as domains and an explicit invariance penalty, so the network cannot rely on family-specific sequence signatures.

Cross-domain import (natural language parsing): secondary structure is a nested bracketing; use a parser with an explicit grammar and learned rule scores, which cannot output physically impossible structures.
Telomerase RNAs are the longest sequences in the set, so test whether the collapse is a length-extrapolation failure by training on artificially lengthened sequences of other families.
Calibrate on an entirely different held-out family than the test family when picking any hyperparameter, so the protocol stays honest and the result transfers.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: RNA secondary structure across families: beat the best published family-fold F1 on ArchiveII, especially telomerase RNA

partial_wins.statement: Telomerase RNA alone: F1 above RNAstructure's 0.50 with a learned model, under the family-fold rule, with the same frozen model's scores on all nine families reported (every published deep model is at or below 0.12 there).
A model under 150M parameters whose nine-family mean beats RNAstructure's 0.60 by at least 0.05 under the family-fold rule, trainable on a laptop.

A reproducible diagnosis of the telomerase collapse (for example sequence length, pseudoknots, or embedding overlap with SRP RNA as the RiNALMo authors note) with a controlled experiment that isolates the cause.

pitfalls: Pretraining corpora (Rfam, RNAcentral, bpRNA) contain the held-out families; using them without filtering breaks the family-fold design even though no labelled structure was seen.
ArchiveII and RNAStralign overlap heavily; training on RNAStralign and testing on ArchiveII is not the family-fold protocol and gives much higher numbers.
Different papers score with different base-pair F1 conventions (shifted pairs allowed, pseudoknots counted or not); use the dl-rna scoring code and say which convention is used.
Reporting only the mean hides a telomerase-style collapse; the criterion requires every family to stay at or above the thermodynamic baseline.
Better secondary-structure prediction is one input to RNA therapeutic design, not a validated design; claims must stop at the benchmark.
targets.statement: Marcell Szikszai, Michael Wise, Amitava Datta, Max Ward and David Mathews (Bioinformatics 2022) showed that deep-learning RNA secondary-structure predictors collapse when tested on RNA families absent from training, and released the family-fold cross-validation split of ArchiveII (3,865 sequences, nine families) with code at github.com/marcellszi/dl-rna. Under that split, thermodynamic RNAstructure averages F1 0.60 while retrained MXfold2 reaches 0.51 and UFold 0.44. The strongest later result is RiNALMo (Rafael Penic and co-authors, arXiv:2403.00043), which reports mean F1 0.71 on the same nine-family evaluation and beats RNAstructure on eight of nine families, but collapses on telomerase RNA at F1 0.12 against RNAstructure's 0.50; its 150M variant reaches 0.08 there and RNA-FM 0.07. A single frozen model that keeps RiNALMo's mean and fixes telomerase, or that raises the mean itself, is an open and laptop-checkable result; the data are a few megabytes and scoring is base-pair F1.
targets.success_criterion: Predicted secondary structures (dot-bracket or base-pair lists) for every sequence of the ArchiveII family-fold evaluation set, produced by models trained strictly under the family-fold protocol (for each test family, no sequence of that family anywhere in training, pretraining corpora declared and checked for that family), whose per-family F1 scores computed by the skeptic with the dl-rna repository's scoring code give a mean over the nine families STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the best published mean for this split (0.71, RiNALMo, arXiv:2403.00043 Table S3, re-fetched live immediately before claiming) by at least 0.02, with no family below the RNAstructure value for that family, and higher than any later published value found by the novelty check.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic takes the ArchiveII family-fold splits from github.com/marcellszi/dl-rna, checks the prediction file covers every sequence, computes per-family base-pair F1 with the repository's scoring code, and audits training logs and pretraining corpora for any sequence of the held-out family (including homologues above a stated identity threshold). Minutes to score; retraining is the attacker's cost.

angles: The published even-n solutions were found by a search that explores few states; reproduce that search and extend it with a better admissible heuristic combining breakpoints, anti-adjacencies and wrong adjacencies as Bouzy's weighted heuristic does.

Cross-domain import (SAT and constraint solving): encode 'sortable in exactly k flips' as a propositional formula with symmetry breaking and hand it to a modern solver, which turns the existence question into a certificate either way.
Cross-domain import (group theory): the stacks form a Cayley graph; use coset enumeration or a subgroup decomposition to prune whole branches instead of searching permutations one by one.

Build constructive sequences from the odd-n proof scheme and test exactly where it fails for even n, as the authors state their construction cannot be applied there; a repaired construction for one residue class would settle a family at once.
Meet in the middle: bidirectional search from I_n and from the identity, with a perfect hash of stacks, is memory-bound but well suited to a laptop with tens of gigabytes.

targets.name: Burnt pancake sorting: settle T(n) for an even n by finding a flipping sequence that attains the lower bound

partial_wins.statement: Re-verify the published n = 24 (37 flips) and n = 26 (40 flips) sequences with an independent checker and publish the checker, since these two values contradict an earlier published table and deserve independent confirmation.
A search that decides T(n) for one further even n by exhaustion, even if the answer is the upper value 3n/2 + 2, with a reproducible certificate and the search's state count.
An improved admissible heuristic for the burnt-pancake graph, demonstrated by solving a published hard stack strictly faster than the reported times in Bouzy's table, with code released.

pitfalls: Confusing T(n), the flips to sort the special stack I_n, with g(n), the diameter of the whole burnt-pancake graph; the OEIS has separate sequences (A078942 and A078941) and they differ at n = 15.
Published tables disagree: the 2016 technical report's values for n = 24 and n = 26 were later shown to be wrong, so a claim must name the source it beats and check the live OEIS entry.
An inadmissible heuristic makes a non-existence claim worthless; admissibility must be proved, not assumed, before a lower-bound certificate counts.
Off-by-one conventions in flip definitions (whether a flip of size 1 counts, whether the spatula goes below or above) change the answer; state the convention and reproduce a known value first.
This is a combinatorial model of genome rearrangement, not a statement about real genomes; a new value says nothing directly about any organism.
targets.statement: Sorting burnt pancakes (prefix reversals with orientation) is the textbook model for genome rearrangement by reversals, and T(n), the number of flips needed to sort the all-burnt-side-up sorted stack I_n = [-1,-2,...,-n], is tabulated in OEIS A078942 with the related diameter in A078941. Gerold Jager and Nacim Oijid (arXiv:2601.09447) closed the odd case by proving the upper bound floor((3n+3)/2) for n = 1 mod 4, matching Josef Cibulka's 2011 lower bound, so for odd n the value is exact. For even n only two values remain possible, 3n/2 + 1 or 3n/2 + 2, and which one holds is open. By explicit search the same authors found sequences attaining the lower bound for n = 24 (37 flips) and n = 26 (40 flips), disproving the values Bruno Bouzy's 2016 technical report listed for those two n, and they note these are the only even n above 2 where the lower bound is known to be attained. Deciding another even n, in either direction, is a checkable new record.
targets.success_criterion: For some even n not already decided in the live OEIS entry A078942 and its references (re-fetched live immediately before claiming), either (a) an explicit flipping sequence that sorts I_n in exactly 3n/2 + 1 flips, verified by a checker that applies each prefix reversal with sign flipping and confirms the final stack is [1,2,...,n] with all burnt sides down, or (b) an exhaustive-search certificate, independently re-runnable within a stated time budget, that no sequence of 3n/2 + 1 flips sorts I_n, hence T(n) = 3n/2 + 2. Either way the value must be strictly new: not already listed for that n in A078942 or in arXiv:2601.09447, and the novelty check must find no later publication giving it.
targets.verification_method: A twenty-line checker applies the claimed flips to [-1,...,-n] and compares with the identity stack; that side is seconds. For a non-existence certificate the skeptic re-runs the released search with the published heuristic and seed, or checks an independently generated proof artefact (for example a pruned-search log with reproducible node counts), and confirms the heuristic used is admissible.

angles: Hard split means the right EC level-3 class has no training reaction, so retrieval must go through another modality: rank candidate ECs by similarity of the query reaction to the reaction CENTRES (atom-mapped bond changes) implied by EC class definitions, which are text and exist for unseen classes.

Cross-domain import (zero-shot classification in vision): describe each EC class by attributes (bond type broken/formed, cofactor, substrate class) parsed from the EC nomenclature and learn a reaction-to-attribute model, as zero-shot learning does for unseen object classes.

Cross-domain import (information retrieval): reciprocal rank fusion of several weak rankers (DRFP similarity, reaction-centre fingerprint, text similarity of EC names) is robust and needs no learned weights.
Exploit hierarchy: predict level 1, then level 2 conditioned on level 1, etc., with a hierarchical softmax; errors at deep levels are less costly to the shallow-level metrics.
Use the optional protein2EC file: embed sequences of enzymes with known ECs (small ESM-2 on CPU) and connect reactions to ECs through predicted substrate-binding residues or Pfam domains.

targets.name: CARE benchmark: beat the best published accuracy for retrieving the enzyme class (EC number) of an unseen reaction

partial_wins.statement: Task 2 hard split: level-3 accuracy above the published best by >= 3 points (predicting EC classes never seen with any training reaction).
Task 2 medium split: level-4 accuracy above the published best by >= 3 points.
Task 1 <30% identity split: level-4 accuracy above CLEAN's published value by >= 3 points with a CPU-feasible method (e.g. small protein language model embeddings plus retrieval).

pitfalls: The hard and medium splits hold out entire EC numbers/classes; using full EC-to-reaction databases (Rhea, BRENDA, KEGG) that include the held-out reactions is leakage even if it looks like 'external knowledge'.
ChatGPT-style baselines were flagged in the paper as possibly leaked; an LLM-based method has the same problem and must be shown not to recall the test reactions.
Promiscuous-split and k=1 accuracy conventions differ (k equals number of true ECs there); use the notebook's exact definitions.
Later papers may already report higher numbers on CARE; the NOVELTY skeptic must search for them before a claim.
targets.statement: CARE (Classification And Retrieval of Enzymes; Jason Yang, Ariane Mora, Shengchao Liu, Bruce Wittmann, Anima Anandkumar, Frances Arnold, Yisong Yue; NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks 2024, arXiv:2406.15669) fixes train/test splits for two tasks. Task 2 asks: given a chemical reaction, rank EC numbers so the correct one comes first. On the medium split (all reactions of the test EC numbers held out) and hard split (all reactions of the test EC level-3 classes held out), published accuracy is low: hard split level-3 accuracy 9.8% and level-2 accuracy 22.2% (CREEP with text), level-1 57.6% (CREEP); medium split level-4 accuracy 7.4%, level-3 59.5% (CREEP with text). The paper itself says 'performance on the harder splits is weak across the board'. Task 1's <30%-identity protein split (CLEAN 55.1% level-4) is a second front. All splits, baselines and per-entry result files (task1_baselines/results_summary, task2_baselines/results_summary) are public.
targets.success_criterion: A ranked EC-number output file for every entry of a CARE test split, in the repository's results_summary format, whose k=1 accuracy at a given EC level, recomputed by the skeptic with the repository's performance_evaluation.ipynb, is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the best method for that split and level in arXiv:2406.15669 Tables 2/4 and the repository results (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) by at least 3 percentage points, and higher than any value for that split and level in later published work found by the NOVELTY check. Training uses only the split's designated train files (plus the optional files the README lists for that split).
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the splits from Zenodo record 14004425 (or the repository), checks the output file covers every test entry exactly once, runs performance_evaluation.ipynb, and confirms from training logs and code that no test-split file or EC-to-reaction mapping that includes test reactions was used. Minutes.

angles: Max-clique search on the GC-constrained Hamming graph with automorphism (coordinate permutation x base-swap A<->T, C<->G) orbit reduction, then clique solvers (e.g. MoMC / cliquer) on quotient graphs.
Variable-neighbourhood search / tabu with conflict-driven replacement, starting from the table's own linear codes in codes/LinearGC.txt.
Linear and additive codes over GF(4)/Z4 with GC-weight selection: search quasi-cyclic generator matrices and take the largest constant-GC coset slice.

Cross-domain import (constant-weight binary codes): map A/T vs G/C to a weight constraint and lift known record constant-weight codes from Brouwer's tables (our bank already confirmed wins there) via product/concatenation constructions.
Cross-domain import (SAT/SMT scheduling): encode 'size >= table+1' as a SAT instance with symmetry-breaking predicates and run kissat/cadical for small n (n<=12).
Cross-domain import (sphere packing/lattice codes): Construction A from quaternary lattices and spherical-code style greedy-with-repulsion annealing.

targets.name: DNA codes with constant GC-content: beat a lower bound in the Gaborit-King A_4^GC(n,d,w) table

partial_wins.statement: Reproduce (tie) an unmarked 'v' (variable-neighbourhood-search) entry with n >= 14 from scratch with our own search, checker-confirmed.
Prove an unmarked entry optimal via exact max-clique with symmetry breaking, producing a checkable certificate (e.g. clique-solver log + upper-bound LP).

pitfalls: The table is stale (2010); later papers (Limbachiya et al. 2016-2018, Montemanni-Smith, Smith-Aboluion-Montemanni-Perkins) may already exceed some cells - a 'win' versus the page alone is not novel.
GC-content w: the table fixes w = floor(n/2); a code with mixed or different GC weights is not admissible.
Do not confuse with the GC,RC table directly below it on the same page (different, stricter constraint).
Entries ending in '.' or ':' are proven optimal; exceeding one indicates a checker bug.
targets.statement: Oliver King's table (rambutan.umassmed.edu/king/dnacodes.html, last updated June 23, 2010) lists best-known lower bounds for A_4^GC(n,d,w): the maximum size of a quaternary (A,C,G,T) code of length n, minimum Hamming distance d, with every codeword containing exactly w = floor(n/2) G/C letters, for 4 <= n <= 20, 3 <= d <= 20. Entries marked '.' or ':' are proven optimal. Construct an explicit code strictly larger than the table entry for an unmarked (n,d). These codes are used for DNA data storage address/primer design and microarray probes.
targets.success_criterion: A plain-text list of codewords for some (n,d) whose table entry on https://rambutan.umassmed.edu/king/dnacodes.html is NOT followed by '.' or ':' such that a checker confirms all words have length n over {A,C,G,T}, exactly the table's GC-content w (w = floor(n/2), confirm from King 2003), pairwise Hamming distance >= d, are distinct, and the count is strictly greater than the table entry re-fetched live immediately before claiming, AND strictly greater than any value for the same (n,d,w) found by a novelty search of post-2010 literature (e.g. Limbachiya-Gupta-Rao altruistic-algorithm papers, Montemanni-Smith, arXiv 1903.03535, 2108.02033).
targets.verification_method: Python checker: read codewords, assert alphabet, length, GC count, uniqueness, all-pairs Hamming distance >= d (n<=20 and sizes <= ~10^5 is seconds with numpy bit tricks), compare size to live table cell. Run on a code file from the page's codes/ directory first.

angles: Build codes as unions of RC-orbit pairs {x, rc(x)}: search on the quotient graph of orbit pairs with max-clique / VNS.
Reversible cyclic and quasi-cyclic codes over GF(4) (Gaborit-King linear constructions, reversible G^k codes) restricted to the GC-weight slice, then greedy completion.
Simulated annealing with tabu over codeword swaps, objective = size with conflict penalty; 10 parallel chains seeded from the page's codes/LinearGCRC.txt.
Cross-domain import (graph colouring/register allocation): Kempe-chain style recolouring moves on the conflict graph to free room for an extra codeword.
Cross-domain import (frequency hopping / radar sequence design): use difference-set and Costas-style algebraic constructions with built-in reversal symmetry as seeds.

targets.name: DNA codes with GC-content and reverse-complement constraint: beat a lower bound in the A_4^GC,RC(n,d,w) table

partial_wins.statement: For an unmarked (n,d), a code of size > half the GC-table entry, beating the GC,RC entry by construction from an RC-closed GC code (checker-confirmed).
Tie a 'v' entry with n >= 15 using our own search from scratch.

pitfalls: Self-constraint: Hamming(x, rc(x)) >= d is required; omitting it inflates sizes and is the most common false positive.
Some authors use the 'Watson-Crick complement' (without reversal) distance instead; that is a different table (Chee-Ling).
Table is from 2010 (footer 'Last updated June 23, 2010'; unlike the GC table, the GC,RC table has no 'x' [SAMP] entries); novelty must be checked against later literature.

Later values (checked 2026-10-18): N. A. Aboluion's thesis (Glamorgan 2011, Tables 10.71-10.72, https://pure.southwales.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/991721/PhD_thesis_Niema.pdf), the basis of Aboluion-Smith-Perkins, Discrete Math. 312 (2012) 1062-1075, is larger than this table in 32 unmarked cells with n <= 20 and smaller in none: (10,4) 860, (10,5) 210, (12,3) 59136, (12,4) 14784, (12,5) 1848, (14,3) 768768, (14,6) 3712, (14,7) 796, (14,8) 208, (14,10) 21, (15,6) 6648, (15,8) 410, (16,6) 55424, (16,7) 13856, (16,8) 3776, (16,11) 68, (17,5) 97520, (18,3) 44933184, (18,4) 11266112, (18,5) 699624, (18,6) 699624, (18,7) 43632, (18,8) 10908, (18,9) 2691, (19,5) 1477796, (19,6) 738772, (19,7) 92252, (19,8) 11542, (20,4) 189432064, (20,5) 11822368, (20,7) 369008, (20,16) 8. Issue #368 reads the same 32 values in the paper's Tables 8-9, plus (17,11) 68 where the thesis has 62. These are maxima over w (the thesis notes that the maximum often, but not always, occurs at w = floor(n/2)), so whether a value holds at w = floor(n/2) must be checked per cell.

Closed cells: (15,12), (16,13) and (20,16) carry no '.' or ':' but cannot give a win. Upper bounds A <= 6, 5 and 8 hold for every GC content (issue #368: a counting argument on C and rc(C), with Lean 4 proofs at https://gist.github.com/MikhailLevit1987/f80776c00af60f6cf376b93b5b3e5f18); 6 and 5 are the table values, and for (20,16) the thesis value 8 and an explicit 8-word code with GC 10 in the same gist reach the bound.
Survey trap: arXiv:1607.00266 (v1) Table XIII gives 20 for (15,12), where this table, the 2011 thesis and the upper bound give 6; take values from primary sources.
Some large-n results in recent papers (n=48..160) are outside this table and not comparable.
targets.statement: Same page as the GC table, second table: A_4^GC,RC(n,d,w) additionally requires Hamming distance >= d between any codeword and the reverse-complement of any codeword (including itself), the constraint that prevents unwanted hybridization in DNA storage/computing. Lower bounds for 4 <= n <= 20 listed; many mid-range 'v' (VNS) and 'c' (linear) entries are not known optimal. Construct a strictly larger code for any unmarked (n,d).
targets.success_criterion: A codeword list for some (n,d) whose A_4^GC,RC entry on https://rambutan.umassmed.edu/king/dnacodes.html is not followed by '.' or ':', checked to satisfy: length n, alphabet ACGT, GC count = floor(n/2), pairwise Hamming >= d, Hamming(x, rc(y)) >= d for all x,y including x=y, distinct; size strictly greater than the live table entry re-fetched immediately before claiming and than any post-2010 published value for the same parameters (novelty search, e.g. arXiv 1903.03535 lists GC,RC improvements).
targets.verification_method: Same checker as the GC table plus the reverse-complement constraint (rc = reverse + A<->T, C<->G) applied to all ordered pairs including self-pairs. Seconds.

angles: Start from the released DREAM-CNN/RNN weights and ensemble or distil them; ensembling well-trained but architecturally different models is the cheapest gain and needs only CPU inference.

Copy the winning idea and push it: Autosome.org recast regression as soft classification over expression bins, mirroring how the measurement was made (sorting cells into bins); model the full binning likelihood (as in MAUDE) instead of a softmax over bins.

Cross-domain import (speech recognition): train on noisy labels with a known measurement channel; use the experiment's sort-bin noise model as a differentiable observation layer (like CTC handles alignment noise).

Cross-domain import (physics-informed models): a thermodynamic layer where predicted expression is a Boltzmann-weighted occupancy of learned transcription-factor motifs, giving interpretable features that generalise to the native and SNV subsets.
Use reverse-complement equivariant convolutions and test-time augmentation over strand and small flank runs.

targets.name: Random Promoter DREAM Challenge: beat the best published Pearson/Spearman score for predicting yeast expression from promoter sequence

partial_wins.statement: Beat the best released model on the SNV subset (Pearson on predicted vs measured expression differences), the subset most relevant to variant effects, under the same rules.

A leakage-free ensemble of the three released Prix Fixe models (weights fitted on val.txt only) that beats each individual released model on both overall scores, with an honest note on whether this exceeds the paper's best.

pitfalls: The test labels are public on Zenodo: selecting a checkpoint or ensemble weight with them is leakage. Use val.txt only.
The challenge weighted Pearson score uses r^2 on some subsets and differences for SNV pairs; any home-made metric will disagree. Use the official notebook only.
Sequences must be scored with the same fixed flanks the challenge used; dropping or changing flanks silently changes inputs.
Matching rather than beating the released models within noise is not a result; the 0.002 margin is small, so report bootstrap intervals over test sequences.
targets.statement: The Random Promoter DREAM Challenge 2022 (Rafi, de Boer and the DREAM consortium, Nature Biotechnology 2024) released 6.7 million random 80-bp yeast promoter sequences with measured expression, and a 71,103-sequence test set with designed subsets (high, low, native yeast, random, challenging, SNV pairs, motif perturbation, motif tiling). Scores are a weighted 'Pearson score' and 'Spearman score' across subsets. The test labels and the evaluation notebook are now public on Zenodo (record 10633252), together with the weights of the Prix Fixe-optimised DREAM-CNN, DREAM-RNN and DREAM-Attn models reported as improving on the individual challenge solutions (Autosome.org, BHI, Unlock_DNA) in Rafi et al. 2024, to be re-scored by the claimant rather than taken on trust. The open question is whether a better model, or a principled ensemble, beats the best released model on the official scoring.
targets.success_criterion: Predictions for all sequences in the official test file whose Pearson score AND Spearman score, computed by the skeptic with the challenge's Evaluation.ipynb from Zenodo record 10633252 (re-fetched live immediately before claiming), are STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the best value reported in Rafi et al. 2024 and than the best released Prix Fixe model re-scored the same way, by at least 0.002 on each score. The model may be trained only on train.txt (and val.txt); hyperparameters and ensemble weights must be chosen without the test labels.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads test sequences, the filtered test labels and Evaluation.ipynb from Zenodo, scores the attacker's prediction file (one value per test sequence, order checked by sequence id), re-scores the released Prix Fixe weights the same way, and checks training logs show no read of the test label file. Minutes for scoring; retraining is the attacker's cost.

angles: Varshamov-Tenengolts-style quaternary constructions (Tenengolts codes) restricted to GC slice, then greedy augmentation.
Max-clique / VNS on the edit-distance conflict graph with symmetry reduction (reversal, complement).
Cross-domain import (bioinformatics read alignment): use banded alignment + seed indexing to make conflict-graph construction fast, enabling larger n.
Cross-domain import (error-correcting codes for racetrack memory / deletion channels): lift known deletion-correcting binary codes via GC-bit / base-pair maps.
Cross-domain import (evolutionary game theory): replicator-dynamics continuous relaxation of max-clique (Motzkin-Straus) for warm starts.

targets.name: Edit-distance DNA codes with GC/homopolymer constraints: beat a published lower bound

partial_wins.statement: Reproduce the largest-n published entry with our own search.
Prove a small cell optimal via exact max-clique with checkable certificate.

pitfalls: The table lives in a thesis PDF behind a repository landing page; the agent must locate and parse the exact table and its constraint definitions.
Edit distance vs insertion/deletion-only distance vs Levenshtein with substitutions: different metrics, not comparable.
Constraint definitions (GC exactly n/2 vs within a band; homopolymer max length) vary between sources.
Tables may be stale; novelty search required.
targets.statement: DNA data storage needs codes robust to insertions/deletions: quaternary codes of length n with minimum Levenshtein (edit) distance d and constant GC-content (optionally no homopolymer runs > 3). Published lower-bound tables exist: the M.Sc. thesis Bounds on edit metric codes with combinatorial DNA constraints by Jing Sun (Brock University, 2010), which tabulates lengths 1 to 9 and minimum distances 1 to 9, and the greedy constructions and bounds of Nabil Bennenni, Kenza Guenda and T. Aaron Gulliver (Greedy Construction of DNA Codes and New Bounds, arXiv:1505.06262). Construct a code strictly larger than the best published lower bound for some (n,d,constraint) cell.
targets.success_criterion: A codeword list for a parameter cell listed in https://brocku.scholaris.ca/items/43d5f016-9190-4ec2-8066-81f3860f672b (thesis tables) or https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.06262, checked for length, alphabet, exact constraint set as defined by that source, all-pairs Levenshtein distance >= d, in a cell that its source does not mark as optimal (the claimant must show this, since many small cells are already exhaustively solved), with size strictly larger than the published lower bound (sources re-fetched live immediately before claiming) and than any later value found by novelty search.
targets.verification_method: Python checker with a C/numba Levenshtein all-pairs loop; n <= 9 for the thesis tables, larger n only if the arXiv:1505.06262 tables list that cell. The checker applies the exact constraint set (reverse-complement, fixed GC content) of whichever source the cell comes from. Minutes.

angles: Decompose and conquer: split the target at multiloops into independent substructures, design each with local constraints, then repair junction conflicts with constrained RNAinverse or a CP-SAT model of base-pair compatibility.

Ensemble-objective optimisation (SAMFEO-style): maximise the Boltzmann probability of the target or minimise ensemble defect with sampled coordinate moves, then polish for exact MFE; ViennaRNA's Python bindings make each evaluation milliseconds.

Cross-domain import (VLSI routing / constraint satisfaction): encode 'target is MFE' lazily as cutting planes. Each time RNAfold returns a rival structure, add a constraint that the target beats that rival, and re-solve with a MaxSAT or ILP solver over sequence choices (counterexample-guided synthesis).

Cross-domain import (protein design): negative design via explicit rival-structure enumeration (RNAsubopt) and boosting GC-closing pairs and loop mismatches that destabilise the specific rivals, as Eterna players do with 'boosts'.
Study the human solutions' motif statistics WITHOUT copying them (e.g. which loop-closing pairs players favour) only from puzzles OUTSIDE the target set, and turn them into priors for the search.

targets.name: Eterna100-V2 under ViennaRNA 2: an automated RNA design algorithm that solves a puzzle no benchmarked algorithm has solved

partial_wins.statement: One of the seven listed puzzles solved de novo under the full criterion.
A single frozen algorithm that solves more Eterna100-V2 targets under Vienna 2 than DesiRNA's 92 (all solutions verified with stock RNAfold), even if it misses the seven hardest.

A machine-checkable undesignability certificate for one of the seven V2 targets under Vienna 2, produced with the released RNA-Undesign code (github.com/shanry/RNA-Undesign), would itself be a result - and would retire that target.

pitfalls: Wrong energy model: loading Turner 1999 parameters into ViennaRNA 2.x leaves dangles=2 and is neither benchmark (the repository README warns this is more permissive). Use stock RNAfold 2.6.4 or 2.1.9 with no flags for Vienna 2.
V1 vs V2 targets: several puzzles differ between Eterna100-V1 and -V2; solving the V1 structure under Vienna 2 does not count for V2. Use the 'Secondary Structure V2' column.
Copying or seeding from the public 'Sample Solution' columns, Eterna player solutions or any database of Eterna designs is not an algorithmic solve.
Degenerate MFE: if the target ties with another structure, RNAfold's traceback decides; the check is the exact string RNAfold returns, not an energy tie.

Novelty: results.tsv covers only six algorithms. Huang-lab methods (SAMFEO and successors) report strong Eterna100 numbers; check their per-puzzle tables before claiming a first. Tristan Cazenave's Montparnasse (arXiv:2606.07562) reports solving all 100 Eterna100 V1 puzzles under Turner 1999 / Vienna 1 (#100 Teslagon in 9,383 s, #90 Gladius the hardest); that does not move this V2/Vienna 2 bar, but a claim must check whether Montparnasse or a successor has since been run on V2.
targets.statement: The Eterna100 is the standard benchmark for RNA inverse folding: for each of 100 target secondary structures, find a sequence whose minimum-free-energy fold is exactly that structure. Koodli, Rudolfs, Romano, Wayment-Steele, Dunlap, Eterna participants and Das redesigned it as Eterna100-V2 for the ViennaRNA 2 energy model, and the eternagame/eterna100-benchmarking repository (last pushed 2026-09-01) publishes per-trial results for RNAinverse, NEMO, DesiRNA, SentRNA, LEARNA and EternaBrain. In data/results.tsv, under Vienna 2 the best algorithm (DesiRNA) solves 92 of the 100 V2 targets, and seven V2 puzzles are solved by no benchmarked algorithm in any trial: #68 Taraxacum officinale, #71 Variation of a crop circle, #79 Shapes and Energy, #86 Methaqualone, #90 Gladius, #99 Shooting Star, #100 Teslagon (the puzzles file ships a Sample Solution (V2/Vienna2) for every V2 target, which a claimant should fold with stock RNAfold to confirm designability of that specific target before attacking it; Tianshuo Zhou, Wei Yu Tang, David Mathews and Liang Huang, arXiv:2402.17206, prove 18 Eterna100 puzzles undesignable under the Turner model in ViennaRNA, including #86, #90 and #99 - but for their V1 structures, and all three are among the 19 puzzles whose V2 structure differs from V1, so the V2 targets are not covered by that proof). A sequence for any one of them, produced de novo by an automated method, is a clean, instantly checkable result.
targets.success_criterion: An automated design program (code released, deterministic given a logged seed) that, given only the dot-bracket target of an Eterna100-V2 puzzle that has no Success=1 row under folder vienna2 in data/results.tsv of github.com/eternagame/eterna100-benchmarking (re-fetched live immediately before claiming), outputs a sequence whose MFE structure from stock ViennaRNA 2.6.4 (or 2.1.9) RNAfold -T 37 with no other flags is EXACTLY the target, within 24 hours on a laptop. The program must not read the Eterna sample solutions, any human player solution, or any sequence database of Eterna designs, and the NOVELTY check must confirm no published algorithm (e.g. SAMFEO, Zhou et al.; Tang et al. arXiv:2412.08751; Gautam et al. arXiv:2602.12470) already reports solving that puzzle under Vienna 2.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic installs ViennaRNA 2.6.4 (not preinstalled on a typical laptop), folds the claimed sequence with stock ViennaRNA 2.6.4 'RNAfold -T 37.0' (no other flags) and compares the dot-bracket string character by character with the target from data/eterna100_puzzles.tsv (seconds). Then re-runs the released program from the logged seed in a clean environment without network access or Eterna solution files and confirms it reproduces a valid design. Checks the NOVELTY literature for per-puzzle results.

angles: Antibodies differ from general proteins mainly in the hypervariable loops; score only the loop residues against an antibody-specific background instead of scoring the whole chain.

Cross-domain import (formulation chemistry): aggregation and polyreactivity are surface-property problems, so compute patch-level hydrophobicity and charge from a predicted structure and regress nothing, which is a mechanism rather than a correlation.

Cross-domain import (credit scoring): with 241 small datasets and inconsistent signs, treat it as a many-small-studies meta-analysis and estimate a pooled effect with random effects, rather than reporting one aggregate number.
Germline distance is a known confound and a known weak predictor; build it as an explicit baseline and require any model to beat it.
Pair heavy and light chains properly: several released scores treat the two chains independently, which cannot capture interface effects that drive aggregation.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: FLAb antibody developability: beat the released zero-shot scores on a therapeutic-property category

partial_wins.statement: Thermostability (25 datasets): beat every released zero-shot method's category mean Spearman by at least 0.05 with a method that runs on a laptop CPU.
A method that is positively correlated on at least 80% of the datasets in a category, where the released language-model scores change sign from dataset to dataset.
A reproducible analysis of how much of any method's apparent skill comes from sequence length or germline distance alone, with a length-and-germline-matched control.

pitfalls: Using the dataset's own fitness values to choose the sign or a per-dataset threshold is label peeking; the direction must come from the documented metadata.
Fifteen datasets with non-standard fitness column names are excluded from automated scoring; silently including or excluding datasets changes the category mean and must match the released protocol.
Many FLAb antibodies are clinical-stage molecules whose sequences appear in public databases and in antibody language model training sets; a memorised ranking is not prediction.
Categories are heavily unbalanced (132 binding datasets against 4 immunogenicity); a single aggregate across categories hides where the method works.
A correlation gain on retrospective developability data is not evidence that a designed antibody will be safe or effective, and must not be described that way.
targets.statement: FLAb (Fitness Landscapes for Antibodies, Gray lab at Johns Hopkins; github.com/Graylab/FLAb, last pushed 2026-08-17) collects 241 public antibody datasets in seven therapeutic-property categories (binding 132 datasets, polyreactivity 33, aggregation 31, thermostability 25, pharmacokinetics 9, expression 7, immunogenicity 4), each a CSV of heavy (and usually light) chain sequences with a measured fitness value. The repository also ships the scoring scripts for about 40 zero-shot methods (AntiBERTy, IgLM, ESM-2 at five sizes, ProGen2 variants, ESM-IF, ProteinMPNN, AbMPNN, IgFold, PyRosetta, and simple biophysical descriptors) and the resulting per-dataset score files under score/, so the current bar for any dataset or category is recomputable from the repository without running a single model. Published analyses of this resource report that general protein language models correlate weakly and inconsistently with antibody developability properties, which is why fifteen datasets with non-standard columns are excluded from automated scoring. Antibody developability is the step where many therapeutic candidates fail.
targets.success_criterion: Scores for every antibody in every dataset of one FLAb property category, produced by a method that never reads the fitness column of any dataset in that category, whose per-dataset Spearman correlations (sign-corrected using each dataset's documented direction of favourable values, taken from the category README, not from the data) give a category mean STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the category mean of every method whose score files are present under score/ in the repository, recomputed by the skeptic from those files (repository re-fetched live immediately before claiming), by at least 0.05, with per-dataset values published and the same method applied to at least two categories.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones the repository (data plus released score files), checks the submitted score file covers every antibody of every dataset in the category exactly once, computes Spearman per dataset with the documented direction, recomputes the same statistic for each released method from the score/ files, and audits the attacker's code for reads of the fitness column. Minutes to recompute, plus the attacker's inference cost.

angles: The benchmark scores a network by how well it predicts held-out perturbation effects, so optimise that objective directly: fit a sparse linear response model from perturbation data and read the network off the coefficients, rather than inferring a network and hoping it transfers.
Cross-domain import (causal inference in economics): CRISPRi knockouts are instrumental variables; estimate edges with two-stage least squares on the perturbation design instead of correlation.

Cross-domain import (compressed sensing): with thousands of perturbations and far more candidate edges, use structured sparsity priors (group lasso over transcription-factor modules) with an explicit recovery guarantee argument.
Use the multiome datasets' chromatin accessibility to restrict candidate edges to accessible motif matches before any statistics, which also makes the laptop version feasible.
Check metric applicability first: the leaderboard marks which metrics pass quality criteria per dataset, and targeting a metric that is merely applicable but not quality-passing wastes effort.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: geneRNIB: beat the best listed gene-regulatory-network inference scores on a perturbation dataset

partial_wins.statement: Beat every listed method's transcription-factor-binding F1 (tfb_f1, around 0.11-0.13 on 300BCG as of 2026-10-15) by at least 10% relative on one dataset without losing on the regression metrics.

Show, with the published scores and your own reruns, that a correlation or regression baseline matches the deep methods on a metric where they are credited with an advantage, and publish the corrected comparison.

A frozen method that beats the best listed method on the same metric in both a CRISPRi knockout dataset (Replogle or Xaira) and an observational dataset, showing it is not exploiting one perturbation design.

pitfalls: Using a curated network database (DoRothEA, ChEA, TRRUST, or the benchmark's own ground-truth resources) as an input feature contaminates the ground-truth metrics; only the dataset's own files may be read.

The overall leaderboard score is a percentile aggregate across datasets and modalities, so a gain in one normalised rank can come from other methods' failures; the criterion therefore uses raw per-dataset metric values.
Negative and positive controls appear in the score table and must be excluded when computing 'the best listed method'.
Some metric columns are empty for some datasets; treating a blank as zero manufactures a false best value.
A better network here is a better hypothesis generator, not a demonstrated regulatory mechanism in any patient or tissue.
targets.statement: geneRNIB (Open Problems gene regulatory network inference benchmark, bioRxiv 2025.02.25.640181) is a living benchmark in which a method outputs a weighted transcription-factor-to-target network from single-cell data, and the network is scored against held-out perturbation data and curated transcription-factor binding evidence. The public raw score table (all_scores.csv linked from the leaderboard page, 120 rows covering 11 datasets including Norman and Replogle CRISPR screens in K562, Xaira CRISPRi in HEK293T and HCT116, 300BCG, Nakatake and two multiome datasets) shows modest absolute values: on 300BCG the best listed gs_f1 is 0.718 (scGPT; then scPRINT 0.681, PORTIA 0.619, Geneformer 0.570) while a plain Pearson-correlation baseline reaches 0.469 and the negative control 0.034, and transcription-factor-binding F1 tops out at 0.128 (Geneformer), with most methods at 0.10-0.12 and scGPT (0.038), scPRINT (0.0) and ppcor (0.0) far below. Several metrics do not separate deep methods from correlation baselines at all. Inputs are public h5ad files on the openproblems-data S3 bucket and the evaluation runs from the repository without Docker for the baseline path.
targets.success_criterion: A network file in the benchmark's expected format for one dataset, produced by a method that reads only that dataset's public input files, whose scores recomputed by the skeptic with the task_grn_inference evaluation components are STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than every non-control method listed for that dataset in all_scores.csv (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) on at least two of the dataset's applicable metrics, by at least 5% relative on each, and no worse than the best listed method on the others; the same frozen method must be run on at least three datasets and all scores reported.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the dataset's inference inputs from the openproblems-data S3 bucket over plain HTTPS, runs the attacker's frozen inference script, then runs the repository's evaluation components (conda path, no Docker needed for evaluation), and compares with all_scores.csv downloaded from the leaderboard page. Hours at most for the smaller transcriptomics datasets.

angles: Pull-move local search + replica exchange Monte Carlo (Thachuk 2007) and FRESS fragment regrowth, seeded from many random starts, 10 cores in parallel on the 3D103/124/136 chains.
PERM/nPERM chain growth with importance sampling and Wang-Landau flat-histogram reweighting to escape the -80 basin on the 136-mer.

Constraint programming: CPSP-style approach (build maximally compact H-cores first, then thread the chain through with a CP-SAT solver) - exact for 48-mers, as a large-neighbourhood move on long chains.
Cross-domain import (VLSI placement/routing): treat the chain as a net routed through a 3D grid and use rip-up-and-reroute of 10-20 residue windows with a SAT/ILP router maximizing H-H adjacency.
Cross-domain import (statistical physics of spin glasses): parallel tempering with population annealing and cluster moves borrowed from Ising spin-glass ground-state search.
Cross-domain import (game AI): Nested Monte Carlo Search / NRPA over move sequences (the method that solved Eterna100 RNA design) with a learned policy prior.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: HP lattice protein folding: beat a best-known energy on a standard 2D/3D benchmark sequence

partial_wins.statement: Independently reach the published best energy (-83 or whatever the table lists) for the 3D cubic 136-mer with our own code from a random start; checker-confirmed; non-trivial because PERM variants stalled at -80.
A new best-known energy for one of the same sequences on the 3D FCC or 2D triangular lattice where a published table (with URL) exists, strictly below the published value.
A machine-checkable certificate (e.g. CPSP-style H-core bound or ILP dual bound) that the 3D103 ground state is >= some value, closing part of the gap to -58.

pitfalls: Run-length notation: H^i/P^i and (s)^i must be expanded exactly; a single off-by-one residue changes the instance. Assert sequence length equals the published length.
Many 2D S1 and all 3D 48-mer values are already proven optimal (CPSP); 'beating' them means the checker is wrong. Only target sequences without an optimality proof.

Energy conventions differ between papers (some count E=-1 per contact, some report positive contact counts; some exclude i,i+2 contacts which are impossible on bipartite square/cubic lattices anyway). Reproduce a published optimum first.
Different papers use differently labelled 3D sequences (the 2025 RL paper relabels and mixes 2D/3D); match the exact string, not the label.
NOVELTY: the tables are static papers; a lower energy might already exist in post-2013 literature. Search before claiming.
targets.statement: The hydrophobic-polar (HP) lattice model (E = -1 per non-bonded H-H lattice contact, self-avoiding walk) has a standard benchmark set: 2D square-lattice S1-1..S1-11 (20-100 residues) and 3D cubic S2-1..S2-10 (48-mers) listed in Chris Thachuk, Alena Shmygelska and Holger Hoos (BMC Bioinformatics 2007, Table 1), plus the longer 3D cubic chains of length 64, 88, 103, 124 and 136 compiled by Thomas Wüst and David Landau (arXiv 1301.3466). For the long 3D chains the best-known energies (e.g. 3D103 = -58, 3D136 = -83 as reported there) are NOT proven ground states. Find a valid conformation with energy strictly lower than the best published value for any benchmark sequence whose optimality is not proven.
targets.success_criterion: A conformation file (sequence + absolute lattice coordinates or relative move string) for a benchmark sequence taken verbatim from https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC2071922/fullTextXML (Table 1) or the 3D long-chain table of https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3466, such that an independent checker confirms (a) the decoded HP string equals the published sequence character-for-character, (b) consecutive residues are unit lattice neighbours, (c) no two residues share a site, and (d) the count of non-consecutive H-H unit-distance contacts gives an energy strictly lower (more negative) than the lowest value published for that sequence in either table AND in any later paper found by a NOVELTY literature search (2013-2026, e.g. arXiv 2504.15634); both tables re-fetched live immediately before claiming, and the sequence must not be one with a published proof of optimality (e.g. CPSP exact results for 3D 48-mers).
targets.verification_method: ~50-line Python checker: expand the H/P run-length notation exactly as printed, decode moves/coordinates, assert self-avoidance and unit steps, count H-H topological contacts (|i-j|>1, Manhattan distance 1). Run first on a known-optimal 2D 20-mer to reproduce -9. Seconds per check.

angles: GreedyMini builds orders greedily on binary alphabets and extends to DNA by interleaving bits; attack the interleaving step directly, since the extension is a design choice rather than an optimum.

Cross-domain import (coding theory): a minimizer order is a covering-style object on the de Bruijn graph, so lower bounds and constructions for covering codes and decycling sets transfer, and the decycling family already in the table came from that tradition.

Cross-domain import (scheduling): choosing one position per sliding window is an interval-covering problem; local search over which window positions are forced can be guided by exchange arguments from scheduling heuristics.
Use exact density computation inside the search loop for small w+k, so the optimiser sees the true objective rather than a sampled estimate, then extend the winning structure to larger parameters.

Target the regimes where the published curves cross (the tables show different schemes winning at different w), because a scheme that is uniformly best across a crossing region is both a record and a practical result.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: Minimizer schemes: beat the lowest published DNA density for a (w, k) pair in the public minimizer density tables

partial_wins.statement: Beat the best listed density for a (w, k) cell with a constant-space scheme (no explicit table of k-mer ranks), which the WABI 2026 authors identify as the practically important regime.
Reproduce a published GreedyMini density for a mid-sized cell (w + k around 20) from scratch with your own search and release the order, confirming the table entry independently.
An exact computation (not sampling) of the density of a published order for a cell where only estimated values are listed, with the method and its error bound published.

pitfalls: Expected density (over random sequences) and particular density (on a specific genome) are different numbers; comparing one against the other is the easiest false win here.
Binary-alphabet densities and DNA densities differ; the tables state which is which and a claim must match.
A table-based order with a huge rank table can beat constant-space schemes trivially; the storage cost must be stated, and the constant-space comparison kept separate.
Sampling-based density estimates have error bars of their own; a 0.1% improvement measured by sampling may not exist, hence the 0.5% relative margin or an exact computation.
Papers report densities at specific (w, k) and sometimes for a fixed sequence such as a human chromosome; reproduce the published value for a known order before claiming to beat a neighbouring cell.
targets.statement: Minimizers are the sampling scheme underneath almost every modern sequence aligner and assembler: for parameters w and k, each window of w+k-1 bases contributes its minimal k-mer under some order, and the density (expected fraction of positions chosen) decides how much memory and time downstream tools use. Two public repositories maintain comparable density tables: OrensteinLab/GreedyMini (Shay Golan, Ido Tziony, Matan Kraus, Yaron Orenstein, Arseny Shur; Bioinformatics 2025) publishes precomputed orders and the densities they achieve, and OrensteinLab/10-minimizers (Shur, Tziony, Orenstein; WABI 2026) publishes CSV tables of DNA densities for GreedyMini, decycling, double decycling, miniception, mod-minimizer and the new spacers across wide ranges of w and k, plus the .gm order files. For example in w_extension_k12.csv at k = 12, w = 10 the listed densities are GreedyMini 0.141413, double decycling 0.149105, miniception 0.164318 and mod-minimizer 0.181827. Lowering any cell is a purely computational, exactly checkable record, and the density of an explicit order can be computed or estimated to tight precision on a laptop.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit minimizer order for a stated (w, k) pair, given either as a complete rank file or as deterministic released code that emits one, whose DNA density, computed by the skeptic with the repositories' own density measurement code, is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the smallest value listed for that (w, k) pair across the tables in github.com/OrensteinLab/10-minimizers and the precomputed minimizers of github.com/OrensteinLab/GreedyMini (both re-fetched live immediately before claiming) by at least 0.5% relative, with the comparison made under the same density definition (expected density for the expected-density tables, particular density on the same sequence otherwise) and with the order's storage cost stated.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic loads the claimed order, verifies it is a total order on all k-mers (or a well-defined constant-space rank function), then computes density either exactly by enumerating windows for small w+k or by the repositories' measurement scripts on the same random or genomic sequence they use, and compares with the live table cell. Seconds to minutes per cell.

angles: Histone-mark tasks are about nucleosome positioning and sequence composition; engineered k-mer and periodicity features with a gradient-boosted tree are a serious baseline and run in minutes.
Cross-domain import (audio): dinucleotide periodicity around 10 base pairs is a helical-phasing signal, so a filterbank or spectral front end may capture what a token-level transformer dilutes.
Cross-domain import (clinical trials): with ten folds and small effects, use paired tests across folds rather than comparing means, and design the experiment to detect a stated effect size.
Reverse-complement equivalence is a free symmetry; averaging over both strands at inference costs nothing and is not standard in all published entries.
Probe cached embeddings from several released genomic models and ensemble them, which separates the value of pretraining from the value of fine-tuning compute.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: Nucleotide Transformer benchmark: beat the best published MCC on a genomic regulatory task

partial_wins.statement: Beat the best listed mean MCC on H3K9me3 (0.4807 as of 2026-10-15) by at least 0.02 with a model under 100M parameters.
Beat the best listed mean MCC on any three of the 18 tasks at once with a single frozen architecture and training recipe.
A reproducible audit of fold-to-fold variance on the histone tasks, showing which published ranking differences are inside the noise, with the per-fold numbers from benchmark.csv.

pitfalls: Genomic regions can be near-duplicated between train and test splits; verify the split as released rather than assuming it is clean, and report any overlap found.
Reporting the best fold instead of the mean over folds is a common inflation; the criterion requires the ten-fold mean and the per-fold values.
MCC, F1 and accuracy rank models differently on imbalanced histone tasks; compare against the same metric the leaderboard lists.

Large pretrained genomic models saw most of the human genome, so they may have seen the test regions unlabelled; this is allowed but must be declared, and a claim of 'no leakage' needs the label check, not a corpus claim.
A gain on a histone-mark classifier is a step in regulatory genomics, not evidence about any disease mechanism.
targets.statement: The Nucleotide Transformer downstream benchmark (Hugo Dalla-Torre and co-authors, InstaDeep; Nature Methods 2024) fixes 18 genomic classification tasks (histone marks such as H3K9me3 and H3K4me2, promoter and enhancer types, splice sites) with published train/test splits and ten-fold results. The public leaderboard space hosts benchmark.csv with 273 rows of per-fold Matthews correlation coefficients, F1 and accuracy for every model and task, so the exact distribution behind each bar is visible rather than a single number. Splice-site tasks are saturated (best ten-fold mean MCC 0.966-0.971) but the chromatin tasks are not: computed from that file, the best ten-fold mean MCC is 0.4807 on H3K9me3 (NT-1000G 2.5B), 0.4991 on H3K4me1 (Enformer), 0.5169 on H3K27ac (Enformer), 0.5186 on H2AFZ and 0.5694 on enhancer types, across 15-16 models per task. The data load from the Hugging Face hub without registration, and sequences are short enough (a few hundred to a few thousand bases) for a small convolutional model or a cached-embedding probe to be trained on a laptop.
targets.success_criterion: Predictions for every sequence of a benchmark task's test split, from a model trained only on that task's training split (pretrained weights allowed if their corpus is declared and contains no test-split labels), whose mean MCC over the benchmark's ten folds, recomputed by the skeptic with the standard MCC definition on the released splits, is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the best mean MCC for that task in the leaderboard's benchmark.csv (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) by at least 0.02 absolute, with the fold-wise values published and a paired comparison over folds favouring the new method.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic loads the task's released splits from the Hugging Face hub, checks the prediction file covers each test sequence per fold exactly once, computes MCC per fold, compares with the per-fold arrays in benchmark.csv, reruns the attacker's training from the released seed for at least one fold, and checks for overlap between training and test sequences. An hour or two.

angles: Isolated labels are, by construction, cell types present in few batches; detect candidate isolated populations without labels (density-based outlier structure) and protect them from mixing, instead of applying one global correction strength.

Cross-domain import (signal separation): treat batch as a nuisance subspace and remove it with an explicit invariance constraint, as in domain-adversarial training, but with a per-cluster strength so rare clusters are not erased.

Cross-domain import (survey calibration): raking and post-stratification align marginal distributions between batches without distorting within-cell-type structure, which is exactly the tension the metrics measure.
Several listed methods are classical (Harmony, Scanorama, fastMNN, Combat); a careful combination of their outputs, chosen without labels, may dominate each one and is cheap to test.
Optimise the actual reported quantity: the metric suite is public, so measure the trade-off curve directly rather than trusting a single hyperparameter default.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: Open Problems batch integration: beat every listed method on the metrics where single-cell integration still fails

partial_wins.statement: Isolated-label F1 on cellxgene_census/tabula_sapiens above the best listed non-control value (0.1336 as of 2026-10-15) by at least 25% relative, without dropping below the median on batch-correction metrics.
A single frozen configuration that beats the best listed method on at least one bio-conservation metric on three different datasets.

A reproducible demonstration of which metric pairs are in genuine tension on these datasets (for example isolated-label F1 against iLISI), with a Pareto front computed from the public score file and your own runs.

pitfalls: Reading the solution file, even to pick the number of clusters or an integration strength, is label peeking; the method must be label-free end to end.
The controls (embed_cell_types, shuffle_integration, no_integration and their variants) must be excluded when computing 'the best listed method'; they are there to bound the scale.
The overall score shown on the website is an aggregate of normalised metrics, so a higher aggregate can come from other methods changing; the criterion uses raw per-metric values.
Some metrics are missing for some methods and datasets in the score file; treating missing as zero manufactures a false bar.
Better integration metrics do not establish that a newly mixed population is biologically real; any claim about a disease-specific cell state needs evidence beyond this benchmark.
targets.statement: The Open Problems batch-integration task asks a method to remove batch effects from single-cell data while preserving biological structure, and scores it with the suite of metrics from the scIB study (Luecken and co-authors) split into batch-correction and bio-conservation groups. In the public run run_2026-08-17_16-18-21 (score_uns.yaml on the openproblems-data S3 bucket, 26 methods over six datasets) several bio-conservation metrics are far from the upper controls: on cellxgene_census/tabula_sapiens the best non-control values are isolated-label F1 0.1336 (scANVI), ARI 0.5125, label silhouette 0.5488 and kBET 0.4017, while the embed-cell-types control reaches 0.9634 label silhouette. Rare and isolated cell types are where every listed method, deep or classical, performs badly, and that is exactly the population that matters when integrating atlases to find disease-specific states. Inputs, solutions and the metric components are public and the smaller datasets run on a laptop.
targets.success_criterion: An integrated embedding (or corrected matrix) for one dataset of the latest batch-integration run, produced by a method that reads only the task's input file (never the solution file with cell-type labels), whose scores recomputed by the skeptic with the official metric components of github.com/openproblems-bio/task_batch_integration are STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than every non-control method listed for that dataset in the newest score file and on the live page (both re-fetched live immediately before claiming) on at least two bio-conservation metrics by at least 5% relative each, while no batch-correction metric falls below the median listed value; the same frozen method must be run on at least three datasets and all metrics reported.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the dataset's input and solution files from the openproblems-data S3 bucket over plain HTTPS, runs the attacker's frozen method in a directory where the solution file is absent, scores the output with the official metric components, and compares with the newest score_uns.yaml and the live page. Minutes to an hour per dataset for the smaller atlases.

angles: Inspect the split first: compare the label sets and batch covariates of train.h5ad and test.h5ad (metadata only); if test batches contain types absent from training or at different granularity, an open-set classifier with hierarchical (Cell Ontology) back-off is the fix.

Cross-domain import (domain adaptation in vision): self-training with confidence thresholds and class-balanced pseudo-labels on the unlabeled test cells (transductive, allowed because test expression is an input), plus batch-statistic re-normalisation (AdaBN).
Cross-domain import (optimal transport): label transfer by entropic OT between train and test cells in a shared embedding with unbalanced marginals, which handles cell-type proportion shift.
Class-imbalance-aware training (logit adjustment, focal loss) directly targets macro-F1, which the listed methods do not optimise.
Ensemble the strongest listed families (scANVI, Seurat TransferData, logistic regression) with weights chosen on a batch-held-out split of the training data.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: Open Problems label projection: beat the best listed accuracy/macro-F1 for transferring cell-type labels on the hardest datasets

partial_wins.statement: gtex_v9: macro-F1 above the listed best by >= 0.02 (rare cell types are where the headroom is).
A checkable explanation of the tabula_sapiens collapse (e.g. label sets that differ between train and test batches, read from train.h5ad/test.h5ad metadata only) plus a method that handles it.

pitfalls: solution.h5ad (the test labels) sits in the same public folder; the skeptic must run the method without it.
Original cellxgene census annotations of the test cells are public elsewhere; looking them up by cell barcode or donor is leakage.
Transductive use of test expression is allowed, but using test-set label distributions estimated from the solution is not.
Datasets are offered in several normalisations (log_cp10k, sqrt_cp10k, l1_sqrt); check which one the leaderboard entry used.
Re-fetch the S3 results listing before claiming; runs are frequent.
targets.statement: The Open Problems label-projection task trains a classifier on annotated single cells from some batches and predicts cell types for held-out batches. Most datasets are near-saturated (accuracy > 0.95), but in the latest public run (run_2026-09-21_17-18-30) two are not: cellxgene_census/tabula_sapiens, where the best accuracy is 0.377 (Seurat TransferData; next MLP 0.247) and best macro-F1 0.167; and cellxgene_census/gtex_v9, where accuracy reaches 0.893 (scANVI scArches) but macro-F1 is only 0.459. The tabula_sapiens result in particular suggests something structural (batch split by tissue or donor, label granularity) that a careful method could exploit.
targets.success_criterion: For cellxgene_census/tabula_sapiens or cellxgene_census/gtex_v9, a frozen method that reads only train.h5ad and test.h5ad (never solution.h5ad) produces labels whose accuracy AND f1_macro, recomputed by the skeptic with the official metric components of github.com/openproblems-bio/task_label_projection, are STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than every non-control method's values for that dataset in the newest score file and on the live page (re-fetched live immediately before claiming), by at least 0.02 absolute on f1_macro and not lower on accuracy.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads train.h5ad and test.h5ad (gtex_v9 about 3 GB; tabula_sapiens about 20 GB, so gtex_v9 is the laptop-friendly target), runs the frozen method with solution.h5ad absent, scores with the official components, compares with the newest S3 score file and live page.

angles: Ensemble the strongest public solutions with weights fitted on a donor-held-out split of the training data; competition winners are often individually close but make different errors.

Cross-domain import (machine translation): treat RNA-to-protein as translation and use kNN-retrieval-augmented prediction (kNN-MT): blend a parametric model with the averaged targets of nearest training cells in a learned embedding.

Cross-domain import (geophysics / data assimilation): use an optimal-interpolation (Kalman-style) correction where the prior is a population-level prediction and the observation is each cell's RNA neighbourhood.
Donor/batch shift is the main difficulty: fit domain-adversarial or simple moment-matching (CORAL) alignment of test_mod1 to the training distribution before prediction; it needs no test labels.
For ATAC-to-RNA, use gene-activity scores (peaks within gene bodies and promoters) as a prior feature set and learn only residuals, which is cheap and robust.

targets.name: Open Problems predict modality: beat the best listed RMSE for predicting protein abundance from RNA (and RNA from ATAC) on NeurIPS 2021/2022 data

partial_wins.statement: Beat the listed best RMSE on neurips2022 pbmc_multiome/swap (where one method leads by a wide margin) or bmmc_cite/normal by >= 0.5% relative under the full criterion.

A leakage-free ensemble of the publicly released top methods (SS-OPM, senkin & tmp, Guanlab-dengkw) with weights chosen on a donor-held-out split of the TRAINING data, beating every individual listed method on one dataset.

pitfalls: test_mod2 is the label and is downloadable from the same bucket; the skeptic runs the method without it present.
Tuning hyperparameters by looking at test RMSE (even through the leaderboard numbers) is overfitting; tune only on held-out donors from the training data.
Normalisation variants (log_cp10k, sqrt_cp10k, l1_sqrt) produce different RMSE scales; compare only against the same dataset/normalisation the leaderboard uses.
The leaderboard is being re-run often (several runs in Sep-Oct 2026), so the record can move under you; re-fetch before claiming.
targets.statement: The Open Problems 'predict modality' task (authors incl. Alejandro Granados, Alex Tong, Bastian Rieck, Daniel Burkhardt, Louise Deconinck, Robrecht Cannoodt, Vladimir Shitov) asks methods to predict one single-cell modality from another on held-out donors/sites of the NeurIPS 2021 (BMMC CITE-seq and multiome) and NeurIPS 2022 (PBMC) datasets. The task is actively re-run (latest public run run_2026-10-10_07-15-14) and the top of the board is tight: on openproblems_neurips2021/bmmc_cite/normal (RNA to protein) the best RMSE is 0.6561 (senkin & tmp), then 0.6576 (SS-OPM), 0.6634 (Guanlab-dengkw); on bmmc_multiome/swap the best RMSE is 0.5143 (Guanlab-dengkw); on neurips2022 pbmc_multiome/swap the best RMSE is 0.3552 (SS-OPM), with a clear gap to second place. Several entries are NeurIPS 2021/2022 competition winners, so a strict improvement is a genuine advance on a well-studied problem.
targets.success_criterion: On a dataset/direction of the latest predict-modality run (live page and newest score file on the openproblems-data S3 bucket, re-fetched live immediately before claiming), a frozen method trained only on train_mod1/train_mod2 and given test_mod1 produces predictions whose RMSE, recomputed by the skeptic with the official metric component of github.com/openproblems-bio/task_predict_modality against test_mod2, is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than every non-control method listed for that dataset by at least 0.5% relative, and whose mean Pearson per cell is not lower than the best listed value minus 0.005.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the train/test h5ad files for the dataset from the public S3 bucket, runs the attacker's frozen code with test_mod2 absent, scores with the official metric component, and compares with the newest score file and the live page. Training data are 0.4-0.7 GB per dataset; laptop-hours.

angles: Start from the strongest listed methods (CellMapper, MAGIC, DCA) and tune the diffusion / neighbourhood human per dataset only via internal molecular cross-validation on a further binomial split of the TRAINING matrix (the same trick the benchmark uses, applied recursively), never the test file.

Exploit the known structure of the metric: binomial thinning means the held-out counts are an independent Poisson draw with known sampling fraction, so the MSE-optimal estimator is a shrinkage estimator of the underlying rate; derive it analytically (James-Stein / empirical Bayes per gene) and use smoothing only to estimate the prior.

Cross-domain import (image denoising): Noise2Self / Noise2Noise-style self-supervised training is exactly molecular cross-validation; borrow BM3D-style 'collaborative filtering' by grouping similar cells and doing low-rank shrinkage within each group rather than one global diffusion.

Cross-domain import (recommender systems / matrix completion): treat the count matrix as implicit-feedback ratings and use Poisson matrix factorisation with optimal hard-thresholding of singular values (Gavish-Donoho), which is cheap and principled.

Cross-domain import (geostatistics): kriging on the cell-cell kNN graph with a variogram estimated from training-split residuals gives a principled gene-specific smoothing bandwidth instead of MAGIC's single diffusion time.

Treat the Poisson-loss failure separately: most smoothers overshrink low counts; a final calibration step that matches each gene's denoised mean and dispersion to the training counts may fix Poisson loss without hurting MSE.
