CROSS-DOMAIN (statistical physics / renewal theory): model epidemic growth as a renewal process with a time-varying reproduction number driven by an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, and propagate parameter uncertainty analytically; this is the physics-style answer to overconfident curve fits.

CROSS-DOMAIN (ecology): borrow empirical-dynamic-modelling/nonlinear-time-series tools (simplex projection, S-map, attractor reconstruction across the 50+ state time series as a spatial replicate ensemble) to forecast by nearest-neighbour analogues of past season trajectories instead of parametric curves.

Hierarchical pooling across locations and seasons: partial pooling (empirical Bayes shrinkage of growth rates toward national and census-division means) is where small-state WIS is won; the ensemble averages models, not information, so a properly pooled single model can beat it.

CROSS-DOMAIN (compression / MDL for model selection): choose among candidate forecast families online by prequential (predictive) code length rather than by in-sample fit, which is exactly a WIS-friendly log-loss analogue and avoids the hindsight tuning that makes retrospective wins fake.

Exploit documented ensemble weaknesses: turning points, holiday-week reporting artefacts, and seasons with early onset; a model that handles reporting-delay backfill explicitly (nowcast the most recent 2 weeks before forecasting) attacks the ensemble where it is structurally weak.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: CDC FluSight hub: beat the FluSight-ensemble's season-average WIS retrospectively on a completed season

partial_wins.statement: Strictly lower season-average WIS than the FluSight-baseline model AND than the median submitted model for the same season/target/locations, under the same as-of data discipline and the hub's scorer, with the bootstrap interval excluding zero.

Beat the FluSight-ensemble's WIS on the subset of forecasts at horizons 2-3 weeks ahead (where the ensemble is weakest) for all locations in a completed season, with the official scorer and the no-look-ahead audit, reported as a horizon-restricted result.

A reproducible scoring audit: independently recompute the hub's published per-model season WIS table for a completed season from model-output/ plus oracle-output.csv with hubverse code, and document any model whose recomputed WIS differs from the published value by more than 1%, with the cause (missing submissions, revised targets, exclusion rules).

pitfalls: Look-ahead/backfill leakage: hospitalisation and ED-visit targets are revised for weeks after first report. Training or fitting on the FINAL time series while claiming a retrospective forecast is the classic false positive here; only as-of snapshots (or the hub's versioned target data) may be used, and the oracle-output must never be read by the pipeline.

Hindsight tuning: picking the model class, window length, or spread multiplier after seeing which choice scores best on that season is overfitting dressed as forecasting. Hyperparameters must be fixed on earlier seasons and frozen, with the commit history or a pre-registration to show it.

Mismatched comparison sets: the ensemble's published WIS covers specific reference dates, locations, horizons and target (hospital admissions vs ED visits), with hub exclusion rules for missing or invalid submissions. Scoring the attacker on an easier subset (e.g. dropping low-count jurisdictions or a bad month) is the commonest way to fake a win.

Scoring-rule errors: WIS must use the hub's exact quantile levels, with counts not rates, non-crossing quantiles, and the same log/natural scale as the official report; an averaging order change (mean of per-location WIS vs pooled) can move results by more than the claimed margin.
Ensemble contamination: using other teams' submitted forecasts, or an ensemble member's output, for the same season turns the result into a post-hoc combination rather than a forecaster.
targets.statement: The CDC FluSight forecast hub (github.com/cdcepi/FluSight-forecast-hub) stores every weekly probabilistic forecast ever submitted by every team (model-output/, one parquet/csv per model per reference date), the ground-truth target data including a hubverse oracle-output.csv (17 MB, fetched 2026-10-13) and time-series.csv (88 MB), the ensemble weights, and the official weighted-interval-score (WIS) evaluation reports (reports/Flu_Hospitalizations_Forecasts_WIS_27 May 2026.html and Flu_ED_Visit_Forecasts_WIS_27 May 2026.html, i.e. the 2025-26 season's end-of-season evaluation). The FluSight-ensemble routinely ranks at or near the top and beating it out-of-sample is a standing open problem in epidemic forecasting. Everything needed to score a new forecaster against every submitted model on a frozen, completed season is public, small and CPU-only, and the scoring rule (WIS over the hub's quantile levels, per horizon/location/target) is implemented in the open hubverse packages.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a released, deterministic forecasting pipeline plus saved quantile forecasts that (a) cover every reference date, location and horizon of ONE completed FluSight season as submitted-format output matching the hub's task-id schema in hub-config/, (b) at each reference date use ONLY data that was available on that date (the pipeline must read from the hub's own versioned/as-of target data or an archived data snapshot, and the code must be auditable for look-ahead, including no parameters tuned on later weeks of the same season), and (c) achieve a season-average WIS, computed with the public hubverse scoring code on the hub's oracle-output.csv for that season with the hub's own exclusion rules, STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the FluSight-ensemble's season-average WIS for the same target, horizons, locations and reference dates as published in the hub's evaluation report in https://github.com/cdcepi/FluSight-forecast-hub/tree/main/reports , re-fetched live immediately before claiming, by at least 2% relative AND outside a stationary-bootstrap 90% interval over reference dates. A forecaster that consumes any other model's submitted forecasts for that season (including the ensemble's) is disqualified.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones the hub at a pinned commit (model-output/, target-data/oracle-output.csv, hub-config/, reports/), validates the attacker's forecast files against the hub's validation schema, recomputes WIS for the attacker and for FluSight-ensemble/FluSight-baseline with the public hubverse scoring code (R hubEvals or an equivalent re-implementation cross-checked on the published numbers), and bootstraps over reference dates. Look-ahead audit: rerun the attacker's pipeline with the data snapshot truncated at each reference date and confirm the forecasts are reproduced bit-for-bit (or within documented stochastic tolerance), and grep the code and configs for any read of future weeks, of oracle-output.csv, or of other teams' submissions. All data is well under 1 GB.

angles: Model the delay distribution properly: a hierarchical negative-binomial delay model with day-of-week effects, state and age-group random effects and a slowly varying reporting-probability curve is the textbook nowcast and still beats most submissions when fitted carefully.

CROSS-DOMAIN (survival analysis): the reporting triangle is right-truncated survival data, so inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting and discrete-time hazard models transfer directly and give calibrated intervals.

CROSS-DOMAIN (queueing theory): treat reports as arrivals through a server with time-varying capacity (weekends, holidays, backlog clearance) rather than as a static delay distribution - backlog dynamics are exactly what breaks naive nowcasts.

CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing / deconvolution): nowcasting is deconvolution of a known-ish delay kernel from a truncated signal; regularised Richardson-Lucy or total-variation deconvolution with uncertainty by bootstrap is an unexploited angle.
Borrow strength across strata: states and age groups share delay structure; partial pooling plus post-stratification stabilises the thin strata where the ensemble is weakest.
Calibration last: conformalise the predictive quantiles on past nowcast errors, since WIS rewards honest spread far more than a better point estimate.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: German COVID-19 hospitalization nowcast hub: beat the hub ensemble's WIS on the published real-time nowcasts

partial_wins.statement: Beat the ensemble by >= 5% relative WIS restricted to the youngest and oldest age strata, where delays are longest and the submitted pool thinnest, over the declared period.
Beat every individual submitted model (not necessarily the ensemble) over the declared period under the as-of discipline, with the bootstrap interval excluding zero.

A reproduction of the hub's published evaluation: recompute per-model WIS for the published period from data-processed and the truth data with a released script, documenting every discrepancy and the exclusion rules needed to reconcile it.

pitfalls: Triangle leakage: using the completed truth for past dates instead of the triangle as it stood is the defining false positive of nowcasting work; the audit must rerun the pipeline on truncated triangles.
Revision definition: the RKI series was itself revised and redefined during the period; the claim must state which truth version it scores against and use the same one for both predictors.
Row mismatch across strata: the ensemble does not cover every state/age/date cell; scoring on an easier subset is the commonest way to fake a win.
Short evaluation windows: the hub's window is limited, so a few weeks of luck can look like skill; the stationary bootstrap over dates and a minimum window length are required.
Consuming other teams' nowcasts turns the result into a post-hoc combination rather than a nowcaster.
A WIS improvement on an archived German series is a methods result, not public-health guidance.
targets.statement: Nowcasting - estimating today's value of a statistic that will only be complete in weeks - is the neglected half of epidemic forecasting, and Germany's seven-day COVID-19 hospitalization incidence was a textbook case because reports arrive with long, age- and state-dependent delays. The Hospitalization Nowcast Hub run by the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology chair of econometrics and statistics with the Heidelberg Institute for Theoretical Studies (github.com/KITmetricslab/hospitalization-nowcast-hub) archives, in a standard format, every submitted real-time nowcast (data-processed), retrospective nowcasts (data-processed_retrospective), and the Robert Koch Institute truth data with its full reporting triangle (data-truth). Daniel Wolffram, Johannes Bracher and colleagues published the collaborative evaluation in 2023 (PMC10446237), scoring models and the ensemble by weighted interval score across states and age groups. The data is tens of megabytes and the whole exercise is CPU-only.
targets.success_criterion: Success means saved quantile nowcasts, in the hub's submission format, for every (forecast_date, location, age_group, delay horizon) row for which the hub ensemble has a nowcast over one declared continuous evaluation period of at least eight weeks within the hub's operating window, produced by a deterministic pipeline that at each date reads ONLY the reporting triangle as it stood on that date (the hub's dated truth files), whose mean weighted interval score against the hub's final truth, recomputed by the skeptic with public scoring code on exactly those rows, is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the ensemble's by at least 5% relative, with a stationary bootstrap over dates at 90% excluding zero. The scorer must first reproduce the ensemble's published scores from https://github.com/KITmetricslab/hospitalization-nowcast-hub and the evaluation of https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10446237/fullTextXML (re-read live immediately before claiming) to within 1%. Submitted nowcasts of other teams may not be consumed.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones the hub at a pinned commit, reconstructs the reporting triangle as of each nowcast date from the dated truth files, validates the attacker's files against the hub format, recomputes WIS for the attacker and the ensemble on identical rows with public code (validated by reproducing the published numbers), bootstraps over dates, and audits for look-ahead by rerunning the pipeline on truncated triangles and by code review. Tens of megabytes, minutes of CPU.

angles: Conventional: replace ridge-on-PCA with a head that matches the data's structure - per-gene shrinkage toward the slide mean, multi-output reduced-rank regression, or a Poisson/negative-binomial likelihood on counts instead of Gaussian regression on normalised values.

Conventional: use the spatial arrangement the published pipeline throws away - neighbourhood averaging of embeddings, conditional autoregressive smoothing of predictions, or multi-scale patches - while keeping the train/test patient split intact.

Cross-domain import (signal processing / super-resolution): expression over a slide is a smooth field sampled on a lattice; borrow deconvolution and total-variation denoising from image restoration to separate the measurable low-frequency field from per-spot shot noise, and predict only the part that is predictable.

Cross-domain import (geostatistics / kriging): this is literally a spatial prediction problem with a known covariance structure; fit a variogram per gene per slide and use kriging with the image embedding as external drift, which is the standard tool in mining and soil science for exactly this data shape.

Cross-domain import (ecology / rarefaction): spot-level counts differ in sequencing depth exactly as ecological surveys differ in effort; coverage-based rarefaction per spot before correlating removes a nuisance axis that currently inflates variance in the weak tasks.

Cross-domain import (compression / MDL): choose the number of PCA factors and the per-gene regularisation by description length rather than validation Pearson; with only a handful of patients per task, validation-based selection is itself extremely noisy.

Ensembling encoders: the table shows 25 encoders whose errors are probably decorrelated; a rank- or precision-weighted ensemble of two or three embeddings, with weights fitted on training patients only, is cheap and untested in the published table.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: HEST-Benchmark: beat the best published Pearson for predicting spatial gene expression from tumour histology

partial_wins.statement: Beat the live best on two of the three weakest tasks (as of 2026-10-15: READ 0.2421, CCRCC 0.2719, LYMPH_IDC 0.2842) by >= 0.015 each with ONE frozen configuration, which is far stronger evidence than a single-task win on the easy IDC or SKCM tasks.

Show that a non-foundation-model pipeline (stains-normalised classical texture/colour features, or a small CPU-trainable encoder) exceeds the published ResNet50 average of 0.3252 by >= 0.03 on at least four tasks, quantifying how much of the foundation-model advantage is reproducible without a large pretrained encoder.

A spatial-leakage audit: re-score the published-style ridge pipeline after enforcing a minimum physical distance between training and test spots within the same slide, and report how much of the reported Pearson on each task is attributable to neighbouring-spot correlation. A benchmark-critique result, checkable from the saved spot coordinates and predictions.

pitfalls: Spot-level leakage within a slide: patches from the same tumour region are strongly correlated, so any split that is not strictly by patient/sample, or any smoothing that crosses the train/test boundary, manufactures correlation. Verify the split files are used exactly as published.

Metric definition drift: the published numbers are Pearson per gene averaged in a specific way after a specific normalisation (ridge on PCA-256 embeddings). Recomputing with a different gene set, different normalisation or a different averaging order moves the number by more than the 0.015 bar.

Encoder provenance and training-data contamination: several listed encoders were pretrained on public cohorts that may overlap HEST slides. A claim built on a new pretrained encoder must state its pretraining corpus; otherwise an apparent win can be memorisation of the same slides.
Single-seed and single-task cherry-picking: with few patients per task, seed and split variance is large. Five seeds, a 2x-std margin and a full nine-task report are required.
Stale-table comparison: the README table has been updated repeatedly (entries dated 30.08.24 and 03.04.26) and accepts community pull requests, so the record must be re-read live before claiming.

Over-claiming: predicting 50 highly variable genes from morphology at Pearson 0.4 is a benchmark result about tissue texture, not a diagnostic assay, and certainly not a substitute for sequencing a patient's tumour.
targets.statement: HEST-1k (Guillaume Jaume, Paul Doucet, Andrew Song and colleagues at Mahmood Lab, NeurIPS 2024 Spotlight) pairs spatial-transcriptomics spots with the matching histology patches and defines HEST-Benchmark: predict the expression of 50 highly variable genes from a 112 x 112 micron patch at 0.5 micron per pixel, in nine tasks covering eight cancer types, scored by Pearson correlation with leave-one-patient-out style public splits. The public result table in the repository README (re-read live on 2026-10-15, table dated 03.04.26) lists 25 publicly available models scored identically with ridge regression on PCA-reduced (256 factors) patch embeddings. The live bests are: average across tasks 0.4229 (H-Optimus-1), with GenBio-PathFM 0.4197 and H-Optimus-0 0.4150; per task, IDC 0.6024 (H-Optimus-1), PRAD 0.3913 (GenBio-PathFM), PAAD 0.5159 (Virchow), SKCM 0.6715 (GenBio-PathFM), COAD 0.3284 (GenBio-PathFM), READ 0.2421 (H-Optimus-1), CCRCC 0.2719 (Virchow2), LUNG 0.5787 (GenBio-PathFM), LYMPH_IDC 0.2842 (GenBio-PathFM); a plain ImageNet ResNet50 reaches 0.3252 on average. Three tasks sit below 0.29 and the gap between a generic ResNet and billion-parameter pathology foundation models is only about 0.10 Pearson, which says the regression head and the spatial statistics - not the encoder - may be where the remaining signal is. The benchmark data are ungated on Hugging Face (MahmoodLab/hest-bench, 42 GB in total but per-task: SKCM 0.49 GB, LUNG 0.82 GB, PAAD 1.2 GB, COAD 2.47 GB), so a single-task attack is laptop-scale, and precomputed CTransPath embeddings ship in the fm_v1 folder.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for one named HEST-Benchmark task, a saved per-spot prediction matrix for the 50 benchmark genes on every test split defined by that task's splits/test_*.csv files in https://huggingface.co/datasets/MahmoodLab/hest-bench, produced by a method trained only on the corresponding train_*.csv patients, and a mean Pearson correlation computed exactly as the HEST-Library's benchmark code computes it (same gene list, same per-gene then per-split averaging), that is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the maximum value in that task's column over ALL model rows of the live HEST-Benchmark table at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mahmoodlab/HEST/main/README.md - re-fetched and re-parsed immediately before claiming - by at least 0.015 absolute, with the gain surviving 5 random seeds reported as mean +/- std and exceeding 2x that std. The attacker must also re-run, in the same environment and splits, at least two published rows (one foundation model with precomputed or recomputable embeddings and the ResNet50 row) and land within 0.01 Pearson of their published values, or the comparison is void. No test-patient patch, expression value or summary statistic may enter training, gene filtering, normalisation, PCA fitting, hyperparameter choice or early stopping. Deliverables: pinned HEST-Library commit, dataset file sha256s, split files used, training and inference scripts, per-split prediction files, and the verbatim benchmark output for all tasks claimed.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the chosen task's folder from the ungated Hugging Face dataset (0.5-3 GB for most tasks), compares sha256s against the attacker's manifest, confirms the train/test patient lists match the published split csv files exactly, loads the attacker's predictions and recomputes the Pearson correlations with the HEST-Library's own benchmark function at a pinned commit (minutes), then re-runs the attacker's training for at least two seeds (laptop-hours) and the two baseline rows. The live record is read by curling the README and parsing the markdown table. Leakage audit: confirm that PCA, scalers, gene selection and any image-level statistics were fitted on training patients only, and that no spot from a test patient appears in training.

angles: Conventional: pan-allele modelling done with modern but small architectures trained from scratch on BD2009 - allele pseudo-sequence plus peptide, with length handling by explicit insertion/deletion encodings rather than separate models per length.

Conventional: measurement-noise-aware loss. Affinities come from different assays with different dynamic ranges; a censored-regression likelihood that respects qualitative and quantitative measurements separately is rarely used and directly addresses what limits small-allele datasets.

Cross-domain import (coding theory / soft-decision decoding): combine per-position scoring matrices for related alleles as unequal-reliability channel observations and decode with a log-likelihood-ratio rule, which is the principled version of 'borrow strength across similar HLA molecules'.

Cross-domain import (statistical physics / Potts models): fit pairwise couplings between peptide positions with pseudo-likelihood direct-coupling analysis, capturing the position-position dependence that position-weight-matrix methods such as SMM-PMBEC assume away, at negligible CPU cost.

Cross-domain import (psychometrics / item response theory): alleles are items with their own difficulty and discrimination and peptides are subjects; IRT-style parameterisation handles the extreme imbalance between well-measured and barely-measured alleles better than per-allele fitting.

Cross-domain import (survey statistics / selection models): IEDB measurements are not a random sample of peptide space - they were chosen by experimenters, often guided by earlier predictors. Model that selection explicitly and reweight, which is exactly the mechanism the published study blames for the optimism gap.

Uncertainty-first: produce calibrated per-dataset confidence and report AUC together with an abstention curve; for neoantigen triage, knowing which alleles the model cannot handle is worth as much as the mean AUC.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: Peptide-MHC class I binding: beat NetMHCpan's blind-set AUC on the frozen public IEDB BD2009-to-Blind benchmark

partial_wins.statement: Beat the best reference blind AUC by >= 0.02 on the 20 smallest Blind datasets (those the published analysis identifies as least reliable, where size and diversity drive the cross-validation-to-blind gap), under the same training restriction, showing that small-allele transfer is improvable.

Shrink the published cross-validation-to-blind optimism gap: report, for the attacker's method, the gap between cross-validated and blind mean AUC and show it is smaller than NetMHCpan's published gap (0.9147 versus 0.8830, i.e. 0.0317) by at least 0.01 while blind AUC is not worse than the reference. A calibration result about honest evaluation, independently checkable.

A leakage-quantification result of record: measure how much apparent blind AUC a modern pretrained predictor gains on this benchmark purely because its training data include the Blind measurements, by comparing it against the same architecture trained only on BD2009. Reported as a methodological finding, not as a record.

pitfalls: Training-data contamination is the defining trap: every modern peptide-MHC predictor was trained on data that include the Blind measurements, so running one of them on this benchmark produces a meaningless number. The claim must document the provenance of every component, including language-model weights.

Near-duplicate peptides between BD2009 and Blind for the same allele: the published analysis shows similarity is not the main driver of the optimism gap, but a claimed win must still report the similarity distribution and show the gain is not confined to near-duplicates.

Dataset-set drift: the published tables cover 87 (allele, length) datasets with both cross-validation and blind values while the Blind set as a whole contains 90; averaging over a different dataset set, or weighting by dataset size instead of averaging per dataset, moves the mean by more than the 0.01 bar.

Threshold and metric conventions: binder/non-binder thresholds (500 nM) and the handling of qualitative measurements change AUC; only the benchmark's own convention counts, and the skeptic must recompute rather than trust reported numbers.

Benchmark age and novelty: this is a 2014 benchmark, so the NOVELTY check must confirm that a claimed method is not simply re-deriving a published post-2014 architecture, and the write-up must not present a win here as state of the art for modern presentation prediction, which is evaluated on mass-spectrometry eluted-ligand data instead.

Over-claiming: binding affinity is only the first filter in neoantigen selection - presentation, T-cell recognition and tumour expression all follow - so a better AUC here does not rank neoantigens for any patient.
targets.statement: Every neoantigen pipeline begins by asking which mutated peptides a patient's HLA molecules can present, so the quality of peptide-MHC class I binding predictors sets the floor for neoantigen ranking. The IEDB Analysis Resource hosts a completely frozen, fully public benchmark for this: Yohan Kim, Bjoern Peters, Morten Nielsen and colleagues (BMC Bioinformatics 15:241, 2014) released BD2009 as a training set and defined Blind as the measurements added to IEDB between 2009 and 2013 - 29,169 data points over 53 alleles and 90 (allele, length) datasets - so a method trained only on BD2009 can be scored on genuinely later data. The benchmark archive at tools.iedb.org ships the predictions of the three reference methods on every dataset plus machine-readable per-dataset AUC tables. Re-read live on 2026-10-15 from the tables in benchmark_mhci_reliability.tar.gz (87 datasets with both cross-validation and blind numbers): mean blind AUC is 0.8833 for NetMHC, 0.8830 for NetMHCpan and 0.8474 for SMM-PMBEC, against cross-validated means of 0.8919, 0.9147 and 0.9025 respectively - the published demonstration that cross-validation systematically overestimates blind performance. Per dataset the spread is large (HLA-A*02:01 9mers 0.9386 blind for NetMHCpan, HLA-A*31:01 9mers 0.8821, HLA-A*02:01 10mers 0.8666). The training data (bdata.20130222.mhci.txt, 7.8 MB) and the whole benchmark archive (26 MB) download with a plain GET, and training a modern-but-small model on 134,645 affinity measurements is laptop-hours on a CPU.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a predictor trained ONLY on the BD2009 measurements distributed with the benchmark (sha256 logged), with no use of any peptide, allele-specific measurement, model weight or embedding derived from data added to IEDB after 2009 - which excludes every modern pretrained peptide-MHC predictor and any protein language model whose training corpus provably contains these later measurements - producing a score for every peptide in every Blind dataset, such that the mean AUC over the same 87 (allele, length) datasets used by the published tables, recomputed by the skeptic with the benchmark's own binder threshold convention, is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the maximum mean blind AUC over the reference methods in the live tables inside https://tools.iedb.org/static/main/benchmark_mhci_reliability.tar.gz - re-fetched and re-parsed immediately before claiming - by at least 0.01 absolute, AND is higher on at least 60 of the 87 individual datasets (a two-sided sign test at p < 0.01). Deliverables: the training script, the exact BD2009 file used, the per-dataset score files, the per-dataset AUC table produced by the skeptic's script, and a documented statement of every external resource the method touched, with evidence that none post-dates 2009.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads binding_data_2013.zip and benchmark_mhci_reliability.tar.gz from tools.iedb.org with a plain GET, compares sha256s with the attacker's manifest, confirms the attacker's score files cover exactly the peptides in each Blind dataset, recomputes the per-dataset AUC with their own script using the benchmark's binder threshold, averages over the same 87 datasets and compares against the reference tables extracted live from the archive. The skeptic then re-trains the attacker's model from BD2009 end to end (laptop-hours) and confirms the scores are reproduced within a documented tolerance. Leakage audit: inspect the training code and any cached artefacts for reads of post-2009 data, check the declared provenance of any pretrained component, and confirm that no Blind peptide (or near-identical peptide for the same allele) appears in the training file used.

angles: Conventional: distance-based classifiers over the full CDR1/CDR2/CDR3 of both chains (the repository ships A1/A2/A3 and B1/B2/B3) with a learned substitution metric; the current leaders are a nearest-neighbour method and a Gaussian process, so the frontier is about the metric, not the architecture.

Conventional: proper handling of the two negative classes - swapped-epitope negatives and healthy-donor control negatives have different statistics, and reweighting or training two heads and combining them is an obvious and untested move.

Cross-domain import (cryptanalysis / distinguisher design): treat specificity prediction as a distinguishing game between two generative sources of CDR3 sequences and build an explicit log-likelihood-ratio distinguisher, where each source is modelled by a V(D)J generation model (the standard IGoR/SONIA machinery) corrected by an epitope-specific selection factor. This directly optimises the quantity the AUC measures instead of a surrogate classification loss.

Cross-domain import (compression / normalised compression distance): define TCR-TCR similarity by the compressibility of concatenated CDR sequences, which needs no alignment, no substitution matrix and no training, and use it as a kernel; parameter-free similarity measures are strongest exactly in the small-sample regime these per-epitope training sets occupy (dozens to a few hundred positives).

Cross-domain import (ecology / species-abundance statistics): a repertoire is a sample from a highly uneven community, so Good-Turing and rarefaction estimators give a principled correction for how much of an apparent epitope-specific motif is sampling depth rather than signal; use the correction to down-weight motifs that look specific only because of unequal sampling.

Cross-domain import (statistical physics): fit a Potts/direct-coupling model over aligned CDR3 positions per epitope and use the statistical energy as the score, capturing pairwise residue couplings that position-weight matrices miss; pseudo-likelihood DCA on a few hundred sequences runs in seconds on a CPU.

Multi-epitope transfer: train one model across all 17 epitopes with the peptide as an input (rather than 17 independent models) and measure whether sharing helps or hurts per-epitope micro-AUC; the published tables mix both styles and never isolate this.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: IMMREP22 TCR-epitope specificity: beat the best published per-epitope micro-AUC on the public paired-chain benchmark

partial_wins.statement: Beat the live best micro-AUC by >= 0.03 on each of the five hardest epitopes (as of 2026-10-15 the columns where the published best stays under 0.80: NQKLIANQF, TTDPSFLGRY, LTDEMIAQY, NLVPMVATV, TPRVTGGGAM), with one frozen configuration chosen without looking at those epitopes' test labels.

Beat the live best average rank in evaluation/epitoperank.csv (3.284, tcrexab, as of 2026-10-15; lower is better) by >= 0.25 under the same no-leakage protocol, which measures consistency across epitopes rather than a single lucky column.

A negative-sampling audit of record: show, with the released control repertoire, how much of each published method's micro-AUC is explained by distinguishing VDJdb-derived TCRs from healthy-donor control TCRs rather than by epitope specificity, by re-scoring the SAME predictions against (a) swapped-epitope negatives only and (b) control-repertoire negatives only. Mechanically checkable from the saved scores and not reported in the published tables.

pitfalls: Negative-set artefacts dominate this benchmark: positives come from VDJdb and many negatives come from one control cohort, so a model can score well by detecting dataset provenance (sequencing protocol, V-gene usage, CDR3 length distribution) rather than specificity. Any claim must include the negative-source ablation, and a win that vanishes when only swapped-epitope negatives are used must be reported as such.

Test-label peeking is trivially easy because the test files ship with labels in the repository. The skeptic must re-run training from the attacker's code rather than trust a score file, and must grep for reads of test_set/.

Near-duplicate TCRs: VDJdb aggregates studies, so clonally related or identical CDR3s can straddle the 80:20 split. Report the maximum similarity (e.g. TCRdist or Levenshtein) between each test TCR and the training set, and show the gain is not confined to the near-duplicate tail.

Metric substitution: micro-AUC pooled over an epitope is not the same as macro-AUC, average precision, or the epitope-rank metric in epitoperank.csv; comparing one against a record from another is a fatal error, and small epitopes swing by far more than the 0.02 bar.

Stale-table comparison: the record must be re-read from the live CSV, and the NOVELTY check must look for later papers reporting higher numbers on this exact benchmark (several re-benchmarks of IMMREP data have appeared since 2023).

Over-claiming: a higher AUC on 17 mostly viral epitopes with laboratory negatives says nothing about finding tumour-reactive TCRs in a patient, where the epitopes are private neoantigens and the negative space is astronomically larger. The write-up must say so.
targets.statement: Deciding which T-cell receptor recognises which peptide is the computational bottleneck of neoantigen-directed cell therapy: once a tumour peptide is nominated, somebody has to guess which TCRs in a patient's repertoire can see it. The IMMREP22 workshop (Working Group 6 of the 2022 Dresden 'Dynamics of Immune Repertoires' workshop, organised by Morten Nielsen, Virag Sharma and colleagues; Nielsen et al., ImmunoInformatics 2023) froze a fully public benchmark for exactly this task: paired alpha/beta TCRs from VDJdb with annotated specificity to 17 peptides, plus an unpublished healthy-donor CD8 control repertoire from A. Eugster used as negatives, split 80:20 into training and test per epitope, with CDR1/CDR2/CDR3 of both chains pre-extracted (Stitchr + ANARCI). Everything needed to score a model is in the repository: training_data/, test_set/ with labels, negativeData_controls/, evaluation/evaluate.py, and the result tables for 22 published method variants. As re-read live on 2026-10-15 from evaluation/microaucs.csv, the best average micro-AUC across the 17 epitopes is 0.8473 (tcrexab), then TCRGP 0.8468, tcrdist3 0.8403, tcrexb 0.8301, netTCR_cdr123ab 0.8246, TCRAI 0.8234; the random baseline sits at 0.4901. Per-epitope the spread is enormous (for ATDALMTGF several methods exceed 0.95 while for NQKLIANQF most sit near 0.5), so the frontier is not one number but seventeen, and the data are a few thousand short amino-acid strings: this is a CPU-only, laptop-hours problem where kernel methods and careful negative handling have repeatedly beaten deep models.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a saved prediction file giving one real-valued score to every TCR in the IMMREP22 test_set/ file for a chosen epitope (or for all 17), produced by a model trained only on that epitope's training_data/ file plus the released control repertoire, scored with the repository's own evaluation/evaluate.py at a pinned commit, whose micro-AUC is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the maximum over ALL method rows in the live https://raw.githubusercontent.com/viragbioinfo/IMMREP_2022_TCRSpecificity/main/evaluation/microaucs.csv - re-fetched and re-parsed immediately before claiming - by at least 0.02 absolute on the _Average column, or by at least 0.03 absolute on a single named epitope column. No test-set TCR, and no label of any test-set TCR, may enter training, feature construction, hyperparameter selection, early stopping or thresholding; hyperparameters may be chosen only by cross-validation inside the training file of OTHER epitopes or inside the training split of the same epitope. The claim must ship: the pinned commit and sha256 of the data files used, the training script, the per-epitope score files, the verbatim evaluate.py output, and a same-environment re-run of at least two published baselines whose micro-AUCs land within 0.01 of the published values (otherwise the comparison is void).
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones the repository at the attacker's pinned commit, checks sha256 of training_data/, test_set/ and negativeData_controls/ against the attacker's manifest, confirms that every test TCR appears exactly once in the attacker's score file and that no test TCR string occurs in the training file used, re-runs evaluation/evaluate.py on the supplied scores (minutes) and then re-trains the attacker's model end-to-end (laptop-minutes to laptop-hours) to confirm the micro-AUC is reproduced. The live record is read by curling microaucs.csv and taking the column maximum with the skeptic's own script. Leakage audit: grep the training code for any read of test_set/, check that no sequence-similarity index was built over the test file, and confirm the control TCRs used as negatives in training are disjoint from those in the test file.

angles: Strong pretrained backbones plus heavy augmentation and multi-crop test-time averaging; most 2017 entries used ResNet-50-era models.
Self-supervised pretraining on the 2,000 training images only (DINO-style) before fine-tuning, which keeps the no-external-data class.
Cross-domain import (few-shot learning): prototype-based heads and episodic training suit a 2,000-image, two-task problem.
Cross-domain import (radiology reader studies): AUC-optimising pairwise losses (as used for screening CAD) target the metric directly.
Multi-task training of the two binary heads with the Part 1 lesion masks as an auxiliary task (masks are part of the official training data).
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: ISIC 2017 Part 3 (melanoma and seborrheic keratosis): beat the challenge-best mean AUC of 0.911 on the public 600-image test labels

partial_wins.statement: Melanoma AUC alone above the best melanoma AUC on the leaderboard's per-category details, no external data.
Mean AUC above 0.911 with an ImageNet-pretrained model fine-tuned on a laptop in under 6 hours, mean over 3 seeds.

pitfalls: Later ISIC releases (2018, 2019 training sets and the ISIC Archive) contain many 2017 test images with labels; any external data must be deduplicated by hash against the 600 test images.
Test labels are public; selecting checkpoints or ensembles by test AUC is leakage.
Some papers report melanoma AUC only, or a 3-class accuracy; only the mean of the two AUCs compares with the primary leaderboard metric.
600 images and roughly 117 melanomas mean AUC differences below about 0.01 are within noise; report bootstrap intervals.
Research benchmark only; no diagnostic claim.
targets.statement: ISIC 2017 Part 3 (Codella et al., ISBI 2018) scored two binary tasks on 600 dermoscopy test images: melanoma vs all and seborrheic keratosis vs all, ranked by the mean of the two ROC AUCs, with only 2,000 training and 150 validation images. The test ground truth is a plain public CSV (ISIC-2017_Test_v2_Part3_GroundTruth.csv) and the official scorer is isic-challenge-scoring. The live leaderboard is led by the Casio and Shinshu University joint team (Kazuhisa Matsunaga and colleagues) at 0.911, then Universidad Carlos III de Madrid (Ivan Gonzalez-Diaz) 0.910 and RECOD Titans 0.908, none flagged as using external data on the board. The small training set makes this a sharp test of data efficiency.
targets.success_criterion: Probability scores for all 600 official test images for both tasks, from a model trained only on the 2,000 official training images (validation images allowed for selection) and frozen before any test scoring, whose mean of melanoma AUC and seborrheic-keratosis AUC computed by the skeptic with isic-challenge-scoring against the public Part 3 test ground truth is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the Part 3 leader on the live 2017 leaderboard (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) and than any official-test value without external data found by the NOVELTY check, by at least 0.005. Claims using external dermoscopy data are reported separately and must be deduplicated against the test images.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the public Part 3 test ground truth CSV, runs isic-challenge-scoring classification on the claim, checks 600 ids, and audits external data for overlap with test images. Minutes.

angles: Optimise the actual metric: thresholded Jaccard punishes outright failures, so add a failure detector (predicted-mask quality regression) and fall back to a second model on low-confidence images.

Modern pretrained encoders (ImageNet ConvNeXt/EfficientNet U-Nets) at moderate resolution with heavy colour and hair augmentation, plus multi-scale test-time augmentation; most 2018 entries predate these.

Cross-domain import (interactive segmentation / SAM-style promptable models): use an automatically generated box prompt from a coarse model and refine with a promptable segmenter, keeping training data rules.
Cross-domain import (cartography): boundary smoothing with active contours or conditional random fields on the probability map, as several top 2018 teams did, now applied to a stronger base.
Exploit the shape prior: lesions are mostly single connected blobs; keep the largest connected component and fill holes, which removes many sub-0.65 failures cheaply.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: ISIC 2018 skin-lesion segmentation: beat the challenge-winning thresholded Jaccard on the public test ground truth

partial_wins.statement: Exceed 0.802 thresholded Jaccard with NO external data and a model trainable on a laptop (CPU/MPS) in under 12 hours.
Reduce the number of test images below the 0.65 cutoff (failures) relative to a reproduced strong baseline, with an analysis of failure types; the thresholded metric is dominated by these failures.

pitfalls: Mean Jaccard is not thresholded Jaccard; many papers report the former (or Dice) and on random training-set splits. Only thresholded Jaccard on the official 1,000-image test set compares to the leaderboard.
Test ground truth is public: choosing epochs, thresholds or TTA settings by test score is leakage. Use the 100-image validation set or a training split.
Images and masks must be evaluated at original resolution; scoring downsampled masks inflates Jaccard.
External data changes the comparison class; the leaderboard marks it, and claims must too.
This is an image-analysis benchmark; it says nothing about clinical melanoma diagnosis and must not be framed that way.

The ISIC Archive and later ISIC releases contain many Task 1 test images, some with lesion masks. Any external dermoscopy data, not only ISIC 2016/2017 masks, must be hash-deduplicated against the test images, or the claim is leakage.
targets.statement: ISIC 2018 Task 1 (lesion boundary segmentation, International Skin Imaging Collaboration; Codella et al. 2019) scored 66 teams on 1,000 dermoscopy test images with the thresholded Jaccard index: per-image Jaccard, set to 0 when below 0.65, then averaged. The final leaderboard (challenge.isic-archive.com/leaderboards/2018) is topped by team MT at 0.802, then Holidayburned and imsight at 0.799. The test images AND test ground-truth masks are now public as plain S3 downloads (ISIC2018_Task1_Test_GroundTruth.zip, 9.7 MB; inputs 2.4 GB; training 11 GB), so the official metric can be recomputed offline. Many later papers claim higher 'Jaccard' on ISIC 2018, but usually mean Jaccard (not thresholded) on random splits of the training set, which is not this benchmark.
targets.success_criterion: Binary masks for all 1,000 official ISIC 2018 Task 1 test images, from a model trained only on the 2,594 official training images (plus optionally the 100 validation images) and frozen before any test scoring, whose thresholded Jaccard (per-image Jaccard, values < 0.65 set to 0, mean over images) computed by the skeptic against ISIC2018_Task1_Test_GroundTruth.zip is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the Task 1 leader on the live leaderboard (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) and than any thresholded-Jaccard value on the official test set found in later literature, by at least 0.005. No external dermoscopy segmentation data (e.g. ISIC 2016/2017 masks, PH2) unless declared, and a declared-external-data claim is reported separately (the leaderboard flags external data).
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads ISIC2018_Task1_Test_GroundTruth.zip from the public ISIC S3 URL and scores the 1,000 claimed masks with the official scorer (pip install isic-challenge-scoring; isic-challenge-scoring segmentation <gt_dir> <pred_dir>). This reports the thresholded Jaccard used for ranking. The skeptic checks mask sizes against the original images, audits training code for any read of test masks, and hash-deduplicates every external training image against the 1,000 test images. Re-runs inference from released weights on a sample. Minutes for scoring.

angles: Dataset-level Jaccard rewards getting the big positives right and not hallucinating on the many images with empty masks; train an image-level presence classifier per attribute and gate the segmenter with it.
Use the Task 1 lesion mask (trained on Task 1 training data only) as an extra input channel or a hard crop: attributes only occur inside the lesion.
Cross-domain import (retinal vessel and road-crack segmentation): thin-structure losses (clDice, topology-aware losses) and multi-scale line filters suit pigment network and streaks.

Cross-domain import (astronomy source detection): milia-like cysts and globules are blob-like point sources; a Laplacian-of-Gaussian detector plus learned refinement may beat dense segmentation for them.
Tune per-attribute probability thresholds on the validation set to maximise accumulated Jaccard, which is not the same threshold as per-pixel accuracy.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: ISIC 2018 Task 2 (dermoscopic attribute segmentation): beat the challenge-best mean Jaccard of 0.307 on the public test masks

partial_wins.statement: Exceed 0.307 with a model trained on a laptop in under 12 hours, no external data.
Beat the leader's per-attribute Jaccard on at least three of the five attributes (from the leaderboard's per-category details), with the mean also above 0.307.

pitfalls: The metric accumulates intersection and union over all images; per-image mean Jaccard (common in papers) gives different numbers and cannot be compared.
Test masks are public: threshold or epoch selection on test scores is leakage.
Many papers on 'ISIC 2018 attributes' report on random splits of the training set; only the official 1,000-image test set compares with the leaderboard.
Annotation is coarse (superpixel-based) and inconsistent; a model that exploits superpixel shapes may gain on the metric without detecting attributes better. Report that honestly.
Attribute masks are a teaching and research aid; better scores do not make a diagnostic tool.
targets.statement: ISIC 2018 Task 2 asked for pixel masks of five dermoscopic attributes that dermatologists use in melanoma assessment (pigment network, negative network, streaks, milia-like cysts, globules) on 1,000 test images, trained on 2,594 images. The metric is the Jaccard index per attribute, accumulated over the whole test set, averaged over the five attributes. The test masks are now a plain public download (ISIC2018_Task2_Test_GroundTruth.zip, 11.8 MB) and the official scorer is the isic-challenge-scoring package. The live leaderboard is topped by NMN_team at 0.307 (no external data), then Le-Health 0.276 and RECOD Titans 0.238. Unlike Task 1 (lesion boundary, about 0.80), this task is far from saturated: the attributes are thin, sparse and inconsistently annotated, and few groups have revisited it with modern segmentation models.
targets.success_criterion: Binary masks for all five attributes on all 1,000 official Task 2 test images, from a model trained only on the official Task 2 training (and validation) data and frozen before any test scoring, whose leaderboard Jaccard computed by the skeptic with isic-challenge-scoring segmentation against ISIC2018_Task2_Test_GroundTruth is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the Task 2 leader on the live leaderboard (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) and than any official-test value found by the NOVELTY check, by at least 0.01.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the public test masks, runs isic-challenge-scoring segmentation on the claimed mask folder (checks naming, image sizes, binary values and that all 5,000 masks exist), and compares with the live leaderboard. Audits that no test mask was read during training or tuning. Minutes.

angles: Optimise the metric: balanced accuracy rewards per-class recall, so tune class-prior offsets on validation (logit adjustment) rather than using argmax of a frequency-biased model.
Modern ImageNet-pretrained backbones (ConvNeXt, EfficientNetV2) at 384-512 px with colour constancy (Shades of Gray) preprocessing, which several top 2018 teams used.
Cross-domain import (long-tailed recognition in ecology / iNaturalist): balanced softmax and deferred re-weighting were built for exactly this class imbalance.
Cross-domain import (ensemble forecasting): weight ensemble members by their validation per-class recall, as forecast hubs weight by skill per target.
Use the lesion-grouping file to keep images of the same lesion together in internal validation splits, so model selection is honest.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: ISIC 2018 Task 3 (HAM10000 diagnosis, 7 classes): beat the best balanced multiclass accuracy on the 1,512-image public test ground truth

partial_wins.statement: No external data: exceed 0.845 with a model trainable on a laptop in under 12 hours, mean over 3 seeds.
Any data class: report per-class recall showing improvement on the three rarest classes without loss on melanoma recall relative to a reproduced strong baseline.

pitfalls: The ISIC Archive and later releases include the test images with diagnoses; any external data from the Archive (or HAM10000-derived sets such as DermaMNIST) must be deduplicated against the test set, or the result is leakage.
Test labels are public: choosing thresholds, epochs or ensemble weights by test score invalidates the claim.
Accuracy, AUC and balanced accuracy differ; many papers report accuracy (~0.9+) or use random splits of HAM10000, which do not compare with the leaderboard.
External-data and no-external-data entries are separate classes on the leaderboard; compare within the declared class.
A dermoscopy benchmark gain is not a validated diagnostic tool and must not be framed as one.
targets.statement: ISIC 2018 Task 3 asked for a 7-way diagnosis (melanoma, nevus, basal cell carcinoma, actinic keratosis/Bowen's, benign keratosis, dermatofibroma, vascular) of dermoscopy images, training on the 10,015-image HAM10000 set (Tschandl, Rosendahl and Kittler 2018) and scoring by balanced multiclass accuracy (mean per-class recall) on 1,512 test images. The test ground truth is now a plain public download (ISIC2018_Task3_Test_GroundTruth.zip) and the official scorer is the isic-challenge-scoring package. The live leaderboard (challenge.isic-archive.com/leaderboards/2018, Task 3) is topped by MetaOptima Technology at 0.885 and DAISYLab (Nils Gessert, Alexander Schlaefer and colleagues) at 0.856, both using external data; the best entry without external data is the Medical Image Analysis Group of Sun Yat-sen University at 0.845. Mean per-class recall is dominated by the rare classes (dermatofibroma, vascular, actinic keratosis), so calibration and class weighting matter more than raw accuracy.
targets.success_criterion: A prediction CSV for all 1,512 official Task 3 test images, from a model trained only on the official training data (and the 193 official validation images) and frozen before any test scoring, whose balanced multiclass accuracy computed by the skeptic with isic-challenge-scoring against ISIC2018_Task3_Test_GroundTruth is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the best value in its comparison class on the live Task 3 leaderboard (re-fetched live immediately before claiming): 0.845 class for no external data, 0.885 class if external data is declared; and higher than any official-test value for the same class found by the NOVELTY check, by at least 0.005.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the public test ground truth, runs isic-challenge-scoring classification gt.csv pred.csv, checks image ids and count (1,512), and audits training data: every external image must be hash-deduplicated against the 1,512 test images. Minutes for scoring.

angles: Treat UNK as open-set recognition: energy scores or Mahalanobis distance on penultimate features, threshold set on held-out training classes (leave-one-class-out simulation), never on test.
Domain-aware training: the three source collections differ in camera and crop; group-DRO or per-source normalisation reduces shortcut learning.
Cross-domain import (anomaly detection in industrial inspection): PatchCore-style memory banks of training-patch features to flag lesions unlike any training class.
Cross-domain import (selective classification in credit scoring): reject-option decision rules trading coverage for accuracy map directly onto when to output UNK.
Exploit balanced accuracy: rare classes (DF, VASC, SCC) and UNK each count as much as nevus, so per-class bias correction on validation data is worth more than backbone size.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: ISIC 2019 skin-lesion diagnosis with an 'unknown' class: beat the best balanced accuracy (0.636; 0.607 without external data) on the public test labels

partial_wins.statement: No external data, images only: exceed 0.607 with a laptop-trainable model, mean of 3 seeds.

Improve UNK recall above every leaderboard entry's UNK recall (from the per-category details) while keeping overall balanced accuracy above 0.60, using an out-of-distribution detector calibrated only on training data.

pitfalls: BCN20000 and the ISIC Archive later published labelled images that include ISIC 2019 test images; any external data must be deduplicated against the test set or the claim is leakage.
Public test labels make test-tuned UNK thresholds tempting; any threshold chosen by looking at test scores invalidates the result.
Papers often report 8-class accuracy on random training splits without UNK; those numbers do not compare with the leaderboard.
Images-only and images+metadata are separate tasks on the leaderboard; compare within the same task and external-data class.
A benchmark gain in open-set skin-lesion classification is not clinical evidence; say so.
targets.statement: ISIC 2019 trained 8-class dermoscopy diagnosis on 25,331 images (HAM10000, BCN20000 and MSK) and tested on 8,238 images that also contain lesions of none of the 8 classes, which must be flagged as 'UNK'; the metric is balanced multiclass accuracy over 9 categories. The test ground truth is now a plain public CSV (ISIC_2019_Test_GroundTruth.csv) and the official scorer is isic-challenge-scoring. On the live leaderboard (images only) DAISYLab (Nils Gessert, Maximilian Nielsen, Mohsin Shaikh, Rene Werner, Alexander Schlaefer) leads with 0.636 using external data, and DysionAI leads the no-external-data class with 0.607; with metadata, DAISYLab 0.634 and Torus Actions 0.597. The open-set UNK requirement and the domain mix keep this well below the 0.85+ of ISIC 2018 Task 3, so it is genuinely unsaturated.
targets.success_criterion: A prediction CSV for all 8,238 official ISIC 2019 test images (9 columns including UNK), from a model trained only on the official 2019 training images (and optionally the official training metadata) and frozen before any test scoring, whose balanced multiclass accuracy computed by the skeptic with isic-challenge-scoring against ISIC_2019_Test_GroundTruth.csv is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the best value in its comparison class (images-only or images+metadata; external data or not) on the live 2019 leaderboard (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) and than any official-test value found by the NOVELTY check, by at least 0.005.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the public ground-truth CSV, runs isic-challenge-scoring classification on the claimed CSV, checks 8,238 rows and image ids, and audits that no external image duplicates a test image (hash or ISIC id). Minutes.

angles: Conventional: strengthen rather than replace the baseline - add per-gene variance modelling, shrinkage toward the control profile, and a count-aware likelihood, and check how much of the deep models' claimed advantage disappears or reverses.

Conventional: use prior biology that the linear model ignores - protein complex membership, pathway co-membership and co-essentiality correlations from public screens - as a structured prior over perturbation vectors, strictly without touching the held-out perturbations' measurements.

Cross-domain import (statistical physics / linear response and cavity method): a knockdown is a field applied to a gene-regulatory network; estimate susceptibilities from the training perturbations with a TAP/cavity approximation, which predicts unseen fields rather than memorising seen ones.

Cross-domain import (control theory / system identification): treat the training perturbations as input-output experiments on an unknown linear-plus-nonlinear system and identify the transfer operator with subspace identification methods, which come with identifiability diagnostics that tell you in advance which unseen perturbations are predictable.

Cross-domain import (compression / MDL): choose the rank and sparsity by two-part code length instead of validation loss; the paper's result suggests the field is over-parameterising a problem whose information content is small, and MDL is the tool that measures exactly that.

Cross-domain import (psychometrics / item response theory): perturbations are 'items' and genes are 'persons'; IRT-style models with discrimination and difficulty parameters handle extremely unbalanced response matrices and provide calibrated uncertainty for unseen items.

Honest ceiling estimation: estimate the irreducible noise floor from biological and technical replicate perturbations in the Replogle data and report how much of the gap between the linear baseline and perfect prediction is even reachable.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: Unseen single-gene perturbations in leukaemia cells: beat the linear baseline that currently matches every foundation model

partial_wins.statement: The same strict improvement on the Replogle RPE1 dataset instead of (or in addition to) K562, under the identical protocol; a method that wins on only one of the two cell lines is a weaker but still reportable result and must be reported as such.

Show that the gain, if any, is concentrated in perturbations whose target gene has close functional neighbours in the training set, by reporting the metric as a function of the distance between the held-out perturbation and its nearest training perturbation in an embedding declared before scoring. This quantifies what 'generalising to unseen perturbations' actually buys and is checkable from saved predictions.

A reproduction of record: re-run the linear baseline and two published deep models on all five splits of both Replogle datasets and report agreement or disagreement with the published Source Data values, with full logs. Reported as a reproduction, not a record.

pitfalls: Pretraining contamination: any foundation model pretrained on corpora that include these Perturb-seq datasets has seen the held-out perturbations' effects. The pretraining corpus must be declared, and an undeclared one voids the claim.

Metric substitution: the published comparison uses L2 over the 1,000 most highly expressed genes and the Pearson delta; switching to correlation over the top differentially expressed genes, or to all genes, changes the ranking entirely and is the single most common way papers in this area manufacture wins.

Control-profile trivia: predicting the control (unperturbed) profile already scores respectably on several of these metrics, so any claim must include the control-only predictor as a baseline and beat it by a stated margin.

Split and dataset drift: GEARS has distributed several versions of these datasets; a different version, gene filter or split seed makes the comparison incomparable. sha256s and split definitions must be logged.

Near-duplicate perturbations: knocking down two members of the same complex produces near-identical profiles, so an apparent generalisation to an 'unseen' perturbation can be retrieval of its complex partner. Report the metric as a function of nearest-training-perturbation distance.
Over-claiming: beating a linear baseline on CRISPRi in K562 is a statement about one leukaemia cell line measured one way, not about predicting a drug's effect in a patient's tumour.
targets.statement: Constantin Ahlmann-Eltze, Wolfgang Huber and Simon Anders (Nature Methods, 2025, doi 10.1038/s41592-025-02772-6) asked whether single-cell foundation models can predict the transcriptional consequence of knocking down a gene that was never perturbed in training, and found that GEARS, scGPT, scFoundation, Geneformer, scBERT and UCE do not beat a deliberately simple linear baseline - a low-rank factorisation with one vector per read-out gene and one per perturbation - on the CRISPRi Perturb-seq datasets of Replogle et al. (K562 chronic myelogenous leukaemia and RPE1) and Adamson et al. (K562), measured as the L2 distance between predicted and observed expression over the 1,000 most highly expressed genes and as the Pearson delta, across five test-training splits. Every input is public and ungated: the Replogle K562 and RPE1 and Adamson datasets as distributed by GEARS on Harvard Dataverse, the analysis code at github.com/const-ae/linear_perturbation_prediction-Paper with the intermediate results archived on Zenodo, and the numeric values behind every figure in the Source Data files, which Europe PMC serves without registration. That makes this one of the few perturbation-prediction frontiers where the bar is a baseline anyone can re-run in minutes on a CPU, and where the honest open question - can anything actually beat it for unseen perturbations in a cancer cell line? - is still unanswered in public.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a model that, trained only on the training perturbations of each of the five published test-training splits of the Replogle K562 dataset as distributed by GEARS (sha256 logged), predicts the expression profile of each held-out perturbation, and whose median L2 distance over the 1,000 most highly expressed genes, computed with the repository's own scoring code at a pinned commit, is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than BOTH (a) the attacker's same-environment, same-splits re-run of the paper's linear baseline and (b) the best value over all methods in the paper's published Source Data for that dataset and metric, re-fetched live immediately before claiming from https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC12328236/supplementaryFiles, by at least 5% of the linear baseline's own value and by at least 2x the across-split standard deviation. The same ordering must hold for the Pearson delta measure reported in the same Source Data. No held-out perturbation's measured cells may enter training, gene selection, normalisation, early stopping or hyperparameter choice, and any pretrained model used must have a declared pretraining corpus that does not include the held-out perturbations of these datasets. Deliverables: pinned commits, dataset sha256s, the split definitions, training and inference code, per-split prediction matrices, and the verbatim metric output for the attacker's model, the linear baseline and at least one published deep model re-run.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the GEARS-distributed Replogle K562 data from Harvard Dataverse (no registration), checks sha256 against the manifest, verifies the five split definitions and that held-out perturbations never appear in training, re-computes the L2 and Pearson delta metrics from the attacker's prediction matrices with the repository's own code at a pinned commit (minutes), then re-trains the attacker's model on at least two splits and re-runs the linear baseline in the same environment (laptop-hours). The live bar is read by fetching the Europe PMC supplementary files and reading the Source Data tables for the relevant figure. Leakage audit: confirm gene filtering and normalisation statistics were computed on training cells only, that no per-perturbation statistic was computed over the full dataset, and that any pretrained weights predate or exclude these datasets.

angles: False-positive reduction is laptop-friendly: extract 3D patches at candidate locations once (small disk footprint), then train compact 3D CNNs or 2.5D multi-view networks per fold.
Cross-domain import (particle physics triggers): cascaded classifiers with increasing cost, as used in detector triggers, cut most easy negatives with a cheap model before an expensive one.
Cross-domain import (astronomy point-source detection): matched filters and scale-space blob detectors on lung-masked CT give a strong, interpretable candidate generator.
Ensembles across folds of different architectures and input scales, combined by rank averaging, typically add the last 0.005-0.01 CPM.
Hard-negative mining focused on vessels and fissures, which dominate false positives at 1/8 and 1/4 FPs per scan where the CPM is weakest.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days
targets.name: LUNA16 lung-nodule detection and false-positive reduction: beat the best CPM (0.951 detection, 0.968 false-positive reduction) under the official 10-fold protocol

partial_wins.statement: False-positive-reduction track: CPM above 0.968 on candidates_V2 with a model small enough to train all 10 folds on a laptop in under 3 days.
Detection track: CPM above 0.951 with all 10 folds released, or a documented reproduction showing that a published claim above 0.951 does or does not hold under the strict protocol.

pitfalls: All labels are public and evaluation is self-run cross-validation, so leakage is easy: any use of a fold's scans for training, early stopping or threshold choice for that fold's predictions invalidates the claim.
Many papers re-split LIDC-IDRI or use different nodule definitions (all nodules, >= 1 radiologist); only the official 1,186-nodule reference and script compare with the results page.
Detection and false-positive-reduction tracks are different tasks with different bars; do not compare a candidate classifier with the detection board.
Pretraining on LIDC-IDRI-derived data (including public nodule datasets built from it) leaks test scans; declare and exclude.
The results page closed to new entries years ago, so later literature claims must be checked; CPM gains do not imply screening benefit.
targets.statement: LUNA16 (Arnaud Setio, Colin Jacobs and co-authors, Medical Image Analysis 2017) is the standard benchmark for lung-cancer screening CT computer-aided detection: 888 LIDC-IDRI CT scans in 10 fixed subsets, 1,186 reference nodules (>= 3 mm, accepted by at least 3 of 4 radiologists), an official evaluation script, and the Competition Performance Metric (CPM: mean sensitivity at 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2, 4 and 8 false positives per scan). Methods are evaluated by 10-fold cross-validation over the fixed subsets. The results page lists PAtech at 0.951 for full detection and PATech at 0.968 for the false-positive-reduction track (classifying the 754,975 supplied candidates in candidates_V2). Data, annotations, candidates and the evaluation script are on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0 (about 120 GB of scans).
targets.success_criterion: Per-subset prediction CSVs for all 888 scans, each subset predicted by a model that never saw that subset's scans or labels in training or selection (strict 10-fold over the official subsets), whose CPM computed by the skeptic with the official LUNA16 evaluation script (with annotations_excluded handling) is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the top score of the same track on https://luna16.grand-challenge.org/Results/ (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) and than any strict-10-fold value for that track found by the NOVELTY check, by at least 0.005.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads annotations.csv, annotations_excluded and the evaluation script from Zenodo, runs the script on the merged predictions, and spot-checks 1-2 folds by retraining or by running released weights on that subset. Audits fold assignment (subset id per scan) and that no fold's model was tuned on its own test subset. Hours for scoring and audit; days for a full retrain.

angles: Conventional: a modern training recipe at 28x28 - cosine schedule, label smoothing, mixup/cutmix, test-time augmentation, stochastic weight averaging - against the official plain-ResNet baselines; most of the published gap on small-image medical benchmarks is recipe, not architecture.

Conventional: colour/stain normalisation for PathMNIST (histology stain variation is the dominant nuisance factor) and intensity standardisation plus aggressive geometric augmentation for the tiny BreastMNIST.

Cross-domain import (signal processing): at 28x28 a learned filter bank is overkill - use a scattering transform (wavelet scattering) or steerable-filter features plus a linear/SVM head, which is translation- and rotation-stable, has almost no parameters, and is extremely strong in the small-sample regime that BreastMNIST represents.

Cross-domain import (compression): classify by minimum compressed-length / normalised-compression-distance against class-conditional dictionaries (learned sparse codes or PPM-style models), and use the compression margin as a confidence score for selective ensembling; parameter-free, CPU-only and genuinely different from a CNN's inductive bias.

Cross-domain import (statistical physics / spin-glass ensembling): treat the ensemble-weighting problem as finding a low-energy configuration over model subsets with an explicit diversity term, solved by simulated annealing on validation predictions only; this is the principled version of ad-hoc ensembling and directly targets the last half-point of accuracy.

Cross-domain import (coding theory): error-correcting output codes for PathMNIST's 9 classes, training binary classifiers on designed codeword splits and decoding by minimum distance, which often beats a single softmax head on small images with confusable classes.

Calibration and decision-threshold work for BreastMNIST's binary task: AUC and ACC reward different things, and optimising the threshold on the validation split alone (never the test split) is legitimate and cheap.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: MedMNIST v2: beat the best published accuracy/AUC on the colorectal-histology (PathMNIST) or breast-ultrasound (BreastMNIST) benchmark

partial_wins.statement: Beat the live best ACC for PathMNIST at 28x28 by >= 0.5 points with a model of fewer than 1M parameters trained from scratch on CPU in under 2 hours, with the full protocol. A compute-efficiency frontier result, independently checkable from the Evaluator output and the training log.

Beat the live best ACC on BreastMNIST at 28x28 by >= 1.0 point as a mean over 5 seeds with the margin exceeding 2x the seed std, with per-seed Evaluator outputs. The small test split makes the published single-run numbers fragile, so a properly seeded improvement is a genuine contribution.

A reproducibility and variance audit of the official table: re-run the published ResNet-18 (28) recipe on PathMNIST and BreastMNIST for 5 seeds each and report the mean +/- std of AUC and ACC, establishing how large a difference is meaningful on each task. A benchmark-methodology result, reported as such, and a prerequisite for believing any small win.

pitfalls: MedMNIST ships test LABELS locally, so leakage is the default failure mode: any use of the test split for early stopping, augmentation search, threshold choice, batch-norm recalibration or ensemble weighting produces a number that is not comparable to the table. The skeptic must verify the test split is read once per seed.

Source-dataset pretraining leakage: PathMNIST derives from the NCT-CRC-HE colorectal histology collection and BreastMNIST from a public breast-ultrasound collection; pretraining on those sources (or on any derivative, including other MedMNIST subsets built from them) means the test images were seen in training. Any pretraining corpus must be declared and audited.

BreastMNIST's test split is ~156 images, so one image is ~0.64 accuracy points. Single-run claims there are meaningless; 5 seeds and a 2x-std margin are mandatory, and even then the result is fragile and must be reported with its uncertainty.

Resolution and version confusion: the 28, 64, 128 and 224 variants have separate published numbers and separate files; comparing a 224-trained model against the 28x28 table (or vice versa) is a false record. The MedMNIST+ line of work publishes stronger numbers than medmnist.com for several subsets, so the official table alone is NOT the frontier.

Metric cherry-picking: PathMNIST's AUC is already 0.990, so an AUC-only claim is uninformative while an ACC-only claim can hide a degraded AUC. Both must be reported and the AUC must not regress materially.
Clinical over-claiming: these are downsampled research images with fixed splits; a benchmark gain says nothing about diagnostic use and the write-up must state that explicitly.
PathMNIST's test set (CRC-VAL-HE-7K) is from a different centre than training. Fitting stain normalisation, colour statistics or batch-norm statistics on test images is transductive leakage.
targets.statement: MedMNIST v2 (Nature Scientific Data 2023) is a standardised, CC-BY, laptop-scale image benchmark with fixed train/validation/test splits and a shipped Evaluator. Two of its subsets are cancer tasks: PathMNIST (colorectal-cancer histology, 9 tissue classes, ~100k images) and BreastMNIST (breast ultrasound, benign vs malignant, 780 images). The official benchmark table on medmnist.com lists, at 28x28: PathMNIST best AUC 0.990 / ACC 0.911 (ResNet-50), with ResNet-18 at 0.983/0.907, auto-sklearn 0.934/0.716, AutoKeras 0.959/0.834, Google AutoML Vision 0.944/0.728; BreastMNIST best AUC 0.919 / ACC 0.863 (Google AutoML Vision and ResNet-18 respectively), with ResNet-18 (28) 0.901/0.863, ResNet-50 (28) 0.857/0.812. At 224x224 PathMNIST ResNet-18 reaches 0.989/0.909 and BreastMNIST 0.891/0.833. The 28x28 variants are tiny (the whole MedMNIST 2D collection is ~708k images in npz form, hosted on Zenodo record 10519652), CPU-trainable in minutes to hours, and the official numbers come from plain ResNets and AutoML tools - so a careful modern training recipe has real headroom, especially on PathMNIST ACC (0.911) where the AUC is already 0.99 and on BreastMNIST where n=780 makes the published numbers soft. The honest difficulty is novelty: MedMNIST+ follow-up work has published stronger numbers, so the criterion must beat the live official table AND the best value the NOVELTY skeptic finds in the literature. Published results already exceed the official table. For example, MedViT-S (Manzari et al., 2023) reports PathMNIST test ACC 0.942 (as tabulated in arXiv:2304.10054, fully supervised table, alongside AUC 0.993; confirmed in the PDF on 2026-10-15). Treat the official table as a floor, not the bar.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a model trained only on the official MedMNIST train split (with the official validation split used for model selection and early stopping, and the official test split untouched until the end), evaluated by the medmnist package's own Evaluator on the official test split at a declared resolution, whose test ACC is STRICTLY HIGHER than the best ACC listed for that task and resolution on https://medmnist.com/ (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) by at least 0.5 percentage points, where the bar is max(live medmnist.com value, best literature value at the same resolution, including MedViT and MedMNIST+) AND whose test AUC is not lower than the live best AUC for that task and resolution by more than 0.002; the value must also strictly exceed the best published ACC for the same task and resolution found by the NOVELTY skeptic in the last 24 months (including the MedMNIST+ line of work, arXiv:2404.15786 and its repository), by the same margin. Because BreastMNIST's test split has only ~156 images, a BreastMNIST claim additionally requires the result as mean +/- std over 5 seeds with the full seed-level Evaluator outputs, and the margin must exceed 2x that std. Deliverables: pinned medmnist version, data sha256 against the Zenodo distribution, training script and exact config, the Evaluator's standard result CSV for each seed, and a log showing the test split was read exactly once per seed. Any use of external pretraining must be declared and must not include any dataset derived from the same source images (for PathMNIST: NCT-CRC-HE; for BreastMNIST: the BUSI collection).
targets.verification_method: Skeptic installs the pinned medmnist package in a clean venv, downloads the npz files from the official Zenodo distribution and compares sha256 against the attacker's manifest, loads the attacker's saved test predictions, and runs the package's own Evaluator (python -m medmnist evaluate --path=...) to recompute AUC and ACC on the official test split (minutes). Then re-trains the attacker's recipe from the training split for at least 2 seeds (laptop-minutes to laptop-hours at 28x28) and confirms the metrics land in the claimed range. Record side: re-fetch medmnist.com and read the live table for that task and resolution, and check the NOVELTY skeptic's literature list.
