Leakage audit: confirm no test image or label was used for augmentation search, early stopping, calibration, batch-norm statistics or ensembling weights; confirm any pretraining corpus excludes the source datasets; confirm the resolution claimed matches the data files used.

angles: Compositional-data discipline: abundances are compositional, so centred log-ratio / balance (ILR) transforms with sparse selection of log-ratio balances (selbal/CoDa-LASSO style) often beat generic learners on relative abundances; this is cheap and directly attacks the published numbers.

CROSS-DOMAIN (ecology, imported as method not metaphor): use diversity partitioning (Hill numbers), co-occurrence network statistics, and neutral-community-model residuals (which taxa deviate from the neutral expectation) as features, rather than raw abundances.

CROSS-DOMAIN (information theory / compression): compress each sample's taxonomic profile against disease-specific and control-specific reference dictionaries and classify by code-length difference (a normalised-compression-distance classifier), which is nearly parameter-free and robust to depth differences.

CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing on graphs): embed the phylogenetic tree as a graph and use graph-Fourier/wavelet transforms of abundance on the tree (phylogenetic multiscale features) so that signal shared across related taxa is pooled - a direct answer to the sparsity of species-level features.

CROSS-DOMAIN (statistical physics): fit a Potts/Ising model of taxon co-occurrence per class and classify by free-energy difference, capturing community states (dysbiosis as a phase) instead of marginal abundances.

Cross-cohort robustness as the real target: batch-correction (ComBat-style, or quantile/rank normalisation within cohort), domain-adversarial training, and leave-one-cohort-out evaluation - the published within-cohort numbers are easier than the honest regime, so improvements there are where new science is.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: Gut-microbiome disease classification: beat the published cross-validated AUC on public non-cancer disease cohorts

partial_wins.statement: A strictly leak-free cross-cohort result for one disease (train on cohorts A..., test on an untouched cohort B of the same disease) with AUC >= 0.70 and a documented pre-registration of the held-out cohort, together with the within-cohort number for context.

Match the best published within-cohort AUC for one disease to within 0.01 using a model with <= 20 named taxa and no nonlinear learner, releasing the taxa and coefficients - an interpretability/parsimony result.

A reproducible confound audit for one disease: quantify how much of the published AUC is recoverable from sequencing-depth, study-of-origin, age/BMI/country covariates alone (and from label permutation within study), with code and numbers, documenting the fraction of apparent signal that is cohort structure.

pitfalls: Study-of-origin confounding: in multi-cohort analyses, disease label correlates with cohort, country and sequencing protocol, so a classifier can achieve high AUC by recognising the study. Leave-one-cohort-out plus metadata-only controls is the only honest test.

Cross-validation leakage: fitting normalisation, batch correction, feature selection or hyperparameters on the whole dataset before splitting is endemic in this literature and inflates AUC by 0.05-0.15. The audit must confirm all fitting is inside folds.

Protocol mismatch: comparing a repeated-stratified-CV mean to a published single-split number, or using a different feature type (strain markers vs species abundance vs pathways) than the published value, is a fake win; cohort, feature type and CV scheme must all match.
Sample-size optimism: several of these cohorts have <150 samples, so AUC differences of 0.02-0.03 are noise; require margin plus a repetition interval, and report per-fold values.
Technical-replicate and household leakage: some cohorts include longitudinal samples or related individuals; samples from the same subject or household must not straddle folds.
targets.statement: Shotgun-metagenomic disease classification (inflammatory bowel disease, type 2 diabetes, liver cirrhosis, obesity, rheumatoid arthritis and other non-cancer conditions) has a public, laptop-scale benchmark lineage: the MetAML study (Edoardo Pasolli, Duy Tin Truong, Faizan Malik, Levi Waldron and Nicola Segata, PLoS Computational Biology 2016) released abundance and marker-presence tables (github.com/SegataLab/metaml/data; no cross-validation fold files are committed) and published cross-validated AUCs per disease and per feature type in the paper itself, and the same cohorts are redistributed as uniformly processed tables in curatedMetagenomicData. Published AUCs for several diseases sit in the 0.6-0.8 range - far from saturated - and cross-cohort generalisation (train on one cohort, test on another of the same disease) is markedly worse and much less studied. The feature tables are megabytes, so the whole benchmark fits on a laptop, and the chief scientific question (is there signal beyond cohort-specific batch structure?) is exactly a question an adversarial verifier can police.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for at least one non-cancer disease cohort of the published benchmark, a released model and saved per-sample predictions obtained with the SAME evaluation protocol as the published number (same cohort, same feature table from the repository, same cross-validation scheme - the repository ships no fold files, so repeated stratified k-fold with the published k and >= 20 repeats, with the claimant's fold files committed and hashed before any model is fitted), whose mean AUC is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best published AUC for that cohort and feature type, read live from the MetAML paper (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4939962/fullTextXML) immediately before claiming, by at least 0.03 AND outside a 95% bootstrap/repetition interval. Any feature selection, normalisation fitting or hyperparameter choice must be inside the training folds only, demonstrated by code. For a cross-cohort claim, the test cohort must be untouched during all model development and the comparator must be a published cross-cohort number (or, if none exists, the claim is a new-result claim and must be reported as a partial win, not a record). Because the comparator is a 2016 printed number rather than a maintained leaderboard, the claimant must also reimplement the paper's own baseline (random forest on species abundances) on the same committed folds and beat that re-run by the same margin.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones SegataLab/metaml (and, for cross-cohort claims, pulls the matching curatedMetagenomicData tables), hashes the feature tables and the claimant's committed fold files, re-runs the reimplemented random-forest baseline on those folds, reruns the attacker's released pipeline to regenerate per-sample predictions, recomputes AUC per fold with the published protocol, and checks the repetition/bootstrap interval. Leakage audit: confirm that normalisation, feature selection and hyperparameter search are fitted inside folds (re-run with a deliberately corrupted test fold and verify training-side outputs are unchanged), and run the metadata-only and permuted-label controls. Minutes of CPU per cohort.

angles: Ensemble with honest grouping: the published tools make complementary errors, so an exon-grouped, calibrated stacker over SpliceAI, Pangolin, MMSplice and SPANR scores plus distance-to-splice-site and exon-context features is the cheapest credible attack - the preprint reports that a naive three-model consensus does not help, which is itself a hint that the combination must be distance-stratified.

CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing): treat exon recognition as matched filtering - build donor, acceptor, branchpoint and polypyrimidine filters, scan the window, and score a variant by the change in the whole filter-response landscape rather than a local site score; the exon interior is where splicing regulatory elements, not splice sites, dominate.

CROSS-DOMAIN (linguistics / distributional semantics): exonic splicing enhancers and silencers behave like a hexamer lexicon; learn hexamer scores by pointwise mutual information between hexamer usage and inclusion in the training exons only, then score a variant by the lexical shift it causes - exactly the exon-interior blind spot.

CROSS-DOMAIN (statistical physics of competition): model site usage as a Boltzmann competition between candidate splice sites in the window, so a variant's effect is a shift in occupancy, which naturally predicts partial inclusion changes instead of a binary flip.

CROSS-DOMAIN (compression / MDL): score the change in description length of the local sequence under exon-trained versus intron-trained universal compressors, a parameter-free cryptic-element detector that needs no annotation.
Ordinal targets: MFASS measures a continuous inclusion index, so regressing the index and thresholding afterwards uses far more information than training on the binary disrupting label.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: MFASS splice-disruption prediction: beat Pangolin's published average precision on the 27,733-variant functional set

partial_wins.statement: Beat the live best average precision restricted to exon-interior variants (more than 10 bp from the nearest annotated splice site), the stratum where the preprint reports recall collapsing, by >= 0.03 with the exon-grouped bootstrap, even if the overall average precision does not improve.

Recover at least 25% of the disrupting variants that the preprint reports are missed by all five tools, at a false-positive rate no higher than Pangolin's at its matched operating point, with the per-variant table released.

An independent reproduction result: recompute all five published AUROC/average-precision values from the public MFASS tables and released tool scores, to three decimal places, with a script, and document every discrepancy and its cause (filtering rule, label threshold, transcript choice).

pitfalls: Exon-level leakage: variants cluster in a few thousand assayed exons, so a variant-level random split puts neighbouring variants of the same exon on both sides. Splits and bootstrap intervals must be by exon.

Training-data overlap: SpliceAI, Pangolin and MMSplice were trained on GENCODE/GTEx data and some MFASS exons appear in their training regions; any supervised component trained on ClinVar or on overlapping data makes the comparison meaningless and must be enumerated and excluded.

Label-threshold games: the disrupting label depends on a cut on the measured inclusion change; moving the cut, or treating intermediate-effect variants as excluded rather than negative, can move average precision by tenths. The rule must be pre-registered and identical for every predictor.
Metric substitution: the class is imbalanced, so AUROC looks good while average precision does not; a claim must beat the live best average precision, with AUROC reported but not substituted.
Assay-specific ascertainment: MFASS measures exon recognition in a minigene reporter, not in a patient; a gain here is a benchmark gain and says nothing about any individual's diagnosis.
targets.statement: MFASS (the Multiplexed Functional Assay of Splicing using Sort-seq) from Kimberly Insigne, Rocky Cheung and Sriram Kosuri's lab measured exon inclusion for ~27,700 rare human exonic and intronic single-nucleotide variants; the cleaned per-variant measurements and the splice-disrupting-variant list are committed in github.com/KosuriLab/MFASS (processed_data/snv/snv_data_clean.txt, 41 MB; sdv_simple_list.txt), with no registration of any kind. A reproducible benchmark preprint posted 2026-07-26 (Europe PMC PPR1286688, doi 10.64898/2026.07.21.739871) scores five public predictors on 27,733 of these variants: Pangolin leads with AUROC 0.888 and average precision 0.421, ahead of SpliceAI (0.819 / 0.321), SpliceTransformer (0.786 / 0.317), MMSplice (0.758 / 0.256) and SPANR (0.748 / 0.228); 19% of the disrupting variants are missed by every tool, and recall collapses in the exon interior. Average precision of 0.42 on an experimentally measured label set is nowhere near saturated, and every predictor involved runs on CPU over a variant list.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a released predictor (code, weights, one fixed inference command) plus a saved score file with exactly one real-valued score for every variant of the benchmark variant set (the MFASS SNV set as defined by the pinned commit of github.com/KosuriLab/MFASS and the preprint's filtering rule, sha256 of the variant list and of the score file published; no variant dropped), whose average precision against the published splice-disrupting-variant labels, computed by a scorer the skeptic reruns, is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best published average precision on that same set, re-fetched live immediately before claiming from https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:PPR1286688&resultType=core&format=json (0.421 for Pangolin as fetched 2026-10-15), by at least 0.02 absolute AND outside a 95% bootstrap interval resampling exons (not variants). AUROC must be reported alongside and must not fall below the live leader's. The predictor may not be trained or tuned on any MFASS measurement, and if it ensembles public tools the exon-grouped split used to fit the combination must be committed before scoring.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones KosuriLab/MFASS at the pinned commit, hashes snv_data_clean.txt and the variant list, rebuilds the label vector with the stated threshold, runs the attacker's released inference to regenerate scores for a random 2,000 variants and checks them against the submitted file, recomputes average precision and AUROC, bootstraps over exons, and re-fetches the preprint record for the live bar. Running Pangolin and SpliceAI themselves on the same variants (CPU, hours) is the cross-check that the comparison set matches. All data is tens of megabytes.

angles: Go beyond presence/absence: amoxicillin-clavulanate failures are driven by promoter mutations, gene copy number, porin loss and bla gene expression, so features counting multiple bla copies, IS elements upstream of ampC and truncated ompF/ompC from the assemblies attack exactly the worst antibiotic.

CROSS-DOMAIN (coding theory / sparse recovery): treat rare determinants as a sparse support-recovery problem with gene-level groups, so alleles carried by a handful of isolates remain identifiable instead of being swamped.

CROSS-DOMAIN (survey statistics): surveillance databases are a biased sample - submitting laboratories, countries and years correlate with resistance. Post-stratification and inverse-probability weighting by submitter/year give an honest estimate and double as a confound control.

CROSS-DOMAIN (phylogenetics): use the SNP clusters both to build honest splits and as evidence - determinants that arise independently in many clusters (homoplasy) are mechanistically causal, unlike clade markers.

CROSS-DOMAIN (measurement-error modelling from psychometrics): AST results come from different methods and breakpoint versions; model the phenotype as a noisy ordinal measurement with laboratory-specific thresholds rather than as truth.
Rule learning for auditability: small boolean rules over determinants (set cover, ILP) give clinically inspectable logic, which is what a diagnostics lab can actually adopt.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: NCBI Pathogen Detection AST: beat the published antibiotic-specific genotype-phenotype F1 for Escherichia coli/Shigella

partial_wins.statement: Beat the published F1 for amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (44.5% as read 2026-10-15) by >= 5 points on a cluster-aware held-out split using only features derivable from the public metadata table (gene calls, point mutations, species, collection metadata), with confusion matrices and bootstrap intervals.

A reproduction result: recompute the published per-antibiotic accuracy and F1 for all eight antibiotics on a fresh export with released code, and document every discrepancy with the published values and its cause (eligibility filter, mapping rule, export date, AMRFinderPlus version).

A leakage demonstration: quantify how much apparent performance a random (non-cluster-aware) split adds over a cluster-aware split for the same model and antibiotic, released as code - the standard trap in surveillance-database benchmarks.

pitfalls: Population-structure leakage: E. coli is clonal enough that random splits put near-identical isolates on both sides; only SNP-cluster-aware splits count and the skeptic must recheck them.

Eligibility-filter drift: the published numbers depend on a specific eligibility rule and phenotype mapping (which intermediate calls are kept, which AST standards are accepted). Changing the filter after seeing results manufactures gains.
Export drift: the metadata table is regenerated continuously and AMRFinderPlus versions change, so a claim on a newer export must recompute the baseline rule on that same export, not quote the paper.
Class imbalance: for several antibiotics resistance prevalence is low, so accuracy and AUROC look fine for trivial models; F1 with confusion matrices and intervals is the only honest report.
Scope creep: this is a database-concordance benchmark for surveillance, explicitly not diagnostic validation, and nothing here supports a treatment decision for any patient.
targets.statement: NCBI Pathogen Detection publishes, with no login, a single metadata table per organism group that links assembly accessions, AMRFinderPlus resistance-gene annotations and laboratory antimicrobial susceptibility (AST) results (ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogen/Results/Escherichia_coli_Shigella/latest_snps/Metadata/, PDG000000004.6375.metadata.tsv, 527 MB, refreshed 2026-10-20; the file name changes with each refresh). Abdullateef Abdullah Alshehri's 2026 study in Int J Mol Sci (PMC13513162, NCBI export of 2026-06-11, AMRFinderPlus 4.2.7) froze such an export, kept 10,201 records meeting prespecified eligibility and scored 56,141 genotype-phenotype comparisons across eight priority antibiotics: concordance is high for tetracycline (accuracy 98.4%, F1 98.1%) and ceftriaxone (97.9%, 94.6%) but collapses for amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (73.6%, 44.5%). The gap between a gene-presence lookup and the measured phenotype for beta-lactam/inhibitor combinations is a real, open diagnostics problem, and the whole benchmark is one tab-separated file plus public assemblies.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for at least one of the eight antibiotics, a released predictor plus a saved per-isolate prediction file on a frozen, hash-pinned export of the NCBI Pathogen Detection E. coli/Shigella metadata (export date and sha256 published), with the paper's eligibility and phenotype-mapping rules reimplemented and published as code and applied identically to both predictors, evaluated on a held-out partition split by SNP cluster (PDS accession; no cluster spans train and test, split file committed with sha256), whose F1 for that antibiotic is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the published genotype-field-inference F1 for that antibiotic, re-read live from https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC13513162/fullTextXML immediately before claiming (e.g. 44.5% for amoxicillin-clavulanic acid as read 2026-10-15), by at least 3 points absolute AND outside a 95% bootstrap interval over clusters, with accuracy no lower than the published accuracy for that antibiotic and the full confusion matrix reported. Because the published numbers come from a 2026-06-11 export, a claim on a newer export must also recompute the published rule on the same new export and beat that recomputation. No clinical or treatment interpretation may be attached.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the frozen metadata table over plain HTTPS, verifies its sha256 against the claimant's, checks the committed split file against the PDS cluster assignments in the table (no cluster on both sides), reruns the attacker's released pipeline to regenerate predictions, independently reimplements the published genotype-field rule, computes both confusion matrices, F1, accuracy and bootstrap intervals over clusters, and re-reads the published table through Europe PMC. Everything is CPU-only on one tab-separated file; adding assemblies is optional and only for the richer feature sets.

angles: Operating-point engineering over architecture: the published work shows the ranking of models changes with the threshold objective, so calibrated probabilities plus an explicit cost-weighted decision rule is the cheapest honest gain.

CROSS-DOMAIN (colour science / spectroscopy): Giemsa staining varies by site and batch; stain normalisation in an optical-density colour space (Macenko/Vahadane deconvolution, imported from histopathology) attacks the main nuisance variable before any learning.

CROSS-DOMAIN (classical computer vision): ring-stage parasites are small chromatin dots - difference-of-Gaussians blob detection, morphological granulometry and Hu moments give interpretable features that a tiny classifier can use on a field laptop.

CROSS-DOMAIN (metrology / measurement error): treat the per-cell call as an input to a parasitaemia estimate and propagate per-cell uncertainty to the slide level, which is what a microscopist actually reports.

CROSS-DOMAIN (domain adaptation): patient codes let one build leave-one-patient-out evaluation and test domain-adversarial or style-transfer training that removes patient-specific staining signatures.
Semi-supervised use of unlabelled cells from the same slides to regularise the small effective sample size once patients, not images, are the unit.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: NIH/NLM thin-smear malaria cells: beat the published sensitivity at matched specificity, and under a patient-grouped split

partial_wins.statement: Publish the patient-grouped split itself: a released, documented mapping from filenames to patient codes, the resulting grouped split, and the measured performance drop of a standard published architecture between image-level and patient-grouped evaluation, with intervals - a methodology result the field currently lacks.

Match the published sensitivity at matched specificity with a model under 100k parameters running CPU-only inference at over 100 cells per second, with timings - the regime a field microscope station can actually run.

A false-negative characterisation: cluster the parasitized cells missed by the published-style model, show at least one visually coherent failure mode (stain intensity, ring-stage size, focus), and exhibit a targeted fix that halves the misses in that cluster without raising the false-positive rate.

pitfalls: Patient leakage: cells from one slide are near-duplicates, so image-level random splits inflate every metric; the patient-grouped protocol is the whole point of this target and the skeptic must verify the grouping.
Threshold peeking: selecting the operating point on the test partition is how 97% sensitivities appear; threshold selection must be demonstrably confined to training/validation data.

Metric substitution: with a balanced set, accuracy and ROC-AUC look excellent while the clinically relevant quantity (missed parasitized cells at acceptable specificity) barely moves; the claim must be sensitivity at matched specificity with counts.
Single-site data: all slides come from one hospital and one staining protocol, so even a patient-grouped gain does not demonstrate transfer; no cross-site claim may be made from this dataset alone.
Clinical overreach: this is cell-level image classification, not a diagnostic device; nothing here supports a diagnosis or a treatment decision for any person.
targets.statement: Microscopy is still the reference test for malaria in most endemic settings, and the NIH/NLM thin-blood-smear cell dataset (data.lhncbc.nlm.nih.gov/public/Malaria/cell_images.zip, 353 MB, downloadable with a plain request) is the standard public benchmark: 27,558 segmented erythrocyte images, half parasitized, from patients at Chittagong Medical College Hospital, released by the Lister Hill National Center for Biomedical Communications. A 2026 study by Fatma Dehbi and Reda Mohamed Hamou in Frontiers in Medicine (PMC13553222) reports, on a fixed stratified 70:15:15 image-level split, a compact CNN with 95.26% accuracy at the default threshold and, after recall-weighted threshold optimisation, 97.05% sensitivity (95% CI 96.23-97.70) with ROC-AUC 0.9876, cutting missed parasitized cells from 177 to 61 - and states plainly that the split is image-level, not patient-level, because the public release has no patient identifiers. In fact the filenames encode patient codes (for example C33P1thinF...), so an honest patient-grouped evaluation is possible and, as far as this bank can establish, unreported: that is the open problem.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a released model plus saved per-image scores for the whole dataset under BOTH protocols, with the split files committed and hashed: (a) the published stratified image-level split regime, where the model's sensitivity at specificity no lower than the published specificity must be STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the published sensitivity, re-read live from https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC13553222/fullTextXML immediately before claiming (97.05% as read 2026-10-15), by a margin whose 95% bootstrap interval over images excludes zero; and (b) a PATIENT-GROUPED split derived from the patient codes in the filenames (no patient's cells in both partitions; the derivation script released), where the same model's sensitivity, specificity and the drop relative to (a) are reported. A claim that reports only (a) is not a win; the honest contribution is the pair. Thresholds must be chosen on training/validation data only, and the claim is about this image benchmark, never about diagnosing any patient.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads cell_images.zip over plain HTTPS, hashes it, rebuilds both split files from the claimant's released scripts and checks the patient-grouped split truly has no shared patient code, reruns the attacker's released inference to regenerate scores, recomputes sensitivity at the matched specificity operating point with bootstrap intervals over images and over patients, confirms the threshold was selected without the test partition (code review plus a rerun with the test partition scrambled), and re-reads the published metrics through Europe PMC. Under an hour on a CPU.

angles: Cascaded 3D U-Nets with the winner's recipe (coarse then fine prediction, heavy flips and rotations, test-time augmentation) as the reproduction baseline; the winning code is public.

Cross-domain import (physics-informed learning): add a differentiable pencil-beam or distance-to-target prior as an input channel, so the network learns a correction to physics rather than dose from scratch.

Cross-domain import (geostatistics / kriging): model the residual dose field as a Gaussian process conditioned on structure distances, and blend with the network prediction where the network is uncertain.
Optimise the metric directly: add a differentiable DVH loss (sorting-based) so the DVH score is trained for, not just voxel error.
Small-data regime: 200 patients is tiny; ensembles of small 3D networks at reduced resolution with careful upsampling may beat one large network on a laptop.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: OpenKBP radiotherapy dose prediction: beat the challenge winner's dose score 2.429 Gy or DVH score 1.478 Gy on the 100 released test patients

partial_wins.statement: Dose score below 2.4294 with DVH score below 1.5393 (better than every challenge team on dose while staying in the top two on DVH), trained on a laptop (CPU or Apple GPU) in under 24 hours.

A reproduction audit of the strongest post-challenge claim (for example the about-2.0 Gy DeepDoseNet test result): rerun with the official evaluator and report whether it holds on the standard 100-patient test split.

pitfalls: Test doses are public: tuning epochs, ensembles or post-processing on test-pats scores is leakage. The README itself warns that post-challenge CodaLab results cannot be trusted for this reason.
Scoring outside the feasible-dose mask, or on a subset of structures, changes the numbers; only the repository's EvaluateDose on all 100 test patients compares with the leaderboard.
Several papers report on the validation split or on their own re-splits; values that look like 2.0-2.3 Gy are often not the standard test split.
The repository's data loader and the original challenge data release must match (file versions changed when the repo was modernised); check patient counts and a sample patient's dose sums.
A better dose prediction is an input to automated planning; it is not a treatment plan and says nothing about clinical outcomes.
targets.statement: OpenKBP (AAPM 2020 grand challenge; Aaron Babier, Binghao Zhang, Rafid Mahmood, Kevin Moore, Thomas Purdie, Andrea McNiven and Timothy Chan, Medical Physics 2021) released CT, structure masks and clinical intensity-modulated radiotherapy dose for 340 head-and-neck cancer patients, split 200 train / 40 validation / 100 test, with the scoring class (EvaluateDose) in the open-kbp repository. Test doses were published after the challenge, so the two official metrics can be recomputed offline: dose score (mean absolute voxel dose error inside the feasible-dose mask, Gy) and DVH score (mean absolute error of the challenge's DVH metrics, Gy); lower is better. The final blinded test leaderboard (an image in the repository README) is topped by LSL AnHui University (Shuolin Liu, Jingjing Zhang, Teng Li, Hui Yan, Jianfei Liu) with dose score 2.4294 and DVH score 1.4776, ahead of SuperPod (2.5635) on dose and PTV - Prediction Team Vienna (1.5393) on DVH. Later papers report dose scores near the winner (for example TrDosePred, 2.426 Gy dose / 1.592 Gy DVH, and nnDoseNet, 2.579 / 1.540); at least one paper (DeepDoseNet, arXiv:2111.00077) reports about 2.0 Gy on the test split, which must be reproduced or explained before any claim.
targets.success_criterion: Predicted dose files for all 100 OpenKBP test patients, from a model trained only on the 200 training patients (validation patients allowed for model selection) and frozen before any test scoring, whose dose score OR DVH score computed by the skeptic with the repository's EvaluateDose class is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the corresponding first-place value on the final test leaderboard shown in https://github.com/ababier/open-kbp (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) AND lower than every test-split value for that metric found by the NOVELTY check (including arXiv:2111.00077 if its protocol is the standard one), by at least 0.02 Gy, with the other score not worse than the winner's by more than 0.05 Gy.

Re-runs inference from released weights on a subset to confirm the files. Audits training code for any read of test-pats dose. Under an hour.

angles: Rotation and reflection equivariance (p4m group convolutions, steerable filters) is the README baseline's key idea; combine it with modern training (long schedules, mixup, EMA weights).
Stain augmentation and stain normalisation computed from the training split only, targeting the slide-level colour shift between splits.
Cross-domain import (noisy-label learning from web-scale vision): co-teaching or small-loss selection to discount the noisy centre-region labels.
Cross-domain import (texture analysis in materials science): wavelet scattering or gray-level co-occurrence features as a parameter-light second model for ensembling.
Use the 64 px context ring explicitly: predict the centre label from a model that sees the whole 96 px patch with centre-weighted attention.

targets.name: PatchCamelyon (lymph-node metastasis patches): beat 89.8% accuracy / 0.963 AUC on the official test split without external pretraining

partial_wins.statement: Exceed 89.8% accuracy (3-seed mean) with a model under 1M parameters trained on a laptop CPU/MPS in under 8 hours.
A documented analysis of the accuracy plateau: per-slide error breakdown using the official meta CSVs, showing which slides drive test errors (a methodology result).

pitfalls: Foundation-model or ImageNet-pretrained results are a different class; mixing classes produces a false record. Pathology foundation models may also have seen CAMELYON16 slides.
Test labels are public; early stopping or seed selection on test accuracy is leakage.
Patches from the same slide share appearance; validation-split tuning is the only honest selection, since the test slides differ.
The README table is short and old; the NOVELTY check must cover from-scratch literature results on the official split before claiming.
Patch classification on a curated benchmark is far from slide-level clinical diagnosis; frame results accordingly.
targets.statement: PatchCamelyon (Bastiaan Veeling, Jasper Linmans, Jim Winkens, Taco Cohen, Max Welling; MICCAI 2018) turns CAMELYON16 breast-cancer lymph-node slides into 327,680 96x96 H&E patches with binary labels (tumour in the centre 32x32), with fixed train (262,144) / validation (32,768) / test (32,768) splits whose test labels are public (Zenodo record 2546921, plain download). The benchmark table in the official repository README lists the rotation-equivariant GDensenet at 89.8% accuracy and 0.963 AUC. Despite its size, PCam has a well-known accuracy plateau around 90% for models trained from scratch, attributed to label noise and slide-level domain shift between splits; foundation models pretrained on large external pathology corpora report higher, but they belong to a different comparison class. The from-scratch cell is laptop-trainable and still informative.
targets.success_criterion: Test-split predictions for all 32,768 PCam test patches from a model trained from random initialisation (no pretrained weights, no external images) on the official train split, with selection on the official validation split only, whose accuracy is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the best from-scratch accuracy in the README benchmark table at https://github.com/basveeling/pcam (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) and than any from-scratch official-test accuracy found by the NOVELTY check, by at least 0.5 percentage points, with AUC not below 0.963; reported as the mean over 3 seeds.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the test labels and meta CSV from Zenodo, checks MD5s against the README, computes accuracy and AUC from the claimed predictions, and re-trains one seed from the released script to confirm. Audits that no pretrained weights or external data were loaded. Hours for one retrain.

angles: Conventional: separate the condition shift from the perturbation effect explicitly - estimate a condition-level transport map from control cells in both conditions (which ARE available) and apply it to training-condition perturbation effects; the published models entangle the two.

Conventional: per-gene shrinkage of logFC estimates toward zero with an empirical-Bayes variance model, which is what makes DEG recall non-zero in practice (recall of differentially expressed genes is destroyed by noisy per-gene estimates, not by the wrong mean).

Cross-domain import (signal processing / optimal transport as filtering): treat the control-to-control condition shift as a channel and estimate it by quantile/Sinkhorn matching on control cells only, then pass predicted perturbation responses through the estimated channel. Label-free, uses only control cells, and is exactly a deconvolution problem.

Cross-domain import (compression / minimum description length): select the latent dimension and the per-gene sparsity by MDL on held-in cells, which is the principled way to avoid the collapse that gives the published models zero DEG recall.

Cross-domain import (ecology / rarefaction): single-cell detection rates differ across conditions exactly like sampling effort differs across ecological surveys; apply rarefaction / Good-Turing coverage correction per gene before computing logFC, so that the predicted and observed logFCs are estimated at matched effort.

Cross-domain import (combinatorial search): the held-out set is 70% of perturbations in one condition, so search over which training perturbations best span the held-out ones (a set-cover / coreset problem on perturbation-effect vectors) and weight training accordingly.

targets.name: PerturBench Frangieh21: beat the published best covariate-transfer metrics for Perturb-seq in melanoma cells

partial_wins.statement: A non-zero DEG recall (>= 0.01 over 5 seeds, per-perturbation list saved) on Frangieh21, where all ten published methods report 0.000. Independently checkable from the predicted anndata with the repo's Evaluator and not implied by any published result.

Strictly beat the published best cosine logFC (0.22) by >= 0.05 absolute over 5 seeds while keeping the cosine-logFC rank no worse than 0.19 + 1 std, i.e. a real transfer improvement rather than a variance trade.

A measured difficulty decomposition: using the same splits, quantify how much of the Frangieh21 transfer error is explained by (i) condition-level global shift, (ii) per-perturbation effect size, (iii) per-gene detection rate, by re-scoring the same predictions after removing each component, and identify which single component dominates. Checkable from saved predictions and logs; a diagnostic result, not a record.

pitfalls: DEG recall of exactly 0.000 for every published method is a red flag about the metric's sensitivity, not only about the models. Any non-zero DEG-recall claim must be recomputed with the repo's Evaluator and the per-perturbation list inspected, or it is almost certainly a metric-implementation difference rather than a result.

Control-cell leakage: using held-out-condition PERTURBED cells (rather than only control cells) to estimate the condition shift is leakage, and the boundary is subtle. The verification must enumerate exactly which cells were used for the transport estimate.

Split provenance: Frangieh21 splits require either the published split csv or a notebook-generated split; a differently generated split makes the published tables incomparable. The exact held-out perturbation list must be logged and verified.
Preprocessing leakage: HVG selection, normalisation and logFC reference statistics computed over all cells including the held-out condition.

Single-seed and cherry-picked-metric claims: with cosine ~0.2 and small published stds, seed noise and metric selection can easily manufacture an apparent record; 5 seeds, a 3x-std margin and an all-metrics report are required.
Stale-table comparison: the arXiv entry has multiple versions and the repo evolves; the published best must be re-read live from the latest version before any claim.
targets.statement: The Frangieh21 task in PerturBench is a cancer-specific perturbation-transfer benchmark: CRISPR Perturb-seq in melanoma cells across experimental conditions, with 70% of perturbations held out in the co-culture condition and the rest used for training (the split file frangieh21_split.csv is published in the ungated Hugging Face repo altoslabs/perturbench, alongside frangieh21_processed.h5ad.gz). The published scoreboard (arXiv 2408.10609v4, Tables 7 and 8) shows every method performing poorly, which makes the frontier unusually soft: best cosine logFC 0.22 +/- 0.003 (SAMS-VAE (S)), best cosine-logFC rank 0.19 +/- 0.03 (CPA* (noAdv); lower is better), best MMD PCA 0.20 +/- 0.003 (BioLord*), DEG recall 0.000 for every single method, best RMSE mean 0.024 (LA and LA (scGPT)), best RMSE-mean rank 0.15 +/- 0.0004 (Decoder), best MMD 1.1 +/- 0.02 (BioLord*). A benchmark where the best cosine is 0.22 and DEG recall is identically zero across ten methods is a textbook low-hanging frontier, and the data are a laptop-scale sparse matrix usable with linear and kernel methods.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a model trained with PerturBench's own Frangieh21 accessor and the published frangieh21_split.csv (or splits regenerated by the repo's documented notebook, with the exact held-out perturbation list logged), scored by the repo's own Evaluator at a pinned commit, that strictly beats the best published value for at least ONE metric in the latest arXiv version of Tables 7-8 (re-fetched live immediately before claiming; per-metric direction as recorded) by at least 3x the published std of the previous best AND over 5 independent seeds reported as mean +/- std, while not being worse than the previous best on any other reported metric by more than 1 published std. Because DEG recall is 0.000 for all published methods, a DEG-recall claim requires a value >= 0.01 over 5 seeds with the per-perturbation recall list saved. Deliverables: pinned commit, dataset and split sha256s, the held-out perturbation list, training script and config, Evaluator output over all metrics and seeds, and same-environment same-split re-runs of the published LA and CPA* (noAdv) baselines landing within 1 published std of the tables (otherwise the comparison is void). No held-out-condition cells may touch training, normalisation, gene selection, early stopping or HPO.
targets.verification_method: Clean venv, perturbench at the attacker's pinned commit, download frangieh21_processed.h5ad.gz and frangieh21_split.csv from the ungated Hugging Face repo and compare sha256 with the attacker's manifest, verify that the held-out perturbation set in the split file matches the attacker's logged list and is disjoint from training, load the attacker's predicted anndata, and run the repo's Evaluator to recompute every metric (under an hour). Re-train at least 2 of the 5 seeds (laptop-hours) and re-run the two published baselines in the same environment to confirm the tables are reproduced. Leakage audit: HVG/normalisation statistics computed on training cells only; controls used exactly as the repo does; no use of held-out-condition cells anywhere outside final scoring.

angles: Conventional: factorise the response as cell-line context x perturbation effect with explicit multiplicative interaction (a bilinear or tensor model), which is the natural model for a 6-cell-line x 5-cytokine design and is far cheaper than the published autoencoders.
Conventional: train with a listwise ranking loss on perturbation identity (the rank metric is the discriminative part of the benchmark) instead of RMSE alone, and report both.

Cross-domain import (cryptanalysis / distinguisher design): the rank metric is literally a distinguishing game - can you match a predicted profile to its true perturbation among all held-out perturbations? Build an explicit likelihood-ratio distinguisher over per-gene response statistics (the standard differential-cryptanalysis framing), which optimises exactly the quantity being measured rather than an L2 proxy.

Cross-domain import (statistical physics / mean-field cavity method): estimate per-perturbation fields and cell-line-specific susceptibilities with a cavity/TAP approximation, giving a transferable linear-response human per cell line; linear-response theory is the right language for 'same perturbation, different context'.

Cross-domain import (combinatorial design): the 30 states (9 with held-out perturbations) form an incomplete factorial design; use design-of-experiments theory (D-optimal weighting of training combinations, Latin-square-style balance) to decide how to weight and augment training data, instead of training on everything uniformly.

Variance control: with published RMSE stds of 1e-5 to 2e-4, metric noise is tiny but model-seed noise is not; measure the attacker's own seed variance before chasing the 3x-std bar, and prefer ensembles that provably reduce it.

targets.name: PerturBench Jiang24: beat the published best cytokine-perturbation transfer metrics across cancer cell lines

partial_wins.statement: Push the RMSE-mean rank metric below 0.25 over 5 seeds (published best 0.32, random 0.5), i.e. demonstrate real perturbation discrimination on this dataset, with the per-perturbation rank list saved and recomputed by the repo's Evaluator.
Beat the published best MMD (3.1, Linear) by >= 0.3 over 5 seeds while keeping RMSE mean no worse than 0.016, i.e. a distributional-fit improvement that does not come from collapsing to the mean.

A cell-line-stratified breakdown: report the three metrics separately for each held-out (cell line x cytokine) state for the attacker's model and for the re-run Decoder baseline, identifying which combinations carry transferable signal. Mechanically checkable from the saved predictions and not reported in the published table.

pitfalls: A rank metric of 0.32 vs random 0.5 means the benchmark is barely above chance; small improvements are extremely likely to be noise or preprocessing artefacts. The 0.02 absolute floor plus 5 seeds exists for this reason.

The published dataset description (30 states: 6 cell lines x 5 cytokines, 9 states held out) and the barcode-level split file carry different information: the split csv has no state column at all. The attacker must log the derived per-state held-out perturbation lists and the skeptic must verify them against the downloaded h5ad rather than against the paper text.

Collapse-to-mean wins: RMSE mean of 0.015 is achievable by predicting almost nothing (the Linear model's 0.038 is the only visibly bad value), so an RMSE claim without the rank metric and MMD is meaningless. All three must be reported.

Preprocessing leakage: normalisation, HVG selection or control-mean statistics computed across all cells including held-out perturbations; and cross-combination leakage where a perturbation held out in one (cytokine, cell line) combination is used in training for the same combination.
Metric reimplementation: recomputing RMSE rank or MMD with the attacker's own code, different PCA dimensionality, or a different kernel bandwidth. Only the repo's Evaluator at a pinned commit counts.
Stale-table comparison against an older arXiv version; the record must be re-read live from the latest version.
targets.statement: The Jiang24 task in PerturBench is perturbation-response transfer across cancer cell lines and cytokine contexts. The live paper (arXiv 2408.10609v4, Table 4) describes 30 biological states (6 cell lines x 5 cytokine treatments) with 70% of the perturbations from 9 of those states held out for validation and testing; the barcode-level split is published as jiang24_split.csv in the ungated Hugging Face repo altoslabs/perturbench (1,628,475 cells: 1,216,452 train, 189,264 validation, 222,759 test), and the state labels must be read from the h5ad obs table. The published scoreboard is remarkably flat. Table 4 (main metrics): best cosine logFC 0.64 +/- 8e-4 (Decoder), best cosine-logFC rank 0.32 +/- 8e-3 (Decoder; lower is better, 0.5 is random), best MMD PCA 0.32 +/- 5e-3 (SAMS-VAE*), best DEG recall 0.005 +/- 6e-4 (CPA* (noAdv)). Table 11 (additional metrics): RMSE mean 0.015 for CPA*, CPA* (noAdv), LA and Decoder, 0.016-0.017 for the SAMS-VAE variants and 0.038 for Linear; RMSE-mean rank best 0.32 +/- 5e-3 (Decoder) with everything else 0.38-0.45; MMD best 3.1 +/- 2e-3 (Linear) with most models at 8.0. A rank metric of 0.32-0.45 against a random baseline of 0.5 means essentially nothing is being learned about WHICH perturbation produces WHICH profile.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a model trained with PerturBench's own Jiang24 accessor and the published jiang24_split.csv, scored by the repo's own Evaluator at a pinned commit, that strictly beats the best published value for at least ONE metric in Table 4 OR Table 11 of the latest arXiv version (re-fetched live immediately before claiming; cosine logFC and DEG recall higher is better, all other metrics lower is better) by at least 3x the published std of the previous best AND over 5 independent seeds reported as mean +/- std, while not being worse than the previous best on either other metric by more than 1 published std. For the rank metric the margin must additionally be at least 0.02 absolute, since a rank metric near 0.5 is uninformative and small moves are noise. Deliverables: pinned commit, dataset and split sha256s, the held-out state (cell line x cytokine) assignment derived by joining jiang24_split.csv to the h5ad obs table, logged with its sha256, training script and config, full Evaluator output over all metrics and seeds, and same-environment same-split re-runs of the published Decoder and LA baselines landing within 1 published std of Tables 4 and 11 (otherwise the comparison is void). No held-out perturbation's cells may touch training, normalisation, gene selection, early stopping or HPO.
targets.verification_method: Clean venv, perturbench at the pinned commit, download jiang24_processed.h5ad.gz and jiang24_split.csv from the ungated Hugging Face dataset and verify sha256s against the manifest, join jiang24_split.csv to the h5ad obs table and confirm the derived held-out perturbation lists per state match the logged ones and are disjoint from training, load the attacker's predicted anndata and recompute all metrics with the repo's Evaluator (under an hour), re-train 2 of 5 seeds (laptop-days at this data size), and re-run the Decoder and LA baselines in the same environment to confirm the published values. Leakage audit as for the other PerturBench targets, plus an explicit check that no cells from a held-out (cytokine, cell line) combination entered training for that combination.

angles: Conventional: strengthen the latent-additive baseline that currently leads - per-perturbation latent offsets with shrinkage toward a learned low-rank basis of single-perturbation effects, plus an explicit learned interaction term for pairs (the whole task is predicting the non-additive part).

Conventional: train directly for the reported metrics (cosine on logFC and the rank metric) rather than for reconstruction RMSE; the published HPO objective is RMSE + 0.1 x RMSE-rank, which is not what Table 3's headline columns measure.

Cross-domain import (coding theory / superimposed codes): single perturbations are codewords and a dual perturbation is their superposition through a non-linear channel. Fit a decoder for the interaction residual using ideas from multi-user detection / successive interference cancellation: subtract the predicted additive part, then decode the residual against a dictionary of interaction motifs learned from the 30% observed duals.

Cross-domain import (statistical physics): treat gene-expression responses as an Ising/Potts system with per-perturbation external fields and learn pairwise couplings between perturbation targets by pseudo-likelihood (the standard direct-coupling-analysis machinery). DCA is cheap, interpretable, CPU-only, and is precisely a tool for inferring pairwise interaction from single-and-pair observations.

Cross-domain import (compression): choose the number of latent dimensions and the interaction sparsity by MDL / two-part code length on held-in cells rather than by validation loss, which is the standard defence against mode collapse (a collapsed model has a short code but terrible residual cost, and MDL sees that trade-off explicitly).

Anti-collapse regularisation: explicitly penalise low variance across predicted perturbation profiles, or train with a rank-based (listwise) loss so that predicting the mean response is heavily penalised; the paper reports collapse in widely used models, so this alone may move the rank metric.

targets.name: PerturBench Norman19: beat the published best combination-perturbation prediction metrics (CRISPR Perturb-seq in a leukemia line)

partial_wins.statement: Beat the published best DEG recall (0.032, CPA*) by >= 2x absolute (i.e. >= 0.064) over 5 seeds without losing more than 1 published std on cosine logFC. DEG recall is near-zero for almost every published model, so a real improvement there is informative and independently checkable from the saved predicted anndata.

Reproduce and then strictly beat the published Linear baseline's numbers with a model of no more parameters (within 10%) over 5 seeds on cosine logFC rank, demonstrating that the leaderboard's simple-model ceiling is not the information ceiling. Requires the same-environment baseline re-run.

A documented mode-collapse audit: for each published model family re-run in the same environment, compute the fraction of held-out perturbations whose predicted logFC vector is within epsilon of the predicted global mean, and report which published Table 3 numbers are compatible with collapse. A benchmark-critique result, reported as such, checkable from saved predictions.

pitfalls: Mode collapse that flatters the metrics: predicting the average perturbation response can give a respectable cosine logFC while the rank metric and DEG recall reveal nothing was learned. Any claim must report all four metrics and the collapse audit.

Split regeneration mismatch: the Norman19 splits are generated by the package, so a different version or seed yields a different held-out set and incomparable numbers. The skeptic must verify the split generator and the exact held-out dual list.

Control/leakage through preprocessing: computing HVG selection, size-factor normalisation, logFC reference means or gene filtering over ALL cells (including held-out duals) leaks the test distribution. logFC is computed against controls, and which control cells are used must be exactly the package's convention.

Metric-definition drift: cosine logFC, the rank metric and DEG recall have specific definitions in the repo's Evaluator; recomputing them with the attacker's own code (different DEG cutoff, different number of top genes, different distance) is the easiest way to manufacture a fake record. Only the repo's Evaluator at a pinned commit counts.

Comparing against a stale table: PerturBench has had four arXiv versions and the repo adds datasets; the published best for a metric must be re-read from the latest version and cross-checked against repo results before any claim.
Single-seed wins: published stds are small (1e-3 to 1e-2) but seed-to-seed variation of a new model can be large; 5 seeds and a 3x-std margin are required.
targets.statement: PerturBench (Altos Labs; NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks; arXiv 2408.10609v4, last updated 2025-10-24) is a standardised framework for single-cell perturbation-response prediction with public datasets, fixed splits, a published metric suite and an Evaluator class. The Norman19 task is combination prediction in the K562 chronic-myelogenous-leukemia line: train on all single CRISPRa perturbations plus 30% of dual perturbations, predict the held-out 70% of dual perturbations. The published Table 3 (arXiv v4) is the public scoreboard: best cosine logFC 0.79 +/- 0.01 (LA, with SAMS-VAE (S) 0.78 and CPA* (noAdv) 0.77), best cosine-logFC rank 0.005 +/- 0.002 (LA; lower is better, 0 perfect, 0.5 random; CPA* (noAdv) 0.0057), best MMD PCA 0.74 +/- 0.05 (SAMS-VAE (S)), best DEG recall 0.032 +/- 0.004 (CPA*). The authors themselves report that several published models suffer mode collapse and that simple models (a latent-additive model, a linear model) are competitive - a strong hint that the frontier is soft. All processed data and splits are public and ungated on Hugging Face (altoslabs/perturbench, last modified 2025-10-21; norman19_processed.h5ad.gz plus split tarballs), the Norman19 splits are generated by the package itself, and the metrics ship in the repo (pushed 2026-08-10). Norman19 is a few GB of sparse counts: CPU-feasible for linear/latent-additive/kernel models, which are precisely the models that currently lead.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a model trained with PerturBench's own data accessors and PerturBench-generated Norman19 combo splits (train = all singles + 30% duals; evaluate on the held-out duals), scored by the repo's own Evaluator class at a pinned commit, that strictly beats the best published value for at least ONE of the four metrics in the latest arXiv version of PerturBench Table 3 (re-fetched live immediately before claiming; direction per metric as recorded above) by at least 3x the published standard deviation of the previous best AND by a margin that survives 5 independent seeds reported as mean +/- std, while not being worse than the previous best on ANY other reported metric by more than 1 published std (so that mode collapse or metric gaming is excluded). Deliverables: pinned perturbench commit, dataset file sha256s from the Hugging Face repo, the split files actually used, the training script and config, the Evaluator output for all four metrics over 5 seeds, and the same Evaluator run on the published LA and Linear baselines in the same environment and splits (whose values must land within 1 published std of Table 3, or the comparison is void). No held-out dual perturbation's measured expression may be used in training, model selection, early stopping, gene filtering, normalisation or the HPO objective.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic creates a clean venv, installs perturbench at the attacker's pinned commit, downloads norman19_processed.h5ad.gz from the Hugging Face repo and compares sha256 with the attacker's manifest, regenerates the splits with the package (or loads the attacker's split files and verifies they match the package's generator and that train/test dual perturbations are disjoint), loads the attacker's predicted anndata objects, and runs the repo's Evaluator to recompute all four metrics (minutes to an hour). Then re-trains the attacker's model for at least 2 of the 5 seeds (laptop-hours) to confirm the metric range, and re-runs the LA and Linear baselines in the same environment to confirm the published values are reproduced. Leakage audit: assert that no held-out dual perturbation appears in training, that highly-variable-gene selection and normalisation statistics were computed on training cells only, and that the HPO objective never read test cells.

angles: Conventional: factorise explicitly into a cell-line context term and a compound-effect term with a low-rank interaction, which is the natural model for a 3-cell-line x 188-compound design and far cheaper than the published autoencoders.

Conventional: per-gene empirical-Bayes shrinkage of predicted log-fold-changes, which is what makes DEG recall non-zero in practice - the published models fail on DEG recall because per-gene estimates are noisy, not because the mean direction is wrong.

Cross-domain import (chemistry / read-across): borrow regulatory read-across methodology - predict an untested compound's effect in a new cell line from structurally and mechanistically analogous compounds with an explicit applicability domain, and abstain outside it, reporting abstention uniformly.

Cross-domain import (coding theory / soft-decision decoding): treat each compound's measured profile in the training cell lines as a noisy codeword observation and decode the held-out cell line's response with a minimum-distance decoder over a learned metric, which gives calibrated confidence instead of a point estimate.

Cross-domain import (statistical physics / linear response): model the cell line as a system with its own susceptibility matrix and the compound as an external field; linear-response theory then predicts transfer as a matrix product, and the susceptibility can be estimated from unperturbed and training-perturbation data only.

Cross-domain import (ecology / rarefaction and Good-Turing): per-cell detection rates differ across cell lines like sampling effort differs across surveys; coverage-corrected log-fold-change estimation puts predicted and observed effects on matched effort before scoring.

Anti-collapse training: optimise a listwise rank loss on perturbation identity rather than reconstruction RMSE, since the rank metric is the discriminative part of the benchmark and the paper itself documents mode collapse (Table 12) on this dataset.
