targets.name: PerturBench Srivatsan20: beat the published best cross-cell-line chemical-perturbation transfer in three cancer cell lines

partial_wins.statement: Raise DEG recall on Srivatsan20 to >= 0.02 over 5 seeds (published best 0.007, with several methods at exactly 0.000), with the per-perturbation recall list saved and recomputed by the repository's Evaluator. Recovering which genes actually move is the part of the task that currently fails completely.

Beat the published best cosine logFC (0.53) by >= 0.05 absolute over 5 seeds while keeping the cosine-logFC rank no worse than 0.09 + 1 published std, i.e. a transfer gain that is not bought by predicting the average perturbation.

A per-cell-line decomposition: report all metrics separately for A549, K562 and MCF-7 for the attacker's model and for the re-run baselines, and identify whether transfer failure is uniform or driven by one lineage. Mechanically checkable from saved predictions and absent from the published table.

pitfalls: Mode collapse flatters cosine and RMSE: predicting the average perturbation response gives a respectable cosine logFC while rank metrics and DEG recall show nothing was learned. The paper quantifies collapse for this dataset in Table 12; any claim must report all metrics plus a collapse audit.

Split regeneration mismatch: Srivatsan20 splits are produced by the package, so a different version or seed yields a different held-out set and incomparable numbers. The exact per-cell-line held-out perturbation lists must be logged and verified.

Preprocessing leakage: highly-variable-gene selection, size-factor normalisation or control-mean statistics computed over all cells, including held-out perturbations, leaks the test distribution into training.

Metric reimplementation: cosine logFC, the rank metric, MMD PCA and DEG recall have specific definitions in the repository's Evaluator (gene subsets, PCA dimensionality, kernel bandwidth). Recomputing them with the attacker's own code is the easiest way to manufacture a fake record.

Single-seed wins and stale tables: published standard deviations are 1e-3 to 1e-2 while a new model's seed variance can be far larger, and PerturBench has had four arXiv versions. Five seeds, a 3x-std margin and a live re-read of the latest version are required.
Over-claiming: better cross-cell-line transfer for 188 compounds in three immortalised cancer lines is a benchmark result about sci-Plex data, not evidence that a drug will work in a tumour.
targets.statement: The Srivatsan20 task in PerturBench (Altos Labs; NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks; arXiv 2408.10609v4, last updated 2025-10-24) asks a question a medicinal chemist would recognise: given how 188 compounds change gene expression in some cancer cell lines, predict what they do in a cell line where those compounds were never tested. The data are sci-Plex single-cell profiles of A549 lung adenocarcinoma, K562 chronic myelogenous leukaemia and MCF-7 breast cancer cells, with 30% of perturbations held out per cell line for validation and test. The published scoreboard is flat and low: in Table 2 the best cosine on log-fold-changes is 0.53 +/- 0.01 (SAMS-VAE* (S)), the best cosine-logFC rank is 0.09 +/- 0.004 (CPA* (noAdv); lower is better, 0.5 is random), the best MMD PCA is 0.49 +/- 0.01 (CPA* (noAdv)), and the best DEG recall is 0.007 +/- 0.002 (CPA*) - essentially zero differentially-expressed-gene recovery across every method. Table 5 adds RMSE mean best 0.017 (LA (scGPT)), RMSE-mean rank best 0.10 (CPA* (noAdv)) and MMD best 2.2 (Linear). A benchmark where ten methods recover under 1% of differentially expressed genes is an open frontier rather than a saturated leaderboard, and the data are ungated: srivatsan20_highest_dose_processed.h5ad.gz (410 MB) in the public Hugging Face repo altoslabs/perturbench, with splits generated by the package itself and the Evaluator shipped in the repo. 410 MB of sparse counts plus linear and kernel models is a CPU-only, laptop-hours problem.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a model trained with PerturBench's own Srivatsan20 accessor and package-generated covariate-transfer splits (train = all cell lines minus the 30% held-out perturbations per cell line; the exact held-out perturbation list per cell line logged), scored by the repository's own Evaluator at a pinned commit, that strictly beats the best published value for at least ONE metric in Table 2 or Table 5 of the latest arXiv version of PerturBench (re-fetched live immediately before claiming; cosine logFC higher is better, all other listed metrics lower is better except DEG recall which is higher) by at least 3x the published standard deviation of the previous best AND over 5 independent seeds reported as mean +/- std, while not being worse than the previous best on any other reported metric by more than 1 published std. For DEG recall, where every published method sits at or below 0.007, a claim requires >= 0.02 over 5 seeds with the per-perturbation recall list saved. Deliverables: pinned commit, dataset sha256, the per-cell-line held-out perturbation lists, training script and config, full Evaluator output over all metrics and seeds, and same-environment same-split re-runs of the published LA and Linear baselines landing within 1 published std of the tables (otherwise the comparison is void). No cell carrying a held-out perturbation may touch training, normalisation, highly-variable-gene selection, early stopping or hyperparameter search.
targets.verification_method: Clean virtual environment, perturbench at the attacker's pinned commit, download srivatsan20_highest_dose_processed.h5ad.gz from the ungated Hugging Face dataset and compare sha256 with the manifest, regenerate the splits with the package (or load the attacker's split files and verify they match the generator and that held-out perturbations are disjoint from training per cell line), load the attacker's predicted anndata and recompute every metric with the repository's Evaluator (under an hour), re-train 2 of the 5 seeds (laptop-hours) and re-run the LA and Linear baselines to confirm the published values are reproduced. Leakage audit: normalisation and gene selection statistics computed on training cells only; control cells used exactly as the package does; no held-out-perturbation cell read outside final scoring.

angles: Information-theoretic phenotype matching done right: the classic scores (Resnik/Lin/Phenomizer) use term information content from annotation frequencies; recompute IC on a pinned HPOA, handle term incompleteness explicitly with a missing-at-random model, and score by likelihood ratio rather than similarity (the LIRICAL idea) with properly calibrated noise terms.

CROSS-DOMAIN (coding theory / nearest-neighbour decoding): treat each disease's annotation set as a codeword over the HPO alphabet and the patient profile as a received word with erasures and substitutions; rank by maximum-likelihood decoding under an explicit erasure/noise channel (erasure probability per term depth), which is exactly the information-poor-profile problem.

CROSS-DOMAIN (compression / MDL): rank candidate diseases by the description length of the patient profile when encoded with that disease's annotation distribution plus the ontology structure (two-part code), which penalises over-general diseases automatically and needs no tuned weights.

CROSS-DOMAIN (linguistics / distributional semantics): learn HPO term embeddings from co-occurrence across the corpus and from ontology structure (node2vec on the DAG, PPMI-SVD on case profiles) and score by soft-cosine matching, capturing the synonymy and granularity mismatch that exact-ontology matching misses.

CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing on graphs): propagate patient phenotype mass over the HPO DAG and the gene-phenotype bipartite graph with heat-kernel/random-walk-with-restart diffusion, then rank genes by received mass - a cheap, strong baseline class that the rare-disease tools largely do not use.

Ascertainment-robust design: weight evidence by whether a gene's annotations predate the case's publication, so the method is scored on prospective-style inference; this attacks the single biggest reason published numbers on literature corpora look optimistic.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: Rare-disease gene prioritisation: beat published ranking performance on a frozen phenopacket-store release

partial_wins.statement: Beat the reference tool's MRR by >= 10% relative on the subset of cases with <= 3 HPO terms (the information-poor regime where phenotype matching is weakest), with bootstrap intervals and identical candidate space.

Beat the reference tool on cases whose causal gene has NO HPO annotation in the pinned HPOA release (i.e. the gene is unannotated, so similarity-to-known-annotations cannot work), demonstrating a genuinely different inference route, with >= 50 such cases and full ranked lists.

A reproducible leakage/ascertainment audit: quantify how much of a reference tool's performance on this corpus is explained by the fact that the same publications generated both the phenopacket and the gene's HPO annotations (e.g. by scoring with annotation releases that predate each case's publication), released as code and numbers.

pitfalls: Circular annotation leakage: the HPO disease annotations are curated FROM the same case reports that the phenopackets come from, so any similarity method is partly recognising its own training data. A claim must pin annotation releases and ideally use pre-publication annotation snapshots; otherwise an apparent win measures curation overlap.

Candidate-space inflation: ranking against a short candidate list (e.g. a 200-gene panel) instead of all protein-coding genes makes MRR look wonderful. The candidate space must be fixed, stated and identical for every method compared.

Case filtering after the fact: dropping cases with few HPO terms, with non-Mendelian inheritance, or where the method failed, silently raises MRR. Exclusions must be pre-registered and applied to all methods.

Release drift: phenopacket-store grows continuously (0.1.27 on 2026-06-09); comparing to a published number computed on an older release, or to a reference tool run with mismatched HPO/HPOA data releases, invalidates the comparison.

Metric sleight of hand: top-1 recall, MRR and top-10 recall move differently; improving top-10 while top-1 falls is not a win here, and per-case bootstrap intervals are needed because corpora are dominated by a few heavily curated genes.
targets.statement: phenopacket-store (github.com/monarch-initiative/phenopacket-store, release 0.1.27 published 2026-06-09, all_phenopackets.zip) is a large, growing, fully public corpus of GA4GH phenopackets curated from published case reports: thousands of individuals with rare Mendelian disease, each with HPO phenotype terms, the diagnosed disease (OMIM/MONDO) and the causal gene/variant. It is the standard public substrate for evaluating phenotype-driven gene and disease prioritisation (Exomiser, LIRICAL, Phen2Gene, phenotype-similarity algorithms), and the natural metrics are mean reciprocal rank and top-k recall of the causal gene/disease. The corpus is small enough to score in minutes, the ontology resources (HPO, MONDO, HPOA) are public, and the algorithmic question - how to rank a gene list from a noisy, incomplete, publication-biased phenotype profile - is wide open and almost entirely untouched by modern methods. No patient-identifiable data is involved: phenopackets are de-identified case descriptions from the literature.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a released ranking method plus saved per-case ranked candidate lists over a FIXED candidate space (all protein-coding genes, or all diseases, stated in advance) for every case in a pinned phenopacket-store release (tag and asset sha256 published), using only ontology/annotation resources whose release dates precede the corpus release and excluding any resource derived from the case reports themselves, such that mean reciprocal rank AND top-1 recall both strictly exceed (direction: max) the values obtained by a publicly available reference tool (Exomiser or LIRICAL, pinned version and pinned data release, run by the claimant AND reproduced by the skeptic on the same corpus and candidate space), by at least 10% relative on MRR and outside a 95% bootstrap interval over cases. If a published evaluation on the same release exists, its best value is the bar instead. Cases must not be filtered after seeing results; any exclusion rule (e.g. cases without HPO terms) must be pre-stated and applied to every method identically.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the pinned all_phenopackets.zip release asset (hash-checked), pins HPO/HPOA/MONDO releases, runs the reference tool (Exomiser or LIRICAL, pinned version and data) themselves on the same corpus and candidate space, runs the attacker's released method to regenerate ranked lists (bit-for-bit or documented tolerance), recomputes MRR, top-1/top-5/top-10 recall and bootstrap intervals over cases, and checks the exclusion rules and candidate spaces are identical between methods. Everything is CPU-only and minutes-scale once the resources are local.

angles: Conventional: better kernels over existing embeddings - the leader is a GP, so composite kernels (Matern over embeddings x Hamming over mutated positions x one-hot amino-acid kernel), automatic relevance determination, and proper marginal-likelihood optimisation inside each training fold are the obvious next step.

Conventional: stack zero-shot scores as a prior mean for the supervised GP (the zero-shot columns are public and label-free), which is the cheapest reliable way to lift supervised Spearman on small assays.

Cross-domain import (coding theory): represent each variant as a codeword over positions and amino acids and use a Hamming-weighted kernel plus syndrome-style features (which positions changed, to which chemical class), i.e. treat the DMS set as a punctured code and exploit its algebraic structure instead of relying on dense embeddings.

Cross-domain import (statistical physics / epistasis): add a Potts-model statistical energy and explicit pairwise-epistasis features from DCA on the protein family as GP input dimensions; supervised models on single proteins rarely include couplings, and the contiguous-fold scheme punishes models that cannot extrapolate across the sequence.

Cross-domain import (compression / MDL): select kernel complexity and feature subsets by description length rather than inner-fold Spearman, which is the right regulariser when the training folds are small (265-1,800 mutants for some assays) and inner-fold selection is itself noisy.

Cross-domain import (signal processing): treat the position-by-amino-acid score matrix as a 2-D signal and denoise it with a separable wavelet or total-variation prior before fitting, exploiting the strong smoothness of DMS landscapes along the position axis.

Uncertainty-aware prediction: because Spearman rewards correct ordering, convert the GP posterior into a rank-optimal point prediction (e.g. the posterior median or an expected-rank transform) rather than the posterior mean.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: ProteinGym supervised benchmark: beat the public best 5-fold Spearman on a cancer-gene DMS assay

partial_wins.statement: Beat the live per-assay best by >= 0.015 on the SAME cancer-gene assay in two of the three fold schemes (random-5, modulo-5, contiguous-5) with one frozen configuration. The contiguous scheme is the hardest extrapolation setting and a win there is substantially stronger.
Beat the live best on MSH2_HUMAN_Jia_2020 (0.665 random-5 as of 2026-10-13, 16,749 mutants) by >= 0.02 Spearman with the full pre-registered protocol.

A same-protocol reproduction of the published leader (Kermut) on one cancer-gene assay, landing within 0.01 Spearman of the published value, with full logs. Independently checkable, non-trivial, and a prerequisite for believing any improvement claim; report it as a reproduction, not a record.

pitfalls: Fold-boundary leakage is the dominant trap and is subtle: any per-position label statistic, label-based clustering, target encoding, or embedding fine-tuned on the full assay crosses the fold boundary while looking like honest feature engineering. The skeptic must re-run the five trainings rather than trust the out-of-fold file.

Fold-scheme confusion: random-5, modulo-5 and contiguous-5 have different records in different CSVs; comparing a random-5 result against a contiguous-5 record (or against the zero-shot CSV, which is a different benchmark entirely) is an easy and fatal error.
Protein-level tuning leakage: PTEN, P53, RASK and VKOR1 each appear in several assays; tuning on one and scoring another shares the same protein's labels. Exclusion must be by UniProt ID.
Cross-benchmark confusion: ProteinGym also publishes clinical_supervised and clinical_zero_shot benchmarks with their own tables; a number from one benchmark never beats a record in another.

Small-assay noise: BRCA2_HUMAN_Erwood_2022_HEK293T has 265 mutants, so 5-fold Spearman swings by far more than 0.015 across seeds. Prefer the large assays, and report seed variability for anything under ~2,000 mutants.
Over-claiming clinical relevance: a supervised model fitted on a laboratory mutational scan is not a clinical variant classifier, and the write-up must say so explicitly.
targets.statement: ProteinGym also publishes a SUPERVISED benchmark with frozen cross-validation schemes (random, modulo and contiguous 5-fold), per-assay Spearman for 11 methods, in plain CSVs in the repo (benchmarks/DMS_supervised/substitutions/Spearman/DMS_substitutions_Spearman_DMS_level_fold_random_5.csv and the modulo/contiguous variants). Because the folds are fixed and published, a claimed improvement is exactly reproducible. The cancer-gene rows in the random-5 scheme as of 2026-10-13: BRCA1_HUMAN_Findlay_2018 best 0.683 (Kermut; ProteinNPT 0.559, Tranception Embeddings 0.573); MSH2_HUMAN_Jia_2020 best 0.665 (Kermut; ProteinNPT 0.526, One-Hot 0.513); P53_HUMAN_Kotler_2018 best 0.791 (Kermut; MSA Transformer Embeddings 0.742, ProteinNPT 0.736); PTEN_HUMAN_Mighell_2018 best 0.647 (Kermut; ProteinNPT 0.632); RASK_HUMAN_Weng_2022_abundance best 0.787 (Tranception Embeddings; ProteinNPT 0.786, Kermut 0.769). Only ELEVEN methods are listed, the leader is a Gaussian-process model over embeddings, and the whole task is regression on a few thousand rows with precomputed embeddings - squarely laptop-scale, and the kind of narrow numeric frontier where a better kernel, better embedding mixture or better uncertainty treatment plausibly wins within laptop-hours.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for one cancer-gene DMS assay and one of the three published fold schemes, out-of-fold predictions for every mutant in ProteinGym's reference file for that assay, produced by training the method five times on the four complementary folds defined by ProteinGym's own published fold assignment column (sha256 logged) and predicting the held-out fold each time, such that the Spearman between the concatenated out-of-fold predictions and the measured DMS scores, recomputed by the skeptic in ProteinGym's convention, is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the maximum over all method columns for that assay in the live CSV for the SAME fold scheme (re-fetched immediately before claiming) by at least 0.015 absolute. All hyperparameters, kernels, embedding choices, feature transforms and early-stopping rules must be fixed before the target assay is scored and pre-registered with a sha256-stamped file; they may be tuned only on assays with different UniProt IDs, or by nested cross-validation INSIDE each training fold (never using the held-out fold). Deliverables: the per-fold prediction files, the fold assignment used, the pre-registration file, the method code, and all five trained-model configs.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the assay's reference file and ProteinGym's published fold assignments, checks sha256s, verifies the attacker's out-of-fold predictions cover every mutant exactly once and that each prediction came from a model trained without that mutant's fold (by re-running the five trainings from the attacker's code and configs; laptop-hours with precomputed embeddings), recomputes the concatenated Spearman in ProteinGym's convention, and re-fetches the live CSV for the same fold scheme to read the per-assay maximum. Leakage audit: confirm the pre-registration predates scoring, that embeddings were not fitted on the assay's labels, that no target-encoding or label-derived feature (per-position mean score, label-based clustering) crossed fold boundaries, and that nested tuning never touched the held-out fold.

angles: Conventional: rank-space ensembling of the ~97 published score columns with weights fitted by leave-assay-out on non-cancer assays (Borda / Copeland aggregation, or a rank-correlation-optimal weighting), which is cheap and frequently beats the single best model per assay.

Conventional: assay-aware calibration - DMS assays measure different properties (abundance vs activity vs organismal fitness, a column in the CSV), so condition the ensemble weights on the assay's declared selection type and MSA depth category, both of which are metadata columns in the public CSV rather than labels.

Cross-domain import (coding theory / soft-decision decoding): treat each public predictor as a noisy channel observation of the true fitness ordering and combine them with a log-likelihood-ratio (soft-decision) decoder whose channel reliabilities are estimated from non-cancer assays; this is strictly better than majority/mean rank fusion and is exactly how one combines unequal-quality observations.

Cross-domain import (statistical physics / Potts models and direct coupling analysis): fit an epistatic Potts model on the protein's MSA (pseudo-likelihood DCA, CPU-cheap) and use its statistical energy as an additional predictor, including pairwise couplings that single-site models miss; for tumour-suppressor domains with deep MSAs this is a genuinely different signal from protein language models.

Cross-domain import (compression): score a variant by the increase in description length of the protein family when the variant is inserted, using a compressor trained on the MSA (e.g. context-mixing or PPM over aligned columns); parameter-free, label-free, and uncorrelated with language-model scores, which is what an ensemble needs.

Structure-aware re-ranking: use a public predicted structure to add solvent accessibility and contact-number features (not labels) as a monotone correction to the ensemble score, with the correction's shape fitted only on non-cancer assays.

Small-model CPU runs: ESM-2 (8M/35M/150M) masked-marginal scoring, site-independent models, and MSA-based methods are all CPU-feasible on single proteins, so the agent can add fresh score columns rather than only recombining old ones.

targets.name: ProteinGym zero-shot: beat the best public Spearman on a cancer-gene deep-mutational-scanning assay

partial_wins.statement: Beat the live per-assay best by >= 0.015 Spearman on at least three cancer-gene assays simultaneously with ONE method and ONE frozen configuration (pre-registered, fitted only on non-cancer assays). Multi-assay consistency with a single configuration is far stronger evidence than a single-assay win.
Beat the live best on MSH2_HUMAN_Jia_2020 (0.409 as of 2026-10-13, the weakest of the large cancer-gene assays, 16,749 mutants) by >= 0.02 Spearman under the same rules.

A leakage-free combination audit: show, with pre-registered weights fitted only on non-cancer assays, how much of the gap between the single best model and the ensemble ceiling is reachable per cancer-gene assay, and publish the per-assay reachable-ceiling estimate (computed by a leave-assay-out protocol over the ~97 public score columns). A methodological result, checkable from the public CSV plus the published score files.

pitfalls: The target assay's labels are PUBLIC, which makes this benchmark trivially leakable: any weight, threshold, model choice or 'validation' decision informed by the target assay's DMS scores invalidates the claim. The pre-registration file with sha256 and the leave-assay-out fitting rule are the only defence, and the skeptic must check timestamps and code paths rather than trusting a claim of blindness.

Protein-level leakage: several cancer genes appear in MULTIPLE ProteinGym assays (two PTEN assays, four P53 assays, two RASK/VKOR1 assays). Fitting on one assay of the same protein and scoring another is leakage even though the assay ids differ. Exclusion must be by UniProt ID, not by assay id.

Scoring-convention drift: Spearman sign conventions, excluded mutants, multi-mutant vs single-mutant subsets, and NaN handling all shift the number by more than the 0.015 bar. The skeptic must recompute with the official convention against the official reference file, not the attacker's own mutant list.

Ensemble selection bias: choosing WHICH of the ~97 columns to ensemble by looking at per-assay performance in the public CSV is itself using the target assay's labels (the CSV reports Spearman against those labels). Column selection must be pre-registered or derived from non-cancer assays only.

Novelty trap: the published columns already include strong ensembles and retrieval-augmented models (TranceptEVE, ProSST, VenusREM, S3F-MSA, PoET, AIDO Protein-RAG, Protriever); matching or marginally exceeding a published ensemble is not a result, and the NOVELTY skeptic must check recent preprints for already-published higher per-assay values.

Clinical over-claiming: a higher Spearman on a laboratory mutational scan of a cancer gene says nothing about any individual's variant interpretation, and the write-up must not frame it as variant classification for patients.
targets.statement: ProteinGym maintains a public, machine-readable benchmark of variant-effect predictors scored against deep mutational scanning assays, with per-assay Spearman correlations for 98 models in a plain CSV in the GitHub repo (benchmarks/DMS_zero_shot/substitutions/Spearman/DMS_substitutions_Spearman_DMS_level.csv; repo last pushed 2026-03-25). Several assays are cancer genes, and the per-assay public bests are far from saturated as of 2026-10-13: BRCA1_HUMAN_Findlay_2018 best 0.560 (S3F-MSA; PoET 200M 0.558, S2F-MSA 0.551) over 1,837 mutants; PTEN_HUMAN_Mighell_2018 best 0.561 (S3F-MSA) over 7,260 mutants; PTEN_HUMAN_Matreyek_2021 best 0.516 (VenusREM) over 5,083; MSH2_HUMAN_Jia_2020 best 0.409 (ESCOTT) over 16,749; P53_HUMAN_Kotler_2018 best 0.722 (ProSST K=1024) over 1,048; RASK_HUMAN_Weng_2022_abundance best 0.470 (Progen2 XL) over 26,012; BRCA2_HUMAN_Erwood_2022_HEK293T best 0.534 (RITA L) over 265; plus ERBB2, additional P53 assays and the RASH/RASK series. Because 98 model score files are distributed with the benchmark, laptop agents can attack this without training any large model: principled combination, calibration and structure-aware re-ranking of existing public scores, or running a small open model (ESM-2 35M/150M, site-independent and MSA-based methods) on CPU, are both in budget. The per-assay frontier for a single cancer gene is a narrow, mechanically checkable record.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a saved score file assigning one real-valued fitness prediction to every mutant in the ProteinGym reference CSV for a chosen cancer-gene DMS assay (the assay's own reference file as distributed by ProteinGym, sha256 logged), produced by a method that is ZERO-SHOT with respect to that assay - it may use sequence, structure, MSAs, and other models' published score files, but no measurement from ANY ProteinGym DMS assay of the same UniProt protein may enter the method, and no hyperparameter, weight, threshold, model-selection decision or combination weight may be chosen using the target assay's labels - such that the Spearman correlation, recomputed by the skeptic with the official ProteinGym scoring convention (same mutant set, same direction convention, same NaN handling), is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the maximum over all model columns for that assay in the live DMS-level Spearman CSV (re-fetched immediately before claiming) by at least 0.015 absolute. Any hyperparameter or combination weight must be fitted on a declared set of NON-cancer-gene assays, or on no data at all, and the fitting set must be logged with a sha256-stamped pre-registration file written before the target assay is scored. Deliverables: the score file, the pre-registration file, the method code, the list of external score files used with their provenance, and the skeptic-recomputable Spearman.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the ProteinGym reference file for the assay and the attacker's score file, checks the mutant sets match exactly (and the sha256 of the reference file), recomputes Spearman with scipy against the assay's DMS_score column following the official convention, and re-fetches the live DMS-level Spearman CSV to read the per-assay maximum over model columns (minutes). Then the skeptic re-runs the attacker's method end-to-end from the logged inputs (laptop-minutes to laptop-hours if it only combines published score files; longer if it runs a model) and confirms the score file is reproduced bit-for-bit or to within a documented tolerance. Leakage audit: confirm the pre-registration file predates the scoring logs, grep the method code and any cached artefacts for reads of the target assay's labels (including through 'validation' splits), and verify that the declared fitting assays share no UniProt ID with the target.

angles: Profile HMMs done properly: the listed HMM scores 0.663 because it is a plain hmmer profile. Deep, taxonomically reweighted MSAs, full forward-algorithm log-odds instead of Viterbi, family-fitted insert/delete priors and length-aware normalisation plausibly close most of the gap to the language models.

CROSS-DOMAIN (string algorithms): score an indel as the cost of the cheapest alignment of the mutant to the family profile under affine gap penalties learned from the family's own gap statistics, with repeat-aware penalties from tandem-repeat detection - in-frame indels in repeats are the classic benign class.

CROSS-DOMAIN (compression / MDL): normalised compression distance between the mutant sequence and the family corpus handles length changes natively, unlike substitution scorers, and costs nothing on CPU.

CROSS-DOMAIN (statistical physics): free-energy difference in a Potts model of the family, with the deletion treated as a column removal and the insertion as an added site sampled from the family's background, gives a principled length-change energy rather than a heuristic.

Structure-informed tolerance: AlphaFold DB models are free for these human proteins, so loop-versus-core location, predicted disorder and local packing give an indel-tolerance prior that no listed baseline uses.

Frame and domain logic: an in-frame indel inside a disordered linker and a frame-preserving deletion of a catalytic loop are different problems; conditioning on Pfam domain boundaries and secondary-structure context is cheap and unexploited.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: ProteinGym clinical indels: beat the leaderboard's best average AUC on insertion/deletion clinical variants

partial_wins.statement: Beat the best alignment-only baseline on the live clinical indel table (Provean, 0.927 as fetched 2026-10-15) by >= 0.010 with a method that uses no neural network at all and runs the whole benchmark on a laptop in under 4 hours, with timings.

Add a genuinely new model class to this table: full-benchmark clinical indel scores from a structure-aware or MSA-based method the table currently lacks, reaching Average_AUC >= 0.92 with code, logs and a reproducible environment.

A per-protein audit: a list of >= 20 clinical proteins where the live leader's released scores give AUC < 0.6, plus a method exceeding AUC 0.8 on those proteins without dropping overall Average_AUC more than 0.005 below the live leader.

pitfalls: Label leakage: most human variant-effect tooling is trained on ClinVar, and this benchmark's labels are clinical. Any supervised pathogenicity component, or a language model fine-tuned on clinical labels, inflates AUC without advancing anything.
Partial coverage: scoring only proteins with many variants, or only in-frame indels, then comparing to an average over the whole benchmark. The repository's aggregation must be rerun on the full set.

No published error bar: because this CSV has no bootstrap standard-error column, differences of 0.003-0.008 can be noise; the claimant must compute and report a resampling interval over proteins, not quote the table.

Table drift: the summary CSV is regenerated as baselines land, and the clinical substitution and clinical indel tables share model names; comparing to a cached number or to the substitutions table is a false positive.
Frequency circularity: benign labels are partly frequency-derived, so any allele-frequency feature re-derives the label definition and must be treated as leakage.
targets.statement: ProteinGym (Pascal Notin, Aaron Kollasch, Debora Marks and colleagues) keeps a separate, much thinner leaderboard for CLINICAL INDELS - benign versus pathogenic insertion/deletion variants in human proteins - alongside its well-known substitution tables. The live summary CSV fetched 2026-10-15 lists only 18 baselines and is led by PoET (200M) at average AUC 0.935, then Provean 0.927, RITA L 0.922, RITA XL 0.916, down to a profile hidden Markov model at 0.663, ProtGPT2 0.649 and Unirep 0.599. Unlike the substitution tables, this file carries no bootstrap standard error column, and almost every strong substitution-benchmark method (GEMME, EVE, ESM-1b/1v, SaProt, ProSST, ESCOTT, VenusREM, RSALOR) is absent because it cannot score length changes. A 0.26 AUC gap between the leader and the plain HMM, in a category where indels dominate unsolved rare-disease exomes, is unusually open ground for alignment machinery that runs on a CPU.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a saved score file with one real-valued score per variant covering EVERY protein and EVERY variant of the ProteinGym clinical indel benchmark (v1.3 release; no protein dropped, mutant identifiers matched exactly, sha256 of the file published), produced by a released method that uses no clinical label source for any benchmark protein (no ClinVar, HGMD, dbNSFP pathogenicity column, gnomAD-derived pathogenicity score and no supervised pathogenicity predictor) and no per-protein tuning, such that the repository's own scoring scripts, run by the skeptic with the repository's aggregation (AUC per protein, then the repository's UniProt/category aggregation), give an Average_AUC STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best Average_AUC in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OATML-Markslab/ProteinGym/main/benchmarks/clinical_zero_shot/indels/AUC/Summary_performance_clinical_indels_AUC.csv , re-fetched live immediately before claiming (0.935 for PoET (200M) as fetched 2026-10-15), by at least 0.010 absolute AND outside a 95% bootstrap interval the skeptic computes by resampling proteins (the live CSV publishes no standard error, so the interval must be computed, not quoted).
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones OATML-Markslab/ProteinGym at a pinned commit, downloads the v1.3 clinical indel benchmark files as the README documents, checks the submitted score file covers exactly the benchmark variant set (per-protein row counts and mutant identifiers), runs the repository's performance scripts to recompute per-protein AUC and the aggregation, resamples proteins for an interval, re-fetches the live CSV for the bar, and greps the attacker's code and model manifest for ClinVar/HGMD/dbNSFP/gnomAD-derived inputs. Reproducing the attacker's scores for 20 random proteins on the skeptic's machine closes the loop. CPU-only, well under an hour of compute.

angles: Cheap-and-strong alignment statistics: rebuild deep MSAs per protein (jackhmmer/MMseqs2 against UniRef) and combine site-specific conservation, pairwise couplings (plmDCA/pseudo-likelihood) and solvent-accessibility weighting in the spirit of RSALOR and GEMME; the open question is whether better MSA construction (depth, diversity reweighting, taxonomic filtering) alone passes 0.920.

CROSS-DOMAIN (coding theory / information theory): treat each protein family alignment as a noisy channel code and score a variant by its syndrome weight under a learned low-density parity-check-style factor graph over coupled columns; minimum-description-length (compression) scoring of 'sequence with variant' versus 'sequence without' gives a parameter-free pathogenicity index that can be computed with gzip/CTW-style universal compressors over aligned columns.

CROSS-DOMAIN (statistical physics): compute variant effects as free-energy differences in a Potts model of the family fitted by pseudo-likelihood, including entropic contributions from a local sampling of the sequence neighbourhood (thermodynamic integration / umbrella sampling over mutational coordinates) rather than a single point energy.

CROSS-DOMAIN (phylogenetics as signal processing): score variants by rate-shift detection on the family tree, i.e. a matched filter over per-site substitution-rate spectra across clades (SiteRM-style ultrafast phylogenetics beat large PLMs on variant effect), which is pure CPU work.

Rank aggregation: ensemble the public per-protein scores of existing baselines with Borda/Copeland voting, Thurstone models, or isotonic calibration per MSA-depth bin; leaderboards aggregate by category, so improving the worst categories (low-MSA-depth, small proteins) matters more than the average.

Target the structure of the metric: AUC is aggregated per protein, so proteins with few variants dominate variance; invest compute in deep MSAs for exactly those proteins, and use conformal/variance-aware shrinkage toward a conservation prior where alignments are shallow.

CROSS-DOMAIN (linguistics): borrow distributional-semantics tests (collocation strength, mutual information between columns, morphological alternation detection) to detect positions under grammar-like constraint, then weight variant penalties by constraint type instead of by raw conservation.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: ProteinGym clinical substitutions (ClinVar benign/pathogenic): beat the leaderboard's best average AUC

partial_wins.statement: Beat the best MSA-free (single-sequence) baseline's Average_AUC on the live clinical substitutions table by > 2 bootstrap SEs using only single-sequence information, no alignments and no structures.

Beat GEMME's live Average_AUC (an alignment-only method) with a method that is itself alignment-only and runs end-to-end on a laptop in under 6 hours wall clock for the whole benchmark, with timing logs.

A reproducible per-protein audit: a list of >= 50 clinical proteins where the leaderboard-leading model's released scores give AUC < 0.6, together with a method that exceeds AUC 0.8 on those same proteins without degrading the overall Average_AUC below the live leader minus 0.005.

pitfalls: Label leakage through dbNSFP-derived features or any pathogenicity predictor trained on ClinVar: the benchmark's clinical labels come from the same curated sources, so any supervised pathogenicity score (or a PLM fine-tuned on ClinVar) inflates AUC without being a real advance. The clinical baselines on this table are deliberately unsupervised or classic conservation tools.

Protein-set cherry-picking: dropping hard proteins, scoring only proteins with many variants, or scoring a subset and comparing to a table computed on all 2,525 proteins. The aggregation (by UniProt ID, then by category) must be rerun with the repository's script on the full set.

Benchmark-version confusion: the summary CSV is regenerated as new baselines land, and the DMS and clinical tables share model names. Comparing to a cached number, to the DMS substitutions AUC, or to the website's rendering instead of the live CSV is a false positive; direction is max and the bar is the live best row.

Bootstrap noise: Average_AUC differences of 0.001-0.003 are inside the reported bootstrap SE; also MSA re-generation changes alignment-based scores run to run, so a single lucky MSA seed is not a record.

Circularity in evaluation: many 'benign' labels are frequency-derived, so a method using allele frequency (gnomAD) re-derives the label definition. Even a weak frequency feature must be treated as leakage.
targets.statement: ProteinGym's clinical substitution benchmark scores variant-effect predictors on annotated human clinical missense variants (benign vs pathogenic) across 2,525 clinical proteins (count to be re-derived from the pinned v1.3 release notes at claim time), aggregated by UniProt ID and by functional category, reported as average AUC with a bootstrapped standard error. The public summary table (fetched 2026-10-13) is topped by PoET (200M) at 0.920, TranceptEVE L 0.920, GEMME 0.919, EVE 0.914, ESM-1b 0.892, then the dbNSFP clinical predictors (Provean 0.886, SIFT 0.878, SIFT4G 0.877, MutationAssessor 0.877, MutPred 0.875, PrimateAI 0.855, LIST-S2 0.842, LRT 0.805). Only a handful of the ~35 baselines present on the DMS leaderboards have been scored on the clinical benchmark at all, and the top of the table is a dead heat between an MSA-conditioned generative model and a 2019 epistatic-conservation method (GEMME), which runs in minutes per family on a CPU. Whether a cheap alignment-statistics or ensemble method can pass 0.920 on this benchmark is open, and the repository explicitly invites new baselines ('How to contribute?').
targets.success_criterion: Success means a saved score file giving one real-valued score per variant for EVERY variant in the ProteinGym clinical substitution benchmark (v1.3 release, all clinical protein files, no proteins dropped), produced by a method whose code and inputs are released, such that the benchmark's own scoring script (scripts/scoring_DMS_zero_shot/*, performance computed exactly as in the repository: AUC per protein, aggregated by UniProt ID then across functional categories) yields an Average_AUC STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best Average_AUC in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OATML-Markslab/ProteinGym/main/benchmarks/clinical_zero_shot/substitutions/AUC/Summary_performance_clinical_substitutions_AUC.csv , re-fetched live immediately before claiming, by at least 0.005 absolute AND by more than twice max(leader SE, runner-up SE, 0.002), with the skeptic recomputing a target-resampling interval (the leader's Bootstrap_standard_error_AUC is 0.0 as of 2026-10-15, so the row SE alone is not a constraint). The method must not use, directly or as a feature, any clinical label source for the benchmark proteins (ClinVar, HGMD, dbNSFP pathogenicity columns, gnomAD-trained pathogenicity scores, or any supervised pathogenicity predictor), and must be applied uniformly to all proteins with no per-protein tuning. A run whose score file omits variants, or re-bins/re-thresholds the labels, does not count.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones OATML-Markslab/ProteinGym at a pinned commit, downloads the v1.3 clinical substitution benchmark (curl from marks.hms.harvard.edu as documented in the repo README), checks the attacker's score file covers exactly the benchmark variant set (row counts and mutant ids per protein, sha256 of the submitted file), runs the repository's own performance scripts to recompute AUC per protein and the UniProt/category aggregation, and re-fetches the live summary CSV for the current leader (its header has a duplicated Model_rank column, so parse it explicitly rather than with a naive read_csv). The protein count and the scoring-script path are re-derived from the pinned v1.3 release notes at claim time. Label-leakage audit: grep the attacker's code and any model weights/manifest for dbNSFP, ClinVar, HGMD or gnomAD-derived pathogenicity inputs, and confirm the released pipeline reproduces the submitted scores for a random sample of 20 proteins on the skeptic's machine.

angles: Profile-HMM done properly: the listed HMM baseline is a plain hmmer profile. Build per-family HMMs from deep, taxonomically reweighted MSAs, score indels with full forward-algorithm log-odds (not Viterbi), calibrate insert/delete state priors per family, and add length-aware normalisation; the table suggests this alone could approach the PLM frontier.

CROSS-DOMAIN (compression / MDL): score an indel by the change in normalised compression distance between the mutated sequence and the family corpus (CTW, PPM, gzip-based NCD, or a family-specific grammar compressor). This is parameter-free, handles length changes natively (unlike substitution-only scorers), and is cheap on CPU.

CROSS-DOMAIN (string algorithms / edit-distance geometry): treat each indel as a move in an edit-distance metric space and score it by the cost of the cheapest alignment of the mutant to the family profile under affine gap penalties learned from the family's own gap statistics (Gotoh with family-fitted gap opening/extension), including repeat-aware penalties from tandem-repeat detection.

CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing): represent the sequence as a multichannel signal of physicochemical property tracks, and treat insertions/deletions as phase runs; score by spectral/periodicity disruption (helical 3.6-residue periodicity, beta-strand alternation), which detects frame-like disruption that substitution models miss.

CROSS-DOMAIN (ecology / community statistics): use MSA column occupancy and gap-pattern co-occurrence as a species-abundance problem (Hill numbers, rarefaction) to estimate how tolerant each region is to length change, giving a per-position indel-tolerance prior.

Ensembling and calibration: combine a cheap alignment score with per-assay-independent rank normalisation and isotonic calibration per functional category; aggregate with rank-fusion rather than score averaging, since the metric is Spearman.

Structure-informed gap tolerance: use public AlphaFold DB models for the target proteins to score indels by loop-versus-core location and by predicted local disorder, filling a model class the indel table currently lacks entirely.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: ProteinGym indel benchmark (zero-shot): beat the best average Spearman on insertion/deletion DMS assays

partial_wins.statement: Beat the live best Average_Spearman in the Low_MSA_depth column (0.283 for PoET (200M) as fetched 2026-10-13) by >= 0.03 while staying within 0.02 of the live overall leader, with the full-benchmark score file and the repo's own aggregation.

Beat every alignment-based baseline on the live indel table (profile HMM 0.389, WaveNet 0.368, Provean 0.347 as fetched 2026-10-13) by >= 0.03 average Spearman with a method that uses no neural network at all, end-to-end reproducible on a laptop in under 4 hours.

Add a genuinely new baseline class to the indel benchmark: full-benchmark scores from a structure-aware or MSA-based method that the table currently lacks, reaching Average_Spearman >= 0.47 (i.e. above ProGen2 M/Base and RITA L as listed on 2026-10-13), with code, logs and a reproducible environment.

pitfalls: Fitting to the labels: indel assays are small, so any per-assay tuning (choosing a gap penalty, a window, or a sign per assay by looking at Spearman) is overfitting and must be rejected; the benchmark is zero-shot by definition.

Partial coverage: scoring only the easy assays, or only single-residue indels, then comparing to an average computed over all 74 assays and all mutants. Low-MSA-depth and viral assays are the hardest and are exactly where the average is won or lost.

Wrong aggregation: taking a plain mean over assays instead of the repository's UniProt-then-category aggregation, or comparing against the substitution leaderboard's numbers (0.5 vs 0.4 scales differ) or against the website rendering instead of the live CSV.

MSA leakage: building alignments with a database or search that includes the assayed mutant sequences themselves (some DMS libraries are deposited), which silently injects labels through homology; search databases must predate or exclude the assay sequences.
Seed and alignment variance: Spearman differences under 0.01 are within run-to-run MSA variance; a record needs margin over twice the listed bootstrap SE and a rerun from a clean environment.

Function_Binding is empty for the leading rows of the indel summary CSV, so category aggregation is effectively over Activity/Expression; a claim must not be aggregated in a way that imputes a Function_Binding score.
targets.statement: ProteinGym's indel benchmark covers ~300k insertion/deletion mutants across 74 DMS assays (plus 1,555 clinical proteins). Indels are the neglected half of variant-effect prediction: the zero-shot indel leaderboard (summary CSV fetched 2026-10-13) has only ~24 baselines, nearly all autoregressive protein language models, and the frontier is PoET (200M) at average Spearman 0.517 (bootstrap SE 0.0), followed by ProGen2 M 0.465, ProGen2 Base 0.464, RITA L 0.457. A profile HMM scores 0.389 and WaveNet 0.368, i.e. plain alignment methods are within 0.13 of models with billions of parameters, and several categories are weak (low-MSA-depth 0.283 for the leader, Function_Expression 0.458). Most of the strong substitution-benchmark methods (GEMME, EVE, ESM-1b/1v, SaProt, ProSST, ESCOTT, VenusREM, RSALOR) are absent from the indel table entirely because they cannot score length changes, so a method that handles indels with alignment-and-profile machinery has unusually large headroom here on a CPU.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a saved score file with one real-valued score per mutant for ALL 74 indel DMS assays of the ProteinGym v1.3 indel benchmark (every assay, every mutant, mutated_sequence matched exactly), produced by a released zero-shot method (no training or tuning on any DMS_score in the benchmark, no per-assay hyperparameters, no use of the DMS_score_bin column), such that the repository's own scoring script (scripts/scoring_DMS_zero_shot/performance_substitutions_indels.sh, with the repo's aggregation: Spearman per assay, then by UniProt ID, then averaged across functional categories) yields an Average_Spearman STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best Average_Spearman in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OATML-Markslab/ProteinGym/main/benchmarks/DMS_zero_shot/indels/Spearman/Summary_performance_DMS_indels_Spearman.csv , re-fetched live immediately before claiming, by at least 0.010 and by more than twice max(leader SE, runner-up SE, 0.005), with the skeptic computing a resampling interval over assays (the leader's Bootstrap_standard_error_Spearman is 0.0 as of 2026-10-15). The Function_Binding column is blank for the top rows, so no aggregation may invent a contribution from that category. Sign conventions must follow the benchmark (higher score = higher fitness); flipping signs per assay to rescue correlations is disqualifying.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the v1.3 indel benchmark files per the repo README, verifies the attacker's score file has exactly one score per mutant for all 74 assays (counts and mutated_sequence hashes per assay, sha256 of the submission), confirms no DMS_score column was read by the scoring pipeline (code review plus running the attacker's scorer on a label-stripped copy of the inputs and checking identical outputs), runs the repository's indel performance script to recompute per-assay Spearman and the aggregation, and re-fetches the live summary CSV. Full re-scoring of 300k indel mutants by an alignment method is minutes to a few hours on CPU.

angles: Structured state-space and dilated-convolution models are current best; combine them with test-time augmentation over random 2.5 s crops, which the benchmark's best entries already use, and average logits across crops and seeds.

Cross-domain import (speech / audio tagging): multi-label audio tagging tricks (mixup between recordings, label smoothing per class, SpecAugment-style time masking per lead) transfer directly to 12-channel 1D signals.

Cross-domain import (physics): use beat-synchronous averaging and vectorcardiogram (3D dipole) features as additional input channels; morphology ('form') labels are about beat shape, which averaging exposes.
Hierarchical label structure: PTB-XL statements form a tree; train on all levels jointly with consistency losses so rare form statements borrow strength from their parents.
Self-supervised pretraining on the unlabeled signal of folds 1-9 only (contrastive predictive coding), then fine-tune.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: PTB-XL ECG classification: beat the best published macro-AUC on the fixed fold-10 test set

partial_wins.statement: Form statements: mean over 5 seeds above the README best by >= 0.005 macro-AUC and above any literature value found.
Match the 0.9417 all-statements state-space-model result within 0.002 with a model that trains on a laptop CPU in under 2 hours, with released code.

pitfalls: Fold 10 has the cleanest labels (human-validated) and is the test set; using it for early stopping, threshold choice or model selection invalidates the result, as the README warns.
Label-set mismatch: papers use 71, 44 or filtered subsets of statements; compare only like-for-like with the benchmark's label preparation (min-sample filtering included).
Reporting the best of many seeds inflates AUC by about the size of the gaps; the criterion uses the 5-seed mean.
Patient leakage: the recommended folds keep each patient in one fold; re-splitting randomly leaks patients and inflates scores.
This is a research benchmark; a higher macro-AUC is not evidence of clinical usefulness and must not be framed as diagnostic advice.

The README table is static (2020 models only); beating it is not a record. The bar is the best fold-10 value in the literature for the same label set, including the 2022-2023 state-space-model papers.
targets.statement: PTB-XL (Wagner, Strodthoff et al., Scientific Data 2020; open access on PhysioNet, no registration) contains 21,799 12-lead 10-second ECGs with cardiologist statements and a recommended stratified 10-fold split (folds 1-8 train, 9 validation, 10 test). Strodthoff, Wagner, Schaeffter and Samek's benchmark (IEEE JBHI 2021) publishes a results table in the helme/ecg_ptbxl_benchmarking README for six label sets (all statements, diagnostic, diagnostic subclass, superclass, form, rhythm). The README table tops out at 0.925 (all), 0.937 (diagnostic), 0.930 (subclass and superclass), 0.899 (form), 0.957 (rhythm); the README table is the benchmark authors' own 2020 results, not a community leaderboard; the best published value we found for all statements is 0.9417 macro-AUC (4S4+1FC structured state-space model, Temesgen Mehari and Nils Strodthoff, arXiv:2211.07579). The form-statement task (morphology, 19 labels) is the least saturated. A 100 Hz version of the data is under 1 GB, so small 1D CNNs train on a laptop in about an hour.
targets.success_criterion: Predictions on PTB-XL fold 10 for one benchmark label set (all, diagnostic, subdiagnostic, superdiagnostic, form or rhythm), from a model trained on folds 1-8 and selected on fold 9 only, whose term-centric macro-AUC computed by the skeptic with utils.evaluate_experiment from the benchmark repository is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the README leaderboard maximum (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) and every fold-10 value for that label set found by the NOVELTY check, by at least 0.003, and the improvement must hold as the mean over 5 training seeds (not the best seed).
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads PTB-XL 1.0.3 from PhysioNet (open access), re-runs the attacker's training for the declared seeds with the benchmark's label preparation, computes macro-AUC on fold 10 with the repository's evaluation code, and checks the training code never loads fold-10 labels before final evaluation. Hours.

angles: Conventional: discrete-time survival with a flexible baseline hazard and proper calibration terms, trained with a loss that mixes a ranking term and a likelihood term, which directly targets the two metrics the tables report.

Conventional: aggressive regularisation and ensembling - these cohorts have fewer than 2,000 patients and a handful of covariates, so variance, not model capacity, is the limiting factor; bagged classical models with monotone spline effects are a serious contender.

Cross-domain import (reliability engineering): accelerated failure time and Weibull mixture models with covariate-dependent shape are the default in equipment-failure analysis and are rarely included in these machine-learning comparisons, yet they handle non-proportional hazards natively.

Cross-domain import (actuarial science / mortality tables): borrow Lee-Carter style factor models for hazard curves, where the time profile is shared and individuals load on it, which is exactly the structure these small cohorts can estimate well.

Cross-domain import (information theory / proper scoring rules): optimise and report strictly proper scores (integrated Brier, right-censored log-likelihood) and treat concordance as a secondary read-out; the published tables show the two disagree, and the field's habit of tuning on concordance is likely why calibration is poor.

Cross-domain import (survey statistics / inverse-probability weighting): model the censoring distribution explicitly and use doubly robust estimation of the survival curve, which protects against the censoring-model misspecification that the integrated Brier score silently depends on.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-minutes
targets.name: Breast-cancer prognosis benchmark: beat the published time-dependent concordance on METABRIC and Rotterdam/GBSG

partial_wins.statement: Achieve the published best C_td on METABRIC (0.675) to within 0.005 while improving the integrated Brier score below 0.172, i.e. resolve the discrimination-calibration trade-off that the two published tables expose, with 10 repetitions.

Beat the classical linear Cox C_td by >= 0.03 on BOTH METABRIC and Rotterdam/GBSG with one frozen method and one tuning protocol, reported with all four published metrics, which no published neural method does on both cohorts simultaneously.

A variance-of-record result: run the published protocol 10 times with different fold seeds for classical Cox, Cox-Time and DeepHit, and report the seed-to-seed spread of C_td on each dataset. If the spread exceeds the gaps between published methods, say so plainly - that is a finding about the benchmark, not a win.

pitfalls: Preprocessing on the full dataset (standardisation, imputation, feature selection, discretisation of the time grid) leaks test-fold information; with gaps between published methods under 0.05 C_td, this alone can fabricate a record.

Metric confusion: Harrell's C-index, Uno's C-index and Antolini's time-dependent C_td give different values; the published bar is C_td as implemented in pycox, and the Brier score is censoring-weighted over a specific time grid.
Tiny cohorts, large variance: METABRIC has 1,904 patients and GBSG 2,232; single-run five-fold estimates move by more than 0.01 between seeds, so repetitions and a 2x-std margin are mandatory.

Dataset-version drift: several METABRIC and GBSG variants circulate with different covariate sets and different censoring; only the pycox-distributed versions used in the paper are comparable, and the sha256 must be logged.
Benchmark staleness and novelty: these datasets are heavily used, so the NOVELTY check must search recent literature for higher published C_td on the same pycox splits before any claim.

Over-claiming: these are retrospective cohorts assembled decades ago under treatment practices that no longer apply; a better concordance is a methods result, not a prognostic tool, and must never be presented as individual risk prediction.
targets.statement: Two small, fully public breast-cancer cohorts - METABRIC (1,904 patients, gene-expression-derived and clinical covariates) and the Rotterdam tumour bank plus German Breast Cancer Study Group set (GBSG) - have become the standard benchmark for survival models, and Havard Kvamme, Ornulf Borgan and Ida Scheel fixed a careful public scoreboard for them (Journal of Machine Learning Research 20(129), 2019). Their Table 2 reports the time-dependent concordance (C_td, Antolini) averaged over five cross-validation folds: on METABRIC, DeepHit 0.675, Cox-Time 0.662, RSF (C_td) 0.652, RSF (Mortality) 0.649, Cox-MLP (CC) 0.643, Cox-MLP (DeepSurv) 0.636 and classical linear Cox 0.628; on Rotterdam/GBSG, Cox-Time 0.677, Cox-MLP (DeepSurv) 0.674, DeepHit 0.670, Cox-MLP (CC) 0.669, classical Cox 0.666. Table 3 reports the censoring-weighted integrated Brier score, where the ordering changes and DeepHit's discriminative win turns into the worst calibration (METABRIC 0.184 versus Cox-Time 0.172). The datasets ship with the pycox package and download without registration; a full five-fold comparison of several model families takes minutes on a laptop CPU. The frontier is narrow - six years of neural survival models have moved METABRIC C_td by under 0.05 over a linear Cox model - and the discrimination-versus-calibration trade-off in the two tables is still unresolved, which is precisely the kind of small, literal, reproducible bar a stranger can check.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for one named dataset (metabric or gbsg as distributed by pycox, file sha256 logged), a saved per-fold risk or survival-function output under a five-fold cross-validation with the published protocol (hyperparameters selected per fold on a held-out validation subset of the training folds only), such that EITHER (a) the time-dependent concordance C_td, computed with pycox's own EvalSurv implementation, exceeds the maximum value in that dataset's column of Table 2 of https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume20/18-424/18-424.pdf - re-fetched and re-read immediately before claiming - by at least 0.015 absolute, with the gain surviving 10 repetitions of the five-fold protocol (mean +/- std) and exceeding 2x that std; OR (b) the censoring-weighted integrated Brier score is lower than the minimum in that dataset's column of Table 3 by at least 0.005 absolute under the same repetition requirement, while C_td is not worse than the published best by more than 0.01. The attacker must include same-environment, same-fold re-runs of classical Cox, DeepHit and Cox-Time and must beat both the re-run and the published values. Deliverables: dataset sha256, fold assignments, training code, per-fold predictions, and verbatim EvalSurv output for every model.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic installs pinned pycox in a clean virtual environment, loads the dataset through the package and compares sha256 with the attacker's manifest, verifies that the fold assignment covers every patient exactly once and that no patient's outcome entered feature preprocessing, recomputes C_td and the integrated Brier score from the attacker's saved survival predictions with EvalSurv (seconds), and re-runs the attacker's training plus the three reference models end to end (laptop-minutes). The live record is read by downloading the JMLR PDF and reading Tables 2 and 3. Leakage audit: standardisation and any entity embeddings fitted on training folds only; no hyperparameter chosen using the test fold; the time grid for the Brier score identical to the published convention.

angles: Span-based rather than token-based decoding: signs are nested, overlapping and discontinuous, which BIO tagging cannot represent; exhaustive span classification, or a grammar over spans, directly targets the 57% class.

CROSS-DOMAIN (parsing / formal languages): parse each sentence with a dependency or constituency parser and define entity candidates as syntactic constituents, so discontinuous signs become coordinated subtrees instead of impossible tag sequences.

CROSS-DOMAIN (information retrieval / ontology lookup): a high-recall dictionary pass over HPO, Orphanet and MONDO labels and synonyms, followed by a learned filter, is a strong and interpretable baseline that neural models rarely beat on recall.

CROSS-DOMAIN (compression / MDL): choose the span segmentation that minimises description length of the sentence under a two-part code (entity lexicon plus residual text), which penalises overgeneration automatically.

Data programming: the corpus is small, so weak supervision over unlabelled NORD and Orphanet text (ontology matches, pattern rules, a label model) can multiply effective training data without touching the test split.
Transfer from clinical NER corpora (BC5CDR, NCBI Disease) with domain-adaptive pretraining on rare-disease text, keeping the RareDis test documents strictly out of every pretraining corpus.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: RareDis corpus: beat the published BioBERT F1 for rare-disease and sign entity recognition on the fixed test split

partial_wins.statement: Beat the published sign F1 (57.2% as read 2026-10-15) by >= 3 points on the official test split with the bootstrap interval over documents excluding zero, releasing the per-span predictions.
Match the published rare-disease F1 to within 1 point with a model that runs CPU-only inference over the whole test split in under 60 seconds, with timings - practical for a clinic without a GPU.

An annotation-quality audit: re-examine the spans the best model gets wrong, classify them into annotation inconsistencies versus genuine errors with a published rubric and a second annotator's agreement statistic, and quantify the ceiling the corpus itself imposes.

pitfalls: Pretraining contamination: NORD texts are on the public web, so a language model pretrained on recent web crawls may have memorised the very documents in the test split; the claim must state the pretraining corpus and its cutoff.

Scorer mismatch: exact-span, relaxed-overlap and token-level F1 differ by many points on nested entities; the published numbers are exact-span micro-F1 and the comparison must use the same scorer, rerun by the skeptic.
Entity-type cherry-picking: improving signs while rare-disease F1 collapses is not a win; all four types must be reported from one model and one run.
Document-level correlation: sentences inside a document are not independent, so intervals must bootstrap documents, not sentences, in a corpus this small.
Benchmark-to-clinic gap: better entity recognition on NORD summaries is not a diagnostic system and says nothing about performance on real clinical notes.
targets.statement: Diagnostic delay in rare disease is partly an information problem: the knowledge sits in unstructured text. Isabel Segura-Bedmar's group at Universidad Carlos III de Madrid released the RareDis corpus - NORD rare-disease texts manually annotated with four entity types (rare disease, disease, sign, symptom) and their relations, with official train/validation/test splits and 9,318 entities - at github.com/isegura/NLP4RARE-CM-UC3M, free to download. Their 2022 study (J Biomed Inform; Europe PMC PMC9258216, open access) benchmarks BiLSTM and transformer models on that fixed split: BioBERT is best with F1 85.2% for rare diseases but only 57.2% for signs, because signs are complex, nested, overlapping and discontinuous noun phrases. A 57% F1 is a long way from saturated, the corpus is a few megabytes, and training a small transformer or a structured span model is laptop work.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a released model plus saved per-token/per-span predictions on the OFFICIAL RareDis test split (pinned commit of github.com/isegura/NLP4RARE-CM-UC3M, sha256 of the split files published; no document dropped), trained only on the official training split (the validation split may be used for model selection, the test split for nothing), whose micro-averaged F1 for a named entity type - computed with exact-span matching as in the published evaluation, by a scorer the skeptic reruns - is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best published F1 for that entity type, re-read live from https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC9258216/fullTextXML immediately before claiming (85.2% for rare diseases, 57.2% for signs as read 2026-10-15), by at least 2 points absolute AND outside a 95% bootstrap interval over documents. Precision and recall must be reported with the F1, and the same model must be scored on all four entity types so that a gain on one is not bought by a collapse elsewhere.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones the corpus repository at the pinned commit, hashes the split files, confirms the attacker's training code never reads the test split (code review plus a run with the test files replaced by scrambled copies, which must leave training outputs unchanged), reruns the attacker's released inference to regenerate predictions, recomputes exact-span micro-F1 per entity type with an independent scorer, bootstraps over documents, and re-reads the published numbers through Europe PMC. Everything is megabytes and minutes on CPU; a small transformer fine-tune is hours.

angles: Nowcast the reporting delay first: ERVISS admissions are revised for weeks, and the near horizons dominate average WIS, so a negative-binomial delay model fitted to snapshot-to-snapshot revisions is probably the single largest gain available.

Pool across countries: a single global model over scaled national series, with partial pooling of growth rates toward a European mean, beats per-country fits when several countries report only a handful of admissions a week.

CROSS-DOMAIN (energy demand forecasting): quantile regression averaging and rolling conformal recalibration of quantiles, the standard recipe of electricity-load competitions, targets WIS directly because WIS rewards calibration over point accuracy.

CROSS-DOMAIN (control theory): a state-space model on log-admissions with a time-varying growth-rate state (Kalman or particle filter) treats revisions as observation noise and emits calibrated intervals by construction.

CROSS-DOMAIN (ecology / nonlinear time series): simplex projection and S-map analogue forecasting across the 25+ country series as replicate trajectories, instead of parametric curves, handles turning points where ensembles are weakest.
Reconciliation: forecast countries jointly and reconcile to an EU aggregate (MinT), which stabilises small countries whose WIS is otherwise dominated by noise.

targets.name: RespiCast COVID-19 hub: beat the hub ensemble's season WIS for COVID-19 hospital admissions in EU/EEA countries

partial_wins.statement: Beat the hub ensemble under the full rules at horizons 1-2 only (the near-term, backfill-dominated horizons) for one complete season, reported as a horizon-restricted result.
Beat the best single submitted model's season-average relative WIS (not only the ensemble) for one season, on matched rows.

Reproduce the hub's published WIS for hubEnsemble and quantileBaseline from the raw forecasts and the truth data to four significant figures, released as a reusable scoring script, documenting the exclusion rules needed to reconcile them.

pitfalls: Vintage leakage: using the current target data rather than the snapshot available at each origin date silently imports revisions; the snapshots folder exists precisely to prevent this and the audit must show it.

Row mismatch: the ensemble's scores cover specific origin dates, countries and horizons; dropping hard countries or weeks is the commonest way to fake a win, so the comparison must be on exactly the ensemble's rows.

Scale mixing: national admission counts differ by orders of magnitude, so a raw mean WIS is dominated by the largest countries; relative WIS must be reported alongside and the row set must be identical.
Season or target selection after seeing results is a forking path; declare both before scoring.

Outlier scores: submitted models occasionally carry absurd WIS values in these files, so any 'beats the average model' framing is meaningless - the ensemble on matched rows is the only legitimate bar.
This is a forecasting-method benchmark, not public-health advice.
targets.statement: The European COVID-19 Forecasting Hub, run by ECDC with the ISI Foundation and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine as part of RespiCast (github.com/european-modelling-hubs/respicast-COVID19), collects weekly quantile forecasts of COVID-19 hospital admissions for EU/EEA countries and - unusually - publishes its own scores: model-evaluation/latest-forecast_scores.csv (5.9 MB, fetched 2026-10-15) carries WIS, relative WIS and rank for every model, origin date, country and horizon from 2024-10-23 onwards, including the hubEnsemble and the quantileBaseline, while target-data holds the ERVISS data with dated snapshots. This is the COVID-19 sibling of the hub's syndromic-indicator track and a separate forecasting problem (admissions counts, different country set, different model pool). Beating a hub ensemble out of sample is a standing open question in epidemic forecasting, and everything needed is a few megabytes of CSV.
targets.success_criterion: For one complete season (2024-25 or 2025-26) and the hospital-admissions target, quantile forecasts in the hub's format for every (origin_date, location, horizon) row for which hubEnsemble has a WIS in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/european-modelling-hubs/respicast-COVID19/main/model-evaluation/latest-forecast_scores.csv (re-fetched live immediately before claiming), produced by a frozen pipeline that at each origin date reads only the target-data snapshot available on that date and no other team's forecasts, whose mean WIS - computed with the hub's own convention, validated by first reproducing hubEnsemble's published WIS on those rows to four significant figures - is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the ensemble's on exactly those rows by at least 3% relative, with a paired bootstrap over origin dates whose interval excludes zero. The season and target must be declared before scoring.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic loads latest-forecast_scores.csv, filters to hubEnsemble rows for the declared season and target, re-scores the attacker's forecast files against the hub's truth with the hub convention (validating the scorer by reproducing the ensemble's published values first), checks via file-access logs that each origin date read only the snapshot available then, confirms no row of another team's model-output was read, and bootstraps over origin dates. Laptop-minutes.

angles: Pool across countries: a global model (gradient boosting or a small neural net) over all countries' scaled series learns season shape far better than per-country models, and the hub's best scorers (e.g. ISI-FluBcast, ISI-SEIR_BRW) hint that cross-country structure helps.
Cross-domain import (retail demand forecasting): the M5-competition recipe of LightGBM on lagged features with Tweedie loss plus quantile post-processing.
Cross-domain import (seismology): treat epidemic onset as an excitation; Hawkes / self-exciting point-process models capture early growth with few parameters.
Calibrate rather than re-model: take the hub's own submitted forecasts available at each date and apply rolling conformal quantile recalibration plus performance-weighted pooling.
Model reporting artefacts: ERVISS revisions and country-specific reporting delays; nowcast the horizon -1 value from snapshot-to-snapshot revisions.
