targets.name: European RespiCast hub: beat the hub ensemble's WIS for influenza-like illness or acute respiratory infection incidence across EU/EEA countries

partial_wins.statement: Beat the hub ensemble on ARI incidence (fewer, newer models, so the ensemble is weaker) for one season under the full rules.
Beat the best single submitted model's season-average relative WIS (not just the ensemble) for one target and season.
Reproduce the hub's published WIS for hubEnsemble from its forecasts and truth to 4 significant figures (a verified scoring pipeline others can reuse).

pitfalls: Using the latest target data (not the snapshot available at each origin date) leaks revisions; the snapshots folder exists to prevent this.
Raw mean WIS mixes countries with incidence scales differing by orders of magnitude; compare on identical rows and also report relative WIS so a few large countries do not decide everything.
Several submitted models have absurd outlier WIS values (e.g. 1e81) in the scores file; any 'beat the average model' framing is meaningless. Compare only to the ensemble on matched rows.
Selecting the season or target after looking at results is a forking path; declare it before scoring.
This is a forecasting benchmark, not public-health advice.
targets.statement: RespiCast's European Syndromic Indicators Forecasting Hub (ECDC with the ISI Foundation and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine; github.com/european-modelling-hubs/RespiCast-SyndromicIndicators, pushed 2026-10-13) collects weekly quantile forecasts of ILI and ARI incidence per 100,000 for EU/EEA countries, horizons 1 to 4 weeks. Unlike most hubs it publishes its own scores: model-evaluation/latest-forecast_scores.csv (32 MB, 276,635 rows, 33 model_ids) lists WIS and AE for every model, origin date, location and horizon from 2024-10-23 to 2026-10-07, including the ensemble (team_id respicast, model_id hubEnsemble) and the quantileBaseline, and target-data/ERVISS/snapshots holds the data vintages. That makes a vintage-honest retrospective comparison against the hub ensemble fully checkable on a laptop. Mean WIS over value_absolute, computed 2026-10-15: ILI 2024-25 ensemble 183.5 vs baseline 206.1; ILI 2025-26 ensemble 157.1 vs baseline 184.8; ARI 2024-25 ensemble 574.3 vs baseline 745.7; ARI 2025-26 ensemble 535.2 vs baseline 522.3, i.e. the quantile baseline currently beats the ensemble on ARI 2025-26 (raw mean WIS mixes countries of very different scale, so this is context, not a ranking).
targets.success_criterion: For one complete season (2024-25 or 2025-26) and one target (ILI or ARI incidence), quantile forecasts in the hub's format for every (origin_date, location, horizon) row where model_id hubEnsemble (team_id respicast) has a WIS in latest-forecast_scores.csv (re-fetched live immediately before claiming), produced by a frozen pipeline that at each origin date uses only the target-data snapshot available on that date, whose mean WIS (computed with the hub's evaluation convention against the same truth data the hub used) is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the ensemble's on exactly the same rows by at least 3% relative, with a paired bootstrap over origin dates excluding zero.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic loads latest-forecast_scores.csv, filters to the ensemble's rows (model_id == "hubEnsemble"; horizons 1-4), re-scores the attacker's forecast files against the hub truth with the hub convention (first reproducing the ensemble's published WIS to validate the scorer), checks via file-access logs that each origin date read only its snapshot, and bootstraps. Laptop-minutes to hours.

angles: Age-structured mechanistic core with statistical calibration: a compact age-stratified SIRS/renewal model with waning immunity, fitted per jurisdiction by particle filtering, then conformalised residual quantiles; RSV's strong immunity-driven biennial-ish pattern rewards mechanism more than flu does.

CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing): seasonal harmonic regression with time-varying amplitude/phase estimated by a Kalman filter or complex demodulation; RSV onset timing runs by weeks between seasons and jurisdictions, so phase estimation (not level fitting) is the real forecasting problem.

CROSS-DOMAIN (ecology / metapopulation): treat jurisdictions as patches with coupled epidemic waves, estimate a spatial coupling kernel from past seasons (gravity model fitted to onset-time lags), and forecast a late-onset state from its already-peaking neighbours.

CROSS-DOMAIN (combinatorial search over model space): run a small genetic-programming / model-lottery search over forecast formulas and spread rules, with prequential (out-of-sample, earlier-seasons-only) selection to avoid hindsight bias; selection by prequential code length (MDL) keeps it honest.

Nowcast the backfill first: RSV surveillance reporting is late and incomplete; a reporting-delay model (negative-binomial delay distribution per jurisdiction, estimated from revision history in the hub's target-data history) that corrects the last 2-3 weeks before extrapolating is probably the single biggest WIS gain available.

Borrow strength from influenza and COVID hubs: fit shared hierarchical priors on growth-rate volatility across respiratory pathogens, then specialise per pathogen, exploiting the much richer flu record to regularise the thin RSV one.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: RSV forecast hub: beat the hub ensemble's season-average WIS retrospectively on a completed RSV season

partial_wins.statement: Strictly lower season-average WIS than every individual submitted model (not necessarily the ensemble) for a completed season, under the as-of data discipline and the public scorer, with a bootstrap interval excluding zero.

Route (a) only: beat the ensemble's WIS restricted to the pediatric (0-4 years) age groups of the HopkinsIDD archive hub, where RSV dynamics are sharpest and the submitted pool is thinnest, across all locations and reference dates of a completed season (the CDCgov hub has no age groups).

An independent recomputation of per-model season WIS for a completed RSV season from the hub's raw model-output and target data, released as a reproducible script, documenting any discrepancy with the hub's own published scores (if any) and the exclusion rules needed to reconcile them.

pitfalls: Revision leakage: RSV hospitalisation targets are revised substantially; fitting on final data and calling it a retrospective forecast is the standard false positive. Only as-of snapshots may be used, and the audit must show it.

Thin-pool illusion: with few submitted models and few seasons, one season's WIS is noisy. A 1-2% margin is meaningless; require a bootstrap interval over reference dates and, if possible, replication on a second completed season.

Target/scale mismatch: age-group and location sets changed across seasons in this hub, as did the target definition and the hub-config task-ids. Comparing a forecaster scored on one task set to an ensemble scored on another is invalid.

Hindsight model selection: choosing the mechanistic structure, waning rate or spread multiplier after inspecting the season is overfitting; parameters must be frozen from earlier seasons with commit evidence.

Ensemble recomputation error: if the hub's ensemble is weighted or trained, recomputing it naively (equal-weight median) can create a strawman that is easy to beat; the ensemble's own submitted output in model-output/ is the only legitimate comparator.

The CDCgov hub removed auxiliary-data/nssp-raw-data/latest.parquet on 2026-10-12, so a pipeline that relied on the hub's own Wednesday NSSP release must switch to data.cdc.gov releases - and must still only read the vintage available at each reference date.

Mixing the two hubs: the HopkinsIDD archive scores RSV-NET counts by age group, the CDCgov hub scores NHSN admissions and NSSP ED-visit proportions without age groups. A forecast scored on one hub's targets cannot be compared with the other hub's ensemble.
targets.statement: RSV forecasting is the thin, under-studied sibling of influenza and COVID forecasting: far fewer teams, far fewer published methods, and strong age-structured seasonality. Two public hubverse hubs cover it. (a) github.com/HopkinsIDD/rsv-forecast-hub is now an archive: from the 2025-26 season the hub was handed to CDC's Center for Forecasting and Outbreak Analytics; its model-output/hub-ensemble has 47 files ending 2025-04-06 (2023-24 files marked -RETRO), it scores RSV-NET-derived hospitalisation counts by state AND age group, and target-data/archive holds 153 dated *_rsvnet_hospitalization.csv vintages (2023-10-16 to 2026-05-29). (b) github.com/CDCgov/rsv-forecast-hub runs the live season with 18 model directories and RSVHub-ensemble (33 files, 2025-09-27 to 2026-10-17 as of 2026-10-15); its targets are wk inc rsv hosp (NHSN confirmed admissions) and wk inc rsv prop ed visits (NSSP) with NO age groups, and its hubverse target-data ships time-series.parquet with as_of plus oracle-output.parquet. Neither hub ships a scores file, so the ensemble's own model-output is the comparator and must be re-scored. Because the submitted model pool is small, the gap between the hub ensemble and a carefully calibrated single model is plausibly larger here than for flu, while the data is tiny and entirely CPU-friendly.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, on ONE of two separately declared routes, saved quantile forecasts in that hub's submission format produced by a released deterministic pipeline that at each reference date reads only data available on that date (as-of vintages; no final revised series, no other team's forecasts, no parameter tuned on later weeks of the same season), whose season-average WIS, computed with the public hubverse scoring code (same locations, horizons, reference dates and, where applicable, age groups; hub exclusion rules applied), is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the hub ensemble's season-average WIS recomputed identically from that hub's own ensemble model-output, re-fetched live immediately before claiming, by at least 3% relative AND outside a stationary-bootstrap 90% interval over reference dates. Route (a), archive: a completed season (2023-24 or 2024-25) of github.com/HopkinsIDD/rsv-forecast-hub, covering every reference date, location, age group and horizon of the hub-ensemble (https://github.com/HopkinsIDD/rsv-forecast-hub/tree/main/model-output/hub-ensemble), with as-of data taken from that hub's target-data/archive vintages. Route (b), live hub: the 2025-26 season of github.com/CDCgov/rsv-forecast-hub for wk inc rsv hosp or wk inc rsv prop ed visits, against RSVHub-ensemble (https://github.com/CDCgov/rsv-forecast-hub/tree/main/model-output/RSVHub-ensemble), with as-of data taken from that hub's time-series.parquet as_of column or from data.cdc.gov releases available at each reference date. Neither hub currently publishes its own scores file; if one appears for the claimed season, its ensemble value becomes the bar instead of the recomputed one.
targets.verification_method: Same mechanics as the FluSight target: pin the hub commit, validate the attacker's files against hub-config task-ids, recompute WIS with public hubverse code for the attacker, each submitted model and the ensemble, bootstrap over reference dates, and audit for look-ahead by rerunning the pipeline against truncated data snapshots and by code review (no reads of future weeks, of the final target series, or of model-output/). Data volume is tens of megabytes; the whole check is minutes on CPU.

angles: Conventional: block-structured regularisation done better - estimate per-block penalties by empirical Bayes rather than by the nested cross-validation the published priority-Lasso and IPF-Lasso use, which is extremely noisy at 100-300 patients.

Conventional: target the metric. Uno's C-index is a rank statistic; train with a smooth concordance surrogate or a partial-likelihood plus rank penalty instead of pure partial likelihood, and calibrate separately for the Brier score.

Cross-domain import (random matrix theory): the RNA and copy-number blocks are wide and noisy; Marchenko-Pastur eigenvalue shrinkage keeps only components outside the noise bulk before the Cox fit, which is the principled version of 'take the top principal components' and costs seconds.

Cross-domain import (econometrics / instrumental thinking about confounding): clinical stage and age carry most of the signal and are correlated with molecular blocks; estimate the molecular contribution orthogonalised against the clinical model (partialling-out / double machine learning) so that the question 'do omics add anything' is answered with a procedure designed for exactly that question.

Cross-domain import (reliability engineering / accelerated life testing): borrow parametric accelerated-failure-time families with covariate-dependent scale, which are standard in reliability and rarely tried in these benchmarks, and which can beat Cox models when hazards are non-proportional.

Cross-domain import (compression / MDL): select the number of features per block by two-part code length rather than cross-validated partial likelihood; with 100-700 patients, selection noise is the dominant error source.

Honest pooling: fit one model across cohorts with cohort-specific baseline hazards (stratified Cox or a hierarchical prior) to borrow strength for the small cohorts, which the per-cohort published protocol never does.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: TCGA multi-omics survival: beat the best published C-index or integrated Brier score for a cancer cohort in the Herrmann benchmark

partial_wins.statement: Beat the clinical-only Cox reference by >= 0.03 Uno C-index on a cohort where Table 5 reports that no molecular learner beat clinical-only (as of 2026-10-15: ESCA, KIRC, STAD, UCEC for the C-index), with the full fold protocol and the same-environment clinical-only re-run. This is the benchmark's central open question, not a leaderboard decimal.
Beat the published best C-index by >= 0.02 on three or more cohorts with ONE frozen method and one hyperparameter protocol, reported across all 18 cohorts so that cherry-picking is visible.

A reproducibility result of record: re-run three published learners (blockForest, priority-Lasso, CoxBoost favoring) on five cohorts with the published code and report the discrepancy against Table 5 with full logs. Independently checkable and useful whether or not any record falls; must be reported as reproduction, not as a win.

pitfalls: Fold-boundary leakage through preprocessing is the dominant trap: variance filtering, imputation, standardisation, PCA or block-weight estimation performed on the whole cohort uses test patients' molecular data and inflates the C-index by far more than the 0.02 bar.

Metric mismatch: Uno's C-index depends on the censoring-distribution weights and the chosen time range; Harrell's C-index, Antolini's time-dependent C-index and IPCW variants all give different numbers. Only the benchmark's definition and time range count.

Small cohorts and wide intervals: several cohorts have fewer than 40 events (COAD 17, BRCA 72), so cross-validation estimates swing wildly. The margin must exceed the published interval half-width, and a win on one cohort with one seed is noise.

Clinical-variable confusion: some published bests ARE the clinical-only Cox model; beating 'the molecular methods' while losing to clinical-only is not a win, and the write-up must state which reference was beaten.

Dataset version drift: the OpenML datasets are split into two or three parts per cohort and must be rejoined exactly as the benchmark code does; a different join or a different feature-block assignment makes the comparison meaningless.

Over-claiming: a better cross-validated C-index on a retrospective TCGA cohort is not a prognostic test for a patient, and these cohorts are old, heterogeneously treated and not representative of current care.
targets.statement: Moritz Herrmann, Philipp Probst, Roman Hornung, Vindi Jurinovic and Anne-Laure Boulesteix (Briefings in Bioinformatics 22(3), bbaa167, 2021) ran the largest honest comparison of survival-prediction methods on multi-omics cancer data: 18 TCGA cohorts, each with clinical variables plus copy number, miRNA, mutation and RNA features (about 100,000 features, 100-735 patients per cohort), 13 learners including Lasso, IPF-Lasso, priority-Lasso, GRridge, SGL, model-based and likelihood-based boosting, random forests, block forests, a clinical-only Cox model and Kaplan-Meier, all compared with repeated 5-fold cross-validation under Uno's C-index and the integrated Brier score. Their headline is sobering and still unbeaten in public: for most cohorts the molecular data add little or nothing over clinical variables alone. The per-cohort records are a literal published table (Table 5), machine-readable from the Europe PMC full-text XML: for example BLCA C-index 0.640 (CoxBoost favoring), BRCA 0.643 (CoxBoost favoring), COAD 0.656 (blockForest, versus clinical-only 0.541), HNSC 0.582 (blockForest), KIRC 0.761 (clinical only), KIRP 0.629 (GRridge), LAML 0.709 (ranger, versus clinical-only 0.596), LGG 0.749 (glmboost), LUAD 0.665 (prioritylasso), LUSC 0.537, OV 0.600, PAAD 0.686, SARC 0.685, SKCM 0.597, STAD 0.598, UCEC 0.686; integrated Brier scores are listed in the same row. The preprocessed data are on OpenML without registration (dataset ids in the repository's data/datset_ids.txt, e.g. BLCA 42279/42280, about 140 MB per part) and the full benchmark code is public, so a laptop can re-run a single cohort in hours.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for one named TCGA cohort of the 18, a saved per-fold risk-prediction file produced under the benchmark's own protocol (the published cross-validation design, the OpenML datasets named in data/datset_ids.txt with their sha256 logged, the same feature blocks), such that EITHER (a) Uno's C-index, computed with the benchmark's own evaluation code over the same folds, is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than that cohort's C-index value in Table 5 of https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC8138887/fullTextXML - re-fetched and re-parsed immediately before claiming - by at least 0.02 absolute AND by more than the half-width of the published confidence interval for that cell; OR (b) the integrated Brier score is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than that cohort's published ibrier by at least 0.01 absolute and by more than the published interval half-width. The attacker must additionally re-run, in the same environment and folds, the clinical-only Cox model and the published best learner for that cohort, and must beat BOTH the re-run values and the published values. Model selection, feature filtering, imputation and hyperparameter tuning must happen inside each training fold only; a single tuning decision made on full-cohort data voids the claim. Deliverables: the OpenML ids and sha256s, the fold assignment, the training code, per-fold predictions, and the verbatim metric output.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the cohort's OpenML parts (about 140-300 MB per cohort, no registration), checks sha256 against the attacker's manifest, verifies the fold assignment matches the benchmark protocol and that no patient appears in both sides of a fold, re-computes Uno's C-index and the integrated Brier score from the attacker's per-fold risk files with their own script using the same evaluation time range convention, and re-fetches the Europe PMC XML to read the live Table 5 values. Then the skeptic re-runs the attacker's training for at least two folds (laptop-hours) and the clinical-only reference. Leakage audit: confirm that feature screening, imputation, standardisation and any block-weight estimation were performed inside training folds only, and that no outcome-derived feature crossed a fold boundary.

angles: Conventional: gradient-boosted trees (LightGBM/XGBoost/CatBoost) on concatenated Morgan/ECFP fingerprints plus physicochemical descriptors for both drugs, plus cell-line expression PCs, with symmetric augmentation (swap drug A/B so the model learns the permutation invariance the MLP has to memorise).

Conventional: explicit mean-effects baseline (global + drug-pair + cell-line + tissue effects) fitted by ridge/ALS, then a learned residual model; this is the single most common reason tabular leaderboards fall, because generic MLPs waste capacity re-learning main effects.

Cross-domain import (coding theory / compressed sensing): treat the drug-pair x cell-line response matrix as a partially observed low-rank tensor and recover it with a syndrome-decoding-style alternating minimisation under an L1/nuclear-norm penalty; combination screens are massively incomplete, and matrix/tensor completion with side information (fingerprints as row/column codes) exploits exactly the redundancy an MLP ignores.

Cross-domain import (statistical physics / ecology): model CSS as a pairwise-interaction (Ising / Lotka-Volterra style) energy over drug-target perturbation vectors, fitting per-target fields and pair couplings with a mean-field or TAP approximation; this gives a physically parameterised interaction term with far fewer free parameters than 7M, which is exactly what small-sample tissue strata (Prostate: 2 cell lines) need.

Cross-domain import (signal processing): dose-response curves are smooth monotone signals; fit a shape-constrained (isotonic / monotone-spline) representation of the per-drug curves and feed the curve coefficients as features instead of scalar summaries, so the model sees the whole response spectrum rather than one summary statistic.

Ensembling and hyperparameter search under the five-seed protocol: because the protocol averages five runs, variance reduction alone (bagging, seed averaging, snapshot ensembling) buys measurable MAE; check how much of the gap is pure variance before building anything clever.
Target the loss: MAE is the metric, so train with L1/Huber or quantile (median) objectives rather than MSE, and calibrate predictions to the conditional median per tissue.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: TDC DrugComb_CSS: lower the leaderboard MAE for drug-combination sensitivity in cancer cell lines

partial_wins.statement: Beat BOTH the leaderboard MAE and the per-cell-line median baseline on at least 4 of the 9 tissue-stratified CSS columns, each by >= 0.30 MAE, under the five-seed protocol.

A benchmark-critique result of record: show with verbatim group.evaluate_many output that the current leaderboard entry is matched by a constant predictor (median of train_val) and beaten by a per-cell-line median, and quantify the symmetry leakage (as of 2026-10-15: 2,321 of 59,708 test triples occur in train_val with the drug order reversed). Reported as a critique, not a modelling win.
Beat the Hema column (leaderboard 28.764) by >= 1.0 MAE while beating the per-cell-line median baseline on every other tissue column.

pitfalls: The single leaderboard entry performs at the level of a constant predictor (measured MAE 16.864 for the train_val median versus 16.858 for the MLP on 2026-10-15), so any criterion anchored only to the leaderboard is cleared by a model that has learned nothing. Trivial baselines must be re-fitted and beaten in the same run.
Quantified symmetry leakage - 2,321/59,708 test triples appear in train_val with drugs swapped; augmenting by swapping, or deduplicating across the split boundary, trains on test rows.

Test labels are shipped locally with the TDC benchmark files, so leakage is trivially easy and invisible: any early stopping, threshold, feature-scaling statistic, drug/cell-line embedding or hyperparameter chosen with reference to the test rows makes the number meaningless. The checker must inspect the code path, not just the output.

Duplicate-row and near-duplicate leakage: DrugComb contains the same drug pair and cell line measured in multiple studies/doses, and the pair is symmetric (A,B) vs (B,A). If the attacker augments or deduplicates across the split boundary, train and test share rows and the MAE collapses for a fake reason. Verify that no (drug A, drug B, cell line) triple in the test set appears in training in either order.

Protocol substitution: reporting a single-run MAE, a custom split, a different seed list, a subset of the test set, or MAE computed by the attacker's own code instead of group.evaluate_many. Only the library's own evaluation on the full TDC test set counts.

Claiming a within-noise gain: the listed std is 0.005, so a 0.02 improvement is noise plus leaderboard staleness. Require the margins in the success criterion (>= 1.0 over the leaderboard, >= 0.30 over the per-cell-line median) and >= 3 sigma.

Wrong endpoint: DrugComb_CSS is a sensitivity score, not a synergy score; the HSA/Loewe/Bliss/ZIP leaderboards have much smaller MAEs (4-9) and are different benchmarks. Mixing endpoints or comparing against the wrong page is a classic crank error.
Treating the result as a therapeutic claim. This is a regression benchmark on public cell-line screens; nothing about it says anything about treating a patient and the write-up must not imply it.
targets.statement: Therapeutics Data Commons hosts the DrugCombo benchmark group, built on the DrugComb dataset of drug-pair screens in cancer cell lines. The main endpoint, TDC.DrugComb_CSS, is the drug-combination sensitivity score (derived from relative IC50 values and areas under dose-response curves) for a (drug A, drug B, cell line) triple. TDC fixes the split: 20% of the data held out by the 'drug combination' split, with a train_val set released and a frozen test set released with labels but with a prescribed evaluation protocol (five independent runs, mean +/- std of MAE via group.evaluate_many). As of 2026-10-13 the public leaderboard has exactly ONE entry: an MLP (7,141,297 parameters, contributed by Yusuf Roohani) at MAE 16.858 +/- 0.005, plus a tissue-stratified table (Kidney 14.570, Lung 15.653, Breast 13.432, Hema 28.764, Prostate 15.692, Ovary 15.263, Skin 15.663, Brain 15.694, Colon 17.729). A single shallow baseline occupying a leaderboard for a tabular regression task with ~300k rows and strong cell-line/drug main effects looks like a soft frontier: gradient-boosted trees on Morgan fingerprints plus cell-line omics, or a factorization/mean-effects decomposition, routinely beat generic MLPs on this data shape. Nothing in the task needs a GPU: the data are a few hundred MB and CPU-only training is laptop-hours. Direct measurement on the downloaded benchmark files (2026-10-15) shows how soft: a constant train_val-median predictor scores MAE 16.864, level with the MLP, and a per-cell-line median scores 15.649, beating it by 1.21 without learning anything about drugs. The open question is therefore whether any model beats the per-cell-line median by a convincing margin.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a saved prediction vector for the TDC drugcomb_css test set obtained exactly as the TDC protocol prescribes (five seeds via group.get_train_valid_split(benchmark='drugcomb_css', split_type='default', seed=s) for s in [1,2,3,4,5], evaluated with group.evaluate_many) whose mean MAE is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than ALL THREE of: (a) the best MAE on the live leaderboard https://tdcommons.ai/benchmark/drugcombo_group/drugcomb_css/, re-fetched immediately before claiming, by at least 1.0 MAE absolute; (b) a constant predictor set to the median of train_val Y (measured at 16.864 on 2026-10-15), by at least 1.0; and (c) a per-cell-line median predictor fitted on train_val only (measured at 15.649 on 2026-10-15), by at least 0.30 MAE absolute and at least 3x the claimed model's reported std. Both trivial baselines must be re-fitted and re-scored by the attacker in the same run and their values printed verbatim. The claim must ship: (a) the exact tdc package version and the sha256 of the downloaded benchmark files, (b) the five per-seed prediction vectors, (c) the training script, (d) the raw group.evaluate_many output printed verbatim. No test-set label may enter training, validation, early stopping, hyperparameter selection, feature construction or any normalisation statistic; a single use of the test labels for any purpose other than the final evaluate call voids the claim. If TDC's leaderboard gains new entries before the claim, the live best value is the bar.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic installs the pinned tdc version in a clean venv, downloads the benchmark (sha256 of data files compared against the attacker's manifest), loads benchmark = group.get('Drugcomb_CSS'), confirms the attacker's prediction vectors have exactly the test-set length and row order, re-runs group.evaluate_many on the five supplied prediction dicts (minutes), and re-fetches the leaderboard page to read the live best MAE. Then the skeptic re-trains the attacker's script end-to-end from the train_val split on a fresh seed set (laptop-hours) and confirms the MAE is in the same range. Leakage check: grep the training code and any cached artefacts for any read of the test split, and confirm feature-scaling statistics are computed on training rows only.

angles: Conventional: train for the metric. Synergy scores are heavy-tailed and near-zero-centred, so an L1/Huber or median-quantile objective with gradient-boosted trees on fingerprints plus cell-line features should dominate an MSE-trained MLP on MAE.

Conventional: multi-task learning across the four endpoints (they are deterministic functions of the same dose-response surfaces) with endpoint-specific heads, exploiting that Loewe/Bliss/ZIP/HSA share almost all of their signal; strictly respect per-endpoint test disjointness.

Cross-domain import (compression / minimum description length): choose model complexity by MDL on the residual stream rather than by validation MAE, encoding the drug-pair x cell-line response matrix as a low-complexity code plus residual; MDL selection is far more robust than validation tuning when the target is mostly noise, which is the regime of Bliss/ZIP (MAE ~4 on a near-zero-centred score).

Cross-domain import (combinatorial search / cryptanalysis-style meet-in-the-middle): search the space of feature-interaction subsets by hashing drug-target profiles into buckets and meeting in the middle on bucket pairs, rather than brute-force hyperparameter sweeps; this finds the few target-pair interactions that actually carry synergy signal within laptop budget.

Cross-domain import (signal processing): model each endpoint as a linear functional of the two-drug dose-response surface and fit the surface (monotone 2-D spline / Hill-equation mixture) rather than the scalar score, then compute HSA/Loewe/Bliss/ZIP analytically from the fitted surface; this imposes the physical consistency constraints among the four endpoints that a scalar regressor cannot see.

Robust loss and outlier handling: identify the heavy-tail rows (extreme Loewe values from poorly fitted curves), down-weight them with a robust (Tukey biweight) loss, and check whether the MAE gain comes mostly from the tail.

targets.name: TDC DrugComb HSA/Loewe/Bliss/ZIP: lower the leaderboard MAE on a cancer drug-synergy endpoint

partial_wins.statement: Clear the bar on three or four endpoints with one method family, reported together with the explicit note that the four endpoints share a single split and are therefore not four independent results.

Beat the per-cell-line median by >= 0.15 MAE on an endpoint using only features that depend on the drug pair (no cell-line-only features), demonstrating that the gain comes from drug-interaction signal rather than from cell-line main effects.
Run the five-seed protocol twice with disjoint seed sets and report both means and stds, showing the gain exceeds between-seed-set variation.

pitfalls: All five DrugComb benchmarks share one split - the test triples are identical across CSS, HSA, Loewe, Bliss and ZIP (verified 2026-10-15), so multi-task training across endpoints does not leak, but winning on several endpoints is close to one result reported several times and must be described that way.

A near-zero-centred target makes the median predictor extremely strong; the leaderboard entry IS effectively that predictor, so any criterion anchored to the leaderboard alone is vacuous. The per-cell-line median must be re-fitted and beaten in the same run.
Test labels are local, so any tuning, early stopping or scaling statistic touching test rows invalidates the result; the evaluation call must be the single use of test labels.

Near-zero-centred targets make a trivial constant/median predictor deceptively strong on MAE for Bliss and ZIP. A gain that disappears when compared against a per-cell-line median baseline is not a modelling result; the write-up must include that baseline.
Protocol substitution: single-seed numbers, custom splits, subset evaluation, or the attacker's own MAE implementation instead of group.evaluate_many.
Scale confusion between endpoints (Loewe MAE ~9 vs ZIP ~4) leading to comparison against the wrong leaderboard page; each endpoint has its own URL and its own bar.
Reading any of this as evidence about combination therapy in patients. It is a benchmark on public cell-line screens and must be reported that way.
targets.statement: Besides the sensitivity endpoint, the TDC DrugCombo benchmark group scores four classical synergy endpoints on the same DrugComb cancer cell-line screens, each with its own leaderboard page: TDC.DrugComb_HSA (highest single agent), TDC.DrugComb_Loewe (Loewe additivity), TDC.DrugComb_Bliss (Bliss independence) and TDC.DrugComb_ZIP (zero interaction potency). As of 2026-10-15 each of the four leaderboards has exactly ONE entry, the same 7,141,297-parameter MLP: HSA 4.453 +/- 0.002, Loewe 9.184 +/- 0.001, Bliss 4.560 +/- 0.000, ZIP 4.027 +/- 0.003. All five DrugComb benchmarks (CSS plus the four synergy endpoints) share one split: the train_val and test tables have identical (Drug1_ID, Drug2_ID, Cell_Line_ID) triples, only the label column differs. Direct measurement on the downloaded benchmark files shows that the leaderboard entry reproduces a constant (train_val median) predictor to three decimals on all four endpoints (4.452 / 9.182 / 4.560 / 4.027) and is beaten everywhere by a per-cell-line median (4.438 / 9.118 / 4.518 / 3.946), so the public state of this benchmark is that no published model demonstrably learns drug-pair interaction at all. The open question is whether anything beats the per-cell-line median by a convincing margin.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for at least ONE endpoint, a mean MAE from group.evaluate_many over the prescribed five seeds that is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than ALL of: the live leaderboard best for that endpoint (re-fetched immediately before claiming), the constant train_val-median baseline, and the per-cell-line median baseline re-fitted by the attacker in the same run, by at least 0.15 MAE absolute for HSA/Bliss/ZIP and 0.30 for Loewe, and by at least 3x the claimed model's reported std. All three baselines' verbatim evaluate_many outputs must ship with the claim. The model may be trained only on that endpoint's train_val split and its seed-specific train/valid partitions; the test labels may be touched exactly once, by group.evaluate_many, at the end. Deliverables: pinned tdc version, data sha256 manifest, five per-seed prediction vectors per endpoint claimed, training script, verbatim evaluate_many output.
targets.verification_method: Identical mechanics to the CSS target: clean venv with pinned tdc, re-download the benchmark and compare file sha256s, confirm prediction vector length and row order against benchmark['test'], re-run group.evaluate_many on the supplied five prediction dicts (minutes), re-fetch the endpoint's leaderboard page for the live best, then re-train from the attacker's script on fresh seeds (laptop-hours) to confirm the number is not a lucky seed. Leakage audit: assert that the set of (drug A, drug B, cell line) triples in each training split is disjoint from the test triples in BOTH drug orders, and that no scaler/encoder was fitted on test rows.

angles: Endpoint-appropriate transforms and mechanistic features: MDR1-MDCK efflux ratio and protein binding are driven by ionisation, lipophilicity and molecular size; model log-transformed endpoints with pKa-derived charge class, logD7.4, TPSA, aromatic-ring count and H-bond descriptors, and fit separate submodels per charge class (acids/bases/neutrals) - a classic DMPK decomposition that monolithic models blur.

Multi-task across the six Fang endpoints (train folds only): clearance, permeability, solubility and protein binding are strongly correlated through lipophilicity, so a multi-output booster or reduced-rank model borrows strength exactly where the per-endpoint folds are small.

CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing / Kalman-style shrinkage): treat each prediction as a noisy measurement with an estimated variance and fuse several models by inverse-variance weighting; optimal linear fusion beats equal-weight averaging on correlation metrics and is free.

CROSS-DOMAIN (compression-based similarity): NCD-kernel SVR over canonical SMILES as an uncorrelated ensemble member - especially useful on the 24-34-compound rppb/hppb folds where any high-variance learner is dangerous.

CROSS-DOMAIN (ecology / environmental niche models): treat physicochemical space as an environment and fit monotone GAM 'niche' responses with ecological-style smoothers plus interaction terms, which extrapolate more gracefully than trees on a different-chemotype test fold.

CROSS-DOMAIN (coding theory / ordinal thresholds): for Pearson-scored endpoints, build the prediction from an ensemble of threshold classifiers (ordinal ECOC) and map decoded ranks back to values by the train-fold quantile function, giving noise-robust, monotone predictions.

Rank-then-calibrate: since pearsonr is scored, fit the ranking first (pairwise loss) and then a monotone calibration from ranks to values on the train fold; separating ordering from scale is a reliable few-point Pearson gain.

targets.name: Polaris ADME-Fang (Biogen 3,521-compound DMPK set): beat the top listed score on an endpoint's public fold

partial_wins.statement: The full strict win on one of the larger folds (polaris/adme-fang-perm-1 or -solu-1, 400-483 test rows; or biogen/adme-fang-perm-reg-v1 / -solu-reg-v1), where the bootstrap has enough rows to be meaningful.

A structure-only result: beating the best listed entry that uses large-scale pretraining or phenomics side-information (the '1B_MPNN_*' / '3B_e50_MPNN_*' / '*-Phenomics' rows) on one endpoint with a model that uses only RDKit descriptors/fingerprints and classical learners, under the same margin and bootstrap rules, even if a community ensemble row remains ahead - reported as a scoped claim.

A multi-endpoint consistency result: one multi-task model trained on the official train folds of the six Fang endpoints that beats the live best on at least two populated endpoint leaderboards simultaneously, with its single-task ablation reported.

pitfalls: Public-CSV label leakage: the entire Biogen dataset (ADME_public_set_3521.csv) is on GitHub, so joining it to the Polaris test rows recovers the labels exactly. Any use of the public CSV for anything other than the official train indices must be treated as leakage, and claims must prove the test endpoint values were never read.

Tiny folds: rppb-1 has 24 and hppb-1 has 34 test compounds; Pearson on 24 points has a 95% CI roughly +-0.15, so 'records' there are nearly meaningless. The stricter margin and bootstrap thresholds for these folds exist to prevent exactly that false positive, and a win there should be reported as fragile.
Empty-leaderboard false win: biogen/adme-fang-rclint-reg-v1 and -hclint-reg-v1 currently list no results; a first entry is not a record.

v1-vs-reg-v1 confusion: polaris/adme-fang-*-1 (Dec 2023) and biogen/adme-fang-*-reg-v1 (Jul 2024) use different splits and sometimes different label columns despite near-identical names; comparing across them is invalid. Always cite the full owner/slug and the API-reported split and targetCols.

Metric column confusion: these leaderboards display MAE, MSE, r2, spearmanr, pearsonr and explained_var simultaneously, and the rows are NOT sorted by the mainMetric (on adme-fang-hppb-1 the row with the best MAE is listed second). Only the API's mainMetric is the record; improvements on other columns are scoped partials.

Pretraining contamination: the phenomics/MolGPS entries and any public ADMET-pretrained encoder may include Fang compounds; an attacker reusing such an encoder must declare it, and the skeptic should treat an undeclared pretrained featuriser as disqualifying.
targets.statement: Polaris hosts the Fang et al. 2023 Biogen DMPK dataset (3,521 compounds, six in vitro ADME endpoints, data public at github.com/molecularinformatics/Computational-ADME) as two generations of benchmarks: polaris/adme-fang-{solu,perm,rppb,hppb,rclint,hclint}-1 (Dec 2023, main metric pearsonr) and biogen/adme-fang-{...}-reg-v1 plus multi-task variants (Jul 2024). Several leaderboards are populated by large pretrained models - polaris/adme-fang-perm-1 best MAE 0.238 / Pearson 0.879 (1B_MPNN_MolGPS), polaris/adme-fang-solu-1 best MAE 0.312 / Pearson 0.770, polaris/adme-fang-rppb-1 Pearson 0.908 on only 24 test compounds, polaris/adme-fang-hppb-1 Pearson 0.888 on 34, biogen/adme-fang-perm-reg-v1 topped by a community 'vidraft-perm-structure-only-ensemble' at MAE 0.316 - while biogen/adme-fang-rclint-reg-v1 and biogen/adme-fang-hclint-reg-v1 are EMPTY. Split indices and table.parquet are served anonymously by the public API (verified 200 for the adme-fang-1 parquet and for the perm-1 benchmark's explicit test index array), so scoring is fully offline. The open question per endpoint: can a CPU-only descriptor model beat the listed best on the official fold?
targets.success_criterion: Pick one named ADME-Fang benchmark whose live leaderboard has at least one entry (empty leaderboards are excluded: a first submission is not a record). Success means a saved prediction file (one prediction per official test row in official order; manifest with the full slug, the sha256 of the downloaded table.parquet and the exact test index array from https://polarishub.io/api/v1/benchmark/<owner>/<slug>) such that (a) the test rows and label column match the API's split and targetCols exactly, (b) the skeptic's own computation of the benchmark's mainMetric is strictly better in that metric's direction than EVERY value listed in the live leaderboard table, re-fetched immediately before claiming, (c) for benchmarks with at least 300 test rows the margin is at least 0.010 absolute (correlation metrics) or 3% relative (error metrics) with a 10,000-resample bootstrap confirming superiority in at least 95% of resamples; for the tiny folds (rppb-1 with 24 and hppb-1 with 34 test compounds) the margin must be at least 0.030 absolute Pearson AND the bootstrap must confirm superiority in at least 97.5% of resamples, (d) fitting used only the official train indices of that benchmark, and (e) the attacker declares every pretrained component and every external dataset and demonstrates zero stereo-stripped-InChIKey overlap between them and the test fold - noting that the full Biogen ADME_public_set_3521.csv is public, so an external copy of the endpoint values for test compounds is the most obvious leak.
targets.verification_method: Plain curl of https://polarishub.io/api/v1/benchmark/<owner>/<slug> (public) for targetCols, mainMetric and split indices; curl of the dataset's table.parquet URL from /api/v1/dataset/...; sha256 check; slice official test rows; recompute the mainMetric with scipy/sklearn from the attacker's prediction file; bootstrap; verify the attacker's train indices are a subset of the official train indices and that declared external data (including ADME_public_set_3521.csv) contain no test-fold InChIKey for that endpoint; re-fetch the live leaderboard page and parse all listed values. 3,521 compounds total, so a full retrain is minutes of CPU.

angles: Classical kitchen-sink QSAR done properly: ECFP4/6 + FCFP + MACCS + RDKit 2D descriptors + Avalon, each with its own kernel, stacked by ridge/LightGBM with nested CV on the train split only; the MoleculeACE paper's own finding is that SVM on ECFP is near-SOTA, so the headroom is in careful ensembling and hyper-parameter search rather than architecture.

Matched-molecular-pair (MMP) residual modelling: enumerate MMPs inside the train split, fit a transformation-effect table (sum of substituent delta-pKi), and predict test molecules as nearest-train-analogue plus learned transformation delta; this directly attacks the activity-cliff failure mode the benchmark was built around.

CROSS-DOMAIN (compression-based similarity / information theory): replace fingerprint Tanimoto with a normalised compression distance between canonical SMILES (or between Morgan-fragment multisets) computed with zlib/bz2, and use it as a kernel in SVR / k-NN; NCD is a parameter-free similarity from Kolmogorov-complexity theory and makes different mistakes than fingerprints, so it adds ensemble diversity cheaply.

CROSS-DOMAIN (coding theory / error-correcting output codes): discretise pKi into ordered bins, train a bank of binary classifiers against a Hadamard/BCH codebook over bin subsets, then decode to a continuous prediction by minimum-distance decoding; ECOC regression is noise-tolerant on small, label-noisy assay data and directly handles the bimodal cliff structure.

CROSS-DOMAIN (statistical physics / replica averaging): train many weak learners at different 'temperatures' (bootstrap fraction, feature dropout, label-noise injection) and combine with a Boltzmann-weighted average whose weights come from out-of-fold likelihood; an explicit variance-bias thermostat tends to beat single tuned models on 100-700-molecule test sets.

CROSS-DOMAIN (linguistics / n-gram language modelling): character n-gram and SMILES-subword (BPE) count features with tf-idf weighting and a linear model; cheap, orthogonal to graph fingerprints, and historically competitive on small ChEMBL regression sets.

Conformal / quantile calibration: fit a conformalised quantile regressor and shrink predictions toward the train mean where the conformal interval is wide; MSE is quadratic, so shrinking uncertain predictions is a guaranteed-in-expectation MSE win on small test sets.

Multi-task borrowing across the 30 MoleculeACE targets (shared ChEMBL assay families: three opioid-receptor sets, two histamine, two JAK, two serine-protease), as a multi-task LightGBM/ridge with target one-hot, with strict InChIKey de-duplication against the test split.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: Polaris MoleculeACE (30 activity-cliff QSAR leaderboards): beat the single listed MSE on an official cliff split

partial_wins.statement: The same strict improvement (live-refetched, >=5% relative, bootstrap-confirmed) on any ONE of the 28 single-entry benchmarks.

A cliff-subset result: on one target, lower MSE than a faithfully reproduced MoleculeACE paper baseline (the repo's own best descriptor+model for that target, run by the attacker and reported with its code) restricted to the test molecules with cliff_mol==1, with at least 40 such molecules, while not being worse on the non-cliff subset.

A sweep result: a single fixed model/featurisation recipe (no per-target tuning on test) that beats the listed best MSE on at least 10 of the 30 benchmarks simultaneously, each verified against its own live leaderboard table.

pitfalls: Split leakage: the MoleculeACE split is cliff-stratified, NOT random; re-splitting randomly (or re-running the repo's splitter with a different seed) produces an easier test set and a meaningless number. The skeptic must take the test rows from the published CSV's split column and match the Polaris nTestDatapoints exactly.

Label leakage from ChEMBL: the labels are public ChEMBL activities, so any model that queries ChEMBL, uses a ChEMBL-pretrained regression head covering the same assay, or uses a public 'autosota' pipeline that ingests ChEMBL can recover test labels. Any pretrained component must be declared with its training-set provenance and checked against the test InChIKeys.

Stereo/salt duplicates: the same compound appears as different SMILES (salts, tautomers, stereo variants) across train and test; nearest-neighbour models then look brilliant. De-duplicate on stereo-stripped InChIKey, not on raw SMILES strings.

Unit confusion: the CSV carries both 'y' (log10 of nM, the training label) and 'y [pEC50/pKi]' (shifted by 9). Scoring against the wrong column leaves MSE unchanged under a pure shift but breaks any mixing of the two, and reporting a number computed in the wrong unit against the leaderboard is a false positive.

Test-set reuse / silent model selection: with 126-733 test molecules, the MSE standard error is roughly 0.05-0.15, so picking the best of many models by test MSE will 'beat' a 0.3-0.5 record by luck. All selection must be out-of-fold on train, the number of test evaluations must be reported, and the 5%-relative + bootstrap margin is mandatory.

Beating only the auto-generated baseline: 'autosota-*' is a machine-produced submission, not the literature state of the art. The NOVELTY skeptic must also compare to the MoleculeACE paper's own published per-target RMSE/MSE table and to any newer activity-cliff paper (e.g. 2023-2026 arXiv/JCIM work citing MoleculeACE) for that same target and split.
targets.statement: Polaris hosts 30 MoleculeACE benchmarks (molecularml/moleculeace-CHEMBL<id>-<Ki|EC50>), one per ChEMBL target from van Tilborg et al., 'Exposing the Limitations of Molecular Machine Learning with Activity Cliffs' (JCIM 2022). Each is a single-task regression of pKi/pEC50 from SMILES with a fixed activity-cliff-stratified train/test split (train 1,0xx-1,9xx, test 126-733 molecules) and main metric mean_squared_error (lower is better). As of 2026-10-13 nearly every one of the 30 leaderboards has exactly ONE entry, an auto-generated 'autosota-moleculeace-<slug>' submission (e.g. chembl2147-ki 0.311, chembl2835-ki 0.166, chembl264-ki 0.342, chembl4203-ki 0.732, chembl233-ki 0.576, chembl231-ki 0.530, chembl287-ki 0.503, chembl237-ec50 0.497); only chembl236-ki and chembl234-ki have 3 entries. The underlying data and the exact split are fully public: MoleculeACE ships one CSV per target (MoleculeACE/Data/benchmark_data/CHEMBL<id>_<Ki|EC50>.csv) with columns smiles, y, cliff_mol and split, and the Polaris train/test sizes match that split column exactly (verified for CHEMBL2147_Ki: 1162 train / 294 test = Polaris 1,162 / 294). So a laptop can train and score offline with no account. The open question per target: can a better descriptor/model combination lower the MSE below the listed best, especially on the cliff_mol subset where the MoleculeACE paper showed all methods degrade?
targets.success_criterion: Pick one named MoleculeACE benchmark (full Polaris slug). Success means a saved prediction file (one predicted y per test molecule, in the official test order, with the benchmark slug, the sha256 of the MoleculeACE CSV used, and the exact test-row indices) such that (a) the test set is EXACTLY the rows with split=='test' in the public MoleculeACE CSV for that target and the label column is the same 'y' column (log10-transformed nM) the Polaris benchmark uses, with the Polaris train/test counts from https://polarishub.io/api/v1/benchmark/molecularml/<slug> matching, (b) the skeptic's own sklearn.metrics.mean_squared_error on that file is strictly LOWER (direction: min) than EVERY mean_squared_error listed in the leaderboard table at https://polarishub.io/benchmarks/molecularml/<slug>, re-fetched live immediately before claiming, (c) the margin is at least 5% relative to the current best AND a paired bootstrap over test molecules (10,000 resamples, same resamples for both prediction sets where the attacker's and a reproduced baseline's predictions are available; otherwise 10,000 resamples of the attacker's squared errors) puts the attacker's MSE below the listed best in at least 95% of resamples, and (d) no test molecule, nor any molecule with the same InChIKey (ignoring stereo) as a test molecule, appeared in training, and no label for a test molecule was looked up from ChEMBL or any other source. The model must be fit on the official train split only; multi-target transfer is allowed only from OTHER MoleculeACE targets' train splits and must be declared, with the union checked for test-molecule leakage.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the MoleculeACE CSV for the target from raw.githubusercontent.com/molML/MoleculeACE/main/MoleculeACE/Data/benchmark_data/<file>.csv, checks sha256 against the manifest, selects split=='test', confirms the count matches nTestDatapoints from https://polarishub.io/api/v1/benchmark/molecularml/<slug>, loads the attacker's prediction vector, recomputes MSE with sklearn, runs the 10,000-resample bootstrap, canonicalises train and test SMILES with RDKit and asserts no InChIKey (stereo-stripped) overlap, then re-fetches the live Polaris leaderboard HTML and parses all listed mean_squared_error values. Optionally re-runs the attacker's training script end-to-end (minutes on CPU for ~1.5k molecules).

angles: Attack the metric directly: AAFE is a geometric-mean absolute error in log space, so train on log10 of the endpoint with an L1 loss, and fit the optimal additive log-space offset (the median log residual) on out-of-fold train predictions; a pure median-offset correction typically removes several percent of AAFE from any mis-scaled model, which is what the 1.013-vs-R2-0.123 pattern implies is available.

Variance-aware shrinkage in log space: predict a log-space mean and variance, then shrink toward the train-set log median proportionally to predicted variance; because AAFE penalises absolute log deviation, shrinking uncertain predictions is near-free improvement.

Metabolism-specific features: CYP3A4 turnover depends on lipophilicity and on the presence of accessible soft spots, so add SMARTS counts for N-dealkylation/O-dealkylation/benzylic-oxidation motifs, logD7.4, aromatic-carbon fraction and fraction-sp3, on top of ECFP; cheap and mechanistically aligned.

CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing / homomorphic filtering): work entirely in the log domain, where multiplicative assay error becomes additive, apply robust (Huber/Theil-Sen) fitting and median filtering across ensemble members, and convert back only at the end - the textbook treatment for fold-error metrics.

CROSS-DOMAIN (coding theory / ordinal ECOC): discretise log-clearance into ordered bins with a Hadamard codebook of binary tasks and decode by minimum distance, which stabilises predictions against the heavy assay noise of microsomal turnover data.

CROSS-DOMAIN (compression / NCD similarity) and CROSS-DOMAIN (linguistics / fragment n-grams) as uncorrelated ensemble members: parameter-free SMILES-compression kernels and BRICS-fragment n-gram models, combined by inverse-variance fusion.

CROSS-DOMAIN (ecology / abundance-weighted sampling): reweight training compounds by inverse scaffold abundance so that the model is not dominated by a few large analogue series, improving generalisation to the test fold's chemotypes.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: Polaris novartis/adme-novartis-cyp3a4-reg: beat the listed absolute-average-fold-error on 368 test compounds

partial_wins.statement: The full strict win on AAFE under the live-refetch, margin, bootstrap and no-ranking-loss rules.

A calibration-only result: take a reproduced baseline's predictions (the attacker's own re-implementation of a descriptor/boosting model, reported with code), apply a monotone recalibration fit ONLY on out-of-fold train predictions, and show that AAFE drops below the live listed best while Spearman is unchanged to within 0.005 - isolating calibration as the mechanism.

A ranking result: beat the best Spearman listed on the same live table (currently 0.410, MolEncoder) by at least 0.030 with the bootstrap rule satisfied, reported as a scoped metric-specific claim rather than as the benchmark record.

pitfalls: Metric definition drift: AAFE has several variants (geometric mean fold error, 10**mean|log10 ratio|, mean of max(p/t, t/p)). Computing a different variant than Polaris does can swing the number by a lot; the exact Polaris metric implementation must be read and used at verification time, and the attacker must report the formula used.

Zero/negative predictions: AAFE is undefined for non-positive predictions, so clipping choices change the score. The clipping rule must be declared and applied identically to all compared prediction sets.

Metric trade-off masquerading as a record: a log-space offset can lower AAFE while the model's ranking is unchanged or worse. The success criterion's no-Spearman-loss clause exists to prevent claiming a pure scaling trick, and any gain must be reported with all five secondary metrics.

Single fold, 368 rows, heavy-tailed clearance labels: a few extreme compounds dominate, so without the bootstrap a 1-2% AAFE 'improvement' is noise. The number of models the attacker evaluated on the test fold must be disclosed.

Leakage via public CYP3A4 data: Novartis released this set publicly and CYP3A4 turnover data for many of these compounds exist in ChEMBL and vendor collections; an undeclared pretrained ADMET model or an external CYP3A4 table can contain the test labels. Declare provenance and check InChIKeys against the test fold.
Empty-companion confusion: novartis/adme-novartis-cyp3a4-cls has no entries; results there are not records, and classification scores must never be compared against this regression table.
targets.statement: Polaris hosts a Novartis CYP3A4 in vitro metabolism benchmark (novartis/adme-novartis-cyp3a4-reg, created 2024-07-15, 368 test compounds) whose main metric is the pharmacokinetics-specific absolute average fold error (AAFE, lower is better). As of 2026-10-13 the leaderboard has only a handful of entries and they are strikingly weak in absolute terms: rank 1 'adme-novartis-cyp3a4-reg-GIRAFFE' AAFE 1.013 with MAE 0.190, MSE 0.062, R2 0.123, Spearman 0.344, Pearson 0.471; 'MolEncoder' AAFE 1.052 with a HIGHER Spearman (0.410) and Pearson (0.545) and R2 0.066; 'AceProp1' AAFE 1.053, Spearman 0.393. The companion classification benchmark novartis/adme-novartis-cyp3a4-cls lists NO results. R2 near 0.1 with Pearson near 0.5 means the listed models are badly mis-scaled rather than uninformative, i.e. the AAFE record is a calibration problem, not a representation-learning problem - exactly the kind of hill a laptop can take. The benchmark's split indices and the dataset parquet download anonymously from the Polaris public API, so scoring is offline and mechanical.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a saved prediction file (one prediction per official test row in official order; manifest with the slug, sha256 of the downloaded table.parquet and the exact test index array from https://polarishub.io/api/v1/benchmark/novartis/adme-novartis-cyp3a4-reg) such that (a) the test rows and the label column match the API's split and targetCols exactly, (b) the skeptic's own AAFE - computed with the same definition Polaris uses (10 ** mean(|log10(pred) - log10(true)|) on the endpoint's own scale, read from the Polaris metric implementation at verification time) - is strictly LOWER (direction: min) than EVERY absolute_average_fold_error listed in the live leaderboard table, re-fetched immediately before claiming, (c) the improvement is at least 1.5% relative AND a 10,000-resample bootstrap over the 368 test rows puts the attacker's AAFE below the listed best in at least 95% of resamples, (d) the attacker ALSO reports MAE, MSE, R2, Spearman and Pearson from the same prediction file and does not lose more than 0.02 Spearman against the best Spearman listed on that table (so the win is not a pure fold-error trick that destroys ranking), and (e) fitting used only the official train indices, with every pretrained component and external dataset declared and shown to contain no test-fold molecule by stereo-stripped InChIKey. The empty companion leaderboard novartis/adme-novartis-cyp3a4-cls is explicitly excluded: a first entry there is not a record.
targets.verification_method: Plain curl of the public benchmark API (targetCols, mainMetric, split indices) and of the related dataset's table.parquet via /api/v1/dataset/novartis/...; sha256 check; slice the official test rows; recompute AAFE with the Polaris metric definition plus the five secondary metrics; bootstrap over test rows; confirm the attacker's training indices are a subset of the official train indices and that declared external sources contain no test InChIKey; re-fetch the live leaderboard HTML and parse every listed AAFE and Spearman. 368 test rows and a few thousand training rows make a full retrain minutes of CPU.

angles: Kinase-family multi-task learning: PKIS2 profiles the same compounds across hundreds of kinases, so the legitimate signal is cross-kinase correlation among the benchmarks' own train splits; a multi-task booster or reduced-rank regression over kinase columns (restricted to training rows) exploits this where single-task pretrained encoders cannot.

Heavy-tailed percent-inhibition handling: labels are bounded percentages with a spike near 0; model logit/arcsine-transformed inhibition, or a two-stage hurdle model (active/inactive classifier times conditional magnitude regressor), then invert - directly attacks the MSE records (849 on KIT means the baseline is dominated by a few large errors).

CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing / matched filtering and whitening): whiten the fingerprint space by the training covariance and use Fisher-discriminant 'matched filters' per kinase as features; detection-theoretic whitening is well-suited to 100-compound problems where plain distances are noisy.

CROSS-DOMAIN (coding theory / ECOC over kinase panels): represent each compound's activity across the panel of training kinases as a codeword, train a decoder for the target kinase bit, and use minimum-distance decoding; panel selectivity patterns are exactly an error-correcting code over targets.

CROSS-DOMAIN (compression / NCD) and CROSS-DOMAIN (linguistics / fragment n-grams): parameter-free SMILES-compression kernels and BRICS-fragment n-gram naive Bayes as uncorrelated ensemble members for a 74-144-row test set, where diversity beats depth.

CROSS-DOMAIN (statistical physics / replica averaging with a tuned noise temperature): bagging with deliberate label-noise injection and Boltzmann weighting by out-of-fold error, to manage the bias-variance trade-off on tiny data far better than a single tuned model.

Conformal shrinkage toward the train mean for compounds whose nearest-neighbour distance exceeds a calibrated threshold - a guaranteed-in-expectation MSE/MAE win when the test fold contains novel chemotypes.

targets.name: Polaris PKIS2/PKIS1 kinase benchmarks (EGFR, KIT, RET, LOK-SLK): beat shallow leaderboards on 74-144 test compounds

partial_wins.statement: The full strict win on polaris/pkis2-kit-wt-reg-v2, the single-entry regression leaderboard (live best MSE 849.611 / MAE 21.480), with the bootstrap rule satisfied.

A multi-task result: one model trained jointly on the train indices of the EGFR, KIT and RET regression benchmarks that beats the live best on at least two of the three under the same margin rules, with the single-task version of the same model reported for ablation.

A classification-ranking result: on polaris/pkis2-kit-wt-cls-v2 or pkis2-ret-wt-cls-v2, beat the live best PR-AUC by at least 0.020 with a model that also does not lose more than 0.010 ROC-AUC against the best listed ROC-AUC, i.e. a genuine ranking improvement rather than a metric trade.

pitfalls: Empty-leaderboard false win: several PKIS variants (and sibling Polaris benchmarks such as polaris/pkis1-egfr-wt-mut-cls-v2, which shows no leaderboard section) have no entries at all; submitting the first number there is NOT beating a record and must never be claimed as one.

Public-source label leakage: PKIS1/PKIS2 percent-inhibition data are published and also present in ChEMBL, so any external kinase-profiling table or kinase-pretrained model can contain the test compounds' labels for the same kinase. Declared provenance plus InChIKey checks against the test fold are mandatory.

Tiny single fold: with 74-144 test compounds, MAE/MSE standard errors are large (MSE on a heavy-tailed label is dominated by two or three compounds), so a 5%-relative margin plus a bootstrap is the minimum, and the count of models evaluated on the test fold must be disclosed.

v1-vs-v2 confusion: the '*-r-1'/'*-c-1' (2023-12) and '*-reg-v2'/'*-cls-v2' (2024-07) benchmarks share a name but differ in split and sometimes label definition; quoting a v1 record against a v2 result (or vice versa) is an invalid comparison. Always cite the exact slug and its API-reported split.

Metric trade: pkis2 classification tables list accuracy, f1, roc_auc, pr_auc, mcc and cohen_kappa; the benchmark's mainMetric is the only record, and an apparent win on one column with losses elsewhere must be reported as a scoped partial, not a record.

Activity-cliff/duplicate structure overlap between train and test folds (PKIS contains close analogue series); report a 1-NN-on-ECFP baseline as a floor so that a 'win' is not just better memorisation.
targets.statement: Polaris hosts 14 kinase-inhibition benchmarks built from the published PKIS1/PKIS2 chemogenomic sets: regression (percent-inhibition) and classification variants for EGFR wild-type, KIT wild-type, RET wild-type and the LOK/SLK pair, in both a v1 ('*-r-1' / '*-c-1') and a v2 ('*-reg-v2' / '*-cls-v2') formulation, with test sizes of 74-144 compounds. The leaderboards are extremely shallow: polaris/pkis2-kit-wt-reg-v2 has a SINGLE entry (CheMeleon, MAE 21.480, MSE 849.611, R2 0.296, Spearman 0.536), polaris/pkis2-kit-wt-cls-v2 has two (CheMeleon PR-AUC 0.646, MHNfs 0.376), polaris/pkis2-egfr-wt-reg-v2 has a handful (best MAE 16.009 by an 'aether-pharmaos' ensemble), polaris/pkis2-ret-wt-reg-v2 best MAE 18.252-18.309 from 1B/3B MolGPS models, polaris/pkis2-ret-wt-cls-v2 best PR-AUC 0.885, and polaris/pkis1-egfr-wt-mut-cls-v2 shows no leaderboard section at all. Data and explicit split indices download anonymously from the Polaris public API, so everything is scorable offline on a laptop. With 74-144 test compounds and percent-inhibition labels, careful classical QSAR plus variance reduction is directly competitive with the pretrained models that currently hold these rows.
targets.success_criterion: Pick one named Polaris PKIS benchmark whose live leaderboard has at least one entry. Success means a saved prediction file (one prediction per official test row in official order; probabilities for classification; manifest with slug, sha256 of the downloaded table.parquet and the exact test index array from the public API) such that (a) the test rows are exactly the indices in the 'split' field of https://polarishub.io/api/v1/benchmark/polaris/<slug> and the label column is that benchmark's targetCols entry, (b) the skeptic's own computation of the benchmark's mainMetric is strictly better in that metric's direction than EVERY value listed in the live leaderboard table, re-fetched immediately before claiming, (c) the margin is at least 5% relative for MSE/MAE or 0.020 absolute for PR-AUC/ROC-AUC/balanced-accuracy, AND a 10,000-resample bootstrap over the 74-144 test rows puts the attacker ahead in at least 95% of resamples, (d) fitting used only the official train indices, with any multi-task borrowing restricted to OTHER kinases' train indices (declared, and checked to contain no test row of the target benchmark), and (e) no external PKIS or ChEMBL kinase-profiling record for a test compound-kinase pair was used; the PKIS data are public, so this must be verified by InChIKey, not assumed. A first entry on an EMPTY leaderboard is NOT a record and does not count.
targets.verification_method: Plain-curl the public API for the benchmark (targetCols, mainMetric, split indices) and for the related dataset (table.parquet URL on data.polarishub.io), hash-check the parquet, slice the official test rows, recompute the mainMetric with sklearn/scipy from the attacker's prediction file, run the bootstrap, verify the attacker's training indices are a subset of the official train indices and that declared auxiliary data contain no test InChIKey, then re-fetch the live leaderboard page and parse every listed value for that metric. Test sets of 74-144 rows and train sets of a few hundred make full re-training a matter of minutes on CPU.

angles: Single-fold means variance reduction wins: average many models and many featurisations (ECFP/FCFP/Avalon/MACCS/RDKit-2D), each tuned by grouped CV on the train indices only, then combine by out-of-fold-weighted stacking. The listed leaders are single large pretrained models with no ensembling across feature families.

Tabular-foundation-model-style priors on CPU: the leaderboards already contain TabPFNv2 rows, and their numbers are beatable on several benchmarks; running TabPFN-class models over multiple descriptor subsets and aggregating (bagging over feature subspaces) is CPU-feasible at these data sizes and is the most direct route.

CROSS-DOMAIN (compression-based similarity): normalised compression distance over canonical SMILES as an SVR/k-NN kernel, used as an ensemble member that errs differently from fingerprint models - parameter-free, no training, seconds of CPU.

CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing / matched filters): build 'matched filter' templates per activity class from the train set in fingerprint space (class-mean fingerprint, whitened by the within-class covariance - i.e. a Fisher/LDA direction in bit space) and use the filter response as a feature; a classical detection-theory view of substructure alerts.

CROSS-DOMAIN (ecology / rarefaction and abundance weighting): weight training molecules by the inverse 'abundance' of their scaffold in the train set (rarefaction-style) so rare scaffolds are not drowned out, since the test fold is a different scaffold community.
CROSS-DOMAIN (coding theory / ordinal ECOC) for the Spearman and PR-AUC benchmarks: threshold-ensemble decoding to produce a robust ranking rather than a point estimate.

Metric-specific post-processing: for MAE benchmarks, median-calibrate; for PR-AUC, rank-optimise the positive class with a pairwise loss; for Spearman, aggregate ensemble members in rank space (Borda) instead of value space.

targets.name: Polaris tdcommons/* ADMET mirrors: beat the top listed score on a single-fold public split (offline-scorable)

partial_wins.statement: The full strict win on one of the tiny-test benchmarks (tdcommons/dili 96, tdcommons/herg 132, tdcommons/cyp2c9-substrate-carbonmangels 135, tdcommons/half-life-obach 135) with the bootstrap rule satisfied.

A no-pretraining result: a model using only RDKit-computable features and classical learners (no pretrained neural encoder, no external labelled data) whose score beats every listed entry that is a large pretrained model (the '1B_MPNN_*', '3B_e50_MPNN_*', 'MolEncoder', 'CheMeleon', 'TabPFNv2-*' rows) on one benchmark, under the same margin and bootstrap rules, even if some other row remains ahead - reported explicitly as a scoped claim.

A cross-benchmark sweep: one fixed recipe (no per-benchmark tuning on test) that beats the live leaderboard best on at least three tdcommons/* Polaris benchmarks at once, each verified against its own live table.

pitfalls: Pretraining contamination is the central trap: these are the standard public TDC/ADMET sets, so '1B_MPNN', 'MolEncoder', 'CheMeleon' and any ADMET-pretrained encoder may have trained on the very molecules in this single test fold, and so may an attacker's chosen pretrained featuriser. Provenance must be declared and InChIKey overlap with the test fold checked; an undeclared pretrained featuriser is grounds to reject the claim outright.

Wrong split: the Polaris fold is NOT the TDC scaffold split (different sizes and indices) and is a single fold, not 5 seeds. Mixing the two protocols - e.g. quoting a TDC 5-seed mean against a Polaris table - is an invalid comparison in both directions.

Single-fold luck: 96-1,478 test rows with one fold means no seed averaging is available; the bootstrap and the absolute/relative margin rules are the only defence, and the number of distinct models the attacker evaluated on the test fold must be reported (any selection on the test fold invalidates the claim).

Metric mismatch: each benchmark has one mainMetric from the API (mean_absolute_error, roc_auc, pr_auc, spearmanr). The leaderboard page may show several columns; beating a non-main metric is not a record, and pr_auc must be computed as average precision exactly as Polaris does.

Label-column confusion in the parquet: several of these datasets carry multiple columns (raw and transformed endpoint values); scoring against a column other than targetCols silently changes the scale.

Novelty trap: the Polaris tables move (new rows appeared through 2025-2026, e.g. 'vidraft-*', 'agentomics-ml-*', 'nextflow-frontier-*' entries), so the table MUST be re-fetched minutes before any claim, and the NOVELTY skeptic must also check for papers reporting the same Polaris fold.
targets.statement: Polaris mirrors 16 TDC ADMET datasets as its own single-task benchmarks (tdcommons/caco2-wang, herg, dili, half-life-obach, vdss-lombardo, clearance-hepatocyte-az, clearance-microsome-az, ld50-zhu, cyp2c9-substrate-carbonmangels, cyp2d6-substrate-carbonmangels, cyp3a4-substrate-carbonmangels, bbb-martins, ames, ppbr-az, lipophilicity-astrazeneca, bioavailability-ma, pgp-broccatelli, solubility-aqsoldb, hia-hou). Unlike TDC these are ONE fixed fold with explicit train/test index lists served by the public API (e.g. caco2-wang 728/182, herg 132 test, dili 96 test, half-life-obach 135 test, cyp2c9-substrate 135 test), and both the table.parquet and the split indices download anonymously over plain HTTPS (verified: https://data.polarishub.io/dataset/polaris/adme-fang-1/table.parquet returned 200 and /api/v1/benchmark/<slug> returns the explicit test index array), so a laptop can score locally with no account and no submission. Leaderboards are active but shallow and dominated by big pretrained models: tdcommons/herg best ROC-AUC 0.915, tdcommons/dili 0.950, tdcommons/caco2-wang MAE 0.270, tdcommons/half-life-obach Spearman 0.625, tdcommons/vdss-lombardo Spearman 0.726, tdcommons/clearance-hepatocyte-az Spearman 0.538, tdcommons/ld50-zhu MAE 0.526, tdcommons/cyp2c9-substrate-carbonmangels PR-AUC 0.478. Single-fold scoring on 96-1,478 test molecules means a careful classical model has a real shot, and the frontier is per-benchmark.
targets.success_criterion: Pick one named Polaris tdcommons benchmark. Success means a saved prediction file (one prediction per official test row in the official order, probabilities in [0,1] for classification, manifest with the benchmark slug, the sha256 of the downloaded table.parquet, and the exact test index array) such that (a) the test rows are exactly the indices in the 'split' field of https://polarishub.io/api/v1/benchmark/tdcommons/<slug> and the label column is that benchmark's targetCols entry, (b) the skeptic's own computation of the benchmark's mainMetric (sklearn: mean_absolute_error, roc_auc_score, average_precision for pr_auc, scipy.stats.spearmanr) is strictly better in the metric's own direction than EVERY value listed in the live leaderboard table at https://polarishub.io/benchmarks/tdcommons/<slug>, re-fetched immediately before claiming, (c) the margin is at least 3% relative for error metrics, or at least 0.010 absolute for ROC-AUC / PR-AUC / Spearman, AND a 10,000-resample bootstrap over test rows puts the attacker's value ahead of the listed best in at least 95% of resamples, (d) the model was fit only on the official train indices (internal validation carved from them), and (e) the attacker declares every pretrained component with its training-data provenance and shows that no test molecule (stereo-stripped InChIKey) appears in any declared training source - which, since these are standard public ADMET sets, must be checked rather than assumed. Reporting a different metric from the benchmark's mainMetric, or a different split, does not count.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic calls https://polarishub.io/api/v1/benchmark/tdcommons/<slug> with plain curl (public, no auth), reads targetCols, mainMetric and the split index arrays, downloads the related dataset's table.parquet from the data.polarishub.io URL given by /api/v1/dataset/tdcommons/<slug>, checks its sha256 against the manifest, slices the official test rows, loads the attacker's prediction vector, recomputes the mainMetric with sklearn/scipy, runs the bootstrap, checks train/test InChIKey disjointness and that the attacker's training indices are a subset of the official train indices, then re-fetches the live leaderboard HTML and parses every listed value. Everything fits in minutes on CPU.

angles: Do classical docking properly: exhaustive sampling budgets, multiple independent runs per complex with different seeds, careful protonation/tautomer enumeration of the ligand, receptor protonation and metal/cofactor handling, and consensus pose selection across runs - the PoseBusters paper's own message is that disciplined Vina beats learned methods, and most of the remaining failures are preparation failures.

Consensus re-scoring: generate many poses with one engine and re-rank with an ensemble of independent scoring functions plus a posebusters-style validity prefilter, selecting the top pose that is both well-scored and physically valid; selecting for validity before RMSD is exactly what the PB-valid metric rewards.

CROSS-DOMAIN (signal processing / matched filtering on grids): precompute receptor interaction-field grids and match ligand pharmacophore 'templates' by cross-correlation (FFT-based docking, as used in protein-protein docking) to seed local optimisation, giving broader coverage of the pocket per CPU second than stochastic search alone.

CROSS-DOMAIN (combinatorial search / cryptanalytic restart strategies): treat torsion angles and rigid-body placement as a discrete-continuous key and run tabu-guided simulated annealing with many short restarts and an elite archive instead of one long stochastic run - a better use of a fixed CPU budget.

CROSS-DOMAIN (statistical physics / replica exchange): parallel-tempered pose sampling across temperatures to cross torsional barriers that single-temperature Monte Carlo misses, then quench the best replicas.

CROSS-DOMAIN (coding theory / covering codes): place starting conformers so that they form a covering code over the pocket's rigid-body and torsional space, guaranteeing a bounded distance from any true pose rather than relying on random initialisation.

Template transfer from non-test structures: for each test receptor, find homologous holo structures NOT in the benchmark and transfer their cognate ligand's binding-mode restraints (shape overlap), which is legitimate as long as no test complex's own crystal pose is used - and must be declared explicitly.
