targets.name: TDC Docking Benchmark Group (DRD3, 5,000-call docking oracle): beat the Graph-GA top-100/top-10/top-1 records

partial_wins.statement: Beat the live rank-1 Top100 value with the %Pass column no worse than the 'Best-in-data' reference row (Graph-GA's own %Pass is 0.393 +- 0.308, far below the data reference 0.780), i.e. a quality-constrained improvement rather than a raw-score one.
A budget-efficiency result: match or beat the live rank-1 Top10 value using at most half the claimed oracle budget, with the full call log proving the budget, verified by re-scoring the final top-10.

An oracle-reproducibility artefact: a documented, pinned docking-oracle configuration (receptor sha256, box, software version, seed) plus a re-scoring script under which a published method's released DRD3 molecules reproduce their reported scores to within 0.3 kcal/mol - a reusable verification harness, reported as infrastructure rather than a record.

pitfalls: Oracle mismatch: docking scores depend on the receptor file, box definition, exhaustiveness, software and seed. A 'record' computed with a different docking configuration than TDC's pyscreener DRD3 oracle is meaningless; the configuration must be pinned, hashed and reproducible by the skeptic, and scores must be reproduced within 0.3 kcal/mol.

Scoring-function exploitation (the classic docking false positive): GAs reliably discover huge, greasy, poly-aromatic or strained molecules that score extremely well and are physically nonsense. This is why the claim is void if %Pass drops below the 'Best-in-data' reference and why Diversity and M1 must be reported - Graph-GA's own %Pass of 0.393 shows the record itself is partly this artefact.

Oracle-budget cheating: calling the oracle during 'development' and then reporting only the final run's calls, caching scores across runs, or using a surrogate trained on out-of-budget oracle calls. The full ordered call log for each of the 3 runs, with repeated SMILES counted as TDC counts them, is the only acceptable evidence.
Single-run luck: Graph-GA's listed stds are large (0.3-0.4 kcal/mol on the score columns, 0.3 on %Pass), so one lucky run can beat the mean. Three seeded runs and the std-based margin are mandatory.

Column shopping: the table has Top100, Top10, Top1, Top1-P, Diversity, Novelty, %Pass and M1. Beating Top1 alone (a single lucky molecule) while Top100 is worse is not beating the benchmark; the claimed column must be stated and the others reported.

Novelty trap: this leaderboard is 2021-era while the molecular-optimisation literature (PMO/mol_opt and later work) has moved on; the NOVELTY skeptic must check whether better DRD3 docking-oracle results under the same budget are already published before anything is claimed.
targets.statement: The TDC Docking Benchmark Group defines a budgeted de novo design task: generate molecules with the best DRD3 docking scores using at most a fixed number of oracle calls (the leaderboard reports 5,000-call and smaller budgets), starting from ZINC 250K, with the oracle being a docking score computed through TDC's pyscreener wrapper. The leaderboard lists only five 2021-era generators plus a 'Best-in-data' reference row (Top100 -12.080, Top10 -12.590, Top1 -12.800, Diversity 0.864, %Pass 0.780, Top1-P -11.700, M1 5.100). Rank 1 is Graph-GA (a fragment-based genetic algorithm with ZERO learned parameters): Top100 -14.811 +- 0.413, Top10 -15.930 +- 0.336, Top1 -16.533 +- 0.309, Diversity 0.626 +- 0.092, %Pass 0.393 +- 0.308, Top1-P -14.267 +- 0.450; then SMILES-LSTM (-13.017 Top100), GCPN, MARS and MolDQN. That a parameter-free GA leads by 1.8 kcal/mol over a 3M-parameter LSTM, and that nothing has been added in years, is exactly the profile of a stale, beatable table; the oracle is CPU docking, so 5,000 calls is laptop-hours to laptop-days on 10 cores.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a saved generation record for the DRD3 benchmark at a declared oracle budget that the leaderboard reports (5,000 calls unless a smaller listed budget is explicitly claimed), consisting of: the full ordered log of every oracle call (SMILES plus returned score, length <= the budget), the final top-100 SMILES dictionary in the format the TDC docking group expects, the exact oracle configuration (pyscreener/docking software name and version, receptor file and its sha256, box centre and size, exhaustiveness, number of poses, random seed), and 3 independent runs with different seeds. It counts only if (a) the skeptic, re-running the SAME documented oracle configuration on the submitted top-100 SMILES, reproduces each molecule's score to within 0.3 kcal/mol, (b) the mean over the 3 runs of Top100 (and separately Top10, Top1) is strictly BETTER, i.e. more negative (direction: min), than the corresponding rank-1 value in the live leaderboard table at https://tdcommons.ai/benchmark/docking_group/drd3/ , re-fetched immediately before claiming, by at least the listed rank-1 std for that column, (c) the number of distinct oracle calls never exceeded the claimed budget (checked from the log, counting repeated SMILES as the benchmark does), (d) the submitted molecules satisfy the benchmark's own auxiliary filters as reported by the leaderboard columns - Diversity, %Pass (the medicinal-chemistry filter rate) and M1 are recomputed and reported, and the claim is void if %Pass falls below the 'Best-in-data' reference row's value, and (e) every submitted molecule is novel with respect to ZINC 250K (no InChIKey match) and chemically valid by RDKit with correct valences. No synthesis route, procurement information or experimental protocol is part of this target; the deliverable is a scored SMILES list only.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic installs the docking stack the attacker pinned (pyscreener plus the named docking binary), downloads the receptor from the attacker's manifest and checks its sha256, re-docks the submitted top-100 SMILES with the identical configuration on 10 CPU cores, compares each score to the attacker's log (tolerance 0.3 kcal/mol), recomputes Top100/Top10/Top1, Diversity, %Pass and M1 with TDC's own definitions, counts the oracle calls in the log against the budget, checks RDKit validity and ZINC-250K InChIKey novelty, then re-fetches the live leaderboard table and compares column by column. Re-docking 100 ligands is well under an hour on CPU; re-running the attacker's whole search is optional and is the laptop-days part.

angles: Replace the protein encoder with cheap sequence statistics: amino-acid composition, dipeptide/tripeptide k-mer counts with tf-idf, CTD (composition-transition-distribution) descriptors, pseudo-amino-acid composition, and binding-site-agnostic physicochemical profiles; concatenate with Morgan/FCFP fingerprints and train LightGBM with target-group-aware CV. This is the single most likely CPU win against a PLM ensemble.

Temporal domain adaptation done simply: sample-weight training pairs by patent recency (exponential recency weighting), or fit on the most recent years only, and calibrate the prediction distribution to the expected 2019-2021 affinity distribution; the leaderboard's own DomainBed baselines show elaborate invariance penalties (IRM 0.284) hurt, while trivial reweighting is untested.

CROSS-DOMAIN (linguistics / n-gram language models and alignment): score drug-target compatibility by an alignment-based kernel between the target sequence and the nearest-neighbour targets in the training set (Smith-Waterman similarity), then predict by similarity-weighted transfer of the ligand's affinities on those neighbours - a translation-by-analogy estimator that handles unseen targets.

CROSS-DOMAIN (compression / information distance): use normalised compression distance between protein sequences (and between SMILES) as a kernel for support-vector regression; NCD approximates an information-theoretic metric and needs no alignment, training or embedding model, and adds ensemble diversity for free.

CROSS-DOMAIN (coding theory / ECOC and rank aggregation): discretise pAffinity into ordered bins with a Hadamard codebook of binary tasks, decode by minimum distance, and aggregate several decoders by Borda count; robust to the heavy label noise and unit heterogeneity of patent-derived affinities.

CROSS-DOMAIN (statistical physics / free-energy additivity): model affinity as a sum of fragment-level contributions (ligand BRICS fragments x target residue-class indicators) with a sparse bilinear interaction term; group-lasso-regularised bilinear models are cheap and extrapolate better across time than black-box encoders.

Ensemble across structurally different models (booster on fingerprints, bilinear fragment model, k-NN by sequence similarity) with weights fit on a strictly temporal inner validation split (e.g. train on 2013-2016, validate on 2017-2018) to mimic the real shift instead of random validation.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: TDC DTI Domain-Generalization (BindingDB patent-year split): beat the listed Pearson correlation

partial_wins.statement: A CPU-only pipeline (no protein language model, no GPU; e.g. Morgan fingerprints + protein k-mer/CTD descriptors + gradient boosting) whose 5-seed mean PCC beats the second-placed listed entry (live value, currently OrangeBalls-ProtBertMorgan 0.538) under the same margin and leakage rules - a 'cheap features beat heavy features' result.

A domain-shift decomposition: per-test-year PCC (2019, 2020, 2021 separately, computed from the official test rows' patent years) for a model that beats the live best overall, plus the same breakdown for a reproduced ERM baseline, showing which year carries the gain - independently checkable and non-trivial since the leaderboard reports only the pooled value.

An unseen-target result: PCC restricted to test pairs whose protein sequence never appears in train_val (count reported, at least 100 pairs) that beats the pooled live best value, demonstrating generalization to genuinely novel targets rather than to new ligands of known targets.

pitfalls: Affinity-label leakage: BindingDB, ChEMBL and Papyrus all contain the same patent-derived measurements, so any external affinity table or affinity-pretrained model can contain the test pairs' labels verbatim. The leading leaderboard entries are knowledge-graph/PLM pipelines, so a 'win' built on an undeclared affinity-trained embedding is the most likely false positive here.

Temporal split violation: using the test years' data (even unlabelled statistics such as the test ligand set's property distribution) for model selection breaks the domain-generalization premise. Validation must be carved from train_val, and the benchmark's 'training-domain validation' convention must be stated.

Pair-level duplication: the same ligand-target pair recurs across patents with slightly different affinity values and units (Ki/Kd/IC50 mixed into one label); a model that memorises the ligand or the target identity scores well without generalising. Report PCC on unseen-ligand and unseen-target subsets alongside the pooled value.

Metric choice: PCC on a heavy-tailed affinity distribution is dominated by a few extreme pairs; clipping, winsorising or dropping outlier test rows (or scoring on log vs linear scale inconsistently) can manufacture a gain. Score only through group.evaluate on all official test rows.

Seed/variance illusion: the listed stds are tiny (0.002-0.021) but they measure training-seed variability, not test-set uncertainty; the bootstrap over test pairs is the binding constraint and must be reported.

Novelty trap: the leaderboard is stale, and 2023-2026 DTI papers (Otter-Knowledge follow-ups, ESM-based affinity models, Papyrus-trained models) may already report higher PCC on this exact split; the NOVELTY skeptic must search for 'BindingDB_Patent' / 'DTI-DG' numbers from the last 24 months.
targets.statement: The TDC DTI_DG benchmark group has a single benchmark, BindingDB_Patent: drug-target affinity pairs from BindingDB that carry patent years, trained on 2013-2018 patents and tested on 2019-2021 patents, scored by Pearson correlation (PCC) - a temporal domain-generalization task, not a random split. The leaderboard has 9 entries, all from 2022-2023 era work: Otter-Knowledge-Ensemble 0.588 +- 0.002, OrangeBalls-ProtBertMorgan 0.538 +- 0.008, then the DomainBed-style baselines MMD 0.433, CORAL 0.432, ERM 0.427, MTL 0.425, GroupDRO 0.384, AndMASK 0.288, IRM 0.284. The gap between the best 'fancy' method and plain ERM is 0.16 PCC, i.e. most of the signal is in representation quality and not in the domain-generalization algorithm, and both leaders are protein-language-model + fingerprint feature pipelines whose features can be replaced by cheap alternatives (k-mer/CTD protein descriptors, Morgan fingerprints) that train on CPU with gradient boosting. The data arrive through PyTDC (group.get('BindingDB_Patent')), the split is fixed, and the leaderboard has had no new entry in years.
targets.success_criterion: Success means 5 saved prediction files (seeds 1-5 from tdc.BenchmarkGroup(name='DTI_DG_Group'), group.get('BindingDB_Patent'), no re-splitting, one predicted affinity per official test pair in the official order, manifest with sha256 of the test (SMILES, protein-sequence) key list and of the TDC data files) such that (a) the test set is byte-identical to the group's own, (b) the mean PCC over the 5 seeds, recomputed by the skeptic through group.evaluate, is strictly HIGHER (direction: max) than the best PCC listed in the live leaderboard table at https://tdcommons.ai/benchmark/dti_dg_group/bindingdb_patent/ , re-fetched immediately before claiming, (c) the improvement is at least 0.010 absolute and exceeds max(listed best std, attacker's 5-seed std), with a 10,000-resample bootstrap over test pairs putting the attacker above the listed best in at least 95% of resamples, (d) training used only the official train_val rows (2013-2018 patents) of the same seed, with validation carved out of train_val as the benchmark prescribes, and (e) no external affinity data for any test (drug, target) pair - in particular no BindingDB/ChEMBL/Papyrus record for a test pair, and no pretrained affinity model whose training data are undeclared - entered the pipeline; protein or molecule representation models pretrained on sequences/structures WITHOUT affinity labels are allowed if declared.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic pip-installs PyTDC, builds BenchmarkGroup(name='DTI_DG_Group'), calls group.get('BindingDB_Patent') for seeds 1-5, hashes the test key list against the manifest, loads the attacker's prediction vectors, calls group.evaluate to obtain PCC mean/std, runs the bootstrap, verifies no test (SMILES, sequence) pair appears in the attacker's training files, and re-fetches the leaderboard page to parse all 9+ listed PCC values. The attacker's full pipeline must be re-runnable on CPU in under a few hours, which is realistic for fingerprint + descriptor features with LightGBM on a few hundred thousand pairs.

angles: Conventional: multi-station template matching (EQcorrscan-style) for each well-sampled deep moonquake nest, scanning windows predicted by the nest's tidal phase.
Conventional: subspace detectors built from the SVD of each nest's catalogued waveforms, more tolerant of waveform variability.
Cross-domain import (astronomy): use the tidal (27.2-day / 206-day) periodicity as a prior, the way periodic transit searches fold light curves.
Cross-domain import (genomics): locality-sensitive hashing of spectrogram fingerprints (as in FAST for earthquakes) to find repeats without templates.
Cross-domain import (structural health monitoring): thermal-moonquake rejection with temperature-cycle models tied to lunar sunrise and sunset.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (Apollo PSE long-period data 1969-1977 via FDSN dataselect, network XA, a few GB per station-year)
targets.name: New deep moonquake or impact in open Apollo Passive Seismic Experiment data, absent from the PDS expanded lunar event catalogue

partial_wins.statement: A new member of a catalogued nest seen on a single station with CC >= 0.6 and the null test passed (single-station detections are weaker evidence).
Recovery of >= 90% of one nest's catalogued events in one year with a measured false-alarm rate, saved and re-runnable.
Relocation of a catalogued nest with formal errors at least 30% smaller than Nakamura 2005, using added arrival picks.

pitfalls: Data glitches, timing jumps and telemetry dropouts are common in Apollo data; reject candidates near gaps or timing discontinuities.
Thermal moonquakes repeat at sunrise/sunset and can correlate with templates; check lunar local time at each station.
Bulow et al. already template-matched many nests; their events are in the Weber catalogue - search it by time, not by event type.
Correlation maxima chosen over long scans need the null test; per-window significance is meaningless without it.
Do not contact PDS or the catalogue authors; claim only the saved package.
targets.statement: The PDS Geosciences Node hosts the Apollo Passive Seismic Experiment expanded event catalogue (bundle by Renee Weber; levent.1008weber.csv, 13,057 events, built on Nakamura's catalogue and including Bulow et al. 2005/2007 template-matched deep moonquakes), plus deep-moonquake location tables (Nakamura 2005). Apollo 12, 14, 15 and 16 seismic data (network XA, stations S12-S16) are served openly by EarthScope FDSN dataselect. Deep moonquakes recur from fixed 'nests' at tidal periodicities, so template matching keeps finding members missed by visual cataloguing. Open task: a new event (deep moonquake nest member, shallow moonquake or meteoroid impact) recorded on >= 2 stations that the PDS catalogue does not list.
targets.success_criterion: A saved event package (UTC time, station/channel list, FDSN request URLs, waveforms, template or detector code) such that: for a deep moonquake, normalised cross-correlation >= 0.5 with the stack of a catalogued nest on >= 2 stations with consistent relative arrival times (within 2 s of the nest's moveout) and occurrence phase consistent with the nest's tidal periodicity; for other types, coherent arrivals on >= 2 stations with a location solution (RMS <= 3 s); the detection statistic exceeds the maximum obtained on a null set (the same templates correlated with time-reversed data and with data circularly shifted between stations by >= 1 h) over the full searched span; data-gap, thermal moonquake (sunrise/sunset) and instrument-glitch checks pass; and no event within +/- 5 min in levent.1008weber.csv and the other tables of https://pds-geosciences.wustl.edu/lunar/urn-nasa-pds-apollo_seismic_event_catalog/data/ re-fetched live immediately before claiming, nor in any published expanded deep-moonquake list of the last 24 months found by search.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic fetches the cited waveform windows, recomputes cross-correlations against the nest stack built from the catalogue times, reruns the time-reversed and shifted nulls, and checks the PDS tables. Under 1 hour.

angles: Conventional: logistic regression or gradient boosting on SWPC region-summary features (McIntosh class, area, spot count) plus recent flare history (counts and peak flux of the last 24-72 h), calibrated with isotonic regression.
Conventional: SHARP-keyword models (total unsigned flux, R-value, free-energy proxies) aggregated over the disk, combined with persistence.
Cross-domain import (seismology): epidemic-type aftershock (ETAS / Hawkes) models of flare self-excitation, giving a background-plus-triggering rate turned into a 24 h probability.

Cross-domain import (sports and election forecasting): forecast combination - a weighted pool of the scoreboard's own historical behaviour is not allowed, but pooling your own diverse models with weights fitted on pre-2023 data often beats any single model in Brier score.
Cross-domain import (credit scoring): monotone-constrained boosting and Platt calibration for rare-event probabilities under base-rate drift across the solar cycle.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (scoreboard forecasts via HAPI in seconds; GOES-16 flare summary 6 MB; SWPC region summaries and HMI SHARP keywords via plain GET)
targets.name: NASA CCMC Flare Scoreboard: a reproducible 24-hour M-class flare forecast that beats every scoreboard model's Brier skill score over 2023-2024

partial_wins.statement: Beat the SIDC_Operator and ASSA_24H_1 BSS (0.1446) on their own windows with the same rules and bootstrap test.
A forecast with BSS > 0.2145 on the NOAA windows whose reliability diagram slope lies within 0.9-1.1 (well calibrated), even if the bootstrap lower bound is not above 0.
Beat the best scoreboard model on the X-class 24-hour forecast (BSS, same windows) for 2023-2024.

pitfalls: Hindsight leakage: training or tuning on 2023-2024 outcomes, or using science-quality data products released months later as if available in real time, inflates skill; the 2-hour cutoff and pre-2023 training rule are mandatory.

Window mismatch: scoreboard models issue at different times (NOAA ~22 UT for 00-24 UT, SIDC 12:30 UT); comparing your 00-24 UT score to a model's differently aligned windows is not like for like - match windows per model.
Probability definitions differ (M-only vs M-or-greater); give each comparator its most favourable reading, as above.
At a 0.57 base rate, small BSS gains are within bootstrap noise; autocorrelated days require block bootstrap, not i.i.d. resampling.
GOES satellite or calibration changes (GOES-16 to GOES-18/19) shift flare counts near class thresholds; use the single stated flsum file.
targets.statement: The NASA CCMC Flare Scoreboard (Leila Mays and the CCMC team; models by NOAA SWPC, SIDC/ROB, ASSA, SPS, AMOS and others) archives real-time full-disk flare probabilities through a public HAPI service. Scored here against GOES-16 XRS science-quality flare peaks (NOAA NCEI flsum v2-2-1; 1,278 M1+ peaks in 2023-2024), using 24-hour windows that start at most 1 h after issue and comparing with climatology over the same windows, the Brier skill scores for 2023-01-01..2024-12-31 are (computed 2026-10-15): NOAA_1 0.2145 when P(M+) = 1-(1-M)(1-X) (0.1727 if its M value is read as M+), SIDC_Operator 0.1446, ASSA_24H_1 0.1446, SPS 0.1141, AMOS_v1 -0.113. A 3-day persistence baseline scores 0.106 on the NOAA windows. Base rate of M+ days is 0.57 (solar maximum). Open task: a forecast built only from data public before each issue time that beats the best of these on the same windows.
targets.success_criterion: A saved forecast file (one 00:00-24:00 UT P(>=M1.0) per day, 2023-01-01..2024-12-31) plus code that regenerates it using only data timestamped at least 2 hours before each window start (GOES XRS 1-min fluxes, NOAA SWPC solar region summaries, HMI SHARP NRT keywords) and training data ending before 2023-01-01, whose Brier skill score against climatology, with outcomes = any GOES-16 flsum EVENT_PEAK of class M or X in the window, is strictly greater (direction: max) than the best full-disk model's BSS on its own matched windows, computed by the skeptic from the HAPI service https://ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/flare-scoreboard/hapi/catalog re-fetched live immediately before claiming, using for each model the most favourable reading of its M probability; the margin must exceed the 95% block-bootstrap (27-day blocks) interval of the BSS difference, i.e. the lower bound of the difference must be > 0.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the HAPI forecasts and the GOES-16 flsum NetCDF, runs a standalone Brier/BSS script with the window matching rule above, regenerates the claimed forecast from code with a data-cutoff harness (inputs read through a function that refuses timestamps later than window start minus 2 h), and runs the block bootstrap. Under 1 hour.

angles: Conventional: pattern scaling with EOF-truncated emission inputs plus a GP correction for regional aerosol effects (the Lutjens et al. finding that linear models are hard to beat).
Exploit ensemble-averaged training targets (Lutjens et al.) to reduce noise in training labels, while keeping the official test target.
Cross-domain import (pharmacokinetics): impulse-response / convolution models of emissions to temperature (as in FaIR) give physically constrained global means; then downscale with patterns.
Cross-domain import (econometrics): distributed-lag and error-correction models for the slow/fast response split.
Cross-domain import (geostatistics): kriging residuals on the sphere with a Matern covariance for spatial NRMSE.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (training data a few GB; pattern-scaling and GP models train in minutes)
targets.name: ClimateBench: beat the best published total NRMSE for climate-model emulation on the SSP2-4.5 test scenario, on CPU

partial_wins.statement: Beat the best published total NRMSE for dtr (10.7, ClimaX) or pr (3.10) with a model of under 1M parameters trained on CPU in under 1 hour; these are the variables where linear pattern scaling loses.
Beat the best published value on the spatial or the global component alone for any variable (Lutjens et al. Table 1 bars).
Match the best published total for tas (0.284) within 2% with a model that trains in under 10 CPU-minutes and uses no global-mean temperature input.

pitfalls: The test target is a 3-member ensemble mean with sizeable internal variability (Lutjens et al.); gains smaller than the seed-to-seed spread are noise. Report 5 seeds.
Using SSP2-4.5 (test) data for early stopping or hyperparameter choice is leakage.
Some papers score against other targets (e.g. MPI-ESM 50-member means, Lutjens et al. Table 2) or other years; compare only like with like.
Pattern-scaling variants that take simulated global-mean temperature as input use part of the target (Lutjens et al. note this about the original LPS); inputs must be emissions only.
The README leaderboard is not the state of the art; check Lutjens et al. Table 1 and any newer ClimateBench paper.
targets.statement: ClimateBench (Watson-Parris et al. 2022, JAMES) asks for emulators mapping emission scenarios to 2015-2100 NorESM2-LM fields of surface temperature (tas), diurnal temperature range (dtr), precipitation (pr) and 90th-percentile precipitation (pr90), scored by spatial, global and total NRMSE (total = spatial + 5 x global) against the 3-member ensemble mean of SSP2-4.5 over 2080-2100. The repository README lists only the 2022 baselines (best totals: tas 0.327, dtr 16.78, pr 3.17, pr90 4.34; CNN-LSTM). Lutjens et al. (arXiv:2408.05288, Table 1) collect all published scores. Best totals as of 2026-10-15: tas 0.284 and pr90 4.03 (linear pattern scaling, Lutjens et al.), dtr 10.7 (ClimaX, Nguyen et al. 2023), pr 3.10 (CNN-LSTM as reproduced by Nguyen et al. 2023). Open task: an emulator trainable on a laptop CPU whose total NRMSE beats the best published value for at least one variable.
targets.success_criterion: A saved, runnable emulator (code, fixed seeds, trained weights) trained only on the official ClimateBench training scenarios, evaluated with the official ClimateBench NRMSE script on the SSP2-4.5 test set (2080-2100), whose total NRMSE for a variable (tas, dtr, pr or pr90) is strictly lower than the best value for that variable in the README leaderboard at https://github.com/duncanwp/ClimateBench (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) AND lower than the best value for that variable reported in any peer-reviewed or arXiv ClimateBench paper (Lutjens et al. 2025 and ClimaX checked explicitly), with the same metric definition (total = spatial + 5 x global); no test-scenario data used in training or model selection; reproduction on CPU within 4 hours.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the ClimateBench data from Zenodo (a few GB), runs the provided training and evaluation scripts from a clean environment, and compares NRMSE to the README and the cited papers. Within 4 hours on CPU.

angles: Conventional: multi-timescale Poisson search (50 us .. 1 ms) on summed BGO+NaI photon lists with a sliding background.
Conventional: restrict to orbits over tropical thunderstorm regions (from orbit position) to raise the prior.
Cross-domain import (neutrino/IceCube burst searches): unbinned maximum-likelihood with a time-clustering test statistic and scrambled-time background.
Cross-domain import (network intrusion detection): change-point detection (Bayesian Blocks, CUSUM) on the photon arrival stream.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: Terrestrial gamma-ray flash in public Fermi GBM TTE data, absent from the GBM TGF catalog

partial_wins.statement: A candidate in 2012-11-26..2016-07-31 with null-test expected false count < 0.5 (rather than 0.05), otherwise vetted as above.
Independent re-detection of >= 95% of catalogue offline-search TGFs for one month with the same pipeline, establishing sensitivity.

A vetted TGF after 2016-07-31 meeting all criteria, labelled 'not yet catalogued' (no public list covers that period), ideally with WWLLN-independent evidence such as a coincident GBM-only lightning-region orbit.

pitfalls: Cosmic-ray air showers and particle events produce short bursts in all detectors - require a TGF-like detector pattern.
Instrumental dead-time and pulse pile-up distort counts of very bright events.
Look-elsewhere: the number of bins searched over years is enormous; per-bin significance is meaningless without trials correction.
The GBM team may maintain a newer TGF list beyond the 2016 catalog; search for it before claiming.
targets.statement: The Fermi GBM TGF catalogue tables at the FSSC (Roberts et al. 2018, JGR Space Physics; the page calls the current tables the second catalogue) list 4,144 TGFs from 2008-07-11 to 2016-07-31, including an offline search of time-tagged-event data; TTE became continuous (CTTE) on 2012-11-26, after which the catalogue is more uniform. GBM daily TTE/CTTE data are public at HEASARC. The catalogue's sensitivity is inhomogeneous. Open task: a statistically significant TGF in public CTTE data inside 2012-11-26..2016-07-31 that the catalogue does not list.
targets.success_criterion: A saved candidate (UTC to 1 microsecond, detector list, TTE file names, photon list, detection code) inside the continuous-TTE period 2012-11-26..2016-07-31 (when the catalogue's offline search ran on full-orbit data) with >= 10 counts in <= 1 ms across >= 2 BGO+NaI detectors, hard spectrum (BGO counts > 100 keV), not during SAA passage, not a cosmic-ray shower signature (simultaneous saturation in all 14 detectors); the same pipeline run on a null set (the photon lists with arrival times scrambled within +/- 1 s blocks, and on orbits over oceans at high geomagnetic latitude where TGFs are rare) yields an expected false count < 0.05 over all searched data at the candidate's statistic; and no entry within +/- 1 ms in all six catalogue tables at https://fermi.gsfc.nasa.gov/ssc/data/access/gbm/tgf/ re-fetched live immediately before claiming, nor in any later public GBM TGF list found by search. Candidates after 2016-07-31 count only as partial win p3.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the cited daily TTE files from HEASARC, re-bins the photon list around the time, recomputes the background from +/- 1 s, recomputes Poisson significance and trials factor, and checks the catalog table. Under 45 minutes.

angles: Conventional: re-implement the published GLM bolide features (group duration, track linearity, energy ratio) with a random forest trained on catalog events vs lightning.
Conventional: search overlap regions of GOES-East/West for stereo coincidences that single-satellite classifiers down-weight.
Cross-domain import (particle physics triggers): a two-level trigger with a loose online cut and an offline likelihood ratio, estimating the false-positive rate on time-shifted data.
Cross-domain import (exoplanet transit search): treat each pixel's group-energy time series like a light curve and apply matched filters (box/Gaussian templates) for meteor-shaped pulses.
Cross-domain import (sports/ball tracking): RANSAC line fitting on event centroids to separate straight bolide tracks from branching lightning.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: Bolide in public GOES GLM lightning-mapper data absent from the NASA GLM bolide catalog

partial_wins.statement: A stereo (two-GLM) candidate whose triangulated altitude is 20-90 km and whose ground track is non-lightning-like, absent from the catalog.
A blind detector run over one month of GLM-16 data that recovers >= 90% of the catalog's events for that month, with the residual non-catalog detections listed and hand-vetted.

pitfalls: Lightning is the dominant false positive; isolated 'bolt from the blue' flashes and sprites can be linear and short.
Glint and instrument artefacts (sun glint over oceans, South Atlantic Anomaly hits, GLM 'blooming') create bright compact events.
Catalog publication lags detection by days; candidates from the last 2 weeks may simply be unpublished - restrict to windows older than 2 months.
Do not report to NASA; claim only the saved verified candidate.
targets.statement: NASA's neo-bolide.ndc.nasa.gov publishes a curated catalogue of bolides detected by the GOES-16/17/18/19 Geostationary Lightning Mappers (public JSON API: 11,611 published events on 2026-10-15, latest event 2026-10-06, published 2026-10-12). GLM L2 LCFA files are public on the NOAA open-data S3 buckets (noaa-goes16/17/18/19). The pipeline uses classifiers on GLM group data plus human vetting, so faint, short or stereo-ambiguous bolides can be missed. Open task: a bolide in public GLM data, older than 2 months, that is absent from the live catalogue.
targets.success_criterion: A saved candidate (UTC time, lat/lon, GLM file names, group/event IDs, extracted light curve, detection code) such that: the light curve lasts >= 100 ms with a smooth single- or multi-peaked meteor shape and a spatial track of >= 3 pixels moving consistently; there is NO co-located lightning (no other GLM flashes within 50 km and +/- 2 min); the same detector run on a null set (one month of data in a lightning-active region, plus the candidate month with group times shuffled within flashes) gives an expected false count < 0.05 at the candidate's score over the searched span; ideally stereo detection by two GLMs; and no event within +/- 2 min / 200 km in the bolide JSON API and the CNEOS fireball API, both re-fetched live immediately before claiming.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the cited GLM L2 files from the NOAA S3 bucket, re-extracts the groups, plots the light curve and track, checks for nearby lightning flashes in the same and adjacent files, and queries both catalogs live. Under 30 minutes.

angles: Conventional: DBSCAN / HDBSCAN in (lambda-lambda_sun, beta, v_g) sun-centred ecliptic coordinates per solar-longitude window, followed by D_SH / D_N refinement; scan low-activity Southern-hemisphere windows where camera coverage grew after 2023.
Conventional: compare yearly activity profiles to find one-night outbursts (the dominant GMN discovery mode, e.g. M2025-Q1).

Cross-domain import (particle physics): treat the radiant map as a 'bump hunt' with look-elsewhere correction (sideband background from adjacent solar longitudes, global p-value via toy Monte Carlo) instead of ad hoc D-criterion thresholds.

Cross-domain import (astronomy/genomics): use the clustering-on-orbital-elements idea from asteroid family detection (hierarchical clustering method, Zappala) or single-linkage with Bonferroni-corrected null shuffles as used for gene-expression clusters.
Cross-domain import (seismology): template matching - take known weak showers' mean orbits as templates and scan other years for repeat 'events' at the same node.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: New meteor shower in public Global Meteor Network orbits, absent from the live IAU MDC shower list

partial_wins.statement: A confirmed new one-year outburst (>= 10 meteors within 6 h, D_SH < 0.08, >= 5 sigma over sporadic background) not in the MDC list nor in eMeteorNews, even if not recurring.

An annual recurrence of a working-list shower in >= 3 GMN years where the MDC entry rests on a single-year detection, with mean orbit consistent (D_SH < 0.1); non-trivial because it moves evidence toward establishment.

A parent-body association: a candidate cluster whose mean orbit has D_SH < 0.15 to a JPL SBDB comet/NEO orbit with a successful meteoroid-stream integration (e.g. via REBOUND) placing ejecta at the observed node.

pitfalls: Most 'new' clusters are already in the MDC working list under an obscure code or in the removed/pending lists - compare against ALL lists in streamfulldata2026.txt, not just established showers.
Single-station or poorly converged trajectories create spurious radiant concentrations; filter on GMN quality columns (convergence angle, number of stations, velocity uncertainty).
Observing-geometry artefacts: camera network growth and lunar phase change detection rates, mimicking 'activity'; the background must be from the same stations/season.
GMN announces showers fast on eMeteorNews; a cluster from 2026 data may already be reported days ago - check the site immediately before claiming.
Do not report to the MDC or GMN; claim only the verified saved cluster.
targets.statement: The Global Meteor Network (GMN) publishes all its multi-station meteoroid orbits openly (traj_summary_yearly_2019..2026, ~3 GB total, refreshed daily). The IAU Meteor Data Center (MDC) maintains the list of all showers (established + working list + pending), last updated 2026-10-19 (944 showers, 172 established; working list up to M2026-S2), with a full-data file streamfulldata2026.txt. GMN itself keeps announcing new showers (M2025-L1/L2, O1, O2, P1, Q1, V1, M2026-P1 per eMeteorNews), which shows that unannounced compact orbit clusters still exist in the open data. Open task: find a statistically significant orbit cluster (new shower or outburst) in the public GMN data that matches no entry in the live MDC list and no GMN/CAMS/eMeteorNews report.
targets.success_criterion: A saved list of >= 15 GMN trajectory IDs (from traj_summary_yearly_*.txt) forming a cluster whose mean orbit has D_SH < 0.10 to each member's median-orbit and whose mean orbit has D_SH >= 0.20 (and radiant separation > 5 deg at matched solar longitude +/- 5 deg) from EVERY entry of streamfulldata2026.txt re-fetched live immediately before claiming; cluster significance must exceed 5 sigma against a sporadic background estimated from the same solar-longitude window in other years (or shuffled-solar-longitude bootstrap); meteors observed by >= 3 independent stations in >= 2 countries; and no eMeteorNews / WGN / arXiv report (last 24 months) of a shower with that radiant, solar longitude and velocity.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the cited traj_summary_yearly file(s) (minutes), extracts the listed IDs, recomputes the mean orbit and pairwise D_SH (Southworth-Hawkins) with a standalone script, re-runs the background estimate with a different random seed, re-fetches streamfulldata2026.txt live and recomputes D_SH to every listed shower; manual search of eMeteorNews and MDC 'new reports'. Under 30 minutes.

angles: Conventional: template matching with V14 high-frequency events (which repeat with similar spectra) across all quiet evening hours, where Martian wind noise is lowest.
Conventional: spectrogram-energy detector at the 2.4 Hz resonance with sol-of-day noise baselines.
Cross-domain import (gravitational-wave searches): chi-square signal-consistency vetoes and time-slide backgrounds to control glitch false alarms on a single noisy station.
Cross-domain import (bioacoustics): animal-call detectors trained with few labels on spectrogram patches (e.g. BirdNET-style), adapted to the HF/VF spectral templates.
Cross-domain import (wind-turbine condition monitoring): regress out wind- and pressure-driven noise from co-located meteorological channels before detection.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (one station, ~1,400 sols of 20-100 sps three-component data, a few tens of GB via FDSN dataselect)
targets.name: Marsquake in open InSight SEIS waveforms absent from the Marsquake Service catalogue V14 and the MarsQuakeNet extension

partial_wins.statement: An event absent from V14 that IS in the MarsQuakeNet list, independently recovered with a different method and the null test above (confirms an ML-only detection).
A new distance or back-azimuth for a V14 event that has none, from re-picked P/S phases with stated uncertainties.
A blind detector that recovers >= 90% of V14 quality-A/B events in one season with a measured false-alarm rate, saved and re-runnable.

pitfalls: Most 'new' low-SNR events are already in MarsQuakeNet's list; that list must be checked, not only V14.
Lander and tether thermal 'donks', glitches and wind gusts create impulsive signals; the polarisation and atmospheric-channel checks are mandatory.
Daytime wind noise dominates; detections clustered in windy hours are suspect - examine the null-test rate by local time.
The mars-event service lists multiple rows per event for some IDs; match by time window, not by row count.
Do not report to MQS; claim only the saved verified package.
targets.statement: NASA's InSight lander recorded Martian seismicity with one station (XB.ELYSE) from 2019 to 2022. The InSight Marsquake Service (MQS; Clinton, Ceylan, Giardini, Stahler, Horleston and colleagues) released catalogue V14 (2023-04-01, DOI 10.12686/a21), served live by the EarthScope mars-event FDSN service (2,715 rows on 2026-10-15). Dahmen et al. (2022, JGR Planets, 'MarsQuakeNet') used a deep denoiser/detector to extend the catalogue by about 60% (1,297 to 2,079 events, mostly low SNR), and Dahmen et al. (2024, GJI) added further low-frequency events; MQS has announced a final reference catalogue (over 1,900 events) that was not found as a public data release on 2026-10-15. Waveforms are open via FDSN dataselect. Open task: a marsquake clearly recorded on SEIS that is in none of these lists.
targets.success_criterion: A saved event package (UTC onset, event class by MQS conventions - LF/BB/HF/VF/24 - with the 2.4 Hz resonance or P/S evidence, spectrograms, FDSN request URLs, detection code) such that: the event has SNR >= 3 in its MQS-class band on the vertical and at least one horizontal channel; it is not a glitch, donk, lander/wind transient or atmospheric pressure signal (checks: polarisation, VBB/SP consistency, co-located pressure and wind sensor data quiet within +/- 10 min); the detector's false-alarm rate measured on a null set (the same pipeline run on time-reversed and phase-randomised data from the same sols) implies an expected false count < 0.05 over the searched span at the event's statistic; and no event within +/- 10 min in the live mars-event service at https://service.earthscope.org/irisws/mars-event/1/query?format=text and in the MarsQuakeNet and Dahmen 2024 supplementary lists and any public MQS final catalogue, all re-fetched live immediately before claiming. If a list cannot be fetched, the result is reported as a partial win only.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the cited waveform windows (and pressure/wind channels) via FDSN dataselect, reproduces spectrograms and polarisation, reruns the detector's null test with a different random seed, and queries the mars-event service and the supplementary lists. About 1 hour.

angles: Conventional: gradient-boosted trees on multi-window solar-wind aggregates (Bz, V, n, coupling functions such as Newell's dPhi/dt and V*Bs) per horizon.

Conventional: physics prior - the Burton/O'Brien-McPherron ring-current ODE (dDst*/dt = Q(VBs) - Dst*/tau) integrated over the 7-day window as a feature or as the backbone, with ML predicting the residual.
Cross-domain import (hydrology): treat solar-wind driving as rainfall and Dst as river discharge; rainfall-runoff LSTMs with a linear-reservoir layer generalise well on extremes.
Cross-domain import (control engineering): identify a nonlinear ARX / Hammerstein-Wiener model of the magnetosphere as a driven system and robustify against sensor dropouts with a Kalman filter.
Cross-domain import (speech enhancement): learned imputation of missing real-time solar-wind samples (the noise the challenge stresses) before forecasting.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (public.zip 287 MB, private.zip 112 MB; LightGBM/1D-CNN models train on CPU in minutes to an hour)
targets.name: MagNet geomagnetic-storm challenge: beat the winning RMSE for real-time Dst forecasting on the released private test set

partial_wins.statement: Re-run the 1st-place code on private.zip and reproduce 11.131 to within 0.02 (validates the local scorer); then beat the 4th-place score 11.529 with a model that trains in under 10 CPU-minutes.
Beat 11.131 on the t1 (one-hour-ahead) RMSE alone, with the winner's t1 RMSE recomputed from its released code as the comparator.
Lower RMSE than the winner restricted to storm hours (Dst <= -50 nT) in the private set, with total RMSE no worse than 11.53.

pitfalls: Leakage: using Dst from dst_labels.csv (past or future) as an input violates the real-time setting; the challenge gave only solar-wind, sunspot and position feeds.
Look-ahead through aggregation: centred rolling windows or resampling that includes data after the prediction timestamp silently uses the future.
Scoring mismatch: the challenge metric pools t0 and t1 errors; reporting only t0 RMSE or a subset of periods is not comparable.
Training on private.zip in any form (feature scaling, early stopping, model selection) is test-set contamination.
A difference of a few hundredths of a nT is within seed noise; report the spread over 5 seeds.
targets.statement: The NOAA/NCEI 'MagNet: Model the Geomagnetic Field' challenge (DrivenData, 2020-21; organised by Manoj Nair and colleagues at CIRES/NOAA) asked for models that forecast the Dst index for the current hour (t0) and the next hour (t1) from real-time inputs (the preceding 7 days of solar-wind data from ACE/DSCOVR, the latest daily satellite positions and the latest monthly smoothed sunspot number), scored by RMSE over both horizons on a hidden test set. Winning scores (private RMSE): 11.131 (Ammarali32, BiLSTM-GRU), 11.253 (belinda_trotta, CNN ensemble), 11.294 (LosExtraterrestres), 11.529 (k_squared). NCEI now serves both public.zip (training) and private.zip, which contains private/dst_labels.csv, so the private test set can be scored locally. As of 2026-10-15 the winners' README (drivendataorg/magnet-geomagnetic-field) is unchanged since the challenge. Open task: a model that obeys the challenge's real-time input rules and scores below 11.131 on the private set.
targets.success_criterion: A saved, runnable model (code, fixed seeds, weights) trained only on public.zip, that produces t0 and t1 Dst predictions for every hourly timestamp in private/dst_labels.csv using only the inputs the challenge's own runner passes for that timestamp t0 (drivendataorg/noaa-runtime, data/main.py): solar_wind records from t0 - 7 days to t0 - 1 minute, the last 7 satellite_positions records stamped at or before t0, and the latest sunspots smoothed_ssn value stamped at or before t0, whatever its age (no Dst values from the label file as inputs), and whose RMSE over all t0 and t1 predictions (the challenge metric, computed with the scorer's own script and checked against the winner's code run on the same file) is strictly lower (direction: min) than the best private score in the README table at https://github.com/drivendataorg/magnet-geomagnetic-field re-fetched live immediately before claiming, by at least 0.05 nT; and lower than any RMSE for this private set reported in a paper from the last 24 months (search 'MagNet Dst' including Nair et al. 2023, Space Weather) with the same metric.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads public.zip and private.zip from NCEI, runs the saved model in a clean environment with a harness that feeds only the inputs the challenge's runner allows (solar_wind from t0 - 7 days to t0 - 1 minute, the last 7 satellite_positions records at or before t0 and the latest smoothed_ssn at or before t0, as data/main.py slices them), computes RMSE with an independent 10-line script, and re-runs the winner's code for the comparator. Look-ahead audit: code reading (including what each saved scaler and weight was fitted on), plus, at several sampled timestamps, re-running the whole pipeline from the raw files in a fresh process with caches cleared, once with every solar_wind row at or after that timestamp and every sunspots and satellite_positions row after it deleted, and once with those rows replaced by other values, some well outside the range of the earlier data, confirming that the t0 and t1 predictions for that timestamp do not change beyond floating-point rounding. Shuffling future rows is not enough: a look-ahead through a mean, max or count over them survives any shuffle. Deletion alone misses a whole-file maximum that lies in the past, and replacement alone misses a row count. Passing these tests is a negative control, not a proof. About 1-2 hours on CPU.

angles: Conventional: 1D CNN on whitened strain with curriculum training on SNR, followed by coincidence and time-slide background estimation.
Conventional: a hybrid - ML pre-filter feeding a reduced template bank matched filter, keeping matched-filter background statistics.
Cross-domain import (radar signal processing): constant-false-alarm-rate detection with learned chirp dictionaries, i.e. sparse matched filtering over a compressed template basis (SVD of the bank).
Cross-domain import (speech recognition): spectrogram transformers with keyword-spotting losses trained on chirps, which handle precession-induced amplitude modulation.
Cross-domain import (particle physics triggers): train against the background estimate directly (time-slid noise) to optimise the low-FAR tail, not classification accuracy.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (one month of two-detector simulated Gaussian noise per test set, tens of GB; generation and evaluation scripts in the repository; ML inference on CPU/Apple GPU)
targets.name: MLGWSC-1 gravitational-wave search challenge: beat the best published sensitive distance at a false-alarm rate of 1 per month on dataset 3

partial_wins.statement: Exceed the Virgo-AUTh dataset-3 value (1240.68 Mpc) at FAR 1/month with a model trained in under 24 laptop-hours.
Beat 1487.67 Mpc on dataset 1 or 2 instead (published bars: dataset 1 ML best 2362.51, dataset 2 ML best 1455.09 Mpc at FAR 1/month).
Match the best ML entry within 2% while analysing the month of data in under 1 hour of wall-clock on a laptop.

pitfalls: Training on noise generated with the challenge seed (or tuning thresholds on the challenge foreground) is test-set contamination.
Estimating background only from the foreground file inflated some entries' sensitivity in the paper; use the separate background set as evaluate.py expects.
Different PyCBC versions change waveform and noise generation; use the repository's pinned requirements.
Sensitive distance at FAR 1/month rests on a handful of loudest background triggers; differences of tens of Mpc can be noise - use the 5-seed check.
Dataset 4 needs real O3a noise from GWOSC, which did not resolve from this network on 2026-10-15; do not substitute other noise and call it dataset 4.
targets.statement: The first Machine Learning Gravitational-Wave Search Mock Data Challenge (Schafer, Zelenka, Nitz, Wang, Wu, and co-authors; Phys. Rev. D 107, 023021, arXiv:2209.11146) evaluates binary-black-hole searches by sensitive distance versus false-alarm rate on one month of simulated two-detector data. Dataset 3 has simulated Gaussian noise whose PSD is drawn per segment from 20 O3a-derived PSDs per detector (files shipped in the repository), and IMRPhenomXPHM signals with isotropic spins (precession) and higher-order modes, component masses 7-50 Msun; its challenge set was generated with seed 470182217, published in the paper, and generate_data.py plus evaluate.py are public. Table IV at FAR = 1 per month on dataset 3: PyCBC (matched filtering) 1577.18 Mpc, TPI FSU Jena (best machine-learning entry) 1487.67 Mpc, cWB 1252.09 Mpc, Virgo-AUTh 1240.68 Mpc. Datasets 1-3 need no detector data download, so the target is reachable even without the GWOSC strain archive. Open task: a search whose sensitive distance at FAR 1/month on dataset 3 exceeds the best published non-PyCBC entry, and (moonshot) the PyCBC entry.
targets.success_criterion: Saved foreground and background trigger files (the challenge HDF5 output format) for the dataset-3 challenge set regenerated with the published seed by the unmodified generate_data.py at the repository's pinned PyCBC version, plus the search code, such that the unmodified evaluate.py gives a sensitive distance at FAR = 1 per month strictly greater (direction: max) than 1487.67 Mpc (main win) by more than the evaluation's Monte-Carlo uncertainty (estimated by re-running evaluate.py on the 5 alternative challenge sets made with seeds 1..5), with the Table IV values in the arXiv/journal version of Schafer et al. and the repository https://github.com/gwastro/ml-mock-data-challenge-1 re-fetched live immediately before claiming, and greater than any dataset-3 FAR-1/month value in later papers (search 'MLGWSC-1 dataset 3'; last 24 months); the search must not be trained or tuned on data generated with the challenge seed. Exceeding PyCBC's 1577.18 Mpc under the same rules is the moonshot win.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic regenerates the dataset-3 challenge set with the published seed, runs the saved search (or checks the saved trigger files hash-match a fresh run), runs evaluate.py, and runs the 5-seed uncertainty check. Laptop-hours to a day.

angles: Conventional: pretrained CNN backbones on stacks of the current and prior frames, plus a sequence model over storm history, with test-time augmentation by rotation (storms are rotation-equivariant up to hemisphere flip).
Conventional: smooth predictions along each storm's timeline with a causal Kalman filter, since intensity changes slowly.
Cross-domain import (Dvorak technique, operational meteorology): explicit features - eye temperature, coldest ring, cloud-top symmetry - as inputs alongside learned features.
Cross-domain import (medical imaging): rotation-equivariant CNNs (polar-coordinate transforms around the storm centre) as used for histopathology.
Cross-domain import (video understanding): temporal shift modules / optical flow between frames to capture intensification.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (about 70k train and 45k test single-band 366x366 IR images, ~20 GB; CNN training on Apple-silicon GPU or CPU for days)
targets.name: NASA/Radiant Earth tropical-storm wind-speed challenge: beat the winning RMSE from GOES infrared imagery on the released test labels

partial_wins.statement: Whole-test RMSE below 6.677 (the winner's public-split score, so below at least one of the winner's two split scores) with a single model trained in under 24 laptop-hours.
Whole-test RMSE below 7.0 with no deep network (e.g. a Dvorak-style feature pipeline with gradient boosting) - a strong interpretable baseline.
Beat the winner's released code re-run on the whole test set (its whole-test RMSE recomputed by the skeptic).

pitfalls: Non-causal use of later frames from the same storm (or bidirectional sequence models) is leakage; the challenge allowed only prior images.
Comparing a whole-test RMSE to a public-split RMSE is not like for like; use the rule above.
Storm-level overlap: random image-level validation splits leak storms; validate by storm.
Labels are best-track wind speeds in 5-kt steps; differences below ~0.05 kt RMSE are noise.
Do not submit to DrivenData; scoring is local.
targets.statement: The 'Wind-dependent Variables: Predict Wind Speeds of Tropical Storms' challenge (DrivenData 2021; data assembled by Radiant Earth Foundation and the NASA IMPACT team, Manil Maskey and colleagues) asks for each storm image the maximum sustained wind speed (kt) using that image and earlier images of the same storm. Winning private RMSE: 6.256 (vecxoz, 51-model ensemble), then 6.417 (KarimAmer), 6.456 (Daniel_FG); the winners' public-split scores were 6.677, 6.867 and 6.839. The full dataset including test_set_labels.csv is downloadable by plain GET from Source Cooperative (data.source.coop/nasa/tropical-storm-competition). The private/public split is not published, so the honest comparison is on the whole test set: the winner's whole-test RMSE must lie between its private and public scores (6.256-6.677). Open task: whole-test RMSE strictly below 6.256 with a causal model.
targets.success_criterion: Saved predictions for every image in test_set_features.csv plus code and weights, where each prediction uses only images of the same storm with relative_time less than or equal to that image's (no future frames, no test labels), trained only on the training set, whose RMSE against test_set_labels.csv over the whole test set is strictly lower (direction: min) than the 1st-place private score in the README at https://github.com/drivendataorg/wind-dependent-variables re-fetched live immediately before claiming (6.256 on 2026-10-15), and lower than any whole-test or private-split RMSE on this dataset reported in a paper of the last 24 months.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the test labels from Source Cooperative, recomputes RMSE with a standalone script, inspects the data loader to confirm causal frame use (and re-runs inference with all future frames of each storm deleted to confirm identical predictions). Under 1 hour for scoring; inference re-run depends on model size.

angles: Conventional: ensemble model output statistics on ECMWF tercile probabilities with spatial smoothing and shrinkage toward climatology where hindcast skill is low.
Conventional: combine ECMWF, NCEP and ECCC ensembles (all in the challenge data) with weights learned per region and lead from hindcasts.
Cross-domain import (finance): Bayesian shrinkage of predictive signals with low signal-to-noise (James-Stein toward climatology) - the main lesson of S2S is that most of the grid has no skill.
Cross-domain import (epidemiology forecast hubs): quantile/probability ensembling with trimmed means, which reliably beats individual models under scoring rules like WIS and RPS.
Cross-domain import (image restoration): treat the global probability fields as images and use a small U-Net on anomaly maps conditioned on MJO/ENSO indices.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (ECMWF hindcasts/forecasts as NetCDF from the ECMWF object store, tens of GB for t2m and tp; post-processing models train on CPU)
targets.name: WMO S2S AI Challenge: beat the best RPSS for week 3-4 and 5-6 temperature and precipitation tercile forecasts in 2020

partial_wins.statement: Reproduce the CRIM score within 0.002 from their released code (github.com/crim-ca/crims2s) and then beat it on one of the two variables alone.
RPSS > 0 for both variables and both lead windows simultaneously (no negative component), which no 2021 entry except CRIM achieved.
A no-neural-network method (e.g. EMOS with spatial smoothing) with RPSS >= 0.040.

pitfalls: Using 2020 observations (directly or via climatology recomputed with 2020) is leakage.
RPSS is averaged in a specific way (by the scorer revised on 2021-10-22); a home-made RPSS will not match - use the template's code.
Forecasts that are overconfident score badly in RPS; many entries were negative because they beat the raw ECMWF on hindcasts but not out of sample.
Precipitation tercile edges come from the challenge files; recomputing them changes the categories.
One test year (2020) is a small sample with La Nina; gains of 0.001-0.002 are within noise.
targets.statement: The WMO Prize Challenge to improve subseasonal-to-seasonal predictions using AI (2021; organised by Andrew Robertson, Frederic Vitart, Aaron Spring and colleagues) scored probabilistic tercile forecasts of 2 m temperature and biweekly precipitation for weeks 3-4 and 5-6, for all 2020 forecast start dates, by RPSS relative to climatology, averaged over the globe land grid. The archived leaderboard (github.com/aaronspring/s2s-ai-challenge-leaderboard, last automated update 2022-11-07) has the best score RPSS = 0.0459475 by the CRIM team (submission-methods-7, Jordan Gierschendorf et al.); the next teams are near 0.0 or negative. Data remain downloadable from the ECMWF object store by plain GET (S2S data licence terms apply; no registration). Open task: a forecast for 2020 built only from the allowed training period that beats 0.0459 with the challenge's scorer.
targets.success_criterion: A saved submission NetCDF in the challenge format (t2m and tp, lead_time weeks 3-4 and 5-6, all 53 2020 start dates, tercile probabilities) plus code, trained only on hindcast/observation data allowed by the challenge rules (no 2020 observations), whose RPSS computed by the challenge's own scoring code (s2s-ai-challenge-template RPSS_verification notebook / scorer, unmodified) against the 2020 terciled observations is strictly greater (direction: max) than the best RPSS on the leaderboard README at https://github.com/aaronspring/s2s-ai-challenge-leaderboard re-fetched live immediately before claiming, by at least 0.002, and greater than any RPSS for the same 2020 test reported in papers of the last 24 months (search 'S2S AI challenge RPSS', including Horat and Lerch's subseasonal post-processing work and the challenge overview by Vitart et al.).
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the needed ECMWF forecast, hindcast and observation files from the object store, runs the unmodified scorer from the template repository on the saved NetCDF, checks that the training code never opens 2020 observation files (sandbox run without them), and compares to the live leaderboard. A few hours.

angles: Conventional: EQcorrscan template matching from ComCat templates in sparse-network regions (Basin and Range, Great Plains induced-seismicity areas, Alaska interior).
Conventional: PhaseNet/EQTransformer via SeisBench on CPU followed by GaMMA association.
Cross-domain import (radio astronomy/pulsar search): matched filtering with a dedispersion-like moveout stack (beamforming across stations) to detect coherent arrivals below single-station SNR.
Cross-domain import (gravitational-wave data analysis): chi-square signal-consistency veto and time-slide background estimation to control false detections.
Cross-domain import (speech recognition): spectrogram fingerprinting (FAST, locality-sensitive hashing) to find repeating events without templates.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.name: Missed local earthquakes in open EarthScope/IRIS waveforms, above the regional completeness magnitude, absent from USGS ComCat

partial_wins.statement: A missed event of magnitude >= Mc - 0.3 with the same location-quality requirements, in a ComCat-authoritative network region (not offshore). The epicentre is in a ComCat-authoritative network region when USGS geoserve returns an ANSS authoritative region for it (https://earthquake.usgs.gov/ws/geoserve/regions.json with type=authoritative; as of 2026-10-28 these are the regions of AK, CI, HV, NC, NM (New Madrid), NN, OK, PR, SE, TX, UU (Utah and Yellowstone) and UW). Where geoserve returns none, NEIC (us) is authoritative only by default and the event does not count for p1, even if a regional network without an authoritative region (for example MB in most of Montana) contributes most local events.

A template-matching catalogue for one sparse-network region and year that recovers >= 95% of ComCat events there and adds >= 3x more detections, each with CC >= 0.6 on >= 3 stations, saved and re-runnable.
A ComCat event demonstrably mislocated by > 20 km (re-location with >= 8 picks and RMS <= 0.3 s), saved with picks.

pitfalls: Most detections are below Mc and trivially 'missed'; the Mc criterion is mandatory.
Quarry/mining blasts and noise bursts (wind, traffic) mimic events - check time-of-day patterns and S/P amplitude ratios; ComCat often lists blasts separately (eventtype=quarry blast).
Teleseismic phases or aftershock coda can be mis-associated as local events.
ComCat updates with delay; very recent windows may be missing events that will appear - use windows older than 6 months.
Never report to USGS or any agency.
targets.statement: USGS ComCat (live FDSN event service) is the authoritative US catalog; open continuous waveforms are served by the EarthScope/IRIS FDSN dataselect service. Template matching and ML pickers routinely find 2-10x more events than standard catalogs, mostly below completeness. The open, non-trivial task: an earthquake at or above the regional magnitude of completeness that ComCat (and ISC) do not list, in a region/time where no published enhanced catalog covers it.
targets.success_criterion: A saved event package (origin time, location, depth, local magnitude with method, >= 8 P/S picks on >= 4 public stations, FDSN request URLs on service.earthscope.org, detection code) such that: the skeptic's independent re-location (e.g. NonLinLoc/HypoInverse-style grid search) gives RMS <= 0.3 s and horizontal error <= 5 km; the detector run on a null set (the same continuous data with station traces circularly time-shifted against each other by >= 10 min, or time-reversed) yields an expected false count < 0.05 over the searched span at the candidate's statistic; the magnitude is >= the regional ComCat completeness magnitude Mc computed by the skeptic (maximum curvature + 0.2) from a live ComCat query for that region over the 5 surrounding years; not a quarry blast (daytime-cluster and S/P amplitude checks; ComCat eventtype filters); and a live ComCat query (and the ISC bulletin if reachable) re-fetched immediately before claiming returns no event within +/- 30 s and 50 km. Must not be inside the space-time window of a published enhanced catalogue (e.g. QTM Southern California, Ross et al. 2019) unless absent there too.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic fetches the listed waveforms from the FDSN dataselect URLs (minutes), hand-checks picks on band-passed traces, re-locates with a 1D regional model, recomputes ML from Wood-Anderson-simulated amplitudes, recomputes Mc from a live ComCat query, and runs the live ComCat absence query. Under 1 hour.

Many 'new' tracks are known comets reported by hunters days or years ago; search all report tables, including retracted and 'additional observations' rows.

targets.statement: The NRL Sungrazer Project homepage reads '5,204 Comets Discovered So Far' (2026-10-15); public report tables include LASCO C2/C3 and GOES-19 CCOR-1/CCOR-2 reports (new reports daily), and confirmations lag by about a year (July-August 2025 confirmations posted 2026-05-28). Meteotsunami hunting: match gauge oscillations with pressure jumps in open surface-pressure data and propagation speeds near sqrt(g h).
Cross-domain import (seismology): STA/LTA triggers and array beamforming across many gauges, treating the gauge network like a seismic array.

targets.name: Tsunami recorded on open tide-gauge data but absent (as an event or at that gauge) from the NCEI Global Historical Tsunami Database

partial_wins.statement: Gauge observations (amplitude, arrival) for a listed NCEI event at >= 2 gauges where NCEI has no runup rows for those stations.
A meteotsunami (atmospheric pressure jump with matching propagation speed) with > 0.3 m amplitude on >= 2 gauges not in NCEI.

A completeness map, reproducible from saved code: of the USGS ComCat M >= 6.5 earthquakes of 2015-2025 that are shallow (ComCat depth <= 70 km) and subsea (epicentre in an ETOPO1 water cell; this drops the NCEI-listed Kaikoura 2016 and Palu 2018 tsunamis, whose epicentres fall on land), the fraction with a tsunami signal on open gauges (IOC SLSMF only; a signal is the main criterion's per-gauge test with its timing window and control days), set against NCEI's listing. The fraction is over the quakes with at least one usable open 1-min gauge within a travel-time range stated before scoring, usability judged only from data availability and the pre-event reference window; the coverage count and bounds on the fraction over all qualifying quakes are reported too.

pitfalls: Seiches and harbour resonances ring at similar periods on most days; the control-day test is mandatory.

Tide-gauge glitches, datum runs and data gaps produce spikes; reject series with level runs, but state before scoring how many identical minutes count as a stuck sensor and in which hours you test for them: gauges that report in 1 cm steps repeat a value for long stretches around high and low water, and during a tsunami. On 2025-07-29/30, IOC petr and nksk (Kamchatka) had 20 and 26 runs of 10 or more identical minutes in the 24 h before the M8.8 origin (the longest 48 and 63 min) and runs of 10-13 min within 6 h after it.
Storm surges and infragravity waves during storms mimic small tsunamis; check weather.
NCEI may list the event under a different source time or as a 'questionable' validity code; search with tolerance and all validity codes.
Do not report to NCEI or IOC; the claim is a vetted candidate.

A +/-10 min arrival window is tight even for real tsunamis. On NCEI's own tide-gauge rows of definite earthquake tsunamis in 2005-2025 with an NCEI travel time of 15-120 min (298 rows, 81 events), first-arrival times from NCEI's epicentre (second-order fast marching with sqrt(g h) on ETOPO1 at 2 arcmin, gauge snapped to the nearest water cell) differ from NCEI's travel time by more than 10 min for 52% of rows (95% CI 36-67%, bootstrap over events), and for 38% of rows of M < 7.5 sources; 74% are within +/-20 min, and 6 of the 44 events with two or more rows have all rows within +/-10 min. A maintainer re-implementation on 2026-10-24 (32-neighbour Dijkstra on a 3.7 km azimuthal grid, at most 1.4% slow on a flat ocean) gave 51% of 300 rows outside +/-10 min (95% CI 36-65%), 34% for M < 7.5, 75% within +/-20 min and 8 of 44 multi-row events with all rows within +/-10 min. Validate the travel-time model against NCEI arrivals and report its error before scoring.

Model travel times depend on the solver and the coast. Grid-graph shortest paths (Dijkstra) are always too slow, by an amount that depends on direction and, on a latitude/longitude grid, on latitude: on a flat ocean over 800 km the worst direction is +8.2% for 8 neighbours and +2.7% for 16 neighbours at the equator, and +15.0% and +6.6% at 60 degrees on a 0.1 degree grid (the 16-neighbour figures were measured by walshne-mit on PR #371 and reproduced independently). Check the claimant's own solver on a flat ocean against the analytic time before scoring. At the coast, gauges snapped to cells shallower than 10 m come out late (median +13 min against NCEI), and snapping to depth >= 20 m lowers the median over all rows from +6.7 to +2.3 min; the #253 models, which treated cells shallower than 5 m as land, came out early (-1.5 to -3.5 min). Fix the solver, depth floor and snapping rule before scoring.

Coverage for p3: of the 264 USGS ComCat M >= 6.5, depth <= 70 km earthquakes of 2015-2025 with an epicentre in an ETOPO1 water cell (2 arcmin), 6 have no IOC SLSMF station of any status within 1,500 km and 42 none within 500 km, and an epicentre-in-water rule drops NCEI-listed tsunamis whose epicentres are on land (Kaikoura 2016, Palu 2018). Count quakes without usable open gauge data explicitly.
targets.statement: The NOAA NCEI/WDS Global Historical Tsunami Database (HazEL) lists ~1,600 confirmed events with runup and tide-gauge observations; NCEI's own completeness studies (Wright, Arcos, Varner and Stroker 2021) note that small tsunamis seen only on tide gauges can be missing. The IOC Sea Level Station Monitoring Facility serves 1-min data from 1,000+ gauges openly. Open task: find a tsunami signal (from an earthquake, landslide, volcano or meteotsunami) clearly recorded on >= 2 open tide gauges that NCEI lists neither as an event nor as a runup/gauge observation at those stations.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (raw IOC SLSMF series for >= 2 gauges, de-tiding code, the travel-time model code, source parameters) showing: on each gauge, a band-passed (2-120 min) signal with peak amplitude > 5x the RMS of the preceding 24 h in the same band; arrival times at all the gauges the claim names in PREREG.md before scoring (at least 2) consistent within a window W with travel times computed from the source. For an earthquake (USGS ComCat) the travel times come from the claimant's own shallow-water model, and W is fixed in PREREG.md before scoring from a held-out check of that model against NCEI tide-gauge arrival times (the NCEI rows used, which exclude the claimed event, the model's errors on them and the rule that turns them into W are recorded there), and is at most +/- 20 min. For a meteotsunami (a pressure jump with propagating-front check) the timing model (the passage of the pressure front, or a reflected branch whose source region and reflection time are taken from meteorological data) is fixed in PREREG.md from meteorological data before scoring and validated on a separate NCEI-listed event named there (for example NCEI 5483 of 2013-06-13, which Wertman et al. 2014, doi:10.1038/srep07143, timed this way), with W set from that validation and capped the same way. W is used unchanged on the control days, where the signals must be absent on the same gauges in the same hours, and in the null test (kit/RUN.md step 3b, at least 400 controls), which reruns the whole pipeline with fake origin times. And the NCEI events API (https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/hazel/hazard-service/api/v1/tsunamis/events) and runups API, re-fetched live immediately before claiming, have no event within +/- 1 day of the source in that region (main win) or no runup row for those gauges (partial win). WORDING OF 2026-10-29 (issue #253): the window W, 'all gauges' as the gauges named before scoring, the meteotsunami timing rule and p3's denominator and terms apply to claims filed after this wording reached the bank on main; claims filed earlier (#642 and #736 among them) are judged on the wording in force when they were filed (arrival times at all gauges within +/- 10 min of the computed travel times, and p3 with no stated denominator).
targets.verification_method: Skeptic re-downloads the IOC SLSMF series (GET service.php query=data), re-runs de-tiding and band-pass, checks the travel-time model's held-out validation and the window W recorded in PREREG.md before scoring (W at most +/- 20 min, the claimed event left out of the validation rows; for a meteotsunami a timing model fixed from meteorological data and validated on a separate listed event), reruns the claimant's frozen travel-time model from the bundle (cross-checking its times against its own bathymetry-based or simple shallow-water estimate), applies the same W to that model's times at the named gauges, on the control days and in the fake-origin null, and re-queries the NCEI API. Under an hour, plus the null rerun.

targets.name: Volcanic thermal anomaly in open Sentinel-2 imagery at a volcano with no corresponding Smithsonian GVP eruption record

partial_wins.statement: A reproducible thermal time series that extends a GVP eruption's end date (activity persisting >= 30 days beyond the listed stop date) in >= 3 clear scenes.

Sun-glint off crater lakes and bright fumarole-free rock in high-sun scenes produce false hot pixels; use night or low-glint tests and baseline per season.
GVP records may lag but local observatories (e.g. PHIVOLCS, KVERT, SERNAGEOMIN) may have reported it; the novelty claim is relative to GVP only and must say so.

The GVP website pages may block scripts; use only the WFS service and do not contact GVP.

Sentinel-2 L2A imagery (open on AWS via the Element 84 Earth Search STAC API) detects hot surfaces (lava, domes, vents) in SWIR bands at 20 m; MIROVA (Coppola et al.) monitors many volcanoes but not all. Remote volcanoes in Melanesia, the Kurils, the Aleutians, South Sandwich and Andes can have unreported low-level activity. targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (Sentinel-2 L2A scene IDs, SWIR band 11/12 chips, detection code) showing a hot-pixel cluster (normalized thermal index or B12 radiance > 5 sigma above the volcano's own clear-sky baseline) within 2 km of a GVP Holocene volcano vent in >= 3 separate clear acquisitions spanning >= 10 days; the same detector run on a null set (the same scenes at >= 300 randomly placed non-volcanic control points of similar terrain, and the volcano's own scenes with dates permuted) gives an expected false count < 0.05 for >= 3-scene detections over the searched span; not explained by wildfires, sun-glint or cloud artefacts (morphology confined to crater/vent); at dates outside every eruption interval for that volcano in the GVP WFS layer GVP-VOTW:Smithsonian_VOTW_Holocene_Eruptions (re-queried live immediately before claiming; open-ended eruptions treated as continuing); and with no GVP Weekly/Bulletin report covering that activity found by text search.

targets.name: Decametric-hectometric type II radio burst in open Wind/WAVES (and STEREO/WAVES) data absent from the CDAW type II list

partial_wins.statement: A listed burst whose end time or end frequency is wrong by > 1 h or a factor 2 in frequency, demonstrated with the same detection and null test.
A blind detector that recovers >= 90% of the list's 2011-2014 bursts with fewer than 1 false lane per month, saved and re-runnable.
A candidate after 2024-12-29 (beyond the list's current end) meeting all criteria, labelled 'not yet catalogued' rather than 'missed'.

The list is human-curated from dynamic spectra, so faint, short or overlapping bursts can be missed. Open task: a DH type II burst in public Wind/WAVES data with a supporting CME that the list does not contain.
targets.success_criterion: A saved candidate (start/end UT, frequency range, drift rate, Wind/WAVES RAD1/RAD2 file names, extracted dynamic spectrum, detection code) such that: an emission lane with negative drift consistent with a shock speed of 300-3000 km/s in a standard coronal density model persists >= 10 min at >= 3 sigma above the frequency-channel background and is seen in both Wind and (after 2006-10) at least one STEREO/WAVES receiver or with fundamental-harmonic structure; the same detector run on time-reversed spectra (positive drifts) and on the full 1996-2024 data gives an estimated false-alarm count below 0.05 at the candidate's statistic; a CME in the CDAW SOHO/LASCO catalog launched within 2 h before the burst with speed >= 400 km/s; and no entry overlapping the burst time in https://cdaw.gsfc.nasa.gov/CME_list/radio/waves_type2.html re-fetched live immediately before claiming, including 'uncertain' rows.
targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the cited Wind and STEREO WAVES files from SPDF, recomputes background-normalised dynamic spectra, re-fits the drift, reruns the time-reversed null, checks the CDAW CME catalog and the type II list. Under 45 minutes.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Erdos #107 (Happy Ending): 33 points with no convex heptagon
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster
targets.statement: f(n), the least N such that any N points in general position contain a convex n-gon, is conjectured to equal 2^{n-2} + 1.
