A lunar-sequence prediction: a model of Guy's Mamari lunar canon (night-name sequence with intercalary insertions), frozen before searching, finds a sequence of 28-30 aligned positions on a tablet other than Mamari (C) whose alignment to the Mamari calendar beats both shuffle nulls at Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.001, absent from the published parallel lists, visually confirmed on the tracings.

A merge set derived without held-out tablets that recovers at least 10% more known parallels on held-out tablets than Horley's basic-glyph map, with p < 0.01 against random merge sets of the same size and the same resulting inventory size, under at least 2 catalogues.

targets.verification_method: The verifier obtains the corpus via jgregoriods/rongopy or ipezygj/rongorongo-catalogue-audit fetch_data.py (recording hashes) and cross-checks against kohaumotu http pages. It reruns Smith-Waterman with the stated matrix, recomputes both shuffle nulls with Bonferroni correction, diffs against the published parallel lists and parallels3 output, and checks the passage image by image on the tracings.

targets.name: Voynich: a manually executable generator that matches held-out structural fingerprints, or a decisive falsification of the Naibbe cipher
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The Voynich manuscript (Beinecke MS 408) is unread. It is still open whether the text is an enciphered natural language, a constructed system, or meaningless. Greshko's Naibbe cipher (Cryptologia, Nov 2025) is a verbose homophonic substitution of Latin/Italian, executable with cards and dice, that reproduces many Voynich statistics at once. Two 2026 papers add structural fingerprints that no generator was designed for. Parisel (arXiv 2604.25979) shows the Currier A/B split reduces to a per-folio boolean switch on the vowel after ch/sh. Rozanova & Temerev (arXiv 2608.17096) show that glyph regularity exceeds simple substitution, that structure concentrates at token edges, and that spaces form two regimes. The open sub-problem: does any historically plausible, hand-executable generator reproduce all known fingerprints, including ones not used in its design? Already published: Naibbe fails edge-glyph coupling (about 0.006 bits vs the manuscript's 0.197) and the singleton-type rate (about 41-42% vs about 70%) per arXiv 2608.17096 Table 7, independently reproduced by voynich-collective PR #16 (2026-09-19); slot and Cardan-grille generators fail the four-signature joint test calibrated per Currier dialect (arXiv 2604.19762, Apr 2026). Status as of 2026-10-03: Unsolved; no accepted decipherment as of 2026-10-03. The leading hand-executable generator, Naibbe (Greshko, Cryptologia 2025), matches glyph-level entropy, BPE gap and token order. It is published to fail edge-glyph coupling and the hapax-rich vocabulary (Rozanova & Temerev arXiv 2608.17096, Aug 2026; voynich-collective PR #16, Sept 2026). Slot and grille generators fail the 4-signature joint test (arXiv 2604.19762, Apr 2026).
targets.success_criterion: Two outcomes qualify. (A) A generator. It must reproduce, per Currier dialect (A and B separately) and on both ZL3b and IT2a, all of the following within the 95% envelope of the Voynich values: (i) the two Naibbe failure statistics as defined in 2608.17096, edge-glyph coupling (bits and share of entropy) and singleton-type rate; (ii) all four signatures of 2604.19762; (iii) Parisel's per-folio switch statistic. It must also reproduce at least 4 further pre-registered statistics never used in tuning (held out). It must be hand-executable: at most 200 table entries plus a written procedure, and at most 1 per-folio state bit beyond the tables. Run it on at least 20 plaintexts from at least 2 period languages x 10 seeds. If space-regime statistics are included, the generator must emit its own uncertain-space channel under a pre-declared rule. (B) A falsification of Naibbe on a pre-registered statistic NOT among edge-glyph coupling, singleton or hapax rate, the 2604.19762 signatures, or limitations in Greshko 2025. Naibbe output (unmodified author code, default parameters, at least 20 plaintexts x 10 seeds) must fall outside the 99.9% Voynich envelope on A and B and on both transliterations. Neither outcome is a decipherment. The 95% and 99.9% envelopes are computed at verification time from ZL3b-n.txt and IT2a-n.txt as then published; any generator or falsification published after 2026-10-03 that already achieves the claimed outcome voids novelty.

partial_wins.statement: A hand-executable generator (at most 200 table entries plus a written procedure, at most 1 per-folio state bit) whose output, over at least 20 plaintexts from at least 2 period languages x 10 seeds, falls inside the 95% Voynich envelope for BOTH Naibbe failure statistics of arXiv 2608.17096 (edge-glyph coupling in bits and share of entropy; singleton-type rate), on Currier A and B separately and on both ZL3b and IT2a, while staying inside the envelope on h2 conditional entropy and the word-length distribution.

A hand-executable generator (same limits) that passes all four signatures of arXiv 2604.19762 jointly, per Currier dialect and on both transliterations, which the published slot and Cardan-grille generators fail.

A single per-folio state bit added to the unmodified Naibbe tables (no other parameter change) that reproduces Parisel's (arXiv 2604.25979) per-folio ch/sh-vowel switch statistic inside the 95% envelope on Currier A and B and both transliterations, while not leaving the envelope on any statistic Naibbe already matches.

targets.verification_method: The verifier downloads ZL3b-n.txt and IT2a-n.txt (both returned HTTP 200 on 2026-10-03; record hashes) and parses IVTFF with Currier tags. It reimplements every statistic independently, including the 2608.17096 and 2604.19762 definitions, and confirms its reimplementation reproduces their published Voynich and Naibbe values before scoring the claim. It runs the submitted generator with its own plaintexts and seeds, checks the pre-registration timestamp in git, and for (B) runs greshko/naibbe-cipher unmodified.

targets.name: MOONSHOT: Voynich manuscript, a key that decrypts held-out folios into meaningful text
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days
targets.statement: Find a key or procedure that maps Voynichese to plaintext in a natural language, and that generalizes to folios not used in building it. Status as of 2026-10-03: Unsolved as of 2026. Multiple 2026 claims (Delgado's Latin, a Galician reading) have no acceptance. The Naibbe cipher (2025) is a generation model, not a decryption.
targets.success_criterion: All of these must hold. (1) The key is fully specified and deterministic, or has bounded ambiguity of at most 2 readings per token, and is frozen before testing. (2) Applied unchanged to at least 10 held-out folios chosen by the verifier, it yields text whose per-character perplexity under a period language model (for example, a 15th-century Latin or Italian corpus) is at least 1.5 bits/char better than the same key applied to glyph-shuffled versions of those folios. (3) Key description length plus plaintext entropy is less than the entropy of the Voynich text under its best compressor (an MDL check against key overfitting). (4) At least 3 plant or star names decrypted on herbal or astro folios match identifications agreed by an independent botanist or astronomer reviewer who has not seen the claimed reading. (5) The frozen key applied to (a) Naibbe-cipher output encrypting a different language and (b) an arXiv 2604.19762-style slot-generator output must give per-character perplexity at least 1.0 bits/char worse than on the held-out Voynich folios. A key that 'decrypts' generated gibberish equally well is rejected.

partial_wins.statement: A frozen key (deterministic, at most 2 readings per token) that, on at least 10 verifier-chosen held-out folios, gives per-character perplexity under an independent period language model at least 1.5 bits/char better than on glyph-shuffled versions of those folios AND at least 1.0 bits/char better than on the verifier-generated structured-gibberish controls (Naibbe output of a different language; slot-generator output), i.e. criteria (2) and (5) without (3) and (4).

Blind illustration match alone: a frozen key decrypts at least 3 plant or star names on verifier-chosen herbal or astronomical folios that match identifications made independently by a botanist or astronomer reviewer who has not seen the claimed reading, while the same key applied to the structured-gibberish controls yields no such matches.

targets.verification_method: The verifier selects held-out folios with its own seed, runs the frozen key, and computes the perplexity against shuffled controls with an independent language model. It checks the MDL accounting and arranges the blind illustration-match review. Additionally, the verifier generates the structured controls itself with fresh seeds and scores them under the same period language model.

targets.name: Condorcet domains: a larger domain than the best published one for some n in 9..25
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: A Condorcet domain on n alternatives is a set of linear orders such that the pairwise majority relation of every profile with an odd number of voters drawn from the set is transitive. Equivalently (Sen 1966), the restriction to every triple of alternatives satisfies a never condition: some alternative of the triple is never first, never middle or never last within that triple. The maximum size is known exactly only for n <= 8 (1, 2, 4, 9, 20, 45, 100, 224; n = 8 by Leedham-Green, Markstrom and Riis, arXiv:2303.15002; all maximal domains for n <= 7 by Akello-Egwel, Leedham-Green, Litterick, Markstrom and Riis, Math. Soc. Sci. 2024). Fishburn's alternating scheme (Social Choice and Welfare 14 (1996) 113-124) gave the long-standing values (488 for n = 9, 1069 for n = 10, 2324 for n = 11); Zhou and Riis (arXiv:2303.06524) raised n = 10 to 1082 and n = 11 to 2349; Karpov and Slinko (Theory and Decision 2023) gave a product construction and the asymptotic bound 2.1890^n; Karpov, Markstrom, Riis and Zhou (arXiv:2308.02817, Discrete Applied Mathematics 370 (2025) 57-70) introduced set-alternating schemes and coherent domains of size above 2.1973^n. The current table is Table 4 of Karpov, Markstrom, Riis and Zhou, 'Improved lower bounds for the maximum size of Condorcet domains', arXiv:2601.07336v1 (12 Jan 2026): for n = 9..20 an inductive search on a supercomputer (stopped at n = 20) gave 492, 1104, 2452, 5520, 12182, 27026, 59430, 131536, 292015, 649079, 1432836, 3155366; for n = 21..25 the Karpov-Slinko construction applied to those domains gave 6674931, 15037178, 33162136, 73279872, 160316046 (marked ks); the asymptotic bound is now Omega(2.198139^n). As of 2026-10-24 the abstract page lists v1 only. Find a larger domain for some n in 9..25.
targets.success_criterion: (1) The object is a never-condition assignment A: exactly one line 'a b c iNj' for each of the C(n,3) triples a < b < c of 1..n, meaning the i-th smallest of {a,b,c} is never in position j (1 = top, 3 = bottom) within the triple. The claimed domain is D(A), the set of ALL linear orders of 1..n obeying every line; it is a Condorcet domain by Sen's theorem, so no separate acyclicity check is needed. This loses no generality: every Condorcet domain lies inside D(A) for an assignment A it satisfies. (2) |D(A)| is counted exactly (not sampled, not estimated) by two independent implementations, for example a forward DP over prefix sets, and both agree with the claimed value. (3) n is in 9..25 and |D(A)| is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than every one of the following, each re-checked at verification time: the n entry of Table 4 of the latest version of arXiv:2601.07336 (status_source; v1 values: n=9 492, 10 1104, 11 2452, 12 5520, 13 12182, 14 27026, 15 59430, 16 131536, 17 292015, 18 649079, 19 1432836, 20 3155366, 21 6674931, 22 15037178, 23 33162136, 24 73279872, 25 160316046), any larger value found by a fresh search of arXiv and the 2025-2026 literature, and any value for the same n already in TROPHY_CASE.md or known-knowns/condorcet-domains/. If the status source cannot be read honestly, the claim is 'PENDING TABLE CHECK', not a record. (4) An explicit list of orders is optional; if shipped it must obey kit/SUBMIT.md (files at most 1 MB, packages at most 50 MB, larger files outside git), and the assignment remains the object that is judged.

partial_wins.statement: Problem 2 of arXiv:2601.07336: determine h(9), the maximum size of a peak-pit Condorcet domain on 9 alternatives, or g_w(9), the maximum size of a Condorcet domain of maximum width (one containing an order and its reverse) on 9 alternatives, by a re-checkable certificate (an exhaustive search with its full log and an independent re-run, or a DRAT/LRAT proof checked with an independent checker); or prove an upper bound on h(9) or g_w(9) smaller than every upper bound published for it at verification time.

targets.verification_method: The verifier writes an independent standard-library checker and does not run the claimant's code: parse the assignment, require exactly one well-formed line per triple (no missing, duplicate or out-of-range triples), then count D(A) by a forward DP over prefix sets: from a placed set S, alternative v may come next unless some line on a triple {v,x,y} forbids v at position 1 + |{x,y} intersect S|; sum counts into S | {v}; |D(A)| is the count at the full set. Only reachable prefix sets need storing (a few thousand for n <= 25), so this runs in seconds in Python. Cross-check the DP with a second method: brute-force enumeration of the restriction of A to the first 9 alternatives must equal the DP count of that restriction, and the DP on Fishburn's alternating scheme (middle element of {a,b,c} never first if b is even, never last if b is odd) must give 488 for n = 9 and 2115186 for n = 20 (Table 4's Fishburn column). Then re-fetch the status source and the trophy case, and claim only if |D(A)| is strictly larger than all of them and equals the claimed value.
angles: Search over assignments, not over lists of orders: D(A) is determined by one never condition per triple and can be counted exactly in milliseconds, so the objective is cheap and exact inside any local search.
Large-neighbourhood search: re-optimise every triple through one or two chosen alternatives at once, exactly (branch and bound or ILP), instead of single-triple moves.
Restrict and extend: delete one alternative from a strong domain on n+1 alternatives, or apply the paper's one-alternative extension step to a strong domain on n-1, then polish.
Rows n = 21..25 of the paper's table come from a product construction rather than search, so they are softer than the n <= 20 rows.
Use the structure of the known maxima (peak-pit conditions 1N3 and 3N1, with some 2N1 and 2N3) as a prior rather than a constraint.
pitfalls: Counting the orders of an assignment with a missing or duplicated triple gives a set that need not be a Condorcet domain; require exactly C(n,3) distinct triples.
Position conventions: whether 1 means top or bottom does not change |D(A)| (reversal is a bijection), but the checker and the claim must use one convention consistently.
Table 4 has other columns (Fishburn's scheme, a formula column ceil((4/5^1.5) * sqrt(5)^n), g(n) for peak-pit domains of maximal width); the record is the f(n) & h(n) column only.
Matching a table value is not a record; neither is a value for n >= 26, where the table has no cell.
Estimating |D(A)| by sampling or by enumerating with a time limit is not an exact count.
The paper's search rows may be superseded by a v2 or a follow-up; always re-read the abstract page's submission history before claiming.

targets.name: Stable marriage: an instance of size n with more stable matchings than the best known (OEIS A357271 and the Ong et al. 2025 instances)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (exact counting through the rotation poset is fast at these sizes; the search is local search over preference lists, embarrassingly parallel)
targets.statement: An instance of the stable marriage problem of size n consists of complete strict preference lists for n men and n women; a perfect matching is stable if no man and woman prefer each other to their partners. How many stable matchings can an instance of size n have? Finding the maximum f(n) is a research problem posed by Knuth (Mariages Stables, 1976) and repeated by Gusfield and Irving (The Stable Marriage Problem: Structure and Algorithms, 1989, Open Problem 1). OEIS A357269 lists exact values for n <= 5 (1, 2, 3, 10, 16; a(5) = 16 by Eilers with a MiniZinc model); M. Jo (Zenodo, 2026-10-13, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23329599, not peer reviewed) claims a computer-assisted proof that f(7) = 85, building on a preprint claiming f(6) = 48, so the exactly known range may extend to n = 7, and Thurber (Discrete Mathematics 248, 2002) proved f(n) strictly increasing; the best general upper bound is Palmer and Pálvölgyi's 3.55^n (arXiv:2011.00915). OEIS A357271 (Dan Eilers, 2022) lists lower bounds for n = 1..28 from Thurber's composition constructions (Appendix C of his 2002 paper): 1, 2, 3, 10, 16, 48, 71, 268, 330, 1000, 1231, 6472, 6720, 20176, 25011, 195472, 200832, 456300, 637336, 3419680, 3506880, 11221136, 15481956, 126112960, 127885440, 262860800, 384418176, 2000043808; a(6), a(8), a(10), a(12) and a(16) are conjectured exact. A file linked from A357271 (Ong, Ang, Ho, Eilers, Marks and Buzi, IFoRE 2024 poster 'Improved Hill Climbing for the Stable Marriage Problem'; the file is dated 2024-11-01 and OEIS labels the link 2025) gives explicit instances that raise the bounds for odd n: 81 (n = 7), 365 (n = 9), 1690 (n = 11), 7123 (n = 13) and 27059 (n = 15). Those gains of 6% to 37% came from plain hill climbing, which suggests that the composition bounds for the other cells are soft. This repository's merged results (known-knowns/stable-marriage-max-stable-matchings/) hold n = 13: 7,698 and n = 15: 30,362 (an earlier n = 15 package has 27,510); merged values count as published values, values in open pull requests do not. As of 2026-10-25 A357271 is at revision #23 (26 May 2025) with the same data line, and the linked instance file still lists 81, 365, 1690, 7123 and 27059.
targets.success_criterion: Success means explicit preference lists for some n >= 6 (n men and n women, each list a permutation of the other side) whose number of stable matchings, counted exactly by two independent methods that agree, is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best known value for that n at verification time. The best known value is the composition closure, not the A357271 data line (which is stale: its odd terms predate the Ong et al. file and its even terms predate composing those instances): the largest count over every instance published for that n (the A357271 data line and its linked file a357271_1.txt, any other OEIS entry or b-file, any paper or preprint, M. Jo's order-7 instance) or merged into this repository (known-knowns/, TROPHY_CASE.md), AND over every composition of such instances (doubling, i.e. the lexicographic product with Knuth's order-2 instance, other products, and Thurber's compositions). The claim must say whether its object is a composition and name its parts; a composition of known instances alone is not a claim. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars, since they can move without anything being published. One cell per claim. A count above a value conjectured exact on A357271 (n = 6, 8, 10, 12, 16) would refute that conjecture and needs an extra independent recount. Submitting a new value to OEIS is an action for a human.

partial_wins.statement: A certified exact maximum for n = 6 (extending A357269): a proof that no instance of size 6 has more stable matchings than the best known value, given as a proof object accepted by a formally verified checker (for example an LRAT proof checked by cake_lpr, or a VeriPB proof) for a constraint model whose correctness is argued in a short note, with symmetry breaking proved sound.

targets.verification_method: Parse the 2n preference lists (or the ranking-table format of the A357271 instance file) and check that each list is a permutation. Count stable matchings with two programs that share no code: (1) the Irving-Leather method, i.e. compute the man-optimal stable matching, its rotations and the rotation poset, and count the closed subsets (down-sets) of the poset; (2) an independent enumeration, for example Gusfield's breakmarriage recursion, or brute force over perfect matchings with a stability check for n <= 10. Calibrate both on A357269 (n <= 5), on the published Ong et al. instances (81, 365, 1690, 7123 and 27059 must be reproduced exactly) and on random instances. Re-fetch A357271, its linked file and the repository before claiming.
angles: Hill climbing with exact recounting: the count is a function of the rotation poset, so a move that swaps two entries of one preference list can be re-scored quickly by recomputing rotations; run many diversified restarts in parallel, as the Ong et al. gains suggest.

Grow structure instead of searching blind: Thurber's compositions combine smaller instances (that is where A357271 comes from), but a product does not simply multiply counts (doubling M. Jo's order-7 instance with 85 stable matchings gives 24,992 at n = 14, not 85 x 85 or 2 x 85 squared); compute the composed count exactly, and Latin-marriage constructions give many stable matchings; seed local search with compositions of the best small instances and with Latin-square-based instances, then perturb.

Search the rotation poset directly: many down-sets need wide, shallow posets with few comparabilities; look for preference structures that realise such posets for the target n, then repair them into valid complete preference lists.
Aim at cells where the table value is a plain composition bound (odd n above 15, n >= 17) rather than at the cells conjectured exact.
pitfalls: Count exactly: sampling or estimating the number of stable matchings is not a check, and the two counters must share no code.
Instances must be complete strict preference lists with equal numbers of men and women; ties, incomplete lists and the roommates problem are different records.

The A357271 data line is not the whole table: the linked Ong et al. file holds larger values for n = 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, and other entries (for example A371810) or newer papers may hold more; compare against every source.
A count above a value conjectured exact (n = 6, 8, 10, 12, 16) is more likely a counting bug than a refutation; recount independently before claiming.

Beating the A357271 data line is not enough: doubling or composing published instances already beats it at n = 14, 18, 22 and 28 with no search. Compute the composition closure for your n first and beat that.

targets.name: Two-item auction determinism threshold: a density pair for which Thirumulanathan's c2*(c1) strictly decreases
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days for polynomial-density search, algebraic root isolation and exact inequality certificates; a general positive proof requires additional analysis
targets.statement: D. Thirumulanathan, On Deterministic Optimal Mechanisms in a Two-Item Setting for Distributions with Nondecreasing Density (arXiv:2608.22371; Journal of Mathematical Economics, DOI 10.1016/j.jmateco.2026.103293), states in the footnote to Section 3.1 (after Theorem 5 and Figure 4): "Whether c*2 is an increasing function of c1 or not is still an open problem." This is the explicitly constructed sufficient threshold of Section 3.1, not the minimal true boundary of deterministic optimality. Fix normalized, strictly positive, nondecreasing C1 densities g_i on [0,b_i]. Values for the two items are independent with translated densities f_i(z)=g_i(z-c_i). For c=c1 in [0,1/g1(0)), write G(x)=integral_0^x g1(u)du and q(c) for the unique optimal single-item price, solving q-(1-G(q-c))/g1(q-c)=0. Define h1=1/[g2(0)G(q-c)], h2=[2+max_{0<=x<=q-c}(c+x)g1'(x)/g1(x)]/g2(0), and R=q(1-G(q-c)). The third threshold h3 is the unique h>=1/g2(0) for which, with t=G^{-1}(1/[h g2(0)]), integral_0^t (c+x)g1(x)dx/G(t)=R. Then c2*(c)=max(h1,h2,h3). Theorem 4 guarantees a deterministic separate-sale mechanism above this threshold. Uniform densities already give the increasing expression 2*b2*b1^2/(b1-c)^2. The threshold depends on g2 only through g2(0), so a counterexample is a question about g1. As of 2026-10-25 the arXiv abstract page lists v1 only. This entry asks for a certified counterexample (a strict decrease); a proof that c2* is increasing for every admissible density pair is outside this repository's scope.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit admissible pair of densities (g1 on [0,b1] and g2 on [0,b2], each normalized, strictly positive, nondecreasing and continuously differentiable, as in Theorem 4 of arXiv:2608.22371), preferably polynomials with rational coefficients, and two shifts 0 <= c < c' < 1/g1(0) with certified values showing c2*(c) > c2*(c') strictly, where c2* = max(c2^th1, c2^th2, c2^th3) exactly as defined in Section 3.1 of the paper (the statement above restates the definitions in shifted coordinates). Every quantity that enters the comparison (the monopoly price q at each shift, the maximum in c2^th2, the root defining c2^th3) must be certified by exact algebra (Sturm sequences, isolating intervals with rational endpoints) or rigorous interval arithmetic, and the two enclosures of c2* must be strictly separated. Alternatively, a positive resolution counts only as a kernel-checked formal proof (Lean, Rocq/Coq or Isabelle, with no sorry, admit or extra axioms, and an axiom audit) that c2* is nondecreasing in the shift for the full density class of Theorem 4, stating whether 'increasing' is meant weakly or strictly and handling the equality case; a written or computer-assisted proof whose analytic steps are not formalised does not count. A strict decrease refutes monotonicity in both the weak and the strict sense. Before claiming, re-check arXiv and the journal version for a later answer.
targets.verification_method: Check normalization, strict positivity and nonnegative derivative of the claimed densities on their entire intervals. For polynomial examples use exact integration, Sturm sequences or rational Bernstein/SOS certificates. Isolate each monopoly-price root and prove it is the required global maximizer. Certify h2's global maximum by checking endpoints and every stationary point, not a grid. Isolate h3 using its defining equation and the source's uniqueness property, bound all three h values at both shifts, and verify a strictly separated max comparison. Such a fixed low-degree algebraic witness takes minutes to hours to check. For a formal positive proof, build it in a clean environment, print the axioms used, and check by reading that the formal c2^th1, c2^th2, c2^th3 and the density class match Section 3.1 and Theorem 4.
angles: Search positive monotone polynomial densities for g1. For fixed g2, its value g2(0) only rescales these three threshold expressions.
Track switches between the three active thresholds. A plot of a single branch is not a plot of the maximum.
Use floating point only to locate candidates; convert a candidate to a rational polynomial and obtain exact root and inequality certificates.
pitfalls: The threshold is sufficient and is explicitly not claimed tight. Changing the question to monotonicity of the true optimal-auction boundary is a different problem.
Keep the densities fixed while translating their supports. Comparing different density shapes at different c is not a monotonicity counterexample.
Do not cross the boundary c=1/g1(0); the expression has a prescribed domain and diverges at that boundary.
A sampled decrease, unchecked stationary maximum, or approximate auction solve does not certify this question.
A proof that c2* is increasing counts only as a kernel-checked formal proof for the full density class; a written argument or a check on sample densities is not a win.

targets.name: Most Nash equilibria in a generic 4-player game with two actions each: find 39 or more (bounds 37 and 65), refuting Hertling-Vujić Conjecture 4.5
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exact equilibrium enumeration of one candidate takes 81 small polynomial systems; search over 32 payoff-difference coefficients is embarrassingly parallel)
targets.statement: For a generic finite game the number of Nash equilibria of its mixed extension is finite and odd. Let mu(n; 2,...,2) be the largest number of Nash equilibria in a generic n-player game in which every player has two pure strategies. Known: mu = 3 for n = 2, and mu = 9 for n = 3 (Jahani and von Stengel, 2024). The maximum number of totally mixed equilibria is the derangement number !n (McKelvey and McLennan, 1997). Vidunas (2017) gives the upper bound V(n) = sum over l of n!/l!, so mu(4) <= 65 and mu(5) <= 326. Hertling and Vujić (arXiv:2412.17890, v1 2024-12-23, v2 2026-09-25) prove the lower bound (V(n) + !n)/2 by small generic deformations of 'product two-action games', so mu(4) >= 37 and mu(5) >= 185 (v2's table prints 187 for n = 5, which does not match the formula (326 + 44)/2 = 185), and they 'optimistically' conjecture equality (Conjecture 4.5): mu(4) = 37. Their v2 dropped a chapter because another of their conjectures (5.2) and a theorem (5.3) had a counterexample. As of 2026-10-25 the arXiv abstract page lists v2 (25 Sep 2026) as the latest version, with Conjecture 4.5 unchanged.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED by an explicit game with rational payoffs (for each of the n players a payoff table over the 2^n pure profiles) that is generic in the sense that every equilibrium is regular (for each equilibrium the indifference system of the players who mix has a nonsingular Jacobian there, and every pure-strategy best-response comparison at the equilibrium is strict) and that has (a) at least 39 Nash equilibria for n = 4, refuting Conjecture 4.5, or (b) at least 189 Nash equilibria for n = 5, exceeding both the formula value 185 and the printed 187. The full equilibrium list must be produced by exact support enumeration (all 3^n combinations of 'plays 0', 'plays 1', 'mixes' per player), each support's polynomial system solved exactly (Gröbner basis or resultants with certified real-root isolation), every candidate checked against all best-response inequalities in exact arithmetic, and the count reproduced by a second, independently written enumerator (for example one using a different computer algebra system). Since generic counts are odd, an even count signals an error. Alternatively, (c) a kernel-checked formal proof (Lean, Rocq/Coq or Isabelle, with no sorry, admit or extra axioms, and an axiom audit) that mu(4) <= 63 is also a full win; a written or computer-assisted upper-bound argument whose analytic steps are not formalised does not count. For the equilibrium-count constructions, also beat any higher count from later published games or valid compositions of published games with the same total player count. Disclose whether the game is a composition and cite its components. Unmerged submissions are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit generic 4-player binary-action game with rational payoffs and exactly 37 equilibria, every equilibrium listed with exact algebraic coordinates and certified as in the success criterion. The published lower bound is proved by a deformation argument; an explicit certified example makes it checkable by anyone and gives the search a verified starting point.

targets.verification_method: Reduce each player's payoffs to the difference function D_i(x_-i) = U_i(1, x_-i) - U_i(0, x_-i), multilinear in the other players' mixing probabilities (8 coefficients per player for n = 4). For every support pattern, players who mix must have D_i = 0 at the point, players fixed at 1 need D_i >= 0 and players fixed at 0 need D_i <= 0, with mixing probabilities strictly in (0, 1). Solve each system exactly (for example msolve, Singular or Sage over the rationals) and isolate real roots with certified intervals; check the inequalities with interval or exact arithmetic; check regularity. Test the enumerator on random 3-player games (the count must be odd and never exceed 9) and on the totally mixed bound !4 = 9. For route (c), build the formal development in a clean environment, print the axioms used, and check by reading that the formal definitions of a binary-action game, genericity (regularity) and Nash equilibrium match the paper's.
angles: Count fast, certify slowly: numerically, each candidate needs only the real solutions of 81 small multilinear systems (at most 9 totally mixed points), so a local search over the 32 coefficients can score candidates quickly in floating point; re-certify exactly only games that score 39 or more.

Start from the paper's maximal product two-action games and their deformations (37 equilibria), then perturb away from the product structure; v2 acknowledges an example that led the authors to modify a conjecture, and dropped Conjecture 5.2 and Theorem 5.3 after a counterexample (arXiv comments), so the authors' structured families are evidently not the last word.

Count by face dimension: Vidunas' bound V(4) = 65 adds the per-face maxima (9 totally mixed, plus contributions from faces where some players are pure); look for games where several face types reach their maxima at once instead of trading off.
The 3-player case (9, proved in 2024) is a calibration: a search that cannot find 9 on n = 3 is not ready for n = 4.
pitfalls: Non-generic games (ties, degenerate equilibria, continua) can show larger naive counts; only regular equilibria of a game in which all equilibria are regular count.
Floating-point solvers miss or duplicate roots near the simplex boundary; every counted equilibrium needs an exact or certified-interval proof, and so does the claim that there are no others.
The paper's table entry 187 for n = 5 disagrees with its own formula (185); state which number a claim beats.
Do not confuse this with the maximum number of equilibria of d x d bimatrix games (a different problem) or with the totally mixed maximum !n, which is already settled.
The field is active (v2 posted 2026-09-25 with a dropped conjecture); check arXiv for newer versions before claiming.
An upper-bound argument (for example mu(4) <= 63) counts only as a kernel-checked formal proof (route (c)); a written or computer-assisted argument is not a win under this entry.

targets.name: Binary polynomial multiplication M(n): fewer AND/XOR gates than the best known circuit for n-term polynomials over GF(2)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (straight-line-program heuristics and SAT-based local improvement on circuits of 100 to 8,000 gates; symbolic verification in seconds)
targets.statement: M(n) is the minimum number of two-input AND and XOR gates that multiply two n-term polynomials over GF(2), computing all 2n-1 product coefficients. Only upper bounds are known beyond tiny n. Bernstein's page 'Minimum number of bit operations for multiplication' (binary.cr.yp.to/m.html) tabulates upper bounds for n = 1..1000 from his 2009 work and earlier sources. Find and Peralta, 'Better circuits for binary polynomial multiplication' (IEEE Transactions on Computers 2019, doi:10.1109/TC.2018.2874662), improved many values and posted circuits for n <= 100 (BinPolMult.tar.gz, linked from Peralta's CMT page). NIST's Circuit Complexity list of circuits currently lists M(11) <= 186, M(12) <= 207, M(15) <= 312, M(16) <= 349, M(18) <= 454, M(19) <= 498 and M(20) <= 527 (checked 2026-10-25), and Peralta's CMT page lists M(10) <= 154 and the history of n = 15 (Bernstein 329, Cenk and Hasan 317, Peralta 312). De Piccoli, Visconti and Rizzo, 'Polynomial multiplication over binary finite fields: new upper bounds' (Journal of Cryptographic Engineering 10 (2020) 197-210), give further upper bounds; it is paywalled and its values must be checked before claiming. The frontier is spread over these sources, so the bar for a given n is the minimum over all of them.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit straight-line program over GF(2) for some 2 <= n <= 100, with inputs f0..f(n-1), g0..g(n-1), each line a two-input AND or XOR of earlier values (no constants, no other gate types), and designated outputs h0..h(2n-2), that a symbolic checker confirms computes every h_k = sum_{i+j=k} f_i g_j exactly, and whose gate count is STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the minimum for that n over: Bernstein's table (binary.cr.yp.to/m.html), the NIST list of circuits, the circuits on Peralta's CMT page and in BinPolMult.tar.gz (each recounted with the verifier's own counter), the tables of Find and Peralta (2019), the values of De Piccoli, Visconti and Rizzo (2020), and any later value found by a literature search at verification time. If a paywalled source cannot be read, the claim is PENDING TABLE CHECK until a human has read it. The bar also includes the best valid composition of published circuits for the same n under the same gate count; state whether the candidate is a composition and name its components and composition rule. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: The same kind of strict improvement for some 101 <= n <= 1000 over Bernstein's table and every later published value for that n (Cenk-Hasan 2015 and De Piccoli-Visconti-Rizzo 2020 must be checked), with priority to cryptographic sizes such as n = 113, 127, 128, 131, 163, 193, 233, 239, 251, 256, 283, 409 and 571.

An exact value: for some n >= 3 with no published optimality proof (check the literature first), a SAT encoding of 'n-term binary polynomial multiplication with at most M - 1 AND/XOR gates', where M is the current best upper bound, shown unsatisfiable with a proof accepted by a formally verified checker (cake_lpr), together with a short argument that the encoding is complete for circuits of that size.

targets.verification_method: Parse the program and evaluate it symbolically in the Boolean polynomial ring: represent each wire as the set of monomials it computes over the 2n input variables (XOR = symmetric difference, AND = product reduced with x*x = x), and compare each designated output with sum_{i+j=k} f_i g_j. This is exact and runs in seconds for n <= 100 because these circuits stay bilinear. Count gates (each AND or XOR line is one; renaming or outputting an existing wire is free). Calibrate the counter by recounting Peralta's published circuits for n = 10, 11, 12, 15 and 16 (154, 186, 207, 312 and 349 gates) and Bernstein's straight-line code for one n. Re-fetch the reference pages before claiming. Recompute comparison compositions using the same checker and resource metric.
angles: Polish the linear layers: a Find-Peralta circuit is a top XOR layer, an AND layer and a bottom XOR layer; each XOR layer is a shortest-linear-program problem where heuristics newer than the 2019 circuits (Boyar-Peralta with all ties explored, Tan-Peyrin, cancellation-allowing searches) often shave gates.

SAT-based local improvement (Kulikov et al., 'SAT-based circuit local improvement', 2021): cut windows of 6 to 12 gates out of a record circuit and ask a SAT solver for a smaller equivalent subcircuit; repeat over thousands of windows in parallel.

Change the bilinear formula, not only its wiring: other choices of the products with the same number of AND gates (Montgomery's five-, six- and seven-term formulae, enumerations of optimal bilinear formulae) can have cheaper linear layers.

Recursion bookkeeping for composite n: combine the best k-term formula with the best m-term circuits for every split of n and count shared XORs across recursive calls (Bernstein's refined Karatsuba overlap); sweep all splits automatically for n <= 100 and propagate improvements upward.
A win at n = 64 or 128 (carry-less multiplication, GHASH) or at a NIST binary-curve size is the one practitioners would notice.
pitfalls: Conventions differ between sources (some circuits on these pages use XNOR or constants); this entry counts only two-input AND and XOR gates, so recount every reference circuit with the same counter.
The frontier is spread over several sources (2009-2020), one of them paywalled; take the minimum per n and keep a claim PENDING TABLE CHECK until every source is checked.
Sources are not monotone in n or in date: a later paper can be worse than an earlier one for a given n.
Random-input testing is not a proof for larger n; use the symbolic check.
Depth is not part of this record.

targets.name: Jehn's adversarial coin-basket games: 'Fill your basket' fair compensation beyond n = 16 (OEIS A392305) and the 3-basket guaranteed win beyond n = 14 (A391538, conjectured formula)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (exact minimax with memoisation over (remaining-coin set, sorted 3-basket sums) states plus alpha-beta or decision-version search; about 2^n * P^2/12 states before pruning; a rough estimate, not measured)
targets.statement: Two perfect-information games on coins worth 1..n and three baskets, both by Ruediger Jehn. (1) 'Fill your basket' (A392305, keywords nonn,more, added Jan 06 2026): each of n turns the presenter chooses one of three baskets and the placer puts one remaining coin of their choice into it; at the end the placer scores the largest basket sum and the presenter the second largest; a(n) is the compensation paid to the presenter that makes the game a draw under optimal play, i.e. the minimax value of (largest - second largest). Known for n = 1..16: 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6. (2) A391538 (keywords nonn,more, Dec 12 2025): each turn the opponent chooses one of three baskets and the player puts a coin of their choice into it; at the end the player takes the largest basket; a(n) is the sum the player can guarantee. Known for n = 1..14: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 21, 25, 29, 34, 39, 44, with the entry's CONJECTURED formula a(n) = floor(n(n-1)/6) + n for n > 4 (it is a problem from the Mathekalender 2025 'Game of Chests' challenge by F. Niessen and S. Rathke). The 2-basket version A391537 has a proved closed form floor(n(n-1)/4) + n and is not a target. OPEN as of 2026-10-25: no term beyond n = 16 (A392305) or n = 14 (A391538), and the A391538 formula is unproved. Checked 2026-10-25: A392305 is at revision #13 (20 Jan 2026) and A391538 at revision #18 (30 Dec 2025), with the terms above, no b-files and no pending drafts.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: the exact values of A392305(17), A392305(18), A392305(19), A392305(20) (K = 4 new terms; direction: new terms) under the entry's definition (presenter chooses the basket, then the placer chooses the coin, each turn; payoff = largest basket sum minus second-largest; placer maximises, presenter minimises; a(n) is that minimax value), each with a game certificate: a placer strategy table guaranteeing margin >= a(n) against every presenter choice AND a presenter strategy table holding the margin <= a(n) against every placer choice, both checked by an independent program that walks the (memoised) game graph exhaustively; plus exact reproduction of A392305 for n = 1..16. The terms must not already be in the OEIS entry, its b-file or edit history at verification time. Submitting to the OEIS is an action for the human only.

partial_wins.statement: A391538 for every n from 15 through 22 with the same two-sided certificate (opponent strategy capping the player's guaranteed sum at a(n), player strategy achieving it), reproducing n = 1..14; this confirms the conjectured formula floor(n(n-1)/6) + n on that range or refutes it at the first n where it fails (a certified counterexample to the formula as stated in the entry).
A392305(17) and A392305(18) only, with the two-sided certificate and calibration.

targets.verification_method: Independent minimax from the definition, memoised on (frozen set of remaining coins, sorted basket sums); a terminal state scores largest minus second largest (A392305) or the largest sum (A391538). For a claimed value v, run two decision searches: 'can the placer force margin >= v' (must be true) and 'can the placer force margin >= v + 1' (must be false); each search returns a strategy table (the placer's move per reachable state for the first, the presenter's basket per reachable state for the second) that a third short program checks by exhaustive play-out against all replies. Calibrate on all published terms first. Exact integers throughout.
angles: Decision version with a known bracket: the terms move by at most 1 per step so far, so test v = a(n-1) and a(n-1) + 1 first; each test is a boolean AND-OR search with heavy pruning.
Canonicalise the three sums by sorting; baskets with equal sums are interchangeable, which also prunes the presenter's choices.
Order the placer's coin choices largest-first and the presenter's baskets smallest-sum-first for early cutoffs.

For A391538, compare optimal play against Jehn's stated strategy (spread the first n-1 coins as evenly as possible over the three baskets, keep coin n for last); the first n where an even split of 1..n-1 into three parts is impossible is where to look for a formula failure.
pitfalls: In A392305 the placer scores the LARGEST basket and the presenter the SECOND largest; the third basket scores for nobody.
The presenter moves first in each turn (chooses the basket), then the placer chooses the coin; reversing this order is a different game.
A392305 is a margin game; do not compute the placer's guaranteed sum (that is A391538, a different payoff).
A391538's formula is labelled conjectured in the entry; matching it for n <= 14 is not evidence for larger n.
Memoisation keys must include the multiset of basket sums, not just their total.

targets.name: Shorter addition chains for elliptic-curve field and scalar inversion exponents (Curve25519, P-256, P-384, secp256k1)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (laptop-days for the field-inversion cells); verification takes milliseconds
targets.statement: An addition chain to exponent E gives a fixed schedule of squarings and multiplications. Brian Smith's ECC inversion page and Michael McLoughlin's addchain results give eight reference exponents. For the P-256, P-384 and secp256k1 field entries, E=N-3 computes the square of the inverse. For Curve25519's field entry and all four scalar entries, E=N-2 computes the inverse. Reference lengths are 265, 266, 396 and 269 for those field entries, and 283, 292, 433 and 290 for the Curve25519, P-256, P-384 and secp256k1 scalar entries. Contributors include Bernstein, Gueron, Krasnov, Dettman, Wuille and Smith. These lengths are not optimality proofs. Compare chains only for the same exact exponent.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit addition chain 1 = a_0, a_1, ..., a_L = E, where E is one of the eight exponents N - d listed in addchain's doc/results.md for Curve25519, P-256, P-384 and secp256k1 field and scalar inversion (d=3 for the P-256, P-384 and secp256k1 field entries; d=2 for the Curve25519 field entry and all four scalar entries), in which every a_i (i >= 1) equals a_j + a_k for some j, k < i (j = k is a doubling), checked with exact integer arithmetic, and whose length L is STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the best of: Brian Smith's live page, addchain's live doc/results.md, and any shorter chain for the same exponent published elsewhere (papers or library source such as BoringSSL, Go crypto, fiat-crypto, RustCrypto, curve25519-dalek, libsecp256k1 before its switch to safegcd), which the claimant must search for and cite. Bars on 2026-10-25 (Smith's page, last updated 3 Sep 2017, and addchain's results.md, whose own Curve25519 scalar chain of 283 beats its Best Known column of 284): Curve25519 field 265, P-256 field 266, P-384 field 396, secp256k1 field 269, secp256k1 scalar 290, P-256 scalar 292, P-384 scalar 433, Curve25519 scalar 283. Include the best valid composition of published objects for the same parameters and metric in the bar, even if it is absent from a printed table. State whether the candidate is a composition. Identify its components and composition rule. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: For one of the twelve field-inversion exponents that addchain lists without a published best (M-221, E-222, Curve1174, E-382, M-383/Curve383187, Curve41417, M-511, P-192, P-224, Goldilocks, secp192k1, secp224k1), a verified chain strictly shorter than addchain's listed length and than any chain the claimant finds in papers or public source code for that exponent.

For one of the eight main exponents, a verified chain of the same total length as the live bar but with strictly fewer additions (multiplications), i.e. a cheaper inversion whenever a squaring costs less than a multiplication.

targets.verification_method: Write the chain as a list of index pairs (j, k), or in addchain's acc format (addchain can parse and evaluate it). Recompute every element with Python integers, check that the last element equals the hexadecimal N - d printed in addchain's results.md (and re-derive N from the curve standards), and count doublings (j = k) and additions. As an end-to-end check, follow the chain to compute x^E mod N for 100 nonzero x. Confirm x*x^E=1 mod N when d=2, and x^2*x^E=1 mod N when d=3. Re-fetch Smith's page and results.md before comparing. Milliseconds. Recompute comparison compositions using the same checker and resource metric.
angles: Scalar inversions are the soft cells: n - 2 has a structured top half (runs of ones, cheap through x^(2^k - 1) ladders) and a random-looking low half of about 128 bits (192 for P-384). Optimise jointly the window decomposition of the low half (dynamic programming over splits) and a shortest addition sequence for the set of odd window values (Bos-Coster, Bergeron-Berstel-Brlek, or exact search for small sets).

Use addchain as the baseline and evaluator; widen its dictionary and hybrid algorithms, try many decompositions, and add simulated annealing or beam search over the dictionary terms. Smith's trick of building odd multiples by repeatedly adding 2 generalises to building the needed table as short arithmetic progressions.

Estimate slack first with Schönhage's lower bound l(n) >= log2 n + log2 v(n) - 2.13 and with the typical length of good chains for random 128-bit numbers; spend compute where the gap to the bar is largest.

Field inversion or inverse-square exponents (p - d with long runs of ones) are near-optimal by construction; search over run-length chains (Bernstein's classical chain for 2^255 - 21 builds runs of 5, 10, 20, 40, 50, 100, 200 and 250 ones; addchain's uses 10, 20, 30, 60, 120, 240, 250) jointly with the head and tail, but treat a one-step gain there as a long shot.
pitfalls: Length counts every step, doublings and additions alike, and not the starting 1. Some sources quote squarings and multiplications separately; compare totals.
The chain must reach exactly E=N-d for its table entry. Congruent but different exponents are different targets, and variable-time methods (binary GCD, safegcd) are not addition chains.

Smith's page records hand-optimised chains from 2017 and addchain's 'Best Known' column is a snapshot; library source code may hold shorter unpublished chains, so the novelty search is part of the claim.
Hex transcription errors: derive N from FIPS 186-5, SEC 2 and RFC 7748, and cross-check against results.md.

targets.name: Multiply two 8-term binary polynomials with 25 products (NIST open problem), or a smaller GF(2^8) AES-field multiplier circuit
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (flip-graph or SAT search over rank-25 decompositions); verification takes milliseconds
targets.statement: The full product of two eight-term binary polynomials is a bilinear map with fifteen output coefficients. NIST's Circuit Complexity project page (research direction 4, 'Recurrence relations for binary polynomial multiplication') records the recursion M(8n) <= 26 M(n) + 147 n - 40 of Find and Peralta (IEEE Transactions on Computers 2019, doi:10.1109/TC.2018.2874662), found by a search in a large space (doi:10.1007/978-3-030-34029-2_22), and states as an open problem whether the division into 8 blocks admits a recursion using fewer than 26 binary polynomial multiplications ('we do not know whether there is a solution with leading term 25'; checked 2026-10-25). Because the coefficients are themselves polynomials, the question is whether the 8-term product has a bilinear algorithm over GF(2) with 25 products. Exhaustive searches for optimal bilinear formulae (Barbulescu, Detrey, Estibals and Zimmermann 2012; Covanov, arXiv:1705.07728) settle smaller sizes. For the partial wins, NIST's list of circuits gives standard-basis field multipliers with 117 gates (48 AND, 69 XOR, depth 6) for GF(2^8) modulo the AES polynomial, 84 for GF(2^7) modulo x^7 + x^4 + 1, 85 for GF(2^7) modulo x^7 + x^3 + 1 and 57 for GF(2^6) modulo x^6 + x^3 + 1, matching Peralta's CMT page.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit bilinear algorithm over GF(2) for the product of two 8-term polynomials using at most 25 products, given as 0/1 matrices U (r x 8), V (r x 8) and W (15 x r), where r <= 25 (zero padding to 25 rows is allowed) such that, over GF(2), sum_t U[t][i] V[t][j] W[k][t] equals 1 if i + j = k and 0 otherwise, for all 0 <= i, j <= 7 and 0 <= k <= 14 (direction: min; best known 26), answering the open problem stated on https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/circuit-complexity, provided no publication has already given such an algorithm or proved it impossible (the claimant searches the literature, including doi:10.1109/TC.2018.2874662 and doi:10.1007/978-3-030-34029-2_22). The other answer also settles the open problem: CONFIRMED equally by a proof that no bilinear algorithm over GF(2) with at most 25 products exists for this map, given as a proof object accepted by a formally verified checker (for example an LRAT proof checked by cake_lpr, or a VeriPB proof checked through CakePB) for an encoding of rank-25 decompositions whose correctness is argued in a short note that a skeptic checks against the definition. Include the best valid composition of published objects for the same parameters and metric in the bar, even if it is absent from a printed table. State whether the candidate is a composition. Identify its components and composition rule. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: A circuit of 2-input AND, XOR and XNOR gates (no other gates, no constants) for multiplication in GF(2^8) modulo the AES polynomial x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1, standard polynomial basis in and out, verified on all 65536 input pairs, with at most 116 gates, i.e. strictly below the 117-gate circuit on the NIST list of circuits and below any smaller published one.

The same kind of circuit for GF(2^7) modulo x^7 + x^4 + 1 with at most 83 gates, or modulo x^7 + x^3 + 1 with at most 84, or for GF(2^6) modulo x^6 + x^3 + 1 with at most 56, verified on all input pairs and below any smaller published circuit.

A computational (not certified) answer that 26 is optimal: two independently written exhaustive searches over rank-25 bilinear decompositions of the 8-term product over GF(2), with stated symmetry reductions proved in a short note, that both complete with no solution and that a skeptic can re-run; labelled computational.

targets.verification_method: Main claim: check the 8 x 8 x 15 tensor identity over GF(2) from U, V and W (960 equations), count the rows of U and V, and as an end-to-end check build the induced circuit and compare with schoolbook multiplication on all 2^16 pairs of 8-bit polynomials. Partial wins: parse the gate list, reject any gate other than AND, XOR, XNOR, evaluate all input pairs against a reference field multiplication (2^16 pairs for GF(2^8), 2^14 for GF(2^7), 2^12 for GF(2^6)), and count gates with the same counter applied to the NIST circuit files (data/slp/gf in github.com/usnistgov/Circuits). Milliseconds. Recompute comparison compositions using the same checker and resource metric.
angles: Flip-graph random walks (Kauers-Moosbauer style) on the 8 x 8 x 15 multiplication tensor over GF(2), started from many 26-term decompositions (two-level Karatsuba variants, Chinese-remainder constructions, the published formula), looking for a reduction step; quotient by the tensor's symmetries (swapping a and b, reversing coefficient order).

SAT or MaxSAT encoding of a rank-25 decomposition with symmetry breaking (fix the first products up to the symmetry group); try restricted families first (decompositions containing many rank-one 'evaluation' products), remembering that a negative answer inside a restricted family proves nothing.

Smaller sizes first: reproduce the best published formulas for 5-, 6- and 7-term products (Montgomery 2005; Barbulescu et al. 2012) with the same search, and study what their decompositions share, before searching at 8 terms.

For the field multipliers, optimise the polynomial product and the reduction modulo the field polynomial jointly (the reduction is a fixed linear map, so merge it into the post-processing XOR layer of the bilinear algorithm and run exact or randomised XOR-SLP minimisation).
pitfalls: Read Barbulescu-Detrey-Estibals-Zimmermann 2012, Covanov 2018 and doi:10.1109/TC.2018.2874662 before investing: if any proves rank 26 optimal for 8 terms, the main target is closed. The NIST page still calls the question open on 2026-10-25.

The algorithm must use GF(2) coefficients only, so that it works when the coefficients are themselves binary polynomials. Formulas over GF(4) or with other scalars, or 25-product formulas for other bilinear maps (short product, middle product, circulant product mod x^8 - 1), do not count.

For the field multipliers, inputs and outputs must be in the standard polynomial basis; a tower-field or normal-basis multiplier (such as the 106-gate tower-field GF(2^8) circuit on the CMT page) is a different function.
Gate counting: AND, XOR and XNOR each count one; NOT gates and constants are not allowed in the NIST basis.

targets.name: Exact Nash values of the ICLR-2026 imperfect-information benchmarks: Phantom Tic-Tac-Toe, Abrupt Phantom Tic-Tac-Toe, Abrupt 3x3 Dark Hex, 2-dice 5-face Liar's Dice
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (one exact gradient/best-response pass over 2-3e10 histories took 27-47 s on a 24-core EPYC with 256 GB in the source; thousands of solver passes are needed; measure the memory footprint on the target machine first)
targets.statement: Rudolph, Lichtle, Mohammadpour, Bayen, Kolter, Zhang, Farina, Vinitsky and Sokota ('Reevaluating Policy Gradient Methods for Imperfect-Information Games', ICLR 2026; arXiv:2502.08938v4, 27 May 2026) introduced five two-player zero-sum benchmark games and released exact exploitability code: exp-a-spiel (MIT licence; sequence form with the payoff matrix generated on the fly). The paper reports each game's Nash value (player 1's expected payoff; win +1, loss -1, draw 0) only to about +-2e-4 (Table 1): 2-dice 5-face Liar's Dice LD2D5F 0.01770 +- 1.8e-4 (235.93M states, 15.73M information states); 3x3 Dark Hex DH3 1.00000 +- 0.0 (19.12B states, 6.07M infostates; already solved, since the first player has a deterministic winning strategy, Appendix B); 3x3 Abrupt Dark Hex ADH3 0.38443 +- 2.1e-4 (29.31B, 27.33M); classical Phantom Tic-Tac-Toe PTTT 0.66665 +- 2.6e-4 (19.93B, 5.99M); Abrupt Phantom Tic-Tac-Toe APTTT 0.55017 +- 1.4e-4 (27.12B, 23.31M). Classical rules make a player who collides with a hidden opponent piece choose another cell; abrupt rules make them lose the turn. Their tabular baselines (Table 3, 512 iterations) reach exploitability, the duality gap, of 0.0004070 (PTTT, DCFR), 0.0003577 (APTTT, DCFR) and 0.0006123 (ADH3, PCFR+). One exact best response takes 27 s (PTTT), 47 s (DH3) or 11 s (LD2D5F) on an AMD EPYC 7413 with 256 GB (Table 2). No exact value for PTTT, APTTT, ADH3 or LD2D5F was found as of 2026-10-25 (arXiv v4 of 27 May 2026 is the latest version; an arXiv search for Phantom Tic-Tac-Toe finds nothing newer). The MIT 6.S890 Fall-2024 Phantom TTT challenge (Farina) used the abrupt rule; its best leaderboard entry had per-seat exploitabilities 0.00034 and 0.00027, from a private grader.
targets.success_criterion: For at least one game G in {PTTT, APTTT, ADH3, LD2D5F}, give explicit behavioural strategies sigma1 and sigma2 (a probability vector for every information state) with ALL action probabilities rational. Rules: for the first three games, exactly as implemented in exp-a-spiel (github.com/gabrfarina/exp-a-spiel, commit 9412882c24e521fad7cbd96fdd68311d9bf6f203, or a later commit named in the claim); for LD2D5F, OpenSpiel's liars_dice with numdice=2 and dice_sides=5 as used by the paper. Certify in exact rational arithmetic, with a checker that shares no code with the solver, that L := min over player-2 strategies of u1(sigma1, .) equals U := max over player-1 strategies of u1(., sigma2). L = U is then the exact Nash value of G. Report it as a reduced fraction; it must lie inside the Table 1 interval of arXiv:2502.08938v4 (PTTT 0.66665 +- 2.6e-4, APTTT 0.55017 +- 1.4e-4, ADH3 0.38443 +- 2.1e-4, LD2D5F 0.01770 +- 1.8e-4). Direction: the width of the certified enclosure of the value, from about 3e-4 to 5e-4 in Table 1, down to 0.

partial_wins.statement: For one of the four games, a certified enclosure [L, U] of the Nash value with U - L <= 1e-6, at least 280 times narrower than the game's Table 1 interval. L and U must be the best-response values of explicit strategies, computed with rigorous error control (exact rationals, or floating point with a proven rounding-error bound) and reproduced both by exp-a-spiel at the pinned commit (where it supports the game) and by an independent best-response implementation.

targets.verification_method: Load the strategies into exp-a-spiel at the pinned commit (Traverser.ev_and_exploitability) and record ev0 and the per-player exploitability terms; their sum is the duality gap U - L. Recompute both best-response values with an independent traversal written in a different code base, in exact rational arithmetic (full win) or with a stated rigorous error bound (p1). Check that the strategies are valid: non-negative, summing to 1 at every information state, and zero on illegal actions. Check that the information-state enumeration matches the game. Before trusting the independent checker, calibrate it on DH3: it must agree within one unit of the last printed digit with exp-a-spiel's README output for uniform play in Dark Hex (ev0 = 0.333684, expl = 1.166488, 0.666318) and value 1 for the paper's deterministic first-player strategy. For LD2D5F (not covered by exp-a-spiel's README), two independent best-response implementations must agree. Calibration against printed decimal numbers must agree within one unit of the last printed digit; exact identities and exact source fractions must agree exactly.
angles: Run the paper's own tabular solvers far longer: Table 3 stops at 512 iterations, while days of laptop time allow thousands. Mix in PCFR+ and DCFR with linear or quadratic averaging, then switch to support identification. Zero out actions whose probability is negligible, solve the restricted indifference conditions at the remaining mixed information states, and rationalize.

PTTT's Table 1 value 0.66665 +- 2.6e-4 contains 2/3. Test the hypothesis that the classical Phantom Tic-Tac-Toe value is exactly 2/3. A clean rational would suggest a structural argument and a small certificate; a certified enclosure that excludes 2/3 would refute the guess.

LD2D5F has two orders of magnitude fewer states (235.93M) than the tic-tac-toe and Dark Hex games. A sparse sequence-form LP with iterative refinement and rational reconstruction (e.g. SoPlex in exact mode) may be within reach on a laptop with tens of GB of memory, which could make it the first exact value.
Quotient by symmetry before solving: the tic-tac-toe board has 8 symmetries and Liar's Dice has face and dice-order symmetries. That shrinks memory and makes exact verification cheaper.

Write the independent exact best-response checker first (integer numerators over a common denominator) and test it on the solved DH3 and on small OpenSpiel games (Liar's Dice 1d4f, 2d3f) before running any solver.
pitfalls: Rule variants are different games: classical vs abrupt collision handling, what the opponent observes about a failed attempt, who moves first, and the draw payoff. APTTT is the paper's own implementation (not in OpenSpiel). Liar's Dice bid-order and wild-face rules must match OpenSpiel's liars_dice exactly.
Running the same solvers longer than Table 3's 512 iterations and quoting a smaller exploitability is not a win; only an exact value (full) or a certified enclosure of width <= 1e-6 (p1) counts.
Floating-point best responses accumulated over about 2e10 histories carry rounding error that can approach 1e-7. For p1 the error bound must be part of the certificate.
exp-a-spiel returns exploitability as a per-player tuple; the duality gap is their sum. Do not compare per-seat numbers with sums, or with the private MIT leaderboard.
Memory: the source machine had 256 GB. Measure the traverser's memory footprint before planning long runs on a smaller machine.
DH3 is already solved (value 1) and does not count.
An 'exact' value outside the Table 1 interval almost certainly signals a rules or implementation mismatch, not a discovery.
Exact verification of the tic-tac-toe and Dark Hex games touches about 2e10 histories; budget the verifier's time and memory before claiming, and prefer LD2D5F for a first exact result.

targets.name: Levine's two-player hat puzzle: tighten the published 7/20 and 81/224 bounds, and certify finite-stack optima
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exhaustive or branch-and-bound search over column partitions of a balanced hint matrix; the exact V_{2,4} cell is laptop-minutes)
targets.statement: Two players each wear an infinite stack of independent fair black/white hats, see only the other player's stack, and simultaneously name a position on their own stack; they win iff both named hats are black. V2 is the supremum of the success probability, V2 = lim V_{2,h} where V_{2,h} restricts both stacks to h hats. Lower bound: V2 >= 7/20 = 0.35 via recursive 'skip monochromatic triples' strategies (Carter-Reyes and Tiefenbruck, OEIS A345255/A345257); Bouquet, Chikhi, Charles, Zhou, Wang (arXiv:2508.01737v2, 19 Apr 2026) add an order-5 recursive strategy S5 and an infinite R_t family, all exactly 7/20. Conjecture: V2 = 7/20 (Buhler et al. Conjecture 2; Bouquet et al. Conjecture 1). Upper bound: V2 <= 81/224 ~ 0.361607, proved by Buhler, Freiling, Graham, Kariv, Roche, Tiefenbruck, Van Alten, Yeroshkin ('On Levine's notorious hat puzzle', INTEGERS 21A (2021), arXiv:1407.4711v8) with the 'matrix hint' game on the 8x14 matrix whose columns are the 14 non-constant affine functions on 3 bits (exhaustive over column partitions; 3920 optimal partitions of 8 types). They write that 81/224 'remains the best provable upper bound to date' and suggest the 16x30 matrix of non-constant affine functions on 4 bits, where hill climbs found no partition better than 0.35625 but 'an exhaustive search over all partitions of the 30 columns of this matrix currently seems infeasible'; the 6x20 matrix of weight-3 columns is worse (partitions reaching 117/320 = 0.365625 exist). Heilman and Tamuz (arXiv:2503.09042, 2025) give a computer-free Fourier-analytic bound, quoted by Bouquet et al. as V2 <= 0.37193. Bouquet et al. (2026) still list V2 as unknown with 81/224 as the upper bound. Finite stacks: brute force has settled only h <= 3 (V_{2,3} = 22/64); Buhler et al. also exhausted SYMMETRIC 4-hat strategies only. Best known lower bounds (Bouquet et al., hill climbing plus their recursive inequality; take the larger of their two tables): V_{2,4} >= 0.34765625 (= 89/256), V_{2,5} >= 0.349609375 (= 358/1024), V_{2,6} >= 0.349853515625, V_{2,7} >= 0.34991455078125, V_{2,8} >= 0.3499755859375, V_{2,9} >= 0.3499908447265625, V_{2,10} >= 0.34999847412109375, V_{2,11} >= 0.34999847412109375, V_{2,12} >= 0.34999942779541016, V_{2,13} >= 0.34999990463256836; they call 4 <= h <= 6 'likely sharp', unproven. OPEN as of 2026-10-25: an arXiv search for Levine's hat problem shows no paper newer than 2508.01737v2. 89/256 is a lower bound for V_{2,4}; no published exhaustive search over all (not only symmetric) 4-hat strategy pairs is known to us.
targets.success_criterion: Fair coin (p = 1/2) throughout. FULL WIN is either (A) or (B). (A) Upper bound: a 0/1 matrix M (any size, duplicate columns allowed) in which EVERY column has exactly half of its entries equal to 1, together with an exhaustive certificate, evaluated in exact rational arithmetic, that the matrix-game value V(M) = max over all partitions ~ of the columns of V(M;~) is at most some U STRICTLY LESS THAN 81/224 (direction: min). Here, per Buhler et al. Section 3.2, V(M;~) = (1/n) * E[max_i r_i . v], where r_i are the rows of M, n is the number of columns, and v in {0,1}^n is constant on each class of ~ with independent fair bits across classes; by their Section 3.4 this proves V2 <= U. (B) Beyond the conjecture: an explicit two-player strategy pair (finite h, or a recursive infinite strategy with its renewal formula written out) whose exact success probability is STRICTLY GREATER THAN 7/20 (direction: max), refuting Conjecture 1 of Bouquet et al. In both cases the result must also beat any newer value found on the status source at verification time. The improvement bar includes the best valid composition of published objects under these same rules, as well as direct published objects. Unmerged submissions are not bars. State whether the submitted object is a composition and identify all components and their sources.

partial_wins.statement: Exact V_{2,4}: an exhaustive, re-runnable search (symmetry reduction allowed if the verifier re-checks it) over ALL pairs of 4-hat strategies, not only symmetric ones, giving the maximum success probability as an exact rational with an optimal pair. If the maximum exceeds 89/256 it is also a new best 4-hat strategy.

Exact V_{2,5} with an exhaustive or branch-and-bound certificate, OR an explicit h-hat strategy pair for some 4 <= h <= 13 whose exact success probability strictly exceeds the larger of the two values listed for that h in Bouquet et al. (arXiv:2508.01737v2, Section 3). Compare with the best valid composition of published strategies for that h and disclose whether the strategy is a composition. Recover exact published win-count fractions where possible; if only a rounded decimal bar is available, clear it by one unit of its last printed digit.

The exact, certified value V(M) of the 16x30 hint matrix (rows: the 16 points of F_2^4; columns: the 30 non-constant affine functions on 4 bits) proposed by Buhler et al., even if it is not below 81/224 (settling the computation they called infeasible).

targets.verification_method: For (A) and p3: re-implement V(M;~) from the definition with exact rationals; check every column of M is balanced; calibrate by reproducing 3/8 for the 4x6 matrix of weight-2 columns and 81/224 for the 8x14 affine matrix (all 190,899,322 partitions of 14 columns, minutes in C). Then re-run the claimant's exhaustive or branch-and-bound search with an independently written checker: every leaf must carry a bound <= U derivable from its partial partition, and every symmetry or dominance reduction must be re-verified (for example, that each claimed group element maps M to itself up to row and column permutations). For (B) and p2: count wins over all 2^(2h) hat configurations with integers; for recursive strategies re-derive the renewal formula (Bouquet et al. give (358 - 1)/((2^5 - 1)^2 + 2(2^5 - 1) - 3) = 7/20 for S5; S3 gives (22 - 1)/60) and evaluate it exactly. For p1: re-run the exhaustive search (4^16 ~ 4.3e9 strategies for one player, exact best response for the other: minutes in C) or check the canonical-form reduction and re-run the reduced search. Calibration against printed decimal numbers must agree within one unit of the last printed digit; exact identities and exact source fractions must agree exactly.
angles: Evaluator first: reproduce 81/224 and the 3920 optimal partitions on the 8x14 affine matrix before touching anything larger.

16x30 affine matrix: AGL(4,2) (order 322,560) acts on rows and columns and preserves the game value; enumerate partitions up to this group by canonical augmentation, prune with an optimistic bound for partially assigned partitions, and use the 0.35625 hill-climb value as the incumbent. B_30 ~ 8.5e23 partitions, so pruning, not brute force, decides feasibility.

Search the space of hint matrices, not only partitions: short (few rows), wide (many columns), balanced matrices from designs, codes or group orbits, ranked by a cheap heuristic estimate of V(M) before any exhaustive certification.

p1: the position-relabelling symmetry (S_4 acting on each player's own stack, with the matching change in the other player's view) plus swapping the players shrinks the 4-hat search; the best response of the second player is computed exactly with bitmasks.

(B): the recursive reset construction of Buhler et al. (Appendix E.4) turns an h-hat base strategy into an infinite one; search base strategies at h = 6 or 7 whose recursive value would exceed 7/20, re-deriving the reset bookkeeping for each candidate.
pitfalls: A hint matrix with an unbalanced column biases the referee and voids the upper bound.
V(M) is a maximum over ALL partitions; a hill climb that finds nothing above U proves nothing (the 0.35625 figure for the 16x30 matrix is exactly such an unproved number).
Bigger hint matrices are not monotonically better: the 6x20 weight-3 matrix admits 117/320 > 81/224.
Finite-stack values V_{2,h} are lower bounds on V2; they never bound V2 from above.
The 2014 exhaustive 4-hat search covered symmetric strategies only; p1 needs all pairs.
Bouquet et al.'s 'continuous Levine game' (value exactly 1/2) is a different game.
Use exact integer win counts out of 4^h; floating point cannot separate values near 7/20.
89/256 is only a lower bound for V_{2,4}; matching it is not p1, which needs the exhaustive certificate.

targets.name: Minimum broadcast graphs on 23–25 vertices: improve the remaining edge bounds
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days for constrained graph search with embedded five-round schedules; certificate checks take seconds
targets.statement: Mohammadhossein Fakharan’s November 2025 Concordia PhD thesis, Dimensional Broadcast Schemes and Their Applications in Broadcast Graphs, section 1.3, printed pages 20–21, lists the remaining gaps through n=32: B(23) in {33,34}, B(24) in {35,36}, and B(25) in {38,39,40}. It credits earlier constructions and degree-based lower bounds, including Bermond and coauthors. In the synchronous telephone model, a simple undirected broadcast graph informs all vertices from every possible source in ceil(log2 n) rounds. Each vertex participates in at most one call per round. A call goes from an endpoint informed at the start of the round to an uninformed neighbor. All three cases allow five rounds. The thesis (pages 20-21) says the values of B(23), B(24) and B(25) have been unknown since 2014: B(24) <= 36 and B(25) <= 40 come from constructions of Bermond et al., and B(24) >= 35 and B(25) >= 38 from degree inequalities plus a computer check of graphs of order 24 and 25.
targets.success_criterion: Give a simple graph and explicit five-round broadcast schedules from every vertex, with either 23 vertices and at most 33 edges, 24 vertices and at most 35 edges, or 25 vertices and at most 39 edges. The first two possibilities settle the corresponding exact values using the published lower bounds; a 39-edge 25-vertex graph improves the record, while 38 edges settles B(25). Every source must have its own valid schedule. Also strictly improve the best comparable published result at claim time, including compatible compositions of published objects. State whether the candidate is a composition and identify its components. Values in unmerged pull requests do not set the bar.
targets.verification_method: Check the graph has exactly n labeled vertices, no loops or parallel edges, and the claimed number of edges. For each of n sources initialize only that source as informed. In each round verify that each listed pair is an edge, pairs form a matching, and one endpoint was informed at the start of the round while the other was not. Update all calls simultaneously. After at most five rounds all n vertices must be informed. The entire certificate contains at most n(n−1) transmissions and is tiny.
angles: Start from known 34/36/40-edge constructions and try edge deletion with local rewiring.
Jointly encode graph edges and per-source schedules in SAT, sharing graph variables across sources.
Exploit a graph automorphism only with a verified orbit argument; expand the final certificate to all sources.
pitfalls: Small diameter does not ensure a five-round broadcast under one-call-per-vertex contention.
A schedule from one source is insufficient.
A newly informed vertex can transmit in the next round.
Allowing six rounds changes the problem.
The thesis gives the published numerical gaps as of November 2025; search for later exact-case results before claiming.

targets.name: Single-item auctions: an asymmetric regular instance where Myerson's revenue exceeds second price with the best anonymous reserve by a factor above 2.1596 (JLTX four-buyer record)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (parameter search over 5-50 triangular buyers; certification is closed-form integrals in interval arithmetic)
targets.statement: For independent regular buyers of one item, compare Myerson's optimal revenue OPT with second-price revenue AR under its best anonymous reserve. Jin, Lu, Tang and Xiao (SODA 2019, arXiv:1804.00480, Theorem 3) give a four-buyer triangular example with numerical ratio about 2.1596. It refutes Hartline and Roughgarden's conjecture of 2. The upper bound is the anonymous-pricing constant near 2.62. Feng and Jin (arXiv:2411.03583) describe the remaining ratio as open. The four-buyer parameters are rounded and the calculation is numerical. The bar 2.1600 includes separation from that numerical value. A certificate must bound AR over every reserve, not a sampled grid. Feng and Jin (Result 3 and Theorem 7) still give AR/OPT in [0.3817, 0.4630] for regular buyers and in [0.2770, 0.4630] for quasi-regular buyers, with the 0.4630 end taken from JLTX Theorem 3 (checked 2026-10-25).
targets.success_criterion: An explicit instance of n >= 2 independent buyers with regular distributions, plus a certificate that a skeptic re-runs with interval or exact arithmetic, showing certified OPT/AR >= 2.1600 (higher is better). The distributions must be triangular Tri(v_i, q_i) with rational parameters (Tri(inf) allowed), or other closed-form distributions accompanied by a written regularity proof. The certificate has three parts. (a) A certified lower bound on OPT. For triangular instances sorted v_1 >= ... >= v_n this is JLTX Lemma 1: OPT = sum_i v_i q_i prod_{j<i}(1 - q_j). Otherwise use Myerson's formula with interval-certified integrals. (b) A certified upper bound on AR = sup over all reserves r >= 0 of the expected second-price revenue with anonymous reserve r.
