For triangular instances, JLTX Lemma 9 puts the supremum at some r = v_i, so it suffices to bound every AR(v_i) (closed-form antiderivatives or interval quadrature). For non-triangular instances, give an explicit argument covering all r. (c) The ratio of the two certified bounds is at least 2.1600. That threshold sits above JLTX's rounded 2.1596, so rounding cannot decide a claim. The certified ratio must also be strictly larger than any certified ratio published after JLTX; re-check arXiv before claiming. Handle Tri(inf) through its exact limiting CDF and revenue contribution, not an undefined product of infinity and zero. Apply the finite-reserve lemma only when its hypotheses cover the proposed limiting instance; otherwise certify every reserve. Include reserve-zero and infinite-reserve endpoint limits when needed. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: The same certificate (certified OPT/AR >= 2.1600) for an instance whose distributions are quasi-regular in the sense of Feng-Jin (arXiv 2411.03583) but not all regular. This improves the upper end 0.4630 of the open quasi-regular interval AR/OPT in [0.2770, 0.4630] (Feng-Jin Result 3); that end is currently inherited from JLTX's regular instance.

targets.verification_method: Python with mpmath interval arithmetic (or python-flint/arb), about 150 lines. For a triangular instance, write each CDF in closed form. Compute OPT by JLTX Lemma 1 exactly. For each candidate reserve v_i, compute AR(v_i) = AP(v_i) + integral from v_i to the top of (1 - D2(x)) dx, as in the proof of JLTX Theorem 3 (D2 is the CDF of the second-highest value; with a single unbounded Tri(inf) buyer the integrand vanishes above the largest finite v_i, while two or more unbounded buyers need a rigorous tail bound). Use closed-form antiderivatives of the rational integrand, or validated quadrature with rigorous tail bounds. Calibrate first on JLTX's three-buyer instance (2.1361, with the v2 equation from the proof) and on the four-buyer instance as printed (about 2.1596; record the certified value of the rounded parameters). Printed calibration outputs use tolerance within one unit of the last printed digit. The 2.1600 threshold is a numerical bar; it does not assert an exact incumbent value of 2.1596.
angles: Extend JLTX's equalisation recursion. Their instances choose each new triangular buyer so that AR(v_i) = 1 at every candidate reserve while OPT grows by v_i q_i prod(1 - q_j). Add a fifth, sixth, ... buyer the same way and optimise the free parameters (2 per buyer) numerically, then certify the best point.

Treat it as an adversary problem: maximise OPT subject to AR(v_i) <= 1 for all i, a smooth nonlinear program in 2n parameters. Use multistart, then a final certified evaluation at rational parameters.

Use the conjectured infinite-buyer limit as a guide: fit the optimised (v_i, q_i) sequences for n = 4..30 and look for a continuum profile whose ratio can be computed exactly. A certified limit value would itself be a strong result.
Reading: Myerson discriminates by buyer while the anonymous reserve cannot. Worst cases pile up many small, steep-revenue buyers just below one equal-revenue whale.
pitfalls: AR is a supremum over ALL reserves. Rely on JLTX Lemma 9 only for genuinely triangular instances; otherwise certify every r.
JLTX's four-buyer parameters are printed to 4 decimals and AR ~ 1.0000 is numerical. Its certified value may differ in the 4th-5th decimal, which is why the bar is 2.1600 rather than 2.1596.
Tri(inf) has unbounded support. With one such buyer every AR integral is over a bounded range, but an instance with two or more unbounded buyers needs certified tail bounds, never truncation.
Do not confuse with anonymous PRICING (AP; tight constant C* ~ 2.62, closed), sequential posted pricing vs AP (closed) or eager/lazy personalized reserves (different cells).

Regularity must hold for each buyer. A 'buyer' made of a point mass plus a tail is regular only in the triangular form; other ad hoc mixtures can be irregular, and those count only toward the quasi-regular partial win.

targets.name: Permutation Penney: a pattern that its right rotation does not beat (counterexample to Elizalde-Lin Conjecture 6.1), or certified k = 4, 5
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (exact consecutive-pattern counts and rational tail certificates for small k; a general proof is harder)
targets.statement: Sergi Elizalde and Yixin Lin, Penney’s Game for Permutations, DMTCS 28:1 (2026), Conjecture 6.1, state: "For any k ≥ 3 and any σ = σ1 . . . σk−1 σk ∈ Sk, the permutation τ = σk σ1 . . . σk−1" satisfies Pr(sigma precedes tau)<1/2. Generate independent draws from any continuous distribution and inspect consecutive length-k windows by relative order. Alice first chooses sigma; Bob chooses its indicated right rotation tau. The first chosen consecutive pattern to appear wins. The paper proves k=3 and reports numerical evidence for k=4,5 from truncation at n=11; it does not prove the general conjecture. This is a probability-game response strategy, not the already solved binary-word version of Penney’s game. As of 2026-10-25 the arXiv abstract page lists v4 (6 Jul 2026) as the latest version. This entry asks for certified computations only: a counterexample, or certified verification of the conjecture for k = 4 or k = 5. A proof for all k is outside this repository's scope.
targets.success_criterion: A specific k >= 4 and sigma in S_k whose right rotation tau = sigma_k sigma_1 ... sigma_(k-1) satisfies Pr(sigma precedes tau) >= 1/2 in the game of arXiv:2404.06585 (independent draws from a continuous distribution; the first of the two consecutive patterns to appear wins), certified by a rigorous lower bound: exact integer counts A, B, R of the permutations of length H in which sigma wins by H, tau wins by H, or neither has appeared, with A/H! >= 1/2. Floating-point values and truncated series without the tail term R/H! do not count. Alternatively, a kernel-checked formal proof (Lean, Rocq/Coq or Isabelle, with no sorry, admit or extra axioms, and an axiom audit) of Conjecture 6.1 for every k >= 3 is also a full win; a written or computer-assisted proof whose analytic steps are not formalised does not count. Before claiming, re-check arXiv and DMTCS for a later version or follow-up.

partial_wins.statement: Certified verification of Conjecture 6.1 for k = 4: for every sigma in S_4 (up to justified symmetries), exact integer counts A, B, R at some length H with (A + R)/H! < 1/2, so that Pr(sigma precedes its right rotation) < 1/2 rigorously, beyond the paper's truncated numerical evidence.
The same certified verification for every sigma in S_5. Reproducing the truncated numerical estimates does not qualify.

targets.verification_method: Check that sigma is a permutation and that tau is exactly its right rotation. The verifier writes its own exact counter from the definition (for example a cluster-method or transfer recurrence for consecutive patterns, or the series of Theorem 3.7 of the paper with exact avoidance counts) and cross-checks it against brute force over all H! permutations for H <= 10. Uniform iid continuous draws induce the uniform distribution on the H! relative orders, so if A, B and R count permutations of length H in which sigma wins by H, tau wins by H, or neither pattern has appeared, then Pr(sigma wins) lies in [A/H!, (A + R)/H!]. A counterexample needs A/H! >= 1/2; p1 and p2 need (A + R)/H! < 1/2 for every sigma in S_4 (resp. S_5), with any symmetry reduction (reversal, complement) justified. All counts and comparisons use integers. Reproduce the paper's k = 3 values and its Pr(2341 precedes 1234) ~ 0.443 for calibration. For a formal proof, build it in a clean environment, print the axioms used, and check that the formal game definition reproduces the k = 3 values.
angles: Start by turning the paper’s k=4 numerical evidence into rigorous intervals; retain the unresolved tail explicitly.
Complement symmetry halves the number of permutations to check. Keep all other symmetry reductions justified.
Look for small margins at k=5 or k=6 to prioritize counterexample search. The rotation need not be Bob’s best response to be a winning response.
pitfalls: The relative order of the most recent k-1 draws, by itself, must not be treated as a Markov state with uniform next-rank insertion after conditioning on avoidance. That defines the different model mentioned at the end of the paper.
These probabilities need not be rational; the source proves irrational examples. Require bounds or symbolic real values, not an unjustified rational linear system.
The source’s example sigma=2341 already shows its rotation is not always the best response; that does not refute Conjecture 6.1.
The k=3 case is solved and is excluded as a win.
Problem 6.2 (Bob's best response) is a different question and is not covered by this entry.
A proof of the conjecture for all k counts only as a kernel-checked formal proof; a written argument is not a win, and certified computations for single k are the partial wins.

targets.name: Random assignments: a finite SD-EF assignment with no Dec-EF decomposition (counterexample to Li-He-Li Conjecture 1)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days; focus counterexample search on 5–8 agents, with 120–40320 permutation columns; exact LP dual checking is small
targets.statement: Keyi Li, Yihao He and Quanyi Li, Envy-Free Decompositions of Random Assignments: Settling Four Agents, and What Lies Beyond (arXiv:2609.35192, September 2026), state Conjecture 1: for every n and every strict preference profile, every stochastic-dominance envy-free (SD-EF) assignment matrix is EF-decomposable. Given n agents, n objects, strict rankings and a bistochastic matrix P, SD-EF means that for every i,j and top-k set U_ik of agent i, sum_{o in U_ik}P_io >= sum_{o in U_ik}P_jo. A decomposition is a distribution p over bijections sigma with marginals P. It is Dec-EF when for all ordered pairs i,j, Pr[sigma(j) is preferred by i to sigma(i)] <= 1/2. The source builds on Kawase et al., Decomposition envy-freeness in random assignment (Mathematical Social Sciences, 2026). Li et al. settle all four-agent matrices, five-agent matrices with at most four distinct preferences, all five-agent probabilistic-serial outputs, and certain larger type patterns. They report adversarial search through seven agents without a counterexample; this does not settle general five-agent inputs. The first remaining five-agent inputs have five distinct preferences and need not be probabilistic-serial outcomes. As of 2026-10-25 the arXiv abstract page lists v1 only.
targets.success_criterion: Produce a finite strict preference profile and nonnegative rational bistochastic P satisfying every SD-EF inequality, together with an exact certificate that NO decomposition of P has all ordered-pair envy probabilities <=1/2. Equivalently certify t*(P)>1/2, where t* is the minimum achievable maximum pairwise envy probability. A bad decomposition of P does not suffice: the claim quantifies over every decomposition.
targets.verification_method: Check P's row and column sums and all SD-EF prefix inequalities in rational arithmetic. Enumerate the n! permutations and their 0/1 pairwise-envy indicators. The feasibility LP has variables p_sigma>=0, marginals sum_sigma p_sigma 1[sigma(i)=o]=P_io, total mass 1, and sum_sigma p_sigma 1[sigma(j) preferred to sigma(i)]<=1/2 for each i!=j. Verify an exact rational Farkas infeasibility certificate by checking its signs, every permutation column and its strictly contradictory right-hand side. Alternatively verify a rational dual bound >1/2 for the minimax LP. For n<=8 this is at most 40320 columns and 56 envy inequalities. Larger witnesses must include a certificate whose full checking still fits the bank's laptop-hours limit.
angles: Search vertices of the SD-EF polytope; Lemma 3.1 proves the minimax value is convex, so vertices suffice for worst cases of a fixed profile.
Concentrate on distinct preferences and matrices with several distinct rows. The source has already solved two-row and several repeated-type cases.
Alternate preference perturbations with primal/dual LP optimization, then rationalize a strict infeasibility margin.
pitfalls: Greedy and maximum-entropy decompositions already have counterexamples. Those are not counterexamples to the existence conjecture.
All four-agent inputs and all five-agent probabilistic-serial outputs are solved in the status paper; do not claim those cases as new.
An approximate LP gap near 1/2 is especially unreliable because repeated preferences often force equality exactly.
The 216-million-vertex positive enumeration in the paper used a server. This entry targets a small obstruction, not a repeat of that computation.

targets.name: Unfair dice games: improve a small Schütte multiple-tournament construction bound
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (SAT/local search on two or three tournaments with at most thirteen vertices; witness checking is sub-second scale)
targets.statement: Joel Jeffries, Schütte’s property for sets of tournaments and an application to dice games (arXiv:2604.08790, April 2026), Definition 2.2, defines f(m,k) as the minimum order of m tournaments on one vertex set such that every k-subset is dominated by a vertex outside that subset in at least one tournament. Section 4 leaves improvement of its construction bound open. Proposition 2.3 composes orders n1,n2 into order n1+n2, with m=m1+m2 and k=k1+k2+1. The published composition bounds in Figure 7 are f(2,5)<=14 and f(3,6)<=13. They follow from two order-7 S2 tournaments, or two order-3 S1 tournaments and one order-7 S2 tournament, respectively. Closing the small published cells under this composition gives the same bars, 14 and 13. Figure 7 marks f(2,4) = 10 and the other small cells as confirmed exact (starred) by a SAT formulation; f(2,5) and f(3,6) are unstarred. The two retained cells are unstarred construction bounds, not claims of proven optimality. The definition is motivated by dice games with a last chooser who selects both a die and a roll mode. Tournament matrices alone do not establish physical dice realization. As of 2026-10-25 the arXiv abstract page lists v1 only.
targets.success_criterion: Give explicit adjacency matrices proving f(2,5)<=13 or f(3,6)<=12, with n>=k+1, and strictly below the best composition of all published constructions available when the claim is checked. The cited-source composition bars are 14 and 13; a later published improvement or its compositions can lower them. Unmerged pull-request values are not bars. Report whether the submitted object is itself a composition, and cite every ingredient if it is. One vertex fewer suffices because orders and the verification are exact. An exact value proved by an UNSAT certificate is partial win p1.

partial_wins.statement: An exact value: an UNSAT certificate (DRAT or LRAT checked by a formally verified checker such as cake_lpr) for a CNF encoding of 'two tournaments on 13 vertices with every 5-subset dominated' (proving f(2,5) = 14) or 'three tournaments on 12 vertices with every 6-subset dominated' (proving f(3,6) = 13), with symmetry breaking proved sound and the encoding's correctness argued in a short note that a skeptic checks against Definition 2.2.

targets.verification_method: Check each matrix has diagonal zero, entries in {0,1}, and A[i,j]+A[j,i]=1 for i!=j. For every k-subset U, check that some single tournament and vertex v outside U have A[v,u]=1 for every u in U. At most C(13,5)=1287 subsets are needed for the proposed witnesses. Regenerate the best composition bar from published ingredients using Proposition 2.3 and compare exact integer orders. For a submitted composition, also check its ingredients and assembly rule; direct checking of the final matrices remains required. A positive SAT search is certified by the matrices independently of the solver. For p1, re-encode the CNF independently from Definition 2.2 (or check the claimant's encoder line by line against it), check every symmetry-breaking clause against its soundness argument, and run the verified checker on the proof.
angles: Seed the search with Proposition 2.3’s block construction, remove one vertex, and repair uncovered k-subsets.
Use symmetry breaking for vertex relabeling and permutation of the tournaments; retain a direct matrix checker independent of the encoding.
Search (m,k)=(2,5) and (3,6), whose Figure 7 cells are unstarred.
pitfalls: Figure 7 marks f(2,4)=10 as exact. No optimality is claimed for 14 or 13; a quick SAT run may settle either cell, so check p1 before a long construction search.
The dominator must be the same vertex for all elements of U in one tournament; allowing a different tournament for each edge changes the property.
A tournament tuple alone does not supply physical dice whose first m roll sums realize it. The paper explicitly leaves that additional realization question open.
Do not retarget the solved m>=k+1 regime, for which the paper proves f(m,k)=k+1.
This is distinct from lottery coverings and covering codes already in the bank, despite the SAT encoding’s covering interpretation.

targets.name: Binary deletion codes: improve the best size at length 15 or 16, correcting two or three deletions
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days for local clique/independent-set search on 32768 or 65536 candidate words; certificate verification is seconds to minutes
targets.statement: Franziska Weindel and Reinhard Heckel, LLM-Guided Search for Deletion-Correcting Codes, arXiv:2504.00613v2 (5 June 2026), Table 2, gives best-known construction sizes and unresolved upper bounds. Maxima across every reported row are (n,s)=(15,2):136, (16,2):215, (15,3):30 and (16,3):42. The LP upper bounds are 277,487,61,99. A binary code corrects s adversarial deletions when distinct codewords have disjoint sets of length n-s subsequences. These unrestricted nonlinear deletion codes differ from the bank's Hamming-metric constant-weight codes and from quaternary edit-metric DNA codes (edit-metric-dna-codes-gc). Checked 2026-10-25: v2 is the latest version.
targets.success_criterion: Provide an explicit set of distinct binary words with respectively at least 137, 216, 31 or 43 codewords for any one of the four specified (n,s) cells, with pairwise disjoint s-deletion subsequence sets. No linearity, constant-weight or decoder-efficiency assumption is imposed. The complete codebook is the certificate. Also strictly improve the best comparable published result at claim time, including compatible compositions of published objects. State whether the candidate is a composition and identify its components. Values in unmerged pull requests do not set the bar.
targets.verification_method: For every word enumerate all choices of s deleted positions, deduplicate the resulting length n−s strings within that word, and insert each string into a map from received string to originating codeword. Reject if a string occurs for two distinct words. Check word length, alphabet and uniqueness, then compare code size to the frozen threshold. Independently cross-check with pairwise dynamic-programming longest common subsequences: LCS(x,y)<n−s. At these four thresholds fewer than 30000 deletion-pattern evaluations suffice for the smallest winning certificates.
angles: Use penalty-guided clique search, but maintain deletion-conflict sets implicitly instead of materializing a dense graph.
Start with the best conventional solver codebooks, then use k-for-(k+1) exchanges and component-wise exact search.
Try priority functions trained jointly on shorter deletion counts and lengths; score the final explicit code with the exact checker.
pitfalls: Beating only the learned-method row is insufficient; take maxima over all rows and comparable later constructions.
Hamming distance alone does not certify deletion correction.
Repeated subsequences within one word are harmless and must be deduplicated.
Naive concatenation need not preserve correction of adversarial deletions across block boundaries.
The June 2026 paper is the numerical source; search for later record literature before claiming.

targets.name: Symmetric rendezvous search: a line strategy below Han et al.'s 4.2574 (unchanged since 2008) or a four-location strategy beating FSD
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (strategy optimisation over distributions on unit-step paths; exact rational evaluation of a candidate takes seconds to hours)
targets.statement: Two searchers start distance 2 apart on a line. They have no common orientation and use the same synchronised random rule with independent randomness, at speed at most 1. Han, Du, Vera and Zuluaga (Operations Research 2008) proved 4.152 <= R <= 4.2574 for agents starting at distance 2 (d = 1; Han et al. show steps of length d suffice) and conjectured R is close to 4.25; Georgiou, Gravel, Kapusin and Mandic (arXiv:2609.13632v2, Sep 2026) restate these as the best known bounds. The separate discrete-location model uses independent random labelings. Cembrano, Fischer and Klimm (arXiv:2604.02058) give an FSD strategy improving Anderson-Weber for n>=4. The target is a line strategy beating Han et al.'s upper bound, or a strategy beating the best exact FSD parameter choice for four locations. Lower bounds are proofs about all strategies and are outside this entry. Printed line bars require numerical separation; a strict comparison with the exact incumbent strategy is a partial target.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED by any one of the following, with the strategy given as a finite explicit object (for the line, for example a distribution over k-step unit-move paths in the sense of Han et al., or a finite-state randomized automaton over moves -1/0/+1 in the agent's own frame; for n locations, a finite-memory randomized rule over location labels) and its expected meeting time computed exactly in rational arithmetic, or enclosed by rigorous interval arithmetic, by a verifier sharing no code with the search. (a) Line, upper bound: expected meeting time <= 4.2573 for initial distance 2 (a margin of 1e-4 below the published 4.2574, so that rounding of the old value cannot matter), counting meetings that happen mid-step. (b) Four locations: a symmetric strategy for n = 4 whose exact expected meeting time is strictly below the minimum over theta in [0, 1) of the exact expected meeting time of the Cembrano-Fischer-Klimm strategy FSD(theta), computed from the exact expression in arXiv:2604.02058 in that paper's time convention (meetings possible from t = 0). In each case the value must beat every bound published at verification time (check arXiv for 'symmetric rendezvous'). The line margins compare against rounded numerical bars. The exact-incumbent comparison in p1 accepts any exactly certified strict improvement. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: Line: an explicit strategy certified strictly better than the exact expected meeting time of Han et al.'s published 15-Markovian strategy (recomputed exactly from the strategy given in their paper), even if the gain is smaller than 1e-4.

Five locations: an explicit symmetric strategy for n = 5 whose exactly computed expected meeting time is below that of FSD(theta) at its best theta, computed exactly by the verifier (the 2026 paper gives only a lower bound on FSD's improvement for n >= 5).

targets.verification_method: Line: write the joint process of the two agents (each agent's automaton state or path index, the relative position, and the relative orientation, which is +1 or -1 with probability 1/2) as an absorbing Markov chain; meeting is absorption when the relative position hits 0, at an integer time or by crossing within a step. For a k-Markovian strategy, enumerate all pairs of paths in the support for both relative orientations, compute the per-round meeting probability and the expected time spent, and solve the renewal equation exactly, as in the worked examples of arXiv:1805.03351 (Alpern's strategy gives exactly 5). Test the verifier on Alpern's 5 and on the simple 2-Markovian strategy (exactly 7) first. Locations: build the chain over (round position, both players' visit histories modulo the random labelings) and compute the expectation exactly; test on Anderson-Weber for n = 3 and on FSD's closed-form improvement for n = 4.
angles: Push k: Han et al. stopped at k = 15 (2^15 paths per agent) with fractional quadratic programming in 2008, and their conjecture that R is about 4.25 suggests the k-Markovian optimum keeps falling with k. Optimise distributions over paths for k = 16 to 24 with sparse supports, many random starts in parallel, and exact re-evaluation of every improvement.

Search over richer strategy classes than renewal-type k-Markovian ones: small randomized automata whose next path depends on the previous round's path; the September 2026 paper's truncated-chain and weak-peek frameworks give ready-made finite-state machinery for evaluating them.

For four locations, start from FSD and Weber's 2009 12-step block idea and optimise over correlated tours across several rounds, guided by negative eigenvalues of the matrix of pairwise meeting times, as Weber did; exact evaluation is a finite sum over pairs of label sequences (15,852 pairs for Weber's block strategy).
pitfalls: Published bounds are rounded to four decimals; a claim within 1e-4 of 4.2574 needs an exact comparison with Han et al.'s actual strategy (partial win p1), not with the rounded number.
Conventions differ: n-location values depend on whether players can meet at time 0 (as in arXiv:2604.02058) or only from time 1. State the convention and compare like with like.
Floating-point evaluation of a strategy is not a certificate; use exact rationals or rigorous intervals, and include meetings that occur mid-step on the line.
Strategies must be symmetric: both agents use the same rule, with independent randomness and independent orientations; any rule that assigns roles (wait-for-mommy) is excluded.
The unknown-distance line problem (best symmetric ratio 13.926, Klimm, Sagnol, Skutella and Tran, SODA 2022) is a different cell and is not covered by this criterion.
Active field: Georgiou's and Klimm's groups both published in 2026; re-check arXiv before claiming.

targets.name: Three-player all-in betting game (Angel-Holmes): is being short-stacked always worse than tying your opponent? Prove or refute Conjecture 9
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours for a pointwise counterexample hunt (certified depth-n recursion, error <= 2^-n); the proof route is a formalisation project (the source's MILP region method stalled beyond depth 6 on 8 cores and only guides a formal proof)
targets.statement: The 'all in' variant of three-player gambler's ruin (the final-table / ICM setting): players 1, 2, 3 hold real stacks x, y, z > 0. Each round an unordered pair of players is chosen uniformly at random (probability 1/3 each) and they bet on a fair coin; the bet is the largest possible, namely the whole stack of the poorer of the two (a heads-up all-in). A player at 0 is eliminated. f(x, y, z) is the probability that player 1 is eliminated first. The game is scale invariant, and from every state the six transitions (pair, coin) each have probability 1/6 (He-Holmes Figure 1). Angel and Holmes (unpublished manuscript ''All In' poker sequences') showed f is NOT monotone decreasing in x (a player can lower their chance of busting first by giving chips away), and conjectured two weaker monotonicity statements. The first, f(x, y, z) > f(y, x, z) > f(z, x, y) for 0 < x < y < z ('you are better off starting with more money than your opponent'), was proved by Angel Y. He and Mark Holmes, 'All In: Give me your money!', arXiv:2410.15329 (v1, 20 Oct 2024, Theorem 1), with a computer-assisted proof (framework MeshItUp: region partition of the simplex plus mixed-integer programs; code github.com/7angel4/betting-game-proof, MIT licence). Their Section 5.3 (Future Work) states the second as open: Conjecture 9 (Angel-Holmes): for x, y, z > 0 with x < y, f(x, y, z) > f(y, y, z), i.e. a short stack is always strictly worse off than a stack tied with the opponent's. They report that their attempt to prove it with the same method 'ran beyond n = 6' and became too slow. On 2026-10-25 only v1 of arXiv:2410.15329 was listed, and a literature search on 2026-10-14 found no proof or refutation; the earlier page review noted that the repository README identifies a yyz module for this comparison but did not establish a resolution. A computer-assisted proof submitted in V3R1T4S PR #192 was closed on 2026-10-24 without a ruling on its correctness: its region certificates reproduced exactly (9,839 nodes, minimum 379/1813985280), but it rests on two analytic lemmas that need peer review. The conjecture is not established.
targets.success_criterion: Settle Angel-Holmes Conjecture 9 as stated in arXiv:2410.15329 Section 5.3 (direction: settle, either way), for the game exactly as defined in that paper's abstract and Section 1. EITHER (A) COUNTEREXAMPLE: explicit positive rationals x < y and z with f(x, y, z) <= f(y, y, z), proved by rigorous enclosures: f(s) lies in [h_n(s), h_n(s) + 2^-n] where h_n(s) is the exact (rational) probability that player 1 is eliminated first within n rounds, so it suffices to exhibit n with h_n(x, y, z) + 2^-n <= h_n(y, y, z), computed in exact rational arithmetic (or interval arithmetic with directed rounding) by a checker that shares no code with the search. OR (B) PROOF: a kernel-checked formal proof (Lean, Rocq/Coq or Isabelle, with no sorry, admit or extra axioms, and an axiom audit) that f(x, y, z) > f(y, y, z) for ALL real x, y, z > 0 with x < y. For the proof route, a written or computer-assisted proof whose analytic steps are not formalised does not count; exact or interval computations may support it only inside the formal proof, where the proof assistant checks them. A region certificate plus hand-proved tail or boundary lemmas is therefore not a full win.

partial_wins.statement: A kernel-checked formal proof (as in (B)) of Conjecture 9 on one of the three orderings of z separately: z >= y (player 3 is the chip leader), or z <= x (player 3 is the shortest), or x < z < y. All three together are the full win (B).

targets.verification_method: Write an exact evaluator: from state (a, b, c) with a, b, c > 0, each of the 6 (pair, winner) outcomes has probability 1/6; the poorer member of the chosen pair either doubles or is eliminated (equal stacks: the loser is eliminated). h_0 = 0; h_n(s) = sum over outcomes of (1/6) * [1 if player 1 is eliminated by that outcome; 0 if another player is eliminated; h_{n-1}(next state) otherwise]. Every round ends the game with probability at least 1/2, so 0 <= f - h_n <= 2^-n, which turns finite-depth exact values into rigorous enclosures. Sanity checks before trusting anything: f(1, 1, 1) = 1/3 (first round always eliminates someone; player 1 is in 2 of the 3 pairs and loses half the time); f(x, y, z) = f(x, z, y); scale invariance f(cx, cy, cz) = f(x, y, z); Monte Carlo agreement at random points; reproduce the sign of He-Holmes Theorem 1 at random 0 < x < y < z. For (A), check the enclosures separate. For (B) and p1, build the formal development in a clean environment, print the axioms used (#print axioms or Print Assumptions), check by reading that the formal definition of f follows the rules above (including the boundary cases x -> 0 and equal stacks), and check that the formal h_n agrees with the exact evaluator at sample rational points.
angles: Counterexample first, it is cheap: f is piecewise defined with discontinuities (transitions change whenever two stacks cross or one doubles past another), so the gap f(x, y, z) - f(y, y, z) may be smallest near such boundaries. Scan a fine rational grid of (x/y, z/y) with depth-12 exact values, then refine wherever the certified lower bound of the gap is smallest; Angel-Holmes's own non-monotonicity example shows where f behaves badly.

If the gap stays bounded away from 0 numerically, the remaining route is a formal proof. The He-Holmes decomposition into h_n plus a tail bound, symmetry (f(x, y, z) = f(x, z, y)), scale normalisation (y = 1) and a partition aligned with the hyperplanes where transitions change can guide it; PR #192's reproduced region certificates show where the margins are smallest.
Split by the position of z relative to x and y (the partial win p1) and formalise the easiest ordering first.
pitfalls: The conjecture compares f(x, y, z) with f(y, y, z): player 1 moves to player 2's stack while player 3 keeps z (the total changes). Do not confuse it with Theorem 1 (already proved) or with plain monotonicity in x (false, per Angel-Holmes).
Bets are all-in for the poorer stack, not unit bets: this is NOT the Diaconis-Ethier unit-step model (proposed target gamblers-ruin-scaling-conjecture).
Floating-point evaluation of h_n is not a certificate; near-ties at region boundaries are exactly where rounding lies.

Before claiming, inspect the 'yyz' folder of github.com/7angel4/betting-game-proof (it may hold partial or complete progress on this very conjecture), search for the Angel-Holmes manuscript if it has appeared, and search papers citing arXiv:2410.15329.
The Angel-Holmes manuscript is unpublished; the binding statement is the one quoted in arXiv:2410.15329 Section 5.3.
PR #192 (closed 2026-10-24) is not a resolution: its certificates reproduced, but its two analytic lemmas were never refereed. A formal proof must cover those steps itself.

targets.name: Three-player Kuhn poker: does the Szafron-Gibson-Sturtevant family contain every Nash equilibrium (on the path of play)?
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (exact algebra and global nonconvex searches over a 48-parameter game); the completeness route is a formalisation of a case-split argument
targets.statement: Three-player Kuhn poker (introduced by Abou Risk and Szafron, 2010; rules as in Szafron, Gibson and Sturtevant, AAMAS 2013, Section 2): a 4-card deck {1,2,3,4}, each player antes 1 chip and gets one card, one betting round with a single fixed bet of 1 chip (check or bet; fold or call when facing a bet; no raises), P1 acts first, showdown among the players who have not folded. A behavioural profile is 48 numbers a_jk, b_jk, c_jk (P1, P2, P3 holding card j in betting situation k = 1..4 of the paper's Table 1). Szafron, Gibson and Sturtevant derived analytically a parameterized family of Nash equilibria (their Tables 2 and 3: three sub-families c11 = 0, 0 < c11 < 1/2 and c11 = 1/2, with 4, 4 and 5 free parameters) with payoffs u1 = -(1+2*beta)/48, u2 = -1/48, u3 = (1+beta)/24, where beta = max{b11, b21} is in [0, 1/4], and in which P1 always checks first. Their conclusion (Section 8) reads: 'It remains open as to whether there exist other three-player Kuhn equilibrium profiles that do not belong to this family.' Wikipedia's Kuhn poker page still says (fetched 2026-10-25): 'It is not known if this equilibrium family covers all Nash equilibria for the game.' Ganzfried, Nowak and Pinales (2018) repeat that there 'may be others beyond those in the family'. Ganzfried (Games 17(1):9, 2026; arXiv:2509.25618v3) reported an equilibrium from Gurobi nonconvex QCP (reported deviation gain at most 1.4e-17; that numerical residual alone is not an exact certificate) of the game with dominated actions removed. It agrees with the family except at two information sets that are reached with probability zero: P1 holding card 3 after check-bet-fold always folds instead of calling with probability 1/2, and P3 holding card 3 facing P1's bet after P2 folds calls with probability 1/2. He concludes that 'additional Nash equilibria exist beyond those in the infinite family previously computed (though perhaps they only differ from the family off the path of play)'. Ganzfried (arXiv:2606.25997v2, June 2026) solves the full game exactly in 1.16 s. Gambit's logit solution and Billingham's numerical continuation (arXiv:1802.04670) also land in the family. The cited work reports off-path differences; the present target asks whether any equilibrium differs from every family member ON the path of play. A candidate completeness proof was closed in PR #201 pending a novelty check of Prisner (2014), chapter "Example: VNM POKER and KUHN POKER", and independent review. Completeness and novelty are not established here.
targets.success_criterion: Settle the question of Szafron, Gibson and Sturtevant (AAMAS 2013, Section 8) in its on-path form, for the game exactly as defined in their Section 2 (cards 1..4, ante 1, bet 1, acting order P1, P2, P3, the betting rules stated there). Direction: settle, either way. EITHER (A) COUNTEREXAMPLE: an explicit profile sigma given as 48 rational action probabilities, such that (1) sigma is an exact Nash equilibrium: for each player i, the exact best-response value against sigma_-i equals u_i(sigma), both computed in exact rational arithmetic over all 24 deals; and (2) sigma differs from every member of the family of Tables 2-3 ON THE PATH OF PLAY, shown by at least one of these witnesses: (W1) u2(sigma) != -1/48; (W2) the payoff vector is not (-(1+2*beta)/48, -1/48, (1+beta)/24) for any beta in [0, 1/4]; (W3) P1 bets first with positive probability with some card (some a_j1 > 0); (W4) an explicit argument, re-derived from Tables 2-3, that for each of the three sub-families no member assigns sigma's action probabilities at every information set that sigma reaches with positive probability. A profile that differs from the family only at information sets of zero reach probability does NOT count (Ganzfried 2026 already found one). OR (B) PROOF: a kernel-checked formal proof (Lean, Rocq/Coq or Isabelle, with no sorry, admit or extra axioms, and an axiom audit) that every Nash equilibrium of the game coincides, at every information set it reaches with positive probability, with some member of the family of Tables 2-3 (equivalently, induces the same distribution over terminal histories as some member). For the proof route, a written or computer-assisted proof whose analytic steps are not formalised does not count; exact or interval computations may support it only inside the formal proof, where the proof assistant checks them.

partial_wins.statement: A kernel-checked formal proof (as in (B)) that P2's expected payoff equals -1/48 in EVERY Nash equilibrium of three-player Kuhn poker. This extends the family's headline property to all equilibria; a single exact equilibrium with u2 != -1/48 is instead a full win under (A).
A kernel-checked formal proof (as in (B)) that in EVERY Nash equilibrium P1 never bets first with any card (a_j1 = 0 for j = 1..4).

targets.verification_method: Write an exact evaluator of about 150 lines (Python fractions.Fraction). Enumerate the 24 ordered deals and the betting tree, compute u_i(sigma), and compute each player's best-response value by backward induction over that player's 16 information sets (card x situation) using opponent-reach-weighted counterfactual values, all in exact arithmetic. sigma is an equilibrium iff BR_i = u_i for i = 1, 2, 3. Validate the evaluator and the transcription of Tables 2-3 on the family itself: sampled members of each sub-family must be exact equilibria with the stated payoffs (Theorem 2 of the paper). Then check the claimed witness W1-W4. For (B) and the partial wins, build in a clean environment, run #print axioms (or Print Assumptions), and check that the formal game model reproduces the family's payoffs and equilibrium property before trusting any statement proved about it.
angles: Aim straight at a witness: add a_41 >= delta (P1 opens with the best card), a_11 >= delta (P1 opens as a bluff), or u2 >= -1/48 + delta to the nonlinear-complementarity equilibrium conditions, and solve globally with an open-source spatial branch-and-bound solver (SCIP). Use Ganzfried's finite bounds on slack and multiplier variables (arXiv:2606.25997), which cut the full-game solve from more than 24 h to about 1 s. Rationalize any solution and verify it exactly.

Support enumeration plus exact algebra: fix which information sets are reached and which actions are mixed; each case is a system of multilinear equalities and inequalities in at most 27 free parameters (Theorem 1 already fixes 21 parameters when reached). Solve the cases with Groebner bases or real-root isolation (msolve, Singular, sympy).

Think like the 2-player game: in 2-player Kuhn, P1 bets the best card with probability 3*alpha and bluffs the worst with alpha. Test whether an analogous opening (a_41 > 0 balanced by a_11 > 0), with P2 and P3 calling ranges re-balanced, can be supported. The family was read off Monte Carlo CFR solutions run with different random seeds, and CFR carries no convergence guarantee in 3-player games, so it may have missed whole regions.

For the proof direction (formal only), follow the case structure of the paper's appendix (four lemmas for Theorem 1). First prove p2 (P1 never opens): every case with some a_j1 > 0 must yield a profitable deviation. Then p1. The rest of the family's structure should follow by restricting to P1-never-opens profiles.
pitfalls: Off-path differences already exist (Ganzfried 2026) and do not count; the claim must change what happens with positive probability.

Card and parameter labels differ between sources: the paper uses cards 1..4, Ganzfried uses J, Q, K, A. One of Ganzfried's off-path parameters is labelled c32 although the situation he describes (P1 bets, P2 folds) is situation 3 of the paper's Table 1. Map situations from the paper's Table 1, not from parameter names.
Take the parameter ranges from the paper (beta <= 1/4), not from secondary summaries.
Solver output with tolerance 1e-13 to 1e-17 is not an exact equilibrium. Rationalize and verify in exact arithmetic.

Nash equilibrium, not a refinement: off-path behaviour may be arbitrary as long as no unilateral deviation pays. Do not impose sequential rationality, and do not discard equilibria because they play weakly dominated actions at unreached information sets.
The PDF renders the fractions in Tables 2-3 badly. Validate any transcription against Theorem 2 (family members are equilibria with the stated payoffs) before using it to judge non-membership.
Check papers citing Szafron et al. 2013 (and Ganzfried's 2025-2026 papers) before claiming; the question is cited by an active line of exact-solver work.

Before attacking or claiming, check Prisner (2014), chapter "Example: VNM POKER and KUHN POKER", for prior results covering the same three-player rules and on-path question. PR #201 was closed pending that novelty check and independent review; the candidate is not established.
A written or computer-assisted completeness argument (such as the one in PR #201) is not a win until it is formalised as in (B).

targets.name: Quadratic APN functions with coefficients in F2 in dimension 11: a seventh CCZ class
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days for a bounded structured counterexample search; roughly four million derivative evaluations per APN check, with invariant checks in minutes to hours; full classification is out of scope
targets.statement: Yuyin Yu, Jingchen Li, Nadiia Ichanska and Nikolay Kaleyski, 'Construction of quadratic APN functions with coefficients in F2 in dimensions 10 and 11' (IACR ePrint 2024/1778; journal version doi:10.1007/s00200-025-00711-8), speed up the search of Yu, Kaleyski, Budaghyan and Li (dimensions up to 9), classify all quadratic APN functions over F_{2^10} with coefficients in F2, and, from partial computations over F_{2^11}, conjecture that the quadratic APN functions over F_{2^11} with coefficients in F2 'form 6 CCZ-inequivalent classes which also correspond to known APN functions' (ePrint abstract). The class is F(x) = sum over 0 <= i < j <= 10 of c_ij x^(2^i+2^j) with c_ij in {0,1}. APN means that for every nonzero a and every b the equation F(x+a)+F(x) = b has at most two solutions. The known quadratic APN functions of this form in dimension 11 include the Gold functions x^(2^k+1), k = 1..5 (pairwise CCZ-inequivalent), and x^3 + Tr(x^9); the paper's own table of class representatives must be read and used at claim time. As of 2026-10-25 a search found no result settling the conjecture. The target is one explicit function of this form in a seventh class, with a certificate; a full classification is not asked for.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit F of the stated form (the list of pairs (i,j) with c_ij = 1) together with a stated irreducible degree-11 binary modulus, such that (1) F is APN, checked exhaustively over all 2047 nonzero a and all 2048 x; and (2) F is CCZ-inequivalent to every class representative listed in the paper (journal version, table of dimension-11 representatives) and to each of x^3, x^5, x^9, x^17, x^33 and x^3 + Tr(x^9), certified by an invariant that differs: for quadratic APN functions CCZ-equivalence reduces to EA-equivalence (Yoshiara, J. Algebraic Combin. 35 (2012) 461-475), and the differential spectrum and the extended Walsh spectrum of the ortho-derivative are EA-invariants of quadratic APN functions. The verifier recomputes these invariants for F and for every representative; F counts only if its invariant histogram differs from each of them. A different truth table, a failed equivalence search or the output of a heuristic classifier is not a certificate.
targets.verification_method: Specify an irreducible binary degree-11 modulus; independently verify irreducibility and build exact field arithmetic. Expand F and each reference function on all 2048 inputs. Check all 2047 nonzero differences and all 2048 inputs, requiring difference counts 0 or 2. For each a≠0, form the linear derivative x↦F(x+a)+F(x)+F(a)+F(0); its image has rank 10. Compute its unique nonzero orthogonal normal vector by GF(2) elimination to obtain the ortho-derivative. Recompute its full differential spectrum and component Walsh spectra. Compare invariant histograms with every reference. Any other inequivalence certificate must cite a published invariant theorem and replay exactly; a failed equivalence search never counts.
angles: Adapt the paper’s reduced-matrix partial-search algorithm, concentrating on matrix patterns omitted by its restriction.
Reject non-APN candidates after the first low-rank derivative, before constructing full invariants.
Use symmetry and algebraic constructions to bias toward a new invariant signature rather than enumerate the full space.
pitfalls: Binary coefficients and dimension 11 are part of the conjecture; an APN function outside the class does not refute it.
Equal spectra do not prove equivalence; a differing valid invariant does prove inequivalence.
The ortho-derivative invariants need the quadratic-APN hypotheses (every derivative is 2-to-1 and affine).
Failure of an equivalence program is not an inequivalence certificate.

On 2026-10-25 the ePrint PDF and the Springer page were behind a bot check, so only the ePrint abstract was read for this entry; read the paper's dimension-11 table of representatives honestly before claiming, and treat its list as the comparison set.

targets.name: Optimal selfish mining in Bitcoin (Sapirshtein-Sompolinsky-Zohar model, gamma = 0): certify an upper bound on the optimal relative revenue below 0.70109 at alpha = 0.45 or below 0.90476 at alpha = 0.475
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (finite MDPs with up to ~10^6 states (a, h, fork); certificates are one exact or interval inequality per state-action pair)
targets.statement: Sapirshtein, Sompolinsky and Zohar ('Optimal Selfish Mining Strategies in Bitcoin', FC 2016, arXiv:1507.06183) model selfish mining as an MDP whose objective is the attacker's share of accepted blocks (REV). Their Table 2 (gamma = 0, truncation T = 95, epsilon = 1e-5) gives epsilon-optimal revenues 0.48866, 0.56808, 0.66891 and 0.80172 at alpha = 0.4, 0.425, 0.45 and 0.475, with upper bounds 0.48904, 0.57226, 0.70109 and 0.90476; at alpha = 0.475 the upper bound is the trivial alpha/(1-alpha). Bar-Zur, Eyal and Tamar (PTO, AFT 2020, arXiv:2007.05614, Table 1, forks capped at 95) report achievable revenues 0.56809, 0.66894 and 0.80184 at alpha = 0.425, 0.45 and 0.475. So at alpha = 0.45 and 0.475 the optimal revenue in the untruncated model is known only to lie in [0.66894, 0.70109] and [0.80184, 0.90476], and the published values are floating-point and uncertified. Sakurai, Nakai and Shudo (arXiv:2607.24415, July 2026) certify bounds on the incentive-compatibility threshold in a model with asymmetric tie-breaking, a different question. As of 2026-10-25 a search found no certified upper bound below SSZ's at these alpha. The target is a certified upper bound for the untruncated SSZ model, obtained from its over-paying finite MDP.
targets.success_criterion: A machine-checkable certificate that max over all policies of REV in the untruncated SSZ model (definitions as in arXiv 1507.06183, Sections 2-4, with gamma = 0) is at most U, where U <= 0.70099 at alpha = 0.45 or U <= 0.90466 at alpha = 0.475. Each bar is 1e-4 below the published SSZ Table 2 upper bound (0.70109, 0.90476); lower is better. The certificate has three parts. (i) A rational rho = U and a truncation T. (ii) The finite over-paying MDP N_rho^T built exactly as SSZ Section 4.2 defines it (same states, actions and transition probabilities; compensation rewards from eq. (7) and the following display). (iii) A rational or outward-rounded interval average-reward dual certificate: a gain g < 0 and a bias vector h over all states of N_rho^T such that, for every state s and every action a allowed in s, r_rho(s,a) + sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) h(s') - h(s) <= g. Here r_rho(s,a) is the expected one-step reward, the transition-probability-weighted w_rho(R_t, honest blocks accepted), including SSZ's truncation compensation. An independent checker rebuilds N_rho^T from the paper's formulas (not from the claimant's files), verifies every inequality, and concludes via SSZ Proposition 3 that max REV < rho. The checker must first reproduce SSZ Table 2's epsilon-OPT values 0.56808 (alpha = 0.425) and 0.66891 (alpha = 0.45) within one unit of their last printed digit with its own model builder. As a sanity test that the over-paying MDP is not mis-built, its own policy-iteration solve of N_rho^T at alpha = 0.45, rho = 0.66 must return a positive optimal gain. These safety margins compare against numerical published bars. If an incumbent is available as an exact certificate, any exactly certified strict improvement over it counts.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit stationary policy, given as an action table on a finite state set with 'adopt' at its boundary, whose relative revenue in the SSZ model at gamma = 0, computed in exact rational arithmetic from its Markov chain, exceeds 0.66894 + 1e-6 at alpha = 0.45 or 0.80184 + 1e-6 at alpha = 0.475. This is strictly above every published value (OSM 2016, PTO 2020), and those values are floating-point and uncertified.
The full certificate format at alpha = 0.4 or 0.425 (gamma = 0), with U below SSZ Table 2's upper bounds 0.48904 or 0.57226 by at least 1e-4.

A certified enclosure of width <= 1e-4 for the selfish-mining profitability threshold in the Ethereum PoW model of arXiv 2007.05614, Section 7 (gamma = 0.5, uncle and nephew rewards as defined there, REV_ARR objective). Equivalently, an exact policy profitable at alpha <= 0.2467, which would show the threshold is below the published 0.2468; that value was computed with forks capped at 20/25 in floating point.

targets.verification_method: Write an independent builder for N_rho^T from SSZ Section 4.2 (Python, under 300 lines; states (a, h, fork) with max(a, h) <= T). Load the claimed (rho, g, h). For every state-action pair, evaluate w_rho(s,a) + sum P h - h - g with fractions.Fraction, or mpmath intervals with outward rounding, and check that it is <= 0. Check g < 0. Then reproduce two calibration facts with the same builder. First, the under-paying MDP solved by policy iteration gives SSZ's epsilon-OPT values 0.56808 (alpha = 0.425) and 0.66891 (alpha = 0.45) within one unit of their last printed digit. Second, the optimal gain of N_rho^T is positive for rho comfortably below those values (e.g. rho = 0.56 at alpha = 0.425 and rho = 0.66 at alpha = 0.45), so no certificate can exist there. Cross-check model semantics against the Bitcoin model in the PTO repository and the OSM Matlab code. Minutes per alpha.
angles: The published upper bound may be loose for numerical rather than structural reasons. SSZ's Algorithm 1 reports rho' + 2(u + epsilon') from an epsilon'-optimal solver run. Start by certifying N_rho^T at T = 95 with an exact dual certificate before raising T.

Certifier lens: solve N_rho^T in floating point by policy iteration, rationalise the bias vector, then repair it. Shift h by a small multiple of a Lyapunov-like function, or use exact policy evaluation of the final policy, until every inequality holds with margin. Binary-search rho downward.

Raise T as needed: the over-paying compensation alpha(1-alpha)/(1-2alpha)^2 is 24.75 at alpha = 0.45 and 99.75 at alpha = 0.475, and Proposition 3 guarantees convergence as T grows. Use sparse structure (at most 3 successors per state-action).

The lower side is a pure exact-evaluation problem: take PTO's or your own optimal truncated policy, compute its stationary revenue in rationals (or via a renewal-reward cycle decomposition), and push T to see if anything clears 0.66894 + 1e-6.
pitfalls: Model variants change the numbers. Use SSZ's gamma semantics (match needs a block prepared in advance), not Eyal-Sirer's SM1 or the 'uniform tie-breaking' variant (where SSZ's 0.2321 threshold lives), nor the gamma-minus/gamma-plus model of arXiv 2607.24415.
Relative revenue is not time-averaged profit before a difficulty adjustment (Grunspan and Perez-Marco), and Ethereum's denominators include uncles. State the objective exactly as SSZ define REV.
A truncated (under-paying) MDP gives only LOWER bounds. An upper bound must go through the over-paying construction or an equally rigorous dominance argument.
Floating-point value iteration is not a certificate: every inequality must be checked exactly or with outward rounding, and the checker must build the MDP itself.
The compensation rewards in eq. (7) are easy to transcribe wrongly (the PDF typesetting is dense). Test the builder by confirming that rho values below the known lower bounds cannot be certified.

targets.name: Jehn's random-basket coin game: exact optimal expected win for 2 baskets beyond n = 22 (OEIS A391791) and 3 baskets beyond n = 18 (A391792)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (exact backward induction over (remaining-coin set, basket-sum profile) states, layer by layer; memory, not time, is the limit: roughly 2^n * T/2 states for 2 baskets, T = n(n+1)/2, so the largest two adjacent layers reach about 1.5e10 entries near n = 26; rough estimates, not measured)
targets.statement: Coins worth 1, 2, ..., n are placed one per turn for n turns. Each turn one of k baskets is chosen uniformly at random and the player then puts one remaining coin of their choice into it; after the last turn the player takes the basket with the largest sum. OEIS A391791 (k = 2) gives a(n) = 2^(n-1) times the maximum expected win and A391792 (k = 3) gives 3^(n-1) times it. Both are by Ruediger Jehn (author of the 'Risk or Safety' sequences A387261/A387262), carry keywords nonn,hard,more, and link his Julia program a391791_1.jl.txt. On 2026-10-25 A391791 (revision #16, last edited 7 Jan 2026) lists n = 1..22: 1, 5, 20, 65, 190, 530, 1407, 3585, 8942, 21819, 52204, 123190, 287044, 661329, 1509949, 3420580, 7688444, 17173896, 38143782, 84262365, 185278522, 405700861; and A391792 (revision #6, last edited 7 Jan 2026) lists n = 1..18: 1, 7, 40, 192, 837, 3423, 13478, 51396, 190809, 693595, 2477822, 8740848, 30419671, 104752091, 357748926, 1211285880, 4074000387, 13615817865. A391791 also states a conjecture: for n > 9 the optimal first move is to put coin floor((n+3)/2) in the first basket.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: the exact integer values of A391791(23), A391791(24), A391791(25) AND A391792(19), A391792(20), A391792(21) (K = 3 new terms of each; direction: new terms), under the entries' own definitions (a(n) = k^(n-1) times the maximum, over all adaptive placement strategies, of the expected largest basket sum; baskets chosen independently and uniformly each turn; coins 1..n each used exactly once), each computed by two independently written exact programs that (i) agree on every new term, (ii) reproduce every published term (A391791 n = 1..22, A391792 n = 1..18), and (iii) use integer or rational arithmetic only (no floating point anywhere in the value recursion). The terms must not already be in the OEIS entries, their b-files or their edit history at verification time. Submitting to the OEIS is an action for the human only.

partial_wins.statement: The three new terms of only one of the two sequences (A391791 n = 23..25, or A391792 n = 19..21), with the same two-program confirmation and calibration.

A settled status for A391791's stated conjecture over a range: for every n from 10 through the largest n computed, the full set of optimal first moves listed exactly, either confirming that coin floor((n+3)/2) is optimal for each n or giving the first n where it is not (a counterexample to the conjecture as stated in the entry).

targets.verification_method: Write the recursion from the definition: V(R, s) = (1/k) * sum over baskets b of max over coins c in R of V(R - {c}, s + c*e_b), with V(empty, s) = max(s); canonicalise s by sorting (baskets are exchangeable) and, for k = 2, use only the difference |s1 - s2| because the total placed is fixed by R. For a state with m = |R| turns remaining, store W(R,s) = k^m V(R,s), so W(empty,s) = max(s) and W(R,s) = sum_b max_c W(R-{c},s+c*e_b) are exact integers. At the empty-basket initial state, the published term is W(R,0)/k because the first random basket is irrelevant by symmetry; verify divisibility by k. Use arbitrary-precision integers or prove fixed-width safety for every intermediate value. Sweep layers by |R| from 0 up to n, keeping two layers in memory. Calibrate on every published term, then compute the new terms with a second, independently written program (different language or different state encoding, e.g. full sorted sum vector instead of differences) and require exact agreement. Optionally publish per-layer SHA-256 hashes of the value tables so a third checker can compare layer by layer.
angles: Two baskets: the state is (remaining set R, |s1 - s2|); the difference has the parity of the placed total, which halves the table; store layer |R| = m as C(n, m) rows indexed by subset rank.
Three baskets: state (R, sorted (s1, s2, s3)); the number of sorted triples for placed total P is about P^2/12, so n = 19..21 is far smaller than it looks.
Evaluator first: reproduce n <= 12 in seconds with a memoised recursion, then switch to the layered sweep and confirm it matches before scaling.
Parallelise inside a layer: each subset R's row depends only on the next layer, so cores split subsets with no locking.
pitfalls: The basket is chosen BEFORE the player picks the coin each turn; reversing the order changes the game (the adversarial siblings A391537/A391538 are different sequences).
The player takes the larger basket at the end (max), not a fixed basket.
a(n) is scaled by k^(n-1), not k^n: the first coin's basket choice does not matter by symmetry. Check the scaling against a(3) = 20 (k = 2) and a(3) = 40 (k = 3).
Do not search only strategies of the conjectured form; the maximum is over all adaptive strategies.
Memory grows as 2^n times the sum range: measure the largest layer before launching.
Check both entries, their b-files and their edit histories at claim time; the two sequences can move independently.

targets.name: Four additive agents: an exact finite counterexample to complete EFX existence
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days for structured counterexample search; 4^10=1048576 to 4^12=16777216 allocations for exact checking; no exhaustive search of all valuations is proposed
targets.statement: Eyad Alkassar, Mahmoud Fouz and Kurt Mehlhorn, 'Complete EFX Allocations Exist for Four Additive Agents and Up to Nine Goods' (arXiv:2608.08590, v1 9 Aug 2026), write that whether complete EFX allocations exist for additive valuations is open for n >= 4 agents; known territory includes two and three agents, four agents with at most one good unallocated, and complete EFX for m <= n + 3 goods (Mahara). Their Theorem 1 covers four additive agents and at most nine goods, even for zero-tolerant EFX0, by reduction lemmas plus a machine-verified certificate corpus. Recent counterexamples (Akrami et al. 2026; Mackenzie and Suzuki 2026) use submodular, not additive, valuations. The target is a counterexample with four agents and strictly positive rational item values, so that EFX and EFX0 coincide: a complete allocation A is EFX if v_i(A_i) >= v_i(A_j) - min_{g in A_j} v_ig for every i, j with A_j nonempty. By the published results any such witness has at least ten goods. As of 2026-10-25 the abstract page lists v1 only. This is a famous open question; long odds.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit strictly positive rational 4 x m additive valuation matrix such that no allocation of all m goods to the four agents is EFX, together with an exact exhaustive or compressed obstruction certificate checkable within a few hours on a laptop. Every good must be assigned once; there are no constraints on bundle size. A witness for non-additive valuations, an incomplete allocation, or EFX plus an extra efficiency condition does not qualify. A witness with m <= 9 would contradict Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.08590 (and, for m <= 7, Mahara's theorem); it counts only after three independently written checkers agree, and the conflict is reported to the authors by the human.
targets.verification_method: Clear denominators and verify strict positivity. Enumerate all 4^m labeled complete allocations and, using exact subset sums, find an i,j,g in A_j with v_i(A_i)<v_i(A_j)-v_ig for each allocation. It suffices to use the good of minimum v_i-value in each envied bundle. Any symmetry reduction must carry a proof that all allocations are covered; unproved canonicalization is not allowed. At m=10..12 a compiled enumerator is a laptop-scale checker. Larger witnesses need a compact proof with independently checked coverage, not just an UNSAT assertion.
angles: The source reports difficult regions with near-identical valuations and a common top good. Search perturbations in those regions rather than uniform random matrices.
Combine adversarial rational valuation search with an exact EFX-allocation separation oracle.
Use the published <=9 theorem as a negative control on any checker; a claimed positive-valued counterexample below ten goods signals a bug or a conflicting claim requiring resolution.
pitfalls: All sizes up to nine goods are already solved for four agents. The original literature's older n+3 frontier is stale.
The source used five 48-vCPU machines for its universal positive result. Extending that exhaustive computation is not the proposed laptop attack.
Three-agent additive existence and recent submodular counterexamples cannot be repackaged as this target.
The strictly positive witness requirement avoids counting a change in zero-good conventions as a disproof.

targets.name: Graph Golf (order/degree and host-switch problems): beat a 2021 best diameter and average shortest path length
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (bit-parallel BFS; one exact evaluation of the n = 158976 instance takes minutes on a multi-core laptop)
targets.statement: Graph Golf, the order/degree problem competition run by the National Institute of Informatics from 2015 to 2021, ranks graphs with a fixed number of vertices and a degree bound by diameter and then by average shortest-path length (ASPL); its host-switch variant measures paths between degree-one hosts attached to switches of bounded radix. The 2021 rankings page (update 2021-10-11) lists the best graphs for each featured problem, with entries by Team RK, EvbCFfp1XB, MODAL-Team, D. Shimizu, SDKY-NITTYM and others, and an ASPL gap to the lower bound for each; only n40d5 and n432d12 have gap 0. The competition is closed, so the table is frozen; later papers may hold better graphs. The target is a strict lexicographic improvement for a featured 2021 problem whose gap is positive, with the incumbent's ASPL recomputed exactly from its published edge file.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit graph for one of the 2021 featured problems other than n40d5 and n432d12 (which meet the lower bound), satisfying the definition on http://research.nii.ac.jp/graphgolf/problem.html (general: simple, undirected, connected, exactly n vertices, every degree <= d; host-switch: exactly n hosts of degree 1, each adjacent to a switch, any number of switches of degree <= r, simple and connected), whose (diameter, ASPL), or (h-diameter, h-ASPL), is lexicographically STRICTLY smaller (direction: min) than the best graph listed for that problem on http://research.nii.ac.jp/graphgolf/ranking.html, with the incumbent's ASPL recomputed exactly (total distance divided by the number of pairs, as a rational number) from its published edge file rather than read from the 5-decimal display, and also smaller than any later published graph for that problem. Ties do not count.

partial_wins.statement: A strict improvement, under that year's rules and verified the same way, on a featured problem of the 2015-2019 Graph Golf competitions (their ranking pages on the same site), against the best graph listed there and any later published one.

targets.verification_method: Read the edge list (calibrate the format by recomputing an incumbent from its published edges.gz file). Check vertex and host counts, simplicity, degree or radix bounds and connectivity. Run BFS from every vertex (bit-parallel BFS for large n; the organisers link Ryuhei Mori's C++ ASPL program and Ryota Yasudo's host-switch program from problem.html) to get the exact diameter and the exact sum of distances, and compare with the incumbent as rationals. Seconds for small cells, minutes for n = 158976.
angles: Start from the published incumbents and run degree-preserving edge-swap local search with an incremental bit-parallel ASPL evaluator; most cells saw only two serious teams over one season, five years ago.

For the large structured cells (n65536d64, n100000d128, n158976d10) use algebraic seeds such as Cayley graphs, lifts of small optimal graphs and voltage graphs; vertex-transitive candidates need only one BFS per orbit to evaluate.

For n1024d5 and n3602d24 the prize is a smaller diameter: check the degree-diameter tables for degree-5 diameter-5 and degree-24 diameter-3 graphs of at least that order, and try vertex deletion or merging while keeping the diameter. Any such graph beats every 2021 entry outright.
Host-switch cells with small radix (h32r4, h80r6) are small enough for exhaustive or SAT-assisted search over switch topologies, which could improve the incumbent or show it is optimal.
pitfalls: The 5-decimal ASPL display hides near-ties; recompute both graphs exactly.
Diameter is compared first: a lower ASPL at a larger diameter loses.
General graphs allow degree <= d (not necessarily regular). Hosts must have exactly one edge, to a switch. Multi-edges and loops are not allowed.

The competition is closed, so the organisers will not list a new record. The claim stands against the frozen 2021 table, and a novelty search ('order/degree problem', 'host-switch graph', 2022-2026) is part of it; any later published graph for the same problem sets the bar.
Cells whose gap is 0 are optimal and cannot be beaten; a result below a lower bound means a bug.

targets.name: Continuous Guts: is the asynchronous coalition value zero for every n >= 4?
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (n=4 payoff analysis, finite-support counterexample search, and exact univariate or chamber certificates)
targets.statement: Kevin Buck, Jessica Babyak, Leah Dichter, David Jiang and Kevin Zumbrun (2024), Remark 5.9 and section 9.1, explicitly conjecture: "VA = 0 also for the n-player game with (n − 1) vs. 1 coalition." Their paper proves the three-player case. This proposal concerns the ordinary ONE-SHOT continuous Guts alpha payoff and n>=4, not a new game and not the already solved n=3 case. Each player sees an independent uniform [0,1] hand and holds above a selected threshold. The zero-sum alpha accounting is defined in section 3 of Kevin Buck, Jae Hwan Lee, Jacob Platnick, Aric Wheeler and Kevin Zumbrun (2022): if h>=1 hold, everybody receives h-2, the highest holder additionally receives n, and each other holder additionally pays n; if nobody holds, alpha=0. For probability measures mu2,...,mun on [0,1], define VA(n)=inf_{mu2,...,mun} sup_{t1 in [0,1]} E[alpha(t1,T2,...,Tn)], where the opponent thresholds T2,...,Tn are independent with these respective laws. This infimum of a best response is the asynchronous coalition value. A symmetric Nash profile supplies the known upper bound zero; the conjecture is that an independent coalition cannot force it lower. As of 2026-10-25 the abstract page of arXiv:2412.19855 lists v1 (25 Dec 2024) only.
targets.success_criterion: EITHER (a) a counterexample: one n >= 4 and explicit independent opponent laws mu_2..mu_n (finite support, with rational or real-algebraic support points and weights) for which sup over t1 in [0,1] of E[alpha(t1, T2, ..., Tn)] < 0, with an exact certificate: the verifier rebuilds the expected alpha as a piecewise polynomial in t1 from the definition, and every candidate maximum (endpoints, breakpoints and every real root of the derivative on each piece, isolated exactly) is shown strictly negative; OR (b) a kernel-checked formal proof (Lean, Coq or Isabelle, with no sorry, admit or extra axioms) that VA(n) = 0 for every n >= 4, over arbitrary independent opponent probability measures. A written or computer-assisted proof whose analytic steps are not formalised does not count. Exhibiting an ordinary Nash equilibrium, or a result for a correlated (synchronous) coalition, does not answer this question.

partial_wins.statement: A kernel-checked formal proof (as in (b)) that VA(4) = 0 for arbitrary independent probability measures on the three opponent thresholds. A check of pure opponent thresholds alone is insufficient unless the formal proof includes the reduction to them.

targets.verification_method: For a finite-support counterexample: verify nonnegative weights summing to 1 for each independent law, form the product distribution, and reconstruct E[alpha] independently from the alpha accounting of section 3 of arXiv:2208.02788 (calibrate on Proposition 3.2 there for n = 3 and on the symmetric equilibrium threshold 2^(-1/(n-1)) of Proposition 3.3, which must give value 0). As a function of t1 it is piecewise polynomial with breakpoints at the opponents' support points; isolate every derivative root exactly, evaluate all roots, breakpoints and endpoints in exact arithmetic, and require every value strictly negative. For a formal proof: build in a clean environment, print the axioms used, and check that the formal definitions of alpha and of VA match the papers by evaluating them on the n = 3 closed forms.
angles: Try to extend the partial convexity/concavity arguments of the solved three-player case to four players.
For counterexample discovery, optimize two- or three-point distributions for each opponent, then rationalize and certify the entire best-response curve.
Keep the product-distribution restriction explicit in the search representation.
pitfalls: The order is inf over opponent product measures, then sup over player 1; swapping these operations gives a different value.
Independent mixing and synchronized mixing are different. The known negative synchronous value does not refute this conjecture.
The follow-up’s Corollary 5.8 contains a repeated-subscript typo; its prose, abstract, and section 9.1 identify the conjecture unambiguously.
This entry concerns the one-shot alpha game. Do not attach an unsupported conclusion about the infinite recursive asynchronous game.
The paper’s suggestions about negotiation are excluded because they do not specify an exact success criterion.

targets.name: Cookson–Shah four-agent key matroids: EF1 with ordered no-envy on 8 or 12 goods
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days for rational MILP/SMT search; a counterexample has only 864 or 31104 feasible labeled allocations to check
targets.statement: Benjamin Cookson and Nisarg Shah, Constrained Fair Allocations via Partition Matroid Reductions (arXiv:2608.31121, August 2026), explicitly leave two finite key-matroid questions open in Section 5 and Appendix B. They write that their computer-aided attempts were "unfruitful" but the result may be within reach with "a smarter brute-force strategy". Four agents have arbitrary nonnegative additive values v_ig and a prescribed order 1,2,3,4. In the size-8 matroid, the goods form groups {1,2,3}, {4,5,6}, {7,8}; each bundle contains at most two goods and at most one from each group. In the size-12 matroid there are four groups of three; each bundle contains at most three goods and at most one from each group. All goods must be allocated. The question is whether an allocation can always be both EF1 and free of envy from every earlier agent to every later agent. EF1 means v_i(A_i) >= v_i(A_j)-max_{g in A_j} v_ig; ordered no-envy means v_i(A_i) >= v_i(A_j) for i<j. Positive resolutions for both key matroids complete the authors' reduction for all four-colorable laminar matroids. There are 864 and 31104 feasible labelled complete allocations, respectively (recounted for this entry); these are search-space sizes, not evidence either way. As of 2026-10-25 the abstract page lists v1 (31 Aug 2026) only.
targets.success_criterion: EITHER a nonnegative rational 4x8 or 4x12 valuation matrix and an agent order for which no complete feasible allocation under the corresponding key matroid is both EF1 and free of envy from each agent towards every later agent, with a complete exact obstruction certificate; OR an existence certificate for BOTH key matroids covering every nonnegative additive valuation matrix and every agent order: either a kernel-checked formal proof (Lean, Coq or Isabelle, no sorry, admit or extra axioms), or a finite partition of the normalised valuation space into rational polyhedra, each with a named allocation and exact linear-arithmetic (Farkas) certificates of coverage and of every EF1 and ordered-no-envy inequality, re-checked by an independent exact checker. A counterexample refutes the stronger key-matroid property the authors' reduction needs, not EF1 existence for laminar matroids.

partial_wins.statement: An existence certificate of the same standard for exactly one of the two key matroids, covering arbitrary nonnegative additive values and any prescribed agent order.

targets.verification_method: For a counterexample, clear denominators and enumerate injective assignments of each group to the four agents, retaining equal loads two or three. Verify completeness of the resulting 864/31104 allocations, then exhibit an exact EF1 or ordered-envy violation in every allocation. Regenerate the enumeration from the group constraints instead of trusting a supplied allocation list. A universal proof may partition normalized valuation space into finitely many rational polyhedra, associate allocations with each region, and supply exact linear-arithmetic/Farkas certificates of coverage and the required inequalities. Include all boundary/tie cases and zero-value rows. A kernel-checked general proof is also acceptable; an unexplained SMT UNSAT exit is not.
angles: Solve the size-8 question first. An adversarial MILP can search valuation matrices while a separation routine finds satisfying allocations.
Exploit within-group item symmetries and per-agent positive scaling. Do not sort agents away when the no-envy order is fixed.
For a positive proof, use small allocation menus on valuation regions and exact linear certificate checking, rather than exhaustively enumerating numerical valuations.
pitfalls: Lemma 12 already disproves the top-i-goods-in-distinct-bundles construction. Rediscovering that example is not a win; it does not disprove the desired EF1/no-envy property.
EF1 alone, or the existence of some acyclic envy order rather than the prescribed order, is insufficient.
All goods must be allocated, and every bundle must obey both its size and group constraints.

targets.name: Lottery numbers L(n,6,6,2) for n >= 71: fewest 6-number tickets that guarantee a 2-match prize (UK-lottery problem, past the published range)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (constraint programming or SAT on a local model around a maximal independent set, as in Cushing-Stewart; checking an explicit design means scanning C(n,6) draws, about 1.3e8 at n = 71 and 6.2e8 at n = 90, which takes seconds to minutes)
targets.statement: L(n,6,6,2) is the minimum number of six-number tickets such that every six-number draw from n numbers shares at least two numbers with some ticket. David Cushing and David I. Stewart, 'Applying constraint programming to minimal lottery designs' (arXiv:2307.12430v3, 17 Jun 2024; journal version Constraints 2024, doi:10.1007/s10601-024-09368-5), determine L(n,6,6,2) for every n <= 70, including L(70,6,6,2) = 35; their program's output for n = 71 reads 'Conjecture L(71,6,6,2) = 38'. Their lower bounds rest on a Prolog constraint-programming run without a proof certificate. As of 2026-10-25 a search found no later paper settling any n >= 71. The target is an exact value for some 71 <= n <= 90: an explicit design plus a certified proof that one ticket fewer is impossible. Upper bounds alone are already covered by the lottery-design partial win of covering-designs-record.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the EXACT value of L(n,6,6,2) for at least one n with 71 <= n <= 90, established by both of the following. (a) An explicit list of L tickets (6-subsets of {1..n}) such that every one of the C(n,6) draws meets some ticket in >= 2 numbers, checked exhaustively. (b) A proof that no design with L - 1 tickets exists, whose computational part comes with a certificate an independent tool checks: an LRAT/DRAT proof checked by cake_lpr or drat-trim, a VeriPB proof, or an exact ILP infeasibility certificate re-verified in rational arithmetic. Any mathematical reduction must be written out in full or cited to a published lemma (e.g. Cushing-Stewart arXiv:2307.12430 Section 3). L must also be no larger than the live upper bound for the cell. Read that bound from coveringrepository.com ((v,k,t,m) = (n,6,2,6)), lottodesigns.altervista.org, and any later paper citing Cushing-Stewart, all re-fetched at claim time. Before claiming, the claimant must also check that no later paper has already settled the cell. The first target is n = 71 (L(71,6,6,2) >= 35 by monotonicity; the published program conjectures 38).

partial_wins.statement: A certified lower bound: for some n in 71..90, a proof (same certificate standard as success criterion part b) that L(n,6,6,2) is STRICTLY greater than max(35, the Füredi-Székely-Zubor bound for n) and strictly greater than any lower bound published for that n after 2024-06-17.
