A certificate-backed re-proof of a Cushing-Stewart value for some n in 60..70 (e.g. L(67,6,6,2) = 34 or L(70,6,6,2) = 35): an explicit design plus an LRAT/DRAT, VeriPB or exact-ILP certificate for the non-existence of a design one ticket smaller. The published proofs rest on an uncertified Prolog CP run, so this is the first independently checkable proof of that value.

targets.verification_method: Upper part: parse the tickets and assert each has 6 distinct numbers in 1..n. Enumerate all C(n,6) draws, or equivalently build the graph G whose edges are pairs sharing a ticket and confirm that G has no independent set of size 6 (a clique search in the complement, run as a second, independent check). Lower part: run the certificate through its checker (cake_lpr or drat-trim for LRAT/DRAT, VeriPB for pseudo-Boolean proofs, exact rational re-verification for ILP), and confirm the encoding's generator matches the written reduction. Re-derive the reduction lemmas against Cushing-Stewart Section 3. Recompute the FSZ bound and the monotonicity bound. Re-fetch coveringrepository.com and lottodesigns.altervista.org for the cell, and search arXiv/Google Scholar for papers citing arXiv:2307.12430.
angles: Start at n = 71. The published program already reduces it to a few exceptional configurations (Figure 1 of arXiv:2307.12430: four 'bad (r,s)' tuples and one degree-pattern exception). Encode only those as SAT/CP with symmetry breaking, and emit LRAT or VeriPB certificates.

Re-implement the paper's local model (structure around a maximal independent set I, with |I| <= 5 forced because 6 independent numbers form a losing draw) in a certificate-producing solver (CaDiCaL plus LRAT, or RoundingSat/VeriPB) rather than Prolog CP. Calibrate by re-proving n = 66 to 70 first (partial win p2).

Equivalent form: L(n,6,6,2) is the fewest 6-cliques whose union graph on n vertices has independence number <= 5. The Turán-type and Shannon chromatic-index arguments in the paper are the obstruction side. Look there for the extra lemma that kills the n = 71 exceptions.

Upper side: a non-disjoint-union design with 37 tickets at n = 71 would also refute the program's conjecture of 38. Try local search seeded from the (14,14,14,14,15) union. Note that an upper-bound record by itself is already a covering-designs-record partial win (lottery (v,k,t,m) tables); here it counts only as part of an exact value.
Sweep n = 71..90 in order. L is monotone in n, so each settled value is a lower bound for the next. n = 90 (SuperEnalotto shape) is the showpiece cell.
pitfalls: Do not confuse L(n,k,p,t) (lottery designs) with covering designs C(v,k,t). The repositories write lottery designs as (v,k,t,m), with t the guarantee and m the draw size, so this entry's cells are (n,6,2,6).
The Cushing-Stewart lower bounds are not certificate-backed, and Bate-van Rees 1998 has known gaps. Do not cite either as a checker.
The FSZ minimum is over unequal partitions: the balanced partition overstates it.
The live repository value for (n,6,2,6) may already be below the disjoint-union bound. Read it before quoting an upper bound.
The Springer journal version (Constraints, 2024) was not read for this entry. Check it for any added values or corrections before claiming.

targets.name: MINLPLib finance and marketing instances still open: beat saa_2 (strategic asset allocation) or close pricing050 (product pricing) with a certificate
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (saa_2 has 4,408 variables and 400 binaries but may reduce to a few asset weights plus a funding scalar; pricing050 has 50 continuous variables)
targets.statement: MINLPLib, maintained by Stefan Vigerske, publishes feasible points and solver-reported dual bounds for each instance; minlplib.solu's '=bestdual=' uses the third-best solver bound. On 2026-10-25: saa_2 (asset management, MBNLP, minimise, in the library since 2001) has best point p4 = 12.1613089 and dual bounds up to 6.02323546 (GUROBI; =bestdual= 1.9954875180); pricing050 (marketing, NLP, maximise, added 2024; source Mohammadreza Kiaghadi; references Davarnia 2021 and Davarnia and van Hoeve 2021) has best point p1 = -1813.829078 and dual bounds down to -1534.3281 (SCIP; =bestdual= -1153.003281), a gap of 15.4% of the primal value against the best solver bound. The target is a better feasible point, or an independently checkable global certificate. A solver status line is not a certificate.
targets.success_criterion: A point file in MINLPLib's text .sol format ('varname value' lines for the nonzero variables, omitted variables read as 0, in the variable space of the posted instance) for saa_2 or pricing050 such that an evaluator written independently from the instance as currently posted at https://www.minlplib.org/gms/<name>.gms (cross-checked against the .py or .nl version) reports: (a) every variable within its bounds and every binary exactly 0 or 1; (b) maximum absolute violation over all algebraic constraints <= 1e-8 in double precision, confirmed with 50-digit mpmath; (c) an objective, recomputed from the model (saa_2: objvar = x4407, minimise; pricing050: objvar = -sum c_i x_i, maximise), strictly better than the '=best=' value for that instance in https://www.minlplib.org/minlplib.solu AND the best primal bound on https://www.minlplib.org/<name>.html, both re-fetched live immediately before claiming, by more than 1e-6 * max(1, |best|). As of 2026-10-25 the bars are saa_2 < 12.1613089 (min) and pricing050 > -1813.829078 (max). The evaluator must first reproduce the posted best point of the same instance (https://www.minlplib.org/sol/<name>.p<k>.sol: saa_2 p4 = 12.1613089, pricing050 p1 = -1813.829078) within one unit of the last printed digit of the reference objective, and must reject a deliberately perturbed copy. Point file, evaluator, instance sha256 and page snapshots are saved together. Sending a point to the MINLPLib maintainer is an action for the human. The displayed incumbents and the stated objective margin are numerical. Keep that margin for comparison to printed numerical values. If the incumbent is reconstructed exactly and candidate feasibility and objective are certified exactly, any strict improvement over that exact incumbent counts.

partial_wins.statement: A machine-checkable certificate that the optimum of pricing050 is at most the best known primal value plus 1e-6 * |value|. Example: (i) an interval-arithmetic (directed-rounding) proof that each of the 250 univariate terms a * x * exp(-b * x^p) is concave on [0,10]; and (ii) multipliers lambda in R^5_+ whose Lagrangian dual value, with each of the 50 separable univariate maximisations bounded rigorously by interval branch-and-bound, is within that tolerance of the primal point. This closes an instance MINLPLib lists as open (against the best solver bound, SCIP -1534.3281, the gap is 15.4% of the primal value).

A certified lower bound on the optimal value of saa_2 strictly above 6.02323546 (the best solver-reported dual bound on 2026-10-25, GUROBI). It must come with a re-runnable certificate: for example an interval branch-and-bound over the 5-asset weight simplex and the funding scalar, whose leaf log a skeptic can re-check in under 24 h on a laptop.

Certified global optimality of the best saa_2 point: a certificate as in partial win p2 whose lower bound is within 1e-6 relative of the best primal value. This closes an instance open since it was added in 2001, even if 12.1613089 turns out to be optimal.

The full success criterion met on any other MINLPLib instance whose application field is Portfolio Optimization, Financial Optimization, Asset Management or Marketing, provided that no solver-reported dual bound on its instance page is within 1e-6 relative of its best primal value at claim time.

targets.verification_method: Download https://www.minlplib.org/gms/<name>.gms (and the .py/.nl versions from the same site for cross-checking) and the posted best point https://www.minlplib.org/sol/<name>.p<k>.sol. pricing050 is a 6-equation model; a 40-line Python evaluator reproduces p1 = -1813.829078 with violation <= 1e-8. saa_2 is GAMS scalar format: parse its 6,206 equations (products of linear factors, bilinear terms and linear rows), or load the Pyomo .py version, set all variable values from the .sol file, and evaluate every constraint body. Reproduce p4 = 12.1613089 first. For certificates: re-run the interval computations with an independent library (mpmath.iv or python-flint/arb) and check that every leaf of the branch-and-bound log is covered. Re-fetch minlplib.solu and the instance page with plain curl before claiming.
angles: saa_2 is low-dimensional underneath. Fix the five weights w and the funding scalar, and every other variable (scenario wealths, products, shortfall binaries) is determined. So the true search is over a 4-simplex times an interval. Build a fast exact evaluator of 'minimal feasible funding given w', then run dense multistart or Lipschitz/interval branch-and-bound over the simplex. Either beat 12.1613089, or certify it (saa2-close). The 200 scenarios are monthly compounding paths, so precompute per-scenario polynomial coefficients.

Read saa_2 as a chance-constrained portfolio. The binaries pick which scenarios may miss each liability date. Enumerate or cut over 'which scenarios fail' with a MILP master for fixed weights, and wrap it in a simplex search.

pricing050: test the convexity reading first (interval second derivatives of x*exp(-b*x^p) on [0,10]). If it holds, any local NLP solve plus KKT multipliers gives the Lagrangian certificate. Separability means the dual function is a sum of 50 one-dimensional maximisations that can be bounded rigorously.
Make the evaluator the deliverable: an independent MINLPLib point checker (GAMS-free) is itself useful and makes every claim cheap to audit.
pitfalls: The instance listing's gap and minlplib.solu's '=bestdual=' use the third-best solver bound, so they overstate how open an instance is. Check every solver bound on the instance page; some instances look open in the listing but are effectively closed.
Solver-reported dual bounds are not certificates (the FAQ says they come 'from some run with some option settings on some machine'). A certified bound must carry its own checkable proof.
pricing050 is a maximisation and saa_2 a minimisation. saa_2's objective variable is objvar = x4407 (equation e4003); do not read another variable as the objective.

Tolerance games: MINLPLib accepts points with infeasibility <= 1e-8 absolute. An 'improvement' obtained by pushing degree-12 polynomial constraints to the edge of that tolerance is not a win; require the 1e-6 relative margin and an mpmath re-check.
If pricing050 is convex (unproven), its posted point is probably already optimal and a primal 'record' there is a bug signal. Aim that cell at the closing certificate.
Use the instance currently posted at minlplib.org (it is revised; the removed-instances archive holds older versions with the same names).

targets.name: NIST Circuit Complexity AES tables: a smaller or shallower {AND, XOR, XNOR} circuit for the AES S-box, inverse S-box, MixColumns or InvMixColumns
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days for the search (SAT and heuristic linear-layer optimisation, basis enumeration); verification takes seconds
targets.statement: NIST's Circuit Complexity project maintains straight-line circuits for the AES S-box, inverse S-box, MixColumns and InvMixColumns over the gate set {AND, XOR, XNOR} with no constants (GitHub usnistgov/Circuits, data/slp/aes/README.md, with subfolders holding more files than the README tables). On 2026-10-25 the README lists, for the S-box, minimum #AND 28 (best total at #AND 28: 124 gates), minimum total 110 gates and minimum gate depth 11; for the inverse S-box, minimum #AND 28 (126 gates at #AND 28), minimum total 112 and minimum gate depth 13; for MixColumns, 88 XOR (depth 5), 90 (depth 4) and 97 (depth 3); for InvMixColumns, 91 XOR (depth 15), 107 (depth 6) and 119 (depth 5). The CSRC page asks for external contributions on a wish list: S-box and inverse S-box with A <= 27, G <= 100, or G <= 120 with GD <= 12; MixColumns with G <= 86, or G <= 93 at GD 3; inverse MixColumns with G <= 105 at GD <= 5. These are construction bounds, not optimality results; contributors are credited in the repository tables. The repository changes often (commits on 2026-10-15 and 2026-10-16).
targets.success_criterion: Success means a circuit, given as a list of 2-input gates of types AND, XOR and XNOR only (NIST Circuit File Format, or one 'GATE out in1 in2' line per gate), with no other gate types and no constants, that computes exactly FIPS 197 SBox(), InvSBox(), MixColumns() or InvMixColumns() under the NIST files' bit conventions (U0 and S0 are the most significant bits of the S-box input and output byte; for [inv]mixcols x_(8b+r) and y_(8b+r) are bit r, LSB = 0, of byte b), verified on all 256 inputs for [inv]SBox and as an exact GF(2)-linear map for [inv]MixColumns, and that meets at least one wish-list target on https://csrc.nist.gov/Projects/circuit-complexity/list-of-circuits as re-fetched at claim time (direction: min in every case; on 2026-10-25: (a) [inv]SBox with #AND <= 27; (b) [inv]SBox with #gates <= 100; (c) [inv]SBox with #gates <= 120 and gate depth <= 12; (d) MixColumns with #XOR <= 86; (e) MixColumns with #XOR <= 93 at gate depth 3; (f) InvMixColumns with #XOR <= 105 at gate depth <= 5). The metric must also strictly improve the best comparable circuit in the live README, the subfolder files, the CSRC page and later publications, under the same gate model. The verifier recomputes all metrics: #gates counts every AND, XOR and XNOR; gate depth is the longest input-to-output path counted in gates; AND depth is the largest number of AND gates on any path.

partial_wins.statement: An [inv]SBox circuit with fewer total gates than the live minimum for that direction (110 for SBox and 112 for InvSBox on 2026-10-25), at any #AND and any depth, verified as in the success criterion.

An [inv]SBox circuit whose #AND equals the live minimum (28 on 2026-10-25) and whose total gate count is strictly below every listed circuit with that #AND (124 for SBox and 126 for InvSBox on 2026-10-25).

A MixColumns or InvMixColumns circuit with strictly fewer XOR gates than every listed circuit of the same function whose gate depth is at most the candidate's depth (on 2026-10-25: MixColumns 88 at any depth, 90 at depth <= 4, 97 at depth 3; InvMixColumns 91 at any depth, 107 at depth <= 6, 119 at depth 5).

An [inv]SBox circuit with gate depth strictly below the live minimum for that direction (11 for SBox and 13 for InvSBox on 2026-10-25) at any size, or with AND depth 3 and at most 34 AND gates (the listed AND-depth-3 circuits use 35).

targets.verification_method: Parse the gate list; reject any gate type other than AND, XOR and XNOR, any wire used before it is defined or defined twice, and any constant. Evaluate the gates in order. [inv]SBox: compare all 256 inputs with the FIPS 197 tables, most significant bit first (calibrate on the listed aes-sbox-a32-ad5-g110-gd22-xx78-3 and aes-mixcols-xor88-depth5 files first). [inv]MixColumns: require XOR gates only, feed the 32 unit vectors and compare the resulting 32x32 GF(2) matrix with the byte matrices [02 03 01 01; 01 02 03 01; 01 01 02 03; 03 01 01 02] and [0e 0b 0d 09; 09 0e 0b 0d; 0d 09 0e 0b; 0b 0d 09 0e] in the files' bit convention (calibrate on a listed file first). Compute #AND, #gates, gate depth and AND depth in one pass, then compare with the live README tables, the subfolder listings (file names encode A, AD, G, GD) and the CSRC page, all re-fetched just before claiming. Seconds on any machine. Condition the comparison bar on the selected target depth or AND budget. For partial p2 compare total gates at the best AND count; for p3 compare XOR counts at depth no greater than the candidate. For p4 compare minimum gate depth without a size limit, or AND count at AND depth at most 3 for its second route.
angles: Treat the listed circuits as data: several 2026 entries were 'derived therefrom via linear optimization' of contributed circuits. Re-optimise the top and bottom linear layers of each listed S-box with exact or randomised linear-circuit methods (Boyar-Peralta exploring all ties, RNBP, Maximov-Ekdahl depth-bounded search, SAT-based exact SLP for small blocks) while keeping the nonlinear core fixed.

Enumerate tower-field and basis choices (polynomial or normal bases for GF(2^2), GF(2^4) and GF(2^8), and the isomorphism matrices) as Canright and Boyar-Peralta did, now with modern SAT/MaxSAT optimisation of each linear layer; the best basis for G need not be the best for A or GD.

For A <= 27, study how the A28 circuits beat the classical split of 32 ANDs (three GF(2^4) multiplications at 9 ANDs each plus a 5-AND GF(2^4) inversion), and search for shared bilinear products across the multiplications with multiplicative-complexity tools for 4- to 6-bit functions.

MixColumns is a byte-circulant matrix: impose its 4-fold rotation symmetry to shrink an exact bounded-depth SAT search (depth 3 is the natural first target), then break the symmetry. For InvMixColumns, seed from the factorisation of InvMixColumns as MixColumns times a sparse matrix.
Run many diversified searches in parallel and keep one Pareto archive over (A, AD, G, GD); improvements in one coordinate often appear as by-products of searching another.
pitfalls: The repository moves fast (commits on 2026-10-15 and 2026-10-16 alone). Re-fetch the README, the subfolder listings, the commit log and the CSRC page immediately before claiming; the CSRC page and the README can differ.
Gate set: NOT, NAND, NOR, OR, MUX and constant inputs are not allowed. Maximov-Ekdahl's 102-gate S-box and Canright's 120-gate S-box use other gates and are not comparable.

Bit order: U0/S0 are the most significant bits for the S-boxes, and MixColumns uses x_(8b+r) = bit r of byte b. A circuit correct under another convention computes a different function until its wires are permuted, and the claim must be about the circuit as submitted.
The README tables show selected circuits only; the subfolders hold more files. Compare against every file and the CSRC page, and recompute metrics yourself rather than trusting file names.
Change-of-basis layers count: a tower-field S-box must take and return standard AES bytes.

Novelty: AI-assisted search is active on this exact table, so the window is short; also check ePrint and arXiv for 2026 AES circuit papers. The maintainers prefer wish-list targets to small increments, so a partial win may beat the table without being listed by them.

targets.name: Octal games: certify the period of one unsettled octal game with at most three code digits in Flammenkamp's table
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days per game (sequential sparse-space sliding window; about 1e15 table lookups to go from 2^43 to 2^44 for the cheapest games; memory is only the window, 1e4 to 1e9 values)
targets.statement: An octal game 0.d1d2d3 (or 4.d1d2d3) is an impartial heap game whose digit d_i says whether removing i tokens may leave zero, one or two heaps; it is conjectured that every finite octal game has an ultimately periodic Sprague-Grundy (nim) sequence. Achim Flammenkamp's table (octal.html, last updated 2026-10-23 20:28 UTC+2) says 'There are still 65 and 8 unsettled' octal games with at most 3 places (and Grundy's game and 0.6111...); its unsettled.txt lists 65 of the form 0.ddd and 8 of the form 4.ddd, for example .6, .14, .36, .64, .76, .167, .174, .205 and 4.045, and the main table also shows .007 (Treblecross) without a period. These have been computed to max n = 2^27 (games with no sparse-space structure, such as .06 and .125) up to 2^43 (.167: 60 rare values, last rare index 1,303, depth 9,407; .174: 57 rare values, last 674; .205; 4.045; 0.6111...), and 2^42 for .015, .245, .324 and 4.367, without a period. In July 2026 Tyler Satchel Orden extended the sequences of many games, and in October 2026 Udo Sprute contributed a parallel C/OpenMP program. Record solved games: .106 (period 328,226,140,474, preperiod 465,384,263,797; 2002-05-21), 4.404 (preperiod 6,872,982,644; 2012-10-29), .104 and .454 (2000-2001). Find the period and preperiod of any game on the unsettled list.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: for one game that is unsettled at verification time, meaning listed in http://wwwhomes.uni-bielefeld.de/achim/unsettled.txt or shown without a period among the non-trivial games of the main table on octal.html (0.ddd or 4.ddd; Grundy's game and 0.6111... excluded because their periodicity criteria differ), an explicit preperiod n0 and period p such that a program sharing no code with the claimant's search computes G(0..N) exactly and verifies G(i+p) = G(i) for every i in [n0, N - p), with N large enough for a published sufficient condition: either the Guy-Smith theorem as quoted in Plambeck, arXiv:math/0501315 (for a finite octal with P places after the point, G(r+p) = G(r) for all r0 <= r < 2*r0 + p + P implies it for all r >= r0; for a 4.ddd game the claimant must justify that the theorem covers splitting without removal, or use the next condition) or Flammenkamp's sparse-space condition (verify over t + max{last, depth} successive values beyond the preperiod, t the largest index of a non-zero digit, p even for a sparse space), stating which one is used. The recomputed sequence must also match Flammenkamp's published value-frequency statistics (nim/stat_<game>) up to his max n. A period claimed from a repeated block without the full window, or from a hash match without exact re-verification, does not count.

partial_wins.statement: The first independent verification of a published record period with a program sharing no code with Flammenkamp's: .106 (period 328,226,140,474, preperiod 465,384,263,797), .104 (period 11,770,282, preperiod 197,769,598), .454 (60,620,715 / 160,949,019) or 4.404 (145 / 6,872,982,644), re-proved under a stated sufficient condition, with the code and frequency statistics published; or a demonstration that one of them is wrong.

targets.verification_method: Write an independent nim-sequence generator from the octal code definition (digit d_i: bit 1 = remove i tokens leaving no heap, bit 2 = leaving one heap, bit 4 = leaving two non-empty heaps; leading 4 = split without removal), check it against easy_octal.txt (first 40 values and the published periods of small solved games such as .45, .156, .644, .16), then run it to N and test G(i+p) = G(i) over the required window exactly. Compare value frequencies with Flammenkamp's nim/stat_<game> file up to his max n. Sparse-space acceleration is allowed in the checker, but its common/rare split must be re-derived, not copied.
angles: Pick games with tiny rare sets and short windows, where a period, if it exists at reachable size, is cheapest to see: .167, .174, 4.045, .245, .015, .166, .374, .774. After the last rare value the game is a finite shift register of length at most last + t (Flammenkamp's remark), so run Brent cycle detection on a rolling hash of the register state instead of storing the sequence, then verify exactly.

Parallelise the mex step: contributions from rare indices r >= R depend only on values at least R steps back, so most cores can precompute the excluded-value sets for a block ahead of the frontier while one core finishes the near contributions; this turns a sequential 1e15-step job into days.
Calibrate on .106: its period (3.3e11) and preperiod (4.7e11) appeared at about 2^40, so the evaluator's speed and correctness can be tested on a known answer (partial win p1) before any open game.

Look at depth and last+t together: games whose depth is close to last (.36: last 11,798, depth 32,322; .374: last 2,354, depth 10,961) have small states, while games such as .64 (depth 6.2e8) are poor bets.
pitfalls: This is a lottery: several cheap games have run to 2^43 (8.8e12) with no period; a week of laptop time reaches perhaps 2^44 to 2^45 for one game.

Active competition: Tyler Satchel Orden extended many sequences in July 2026, Udo Sprute contributed a parallel program in October 2026, and the page was updated on 2026-10-23; re-fetch the table and the game's stat file before and after a run.
Many codes are the same game (comp_octal.txt maps all 1024 codes to 167 standard forms), but not all apparent twins are: .161 differs from .36 from index 520 on (Czajka, 2020).
The games marked '?' (11 in unsettled.txt on 2026-10-25, among them .06 and .125) have no known sparse-space structure; without it the computation is quadratic and stuck near 2^27.

unsettled.txt lists .64 twice; the main table also shows .74 without a period, so the second entry is probably .74. Use the main table's list of non-trivial games without a period as the authority and say which game is claimed.
Flammenkamp's stat files cover heap sizes 0 to 2^k - 1; the 'max n' column encodes 2^k as k (for example 243 means 2^43).
A long repeated block, or an equal rolling hash, is evidence, not proof; only the exact window check counts.

targets.name: QOBLIB minimum Birkhoff decomposition: an exact decomposition of B5_25_2 with at most 13 terms or B6_36_10 with at most 18
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days for search; exact checking takes seconds; 5x5 and 6x6 integer matrices, respectively 120 and 720 possible permutation columns
targets.statement: QOBLIB's Minimum Birkhoff Decomposition problem (ZIB-AOPT/QOBLIB, 03-birkhoff) asks for the fewest permutation matrices in an exact convex decomposition of a doubly stochastic matrix (Kulkarni, Lee and Singh, IPCO 2017; Dufosse and Ucar, Linear Algebra Appl. 2016). On 2026-10-28 the auto-generated best-known table (last updated 2026-10-19) lists B5_25_2 at 14 and B6_36_10 at 20, both from the 20260111_MIP_Schicker submission (Maximilian Schicker, 2026-01-10). The table lags for B6_36_10: András Czégel (arXiv:2610.25837, 2026-10-19, Appendix D, Table 8) reports exact integer-weight decompositions of length 14 for B5_25_2 and 19 for B6_36_10. The 19-term decomposition is public in the paper's data repository (tg90000/rcs-birkhoff) and in QOBLIB PR #95 (submission 20261020_RecoverCertifySearch_Czegel, opened 2026-10-20, unmerged on 2026-10-28) and reconstructs B6_36_10 exactly (re-checked for this entry), so the published bars are 14 for B5_25_2 and 19 for B6_36_10. Both matrices are integer matrices with row and column sums 10000 (scale 10000) in qbench_05_dense.json and qbench_06_dense.json. The current solutions/B5_25_2.bst.json and B6_36_10.bst.json files list 13 and 17 terms with floating-point weights, but neither support reconstructs its matrix exactly over the rationals (re-checked for this entry: the exact linear systems are inconsistent, residuals about 12 and 24 in the scaled entries), so they do not settle these cells.
targets.success_criterion: For either named matrix A, give pairwise distinct permutations and strictly positive rational weights w_k summing to 10000 such that A=sum_k w_k P_k entrywise exactly, with at most 13 terms for B5_25_2 or at most 18 for B6_36_10. This is a record win; global minimality need not be proved. Alternatively, close either exact optimum by an attaining decomposition and an independently checkable lower-bound certificate valid for arbitrary nonnegative real weights. A certificate restricted to integer weights does not establish the latter claim.
targets.verification_method: Locate instances by their id, not JSON insertion order. Check integer matrix entries, common row/column sum 10000 and each submitted permutation of 1..n. Merge duplicate permutations and discard zero weights before counting. Clear rational denominators and check all 25 or 36 reconstruction equations and the weight sum with arbitrary-precision integers; tolerance must be zero. Use row-major storage, as confirmed against the exact MIP incumbents. For an optimality claim, a rational MILP branch proof over all n! support indicators and continuous weights can be checked node by node using Farkas/dual certificates. The small audit script checks fixed supports, not optimality, and is not a substitute for a general lower-bound proof.
angles: Start with a support-selection MILP over 120 or 720 permutations, then solve its weights exactly. Integer-only models are useful for finding witnesses but restrict the mathematical problem.
Use the approximate 13/17-term supports only as search seeds. They cannot be made exact just by increasing numerical precision; their exact systems are inconsistent.
Favor local support replacement and exact nullspace reductions. Keep all matrix equations, not only row and column totals.
pitfalls: The instance description and checker use different storage-language conventions; these MIP witnesses reconstruct the target in row-major order.
A smaller approximate support is not an exact decomposition.

The Schicker submission's 'optimality bounds' (13 for B5_25_2, 11 for B6_36_10) come from an integer-weight model solved numerically by Gurobi; they bound integer decompositions, not decompositions with real weights.
Exact rational weights, including any strict improvement, require zero reconstruction tolerance.
Benchmark libraries are open targets: publish the exact decomposition in full.

The table lags: B6_36_10 at 19 terms is already published (Czégel, arXiv:2610.25837; the object is in QOBLIB PR #95 and tg90000/rcs-birkhoff) although the auto-generated table shows 20 while that PR is unmerged; reproducing 19 terms is NOT new. Check recent preprints and open QOBLIB submissions, not only the table.

targets.name: Risk or Safety: exact optimal-play win probabilities beyond n = 30 (OEIS A387261/A387262)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (exact policy iteration over O(n^3) positions with big rationals, one strongly connected component at a time; measure growth at n >= 31)
targets.statement: Two players race to n banked points. On a turn the player tosses a fair coin: each head adds one open point and the player may then stop, banking the open points (turn passes), or toss again; a tail loses all open points and passes the turn. First to n points wins. Jehn ('Optimal strategy in the game Risk or Safety', arXiv:2603.01002, March 2026) proves the solution is unique (following Glenn, Fang and Kruskal's argument for Can't Stop), solves n <= 6 analytically (first-player win probability 6/11 for n = 3, 2236/4165 for n = 4, 1026/1925 for n = 5, 275848876/521145625 for n = 6) and gives optimal strategies up to n = 20 (paper Table 1; OEIS A394776, b-file of 400 terms). On 2026-10-25 OEIS A387261 (numerators) and A387262 (denominators), keyword 'hard', list n = 1..15 (last edited 10 Apr 2026). Exact terms for n = 16..30, each with a Bellman certificate, are in this repository at known-knowns/risk-or-safety-exact-optimal-play/ (merged 2026-10-15, pull request #169). The rules appear to coincide with the coin variant of Pig ('Piglet') analysed by Neller and Presser; check that work for prior exact values before claiming novelty. The open extension starts at n = 31.
targets.success_criterion: Exact reduced rationals A387261(n)/A387262(n) - the starting player's win probability from (0 open, 0 banked, 0 banked) under optimal play by both players - for EVERY n from 31 through 45 (direction: new terms), each with a certificate: the claimed value P(a, b, c) for every position (a open and b banked points of the player to move, c banked by the opponent) and the claimed action, satisfying exactly P(a, b, c) = max(continue, stop) for a >= 1 and the forced toss for a = 0, where continue = (1/2)(1 - P(0, c, b)) + (1/2) P(a + 1, b, c) and stop = 1 - P(0, c, a + b), with P = 1 when a + b >= n (equations of Sections 3-4 of arXiv:2603.01002), all checked in exact arithmetic. The same code must reproduce the published terms (n <= 15) and the terms in known-knowns/risk-or-safety-exact-optimal-play/ (n = 16..30), or certify a correction (see p1). Check the OEIS entries, b-files, edit histories and the repository's known-knowns before claiming; terms already established there do not count as new terms.

partial_wins.statement: A certified correction: an exact Bellman certificate showing that a published value (A387261/A387262 for n <= 15, or the repository's terms for n = 16..30) or a published optimal action (paper Table 1 / A394776, n <= 20) is not optimal.
Certified exact terms for every n = 31..35 with complete independently checked Bellman value/action tables, after calibration on the published and repository terms through n = 30.

targets.verification_method: A short checker in Python fractions reads the claimed value and action tables, checks terminal positions, then checks at every non-terminal position that the claimed value equals the maximum of the two action values computed from the table itself (only the toss at a = 0) and that the claimed action attains it. Every strategy pair ends the game with probability 1 (banked totals never fall and each turn has positive probability of progress), so these equations have a unique solution (Jehn Section 2) and the check proves optimality. Reduce P(0,0,0) and compare with OEIS; calibrate on the closed forms for n <= 6, the OEIS terms for n <= 15 and the repository's terms for n = 16..30.
angles: Banked scores never decrease, so positions split into components with a fixed pair {b, c}; solve components in decreasing b + c, each a small two-player stochastic game, by exact policy iteration.
Find the policy in floating point first, then do one exact rational solve per component and an exact policy-improvement check.
Numerators reach 38 digits at n = 15 and keep growing: use GMP or FLINT rationals.
Cross-check the action table against A394776's encoding (n = (j-1)^2 + i if i < j, else i^2 - j + 1, for i points needed by the mover and j by the opponent).
pitfalls: At a = 0 the player must toss; stopping with no open points is not an action.
Reaching n with open points counts as a win (the paper sets P = 1 when a + b = n).
Near-ties can flip a floating-point policy choice; decide actions only after an exact comparison.
OEIS 'hard' reflects the original method, not the problem; the main risk is a rules mismatch (who moves first, banking at n), so reproduce n <= 6 exactly before scaling up.
If the game is exactly Neller-Presser's Piglet, earlier exact or numerical work may exist for some n; check before claiming.

targets.name: Minimum-comparison selection: settle V8(16) in {28, 29}, or beat the new n = 17 upper bounds (V6..V9 of 17)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (single-threaded proof-number or depth-first construction search in Rust, many workers in parallel; certificates check in seconds; refuting a budget is far more expensive than finding an algorithm)
targets.statement: V_i(n) is the minimum worst-case comparison count for finding the i-th smallest of n distinct elements. Jonathan Cremer, 'Selecting the 7th Smallest of 16 Elements Takes Exactly 28 Comparisons' (arXiv:2610.18740, v1 13 Oct 2026; certificates, checkers and a Lean 4 development at github.com/JCremerr/selection-7-of-16), reports V_7(16)=28 and 28 <= V_8(16) <= 29. For n=17 and ranks 6 through 9, reported upper bounds are 29, 30, 31 and 31; lower bounds are 28, 29, 29 and 29. The lower bounds and the search code are from Dörrer et al. (SEA 2025, doi:10.4230/LIPIcs.SEA.2025.16). As of 2026-10-25 the arXiv abstract page lists v1 only. The target is an explicit decision graph improving one of these five upper bounds. A 28-comparison algorithm for V_8(16) closes that cell if the reported lower bound remains current.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit comparison-selection algorithm for one cell (n, i) in {(16, 8), (17, 6), (17, 7), (17, 8), (17, 9)} (1-based rank i; the mirror rank n+1-i is the same cell), written as a decision graph in the Rust certificate format of Cremer's repository and of the Dörrer et al. search code (functions that compare two arguments, discard arguments that cannot be the answer, call another function on the remaining arguments, or return an element), or in a format converted losslessly into it, whose worst-case number of comparisons is STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the best upper bound for that cell on the status sources re-fetched at verification time (on 2026-10-25: V8(16) <= 29, V6(17) <= 29, V7(17) <= 30, V8(17) <= 31, V9(17) <= 31, all from Cremer arXiv:2610.18740v1) and than any lower value in a newer arXiv version or in any paper citing it. The certificate must be accepted, with the claimed worst case, by (1) Cremer's static checker (python3 -I code/verifier/verify_rs_algorithm.py CERT.rs --expect-n N --expect-i I --expect-worst W, where --expect-i is 1-based) and (2) a second checker written from the definition without Cremer's code. A reported worst case below the proven lower bound (V8(16) >= 28; V6(17) >= 28; V7(17), V8(17), V9(17) >= 29) means a checker or parser bug, not a record. A 28-comparison certificate for the 8th smallest of 16 settles V8(16) = 28 and is the headline result; a certificate meeting the lower bound for an n = 17 cell settles that cell.

partial_wins.statement: A raised lower bound for one of the open cells (V8(16) >= 29; V6(17) >= 29; V7(17), V8(17) or V9(17) >= 30) established either by a proof object accepted by a formally verified checker (for example a Lean 4 proof, or a DRAT/LRAT/VeriPB proof of an encoding whose correctness is argued in a short note), or by two independently written exhaustive searches (for example a forward minimax search and a backward search, as Dörrer et al. did) that complete with the same answer and whose runs a skeptic can repeat on comparable hardware; the second route is labelled computational, not certified.

An explicit certificate for a cell (18, i) with 5 <= i <= 9 whose worst case is strictly below the Hadian-Sobel bound n - i + (i - 1) * ceil(log2(n + 2 - i)) and below every value for that cell in Gasarch-Kelly-Pugh 1996 Table 3 and later sources (a claimant must locate and read that table), verified by the same two checkers.

targets.verification_method: Fetch the certificate and run Cremer's tooling as in his README quick start (SHA-256 check; code/verifier/verify_rs_algorithm.py with --expect-n/--expect-i/--expect-worst; code/independent_checks/checker/pathcheck.py; Python standard library only, seconds). Then run an independent checker written from the definition: start from the empty order on n elements, follow both outcomes of every comparison while maintaining the transitive closure, compute each function's precondition as the relations common to all its call sites (never trust doc comments), require each discarded element to have at least r+1 known predecessors or at least m-r known successors (0-based rank r among m remaining elements), require each returned element to have exactly r known predecessors and m-1-r known successors, require call arguments to be distinct and the callee rank to be adjusted correctly, require an acyclic call graph, and take the maximum number of comparisons over all paths. Optional third and fourth checks: compile the Rust certificate and run it on 10^7 or more random permutations, and replay Cremer's Lean 4 development (code/lean; about 3 minutes and 1.8 GB for his seven bounds) on the new certificate. Calibrate both checkers on Cremer's certificates (they must report exactly 28 for V7(16) and 29 for V8(16)) and on optimal algorithms published by Dörrer et al. Re-fetch the repository README and the arXiv listing immediately before claiming.
angles: Proof-number search with a better initialisation: Cremer seeds unexplored df-pn nodes from a cost predictor fitted to exactly solved small problems, shifted pessimistically, and reports that this mattered by factors of 10-100. Fit a stronger predictor on a larger corpus of exactly solved reduced posets (n <= 12-13, generated with the Dörrer et al. code) and run many df-pn workers in parallel with different predictor shifts, tie-breaks and comparison orderings at one fixed budget.

Leave the runner-up opening for V8(16): Cremer's search found no 28-comparison completion from his 15-comparison opening R16 (a search-level result, stated as such), so a 28-comparison median-of-16 algorithm, if it exists, opens differently. Enumerate openings of 10-16 comparisons up to isomorphism, rank them by the combined Fussenegger-Gabow weight and the KEY bound (Cremer, Section 5), and run df-pn from each opening state at the remaining budget.

This is an AND/OR game against an adversary: game-solving machinery transfers directly (df-pn+ with threshold control, transposition tables keyed by canonical reduced posets shared across workers, dual problems (P, i) and (P reversed, n+1-i) sharing entries, retrograde tables of all small reduced problems).

For n = 17, start from Cremer's certificates (his Table 3: 266 to 1,493 functions, found in 89 s to 63 min single-threaded) and ask for one comparison less; V6(17) is one comparison above its lower bound 28, so a 28 certificate settles that cell outright.

Feed the refutation side too: any state lower bound stronger than Cremer's combined weight (for example weights on solutions rather than counts, as he suggests) prunes the construction search and is the only road to p1.
pitfalls: Index conventions differ: Cremer's checker flag --expect-i is 1-based, while the doc comments and the Dörrer et al. program use 0-based ranks; V_i(n) = V_{n+1-i}(n), so (16, 9) is the same cell as (16, 8).

The status moved on 2026-10-13 and the field has at least two active groups; re-fetch the README, the arXiv listing and papers citing arXiv:2610.18740 immediately before claiming. A tie is not a record.

A checker that reads the relations stated in doc comments instead of propagating them from the call sites accepts wrong programs; Cremer's checker intersects preconditions over all callers for this reason.
Random-permutation testing is not a proof; the exhaustive propagation check (or the Lean replay) is.
Refutations under a fixed opening, timeouts and search logs are not lower bounds; only the routes listed in p1 count, and the two-program route is labelled computational.
A worst case below a proven lower bound (28 for V8(16)) means a bug in the certificate, its parser or the checker.

targets.name: SMT-COMP 2026 P4/DFA bit-vector holdouts: one exact SAT model or UNSAT certificate
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days using alternative preprocessing and solver configurations; require model/proof checking within laptop-hours
targets.statement: The SMT-COMP 2026 benchmark metadata (benchmarks-2026.json.gz in the SMT-COMP/smt-comp.github.io repository) gives SMT-LIB status 'unknown' to 79 QF_BV files of the family 20221214-p4dfa-XiaoqiChen (P4 / DFA packet-processing benchmarks by Xiaoqi Chen). Eight of them were run in the 2026 single-query track, 23 runs each, all Timeout or unknown: under QF_BV/20221214-p4dfa-XiaoqiChen/, Composition/compose.s4._bit8_na6_nr4_paired.smt2; StringMatching/string2x16.10._bit8_na6_nr3_paired.smt2; StringMatching/string4x16.2._bit8_na6_nr4_pairedtwobranch.smt2; StringMatching/string4x8.2._bit8_na6_nr3_paired.smt2; StringMatching/string4x8.3._bit16_na6_nr4_paired.smt2; StringMatching/string4x8.5._bit8_na6_nr3_paired.smt2; StringMatching/string4x8.8._bit16_na6_nr4_paired.smt2; TCP/tcp_full_split4_bit8_na6_nr4_paired.smt2 (4969 assertions). Re-checked on 2026-10-25: none of the 79 unknown-status files has a sat or unsat result in the 2026 single-query, model-validation, parallel or unsat-core logs, and those of the eight that appear in the 2023-2025 single-query logs were never decided there either. Public timeouts do not exclude private results.
targets.success_criterion: Decide any one of the eight exact benchmark instances with an independently checked SAT model or UNSAT certificate. Identify the official SMT-LIB file path and SHA-256 of the unmodified downloaded input. A SAT answer needs a total assignment satisfying every assertion under exact SMT-LIB bit-vector semantics. An UNSAT answer needs a checked bit-blasting translation plus a replayable SAT proof, or another independently checkable theory proof. A bare solver answer, timeout change or solution of a simplified non-equivalent instance does not win.

partial_wins.statement: The same standard of certificate for any other file of the 20221214-p4dfa-XiaoqiChen family whose status is 'unknown' in the SMT-COMP 2026 benchmark metadata and which has no sat or unsat result in any SMT-COMP 2023-2026 log at claim time.

targets.verification_method: For SAT, parse the original SMT-LIB input and evaluate all terms under the submitted assignment using width-bounded integers, including signed operations, shifts, overflow and division-by-zero semantics. For UNSAT, independently reconstruct or certify every preprocessing/bit-blasting step, and validate the resulting LRAT or comparably explicit proof. Verify that the CNF proved UNSAT is equisatisfiable with the original assertions. Accept only certificates that a reviewer can check within hours on one laptop; search runtime itself is not evidence.
angles: Inspect the TCP and smaller string-matching constraints first, identify repeated automaton structure, and derive semantics-preserving preprocessing.
Try word-level simplification before bit-blasting and switch between eager and lazy bit-vector reasoning.
Use failed runs to choose a different encoding or branching strategy; prioritize SAT models because their certificates are smaller.
pitfalls: Unknown metadata alone is insufficient; check corresponding result logs.
The original input must be downloaded and hashed before attacking or claiming; metadata is not input verification.
A public timeout does not prove no private solution exists.
Every UNSAT preprocessing and translation step needs independent checking.
SMT-LIB status fields change between releases; check the current SMT-LIB release and the SMT-COMP results of the latest year before claiming.

targets.name: Three agents dividing additive chores: does a complete EFX allocation always exist?
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days for adversarial integer-cost search; checking a 3-agent, 13–15-chore counterexample means 1594323–14348907 allocations
targets.statement: Wentao He and Biaoshuai Tao, 'EFX for Additive Chores: Nonexistence, Pareto Incompatibility, and Bi-Valued Existence' (arXiv:2606.08872, v1 7 Jun 2026, v2 9 Jul 2026), explicitly state in Section 6: "It is open whether an EFX allocation always exists for three agents." They show nonexistence for every n>=4, using a four-agent, thirteen-chore, three-cost-level example, and prove existence for four agents with bi-valued costs. Thus neither the general four-agent nonexistence question nor four-agent bi-valued existence is a new target. The remaining three-agent problem has nonnegative additive costs c_ig. A complete allocation X is EFX if, whenever X_i is nonempty, c_i(X_i)-min_{g in X_i}c_ig <= c_i(X_j) for every i,j. This is Definition 2 in the paper, including zero-cost chores. No Pareto or efficiency condition is imposed. As of 2026-10-25 the abstract page lists v2 as the latest version.
targets.success_criterion: Settle the stated three-agent existence question: EITHER an explicit nonnegative rational 3 x m cost matrix with no complete EFX allocation (Definition 2 of the paper) and a complete exact obstruction certificate; OR a kernel-checked formal proof (Lean, Coq or Isabelle, no sorry, admit or extra axioms) that a complete EFX allocation exists for every m and all nonnegative additive costs. A written proof whose steps are not formalised, bounded tests, or a bounded-size UNSAT search do not establish existence. The preferred computational route is a small counterexample with a strict violation in every allocation.
targets.verification_method: For a finite counterexample clear denominators, precompute exact subset costs for each agent and enumerate every assignment of every chore to one of the three labeled agents. For each allocation, verify an ordered pair i,j with nonempty X_i and c_i(X_i)-min_{g in X_i}c_ig > c_i(X_j). Empty bundles are handled exactly as in Definition 2. Enumeration with incremental subset sums takes minutes to hours for the suggested sizes. If chores have identical cost columns, an independently verified multiplicity enumeration can replace labeled enumeration. Positive general proofs require a proof kernel; bounded tests or a bounded-size UNSAT search do not prove existence for arbitrary m.
angles: Use the published four-agent, three-type obstruction as structural guidance, while recognizing that simply deleting an agent changes the problem.
Search integer cost matrices with a few repeated chore types and a separation routine that returns an EFX allocation to rule out the current candidate.
Require a positive exact obstruction margin and simplify a found instance before certifying all allocations.
pitfalls: For chores, remove an item from the envious agent's OWN bundle. The goods convention removes an item from the envied bundle.
EFX tests removal of every item, equivalently the cheapest own chore, not the most expensive one.
The source's general n>=4 counterexamples are already published. Bi-valued instances with up to four agents are already covered by existence results.
A failure of EFX plus Pareto optimality is not a failure of EFX existence.

targets.name: Single-error-correcting codes for the Z-channel: beat 112, 198 or 379 (Sloane's 1zc challenge graphs), or certify a tighter upper bound
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (maximum-independent-set heuristics and exact solvers on graphs with 1,024 to 4,096 vertices; verification in milliseconds)
targets.statement: A Z-channel can change a transmitted 1 into 0, never 0 into 1. For distinct binary words x, y let N(x,y) count positions with x_i = 1 and y_i = 0; a code corrects one such error iff max(N(x,y), N(y,x)) >= 2 for every pair (asymmetric distance 2). OEIS A010101 (N. J. A. Sloane) gives the maximum code sizes 1, 2, 2, 4, 6, 12, 18, 36, 62 for n = 1..9 and says the next three terms lie in 112-117, 198-210 and 379-410 (last edited 24 Aug 2020); Sloane's 'Challenge Problems: Independent Sets in Graphs' page lists the equivalent graphs 1zc.1024, 1zc.2048 and 1zc.4096 (1zc.1024 'Most wanted!'), with the lower bounds from Etzion and Ostergard (IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 44 (1998)) and, for n = 12, Butenko, Pardalos, Sergienko, Shylo and Stetsyuk (379, 2001). Lebedev, Vorobyev, Lebedev and Deppe (arXiv:2202.00136v2, 2022, Table I) give the same ranges for non-adaptive codes. As of 2026-10-25 a search found no improvement.
targets.success_criterion: Success means either (a) RECORD: an explicit set of distinct binary words of length n in {10, 11, 12} with max(N(x,y), N(y,x)) >= 2 for every pair (checked for all pairs), also verified as an independent set of the DIMACS graph 1zc.1024, 1zc.2048 or 1zc.4096 from Sloane's page, whose size is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best lower bound shown on OEIS A010101 and on the challenge page, both re-fetched at verification time, and than any later published value found by a literature search (on 2026-10-25: 112, 198 and 379); or (b) CLOSURE: a proof that 112 is optimal for n = 10 (the independence number of 1zc.1024 is 112), with a certificate checkable without trusting the search: a VeriPB proof log of a maximum-independent-set or clique solver run verified by VeriPB (and preferably CakePB), or a DRAT/LRAT proof for a CNF or pseudo-Boolean encoding whose correctness is argued in a short note and whose proof is accepted by cake_lpr.

partial_wins.statement: A certified upper bound strictly below the published one for n = 10, 11 or 12 (below 117, 210 or 410): an exact rational dual certificate of an LP or semidefinite relaxation adapted to asymmetric distance (exploiting the symmetric group on coordinates), checked by a standalone exact-arithmetic program that rebuilds the relaxation from the definition, or a verified proof log as in (b).

targets.verification_method: Parse the words (or the DIMACS node numbers, where node = 1 + decimal value of the word). Check the asymmetric-distance condition directly for every pair (O(M^2 n), milliseconds). Separately rebuild the graph from the definition, confirm that its edge set equals the downloaded 1zc file (this pins the bit-order convention), and check independence in the file. For a closure or upper bound, run VeriPB (and CakePB) on the proof log, or the exact rational checker on the dual certificate after rebuilding the relaxation from the definition. Re-fetch OEIS A010101 and the challenge page, and search the literature on asymmetric (Z-channel) single-error-correcting codes, before claiming.
angles: Use the symmetry: the problem is invariant under permutations of coordinates (not under complementation); prescribe a subgroup (cyclic shifts, products of cycles; for n = 11 the cyclic group of prime order) so the code is a union of orbits, then solve the orbit-weighted independent-set problem exactly with an ILP or CP-SAT.

Layer by weight: two words of equal weight conflict only when they differ in exactly two positions, and words of adjacent weights conflict when one covers the other with one extra 1; seed each weight layer from good constant-weight codes of minimum distance 4 and solve the inter-layer conflicts exactly.

Modern maximum-independent-set machinery, many runs in parallel: kernelization and reduce-and-peel (KaMIS-style), long local-search runs (NuMVC/FastVC-style vertex-cover search) with many seeds; the graphs are small enough for millions of moves per second.

Closing n = 10 (112 against 117): exact branch-and-bound with orbital branching or symmetry-breaking constraints and clique cuts from Z-channel balls, with VeriPB proof logging (supported by the Glasgow subgraph/clique solvers), so the closure is checkable.

Bounds: Delsarte-type LP and Schrijver-type SDP bounds for asymmetric distance (the metric is not translation-invariant, so reduce by the symmetric group acting on weight classes); a certified rational dual giving 116 would be a new upper bound (p1).
pitfalls: Do not confuse asymmetric distance 2 (this entry) with Hamming distance 3 codes or with codes for unidirectional errors; check the definition against the graph file.
Node numbering is 1 + decimal value of the word, but the bit order must be pinned by comparing a rebuilt graph with the file.

Sloane's challenge page is stale in places (it still lists 1dc.2048 as open, although arXiv:2309.14736 settled it in 2023); use OEIS A010101 for the current range and search the literature before claiming.
Maximum-clique benchmark tables list these graphs as complements; make sure the claimed set is independent in 1zc (a clique in the complement).
A branch-and-bound log without a proof certificate is not a closure.
Codes for a single deletion, or for adaptive or two-stage (feedback) Z-channel coding, are different problems.

targets.name: Regret matching+ inside CFR+/PCFR+: does alternating predictive RM+ converge ergodically? Prove RM+ non-convergence on the 3x3 counterexample game
targets.compute_profile: pure thought plus a formalisation effort (exact rational simulation of candidate games helps find the argument)
targets.statement: Regret matching+ (RM+) with alternating updates is the regret minimizer inside CFR+, the algorithm that essentially solved heads-up limit hold'em (Tammelin, Burch, Johanson, Bowling, IJCAI 2015). Predictive RM+ (PRM+) with alternation is the core of PCFR+, a state-of-the-art tabular solver (best on 3x3 Abrupt Dark Hex in Table 3 of arXiv:2502.08938). Cai, Farina, Grand-Clément, Kroer, Lee, Luo and Zheng ('Last-Iterate Convergence Properties of Regret-Matching Algorithms in Games', ICLR 2025, arXiv:2311.00676v2) state: 'Despite its strong empirical performance, it is unknown if alternating PRM+ enjoys ergodic convergence', and call alternating PRM+ 'an algorithm for which neither ergodic nor last-iterate convergence guarantees are known'. For simultaneous RM+, alternating RM+ and simultaneous PRM+ the average iterate converges at O(1/sqrt(T)), but the paper shows only NUMERICALLY that their last iterates fail to converge on A = [[3,0,-3],[0,3,-4],[0,0,1]]. That game has a unique, fully mixed, non-strict equilibrium x* = (1/12, 1/12, 5/6), y* = (1/3, 5/12, 1/4), with value 1/4. From R = 0 and uniform strategies the duality gap stays about 1e-1 after 1e5 iterations (their Figure 1), while alternating PRM+ converges there in practice. The paper proves last-iterate convergence of RM+ only when a strict equilibrium exists (Theorem 1); divergence of RM+ was proved earlier only for rock-paper-scissors (Lee et al. 2021, cited there). A literature search on 2026-10-14 found no proof for either question. The positive last-iterate results in that paper, and in later work that searches surfaced, concern smoothed or extragradient variants (SPRM+, ExRM+), not these algorithms. On 2026-10-25 the arXiv listing of 2311.00676 still shows v2 as the latest version.
targets.success_criterion: Settle the published question: does alternating PRM+ (Algorithm 8 of arXiv:2311.00676v2, self-play on a two-player zero-sum matrix game, initialized at R = 0 with uniform strategies, uniformly averaged iterates) enjoy ergodic convergence, i.e. does the duality gap of the averaged strategies tend to 0 in every matrix game? Direction: settle, either way. EITHER (a) an explicit matrix game with rational entries and a kernel-checked formal proof (Lean, Rocq/Coq or Isabelle, with no sorry, admit or extra axioms, and an axiom audit) that the averaged duality gap of alternating PRM+ on it does NOT tend to 0, OR (b) a kernel-checked formal proof (Lean, Rocq/Coq or Isabelle, with no sorry, admit or extra axioms, and an axiom audit) that it tends to 0 in every matrix game (any rate). For the proof route, a written or computer-assisted proof whose analytic steps are not formalised does not count; exact or interval computations may support it only inside the formal proof, where the proof assistant checks them.

partial_wins.statement: A kernel-checked formal proof (as in the success criterion) that alternating RM+ (Algorithm 7 of arXiv:2311.00676v2, the matrix-game core of CFR+), started from R = 0 and uniform strategies, does not converge in the last iterate on A = [[3,0,-3],[0,3,-4],[0,0,1]]: the liminf over t of the duality gap of (x_t, y_t) is positive. This turns the paper's Figure 1 into a theorem.
The same kernel-checked last-iterate non-convergence proof on A for simultaneous RM+ (Algorithm 1) or for PRM+ (Algorithm 2), from R = 0 and uniform strategies.

targets.verification_method: Build the formal development in a clean environment and run #print axioms (or Print Assumptions). Diff the formal update rules against Algorithms 1, 2, 7 and 8 of the paper, and test the formal definitions by executing the first 1,000 iterations on A and matching an independent floating-point implementation. Any exact or interval computation the argument relies on must be checked inside the proof assistant (kernel evaluation or a verified checker). Plots and long simulations never count.
angles: RM+ is scale-invariant. Normalize the cumulative regrets and study the piecewise-smooth map on the normalized regret simplex, whose effective step size decays like 1/t. Show that the continuous-time RM+ dynamics on A have an attracting set that excludes the equilibrium, then control the discretization (asymptotic pseudotrajectories), or look for exact invariants of the discrete map.

Simulate in exact rational arithmetic (the updates are rational) and record the sequence of positive-part clipping events. An eventually periodic clipping pattern with linearly growing regret would give a finite core that a formal proof can check by computation, both for p1 and for a counterexample to ergodic convergence of alternating PRM+.

Search small games (2x2, 2x3, 3x3 with small integer entries) for alternating PRM+ runs whose average-iterate regret grows linearly. Seed the search with A and with rock-paper-scissors perturbations, where non-alternating variants are known or observed to cycle.

Start from the two proofs in hand: Lee et al.'s RPS divergence for RM+, and Theorem 1 (convergence under a strict equilibrium). Find exactly which step fails for A's fully mixed, non-strict equilibrium.
pitfalls: Numerical non-convergence on A (a duality gap of about 0.1 after 1e5 iterations) is already published and is not a result.

Variants matter: simultaneous vs alternating updates, which player updates first, uniform vs linear averaging, the initialization, and the prediction used by PRM+. Match Algorithms 1, 2, 7 and 8 of the paper exactly and state the averaging used.

Ergodic (average), last-iterate and best-iterate convergence are different questions. Alternating PRM+ converges well in practice, so a counterexample to its ergodic convergence may not exist; the convergence proof (b) is the likelier truth and the harder formalisation.
The positive-part clipping makes the maps non-smooth; arguments for smooth dynamics (replicator, mirror descent) do not transfer automatically.
Extragradient and smooth variants (ExRM+, SPRM+) already have last-iterate guarantees; results about them do not answer this question.
Check 2025-2026 papers from the Farina, Kroer, Grand-Clément and Luo groups before claiming.

targets.name: Three-player von Neumann poker (Krityakierne-Thanatipanonda-Zeilberger 2024): is the conjectured threshold equilibrium a Nash equilibrium at bet size 2?
targets.compute_profile: laptop-minutes to laptop-hours for exact algebra over piecewise-polynomial payoffs and finite-deck LP/NLP cross-checks; the confirmation route (A) also needs a formalisation effort
targets.statement: Krityakierne, Thanatipanonda and Zeilberger, 'von Neumann and Newman Pokers with Finite Decks', arXiv:2407.16155 (v1, 23 Jul 2024; Maple packages FinitePoker and ThreePersonPoker), Section 4, extend von Neumann's poker to three players: each antes 1 and receives an independent uniform(0,1) hand; Player I checks (three-way showdown for the pot of 3) or bets b; if I bets, Players II and III each call or fold, the call/fold of each not depending on the other's action (their Call2/Call3 payoffs and Fast NLP give II and III strategies that depend only on their own card), and the highest hand among the non-folded players wins. They write that 'the dynamics of the three-player game therein remain unexplored', guess the form of the continuous equilibrium from finite-deck data ('conjectured Nash equilibrium strategies', Figure 2): I bets iff x < A or x > B, II and III call iff their hand > C, with II and III symmetric, and obtain A, B, C from three indifference equations only (Eq. A, B, C). For b = 2 they report A = 0.137058194328370, B = 0.829422249795391, C = 0.641304115985175, value to I 0.122557074714865, and an optimal bet b* ~ 2.07 with value 0.122590664136184. The paper does not verify the global best-response conditions (only indifference at the three cut points), does not discuss asymmetric equilibria of II and III, and gives no exact closed form. The proposal found no later work on this game, and on 2026-10-25 the arXiv listing still shows v1 only. A written proof for every b > 0 with simultaneous callers was submitted in V3R1T4S PR #196 and closed on 2026-10-24 because its analytic steps need peer review; its b = 2 values reproduced exactly, so it is no refutation, but it is not an established proof either.
targets.success_criterion: For b = 2 in the game exactly as defined in arXiv:2407.16155 Section 4 (II and III decide without observing each other's decision), EITHER (A) a kernel-checked formal proof (Lean, Rocq/Coq or Isabelle, with no sorry, admit or extra axioms, and an axiom audit) that the profile (A, B, C) defined by the paper's Eq. A-C (with A, B, C given as exact real algebraic numbers, isolating intervals included) is a Nash equilibrium: for every hand value, each player's prescribed action is a best response against the other two, over ALL measurable deviations (for the proof route, a written or computer-assisted proof whose analytic steps are not formalised does not count; exact or interval computations may support it only inside the formal proof, where the proof assistant checks them); OR (B) a refutation: an explicit hand interval and deviation for one player that strictly improves that player's payoff against the other two players' profile, certified in exact or interval arithmetic. Direction: settle, either way. In case (A) the exact game value at b = 2 must be stated as an algebraic number agreeing with the printed 0.122557074714865 within one unit of its last printed digit (10^-15).

partial_wins.statement: Settle the same question for every b > 0 (or for every b in a stated interval containing 2): a kernel-checked formal proof (as in (A)) that the threshold profile from Eq. A-C is a Nash equilibrium, or, for a certified explicit b, a refutation certified as in (B).

targets.verification_method: Write the three payoff functions in closed form: against threshold opponents, each player's payoff from each action is a piecewise polynomial in their own hand with breakpoints at A, B, C, so best-response checks reduce to sign conditions of explicit polynomials on finitely many intervals, decidable exactly (Sturm sequences or real-root isolation in sympy, msolve or Mathematica). Validate the evaluator by reproducing the paper's two-player special case (von Neumann: a = 1/9, b = 7/9, c = 5/9, value 1/9 at bet 2) and the reported three-player numbers. Cross-check with the paper's finite-deck solutions, e.g. FastMNE(4,1): value 1/24 for I and -1/48 for II and III, recomputed by exact LP or exact best responses on the finite game. Calibration against printed decimal numbers must agree within one unit of the last printed digit; exact identities and exact source fractions must agree exactly. For (A) and p1, build the formal development in a clean environment, print the axioms used, and check by reading that the formal payoff functions follow Section 4 of the paper (simultaneous callers) and reproduce the two-player von Neumann values.
angles: Check the regions the indifference equations do not cover: I's check region (A, B) against betting, II's fold region below C (including hands below A, which beat I's bluffs), and whether a hand between C and B prefers to fold when the other caller's range is accounted for.
If the symmetric profile fails, solve for the true equilibrium with an exact finite-deck NLP sequence (n up to a few hundred) and lift its pattern, the method the paper itself used.
pitfalls: The observation structure matters: if Player III sees Player II's decision before acting (as at a real table), the game is different and the paper's profile does not even have the right strategy space. Stick to the paper's simultaneous reading, or state clearly that a sequential-variant result is a different target.
Ties have probability zero in the continuous game; in finite decks the paper deals distinct cards, which matters for cross-checks.
A modest target: the most likely outcome is a clean confirmation (A). Do not overstate it; the novelty is the first full verification, not a new strategy.
PR #196 (closed 2026-10-24) is not a resolution of the b = 2 target or of the all-b partial win; a formal proof must cover its analytic steps itself.

targets.name: Losing chess (antichess): solve one of White's six first moves still marked Unknown (1.a4, 1.b3, 1.c4, 1.g3, 1.g4, 1.Nh3)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (published first-move proof files are 4 MB to 1.3 GB of bz2; the final leg of 1.e3 b6 took a few hours on 128 cores); a move that turns out easy could fall in laptop-days
targets.statement: Losing chess, main variant (captures compulsory, the king is an ordinary piece that can be captured, no check or castling, pawns may promote to king; a player wins by losing all pieces or by being stalemated; fifty-move rule and repetition draws as in chess), was weakly solved by Mark Watkins in October 2016: 1.e3 wins for White under both FICS and International stalemate rules (final proof about 900 million positions; ICGA Journal 39/2). Of White's 20 legal first moves, 13 are known Black wins: 1.e4, 1.d4 and 1.d3 classically; 1.Nc3, 1.Nf3, 1.f4 and 1.h4 (proofs in the Nilatac opening book); 1.b4, 1.c3, 1.f3 and 1.h3 by computer (Nye, Steenhuis); 1.a3 (Klaas Steenhuis, October 2015, via 1...e6) and 1.Na3 (Steenhuis, June 2020, via 1...e6, a 1.3 GB proof file). Wikipedia's 'Losing chess' article names the 13 first moves after which Black is known to win and Watkins' 1.e3, and shows the rest as 'Unknown' in its solution diagram; by elimination these are 1.a4, 1.b3, 1.c4, 1.g3, 1.g4 and 1.Nh3. Task: settle one of these six, either as a forced Black win after it or as a forced White win with it. Status checked 2026-10-25: the Wikipedia article still says a Black win is known after 13 of White's 20 first moves and names them, and Watkins' page (proof files through May 2021) lists no proof after any of the six.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: for one first move X in {1.a4, 1.b3, 1.c4, 1.g3, 1.g4, 1.Nh3} that is still not listed as solved on Wikipedia's 'Losing chess' page and on Watkins' Losing Chess page at verification time, a complete proof tree that the unmodified verifier verify_win.c from Watkins' current source tarball (CombinedJan05.tar on his page, which includes the April 2019 double-en-passant fix) accepts, proving a forced win for one side after 1.X under International stalemate rules (stalemated player wins) AND under FICS rules (stalemate won by the side with fewer pieces, equal counts drawn), as Watkins' 1.e3 proof does; a Black-win proof may use the tarball's NULL-move inversion (proof_invert) as Watkins' 1.h3 and 1.b4 files do. Every tablebase leaf must be resolved by tablebases rebuilt from scratch by the verifier (4- and 5-unit with the 2019 fix) or by a second, independently generated tablebase set, or else expanded to terminal positions. A second check by an independently written antichess move generator over all leaves and a random 1% of internal nodes must agree.

partial_wins.statement: The same proof for one of the six moves under ONE stalemate ruleset only (International or FICS), verified exactly as in the success criterion and labelled with its ruleset.

An independent re-verification of a published first-move proof that has only been checked with Watkins' own code (for example Na3e6.proof.bz2, a3e6_rev_new.proof.bz2 or c3e5.rev.bz2), using a verifier and tablebases that share no code with Watkins' tarball, with every disagreement (tablebase errors included) reported; or a proof that one of these files is wrong.

targets.verification_method: Download the proof (.bz2) and check its md5. Build Watkins' tarball, regenerate the 4- and 5-unit tablebases with its builder (the Apr 2019 version fixes double en passant), uninvert NULL-move files with ./proof_invert uninvert, and run verify_win. The verifier checks that every reply of the losing side is present, that hash-identified nodes are the same position, and that terminal nodes are wins under the stated ruleset. Then run an independent checker: an antichess move generator (for example python-chess's antichess variant, after confirming its stalemate rule matches the claimed ruleset) regenerates the losing side's moves at every node of a 1% random sample plus all leaves, and an independently built tablebase set (or explicit expansion) scores the leaves.
angles: Reuse Watkins' machinery (source tarball): an upper-level best-first tree whose leaves are expanded by bounded proof-number searches (1e7 to 1e8 nodes each), N independent pn-searches in parallel, the 'NULL move' trick for Black-win proofs, and 4-6-unit tablebases. On a many-core machine this is the same shape of run that produced 1.e3 b6's final leg in hours on 128 cores.

Choose the move first: run a strong antichess engine (for example Fairy-Stockfish or the Nilatac book) on each of the six moves and start with the one whose evaluation is most lopsided; a Black win after 1.X needs only one refuting reply, a White win needs all Black replies.

Look for transpositions into solved territory: many antichess lines become forced capture chains within a few moves; positions reached after 1.X may coincide with nodes of the published 1.e3 or 1.a3/1.Na3 proof trees, whose subtrees can be reused after re-verification.
Build selective 6-unit tablebases for the endgames the search keeps reaching, as Steenhuis's long 1.a3 and 1.Na3 proofs suggest is necessary.
pitfalls: Stalemate rulesets differ (International, FICS, joint); a proof is valid only for the ruleset it names, and the full win needs both.

Tablebase bugs: a double-en-passant bug corrupted 40 positions of the 2016 proof (fixed 2019), and Steenhuis reports other wrong 4-piece tablebases. Leaves scored by an unverified tablebase are not proof.
Inverted (NULL-move) proof files break the verifier unless uninverted first.
Fifty-move-rule and repetition handling: a line that only 'wins' by a repetition or a 50-move shuffle the rules count as a draw is not a win.
The six moves may be large: Steenhuis's 1.Na3 proof file is 1.3 GB of bz2, larger than the whole 1.e3 proof, so a week of one machine may only reach partial win p1 or nothing.

Wikipedia names the 13 Black wins in its text but marks the remaining six as 'Unknown' only in a diagram; confirm on Watkins' page and in recent antichess literature that the chosen move is still unsolved before claiming (asking the antichess community is a human action).

targets.name: Bilateral trade: an instance where the better of seller-offering and buyer-offering earns less than 3/4 of second-best gains from trade (open gap [1/2, 3/4], Babaioff-Dobzinski-Kupfer 2021)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (exact rational LPs over supports of 3-30 points per side; one large instance of 20,000 support points only for the AlphaEvolve angle)
targets.statement: A seller and a buyer have independent private values. Seller-offering and buyer-offering each select a profit-maximising price. Their better gains from trade are compared with second-best gains from trade under Bayesian incentive compatibility, interim individual rationality and ex-ante budget balance. Babaioff, Dobzinski and Kupfer (arXiv:2111.07790, Section 3) give a limiting ratio of 3/4, against the 1/2 guarantee credited to Brustle, Cai, Wu and Zhao. Their two-by-two example uses adverse offer ties; favourable ties give ratio 1. The open target is a ratio strictly below 3/4 that survives favourable ties. The 2026 random-offerer papers (M. Jo, arXiv:2607.13959; Bei et al., arXiv:2609.37997; Shang and Chen, arXiv:2610.06547) and the 2026 second-best versus first-best papers (arXiv:2606.03849, 2609.18724, 2609.30702, 2609.37366) use first-best as the benchmark or bound SB itself; an arXiv search on 2026-10-25 found no newer bound on best-of versus second-best.
targets.success_criterion: An instance given by two finite-support distributions (rational support points and rational probabilities) for s and b, independent, plus an explicit mechanism M, such that a checker in exact rational arithmetic confirms all of the following. (a) M is feasible. Either M is a posted price p (trade iff s <= p <= b), which is incentive compatible, individually rational and budget balanced by construction. Or M is given by allocation probabilities x(s,b) in [0,1] and interim expected transfers, and every BIC constraint (each type against each misreport) and every interim IR constraint holds for both agents, together with ex-ante budget balance (E[buyer payment] >= E[seller receipt]). This makes GFT_M = E[(b - s) x(s,b)] a lower bound on SB. (b) GFT_SO and GFT_BO are computed exactly. Seller offers range over the buyer's support points and buyer offers over the seller's support points. Among tied profit-maximising offers, each agent takes the one giving the LARGEST GFT, so the claim holds under every tie-breaking rule. (c) GFT_M > 0 and max(GFT_SO, GFT_BO) < (3/4) * GFT_M. Direction: lower ratio is better. The bar is 3/4 from BDK, arXiv 2111.07790, Section 3. Before claiming, re-run the status search and compare against any newer bound. The checker must first reproduce two calibration values. On BDK's 2x2 instance it must report ratio 1 under the GFT-favourable tie rule and 3/4 under BDK's adversarial rule. On the AlphaEvolve instance (appendix code of arXiv 2603.08679) it must reproduce FB ~ 1.2322, SO ~ 0.3312 and BO ~ 0.8565 under that paper's own tie rule. Any exact rational certificate of this strict inequality counts, however small the improvement. Match printed numerical calibration values within one unit of the last printed digit. The exact BDK calibration fractions remain exact. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit instance whose certified ratio FB/RO exceeds 2.28862548 + 1e-6, where RO = (GFT_SO + GFT_BO)/2 with GFT-favourable tie-breaking. Supports may be finite and checked exactly, or distributions closed-form with interval-arithmetic integrals in the style of M. Jo 2026. This pushes the worst-case random-offerer ratio below 0.436943488, the limit of Shang-Chen's recursive families (arXiv 2610.06547); Bei et al. (arXiv 2609.37997) show RO >= FB/e, so the open window for FB/RO is (2.28862548, e]. The cell is crowded (several 2026 papers, one using AI-guided evolutionary search).

Exact second-best values, each an LP optimum with a rational primal-dual certificate, for the published hard instances. These are the AlphaEvolve instance in the appendix code of arXiv 2603.08679 and BDK's Section 2 family for H = 3..20. Report max(SO,BO)/SB for each. No second-best figures for these instances are published, so the table settles whether the first-best-hard instances are also second-best-hard.

targets.verification_method: Python with fractions.Fraction, under 200 lines. (1) Read the two distributions. (2) For each seller type, evaluate profit at every buyer support point, keep the maximisers and take the GFT-maximising one; do the mirror image for buyer types; sum to get GFT_SO and GFT_BO exactly. (3) If M is a posted price, compute E[(b - s) 1{s <= p <= b}]. Otherwise check every BIC and interim-IR inequality and the ex-ante budget inequality exactly, then compute GFT_M. (4) Check GFT_M > 0 and max(GFT_SO, GFT_BO) < (3/4) * GFT_M. Reproduce BDK's 3/4 (adversarial ties) and ratio 1 (favourable ties) on the 2x2 instance first. An optional second check solves the full SB LP with an exact rational solver (SoPlex in exact mode, or a sympy/fractions simplex for small supports) and confirms SB >= GFT_M.
angles: Cheapest first move: compute SB on the AlphaEvolve instance (FB ~ 1.2322, max(SO,BO) = BO ~ 0.8565). If SB > 0.8565 / 0.75 ~ 1.1420, i.e. SB/FB > 0.927, the 3/4 bar falls to a published object nobody has evaluated against second-best.

Small-support adversary search: anneal over 3-10 support points per side with SB computed exactly (LP, or the discrete Myerson-Satterthwaite virtual-value characterisation with a one-dimensional multiplier search), maximising SB / max(SO,BO). Keep ties robust by always scoring with GFT-favourable tie-breaking.

Pricing view: max(SO,BO) is the better of two one-sided monopoly quotes. Look for instances where both monopolists' optimal quotes shade far from the efficient price while one posted 'mid' price, or a randomised IC mechanism, still trades almost all profitable pairs.
