Seed from equal-revenue-type families (BDK Section 2, M. Jo 2026, Shang-Chen 2026), which already make one side's offer badly distorted, and perturb them toward instances where a single price nearly separates s < b, so SB stays close to FB.
pitfalls: Tie-breaking is the whole game at the bar. BDK's 3/4 exists only with ties broken against trade (implemented by perturbation); scoring SO/BO with adversarial ties produces false records. Use GFT-favourable ties or strictly unique optimal offers.

Benchmark confusion: this cell is versus SECOND-best (BIC, interim IR, ex-ante budget balance, per BDK); 2026 papers use other budget-balance notions for SB, so do not import their constants. The 2026 random-offerer papers and the AlphaEvolve instance report ratios against FIRST-best. A first-best ratio below 3/4 says nothing here unless SB is certified.
A posted price or any explicit feasible mechanism only lower-bounds SB, which suffices for the claim. Do not claim SB itself without an exact dual certificate.
Best-of means max(SO, BO), not the random-offerer average (SO+BO)/2. Ratio direction varies across papers (RO/FB 0.4369 vs FB/RO 2.2886).
Continuous distributions need interval-certified integrals; floating-point ratios do not count.
Neighbouring cells moved monthly in 2026, including an AI-guided evolutionary search (arXiv:2603.08679). Re-check arXiv the day of any claim.

targets.name: Binary minimal codes for secret sharing: shorten the dimension 10–13 records
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days for structured generator-matrix search; exact minimality checking over at most 8191 nonzero messages takes seconds to minutes with GF(2) rank tests
targets.statement: Vladimir Chubenko and Sascha Kurz, Divisible Minimal Codes, Serdica Journal of Computing 18(2), 97–124 (issue year 2024; published 25 June 2025), Table 2, give m(10,2)=28–29, m(11,2)=31–35, m(12,2)=34–38 and m(13,2)=39–43. Here m(k,2) is the minimum length of a k-dimensional binary linear minimal code. Minimality means no distinct nonzero codewords have one support contained in the other. The paper relates these codes to secret sharing and uses generalized circulant constructions. Dimensions 7–9 are exact and excluded. An arXiv search on 2026-10-25 found no later values for these dimensions. This optimizes minimal-code length; the upstream codetables target optimizes Hamming minimum distance.
targets.success_criterion: Give a full-rank binary generator matrix for a minimal [n,k] code with k=10 and n≤28, k=11 and n≤34, k=12 and n≤37, or k=13 and n≤42. The resulting code must satisfy minimality for all nonzero codewords. No divisibility, quasi-cyclic structure, projectivity or minimum-distance assumption beyond what follows from minimality is imposed. A valid dimension-10 construction would settle m(10,2)=28 using the published lower bound; the other cases improve a published upper bound. Also strictly improve the best comparable published result at claim time, including compatible compositions of published objects. State whether the candidate is a composition and identify its components. Values in unmerged pull requests do not set the bar.
targets.verification_method: Check that the supplied k-by-n matrix is binary and has rank k over GF(2). For every nonzero message a in GF(2)^k, compute c=aG and collect the columns of G at positions where c is zero. Their rank must be k−1. This is an exact minimality test: a codeword bG is supported within supp(c) precisely when b annihilates those columns; a one-dimensional kernel must be {0,a}. Independently cross-check by enumerating all nonzero codewords and rejecting any pair with a proper support inclusion. The rank version avoids a quadratic pair scan and uses at most 8191 small elimination problems. Check n against the corresponding record after validation.
angles: Reproduce the paper’s generalized circulant constructions, then puncture, repair and replace columns while tracking low-rank hyperplane intersections.
Use the exact rank criterion as a counterexample-guided search objective; each failing message gives a concrete missing-span constraint.
Search small projective strong blocking sets in GF(2)^k with local trades and occasional exact repair; output a generator matrix for the final unrestricted check.
pitfalls: Good minimum distance alone does not imply minimality.
Minimality concerns support inclusion, not the size of a generator matrix.
The Ashikhmin–Barg sufficient weight-ratio condition is not necessary.
The actual publication date is June 2025; the issue year is 2024.

Later constructions and compatible combinations of published constructions must be checked before claiming. The lower bounds 28, 31, 34 and 39 come from codetables.de minimum-distance data and move if that table moves.

targets.name: Card guessing with yes/no feedback: exact optimal expected scores for two-copy decks beyond n = 10
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (exact backward recursion over label-symmetric (r, f) states with big-rational arithmetic; memory, not time, is the limit)
targets.statement: A deck with n labels and m copies of each is uniformly shuffled; a guesser names each card before it is turned and learns only whether the guess was right (yes/no, or partial, feedback). P+_{m,n} is the maximum expected number of correct guesses over adaptive strategies. Diaconis and Graham (Ann. Statist. 9 (1981)) solved m = 1; for m >= 2 the optimal strategy is not greedy and has no closed form. Diaconis, Graham and Spiro ('Guessing about guessing', Amer. Math. Monthly 129(7) (2022) 607-622, arXiv:2012.04019, Tables 2-3) report optimal values for m = 2, rounded to four decimals: n = 2: 2.8333, 3: 3.0111, 4: 3.0452, 5: 3.0467, 6: 3.0376, 7: 3.0323, 8: 3.0260, 9: 3.0219, 10: 3.0186 (non-monotone; computed with Gatto's algorithms), and 6.65 for the ESP deck m = n = 5. Diaconis, Graham, He, Spiro (Combin. Probab. Comput. 31 (2022), arXiv:2010.05059) proved P+_{m,n} = m + O(m^{3/4} log m) for large n. Luo (arXiv:2609.25062, 14 Sep 2026) proved P+_{m,n}/m <= sum_{k=1..n} 1/k! < e - 1 and posed Question 5.1: for fixed m >= 2 does lim_n P+_{m,n} exist, and what is it for m = 2? Current bounds: 2.91 <= liminf P+_{2,n} <= limsup P+_{2,n} <= 2(e - 1) ~ 3.4366. Luo's Appendix A gives an exact recursion on a sufficient state (r, f) - per label, the remaining undetermined multiplicity r_i and the number f_i of past positions forbidding it - with a closed inclusion-exclusion count C(r, f) (his eq. A.1). An arXiv search on 2026-10-25 ('card guessing') found no published exact value of P+_{2,n} for n >= 11, and Luo names the exact extrema at fixed parameters among the principal remaining questions. Exact n = 11..13 values submitted in V3R1T4S PR #200 are under review and are not established.
targets.success_criterion: Exact values of P+_{2,n} (two copies of each of n labels, yes/no feedback, maximise the expected number of correct guesses) as reduced rationals for EVERY n from 11 through 16 (direction: exact values; submissions for n = 11..13 are under review, not established), each accompanied by a Bellman certificate: the table of V+(r, f) over all reachable canonical states, which a checker verifies state by state against Luo's recursion (arXiv:2609.25062, Appendix A: p_i = C(r - e_i, f)/C(r, f), V+(r, f) = max_i { p_i [1 + V+(r - e_i, f)] + (1 - p_i) V+(r, f + e_i) }, V+ = 0 when no free position remains). The same code must reproduce Table 3 of Diaconis-Graham-Spiro for n = 2..10 within one unit of the last printed digit (0.0001 for four decimals), and any newer published values found via the status source must be matched or exceeded in range.

partial_wins.statement: Certified exact P+_{2,n} for n = 11, 12 and 13, checked independently over all reachable states. Values submitted in PR #200 remain under review and must not be treated as established.

An exactly verified counterexample, inside the m = 2 yes/no game, to the 'persistence conjecture' as stated in the sources (Chung-Diaconis-Graham-Mallows 1981; Diaconis-Graham-Holmes 2001, as summarised by Diaconis-Graham-He-Spiro: after an incorrect guess of label i, guessing i again is optimal): a reachable state where, right after a failed guess of i, every optimal next guess differs from i. The precise wording and status of that conjecture must be checked in the 1981/2001 sources first.

targets.verification_method: Independent implementation of Luo's Appendix A: C(r, f) from (A.1) with exact integers, p_i = C(r - e_i, f)/C(r, f), V+ by backward recursion on L (the number of free positions, which drops by one each round), with Python fractions or FLINT. Canonicalise states by sorting the (r_i, f_i) pairs (labels are exchangeable). Calibrate against Diaconis-Graham-Spiro Table 3 (n = 2..10, four decimals) and Table 2. Certificate check: for every state in the claimed table, recompute the right-hand side of the recursion from the table's own successor values and confirm equality, then confirm the initial state r = (2,...,2), f = 0 carries the claimed value; this costs one pass over the table and needs no search. Calibration against printed decimal numbers must agree within one unit of the last printed digit; exact identities and exact source fractions must agree exactly.
angles: Evaluator first: C(r, f) from (A.1) with memoised falling factorials; check it against brute-force permutation counts for tiny decks.
Process the recursion layer by layer in L and stream finished layers to disk; states are multisets of (r_i, f_i) pairs, and a label with r_i = 0 is inert.
Count reachable canonical states for each n before running, to choose how far to push.
Use the exact tables to test the 'card counting' heuristic c_i + beta g_i of Diaconis-Graham-Spiro and the persistence property on every reachable state; both come free with the recursion.
pitfalls: Yes/no feedback reveals the card only when the guess is right; complete-feedback formulas do not apply.
P+ (maximise) and P- (misere, minimise) are different problems.
The published Table 3 values are rounded to four decimals; agree within one unit of the last printed digit (0.0001), rather than requiring identical rounded digits.
Two-label decks are degenerate (a wrong guess reveals the card); do not extrapolate from them.
Exact numerators and denominators grow quickly; use big integers end to end.

targets.name: Covering codes K_q(n,R) for q = 2, 3, 4 (hypercube domination, football pool): beat an upper bound in Kéri's tables
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (local search and large-neighbourhood search with exact coverage counts; exhaustive verification over q^n words takes seconds for ternary and up to minutes for binary n <= 33 with a 1 GiB bit array)
targets.statement: K_q(n,R) is the minimum number of q-ary words needed so that every length-n word is within Hamming distance R of one of them. Gerzson Kéri's tables cover binary, ternary and quaternary cells. Kéri's ternary table (3_tables.pdf, file date 2011-11-24) gives 71 <= K_3(6,1) <= 73 and credits Laarhoven, Aarts, van Lint and Wille for the upper construction. Márk Marosi (arXiv:2608.19872) gives newer search methods and 83 improved bounds for alphabets 5 <= q <= 21. Tamal Maharaj (arXiv:2610.03760) gives K_4(8,2) <= 256 and K_4(6,2) <= 48. The target is a smaller explicit code for a still-open cell. Reference tables alone do not establish the full current frontier; compositions and later publications must also be checked.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit code C contained in Z_q^n with q in {2, 3, 4}, given as a list of distinct words, whose covering radius is at most R (every one of the q^n words lies within Hamming distance R of a codeword, checked exhaustively), for a cell inside the ranges of Kéri's tables (q = 2: n <= 33, 1 <= R <= 10; q = 3: n <= 14, 1 <= R <= 8; q = 4: n <= 11, 1 <= R <= 8), such that |C| is STRICTLY SMALLER (direction: min) than (a) the upper bound for (q, n, R) in Kéri's table re-fetched at verification time, read from the rendered PDF, and (b) every later published upper bound for that cell, including the values implied through K_q(n+1, R+1) <= K_q(n, R) and K_q(n+1, R) <= q * K_q(n, R) by newer codes (later bounds known on 2026-10-25: K_4(8,2) <= 256 and K_4(6,2) <= 48, Maharaj arXiv:2610.03760), found by a search of arXiv and Google Scholar for covering codes with the cell's parameters (2012-present). |C| must be at least the best published lower bound for the cell; a smaller code means a checker bug. Cells with a perfect code (key h) are closed. For compositions, include direct products and direct sums with added radii, plus valid coordinate-extension constructions. Include the best valid composition of published objects for the same parameters and metric in the bar, even if it is absent from a printed table. State whether the candidate is a composition. Identify its components and composition rule. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: A strictly smaller explicit code for a cell of Kéri's mixed binary/ternary table (mixed_tables.pdf, file date 2011-11-24), below that table's upper bound and any later published value, checked exhaustively in the same way.

A certified lower bound strictly above the best published lower bound for a cell with q in {2, 3, 4} (for example from a higher level of the Gijswijt-Polak semidefinite hierarchy), delivered as an exact rational dual certificate verified by a standalone exact-arithmetic checker that rebuilds the program from (q, n, R), as in Marosi's pipeline.

targets.verification_method: Parse the code (one word per line, symbols 0..q-1), assert the length n, the symbol range and distinctness, and count M. Method 1: mark the radius-R ball of every codeword in a q^n-entry array (M * sum_{j<=R} C(n,j)(q-1)^j updates) and confirm that no word is unmarked. Method 2 (shares no code with method 1): R rounds of coordinate-wise dilation of the code's indicator array, which computes no distances (one of the four checks Marosi used). Binary n <= 33 needs at most 2^33 bits (1 GiB); ternary n <= 14 needs about 4.8 million entries. Re-fetch Kéri's directory listing and the cell's PDF, read the cell from the rendered PDF, and repeat the literature search before claiming. Recompute comparison compositions using the same checker and resource metric.
angles: Transfer Marosi's two searches (arXiv:2608.19872 Sections 4-5) to q = 2, 3, 4: a focused local search seeded with structured codes, and a large-neighbourhood search that scores every candidate codeword position at once by exact coverage counts computed with a coordinate-wise transform. Kéri's largest binary cell has 2^33 (about 8.6 * 10^9) words and the largest ternary cell 3^14 (about 4.8 * 10^6), so exact full-space coverage transforms fit on a laptop.

Aim first at cells whose upper bound is an old direct sum or algebraic construction far above the sphere-covering bound (for example K_2(13,2) <= 128 from 1985 against a lower bound of 97, K_3(8,2) <= 81 against 54, K_3(8,3) <= 27 against 14); Marosi's largest gains came from cells whose tabulated bound was a direct sum.

Prescribe automorphisms (cyclic shifts, a subgroup of coordinate permutations, a linear subcode acting by translation: the matrix method of Östergård and Kéri) so the code is a union of orbits, then solve the orbit set-cover exactly with CP-SAT or an ILP.

Propagate every win automatically: a new code for (n, R) gives bounds for (n+1, R+1), (n+1, R) via the factor q, and direct sums with other table codes; sweep the neighbours before claiming each cell once.

Moonshot cell inside the harvest: the football pool K_3(6,1) in [71, 73]; a 72-word ternary code of length 6 with covering radius 1 would improve the upper bound. It would not establish optimality against the reported lower bound 71.
pitfalls: In text extraction of Kéri's PDFs the key letters and footnote marks are glued to the numbers (for example '2717' for an exactly known cell of 27 with marks); always read the cell from the rendered PDF.

The q >= 5 cells moved in August 2026 (Marosi) and two q = 4 cells moved in October 2026 (Maharaj); Kéri's binary and quaternary tables date from 2009 and the ternary table from 2011, so a literature search is part of every claim and a tie is not a record.
Covering radius is a maximum over all q^n words: sampling words is not a check.
Count distinct codewords; duplicates do not count.

Do not mix tables: unrestricted codes K_q(n,R) (this entry), linear covering codes and the length function l(r,R) (e.g. Davydov-Marcugini-Pambianco, arXiv:2511.02542), mixed binary/ternary codes (p1) and Lee-metric or Z4-linear Gray-image codes are different records.
A code smaller than a certified lower bound means a checker bug.

targets.name: Three-player gambler's ruin (the final-table ICM problem): a counterexample to the Diaconis-Ethier 0.0004 scaling conjecture
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (exact sparse linear solves for N up to a few hundred; interval-certified iteration beyond)
targets.statement: Three players hold A, B, C units, N = A + B + C. Each round a pair of surviving players is chosen uniformly at random and a fair coin moves one unit between them; after the first elimination the other two play ordinary fair gambler's ruin. P_{A,B,C}(sigma), sigma in S3, is the probability of elimination order sigma (sigma = 132: player 1 out first, then player 3). These are the probabilities final-table deals and the Independent Chip Model (ICM) try to approximate. Diaconis and Ethier ('Gambler's ruin and the ICM', Statistical Science 37(3) (2022) 289-305, arXiv:2011.07610v3) show the ICM is inadequate, compute exact values for N <= 200 and near-exact values for N = 300 (WSOP 2019 Main Event final three as the worked example), and state the scaling conjecture P_{nA,nB,nC}(sigma) ~ P_{A,B,C}(sigma). Their Conjecture 4.2(a): for each A, B, C >= 1, sigma in S3 and n >= 2, |P_{nA,nB,nC}(sigma) - P_{A,B,C}(sigma)| < 0.0004; they report differences 'as large as 0.000383'. Conjecture 4.2(b): |P_{nA,nB,nC}(sigma) - P^BM_{A,B,C}(sigma)| = O(1/(nN)^4). Denisov and Wachtel (arXiv:2212.11526; Ann. Appl. Probab. 34(5), 2024) confirmed the exact asymptotic (Brownian-motion) behaviour with a rate of convergence; that does not settle the numerical inequality 4.2(a). Open as of 2026-10-25: an arXiv search found no proof or refutation; later three-gambler papers (arXiv:2309.08762, 2406.07878) treat other questions.
targets.success_criterion: Integers A, B, C >= 1, n >= 2 and an elimination order sigma in S3 with |P_{nA,nB,nC}(sigma) - P_{A,B,C}(sigma)| >= 0.0004 (direction: max; a counterexample to Diaconis-Ethier Conjecture 4.2(a)), under exactly the rules of arXiv:2011.07610 Section 1, with both probabilities given as exact rationals or as interval enclosures with directed rounding whose separation proves the inequality. A specific finite n must be named; the n -> infinity limit does not count.

partial_wins.statement: A certified discrepancy |P_{nA,nB,nC}(sigma) - P_{A,B,C}(sigma)| strictly greater than 0.000383 (the largest the authors report) but below 0.0004, with exact or interval-certified values: a new largest known discrepancy that narrows the conjecture's margin. This is a numerical-bar comparison: certify strict separation from the reported decimal and check for newer published discrepancies before calling it a record.

targets.verification_method: Recompute both probabilities with an independent code: interior states (a, b, c) with a, b, c >= 1 and a + b + c = N; each of the six moves (three pairs, two coin outcomes) has probability 1/6; on reaching a state where one player has 0, the remaining order is decided by two-player fair ruin (the player holding x of the remaining x + y units outlasts the other with probability x/(x + y)). Solve the absorbing chain in exact rationals (sparse elimination or FLINT) for N up to about 100, or by interval-certified Jacobi iteration beyond. Sanity checks before comparing: the six sigma sum to 1; P_{i,i,N-2i}(123) = (1 - 2i/N)/2 (their eq. 4.5); P_{1,1,2}(312) = 1/14; the paper's Table 9 entries (e.g., (2,3,5), sigma = 213: 0.190419015064). The authors' Mathematica programs listed in Section 6 of the paper are a second reference. Calibration against printed decimal numbers must agree within one unit of the last printed digit; exact identities and exact source fractions must agree exactly.
angles: Discreteness effects are largest for small N: tabulate every base triple with N <= 40 exactly and compare with multiples up to nN ~ 600 (certified iteration), and with the Brownian limit where the Ferguson/Hajek conformal-map formula is computable (the paper's Figure 5 covers A = B).
Rank (base triple, sigma) cells by the discrepancy at n = 2 and at the limit; spend compute only on the top cells.
Kill early: if the certified maximum over all bases with N <= 40 sits below 0.0004 and is decreasing in N, record it (p1 if above 0.000383) and park the line.
pitfalls: The conjecture is about each finite n >= 2; a counterexample must name n.
sigma is the elimination order (first out listed first), not the finishing order used in many ICM tools.
While three players survive the pair is uniform over the three pairs; after the first bust the game is two-player.
Orders covered by (4.5) are exactly scale-invariant; do not search there.
Double-precision solves at N = 300 carry errors far below 1e-4 but are not certificates; certify the final numbers.
Denisov-Wachtel's confirmation concerns asymptotics, not the 0.0004 constant; re-check papers citing arXiv:2011.07610 before claiming.

targets.name: Sponsored-search GSP auction: a full-information pure Nash equilibrium (no overbidding) with welfare ratio above 1.259134, refuting the 2010 Lucier-Paes Leme conjecture (proven upper bound 1.28216)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (search over values, click-through rates and rankings for n = 5-8 bidders; each candidate equilibrium is checked by a few hundred exact rational inequalities)
targets.statement: In a full-information GSP auction, slots have decreasing click-through rates and bidders pay the next bid per click. Each bidder obeys b_i <= v_i. Lucier and Paes Leme (arXiv:1011.3268) conjectured that the worst pure-equilibrium welfare ratio for any slot count equals the three-slot supremum. Caragiannis, Kaklamanis, Kanellopoulos, Kyropoulou, Lucier, Paes Leme and Tardos (JET 2015, arXiv:1201.6429) establish the three-slot value near 1.259134 and the general upper bound (61+7*sqrt(217))/128. Ding, Wu, Qin and Liu (arXiv:1305.5404, unrefereed) claim PoA_4 = 1.259 but give details for one ranking only. Kroll, Schäfer and Tsikiridis (arXiv:2609.39532) study budget-constrained and budget-free GSP under other overbidding notions (budget-free PNE lower bound 2, Prop. 6.1); their bounds do not change this per-bidder target.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit instance (n bidders, rational values v_i, rational CTRs alpha_1 >= ... >= alpha_n >= 0), a bid vector b with 0 <= b_i <= v_i, and a stated deterministic tie-breaking rule. An exact-rational checker must confirm that b is a pure Nash equilibrium of the full-information GSP auction under that rule: no bidder i can strictly increase alpha_slot * (v_i - price) by moving to any slot via any bid in [0, v_i]. It must also confirm that OPT(v)/SW(b) > 1.259134, where OPT sorts values against CTRs. Direction: higher is better. The bar is the 3-slot supremum bound 1 + 2*zeta, reported numerically as approximately 1.259134 of arXiv 1201.6429 (Theorem 4.2 / App. B.1), which the 1.25913 conjecture of arXiv 1011.3268 says holds for all n. Re-check arXiv for newer GSP equilibrium bounds before claiming. The checker must first reproduce the published 3-bidder instance (ratio >= 1.259133, NE verified exactly) and the 2-slot instance (v = (1, 1/2), alpha = (1, 1/2), b = (0, 1/2), ratio 5/4). The decimal bar is numerical. Alternatively an exact symbolic certificate that the ratio exceeds the exact three-slot supremum defined in Theorem 4.2 counts, without a minimum gap. If transcribed printed parameters fail an exact Nash check, calibrate on the source-defined exact instance; printed numerical outputs use tolerance within one unit of the last printed digit. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: A coarse correlated equilibrium (finite-support distribution over bid profiles, each with b_i <= v_i, rational probabilities) of a full-information GSP instance with OPT/E[SW] > 1.259134. A mixed Nash equilibrium is a special case. The checker verifies the CCE inequality for every bidder against every deviation bid in [0, v_i]; this reduces exactly to finitely many breakpoints at the other bidders' support bids, with each tie side checked. This raises the best lower bound for the GSP mixed and CCE PoA under per-bidder no-overbidding; the upper bound is 2.310.

An exhaustive, machine-checkable proof for n = 4 (all rankings, exact LP or SMT certificates) that the pure PoA with per-bidder no-overbidding is at most 1.259134, or a 4-bidder counterexample. This independently settles the unrefereed claim of arXiv 1305.5404 and tells a search where to start.

targets.verification_method: Exact rational arithmetic, under 100 lines. Sort bids, assign slots under the stated tie rule, and compute payments (the next bid). For each bidder i and each target slot j, compute the cheapest deviation bid in [0, v_i] that lands i in slot j under the same tie rule. Moving up costs the bid of the bidder currently in slot j; moving down costs the bid of the bidder who ends up just below. Check that utility does not strictly increase. Then compute OPT and SW exactly and compare against 1.259134. For a CCE, enumerate profiles in the support and check deviations at all breakpoints. Calibrate on the JET 3-bidder instance and the 2-slot example first. For the symbolic route compare with the exact three-slot supremum defined in the source theorem, using certified algebraic or symbolic inequalities. Do not replace that value with a fixed decimal threshold.
angles: Cheapest first move: Ding et al.'s own weakly feasible 4-bidder example in arXiv 1305.5404 has v = (1.00, 0.53, 0.25, 0.16), alpha = (1.00, 0.57, 0.47, 0.19), ranking (2,3,1,4) and ratio 1.269. Whether bids b <= v make it a Nash equilibrium is one small exact LP. Their unrefereed PoA_4 = 1.259 proof (details shown for one permutation only) says no; checking it, and its neighbourhood, costs minutes.

For a fixed ranking pi and fixed CTRs, the equilibrium conditions are linear in the bids, and with values free they are bilinear. Fix pi and alpha, then maximise OPT - r*SW over (v, b) with an LP or bilinear solver, and binary-search r. Enumerate non-cyclic rankings for n = 5, 6, 7 (Ding et al. claim the cyclic one and n = 4 are safe).

Weakly feasible allocations (the relaxation behind the 1.28216 upper bound) reach 1.269 at n = 4 per arXiv 1305.5404. Use the gap between weak feasibility and true NE constraints to see which constraint blocks each candidate, and design rankings where it is slack.

Intuition: inefficiency comes from a high-value bidder underbidding into a low slot while lower-value bidders sit above at cheap prices. Search instances with long chains of such underbidders and geometric CTR profiles.
For the CCE partial, the LP 'minimise E[SW] subject to the CCE constraints' over a discretised bid grid is exact once deviations are restricted to breakpoints; this alone may beat 1.259.
pitfalls: The no-overbidding variant changes the answer: per-bidder pointwise b_i <= v_i (this cell, bar 1.259134) vs the weaker notions of arXiv:2609.39532 (bar 2). Never compare across them.

Ties: the published worst cases sit exactly on indifferences. Fix and state the tie rule, verify the NE under that rule, and prefer instances whose inequalities hold strictly so the claim survives any tie rule.
Weakly feasible is not Nash. Ding et al.'s 1.269 n = 4 allocation is only weakly feasible, and a claim needs actual equilibrium bids checked exactly.
The 3-slot supremum is irrational, so rational instances cannot match it exactly. Any claim at n = 3 above 1.259134 is a checker bug, since Theorem 4.2 proves the bound there.
Quality factors and 'squashing' variants change the model. Use the plain separable-CTR GSP of arXiv 1201.6429 Section 2.

targets.name: Levine's hat puzzle with 3 to 12 players: beat a best-known success probability in the Buhler et al. record table (or lower V3 <= 89/256)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (an exact evaluation of a t-level strategy enumerates 2^(n*t) hat configurations: 2^15 for n=3, t=5; 2^18 for t=6; 2^20 for n=4, t=5)
targets.statement: n players each wear an infinite stack of independent fair black/white hats, see every stack but their own, and simultaneously name a position on their own stack; the team wins iff every named hat is black. V_n is the supremum of the success probability. No V_n is known exactly for n > 1; V_n is strictly decreasing in n (Buhler et al. 2021; Alon, Friedgut, Kalai, Kindler, arXiv:2208.06858), and Levine conjectured V_n -> 0 (the best general lower bounds behave like 1/log2(n), via Winkler-type strategies). Buhler, Freiling, Graham, Kariv, Roche, Tiefenbruck, Van Alten, Yeroshkin (INTEGERS 21A (2021), arXiv:1407.4711v8, Section 5 'Best Current Lower Bounds', offered 'for puzzle aficionados ... who would like to improve upon existing strategies') list: V3 >= 9119/32670 ~ 0.279124, V4 >= 14844/64120 ~ 0.231503, V5 >= 205447/1012494 ~ 0.202911, V6 >= 2984604/15946868 ~ 0.187159, V7 >= 43930663/250593742 ~ 0.175306, V8 >= 651583632/3929765616 ~ 0.165807, V9 >= 0.158764..., V10 >= 0.153517..., V11 >= 0.149025..., V12 >= 0.145047... (decimals rounded down). Provenance: V3 and V4 come from 2014 hill climbs (Reyes and Carter) over SYMMETRIC strategies only: for n = 3 a symmetric 32x32 table with values in 1..5 (5 levels) wins 9120 of 32768 configurations, and white-and-black recursive resets give (9120 - 1)/(31^3 + 3*31^2 - 4); for n = 4 a symmetric 4-level 16x16x16 tensor wins 14845/65536, then resets. V5..V12 come from generalized Winkler strategies (Latin-square 'sums' of lowest-black-hat levels over t ~ log2(n) levels, counting bonus wins) with resets; the reset denominators are (2^t - 1)^n + n(2^t - 1)^(n-1) - (n + 1). Upper bounds: V3 <= 89/256 = 0.34765625 (their Theorem 9, a hint argument) and V_n <= V2 <= 81/224. The 2025 papers (Heilman-Tamuz arXiv:2503.09042; Bouquet et al. arXiv:2508.01737v2) give new values for n = 2 only (plus an uncountable-stack variant); an arXiv search on 2026-10-25 found no newer n >= 3 values, so the table appears unchanged since 2021.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit strategy for some n with 3 <= n <= 12 - a finite t-level strategy (for each player, a function from the other players' first t hats to a level in 1..t), optionally extended by recursive resets whose renewal bookkeeping is written out in full - whose EXACT success probability, computed by enumerating all 2^(n*t) configurations of one tier and solving the renewal equations in exact rational arithmetic, is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the value for that n in Buhler et al. Section 5 (arXiv:1407.4711v8) and than any newer published value found via the status source at verification time. For n = 3..8 compare with the printed fractions; for n = 9..12, where only 6-decimal round-downs are printed, the claim must reach at least the printed decimal + 0.000001 (0.158765, 0.153518, 0.149026, 0.145048) unless the exact table fraction is recovered from the paper's construction and strictly beaten. The improvement bar includes the best valid composition of published objects under these same rules, as well as direct published objects. Unmerged submissions are not bars. State whether the submitted object is a composition and identify all components and their sources.

partial_wins.statement: A certified upper bound V3 < 89/256 = 0.34765625: a hint or matrix-game construction in the style of Buhler et al. Theorem 9 whose value is computed by an exhaustive, re-runnable search in exact arithmetic.

targets.verification_method: Write an evaluator from the definition: for a t-level strategy, loop over all 2^(n*t) hat assignments, compute each player's named level from the OTHER players' hats only, and count the assignments in which every named hat is black; the base success probability is count/2^(n*t), exact. If resets are claimed, model the play tier by tier as an absorbing Markov chain (state: which players have not yet named a level, and whether every level already named was black), with one-tier transition probabilities obtained from the same exhaustive enumeration, and solve it in exact rationals; cross-check against the paper's closed form (W - 1)/((2^t - 1)^n + n(2^t - 1)^(n-1) - (n + 1)) where it applies. Calibrate on n = 2 (the 3-level S3 strategy: W = 22 of 64, value 21/60 = 7/20) and by re-deriving 9119/32670 from a re-searched symmetric 5-level n = 3 strategy. Calibration against printed decimal numbers must agree within one unit of the last printed digit; exact identities and exact source fractions must agree exactly.
angles: Drop the symmetry assumption: the 2014 V3/V4 searches were over symmetric strategies; seed asymmetric local search from symmetric optima.

More levels: n = 3 with t = 6 (2^18 configurations) and n = 4 with t = 5 (2^20); changing one entry of a player's table (one view of the others' hats) touches only the 2^t configurations in which that view occurs, so incremental exact scoring makes local search fast.
Run many diversified hill climbs or annealers in parallel, mark each by improvement per CPU-minute, keep the best, then apply the white/black reset construction to every finalist.
For n >= 5, search over quasigroups (Latin squares of order t) and over which levels count, including the 'bonus' wins when the target sum is missed.
Exact local completion: fix most of a strategy and solve the best assignment of a block of views with an ILP or MaxSAT model.
pitfalls: The team wins only if ALL players name black hats.
A player's choice may depend only on the other players' hats; full-configuration enumerators make it easy to leak a player's own hats into their own decision.
Players may reset at different tiers; renewal bookkeeping must cover mixed cases, not only simultaneous resets.
V9..V12 are printed as rounded-down decimals; clear them by at least 1e-6 or recover the exact fractions.
Use exact integer counts; never compare rounded floats against the table.
p1 is a maximum over all strategies of a hint game; heuristic search cannot certify it.
Recursive resets and any other valid composition of published strategies belong in the comparison bar; identify the submitted strategy as composed when it is composed.

targets.name: Median selection networks: reduce a current comparator count for 10–25 inputs
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days for evolutionary search or SAT-assisted local replacement; exhaustive zero-one verification at n≤25 fits laptop memory and minutes to hours
targets.statement: Bert Dobbelaere’s maintained List of median selection networks gives explicit size/depth trade-offs. On 2026-10-25 (page updated that day), the least listed comparator counts for n=10 through 25 are respectively 22,25,29,32,38,41,46,49,55,58,63,66,74,77,82,85. These are construction records, not proofs of optimality. Its history lists updates through 2026-10-25 (that day: smaller networks for 46 to 49 and 61 inputs, and minor improvements for sizes between 22 and 54) and credits Mason Hemmer and Touko Ursin. Re-read the page on the day of any claim. For odd n one designated output is the middle order statistic. For even n two designated outputs are the two middle order statistics, possibly unordered. The page also describes reductions from networks with nearby input sizes. Median selection differs from full sorting and adaptive comparison selection.
targets.success_criterion: For any listed n, give an input-independent sequence of compare-exchange pairs, output positions, and an exact correctness certificate, using strictly fewer comparators than the listed minimum for that n. A comparator replaces its ordered pair of wires by (min,max). For even n return the two middle input values as an unordered pair; averaging is outside the network. Count every comparator including any added at the outputs. Depth is reported but unconstrained. Also strictly improve the best comparable published result at claim time, including compatible compositions of published objects. State whether the candidate is a composition and identify its components. Values in unmerged pull requests do not set the bar.
targets.verification_method: Check pair indices and count comparators, then evaluate every binary input in {0,1}^n using packed bitsets or batches. For odd n the selected bit must be 1 iff the input contains at least (n+1)/2 ones. For even n compare the sorted selected pair with binary order statistics n/2 and n/2+1. The threshold principle for comparator circuits extends this exhaustive binary check to all totally ordered inputs, including ties. A SAT UNSAT certificate for a violating input is an alternative, provided the encoding is independently reconstructed and the proof checked.
angles: Delete or reroute comparators in the recent records and use counterexamples to repair the network.
Seed from nearby input sizes using the table’s documented trimming and central-pair constructions.
Resynthesize a small suffix exactly while freezing the prefix; verify the resulting whole network.
pitfalls: Count comparator elements, not the separate min/max subcomponent cost.
For even n the middle two outputs may be unordered; averaging is outside the network.
Random testing is not a correctness certificate.
Nearby-size constructions are part of the comparison bar.
The upstream full sorting-network target shares SorterHunter, but asks a different question.
The page is actively improved, including AI-assisted contributions in October 2026 for n >= 25; re-read it the day of any claim.

targets.name: Misère Sprouts: settle the 21-spot game (first unknown since 2011)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (the 20-spot proof database of 2011 holds 73,258 positions and was found by human-guided search; no CPU time is published)
targets.statement: Sprouts (Conway and Paterson, 1967) starts with n spots in the plane; a move joins two spots (or one spot to itself) by a curve that crosses nothing and puts a new spot on it, and no spot may have more than 3 lines. In misère play the player who makes the last move loses. Starting-position outcomes are known only for n <= 20: Applegate, Jacobson and Sleator (1991) to 9 spots, then 10 to 16 in 2006-2009 (credited to Purinton and Khorkov on the Glop records page, to Josh Jordan and Roman Khorkov on Wikipedia), then Lemoine and Viennot's program Glop: 17 win (2009-08-30), 18 win and 19 loss (2010-12-18), 20 loss (2011-03-18). The Glop records page lists 21 as '?', and Wikipedia's Sprouts article still gives 20 spots (2011) as the misère frontier. Lemoine and Viennot (arXiv:0908.4407, Conjecture 3) conjecture that the first player wins exactly when n mod 6 is 0, 4 or 5, except that n = 1 is a win and n = 4 a loss; this predicts 21 = loss, 22 = win, 23 = win. Normal-play Sprouts moved far ahead in 2025 (Čížek, Balko and Schmid's SPOTS solver, 480-1024 cores: all n <= 62 plus 27 cases up to 104), but SPOTS handles normal play only, and its nimber reductions do not apply to misère play. Checked 2026-10-25: the Glop table lists 21 as '?' and Wikipedia's misère section ends at 20 spots (2011).
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: the misère outcome (first-player win or loss) of the 21-spot starting position in the plane, under standard rules (at most 3 lines per spot; the last player to move loses), with BOTH of the following. (1) A complete solution tree (OR nodes: one named child proven lost for the player to move; AND nodes: every child proven won), in Lemoine-Viennot string notation or another documented notation, that a checker which shares no code with the solver accepts, where the checker regenerates the full child list of every AND node with its own move generator. If the certificate uses Lemoine-Viennot reduced canonical trees (RCTs) to split positions into independent lands, the checker recomputes every RCT it relies on from scratch; nimber (Grundy) reductions are not valid in misère play and may not be used. (2) The outcome reproduced by a second, independent implementation (for example Glop 2.2 from the official tarball, run on the same certificate or from scratch). The 21-spot misère value must be unknown at verification time on Wikipedia's Sprouts article, the Glop records page and arXiv (search 'misère Sprouts'). A first-player win at n = 21, refuting the conjecture, is an equally full win.

partial_wins.statement: The misère outcome of the 22-spot or 23-spot starting position (both predicted first-player wins, where the root needs only one proven-losing child), certified exactly as in the success criterion, while n = 21 is still open.

The first independent confirmation of the 2009-2011 misère values for n = 17, 18, 19 and 20: solution trees produced by a solver that shares no code with Glop, each accepted by a checker as in criterion (1) and agreeing with the Glop records table.

targets.verification_method: Build an independent Sprouts move generator and test it first: reproduce the published normal-play outcomes for n <= 14 and the misère outcomes for n <= 12 from scratch, and compare child counts of random small positions with Glop 2.2 (GPL v2; source at http://download.tuxfamily.org/sprouts/glop-2.2.tar.bz2). Then walk the claimed solution tree: at every AND node regenerate all children and check each is a proven win in the certificate; at every OR node check that the named child is legal and a proven loss; terminal positions (no legal move) are wins for the player to move in misère play. Recompute any RCT the certificate uses. Finally run Glop 2.2 (or another independent solver) on the same position and compare outcomes.
angles: Lemoine and Viennot wrote that the bottleneck for larger Sprouts games was human time spent guiding the search, not CPU or memory, and suggested proof-number search. Port SPOTS (open source, PNS-PDFPN, two-level parallelism) to misère play: replace its nimber reductions with RCT-based land splitting, or start with whole-position PN search and canonical-string transpositions, run in parallel.

Attack 22 and 23 first: a predicted win needs one proven-losing child at the root. In normal play the easy refutations for p = 5 mod 6 linked one spot to itself and split the remaining spots into two equal sets; test the misère analogue of that child first.

Warm-start from the published misère databases (Records Sprouts misère - n6rct and the 6-spot RCT database on download.tuxfamily.org/sprouts/bases/) so that all positions already solved for n <= 20 cost nothing.
For 21 (predicted loss) every root child must be proven a win; order children by the authors' 'lives' measure and solve the cheapest first, sharing a transposition table across workers.

Keep a solution-tree export from day one (Glop's 'check computation' idea: re-run guided by the database and store only one losing child per winning node), so the certificate is small enough for an independent checker.
pitfalls: Normal and misère results must never be mixed: Sprague-Grundy sums do not hold in misère play, and only RCT reductions proved in arXiv:0908.4407 are sound.
The Glop records page's prose still says the first unknown misère value is the 20-spot game; its table shows 20 solved (loss, 2011-03-18) and 21 as '?'.
The record databases are not compatible with Glop 2.2 (page note); use the matching Glop version or recompute.
The 'positions' column counts stored database entries (including the whole 6-spot game tree), not search effort.
The record is for the plane (sphere); results on other compact surfaces are a different table.
A single solver run proves nothing: a move-generator bug gives a wrong outcome. Two independent implementations are required.
Crowding risk: the SPOTS team (Charles University) titled its paper 'Impartial Games and Beyond' and could move to misère play; check arXiv and the SPOTS repository before and after a run.

targets.name: Odd-variable Boolean nonlinearity: exceed 242, 996 or 4040
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days for symmetry-restricted search and local modifications; a full Walsh certificate takes milliseconds to seconds
targets.statement: Claude Carlet, Marko Ðurasevic, Domagoj Jakobovic, Stjepan Picek and Luca Mariot, A Systematic Study on the Design of Odd-Sized Highly Nonlinear Boolean Functions via Evolutionary Algorithms (arXiv:2504.17666v1, April 2025; journal publication December 2025), describe maximum nonlinearity for odd n>7 as open. Table 1 gives unrestricted best-known values 242,996,4040 for n=9,11,13, and upper bounds 244,1000,4050. Nonlinearity is minimum Hamming distance to an affine Boolean function. The n=9 construction is credited to Kavut and Yücel. Direct sums of an n=9, nonlinearity-242 function with two- or four-variable bent functions already give 996 and 4040. These compositions belong to the bar. Author spellings here follow the cited preprint.
targets.success_criterion: Supply the complete truth table of f:{0,1}^n→{0,1}, for n=9,11 or 13, with nonlinearity strictly greater than 242,996 or4040 respectively. No balancedness, rotation symmetry or algebraic-degree restriction is imposed. Report the full Walsh spectrum and the exact achieved nonlinearity; the checker recomputes it. Also strictly improve the best comparable published result at claim time, including compatible compositions of published objects. State whether the candidate is a composition and identify its components. Values in unmerged pull requests do not set the bar.
targets.verification_method: Validate 2^n Boolean table entries in explicitly specified lexicographic bit order. Apply the integer fast Walsh–Hadamard transform to (-1)^f(x). Compute NL(f)=2^(n−1)−max_a |W_f(a)|/2, which includes distances to both affine constants. Check Parseval sum_a W_f(a)^2=2^(2n) and compare the exact integer result with the threshold. This requires at most 8192×13 additions and no floating-point tolerance.
angles: Explore generalized rotation-symmetric orbits, but verify the expanded unrestricted truth table.
Use incremental Walsh updates for small truth-table moves and optimize the largest coefficients first.
Search secondary constructions from the n=9 examples while tracking exact spectral changes.
pitfalls: Balanced-function records do not set unrestricted thresholds.
Semi-bent values are below the records here.
A Walsh spectrum alone is not a function certificate; include the truth table.
The established bent-function compositions already attain 996 and 4040.
Re-check the literature before claiming; an arXiv search on 2026-10-25 found no improvement of 242, 996 or 4040.

targets.name: QOBLIB ten-asset portfolio: close the exact optimum gap for a010_t10_orig_b004_l1e-03
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days; 10 assets, 10 periods, 600 position binaries before presolve, plus 110 slack bits; exploit interchangeable unit copies and the four-position budget
targets.statement: Thorsten Koch and colleagues’ Quantum Optimization Benchmarking Library publishes a multi-period Markowitz benchmark with transaction costs, cash interest and short positions. On 2026-10-25 the portfolio table labels a010_t10_orig_b004_l1e-03 best known with incumbent -8397. Maximilian Schicker’s 2025-08-19 submission reports -8397 and numerical bound -15342.65126758 after 3600.03 seconds; that bound is not an exact proof. The canonical schedule file repeats instance po_a010_t10_orig, budget 4, lambda 0.001 and objective -8397. Fix the shipped rounded integer-coefficient BQP, dataset po_a010_t10_orig, a=10, t=10, B=4 and lambda=1/1000; keep the other parameter_u3_c10.zpl settings, including unit=100000, cash=1000000, ub=3, delta=0.001, nu=0.0001, rho=0.000025 and upscale=1. There are three interchangeable copies per asset, direction and period, plus four-bit cash and seven-bit budget slack registers. The exact global optimum remains unproved in the source table.
targets.success_criterion: Give a globally optimal feasible position schedule for this exact instance, its integer objective v <= -8397, and an independently checkable matching lower-bound certificate. A solution equal to -8397 is a full win only with an exact global optimality certificate. Certificates may be a complete dynamic-programming/Bellman certificate or an exact rational branch-and-bound proof for the published BQP; a solver status or floating-point gap alone does not qualify.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit feasible canonical schedule with recomputed integer objective at most -8398, strictly improving the published -8397 incumbent, even without proving optimality. Also strictly improve the best comparable published result at claim time, including compatible compositions of published objects. State whether the candidate is a composition and identify its components. Values in unmerged pull requests do not set the bar.

targets.verification_method: Read the original price and covariance decimal strings as rationals. Reproduce the coefficients of bqp_u3_c10.zpl using Zimpl round-half-away-from-zero, at the same places as the model. Check every unit count is an integer in 0..3, per-period total count <=4, cash slack 10-net in 0..15 and budget slack 4-total in 0..127. Reconstruct canonical copy slots, slack bits and the complete objective, including initial purchases, final liquidation and the model's actual indexing/multiplicities. Cross-check with the public exact Rust checker. For optimality, enumerate per-period count states and verify all Bellman lower-bound inequalities and a matching attaining path. There are 10606 count states before any additional pruning: 20 direction/asset counts in 0..3 with total <=4. Direct comparisons are about a billion small integer operations; a certified weighted-L1 distance transform can reduce this substantially. A verifier should take minutes to hours in compiled code.
angles: Use long/short unit counts, not permutations of the three identical copies. The source checker explains why canonical aligned slots preserve the optimum.

Build an exact dynamic program over daily states. Transaction costs are weighted absolute count changes; shortest-path distance transforms on the count-state graph may avoid an all-pairs transition loop.
Use the -8397 schedule as a reproducibility check before searching. Optimize the rounded shipped objective, with its exact boundary terms.
pitfalls: The source table is not an optimality certificate. Likewise the reported Gurobi lower bound is floating-point evidence, not a proof.
The high-level README simplifies the model. The Zimpl source and parameter file define the actual instance, including any repeated summands; do not silently repair the economics.
Long and short holdings in the same asset are not forbidden by the published constraints. Adding that prohibition changes the benchmark.
The time-index convention matters: price data and objective return/liquidation indices must follow the source exactly.

targets.name: SAT Competition 2026: first certified solve of a Main-track instance whose result is unknown
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days per instance (portfolio of CDCL and local-search solvers, cube-and-conquer on a multi-core machine); an UNSAT proof from a multi-day run can need tens to hundreds of GB of disk
targets.statement: SAT Competition 2026's Main track contains 400 CNF formulas. On 2026-10-25 the GBD track page lists 40 of them with result 'unknown'; one, 3c51a565526faa922fb298a2658440e9 (hard-cep), was answered unsat without a checked proof by an experimental-track configuration in scores.csv, leaving 39 eligible candidates. An unknown database row alone does not establish eligibility. A target formula must still have no SAT or UNSAT answer from any configuration in the cited competition scores and no later published answer. Either a complete satisfying assignment or a checked proof of unsatisfiability answers the exact original formula. The competition organisers and benchmark contributors provide the reference files and proof rules.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for one instance whose GBD result attribute is 'unknown' on https://benchmark-database.de/?track=main_2026 when re-fetched at verification time and that received no sat or unsat answer from any configuration in https://satcompetition.github.io/2026/downloads/scores.csv (39 instances on 2026-10-25: exclude 3c51a565526faa922fb298a2658440e9 and re-derive the eligible list from the linked database and scores), downloaded from http://benchmark-database.de/file/<hash> and matched to that hash: (a) if satisfiable, a complete assignment that satisfies every clause of the original (unpreprocessed) CNF, checked by a model checker written independently of the solver; or (b) if unsatisfiable, a proof of unsatisfiability of that exact CNF accepted by a formally verified checker from the competition's pipelines (LRAT checked by cake_lpr, for example after elaboration with drat-trim or dpr-trim; GRAT checked by gratchk; or a VeriPB proof checked through CakePB), with the checker's accepting output, its version and the proof's SHA-256 saved. The instance must not have been reported solved elsewhere (search arXiv and the web for the hash and file name; check any published 2026 parallel or cloud track results). Either answer counts; the result is the first certified solve. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: An UNSAT proof for one of the 39 instances accepted by an unverified checker (drat-trim or dpr-trim) when the formally verified checker does not finish within 72 hours on the claimant's machine, labelled as such.

A certified answer under the same certificate and checker standards as the full win, with the following explicit eligibility exception, of an instance tagged main_2025 on GBD whose result is 'unknown' at verification time and which is not among the 40 main_2026 instances.

A certified answer under the same certificate and checker standards as the full win, with the following explicit eligibility exception, of 3c51a565526faa922fb298a2658440e9 (hard-cep), the one GBD-unknown main_2026 instance that the 2026 experimental-track configuration reported unsat without a checked proof: a proof accepted by a formally verified checker (or a model, which would contradict that report).

targets.verification_method: Download the CNF by hash (xz-compressed DIMACS), confirm the normalised GBD hash with GBD's open-source tools, then: SAT: parse the v-lines, confirm every variable is assigned (or extend unassigned variables arbitrarily and re-check) and that every clause contains a true literal (a short independent script, seconds); UNSAT: run the verified chain on the claimed proof against the same CNF (for example drat-trim in LRAT-output mode followed by cake_lpr, or the VeriPB/CakePB chain), recording versions, wall time and the accepting line. Re-fetch the GBD track page and confirm the result column still reads 'unknown' for that hash.
angles: Triage first: for all 39 record size, family and structure, give each a short portfolio run (kissat, CaDiCaL, a stochastic local-search solver for satisfiable-looking families), then concentrate the nights on the three to five that move.

About 18 eligible instances carry only 2026 tags and have had one competition's worth of attention (33 configurations at a 5000 s limit); scheduling-like families (school-timetabling, station-repacking from spectrum repacking) and colouring families (van der Waerden, cyclic anti-bandwidth) are where long local-search runs or symmetry breaking most often succeed.

Cube-and-conquer for UNSAT-leaning combinatorial families (greentao, erdos-discrepancy, van der Waerden, Tseitin, xor-chain): split with a lookahead cuber, solve cubes in parallel, emit per-cube proofs and a proof of the cube cover, and check the merged proof.

Re-encode at the application level when CDCL stalls: Gauss-Jordan/XOR reasoning for xor-chain, Tseitin and syndrome-decoding instances; a bit-level view of the cryptography and bitvector instances; any model found must still be checked against the original CNF.
The crypto_2021 instance and the syndrome-decoding instance are attack encodings; understanding the cipher or code suggests variable orders and guessing strategies (cube on key or error bits).
Plan disk: use binary DRAT, compress, keep only the proof of the run that finishes, and check incrementally.
pitfalls: The criterion is GBD's 'unknown', not 'unsolved in 2026': GBD already records results for instances no 2026 solver finished.
Instances are identified by GBD hash of the normalized CNF; download by hash and verify before running checkers, or the result may be for a different file.
A solver's 's UNSATISFIABLE' line is not a result; only an accepted proof counts, and the formally verified checker is the bar for the full win (p1 covers acceptance by unverified checkers).
Check models against the original CNF, not a preprocessed or re-encoded file.

Some families encode open mathematical questions (Green-Tao, van der Waerden, Erdős discrepancy, matrix multiplication); a SAT answer there may be a mathematical result in its own right and deserves an independent cross-check and a literature search.
Results may exist outside GBD (papers, solver authors' private runs, the 2026 parallel and cloud tracks); search before claiming.

The hard-cep instance 3c51a565526faa922fb298a2658440e9 is GBD-unknown but was answered (unsat, unverified) in the 2026 experimental track; it counts only as partial win p3, and scores.csv must be re-read for any newer answer.

targets.name: Price of stability of undirected Shapley network design with three players: an instance above 1769/1126 (upper bound 286/175)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (exact enumeration of all strategy profiles on graphs with 5-9 vertices, inside a search over topologies and edge costs)
targets.statement: Three players choose simple paths in an undirected graph and split each used edge's positive cost equally. Price of stability is the cheapest Nash-equilibrium social cost divided by the cheapest profile's social cost. Disser, Feldmann, Klimm and Mihalák (TCS 2015) give a five-vertex construction with ratio 1769/1126. Bilò and Bove (2011) give upper bound 286/175. The cited paper leaves the three-player value open. The target is an explicit rational instance with a larger exact ratio, verified by enumerating all paths, profiles and unilateral deviations. An arXiv search on 2026-10-25 found no later three-player lower bound; later publications must still be checked.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: an explicit instance with exactly three players (undirected graph, positive rational edge costs, three source-target pairs) whose price of stability is strictly greater than 1769/1126, computed exactly: every simple path for every player is listed, every strategy profile is evaluated with exact rational cost shares, every profile is tested for the Nash condition against all of the deviating player's simple paths, the optimum is the minimum social cost over all profiles, and the ratio (cheapest equilibrium cost) / (optimum) is reported as an exact fraction. Two independently written checkers must agree, and the value must exceed every 3-player lower bound published at verification time (search for papers citing Disser et al. 2015). Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: An independent exact reproduction, with published code, of the 1769/1126 instance of Disser et al. (all profiles enumerated, the equilibrium shown unique, the optimum confirmed at 1126) and of their potential-optimal family whose ratio approaches 286/175, establishing a verified baseline that the literature currently states only in prose and figures.

targets.verification_method: Read the instance; enumerate all simple s_i-t_i paths per player (graphs are small); for every profile compute each player's cost as the sum over her edges of c_e divided by the number of players on e, using exact fractions; mark a profile as an equilibrium if no player has a path with strictly smaller cost given the others' paths; compute the optimum as the minimum over profiles of the total cost of edges used by at least one player; output min equilibrium cost / optimum as a fraction and compare with 1769/1126. Sanity checks: the 2-player worst case 4/3 and Disser et al.'s 5-vertex instance (equilibrium 1769, optimum 1126).
angles: Adversary search: fix a small topology (5 to 8 vertices, the 1769/1126 example being 5), then optimise the edge costs with an LP or local search that keeps a chosen bad profile an equilibrium while pushing every cheaper profile out of equilibrium; each step's exact ratio comes from full enumeration, which is milliseconds at this size.

The record has a simple structure (in its unique equilibrium each player uses the direct edge s_i t_i, while the optimum uses all the other edges): enumerate small gadget families of this kind and solve for the edge costs that make the expensive profile the unique equilibrium.

Use the gap: Bilò and Bove's 286/175 is tight only for potential-minimising equilibria, so a better instance must make every potential minimiser expensive while a cheaper non-minimising equilibrium does not exist; search for instances where the potential minimiser is the unique equilibrium.

Scale out: the search is embarrassingly parallel over topologies and source-target placements; many cores can run a cost optimisation for every connected graph on up to 6 vertices and every placement of three pairs, then sample 7- and 8-vertex graphs.
pitfalls: Price of stability, not anarchy: the ratio uses the CHEAPEST equilibrium, so every equilibrium of the instance must be found and costed.
Strategies are simple paths; a player who uses a non-simple walk or two parallel routes is outside the model.
Cost shares are equal splits among the players actually using the edge (Shapley), and the social cost counts each used edge once.
Directed instances do not count (directed PoS is H_k and is known to be tight).
Floating-point ratios hide ties; an equilibrium test that is off by a tie changes the answer. Use exact fractions throughout.
Cite and beat the newest 3-player bound: check papers citing Disser et al. 2015 before claiming.

targets.name: Subtraction games: longest eventual period for largest move n (OEIS A389689: 1036 at n = 25 is recorded in Flammenkamp's dissertation; n = 31 is the next candidate, subject to the unchecked enlarged 1997 book edition; A389690 beyond n = 22)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (exhaustive over 2^(n-1) move sets; about 5.4e8 sets at n = 30, 1.1e9 at n = 31)
targets.statement: In the subtraction game with finite move set S (a player removes s in S tokens from one heap; whoever cannot move loses), the outcome sequence and the Sprague-Grundy sequence are eventually periodic (Golomb, 1966), but the only general bound on the period is exponential; Althöfer and Bültermann (TCS 148, 1995) gave sets with cubic periods, and Flammenkamp (1997) conjectured at most quadratic periods for 3-move sets. OEIS A389689 (Rui Yao, Oct 2025) lists, for each n, the longest eventual period of the win/lose sequence over all S with max S = n: n = 1..23 known (2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 22, 25, 28, 45, 54, 61, 76, 94, 168, 168, 204, 314, 309, 266, 444, 516, 446). A389690 does the same for the Sprague-Grundy sequence, n = 1..22 known (2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 22, 25, 28, 58, 54, 87, 114, 144, 189, 336, 306, 456, 728, 1178, 1180, 4464). Both entries carry the 'more' keyword and have not been extended since October 2025 (as of 2026-10-28); the terms come from exhaustive Python searches over all 2^(n-1) sets. Both entries were re-read on 2026-10-28 and show these terms. Further A389689 terms were published long before, in a source neither entry cites: Achim Flammenkamp's dissertation, Lange Perioden in Subtraktions-Spielen (Universität Bielefeld, 1997; the author's PostScript diss.ps.gz is linked from OEIS A014588; an enlarged book edition, not checked here, appeared in 1997, Hans-Jacobs-Verlag, ISBN 3-932136-10-1). On printed pp. 40-41 he computes the periods of all move sets with max S < 30 and lists the 44 record holders as max S grows. Its last line for each max S is the maximum for that n: A389689(24) = 1107 ({1, 3, 12, 21, 23, 24}) and A389689(26..29) = 1256, 1937, 3624, 4896, and the list agrees with OEIS at every n <= 23 where it has a line. The pp. 40-41 record list has no max S = 25 row, so by itself it implies only A389689(25) <= 1107. The dissertation's symmetric 5-move data record p = 1036 at s5 = 25: dia5.eps (Bild ix, p. 52) plots ln p(L) = 6.943122, and the embedded s5 = 5..117 data table in dia55.eps (Bild x, p. 55) contains '25 133.05 % 1036 0.278 0.1956' (the integer follows a PostScript % comment; the typeset table on pp. 52-54 starts at s5 = 40). The dissertation therefore gives 1036 <= A389689(25) <= 1107. The list's final line, {4, 10, 15, 20, 26, 30} with period 5296, is ambiguous: the text twice puts the exhaustive range at max S < 30 (pp. 40 and 43) yet counts this line among the 44, and the same line opens his search of symmetric sets only (n - s in S for every s < n in S) up to max S = 60 (p. 43), whose periods are lower bounds, not terms. Here 5296 at n = 30 counts as published, although it may be only a lower bound. Likewise 1036 at n = 25 counts as published here, although the dissertation records it only as a symmetric-5-move lower bound; an exhaustive all-set computation gives 1036, so the bound is tight. The dissertation gives no Sprague-Grundy period maxima, so A389690 is unaffected.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: the exact value of the next candidate A389689 term beyond the dissertation's recorded values (n = 31, after the pp. 40-41 record-list values at n = 24 and 26..30 and the recorded 1036 at n = 25; subject to checking the enlarged 1997 book edition for prior publication), or A389690 at n = 23, or of any later unpublished term once those are filled, using the entries' own definitions (S ranges over all subsets of {1, ..., n} that contain n; the period is the minimal eventual period, found as the first repeat of the length-n window of outcomes or Sprague-Grundy values), with all of: (1) an explicit maximising set S whose period an independent program recomputes exactly; (2) two independently written exhaustive searches over all 2^(n-1) sets that agree on the maximum AND on the full histogram of periods (number of sets with each period); (3) the term is not yet in the OEIS entry, its b-file or its history at verification time, and does not merely equal a value already recorded for that n in Flammenkamp's 1997 dissertation diss.ps.gz: A389689 at n = 24 and 26..29 and 5296 at n = 30 on pp. 40-41, 1036 at n = 25 in the embedded Bild ix/x symmetric-5-move data, and the symmetric-set lower bounds explicitly recorded for n >= 31 on pp. 43-44 and in the Bild ix/x data (for example 1800 at n = 31 and 8530 at n = 32). Those recorded numbers count as published although the OEIS entry lacks them; an unprinted value at n >= 31 that strictly exceeds the recorded lower bound for that n counts as new against diss.ps.gz. The enlarged 1997 book edition remains an unresolved source. Submitting to OEIS is an action for the human only.

partial_wins.statement: A correction of a published term: for some n already listed (n <= 23 in A389689, n <= 22 in A389690, n = 24 and 26..30 in Flammenkamp's 1997 pp. 40-41 record list, or n = 25 where 1036 is recorded in the embedded Bild ix/x symmetric-5-move data), an explicit set S with max S = n whose eventual period exceeds the listed value, confirmed by the OEIS Python program and one independent program.

targets.verification_method: Recompute the eventual period of each claimed maximising set with the Python program linked from the OEIS entry (a389689_1.txt or a389690_2.txt) and with an independent implementation. For the maximum, rerun an independent exhaustive search (C or Rust; bit-parallel windows for A389689) and compare the period histogram line by line with the claimant's; also confirm that the search reproduces every published term for smaller n, including Flammenkamp's (for example 1107 at n = 24, for {1, 3, 12, 21, 23, 24}).
angles: Win/lose sequence as bit operations: with the last n outcomes in a machine word w, the next outcome is ((~w) & maskS) != 0; Brent's cycle detection on w needs no hash table, so each set costs a few thousand word operations and 2^(n-1) sets split perfectly across cores.
For Sprague-Grundy values the window holds small integers (values are at most |S|); pack them ceil(log2(n+1)) bits per entry (five bits are needed once n >= 16) and use the same cycle detection.

Study the maximising sets for n <= 23 first (small-data) and seed a running maximum with the analogous sets and with Althöfer-Bültermann-type sets at the new n; this gives an early lower bound for the report, but the exhaustive pass must still cover every set.
Keep and publish the per-set periods for a random 1% sample plus all sets within 10% of the maximum, so that a checker can spot-check cheaply before a full rerun.
pitfalls: The minimal period is the first repeat of the full length-n window, starting only once n values exist; a repeat of a shorter block, or one found inside the padded prefix, is wrong.
Off-by-one in the convention: position 0 is a loss (no move), moves may not go below 0, and n itself must be in S.
A389689 is not monotone (for example 314, 309, 266 at n = 18..20), so a search capped by the previous term is invalid.

OEIS is not the only record: Flammenkamp's 1997 dissertation already gives A389689 at n = 24 and 26..29, lists 5296 at n = 30 (pp. 40-41), and records 1036 at s5 = 25 in the embedded Bild ix/x symmetric-5-move data (dia5.eps p. 52; dia55.eps p. 55; the typeset table on pp. 52-54 starts at s5 = 40), so recomputing those values is a calibration, not a new term. His symmetric-set lists (pp. 43-44 for max S = 30..60 and the Bild ix/x data for symmetric 5-move sets up to s5 = 117, including 1800 at s5 = 31 and 8530 at s5 = 32) give lower bounds; an all-set maximum at n >= 31 must strictly exceed the bound recorded for that n to count as new against diss.ps.gz. His enlarged 1997 book edition has not been checked; a value found there is published too.
Some periods grow fast (A389690 jumps from 1180 to 4464 at n = 22); detection must not assume a period bound below 2^n (win/lose) or (n+1)^n (Sprague-Grundy).
This is a modest table: the value of a win is a correct, independently reproduced new term, not a theorem about period growth.

targets.name: 3-handed no-limit hold'em jam/fold sit-and-go endgame (Ganzfried-Sandholm): a certified epsilon-equilibrium well below $0.0488
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (exact preflop all-in outcome tables for all 169-class pairs and triples with card removal, about 1e13-1e14 seven-card evaluations; then a 946-state stochastic-game solve and an exact ex post best-response check)
targets.statement: Ganzfried and Sandholm (AAMAS 2008, IJCAI 2009) model a three-handed hold'em sit-and-go endgame with jam/fold actions. There are 13,500 chips, blinds 300/600, 946 nonterminal stack vectors and payouts of 50, 30 and 20 dollars. Terminal values use the Independent Chip Model. Their reported maximum unilateral improvement is 0.0488 dollars across starting states and players. The target is an explicit stationary profile with a certified maximum gain at most 0.0010 dollars, using exact all-in outcome probabilities. The proposal checks both stated same-hand elimination conventions. Later variants with other payouts or approximate equities do not move this model's bar.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit stationary jam/fold profile for G: for each of the 946 stack vectors, the jam probability of the button, the small blind and the big blind for each of the 169 hand classes in every decision situation. Its ex post epsilon must be at most $0.0010, at least 48 times below the published $0.0488 (direction: lower). Epsilon is the maximum, over all 946 starting states and all three players, of the player's best-response value in the induced undiscounted MDP minus the player's value under the profile, in dollars of the $100 pool, computed as in Ganzfried's thesis section 9.4. All-in outcome probabilities must be exact: full enumeration of boards and of the remaining cards. The sources do not say how two players eliminated in the same hand are ranked, so the bound must hold under both readings: (i) the player who started the hand with more chips takes the higher place, and equal starting stacks split the two prizes; (ii) all players eliminated in the same hand split their prizes equally. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: A profile whose certified ex post epsilon is strictly below $0.0488 (but above $0.0010) under both readings, verified exactly as in the success criterion. This is a new record for the published model, though not the full win.

targets.verification_method: Build an independent checker in four steps. (1) Recompute the two- and three-way preflop all-in outcome probabilities by exhaustive enumeration with a fast 7-card evaluator; cross-check a second evaluator on random deals and on standard heads-up equities. (2) For each player, build the MDP the profile induces (946 x 3 position-states plus terminal ICM states), with blinds moving clockwise, the split-pot rule, and short-stack blind posting. (3) Compute the player's best-response value with policy iteration for the undiscounted total-reward criterion, taking the minimal non-negative solution as in thesis section 9.4.1, or with value iteration from a pessimistic start (thesis Theorem 2). Compute the profile's own values by solving the linear system in exact rational arithmetic or rigorous outward-rounded intervals. A residual alone is insufficient; prove bounds on strategy and best-response values. (4) Epsilon is the largest gap over states and players; repeat for both elimination readings.
angles: Write the ex post checker first, then the solver. The checker is the certificate, and it also defines every convention (blind posting, side pots, splits, eliminations).

Equity tables: in 2008 the 3-way rollout took 'a month using 16 processors'. With suit canonicalisation, a table-based 7-card evaluator and a multi-core laptop it should take hours. Store the 13 outcome probabilities per class triple, as the source does, with checksums.

Solve each state's 3-player jam/fold game (169, 338 and 507 information sets) with CFR+ or fictitious play inside a policy-iteration outer loop (PI-FP from IJCAI 2009). Then polish: identify the indifferent hands and solve the indifference equations by Newton's method, driving epsilon toward machine precision.

Report where the exact equilibrium values deviate from ICM. AAMAS 2008 Table 1 lists the ICM deviations of their profile (mean $0.3703 over 2,838 state-seat pairs), which gives a reproducibility cross-check.
pitfalls: Terminal states use ICM payoffs (thesis section 9.4), not heads-up jam/fold equilibrium values; the conference papers only say 'substitute the corresponding payoffs'. The ranking of players busted in the same hand is unstated, hence the two readings.
Split pots must keep stacks in multiples of 300 via the random 300-chip rule. Any other rounding defines a different game with a different state space.
Short stacks: a player with 300 chips in the big blind is all-in for less, which creates side pots. Fix and document the convention, and keep it identical in solver and checker.
The MDP is undiscounted. Naive value iteration from an optimistic start can converge to wrong values (Ganzfried's thesis gives an example); use the minimal non-negative solution.
Epsilon is the maximum over ALL 946 starting states and all three players, in dollars of a $100 pool ($10 entry). A per-hand or average figure is not the published quantity.
Equities must be computed over actual cards with card removal; strategies depend only on the 169 classes.
Search papers citing Ganzfried-Sandholm 2008/2009 before claiming; 'ICM Out!' (2026) shows renewed interest in this exact state space.

targets.name: Lotteries vs item prices for a unit-demand buyer with independent values: an explicit menu earning more than (1 + ln2/5) ~ 1.1386 times any item pricing (gap [1.1386, 3])
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (lottery-pricing LPs over 10^3-10^4 discrete types with lazily added IC constraints; certification is exact enumeration)
targets.statement: A unit-demand buyer values independent items and can buy at most one. Compare optimal lottery-menu revenue with optimal deterministic item-pricing revenue. Chawla, Malec and Sivan (EC 2010, arXiv:1002.3893) give lower bound 1+ln(2)/5 using capped equal-revenue items and a three-entry menu. Jin and Lu (arXiv:2606.10169, Corollary 2(ii)) give upper bound 3 and retain that lower bound. The source appendix's rounded revenue calculation must be recomputed before close calibration. The target is a finite explicit menu whose certified ratio is strictly larger than the symbolic lower-bound constant. Independence and conservative buyer tie-breaking are essential.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit instance (k >= 2 independent item-value distributions, given either with finite rational supports or as closed-form CDFs) and an explicit finite menu of lotteries with rational entries (x >= 0, sum_i x_i <= 1, price l). A checker must confirm three things. (a) The menu's revenue R is computed exactly. With finite supports, enumerate all value profiles; the buyer picks a utility-maximising entry, ties go to the LOWEST-priced maximiser, and the buyer buys nothing when the best utility is <= 0. With closed-form CDFs, use interval-certified integration over the regions where each entry is chosen. (b) An upper bound D on optimal item-pricing revenue: either D = sum_i max_p p * Pr[v_i >= p], always valid for a unit-demand buyer, or the exact OIP from a search over a price set proved sufficient in the write-up. (c) D > 0 and R/D > 1 + ln(2)/5. Direction: higher is better. The bar is the Chawla-Malec-Sivan constant as restated in Jin-Lu, arXiv 2606.10169, Corollary 2(ii); re-check arXiv for newer lower bounds before claiming. The checker must first reproduce the CMS menu's revenue on CMS's capped equal-revenue pair for several n. Use interval integration of the continuous version, or exact enumeration of a fine rational discretisation with the discretisation error bounded. Derive the source menu revenue independently. Match printed finite numerical calibration values within one unit of the last printed digit. Do not turn a rounded appendix calculation into an exact identity. An exact rational or symbolic certificate of any strict improvement counts. For floating-point certificates require a certified ratio at least 1+ln(2)/5+1e-4. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: For the discrete two-item i.i.d. equal-revenue instance with P(v>=x)=1/x on {1,...,n} and some n>=8, certify the exact lottery-revenue and deterministic item-pricing revenue suprema.
