Give a rational primal-dual certificate for the lottery LP and prove its value is the supremum under the stated tie rule. For item pricing, give an exact exhaustive price-region proof or an appropriate integer/global certificate covering all prices. If conservative ties prevent attainment, provide epsilon-achieving menus or prices with a proved revenue gap. Compare existing published values before claiming novelty.

targets.verification_method: Python with fractions.Fraction, under 150 lines. Read the item distributions and the menu. Check x >= 0 and sum x <= 1 for every entry. Enumerate the product of supports, apply the conservative tie rule, accumulate the revenue exactly, and compute D as the sum of the single-item monopoly revenues. Prove R/D > 1 + ln(2)/5. Refine rigorous bounds on ln 2 until the strict comparison is certified; a fixed decimal approximation must not set a minimum improvement. Calibrate on the CMS menu first. For the partial win, check the lottery LP primal and dual feasibility exactly, with equal objective values, and the argument connecting it to the revenue supremum under conservative ties. Independently verify the complete deterministic-price region enumeration or global certificate. Distinguish an attained optimum from a supremum approached by epsilon-achieving menus or prices.
angles: Let the LP find the menu. For discretised equal-revenue pairs with n = 8, 16, 32, ..., solve the lottery-pricing LP (one allocation vector and payment per type; IC constraints added lazily). The item-pricing bound stays exactly 2, so any LP optimum above 2 * (1 + ln(2)/5) ~ 2.27726 is a record after extracting and verifying the menu.

Thanassoulis' intuition, as CMS summarise it: a 50/50 lottery sells to buyers nearly indifferent between items who cannot afford either item. Richer menus (many split lotteries at graded prices) should harvest more of the middle of the value square without leaking the high tail.
Go beyond two items: with k i.i.d. equal-revenue items the item-pricing bound is k, and lotteries can split across more items. Test whether OLP/k grows with k.
Asymmetric pairs: one equal-revenue item plus one item with a different tail (uniform, two-point) may break the symmetry that limits the CMS menu.
pitfalls: This is the UNIT-DEMAND cell. The additive-buyer gaps (Rev vs SRev/BRev, Rev vs DRev for additive valuations) are different problems with different constants.
Correlated item values make the gap unbounded (Briest et al.). The instance must be a product distribution.
1.1386 is a LIMIT (n -> infinity) of the CMS construction (their revenue 2.275 + o(1) against item-pricing bound 2). Finite truncations fall short, so a finite instance must strictly exceed the bar.
Tie-breaking toward the seller inflates menu revenue. Use lowest-price-among-maximisers and buy-nothing at zero utility.
Learned or 'approximately IC' mechanisms do not count. A menu with true buyer best-responses is IC by construction, and that is what must be scored.
If exact OIP is claimed instead of the sum-of-monopoly bound, the candidate price set must be provably sufficient; prices at support points alone may not be, because of cross-item indifferences.

targets.name: Guts with the Weenie rule: does the symmetric threshold resist every coalition for n >= 4?
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days for the n=4 and n=5 certificates (exact polynomial integration and chamber certificates in three or four opponent thresholds); the all-n route is a formalisation project
targets.statement:
Kevin Buck, Jae Hwan Lee, Jacob Platnick, Aric Wheeler and Kevin Zumbrun, Continuous Guts Poker and Numerical Optimization of Generalized Recursive Games (2022), Appendix B.3, explicitly conjecture min_{t2,...,tn in [0,1]} alpha(3^(-1/(n-1)),t2,...,tn) >= 0 for every n >= 2. Their words are: "We conjecture that this property holds for general n ≥ 2". Appendix B.2 proves the cases n=2,3; B.3 reports numerical tests for n=3,4,5, not a proof for n>=4. The model gives each player an independent uniform [0,1] hand on every deal. A player holds exactly above their threshold. A sole holder wins and ends the game; otherwise the highest holder wins the pot, each losing holder matches it, and play continues. Under the Weenie rule, when everybody drops, the highest-hand player must match the pot, doubling it for the next deal. Alpha is the paper’s expected zero-sum immediate payoff including virtual-ante adjustments, in units of one player’s current ante. Explicitly, for h>=1 holders, each player receives the virtual amount h-2, the highest holder additionally receives n, and each other holder additionally pays n. For h=0 under the Weenie rule, each receives 1 and the highest-hand player additionally pays n. The target is this published alpha inequality, which underlies the claimed resistance to a coordinated coalition.

Source check, 2026-10-24 UTC (arXiv still lists v3 as the latest version on 2026-10-25): the retrieved status source still presents the question as open. This confirms the cited source, rather than establishing that no later result exists elsewhere. Recheck current literature before claiming a new result.
targets.success_criterion: EITHER (a) a refutation: one n >= 4 and an explicit threshold vector (t2, ..., tn) for which the exact alpha value alpha(3^(-1/(n-1)), t2, ..., tn) is strictly negative. A counterexample must specify every threshold as a rational or real algebraic number with isolating data; the distinguished threshold is the positive root of 3*a^(n-1)-1=0. OR (b) a kernel-checked formal proof (Lean, Rocq/Coq or Isabelle, with no sorry, admit or extra axioms, and an axiom audit) of the displayed inequality for every integer n >= 2 and every opponent threshold vector. For the proof route, a written or computer-assisted proof whose analytic steps are not formalised does not count; exact or interval computations may support it only inside the formal proof, where the proof assistant checks them. A finite grid with no counterexample is not a proof.

partial_wins.statement: The inequality for n=4 for ALL (t2,t3,t4) in [0,1]^3, with an exact global nonnegativity certificate: on every ordering chamber and boundary, a rational sum-of-squares, Bernstein or Positivstellensatz identity (or a replayable real-algebraic decision certificate) that an independent checker verifies in exact arithmetic.
The same exact global nonnegativity certificate for n=5, for ALL four opponent thresholds.

targets.verification_method: Independently integrate the event payoffs over the unit cube of dealt hands, partitioning at the thresholds and the possible highest hand. This yields piecewise polynomials with rational coefficients. Substitute a=3^(-1/(n-1)) using its polynomial and a rational isolating interval. For a negative witness, evaluate in the real algebraic field and certify its sign. For a finite-n proof, check every ordering chamber and boundary using a supplied exact identity (for example a rational sum-of-squares/Bernstein certificate after mapping the ordered chamber to a simplex), or a replayable real-algebraic proof. A general-n proof must be a formal development (induction or other symbolic argument inside the proof assistant): build it in a clean environment, print the axioms used, and check that the formal alpha matches Appendix B and reproduces the proved n = 2, 3 cases. Finitely many positive samples cannot verify it. Small-n certificates should check in minutes to hours.
angles: Start with n=4. Opponent exchange symmetry reduces the cases to the position of a among the sorted opponent thresholds.
Reconstruct payoffs from the event definition before optimizing; Appendix B.1 gives useful n=2,3 cross-checks.
Search numerically for negative regions, then use exact algebraic arithmetic to validate a witness; if none appears, attempt a symbolic chamber certificate.
pitfalls: The abstract sounds more general than the proved body: Appendix B.3 explicitly leaves n>=4 conjectural.
The 2024 solution of ordinary three-player Guts does not prove this different-rule, higher-player conjecture.
The one-shot alpha includes virtual-ante accounting. Simply summing cash won during a deal computes a different expression.
The source has typographical slips in some formulas; derive the definition independently and distinguish any corrected identity from a quotation.
A proof of the alpha inequality is the precise target. Additional claims about infinite-play utilities require the source’s recursive-game justification.

targets.name: Unrestricted binary codes A(n,d), n <= 28: new lower bound in Brouwer's table
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: A(n,d) is the maximum size of a binary code (not necessarily linear) of length n and minimum Hamming distance d. Brouwer's 'Table of general binary codes' (updated version of Best-Brouwer-MacWilliams-Odlyzko-Sloane 1978; page last modified 2026-10-21) gives lower-upper ranges for n=17..28 (even d only, since A(n,2e-1)=A(n+1,2e)), e.g. on 2026-10-28: A(21,10) 42-47, A(22,10) 64-84, A(23,10) 84-150, A(24,10) 136-268, A(25,10) 196-466, A(25,12) 52-55, A(26,12) 65-96, A(27,12) 128-169, A(28,12) 192-288, A(25,8) 4096-5421. Lower-bound improvements since 1978 came from computer searches (Kaikkonen, Ostergard, Laaksonen-Ostergard, Elssel-Zimmermann, Milshtein), and the table is moving fast in October 2026: Kazuki Ota, Takayuki Osa and Tatsuya Harada (arXiv:2610.11609, 8 Oct 2026) gave A(23,10) >= 84, A(25,10) >= 196, A(26,12) >= 65; Oscar Sanchez (email to Brouwer, 2026-10-17) gave A(18,4) >= 6144; Moshe Milshtein (arXiv:2610.23626, 16 Oct 2026) gave (16,3072,3), (17,6144,3), (18,12288,3) and (19,24576,3) codes, i.e. A(17,4) >= 3072, A(18,4) >= 6144, A(19,4) >= 12288, A(20,4) >= 24576; Zhiyang Chen (email, 2026-10-21) gave A(28,12) >= 192, A(21,6) >= 3072, A(27,6) >= 81920, A(28,6) >= 139264. This is the unrestricted A(n,d) table, distinct from the constant-weight A(n,d,w) table already in the bank.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit list of M distinct binary words of length n such that an independent script confirms all pairwise Hamming distances >= d (exhaustive over all M(M-1)/2 pairs, bit operations) and M is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the lower bound for A(n,d) in https://aeb.win.tue.nl/codes/binary-1.html re-fetched live immediately before claiming (the table lists even d only: for odd d compare against the even-d cell A(n+1,d+1), since A(n,d) = A(n+1,d+1)), M does not exceed the table's upper bound for that cell, and no arXiv/journal result found on the day already gives >= M.

partial_wins.statement: A code meeting the live lower bound for some (n,d) with n in 21..28 that is provably inequivalent to the published code (different distance distribution or automorphism group order), verified exactly.
A strictly improved lower bound for A(n,d) with n = 29..32 (outside the table) beating the best value in the literature (e.g. Kaikkonen's A(29,10) >= 1460), with literature check.

targets.verification_method: Load words as Python ints; check M distinct, all lengths n; pairwise popcount(x^y) >= d via numpy uint32 XOR + popcount (M up to ~10^4 is 5*10^7 pairs, seconds); fetch the live table and parse the cell. Minutes.
angles: Codes invariant under a prescribed permutation group (Kaikkonen's affine permutation groups; Laaksonen-Ostergard): choose a group G of order 20-500 acting on n coordinates, compute orbits of words, then solve maximum-weight clique on the orbit compatibility graph (Cliquer / KaMIS).
Unions of cosets of a good linear code (e.g. punctured/shortened BCH or QR codes) selected by clique search on coset representatives.
Construction X / Plotkin (u|u+v) and concatenation from the best ternary or quaternary codes via Gray maps (Z4-linear codes give nonlinear binary codes beating linear ones, cf. Nordstrom-Robinson).

Cross-domain import (combinatorial chemistry / max independent set heuristics from graph ML): use ReduMIS / KaMIS evolutionary MIS solvers, which dominate on huge sparse graphs, on the 'distance < d' conflict graph restricted to an orbit space.

Cross-domain import (statistical physics, hard-core lattice gas): simulated annealing / parallel tempering of a hard-core gas on the hypercube with fugacity schedule, a direct analogue of packing particles.
Cross-domain import (SAT / exact cover from puzzle solving): Knuth's dancing-links or SAT with symmetry breaking to extend a large partial code by the last few words.
pitfalls: Verify the minimum distance over ALL pairs (nonlinear codes) or all codewords (linear), never by sampling.

Literature-ahead-of-table trap: Brouwer's pages are updated irregularly but are very active right now (binary table last modified 2026-10-21, ternary and 5-ary 2026-10-17, mixed binary/ternary 2026-10-17, quaternary not since 2017-09-07, with four independent groups sending improvements in October 2026); search arXiv for the specific (n,d) and re-fetch the page immediately before claiming.
Odd-d cells are equivalent to the even-d cell of length n+1; claim against the correct cell.
A code for (n,d) obtained by trivially shortening/puncturing a known record is implied by known results, not a win.

targets.name: Mixed binary/ternary codes N(m,n,d): new lower bound in Brouwer's mixed-code tables
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: N(m,n,d) is the maximum number of words with m binary and n ternary coordinates at mutual Hamming distance >= d. Brouwer's page (tables copied from Brouwer-Hamalainen-Ostergard-Sloane 1998 with later improvements; HTTP Last-Modified 2026-10-17, no visible date on the page) tabulates bounds for d = 3..10; on 2026-10-28 the grids contain 253 cells still given as lower-upper ranges (counting the pure m=0 / n=0 border cells shown in the grids). Lower-bound improvements came from Ostergard and others and from football-pool enthusiasts (Codigo, PacoHH, Pucho, ehl555, Pedro fdez, 2010-2013), and most recently from Oscar Sanchez (2026, e.g. N(12,2,3) >= 1552, N(10,3,3) >= 1176, N(7,5,5) >= 104, N(5,8,5) >= 513, N(3,10,5) >= 736, N(5,9,7) >= 73, N(2,11,7) >= 77). The upper bounds of Naszvadi-Koniorczyk (arXiv:2310.01883) appear only in an HTML comment in the page source, marked 'not better than PRJÖ' (Östergård); they are not shown on the rendered page. The problem is the packing side of the football-pool problem and has received far less computation than pure binary codes.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit list of M distinct words in {0,1}^m x {0,1,2}^n (m >= 1, n >= 1) with all pairwise Hamming distances >= d (checked exhaustively by an independent script), where M is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the lower bound for N(m,n,d) on https://aeb.win.tue.nl/codes/23codes.html (grid and notes) re-fetched live immediately before claiming, and not already exceeded in an arXiv/journal search done on the day.

partial_wins.statement: A new code meeting a lower bound in a cell where the page records no explicit construction (only an existence argument or an announcement, e.g. the d=3 bounds announced by Código for which the page says 'No explicit construction was given'), giving the explicit word list, verified exhaustively.

targets.verification_method: Parse words, check coordinate alphabets (first m binary, last n ternary), pairwise distances in numpy; parse the live table cell. Minutes.
angles: Start from the best pure ternary code of length m+n and binarise m coordinates (map ternary symbols to binary with a partition maximising retained distance) then re-optimise; and conversely extend binary codes.
Prescribed automorphism groups acting separately on binary and ternary coordinate blocks; clique search on orbits.
Exploit the d=3 cells' link to perfect/mixed perfect codes (sphere-packing bound is often near tight); search near-perfect codes by tabu.
Cross-domain import (sports betting / football-pool systems): pool-system enthusiasts' packing heuristics and published 'reduced systems' are a source of seeds.
Cross-domain import (crystal structure prediction): treat the mixed Hamming space as a product lattice and use symmetric 'Wyckoff-orbit' generation to produce candidate structures.
Cross-domain import (integer programming from scheduling): column generation over orbit 'patterns' with Gurobi-free solvers (HiGHS/SCIP).
pitfalls: Verify the minimum distance over ALL pairs (nonlinear codes) or all codewords (linear), never by sampling.

Literature-ahead-of-table trap: Brouwer's pages are updated irregularly but are very active right now (binary table last modified 2026-10-21, ternary and 5-ary 2026-10-17, mixed binary/ternary 2026-10-17, quaternary not since 2017-09-07, with four independent groups sending improvements in October 2026); search arXiv for the specific (n,d) and re-fetch the page immediately before claiming.
Confusing (m binary, n ternary) order in the table axes is an easy way to compare against the wrong cell.
Cells with m=0 or n=0 are the pure tables, handled by separate entries.

targets.name: Unrestricted ternary, quaternary and 5-ary codes A_q(n,d): new lower bound in Brouwer's small q-ary tables
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Brouwer's tables of general (nonlinear) codes over alphabets of size 3, 4 and 5 (from Brouwer-Hamalainen-Ostergard-Sloane 1998, Bogdanova-Brouwer-Kapralov-Ostergard 2001, Bogdanova-Ostergard 2001, with later improvements by Laaksonen-Ostergard 2017/2019 and others) list lower/upper bounds for n up to 16 (q=3), 12 (q=4) and 11 (q=5) with wide gaps, e.g. on 2026-10-28: A3(12,7) 60-108, A3(16,8) 387-1923, A3(15,10) 27-39, A5(9,5) 893-2152, A5(10,6) 625-1625. The ternary table credits football-pool enthusiasts ('found by ehl555', 'found by Codigo', 'spaik', 'PacoHH', 'Joan'), so local search on a laptop has produced records here; the ternary and 5-ary pages were updated on 2026-10-17 with new lower bounds from Oscar Sanchez (A3(14,8) >= 123, A3(15,5) >= 7929, A5(7,3) >= 1601, A5(9,4) >= 4500, A5(9,5) >= 893, A5(10,4) >= 18750). The quaternary page was last modified 2017-09-07.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit list of M distinct words over {0..q-1}^n (q in {3,4,5}) such that an independent script confirms all pairwise Hamming distances >= d, and M is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the lower bound for A_q(n,d) in the corresponding live table (https://aeb.win.tue.nl/codes/ternary-1.html, https://aeb.win.tue.nl/codes/quaternary-1.html or https://aeb.win.tue.nl/codes/5ary-1.html), re-fetched live immediately before claiming; '=' entries are exact and cannot be beaten; the improvement must not appear in the notes under the table or in an arXiv/journal search done on the day.

partial_wins.statement: An improved lower bound for a ternary cell with n = 17 or 18 (just beyond the table) over the best value in the literature.
An exact upper-bound improvement certified by a checkable LP/Delsarte certificate in rational arithmetic for one cell.

targets.verification_method: Parse codewords; pairwise Hamming distances vectorised in numpy (M up to ~2*10^4 fine); parse the live table cell (note 'ub'/'lb' rows and '=' convention). Minutes.
angles: Prescribed-automorphism clique search: pick a group (cyclic runs x alphabet permutations, or PSL(2,p) on n=p+1 coordinates), compute orbits, max-weight clique on orbits.
Unions of cosets of linear codes from codetables.de over GF(3)/GF(4)/GF(5) (a linear [n,k,d] code gives q^k words; unions of compatible cosets add more).
Target cells with the widest relative gap (ub/lb) and moderate size (lb < 5000) first, e.g. A3(12,7), A3(13,7..8), A5(8..9,5..6).

Cross-domain import (football-pool / lottery wheel design): the pool community's covering/packing heuristics (tabu search on forms) have already produced table entries; reuse their local-search with 'remove k, re-insert greedy' moves.
Cross-domain import (quantum annealing / QUBO): formulate packing as QUBO on orbit variables and run classical simulated bifurcation / parallel tempering QUBO solvers.
Cross-domain import (molecular dynamics): treat codewords as particles with repulsive potential on the Hamming graph and anneal, then repair violations.

Literature-ahead-of-table trap: Brouwer's pages are updated irregularly but are very active right now (binary table last modified 2026-10-21, ternary and 5-ary 2026-10-17, mixed binary/ternary 2026-10-17, quaternary not since 2017-09-07, with four independent groups sending improvements in October 2026); search arXiv for the specific (n,d) and re-fetch the page immediately before claiming.

The tables' text notes list improvements that may not yet be reflected in the grid, and some older notes are superseded by the grid (e.g. the ternary notes still mention A3(13,4) >= 8559 and A3(14,4) >= 24786, while the grid now shows 13122 and 27702); compare against the max of grid and notes.

targets.name: Circulant weighing matrices: settle an 'Open' CW(n,k) in Gordon's La Jolla repository
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: A circulant weighing matrix CW(n,s^2) is an n x n circulant matrix with entries in {-1,0,1} and W W^T = s^2 I; equivalently a {-1,0,1} sequence of length n with s(s+1)/2 entries +1, s(s-1)/2 entries -1 and zero periodic autocorrelation. Daniel Gordon's La Jolla Circulant Weighing Matrices Repository (Zenodo v1.3, 2026-04-24; GitHub dmgordo/circulant-weighing-matrices) records the existence status of proper CW(n,k) (not contained in a coset of a proper subgroup) for n < 1000 and k <= 19^2. Its data file cwm.json (keys written CW(n,s), i.e. weight k = s^2; last commit 2026-04-24) lists 2,773 parameter pairs with status 'Open' on 2026-10-28; the project page itself only shows the summary table of known proper CWs. cwm.json lags the literature: Ming Ming Tan (arXiv:2608.18468, v2 1 Sep 2026) proves that CW(105,36), CW(140,36), CW(116,49), CW(120,49), CW(192,49), CW(140,64), CW(180,64) and CW(196,64) do not exist, and seven of these are still 'Open' in cwm.json, leaving 2,766 pairs open. The smallest-weight open cases include CW(155,25), CW(165,25), CW(186,25); for k = 36: CW(96,36), CW(112,36), CW(117,36), CW(180,36); for k = 49: CW(228,49), CW(240,49). Construct a proper CW for an open pair, or prove non-existence with a checkable certificate.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a first row w in {-1,0,1}^n with exactly k nonzeros, zero periodic autocorrelation at every nonzero shift (so W W^T = kI), that is proper (its support is not contained in a coset of a proper subgroup of Z_n), verified by two independent programs, for an (n,k) whose status is 'Open' in the live La Jolla repository (https://dmgordon.org/circulant-weighing-matrices/ and the latest cwm.json on GitHub dmgordo/circulant-weighing-matrices or Zenodo, re-fetched live immediately before claiming) and that is not settled in the literature (not among the non-existence results of Tan, arXiv:2608.18468, and with no existence or non-existence result found by a fresh arXiv search for that CW(n,k)).

partial_wins.statement: A non-existence proof for a CW(n,k) that is 'Open' in the live cwm.json and not already settled in the literature (e.g. not one of the eight cases of Tan, arXiv:2608.18468), delivered as a checkable certificate (an exhaustive search with a DRAT/LRAT-verified UNSAT proof, or an explicit multiplier/field-descent argument whose computational part a skeptic re-runs).

A new signed or relative difference set for a parameter set listed as open in Gordon's La Jolla signed difference set or relative difference set repositories (same site), verified by the group-ring equation.

targets.verification_method: Load the sequence, check entries are in {-1,0,1} and the counts of +1 and -1 are s(s+1)/2 and s(s-1)/2. Compute the periodic autocorrelation sum_i w_i w_{i+t mod n} for every t = 1..n-1 and require all zero (or W W^T = kI directly). Check properness by testing, for each proper divisor d of n, whether the support lies in one coset of dZ_n. Use two independently written checkers; the repository's is_cwm in cwm_code.py may be read as a reference for the conventions but downloaded code is not executed. Then confirm the pair is 'Open' in the live data and not settled by Tan (arXiv:2608.18468) or a newer paper.
angles: Multiplier orbits: assume the support is a union of orbits of a multiplier group (x -> t*x mod n) and solve the reduced autocorrelation equations exactly with SAT or ILP; this is how many sporadic CWs were found.

Spectral filtering from signal processing: a CW has flat periodic power spectrum |DFT(w)|^2 = k at every frequency. Use this as a strong pruning test in backtracking (partial sums cannot exceed the bound), as in perfect-sequence searches.

Compression (Djokovic-Kotsireas): project the sequence to Z_m for m | n, enumerate compressed sequences satisfying the compressed autocorrelation, then lift with SAT. This turns length-150 searches into length-30 searches plus lifting.
Product and RDS constructions: check whether an Open pair follows from combining known CWs or relative difference sets in ways not yet recorded in cwm.json, then verify the explicit matrix.
Field descent and character sums (Schmidt): for non-existence, compute the necessary conditions for each Open pair automatically to find ones that are actually excluded.
pitfalls: Improper matrices: a CW whose support lies in a coset of a proper subgroup is derived from a smaller one and does not settle the Open entry for proper CWs.
Confusing periodic and aperiodic autocorrelation. CW needs periodic (cyclic) autocorrelation zero.
Weight convention: the repository uses k = s^2; CW(n,s) versus CW(n,s^2) mix-ups lead to the wrong row.
The repository is updated (v1.3 in April 2026). Re-download cwm.json and check the status of the exact pair before claiming.

cwm.json lags the literature: Tan (arXiv:2608.18468, Sep 2026) proves non-existence of CW(105,36), CW(140,36), CW(120,49), CW(192,49), CW(140,64), CW(180,64), CW(196,64), all still 'Open' in the April 2026 json. Search arXiv for the exact pair before claiming either direction.
A 'non-existence' result from an unverified search run without a certificate is not a win.

targets.name: Entanglement-assisted qubit codes [[n,k,d;c]]: raise a lower bound in Grassl's EAQECC table
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: codetables.de (Markus Grassl) hosts a table of bounds on the minimum distance of entanglement-assisted qubit codes [[n,k,d_lower-d_upper;c]] (non-catalytic setting) for n <= 64, last changed 10.07.2025. On 2026-10-28 the table has 7,752 parameter cells, of which 6,715 show a gap d_lower < d_upper; 5,354 of those gap cells have c >= 1, 616 of them with n <= 25 (e.g. [[5,2,3-4;3]], [[6,1,4-5;1]], [[7,0,5-6;4]]). Small-n gaps are within reach of exhaustive or SAT search; any explicit code with larger d is mechanically checkable. Only cells with c >= 1 count here: c = 0 cells are ordinary qubit stabilizer codes, covered by the codetables qubit entries already in the bank, and the companion qutrit table is its own bank target (eaqecc-qutrit-codetables-gaps).
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for a cell with c >= 1, an explicit stabilizer matrix S over GF(2) in symplectic form, with n-k+c rows and 2n columns (the standard EA representation), such that an independent script verifies (1) GF(2)-rank of S is n-k+c, (2) the symplectic Gram matrix S Omega S^T has GF(2)-rank exactly 2c (so exactly c ebits are needed), and (3) the EA minimum distance d, defined as in the table (minimum symplectic weight of a vector in the symplectic dual of rowspace(S) that is not in rowspace(S) ∩ its symplectic dual), is computed EXACTLY by full enumeration; and d is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than d_lower for (n,k,c) in http://www.codetables.de/EAQECC/qubit.php re-fetched live immediately before claiming, with d <= d_upper.

partial_wins.statement: Close a gap from above for a small cell (n <= 12): exhaustive, re-runnable non-existence search proving no [[n,k,d_upper;c]] code exists, lowering d_upper.

targets.verification_method: Symplectic linear algebra over GF(2) in Python (galois or hand-rolled bit ops); enumerate the symplectic dual of rowspace(S) (2^(n+k-c) vectors; feasible for n <= ~25) for minimum symplectic weight outside the isotropic part; parse the cell from the live table HTML (format [[n,k,dl-du;c]]2). Minutes.
angles: Exhaustive search for small n via the classical-code correspondence: an EA qubit code with c ebits comes from any additive (n, 2^(n-k+c)) code over GF(4) whose symplectic Gram rank is 2c; search quasi-cyclic additive codes and compute both quantities.
Start from best classical GF(4)-linear codes in codetables.de and choose c to trade ebits for distance (Brun-Devetak-Hsieh construction), then puncture/shorten using the table's propagation rules.
SAT/ILP for small cells: encode existence of S with rank and weight constraints, solve with kissat with symmetry breaking (column permutations, local Cliffords).

Cross-domain import (quantum chemistry graph states): EA codes with k=0 relate to graph states plus Bell pairs; use graph-state local-complementation orbit enumeration (as in Danielsen's database) to search.
Cross-domain import (machine learning for code search, RL decoders): use a learned surrogate of min-distance from symplectic-weight enumerator features to prioritise candidates before exact checks.
Cross-domain import (lattice basis reduction): search over Construction-A lattices of the codes and use short-vector counts as a quick distance proxy.
pitfalls: The EA distance definition (catalytic vs non-catalytic, degenerate vs not) must match the table's explanation; the table states the non-catalytic setting.
Propagation rules in the table (subcode, lengthening, puncturing, teleportation) mean a new code in one cell may already be implied; the claim must beat the live d_lower of its own cell.
A code where the Gram rank is not exactly 2c uses a different number of ebits and belongs to another cell.
Distance by random sampling of logical operators is not a proof; enumerate.

targets.name: Qudit stabilizer codes [[n,k,d]]_q for q = 3, 4, 5, 7, 8: raise a lower bound in Grassl's extended tables
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Since May 2024 codetables.de has extended tables of bounds for qudit stabilizer codes [[n,k,d]]_q for q = 3,4,5,7,8 up to n = 100 (mainly based on Ezerman-Grassl-Ling-Ozbudak-Ozkaya, arXiv:2405.15057, and Bierbrauer-Edel twisted codes). These tables are young and far less mined than the qubit table: the qutrit table alone has 503 gap cells (d_lower < d_upper) for n <= 40 on 2026-10-28 (page last change 23.05.2024). The existing bank entry codetables-binary-linear counts a record in any codetables.de quantum-code table only as its partial win p1; this entry makes the non-binary qudit tables (q = 3,4,5,7,8) a full target. Claim a qudit record once, here.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit stabilizer generator matrix over GF(q) in symplectic form (n-k) x 2n such that an independent script verifies symplectic self-orthogonality exactly, rank n-k, and the exact minimum distance d (minimum symplectic weight over C^perp_s \ C, computed by full enumeration or two independent exact algorithms), with d STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the lower bound for [[n,k]]_q in the live table obtained from http://www.codetables.de/QECC/Tables_color.php?q=<q^2>&n0=1&n1=100&k0=0&k1=100 re-fetched immediately before claiming, and no newer arXiv result giving d.

partial_wins.statement: Lower an upper bound d_upper for some [[n,k]]_q cell (q in {3,4,5,7,8}) via an exact, independently re-runnable certificate (an LP/shadow-type dual certificate verified in rational arithmetic, or an exhaustive non-existence search a skeptic re-runs), compared with the live table.

targets.verification_method: GF(q) arithmetic (q prime or GF(4), GF(8) via galois); symplectic inner product check; distance by enumeration of the symplectic dual modulo stabilizer (q^(n+k) vectors; feasible when n+k small) or by Brouwer-Zimmermann on the associated additive code; parse table HTML cell. Minutes to an hour.
angles: Hermitian/symplectic self-orthogonal quasi-twisted codes of index 2-4 over GF(q^2) (the construction that populated the tables); vary twist constants and generator polynomials systematically.
Nearly self-orthogonal codes plus extension (the 2405.15057 method) applied to cells the paper did not reach.
Propagation: apply lengthening/puncturing/shortening rules to any new code to improve neighbouring cells.
Cross-domain import (number theory, algebraic curves): AG-code constructions from curves with many points (Hermitian, Suzuki) give self-orthogonal codes for q=4,8; compute small cases explicitly.
Cross-domain import (evolutionary algorithms / LinCodeEvolve-style program search): evolve generator programs for QT codes with exact distance as fitness.
Cross-domain import (combinatorial designs): codes from orbit matrices of designs / strongly regular graphs with self-orthogonality.
pitfalls: Table parameter q in URLs is q^2 (q=9 for qutrits); compare against the right local dimension.
Degenerate vs pure distance: the table uses the stabilizer (degenerate) distance; compute that.
Over GF(4) vs GF(2)^2 representation errors in symplectic form are a common false positive.
Never sample codewords for distance.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - denser sphere packing than Cohn's table in some dimension 10..48
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Henry Cohn maintains a table of the best known sphere packing densities (center density, number of translates, density, upper bound, ratio) in dimensions 1-48, with archived data and explicit coordinates. Only dimensions 1, 2, 3, 8, 24 are proven optimal. Improvements in mid dimensions (e.g. 10, 11, 13, 18-23) came from non-lattice periodic packings and new lattices, and the table is still moving: Chen, Hu, Li, Wang and Wu (arXiv:2505.02394, antipode construction, 2025) hold the records in dimensions 19, 20, 21, 23, 44, 45 and 47, and Dorofeev, Sun and Wang (arXiv:2607.20359, v4 29 Aug 2026) hold them in every dimension from 38 to 43. Any denser packing in a listed dimension is a famous result but is checkable from a periodic packing description.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a periodic packing in R^n, 10 <= n <= 48 (lattice basis L plus k translates t_i, all with exact rational or algebraic coordinates), such that an independent script computes exactly the minimal distance 2r between distinct centers (min over lattice vectors and translate differences, by exact Fincke-Pohst enumeration in rational arithmetic) and the resulting center density k*r^n/covol(L) is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the center density for dimension n on https://cohn.mit.edu/sphere-packing/ re-fetched live immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: A new non-isometric packing matching the best known density in some dimension 10-31 (different kissing configuration), certified exactly.
A lattice (not just periodic packing) matching a non-lattice record density in some dimension, certified exactly.

targets.verification_method: Exact rational lattice arithmetic (fpylll for enumeration with rational Gram, cross-checked with PARI qfminim); compute packing radius and covolume; compare with the table's center density. Under an hour for n <= 32.
angles: Codes-to-lattices: Construction A/B/D from the best binary/ternary codes in codetables.de and Brouwer's tables, including newly found codes from the other coding-theory entries.
Non-lattice periodic packings: start from the record lattice, add a coset (glue vector) at deep holes and optimise the scaling exactly (the method behind several mid-dimension records).

Cross-domain import (materials science / crystal structure prediction): apply random-structure search (AIRSS-like) in R^n with soft repulsive potentials and periodic cells, then snap to exact rational coordinates.
Cross-domain import (machine learning / AlphaEvolve-style program search): evolve programs that output Gram matrices, with exact density as fitness.
Cross-domain import (algebraic number theory): ideal lattices of number fields with small discriminant (Craig-type and Mordell-Weil lattices) evaluated exactly.
pitfalls: Center density vs density vs kissing number confusion (the table's 'center density' is the number of unit-radius spheres per unit volume, i.e. k*r^n/covolume with r half the minimal distance).
Floating-point minimal-norm computation can miss a short vector; use exact enumeration.
A periodic packing's density must account for all k translates and their mutual distances, not only lattice vectors.
The kissing-number tables (already in the bank) are a different record.

targets.name: Degree-diameter problem for bipartite graphs: a larger bipartite (d,k)-graph than the Combinatorics Wiki table
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Nb(d,k) is the largest order of a bipartite graph with maximum degree d and diameter k. The Combinatorics Wiki page 'The Degree Diameter Problem for Bipartite Graphs' (Loz, Pérez-Rosés, Pineda-Villavicencio; table 'as of January 2012', page last modified Feb 2022) lists the largest known bipartite graphs for 3 <= d <= 16 and 3 <= k <= 10 (examples: (3,5) = 56, (3,7) = 168, (3,10) = 800, (4,7) = 840, (5,10) = 90,068) and upper bounds. Known later results include Feria-Purón, Miller and Pineda-Villavicencio (order 190 for (11,3); Nb(7,3) = 80). Find a bipartite graph with maximum degree at most d and diameter at most k with strictly more vertices than the table entry and any later published value. The bank's general degree-diameter-table target counts a beat of a bipartite table as its partial win p2; a bipartite record is claimed once, here, not under both.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit graph (edge list) that is bipartite (2-colouring verified), has maximum degree at most d and diameter at most k (all-pairs BFS), with STRICTLY MORE vertices (direction: max) than the entry for (d,k) at http://combinatoricswiki.org/wiki/The_Degree_Diameter_Problem_for_Bipartite_Graphs re-fetched live immediately before claiming, AND than every value for that (d,k) found by a fresh literature search covering 2012-2026 (the wiki table is dated January 2012, so later papers may hold larger graphs). Graphs exceeding the listed upper bound (bipartite Moore bound or better) mean the checker is wrong.

partial_wins.statement: A record for a small (d,k) with d <= 5 and k <= 6 (where exhaustive verification is instant), beating both the wiki table and the literature.
A checkable optimality proof for a small open (d,k) cell whose upper bound in the wiki is above the largest known order, via exhaustive search with a reproducible certificate.

targets.verification_method: Load the edge list; check simplicity, maximum degree, a proper 2-colouring by BFS, and all-pairs BFS diameter at most k; count vertices. Two independent implementations (e.g. networkx and a C BFS) must agree. Compare with the live wiki table and a literature search for that (d,k) since 2012.
angles: Lifts (voltage graphs) of small bipartite base graphs over cyclic and metacyclic groups: exhaust voltage assignments for base graphs with 2-6 vertices; this is how many general-graph records were found and the bipartite table is less picked over.

From finite geometry: incidence graphs of generalized polygons are bipartite Moore graphs for k = 3, 4, 6; delete structured point/line subsets or take incidence graphs of partial geometries and nets for nearby (d,k).

Bipartite Cayley-type graphs (bi-Cayley / Haar graphs) on groups of order n: a connection set S defines a bipartite graph; search groups from the SmallGroups library and random S with diameter checks.

From coding theory: bipartite graphs of large girth and small diameter come from LDPC-code Tanner graph constructions (quasi-cyclic, protograph lifts). Repurpose QC-LDPC search code with a diameter objective.
Computer search in the style of Exoo: start from a random d-regular bipartite graph on N vertices and do edge swaps that reduce the number of pairs at distance greater than k.
pitfalls: The table is dated January 2012; beating it is not enough if a later paper has a larger graph. Search the literature for each cell.
Bipartite diameter subtlety: in a bipartite graph, vertices on the same side are at even distance. Compute the true diameter over all pairs, not just across the bipartition.
The wiki's HTTPS certificate does not match the host; use the http:// URL.
Maximum degree at most d is allowed; do not compare a non-regular graph against a regular-only table or vice versa.
Exceeding the bipartite Moore bound 2((d-1)^k - 1)/(d-2) means the checker is wrong.

targets.name: Degree-diameter problem for planar graphs: a larger planar graph than the Combinatorics Wiki table
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: For maximum degree d and diameter k, find the largest planar graph. The Combinatorics Wiki page 'The Degree Diameter Problem for Planar Graphs' (Loz, Pérez-Rosés, Pineda-Villavicencio; last modified Feb 2022) lists the largest known planar graphs for 3 <= d <= 10 and 2 <= k <= 10 (examples on 2026-10-13: (3,10) = 157, (4,10) = 728, (5,6) = 158, (6,5) = 117), with constructions by Fellows-Hell-Seyffarth, Yang-Lin-Dai, Exoo, Tishchenko, Feria-Purón and Pineda-Villavicencio (2013) and others, and a separate table for regular planar graphs (3 <= d <= 5). Most entries are not known to be optimal. Find a planar graph with maximum degree at most d and diameter at most k with strictly more vertices than a table entry.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit graph (edge list) that is planar (checked by two independent planarity tests, e.g. networkx check_planarity and a Boyer-Myrvold or SageMath implementation, plus an explicit combinatorial embedding), has maximum degree at most d and diameter at most k (all-pairs BFS), and has STRICTLY MORE vertices (direction: max) than the entry for (d,k) in the general or regular planar table at http://combinatoricswiki.org/wiki/The_Degree_Diameter_Problem_for_Planar_Graphs re-fetched live immediately before claiming, and than any value found by a fresh search (Feria-Purón and Pineda-Villavicencio 2013 and later papers on large planar graphs). Matching an entry does not count.

partial_wins.statement: A record in the regular planar table (d-regular planar graph of diameter k, 3 <= d <= 5) beating the live entry and any later paper, verified as above plus regularity.

An exact value: a checkable proof (exhaustive enumeration with plantri plus a reproducible log, or an UNSAT certificate) that a current entry for some small (d,k) is optimal, where the page does not already mark it optimal.

targets.verification_method: Load the edge list, check simplicity, the maximum degree and the vertex count; compute all-pairs BFS distances and check the maximum is at most k; run two independent planarity tests and output a planar embedding (rotation system) checked by Euler's formula on its faces. Then compare with the live wiki table and a literature search.
angles: Recursive 'replace vertex by gadget' constructions (Fellows-Hell-Seyffarth, Feria-Purón-Pineda-Villavicencio): search over small planar gadgets with a SAT/ILP model for the best gadget at each (d,k), since the published gadgets were hand-designed.

From network design: planar graphs of small diameter look like hierarchical 'hub and spoke' or nested-ring layouts. Parametrise nested rings with chords and search the parameters exhaustively for each (d,k).
Local search on planar triangulations with plantri-generated seeds: flip edges and add vertices while maintaining planarity and degree, scoring by diameter violations.
Rotationally symmetric planar graphs (cyclic symmetry around a centre face or vertex) reduce the search to a fundamental sector; this matches the shape of many record graphs.
For large k, combine good small-diameter blocks by identifying boundary vertices, then repair degree and diameter with SAT.
pitfalls: The wiki serves HTTPS with a certificate for a different host; use the http:// URL. Do not ignore a stale page: it was last modified in 2022, so also search for later papers on large planar graphs.

The wiki links to 'Tables of the largest known planar graphs maintained by James Preen' (http://faculty.cbu.ca/jpreen/degdiam.html), which may hold newer values; it did not connect on 2026-10-28. Try it once honestly and, if unreachable, record the comparison against it as pending rather than skipping it.

Diameter 3 is nearly settled: Dailly, Darmon, Giocanti, Hilaire and Valicov (arXiv:2507.18797, 2025) prove the maximum order is at most 9Δ/2 + c, matching the Fellows-Hell-Seyffarth lower bound 9Δ/2 - 3 that the k = 3 column already attains; expect at most a constant gain there.
Maximum degree versus regular: the general table allows degree at most d, the regular table requires exactly d at every vertex. Compare with the right table.
Planarity checked only by a drawing or a single library call with a bug: use two independent tests and an explicit embedding.
Diameter computed on a directed or weighted interpretation, or ignoring disconnected graphs (infinite diameter).
Off-by-one in the table indices: rows are degree d, columns diameter k.

targets.name: Erdős distinct subset sums: an n-element set with distinct subset sums and smaller maximum than the best known
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Erdős Problem #1 asks how small the largest element of an n-element set of positive integers with all subset sums distinct can be. Its asymptotic form (is max(S) >> 2^n?) is now marked disproved on erdosproblems.com/1 (last edited 2026-09-03), by a construction from an OpenAI model ('GPT-6 Astra') giving max(S) <= eps*2^n for arbitrarily large n; that does not settle any small-n value. OEIS A276661 gives the exact minimum a(n) for n <= 10 (Lunnon a(0..8), J. P. Grossman a(9), Paul W. Dyson a(10) = 309 in 2025). For n >= 11 only bounds are known: the Conway-Guy sequence (A005318) gives a(11) <= 594, and Bohman showed it is not always optimal; Dubroff, Fox and Xu give a(n) >= A001405(n) = C(n, floor(n/2)), which Hasratyan and Ruszinkó (arXiv:2610.32580, 23 Oct 2026) improve for odd n to a(n) >= 2*C(n-1,(n-1)/2) (504 for n = 11). As of 2026-10-28, A276661 records sets below Conway-Guy: Ven Popov (Nov 2025) a(12) <= 1157 and a(13) <= 2249; Zachary Sharp (Oct 20 2026, witness sets in the a-file) a(14) <= 4403, a(15) <= 8635, a(16) <= 16946, a(17) <= 33280, a(18) <= 65412, a(19) <= 129517, a(20) <= 256715. Find, for some n >= 11, a set of n positive integers with distinct subset sums whose largest element is strictly smaller than the best known upper bound.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit set S of n >= 11 distinct positive integers whose 2^n subset sums are pairwise distinct, verified by two independent programs, with max(S) STRICTLY SMALLER (direction: min) than the best known upper bound for a(n) at verification time: the minimum over https://oeis.org/A276661 (data, comments and a-files, including Sharp's n = 14..20 witnesses) re-fetched live immediately before claiming, the Conway-Guy value A005318(n), Bohman's constructions, https://www.erdosproblems.com/1 and a fresh arXiv search for distinct-subset-sum constructions. Sets that are just a scaling or the {1} U 2S doubling of a known set do not count unless they beat the bound.

partial_wins.statement: Determine a(11) exactly: an exhaustive search with a reproducible, independently re-runnable enumeration (or a checkable certificate) proving that no 11-element distinct-subset-sum set has maximum below some value, matched by an explicit set attaining it.

A certified lower bound for a(11) above every published one (currently 2*C(10,5) = 504 from Hasratyan-Ruszinkó, arXiv:2610.32580, improving A001405(11) = 462 of Dubroff-Fox-Xu; plus any exhaustive-search bound in A276661 or a fresh arXiv search): an independently re-runnable exhaustive search proving that no 11-element distinct-subset-sum set has maximum <= M, for a stated M larger than the best published lower bound.

targets.verification_method: Compute all 2^n subset sums (n <= 40 with meet-in-the-middle: sort the 2^(n/2) half-sums and check that no two differences coincide, or use a bitset of size sum(S) for n <= 25) and check there are no repeats. Two implementations must agree. Equivalently, verify that no nonzero vector in {-1,0,1}^n gives a zero signed sum. Then compare max(S) with the live OEIS entry and Erdős problems page.
angles: Popov's n = 12, 13 sets cluster near the maximum with a few small elements, like Conway-Guy sets. Local search: start from the Conway-Guy or Popov set, lower the maximum by 1, and repair by moving 1-3 elements, using a fast incremental test of signed-sum collisions.

From coding theory: distinct subset sums means the integer vector is a 'detecting matrix' for the coin-weighing problem. Borrow constructions of small-entry detecting matrices and Lindström-type sequences, and convert.

From lattice reduction: write the condition as 'no nonzero {-1,0,1} vector is orthogonal to S'. Use LLL/BKZ on a lattice built from a candidate S to find short orthogonal vectors quickly, as a fast rejection filter inside a search.

SAT/ILP over the binary representations of the elements with a pseudo-Boolean constraint per signed combination is too large, but cube-and-conquer on the top few elements with a dynamic-programming check below is feasible for n = 11.
Recursive improvements: if a smaller set is found at n, the {1} U 2S rule and Bohman's recursions give bounds at n+1, n+2; check whether a direct search beats those propagated bounds.
pitfalls: Off-by-one in indexing: A276661 starts at n = 0 (a(0) = 0). Check that the set has exactly n elements.
Allowing 0 or repeated elements: S must be a set of distinct positive integers.
Distinct subset sums is not the same as distinct sums of pairs (Sidon) or distinct subset products. Check all 2^n subsets.
Popov's n = 12, 13 and Sharp's n = 14..20 sets already beat Conway-Guy; beating Conway-Guy alone is not a record. Compare against the best value in the OEIS comments and a-files.

The 2026 asymptotic disproof on erdosproblems.com/1 is about large n; it gives no small-n record by itself. Compare per n, and check whether any explicit set from that construction or its expositions beats a small-n bound.
Overflow in subset-sum computation for large n: use 64-bit or big integers and test the checker on a known collision.

targets.name: Equiangular lines: more equiangular lines in R^18, R^19, R^20 or R^42 than the best known
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The maximum number of equiangular lines in R^d is known exactly for d <= 17 and d = 21..41, 43 (OEIS A002853). Open cases include d = 18, 19, 20 and 42. On 2026-10-28 the best bounds are 57 <= a(18) <= 59 (lower bound Greaves-Syatriadi-Yatsyna 2021, arXiv:2104.04330; upper bound Greaves-Syatriadi, JCTA 2023, arXiv:2206.04267), 72 <= a(19) <= 74, 90 <= a(20) <= 94 (upper bounds Greaves-Syatriadi-Yatsyna 2020, arXiv:2002.08085) and 276 <= a(42) <= 288. The OEIS comment still gives a(18) <= 60, so it lags on the upper bound; its lower bounds are current. Lin, Munemasa, Taniguchi and Yoshino (arXiv:2503.06377, 2025) found at least 246,896 sets of 57 equiangular lines in R^18, and Munemasa, Szöllősi and Yoshino (arXiv:2606.10421, v2 Oct 2026) constructed further 57-line sets from Latin squares of order 6, but no larger set is known. A configuration is a Seidel matrix with smallest eigenvalue of multiplicity N - d, checkable exactly.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a symmetric N x N Seidel matrix S (zero diagonal, +-1 off-diagonal) whose smallest eigenvalue lambda_min has multiplicity >= N - d, established in exact arithmetic (exact characteristic polynomial and exact rank of S - lambda_min*I over the field of lambda_min, via sympy or PARI), so that the N lines live in R^d; and N is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the larger of the lower bound stated in OEIS A002853 (https://oeis.org/A002853, re-fetched live immediately before claiming) and the best lower bound found in an arXiv search on the day.

partial_wins.statement: A configuration achieving the best known count in d = 19 (72 lines) or d = 20 (90 lines) that is not switching-equivalent to any configuration in the literature, certified by exact rank and a switching-class invariant (e.g. Seidel spectrum or canonical form of the associated two-graph).

A lowered upper bound: an exact, independently re-runnable certificate (exhaustive enumeration in exact arithmetic, or an SDP/LP dual certificate verified in rational arithmetic) proving a(18) <= 58, a(19) <= 73 or a(20) <= 93.

targets.verification_method: Load S; check symmetry/entries; compute exact characteristic polynomial (integer matrix, sympy or PARI) and the multiplicity of its smallest root via exact rank over the minimal polynomial's field; N - mult <= d. Minutes.
angles: Greaves-style approach: enumerate Seidel matrices with prescribed characteristic polynomial modulo small primes (mod-4 / mod-p constraints) and extend cliques of compatible blocks.
Start from known 57/72/90-line systems, apply switching and try to add lines via exact feasibility (each added line must keep the rank condition), using lattice/Gram completion.

Cross-domain import (frame theory / signal processing): use alternating projection algorithms for Grassmannian frames to find near-equiangular numerical configurations, then round to +-alpha Gram entries and certify exactly.
Cross-domain import (quantum information, SIC-POVM search): reuse numerical Gram-matrix optimisation pipelines and exact-recognition (PSLQ/LLL) from SIC research.

Cross-domain import (spectral graph theory / two-graphs from strongly regular graph catalogues): search regular two-graphs and their descendants from Brouwer's SRG tables for large switching classes with the right spectrum.
pitfalls: Stale scoreboard: the OEIS comment lags the literature on upper bounds (it still says a(18) <= 60; Greaves-Syatriadi proved a(18) <= 59). Check the Greaves et al. papers and a fresh arXiv search before claiming.
Numerical eigenvalue multiplicity is not proof; use exact arithmetic.
Lines vs vectors: N lines means N unit vectors up to sign; antipodal duplicates do not count.
Configurations in d dimensions that actually span fewer dimensions are still valid, but a rank miscount in floating point creates fake records.

targets.name: Hales-Jewett numbers: beat HJ(3,3) >= 22 or HJ(4,2) >= 14 with an explicit line-free colouring
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: HJ(t,r) is the least n such that every r-colouring of the grid [t]^n contains a monochromatic combinatorial line. Younes Mouhib (arXiv:2606.22155, v2 24 Jul 2026) raised HJ(3,3) >= 22 (previous record 14) and HJ(4,2) >= 14 (previous record 12) using colourings that are invariant under coordinate permutations, so a colouring depends only on the letter-count vector; certificates are in the GitHub repository ysmouhib/hj-certificates. The same paper reports new Gallai and Rado numbers and lists open cells such as G_4({0,1,3}) >= 94. Exact values are known only for tiny cases (HJ(2,r)=r, HJ(3,2)=4). Find an explicit line-free colouring of [t]^n for some small (t,r) with n at or above the current record, i.e. proving HJ(t,r) > n with n strictly larger than the best known lower bound minus one.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit r-colouring of [t]^n (given as a full table, or as a function of the letter-count vector if it is symmetric) with no monochromatic combinatorial line, verified by two independent checkers, proving HJ(t,r) >= n+1, where n+1 is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best lower bound for that (t,r) at verification time: the maximum over the latest version of https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22155 re-fetched live immediately before claiming, the ysmouhib/hj-certificates repository, and a fresh arXiv search for 'Hales-Jewett' lower bounds over the last 24 months. Bounds that only hold for a restricted line family (bracket, q-fold or interval lines) do not count.

partial_wins.statement: A new exact or improved Gallai number listed as open in arXiv:2606.22155 (for example a 4-colouring of a window of length 94 or more with no monochromatic homothet of {0,1,3}, beating G_4({0,1,3}) >= 94), verified by exhaustive homothet enumeration.

An improved lower bound for some other small Hales-Jewett cell (for example HJ(3,4), HJ(4,3) or HJ(5,2)) beating both the van der Waerden shadow bound and any value in arXiv:2606.22155 and a fresh search, with an explicit checked colouring.

targets.verification_method: For symmetric colourings: a combinatorial line in [t]^n with active set size m and fixed part having letter counts v corresponds to the t letter-count vectors v + m*e_i; enumerate all (v,m) pairs with m >= 1 and |v|+m = n and check that the t colours are not all equal. Cross-check this reduction on n <= 6 against brute force over all lines of the full grid ((t+1)^n - t^n lines). For non-symmetric colourings, brute force over all lines (feasible for [4]^13, about 1.2e9 lines, in C on a laptop). Two independent implementations must agree. Then re-fetch arXiv:2606.22155 and search arXiv for newer records.
angles: Search the symmetric (equivalently one-weight) class directly with SAT: variables are colours of the letter-count simplex points, clauses forbid monochromatic corner tuples v+m*e_i. For (3,3) at n=22 this is about 276 cells, tiny for CaDiCaL. The paper proves the symmetric class equals the one-weight class, so check its results tables and SAT logs for which cells it already exhausted before repeating a search.

Go beyond symmetry: colourings invariant under a smaller group (for example S_a x S_b acting on two blocks of coordinates) give a two-simplex reduction with more freedom; encode lines across the blocks and SAT-solve.

From additive combinatorics: one-weight colourings reduce to Gallai homothety problems in Z. Import Behrend-style and Rankin-type constructions for sets free of homothets of {0,1,2} or {0,2,3,5}, then lift.

From coding theory: treat a colour class as a code in [t]^n avoiding lines (a cap-set-like condition). Use known large line-free sets (density Hales-Jewett constructions, Polymath DHJ(3) data) as colour classes and complete the rest with SAT.
Cube-and-conquer over 10 cores on the symmetric encoding for (3,3) at n=22 and (4,2) at n=14, splitting on the colours of the simplex corners.
pitfalls: A colouring that is line-free only for a restricted line family (bracket lines, q-fold lines, interval lines) gives no bound on HJ(t,r). Check all combinatorial lines.
Off-by-one: a line-free colouring of [t]^n proves HJ(t,r) >= n+1. Matching the record dimension is not an improvement.
Trusting the symmetric reduction without testing it: cross-check the corner-tuple checker against brute force on small n, since an indexing bug silently drops lines.
The records are from one recent single-author preprint. Re-check its certificates yourself and search for any correction or newer version before taking its numbers as the baseline.
Confusing combinatorial lines with geometric lines (which also include reversed coordinates). The Hales-Jewett number uses combinatorial lines only.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Strongly regular graphs: construct an srg for an open parameter set in Brouwer's table
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Andries Brouwer's online tables list feasible parameter sets (v,k,lambda,mu) of strongly regular graphs up to 1300 vertices, marking each as known to exist, known not to exist, or unknown ('?'). On 2026-10-28 the pages for 51-1300 vertices contain 1,361 rows marked '?'; the smallest are srg(88,27,6,9), srg(99,14,1,2) (Conway's 99-graph, already a separate target), srg(100,33,8,12), srg(111,30,5,9), srg(115,18,1,3), srg(121,36,7,12) and srg(121,48,17,20). The table is actively maintained: recent entries credit Gritsenko for an srg(65,32,15,16), Jose Yip Zheng Ho for an srg(117,58,28,29) (open on the 2026-10-13 draft, now '+'), and 'Kovaľ + AI' and 'Akiyama + AI' for many non-existence and uniqueness results. Construct an srg for any parameter set currently marked '?', excluding (99,14,1,2), which is covered by its own target.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit adjacency matrix (or edge list) on v vertices that is k-regular, where every adjacent pair has exactly lambda common neighbours and every non-adjacent pair exactly mu, verified by two independent programs, for a parameter set that is marked '?' (existence unknown) in Brouwer's table at https://aeb.win.tue.nl/graphs/srg/srgtab.html (the relevant sub-page re-fetched live immediately before claiming), excluding srg(99,14,1,2), and with no construction or non-existence proof found by a fresh arXiv/Google Scholar search for those parameters. A graph for the complementary parameters counts for the same table row.

partial_wins.statement: A machine-checked non-existence proof for a parameter set currently marked '?' (for example via an exhaustive search with a DRAT/LRAT-checkable UNSAT certificate or an exact ILP certificate) that an independent checker re-verifies on a laptop.

A new graph for a row marked '+' (exists) whose number of known non-isomorphic graphs is listed as a single construction, with a canonical-form (nauty/Traces) certificate that it is not isomorphic to any graph the table or its cited sources already give.

targets.verification_method: Compute A^2 and check A^2 = k*I + lambda*A + mu*(J - I - A) with A symmetric 0/1, zero diagonal; this is O(v^3) and instant for v <= 1300. Recompute the eigenvalues and multiplicities and compare with the table row. Confirm the row still shows '?' on the live page and search arXiv for the parameters.
angles: Prescribed automorphism groups: assume a group G of order dividing v (or acting with few orbits) and solve for a union of orbitals with the right intersection numbers. This is the Kramer-Mesner trick from design theory and turns the search into a small exact cover / ILP.

From coding theory: projective two-weight codes give srgs. Search for new two-weight codes over GF(q) with the right length and dimension (the table's comments name many such codes) using Kohnert-style prescribed-group ILP.

From finite geometry: partial geometries, generalized quadrangles and hemisystems give srgs; for rows with geometric-looking parameters, search for the underlying point-line structure instead of the graph.
Switching: Godsil-McKay or Wallis-Fon-Der-Flaass switching of known graphs with nearby parameters can produce graphs with new parameters; enumerate switching sets with a SAT solver.
Cyclotomy and Cayley graphs on abelian groups of order v (partial difference sets): exhaust small unions of cyclotomic classes for prime-power v.
pitfalls: Building a graph for a parameter set already marked '+' or '-' and calling it new. Re-read the live row, including the complement row.
Floating-point eigenvalue checks are not proof; use the exact matrix identity A^2 = kI + lambda A + mu(J-I-A).
Conway's 99-graph srg(99,14,1,2) is a separate target; do not double-claim it here.
A table-row non-existence claim produced by an unverified solver run is not a result; it needs a checkable certificate (partial win p1).
The table is updated often (for example 'Kovaľ + AI' entries in 2026). Check the live page and recent arXiv for the exact parameters before claiming.

targets.name: Turan numbers for forbidden cycles: beat an 'at least' entry in the Afzaly-McKay extremal graph tables
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Narjess Afzaly and Brendan McKay maintain tables of extremal graphs ex(n,H) for many families H of forbidden cycles: {C4}, {C5}, ..., {C3,C4} (girth 5), {C3,...,Ck}, {C4,C6}, bipartite families {C_odd,C4}, and more. Entries are exact where proved; for larger n they give lower bounds marked '>=' from graphs found by search (the page was last modified 2026-10-09). Examples on 2026-10-13: ex(n,C4) >= 132, 137, 142 for n = 41, 42, 43 (Max Alekseyev's upper bounds in OEIS A006855 are 133, 139, 145); girth-5 graphs ex(n,{C3,C4}) >= 185, 189, 193 for n = 54, 55, 56 (OEIS A006856). Find a graph on n vertices with no forbidden cycle and strictly more edges than a '>=' entry in any of the tables.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit simple graph on n vertices (edge list) containing none of the forbidden cycles of a family H on the Afzaly-McKay page, verified by two independent cycle checkers, whose edge count is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the table entry for (H,n) on https://users.cecs.anu.edu.au/~bdm/data/extremal.html re-fetched live immediately before claiming, and also greater than the matching OEIS entry (A006855 for C4, A006856 for girth 5, and so on) and any value found by a fresh arXiv search. Edge counts above a proved upper bound (for example Alekseyev's ex(41,C4) <= 133) mean the checker is wrong.

partial_wins.statement: Determine an exact value: a graph attaining a proved upper bound (for example a C4-free graph on 41 vertices with 133 edges, which would settle ex(41,C4) = 133), or a checkable proof that the '>=' entry is exact for some (H,n) via an UNSAT certificate verified by drat-trim/LRAT.

A bipartite C4-free graph with parts of sizes m and n and more edges than the best known value of the Zarankiewicz number z(m,n;2,2) in OEIS A072567 or a fresh search, for some m,n beyond the exactly known range (n x n case known to n = 24).

targets.verification_method: Parse the edge list, check simplicity (no loops, no multi-edges) and the vertex count. For each forbidden cycle length L, run an exact search: for C4, check that no two vertices share two neighbours (adjacency-matrix product); for longer cycles, run an independent DFS-based cycle detector and also networkx's simple_cycles with length bound, and require both to find none. Compare the edge count with the live Afzaly-McKay table, the OEIS entry and the proved upper bound.
angles: Start from algebraic extremal graphs: polarity graphs of projective planes (Erdős-Rényi graphs ER_q, q^2+q+1 vertices) are near-optimal for C4. Delete or add vertices carefully, then repair with SAT. The '>=' entries near q^2+q+1 for q = 5, 7 (31, 57 vertices) are natural starting points.

From coding theory and finite geometry: generalized polygons and their subgraphs are extremal for {C3,...,C_{2k}}. Take an incidence graph of a generalized quadrangle or hexagon, then search for large induced subgraphs on the target vertex count.

Tabu search on edge sets with an incremental count of forbidden cycles through each new edge (cheap for C4 via common-neighbour counts), seeded with the downloaded sparse6 extremal graphs from the page for n-1 and n+1.

Vertex-extension SAT: take a record graph on n-1 vertices and solve for the neighbourhood of a new vertex that maximises degree without creating forbidden cycles, then allow a few edge flips in the old graph.

Prescribed symmetry: assume a cyclic or dihedral automorphism of order n or n-1, so the graph is circulant or bi-circulant, and exhaust connection sets; this is the same reduction that works for Ramsey graphs.
From statistical physics: simulated annealing at fixed edge count with a penalty for cycles, then greedy edge addition at zero penalty.
pitfalls: Confusing families: {C4} allows triangles; {C3,C4} (girth 5) does not; bipartite families forbid all odd cycles. Check the exact family heading on the page.
Equalling the '>=' value is not a record; the page already lists such graphs. You need strictly more edges.
A heuristic cycle detector that misses some cycles gives false positives. Use an exact method and two independent implementations.
Exceeding a proved upper bound (Alekseyev's bounds in OEIS A006855) signals a bug, not a breakthrough.
The page and OEIS can disagree in timing; check both and any newer paper (for example on the Zarankiewicz problem) before claiming.

targets.name: Erdős unit distance problem for small n: more unit distances among n points than the best known (n = 22..100)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: u(n) is the maximum number of pairs at distance exactly 1 among n points in the plane (Erdős Problem #90, OEIS A186705). Alexeev, Mixon and Parshall (arXiv:2412.11914, v2 Feb 2025) determined u(n) exactly for n <= 21 and proved upper bounds for 22 <= n <= 30; the best lower bounds are u(22) >= 60, u(23) >= 64, u(24) >= 68, u(25) >= 72, u(26) >= 76, u(27) >= 81, u(28) >= 85, u(29) >= 89, u(30) >= 93 (from Schade, Ágoston-Pálvölgyi and Engel et al.), against upper bounds 61, 66, 72, 78, 84, 90, 96, 103, 110. Engel, Hammond-Lee, Su, Varga and Zsámboki (arXiv:2406.15317) gave lower bounds for 30 < n <= 100 by beam search in the Moser ring. The asymptotic problem moved in 2026 (erdosproblems.com/90 now marks Erdős's n^(1+o(1)) conjecture disproved, via an OpenAI-hosted proof with details in Will Sawin's arXiv:2605.20579 and remarks by Alon et al. in arXiv:2605.20695), but small-n values are separate and still open. Find n points with more unit distances than the best known lower bound for some n in 22..100.
targets.success_criterion: Success means n explicit points in the plane, given exactly (coordinates in a stated number field, e.g. Q(sqrt3, sqrt11, ...) or as an algebraic embedding certificate), with E pairs at distance exactly 1 verified by exact arithmetic in two independent implementations, where E is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best known lower bound for u(n) at verification time: the maximum over https://oeis.org/A186705 re-fetched live immediately before claiming, arXiv:2412.11914 (latest version), arXiv:2406.15317 (latest version), https://www.erdosproblems.com/90, and a fresh arXiv search. E must not exceed the proved upper bounds in arXiv:2412.11914 for n <= 30.

partial_wins.statement: Settle u(22) (is it 60 or 61?) or u(23): either 22 points with 61 unit distances, verified exactly, or an independently re-runnable exhaustive computation extending the Alexeev-Mixon-Parshall method showing 61 is impossible.

A unit-distance graph for some 31 <= n <= 100 that matches or beats the Engel et al. lower bound for that n, verified exactly, whose embedding is not an isometric copy of a Moser-ring configuration: certified by exhibiting two unit edge vectors u, v (as complex numbers) such that the ratio v/u lies neither in the Moser ring (as defined in Engel et al., arXiv:2406.15317) nor in its complex conjugate, with the ring-membership test done in exact arithmetic and re-runnable.

targets.verification_method: Represent coordinates exactly (sympy algebraic numbers or a number-field library). For every pair, compute the squared distance exactly and count pairs equal to 1; check all points are distinct. Two independent implementations (e.g. sympy and PARI/GP or Sage) must agree. Floating-point checks (|d-1| < 1e-12) may be used only as a filter, never as proof. Compare with the live OEIS page and the latest versions of the two arXiv papers.
angles: Search rings beyond the Moser ring: point sets in rings generated by several unit-length rotations (unit complex numbers in fields such as Q(sqrt(-3), sqrt(-11)) or Q(sqrt(-3), sqrt(-15))). The 17-vertex exception found by Alexeev-Mixon-Parshall shows good graphs exist outside the Moser ring.

From number theory (the 2026 asymptotic breakthroughs): points in lattices of number fields with many elements of norm 1. Enumerate small 'unit-distance-rich' subsets of such lattices for n up to 100.

Combinatorial-first: generate dense graphs that avoid known non-embeddable subgraphs (K4, K_{2,3}, the forbidden family F of Alexeev-Mixon-Parshall), then test embeddability with exact algebra, as in their pipeline.
Minkowski sums and unions of rotated copies of good small configurations (Hamming graph H(3,3) gives 27 points with 81 unit distances) followed by greedy point addition/removal.
Beam search (Engel et al.) with different scoring, e.g. reward for future potential edges, and with different generating rotation sets.
pitfalls: Floating-point 'unit distances' that are only approximately 1. Use exact arithmetic; many near-coincidences exist in dense configurations.
Duplicate points: coincident points can inflate the count. Check distinctness exactly.
Exceeding a proved upper bound for n <= 30 means the checker is wrong.
The asymptotic result (n^(1+c) unit distances for infinitely many n) does not give small-n records; compare per n. erdosproblems.com/90 says 'disproved' for the asymptotic conjecture only.
Comparing with OEIS A186705 data alone: OEIS lists only exact values to n = 21; the lower bounds for n >= 22 live in the papers.

targets.name: Van der Waerden numbers: beat a small-parameter lower bound W(r,k) or w(2;k1,k2)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The van der Waerden number W(r,k) is the least N such that every r-colouring of {1..N} contains a monochromatic k-term arithmetic progression. Only seven nontrivial diagonal values are known exactly (W(2,3..6), W(3,3), W(3,4), W(4,3)). For other small cells the best lower bounds come from explicit colourings: Rabung and Lotts (2012, cyclic zippers), Daniel Monroe (arXiv:1603.03301, v7 2022, distributed search over primes up to 9.5e8; the arXiv comment says 'Version as published'), Heule ('Avoiding triples in arithmetic progression', J. Combinatorics 2017; certificates at github.com/marijnheule/vdWaerden) and Herwig-Heule-van Lambalgen-van Maaren (2007). Examples from the Wikipedia table on 2026-10-28: W(2,7) > 3,703; W(2,8) > 11,495; W(3,5) > 2,173; W(4,4) > 1,048; W(5,3) > 170; W(6,3) > 225. Off-diagonal two-colour values w(2;3,k) are exact up to k=20 (k=19 Ahmed-Kullmann-Snevily; w(2;3,20) = 389, conjectured by them and verified by Kouril 2015), w(2;4,k) up to k=9 and w(2;5,k) up to k=7; beyond those only conjectured or lower-bound values exist. Recent work by Fox and Hunter (arXiv:2606.02541, Jun 2026) and Cao (arXiv:2609.31798, Sep 2026) is asymptotic and does not settle small cells. Find an explicit colouring of {1..N} with no monochromatic forbidden progression where N+1 beats the best known lower bound for some small (r,k) or off-diagonal cell.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit colouring c:{1..N}->{1..r} (plain text, one colour per integer) with no monochromatic k-term arithmetic progression (or, for an off-diagonal cell w(r;k1,...,kr), no colour-i progression of length k_i), checked exhaustively by two independent programs, where N+1 is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best lower bound for that cell at verification time. The best lower bound is the maximum over Monroe's tables (https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.03301, latest version, re-fetched immediately before claiming), the live table at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Waerden_number, Rabung-Lotts (E-JC 2012), Heule's certificate repository, and a fresh arXiv/Google Scholar search for that exact cell. Off-by-one: a colouring of {1..N} proves W > N, i.e. W >= N+1. Bounds derived only from product or recursive formulas, without an explicit checked colouring, do not count.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit 2-colouring of {1..N} with no blue 3-term and no red k-term progression proving w(2;3,k) > N for some k >= 21 (or w(2;4,k) for k >= 10, w(2;5,k) for k >= 8), where N strictly exceeds every lower bound and conjectured value published for that cell (Ahmed-Kullmann-Snevily tables and any newer paper found by a fresh search).

An exact new value: a certified determination of a currently open small off-diagonal number (for example w(2;3,21), w(2;4,10) or w(2;5,8)) via an explicit colouring of {1..N-1} plus an UNSAT proof at N that is checked with drat-trim or an LRAT checker on a laptop.

targets.verification_method: Write two independent checkers: (a) for each difference d and start a, test whether a, a+d, ..., a+(k-1)d all have the same colour (O(N^2/k) per colour); (b) a bitset-based checker that, for each colour class, ANDs shifted bitsets. Both must report zero monochromatic progressions. Confirm the colouring has exactly N entries and uses only r colours. Then re-fetch the Wikipedia table and grep arXiv for the exact cell (e.g. "W(3,5)", "w(3;5)") over the last 24 months before claiming.
angles: Rabung's method with a twist: colour x by the discrete logarithm of x modulo a prime p, reduced mod r, then repeat the block. Monroe searched primes up to 9.5e8 for the plain version; search instead over composite moduli, two-prime CRT colourings, or Rabung colourings followed by SAT repair of the last few hundred cells.
Cyclic zippers (Rabung-Lotts) generalised: interleave two or three good cyclic colourings of smaller length and use a SAT solver (CaDiCaL, kissat) to fix the junction cells.

From coding theory: a k-AP-free colouring is like a code avoiding a fixed pattern on every arithmetic 'line'. Borrow quasi-cyclic and multiplier-group constructions from code tables, i.e. require the colouring to be invariant under x -> g*x mod p for a subgroup g, which shrinks the SAT instance by the subgroup order.

From statistical physics: run parallel tempering or population annealing with an energy equal to the number of monochromatic progressions, starting from the best published colouring padded by a few cells.
Incremental SAT: fix a known record colouring on {1..N}, append cells N+1..N+m as free variables plus a free window at the end of the old colouring, and solve with assumptions; slide the window.

For multicolour cells such as W(5,3) and W(6,3), try colourings that are products or lifts of good colourings modulo small primes, then use local search, since small-k multicolour cells have been searched less than 2-colour ones.
pitfalls: Off-by-one: a valid colouring of {1..N} proves W > N. Claiming W >= N or W > N+1 is a false record.
Mixing up notations: W(r,k) (colours first) versus W(k;r), and diagonal versus off-diagonal w(2;3,k). Read the table header carefully.
Checking only progressions with common difference up to some limit, or only progressions starting at 1. The checker must cover every start a >= 1 and every difference d >= 1 with a+(k-1)d <= N.
Comparing with a stale table: neither Wikipedia (last edited 2026-07-14) nor Monroe's arXiv tables (v7, 2022) is guaranteed current. Do a fresh search for the specific cell.
Claiming an asymptotic bound (Green, Hunter, Fox-Hunter, Cao) as a small-cell record. Only explicit colourings count here.
A periodic colouring of length p verified only on one period: progressions that wrap around the period boundary must be checked on the actual interval {1..N}.

targets.name: fev-bench forecasting: beat the best posted scaled quantile loss on a task with locally run open-weight models
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: fev-bench (Oleksandr Shchur, Abdul Fatir Ansari, Caner Turkmen and colleagues at AWS, with the fev library; arXiv:2509.26468) is a forecasting benchmark of 100 tasks with fixed rolling evaluation windows. Its GitHub repository stores one results CSV per model: 44 files on 2026-10-28 (iAmTime was added that day), including Chronos-2, TimesFM-2.5/3, TiRex, Toto 2.0, Moirai 2.0, TabPFN-TS, TimeH2O-v1, Timestral, t0-gamma, statistical baselines and four entries that benchmarks/fev_bench/models.yaml marks closed-api (ChakraTS, Lingjiang2.0, TimeRSI-1.0, TimeRSI-1.5). Each row gives test_error (scaled quantile loss, SQL) per task and a trained_on_this_dataset flag.
