Ignoring leaked rows (trained_on_this_dataset = True, mostly Moirai-2.0, TimesFM-2.5, Toto-1.0 and FlowState), closed-api systems lead 30 of the 100 tasks (TimeRSI-1.0 alone leads 20). On many tasks the best and second-best models are within 0.1%, but on others the leader is several percent ahead, e.g. rohlik_orders_1W (timeh2o-v1 1.1157 vs FlowState 1.2428), us_consumption_1Q (t0-gamma 1.5001 vs TimeRSI-1.0 1.5885), favorita_transactions_1D (Chronos-2 0.6846 vs Timestral-209M 0.7229), solar_1W (TimeRSI-1.0 0.6727; best open-weight citras-fm 0.7992). Can a locally run combination of open-weight models and classical methods beat the best posted non-leaked SQL on some task?
targets.success_criterion: For a named fev-bench task T: a forecast produced by running the fev library's task definition for T (all evaluation windows, the official horizon and quantile levels) on a laptop, using only open-weight models and classical methods run locally whose training data did not include T's dataset (documented), whose fev-computed test_error (SQL) is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the minimum test_error for T over all rows with trained_on_this_dataset not True in all CSV files in https://github.com/autogluon/fev/tree/main/benchmarks/fev_bench/results, re-fetched live immediately before claiming (fetch each CSV via raw.githubusercontent.com). Closed-api rows count toward this minimum. Saved forecasts plus the script must reproduce the score.

partial_wins.statement: On a task whose non-leaked leader is a closed-api entry (one marked model_type: closed-api in benchmarks/fev_bench/models.yaml, which on 2026-10-28 lists ChakraTS, Lingjiang2.0, TimeRSI-1.0 and TimeRSI-1.5), a test_error strictly below the minimum over all non-leaked rows of the other (open-weight and classical) entries, under the same protocol as the full win.
A single fixed ensemble recipe that, under the full-win protocol, beats the best posted non-leaked SQL on at least three tasks.

targets.verification_method: Install the pinned fev version, load task T from the benchmark's tasks.yaml, load the saved per-window forecasts (or re-run the saved script), and compute SQL with fev's evaluator. Re-download every results CSV and take the minimum test_error for T over rows whose trained_on_this_dataset is not True. Confirm each model's training corpus documentation does not list T's dataset and that no model received future values.
angles: Forecast combination from the M-competition literature: median or quantile-averaged ensembles of Chronos-2, TiRex, TimesFM-2.5 and Toto open checkpoints (quantile averaging, sometimes called Vincentization) usually beat each member on probabilistic loss.
Weather-forecasting style post-processing: fit isotonic or EMOS-type quantile recalibration on the earlier, non-evaluated history of each series, then apply it to the final windows.

Use covariates the zero-shot models ignore: for tasks with known dynamic columns (holidays, prices, weather), feed them to a covariate-aware model (Chronos-2 with covariates, TabPFN-TS, LightGBM quantile regression) and blend.
Hierarchical reconciliation from official statistics (MinT) on hierarchical_sales and tourism tasks.
Pick tasks where the leader's margin is large (several percent) rather than tasks where many models tie within 0.1%.
pitfalls: Leakage through pretraining: some foundation models were trained on corpora containing these datasets (GIFT-Eval, Monash, M5); using one whose training data covers T's test period is not a legitimate win.
Window misuse: fitting or calibrating on data from later windows before forecasting earlier ones leaks the future; fev's rolling windows must be respected in order.
Metric mismatch: SQL depends on the quantile levels and on the seasonal-naive scaling; compute it with fev, not a re-implementation.
Per-task cherry-picking across hundreds of ensemble variants overfits the test windows; fix the recipe on validation windows carved from training history before scoring.

Results CSVs change often (eight result additions between 2026-10-06 and 2026-10-28); re-fetch all of them right before claiming, and exclude rows flagged trained_on_this_dataset = True from the bar exactly as the criterion says.

targets.name: MadryLab CIFAR-10 challenge (white-box, Linf 8/255): push the secret model's accuracy below 43.95%
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The MadryLab CIFAR-10 Adversarial Examples Challenge keeps a white-box leaderboard for its adversarially trained wide ResNet (the 'secret' model, released 2017-12-10): the lowest accuracy on the 10,000 CIFAR-10 test images under an L-infinity budget of 8 on the 0-255 scale. Siyuan Yi's 'Guided Local Attack' leads at 43.95% (2021-08-02), one image ahead of Ye Liu's EWR-PGD at 43.96%, followed by Yusuke Tashiro's ODI-PGD at 43.99% and Sven Gowal's MultiTargeted at 44.03%. The last three improvements were 1-4 images each. Can any attack find a single further adversarial image that the leaders missed, reaching 43.94% or lower?
targets.success_criterion: A saved attack.npy of shape (10000, 32, 32, 3) on the 0-255 scale with every value in [0, 255] and max |x_adv - x_nat| <= 8.0 exactly (not using run_attack.py's 0.0001 tolerance), in the official test order, for which the repository's run_attack.py with the 'secret' checkpoint reports an accuracy STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the lowest entry in the 'White-Box Leaderboard' table of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MadryLab/cifar10_challenge/master/README.md re-fetched live immediately before claiming, and lower than any figure the skeptic finds published for this exact model and budget on all 10,000 images.

partial_wins.statement: At least 3 test indices where the secret model survives a fixed, saved strong baseline (AutoAttack standard plus 20-restart MultiTargeted, seeds saved) but you hand over a saved valid adversarial image.
A fully reproducible attack reaching 44.00% or lower within 48 laptop-CPU hours with code and seeds saved.

targets.verification_method: Clone MadryLab/cifar10_challenge, fetch the secret model with fetch_model.py, check the array's shape, range and L-infinity bound in float64, run run_attack.py (TF 1.x, or a PyTorch port whose logits match the checkpoint on all clean images), and recount correct predictions. Re-fetch the README table and search for newer numbers on this exact model.
angles: Triage first: run cheap APGD-DLR on all 10,000 images, then spend almost all compute on the few hundred correctly classified points with the smallest worst-case margin. A record only needs one more image.

Ensemble the published leaders' ideas (ODI starts, MultiTargeted, EWR-PGD's example-wise reweighting, Square Attack's random search) on the low-margin points, with many seeds. Their union may beat each one alone.

Bring in a technique from numerical optimisation: run Frank-Wolfe or mirror descent with line search on the CW margin, and switch to exact coordinate search on the pixels saturated at the box boundary in the final steps.

Black-box evolutionary search from evolutionary computation (CMA-ES in a low-frequency colour-DCT subspace, or the Parsimonious attack's lazy greedy corner search), which sidesteps any residual gradient obfuscation in this TF model.
Use the CPU's ability to run many small processes: each core attacks a disjoint shard of the hard points with a different random portfolio, and results are merged per index.
pitfalls: Scale confusion: this challenge uses 0-255 pixels and epsilon 8.0; an attack built for [0,1] inputs and epsilon 8/255 must be rescaled exactly, or rounding can exceed the budget.
Tolerance slack: run_attack.py accepts 8.0001 and 255.0001; the target requires the strict bounds.
Only the 'secret' checkpoint counts; 'adv_trained' and 'natural' are different models.
A PyTorch port of the TF wide ResNet (batch-norm in inference mode, padding) can differ; confirm the logits match before trusting extra errors.
RobustBench lists a different Madry-style CIFAR-10 model; numbers from RobustBench do not transfer to this checkpoint.

targets.name: MadryLab MNIST challenge (white-box, Linf 0.3): push the secret model's accuracy below the leaderboard's best attack
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The MadryLab MNIST Adversarial Examples Challenge (Madry, Makelov, Schmidt, Tsipras, Vladu) released an adversarially trained two-conv-layer CNN (the 'secret' model, weights public since 2017-10-19) and keeps a white-box leaderboard: the lowest accuracy any attack achieves on the 10,000 MNIST test images under an L-infinity budget of 0.3. The README table, frozen since submissions closed on 2022-05-03, is led by Siyuan Yi's 'Guided Local Attack' at 88.00% (2021-08-30), ahead of Chen Wan's PCROS attack at 88.04%, Tianhang Zheng's adaptive Distributionally Adversarial Attack at 88.06%, Yusuke Tashiro's ODI-PGD at 88.13% and Francesco Croce's Square Attack at 88.25%. Since May 2018 the record has improved eight times, by 0.02-0.77 points each; the last two improvements (2020-10-28, 2021-08-30) were 0.02 and 0.04 points (2 and 4 images), and about 8,800 test points are still unbroken. Is the true robust accuracy below 88.00%? One more adversarial image is enough: 87.99% means 8,799 correct out of 10,000.
targets.success_criterion: A saved attack.npy of shape (10000, 784) such that (1) every pixel lies in [0, 1] exactly and max |x_adv - x_nat| <= 0.3 exactly (no use of the 0.0001 tolerance in run_attack.py), against the challenge's own test-set ordering; (2) the repository's run_attack.py with the 'secret' checkpoint fetched by fetch_model.py reports an accuracy STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the lowest accuracy in the 'White-Box Leaderboard' table of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MadryLab/mnist_challenge/master/README.md, re-fetched live immediately before claiming; and (3) strictly lower than any figure the skeptic finds in a paper or repository for this exact secret model, the full 10,000 images and an L-infinity budget of 0.3. Submitting to MadryLab is not part of the target.

partial_wins.statement: A list of at least 5 test indices on which the secret model stays correct under a fixed, re-runnable strong baseline (AutoAttack standard version plus 100-restart PGD on the CW margin loss, seeds saved), but for which you hand over a saved valid adversarial image. Each image is checked independently.

A deterministic, documented attack that reaches 88.05% or lower on the full set in at most 24 hours on a laptop CPU, with code and seeds saved, so that it matches the top three entries using an attack anyone can reproduce.

targets.verification_method: Clone MadryLab/mnist_challenge, run `python fetch_model.py secret`, load the saved attack.npy, assert shape, range [0,1] and L-infinity <= 0.3 with numpy in float64, then run `python run_attack.py` (TensorFlow 1.x environment or a PyTorch port whose logits match the TF checkpoint to 1e-5 on all 10,000 clean images) and read the accuracy. Recount the correct predictions independently from the logits. Re-fetch the README table and search for later published numbers on the same model.
angles: Treat it as combinatorial search, imported from SAT/MAX-SAT local search: the optimum of a piecewise-linear network inside an L-infinity box usually sits at a box corner, so run WalkSAT-style local search over sign patterns of the 784 pixel perturbations (flip blocks of pixels, accept on margin decrease), seeded from PGD solutions.

Use a verifier as an attacker (from formal methods): run branch-and-bound with alpha-beta-CROWN or a MILP solver restricted to the roughly 1-2% of points where PGD margins are smallest; this small CNN is close to tractable, and an exact counterexample on even one point beats the record.

Search in a compression basis (from image coding): parameterise the perturbation in a DCT or wavelet subspace and run CMA-ES or another derivative-free search, which is immune to the gradient masking that max-pooling and ReLU dead zones cause on this adversarially trained model.

Use diverse start points: output-diversified initialisation (Tashiro), many targeted restarts on each wrong class (Gowal's MultiTargeted), and a portfolio over loss functions (CE, CW margin, DLR). Spend the CPU budget only on the low-margin points.
Borrow the 'temperature' trick from statistical physics: anneal a smoothed surrogate (softplus ReLUs, soft max-pool), take gradients through it to reach a basin, then finish with exact-model PGD.
pitfalls: Tolerance exploitation: run_attack.py accepts L-infinity up to 0.3001 and pixels up to 1.0001; a 'win' that depends on that slack is not a win here. Clip in float64, then cast.
Wrong checkpoint: the 'adv_trained' public model and the 'natural' model are easier; only the 'secret' checkpoint counts.

Port mismatch: a PyTorch re-implementation with slightly different padding or max-pool rounding can report extra errors that the original TF model does not make; verify logits agree with the TF checkpoint on every image.

Unrestricted attacks such as spatial transforms or structure-preserving transformations report far lower accuracy (one 2018 paper reports 9.79%) but do not respect the L-infinity 0.3 threat model and do not count.
Index or label misalignment: the attack file must follow the official test-set order; reordering or using a subset changes the denominator.

targets.name: OGB ogbg-molhiv: beat the leaderboard's top mean test ROC-AUC under the official protocol
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: ogbg-molhiv from the Open Graph Benchmark (Weihua Hu, Matthias Fey, Marinka Zitnik, Yuxiao Dong, Hongyu Ren, Bowen Liu, Michele Catasta, Jure Leskovec) asks whether each of 41,127 molecules inhibits HIV replication, with a fixed scaffold split, scored by test ROC-AUC averaged over 10 random seeds with model selection on validation. The leaderboard is led by 'Multi-RF Fusion + Multi-GNN' (Zacharie B., 2026-03-21) at 0.8476 ± 0.0002 (listed with 993,331,107 parameters on an NVIDIA H100), then HyperFusion (Xinwei Zhang, 2024-02-24) at 0.8475 ± 0.0003 (5.9 million parameters, RTX 3080) and PAS+FPs (Xu Wang) at 0.8420. Several top entries combine random forests over molecular fingerprints with GNNs; a fingerprint random forest on its own ('Molecular FP + Random Forest', Luca Hagemeyer, the only CPU entry in the top ten) reaches 0.8208. Can a model without external data beat 0.8476 under the rules?
targets.success_criterion: Saved code, seeds and per-seed test predictions such that, using the official ogbg-molhiv scaffold split and the ogb Evaluator, the mean test ROC-AUC over 10 runs with seeds 0-9 (each run's checkpoint or ensemble chosen by validation ROC-AUC only) is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the top 'Test ROC-AUC' value among no-external-data entries in the ogbg-molhiv table of https://ogb.stanford.edu/docs/leader_graphprop/ re-fetched live immediately before claiming. Only the training split's labels may be used for fitting; no external labelled data or models pretrained on molecular property labels.

partial_wins.statement: Mean test ROC-AUC over 10 seeds strictly above the second-ranked no-external-data entry, with every component trained on the laptop CPU in under 12 hours total.
A model with fewer than 1 million learned parameters whose 10-seed mean test ROC-AUC beats every leaderboard entry with fewer than 10 million parameters.

targets.verification_method: Install ogb, load PygGraphPropPredDataset or the raw SMILES with the official split, re-run the saved script for 2 of the 10 seeds to confirm per-seed numbers, compute test ROC-AUC with ogb's Evaluator on the saved predictions for all 10 seeds, and check that model selection used validation only (inspect logs). Re-fetch the leaderboard.
angles: Cheminformatics feature diversity: combine Morgan counts at several radii, MACCS, RDKit 2D descriptors, Avalon and atom-pair fingerprints in rotation forests or extremely randomised trees, then rank-average with a GNN.
Rank-based losses from information retrieval: optimise AUC directly (LibAUC's AUC-M loss, pairwise ranking with LightGBM's lambdarank objective) since the metric is ROC-AUC.
Scaffold-split robustness from domain adaptation: reweight training molecules to match the validation scaffold distribution (covariate-shift importance weights).
Use self-supervision only on the unlabelled molecules of this dataset (allowed, no external labels): masked-atom pretraining or graph contrastive pretraining on the 41k SMILES before fine-tuning.
Stacking with nested validation: train many diverse base models and fit the blender on validation predictions, then re-check that the same blender, not test-tuned weights, is used for all 10 seeds.
pitfalls: Test-set model selection: picking epochs, blend weights or seeds by test ROC-AUC inflates scores; the rules allow validation only.
Seed games: reporting the best 10 of 50 seeds is not the protocol; seeds 0-9 or the first 10 runs, all reported.

External data: fingerprints are computed from the molecules themselves and are fine; models pretrained on labelled bioactivity data (ChEMBL, PCBA) count as external data and belong in a different comparison.
ROC-AUC differences of 0.0001 are within seed noise; the claim must exceed the record mean, and the skeptic should report the standard deviation too.

targets.name: Smallest neural network reaching 99% test accuracy on MNIST (record: 697 parameters)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: How few learned parameters does a network need to reach 99% accuracy on the standard 10,000-image MNIST test set? Ruslan Grimov's mnist-minimal-model project reached 99.1% with 1,936 parameters (a Keras CNN with separable convolutions and instance normalisation). Josh Warn's Parameter-Efficient-MNIST, with models contributed by Thomas Warn, lowered this to 697 parameters at 99.03% after training about 700 models with five convolution layers; the saved weights are in the repository as 697_mnist_0.9903.h5 with load_and_test_model.py. No smaller verified model is known. Can a network with 696 or fewer parameters reach 99.00%?
targets.success_criterion: A saved model file plus a standalone inference script such that (1) on the official MNIST test set (10,000 images, standard order and labels), plain argmax predictions with no test-time augmentation and no ensembling give accuracy >= 99.00%; (2) the parameter count is STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the record stated in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JoshWarn/Parameter-Efficient-MNIST/main/README.md re-fetched live immediately before claiming (and less than any smaller verified claim the skeptic finds); counting is conservative: every number in the forward pass that is not a universal constant counts (weights, biases, normalisation scales and runs, stored running statistics, fixed hand-designed filters, lookup tables and thresholds), whereas only architecture integers (kernel sizes, strides) and the input scaling 1/255 are free; (3) the weights were learned by a generic training procedure on the 60,000 training images only (training script and seed saved).

partial_wins.statement: A model at or below 697 counted parameters (under the conservative rule above) whose accuracy on the test set is at least 99.10%, which beats the record holder's 99.03% at equal or smaller size.
A model with at most 500 counted parameters reaching at least 98.80%, giving a new public point on the size-accuracy curve with reproducible training.

targets.verification_method: Load the saved weights in a fresh environment, enumerate every tensor and constant used in forward() and sum their element counts (tied tensors once), run inference on the official MNIST test set with argmax, and compare accuracy and count. Read the script for test-time augmentation, ensembling or test-set use during training. Re-run the training script with its seed to confirm a passing checkpoint is reproducible (or at least that training never touches test images).
angles: Weight sharing from signal processing: steerable or rotation-tied convolution kernels and depthwise kernels shared across layers (as in the 1,936-parameter design's shared separable block) cut counts while keeping receptive field.
Knowledge distillation: train a large teacher, then train the tiny student on soft labels and on augmented inputs; on tiny models distillation often adds the last 0.1-0.3 points.

Architecture search on CPU: an evolutionary search over kernel shapes (1x3/3x1 factorisation), channel counts and pooling placement, each candidate trained for a few minutes with many seeds in parallel.

Borrow from compressed sensing and coding theory: low-rank or Kronecker-factored kernels and a final layer that is a tied, structured projection, then check exactly how the conservative rule counts each factor.
Training-side levers that add no parameters: long schedules with cosine annealing, label smoothing, elastic-distortion augmentation of training images and stochastic weight averaging.
pitfalls: Free-constant smuggling: fixed Gabor or scattering filters, hard-coded normalisation statistics or lookup tables are counted under the conservative rule; a model that is small only because constants are hidden is not a win.
Test-set selection: choosing the checkpoint or seed by test accuracy is weak evidence; report the selection on a validation split of the training set and re-check on test.
Accuracy rounding: 98.995% is not 99%; the count of correct images must be at least 9,900.
Test-time augmentation or ensembling of several tiny models multiplies the effective parameters and is excluded.
Using EMNIST, QMNIST or extra digits for training changes the task; only the 60,000 MNIST training images may be used.

targets.name: SRBench 2025 black-box: a symbolic regressor that Pareto-dominates the best-accuracy method on a dataset
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: SRBench (William La Cava, Patryk Orzechowski, Bogdan Burlacu, Fabrício Olivetti de França, Marco Virgolin, Ying Jin, Michael Kommenda, Jason Moore; 2025 edition led by Guilherme Imai Aldeia, Hengzhe Zhang, Geoffrey Bomarito, Miles Cranmer, Alcides Fonseca, Bogdan Burlacu, William La Cava and Fabrício Olivetti de França) benchmarks symbolic regression. The 2025 black-box track ran 28 methods on 12 PMLB datasets with 30 fixed train/test splits each and published every returned model with its test R² and model_size (SRBench's sympy node count, or the method's own complexity where sympy parsing failed). The best median R² is often bought with very large models, e.g. 1028_SWD PS-Tree 0.380 at size 3270, 522_pm10 PS-Tree 0.301 at size 4996, 1193_BNG_lowbwt EQL 0.602 at size 188; elsewhere small models lead, e.g. 210_cloud Genetic Engine 0.8465 at size 7. Can a symbolic regression procedure beat the best median test R² on a dataset while also matching or undercutting that method's median model size?
targets.success_criterion: For a named dataset D among the 12 SRBench 2025 black-box datasets: a symbolic regression procedure run on each of the 30 splits used in results.feather (train_test_split with train_size 0.75 and random_state equal to each listed seed, as in experiment/evaluate_model.py on the srbench_2025 branch, including its training subsampling rule) that returns one closed-form expression per split, such that (a) the median test R² over the 30 splits is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the highest median r2_test of any algorithm for D in https://github.com/cavalab/srbench/tree/srbench_2025/results/black-box-tuning (results.feather, re-fetched live immediately before claiming), and (b) the median complexity of the 30 expressions, computed with SRBench's own symbolic_utils.complexity, is less than or equal to that leading algorithm's median model_size. The procedure must be fixed before scoring (no per-split hand edits).

partial_wins.statement: For a dataset D, a procedure whose (median R², median complexity) point is not dominated by any algorithm's point in results.feather and strictly dominates at least one point currently on the Pareto front.
For a dataset D, a procedure with median complexity at most 20 whose median test R² beats every algorithm whose own median model_size is at most 20.

targets.verification_method: Download the PMLB dataset, rebuild the 30 splits from the seeds in results.feather with evaluate_model.py's code, load the saved expression for each split, evaluate test R² with numpy, compute complexity with symbolic_utils.complexity after the same sympy parsing, take medians, and compare with the medians recomputed from results.feather (excluding rows with model_size -1 only when computing sizes). Re-run the procedure on two splits to confirm it returns the saved expressions.
angles: Distil a strong black-box model into a formula: fit gradient boosting or a tabular foundation model, then run symbolic regression (PySR, Operon) on its smoothed predictions with additive structure found by partial dependence, the 'symbolic distillation' idea from Cranmer's work.
Generalised additive models from statistics: fit a GAM, then replace each shape function by a short closed form (piecewise-linear with max/min, logs) and refit constants jointly.
Target the datasets where the leader is huge (1028_SWD, 522_pm10, 1193_BNG_lowbwt): an expression of size a few hundred only needs to edge past the leader's R² to dominate it.

Multi-objective evolutionary search from engineering design (NSGA-II with complexity as an explicit objective) plus constant refitting with Levenberg-Marquardt, as in Operon, run with a longer budget than the benchmark's.
Robust losses from statistics (Huber, trimmed) for noisy targets like pm10 and visualizing_environmental, since outliers dominate R².
pitfalls: Split mismatch: the 30 seeds and the training subsampling in evaluate_model.py must be reproduced exactly; using different splits makes medians incomparable.
Complexity mismatch: SRBench measures size after its own sympy parsing; an expression that looks small but expands under sympy (e.g. nested powers) may count larger. Use symbolic_utils.complexity.
Non-symbolic models: a formula embedding a lookup table, piecewise definitions with hundreds of branches or a numeric array literal is not a closed-form expression in the benchmark's sense.
Test-split tuning: choosing hyperparameters by test R² across the 30 splits is leakage; tune inside the training part.
model_size is -1 for rows where SRBench failed to parse a model; exclude those only from size medians, not from R² medians, and say so.

targets.name: TRADES MNIST white-box leaderboard (Linf 0.3): push the TRADES SmallCNN's robust accuracy below 92.46%
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Hongyang Zhang, Yaodong Yu and co-authors of TRADES (ICML 2019) published their MNIST SmallCNN checkpoint and test arrays with a white-box attack leaderboard (L-infinity epsilon 0.3, 10,000 test images). Hong Lei's ITA attack leads at 92.46% robust accuracy (2021-08-27), one image ahead of Ye Liu's EWR-PGD at 92.47% (2020-12-20), then 92.52% (EWR-PGD, first entry), Maksym Andriushchenko's Square Attack at 92.58% and Francesco Croce's FAB at 93.33%. Is there an attack that breaks at least one more image, reaching 92.45% or below? This model is not on RobustBench (which has no MNIST track), so it is separate from the RobustBench targets.
targets.success_criterion: A saved mnist_X_adv.npy built from the repository's mnist_X.npy (same order) with every value in [0, 1] and max |x_adv - x| <= 0.3, for which the repository's evaluate_attack_mnist.py with model_mnist_smallcnn.pt reports a robust accuracy STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the lowest 'Robust Accuracy' in the MNIST 'White-box leaderboard' table of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yaodongyu/TRADES/master/README.md re-fetched live immediately before claiming, and lower than any figure the skeptic finds published for this exact checkpoint, budget and full test set.

partial_wins.statement: At least 5 test indices where the TRADES SmallCNN survives a fixed, saved strong baseline (AutoAttack standard plus 100-restart PGD on the CW margin, seeds saved) but you hand over a saved valid adversarial image.
A reproducible attack that reaches 92.50% or below on a laptop CPU in at most 12 hours, with code and seeds saved.

targets.verification_method: Download model_mnist_smallcnn.pt, mnist_X.npy and mnist_Y.npy from the README links (plain GET), load SmallCNN from models/small_cnn.py, run evaluate_attack_mnist.py on the saved adversarial array (it checks the delta and the [0,1] range), and recount errors independently from the logits on CPU. Re-fetch the README table.
angles: The SmallCNN is small enough for exact methods from operations research: encode the network as a MILP (or use alpha-beta-CROWN's BaB-attack) for the lowest-margin images and let the solver either find a counterexample or prove the point safe, which shrinks the search set.
Corner search from discrete optimisation: L-infinity optima on piecewise-linear nets tend to lie on box vertices, so run local search over pixel sign patterns (block flips, tabu lists) seeded by PGD.
Combine the leaders' tricks (ITA, EWR-PGD reweighting, Square Attack random search, FAB minimum-norm boundary search) as a portfolio per image; since every new image counts, union the successes.

Use an idea from the physics of glasses, parallel tempering: run several PGD chains at different step sizes and noise levels and swap states, to escape the flat loss plateaus that TRADES training creates.
Transfer from surrogates: fine-tune a surrogate on the TRADES model's soft labels and use its adversarial directions as starting points for white-box refinement on the real model.
pitfalls: Range and budget: the evaluator rejects values outside [0,1] and deltas above 0.3; float32 rounding after clipping can push a delta to 0.30000001, so clip in the final dtype.
Use the checkpoint and the arrays from the README links; retraining a TRADES model yourself gives a different, easier model.
The CIFAR-10 TRADES WRN-34-10 model is also on RobustBench (already covered there); this target is only the MNIST SmallCNN.
A model in train mode (dropout active) gives random errors; the evaluator must use model.eval().

targets.name: TSB-AD multivariate anomaly detection: beat the leaderboard's best average VUS-PR on the evaluation set
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: TSB-AD (Qinghua Liu and John Paparrizos, NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks; maintained by TheDatumOrg) is a curated time-series anomaly detection benchmark with a fixed split of series into a tuning set and an evaluation set and a recommended metric, VUS-PR (volume under the precision-recall surface). The community leaderboard (open to submissions since 2026-04-01; last updated 2026-10-20, when Syntropic, CHARM (kNN/ZS), VERITY-AD and AxonAD were added) ranks methods by average VUS-PR. On the multivariate track TSB-AD-M, the pretrained CHARM (kNN) leads at 0.54, followed by AxonAD at 0.50 (the best method not marked pretrained), CHARM (ZS) at 0.46 and StreamVAE at 0.44, while the classic PCA baseline scores 0.31. On the univariate track the best is CHARM (kNN) at 0.68, then Syntropic at 0.67 and VERITY-AD at 0.61 (the best not marked pretrained). Can a method with hyperparameters chosen only on the tuning set beat the best TSB-AD-M average?
targets.success_criterion: A detector whose hyperparameters and any model selection used only the TSB-AD-M tuning-set file list, run on every series in the TSB-AD-M evaluation-set file list from the repository's Datasets/File_List, with anomaly scores saved per series, such that the average VUS-PR computed by the repository's get_metrics over all evaluation series is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the highest TSB-AD-M value in https://thedatumorg.github.io/TSB-AD/static/leaderboard/TSB-AD-updated.html re-fetched live immediately before claiming, and also greater than that leader's unrounded score if the repository's benchmark results files give one. No evaluation-set labels may be used before scoring.

partial_wins.statement: Beat the best average VUS-PR on TSB-AD-M among methods marked as not pretrained on the live leaderboard (AxonAD, 0.50 on 2026-10-28) with a CPU-only method that runs on all evaluation series in under 6 hours, under the full-win protocol.
Beat the leaderboard's best TSB-AD-U value among methods marked as not pretrained (VERITY-AD, 0.61 on 2026-10-28) on the univariate track, under the same tuning-set-only rule.

targets.verification_method: Clone TheDatumOrg/TSB-AD, download the datasets, read the tuning/evaluation file lists, re-run the saved detector script with its fixed hyperparameters on a random 10% of evaluation series to confirm the saved scores, then compute VUS-PR with TSB_AD.evaluation.metrics.get_metrics for every saved score file and average. Inspect the script for any read of evaluation labels. Re-fetch the leaderboard.
angles: Ensembles of complementary detectors (reconstruction VAE, PCA residuals, isolation forest on lagged windows, matrix-profile discord scores) with rank normalisation, a standard trick in outlier-detection ensembles (Aggarwal and Sathe).
Process-control statistics from industrial engineering: multivariate CUSUM and Hotelling T² on PCA scores with robust (MCD) covariance, tuned only on the tuning set.
Score post-processing matters for VUS-PR: smooth scores with windows matched to the series' period and apply per-channel normalisation before aggregating.
Spectral residual methods from computer vision saliency detection (as used in Microsoft's SR-CNN) applied per channel.
Graph-structured models: learn a sparse dependency graph among channels on the first part of each series (unsupervised) and score residuals from graph-based predictions.
pitfalls: Label peeking: evaluation labels are public; tuning thresholds, windows or model choice on them makes the claim void. All choices must be fixed from the tuning set, and the script must be inspected.
Rounding: the leaderboard shows two decimals; beating '0.54' needs an exact comparison with the leader's unrounded score where available, or a margin of at least 0.005.
Metric implementation: VUS-PR has parameters (sliding window, version); use the repository's get_metrics defaults exactly.
Fine-tuned foundation models that were trained on data overlapping the evaluation series are leakage.
Skipping series that crash the method lowers the denominator; every evaluation series must have a score file.

targets.name: Time series extrinsic regression (TSER archive): beat the best reference regressor's 30-resample mean RMSE on a dataset
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The Time Series Extrinsic Regression archive (Chang Wei Tan, Christoph Bergmeir, François Petitjean, Geoffrey Webb; extended by David Guijo-Rubio, Matthew Middlehurst, Anthony Bagnall and others to 63 datasets) predicts a continuous value from a whole time series. timeseriesclassification.com hosts reference RMSE results for 19 regressors (estimators.txt: 1NN/5NN-DTW and -ED, CNN, DrCIF, FCN, FPCR, FPCR-b-spline, FreshPRINCE, GridSVR, InceptionTime, RandF, ResNet, Ridge, ROCKET, RotF, SingleInceptionTime, XGBoost) over 30 resamples of all 63 datasets. Newer methods such as MultiROCKET-Hydra and QUANT are not in the reference set. tsml-eval's TSER archive-expansion results (publications/y2023/tser_archive_expansion) add MultiROCKET, TSF and an InceptionTime ensemble, which beat the reference minimum on 7 datasets (e.g. GasSensorArrayAcetone 0.1435 vs DrCIF 0.1845), so on those datasets the bar is lower than the reference files show. For many datasets the gap between the best and the second-best is several percent, for example WindTurbinePower (FreshPRINCE 44.66 vs RotF 74.25), DhakaHourlyAirQuality (1.784 vs 2.702), SodiumConcentration (DrCIF 312.8 vs GridSVR 362.6). Can a new regressor beat the best reference and published 30-resample mean RMSE on some dataset?
targets.success_criterion: For a named TSER dataset D: saved test predictions for all 30 resamples (resample r from tsml-eval's regression resampling with random_state = r applied to the default split, resample 0 = default split), each from a model fit only on that resample's training part, whose mean test RMSE over the 30 resamples is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the smallest 30-resample mean for D across every *_rmse.csv file at https://timeseriesclassification.com/results/ReferenceResults/regression/rmse/ re-fetched live immediately before claiming, and below any credible published 30-resample mean for D the skeptic finds (including the TSER archive-expansion results in tsml-eval's publications/y2023/tser_archive_expansion).

partial_wins.statement: Beat the best reference RMSE on the default split (resample 0) and the best reference mean over resamples 0-9 for a dataset D.
One fixed regressor configuration that beats the reference best mean RMSE on at least three datasets.

targets.verification_method: Recreate the 30 resamples with tsml-eval's resampling utilities, align saved predictions with each resample's test cases, recompute RMSE per resample and the mean, re-run training on two resamples from the saved script and seed, and re-download all reference *_rmse.csv files to take the minimum mean for D.
angles: Run modern convolution-kernel regressors (MultiROCKET-Hydra, QUANT with extra-trees) that are missing from the reference set, then stack them with FreshPRINCE and DrCIF using out-of-fold predictions inside each training set.

Chemometrics for the element-concentration sets (SodiumConcentration, PotassiumConcentration and the rest): if the series are spectra, as their names suggest, PLS regression, Savitzky-Golay derivatives and multiplicative scatter correction are standard spectroscopy preprocessing and are absent from the reference methods. Check the dataset descriptions first.

Physics-informed features for the energy and weather sets (WindTurbinePower, Solar, AustraliaRainfall): power-curve transforms of wind speed (cubic law), clear-sky normalisation, daily cycle harmonics.
Target transforms from econometrics: model log or Box-Cox of skewed targets and correct the back-transform bias (smearing estimator) before computing RMSE.
Gradient-boosted trees on catch22 or tsfresh summary features with monotonic constraints where domain knowledge allows.
pitfalls: RMSE is scale-dependent; a mistake in un-normalising the target (fitting the scaler on all data, or forgetting the inverse transform) gives fake wins or losses.
Default-split-only results are not the record; all 30 resamples are required.
The reference set excludes some newer published methods; a claim must also beat the best credible published 30-resample mean for D (search Guijo-Rubio et al.'s TSER bake-off and later papers).
Some datasets have missing values ('_nmv') or unequal lengths ('_eq'); use the same processed version as the reference files.
Hyperparameter tuning must be nested within each resample's training data.

targets.name: UCR univariate time series classification: beat the best reference classifier's 30-resample mean accuracy on a dataset
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The UCR/UEA archive (Hoang Anh Dau, Eamonn Keogh, Anthony Bagnall and colleagues) has 128 univariate classification datasets with fixed default train/test splits. The time-series machine learning group at timeseriesclassification.com (Matthew Middlehurst, Anthony Bagnall, Patrick Schäfer and others) host reference results generated with the aeon toolkit for 40 classifiers (estimators.txt; the *_accuracy.csv files cover 142 univariate datasets), including HIVE-COTE 2, MR-Hydra, QUANT, InceptionTime, WEASEL 2.0, RDST and TS-CHIEF, each on 30 resamples (resample 0 is the default split). For many datasets the best 30-resample mean accuracy is far from 100%, for example Phoneme 0.4172 (DrCIF), Haptics 0.5707 (RDST), InsectWingbeatSound 0.6669 (MR-Hydra), Worms 0.7944 (WEASEL 1.0), FiftyWords 0.8456 (MR-Hydra). Can a new classifier beat the best reference mean on some dataset?
targets.success_criterion: For a named univariate dataset D: saved test predictions for all 30 resamples (resample r produced by tsml-eval's stratified resampling with random_state = r applied to the default train/test split, resample 0 = default split), each from a model fit only on that resample's training part, whose mean test accuracy over the 30 resamples is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the largest 30-resample mean for D across every *_accuracy.csv AND every *_TESTFOLDS.csv file listed at https://timeseriesclassification.com/results/ReferenceResults/classification/accuracy/ re-fetched live immediately before claiming, and greater than any credible published 30-resample mean for D (same resampling) that the skeptic finds in the literature. Missing resamples count as failures.

partial_wins.statement: On a dataset D whose reference best mean is below 0.95, beat the best reference accuracy on the default split (resample 0 column) and also beat the best reference mean over resamples 0-9.
One fixed classifier configuration (no per-dataset tuning outside training data) that beats the reference best mean on at least two datasets.

targets.verification_method: Rebuild the 30 resamples with tsml-eval's resampling function (stratified, random_state = resample id) from the archive's default split; check the saved predictions line up with each resample's test cases and labels; recompute mean accuracy; re-run training for two random resamples with the saved script and seed; re-download the reference CSVs and take the max mean for D.
angles: Ensemble across representation families (HIVE-COTE style) but with the newest members: QUANT, MR-Hydra, RDST and WEASEL 2.0 probabilities weighted by training-set cross-validation accuracy.
Speech-processing features for audio-derived sets (Phoneme, InsectWingbeatSound, Haptics): MFCCs, log-mel spectrogram statistics and pitch features fed to a ridge or tree classifier.

Shape-based tricks from computer vision for outline datasets (FiftyWords, phalanx outlines): convert series to images (Gramian angular fields, recurrence plots) and use a small CNN, or use elastic shape analysis from computational anatomy.

Semi-supervised and transductive learning from NLP: self-train on the unlabelled test series of each resample (legal, since labels are not used), which helps small-train datasets such as Worms and Beef.
Data augmentation from audio (time warping, window slicing, mixup) for the deep models when training sets are tiny.
pitfalls: Default-split cherry-picking: beating the best on one split is easy noise; the record is the 30-resample mean.
Resampling mismatch: using sklearn's train_test_split instead of tsml-eval's stratified resampler gives different resamples and is not comparable.
Test-set leakage through z-normalisation or feature scaling fitted on train plus test is acceptable only per-series (instance-wise); fitting scalers on test labels or tuning on test accuracy is not.

Newer published results (papers after the reference upload) may already beat the hosted maximum; the novelty check must search the literature for D, and a claim must also beat any credible published 30-resample mean for D.
Variable-length and missing-value datasets have '_eq'/'_nmv' processed versions in the reference files; use the same version.

targets.name: UEA multivariate time series classification: beat the best published 30-resample mean accuracy on a dataset
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The UEA multivariate archive (Bagnall, Dau, Lines, Flynn, Large, Bostrom, Southam, Keogh) has 26 equal-length multivariate classification datasets with default splits. Alejandro Pasos Ruiz, Michael Flynn, James Large, Matthew Middlehurst and Anthony Bagnall's multivariate bake-off (2021) and the HIVE-COTE 2 paper (Middlehurst et al. 2021) published 30-resample accuracies for about 20 classifiers, hosted at timeseriesclassification.com. Best means include Handwriting 0.6121 (DTW_D), LSST 0.6370 (HC2), FaceDetection 0.7135 (HC2), SelfRegulationSCP2 0.5369 (DTW_D), EigenWorms 0.9056 (DrCIF), Heartbeat 0.7652 (CIF). Newer methods (MR-Hydra, QUANT, convolutional transformers) have not been posted to this table. Can a new classifier beat the best published mean on some dataset?
targets.success_criterion: For a named UEA multivariate dataset D: saved test predictions for all 30 resamples (tsml-eval stratified resampling with random_state = r on the default split, r = 0..29), each model fit only on that resample's training part, with mean accuracy STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the largest 30-resample mean for D across every *_TESTFOLDS.csv in https://timeseriesclassification.com/results/PublishedResults/Bakeoff2021/ and https://timeseriesclassification.com/results/PublishedResults/HIVE-COTEV2/ re-fetched live immediately before claiming, and greater than any credible published 30-resample mean for D that the skeptic finds (including any multivariate files later added under ReferenceResults).

partial_wins.statement: Beat the best published accuracy on the default split (resample 0) and the best mean over resamples 0-9 for a dataset D.
One fixed classifier configuration that beats the best published mean on at least two datasets.

targets.verification_method: Recreate the resamples with tsml-eval's stratified resampling, align predictions and labels, recompute per-resample accuracy and the mean, re-run training for two resamples from the saved script and seed, and recompute the published maximum from the downloaded CSVs.
angles: Run the modern convolution-kernel family (MultiROCKET-Hydra, QUANT) channel-wise and jointly; these routinely beat ROCKET and HC2 on univariate data but are absent from this table.

EEG and BCI methods for SelfRegulationSCP1/2, MotorImagery, FingerMovements: Riemannian geometry on covariance matrices (tangent-space logistic regression, minimum distance to Riemannian mean) and common spatial patterns from brain-computer-interface research.
Astronomy features for LSST: the PLAsTiCC-challenge winners used Gaussian-process light-curve interpolation and redshift-aware features; the series here are LSST simulated light curves.
Handwriting and gesture sets: rotation-invariant and path-signature features (rough path theory) of the 3D accelerometer trajectories.
Channel selection (from feature selection literature) to drop noisy dimensions before the classifier, chosen by cross-validation on the training part.
pitfalls: The hosted table is from 2021; later papers may already report higher 30-resample means; the novelty check must search the literature for D.
Unequal-length datasets (e.g. JapaneseVowels, CharacterTrajectories) are not in this 26-dataset set; use the equal-length versions the bake-off used.
Default-split wins are noise on small test sets (AtrialFibrillation has 15 test cases).
Do not tune on resample test accuracy; nest all tuning inside the training part.

targets.name: Cubature: a positive-interior (PI) rule with fewer points than the best known for a standard region and degree
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Ronald Cools' Encyclopaedia of Cubature Formulas (nines.cs.kuleuven.be/ecf, KU Leuven) tabulates, for each standard region (square, cube, disk, ball, triangle, tetrahedron, hexagon and others) and polynomial degree, the known numbers of points N and their quality (P = positive weights, I = all points inside; '*' marks a rule attaining a known lower bound). The public overview tables are free to read, while the point files need a login. The site index was last modified 2022 and the tables page 2004. Later literature improved some entries, e.g. symmetric rules by Witherden-Vincent 2015 (polyquad), Xiao-Gimbutas 2010, Papanicolopulos 2015-2016 and Jaśkowiec-Sukumar 2019-2020. For many (region, degree) pairs the best PI rule is not known to be minimal. Can a PI rule be found with strictly fewer points than every published PI rule for some region and degree?
targets.success_criterion: For a region R with an ECF overview table and a degree d whose best PI entry in that table is not marked '*': a saved rule (points, weights) with every weight > 0 and every point strictly inside R, exact for all polynomials of degree <= d. Exactness is checked in mpmath at 50 digits against the exact integral of every monomial of degree <= d, with maximum absolute error below 1e-30 times the integral of 1 over R, after Newton polishing. The rule's point count N must be STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than both (a) the smallest PI entry for (R,d) in the ECF table, re-fetched live immediately before claiming, and (b) the smallest PI rule for (R,d) published in Witherden-Vincent (polyquad), Xiao-Gimbutas, Papanicolopulos, Jaśkowiec-Sukumar, or any other paper or software collection (e.g. quadpy) the skeptic finds. N must not fall below a proven lower bound (Möller, Mysovskikh); a rule below one means a bug.

partial_wins.statement: A fully symmetric PI rule for (R,d) whose N equals the best known N, where every published rule with that N is only PO, NI or worse, upgrading the quality. Checked by the same exactness, positivity and interiority tests.
A PI rule for the square or triangle at degree >= 25 with fewer points than any published fully symmetric PI rule for that degree, under the same checks.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic evaluates the rule on all monomials up to degree d in mpmath (exact monomial integrals over R), checks positivity and interiority, and compares N to the live ECF table and cited papers. Minutes.
angles: Conventional: symmetry-orbit ansatz + Levenberg-Marquardt on moment equations with point-elimination (Xiao-Gimbutas node elimination).
Conventional: start from the best known rule and try to delete one orbit, re-solving with Newton.
Cross-domain import (sparse signal recovery): L1 / Caratheodory-Tchakaloff compression of a dense rule (NNLS / LP) to a minimal positive support.
Cross-domain import (molecular conformer search): basin-hopping over orbit parameters with repulsion terms to keep points interior.
Cross-domain import (coding theory): treat rules as designs and use linear-programming bounds to target degrees where the gap to the lower bound is largest.
pitfalls: The ECF tables are stale; many entries were beaten after 2002 - compare against the literature sources too.
Numerical exactness at 1e-12 is not exactness; polish to high precision and check all monomials.
Points on the boundary or slightly outside (I vs O quality) and tiny negative weights disqualify a PI claim.
The ECF point files are password-protected; do not request credentials - use the public overview tables only.

targets.name: KnotInfo: close one of the last interval-valued smooth 4-genus entries (13 crossings) by an explicit ribbon disk or genus-1 cobordism
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: KnotInfo (Charles Livingston and Allison Moore, knotinfo.org) lists the smooth 4-genus of prime knots up to 13 crossings. All entries through 12 crossings are now determined, the last ones by Brittenham and Hermiller, Stoimenow's ribbon searches, Lamm and Herald-Kirk-Livingston. In database_knotinfo 2026.10.5 (the monthly mirror, released 2026-10-05) exactly 19 entries are still intervals, all 13-crossing knots. Six are [0,1]: 13n_65, 13n_3871, 13n_3872, 13n_3897, 13n_3936, 13n_4582. Thirteen are [1,2], e.g. 13a_2554, 13a_2844, 13a_4184, 13n_459, 13n_863, 13n_2496. Dunfield and Gong (arXiv:2512.21825) ran large ribbon and slice-obstruction searches over all 352.2 million prime knots up to 19 crossings and left smooth sliceness undetermined for about 11,400 of them, so the [0,1] cases have survived serious search. Upper bounds are constructive and mechanically checkable. Band moves that produce an unlink certify a ribbon disk. A genus-g cobordism to a slice knot certifies g4 <= g. Can an explicit construction realise the lower bound for one of these 19 knots?
targets.success_criterion: For a knot K whose smooth_four_genus is an interval [a,b] in the live KnotInfo database (https://knotinfo.org/, or its database_knotinfo mirror when that is not older than the site), re-fetched immediately before claiming, and not resolved in any paper the skeptic finds: a saved sequence of band moves on a verified diagram of K that realises the lower bound a. (i) If a = 0: n bands producing an (n+1)-component link that Regina certifies is the unlink (each component unknotted and the link split), which is a ribbon disk. (ii) If a = 1: a genus-1 cobordism, given as band moves, from K to a knot that KnotInfo lists with smooth_four_genus 0. Every intermediate identification must be checked by SnapPy and Regina.

partial_wins.statement: A ribbon certificate in the sense of (i) for a 14- or 15-crossing knot that Dunfield-Gong (arXiv:2512.21825) list as of unknown smooth sliceness, checked the same way.

A concordance, given as band moves checked by SnapPy and Regina, between two of the six [0,1] knots, or between one of them and a knot of 14 or 15 crossings, so that a future ribbon disk for one settles both.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic replays the band moves in SnapPy (link diagrams via PD codes), identifies each result with Regina (unknot/unlink recognition, knot identification), and checks genus bookkeeping. Under 30 minutes.
angles: Conventional: exhaustive search of short bands between diagram arcs (Herald-Kirk-Livingston style computer search for ribbon disks).
Conventional: symmetric-union and 2-bridge ribbon templates (Lisca's classification) applied to near-template knots.
Cross-domain import (reinforcement learning, as in the 'RL for ribbon knots' work): agents choosing band moves with rewards from simplification of hyperbolic volume.
Cross-domain import (graph rewriting / chemistry reaction search): treat band moves as reactions and run beam search over the reaction network with canonical PD hashing.
pitfalls: Topologically slice vs smoothly slice: constructions here are smooth; lower bounds from Freedman-type results do not apply.
Unlink recognition must certify split + trivial components; a link with unknotted components can still be non-trivial.
Several entries were resolved by personal communications or new papers not yet installed; search arXiv before claiming.
The six [0,1] knots have survived Dunfield-Gong's ribbon search; expect long odds and record negative results honestly.

targets.name: KnotInfo: determine an unknotting number currently listed as an interval
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: KnotInfo (Charles Livingston and Allison Moore, knotinfo.org) lists unknotting numbers of prime knots up to 13 crossings. In database_knotinfo 2026.10.5 (the monthly mirror, released 2026-10-05), 4,991 of them are intervals: 10 with 10 crossings, 65 with 11, 548 with 12 and 4,368 with 13. The most common are [1,2] (2,577), [2,3] (1,607), [1,3] (416) and [3,4] (271), e.g. 10_6, 10_11 and 10_47 at [2,3]. Upper bounds come from explicit crossing-change sequences (Jablan-Sazdanović, Brittenham-Hermiller). Lower bounds come from signatures, Heegaard Floer obstructions, and the results of McCoy and Owens as applied by Kawano and Gebel-Pragley. KnotInfo's unknotting-number page says that Dranowski, Kabkov and Tubbenhauer (arXiv:2603.07955, 'RL unknotter, hard unknots and unknotting number', v4 2026-09-09) found new upper bounds on many unknotting numbers, and that 'This work is pending and the results are not installed.' Applebaum et al. (arXiv:2409.09032) also report reinforcement-learning upper bounds. Can an explicit unknotting sequence close an interval, or lower an upper bound below every published one?
targets.success_criterion: For a knot K whose unknotting_number is an interval [a,b] in the live KnotInfo database (https://knotinfo.org/, or its database_knotinfo mirror when that is not older than the site), re-fetched immediately before claiming: a saved planar diagram code D of K, verified as K by SnapPy/Regina identification (mirror image and orientation handled), and a set of c crossings of D whose change gives a diagram that Regina's unknot recognition certifies as the unknot, where c is STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than b and than every upper bound for K published in arXiv:2603.07955, arXiv:2409.09032 or any other source the skeptic finds. c = a closes the interval.

partial_wins.statement: Lower the KnotInfo upper bound b by at least 1 for an interval-valued knot (c < b) with the same certificate, even if c > a and even if a pending published result already matches c (say which).

For a knot listed as [1,2], a single crossing change in some diagram (not necessarily minimal) that Regina certifies yields the unknot. This closes the entry at 1, and is reported separately because it needs no published-bound comparison beyond KnotInfo and the two arXiv papers.

A demonstrated KnotInfo data inconsistency: a certified computation (e.g. |signature|/2, computed reproducibly in SnapPy or Sage from a verified diagram) that exceeds a listed upper bound, or a certified crossing-change sequence shorter than a listed lower bound, with the inputs saved.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic loads D in SnapPy/Regina, confirms identification as K (isometry of hyperbolic exteriors or Regina knot signature), applies the listed crossing changes, and runs Regina's unknot recognition. Minutes.
angles: Conventional: randomised Reidemeister-move diagram exploration (increase crossings, then search all crossing-change subsets) as in Brittenham-Hermiller.
Conventional: crossing changes to a known knot with known u (u(K) <= 1 + u(K')) using KnotInfo's own table for K'.
Cross-domain import (reinforcement learning / game search): MCTS over Reidemeister moves + crossing changes with a cheap value function (signature, determinant, hyperbolic volume).
Cross-domain import (chemistry / molecular dynamics): simulate the knot as a polymer under energy minimisation (KnotPlot-like) to find simplifying diagrams.
Cross-domain import (computer vision hashing): canonical diagram hashing to deduplicate the search space.
pitfalls: Diagram identification errors: mirror images and orientation matter for some invariants; verify the knot type with Regina/SnapPy, not by invariants alone.

Pending published results (Dranowski-Kabkov-Tubbenhauer, arXiv:2603.07955; Applebaum et al., arXiv:2409.09032) may already match or beat your bound; the KnotInfo page says the former are not installed, so check the papers and their data before claiming.
An upper bound equal to the listed lower bound is a win; an upper bound equal to the listed upper bound is not.
Do not email KnotInfo maintainers.

targets.name: Matbench v0.1: beat the per-task leaderboard on a small-data task (steels, jdft2d, expt_gap, glass) with CPU-only models
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Matbench v0.1 (Alexander Dunn, Qi Wang, Alex Ganose, Daniel Dopp and Anubhav Jain, npj Comput. Mater. 6, 138, 2020) scores materials-property models by nested 5-fold cross-validation with fixed folds. Its per-task leaderboards, which include specialised algorithms that the general-purpose front-page table leaves out, list for the four smallest tasks: matbench_steels (312 compositions, yield strength) MAE 79.9468 ± 13.5883 MPa by TPOT-Mat, then AutoML-Mat 82.3043 and MODNet v0.1.12 87.7627; matbench_jdft2d (636 structures, exfoliation energy) MAE 33.1918 ± 7.3428 meV/atom by MODNet v0.1.12; matbench_expt_gap (4,604 compositions) MAE 0.2865 ± 0.0083 eV by Darwin; matbench_glass (5,680 compositions, classification) 0.9603 ± 0.0075 by MODNet v0.1.12. The glass page warns that its listed 'ROC-AUC' values were computed on predictions thresholded at 0.5, so they equal balanced accuracy. These tasks are trainable on a laptop CPU. The six medium-size tasks are a separate entry (matbench-medium-structure-tasks-cpu).
targets.success_criterion: For one of matbench_steels, matbench_jdft2d, matbench_expt_gap or matbench_glass: saved code and per-fold predictions that the skeptic re-runs with the official matbench package (MatbenchBenchmark v0.1, the fixed folds, hyperparameters chosen only inside training folds, no test leakage). The mean score must be STRICTLY BETTER than the best entry on that task's live per-task leaderboard (https://matbench.materialsproject.org/Leaderboards%20Per-Task/matbench_v0.1_<task>/), re-fetched immediately before claiming. Better means: for the three regression tasks, mean MAE lower (direction: min); for matbench_glass, mean balanced accuracy of predictions thresholded at 0.5 higher (direction: max), which is the quantity the page's 'rocauc' column actually reports. The margin must exceed the larger of 2% relative and the best entry's fold standard deviation divided by sqrt(5). The claim must also beat every Matbench-v0.1-protocol score for that task the skeptic finds published.

partial_wins.statement: Beat the per-task leaderboard best on matbench_steels, under the full-win protocol and margin, with a model of under 10,000 learned parameters or a closed-form symbolic formula (e.g. SISSO-like).

One fixed method (no per-task tuning outside training folds) that, under the full-win protocol, scores better than every listed entry except the AutoML pipelines (TPOT-Mat, AutoML-Mat, AMMExpress v2020) on two of the four tasks.
A re-run of the top per-task entry's published code and folds that reproduces a mean score differing from the posted score by more than 2 posted fold standard deviations, with all outputs saved.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic installs matbench, runs the saved script with the official benchmark object (record per fold), recomputes the task's metric (MAE, or balanced accuracy at a 0.5 threshold for glass) from the saved per-fold predictions, compares it with the live per-task leaderboard, and audits that only training-fold data was used for tuning. 10-60 minutes on CPU.
angles: Conventional: Magpie/matminer features + gradient boosting / TabPFN-style ensembles with careful inner-fold tuning.
Conventional: metallurgy-informed features for steels (solid-solution strengthening terms, carbon equivalent, element pair interactions).
Cross-domain import (NLP): pretrained element/composition embeddings (mat2vec) or LLM text embeddings of formulas as features.
Cross-domain import (physics-informed ML / symbolic regression): PySR / SISSO formulae as low-variance models for 300-sample tasks.
Cross-domain import (genomics small-n statistics): Gaussian-process regression with composition kernels and empirical-Bayes hyper-priors.
pitfalls: Test leakage via hyper-parameter tuning on all folds or via deduplicated-composition overlaps; only the official nested protocol counts.
Pretrained models can leak labels: jdft2d comes from JARVIS-DFT, so models pretrained on JARVIS data are suspect there; audit the pretraining data of any pretrained component.
Leaderboard differences within fold std are noise; the margin rule is there for that reason. For glass, the page's rocauc column is balanced accuracy, so compare like with like.
Submitting to the leaderboard needs a GitHub PR - do not submit; claim the verified local result.

targets.name: TPTP: prove (or refute) a problem with status Unknown/Open or rating 1.00, with an independently checked proof
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The TPTP problem library (Geoff Sutcliffe; tptp.org) is at v9.3.1, which the TPTP home page dates Fri 21 Aug 2026 (the distribution tarball was last modified 2026-09-08 and the BuggedProblems list 2026-10-21); it is still the current release on 2026-10-28. It annotates each problem with an SZS status (Theorem, Unsatisfiable, Satisfiable, CounterSatisfiable, Unknown, Open, ...) and a difficulty rating. Rating 1.00 means no system solved the problem in the rating runs. Status Unknown or Open means the library knows no proof or countermodel. These are machine-readable frontiers for automated reasoning. Can an independently verified proof, or a finite countermodel, be produced for such a problem?
targets.success_criterion: For a TPTP problem whose header in the live library (https://seetptp.tptp.org/?folder=TPTPWorld/TPTP/Problems/, re-fetched immediately before claiming) shows Status Unknown or Open, or Rating 1.00, and that is not listed in BuggedProblems for that version: either (a) a saved TSTP derivation of the conjecture, or of a contradiction for CNF/unsatisfiability problems, whose every inference step is independently checked (GDV-style step verification by a different prover, or reconstruction in Isabelle/Metis or Lean), or (b) for a Satisfiable or CounterSatisfiable claim, a saved finite model checked by an independent model evaluator against all axioms and the negated conjecture. For a Rating 1.00 problem the claim counts only if no system's solution for it appears in the TSTP solution library on SeeTPTP for the current version.

partial_wins.statement: A checked proof of a rating >= 0.95 Theorem problem with a non-trivial derivation produced on a laptop in < 4 h.
A finite countermodel (size <= 20) for a problem with status Unknown, checked by an independent evaluator.
A checked proof of an Open problem in a single domain (e.g. LAT, GRP, ALG) using a lemma-discovery loop, with all lemmas also checked.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the problem file, re-runs the proof checker (e.g. GDV or re-proving each inference step with E/Vampire in a short time limit, or Isabelle reconstruction), or evaluates the model; confirms status/rating in the live header. Under 1 hour.
angles: Conventional: long runs of Vampire/E/iProver portfolios with tuned strategies (CASC schedules) on the 10 cores, plus Mace4/Paradox for countermodels.
Conventional: axiom selection (SInE/premise selection) for large-theory problems that fail by timeout.
Cross-domain import (program synthesis / AlphaProof-style): LLM-proposed intermediate lemmas, each discharged by an ATP, assembled into a checked derivation.
Cross-domain import (computer algebra): Knuth-Bendix completion / Groebner-style rewriting for equational ALG/GRP/LAT problems (Waldmeister-style ordered completion).
Cross-domain import (SAT solving): finite model finding by SAT encoding with symmetry breaking for countermodels.
pitfalls: Rating 1.00 is relative to the systems in the rating runs; newer provers may already solve it - check the latest CASC results and SystemOnTPTP solutions (TSTP library) first.
Unsound proof steps (prover bugs, mis-parsed input, axioms dropped by selection) - only an independent check counts.
Bugged problems (BuggedProblems list) and problems with inconsistent axioms make 'proofs' trivial.
Do not submit to TPTP/SystemOnTPTP web services; run locally.

targets.name: Relevant variables of degree-d Boolean functions (C_44): beat the 3/2 lower bound with an explicit function
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Tao's optimization-constants repository, constant 44: R_d is the maximum number of relevant variables of a Boolean function f:{0,1}^n -> {0,1} whose real multilinear degree is at most d, and C_44 = sup_d R_d / 2^d. Upper bounds: 6.614 (Chiarelli-Hatami-Saks 2020), 4.416 (Wellens 2019), 4.394 (Wellens, Discrete Analysis 2022, best published), then two unrefereed exact-certificate refinements of Wellens's recurrence listed with asterisks: 4.3654674227* (BakeLab/Epi, reviewed 11 Sep 2026) and 4.3576549226* (Ricardo Pinho, 23 Oct 2026, degree-three weighted cap 5/4). Lower bound 3/2 from the Chiarelli-Hatami-Saks construction R_d >= 3*2^{d-1} - 2 (also observed by Shinkar and Tal), unchanged on the page as of 2026-10-28. Exact small values: R_3 = 10 (Tarannikov-Kirienko via the translation R_d = p(d+1) to correlation-immune functions, cf. Krotov-Valyuzhenich 2024). Target: an explicit Boolean function f of some degree d with more than 1.5 * 2^d relevant variables, or (partial) a new record R_4 >= 23.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit Boolean function f (truth table, or a circuit/decision tree that is expanded to a truth table) on n variables such that (i) its multilinear polynomial over the reals, computed exactly by Mobius inversion of the truth table, has degree d, (ii) all n variables are relevant, and (iii) n / 2^d is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the lower bound listed on the live page https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/44a.html and in any open pull request touching constants/44a.md at https://github.com/teorth/optimizationproblems/pulls, both re-fetched live immediately before claiming. An infinite family counts if a proof of the recursion is supplied and its base case is checked by computer.

partial_wins.statement: A degree-4 Boolean function with at least 23 relevant variables (beating the CHS value 22 = 3*2^3 - 2 at d = 4), provided a literature search (correlation-immune / resilient function tables, the quantity p(5)) shows 23 is not already known.
A computer proof that R_4 = 22 (or the exact value of R_4), with a checkable certificate (for example an ILP/SAT unsatisfiability proof with DRAT/LRAT output).

targets.verification_method: Given the truth table on n <= 30 variables, compute the Mobius transform over the reals (integer arithmetic) in O(n 2^n), read off the maximal monomial size, and check each variable appears in some nonzero monomial. Two independent implementations (e.g. numpy and a C bit-sliced version). Seconds to minutes.
angles: Search in the correlation-immune world: by the R_d = p(d+1) translation, look for unbalanced perfect colourings / correlation-immune functions of the needed order with more variables, using the Krotov-Valyuzhenich framework and existing tables.

Composition: study which compositions f(g_1,...,g_k) multiply degree and relevant-variable counts favourably; the CHS construction is a recursion, so a better base case at d = 4 or 5 may lift to all d.

Cross-domain import (cryptography): resilient and plateaued Boolean functions are designed for spectral constraints that are equivalent to low Fourier degree on subcubes; port cryptographic search tools (e.g. evolutionary search for bent/resilient functions) with degree as a hard constraint.

Cross-domain import (SAT/ILP): encode 'degree <= 4' as linear constraints on the truth table (all Mobius coefficients of size >= 5 vanish) and maximise the number of relevant variables with an ILP solver on n = 23..25; symmetry-break by assuming invariance under a chosen permutation group to shrink the search.
Decision-tree view: functions with small decision-tree depth have small degree; search non-read-once trees and sensitivity-style constructions where the degree is less than the depth.
pitfalls: Degree over GF(2) vs over R: the constant uses the real multilinear degree; algebraic degree over GF(2) is different and usually smaller.
A variable that appears only in cancelled monomials is not relevant; check by Mobius coefficients, not by syntactic occurrence in a formula.
R_d / 2^d > 3/2 must hold strictly; 3*2^{d-1}-2 approaches 3/2 from below, so matching the CHS family at a larger d is not a win.
Known values in another language: correlation-immunity tables may already list the value you find; search that literature before claiming p1.

targets.name: Centred Hardy-Littlewood maximal constant for squares in the plane (C_47): a measure beating Lin's 1.6855099933
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Tao's optimization-constants repository, constant 47: c_2 is the optimal weak-type (1,1) constant of the centred maximal operator over axis-parallel squares in R^2. No best constant is known in any dimension d > 1 (Melas solved d = 1: (11+sqrt 61)/12). Bounds: upper 3.879 (Yongxi Lin 2026, Lean-formalised, improving the covering bound 4); lower bound Phi ~ 1.6855099933 (Lin 2026, Lean on Palomar), from a periodic measure with masses 1 and w = (17+4 sqrt 22)/9 on alternating columns, improving Aldaz's 1.6211915 (2000). Discretisation (Aldaz 2011) means sums of Dirac masses suffice. Target: an explicit (finite or periodic) measure giving a strictly larger certified lower bound.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit measure mu (finitely many point masses, or a periodic arrangement with a finite period cell) with exact algebraic or rational parameters, plus a proof-carrying computation showing alpha |{x : M mu(x) >= alpha}| / ||mu|| > L, where L is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the largest lower bound on the live page https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/47a.html and in any open pull request touching constants/47a.md at https://github.com/teorth/optimizationproblems/pulls, both re-fetched live immediately before claiming. The area of the super-level set must be computed exactly (polygonal regions bounded by lines where square averages equal alpha, which for point masses are piecewise axis-parallel/diagonal) or enclosed by interval arithmetic with a strictly positive margin, in two independent implementations. For periodic measures the reduction to a period cell must be stated and checked.

partial_wins.statement: A rigorous upper bound on the best ratio achievable within Lin's two-mass alternating-column family (all choices of the two masses, column spacing h and row spacing V), showing the family is exhausted (a computer-assisted proof).

targets.verification_method: For point masses at exact coordinates: the maximal function at x is a max over finitely many critical side lengths (where the square boundary hits a mass), so {M mu >= alpha} is a finite union of polygons computable exactly with rational/algebraic arithmetic (e.g. in Sage or with interval arithmetic on a fine adaptive grid with certified inclusion). Two implementations must agree; compare to the live record.
angles: Generalise Lin's lattice: three or more mass values, non-rectangular periodic lattices (sheared or rotated by 45 degrees), and optimise parameters by gradient-free search on the exact area functional.
Lift Melas's one-dimensional extremisers: products and tensorised versions of the d = 1 extremal configurations, then perturb.

Cross-domain import (crystallography / sphere packing): treat the period cell as a crystal and search space groups (wallpaper groups) for the mass arrangement, as packing records are found by symmetry-constrained search.

Cross-domain import (topology optimisation in engineering): represent the measure as a density on a fine grid, optimise the smoothed ratio with adjoint gradients, then 'snap' the result to point masses and certify exactly.
Use the Lean development in Lin's repository as a template for a formal certificate once a numeric improvement is found.
pitfalls: Wrong operator: the constant is for centred squares (l_inf balls), not Euclidean discs or uncentred squares; Lin's repository also has disc bounds that are a different constant.
Normalisation: weak type (1,1) uses alpha |{M f >= alpha}| / ||f||_1; using > alpha vs >= alpha or forgetting to divide by the period-cell mass inflates the ratio.
Grid estimates of the area: sampling the plane on a grid gives a number, not a bound; the area must be exact or rigorously enclosed.
Periodic measures are infinite: the reduction to one period cell must be justified (as in Lin's construction) or a finite truncation with boundary loss accounted for.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Earth-Moon problem: a biplanar (thickness-2) graph with chromatic number 10
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Ringel's Earth-Moon problem asks for the largest chromatic number of a biplanar graph (edges split into two planar graphs). Euler's formula gives an upper bound of 12; Sulanke (1980, via Gardner) found a 9-chromatic biplanar graph (the join of K_6 and C_5, 11 vertices); Gethner conjectures the answer is 11. Tao's constant 27b lists 9 <= C_27b <= 12, and Epoch AI's FrontierMath open-problems page lists 'construct a biplanar graph with chromatic number at least 10' as unsolved. Target: an explicit biplanar graph with chromatic number at least 10.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit graph G with an explicit partition of its edges into E1 and E2, such that (i) (V,E1) and (V,E2) are each certified planar by two independent planarity testers (e.g. networkx check_planarity and Boost/OGDF, with the combinatorial embeddings saved and re-checked by Euler's formula on the rotation systems), and (ii) G is not 9-colourable, proven by a SAT solver's UNSAT result with a DRAT/LRAT proof checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr on a CNF regenerated by the skeptic. The live pages https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/27b.html and https://epoch.ai/frontiermath/open-problems/earth-moon must still list 9 as the best lower bound / the problem as unsolved, re-fetched live immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: A biplanar graph with fractional chromatic number strictly greater than 8.5 (the value for K_6 + C_5) and above any value found in a literature search on fractional colourings of thickness-two graphs, certified by an exact rational LP solution of the fractional colouring LP and its dual.
A 9-critical biplanar graph not isomorphic to any graph in Boutin-Gethner-Sulanke's published lists (checked by canonical labelling), with exact verification of criticality and biplanarity.

targets.verification_method: Check each edge class for planarity (two independent implementations, plus Euler-formula check on the produced embeddings); check that E1 and E2 partition E; build the 9-colouring CNF with symmetry breaking on a clique, solve with proof logging, verify the proof. Minutes to an hour for graphs up to a few hundred vertices.
angles: Search graphs with independence number small relative to n: chi >= n / alpha, so a biplanar graph with n > 9 alpha forces 10 colours; biplanar graphs have fewer than 6n edges, so search dense near-6n-edge graphs (blow-ups and joins of planar triangulations) with small alpha via SAT.

Join constructions: K_6 + C_5 is a join; search joins and generalised joins of small planar pieces whose two planar layers can absorb the cross edges, using SAT with planarity encoded through Schnyder woods or a fixed rotation system.

Cross-domain import (VLSI two-layer routing): a biplanar graph is a two-layer wiring with no vias; reuse two-layer routing heuristics to decide whether a candidate dense graph splits into two planar layers.

Cross-domain import (frequency assignment in cellular networks): interference graphs of two overlaid planar cell layouts are biplanar; known hard instances for frequency assignment may contain high chromatic structure.
Fractional relaxation first (partial win p1): maximise n/alpha-type LP bounds, which guide the search toward graphs that can possibly need 10 colours.
pitfalls: Thickness vs biplanarity on the sphere vs plane is the same, but 'Earth-Moon' variants with countries of several regions are different problems; the target is graphs of thickness at most 2.
A planarity claim from a drawing is not a proof; use two independent planarity algorithms and check the embeddings.
Unverified UNSAT: a solver saying 'not 9-colourable' must come with a checked DRAT/LRAT proof.
Multigraph edges or loops created by merging vertices are not allowed; the graph must be simple.

targets.name: Erdos #213: eight points in the plane, no three on a line, no four on a circle, all distances integers
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Are there n points in the plane, no three collinear and no four concyclic, with all pairwise distances integers, for every n?
