Anning and Erdos (1945) showed no infinite set exists; Harborth found n = 5; the best known is n = 7, found by Kreisel and Kurz (2008) by computer search. Greenfeld, Iliopoulou and Peluse (2024) showed such sets in [-N,N]^2 have size (log N)^{O(1)}; Ascher, Braune and Turchet showed a uniform bound conditional on Bombieri-Lang. A September 2026 forum post reports AI-assisted relaxed searches for n = 8 only found sets with all points on a line or circle. Target: an explicit 8-point set in general position with integer distances.
targets.success_criterion: Success means 8 points given by exact coordinates (integer distances force coordinates of the form (a, b sqrt(q)) up to rigid motion; give them in that exact form) such that, in exact integer arithmetic: all 28 pairwise squared distances are perfect squares of positive integers, no three points are collinear (all orientation determinants nonzero), and no four points are concyclic (all 70 four-point incircle determinants nonzero). The live page https://www.erdosproblems.com/213 (and its forum thread) must still report 7 as the best construction, re-fetched live immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: A 7-point integral set in general position with a smaller diameter than every 7-point example in the literature (Kreisel-Kurz 2008 and later work by Kurz and coauthors, located by literature search before claiming), with exact verification.

An 8-point integral set with no three collinear and at most one concyclic quadruple (strictly better than the forum's reported C+Q = 5 relaxation), verified exactly; labelled as a relaxation, not a solution.

targets.verification_method: Check squared distances are integer squares (isqrt), orientation determinants nonzero, and the 4x4 concyclicity determinants (x^2+y^2, x, y, 1) nonzero, all in exact integers after scaling sqrt(q) components. Instant.
angles: Follow Kreisel-Kurz: all points share a characteristic (squarefree q with coordinates in Z x sqrt(q) Z); enumerate Heronian triangles with a fixed characteristic and grow cliques of mutually integral points, pruning collinear and concyclic configurations; push the diameter bound and the set of characteristics further with modern hardware.

Cross-domain import (database joins / clique search): the problem is a maximum-clique search in the 'integer distance' graph on candidate points; use bitset clique solvers (as in coding-theory record searches) with incremental candidate generation.

Cross-domain import (elliptic curves): adding a point at integer distances to three fixed points is a rational point problem on a curve; use Mordell-Weil generators of the associated elliptic curves to produce candidates instead of brute force.
Extend each known 7-point set: for each, search for an 8th point with integer distances to all 7 via the elliptic-curve parametrisation of points at integer distance from two fixed points.
Search characteristic-mixed relaxations first (allow exactly one concyclic quadruple) to learn structure, as the forum post began.
pitfalls: Concyclic quadruples are easy to miss: all 70 four-point subsets must be checked with an exact determinant, not a floating-point circle fit.
Collinear triples hidden by scaling: check orientation determinants exactly after clearing sqrt(q).
Sets with almost all points on a line or circle (Anning-Erdos families) satisfy integrality but not general position.
Floating-point distances that are 'almost integers' (1e-9 off) are not integer distances.

targets.name: Erdos #513 (maximum-term constant C_51): a transcendental entire function with liminf mu(r)/M(r) above the record
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: For transcendental entire f, beta(f) = liminf_{r->inf} mu(r,f)/M(r,f), where mu is the largest term |a_n| r^n and M the maximum modulus. B = sup beta(f) (Erdos #513, Tao's constant 51) satisfies 4/7 < B <= 2/pi - c (Clunie-Hayman 1964). He and Tang (arXiv:2602.12217) generalised the Clunie-Hayman scaling-identity construction to a two-parameter family and certified B > 0.5850724 with ball arithmetic; Sothanaphan's GPT-assisted run nudged it to 0.5850788 and reported that more ambitious attempts failed; open pull request #184 claims 0.5850788196744* with exact parameters in the same family. The He-Tang family looks exhausted; a real improvement needs a new family. Target: a certified lower bound strictly above the best live value.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit construction of a transcendental entire function f (or a family with a proven formula for beta(f), as in He-Tang's identity beta = 1/max_{|z|=1}|k(z)|) together with a rigorous ball/interval-arithmetic certificate that beta(f) >= L with L STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the largest lower bound listed on the live page https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/51a.html and in any open pull request touching constants/51a.md at https://github.com/teorth/optimizationproblems/pulls, both re-fetched live immediately before claiming, by at least 1e-9. The proof of the reduction from beta(f) to the certified quantity must be written out and checked by the skeptic; the maximum over the circle must be enclosed rigorously (not sampled).

partial_wins.statement: A new multi-parameter generalisation of the Clunie-Hayman/He-Tang construction (three or more parameters) with a proven beta-formula that reproduces the record within the new family, even if it does not beat it.
An independent rigorous replay of the open PR #184 value (exact parameters, circle maximum enclosed by arb), confirming or refuting it.

targets.verification_method: Recompute max_{|z|=1}|k(z)| for the stated Laurent series k with arb (python-flint) using a certified branch-and-bound on the circle and an explicit tail bound for the series; check the claimed functional identity numerically on random points as a sanity check; compare 1/max to the live record.
angles: Replace the single scaling identity k(Kz) = (stuff) k(z) by a two-scale or matrix-valued identity (a vector of Laurent series satisfying a linear system under z -> Kz), which still allows exact M(r) on a geometric sequence of radii.

Cross-domain import (signal processing, filter design): maximising the peak term against the sup norm on the circle is a 'peak-to-average' problem; borrow Chebyshev/minimax filter design (Remez exchange) to shape |k| on |z| = 1.

Cross-domain import (dynamical systems): the scaling identity is a renormalisation fixed point; look for other fixed points of the renormalisation operator by Newton's method in a space of Laurent coefficients.
Upper-bound side for context: work out the explicit c in Clunie-Hayman's 2/pi - c (noted as missing on the forum); a numeric value would bound how much room there is.
Gap structure: use lacunary power series with geometrically growing gaps where mu and M are both controlled by a few dominant terms, then optimise the coefficients.
pitfalls: Polynomials are excluded (they give 1); truncations used in computations must still correspond to a transcendental function with the stated liminf.
Sampling the circle: max |k(z)| on |z| = 1 must be enclosed rigorously; a sampled max underestimates it and overstates beta.
liminf vs limsup: the ratio along a favourable sequence of radii only bounds limsup; the reduction must control all large r.
Rounding: records differ in the 7th-12th decimal; compare exact or certified values, not printed roundings, and include open PR #184.

targets.name: Furstenberg-Sarkozy exponent C_4b: a larger square-difference-free set exponent
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Tao's optimization-constants repository, constant 4b: C_4b is the least constant with r(N) <= N^{C_4b+o(1)}, where r(N) is the largest subset of {1..N} with no difference equal to a nonzero perfect square. For forty years the lower bound sat near 0.7334 (Ruzsa 1984; Beigel-Gasarch 2008 / Lewko 2015, base 205). In August-October 2026 it moved fast: Krachun 0.752796 (Paley chains, arXiv:2608.01325), JD Jones 0.753742 and 0.75806770413 (Lean-formalised), Naslund 0.75806746 and then 0.7580758 (exact 473797394875551/625000000000000; interval-moment criterion with new finite witnesses, Hexagon preprint 2610.00151, Lean on Palomar), which is now the page record after pull request #219 was merged on 18 Oct 2026. Naslund notes this is close to the limit of the current approach. The page also records OpenAI's first power-saving upper bound C_4b <= 1 - c (preprint of 24 Sep 2026), with no useful numerical c. As of 2026-10-28 no open pull request touches constants/4b.md. Target: a certified lower bound strictly above the best live value, including open pull requests.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a construction (base-expansion components, chains, codes or a new mechanism) with an exact rational exponent alpha and a machine-checkable certificate showing r(N) >= c N^alpha for all large N, such that alpha is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the largest lower bound listed on the live page https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/4b.html and in any open pull request at https://github.com/teorth/optimizationproblems/pulls touching constants/4b.md, both re-fetched live immediately before claiming. The certificate must be checked in exact arithmetic by an independent verifier written from the criterion's statement (for interval-moment constructions: every modular square edge respects the interval order, every moment inequality holds exactly, and sum of moment powers exceeds alpha), and a brute-force check must confirm that the finite blocks are square-difference-free modulo their bases.

partial_wins.statement: A strictly better finite component for an existing criterion (for example a longer Paley chain at some prime p = 3 mod 4, or a composite-modulus digraph with larger longest-path ratio) that provably increases that component's moment power, even if the total exponent does not pass the record.

targets.verification_method: Recompute every finite object: for each component (base m, digit set or chain), check all pairwise differences of residues for being nonzero squares mod m (or mod p for each prime factor), check the claimed interval/moment inequalities in exact rationals, and recompute alpha. Optionally build the set for N up to 10^7 and verify no square difference by a sieve over squares. Minutes on a laptop.
angles: Search new components: exhaustive or SAT search for longest Paley-type chains (every forward difference a nonzero square mod p) at primes p = 3 mod 4 beyond 103, and for acyclic square-difference digraphs on square-free composite moduli (the 235 and 299 examples came from such searches).

Cross-domain import (scheduling / longest-path in DAGs): the interval-moment criterion is an interval-scheduling problem on a digraph; use LP duality to find the optimal widths for a fixed digit set, then local-search the digit set.

Cross-domain import (coding theory): the composite three-low-digit codes at 215^6 and 437^6 are codes avoiding a 'square difference' metric; search better codes with clique-finding (cliquer / max-clique on the compatibility graph) as for constant-weight code records.

Re-optimise the binary 25-state recursion: treat its transition weights as a matrix and maximise the spectral radius (growth factor) with exact rational certification, as the 0.75806770413 entry did by reallocation.
Look for a genuinely new mechanism (e.g. using residues mod p^2 that are non-squares but where higher digits repair the difference) since Naslund reports the current approach is near its limit.
pitfalls: Confusing the finite-N record with the exponent: a large finite set does not prove an exponent; only a construction valid for all N does.

Squares modulo m vs squares in Z: a block free of square differences mod m may still have differences that are squares in Z when digits carry; the criterion's lifting lemma must actually apply to the new component.
Ignoring pending pull requests: always check open PRs touching constants/4b.md; beating an older page value (for example 0.75806770413) is not a record once 0.7580758 is listed.
Floating-point exponents: the record entries are exact rationals; compare exactly, not to 6 decimals.
Using composite moduli where 'z^2 mod m' squares include zero divisors without checking the lemma's hypotheses (the Jones construction states 'any nonzero z^2 mod m counts as a square').

targets.name: Hadwiger-Nelson finite witnesses (Erdos #508 context): a 5-chromatic unit-distance graph with fewer than 509 vertices
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The chromatic number of the plane (Erdos #508, Tao's constant 27a) is now known to be 6 or 7: OpenAI's preprint 'The Euclidean plane is not five-colorable' (23 Sep 2026, Lean formalisation in github.com/openai/math, linked from erdosproblems.com/508, which lists 6 <= chi <= 7) proves no proper 5-colouring exists. That proof is non-constructive (a measurable-transfer argument plus graph compactness), so it exhibits no small finite graph. The finite-witness record question for 5 colours remains: de Grey's 2018 1581-vertex graph first showed chi >= 5; Heule's SAT-based shrinking reached 553 vertices and Parts (arXiv:2010.12665) reached 509 vertices and 2442 edges, which MathWorld's de Grey graphs page (last updated 27 Oct 2026) still lists as the smallest known 5-chromatic unit-distance graph; Haugland 2026 (arXiv:2608.04542) gives a larger Moser-spindle-free example. Lower bounds on the order of such graphs are studied in arXiv:2303.14714. Target: a unit-distance graph in the plane with chromatic number 5 (not 4-colourable) and fewer vertices than the live record.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit graph G with exact algebraic coordinates for each vertex (in a stated number field, e.g. Q(sqrt3, sqrt5, sqrt11, ...)), such that (i) all vertices are distinct, (ii) every listed edge joins two points at distance exactly 1 (exact arithmetic), (iii) G is not 4-colourable, proven by a SAT solver's UNSAT result with a DRAT or LRAT proof checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr, and (iv) the number of vertices is STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the smallest 5-chromatic unit-distance graph reported on the live page https://mathworld.wolfram.com/deGreyGraphs.html, the Wikipedia Hadwiger-Nelson page, the Polymath16 wiki and any newer arXiv paper (search 'unit distance graph chromatic number 5'), all re-fetched live immediately before claiming. Graphs on a sphere or in higher dimensions do not count.

partial_wins.statement: A 5-chromatic unit-distance graph with at most 509 vertices and fewer than 2442 edges, with the same exact-coordinate and DRAT/LRAT checks.
An exact recount/recheck of Parts' 509-vertex graph from its published coordinates that confirms or corrects the record (replay note).

targets.verification_method: Parse coordinates as exact algebraic numbers (sympy/Sage); check pairwise distinctness and that each edge has squared length exactly 1 (and optionally add all unit pairs present, which can only help non-colourability); encode 4-colouring as CNF with symmetry breaking on a known triangle; run CaDiCaL/kissat with proof output; check the proof with drat-trim or an LRAT checker. Minutes to an hour.
angles: SAT-core shrinking with stronger tools: compute minimal unsatisfiable cores of the 4-colouring CNF of Parts' graph with modern MUS extractors and different symmetry breaking; then re-add unit pairs that appear 'for free' between remaining vertices.

Rebuild from different spindles: Parts' method uses specific 'gadget' subgraphs forcing monochromatic pairs at certain distances; search new gadgets in other algebraic fields (e.g. involving sqrt 7 or sqrt 33).

Cross-domain import (VLSI circuit minimisation): treat vertex removal as logic minimisation with don't-cares; iterative 'remove, re-solve, keep if still UNSAT' with learned clause reuse (incremental SAT) is how circuit minimisers scale.

Cross-domain import (protein design / inverse folding): the graph must stay realisable while losing vertices; alternate a combinatorial step (drop a vertex set) with a continuous realisation step (keep unit edges exact via algebraic closure), like sequence-structure co-design.
Use rotations by angles whose cosines lie in the existing field to create many new unit coincidences in a small Minkowski sum before pruning.
pitfalls: Numerical unit distances: an edge at distance 1 + 1e-15 is not an edge; coordinates must be exact algebraic numbers.
Abstract vs geometric: a graph that is 4-chromatic-free as an abstract graph but not realisable as a unit-distance graph (or realisable only with coincident vertices) does not count.
Unchecked UNSAT: the solver's verdict alone is not enough; the DRAT/LRAT proof must be verified, and the CNF must be regenerated from the coordinates by the skeptic.
Counting the record wrongly: the record is by vertices (509); edge-count improvements are only partial win p1.

Wrong target: since chi(R^2) >= 6 is now proved, a smaller 5-chromatic graph is a finite-witness record, not progress on the 6-vs-7 question; a 6-chromatic finite graph is a different question (see the separate Hadwiger-Nelson six-or-seven proposal).

targets.name: Kakeya-type sum-difference constants C_3b and C_3c: beat the entropy-certificate lower bounds
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Tao's optimization-constants repository, constants 3b and 3c (Katz-Tao arithmetic Kakeya). C_3b is the least exponent with |A -_G B| <= max(|A|,|B|,|A +_G B|)^{C_3b}; equivalently (entropy form) H(X-Y) <= C_3b max(H(X),H(Y),H(X+Y)) for all discrete random variables X, Y. Every recent lower bound is an explicit finite joint distribution of (X,Y): 3b stands at 1.77898884 (Mosaic Intelligence, 13-point support, independently replayed by Toledo; Lemm 2015 had 1.77898; AlphaEvolve improved the 8th decimal) with upper bound 2 - 1/6. C_3c adds the constraint H(X+2Y): after pull request #221 was merged on 18 Oct 2026 the page record is 1.674894211307116 (Manvir Jaswal, n = 10^20 independent base-55 digits drawn from two laws on 51 and 47 points, independently replayed by Toledo), a jump of 1.6e-4 over Lin's 1.6747338950414058 (147-point support) after months of 1e-11 gains; PR #216 (merged) removed the asterisks on 3b and 3c. Upper bound for 3c: 2 - 1/4. As of 2026-10-28 the only open PR touching these pages (#282) corrects the 3b definition, not a bound. Target: a larger certified lower bound for C_3b (main), or for C_3c beyond the best live value including open pull requests.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit integer-valued law for (X,Y) with exact rational probabilities, saved as a file, given EITHER (a) as a finitely supported joint distribution, OR (b) as a product construction X = sum_i b^i X_i, Y = sum_i b^i Y_i of independent digit pairs (X_i, Y_i) drawn from finitely many explicit component laws (each saved as a file with exact rational weights) with stated exact multiplicities, where b >= 2K+1 and K is the largest absolute value taken on any component support by x, y, x+y, x-y (and, for 3c, x+2y), so that every form's digit map is injective and each entropy equals the multiplicity-weighted sum of the component entropies (the mechanism of Jaswal's 3c record, PR #221). The ratio H(X-Y) / max(H(X),H(Y),H(X+Y)) (for 3b; for 3c the max also includes H(X+2Y)) must be certified by outward-rounded interval arithmetic in two independent implementations to be STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the largest lower bound for that constant on the live page (https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/3b.html or .../3c.html) AND in any open pull request at https://github.com/teorth/optimizationproblems/pulls touching that constant, all re-fetched live immediately before claiming, by at least 1e-9 for 3b and 1e-9 for 3c. The entropies are computed from exact pushforward distributions (all collisions in X-Y, X+Y, X+2Y merged exactly) of the finite law in case (a), or of each component law in case (b), where the injectivity bound b >= 2K+1 is also checked exactly. A main win is on 3b; a 3c win must beat the best live 3c value (1.674894211307116 as of 2026-10-28, or any later value or open PR).

partial_wins.statement: A C_3b certificate that beats 1.77898884 by less than 1e-9 but strictly, under the same exact-pushforward interval verification (an exact sub-threshold record).

A C_3c certificate that beats the live 3c record (1.674894211307116 as of 2026-10-28) by less than 1e-9 but strictly, under the same exact-pushforward interval verification (an exact sub-threshold record).

targets.verification_method: Read the support points and rational weights (for a product construction: each component law, its multiplicity and the base b). Compute pushforwards of X, Y, X+Y, X-Y (and X+2Y) with exact rational masses keyed by exact integer values, per component in the product case, and check b >= 2K+1 exactly. Evaluate -sum p log p with mpmath interval arithmetic (or arb) at 100+ bits in two independent codes, combining component entropies with their exact multiplicities. Compare the ratio's lower endpoint to the live record. Runs in seconds for finite supports (or component supports) up to 10^5 points.
angles: Port the 'two independent digit laws' idea of Jaswal's merged 3c record (PR #221) to 3b: take X, Y as sums of independent scaled copies (base-b digits) of two different small distributions and optimise the pair jointly; entropy is additive under such products only when no carries collide, so search for bases where carries are rare.

Grow the 13-point support by continuation: start from the published 13-point certificate, add points one at a time on a lattice neighbourhood and re-optimise weights by mirror descent on the ratio (a smooth objective once the max is replaced by a soft-max).

Cross-domain import (information theory, channel capacity / Blahut-Arimoto): the problem is a max of a ratio of entropies over a polytope of joint distributions; alternating-maximisation updates of Blahut-Arimoto type often find better fixed points than generic gradient methods.

Cross-domain import (statistical physics): treat log-weights as a field on Z^2 and anneal (parallel tempering) with the ratio as negative energy; low-temperature samples tend to form quasi-periodic, self-similar supports like the record certificates.
Exploit the known structure behind Lemm's and Ruzsa's constructions (product sets in high dimensions projected to Z) and search over projection vectors rather than point weights.
pitfalls: Rounding the weights after optimisation: the claimed ratio must be recomputed from the exact rational weights that are published, not from the floats used in the search.
Missing collisions: X-Y and X+Y pushforwards must merge equal values exactly; hashing floats of x-y can split one atom into two and inflate H(X-Y).

Mixing up the constants: 3b uses max(H(X),H(Y),H(X+Y)); 3c adds H(X+2Y); 3a (Gyarmati-Hennecart-Ruzsa, already a separate target) has a different normalisation. A 3c-type distribution scored with the 3b formula is not a 3b record.
Beating the page while an open pull request already claims more: the bar is the maximum over the page and open PRs.
Natural log vs log base 2 does not matter for the ratio, but mixing them between numerator and denominator does.

targets.name: Romanoff's constant C_45: a smaller certified upper bound for the density of odd n = p + 2^k
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Tao's optimization-constants repository, constant 45: C_45 is the asymptotic density of odd integers of the form p + 2^k (p prime, k >= 0). Erdos (1950) showed it is below 1/2 using covering congruences; later upper bounds are finite 'obstruction certificates': choose a finite prime set P, look at residue classes a mod M = prod P, count how many exponents r mod T = lcm ord_q(2) keep a - 2^r coprime to M, and sum a sieve-type bound. Records on the page: 0.490941 (Habsieger-Roblot 2006), 0.490341088858244 (Chen-Dai-Li 2024), 0.490249407811155 (Griego 2026, 36 primes), 0.490180063290061 (Andrew Yoo 2026, 38 primes, optimised from Griego's set, exact-rational verifier). Open pull request #281 (27 Oct 2026) claims 0.489596115074071 with 39 primes (a 21-prime base with orders dividing T_0 = 5040, Yoo's 14 plus 43, 127, 241, 113, 109, 97, 151, together with the union of Griego's and Yoo's clusters), checked by two independently written checkers that also reproduce Griego's and Yoo's values. Lower bound 0.107648 (Elsholtz-Schlage-Puchta 2018). Target: a strictly smaller certified upper bound than the best of the page and open PRs (main), or a better lower bound (moonshot side). Variants appear as Erdos problems #205, #244 and #851.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a finite prime set P and a verifier that computes, in exact rational arithmetic with a rigorous lower bound for log 2, an upper bound U on the upper density of {odd n : n = p + 2^k} via the obstruction inequality printed on the live page https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/45a.html, with U STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the smallest upper bound listed on that page and in any open pull request touching constants/45a.md at https://github.com/teorth/optimizationproblems/pulls, both re-fetched live immediately before claiming. The skeptic re-derives the residue histogram with an independently written program (at least for a seed subset of primes, plus exact replay of the cluster-update step) and recomputes U. A lower-bound improvement above the page's best lower bound also counts, with its full proof.

partial_wins.statement: An independent from-scratch reimplementation that reproduces the open PR #281 value 0.489596115074071 exactly (same rational) from its stated 39-prime set, or finds an error in it, documented as a replay note (not a record).

targets.verification_method: Clone the published verifier style (Griego's repository describes seed histogram + exact coprime-order cluster updates); rewrite the histogram step independently in another language for the first 13-20 primes and cross-check; run the exact-rational evaluation and compare to the live record. Expected minutes to an hour on a laptop.
angles: Prime-set search: add primes q whose multiplicative order of 2 divides the current T (cheap to add because T does not grow), e.g. Mersenne and Fermat-type factors of 2^d - 1 for d | T; this is how covering-system builders choose moduli.

Cross-domain import (combinatorial optimisation / feature selection): treat the choice of P as subset selection with an expensive objective; use beam search or simulated annealing with a cheap surrogate (the seed-histogram bound) and certify only the best candidates exactly.

Cross-domain import (covering systems research, Erdos #7 and Hough's work): reuse the large lists of moduli with small lcm used in covering-system searches to pick primes with highly composite ord_q(2).
Change T: allow T to be a multiple of the lcm (padding) so more primes fit with the same structure; check whether the inequality benefits from coarser exponent classes.
Lower-bound side: re-run the Elsholtz-Schlage-Puchta counting with a better Selberg-sieve upper bound for pairs p1 + 2^{k1} = p2 + 2^{k2}, computed numerically with rigorous error terms.
pitfalls: Floating-point log 2: the bound needs a rigorous lower bound for log 2; using double log(2) can flip the last digits.
Silently changing the inequality: the obstruction bound has min(1/(2M), nu/(T phi(M) log 2)) per class; dropping the min or the factor 1/2 for odd n gives a fake improvement.

Comparing to the certificate printed on the page (Griego's superseded 0.490249...) or to Yoo's page record instead of the best value including open pull requests (PR #281 claims 0.489596115074071 as of 2026-10-28).
Histogram overflow: residue counts over M (a product of 38 primes) exceed 64 bits; use exact big integers or the cluster-update method.
Claiming a density statement for all n instead of odd n (the page's set is odd integers).

targets.name: Spencer discrepancy constant C_10c: an n x n matrix in [-1,1] whose discrepancy beats the record ratio disc(A)/sqrt(n)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Tao's optimization-constants repository, constant 10c: C_10c is the least K with disc(A) <= K sqrt(n) for every n and every A in [-1,1]^{n x n}, where disc(A) = min over x in {+-1}^n of ||Ax||_inf (Spencer's 'six standard deviations suffice'). Upper bounds: 5.32 (Spencer 1985), 4.1 algorithmic (Pesenti-Vladu, corrected v2). Lower bounds are explicit small matrices with an exhaustively checked discrepancy: 4/sqrt(6), 5/3, 7/sqrt(17), and the current record 5/sqrt(8) ~ 1.767767 (an 8 x 8 matrix over {-1,0,1} built from the perfect [7,4] Hamming code, submitted to the repository on 5 Sep 2026; the page proves 5 is optimal at n = 8). Target: any explicit square matrix with entries in [-1,1] (rational entries allowed, not only signs) whose exact discrepancy divided by sqrt(n) strictly exceeds the live record.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit n x n matrix A with rational entries in [-1,1] (n arbitrary), saved as a file, such that the exact discrepancy d = min over all 2^n sign vectors x of max_i |(Ax)_i|, computed by exhaustive enumeration in exact rational arithmetic by two independent programs, satisfies d / sqrt(n) STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the largest lower bound listed on the live page https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/10c.html and in any open pull request touching constants/10c.md at https://github.com/teorth/optimizationproblems/pulls, both re-fetched live immediately before claiming; the comparison d^2 / n > (record)^2 is done exactly. A rectangular or padded matrix counts only after it is made square without lowering d (duplicate rows or zero columns are allowed, as on the page).

partial_wins.statement: A sign matrix (entries exactly +-1) whose discrepancy ratio strictly beats the best sign-matrix entry on the live page (7/sqrt(17) as of 2026-10-28), showing that zeros/real entries are not needed to pass it.

For some specific n in 9..40, an n x n matrix with entries in [-1,1] whose exact discrepancy d satisfies d/sqrt(n) strictly greater than the best value obtainable at that same n from Keri's covering-code table by the page's reduction C_10c >= (n-2r)/sqrt(max(n,P)) (the claim computes and states that per-n value from the table), with exhaustive two-implementation verification; this is a per-size improvement, not a record unless it also beats the main bar.

targets.verification_method: Load the matrix as exact rationals; enumerate all 2^n sign vectors (Gray-code order, incremental update of Ax, exact integers after clearing denominators) and record min ||Ax||_inf; a second implementation in a different language (or a covering-radius check when the matrix is a sign matrix) must agree. Compare d^2*8 > 25*n style integer inequality against the live record. n up to about 40 runs in minutes on a laptop with bit-parallel code.
angles: Leave the covering-code world: the page's reduction only covers sign rows. Real-valued rows can carve the cube into regions that no Hamming ball shape allows. Run local search on A in [-1,1]^{n x n} with the exact discrepancy as the objective for n = 9..24, using an LP inside the loop: fix the set of x that each row is responsible for and maximise the margin by linear programming over the row entries.

Cross-domain import (coding theory, covering codes with weights): the n=8 record is the perfect Hamming code. Try weighted or nonbinary covering objects (ternary Golay, perfect codes over mixed alphabets) and translate them into rows with entries in {-1,-1/2,0,1/2,1}.

Cross-domain import (adversarial ML / robust optimisation): treat x as the adversary and A as the defender; alternate a max-min game (best-response x by branch-and-bound, then a gradient or LP step on A against the current active set of worst x), which is how certified-robust training finds hard instances.

Cross-domain import (SAT/MaxSAT): for a fixed sign pattern support and target discrepancy d, encode 'every x has some row with |<a_i,x>| >= d' as a covering problem and hand it to a MaxSAT or ILP solver; zero entries become 'don't care' literals.
Kronecker and direct-sum constructions: check whether tensoring the 8 x 8 record with small matrices (or block-diagonal mixtures) keeps the ratio, and search for gluings that gain.
pitfalls: Floating-point discrepancy: a matrix with irrational or float entries can show a spurious ratio from rounding; only exact rationals and exhaustive enumeration count.
Non-square matrices: more rows than columns trivially raise the discrepancy; the definition is n x n. Padding with duplicate rows is allowed only while rows <= columns are made square as on the page.
Sampling x instead of enumerating all 2^n sign vectors overestimates the discrepancy.
Comparing against a stale record: the page and its open pull requests move weekly; compare against the maximum live value, not the number in this entry.
Entries outside [-1,1] (for example 1.0000001 after scaling) void the claim.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Equational Theories Project: settle the last 2 finite-magma implications (Eq677 ⇒ Eq255, Eq2910 ⇒ Eq47)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The Equational Theories Project dashboard (re-fetched 2026-10-28) shows the general implication graph 100% complete and the finite graph 99.99999% complete with exactly 2 implications having no proof and no conjecture. Its raw_data/finite_outcomes.json.gz marks exactly two finite implications 'unknown': Equation677 => Equation255 and Equation2910 => Equation47. Partial progress on 677 => 255 sits in open ETP issues, not yet merged: #1464 (July 2026) gives a Lean orbit lemma and 45 DRAT-certified order-10 UNSAT cases, claiming every finite counterexample has at least 11 elements; #1517 (Oct 2026) gives a Lean-checked conditional proof assuming the left translations are closed under conjugation. Settle either implication: a Lean proof that every finite magma satisfying the first law satisfies the second, or a finite magma satisfying the first and violating the second (a finite counterexample, Lean-checkable by `decide`).
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for one of the implications listed with 'no proof' on https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/dashboard/ (finite graph, re-fetched live immediately before claiming, and still 'unknown' in raw_data/finite_outcomes.json.gz): EITHER an explicit finite magma (operation table) that satisfies the hypothesis law and violates the conclusion, verified by an independent exhaustive Python check AND a Lean `decide` proof compiled in the ETP repository at its pinned toolchain; OR a Lean proof of the finite implication, sorry-free, no new axioms, `#print axioms` only propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound.

partial_wins.statement: Exhaustive exclusion of counterexamples up to a new size bound beyond any bound documented in the ETP paper, blueprint or issues for that implication (for 677 => 255 this means excluding order 11 or more, since issue #1464 claims order 10), with a reproducible SAT/DRAT certificate per size and the symmetry-breaking argument written out.

A Lean proof of the implication under an additional natural hypothesis (e.g. the magma is a quasigroup, or left-cancellative) that is neither implied by nor equivalent to a hypothesis already proved in the ETP issues (e.g. the translation-conjugacy closure of issue #1517), stated as a separate theorem.

targets.verification_method: Counterexample: load the table, check the hypothesis law on all n^k assignments and find a violating assignment for the conclusion (Python, seconds); compile the `decide` proof in ETP. Proof: build in ETP checkout, `#print axioms`.
angles: Read the ETP paper's section on 677/255 first: infinite counterexamples exist (that is why the general implication is false), so the finite question is about whether finiteness forces the conclusion; known structure results (677 magmas are quasigroup-like) narrow the search.
SAT/SMT search for finite counterexamples with symmetry breaking (Mace4/Kissat with lex-leader constraints), pushing sizes beyond the published bound.

Cross-domain import (coding theory): treat the operation table as a code over an alphabet of size n and use the law as parity-check constraints; algebraic constructions (linear magmas x◇y = ax+by over finite rings, then twisted versions) mirror code construction over GF(q).

Cross-domain import (dynamical systems): finiteness arguments often come from iterating a self-map (here the left/right translations) and using pigeonhole/permutation cycle structure; model translations as permutations and look for an invariant like a conserved quantity.
Translate the known infinite counterexample into a profinite/inverse-limit family and test whether any finite quotient survives.
pitfalls: The general (infinite) implication is already refuted; an infinite counterexample does not count.
Equation numbering is ETP-specific; verify the laws by reading equations.txt, not from memory.
Lean `decide` over large tables can be slow; native_decide is forbidden.
The project may close these at any time; re-fetch the dashboard before claiming.

targets.name: Formal Conjectures: research-solved sorries closable by an explicit finite witness (R(5,5) > 42 graph, small Hadamard orders, ...)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: In formal-conjectures (commit 5a2fb85, 2026-10-28, toolchain v4.33.1) a scan finds about 517 theorems tagged `research solved` outside the ErdosProblems, WrittenOnTheWallII and OEIS folders (those have their own bank entries) that still end in `sorry` with no `formal_proof` attribute. A subset are existential or finite statements whose known proof is an explicit object plus a finite check, e.g. Wikipedia/RamseyNumbers.lean `ramsey_number_five_five_lower_bound` (a graph on Fin 42 with no 5-clique and no 5-independent set; Exoo 1989). A much harder finite item is Wikipedia/Hadamard.lean `HadamardConjecture.variants.first_cases`, stated on main as `668 ≤ hadamardConstant`: a Hadamard matrix (FC's IsHadamard, defined via |det M| = n^(n/2)) must exist for every order 4k with k ≤ 166. That needs explicit matrices for all such orders, including ones that need Williamson-type or later constructions (e.g. order 428), far beyond Sylvester and Paley alone. Several earlier examples are now taken: the non-abelian Leinster group and R(3,3), R(3,4), R(3,5), R(4,4) have formal_proof links proposed in open FC PRs #6953 and #7660, and the Steiner system S(5,8,24) in #7660. Textbook-tagged items (BB(2), the irregular prime 37, OEIS textbook facts) belong to the separate textbook-sorries entry. Target: prove one in-scope research-solved finite-witness statement with kernel-checked computation.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a Lean file that restates one FC theorem verbatim (diffed against the live main branch of https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures re-fetched immediately before claiming) where that theorem is tagged research solved, lives outside FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems, WrittenOnTheWallII and OEIS, ends in `sorry`, has no `formal_proof` attribute, and is not the subject of any open FC pull request that proves it or adds a formal_proof link for it (searched on GitHub immediately before claiming), and proves it. Lean's kernel is the referee: the submitted file must compile with `lake build` against the repository's pinned lean-toolchain and lake-manifest (Mathlib rev as pinned, no edits to the statement, no new `axiom`, no `sorry`/`admit`, no `native_decide`/`Lean.ofReduceBool`, no `implemented_by`/`extern` tricks, no `set_option debug.skipKernelTC`), and `#print axioms <thm>` must list only a subset of {propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound}. Heavy computation must go through `decide`, `Decidable` instances or proof-by-reflection checked by the kernel; `native_decide` is forbidden.

partial_wins.statement: HadamardConjecture.variants.first_cases restricted to a proved range k <= K with K >= 8 (orders up to 32), stated as a separate Lean theorem with the same IsHadamard predicate, kernel-checked.

A kernel-checked proof of a reusable decision procedure (e.g. a reflected clique-freeness checker for graphs on Fin n, or a Hadamard-matrix verifier) that an in-scope FC statement reduces to, plus the instance check for a smaller case (e.g. the Paley graph on 17 vertices has no 4-clique and no 4-independent set).

targets.verification_method: Same as Lean rule: compile in a clean FC checkout at the pinned toolchain with the Mathlib cache, `#print axioms`, forbidden-token grep, statement diff against live file. Kernel `decide` runs must finish within the default or an explicitly raised `maxRecDepth`/`maxHeartbeats` (raising limits is allowed; `native_decide` is not).
angles: R(5,5) > 42: encode Exoo's 42-vertex graph as a bit-packed adjacency Nat, prove once that a reflected checker over all 5-subsets is sound, and let the kernel run it; split the 850,668 5-subsets by first vertex to keep each `decide` within heartbeat limits.

Cross-domain import (cryptographic proof systems / zero-knowledge 'certificate + cheap verifier'): ship a compact certificate (e.g. the Hadamard matrix as a bit-packed Nat) and a tiny verifier whose soundness is proved once; the kernel only runs the verifier.

Cross-domain import (database query optimisation): rewrite brute-force decide checks as joins over sorted lists with proved index lemmas (merge-join instead of nested loops) so kernel reduction stays under heartbeat limits.

Hadamard small orders (partial win p1): Sylvester doubling for powers of 2 plus Paley I/II for q = 3 mod 4 / q = 1 mod 4; proving Paley in general gives many orders at once. The full first_cases statement (`668 ≤ hadamardConstant`) needs every order up to 664 and is a long project. FC's IsHadamard is stated via the determinant; the proved direction of `isHadamard_equiv_isHadamard'` and the proof of `isHadamard_H12` on main show how to get it from M^T M = n I. Open FC PR #4900 (order 668) touches this file; do not duplicate it.
Triage the ~517 in-scope sorries by statement shape (`∃ x, ...` over a finite type, or an equality of a computable function at a numeral) to find more finite-witness items.
pitfalls: FC definitions can differ from textbook ones; a proof about the wrong definition does not count.
`native_decide` makes huge checks easy and is forbidden; also ban `Lean.ofReduceBool` and `implemented_by`.
Items get claimed fast: Leinster, small Ramsey numbers and S(5,8,24) were taken by open PRs within two weeks. Check open FC PRs and the formal_proof attribute on live main before claiming.
Upper-bound Ramsey statements (e.g. R(5,5) <= 46) are not finite-witness items; they need exhaustive search certificates far beyond kernel reach.

targets.name: Formal Conjectures WrittenOnTheWallII (Graffiti) and OEIS collections: research-solved conjectures without any Lean proof
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: FC's WrittenOnTheWallII collection (Fajtlowicz's Graffiti graph-theory conjectures) has, at commit 5a2fb85 (2026-10-28), 14 research-solved theorems ending in `sorry` with no formal_proof attribute: GraphConjecture3, 4, 5, 6, 13, 16, 17, 18, 23, 24, 25, 33, 91 and 291. Four are claimed by open FC PRs as of 2026-10-28: 5 (#6956 adds a formal_proof link), 17 (#4161 adds a formal_proof), 91 (#7394, a Lean disproof) and 291 (#7248, links a Lean refutation). That leaves 10 unclaimed: 3, 4, 6, 13, 16, 18, 23, 24, 25 and 33. The OEIS collection has 8 more (OEIS/109074, 100478, 287616, 111291, 53175, 1818, 2454 and 38552 `starkHeegner_classNumberOne`, the last a deep theorem), none touched by an open FC PR on 2026-10-28; the other research-solved OEIS items link external proofs. These were settled in papers, often by short graph-theoretic or elementary arguments. Target: prove one unclaimed item in Lean.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a verbatim restatement (diffed against the live FC main branch re-fetched immediately before claiming) of one WrittenOnTheWallII or OEIS theorem tagged research solved, ending in `sorry`, with no formal_proof attribute and not the subject of any open FC pull request that proves it or links a proof (searched on GitHub immediately before claiming), proved in full. Lean's kernel is the referee: the submitted file must compile with `lake build` against the repository's pinned lean-toolchain and lake-manifest (Mathlib rev as pinned, no edits to the statement, no new `axiom`, no `sorry`/`admit`, no `native_decide`/`Lean.ofReduceBool`, no `implemented_by`/`extern` tricks, no `set_option debug.skipKernelTC`), and `#print axioms <thm>` must list only a subset of {propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound}.

partial_wins.statement: A proof of the conjecture for all graphs with at most n vertices (n >= 7) by a kernel-checked enumeration, stated as a separate theorem (bounded verification, not a win).

A Lean library lemma relating FC's Graffiti invariants (e.g. independence number, residue, average distance) to Mathlib's SimpleGraph API, proved and reused by at least one closed conjecture's proof skeleton.

targets.verification_method: Clean FC checkout; compile; `#print axioms`; forbidden-token grep; diff statement vs live file.
angles: Read the solved-by reference in each docstring; pick ones whose published proof is a single inequality chain on degrees/independence number.
Bounded enumeration first (nauty geng to n=9) to make sure the FC statement agrees with the literature on small graphs before investing in a proof.

Cross-domain import (spectral methods from physics / vibration analysis): several Graffiti invariants are eigenvalue-based; use Rayleigh-quotient bounds as the proof backbone and formalise only the variational inequality needed.

Cross-domain import (electrical network theory): resistance-distance and average-distance invariants obey Kirchhoff/Rayleigh monotonicity; port a monotonicity argument rather than a combinatorial one.
For OEIS items, identify a closed form or recurrence and prove it by induction with `decide` base cases.
pitfalls: Graffiti conjectures are often stated for connected graphs only; FC may encode connectivity differently from the paper.
Small-graph enumeration is a sanity check, not a proof of the universal statement.
Some 'solved' Graffiti conjectures were solved by counterexample: then the FC statement should be the negation; check the docstring.
Mathlib's SimpleGraph API changes often; pin to FC's lake-manifest.
Open PRs claim items quickly (on 2026-10-28: #6956 for GraphConjecture5, #4161 for 17, #7394 for 91, #7248 for 291); search the FC PR list for the file name before starting and again before claiming.

targets.success_criterion: Success means a verbatim restatement (diffed against the live FC main branch re-fetched immediately before claiming) of one theorem tagged `textbook` that ends in `sorry`, has no formal_proof attribute and is not the subject of an open FC pull request proving it or linking a proof (searched on GitHub immediately before claiming), proved in full. partial_wins.statement: Wikipedia/BusyBeaver `BB_2` in the FC formulation (every 2-state 2-symbol machine either halts within the champion's step count or provably never halts), kernel-checked.
Two or more textbook sorries in one FC file closed, sharing one new helper lemma proved from Mathlib.

targets.verification_method: Clean FC checkout at pinned toolchain; compile; `#print axioms`; forbidden-token grep; statement diff; `exact?` probe to check the result is not already a direct Mathlib lemma.
angles: Rank the ~80 items by statement length and by Mathlib API proximity (Finset sums, ZMod, Nat.choose) and attack the shortest first.

BB(2)/BB(3): encode the champion machines and the finite list of all 2-state/3-state machines up to symmetry; prove non-halting of the rest via translated-cycler / bounded-loop certificates checked by a verified decider (mirror the Coq bbchallenge deciders).
Irregular prime 37: compute B_32 via Mathlib's `bernoulli` with a reflected rational evaluator, or use Kummer's criterion if FC defines regularity via class numbers (check the definition first).

Cross-domain import (program synthesis / superoptimisation): run a bounded search over tactic scripts (stochastic superoptimiser style: random mutations of a tactic sequence scored by remaining goals) instead of only LLM sampling.

Cross-domain import (structural engineering 'load path' analysis): draw the dependency DAG of the informal proof, identify the single lemma carrying most of the load, and prove it in isolation first; the rest is glue.
Search Loogle/Mathlib for near-identical statements; many textbook items are a bridge between FC's custom definitions and existing Mathlib notions.
pitfalls: A 'proof' that changes FC's custom definition or adds an instance assumption is not a proof of the FC statement.
Textbook facts sometimes landed in Mathlib after FC was written; a one-line `exact Mathlib.lemma` is real but not a research win.
Analytic items (real-number inequalities) tempt `nlinarith`/`polyrith` with external oracles; only the kernel-checked certificate counts.
Statement-level typos in FC (off-by-one bounds) can make a textbook item false; prove the negation only as a misformalisation note, not a 'win'.
BB(3) involves 3-state 2-symbol machines with a specific FC encoding of halting; mis-encoding the champion's step count is a common silent error.

targets.name: PrimeNumberTheoremAnd (PNT+): close an unassigned open formalisation issue (IK identities, Rosser-Schoenfeld prime sums, Dusart table bounds)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The PNT+ project (AlexKontorovich/PrimeNumberTheoremAnd, toolchain v4.35.0) tracks remaining `sorry`s as GitHub issues. On 2026-10-28 there are 27 open issues, 11 of them unassigned (#1240, #1685, #1688, #1690, #1692, #1694, #1762, #1773, #1774, #1775, #1796). Several of those are already claimed. #1685 isCompletelyMultiplicative_liouville and #1690 zeta_pow_four_eq (IK 1.29) are in PR #1772. #1762 pi_inequality and #1773-#1775 (theta bounds from Dusart Table 4.2) are in PR #1799. #1688 zeta_mul_zeta_mul_zeta_mul_zeta_eq (Ramanujan identity, IK 1.28) is in open PR #1730 (Robby955, since 1 Aug 2026), and the same declaration is tracked by issue #1242, assigned to KanCup. #1240 (upstream a lemma to Mathlib) and #1796 (attribution) are not sorry-filling tasks. That leaves #1692 RS_prime.theorem_d (sum log p / p < log x for x > 1) and #1694 RS_prime.theorem_c (sum 1/p > log log x for x > 1), both in PrimeNumberTheoremAnd/IEANTN/TMEEMT.lean, as unassigned sorries with no open PR. Target: fill one such sorry.
targets.success_criterion: Success means: for one issue that is still open and unassigned on https://github.com/AlexKontorovich/PrimeNumberTheoremAnd/issues, whose named declaration is not targeted by any open pull request or by any other open, assigned issue (including PRs and issues that name the declaration without citing this issue number), all re-fetched live immediately before claiming, the named declaration on live main still contains `sorry`, and a patch to that declaration only (statement unchanged, diff-checked) makes the project compile with `lake build` at the pinned toolchain, with `#print axioms` on the declaration showing only propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound (no sorryAx, no new axiom, no native_decide). No PR is opened; the claim is for the checked patch.

partial_wins.statement: RS_prime.theorem_c (#1694) or RS_prime.theorem_d (#1692) proved for all x >= X0 for an explicit X0, derived from statements already formalised in the project (Mertens-type, Rosser-Schoenfeld or Dusart bounds), with the remaining range 1 < x < X0 stated as a separate, clearly named lemma; kernel-checked, statement unchanged, if no open PR claims the declaration at verification time.

A kernel-checked proof (no native_decide) of the finite-range part 1 < x < X0 of RS_prime.theorem_c or RS_prime.theorem_d for an explicit X0 >= 10^4, via a reflected prime table and rational interval bounds for the logarithms, stated as a separate lemma that composes with the large-x part.

targets.verification_method: Clone PNT+ main, `lake exe cache get`, apply patch, `lake build` (or build only the affected module and dependents), `#print axioms` on the target, grep diff for forbidden tokens, confirm the statement text is unchanged.
angles: RS prime-sum bounds: split into x >= X0 (from already-formalised Rosser-Schoenfeld/Dusart/Mertens-type statements in the project) and 1 < x < X0 by a kernel-checked prime table via reflection.

Cross-domain import (numerical analysis / validated numerics in control engineering): use interval arithmetic with outward rounding encoded in rationals to certify the finite-range inequalities, the same way flight-control verification certifies polynomial bounds.

Cross-domain import (accounting reconciliation): treat the explicit-constant chain as a ledger: tabulate every constant from the source tables with its source row and cross-foot them before formalising, catching transcription errors early.

Check each issue's linked PRs, the open PR list and other issues naming the same declaration first: in 2026 contributors bundled several issues into single PRs (#1772, #1799), and IK 1.28 is claimed by PR #1730 and by assigned issue #1242.
pitfalls: Issues get assigned or closed, or bundled into other people's PRs, quickly; re-check the live issue state, open PRs and the main branch before claiming.
Changing the declaration's statement (e.g. weakening a constant) is not a fix.
Building all of PNT+ is long; partial module builds can miss downstream breakage: run the full `lake build` before claiming.
Explicit constants: a misread table row (e.g. 0.78 vs 0.078) gives a false or unprovable bound.

targets.name: Blanking and Beeping Busy Beavers: beat a small-domain champion (BLB(2,4), BLB(2,5), BBB(2,4)) or settle BLB(4)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Variants of the Busy Beaver game tracked on the bbchallenge wiki. Blanking Beaver BLB(n,m): most steps an n-state m-symbol Turing machine takes before the tape first becomes all blank (halting or not). Beeping Busy Beaver BBB(n,m) (Scott Aaronson, 2020): most steps before the last visit to a 'beep' state for machines that beep finitely often (quasihalt; term coined by Nick Drozd). As listed on 2026-10-28 (Blanking_Beaver page last edited 2026-10-17, Beeping_Busy_Beaver page last edited 2026-10-25), with most small-domain champions from Nick Drozd's searches: BLB(2) = 8, BLB(3) = 34, BLB(4) >= 32,779,477 (listed as a lower bound, not proven exact), BLB(5) > 10^14,006, BLB(2,3) = 77, BLB(2,4) >= 1,367,361,263,049, BLB(2,5) > 10^32, BLB(3,3) > 10^^6.54 (Drozd, September 2026); BBB(3) = 55, BBB(4) = 32,779,478 (Coq-BBB4), BBB(2,3) = 59, BBB(2,4) > 2 x 10^23, BBB(3,3) > 10^^6.74. 2-state, 4- and 5-symbol spaces are small enough for laptop enumeration in tree normal form, unlike the 5- and 6-state domains.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a Turing machine in standard bbchallenge text format with the stated number of states and symbols that (a) blanks the tape for the first time at a step count STRICTLY greater than the champion listed for that domain on https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Blanking_Beaver, or (b) quasihalts at a step count strictly greater than the BBB champion listed on https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Beeping_Busy_Beaver, both pages re-fetched live immediately before claiming; the step count is verified by direct simulation (counts up to about 10^13) or, for larger counts, by a machine-checkable accelerated proof (e.g. a Coq/Lean proof, or an exact macro-machine simulation whose rules are independently re-derived) and, for quasihalting, a translated-cycler certificate showing no further beeps. OR (c) an exact value BLB(4) = 32,779,477 (or a larger value with a new champion): every 4-state 2-symbol machine in tree normal form either blanks by that step, never blanks (with a checkable certificate), as reproduced by an independent decider.

partial_wins.statement: A new BLB(2,4) champion (criterion (a)), verified by direct C simulation with step count printed.
The exact value of BLB(4), with certificates, if the page still lists it with '>='.
A full enumeration of the 2-state 4-symbol domain in tree normal form with a published list of fewer than 1000 machines whose blanking status is undecided, plus the decider code.

targets.verification_method: Simulate the machine with an independent C or Rust simulator on a two-way infinite tape (blank symbol 0), counting steps until the tape is all 0 (blanking) or until the last beep; for very large counts, use an independent macro-machine/accelerated simulator and cross-check the first 10^9 steps against direct simulation. For non-blanking or non-quasihalting certificates (exact-value claims), re-run independent deciders (cyclers, translated cyclers, backward reasoning, finite automata reduction) and check every holdout is closed.
angles: Exhaustive tree-normal-form enumeration of 2-state 4-symbol machines (roughly 10^8-10^9 candidates after TNF) with a cheap 'tape returns to blank' detector; run every candidate to 10^7 steps and promote survivors to accelerated simulation.
Look for blanking machines among known BB(2,4) and BBB(2,4) long-runners: Shawn Ligocki's 2x4 machine lists contain machines whose tape may blank later than the current BLB champion.

Import from cellular-automaton glider analysis: blanking events come from 'counters' that sweep and erase; model the macro behaviour as a recurrence (Collatz-like) and solve it in closed form to predict the blanking step exactly, as done for BB(5)/BB(6) champions.

Import from model checking: encode 'tape blank at step t' as a bounded model-checking query with a SAT solver over the TNF parameters, to search for machines with long blanking times without simulating each.
For BLB(4) exactness, reuse bbchallenge's BB(5) decider stack (cyclers, translated cyclers, backward reasoning, FAR) adapted from halting to blanking.
pitfalls: Blanking means the WHOLE tape is blank at some step after the start; a machine that halts with ones on the tape does not blank, and step 0 does not count.
BBB counts steps until the LAST beep; a machine that beeps forever never quasihalts, and claiming quasihalting needs a proof that no later beep occurs.

Champion step counts are off-by-one sensitive (whether the final transition counts); calibrate your simulator on the listed champions first (e.g. BLB(2,3) = 77, BLB(3) = 34, BBB(3) = 55, BBB(2,3) = 59).
Machine format and symbol/state counting must match the wiki's (TNF, '---' for undefined transitions, Z for halt).
These variants are actively studied on the Busy Beaver Discord and wiki; re-fetch the champion tables immediately before claiming.

targets.name: Game of Life: a cheaper glider synthesis than Catagolue's best-known cost for a still life or oscillator
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: A glider synthesis builds a Game of Life (B3/S23) object by colliding gliders only; its cost is the number of gliders. Catagolue's Syntheses section (Adam P. Goucher's Catagolue, assembled from Jeremy Tan's Shinjuku database of synthesis components with contributions from Mark Niemiec, Martin Grant, Goldtiger997 and many others) lists the cheapest known synthesis cost for every synthesised object. Coverage includes every strict still life up to 22 cells (the xs22 tabulation lists 680,289 objects) and a partial set of larger still lifes: the xs24 tabulation lists 118,117 objects, far fewer than the roughly 4.05 million strict 24-cell still lifes (OEIS A019473). The most expensive xs24 entry, xs24_03lozg5u05b8oz11, costs 167 gliders (true synthesis) as of 2026-10-28. Oscillators are listed by period (xp2, xp3, ...). The tables are recomputed every four hours as new components arrive. Many costs are far above what the component library could achieve with a smarter assembly. Open target: a valid all-glider synthesis of some tabulated object that uses STRICTLY fewer gliders than the live listed cost, or a first synthesis of a still life/oscillator the tables do not list.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an RLE pattern in rule B3/S23 that (1) at generation 0 consists ONLY of gliders, each a separate connected component, (2) is a valid synthesis: rewinding every glider backwards by at least 4*(bounding box diameter) generations along its own trajectory produces a pattern with no glider-glider interaction during the rewound interval (so the gliders genuinely come in from infinity), (3) after running forward until the population is periodic, contains exactly the target object (apgcode match, via lifelib or an independent simulator) with NO other live cells and no escaping gliders or spaceships (unless the page's own synthesis convention for that object explicitly allows outgoing gliders, in which case follow it literally), and (4) uses STRICTLY fewer gliders than the cost shown for that apgcode on its Catagolue object page and tabulation (https://catagolue.hatsya.com/census/b3s23/synthesis-costs/<class>), re-fetched live immediately before claiming. For objects listed with a '(pseudo)' cost, compare against that listed number but report the result as a true synthesis improvement only if the new synthesis is all-glider. A first synthesis of a strict still life or oscillator absent from the tables also counts if its apgcode does not appear on the tabulation page for its class.

partial_wins.statement: A strictly cheaper true glider synthesis for any object whose current listed cost is at least 60 gliders, verified as above.
A strictly cheaper synthesis for an oscillator class page (xpN) object, verified with the same checker, including a check that the final object oscillates with the listed period.

A reusable new synthesis component (a converter from an object with a known synthesis to another object, at a stated glider cost) that, combined with existing listed costs, lowers the cost of at least 10 distinct tabulated objects, each re-verified end-to-end as a full all-glider synthesis.

targets.verification_method: Install python-lifelib (Adam P. Goucher). Load the claimed RLE, decompose generation 0 into connected components and confirm every component is a glider (apgcode xq4_153 in some phase/orientation). Rewind each glider independently along its direction and check by forward simulation that the rewound pattern evolves into the generation-0 pattern unchanged (no early interaction). Run forward until periodic, classify with lifelib's apgcode function, and confirm the result is the single target object with nothing else. Count gliders. Fetch the object page https://catagolue.hatsya.com/object/<apgcode>/b3s23 and read the '#CSYNTH <apgcode> costs N gliders' line. Cross-check with an independent numpy Life simulator.
angles: Shortest-path view: treat Shinjuku components as weighted edges between apgcodes and run Dijkstra from the empty board; any object whose shortest path is cheaper than its listed cost is an immediate candidate (the published tables are a running min, not always a global shortest path after new components arrive).
Target the most expensive objects first (xs24 ranks 1-50 cost 90-167 gliders): look for a cheaper predecessor still life that differs by one 'tail' or 'hook' and a known cheap converter.

Import from organic chemistry retrosynthesis: run a retrosynthetic search (Corey-style disconnections, Monte Carlo tree search as in AiZynthFinder) from the target backwards to cheap 'reagent' objects, where each reaction is a Shinjuku component.

Import from compiler peephole superoptimisation: exhaustively enumerate 2- and 3-glider collisions against small objects near the target's frontier cells (a bounded 'superoptimiser' over glider phases and lanes) to discover new one-step converters.

Soup mining: Catagolue's census of random soups contains natural formations of many objects; search the census for small 'seed' constellations (2-4 still lifes) that evolve into the target, then synthesise the seed cheaply.
pitfalls: A pattern that contains anything other than gliders at generation 0 (a block, a boat, a stray cell) is not a glider synthesis, even if it builds the object.
Gliders that already overlap or interact when rewound are an impossible 'from infinity' setup; skipping the rewind check gives false records.
Leftover debris, a stray blinker, or an escaping glider means the target was not built cleanly; the final apgcode must match exactly.

The CSV textcensus encodes costs with an offset: values of 10^17 or more are true syntheses with cost value-10^17, smaller values are '(pseudo)' costs. Read the object page's #CSYNTH line instead of the raw CSV number.
Costs drop often as people submit new components. A cost that was beatable yesterday may already be lower; re-fetch the object page immediately before claiming.
Pseudo still lifes and strict still lifes are different classes; a synthesis of a pseudo still life is not a synthesis of a strict one with the same cell count.

targets.name: Knight covering (domination) of the n x n board: fewer knights than Frank Rubin's records for n = 22..50
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The knight domination number of the n x n board is the fewest knights that occupy or attack every square (OEIS A006075). Exact values are known up to n = 21 (a(20) = 62, verified optimal by Lee Morgenstern per the Contest Center; a(21) = 68 added by Andy Huchala in 2021). For larger boards the best known coverings are Frank Rubin's, mostly from 2000-2004, on his Contest Center pages: 22x22: 75, 23x23: 82, 24x24: 88, 25x25: 96, 26x26: 102, 27x27: 111, 28x28: 119, 29x29: 126, 30x30: 135, 31x32: 148, 35x35: 182, 40x40: 230, 45x45: 291, 50x50: 350. These were found with hand-designed patterns (tetrads, Monier's pattern, 'cup' patterns) and partial search. A web search on 2026-10-28 found no published SAT/MaxSAT/ILP or local-search improvement for these sizes. Open target: an explicit covering of some listed board with STRICTLY fewer knights.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a list of knight squares on an n x n board (n among 22..30, 35, 40, 45, 50, or the 31x32 board) such that every square is occupied or attacked by a knight, checked by an independent exact checker, with STRICTLY fewer knights than the smallest of: Rubin's count for that board on https://www.contestcen.com/knight.htm and its linked board page (e.g. https://www.contestcen.com/kn27.htm), the upper bounds in OEIS A006075 (https://oeis.org/A006075), and any newer published covering found by a literature search, all re-fetched live immediately before claiming. For n = 22, a covering with 74 or fewer knights also settles that A006075's listed upper bound is not optimal.

partial_wins.statement: A certified optimality result: a(22) = 75 (or a smaller exact value with matching covering) proved by an ILP or SAT solver with a checkable certificate (DRAT/VeriPB proof, or an LP dual bound proof).
A strictly better covering for a rectangular m x n board with 20 <= m, n <= 50 that appears on Rubin's or Morgenstern's pages (archived), verified the same way.

targets.verification_method: Parse the knight list, mark each knight square and its up to 8 attacked squares, and confirm all n^2 squares are marked. Count knights. Fetch the Contest Center board page and OEIS A006075 live and compare. The check takes milliseconds.
angles: Set cover with CP-SAT or a MaxSAT solver, warm-started from a periodic tiling (Monier pattern interior) with free variables only in a border strip of width 4-6; the interior is near-optimal, the border is where Rubin's records leave slack.
Large-neighbourhood search: repeatedly free a random k x k window (k ~ 8-12), re-solve it exactly with ILP given the fixed knights outside, accept improvements.

Import from wireless sensor networks / facility location: knight covering is a minimum dominating set on a regular graph; apply the 'Lagrangian heuristic plus subgradient' methods from facility location and the dominating-set heuristics from ad-hoc network backbones.
Import from crystallography: enumerate wallpaper-group-periodic patterns with density close to 1/8 (Monier) and stitch them with optimised boundary layers, like crystal-surface reconstructions.
Lower-bound side: LP relaxation with the 3x3 'needs 4 knights' cut from Rubin's optimality proofs gives instant bounds to see which boards have the biggest gap.
pitfalls: Rubin's board pages draw each covering as an HTML table (one cell per square); parse it carefully and compare against the stated knight count in the page heading, not your own reading of the table.
A covering of the torus or of an infinite pattern clipped to the board is not automatically a covering of the bounded board: knights near the edge attack fewer squares.
Squares occupied by knights must also be counted as covered (domination), but do not confuse with 'total domination' where knights must be attacked too; the record is the ordinary domination version.
Lee Morgenstern's or later authors' results may beat a Rubin number without being on the Contest Center page; search the archived Morgenstern site and recent literature before claiming.
Some board pages show several coverings (e.g. 30x30: 136 then 135; 40x40: 232, 232, 230; 45x45: 292 and 291; 50x50: 360 down to 350); the record is the smallest count on the page.
A 'covering' found by a heuristic that leaves a single uncovered corner square is the commonest false win; always run the exhaustive checker.

targets.name: Peaceable queens: beat Clinch-Drescher-Huynh-Saffidine's odd-torus records (n = 19..63), or determine a(16)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Peaceable queens: place white and black queens so that no queen attacks one of the opposite colour, maximising the smaller army. On the ordinary n x n board, a(n) (OEIS A250000) is known exactly only through n = 15 (a(14), a(15) = 28, 32 by Paul Tabatabai with integer programming, 2018). For n >= 16 only bounds are known. Rob Pratt's 2014 IP gives 37 <= a(16) <= 64. Stephen Ainley's 1977 constructions (values for n <= 30, general lower bound floor(7n^2/48)) have been beaten only once, by Dmitry Kamenetsky's n = 27 solution with 106 queens against Ainley's 105. Peter Karpov notes that all known values equal floor(7n^2/48) except at n = 5, 9. On the toroidal board, Katie Clinch, Matthew Drescher, Tony Huynh and Abdallah Saffidine (arXiv 2406.06974, latest v3 of 27 Oct 2024) give bounds. In Appendix A they list their best odd-torus solutions, found by local search, for every odd n from 13 to 63 (e.g. 19: 32, 25: 56, 41: 156, 43: 162, 45: 184, 51: 252, 53: 250, 63: 348). The authors note there is no regular pattern and that n = 53 is below n = 51, so improvements are plausible. The toroidal sequence OEIS A279405 (m white and m black queens, equivalent to maximising min(|B|,|W|)) is now exact through n = 18 (a(13)-a(14) from Jaideep Padhi, Jun 2026; a(15)-a(18) from Jan P. Harries, Jul 2026). Its values a(13) = 16, a(15) = 20, a(17) = 28 equal Appendix A, so the open odd-torus cases start at n = 19. Score on the torus is min(|B|, |W|).
targets.success_criterion: Success means one of three things. (a) For some odd n in 19..63: sets B, W of cells of the n x n TORUS (rows, columns, and both diagonal families taken mod n) with no queen in B attacking a queen in W along any wrapped line, and min(|B|,|W|) STRICTLY greater than all of: the value listed for that n in Appendix A of the latest version of https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06974 (v3 as of 2026-10-28), any term for that n in OEIS A279405 (https://oeis.org/A279405), and any later published value found by search, all re-fetched live immediately before claiming. (b) For some n >= 16 on the ordinary board: a peaceful configuration with min(|B|,|W|) STRICTLY greater than both floor(7n^2/48) and every lower bound or construction cited for that n in OEIS A250000 (https://oeis.org/A250000), re-fetched live (comments, links and b-file; e.g. 106 for n = 27). (c) A certified determination of a(16): a configuration achieving the claimed value plus an upper-bound proof for value+1 (ILP with an exact-arithmetic certificate such as VeriPB, or SAT with DRAT checked by drat-trim), with two independent encodings.

partial_wins.statement: An odd-torus record improvement for any single odd n in 19..63 (criterion (a)) - the most realistic target.

Even-torus: for an even n larger than every n in the live DATA of OEIS A279405 (n >= 20 as of 2026-10-28), a configuration on the n x n torus beating the paper's Theorem 1.1 construction value for that n and not dominated by any configuration the paper or a later source (e.g. Harries 2026 on even tori) reports (state the value used).
A certified upper bound a(16) <= 38 (or any improvement on the best published upper bound), without the matching construction.

targets.verification_method: Read B and W as cell lists; check B and W are disjoint; for every b in B and w in W check they do not share a row, column, diagonal (i-j) or anti-diagonal (i+j) - mod n on the torus, plain on the board. Count. Milliseconds. For a(16), re-run the certificate checker.
angles: Exploit the irregularities: n = 43 and n = 53 sit well below the trend of their neighbours; start local search from the n = 41/45 and n = 51 solutions rescaled or with rows/columns inserted.

Torus symmetry: impose invariance under a translation subgroup (Z_n acts transitively), turning the problem into choosing periodic 'argyle' or 'plaid' motifs plus a defect; enumerate motifs exactly, then repair defects with CP-SAT.
Import from statistical physics: this is a two-species hard-core lattice gas with long-range exclusion; use parallel tempering / replica exchange with cluster (swap-colour region) moves.

Import from image segmentation: the two armies occupy regions bounded by lines of four slopes; optimise region shapes as polygons (graph-cut style) in the continuum limit, then discretise, as Jubin's and Ainley's pentagon constructions do.
For a(16): IP with orbital branching over the 16-element symmetry group (rotations, reflections, colour swap), plus cuts from the 'amicable rooks' bound.
pitfalls: On the torus, lines wrap around: a queen at (0,0) attacks (n-1,n-1) diagonally. Checking with board (non-wrapped) lines gives fake torus records.
The score is the SMALLER army, min(|B|,|W|); a bigger total with an unbalanced split is not a record.
Even and odd tori behave very differently; Appendix A lists only odd n.
Odd tori n = 13, 15, 17 are already settled by OEIS A279405 (exact values equal Appendix A); do not target them. A279405 is actively extended (2026 additions), so re-check its DATA for n = 19 and up.

The paper may be revised (v4+) with better numbers, and later papers or apps by the same authors or others (e.g. Harries 2026) may host newer results; re-fetch the latest arXiv version and search before claiming.
On the ordinary board, matching floor(7n^2/48) is the known best, not a record; for n = 27 the bar is already 106 (Kamenetsky).

targets.name: Polyform compatibility: solve an open ('?') pair or shrink a smallest-known common figure on George Sicherman's tables
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Two polyforms are compatible if some figure can be tiled by copies of each. George Sicherman's Polyform Curiosities maintains tables of the smallest known compatibility figures, in number of tiles, for every pair in many families: heptiamonds (with and without holes), hexiamonds, holeless hexominoes, holeless pentomino-hexomino pairs, pentahexes and more, continuing work by Andris Cibulis, Andy Liu, Bob Wainwright, Uldis Barbans, Gilbert Lee, Giovanni Resta and Erich Friedman. Cells marked '?' are pairs with no known compatibility figure but no impossibility proof; '×' marks pairs believed impossible. The heptiamond table (revised 2012-01-04) and holeless hexomino table (2020-06-18) still contain many '?' cells. Open target: a figure for a '?' pair, or a figure with fewer tiles than listed for a solved pair.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for a pair of polyforms (P, Q) in a table linked under the Polyominoes, Polyiamonds or Polyhexes headings of http://sicherman.net/pairwise.html (square, triangular or hexagonal lattice). Tables under 'Other Plane Polyforms' and 'Solid Polyforms' are excluded because the verification method does not cover their grids. A win needs a figure F (a set of lattice cells) together with an explicit tiling of F by copies of P (rotations and reflections allowed unless the page says otherwise) and an explicit tiling of F by copies of Q. Both must satisfy the page's side conditions (e.g. 'holeless', connected), verified by an exact checker. AND either the pair's cell on the live page is '?', or F uses STRICTLY fewer tiles than the page's listed minimum for that pair. Use the page's own count convention: the number of tiles of each kind, i.e. area / order for equal-order pairs, or the pair of counts shown for mixed-order tables. The page must be re-fetched live immediately before claiming, and Friedman's Math Magic and Resta's Polypolyominoes checked for an existing smaller figure.

partial_wins.statement: Any '?' cell resolved by an explicit compatibility figure on any of the tables (heptiamond, hexiamond, holeless hexomino, holeless pentomino-hexomino, pentahex).
A smaller figure for a pair whose listed minimum is at least 10 tiles.
A computer-certified impossibility (SAT/DLX exhaustive, with checkable proof) up to a stated figure size for a '?' pair, clearly labelled as bounded.

targets.verification_method: Represent cells on the square, triangular or hexagonal lattice with integer coordinates. Check that tiling 1 uses only congruent copies of P (canonicalise each piece under the allowed symmetry group), tiling 2 only copies of Q, that both cover F exactly with no overlaps, that F satisfies the page's conditions (holeless: complement connected to infinity; connected). Compare tile counts with the live page. Milliseconds.
angles: Joint SAT model: variables for which cells are in F (bounded box), plus placement variables for P-copies and Q-copies; constrain both tilings to cover exactly F. Increase the tile count k until SAT. Symmetric F (mirror or rotational) shrinks the search a lot.

Grow from known 'euphoric' polyforms: Sicherman lists polyforms compatible with every member of a family; chaining P -> euphoric -> Q does not directly give a figure, but their common figures are good seeds for local search.

Import from crystallography: look for F as a fundamental domain of a periodic tiling shared by P and Q (find a common lattice of periods first, then cut a finite patch), as is done for co-tiling in quasicrystal studies.
Import from VLSI placement: use rectangle-packing style simulated annealing over the boundary of F, alternating 'P-tile F' and 'Q-tile F' feasibility checks via DLX.
Triage by staleness: the heptiamond page is from 2012, so modern SAT solvers have likely not been run across all its '?' cells.
pitfalls: Check whether reflections are allowed for the specific table; most allow them, but some variants (e.g. 'odd pairs', 'holeless') add constraints.
'Holeless' variants forbid holes; a figure with an enclosed hole does not count for the holeless table, but may count for the unrestricted one.
