Tile counts: compare like with like (number of P-tiles, number of Q-tiles, or area) as the page states; mixed-order tables use different conventions.
Many 'smaller' figures already exist in Erich Friedman's Math Magic (Sept 2004) or Giovanni Resta's pages without being on Sicherman's page; check them before claiming.
A '×' cell means 'almost surely no solution'; a claimed solution there is more likely a checker bug (wrong piece shape) than a discovery.

targets.name: Queen domination of the 26 x 26 board: 13 or 14 queens? (first open value of OEIS A075458)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: gamma(Q_n), the fewest queens that occupy or attack every square of the n x n board, is known through n = 25 (OEIS A075458; values to n = 24 from William Bird's 2017 thesis, a(25) = 13 from Dmitry Kamenetsky's file). It is known that gamma(Q_n) is ceil(n/2) or ceil(n/2)+1 for n <= 132 (Ostergard and Weakley), so gamma(Q_26) is 13 or 14; Kamenetsky's best-known file lists a(26) <= 14. William D. Weakley ('Queen Domination of Even Square Boards', Electron. J. Combin. 29(2) (2022) P50) showed that a dominating set of size n/2 on an even board is either monochromatic (all queens on squares of one colour, by parity of x+y) or bichromatic with colour classes differing in size by at most 2. Below 238, monochromatic sets of size n/2 exist only for n = 2, 4, 6, 10, 12, 18, 30, 130, which rules out a monochromatic 13-queen set for n = 26. He conjectures that bichromatic sets of size n/2 do not exist for n > 4. So a 13-queen solution would have to be bichromatic (6 and 7 queens on the two colours) and would refute Weakley's conjecture. Taha Rostami and Curtis Bright (arXiv 2508.11945, v2 29 Jul 2026) built proof-producing SAT for queen domination, corrected the n = 16 solution count and resolved the previously open n = 19 enumeration case, but A075458 still stops at n = 25. Open target: either a 13-queen dominating set of the 26 x 26 board, or a certified proof that none exists.
targets.success_criterion: Success means either (a) 13 squares of the 26 x 26 board such that every square is occupied or attacked by a queen on one of them, verified by an exact checker, or (b) a proof that 13 queens cannot dominate the 26 x 26 board: an UNSAT result for a validated CNF/ILP encoding with a DRAT/LRAT proof checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr (or a VeriPB certificate), with a second independent encoding agreeing; in both cases OEIS A075458 (https://oeis.org/A075458) re-fetched live immediately before claiming must still lack a(26), and a literature search (arXiv, Ostergard/Weakley/Bird follow-ups) must find no earlier resolution.

partial_wins.statement: Independent queen domination: a(32) of OEIS A075324 (the independent domination number, known through n = 31 from Langlois-Remillard, Mussig and Roldan), determined with a construction and a certified lower bound.

A DRAT-certified proof that every 13-queen dominating set of the 26 x 26 board, if any exists, must have a stated structural property (e.g. occupies every row of one parity), proved for a sound case split covering all cases.

targets.verification_method: For (a): mark rows, columns, diagonals and anti-diagonals of the 13 queens and check all 676 squares are covered. For (b): independent CNF generation, CaDiCaL/kissat with proof output, drat-trim check; compare with Rostami-Bright's published encoding on n = 24, 25 known values.
angles: Weakley structure: by Weakley (EJC 2022) any 13-queen dominating set of the 26 x 26 board is bichromatic with 6 queens on one square colour and 7 on the other; add that cardinality split as a constraint (citing the theorem) and enumerate the remaining structure with SAT. Weakley's own analysis of the bichromatic case is the natural starting point.

Reuse the Rostami-Bright encoding (auxiliary line-occupancy variables, literal ordering, cube-and-conquer) and add symmetry breaking for the 8 board symmetries; split cubes over which columns are empty.

Import from radar coverage / art-gallery problems: queen domination is a line-cover problem; use an LP 'line-weight' relaxation (weights on rows, columns and diagonals that every queen can cover only a bounded amount of) to prune cubes before SAT.
Import from error-correcting codes: dominating sets of queen graphs resemble covering codes; search for 13-sets with additive structure (subsets of cosets of a line mod 26) and repair locally.
Independent domination side (p1): Langlois-Remillard et al. published Julia ILP code; run it with stronger symmetry breaking for n = 32.
pitfalls: Domination counts squares occupied by a queen as covered; independent domination additionally forbids queens attacking each other. Do not mix A075458 and A075324.
Diagonals and anti-diagonals both count; board edges cut them (no wrap-around).
An UNSAT run with unchecked symmetry breaking or without a proof certificate is not a proof that a(26) = 14.
An UNSAT proof that adds Weakley's 6/7 colour-split constraint relies on his 2022 theorem; state that dependency explicitly, or prove the split inside the certified pipeline.

Bird's 2017 thesis (https://dspace.library.uvic.ca/handle/1828/8634, reachable on 2026-10-28), Weakley's 2022 paper and later papers may contain more than A075458 shows; check them and any follow-ups before claiming.

targets.name: Is the 27 x 27 queens graph 27-colourable? (first open chromatic number of the queens graph)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The n x n queens graph has the squares as vertices, adjacent when a queen on one attacks the other. Its chromatic number is at least n; it equals n whenever n mod 6 is 1 or 5 (Gardner/Iyer-Menon construction), and Michel Vasquez and Gunter Stertenbrink found n-colourings for many other n by computer search (Vasquez found a 26-colouring of the 26 x 26 board). OEIS A088202 records the values through n = 26 (a(26) = 26 added 2016 from Chvatal's site) and states that a(27) is the first open case; Vasek Chvatal's page poses 'Problem 1. Is the 27 x 27 queen graph 27-colourable?'. A 27-colouring is the same as a partition of the 27 x 27 board into 27 disjoint non-attacking 27-queen solutions. Bernardo Subercaseaux, Przybocki and Marijn Heule (arXiv 2609.27674) benchmarked 1584 SAT encodings of queen colouring but did not report settling n = 27.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit 27 x 27 array of colours 0..26 such that no two squares in the same row, column, diagonal or anti-diagonal share a colour, verified by an independent checker, while OEIS A088202 (https://oeis.org/A088202), re-fetched live immediately before claiming, still says a(27) is open (also check Chvatal's page http://www.cs.concordia.ca/~chvatal/queengraphs.html if it is reachable, and a literature search); OR a certified proof that no 27-colouring exists (an UNSAT result for a validated encoding with a DRAT/LRAT proof checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr, plus a second independent encoding agreeing).

partial_wins.statement: An n-colouring of the n x n queens graph for some n > 27 that OEIS A088202 or Chvatal's page lists as open at verification time (check the page for which n are known via compositions).

A 27-colouring of the 27 x 27 queens graph with exactly one row, column or diagonal relaxed (e.g. the 27 x 27 board with one wrapped diagonal family, i.e. a partial-torus variant), stated clearly as a relaxation, together with a reproducible search showing how close a full solution is (number of violated pairs), as a benchmark rather than a record.

targets.verification_method: Read the 27 x 27 array; for each row, column, each of the 53 diagonals and each of the 53 anti-diagonals check colours are distinct. Milliseconds. For an impossibility claim, check the DRAT proof and re-derive the CNF independently.
angles: Two-stage exact cover: enumerate many 27-queen solutions with strong symmetry (e.g. invariant under 180-degree rotation, or 'linear-like' solutions j = a*i + b mod p perturbed), then solve the exact-cover problem of choosing 27 disjoint ones with DLX or SAT.

Use the best encodings from Subercaseaux-Przybocki-Heule (symmetry-breaking choice, clique hints, blocked-clause exactly-one) and add a 3-fold or 9-fold symmetry assumption because 27 = 3^3; symmetric solutions shrink the search by orders of magnitude.

Import from Latin-square and Sudoku generation: a 27-colouring is a Latin square whose colour classes also avoid repeated colours on every straight diagonal; reuse simulated annealing and Jacobson-Matthews style Markov moves from Latin-square sampling, with diagonal conflicts as the energy.

Import from frequency assignment (radio channels): tabu-search colouring algorithms like Vasquez's own (which found the 26-colouring) with modern partial-assignment crossover (hybrid evolutionary 'HEA' of Galinier and Hao).

Composition: Chvatal's page explains composing r- and s-colourings into rs-colourings; look for 'near-composition' ideas such as a 3 x 3 block of 9 x 9 boards with twisted offsets, repaired by local search.
pitfalls: Diagonals must include ALL diagonals of the square board (not wrapped/toroidal ones, which would be a harder problem, and not only the two main diagonals).
A colouring of the 27 x 27 torus is impossible in general for n divisible by 3; do not confuse torus and board results.
Partial colourings with a few conflicts left are not solutions, however close.
An UNSAT result from an encoding with a symmetry-breaking assumption only excludes symmetric solutions; it proves nothing about chi(Q_27) unless the symmetry breaking is proven sound.

targets.name: Domatic, idomatic and total domatic numbers of the n x n queens graph for n = 10..12 (close Lauri's gaps)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The domatic number dom(Q_n) is the largest k such that the squares of the n x n chessboard split into k disjoint sets, each dominating the queens graph (every square holds a queen of the set or is attacked by one). idom requires each set to also be independent; tdom requires total domination. Juho Lauri settled many small cases by SAT (Discrete Math. Lett. 16 (2025) 94-99). His Corrigendum (Discrete Math. Lett. 18 (2026) 34-35, published 26 Aug 2026, doi 10.47443/dml.2026.195) fixes a programming error and gives the current table: dom(Q_9) = 15, dom(Q_10) = 17, dom(Q_11) in {18, 19, 20}, dom(Q_12) in {20, 21}; idom(Q_9) = 15, idom(Q_10) = 16, idom(Q_11) = 18, idom(Q_12) in {18, 19, 20}; tdom(Q_9) = 14, tdom(Q_10) in {15, 16}, tdom(Q_11) in {16, 17}, tdom(Q_12) in {18, 19, 20}. Six (invariant, n) pairs are still open. OEIS A292192 (dom(Q_n)) still shows the pre-corrigendum a(9) = 13 and a(10) = 16 as of 2026-10-28. Each open value can be settled from below by an explicit partition (checkable in milliseconds) or from above by an UNSAT proof.
targets.success_criterion: Success means settling or narrowing one of the six intervals still open in Table 1 of Lauri's Corrigendum, Discrete Math. Lett. 18 (2026) 34-35 (https://doi.org/10.47443/dml.2026.195): dom(Q_11) in {18,19,20}, dom(Q_12) in {20,21}, idom(Q_12) in {18,19,20}, tdom(Q_10) in {15,16}, tdom(Q_11) in {16,17}, tdom(Q_12) in {18,19,20}. The interval must still be open in any later erratum or paper found by a search and in the live OEIS entries (A292192 and related), all re-fetched immediately before claiming. A raised lower bound requires an explicit partition of all n^2 squares into k classes, each class dominating (resp. independent dominating, total dominating) Q_n, with k above the current lower bound. A lowered upper bound requires a CNF encoding of 'a partition into k classes exists' that a solver reports UNSAT, with a DRAT/LRAT proof checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr, and the encoding cross-checked by finding the known (k-1)-partitions as SAT. Determining dom(Q_11) or dom(Q_12) exactly also extends A292192.

partial_wins.statement: Any single raised lower bound (an explicit partition beating the Corrigendum's lower bound for one of the 6 open (invariant, n) pairs).
A DRAT-certified upper bound improvement for one of the open pairs, with two independently written encodings agreeing.
Exact values for n = 13 for any of the three invariants, with a constructive lower bound and a certified upper bound, if not already published.

targets.verification_method: For a partition: check it covers each square exactly once; for each class, check every square is in the class or shares a row, column or diagonal with a class member (for tdom, every square including members must be attacked by a different member; for idom, no two members attack each other). For an upper bound: rerun the CNF through CaDiCaL/kissat with proof output and check with drat-trim; separately regenerate the CNF from an independent script and compare satisfiability on k-1.
angles: Symmetry-aware SAT: impose that the partition is invariant under a subgroup of the board's dihedral group (classes mapped to classes), which shrinks the search hugely for constructive lower bounds.

Upper bounds by counting: as in the Corrigendum's proofs, enumerate all minimum dominating sets (e.g. Q_11 has exactly two of size 5, Q_12 eight of size 6) and use size-distribution counting plus set-packing SAT; add clique hints (as in Subercaseaux, Przybocki and Heule's queen-colouring encodings).

Import from frequency assignment in cellular networks: domatic partitions are 'cluster-head rotations'; graph-colouring-style tabu search (TabuCol) adapted to the domatic objective finds partitions fast.

Import from coding theory: a domatic partition of a vertex-transitive graph often comes from a perfect-code-like lattice; try cosets of sublattices of Z^2 mod n as candidate classes and repair with SAT.
Cube-and-conquer on the UNSAT side, splitting on which class occupies the 4 corners and the centre.
pitfalls: dom, idom and tdom are three different invariants; a partition valid for dom may not be independent (idom) or total (tdom). Check the exact definition for the claimed one.
Total domination requires every square, including those in the class, to be attacked by another member of the same class.
An UNSAT result without a checked proof, or from an encoding never validated on known SAT cases, is not a certified upper bound.

The original 2025 paper had a programming error; several of its values (dom(Q_9), dom(Q_10), idom(Q_9), idom(Q_10), idom(Q_11)) were corrected in the 2026 Corrigendum, and OEIS A292192 had not caught up as of 2026-10-28. Use the Corrigendum's table, and search for any later erratum before claiming.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Rubik's Cube in the quarter-turn metric: a new position at distance 26, or a third distance-25 position
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: God's number for the 3x3x3 Rubik's Cube in the quarter-turn metric (QTM) is 26 (Tomas Rokicki and Morley Davidson, 2014, about 29 CPU-years). Yet only ONE position is known to need 26 quarter turns (superflip composed with fourspot, proven by Michael Reid in 1998, with its two rotations), and at distance 25 only two positions (and their rotations) are known; about 150,000 positions are estimated at distance 24. Rokicki's cube20.org states that despite significant effort no additional distance-26 positions have been found. cube20.org/symmetry also gives the optimal QTM distance of EVERY position with a nontrivial symmetry or antisymmetry: 78,820 such positions at distance 24, 36 at distance 25 and 3 at distance 26. So all known 25s and 26s are symmetric, and any new one must have trivial symmetry. Open target: a new antipode at distance 26, or a third distance-25 position, inequivalent under the 48 cube symmetries and inversion to the known ones.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a cube position, given as a scramble and a facelet string, that two independently written optimal QTM solvers (e.g. Rokicki's and Kociemba's or an independent IDA* with verified pattern databases) both prove requires exactly 25 (or 26) quarter turns, and that is not equivalent under the 48 spatial symmetries combined with inversion to any position listed as known at that distance on https://www.cube20.org/qtm/ re-fetched live immediately before claiming (and not reported in later literature or the cube forums found by search).

partial_wins.statement: A distance-24 QTM position with trivial stabiliser under the 96-element symmetry/antisymmetry group (so not among the symmetric positions tabulated at https://cube20.org/symmetry/sum2-q.html), proved distance-24 by two independent optimal solvers and not listed on cube20.org or its linked Cube-Lovers/cubeman posts, with a search log showing how its quarter-turn neighbours were screened for distance 25.

targets.verification_method: Run both optimal solvers on the position; each must return a 25- (or 26-) move solution and exhaust depth 23 (resp. 24) without a solution (parity fixes odd/even). Check the solution by applying it to the scramble. Canonicalise the position under the 96-element symmetry/antisymmetry group and compare with the known positions (superflip*fourspot and the two distance-25 positions from the cube20 page and its linked Cube-Lovers/cubeman posts). A depth-25 optimal proof can take hours per position on a laptop, so budget accordingly.
angles: Symmetric positions are exhausted (cube20.org/symmetry), so target asymmetric positions. Every distance-25 position is one quarter turn from some distance-24 position, so screen the asymmetric quarter-turn neighbours of the 78,820 symmetric distance-24 positions (and of newly found asymmetric 24s) with a fast suboptimal solver, then run optimal solvers on survivors.

Perturb the known antipodes: apply short asymmetric move sequences or conjugations to superflip*fourspot and the two known 25s, and screen the results for positions whose best suboptimal solution stays at 24+ before optimal solving.

Import from cryptanalysis (meet-in-the-middle): screen candidates by checking whether they are within distance 12 of a large table of distance-13 positions from both sides; positions that fail are distance-25/26 candidates.

Import from extreme-value search in large graphs: run a random walk or simulated annealing biased towards positions with high pattern-database lower bounds (heuristic 'deepness'), using the admissible heuristic itself as the energy, and send only high-scoring positions to the optimal solvers.
pitfalls: Half-turn metric (HTM) distance-20 positions are plentiful; claims must be in the quarter-turn metric, where a half turn counts as 2.
Positions related by one of the 48 symmetries or by inversion are the same for this purpose; canonicalise before claiming novelty.
Every position with any nontrivial symmetry or antisymmetry has already been solved optimally on cube20.org/symmetry; a 'new' symmetric distance-25/26 position means a canonicalisation or solver bug.
A suboptimal solver failing to find a short solution is not a lower bound; only an exhaustive optimal search proves distance.
QTM parity: odd-parity positions have odd distance; a solver reporting an even distance for an odd position has a bug.

targets.name: Busy Beaver for SKI combinator calculus: beat a listed lower bound for size 7..11, or settle Xi_0(7) exactly
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Xi_0(n) is the largest normal-form size of a terminating SKI combinator term with n combinators (leaves), reduction rules Sfgx = fx(gx), Kfx = f, Ix = x. The bbchallenge Busy Beaver wiki's 'SKI Calculus' page (last edited 2026-10-23) lists exact values for n <= 6 (Xi_0(6) = 17, SSS(SI)S) and only lower bounds above: n = 7: >= 41 (SSS(S(SS))S), 8: >= 80 (SSK(S(SS)S)S), 9: >= 1561 (S(SI)(SS)(SS)SS), 10: >= 1562, 11: >= 1563, then astronomically large lower bounds from n = 12. It also tabulates the SK-only calculus (exact through n = 7, Xi = 41; then 8: >= 80, 9: >= 169, 10: >= 1561, ...) and BCKW (exact through n = 5 = 47; n = 6 is already astronomically large). The small sizes are enumerable on a laptop: there are Catalan(n-1)*3^n SKI terms of size n (about 2.9e5 for n = 7, 2.8e6 for n = 8, 2.8e7 for n = 9, 2.9e8 for n = 10). Open targets: a terminating term of size n in 7..11 whose normal form is STRICTLY larger than the listed bound, or an exact value Xi_0(7) (or 8) with every non-terminating term certified.
targets.success_criterion: Success means (a) an SKI term with exactly n combinator leaves, 7 <= n <= 11, that reaches a normal form under leftmost-outermost (normal-order) reduction, whose normal form has STRICTLY more combinator leaves than the lower bound listed for that n on https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/SKI_Calculus re-fetched live immediately before claiming (same size convention as the page: size = number of S/K/I leaves); or (b) an exact value: a complete enumeration of all SKI terms of size n (n = 7 or 8) in which every term is either normalised (with its normal-form size recorded) or carries a machine-checkable non-termination certificate, the maximum normalised size matching the page's listed champion, while the page still shows '>=' for that n. The same rules apply, reported separately, to the SK-only table for 8 <= n <= 12, where the page lists a lower bound.

partial_wins.statement: Exact Xi_0(7) for SKI (expected 41 if the listed champion is optimal), with all non-normalising size-7 terms certified.
Exact Xi_0 for the SK-only calculus at n = 8 (all size-8 SK terms classified with certificates), if the page still lists '>= 80'.
A complete classification of size-8 SKI terms leaving at most 20 unresolved holdouts, with the holdout list published for others.

targets.verification_method: Parse the term, reduce with an independent normal-order reducer (graph reduction with sharing is fine, but the normal form must be printed in full and its leaves counted). Confirm the normal form has no redex (no S with 3 args, K with 2, I with 1). For exact-value claims: re-run the enumeration with an independently written enumerator, confirm the count Catalan(n-1)*3^n, and re-check each non-termination certificate (e.g. a reduction sequence from t to a term containing an instance of t in head position, or a proven-looping pattern like SII(SII) reached).
angles: Exhaustive enumeration with memoised reduction: reduce every subterm bottom-up once, hash-cons normal forms, and reuse results across the Catalan shapes; sizes 7-9 take minutes.

Non-termination certificates borrowed from Busy Beaver Turing-machine deciders: cycle detection, 'translated cycler' style growth detection (term t reduces to C[t'] with t' an instance of t), and loop-pattern libraries (omega-like subterms SII(SII), S(SI)(SI)...).

Import from term rewriting: use AProVE/TTT2-style termination provers on the non-normalising holdouts (dependency pairs, matrix interpretations) to certify non-termination or termination automatically.

Import from program synthesis: search sizes 10-11 by genetic programming over term trees with fitness = normal-form size under a step budget, seeded with the champions of sizes 8-9 (champions tend to be extensions of smaller ones).
Use the SK-only and BCKW tables as cross-checks: an SK term with I replaced by SKK is size-inflated, so champions transfer between tables in a known way.
pitfalls: Size is the number of combinator leaves, not the number of characters or applications; normal-form size is counted the same way.

Applicative-order (innermost) reduction can loop on terms that DO have a normal form; only normal-order reduction is complete. A term judged non-terminating because an innermost reducer looped is a classic error.
Terms that grow without bound but never reach a normal form are not terminating, however large they get.
The page was edited repeatedly in October 2026 (footer: last edited 2026-10-23), and the n = 9..11 SKI bounds now read 1561-1563; champions change often. Re-fetch before claiming.
Do not mix the SKI, SK-only and BCKW tables; each has its own size convention and champions (BCKW is out of reach beyond n = 5).

targets.name: Erich Friedman's Math Magic archive: beat a best-known entry on a monthly-problem page (non-packing categories)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Math Magic (1998-2020 monthly unsolved problems, archive at erich-friedman.github.io/mathmagic) keeps per-problem tables of best-known answers for each n (tilings, reptiles, numbers, digits, matrices, graphs, chess, games). Many were updated years after posting; the index's latest per-entry update is 3/25/23. Its 'Unsolved Problems from Math Magic' page lists 34 open questions with credited later progress (e.g. #8 proven in 2026 by Alec Kriebel, #19 found by Bryce Herdt, #20 proved by Vamshi Jandhyala, #33 disproved by Konstantin Kopp). Many still open items could be refuted or advanced by a single finite construction, e.g. #2: do any of 7 length-9 disconnected linear polyominoes tile a rectangle; #5: products of powers using 1..2n exactly once for n >= 2; #7: another shape with partridge number 4. Distinct from the bank's friedman-packing-records (the Packing Center). Target: a construction strictly improving a listed best-known value for some n on a Math Magic page, or a finite witness settling an item on unsolved.html.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit object (tiling coordinates, number, matrix, sequence) for one problem page linked from https://erich-friedman.github.io/mathmagic/index.html (excluding problems in the index's Packing category and anything under erich-friedman.github.io/packing, which friedman-packing-records covers) and one n, which (1) satisfies that page's stated rules as verified by an independent exact checker, and (2) is STRICTLY better in the page's own direction than the best entry for that n on the page re-fetched live immediately before claiming (or fills an n the table marks as unknown/blank within the range the page tabulates); OR an explicit finite witness that settles a question still listed as open on https://erich-friedman.github.io/mathmagic/unsolved.html re-fetched live (not one the page already credits as solved). The object must not appear in later literature found by searching the problem name. Emailing Friedman is NOT part of success.

partial_wins.statement: Extend a page's table to a new n just beyond the largest tabulated n with a verified construction plus a reproducible exhaustive-search log showing it is optimal for that n.
Unsolved #5: a verified solution for every n up to a bound beyond any n shown on the December 2000 page, with the search code.
Unsolved #2: a SAT/DLX-certified proof that one of the 7 disconnected polyominoes cannot tile any rectangle up to a stated size bound (bounded result, clearly labelled).

targets.verification_method: Write a per-page exact checker (integer coordinates / exact arithmetic), re-run it on the claimed object, fetch the live page and parse the table row for n, compare in the page's direction. Literature search on the problem title.
angles: Triage: crawl every monthly page, extract tables with 'best known'/'?' cells, and rank by last-updated date (stale pages from 1999-2010 with blank cells are the softest).
Exact cover / DLX and SAT (Kissat with cardinality encodings) for tiling and digit-arrangement problems; CP-SAT for matrix problems.
Cross-domain import (VLSI floorplanning): rectangle-packing and tiling pages map directly onto floorplanning B*-tree / sequence-pair representations with simulated annealing.
Cross-domain import (protein folding Monte Carlo): pull-move and replica-exchange Monte Carlo from HP-lattice protein folding for polyomino/polyform-shape optimisation pages.
Number pages: meet-in-the-middle and modular sieving (as in sums-of-cubes searches) for digit/number records.
pitfalls: Each page has idiosyncratic rules (e.g. 'distinct', 'non-trivial', reflections allowed?); misreading them is the commonest false record.

Updates to the pages are sporadic (latest index update 3/25/23, though unsolved.html credits a 2026 result); improvements may exist in later literature or OEIS but not on the page. Search before claiming.
Direction varies per page; a 'larger' value is not always better.
Do not overlap the Packing Center target (friedman-packing-records): packing pages under erich-friedman.github.io/packing and Math Magic problems in the Packing category are excluded here.

targets.name: Multimagie.com: smaller best-known multiplicative or additive-multiplicative magic squares (orders 7-17)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Christian Boyer's multimagie.com tables list the best known (mostly not proven minimal) multiplicative magic squares (smallest magic product P and/or smallest maximum entry 'Max nb'), pandiagonal multiplicative squares and additive-multiplicative squares for orders 3-17. Examples: 8x8 smallest known Max nb <= 117 and 9x9 <= 153 (Toshihiro Shirakawa, 2013), orders 10-17 products and Max nb (Shirakawa 2013, from his add-mult squares, plus Boyer and Luke Pebody 2005), a 9x9 pandiagonal multiplicative square with Max nb 1365 (Elbert Krison, 2017), and add-mult squares of orders 7 (Sebastien Miquel, 2016), 8-9 (Boyer 2005, after Walter Horner) and 10-17 (Shirakawa 2013). Target: a square of a listed type and order with strictly smaller P, Max nb or S (per the table's criterion) than the best known. Whether a 5x5 or 6x6 add-mult square exists is a live prize enigma, tracked separately and excluded here.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit n x n array of DISTINCT positive integers which an independent checker confirms has the type's properties (all rows, columns and both main diagonals with equal product; additionally equal sums for add-mult; all broken diagonals for pandiagonal), and whose criterion value (P, Max nb or S as named on the page) is STRICTLY SMALLER (direction: min) than the best-known value for that type and order on the relevant page among http://www.multimagie.com/English/Multiplicative.htm, Multiplicative6_7.htm, Multiplicative8_9.htm, Multiplicative10_.htm, AddMult10_.htm and SmallestAddMult.htm, re-fetched live immediately before claiming. Objects that would solve an enigma on http://www.multimagie.com/English/Enigmas.htm (e.g. any 5x5 or 6x6 add-mult magic square) are excluded. A literature search (arXiv, OEIS, Shirakawa/Miquel follow-ups) must also find no smaller published example.

partial_wins.statement: A pandiagonal multiplicative square improving a pandiagonal best-known entry.
An improvement in a secondary criterion (e.g. equal P but smaller MaxNb) where the page tracks both.

targets.verification_method: Python with exact integers: check distinctness, all line products (and sums), compute P, MaxNb, S, compare with the parsed live page. Seconds.
angles: Exponent-vector reduction: a multiplicative square is an additive magic 'square' of exponent vectors over the primes used; build additive Latin-square-based magic squares for each prime's exponents and combine (Graeco-Latin products).
For add-mult, start from Shirakawa/Miquel constructions and run local search (swap/scale moves) minimising MaxNb with CP-SAT feasibility repair.
Cross-domain import (MIMO / orthogonal space-time codes): orthogonal-design combinatorics (Latin and Graeco-Latin structures used in coding) give systematic exponent layouts.
Cross-domain import (portfolio optimisation): choosing the multiset of entries with fixed product as a knapsack on log-values; branch-and-bound on log-space with exact integer back-checks.
Restrict to smooth numbers with small prime support (2,3,5,7,11,13) and enumerate entry multisets with the right prime-exponent totals.
pitfalls: Distinctness is mandatory; repeated entries invalidate the square.
Semi-magic (rows/columns only) vs magic (plus diagonals) vs pandiagonal are different tables.
The site is updated rarely and 'best known' may have been improved in print; search the literature before claiming. Fetch the pages over plain http (the https certificate does not verify).
Do not confuse P (magic product) with MaxNb; the page may track both separately.
5x5 and 6x6 add-mult magic squares are live prize enigmas (Enigmas.htm), not table improvements; they are excluded from this target.

targets.name: OEIS 'keyword:more' sequences: compute the next term(s) beyond the live entry and b-file
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The OEIS flags sequences needing more terms with keyword 'more': on 2026-10-28 the search keyword:more returned 27,020 sequences, and keyword:more keyword:nice alone returned 845. Many are combinatorial counts or searches whose next term is within laptop reach with a better algorithm. Target: a new term (the next unknown index) for a 'more' sequence, computed by two independent programs.
targets.success_criterion: Success means one new term for one OEIS sequence A-number that carries keyword 'more' in its live entry (https://oeis.org/Annnnnn and its b-file, re-fetched immediately before claiming). The term must be at least one new value at the first index not present in DATA or the b-file. It must be computed by two independently written programs (different algorithms or languages) that agree, and both must reproduce all existing terms. The term must not appear in the entry's comments/links/extensions, in the OEIS edit history (https://oeis.org/Annnnnn/history, including pending drafts), or in an OEIS search for the term value. Excluded: any A-number named in another entry of the V3R1T4S bank (bank/targets.json or an open bank proposal), e.g. A075458, A088202, A292192, A250000, A279405, A006075, A028420, A389689, A389690, A392305, A391791, A387261, A387262, A357271; those terms count only under their own targets. Near-repdigit/repunit prime-index sequences are excluded unless the claimed term lies beyond the searched limit reported by the external search project that covers them (e.g. Makoto Kamada's pages), checked live. No submission to the OEIS.

partial_wins.statement: An independent verification that FAILS to reproduce an existing term (an error in the OEIS entry), with both programs and a hand-checkable explanation.
A proven lower or upper bound for the next term (e.g. exhaustive search to a limit with no hit) for a 'search' sequence, with logs.

targets.verification_method: Run both programs from a clean checkout on the skeptic's machine (≤ 1 hour, choose sequences accordingly); diff against the live b-file; fetch the history page for drafts.
angles: Mine the JSON search API for 'more' sequences whose last term was added long ago, with small terms and a short definition (counting problems on graphs, permutations, polyforms).
Transfer-matrix and dynamic-programming rewrites of brute-force counts (often gain 2-3 terms).
Cross-domain import (statistical physics): enumerations of lattice objects via the corner transfer matrix / finite-lattice method used for Potts and self-avoiding-walk series.
Cross-domain import (database engines): meet-in-the-middle with hash joins and columnar bitsets for 'number of solutions' searches; treat the count as a join cardinality.
Use SAT/#SAT model counters (ganak, d4) for constraint-defined counts.
pitfalls: Ambiguous definitions: the OEIS entry's DATA defines the sequence; reproduce all existing terms before trusting a new one.
Terms may be in the b-file or a pending draft but not in DATA; check both and the history page.
Off-by-one offsets (index base) produce a 'new' term that is actually an existing one.
Prime-search 'more' sequences (repunit-like) have external searched limits; a 'new' term below that limit would already be known.

targets.name: Prime Gap List: improve the record merit for some gap size
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The community Prime Gap List (github.com/primegap-list-project/prime-gap-list, file allgaps.sql, 3,930 commits, continuing Thomas Nicely's tables) records the largest known merit g/ln(p1) of a gap between consecutive primes for each even gap size g it lists. Endpoints may be certified primes or probable primes, per the primecat column. On 2026-10-28 allgaps.sql held 124,966 gap sizes: every even g up to 122,288, then sparse coverage up to 16,045,848 (the first missing even size was 122,290). It is updated several times a day; commits on 2026-10-27/28 include '48 updates by S.Troisi', 'New record 206048 merit=20.7850 found by M.Jansen', 'New record 296626 merit=5.0928 found by PDeGeest', 'new gaps by A.Renyer' (gaps up to 2,477,052) and '7 updates by Gapcoin'. Target: find a prime gap of some size g whose merit strictly exceeds the live table's merit for g, or a gap of an even size with no entry.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a pair (p1, g) such that an independent checker confirms three things. (1) p1 and p1+g are prime or strong probable prime (BPSW plus Miller-Rabin with at least 20 random bases; a primality certificate via PARI primecertify/ECPP is required only if the claim says 'certified'). (2) Every integer strictly between them is composite (sieve plus BPSW on survivors). (3) Either g/ln(p1), computed in mpmath, is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the merit recorded for g in allgaps.sql on the live master branch, or g is an even gap size with no row in allgaps.sql. The comparison uses allgaps.sql re-fetched immediately before claiming; also check the last 48h of commits, open PRs and the offsite https://primegaps.cloudygo.com/merits.txt for the same g. No submission is made.

partial_wins.statement: A gap with merit >= 20 (any size) verified by the checker, even if the size already has a higher-merit record (calibration of the search).
A record for a gap size in a band where the table's merits are locally low (a 'merit hole'), verified.

targets.verification_method: Use the repo's own check.py logic re-implemented independently with gmpy2: is_prime(p1), is_prime(p1+g), all interior numbers composite (trial sieve + gmpy2.is_prime), merit in mpmath; then parse allgaps.sql from a fresh clone. Minutes.
angles: Plot merit vs g from allgaps.sql and target 'holes' (sizes whose merit is far below neighbours); those are cheap to beat.
Primorial-offset search: candidates N = m·P#/d − a with combined sieving over a long interval (Troisi's combined_sieve approach), then BPSW on survivors at both ends.
Cross-domain import (radio astronomy / SETI dedispersion): run many trial offsets through one shared sieve pass the way dedispersion pipelines share FFT work across trial DMs.

Cross-domain import (reliability engineering 'weakest-link' statistics): model expected merit from the Cramér/Gumbel extreme-value distribution to allocate CPU only to (m, P#) bands with the highest expected record yield.
GPU-free: use 10 cores with gmpy2 and a segmented wheel sieve; avoid duplicating heavy-hitters by choosing primorials they do not use (inspect discoverer/primorial patterns in allgaps.sql).
pitfalls: The list is updated daily by heavy-compute contributors; a 'record' found today may already be superseded or pending. Re-fetch allgaps.sql and recent commits immediately before claiming.
PRP vs proven primes: the list records the endpoint category (primecat); an interior number misclassified as composite, or an endpoint that is only a weak Fermat PRP, invalidates the gap.
Merit uses natural log of the FIRST prime p1; using p2 or log10 gives inflated merits.
A gap is only valid if the interval contains NO prime; a sieve bug that skips one candidate creates fake huge gaps.

targets.name: Prime k-tuplets: a larger proven prime k-tuplet than the largest known for a stale (k, pattern) row (k = 11..17)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Norman Luhn's pzktupel.de 'Largest known prime k-tuplets to given pattern' table (last updated 18 Oct 2026) lists, for each k and admissible minimal pattern, the largest known proven prime k-tuplet. Small k are dominated by Riecoin (whose 8- and 9-tuplets fill the 2026 history) and by Ryan Propper and Serge Batalov (k = 11, May 2026), but some rows for k >= 12 are old and small (e.g. k=12 pattern d = 0,6,10,12,16,22,24,30,34,36,40,42: 75 digits, Michael Stocker, 30 Sep 2014). Target: a proven prime k-tuplet for some (k, pattern) row with more digits/larger value than that row's entry.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit integer n such that n + d is prime for every offset d of one admissible minimal pattern row on https://pzktupel.de/largest.php (re-fetched live immediately before claiming), with each member PROVEN prime (PARI/GP `primecertify` ECPP certificate verified by an independent run of `primecertify`/`checkprimecert`, or Primo certificate), and n STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the start of that row's listed tuplet; also not in the page's 'Recent additions' or kthist2026 history.

partial_wins.statement: Any proven k-tuplet that would enter the site's top-10 list for that k (top10.php), verified.
A proven tuplet beating a row for a SECOND pattern of the same k.

targets.verification_method: Independent PARI/GP: for each member isprime() and primecertify(); check pattern offsets equal the row's admissible pattern; compare against the live table. Seconds to minutes for <= 150-digit numbers.
angles: Search form n = m·P# + c with c chosen so the pattern is admissible mod every prime ≤ P (CRT on residue classes), then sieve m over a large range for all k offsets simultaneously.

Pick rows with the smallest digit counts relative to neighbours (stale rows), estimate expected time from the Hardy-Littlewood constant for that pattern (the site's ktpatt_hl.php) and pick the cheapest.
Cross-domain import (bioinformatics k-mer seeding / spaced seeds): treat the pattern as a spaced seed and use bit-parallel shift-and over sieve bitmaps to find positions where all k offsets survive.

Cross-domain import (lottery/wheel design in operations research): choose the primorial wheel and residue classes by a covering-design-style optimisation to maximise surviving density per unit of sieve work.
Fermat-test (base 2) filter in gmpy2 on survivors, BPSW, then ECPP only on full hits.
pitfalls: Patterns must be the exact admissible minimal pattern listed (different patterns of the same k are different rows).
PRP is not enough for this table; all members must be proven.
The table also lists 'early discoveries'; compare against the 'largest known' column only.
Riecoin miners can produce large 9/10-tuplets daily; avoid those rows and re-fetch before claiming.

targets.name: Gavin Theobald's Geometric Dissections: a dissection with fewer pieces than the catalogue's best
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Gavin Theobald's site catalogues 786 geometric dissections (regular polygons, stars, Greek crosses, etc., 2D and 3D) with the fewest pieces known, last updated 11 June 2026; the History page shows steady improvements (e.g. 'Improved dissection of {4} to 2×{7}', 7 Dec 2025; new {4}→rotated {6}, 30 Mar 2026). Target: a valid dissection between two shapes listed in the catalogue using strictly fewer pieces than the catalogue's entry (same rules: free / hinged / turn-over-allowed as on that page), or the same count without turning pieces over where the catalogue needs a turnover.
targets.success_criterion: Scope: plane (2D) polygon dissections on the catalogue whose record is an ordinary free dissection. 3D, spherical, hinged and locked dissections are excluded because the verification method does not check them. Success means explicit pieces (vertex coordinates in exact form: rationals or explicit algebraic numbers in Q(sqrt2, sqrt3, sqrt5, ...) as sympy expressions) together with two rigid-motion placements, such that an exact checker confirms two things. First, each placement tiles the respective target polygon exactly (union equals target up to measure zero; pairwise interiors disjoint; total area equal). Second, the shapes have the catalogue's normalisation (equal area). The piece count must be STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the count on the relevant catalogue page on https://www.gavin-theobald.uk/, re-fetched live immediately before claiming, with turnover allowed only if that page's record allows it. Alternatively, an equal count with no piece turned over counts where the live record requires a turnover. The dissection must not be previously published (check Frederickson's books and the site's History).

partial_wins.statement: Matching a catalogue piece count with a genuinely different dissection (non-congruent piece set), exactly verified.
A turnover-free dissection where the catalogue's best of the same count needs a turnover.

targets.verification_method: Exact polygon geometry in sympy (or exact algebraic-number Shapely-free code): verify each placed piece is a rigid motion (orientation-preserving unless turnover allowed) of the piece polygon, check pairwise interior-disjointness via exact segment intersection, and check union area = target area plus every target boundary point covered (vertex/edge-matching). Under an hour.
angles: Classic strip and tessellation superposition (Frederickson's T-strip/P-strip methods): automate overlaying two strips at varying offsets/angles and count resulting pieces.
Target the families the History shows as still moving (polygon-to-2×polygon, rotated copies, stars {n/k}) where the record is recent and seldom minimal.
Cross-domain import (image registration in medical imaging): treat the two tessellations as images and optimise the overlay transform to maximise boundary coincidence, which minimises piece count.
Cross-domain import (garment/sheet-metal nesting): nesting heuristics (no-fit polygons) to place pieces of the first shape into the second.
Exhaustive search over small hinged-dissection combinatorics for 4-5 piece targets.
pitfalls: Floating-point coordinates that 'almost' fit are the classic false dissection; only exact arithmetic counts.
Turnover rules: reflected pieces are not allowed when the record is turnover-free.
Area normalisation: dissections are between shapes of EQUAL area; a scaled target is invalid.
Frederickson's books and Theobald's site may contain the dissection already under a different shape name; check both.

targets.name: Amicable pairs: beat the smallest known ratio m/n
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Sergei Chernykh's amicable-pairs site (sech.me/ap) announces on its news page that the BOINC search for all pairs with smaller member below 10^21 finished on 2026-04-08. The main page still describes the list as complete below 10^20, and the downloadable database is dated 2023-01-01. The site also holds over a billion larger constructed pairs. The record for the most unbalanced pair (smallest m/n with m < n) was set on 2023-10-16 by 149251425686668100950 / 255075095917125253802 (ratio about 0.58512739, credited on the news page to 'BOINC: Science United, BudgieSoft'). Before it, the best even-even pair had ratio about 0.60512272 (Chernykh, 2015). The best odd-odd pair, about 0.59834304 (1997), is still the odd-odd record. A smaller ratio is a clean, checkable record. It must come from constructions beyond 10^21, since everything below has been searched exhaustively.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for positive integers m < n with complete proven factorisations such that sigma(m) = sigma(n) = m + n exactly and m/n, compared as an exact rational, STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the smallest ratio stated on https://sech.me/ap/news.html (re-fetched immediately before the claim) and than any smaller ratio found in a same-day check of sech.me pages and the literature.

partial_wins.statement: Odd-odd record: a new amicable pair with both members odd whose ratio m/n is STRICTLY LESS than the best odd-odd ratio stated on the news page at verification time.

New unbalanced pair: an amicable pair with m/n < 0.6 that is absent from the downloadable non-trivial pairs file c2_filtered.7z on https://sech.me/ap/ and is NOT of a type (3,2) to (10,2) with more than 30 digits (that file omits those types; such a pair counts only after a check against the full downloadable database). Labelled 'new relative to the public download'.

targets.verification_method: Prove every prime factor (BPSW + PARI isprime/ECPP), compute sigma(m) and sigma(n) from the factorisations, check both equal m+n, compare m*q < p*n with the record ratio p/q as exact integers. For p2 grep the pair in the downloaded non-trivial list.
angles: Borho-Hoffmann breeders and te Riele's rules: a pair (a*u, a*p) built on a common factor a; very abundant a with small extra primes drives sigma(m)/m up, which is what a small ratio needs (sigma(m)/m = 1 + n/m).
Integer programming (imported from operations research): choose a set of prime powers for the common part to hit a target abundancy window, as a knapsack over log(sigma(p^e)/p^e).

Meet-in-the-middle on abundancy (imported from cryptanalysis): tabulate products of small prime powers by their sigma/n ratio in two halves and match halves whose product lands in the narrow window the ratio record needs.
Simulated annealing over prime-signature templates (imported from statistical physics), scoring by distance of the resulting equation from solvability.
Study the 2023 record's structure (a 2*5^2*7^2*11*17*23*31*313*523*1487*1877 shape against 2*31*53*313*743*4463*74789471) and look for the same common factor with other cofactor splits.
pitfalls: Ratio defined with m < n; inverting gives a number above 1.
Incomplete factorisation fakes sigma; every factor must be proven prime.
Pairs below 10^21 are all known (BOINC search finished 2026-04-08); a 'new' small pair is a bug.

The 446 MB non-trivial file covers all known pairs up to 30 digits but omits types (3,2)-(10,2) for longer pairs; the full database (25.44 GB compressed, 714 GB unpacked, dated 2023-01-01) is downloadable but heavy. State exactly which list novelty was checked against.

targets.name: Conjectures 'R Us: eliminate a remaining k from a Riesel or Sierpinski base conjecture
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: For each base b <= 1030 the Riesel (resp. Sierpinski) conjecture says a specific conjectured k is the smallest k for which k*b^n-1 (resp. k*b^n+1) is composite for every n. Proving it means finding a prime for every smaller eligible k. The Conjectures 'R Us project (Gary Barnes, Mark Rodenkirch and contributors) lists for each base the k's still without a prime and the n-range tested; the unproven page is regenerated continually (last update 2026-10-28). Several Riesel bases still have hundreds of thousands of k's tested only to n = 2500 (on 2026-10-28: base 891 with 763087 k's, 690 with 739852, 876 with 612567, 756 with 604445, 801 with 494394), where candidates have about 7000 digits and a probable-prime test takes about a second.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a base b and a k that is listed as remaining for b on the live CRUS Riesel or Sierpinski pages (http://www.noprimeleftbehind.net/crus/vstats_new/crus-unproven.htm and the per-base remaining-k files it links), re-fetched immediately before the claim, plus an exponent n STRICTLY GREATER than the tested n-limit listed for that k, such that k*b^n-1 (Riesel) or k*b^n+1 (Sierpinski) is PROVEN prime (an N+1 or N-1 proof, since b^n is fully factored; probable-prime results alone do not count). Each such prime removes one k (direction: min on the remaining count). Work only on k's or bases marked available, not on reserved ones.

partial_wins.statement: Base proven: the last remaining k of some base b eliminated, so the base appears among unproven conjectures at verification time but now has a prime for every remaining k.

Range extension certificate: an available k (or a whole available base) sieved and tested with no prime from the listed limit up to at least 1.5 times that limit, with the sieve file and test residues saved so a verifier can re-test a random 2% sample of survivors and re-sieve a random sub-range.

targets.verification_method: Check k is listed as remaining on the live page and n exceeds its listed limit. Prove primality: Sierpinski form with PFGW -tp/-tm or LLR/PRST (Proth/Pocklington N-1 test), or PARI isprime(N,1) for small cases; Riesel form with LLR/PRST (Lucas-Lehmer-Riesel / N+1 test) or PFGW -tp. Confirm k is not a multiple of b (MOB) that maps to another listed k, and that k is not excluded for algebraic factors.
angles: Pick available bases with huge k-counts at n = 2500: sieve all k together with srsieve2/sr2sieve to depth ~1e9, then PRP-test in n order. Each prime found removes a k, so expected yield per hour is high.

Portfolio allocation (imported from finance, Kelly criterion): weight each k by its Nash weight / expected primes per CPU-second given candidate size, and rebalance the queue every hour as k's drop out.
Survival analysis (imported from biostatistics): model 'time to first prime' per k from its sieve survival rate and stop testing k's whose hazard falls below the base average.
Error-checked arithmetic (imported from numerical analysis): use PRST/LLR with Gerbicz error checking so a hardware glitch never produces a false prime or a false composite.

Look for k's with partial algebraic factorizations (k = m^2 for Riesel, k = m^4 forms, etc.) on the remaining lists: proving such a k can never yield a prime for an n-class also shrinks the problem, but must follow CRUS conventions.
pitfalls: A probable prime is not a proof; CRUS-style eliminations need an N-1 or N+1 primality proof.
Multiples of the base (k divisible by b) duplicate another k at n+1; they are excluded from the lists and do not count.
A prime with n below the listed test limit means a transcription error or a wrong k, not a discovery.
Confusing Riesel (-1) with Sierpinski (+1), or base b with base b^2 lists.
Working on reserved k's duplicates someone's running effort; the claim may already exist unreported.

targets.name: Cunningham chains: beat a largest-known record for some length, or find a chain of length 21
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: A Cunningham chain of the first kind of length L is p, 2p+1, 4p+3, ... (L primes); of the second kind p, 2p-1, 4p-3, .... The records page at pzktupel.de (continuing the list originally created and maintained by Dirk Augustin; last updated 2026-10-22) lists the largest known chain of each length and kind and the smallest chains. Active 2026 record setters include Serge Batalov (many lengths 3-17), Ryan Propper with Serge Batalov (length 3, first kind, 2026-10-19), John Armitage (lengths 19 and 20) and Nenad Mićić (length 18, first kind). Length 11-14 records (98-149 digits) date from 2013-2018 (Primecoin, Andrey Balyakin), lengths 15-20 records are 25-45 digits, and the longest known chains have length 20 (John Armitage, 2026-03-29 for the second kind and 2026-04-18 for the first kind). No length-21 chain is listed.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a chain of length L >= 3 and kind K whose L members are all PROVEN prime and whose initial prime is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max, compared as integers) than BOTH (a) the initial prime of the largest known chain of length L and kind K on https://pzktupel.de/CC/cc.php, re-fetched immediately before the claim, AND (b) the initial prime of every length-L run of consecutive members of any longer chain of kind K listed anywhere on that page (both tables). Part (b) is needed because the page does not always list sub-chains: on 2026-10-28 the listed length-20 first-kind chain 75949683268775452969189500*2^k-1 contains length-19 sub-chains larger than the listed length-19 first-kind record. A longer new chain counts toward a shorter length L under the same comparison.

partial_wins.statement: Longest chain ever: a proven Cunningham chain of length 21 or more of either kind (no length-21 chain is listed at verification time). Headline result.

New length-19 or length-20 chain of either kind, any size, whose initial prime is not listed on the page at verification time AND which is not a run of consecutive members of any chain listed on the page (dropping the first member of a listed length-20 chain gives a length-19 chain that is not new).

targets.verification_method: Recompute each member from the initial prime. Prove the first prime (PARI isprime with certificate, or N-1/N+1 proof using the primorial*2^k structure); then each next member q = 2p+1 (resp. 2p-1) has q-1 = 2p (resp. q+1 = 2p) with p already proven, so a Pocklington (resp. Morrison) step proves it. Check the chain cannot be extended backwards in a way that changes its listed length, and compare the initial prime with the live record.
angles: Primorial-form search: p = k * P# * 2^j - 1 (first kind) with a sieve over k that removes every k for which some member is divisible by a prime up to 10^9 before any primality test.

Multi-modulus wheel sieving: precompute the admissible residues of k modulo primorials so that every surviving k has no small factor in any of the L members; this is how the length 19-20 chains were found.

GPU-style bit-sliced sieving (imported from high-performance computing / bitcoin-era Primecoin miners, which set the length 11-14 records): even on a laptop, a vectorised sieve on the CPU cores can test billions of k per hour.

Extreme-value statistics (imported from risk modelling): fit the distribution of chain lengths found per sieve batch to estimate how many candidates a length-21 hit needs, and choose the primorial size that maximises expected record digits per hour.
Bi-twin and mixed constellations: a bi-twin chain search also produces long chains of both kinds as a by-product.
pitfalls: Probable-prime members are not proof; but here proofs are cheap through the chain structure, so insist on them.
A chain that extends further than claimed (or starts earlier) may already be listed under a different length or initial prime.
Shifting a known chain (starting at its 2nd, 3rd, ... member) gives a shorter chain with a new initial prime that is not a discovery; check every listed chain for containment.
Mixing up first kind (2p+1) and second kind (2p-1).
Comparing digit counts instead of exact integers when two chains have the same number of digits.

targets.name: High-rank elliptic curves over Q with prescribed torsion: beat a cell of Dujella's table
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: For each of Mazur's 15 torsion groups T, Andrej Dujella's table gives the best known lower bound B(T) for the rank of an elliptic curve over Q whose torsion subgroup is exactly T. On 2026-10-28 the table reads: trivial 32 (Elkies-Klagsbrun-Li, October 2026; the rank history page lists rank >= 30 and >= 31 by Alpoge-Howell, August 2026, before it), Z/2 22 (Li 2026), Z/3 15 and Z/4 13 (Elkies-Klagsbrun 2020; Li 2026), Z/5 9 (Klagsbrun 2020), Z/6 9 (Klagsbrun 2020, Voznyy 2020, Dujella-Peral 2026), Z/7 6 (Klagsbrun 2020), Z/8 6 (Elkies 2006, Dujella-MacLeod-Peral 2013, Voznyy 2021), Z/9 4 (Fisher 2009, van Beek 2015, Dujella-Petricevic 2021, Dujella-Petricevic-Rathbun 2022, Voznyy 2026), Z/10 4 (Dujella 2005, 2008; Elkies 2006; Fisher 2016), Z/12 4 (Fisher 2008), Z/2xZ/2 15 (Elkies 2009, Li 2026), Z/2xZ/4 9 (Dujella-Peral 2012, 2019; Klagsbrun 2020), Z/2xZ/6 6 (Elkies 2006; Dujella-Peral-Tadic 2015; Dujella-Peral 2020), Z/2xZ/8 3 (Connell 2000 and many later authors, most recently AttarBashi, Fisher, Rathbun and Voznyy 2022). The trivial-torsion and Z/2 cells are being pushed by large 2026 campaigns and are not laptop targets; the small-family cells (Z/7 through Z/12, Z/2xZ/6, Z/2xZ/8) are searched by Mestre-Nagao sieving over one- or two-parameter Kubert families, which is laptop-scale. A rank-4 curve with torsion Z/2xZ/8 would settle a question asked in print since 2000.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for an elliptic curve E over Q, given by integral Weierstrass coefficients, whose torsion subgroup computed exactly (PARI elltors) is isomorphic to T, together with r explicit rational points whose Neron-Tate height-pairing matrix has determinant > 0 (computed at 100 and again at 200 decimal digits, agreeing, and bounded away from 0 by at least 10^-20 relative to the product of the diagonal), where r is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the value of B(T) shown for that T on https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~duje/tors/tors.html, re-fetched live immediately before the claim, and greater than any higher value found in a same-day literature check (arXiv, Dujella's history page). Rank lower bounds only: analytic-rank, Nagao-sum or parity arguments never count.

partial_wins.statement: Record tie with a new curve: torsion exactly T for T in {Z/7, Z/8, Z/9, Z/10, Z/12, Z/2xZ/6, Z/2xZ/8}, r independent points with r equal to the live B(T), and the curve not isomorphic over Q (different minimal model after ellminimalmodel and not related by ellisomat) to any curve on Dujella's page for T at verification time.

Family record: an elliptic curve over Q(t) with torsion T and r independent Q(t)-points, r STRICTLY GREATER than G(T) on https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~duje/tors/generic.html at verification time; independence certified by specializing at one rational t0 where the torsion is still T and the r specialized points have positive regulator.

targets.verification_method: PARI/GP: E=ellinit(a); check discriminant != 0; elltors(E) gives T exactly; ellisoncurve for every point; M=ellheightmatrix(E,P) at \p100 and \p200; matdet(M) > 0 with the stated margin and stable between precisions. Compare ellminimalmodel(E) and j-invariant against every curve scraped from the T page (z7.html, z8.html, ...). For p2 substitute t0, re-run the same checks, and verify the points satisfy the generic equation symbolically.
angles: Mestre-Nagao sieve: run the Kubert parametrization for T over millions of small-height parameters, rank by Nagao sums S(N) = sum over p<N of (1 - (p-1)/#E(F_p)) * log p, then run 2-descent (PARI ellrank) only on the top 0.01%.

Ranking as a learning problem (imported from machine learning): train a gradient-boosted model or small transformer on the first few hundred a_p of curves with known rank (the murmurations work of He, Lee, Oliver and Pozdnyakov shows a_p sequences carry rank signal) and use it to reorder the sieve queue.

Bayesian optimisation / bandits over the parameter plane (imported from experimental design): treat the Nagao sum as a noisy objective, fit a Gaussian process over (u, v) parameters in two-parameter families, and spend sieve budget where the posterior upper bound is highest.

Fibre in a richer family: for Z/2xZ/6 and Z/2xZ/8 use Dujella-Peral style sub-families with forced extra points (Diophantine triples, Heron triangles), so the generic rank starts higher before sieving.

Signal-processing view of the sieve: Nagao sums are matched filters; replace them by a weighted sum tuned on known record curves (learned weights per p) and check whether it separates rank-r from rank-(r-1) curves better.
pitfalls: The torsion is larger than T (e.g. a Z/8 curve that actually has Z/2xZ/8): it then belongs to a different row and is not a record for T.
Points that are dependent (multiples, sums with torsion) give a singular height matrix; low-precision determinants can look positive. Require two precisions and a margin.
Rank 'found' by analytic rank, Nagao sums, root number/parity or BSD heuristics is not a lower bound. Only explicit independent points count.
A change of Weierstrass model or a twist that is actually isomorphic over Q re-presents a listed curve; always compare minimal models.
The trivial and Z/2 cells move monthly in 2026 (large GPU campaigns); a claim there must be checked against the live page and the rank history page the same day.

targets.name: High-rank elliptic curves with prescribed torsion over quadratic fields: beat or certify a cell
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Over quadratic fields K = Q(sqrt d) there are 26 possible torsion groups (Kenku-Momose, Kamienny). Dujella's table lists, for each T, the best known lower bound B(T) for the rank of a curve over some quadratic field with torsion T, the squarefree d of the field Q(sqrt d) for the record, and in brackets bounds that are only conditional on the parity conjecture (on 2026-10-28 only T = 0, 34 (35), and Z/2xZ/10, 4 (5), have bracketed values). Small cells on 2026-10-28 include Z/11 (3, d = 12601), Z/13 (2, d = 193), Z/14 (3, d = 430), Z/15 (2, d = 190), Z/16 (4, d = -183443183), Z/18 (2, d = 9049), Z/2xZ/10 (4, conditional 5), Z/2xZ/12 (5, d = -295935), Z/3xZ/3 (9, d = -3), Z/3xZ/6 (6, d = -3), Z/4xZ/4 (8, d = -1). Most recent entries are by M. Voznyy (personal communications 2021-2026); S. Li raised Z/2xZ/2 to 22 in October 2026.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a quadratic field K = Q(sqrt d) (d squarefree), an elliptic curve E over K with torsion subgroup over K computed exactly as T, and r explicit K-points with positive height-regulator (two precisions, margin as for the Q table), where r is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the unconditional value B(T) on https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~duje/tors/torsquad.html, re-fetched live immediately before the claim. Bracketed (parity-conditional) values are not the bar; the unconditional value is.

partial_wins.statement: Unconditional upgrade: for a cell whose table entry has a bracketed conditional value, exhibit that many independent K-points explicitly (e.g. Z/2xZ/10 at rank 5), making the conditional value unconditional.
Smaller field: a curve with torsion T reaching the live record rank B(T) over a quadratic field with |d| STRICTLY SMALLER than the d listed for T at verification time.

targets.verification_method: PARI/GP: K=nfinit(y^2-d); E=ellinit(a,K); elltors(E) over K; check each point on E; ellheightmatrix(E,P) over K at two precisions; matdet > 0 with margin. Check d squarefree and compare against the listed d. If E is defined over Q, cross-check with rank E(K) = rank E(Q) + rank E^d(Q) using independent points on E and on the twist.
angles: Quadratic points on modular curves X1(N) (hyperelliptic or bielliptic for the relevant N) give explicit families of curves with torsion Z/N over quadratic fields; sieve over small-height points of these parametrizations.
Base-change trick: for torsion groups realisable by curves defined over Q, rank E(Q(sqrt d)) = rank E(Q) + rank E^d(Q); search for a high-rank Q-curve and a twist d that also has many points.

Treat d as an arm of a multi-armed bandit (imported from reinforcement learning): allocate 2-descent effort across candidate fields by the upper confidence bound of Nagao-type sums computed over split primes of K.

Metropolis random walk over family parameters (imported from statistical physics) with energy = minus the Nagao sum, cooling slowly; good for the small Z/13, Z/15, Z/18 families where exhaustive grids are sparse.

For p1, search for missing points by height-bounded enumeration plus LLL on the Mordell-Weil lattice of the known points (the lattice-reduction idea from cryptanalysis), since the conditional rank already tells you a further point exists.
pitfalls: Torsion over K larger than T, or points defined only over a bigger field (check every coordinate lies in K).
Parity-conjecture or analytic-rank arguments do not count; explicit points only.
d not squarefree, or d and d*k^2 treated as different fields.
Confusing rank over Q with rank over K, or quoting a Q-record as a quadratic-field record.

targets.name: Giuga numbers: find one not yet known
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: A Giuga number is a composite n such that p divides n/p - 1 for every prime p dividing n (equivalently, sum of 1/p over p | n minus 1/n is a positive integer). Giuga's primality conjecture says no Giuga number is a Carmichael number. OEIS A007850 (credited to D. Borwein, J. M. Borwein, P. B. Borwein and R. Girgensohn) lists 12 terms up to 1910667181420507984555759916338506, records Fred Schneider's 2006 exhaustive search showing no further Giuga numbers with 8 or fewer prime factors, and mentions one further 97-digit Giuga number with 10 prime factors (Butske, Jaje and Mayernik, 2000) that may not be the next term. All known Giuga numbers have sum 1/p - 1/n = 1.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a squarefree composite n given with its complete proven prime factorisation such that for every prime p | n, (n/p - 1) mod p == 0, and n is absent from the data, comments and b-file of https://oeis.org/A007850 (re-fetched immediately before the claim), from the Butske-Jaje-Mayernik paper's list, and from the mersenneforum Giuga thread.

partial_wins.statement: Exhaustive 9-factor certificate: a complete search, reimplemented by the verifier, listing every Giuga number with exactly 9 prime factors (extending Schneider's 8-factor search), with the search tree logs saved so that random branches can be rerun.
A Giuga number with sum 1/p - 1/n = 2 (or larger); none is known.

targets.verification_method: Python big integers: multiply the primes, prove each prime (BPSW + PARI isprime), check squarefree, check (n//p - 1) % p == 0 for every p, compute sum 1/p - 1/n with fractions.Fraction. Diff n against the OEIS data, b-file and comments.
angles: Borwein-Girgensohn completion: fix the first m-2 primes; the last two primes are determined by factoring a single explicit integer, so the search is a tree whose leaves are factorisations.
Branch-and-bound on Egyptian fractions (imported from operations research): the condition sum 1/p - 1/n = 1 is an Egyptian-fraction equation over primes; bound remaining sums tightly to prune.
Arithmetic-derivative fixed points (Grau and Oller-Marcen): n is Giuga iff n' = a*n + 1; search for fixed points of the map n -> n' - n with structured n.

Perfectly weighted graphs (Butske, Jaje, Mayernik): use the graph-theoretic reformulation to enumerate compatible prime sets as a constraint-satisfaction problem (imported from combinatorial search / SAT).
Use ECM/SIQS-friendly ordering: choose search branches whose completion integer is smooth or small so the factoring at each leaf finishes in seconds.
pitfalls: Non-squarefree n are not Giuga numbers.
Primary pseudoperfect numbers satisfy sum 1/p + 1/n = 1 (plus sign) and are a different sequence (A054377).
The 97-digit 10-factor example is already known (in the OEIS comments); rediscovering it is not new.
An unproven large prime factor leaves the claim unproven.

targets.name: Curves over finite fields with many points: raise a lower bound on manYPoints
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: N_q(g) is the largest number of F_q-rational points on a smooth, projective, absolutely irreducible curve of genus g over F_q. The manYPoints table (Gerard van der Geer, Everett Howe, Kristin Lauter, Christophe Ritzenthaler) lists for small q (primes up to 97 and prime powers) and g up to 50 either the exact value or an interval [lower, upper]. Interval cells are open; the table was updated as recently as 2026-09-14 and Everett Howe added constructions in April 2026. Raising a lower bound needs one explicit curve and a point count.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for an explicit curve C over F_q (equations given) that is smooth projective and absolutely irreducible after normalisation, of geometric genus exactly g, with N rational points on its smooth projective model, where (direction: max) N is STRICTLY GREATER than the lower bound for cell (q, g) on https://manypoints.org/ (and in https://manypoints.org/Download.ashx), re-fetched live immediately before the claim. For a cell with no listed lower bound (blank on the table, 'm' in the download; 1488 of 2950 cells on 2026-10-28), N must be at least the site's admissibility threshold floor((U - q - 1)/sqrt(2)) + q + 1 stated on https://manypoints.org/Info.aspx, where U is the cell's listed upper bound. A curve below that threshold is not a win. N above the cell's upper bound is a BUG, not a win.

partial_wins.statement: Family-exhaustion certificate: for one non-exact cell, a complete enumeration of an explicitly defined family (for example all genus-g hyperelliptic curves over F_q up to isomorphism, or all plane quartics over F_q for g = 3) proving that no member exceeds the current lower bound, with code the verifier reruns in under an hour.

targets.verification_method: Compute the genus (Sage/Singular normalisation or Riemann-Hurwitz for covers) and count points of the smooth model over F_q, F_q^2, ..., F_q^g; reconstruct the L-polynomial and check it satisfies the Weil bounds and functional equation (a consistency check that catches miscounts). For hyperelliptic curves use PARI hyperellcharpoly. Compare N with the live cell.
angles: Fibre products of Artin-Schreier or Kummer covers of P^1 (van der Geer-van der Vlugt style): choose additive or multiplicative polynomials whose fibres split over many F_q-points, and take fibre products to multiply points faster than genus.
Quotients of curves with large automorphism groups (Hermitian, Suzuki, Deligne-Lusztig, modular curves X0(N) over F_p) by subgroups: Riemann-Hurwitz gives genus, point counts drop predictably.

Evolutionary search (imported from optimisation): CMA-ES or genetic search over coefficient vectors of plane curves or superelliptic equations with fitness = rational point count, keeping the genus fixed by construction.
Constraint solving (imported from SAT/SMT): encode 'f(x) is a square for at least N values of x in F_q' for hyperelliptic y^2 = f(x) as a pseudo-Boolean problem and let a solver look for f.
Algebraic-geometry codes view (imported from coding theory): curves with many points give long AG codes, so known record codes from codetables.de constructed via curves can point at candidate curves.
pitfalls: Counting points on a singular plane model instead of its normalisation: singular points may split into several places or none.
Missing points at infinity, or counting the affine model only.
Curve not absolutely irreducible (it splits over an extension), so it is not a genus-g curve at all.
Using the arithmetic genus of a plane model instead of the geometric genus.
Reading the wrong column: q = 2^3 and q = 8 style headers, or the A(q) asymptotic rows, are different cells.

targets.name: Sociable numbers: find an aliquot cycle not on Moews' list
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: An aliquot cycle of length L >= 3 (sociable numbers) is a cycle of the map s(n) = sigma(n) - n. David Moews' list (updated 11-IX-2026) has 5446 cycles: 5433 of length 4, one of length 5, five of length 6, five of length 8, one of length 9 and one of length 28. Exhaustive searches: all cycles whose number before the largest member is below 10^14 (Dmitry Bodyagin, 2016), and all cycles with odd smallest member up to 10^16 (a mersenneforum.org group using Bodyagin's program, 2016). Most of the 4-cycles are of Borho's form (cycles 121-5446 among them); the list credits the bulk of these to Robert Gerbicz, with many by Karsten Blankenagel and Wieland Borho, Andreas vom Stein, Ren Yuanhua and others, so new large 4-cycles keep appearing.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a list of L >= 3 distinct positive integers n_1..n_L, each with a complete factorisation into proven primes, such that s(n_i) = n_{i+1} and s(n_L) = n_1 exactly, and such that no member appears anywhere in https://djm.cc/sociable.txt re-fetched immediately before the claim (direction: max on the count of known cycles).

partial_wins.statement: A new cycle of length other than 4 (5, 6, 8, 9, 28 or any new length), absent from the list; report as the headline result.

A new cycle whose smallest member is below 10^20, which would expose a gap in the region the list is closest to complete; label it separately and double-check against the exhaustive-search statements in the list header.

targets.verification_method: Multiply out each factorisation, prove every prime factor (BPSW below 2^64, PARI isprime or ECPP above), compute sigma exactly from the factorisation, check the cycle closes, check all members distinct and not perfect/amicable, and grep every member against the live list.
angles: Borho's rule for 4-cycles (the analogue of Euler's rule for amicable pairs): fix a common part a and solve for the prime structure of the other part; Gerbicz's large harvest came from systematically running such rules.

Cycle detection on functional graphs (imported from algorithm design): run Brent's cycle finder on s(n) from structured seeds (products of a known-cycle common part with new primes) rather than from random n.

Constraint solving (imported from SMT): encode the prime-exponent pattern of each member and the sigma equations modulo many small primes as constraints; let a solver propose patterns, then confirm with exact arithmetic.

Meet-in-the-middle (imported from cryptanalysis): split each member into a fixed smooth part and an unknown part; tabulate sigma-ratios of candidate unknown parts and look for matches across the four members.
Mine the 'breeders' and near-misses of amicable searches (Chernykh's database) as seeds for 4-cycles.
pitfalls: Amicable pairs (length 2) and perfect numbers (length 1) do not count.
A rotation of a known cycle is the same cycle; check every member, not just the smallest.
Incomplete factorisation gives a wrong sigma; every factor must be proven prime.
Floating-point or truncated arithmetic in sigma for 30+ digit members.

targets.name: Multiply perfect numbers: find a new 9-, 10- or 11-perfect number
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: n is k-perfect when sigma(n) = k*n. Achim Flammenkamp's Multiply Perfect Numbers page (built on Richard Schroeppel's archive; page last updated 2026-02-20) lists 5932 known MPNs in its database snapshot of 2022-12-31 (its yearly table counts 5933 for 2024 and 2025, adding the 2024 perfect number credited on the page to 'Lurant&Woltman&Kurowski et al.'): 1136 8-perfect (estimated about 1140; the page answers 'probably yes' to whether all are discovered), 2164 9-perfect (estimated about 2200), 1710 10-perfect (estimated about 4500) and only 2 11-perfect (estimated about 10000; the first found 2001-03-13 by G. F. Woltman, the second 2022-09-07). George Woltman is credited with 2416 discoveries (1997-2013, 2021-2022). The claims file mpn_current.txt lists 0 claimed-but-unmerged numbers since 2023-01-12. Verification is cheap: given the factorisation of n, sigma(n) needs no further factoring.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a positive integer n given as a product of proven primes with exponents, such that sigma(n) = k*n exactly with k >= 10, and n absent from the database file mpn.gz and the claims file mpn_current.txt linked from https://wwwhomes.uni-bielefeld.de/achim/mpn.html (both re-fetched immediately before the claim) and from OEIS A007691 (multiply-perfect numbers) and its b-file.

partial_wins.statement: New 9-perfect number: sigma(n) = 9n exactly, n absent from mpn.gz and mpn_current.txt at verification time.
New 8-perfect number (the page calls the 8-perfect list 'probably' complete, so this would be surprising): same checks; double-check before claiming.

targets.verification_method: Prove each prime (BPSW + PARI isprime/ECPP). Compute sigma(n) = prod (p^(e+1)-1)/(p-1) exactly with Python big integers; check sigma(n) mod n == 0 and k = sigma(n)/n. Compute ln(ln(n)) to 7 decimals and the factorisation string and search both in mpn.gz and mpn_current.txt.
angles: Systematic substitution: the page lists 'substitution pairs' (X, Y) with equal fractional abundancy; apply every pair to every known MPN containing X, and compose substitutions. Check which combinations are absent from the database.
