Term rewriting (imported from programming-language theory): treat substitutions as rewrite rules on factorisation strings and search the closure of the known set under the rules with deduplication by ln(ln(n)).

Best-first search with an admissible heuristic (imported from AI planning, A*): state = partial factorisation with an unbalanced sigma; heuristic = how far the remaining abundancy is from the target; expand by adding the largest unresolved prime from sigma(p^e).
Use Cunningham-table factorisations of p^e - 1 (Wagstaff's tables) as a free oracle so the search never stalls on factoring sigma(p^e).
Times-k trick from the page: if n is k-perfect, k is prime and k does not divide n, then k*n is worth testing for (k+1)-perfection; scan the 10-perfect list for 11-perfect candidates.
pitfalls: Duplicates written with a different factor order or exponent layout; dedupe by the full integer or ln(ln(n)).
A factor that is only a probable prime makes the claim unproven.
Numbers known on forums or in OEIS but not yet merged into Flammenkamp's file; check OEIS and the claims file too.
Abundancy miscounted when sigma(n)/n is not an integer (a 'near' MPN).

targets.name: Generalized Cullen and Woodall primes: first prime for a base with none known
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Generalized Cullen numbers are n*b^n+1 and generalized Woodall numbers are n*b^n-1. Gary Barnes's tables (No Prime Left Behind, started 2025-08-09; the bases <= 1000 Cullen page was last updated 2026-10-25, the bases <= 1000 Woodall page 2026-05-11) list, for every base b up to and beyond 10000, the n giving primes and the contiguous test limit; Gunter Loh's older status page and Norman Luhn's pzktupel tables are the history. In the bases 9001-10000 page (unchanged since 2025-08-09), every base is tested only to n = 10K and 365 of the 1000 bases had no known Cullen prime on 2026-10-28; the bases <= 1000 Cullen page has 258 bases with no known prime (205 of them tested only to 10K) and the Woodall page 64. Candidates near n = 10K, b ~ 9000 have about 40 000 digits; Cullen primes are provable by an N-1 test because N-1 = n*b^n is fully factored.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a base b marked as having no known primes (zero primes listed) on the live NPLB Generalized Cullen or Woodall page for its range (index at http://www.noprimeleftbehind.net/Generalized-Cullen-primes-1000.htm), re-fetched immediately before the claim, and an n STRICTLY GREATER than that base's listed test limit such that n*b^n+1 (Cullen) or n*b^n-1 (Woodall) is PROVEN prime (N-1 or N+1 proof). Each such base leaving the no-prime list counts (direction: min on the count of bases with no known prime).

partial_wins.statement: New prime for a base that already has primes: proven prime n*b^n+-1 with n greater than the listed contiguous test limit and not listed (including not inside a '(...)' missing-range note) at verification time.

Test-limit extension certificate: one unreserved base tested with no prime from the listed limit to at least twice that limit, with sieve file and residues saved for a 2% random retest by the verifier.

targets.verification_method: Check the base row on the live page (zero primes, limit). Recompute N exactly. Cullen: N-1 = n*b^n, factor n and b, run a Pocklington/Proth-style proof (PFGW -tp/-tm, PRST, or PARI isprime(N,1) where feasible). Woodall: N+1 = n*b^n, N+1 proof with PFGW -tp or LLR/PRST. Confirm no trivial factor from parity (b odd and n odd makes n*b^n+1 even) or from b being a perfect power that maps to a different listed form.
angles: Sieve all no-prime bases of one page together (gcwsieve / MultiSieve handle many bases at once) from n = 10K to 20K, then PRP in increasing n so the first hit per base ends work on that base.

Scheduling theory (imported from operations research): candidate test time grows like (n log b)^2 log(n log b); order the queue by expected primes per second (sieve survivors times 1/ln N) rather than by base number.

Heuristic prime-count models (Wagstaff-style, imported from probabilistic modelling): estimate each base's expected number of primes in a range from its sieve density and spend effort where the posterior chance of a first prime is highest.

Covering-set analysis: for a stubborn base, look for a finite covering set or algebraic factorisation that makes every n*b^n+1 composite on some residue class; proving such a class is barren is a different but checkable result.
Error-checked big-integer arithmetic (Gerbicz checks in PRST) so a single bit flip never produces a false prime at 40 000 digits.
pitfalls: PRP is not proof; Cullen needs an N-1 proof and Woodall an N+1 proof.
Odd b with odd n gives an even Cullen number: trivial compositeness; similar parity traps for Woodall.
Exponents already shown in the '(...)' missing-range notation or above the contiguous limit may already be known.
Bases that are perfect powers can be the same numbers as another base's form; check the page notes.
Reserved bases (yellow or green) are being worked by others; claims there may duplicate unreported work.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - a rational Diophantine septuple
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: A rational Diophantine m-tuple is a set of m nonzero rationals such that the product of any two, plus 1, is the square of a rational. Euler knew infinitely many quintuples; Philip Gibbs found the first rational sextuples; Dujella, Kazalicki, Mikic and Szikszai (2017) proved there are infinitely many, and Piezas gave a simpler parametrisation. Andrej Dujella's survey (section 5.2) states it is still not known whether any rational Diophantine septuple exists. The problem is also listed as unsolved on Epoch AI's FrontierMath Open Problems page (no prize); Dujella's page's most recent dated item is Rathbun's 2024 sextuples.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for seven distinct nonzero rationals a_1..a_7 such that a_i*a_j + 1 is the square of a rational for all 21 pairs i < j, checked with exact rational arithmetic, and no septuple is reported on https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~duje/ratio.html or https://epoch.ai/frontiermath/open-problems/diophantine-septuple (both re-fetched immediately before the claim) or in a same-day literature check. Any pair with a_i*a_j + 1 = 0 must be reported and flagged; a septuple relying on it is a degenerate case and only counts if the literature definition admits it.

partial_wins.statement: A cube Diophantine quadruple: four distinct positive integers with all six a*b + 1 perfect cubes (Bugeaud and Dujella prove at most 7 elements are possible; the survey's section 7.1 gives only triples such as {2, 171, 25326}), absent from section 7.1 of https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~duje/gener.html and the Bugeaud-Dujella paper at verification time.

targets.verification_method: Python fractions.Fraction: for each pair compute a*b + 1 = u/v in lowest terms and check u and v are perfect squares with math.isqrt. For p1, integers and integer cube roots with exact cubing.
angles: Extend known sextuples: for each sextuple from the Dujella-Kazalicki-Mikic-Szikszai and Piezas families, the seventh element must lie on a curve given by six square conditions; search for rational points on its genus-1 or genus-2 quotients first.
Elliptic curves induced by Diophantine triples: triples whose induced curve has high rank give more room for extensions; rank by the techniques of the torsion-record tables.

Hash-join search (imported from databases): enumerate rationals of bounded height, hash a*b+1 squareness by residue fingerprints modulo many primes, and join candidate sets as a clique search in the 'square-product graph'.

Maximum-clique heuristics (imported from graph algorithms): the problem is a 7-clique in the graph whose vertices are rationals and edges mean ab+1 is a square; use modern clique solvers on large height-bounded vertex sets.
Groebner-basis and homotopy methods (imported from computer algebra and robotics kinematics) on the variety of sextuples with a free seventh coordinate, to find special subvarieties of low genus.
pitfalls: Repeated elements or zero elements make 'septuples' trivially.
a*b + 1 = 0 is a degenerate square; flag it rather than count it silently.
Floating-point squareness checks; use exact rationals only.
Extending a set that is actually a sextuple with one condition failing (20 of 21 squares) is not a septuple.

targets.name: APN functions: a new CCZ-inequivalent APN function (or APN permutation) in dimension 9 or 10
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: An (n,n)-function F is APN if every derivative equation F(x+a)+F(x)=b (a!=0) has at most 2 solutions. CCZ classes are classified only for quadratic n<=7. In dimension 8, Beierle, Langevin, Leander, Polujan and Rasoolzadeh (arXiv:2508.04644, v2 2026-08-27) constructed 3,775,599 inequivalent quadratic APN functions (32,892 were known before; they estimate about six million), and Kuznetsov (arXiv:2606.11967, June 2026) reports four further classes. In dimensions 9 and 10 only the infinite families plus a modest number of sporadic quadratic instances are known: Beierle and Leander (IEEE TIT 2022, arXiv:2009.07204) found 35 new quadratic APN functions in dimension 9 (two of them APN permutations) and 5 in dimension 10; Yu, Kaleyski, Budaghyan and Li classified quadratic APN functions with coefficients in F2 up to n = 9, and Yu, Li, Ichanska and Kaleyski (IACR ePrint 2024/1778) did so for n = 10. The UiB Boolean Functions wiki lists CCZ-inequivalent representatives from the known families up to n = 11 and only one APN function CCZ-inequivalent to quadratics and monomials (in dimension 6). APN permutations are known only from monomials in odd n, one quadratic family in dimension 3k, Dillon's dimension-6 permutation and the two sporadic quadratic permutations in dimension 9. Finding a further CCZ class in n = 9 or 10 is checkable from a lookup table plus CCZ invariants. Dimension 11 with coefficients in F2 is the separate bank target binary-coefficient-apn-dimension-11.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a lookup table (or polynomial with a stated irreducible modulus) F over GF(2^n), n in {9,10}, such that (1) an independent script confirms differential uniformity exactly 2 by exhaustive count over all a!=0 and all b; (2) at least one CCZ invariant, computed exactly (extended Walsh spectrum, Gamma-rank or Delta-rank, or for quadratic F the differential and extended Walsh spectra of the ortho-derivative), takes a value for F that differs from its value for: every representative listed on https://boolean.wiki.uib.no/Tables and its linked pages (re-fetched live immediately before claiming); EVERY instance (not only the wiki's representatives) of every known infinite APN family in dimension n, including the family C11 instances in dimension 10 that the wiki says have not all been checked; every function in the published datasets of Yu-Kaleyski-Budaghyan-Li (IACR ePrint 2019/1491, F2 coefficients up to n = 9), Beierle-Leander (IEEE TIT 2022) and Yu-Li-Ichanska-Kaleyski (ePrint 2024/1778); and every function in any other arXiv or ePrint dataset for that n, of any date; with the verifier recomputing the invariant for F and for every compared function; (3) a literature search on arXiv/ePrint for that n finds no prior instance with the same invariants. A failed equivalence search, a different truth table or the output of a heuristic classifier is not a certificate of inequivalence.

partial_wins.statement: A new APN permutation in dimension 9 CCZ-inequivalent to monomials, the 3k-family and both Beierle-Leander sporadic permutations (verified bijectivity + APN + distinguishing invariant).

A new quadratic APN function in dimension 10 whose ortho-derivative differential spectrum differs from all known dim-10 instances in the wiki tables and published datasets (including the F2-coefficient classification of ePrint 2024/1778).

A new CCZ class of APN functions in dimension 8 that is neither CCZ-equivalent to a quadratic function nor to a monomial (the wiki's list of APN polynomials CCZ-inequivalent to quadratic functions and monomials has a single entry, in dimension 6, and none in dimension 8). Certificate: (i) the extended Walsh spectrum of F contains a nonzero absolute value that is not a power of 2, which no function CCZ-equivalent to a quadratic one can have (quadratic components are plateaued with power-of-two amplitudes), and (ii) an exactly computed CCZ invariant of F differs from that of every APN power function in dimension 8 (the Gold functions and the Kasami function x^57).

targets.verification_method: Python/numpy or C: exhaustive differential table (2^n x 2^n counts, n<=11 is 4M cells, seconds). Walsh spectrum via fast Walsh-Hadamard of each component. Ortho-derivative for quadratic F: for each a, the unique pi(a) with pi(a).(F(x)+F(x+a)+F(a)+F(0))=0; compute its differential and extended Walsh spectra as CCZ invariants and compare to invariants recomputed from the known lists. Minutes.
angles: Beierle-Leander self-equivalence search: fix a linear self-equivalence (e.g. cyclotomic x -> a x or Frobenius-like) and search quadratic APN with that symmetry via a recursive tree over coordinate bilinear forms; dim 9 with a degree-3 extension structure is the sweet spot.
QAM (quadratic APN matrix) method of Yu-Wang-Li: search symmetric matrices over GF(2^n) with the QAM rank property; prune by subspace counting.
Switching neighbours: F + f(x)*u for Boolean f, starting from known dim-9/10 instances (Edel-Pott switching), keeping APN with incremental derivative checks.

Cross-domain import (SAT/constraint programming from hardware verification): encode quadratic APN as bilinear-form constraints with symmetry breaking (CCZ canonical forms) and use CaDiCaL/kissat with cube-and-conquer across 10 cores.

Cross-domain import (coding theory/ graph isomorphism tools from chemistry): use canonical labelling (nauty/bliss) of the associated design/code to decide CCZ inequivalence quickly, like molecule deduplication in chemical databases.

Cross-domain import (evolutionary program synthesis): evolve small polynomial expressions over GF(2^n) (few terms, coefficients) with APN-ness as hard filter and novelty (distance in invariant space) as fitness, MAP-Elites style.
pitfalls: The wiki's dimension-8 instance list is far behind the literature (millions of quadratic classes in arXiv:2508.04644 and its Zenodo data, more in arXiv:2606.11967); any 'new' dim-8 claim must be checked against those datasets. Prefer n = 9 or 10.
Same invariant does not prove equivalence, but DIFFERENT invariants prove inequivalence; the claim must rest on a differing invariant, not on failing to find an equivalence.
EA-inequivalence is not CCZ-inequivalence; compositions with permutations' inverses can be CCZ-equivalent to known functions.
Field-representation bugs: the lookup table must be with respect to a stated primitive polynomial; recompute everything from the table, not from the polynomial.
A function that is APN only on a subset or with off-by-one counting (counting a=0) is the classic false positive.

targets.name: ITC2021 sports timetabling: lower the best known penalty of an open instance
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The 2021 International Timetabling Competition (organised by David Van Bulck and Dries Goossens of Ghent University, Jeroen Belien of KU Leuven and Morteza Davari of SKEMA Business School) left 45 double round-robin instances (16-20 teams, Early/Middle/Late) whose live table at the RobinX repository lists the best lower and upper bound as (infeasibility, penalty). After the competition, records were lowered by Krystallidis and Musliu, Team UoS, Fonseca and Toffolo, Van Bulck and Goossens, Premananda and Muklason and others, with the newest change on 11 July 2026 (Early_1 and Late_11). On 2026-10-28 the table shows 3 instances closed (Middle_4 at 7, Late_4 and Late_15 at 0) and 42 of 45 with best known penalty above the best lower bound (e.g. Middle_3: LB 3378 vs UB 8648; Early_7: 1296 vs 4744; Late_12: 203 vs 3226). The page says submissions are open again (by email to the organisers; a human-only step). Find a feasible timetable with a strictly lower penalty.
targets.success_criterion: A solution XML for an ITC2021 instance listed on https://robinxval.ugent.be/ITC2021/instances.php that the open-source RobinX/ITC2021 validator (github.com/Robin-X/RobinX) evaluates to infeasibility 0 and a penalty strictly below that instance's 'Best UB' value, also reproduced by a second, independently written evaluator, with the table and the instance's history page re-fetched live immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: Strict improvement on any Middle or Late instance whose UB is more than 500 above its LB (e.g. Middle_1/2/3, Late_2, Late_12), validated by the RobinX validator.

A strictly higher lower bound for any open instance, given as a saved MIP/CP model file plus solver log and seed whose dual bound a skeptic re-runs to the same value (or better) in a fresh session; or, more strongly, a feasible timetable whose penalty equals the listed Best LB, which closes the instance and is checked by the validator alone.
Build the RobinX validator and reproduce the listed penalty of every posted best solution (45 files) exactly; a prerequisite that also catches stale table entries.

targets.verification_method: Instances: https://robinxval.ugent.be/validator/Repository/ITC2021/Instances/<name>.xml (redirect from sportscheduling.ugent.be, plain GET). Posted best solutions: .../ITC2021/Solutions/<file> (linked per row). Build RobinX with make (C++, GPL), run ./RobinX -i instance.xml -s solution.xml; first confirm it reproduces the posted best solution's penalty, then run it on the claim. Seconds.
angles: Two-phase decomposition used by strong ITC2021 entries: first fix the home/away pattern set (which teams play home in each slot) with a MIP that respects break constraints, then assign opponents with a second MIP or CP model; iterate with fix-and-optimize over windows of slots.

Combinatorial design theory: 1-factorizations of K_n (e.g. the canonical 'circle' and its isomorphism classes) give structurally different starting timetables than random; enumerate many non-isomorphic factorizations as seeds.

Satisfiability: encode one instance as weighted MaxSAT (hard constraints hard, soft penalties weighted) and run modern MaxSAT solvers (core-guided plus local search); Late and Middle instances with small LB/UB gaps are good first tests.

Neural guided search import from chip placement: learn which slots/teams to free in each large-neighbourhood step from improvement history across instances (bandit or simple classifier), rather than choosing uniformly.
Start from the posted best solutions (downloadable) rather than from scratch; the cheapest wins usually come from long polishing runs on instances whose record was set by a short competition run.
pitfalls: Lexicographic objective: (infeasibility, penalty). A low-penalty timetable with any hard violation is worse than every feasible one; only infeasibility 0 counts.
Version mismatch: the instance archives exist in versions (EarlyInstances_V2/V3, TestInstances_V2/V3); validate against the exact XML linked from the live table row.
Test instances (Test1-Test8, Demo) are not competition instances; improving them is not an ITC2021 record.
Self-reported lower bounds are not checkable by themselves; never claim a 'gap closed' without a feasible timetable whose validated penalty equals the bound.
Re-fetch the table and the instance's history page before claiming; records changed as recently as 11 July 2026.

targets.name: Multi-activity multi-day shift scheduling (Curtois-Qu MATSP instances 1-225): beat a best known penalty
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The Shift Scheduling Benchmark site run by Tim Curtois (schedulingbenchmarks.org) hosts 225 multi-activity, multi-day retail staff-scheduling instances (Curtois and Qu; 7, 14 or 28 days, 10-150 staff, 1-19 tasks). On 1 Sept 2026 every best known solution was replaced by results from a multi-neighbourhood simulated annealing by Laszlo Kalman Trautsch and Bence Kovari (Budapest University of Technology and Economics, J. Sched. 2026); no lower bounds are published, and a command-line verifier was released on 7 Oct 2026. Checked 2026-10-28: all 225 rows still credit TRA26 and the Changes page has no multi-activity update after 7 Oct 2026 (later entries, the newest dated 21 Oct 2026, concern the separate nurse-rostering instances). Instance 5 already has best known 0 and cannot be improved. Find a solution for any instance with positive best known value whose total penalty is strictly lower than the listed best known value.
targets.success_criterion: A solution in the site's XML solution format for one instance listed on https://www.schedulingbenchmarks.org/matsp/ with a positive 'Best known' value, such that an independent checker written from the published ProblemDefinition.pdf (which first reproduces penalty 889 on the site's example file 8_7_20_2.Solution.889.xml) reports all hard constraints satisfied and a total penalty strictly below that instance's 'Best known' value, with the table and https://www.schedulingbenchmarks.org/changes.html re-fetched live immediately before claiming. Cross-checking with the site's own RosterViewer or command-line verifier (closed-source binaries) is optional and done by the human, not the agent; nothing is emailed or submitted by the agent.

partial_wins.statement: Strict improvement on any instance with at most 20 staff and positive best known value (instances 1-4, 6-10, 76-85, 151-160), checked by the independent evaluator; non-trivial because the current values are fresh 2026 SA results.

A proof of optimality for any instance with positive best known penalty: an exact MIP/CP model file plus a solver log (and seed) whose matching lower bound a skeptic re-runs to the same value in a fresh session, or a VIPR-style certificate checked by an independent checker; the site lists no lower bounds, so this is new information even without a better solution.
An open-source evaluator that reproduces the site's posted penalty for the example file and for a TRA26 best known solution if one is published; checkable by running it.

targets.verification_method: Download the instances (https://www.schedulingbenchmarks.org/matsp/data/instances1_225.zip, text and XML) and the formal definition (ProblemDefinition.pdf). Write an independent penalty evaluator and confirm it reproduces the penalty 889 of the site's example solution file https://www.schedulingbenchmarks.org/matsp/data/8_7_20_2.Solution.889.xml before trusting it. Evaluate the claimed solution with that evaluator. The official MATSP_Verifier and RosterViewer are closed-source binaries (MATSP_Verifier.zip); agents do not download and run them (kit/RULES.md rule 10), but the human may cross-check with them; a disagreement means the claim is not claimed. Minutes.
angles: All 225 records come from one method run once; a second, structurally different method is the obvious lever: column generation over individual weekly shift patterns (as in the Strandmark-Qu-Curtois work on the sibling nurse instances) with a restricted-master MIP to pick one pattern per employee.

Small instances first: instances with 10-20 staff and 1-2 tasks (e.g. 1-10, 76-85, 151-160) are small enough for an exact CP-SAT or MIP model of the full problem; proving or improving them gives quick, checkable records.
Large-neighbourhood search that frees all assignments of one day or one task at a time and re-solves that slice exactly with CP-SAT, keeping the rest fixed.

Telecom / call-centre workforce management import: staffing curves per 15-minute interval are a classic set-covering problem; solve the coverage layer as a min-cost flow over time intervals first, then assign people.

Music/sequence modelling import: treat each employee's week as a string over a small alphabet of shift/task tokens and use a learned or n-gram proposal distribution inside the annealer, so moves stay in the space of plausible rosters.
pitfalls: Instance numbering: files are named <id>_<days>_<staff>_<tasks> (e.g. 8_7_20_2); the example solution 8_7_20_2.Solution.889.xml (2019) is NOT the current best (763), so beating 889 is not a win.

The closed-source verifier is a convenience, not a proof, and agents do not run it: the independent evaluator must reproduce 889 on the example file before it is trusted, and any later disagreement with the official tool (run by the human) withdraws the claim.
Hard constraints are not penalties: a solution that trades a hard-constraint violation for a low penalty is infeasible; the checker must report hard feasibility separately.
The nurse rostering instances 1-24 on the same site are a different problem with a different format; Instance 24's 1-unit gap (LB 40438, UB 40439) is not part of this target.
Re-fetch the table and the Changes page right before claiming: all 225 values changed on 1 Sept 2026 and could change again.
Instance 5 (7 days, 10 staff, 2 tasks) has best known 0: it is already optimal and cannot be improved.

targets.name: MINLPLib: better feasible point for an open mixed-integer nonlinear instance
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: MINLPLib (Stefan Vigerske, ZIB/GAMS, with Ambros Gleixner and others; last updated 14 Sept 2026, new points added 2026-05 to 2026-09) is the standard library of 1,633 mixed-integer and continuous nonlinear programs. Each instance page lists the best known feasible point (maximum absolute constraint violation at most 1e-8) and dual bounds from global solvers. Re-checked 2026-10-28: the instance data CSV (1,633 rows) still shows 538 instances with relative gap above 1e-4 and 49 with no primal bound; the newest points are dated 2026-09-14 (nd_netgen-2000-2-5-a-a-ns_7, sporttournament48). The finance/marketing instances saa_2 and pricing050 are a separate bank target (minlplib-finance-open-instances) and are excluded here. Find a point that is feasible within the library's tolerance and has a strictly better objective than the listed primal bound.
targets.success_criterion: A solution point for an instance listed on https://www.minlplib.org/instances.html, other than saa_2 and pricing050 (bank target minlplib-finance-open-instances), whose instance page shows no dual bound equal to the primal bound, such that an independent evaluation of the instance's .gms/.py/.nl model at that point (with integers exactly integral and bounds exactly satisfied) gives maximum absolute constraint violation <= 1e-8 and an objective strictly better (in the instance's objective sense) than the listed primal bound by more than 1e-6 relative, with the instance page re-fetched live immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: Strict primal improvement on any open instance with at least 50 variables, checked by the independent evaluator.
A feasible point (violation <= 1e-8) for an instance that currently lists no feasible point at all, checked the same way.
An independent evaluator that reproduces the listed objective and violation of the posted .sol points for 20 randomly chosen instances; prerequisite and useful public check.

targets.verification_method: For the instance, download the model (gms/<name>.gms, py/<name>.py or nl/<name>.nl) and the posted best point (sol/<name>.pN.sol). Evaluate objective and constraint violations with Pyomo (py format) or the AMPL Solver Library via the .nl file, matching variables by name. First reproduce the posted best point's objective and violation; then evaluate the claimed point. Minutes.
angles: Filter for instances where all listed dual bounds are far from the primal bound and the problem is nonconvex with many continuous variables; run multistart local NLP (Ipopt, Knitro-free alternatives) from thousands of random or Latin-hypercube starts, then polish to 1e-9 violation.

Use global solvers available for free (SCIP 9/10 with its MINLP features) with long time limits and primal heuristics emphasis on mid-size open instances; even without closing the gap they often find better incumbents than older runs.

Chemical-process design import: many MINLPLib instances (syn*, rsyn*, water*, pooling) are flowsheet or pooling problems; known structure-specific heuristics (multi-commodity reformulations for pooling, successive linear programming) often beat generic solvers.

Applied-physics import for the geometric instances (kall_*, pointpack*, cvxnonsep*): use the Packomania-style billiards / repulsion methods instead of MINLP solvers; but check first whether the primal value already matches a proven optimum from the packing literature.
Rescaling trick: solve a better-scaled equivalent model, map the point back, and re-verify violation in the original formulation, since the 1e-8 tolerance is absolute.
pitfalls: The CSV 'gap' is not 'open': the library calls an instance solved only when 3 solvers agree, so an instance with large CSV gap may already have one solver's dual bound equal to the primal bound (e.g. like: GUROBI dual bound = primal bound), in which case no improvement exists. Read the instance page.
Tolerance exploitation: a point with violation 1e-6 can look better than the best 1e-8 point; the library lists such points separately as 'Other points' and they do not count.
Variable naming: .sol files are keyed by the GAMS names; evaluating them against a reordered format by index gives garbage. Always evaluate by name.
Several instances are listed as min with a negative objective; 'better' means lower for min, higher for max; read objsense.
Floating point: report the objective recomputed in double precision from the model, not the solver's reported value, and require the improvement to exceed 1e-6 relative to rule out round-off.

targets.name: MMLIB / Boctor multi-mode resource-constrained project scheduling: shorter makespan for an open instance
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The multi-mode RCPSP lets each activity run in one of several modes (duration and renewable/non-renewable resource use). Mario Vanhoucke and Jose Coelho's SolutionsUpdate site tracks open instances in MMLIB (Van Peteghem and Vanhoucke 2014) and Boctor's sets (Boctor 1996): its MMRCPSP table (headed September 2026, re-checked 2026-10-28) gives MMLIB50 54 of 540 open, MMLIB100 114 of 540, MMLIB+ 1,965 of 3,240 (average gap 14.7%), and Boctor100 33 of 120 (average gap 14.8%). Each SolutionsUpdate dataset page (e.g. http://solutionsupdate.ugent.be/dataset/boctor100) publishes a per-instance best-known-solution CSV; recent Boctor100 bounds were submitted by Shichen Tian (June and September 2026). The MMLIB GitHub release (v2.1, published 23 June 2026; README updated 23 July 2026) contains the MMLIB50, MMLIB100 and MMLIB+ instances and an Excel file of LB-lit/UB-lit values that lags the site (on 2026-10-28 the Excel still has 82 MMLIB50 and 52 Boctor100 rows with LB-lit < UB-lit); the Boctor instances themselves are distributed by SolutionsUpdate and PSPLIB, not in that release. Find a feasible mode assignment and schedule with makespan strictly below the best known upper bound of an open instance.
targets.success_criterion: A mode assignment plus start times for one MMLIB50, MMLIB100, MMLIB+ or Boctor100 instance that is open (LB < UB) on its SolutionsUpdate dataset page, that an independent checker confirms satisfies precedences, renewable capacities in every period and non-renewable totals, with makespan strictly below both that instance's value in the best-known-solution CSV linked from http://solutionsupdate.ugent.be/dataset/<mm50|mm100|mmplus|boctor100> and its UB-lit in the latest MMLIB release Excel, all re-fetched live immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: Strict UB improvement on any open MMLIB+ instance, verified by the checker.
Strict UB improvement on any open MMLIB100 or Boctor100 instance, verified by the checker.
A schedule matching the listed lower bound of an open instance (closing it), verified by the checker.

targets.verification_method: MMLIB instances: the release at https://github.com/MarioVanhoucke/MMLIB-Multi-Mode-Resource-Constrained-Project-Library/releases/latest (MMLIB50.zip, MMLIB100.zip, MMLIB+.zip and 'MMLIB (Parameters and BKS).xlsx'). Boctor instances are not in that release: use the Boctor.zip linked from http://solutionsupdate.ugent.be/dataset/boctor100 (or the PSPLIB multi-mode data page). Current per-instance values: the *_BKS.csv linked from each SolutionsUpdate dataset page (e.g. Boctor100_0_BKS.csv, MM50_7_BKS.csv; columns ID;Type;Value;Time;Solution). The checker reads the instance (activities, modes, durations, renewable and non-renewable demands, availabilities, successors), verifies one mode per activity, total non-renewable use <= availability, precedences and per-period renewable usage, then reports makespan; first confirm it accepts a posted BKS schedule and reproduces its value. Seconds.
angles: CP-SAT with optional interval variables per mode (one present per activity) and cumulative plus non-renewable knapsack constraints; seed with a mode assignment from a fast non-renewable-feasibility MIP.

Two-level search: an outer mode-assignment local search (flip one activity's mode, keep non-renewable feasibility) and an inner single-mode RCPSP solved by a fast schedule generation scheme with forward-backward improvement.

Cloud-computing import: multi-mode activities are like jobs with alternative VM shapes; bin-packing heuristics for VM placement (best-fit decreasing on resource vectors) give good initial mode choices.

Statistics import: fit a simple regression of makespan on instance indicators (provided in the Excel) to pick the instances whose current UB is most anomalous relative to similar instances; attack those first.
Large-neighbourhood search that frees all activities in a time window, including their modes, and re-solves exactly.
pitfalls: Non-renewable resources: a schedule that respects renewable capacities but overspends a non-renewable budget is infeasible; many heuristics repair this with penalties and can output infeasible incumbents.

MMLIB+ instances use different numbers of modes and resources than MMLIB50/100; parse each file's header rather than hard-coding. Boctor files (.prb) have their own format and no non-renewable resources.

The release Excel lags the live site (2026-10-28: 82 vs 54 open MMLIB50, 52 vs 33 open Boctor100); an instance open in the Excel may already be closed or improved on SolutionsUpdate. Compare against the dataset page's BKS CSV, re-fetched before claiming.
The summary table and the dataset pages can differ by one (MM50 54 vs 55, MM100 114 vs 115 on 2026-10-28); the per-instance CSV value is what counts.
PSPLIB multi-mode sets (J10-J30) and Boctor50 are all closed; they are not targets.
Lower bounds are not mechanically checkable here; only UB improvements or LB-matching schedules count.

targets.name: QPLIB: better solution point for a quadratic (including QAP-type and Max-Cut-type binary) instance
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: QPLIB (Furini, Traversi, Belotti, Frangioni, Gleixner, Gould, Liberti, Lodi, Misener, Mittelmann, Sahinidis, Vigerske, Wiegele; hosted at ZIB) collects 453 quadratic programming instances, many with binary variables (quadratic assignment, Max-Cut, QUBO, quadratic knapsack). Each page lists the best known solution point. The library is actively updated: new better points were added on 12 Oct 2026 (QPLIB_2880, a 25x25 quadratic assignment instance, by Yuan Wang, Shenzhen Research Institute of Big Data; its value 1167256 equals the proven optimum of QAPLIB tai25a, so it is closed), 5 Oct 2026 (QPLIB_2096, contributed by ZiYor with an exact optimality certificate, so it is closed), 14 Sept 2026 (QPLIB_2174, QPLIB_5442 by Xiang He and Shaowei Cai's Qseek), 7 Aug 2026 (QPLIB_2036, Quplane, Todd J. Hendricks) and 28 July 2026 (QPLIB_2166, 2205, 10031-10033, Qseek); no newer History entry as of 2026-10-28. QPLIB pages do not mark which points are proven optimal. Find a feasible point with strictly better objective than the listed one (impossible where the listed value is already optimal, as for QPLIB_2096 and QPLIB_2880).
targets.success_criterion: A solution point for an instance listed on https://qplib.zib.de/instances.html, evaluated independently from that instance's .lp or .gms file (variables matched by name; binaries and integers exactly integral; variable bounds exactly satisfied; maximum absolute violation of linear and quadratic constraints <= 1e-9), whose objective is strictly better in the instance's sense than the 'Solution point objective value' on its QPLIB_<id>.html page by at least 1e-6 relative, with the instance page and the History section of https://qplib.zib.de/ re-fetched live immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: Strict improvement on any pure-binary instance (probtype whose second letter is B, e.g. QBL, QBN, LBQ) with at least 100 variables, checked by the evaluator.

Strict improvement on any quadratic-assignment-structured instance (n^2 binaries with 2n assignment equalities) whose underlying QAPLIB instance is not marked (OPT) on the QAPLIB page, checked by the evaluator; QPLIB_2880 (tai25a, proven optimal) does not qualify.

A machine-checkable optimality certificate for an instance whose current point has no proof: an exact-arithmetic certificate (e.g. VIPR from exact SCIP) checked by an independent checker, or a model file plus open-source solver log and seed that a skeptic re-runs to the same bound in a fresh session.

targets.verification_method: Download qplib.zib.de/lp/QPLIB_<id>.lp (LP-format with the quadratic objective in [ ... ]/2) and sol/QPLIB_<id>.sol. Parse the objective and constraints by variable name and evaluate. Verified 2026-10-13: parsing the .lp of QPLIB_2880 and the posted .sol by name reproduces 1167256 exactly (evaluating the .qplib file by index does not, see pitfalls). Seconds.
angles: Recent records came from strong binary local search (Qseek; permutation-based SA for QAP); for QAP-structured instances use robust tabu search (Taillard) and Misevicius' iterated tabu / hybrid genetic algorithms, the methods behind most QAPLIB records.

Physics import: QUBO/Max-Cut instances are Ising spin glasses; use parallel tempering, population annealing or simulated bifurcation (the quantum-inspired dynamics behind Toshiba's SQBM+) on the binary instances.
Reformulate small-to-mid binary instances exactly as MaxSAT or pseudo-Boolean problems and run modern anytime solvers (e.g. NuWLS-style local search plus core-guided search).
For mixed-continuous nonconvex instances, alternate between fixing the binaries and solving the continuous QP to global optimality with an open-source spatial branch-and-bound.
Mine the History section: instances improved in 2025-2026 show where incumbent quality is weak; neighbours in the same family (same donor, same structure) are likely to have slack too.
pitfalls: Variable order: .sol files use GAMS names (b1..bn); the .qplib file indexes variables in a different order, so evaluating a .sol against .qplib by index gives a wrong objective (on QPLIB_2880 it gives 2892328 instead of 1167256). Evaluate by name from .lp or .gms.
Quadratic objective scaling: the LP format writes the quadratic part as [ ... ]/2; forgetting the /2 doubles the objective.
Objective sense: some instances maximise; check 'Objective Sense' on the page.

QAP-structured instances are QAPLIB instances in disguise: QPLIB_2880 is tai25a (same value 1167256), which the QAPLIB page at https://coral.ise.lehigh.edu/data-sets/qaplib/qaplib-problem-instances-and-solutions/ marks (OPT), so it cannot be improved. Check the underlying QAPLIB entry (OPT or bound) before attacking any QAP-type instance.
QPLIB pages show no dual bounds or optimality marks; many listed points are already optimal. A tolerance-exploiting point (violation above 1e-9) is not a win even if its objective is better.
Re-fetch the History section before claiming: points were updated on 2026-10-12 and 2026-10-05; QPLIB_2096 now carries an exact optimality certificate and cannot be improved.

targets.name: RCPLIB (Vanhoucke-Coelho) RG300 and DC2 resource-constrained project scheduling: shorter makespan for an open instance
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Mario Vanhoucke and Jose Coelho (Ghent University) maintain RCPLIB and the SolutionsUpdate site, which tracks open instances for single-mode RCPSP datasets beyond PSPLIB. On 2026-10-28 the live table (headed October 2026) reports 334 open instances out of 480 in RG300 (300 activities, Debels and Vanhoucke 2007; average gap 28.2%; newer contributions coded 4C, 4Cb and ZV) and 140 of 720 in DC2 (Vanhoucke 2010). The current RCPLIB release (v2.4, published 28 January 2026; README updated March 2026) gives per-instance best lower bound (LB-lit) and best upper bound (UB-lit). Find a feasible schedule with makespan strictly below UB-lit for an instance with LB-lit < UB-lit.
targets.success_criterion: A start-time vector for one RG300 or DC2 instance (original-version Patterson .rcp file from the latest RCPLIB release) that is open (LB < UB) on its SolutionsUpdate dataset page, that an independent checker confirms satisfies all finish-to-start precedences and all renewable resource capacities at every time unit, with makespan strictly below both that instance's UB-lit in the latest RCPLIB release Excel and its value in the best-known-solution CSV linked from http://solutionsupdate.ugent.be/dataset/RG300 or http://solutionsupdate.ugent.be/dataset/DC2 (e.g. RG300_3_BKS.csv), all re-fetched live immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: Strict UB improvement on any open RG300 instance, verified by the checker.
Strict UB improvement on any open DC2 instance, verified by the checker.
Closing an open instance by finding a schedule whose makespan equals LB-lit (proving optimality without a new bound), verified by the checker.

targets.verification_method: Download the release zip (https://github.com/MarioVanhoucke/RCPLIB-Resource-Constrained-Project-Library/releases/latest, 86 MB; contains RG/RG300.zip, DC/DC2.zip and 'RCPLIB (Parameters and BKS).xlsx', whose RG300 sheet has LB-lit in column BG and UB-lit in column BH: 347 rows with LB < UB in v2.4). Current per-instance values: the *_BKS.csv linked from the SolutionsUpdate dataset pages (columns ID;Type;Value;Time;Solution; RG300 334 open and DC2 140 open on 2026-10-28, so the site is newer than the Excel). A 40-line checker parses the Patterson file (activities, durations, renewable demands, successors), verifies precedence and per-period resource usage, and reports makespan; first confirm it accepts a posted BKS schedule with the posted value. Seconds.
angles: Run open CP-SAT (OR-Tools) with interval variables and cumulative constraints, warm-started from a good serial-schedule-generation-scheme solution; CP-SAT's LNS is strong on 300-activity RCPSP and the RG300 average gap of 28.2% suggests large slack.
Forward-backward improvement (justification) plus decomposition-based GA in the spirit of Debels and Vanhoucke, but with much longer runs than the original papers' schedule limits.
Signal processing import: treat the resource profile as a time series and use convolution-based 'peak shaving' to choose which activities to delay, as in power-grid load levelling.

Sequence-to-schedule learning import from compiler instruction scheduling: list-scheduling priority rules learned per instance (genetic programming of priority rules, as in Luo, Vanhoucke, Coelho and Guo 2022) to seed CP search.
Use the 'lowRU/highRD' and 'keepOPT' equivalent versions supplied in the release to search on the reduced instance, then map back and verify on the original.
pitfalls: Per-instance values in the Excel lag the live site (347 open in v2.4 vs 334 open live on 2026-10-28): a 'win' against UB-lit may already be matched by a newer upload; compare against the dataset page's BKS CSV before claiming.

Instance versions: each instance comes in original, lowRU, highRD and keepOPT versions; records refer to the original version, and a makespan on a transformed version is a win only after mapping back and re-checking on the original.
PSPLIB J120 is a separate bank target; J60/J90/J120 rows on the same page are not part of this target.

Patterson format details: the dummy start and end activities have zero duration; resource availabilities are on the line after the activity count; misreading successor lists silently drops precedences.
Do not count lower-bound improvements; they are not mechanically checkable from a saved object.

targets.name: Traveling Tournament Problem (RobinX repository): shorter total travel for an open NL, NFL, GAL, CIRC, SUP, BRA or CON instance
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The Traveling Tournament Problem (Easton, Nemhauser and Trick, 2001) asks for a double round-robin schedule minimising total team travel, with at most three consecutive home or away games and no immediate rematches. Michael Trick's original challenge page was frozen in 2022 and handed to the RobinX repository maintained by David Van Bulck (Ghent), which lists validated best upper bounds, best lower bounds and literature-only upper bounds. Many instances remain open, e.g. GAL40 (LB 227134, UB 240063), NFL32 (836031 vs 914620 in the literature), CIRC20 (1600 vs 1724), BRA24 (470496 vs 499804). Find a feasible schedule with strictly smaller total travel than both the repository's best UB and any literature UB for that instance.
targets.success_criterion: A schedule (RobinX solution XML) for a classic TTP row on https://robinxval.ugent.be/RobinX/travelRepo.php (classification '2RR, C, ∅ | CA3, SE1 | TR'; not a Mirrored or other variant row) whose Best LB is below min(Best UB, Best UB literature), such that the RobinX validator and an independent checker both report a valid double round robin with no more than three consecutive home or away games, no repeaters, and total travel (each team starts and ends at home) strictly below min(Best UB, Best UB literature) for that row (a '/' entry is ignored), with the page re-fetched live immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: Strict improvement on any GAL (12-40 teams) or CIRC (12-40 teams) instance whose literature column is empty, so the repository value is the record.

A validated schedule matching or beating a literature-only UB (e.g. NL16 261687, NFL24 463657) where the repository holds only a worse validated schedule; checkable and fills a public verification gap.
Strict improvement on the mirrored or unconstrained variant of an open instance listed on the same page (separate rows), validated with the same checker using that variant's rules.

targets.verification_method: Download instance and posted best solution XML from https://robinxval.ugent.be/validator/Repository/TravelOptimization/Instances/<name>.xml and .../Solutions/<file>. A 40-line checker (verified 2026-10-13: it reproduces GAL40_240063.xml = 240063 and CIRC20_1724.xml = 1724 exactly with 0 violations) sums distances along each team's venue sequence, starting and ending at home, and checks round-robin, at-most-three, and no-repeater rules. Cross-check with the RobinX C++ validator (github.com/Robin-X/RobinX). Seconds.
angles: Simulated annealing on the classical TTP neighbourhoods (swap homes, swap rounds, swap teams, partial swap rounds/teams; Anagnostopoulos, Michel, Van Hentenryck and Vergados) with strategic oscillation between feasible and infeasible regions; the larger GAL and CIRC records were set by short SA runs and likely have slack.

Exploit symmetry in CIRC: the circular distance instances are invariant under rotation and reflection; search only over schedules generated from structured patterns (e.g. modified canonical schedules) and lift them.

Vehicle-routing import: each team's away trips are short tours of at most three cities; evaluate and re-optimise trips as a small set-partitioning / TSP-with-capacity problem, then repair the round robin with an exact matching model per slot.

Astronomy/geometry import for GAL: distances come from 3-D positions of exoplanets; cluster teams by position and build trips that visit clusters, as in hierarchical clustering heuristics for the Euclidean TSP.

Column generation over away-trip sets, followed by a CP model that assembles trips into a valid schedule, which is the structure behind the strongest published lower bounds and can also produce good upper bounds on mid-size NL/NFL instances.
pitfalls: Two UB columns: an improvement over 'Best UB' that is still above 'Best UB literature' (e.g. NL16: 271476 vs 261687) is not a record; criterion is strictly below both.

Mirrored, unconstrained and incomplete variants are separate rows with different rules; they count only for the variant partial win, validated with that variant's rules; a mirrored schedule claimed against the plain TTP row, or vice versa, is invalid.
Travel must include the final trip home after the last slot and start from home; omitting either gives artificially small totals.
Asymmetric data handling: distance files list team1/team2 pairs; build the matrix from the file rather than assuming symmetry or a particular team order (team ids are not in city-name order).
Some rows are closed only via the literature column (e.g. CON22, CON28, CON34, CON40 have Best LB equal to the literature UB); they cannot be improved.

Re-fetch the repository page before claiming; it is maintained (the RobinX GitHub backup was updated on 22 Oct 2026), although the classic-row histories checked on 2026-10-28 show no change since 2024.

targets.name: SINTEF VRPTW (Gehring-Homberger, hierarchical objective): fewer vehicles, or equal vehicles and shorter distance, on a 200-1000 customer instance
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: SINTEF's TOP pages (maintained by Geir Hasle) list best known solutions for the 300 Gehring-Homberger VRPTW instances under the classic hierarchical objective: first minimise the number of vehicles, then total distance in double precision. Records keep moving: on the 1000-customer page (checked 2026-10-28), Seiya Takahashi, Tsubasa Kumamoto, Ryotaro Shin, Masahiro Nomura and Isao Ono (Institute of Science Tokyo, 'ISCT') set R1_10_5, R1_10_7..R1_10_10 and RC1_10_3, RC1_10_6, RC1_10_7 between 6 and 14 Sept 2026; Tobias Linke (Enpal Fulfillment, 'TL') then set R1_10_3 (91 vehicles, 44689.19) on 1 Oct 2026, and R1_10_6 (91, 46928.44) is credited to ISCT and TL independently (8 Sept / 3 Oct 2026). On the 200-customer page SINTEF noted on 22 Oct 2026 that four old MB/MB2 values not backed by detailed solutions (C1_2_10, R1_2_2, R2_2_4, RC2_2_10) were replaced by marginally higher values with checked detailed solutions from Victor Allis (Saviter, 'VAS', dated 17-19 Sept 2026), which coincide with values reported earlier by several authors. Earlier records include NVIDIA cuOpt (Jan 2024), SCR (Emapa) and CAINIAO. This is a different record set from the CVRPLIB DIMACS distance-only table (bank entry cvrplib-vrptw-gh-dimacs-bks). Find a feasible solution that is lexicographically better than the listed best for any instance.
targets.success_criterion: A route file for one Gehring-Homberger instance that an independent checker confirms visits every customer exactly once, respects vehicle capacity, all time windows (service may start no earlier than ready time; waiting allowed; arrival no later than due date, including return to the depot) and the instance's vehicle limit, and that is lexicographically better than the (vehicles, distance) pair listed for that instance on the matching SINTEF page (fewer vehicles, or equal vehicles and distance lower by at least 0.01 in double precision), with the page re-fetched live immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: Equal vehicles and strictly shorter distance on any 600-1000 customer instance, verified by the checker.
One fewer vehicle on any instance (distance irrelevant), verified by the checker; the rarer and more valuable kind of improvement.
Independently reproducing (tying) one of the September-October 2026 1000-customer records (ISCT or TL) from scratch in under 24 laptop-hours, verified by the checker.

targets.verification_method: Instances: https://www.sintef.no/globalassets/project/top/vrptw/homberger/1000/homberger_1000_customer_instances.zip (and the 200-800 analogues linked from the size pages). Posted best solutions are linked per row (e.g. .../r1_10_3.91-44689.19.txt as of 2026-10-28). A 30-line checker computes Euclidean distances in double precision, travel time = distance, service times from the file, and checks capacity, windows, coverage and vehicle count; first confirm it reproduces the vehicles and distance of the currently posted file for the row, then run it on the claim. Seconds.
angles: Route minimisation first: the Nagata-Braysy ejection-pool heuristic with squeeze and insertion-ejection is still the strongest tool for removing a vehicle; run it for long times on instances whose vehicle count has not changed since 2018-2019 (many SCR/CAINIAO rows).
Distance phase: EAX-based memetic algorithms (Nagata, Braysy and Dullaert) and edge-diversity variants like the 2026 Institute of Science Tokyo method; start from posted best solutions and polish.

Seed from the CVRPLIB DIMACS-objective BKS files for the same instances: those distance-optimised solutions often use more vehicles but contain excellent route fragments for the hierarchical objective.

Logistics-from-biology import: ant-colony pheromone matrices built from all posted best solutions across the 10 instances of a family (e.g. R1_10_1..10 share customer locations) as a prior on good edges.
GPU import: batch evaluation of millions of 2-opt*/or-opt moves per second on a laptop GPU (Apple Metal) as in the NVIDIA cuOpt records of Jan 2024.
pitfalls: Hierarchical objective: a shorter distance with one more vehicle is worse; a vehicle reduction counts even with a much longer distance.

Precision: SINTEF uses unrounded Euclidean distances; the CVRPLIB table for the same instances truncates to one decimal and ignores vehicle count, so a result must be scored against the SINTEF row only.
Time windows include the return to the depot by its due date and service times at customers; omitting either accepts infeasible routes.

Old table values can be infeasible: in Oct 2026 SINTEF replaced four 200-customer MB/MB2 entries that were not backed by feasible detailed solutions with slightly higher VAS values; matching an older, lower literature value is not a win unless the checker accepts the routes.
File naming: posted solution files use inconsistent names (dots, hyphens, '-converted'); read the row's numbers from the page, not from the file name.

Re-fetch the page before claiming; records changed repeatedly in Sept and Oct 2026 (latest 1000-customer change 3 Oct 2026; 200-customer page revised 22 Oct 2026), and independent groups have tied the same value.

targets.name: Walshaw Graph Partitioning Archive: beat a best known edge cut (k = 2..64, 0/1/3/5% imbalance)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Chris Walshaw's Graph Partitioning Archive (running since 2000, last updated 25 March 2026, unchanged on 2026-10-28; the page notes its own graph and partition files are offline and available only on request from the maintainer, so 17 of its 34 graphs come from the SuiteSparse DIMACS10 copies and the rest need the maintainer's files, a human-only request) lists, for 34 benchmark graphs, the smallest known edge cut for partitioning into k = 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 parts under four balance tolerances (0%, 1%, 3%, 5% imbalance): 816 records in total. The entries were set by KaFFPa/KaFFPaE and KaBaPE (Sanders and Schulz), ILP-polishing (Henzinger, Noe and Schulz), Jet (Gilbert et al., SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 2024), KaHyPar-E, IPMNE2 (Hein and Setzer) and others, and keep being lowered by improvement runs that start from archive partitions. Find a partition of one listed graph into k parts that respects the archive's balance bound and cuts strictly fewer edges than the table entry for that (graph, k, imbalance) cell.
targets.success_criterion: A partition file (one block id 0..k-1 per vertex) for a graph and k listed on https://chriswalshaw.co.uk/partition/, such that an independent checker (a) evaluates it on the SuiteSparse DIMACS10 copy of that graph (https://sparse.tamu.edu/DIMACS10/<name>, vertex order as in that file) or, for an archive graph with no DIMACS10 copy, on the archive's own graph file obtained by the human from the maintainer, after confirming that |V| and |E| equal the archive's graph table, (b) confirms every block has weight at most floor(S_opt * (100 + x) / 100) with S_opt = ceil(|V| / k) and x the imbalance of the table being claimed, and (c) counts cut edges strictly below the entry in that table cell, with the archive page re-fetched live immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: Strict improvement of any cell of the 0% (perfect balance) table; these are the most contested cells and a confirmed improvement is a new archive record by itself.
Strict improvement of any 1/3/5% cell currently credited to Jet (the newest solver in the archive, e.g. auto k=16..64), independently checkable with the same checker.

A partition that exactly ties a k>=32 cell on a graph with |V| >= 100,000 that is available in the SuiteSparse DIMACS10 group (auto, 144, m14b, fe_ocean) produced from scratch in under 12 laptop-hours, verified by the checker; non-trivial because these entries come from long evolutionary plus ILP polishing runs.

targets.verification_method: Download the graph in Matrix Market form from the SuiteSparse DIMACS10 group (the 10th DIMACS Challenge copy of the Walshaw graphs, e.g. https://sparse.tamu.edu/DIMACS10/fe_4elt2; verified 2026-10-13 that its header gives 11143 vertices and 32818 edges, matching the archive). A 30-line script reads the edge list (symmetric pattern, ignore the diagonal), reads the partition, checks block sizes against floor(ceil(|V|/k)*(100+x)/100) and counts edges whose endpoints lie in different blocks. Compare with the live table cell. Runs in seconds.
angles: Start from the strongest open-source pipeline (KaHIP's KaFFPaE / KaBaPE with the 'strong' preset, and the ILP improver from Henzinger, Noe and Schulz) on the mid-sized graphs where the 0% cells were last set by older tools (FSMAGP, MAHMBCDP, JE): those are the cells most likely to have slack.

Statistical physics: treat partitioning as a Potts-model ground-state search; parallel tempering with a balance-preserving Kawasaki (pair swap) move set is a natural fit for the 0% table, where single-vertex moves are illegal.

Spectral and geometric seeding from numerical analysis: most archive graphs are finite-element meshes; recursive coordinate or inertial bisection on recovered mesh geometry (via a spectral embedding) gives very different starting partitions for multilevel refinement than random matching.

Image segmentation import: graph-cut / max-flow based boundary refinement (FlowCutter-style most-balanced minimum cuts on a band around each block boundary) can shave edges that FM-style refinement cannot reach.

Exploit the integer slack in the balance bound: for many (|V|, k) the bound floor(S_opt*(100+x)/100) allows one or two more vertices than a naive percentage calculation; search over which blocks carry the slack.
pitfalls: Balance bound arithmetic: the archive uses S_opt = ceil(|V|/k) and allows |S_p| <= S_opt*(100+x)/100, i.e. floor(S_opt*(100+x)/100) for integer block sizes; a checker that drops the ceiling rejects valid partitions, and one that rounds the bound up instead of down accepts partitions the archive would reject.

Graph identity: only 17 archive graphs are in the SuiteSparse DIMACS10 group (data, uk, wing_nodal, fe_4elt2, fe_sphere, cti, cs4, fe_body, t60k, wing, fe_tooth, fe_rotor, 598a, fe_ocean, 144, m14b, auto). add20, 3elt, add32, bcsstk29-33, whitaker3, crack, vibrobox, 4elt, memplus, fe_pwt, brack2, finan512 and wave are not, and same-named matrices in other SuiteSparse groups (e.g. Hamm/add20) are not guaranteed to be the archive graph; matching |V| and |E| alone does not prove identity.

Wrong table: a cut that beats the 5% cell but violates the 3% bound is a 5% record only; claims must name the exact (graph, k, imbalance) cell, and an improvement in a looser table never counts for a tighter one.

Self-loops and duplicate edges: Matrix Market symmetric files store each edge once and may include diagonal entries; counting both triangles or the diagonal doubles or inflates the cut and can hide a non-improvement.
Re-fetch the archive before claiming: entries are improved in batches and the page was last updated in 2026.

targets.name: Anarchy Golf: a strictly shorter solution than the best-ranked one in some language on a post-mortem problem
targets.compute_profile: laptop-minutes
targets.statement: golf.shinh.org (anarchy golf, run by shinh; 116 languages, active today: recent records dated 2026-10-28 JST, eight active problems up to #1831) keeps per-problem, per-language rankings of shortest correct programs. Only problems in post-mortem state are targets: after the deadline the page says 'all source codes will be revealed', so the full ranking and code are public. Active problems (solutions hidden until the deadline) and endless problems (no deadline, submissions never revealed) are live contests and are out of scope. Find a program in some language that is strictly shorter (bytes) than the current best for that post-mortem problem+language and passes all of the problem's published test cases on the same interpreter version.
targets.success_criterion: A source file for a named anagol problem whose page http://golf.shinh.org/p.rb?<Problem> shows post-mortem state ('now post-mortem time, all source codes will be revealed'), and a language, such that (a) running it locally with the interpreter version listed on http://golf.shinh.org/version.rb against every published test input of that problem produces byte-identical expected output (trailing-whitespace rules as the server defines), and (b) its byte size is strictly smaller than the best entry for that language on the problem page re-fetched live immediately before claiming. No submission to the server is made by the agent.

partial_wins.statement: Improve the best Python 3, Ruby, Perl or JavaScript solution on any post-mortem problem (strong-competition languages), checked the same way.
A solution shorter than the overall #1 across all languages for some post-mortem problem, checked the same way.

targets.verification_method: Download test inputs/outputs from the problem page, run with the matching interpreter version in a sandbox, diff outputs, count bytes with wc -c. Minutes.
angles: Target languages with few golfers per problem (from l.rb per-language result pages) and port the overall-best algorithm from a terse language into them.
Brute-force superoptimization of short expressions (e.g. magic-number/modular lookup tricks) with a search over Python expression grammars.
Kolmogorov problems (fixed output): try zlib/base-N string compression with language-native decompressors vs hand-crafted generators.
Cross-domain import (data compression): use LZ77/arith-coding analysis of the target output to find repeated structure, then encode via language string-repetition idioms.
Cross-domain import (genetic programming / evolutionary computation): evolve programs with byte-length fitness under test-case constraints.
Cross-domain import (number theory/hash design): search for perfect-hash magic constants mapping inputs to outputs (classic golfing 'magic formula' search) using SAT/brute force on 10 cores.
pitfalls: Interpreter version mismatch: a program passing on a newer local Python may fail on the server's version; use the exact versions on version.rb.
Problems with hidden/randomized tests: only use post-mortem problems whose full test sets are visible.
Trailing newline/whitespace rules; byte vs character counting for non-ASCII.

Active and endless problems are out of scope: their code is hidden and they are live contests; never publish a solution to one. Post-mortem rankings also keep changing, so re-fetch the problem page before claiming.

targets.name: Brainfuck constants: a shorter BF program producing a constant than the esolangs table
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The esolangs.org 'Brainfuck constants' page (last edited 25 June 2025) lists the shortest known Brainfuck code to leave value n in the cell (8-bit; separate wrapping and non-wrapping lists) for n = 0..255 plus larger numbers, with instruction count and cells used, under the convention that the code never touches cells left of the start. This is a Kolmogorov-complexity record table with a trivial mechanical checker. Find a program strictly shorter than the listed shortest for some n in the same category (wrapping / non-wrapping).
targets.success_criterion: A Brainfuck string for some n listed on https://esolangs.org/wiki/Brainfuck_constants (re-fetched live immediately before claiming) such that a reference interpreter with unbounded right tape, 8-bit cells (wrapping only if claimed in the wrapping category), starting at all zeros, halts with the pointer on a cell holding n (mod 256 rules exactly as the page defines), never moves left of the start cell, and whose instruction count is strictly less than the smallest listed count for n in that category (and for numbers > 255, the page's stated cell-size conventions).

partial_wins.statement: Improve any non-wrapping entry for n in 128..255.

An exhaustive search certificate (enumeration log + checker) proving the listed wrapping program is optimal for all n up to some length L (e.g. all programs of length <= 14), publishing optimality for a range of n.
A shorter program for one of the listed constants above 255.

targets.verification_method: 20-line Python BF interpreter with step limit (e.g. 10^7), asserting final pointer cell value, no left-of-origin access, and length; the skeptic runs each candidate in milliseconds.
angles: Exhaustive enumeration of all syntactically balanced programs up to length 16-18 with a fast C/Rust interpreter, pruning by canonical forms (no '+-', '<>' adjacent pairs) and memoizing tape states; collect min length per n.
Grammar-guided search over loop templates (multiplication loops, wrapping 'divide' loops like -[----->+<]) with parameter sweeps.
Cross-domain import (superoptimization in compilers, e.g. STOKE/Souper): stochastic MCMC over programs with a cost = length + distance-to-target, then exhaustive verification.
Cross-domain import (number theory/addition chains): use modular-inverse wrapping tricks (k*x == n mod 256) to design 1-loop programs; search over pairs (step, decrement) solving linear congruences.
Cross-domain import (program synthesis / RL in AlphaDev style): Monte Carlo tree search over instruction sequences with interpreter feedback.
pitfalls: Convention: must not modify or rely on cells left of the starting pointer; some short programs violate this.
Wrapping vs non-wrapping vs '(soft)' entries are different categories; compare within category.
Final pointer position matters: the value must be in the cell under the pointer at halt.
Programs must halt; the step limit must not be tight enough to reject a valid long-running program, nor loose enough to hang.
Small n are likely already exhaustively optimal; check the talk page/history for prior exhaustive results before claiming.

targets.name: LODA: a new verified LODA program for an OEIS sequence that has none
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The LODA project (loda-lang.org; programs repo loda-lang/loda-programs, last program maintenance commit 2026-09-30, last commit 2026-10-18; loda-cpp release v26.8.1 of 1 Aug 2026) mines short assembly-like programs that generate OEIS sequences and checks them mechanically against the OEIS b-files. LODA does not rank programs by length: loda-cpp's Checker::isOptimizedBetter replaces a program only when the new one is simpler by static checks (shorter only for sequences with at most 100 known terms), corrects it, computes more terms, or runs faster, so the repo often keeps longer, faster programs (A000045's is a 31-operation logarithmic-time method) and a shorter program is not a LODA record. Produce a LODA program for an OEIS sequence that has no program in the repo and is not on its deny list, verified against the OEIS b-file.
targets.success_criterion: A .asm program for an OEIS id such that the official loda evaluator (loda-cpp, latest release built from source) reproduces every term of the OEIS b-file https://oeis.org/A<id>/b<id>.txt exactly, the b-file having at least 100 terms, where no file oeis/<NNN>/A<id>.asm exists on https://github.com/loda-lang/loda-programs main and the id is not listed in that repo's oeis/deny.txt, both re-fetched live immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: Ten new programs for sequences with no LODA program and not in deny.txt, each verified on >= 200 b-file terms.
A new program for a sequence in A000001-A099999 that has no LODA program and is not in deny.txt, verified the same way.

targets.verification_method: Build loda-cpp from its GitHub source, run 'loda eval' on the program for as many terms as the b-file has, and diff against the b-file; then confirm on loda-programs main that oeis/<NNN>/A<id>.asm does not exist and the id is not in oeis/deny.txt. Seconds to minutes.
angles: Run the LODA miner locally (mutation + pattern templates) focused on OEIS keyword:easy sequences lacking programs.
Formula-to-program compiler: parse OEIS FORMULA fields (linear recurrences, products, gcd/divisor sums) and emit LODA code directly.
Cross-domain import (symbolic regression in physics): use PySR-style equation search on sequence terms, then compile the found formula to LODA.

Cross-domain import (program reuse): many sequences are transforms (partial sums, binomial transforms, characteristic functions) of sequences that already have programs; LODA's seq operation can call them.
Cross-domain import (linear-feedback shift registers / coding theory): Berlekamp-Massey to detect linear recurrences (also modulo primes) and emit minimal recurrence loops.
pitfalls: Matching the b-file is not a proof of correctness for all n; the claim is 'verified on N terms', not 'proved'.
The repo moves quickly (miners run continuously and add programs daily); re-fetch before claiming absence.
Some sequences are excluded by LODA deliberately: check the repo's oeis/deny.txt (not suitable for LODA) before claiming.
Shorter is not better in LODA: the project prefers simpler, correct and faster programs, so a shorter program for a sequence that already has one is not a win here.
A program that uses seq to call the target sequence itself is rejected by LODA's checker; calls to other sequences must reference programs that exist in the repo.

targets.name: Silesia corpus: beat the best per-file compressed size with a specialized open-source model
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Matt Mahoney's Silesia Open Source Compression Benchmark (programs as of Oct. 10, 2026) lists per-file compressed sizes (KB, truncated) for the 12 Silesia files. Per-file column minima today come from paq8px_v206/v217, precomp|cmix v21 and gleipnir 1.0.2 (sao). Several files are highly structured binaries where a format-specific model can plausibly beat general CM: sao (SAO star catalog, fixed 28-byte records), osdb (synthetic MySQL-style database), x-ray and mr (16-bit / DICOM medical images), nci (SMILES-like chemical database). Produce a byte-exact round trip on one file whose total (compressed file + zipped decompressor source) is strictly below that file's column minimum.
targets.success_criterion: For one Silesia file (md5 as listed on https://mattmahoney.net/dc/silesia.html), an open-source compressor/decompressor where: decompress(compressed) reproduces the file byte-exactly (md5 match), run by a skeptic from a clean build; and size(compressed) + size(zip -9 of the decompressor source tree including any dictionaries/models) is strictly less than 1000 x (the minimum KB value in that file's column of the live table, re-fetched immediately before claiming). Decompressor must not embed file-specific data beyond what is counted in its zipped size; runtime <= 24 laptop-hours, RAM <= 32 GB.

partial_wins.statement: A specialized sao model beating every paq8px/cmix row (not necessarily gleipnir) by the same counted-size rule.
An open preprocessor (e.g. record transposition for osdb/sao, delta+bitplane for x-ray) that makes paq8px_v217 -12L output strictly smaller than its own listed size on that file, round-trip verified.
Strictly beat the top Silesia total (27682006 bytes today, re-fetch) with the same per-file-counted rule - stretch.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic builds the decompressor from the zipped source, decompresses, md5sum compares against the corpus md5 on the page, then sums sizes. One run of a CM decompressor on a <=10 MB file is minutes to an hour.
angles: sao: parse the fixed-length SAO star catalog records into fields (RA, Dec, magnitudes, spectral type, proper motions) and model each with field-specific contexts (sorted RA deltas, Dec correlation), mixing with a paq-style logistic mixer.
osdb / nci: column/record transposition preprocessing then paq8px_v217 or cmix; tune column contexts.
x-ray / mr: 16-bit lossless image models (CALIC/GraLIC-style gradient-adjusted prediction + context mixing on residual bitplanes), DICOM header handled separately.

Cross-domain import (astronomy): exploit the sky-sorting structure of the star catalog - HEALPix/zone ordering of stars makes coordinates nearly monotone; model proper motions with priors from Gaia-like distributions (computed from the file itself, no external data).
Cross-domain import (genomics/bioinformatics): SMILES-aware tokenization for nci, borrowing grammar-based compressors used for chemical/biological sequence data.
Cross-domain import (medical imaging/MRI reconstruction): slice-to-slice motion-compensated prediction for the 3-D mr volume, like video codecs.
pitfalls: Table sizes are in KB truncated; compare total bytes to 1000 x KB minimum strictly (a value equal to the truncated KB could still be larger in bytes).
Embedding file data in the decompressor: count the zipped decompressor source; a giant model file is counted too.
Closed-source programs are not listed; the record is among open-source programs only - a closed program's better result does not move the table, but our claim must be open source.
md5 must match the page's listed md5; some mirrors ship altered files (e.g. CRLF).

targets.name: Reliable rotation periods for asteroids with no entry in the Asteroid Lightcurve Database, from public survey photometry
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (per-object photometry is KB-MB; batch of thousands overnight)
targets.statement: The Asteroid Lightcurve Database (LCDB; Warner, Harris and Pravec) lists rotation periods with reliability codes. Its latest public release is dated 2023 October 1 (still the current release on the LCDB page, re-checked 2026-10-28). Survey photometry has been mined heavily since then: ATLAS bootstrap convex inversion (Durech, Vavra, Vanco and Erasmus 2022, Front. Astron. Space Sci. 9, 809771), Gaia DR3 spin states (Durech & Hanus 2023, J/A+A/675/A24), and Gaia DR3 light-scattering inversions for over 8,000 asteroids (MacLennan et al. 2026, J/A+A/707/A131). Durech & Hanus 2026 (A&A 714, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202662316, arXiv:2610.06082; previewed as EPSC2026-425) combined Catalina, Mt. Lemmon, Pan-STARRS, ZTF, USNO, ATLAS, ASAS-SN, TESS and Gaia photometry with Asteroids@home into about 30,000 models, including about 22,000 unique spin-state solutions. Smaller 2026 period sets include KMTNet bulge-field periods for 96 asteroids, 84 of them new (Huang et al., arXiv:2606.26184), periods from MPC-circular photometry (Nagainis & Eglitis, arXiv:2610.13223) and early Rubin Observatory science-validation periods (Carruba et al., arXiv:2609.29841). Dense public data still exist for many objects with no published period. Open task: derive an unambiguous rotation period (LCDB quality U >= 3-equivalent) for asteroids with no LCDB entry and no published period.
targets.success_criterion: For each claimed object, a saved bundle (designation, raw photometry with times, filter, observer-centric geometry from JPL Horizons, phase-angle-corrected reduced magnitudes, period-search code) in which all of the following hold. (1) The best period has a Lomb-Scargle / Fourier-series FAP < 1e-4. (2) The folded curve at P shows two maxima and two minima of amplitude > 0.1 mag. (3) The P/2 and 2P aliases are tested and rejected by chi^2 (delta chi^2 > 25). (4) The period is recovered independently, within 1%, in two separate apparitions or two separate surveys. (5) The object has no period in any of these: the LCDB release linked at https://www.minorplanet.info/php/lcdb.php (re-fetched live immediately before claiming); DAMIT; J/A+A/707/A131; J/A+A/675/A24; the ATLAS inversion catalogue of Durech et al. 2022; Durech & Hanus 2026 (arXiv:2610.06082, A&A 714) or any released model or period table from that work; arXiv:2606.26184; arXiv:2610.13223; arXiv:2609.29841; and ADS (search by number/designation).

partial_wins.statement: Ten or more new periods meeting all criteria (one is the main win; a batch shows a reusable pipeline).
A new very slow rotator (P > 500 h) or a new candidate binary asteroid (two-period solution, eclipse/occultation-like events) meeting all checks.
A demonstrable correction of an LCDB U=2 period, with the new period confirmed in two independent data sets and the LCDB value excluded at delta chi^2 > 25.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic re-queries the photometry (IRSA ZTF, TESS FFI cutouts or Gaia DR3 SSO tables), recomputes geometry from Horizons, reruns an independent periodogram, and checks the LCDB file and DAMIT. Minutes per object.
angles: Conventional: multi-band Fourier-series fits with an H-G12 phase function on ZTF g/r forced photometry, prioritising objects with > 200 detections in one apparition.
TESS full-frame images contain thousands of asteroids with dense 10-min or 200-s cadence; extract them with moving-aperture photometry (as in the TSSYS work of Pal et al.).
Cross-domain import (radar/sonar): treat sparse multi-survey data with a joint likelihood over a period grid (like a matched filter across sensors) rather than separate periodograms.
Cross-domain import (circadian biology): chronobiology's methods for noisy, unevenly sampled rhythms (JTK_CYCLE, cosinor) are robust to sparse sampling and give honest p-values.
Cross-domain import (compressed sensing): recover periods from very sparse Gaia DR3 photometry by sparse-frequency recovery with a dictionary of physical lightcurve shapes.
pitfalls: Half/double-period ambiguity: a monomodal fold at P/2 is the classic false period; require bimodal shape and alias rejection.
Sidereal/synodic and 1-day aliases from nightly sampling; check the window function.
Phase-angle and aspect changes alter amplitude between apparitions; do not combine raw magnitudes without geometry correction.
LCDB public release is from 2023; newer published periods exist - search ADS/DAMIT/Gaia inversion catalogue, not just LCDB.
