Blends with background stars in ZTF produce spikes; reject points near catalogued stars.

targets.name: Hidden repeating FRB source among apparently one-off bursts in CHIME/FRB Catalog 2
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (catalog is a few MB; localisation maps tens of MB; Monte Carlo is minutes)
targets.statement: The second CHIME/FRB catalog (CHIME/FRB Collaboration, arXiv:2601.09399, published 2026-01-14; catalog version 20251231; public table at https://assets.chime-frb.ca/catalogs/catalog2/releases/20251231/data/chimefrbcat2.csv, archive DOI 10.11570/25.0066) lists 4,539 bursts observed 2018 July 25 to 2023 September 15 (5,045 table rows counting sub-bursts) from 3,641 unique sources. These include 981 bursts from 83 repeating sources. Cook et al. (arXiv:2605.08410) present 30 newly discovered repeating sources and say these bring CHIME/FRB's total number of observed repeaters to 80. They find only 2.4 +/- 0.4% of sources observed to repeat, but the data fit equally well with 50-100% of the population repeating at low rates. Later Catalog-2 papers model the population (Sirota & Lorimer, arXiv:2610.18710), classify morphology (Fan et al., arXiv:2607.13148) or study single known repeaters; as of 2026-10-28 none reports new repeaters found by grouping one-off bursts. Open task: find a pair (or larger group) of catalogued bursts that are treated as separate one-off sources, are not among the published repeaters, and whose positions, dispersion measures and other properties are consistent with a single repeating source, at a chance-coincidence probability low enough to survive the trials factor.
targets.success_criterion: A saved file listing >= 2 Catalog 2 (version 20251231) burst TNS names that the catalog assigns to different sources (empty or different repeater_name), all with sidelobe_flag = 0 and excluded_flag = 0, such that: (1) for every pair in the group, |delta RA * cos(dec)| and |delta Dec| are each <= 1.96 * sqrt(err1^2 + err2^2), using the catalog's ra_err and dec_err columns (or the 95% regions overlap in any localisation product the collaboration publishes for these bursts); (2) |dm_fitb difference| <= 1.96 * sqrt(dm_fitb_err1^2 + dm_fitb_err2^2) + 2 pc/cm^3; (3) the chance-coincidence false-alarm probability is < 1e-3 AFTER the full look-elsewhere factor of all pairs tested, computed by a Monte Carlo over the whole catalog with sky positions shuffled within CHIME's exposure map and DMs drawn from the catalog; and (4) the group is absent from the repeater assignments of Catalog 2, of Cook et al. (arXiv:2605.08410) and of any CHIME/FRB repeater paper on arXiv up to the claim date (https://chime-frb.ca/catalog2 and arXiv re-fetched live immediately before claiming).

partial_wins.statement: A complete, reproducible catalog-wide pair search that independently recovers >= 90% of the Cook et al. new repeaters with the same false-alarm machinery (validates the method; checkable against their table).
A candidate group meeting every criterion except the false-alarm threshold (1e-3 < FAP < 1e-2 after trials), with morphology (narrowband, downward drift) supporting repetition.
A Catalog-1 one-off whose position and DM match a Catalog-2 burst from a different source ID, giving a multi-year repetition baseline, with FAP < 1e-2 after trials.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the Catalog 2 CSV/FITS from https://chime-frb.ca/catalog2 (minutes), reruns the supplied pair-FAP script with a new random seed and an independently written trials count, recomputes the position and DM agreement from the catalog columns, checks the sidelobe and excluded flags, and greps the published repeater tables. Under an hour.
angles: Conventional: pairwise overlap of localisation contours with a DM window, then a catalog-wide shuffled-sky Monte Carlo for the false-alarm rate (the method used for CHIME repeater discovery).

Use morphology as a prior: Sun et al. and the semi-supervised Catalog 2 classification find repeater-like narrowband bursts cluster separately; rank one-offs by repeater-likeness and search those first to cut the trials factor honestly (pre-registered ranking).
Cross-domain import (record linkage / genealogy): treat bursts as noisy records and use Fellegi-Sunter probabilistic linkage with match weights from position, DM, scattering and spectral index.

Cross-domain import (gamma-ray astronomy): borrow the 'stacking' likelihood used to find weak neutrino or GRB counterpart clusters - an unbinned likelihood over all bursts near a trial position, instead of pair counting.
Cross-domain import (seismology): repeating-earthquake detection uses waveform similarity; use dynamic-spectrum template similarity between bursts at the same position as extra evidence.
pitfalls: CHIME has huge, elongated sidelobe-shaped localisation regions near the zenith band; overlapping contours are common by chance - the trials factor over all pairs dominates.
Low-DM Galactic-plane bursts and RRAT-like Galactic sources contaminate; check DM against the NE2001/YMW16 Galactic maximum.
Some 'new' groupings are already merged in Cook et al. or later CHIME repeater papers under a different source name; compare TNS names, not internal IDs.
Sidelobe detections are assigned wrong positions; the catalog flags them - exclude flagged events.
Do not post to TNS or contact CHIME; the claim is a vetted candidate only.

targets.name: Unreported historical outburst (nova, dwarf nova or large-amplitude event) in DASCH DR7 century-long plate light curves
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (API queries per field; cutouts are MB each)
targets.statement: DASCH Data Release 7 (Grindlay, Williams and team; released 2024 December 29) provides ~23.6 billion photometric measurements of 252 million sources from Harvard plates, ~1880-1990, via the daschlab client and public web APIs. Only a handful of DR7-era discoveries are published (e.g. a candidate 1951 superoutburst of GOTO065054+593624, arXiv:2501.11524). Open task: find a source with a significant historical outburst (>= 2 mag, on multiple plates) that is not recorded in VSX, the AAVSO International Database summary, the CBAT/Duerbeck nova lists or the literature.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (DASCH DR7 light curve table as returned, plate identifiers, cutouts of every outburst plate and the nearest pre/post non-detection plates, analysis code) showing an outburst of amplitude >= 2.0 mag above the quiescent median seen on >= 3 distinct plates from >= 2 different plate series (telescopes) within the event, with every outburst point passing DR7 quality flags, visual inspection of cutouts showing a stellar PSF (not a plate defect, emulsion flaw or neighbour blend), and no listing of an outburst at that epoch for that position in VSX, the Duerbeck/CBAT nova lists, or ADS full-text (status pages re-fetched live immediately before claiming).

partial_wins.statement: A new dwarf nova recurrence time measured from >= 5 DASCH outbursts for a known CV with no published recurrence time.
A previously unreported historical outburst of a known CV/symbiotic (object known, epoch new), on >= 3 plates from >= 2 series.
A published reproducible false-positive census: the fraction of DR7 'outbursts' that are plate defects, with a classifier that keeps >= 90% of known historical novae in DR7.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic re-queries the light curve and plate cutouts via daschlab, checks the flags and cutouts by eye, and searches VSX/ADS by coordinates. Under an hour.
angles: Conventional: target positions of known quiescent CVs (from the Ritter-Kolb catalogue and Gaia CV candidates) and scan their DASCH light curves for > 2 mag brightenings on multiple series.
Blind search near the Galactic plane for single-epoch multi-plate brightenings at positions with faint Gaia counterparts (G 17-20), the regime of unrecorded classical novae.
Cross-domain import (archival manuscript studies): codicology-style provenance checks - use plate jackets and logbook photos to rule out double exposures and plate annotations.
Cross-domain import (fraud detection): isolation forests over per-plate residuals flag points that are anomalous relative to the plate's own calibration, separating defects from real variability.
Cross-domain import (epidemiology): outbreak-detection CUSUM charts over the light curve give principled thresholds for 'outburst' with a controlled false-alarm rate.
pitfalls: Plate defects, dust and emulsion flaws masquerade as single-plate brightenings; require multiple plates from different telescopes.
Source splitting and ATLAS-refcat2 calibration artefacts (DASCH documents 'false ATLAS trends') fake long-term changes; use the APASS-referenced light curves and read the DR7 known-issues pages.
Blends with bright neighbours on low-resolution patrol plates; inspect cutouts.
Known novae and CV outbursts are catalogued under historical names; search VSX and the literature by coordinates.
The DR7 lightcurve endpoint is a read-only POST JSON query used by the official client; no account is needed, but if it ever requires registration, the target is off limits.

targets.name: Gamma-ray pulsations from a known radio pulsar not yet on the public list of LAT-detected pulsars
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (LAT weekly photon files total ~100 GB for the mission; an ROI selection is far smaller)
targets.statement: The public list of LAT-detected gamma-ray pulsars (created by Paul Ray, maintained with David A. Smith; content 'Updated 3 July 2025', page last edited 2025 July 16) holds 323 pulsars (83 young radio/X-ray selected, 71 young gamma selected, 159 radio-selected MSPs, 10 gamma-selected MSPs); the Third Fermi-LAT Pulsar Catalog (3PC, Smith et al. 2023) describes most of them. Hundreds of new radio pulsars (e.g. FAST GPPS and CRAFTS, MeerKAT TRAPUM, many in 4FGL unassociated sources) have published timing solutions. Open task: detect significant gamma-ray pulsations by folding public Fermi-LAT photons with a published radio ephemeris for a pulsar absent from the public LAT list and from later papers and ATels.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (published ephemeris .par file with citation; LAT photon selection: event class, ROI, energy range, time range; the weighted photon list; the folding code) in which: (1) the weighted H-test (de Jager; photon weights as in Kerr 2011) on photons folded with the ephemeris inside its validity span gives single-trial H > 36 (chance probability about exp(-0.4H) ~ 6e-7, about 5 sigma before trials); (2) after multiplying by the number of selection choices (ephemerides, energy cuts, ROIs, weightings) declared in advance, the post-trials significance is still >= 4 sigma; (3) the pulse profile is stable across the two halves of the data; (4) folding at slightly wrong spin parameters destroys the signal; and (5) the pulsar is absent from https://confluence.slac.stanford.edu/spaces/GLAMCOG/pages/108698084/Public+List+of+LAT-Detected+Gamma-Ray+Pulsars and from ADS/ATel (re-fetched live immediately before claiming).

partial_wins.statement: A 3-4 sigma pulsation candidate (H between 20 and 36) with consistent profiles in both data halves.
A reproducible pipeline that recovers pulsations for >= 20 listed LAT pulsars from their public ephemerides with the stated H thresholds.
A significant (> 5 sigma) gamma-ray point source, from a likelihood analysis, at the position of a new radio pulsar that is absent from 4FGL-DR4 and from the LAT FL16Y 16-year source list.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the LAT weekly photon and spacecraft files for the span, reruns the weighting (photon probabilities from a 4FGL model or simple PSF weights) and folding with PINT, and recomputes the H-test. One to a few hours on a laptop.
angles: Conventional: rank pulsars with published phase-connected timing (FAST, MeerKAT, Parkes papers) by spin-down flux Edot/d^2 and fold LAT photons only within each ephemeris's validity span.
Prioritise pulsars inside 4FGL-DR4 unassociated source error ellipses (the population where radio surveys targeted gamma-ray sources).

Cross-domain import (communications engineering): weighted H-test is a matched filter; use optimal photon weights computed from a source model (Kerr 2011 weighting), the analogue of SNR-weighted combining.
Cross-domain import (gravitational-wave searches): semi-coherent stacking across short segments allows modest ephemeris error, recovering signal where the ephemeris drifts outside its fit span.
Cross-domain import (pharmacology dose-response): pre-register the energy and ROI cuts to avoid trying many selections until something crosses threshold.
pitfalls: ATNF catalogue ephemerides are often from short spans years before the LAT era; folding outside the validity span smears pulsations.
Trying many energy cuts, ROIs and weightings inflates significance; count trials.
Nearby bright gamma-ray pulsars or blazars leak into the ROI; check that the pulse profile is not from a neighbour (fold the neighbour with its own ephemeris).
The public list may lag recent ATels/papers; search ADS and ATel before claiming novelty.

targets.name: First true (dynamical) mass for an RV-detected companion from Hipparcos-Gaia accelerations plus public radial velocities
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (an orvara fit is minutes to an hour; data are KB)
targets.statement: Radial velocities give only m sin i. Combining public RVs with the Hipparcos-Gaia Catalog of Accelerations (HGCA; Brandt 2021) using orvara (Brandt et al. 2021) or kepmodel yields the inclination and true mass. Large applications exist (Xiao et al. 2023 for 115 substellar companions, arXiv:2303.12409; Feng et al. 2022; Piccinini et al. 2026, arXiv:2601.09401), but on 2026-10-28 the NASA Exoplanet Archive composite table (PSCompPars) still had 924 of its 6,451 planets with mass provenance pl_bmassprov = 'Msini'. Open task: produce a robust true-mass measurement for a companion whose archive entry has no published true mass and no published astrometric inclination.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (HGCA EDR3 row, all RV data with provenance, orvara/kepmodel config and posterior chains) for a companion whose live archive row (https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/cgi-bin/TblView/nph-tblView?app=ExoTbls&config=PSCompPars, re-fetched immediately before claiming) has pl_bmassprov = 'Msini' (checkable with the TAP query https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/TAP/sync?query=select+pl_name,hostname,pl_bmassprov+from+pscomppars+where+pl_bmassprov='Msini'&format=csv), with: HGCA proper-motion anomaly chi^2 > 11.8 (3 sigma, 2 dof); converged chains (Gelman-Rubin < 1.01 across >= 4 independent runs); true mass with fractional 1-sigma uncertainty < 30% and inclination excluding 90 +/- 10 deg or a mass ratio that changes the object's class; no unexplained additional companion in residuals; and no prior paper (ADS/arXiv full-text search on host name with 'inclination' or 'Hipparcos-Gaia') reporting a true mass.

partial_wins.statement: A reproducible table re-deriving true masses for >= 10 companions from Xiao et al. 2023 within 1 sigma (validates the pipeline).
A significant (3 sigma) HGCA acceleration that is inconsistent with all known companions in the system, implying an additional unseen companion, with a mass-separation curve.
An archive companion with m sin i < 13 MJup shown to have true mass > 13 MJup (or > 80 MJup) at > 3 sigma, not previously reported.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic reinstalls orvara, runs the saved config on the saved RVs and HGCA row with new seeds, checks the posterior and chi^2, re-fetches the archive row and searches ADS. Under an hour per object.
angles: Conventional: rank archive companions by predicted HGCA signal (m sin i, period, distance) and run orvara on those with significant proper-motion anomalies and public RVs (HARPS RVBank, published tables on VizieR).
Add Gaia DR3 NSS acceleration or orbital solutions as a third constraint where available.
Cross-domain import (satellite orbit determination): use a square-root information filter / batch least squares with covariance analysis to show which observations actually constrain inclination.
Cross-domain import (structural engineering): sensitivity analysis via Sobol indices on the posterior to expose priors driving the inclination.
Cross-domain import (election forecasting): pre-register selection rules and report all fits, not only the striking ones, to avoid a forking-paths win.
pitfalls: The HGCA anomaly can come from a different, wide stellar companion; check Gaia for co-moving neighbours and imaging literature.
Archive 'Msini' flags can lag the literature; the novelty check must be a paper search, not just the archive flag.
Poorly sampled long-period orbits give bimodal inclination posteriors; a single mode reported as a mass is a false win.
HARPS 2015 fibre upgrade offset must be a separate instrument offset; forgetting it fakes a trend.
Prior choice (uniform in cos i vs uniform in i) can drive results when data are weak; report prior sensitivity.

targets.name: New hierarchical triple from eclipse-timing variations of a TESS eclipsing binary
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (2-min and FFI light curves for a few thousand EBs; per-system timing is seconds)

partial_wins.statement: A third-body detection that meets every criterion but with outer-period coverage < 1.5 cycles (period lower limit only), with the anti-correlated/in-phase primary-secondary test passed.
Detection of a previously unreported tertiary eclipse in a TESS EB, confirmed by flux-centroid analysis to be on target.
A new apsidal-motion rate for an eccentric TESS EB not in published apsidal-motion compilations, with primary/secondary anti-correlated ETVs at > 10 sigma.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic re-extracts the TESS light curves (lightkurve/eleanor from MAST), re-measures a random subset of eclipse times with an independent template, refits the LTTE model and BIC comparison, and checks the catalogues by coordinates. Under an hour per system.
angles: Conventional: measure eclipse times per sector with a fixed per-system template, fit LTTE with an MCMC, and prioritise EBs with >= 6 sectors and long baselines (2018-2026).
Add pre-TESS times from SuperWASP, KELT, ASAS-SN or Hipparcos epoch photometry to stretch the baseline for long outer periods.
Cross-domain import (pulsar timing): use a timing-residual formalism with red-noise modelling (as in pulsar timing arrays) so spot-induced timing noise does not masquerade as a third body.
Cross-domain import (geodesy / GNSS): treat eclipse times as a clock time series and use Allan-variance-style analysis to separate white timing noise from coherent signals.
Use Gaia DR3 RUWE and astrometric acceleration solutions as independent priors pointing to triples.
pitfalls: Starspots shift measured eclipse times in anti-correlated fashion between primary and secondary; a third body produces in-phase runs.
TESS sector-to-sector systematics and the 2-min vs 200-s/10-min cadence change can create offsets that a sparse ETV fit absorbs as signal.
Blended EBs in large TESS pixels: the EB may not be the target star; centroid tests needed before any physical interpretation.
Many TESS EB triples are already in Mitnyan 2024 / Zasche 2022 / the Gaia-NSS cross-match under a TIC ID or a GCVS/ASAS name; search by coordinates.

targets.name: New exocomet-transit candidate (asymmetric single dip) in public TESS light curves
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (bright-star QLP/SPOC light curves for selected sectors are a few GB)
targets.statement: Transiting exocomets produce shallow, asymmetric dips (sharp ingress, slow egress), first seen in Kepler (Rappaport et al. 2018) and in TESS around beta Pic (Zieba et al. 2019). Norazman et al. (arXiv:2508.04673, MNRAS) searched a magnitude-limited sample in TESS Sectors 1-26. They recovered beta Pic and found 5 new candidates: TIC 280832588, 73149665 and 143152957 on the main sequence, TIC 229790952 (a giant) and TIC 110969638 (a probable supergiant). Gibson et al. (arXiv:2510.09920) found 24 exocomet transits of RZ Psc in a targeted TESS survey of extreme debris disks. Dobrycheva et al. (arXiv:2402.19075, 2602.02701) flagged 32 Sector-1 candidates with a random-forest search. No published magnitude-limited systematic search covers Sectors 27 onward. Open task: a new, vetted exocomet-like dip on a star absent from those lists.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (TIC ID, TESS SPOC/QLP light curves and target-pixel cutouts as downloaded, code) with a single dip of depth > 300 ppm, asymmetric by a one-sided exponential-tail model preferred over a symmetric model by delta BIC > 10, duration within the range computed for a body on a bound or parabolic orbit around the host (using the TIC mass and radius; computation included), on-target by difference-image centroids (offset < 1 pixel/3 sigma), not coincident with momentum dumps, scattered light or other stars' simultaneous dips in the same camera/CCD, and absent from arXiv:2508.04673, 2510.09920, 2402.19075, 2602.02701 and from ADS/arXiv by TIC/coordinate search (status query https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=abs:exocomet+AND+abs:TESS&sortBy=submittedDate&sortOrder=descending&max_results=50 re-run immediately before claiming).

partial_wins.statement: Recovery of every published TESS exocomet event in the searched sectors with the same pipeline, plus a quantified false-alarm rate from injection tests.
A second dip on one of the published candidates (Norazman 2025 list) in later sectors, meeting the asymmetry and centroid tests.
An occurrence-rate estimate for sectors 27+ with injection-recovery completeness, reproducible from saved code.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic re-downloads light curves and TPFs from MAST, refits asymmetric vs symmetric models, reruns centroid tests and checks the spacecraft quality flags and neighbour light curves. Under an hour.
angles: Conventional: matched filter with the Lecavelier des Etangs/Brogi exocomet profile on A/F stars brighter than T=9 in sectors 27+.
Focus on young debris-disk stars (WISE IR excess) that earlier searches dropped for stellar activity, using GP detrending of pulsations.
Cross-domain import (gravitational-wave glitch classification): use a Gravity-Spy-style classifier trained on known systematics (momentum dumps, scattered light) to veto dips.
Cross-domain import (hydrology): asymmetric rise/recession of a storm hydrograph is the same shape; use recession-curve analysis to fit egress tails.
Cross-domain import (structural health monitoring): use multi-star simultaneous events on the same CCD as a 'common-mode' signal and subtract it before searching.
pitfalls: Momentum dumps, scattered light and thermal events produce asymmetric dips; check quality flags and neighbours on the same CCD.
Delta Scuti/gamma Dor pulsations in A/F stars beat to make dip-like features; detrend carefully and test injection recovery.
Contaminating eclipsing binaries in the aperture; difference-image centroids are mandatory.
No central catalogue exists; novelty depends on a literature search by TIC and coordinates.

targets.name: New white dwarf with transiting planetary debris in public ZTF or TESS light curves
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (ZTF light curves for ~100k WDs is a few GB via the IRSA light-curve service; TESS for the brightest few thousand)
targets.statement: White dwarfs with transits by disintegrating planetary debris are rare: WD 1145+017 (Vanderburg et al. 2015); ZTF J0139+5245 and ZTF J0328-1219 (Vanderbosch et al. 2020/2021); the Guidry et al. 2021 systems; WD 1054-226 (Farihi et al. 2022; Korth et al. 2026, arXiv:2603.07677); SBSS 1232+563 (Hermes et al. 2025); the six Bhattacharjee et al. 2025 ZTF candidates (arXiv:2502.05502; ZTF J1944+4557 confirmed by Guidry et al. 2025, arXiv:2508.18348); and six previously non-variable white dwarfs with deep, long-lived single obscuration events found in ZTF negative alerts by van Roestel et al. 2026 (arXiv:2609.08923), which bring the confirmed count to 20. Bhattacharjee et al. searched only within 500 pc and only the top 1% most variable objects. Open task: identify a new white dwarf (Gentile Fusillo Gaia catalog) whose public ZTF and/or TESS photometry shows irregular or periodic dimming events with the depth/shape signature of debris transits, not in any published list.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (Gaia DR3 source_id, white-dwarf probability > 0.75 from the Gentile Fusillo catalog, raw ZTF/TESS light curves as downloaded, analysis code) showing either (a) a periodic dimming signal (FAP < 1e-3 after trials over the searched sample) with depth > 3% in >= 2 independent data sets or seasons, or (b) >= 3 aperiodic dips each > 10% deep and > 5 sigma below the local median in a single filter, confirmed in a second filter or second survey within the same epoch; plus checks excluding blending (no Gaia neighbour within 10 arcsec brighter than G+3), eclipsing-binary/companion explanations (no secondary eclipse, no ellipsoidal variation, no IR excess implying M dwarf) and instrumental flags; and the source is absent from the tables of arXiv:2502.05502 and arXiv:2609.08923, from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_exoplanets_and_planetary_debris_around_white_dwarfs, and from arXiv/ADS search on its Gaia/ZTF/WD name and coordinates (status query https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=abs:%22white+dwarf%22+AND+abs:debris+AND+abs:transit&sortBy=submittedDate&sortOrder=descending&max_results=50 re-run immediately before claiming).

partial_wins.statement: Extend the Bhattacharjee et al. variability-metric search beyond 500 pc (or to the 1-5% variability tail) and publish a ranked, reproducible list where every published system that falls in scope is recovered in the top N.
Measure a previously unreported period (FAP < 1e-3) for one of the published transit candidates that lacks a period.
A new candidate with a single deep (>20%) dip event confirmed in two filters, without the multiplicity required for the full criterion.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic re-downloads the ZTF light curves (IRSA) and TESS FFI/2-min data (MAST) for the source_id, re-runs the periodogram or dip detector, checks Gaia neighbours and flags, and searches ADS/arXiv for the name. Under an hour.
angles: Conventional: compute a multi-band variability metric (Gaia flux-error excess plus ZTF g/r scatter) and box/dip searches over the full Gentile Fusillo WD sample, prioritising metal-polluted (DZ/DAZ) and IR-excess objects.
Search beyond the 500 pc cut and in the 1-5% variability tail that earlier work left out; use TESS 200-s FFIs for the few hundred brightest WDs.
Cross-domain import (finance): change-point and drawdown statistics from trading-risk analysis detect irregular, asymmetric dips better than periodograms for aperiodic debris.
Cross-domain import (fault detection in machinery): use spectral-kurtosis or matrix-profile motif discovery to find repeated dip shapes at unknown period.
Cross-domain import (epidemiology): treat each object as a 'case' and use scan statistics over time windows (Kulldorff) with a per-object background to control false alarms across 100k light curves.
pitfalls: Faint WDs near the ZTF limit give spurious dips from bad photometry; require catflags==0 and check the same nights on neighbouring stars.
Eclipsing WD+M-dwarf binaries and CVs mimic periodic dimming; check for secondary eclipses, emission lines (if a public spectrum exists) and IR excess.
Blending in crowded fields or TESS's 21-arcsec pixels attributes a neighbour's variability to the WD.
Many candidates appear in Guidry et al. 2021, Bhattacharjee et al. 2025 or van Roestel et al. 2026 lists under ZTF names; cross-match by coordinates, not by name.
Do not report to any agency or team; the claim is a vetted candidate.
The Wikipedia list lags the literature (on 2026-10-28 it listed 14 transiting systems and omitted the six van Roestel et al. 2026 objects); never use it as the only novelty check.

targets.name: New microlensing event in public ZTF light curves absent from published ZTF, Gaia and OGLE/KMTNet microlensing catalogues
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to overnight (ZTF light-curve parquet files for selected fields are tens of GB)
targets.statement: ZTF public data releases contain light curves for over a billion objects. The latest, DR24 (IRSA, 2026 January), covers about March 2018 to July 2024 for partnership and Caltech data, plus public-survey data to 2025-10-22. Published searches are Rodriguez et al. 2022 (Galactic plane, arXiv:2112.07684), Medford et al. 2023 (60 events in ZTF DR5, arXiv:2201.08335) and Zhai et al. 2025 (ApJ 978, 76, arXiv:2311.18627: 124 high-confidence plus 54 possible events in DR17 Galactic-plane fields). Other sources are the Gaia DR3 microlensing catalogue (Wyrzykowski et al. 2023, 363 events) and Gaia Science Alerts (about 27,000 alerts; the stream ended with Gaia25aeh on 2025-01-15). Later ZTF releases add years of data that no published catalogue covers. Open task: find a microlensing event in public ZTF light curves that is in none of these catalogues or alert streams.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (ZTF object IDs per filter, light curves as downloaded from IRSA, fit code) where a point-source point-lens (or finite-source / parallax) model fits g and r jointly with achromatic magnification (blend fractions allowed per filter), delta chi^2 versus a constant + linear model > 500, the rise and fall are each sampled by >= 5 points, the baseline is flat (RMS < 0.05 mag) for >= 1 year either side, the event is not a CV/YSO/Be outburst (achromaticity test, no repeat in the full baseline), and no entry exists within 2 arcsec in the Gaia Science Alerts list (http://gsaweb.ast.cam.ac.uk/alerts/alerts.csv), the Gaia DR3 microlensing table, the published ZTF catalogues (arXiv:2112.07684, 2201.08335, 2311.18627), or ADS/TNS-by-coordinate literature (arXiv status query https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=abs:microlensing+AND+abs:ZTF&sortBy=submittedDate&sortOrder=descending&max_results=50 re-run immediately before claiming).

partial_wins.statement: A reproducible pipeline that recovers >= 80% of the Medford et al. 2023 events from the public light curves with < 10 false positives per recovered event after vetting.
A new event with Einstein time tE > 100 d showing a significant annual-parallax signal (delta chi^2 > 50), a black-hole lens candidate class.
A new event off the Galactic plane (|b| > 15 deg) meeting every criterion.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic re-downloads the ZTF light curves, refits with an independent microlensing code (e.g. MulensModel or pyLIMA), checks achromaticity and baseline, and cross-matches catalogues by coordinates. Under an hour.
angles: Conventional: run the Medford-style cuts (von Neumann ratio, chi^2 of flat fit, Paczynski fit) on the newest public DR light curves for epochs after the DR17 search.
Search the outer disk and halo fields where survey teams rarely look; long-tE events give parallax and lens masses.
Cross-domain import (particle physics): template bank of Paczynski curves in (t0, tE, u0) scanned like a trigger, with a background estimated by time-reversed or scrambled light curves.
Cross-domain import (anomaly detection in industrial telemetry): autoencoders trained on 'normal' light curves score the symmetric single-bump shape as an anomaly class.
Cross-domain import (medical imaging): use the g/r achromaticity test as a 'dual-energy' discriminator, analogous to separating tissue types by spectral response.
pitfalls: CVs, Be stars and young stellar objects produce symmetric bumps; check colour change and repeated outbursts over the 7+ year baseline.
ZTF ref-image changes and fields/CCD edges produce step-like artefacts; require consistency across ZTF field IDs.
Events already reported by Gaia alerts, OGLE or KMTNet near the bulge appear under other names; cross-match by coordinates.
Short events sampled only at peak can fit almost any bump; demand the rise/fall sampling criterion.

targets.name: Inka khipus: frozen structural model that predicts masked cord values on khipus outside khipu.db (Open Khipu Repository)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.success_criterion:
Protocol (all frozen before touching held-out data):
1. Train only on data/khipu.db.
2. Held-out set: every khipu recorded in an .xlsx recording sheet in an OKR data/ folder numbered KH0631 or higher (these are not in khipu.db) with at least 20 valued cords. Excluded: image-only and PDF-only records (such as KH0653-KH0663 and KH0674-KH0675), the KH0002_0010 re-recordings, and any held-out khipu whose cord-value sequence matches a training khipu (the number removed is reported). A sheet covering two KH numbers is scored as one unit.
3. Parsing of the held-out sheets is validated by hand on at least 3 khipus, and the share of unparseable cords is reported.
4. For each held-out khipu, mask a random 20% of cords' total knot values with a published seed. The model sees everything else (other values, colours, structure).
5. Score = exact-match accuracy of predicted integer values on masked cords.
6. Baselines run on the same masks: (b1) the most common value in that khipu; (b2) an exact Ascher-style sum-relation solver that fills a masked cord only when an observed relation forces it; (b3) b2 plus the nearest-neighbour value within the cord group.
7. CONFIRMED if the frozen model beats the best baseline by at least 5 percentage points of exact-match accuracy, with a 95% bootstrap CI over khipus that excludes 0, AND the gain survives removing any single held-out collection.
8. The model hash, seeds, the OKR commit and the held-out file hashes are published before scoring.
9. Re-check the OKR repository live before claiming, to make sure the held-out khipus have not been merged into khipu.db with changed data.

partial_wins.statement: Pre-registered relation prediction: a rule set learned only from khipu.db (for example 'cords of colour pattern P at group position k sum the preceding group') that predicts, before inspection, at least 10 exact sum relations in held-out khipus, with fewer than 20% false predictions, beating a permutation null that shuffles cord positions within khipus at p < 0.01.

Non-numeric signal: a frozen model shows that a non-numeric feature (colour, attachment direction or ply) improves held-out masked-value accuracy over the same model without it by at least 2 points, CI excluding 0.

targets.verification_method: Clone the OKR repository at the recorded commit, hash khipu.db and the held-out spreadsheets, regenerate masks from the published seed, run the frozen model and the three baselines, and recompute accuracy and the bootstrap CI. Confirm by date and commit that no held-out file was used in training.

targets.name: WWII British censorship manual steganograms: locate the Morse code in the fashion drawing and recover the German text in the Amsterdam map
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: A 1939 British censorship training manual (UK National Archives KV 2/2424; Klaus Schmeh links a scan, and he photographed the original fashion drawing in high resolution at the archive and posted a high-resolution photo of the map) shows two pictures with hidden messages. It gives their meanings but not the full methods. (1) Fashion drawing, page 14: the hidden message is 'Heavy reinforcements for the enemy expected hourly. Before Arras.' The first part is said to be in Morse code and the second in shorthand (Schmeh calls it French shorthand). Blog reader Gerry read 'von aras' in German shorthand in the signature surname 'Shaw', and Schmeh accepted this reading ('Vor Arras') in May 2017. Where the Morse dots and dashes are hidden is still unknown. Commenter Thomas Ernst's 'EINE' reading of the collar is an unconfirmed guess. (2) Amsterdam city map, page 17: the manual says the message is in 'the morse alphabet (plus a transposition of 11 positions forward)' and gives it only in English: 'Oil has arrived, everything is ready. Gustav available for the appointed day.' The German original is not given. In October 2016 a reader called 'm' found pen-mark Morse below the dashed line along Raadhuisstraat, starting near Keizersgracht, with single strokes as dots and small filled boxes as dashes. The reading 'aathut' becomes 'llesfe' after the shift. 'm' also saw possible Morse between Kalverstraat and Rokin. Commenter Norbert reproduced 'llesfertig' and a few more fragments, and in September 2023 commenter Bugfish also read 'Alles Fertig' with only partial text around it. The full German original has not been recovered. Schmeh lists this as no. 33 of his Top 50 unsolved encrypted messages and calls the map result an 'almost solution'. No later solution appears on his blog, either the scienceblogs.de posts or klausschmeh.net since April 2026 (checked 2026-10-28). The plaintext meanings are known, so any solution can be checked mechanically.
targets.success_criterion: Before reading, name one public image of each page (URL and SHA-256). For each page, state the reading rule: which strokes count as dots and dashes, and the reading order. Also state the Morse table, including any signs used for German umlauts and CH and how they are treated by the shift. (A) Map CONFIRMED if all hold: (1) a published mark list, with pixel bounding boxes on the page-17 image, each labelled dot, dash, letter gap or word gap and given in reading order, is decoded by a published script (the stated Morse table, then a forward shift of 11 on A-Z) into a German string; (2) the string contains a word for oil (OEL, OL or ÖL), FERTIG and GUSTAV in that order, and its 'llesfertig' part comes from the Raadhuisstraat marks; (3) it differs from a German sentence stated by the claimant by at most 3 symbol errors, and that sentence is a faithful translation of the manual's English text. (B) Fashion drawing CONFIRMED if a published mark list on the page-14 image, read under the stated rule, decodes by the stated Morse table to HEAVYREINFORCEMENTSFORTHEENEMYEXPECTEDHOURLY, or to a German translation stated before reading, with at most 2 symbol errors. For both: (i) the same rule applied to 20 control images of similar line density, chosen and hashed before reading, must never decode to a string with 3 or more consecutive dictionary words of 4 or more letters; (ii) a second reader given only the rule and the image must reproduce the mark list within the stated error allowance. Re-fetch the status page and Schmeh's solved-cryptogram category on klausschmeh.net before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: Map only: a published mark list on the page-17 image that the decoding script (stated Morse table, forward shift 11) turns into one contiguous German string of at least 30 letters, containing 'llesfertig' and at least one of OEL/OL/ÖL and GUSTAV, reproduced by a second reader from the rule and image alone.

Fashion drawing: a mark list under the pre-stated rule that decodes by the stated Morse table to HEAVYREINFORCEMENTSFOR (or the first three words of a German translation stated before reading) with at most 1 symbol error, reproduced by a second reader from the rule and image alone.

targets.verification_method: Fetch the named images and check their SHA-256. Overlay the claimed bounding boxes, re-label the marks blind under the stated rule, and run the published decoding script (Morse table, plus the shift of 11 for the map). Diff the output against the required keywords or the target string and count symbol errors. Run the same rule and script on the 20 pre-hashed control images and apply the dictionary-run threshold.

targets.name: Chaocipher: break a single ciphertext-only message, and known-plaintext attack on the Extended variant (open per the Chaocipher Clearing House)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Chaocipher, invented by John F. Byrne in 1918, uses two dynamically permuted 26-letter alphabets. Its algorithm was revealed in 2010 after his family gave the papers to the National Cryptologic Museum. Moshe Rubin's Chaocipher Clearing House keeps the 'Current State of Chaocipher Research' table, created in Progress Report #25 and last updated 13 January 2023. Solved per the table: key recovery from ciphertext plus plaintext for the Classic system (Scheffler 2010, Rubin 2011, Crypto Forum 2015); in-depth messages with plaintext (Lasry/Rubin 2016, at least 10 messages Classic, 20 Extended); in-depth ciphertext-only messages (Classic needs 60-80 messages, Extended 600-800; a 2015 Crypto Forum hill-climbing attempt failed). George Lasry, Moshe Rubin, Nils Kopal and Arno Wacker (Cryptologia 40(6), 2016) solved Exhibit 6, a real-life challenge by Lou Kruh and Cipher Deavours; whether it can be done with fewer messages is still asked. Still OPEN: (a) recovering the key from a SINGLE ciphertext-only message, for both the Classic and Extended systems; (b) recovering the key from ciphertext plus plaintext for the Extended system ('not yet tackled'). Progress Report #29 (19 April 2026) repeats that 'no method is currently known for solving a single, long Chaocipher ciphertext message'. The task is a reproducible, publishable attack, measured on a frozen benchmark.
targets.success_criterion: Freeze a benchmark BEFORE attacking: 100 English plaintexts of a stated length L, drawn from a public corpus not used in development. Encipher each under a fresh, uniformly random Chaocipher key (independent random permutations for both alphabets, plus a uniformly random left/right selection key for Extended). Use an independent reference implementation that has first been checked against Byrne's Exhibit 1 and the solved Exhibit 6 data. (A) Classic single-message ciphertext-only: CONFIRMED if the attack recovers at least 98% of the plaintext letters for at least 50 of 100 messages with L <= 1000, within 2 laptop-hours per message. (B) Extended known-plaintext: CONFIRMED if the attack recovers the starting alphabets and the left/right selection key for at least 90 of 100 pairs with L <= 500. For both, re-fetch the Clearing House table live before claiming and confirm the cell still says 'Open'. Publish the code, the benchmark seeds and the per-message logs.

partial_wins.statement: Classic single-message attack that succeeds on at least 50 of 100 frozen benchmark messages at some length L <= 3000, each message under an independent uniformly random key.
Extended known-plaintext attack that succeeds on at least 50 of 100 frozen benchmark pairs at L <= 1000.

Fewer messages for Exhibit-6-style depth: recover the key from at most 30 in-depth Classic ciphertext-only messages (the Clearing House table lists 60-80 as required) on a frozen benchmark, with at least 80% success.

targets.verification_method: Use a reference Chaocipher implementation checked against the Clearing House exhibits. Regenerate the benchmark from the published seeds, confirm the keys are uniformly random, run the attack code unchanged, count recoveries with a letter-accuracy script and check wall time per message.

targets.name: Moustier altar inscriptions (two 19th-century coded inscriptions, St Martin's Church, Belgium)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Two carved letter inscriptions on the side altars (St Mary's and St Martin's) of St Martin's Church in Moustier, Frasnes-lez-Anvaing, Hainaut, Belgium, which Klaus Schmeh dates to the 19th century (parish records mention altar repairs in 1836-1840). Each is set in ten lines (two blocks of five) of about 80 characters, one inscription four characters longer than the other, including special signs (^, [ and an HP/FHP group). Cryptologists learned of them through 'Secrets of the Altars' in the September 1974 issue of the NSA newsletter Cryptolog, which Nick Pelling (Cipher Mysteries) found in 2013. Pelling made the standard transcriptions. Schmeh photographed the altars in 2015 and lists them as no. 18 of his Top 50 unsolved encrypted messages. Jean Connart worked on them from 1961. His booklet's Trithemius-based Latin reading, Rudy Cambier's Nostradamus/consonant-script theory (from his book of about 2002, discussed by Pelling in 2013) and Philippe Connart's lettering theory (2016) are not accepted. Dirk Huylebrouck's 2022 EOS article reviews the proposals, with comments from Jarl Van Eycke, who notes that the lines repeat unusually few letters. Pelling and Schmeh both reported the inscriptions unsolved in April 2022. As of October 2026 no solution has been accepted by either. Unverified readings posted as blog comments (for example German-based readings in April 2026 and partial key claims by other commenters) have not been confirmed. Find the method and plaintext of either inscription.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED only if ALL hold. (1) A transcription is frozen and published before solving. It starts from Pelling's, is checked against Schmeh's 2015 photographs, and gives every ligature and special sign a declared reading. (2) One method, declared before solving together with a plaintext language and a lexicon for it named before solving (for example Whitaker's Words for Latin), decrypts every character of one inscription into text in which at least 90% of plaintext letters belong to words found in that lexicon. Abbreviations count as explained only if they come from a standard list for that language (for example an ecclesiastical abbreviation list), fixed before solving, and expand deterministically. At most 3 characters may be unexplained. A language model or a reader saying the text 'makes sense' is not evidence. (3) Key bits stay below 0.5 x length x 3.5. The same method family applied to the second inscription either decrypts it under the same rule or is shown to need a different key of the same form. (4) Under the same solver budget, 1,000 random strings with the same character frequencies never reach the lexicon-coverage score of the claimed plaintext. Re-fetch the status page live before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: Structural proof: a mechanically checkable demonstration that the two inscriptions share a key or a plaintext (for example aligned repeats, an isomorph, or one being a transposition of the other), with a shuffle null at p < 0.001.

Over-budget candidate: a method declared before solving that decrypts one full inscription with at least 90% lexicon coverage (as in criterion 2) and passes the 1,000-string null, but exceeds the key-bit limit by less than 50%. Reported as a candidate only.

targets.verification_method: Check the frozen transcription character by character against Schmeh's 2015 photographs and Pelling's transcription. Re-implement the method, decrypt, compute lexicon coverage against the named lexicon and abbreviation list, recompute key bits, and run the 1,000-string frequency-matched null with the same budget.

targets.name: Salem-Spencer sets: settle r_3(212) in {43, 44}, or beat a Wróblewski nonaveraging record a(n)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster for a complete UNSAT certificate (Ergezer's campaign used Slurm nodes and still left 26 of 6,071 chunks open); a 44-set search or a better split is laptop-days
targets.statement: r_3(N) is the largest subset of {1..N} with no 3-term arithmetic progression (OEIS A003002). Exact values are known for N <= 211 (Dybizbański 2012 to 120; Fausto A. C. Cariboni's b-file to 211, r_3(211) = 43). The first open case is N = 212. Mehmet Ergezer (arXiv:2606.04016, v1 31 May 2026; Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.21413746, 17 Jul 2026; GitHub README snapshot mpc-submission-v1.3) gives a verified 43-element witness and a large CP-SAT/HiGHS/CaDiCaL/kissat campaign. No 44-set was found, but the complete cube cover has not been certificate-checked: 6,045 of 6,071 T2 chunks closed without proof logging, 26 UNKNOWN. So r_3(212) is in {43, 44}, an explicitly stated open unit gap. Equivalently, the threshold A065825(44) (least M with a 44-element 3-AP-free subset of [1..M]) is in [212, 215]. Jarek Wróblewski's nonaveraging-sets site keeps best-known a(n) for n <= 1024 (BEST.TXT, last modified 2023-08-31) and modular records m(n) (BESTMOD.TXT). It lists a(44) <= 215, a(45) <= 227, a(100) <= 762 and a(1024) <= 25958, from searches and constructions by Gavin Theobald, Clyde Kruskal, William Rex Marshall, Fumitaka Yura and Rodolfo Niborski. Target: decide r_3(212).
targets.success_criterion: Success means either (a) an explicit 44-element subset of {1..212} with no three elements a < b < c satisfying a+c=2b, checked exhaustively by two independent programs (this proves r_3(212) = 44 and beats Wróblewski's a(44) <= 215); or (b) a complete proof that no such 44-set exists: a cube or chunk cover of the whole search space whose completeness is checked by an independent script, with every cube UNSAT by a DRAT/LRAT proof accepted by drat-trim or cake_lpr, on a CNF that an independent generator reproduces byte for byte from the definition (all 3-APs in [1,212], cardinality 44). Together with the known 43-witness this proves r_3(212) = 43. Before claiming, re-fetch https://oeis.org/A003002 (b-file), https://oeis.org/A065825 and the Ergezer README/Zenodo/arXiv versions: success needs r_3(212) to be undetermined there on the day.

partial_wins.statement: A Wróblewski integer record: for some n with 44 <= n <= 1024, an n-element 3-AP-free subset of {1..M}, checked by two programs, with M STRICTLY SMALLER (direction: min) than the effective bar for n. The bar is the minimum over k >= n of a(k) - (k - n) and m(k) - (k - n), with a(k) from http://www.math.uni.wroc.pl/~jwr/non-ave/BEST.TXT and m(k) from http://www.math.uni.wroc.pl/~jwr/non-ave/BESTMOD.TXT, both re-fetched live. This works because deleting the largest element of a k-set lowers its maximum by at least 1, and a k-set mod m lifts to a k-set in [1..m]. M must also be smaller than any value for that n in OEIS A065825 (including drafts shown in its history) or a newer paper. For n = 44 the bar is 215, so a 44-set with maximum 213 or 214 counts here; maximum 212 is the full win. On 2026-10-30 the bar is below the listed a(n) only at n = 59 (330), 254 (3178) and 255 (3179).

A Wróblewski modular record: for some n <= 1024, an n-element subset of Z_m with no 3-term progression mod m (no x, y, z, not all equal, with x + z = 2y mod m), with m STRICTLY SMALLER (direction: min) than m(n) in http://www.math.uni.wroc.pl/~jwr/non-ave/BESTMOD.TXT re-fetched live, checked by two programs over all pairs modulo m.

targets.verification_method: For (a) and p1, enumerate all pairs (a,c) with a+c even and test whether (a+c)/2 is in the set, in two independently written programs; check size, range and distinctness. For p2, check all ordered pairs mod m, including the even-m case where x and x+m/2 exclude each other. For (b), regenerate the CNF from the definition with a separate script, check cube-cover completeness (every assignment of the split variables is covered, or the union of cube constraints is a tautology, checked by SAT), and run drat-trim or cake_lpr on every proof. Calibrate the pipeline by reproducing r_3(211) = 43 (or Ergezer's regressions at N = 80, 90, 100). Then compare with the live OEIS b-file and Wróblewski files.
angles: Start from Ergezer's released split and the 26 UNKNOWN chunks. Try a different split (endpoint plus middle-window cardinalities from A003002) together with kissat or CaDiCaL with proof logging, then close the leftovers with cube-and-conquer (march_cu) instead of CP-SAT.

Use window-cardinality constraints from the exact r_3 values: every interval of length L inside [1,212] holds at most r_3(L) elements. Add them as native cardinality constraints and also as clauses, and compare.
To look for a 44-set, take the Wróblewski records near a(44) = 215 (Theorem 22 construction), shrink by local search and SAT repair, and use the 3-AP hypergraph's reflection symmetry.
For p1, many Wróblewski records come from product/split methods (methods.htm) and never had a dedicated search: run modern SAT/local search at mid-range n (100-300) seeded by the modular records.
pitfalls: Wróblewski's index page (non-ave/index.htm) warns that some 'Search' records have no stored solution and that the published results 'are not reliable'. BEST.TXT is also not monotone-consistent: a(59) = a(60) = 331, and a(254), a(255) exceed what a(256) = 3180 implies. So p1 uses the effective bar, not the raw listed value. Beating a value only counts if no newer source (OEIS A065825, papers) already lists a smaller one.
Ergezer's no-proof closures (kissat without proof logging) are solver-attested, not certified. A full proof needs proofs for every cube plus a checked cover.
Offsets: A003002 has offset 0, and A065825(n) is the least M (not M-1). A 44-set in [1,212] means A065825(44) <= 212.
A CNF must forbid every triple a < b < c with a+c=2b in [1,212]; a missed triple gives a fake SAT witness.

A fresh search on 2026-10-30 found nothing that settles r_3(212). It covered arXiv, the A003002 and A065825 histories, the Ergezer README and the erdos-frontier-atlas gap map, which lists the cell as open. A pending A065825 draft (Zachary Sharp, 20 Oct 2026) lists upper bounds for a(49..60), none below Wróblewski's. Other groups are working on this cell, so repeat the search before claiming.

targets.name: Largest k-AP-free subsets of [1..n] for k = 4, 5, 6: the next exact terms of A003003 (n = 143), A003004 (n = 116) and A003005 (n = 148)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exact search; SAT with proof logging); a lucky witness is laptop-hours
targets.statement: r_k(n) is the largest subset of {1..n} with no k-term arithmetic progression (Erdős problems #3, #139, #142 for the asymptotics). Exact small values for k = 4, 5, 6 are OEIS A003003, A003004 and A003005. Their b-files come from Fausto A. C. Cariboni (2018), who also posted the extremal sets: A003003 to n = 142 (r_4(142) = 58; a(52)-a(72) earlier from Rob Pratt, 2015), A003004 to n = 115 (r_5(115) = 67) and A003005 to n = 147 (r_6(147) = 95). Earlier work is by Wagstaff (1972), Karl Rubin (1973) and Shao-Deng-Liang-Xu (J. Comput. Syst. Sci. 2012). None of these entries has changed since 2018 (no %E after 2018, as fetched on 2026-10-30), and the k = 3 case is a separate bank target (r3-212-salem-spencer-unit-gap). Each sequence is nondecreasing with steps of at most 1, so the next term is one of two values: either a witness one larger than the last term or an exhaustive certificate settles it. Target: a new exact term of one of the three sequences.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for some k in {4, 5, 6}, the exact value of r_k(n) at the first index n beyond the live b-file (n = 143 for A003003, n = 116 for A003004, n = 148 for A003005, re-fetched immediately before claiming). The proof needs (i) an explicit witness set of the claimed size in {1..n} with no k-term AP, checked by two programs, and (ii) unless the witness is one larger than r_k(n-1), a certificate that no set one larger exists: a DRAT/LRAT UNSAT proof checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr on a CNF regenerated independently from the definition, or two independently written exact searches that agree. The value must not already appear in the entry's data, b-file, a-files or history, or in a newer paper found by a fresh search.

partial_wins.statement: A certified exact value r_k(N) for some k in {4,5,6} and some N beyond the live b-file that is not the next index (N at most 30 beyond the b-file end), with witness plus UNSAT/exhaustive certificate as in the main criterion.
An independently certified discrepancy: a witness set or UNSAT certificate showing that a value in the live A003003/A003004/A003005 b-file is wrong, reproduced by two independent programs.

targets.verification_method: Two independent checkers enumerate every start a and difference d with a+(k-1)d <= n and test membership of all k terms. For the upper bound, regenerate the CNF (one clause per k-AP forbidding all k true, plus a cardinality encoding checked on small n), run drat-trim/cake_lpr, and calibrate by reproducing the last three b-file values. Compare with the live entries and their history pages.
angles: Reuse the r_3 machinery: window-cardinality pruning from the known exact values (every interval of length L holds at most r_k(L)), endpoint forcing, and reflection symmetry.
Seed the witness search with Cariboni's extremal sets at n-1 and try to extend by one element with SAT repair of a sliding window.
For k = 5 the b-file stops at the shortest n (115). Its last terms sit on a plateau (67 for 113..115), so the next term is likely to stay at 67 and needs only the UNSAT side.
pitfalls: Offsets: A003003, A003004 and A003005 start at n = 1, unlike A003002 (n = 0).
A progression means k distinct terms in AP with d >= 1. Check every difference, not only d <= n/(k-1) for a fixed start.
A heuristic search that finds no larger set is not a proof. The upper bound needs a checkable certificate.
WebSearch was unavailable when this entry was written: do a fresh literature search (e.g., later Shao/Cariboni-style computations) before claiming.

targets.name: Sparse rulers (minimal difference bases): fewer marks than Pegg's best-known table at some length n >= 245
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours for constructive search at a given length; exhaustive minimality proofs (partial wins) need cluster
targets.statement: A sparse ruler of length n is a set of integer marks 0 = m_0 < ... < m_{k-1} = n whose pairwise differences cover 1..n. A046693(n) is the fewest marks. Erdős problem #170 asks for lim A046693(n)/sqrt(n). Erdős-Gál showed the limit exists, and it lies in [1.56, sqrt(3)] (Leech 1956; Wichmann 1963). Exact values are verified for n <= 213 (Arch D. Robison 2014; A046693 b-file 0..213 by Ed Pegg Jr). The maximal lengths A004137(25) = 213 (Robison with Peter Luschny) and A004137(26) = 232 (Fabian Schwartau, Yannic Schröder, Lars Wolf, Joerg Schoebel, 2021) are proven. A004137(27) is unknown; Wichmann gives 251. The Schwartau et al. IEEE DataPort files (login required, not checked here) reportedly give the length/mark-count combinations up to length 244, so lengths 214..244 are left out. Write E(n) = marks - round(sqrt(3n + 9/4)) for the excess (A326499). Ed Pegg Jr's table (A326499 a-file a326499_2.txt, n = 1..10501; E <= 1 proved by Pegg, 2019) lists best-known rulers. 4,890 of the lengths 214..10501 have E = 1 (re-counted 2026-10-30). The entry says terms over n = 213 are unverified minimal; for example, n = 474 has E = 1, but an E = 0 ruler may exist. The smallest in-scope lengths listed with E = 1 are 245..249 (28 marks listed; 27 would be E = 0), then 262..268 and 282..287. Luschny's conjecture says the length-58 ruler 1^3 24^1 5^1 4^5 3^2 is the last non-Wichmann optimal ruler. It would imply many E = 1 entries are optimal, but it is unproven. Target: a ruler with fewer marks than the table at some n >= 245.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for some n >= 245, an explicit list of k integer marks 0 = m_0 < ... < m_{k-1} = n whose pairwise differences cover every integer 1..n, checked exhaustively by two programs. k must be STRICTLY SMALLER (direction: min) than the best-known mark count for n at verification time. That count is the minimum over Pegg's table https://oeis.org/A326499/a326499_2.txt, the A046693, A326499 and A308766 entries, Pegg's Wolfram Community 'Sparse ruler data' post, Luschny's ruler pages, and any newer paper or table found by a fresh search, all re-fetched live. Lengths 214..244 do not count. A count that contradicts the proven A004137 values (k <= 26 for any n >= 233) means a bug, not a win.

partial_wins.statement: A certified exact minimal mark count for some n in 245..249, currently listed with 28 marks (E = 1). This needs an independently re-runnable exhaustive search, with logs, proving that no 27-mark sparse ruler of that length exists, provided no live source already settles it.

A certified value of A004137(27), the maximum length of a 27-mark complete ruler. Either an exhaustive, independently re-runnable search proving that no 27-mark ruler of length 252 or more exists (confirming the Wichmann value 251), or an explicit 27-mark ruler of length >= 252 checked by two programs.

targets.verification_method: Compute all k(k-1)/2 differences into a boolean array of size n+1 and check that every 1..n appears; confirm 0 and n are marks and k is as claimed; two independent implementations. Recompute round(sqrt(3n+9/4)) exactly in integer arithmetic. For partial wins, rerun the exhaustive search independently and calibrate it by reproducing A004137(24) = 198 and A004137(25) = 213 or Robison's counts.
angles: Non-Wichmann families: search over 'gap-word' templates 1^a x^b y^c z^d ... with more blocks than Wichmann's six, solving for block lengths by integer programming and then checking coverage exactly.
Local repair: take an excess-1 ruler, delete one mark, and use a SAT model (marks as booleans, each difference covered by at least one pair) restricted to a window to recover full coverage.
Target lengths where Pegg's table switches between excess 0 and 1 inside one batch of A289761; boundary lengths are the most plausible to drop.
pitfalls: Excess is defined with round(sqrt(3n + 9/4)), and Pegg's table rounds half to even (Mathematica Round). That differs from round-half-up at the 29 lengths n = 6, 36, 90, 168, 270, ... where sqrt(3n + 9/4) is a half-integer. Compare mark counts, not excess, using exact integer arithmetic.
Pegg's table notation lists gap multiplicities (e.g., 1^4 4^1 8^5 ...). Expand to marks before comparing, and check the expanded ruler.
Lengths 214..244 are out of scope because Schwartau et al.'s login-gated data reportedly cover them. 214, 215 and 233 are provably E = 1 in any case, from A004137(25) = 213 and A004137(26) = 232.
Golomb rulers (distinct differences) are a different problem and are held separately; this target is about covering every difference.

targets.name: Erdős #156 small cases: minimum size of a maximal (saturated) Sidon set in {1..n}: settle a(189) in {9, 10}, and the nine-mark threshold
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days to needs cluster (exhaustive nine-mark saturated-Sidon search with blocker pruning); a witness search is laptop-hours
targets.statement: Erdős problem #156 (Erdős-Sárközy-Sós) asks whether some maximal Sidon set in {1..N} has size O(N^(1/3)). Ruzsa constructed one of size O((N log N)^(1/3)). OEIS A382397(n) is the minimum size of an inclusion-maximal (saturated) Sidon subset of {1..n}. Felix Huber (Aug 2026) extended it to n = 183 (b-file 0..183, a(n) = 9 for 145 <= n <= 183). His preprint 'Saturated Sidon Sets in Consecutive Intervals: The Eight-Mark Threshold Is 144' (A399118 a-file) proves that an 8-element saturated Sidon set exists for interval length 144 and never for any larger length. Writing E_k for the lengths admitting a saturated k-set, he records that E_9 contains [45, 183]. A k-set blocks at most (k^3-k)/2 outside points, so sets of size <= 7 cannot be saturated for n >= 176. The table has moved past the b-file outside OEIS. The erdos-frontier-atlas gap map (curation 2026-09-27) gives the 9-set {39,43,72,78,99,100,112,119,143}, which is saturated in {1..n} for 143 <= n <= 188, so A382397(n) = 9 for 184 <= n <= 188 and max E_9 >= 188. The d3lefts project (GitHub issue #46, 29 Oct 2026) gives the 10-set {50,51,57,79,94,105,126,140,150,167}, which is saturated in {1..189}. Both were re-checked on 2026-10-30. So 9 <= a(189) <= 10, and a(189) = 9 exactly when 189 is in E_9. Huber's open questions ask for terminal values max E_k for other k. In the forum (16 Sep 2026), veljjanoski computed the cyclic analogue: the largest n with an inclusion-maximal k-element Sidon set in Z_n is c(3..7) = 14, 30, 50, 84, 126. Target: decide a(189).
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact value of A382397(189). If a live source has settled it, the target is instead a(n) at the first n >= 189 that no live source settles. Re-fetch https://oeis.org/A382397, the forum thread and the erdos-frontier-atlas gap map before claiming. If the value is 9, give an explicit 9-element Sidon subset of {1..189} that is inclusion-maximal (adding any other x in {1..189} creates a repeated difference), checked by two programs. The lower bound 9 then follows from Huber's theorem (no saturated 8-set for n >= 145) and the counting bound (k <= 7 impossible for n >= 176). The verifier must confirm both, including Huber's {0..n-1} versus {1..n} convention. If the value is 10, the 10-element witness is already public, so success needs a certificate that no saturated 9-element Sidon set exists in {1..189}: two agreeing, independently written exhaustive searches, or a DRAT/LRAT-checked UNSAT proof on an independently regenerated CNF.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit saturated 9-element Sidon set in {1..n} for some n >= 190, checked by two programs, provided no live source already lists such an n. Sidon means all positive differences are distinct; saturated means adding any further x in {1..n} breaks this. This shows max E_9 >= n, beyond the public n = 188 witness and Huber's [45,183]; n = 189 itself is the main target.

The cyclic analogue c(8): the largest n such that Z_n contains an inclusion-maximal 8-element Sidon set (a+b = c+d mod n only trivially, sums with a <= b including a = b). It needs a witness and an exhaustive search over all n up to the trivial bound (k^3+k^2+2k)/2 = 296 stated in the forum, by two independent programs, extending veljjanoski's c(3..7) = 14, 30, 50, 84, 126.

targets.verification_method: Check the Sidon property by computing all C(k,2) differences (or all sums a+b with a <= b). Check saturation by trying every x not in A and confirming that a repeated difference appears. Calibrate first. Exhaustive searches must reproduce a(n) for 140 <= n <= 183 and the 8-mark threshold 144. The checker must accept {39,43,72,78,99,100,112,119,143} as saturated in {1..188} and reject it in {1..189} (189 is addable), and must accept {50,51,57,79,94,105,126,140,150,167} as saturated in {1..189}. Then check the new claim. For p2, calibrate on c(7) = 126 with its witness {0,21,50,103,104,119,121}.
angles: Use Huber's blocker criterion: a set is saturated iff each outside point x is blocked by some (a,b,c) with x = a+b-c, x = 2a-b or x = (a+b)/2. Build sets by choosing minimal witnesses that block the new endpoint, as in his canonical search classes.

Use the capacity bound: a 9-set blocks at most (9^3-9)/2 = 360 outside points. Huber's first-return lemma (a saturated witness at a new length must contain both endpoints) cuts the search for {1..189} sharply; adapt his endpoint-root enumeration from 8 to 9 marks.
For p1 or a 9-mark witness at 189, start from the public 9-set saturated in {1..188} and the 10-sets saturated at 184 and 189, then perturb or delete marks with an exact saturation check.
pitfalls: Inclusion-maximal is not maximum: the target is the smallest saturated set, not the largest Sidon set (Golomb ruler problems are separate and held).
Huber uses [n] = {0..n-1}; OEIS uses {1..n}. Both have n points, but a mismatched convention can shift a threshold by one.

A set saturated in {1..n} stays saturated in {1..n'} for max(A) <= n' <= n, because blocking depends only on A and x. Saturation can fail as n grows, and a cardinality can reappear after disappearing, so a failed search at one n says nothing about larger n.

At least two public AI-agent efforts (d3lefts issues #46/#91 and erdos-frontier-atlas) are working this cell. Their annealing near-candidates at n = 184..200 were not saturated, and their timeouts are not UNSAT proofs. Re-check any third-party witness before relying on it.

targets.name: Erdős #773 small cases: largest Sidon subset of the first n squares, a(72) and beyond (OEIS A390813)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (maximum independent set / ILP on the sum-collision hypergraph)
targets.statement: Erdős problem #773 (Alon-Erdős) asks for the size of the largest Sidon subset of {1^2, 2^2, ..., N^2} and whether it is N^(1-o(1)). Known: >> N^(2/3) (Lefmann-Thiele 1995) and <= N exp(-c log N / log log N) (Croot, Mao and Yip, announced on the problem's forum, Apr 2026). OEIS A390813 (submitted by Giorgos Kalogeropoulos, Nov 2025) gives the exact maximum a(n) for n <= 68, with a(43)-a(68) from Christian Sievers (27 Nov 2025); a(68) = 32. Sievers also noted that up to at least n = 68, n = 32 is the only n where no maximum subset contains n^2. Erdős Problem a Day (erdosproblemaday.com, 12 Aug 2026) reports a(69) = 32, a(70) = 33 and a(71) = 33. These come from exhaustive searches conditional on the published OEIS prefix, with a size-33 witness and an independent audit; they are not yet in OEIS and were not re-run for this entry. So a(72) is 33 or 34. The sum-collision structure comes from representations x^2 + y^2 = z^2 + w^2, which are plentiful, so exact values need a genuine combinatorial search. Target: the next exact term a(72).
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact value of A390813(72). If the live b-file or the Erdős Problem a Day #773 page has grown past 71, the target is a(n) at the first index beyond both, re-fetched immediately before claiming. If a(72) = 34, give an explicit 34-element subset of {1..72} whose squares form a Sidon set (all sums x^2+y^2 with x <= y distinct), checked by two programs. This suffices since a(n+1) <= a(n)+1 and a(71) <= 33. If a(72) = 33, give a 33-element witness and a certificate that no 34-element subset exists. The certificate is either two independently written exact searches that agree (e.g., branch and bound and an ILP with all collision constraints), or a DRAT/LRAT-checked UNSAT proof on an independently regenerated CNF. Any prefix values a(k), k <= 71, used as pruning bounds must come from the OEIS b-file or be re-certified in the same run. The value must not appear in the entry, its history, the erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/773 comments or the Erdős Problem a Day #773 page.

partial_wins.statement: A certified exact value a(N) for some N with 73 <= N <= 100 (not necessarily consecutive with the known values), with witness and exhaustive/UNSAT certificate as in the main criterion.

A second n with 69 <= n <= 100, after Sievers' n = 32, where no maximum Sidon subset of {1^2..n^2} contains n^2. It needs the certified exact value a(n), as in the main criterion, re-certified rather than taken from an unverified source. It also needs a certificate, from the same two-method exact pipeline, that every Sidon subset of {1^2..n^2} containing n^2 has at most a(n) - 1 elements.

targets.verification_method: Enumerate all collisions x^2+y^2 = z^2+w^2 with x <= y, z <= w, {x,y} != {z,w}, in 1..N (including x = y cases) by hashing sums; a set is Sidon in squares iff it contains no collision quadruple. Use two independent implementations. Calibrate the exact searches by reproducing a(60..68) from the b-file and the reported a(69..71) = 32, 33, 33, then run the new N.
angles: Model it as a maximum independent set in a 4-uniform (and 3-uniform for x = y repeats) hypergraph and solve it with an ILP (HiGHS/CBC) using clique-like cover cuts from parametrised families of collisions (Brahmagupta identities).
Do incremental search over n: an optimal set at n-1 plus warm starts gives fast lower bounds; only the upper bound needs a full proof.
Use the many multiplicative symmetries of the collision structure (which are not global symmetries of [1..n]) for cutting planes rather than symmetry breaking.
pitfalls: Sidon here means all sums a+b with a <= b distinct, so 2x^2 = y^2 + z^2 collisions (x = y on one side) count.
Squares of the indices, not the indices themselves: the set is {x^2 : x in S}.
A heuristic that fails to find a 34-set proves nothing.

The Erdős Problem a Day values a(69..71) depend on the OEIS prefix and have not been independently re-run. If an independent exact search disagrees with them, report it, but a disagreement is not a listed win.

targets.name: Restricted additive 2-bases (restricted postage stamp, A006638): beat the Challis-Robinson symmetric-basis ranges for 48 <= k <= 82, or settle a(48)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days for preamble searches (s = 27, 28) and constructions; an exhaustive a(48) needs cluster (about 4,000 CPU-hours extrapolated from Kohonen's 812 h at k = 47)
targets.statement: An additive 2-basis A = {0 = a_0 < a_1 < ... < a_k} has range n_2(A), the largest n with {0..n} in A+A. It is restricted if n_2(A) = 2a_k. OEIS A006638 gives the largest range of a restricted basis with k positive elements. Jukka Kohonen determined it exactly for k <= 41 (J. Integer Seq. 17, 2014) and k <= 47 (arXiv:1503.03416, 2015). For k = 42..47 the values are 588, 614, 644, 674, 704 and 734; the k = 47 prefix search took 812 CPU-hours. All extremal bases there are symmetric and are exactly those of the preamble-amble construction of Michael F. Challis and John P. Robinson (J. Integer Seq. 13 (2010) 10.2.3, corrected Tables 2 and 3). Their Table 3 gives the best symmetric ranges as piecewise-linear formulas: 30k-676 for 43 <= k <= 52 (764 at k = 48), 32k-780 (52-56), 34k-892 (56-58), 38k-1124 (58-62), 40k-1248 (62-67), 44k-1516 (67-80), 48k-1836 (80-82), and an open-ended 52k-2164 from k = 82. They come from the most efficient preambles PA(s, a_s), known up to s = 26. No exact value is known for k >= 48 (A006638 b-file 1..47). The formulas are linear, while quadratic constructions in the literature (e.g., Mrose 1979, about (2/7)k^2) overtake them for k beyond roughly 100. This target is therefore limited to 48 <= k <= 82, where Table 3 is the best published range found. It differs from the unrestricted postage-stamp numbers n(2,k) (A001212). Target: a restricted basis beating the best published range for some 48 <= k <= 82.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for some k with 48 <= k <= 82, an explicit set A = {0 < a_1 < ... < a_k} of integers with {0..2a_k} in A+A, checked by two programs. That is, every integer 0..2a_k is a sum of two not necessarily distinct elements of A. Its range 2a_k must be STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best published restricted (or symmetric) range for that k, all checked live. The sources are the Challis-Robinson Table 3 formula value, OEIS A006638 and its links, Mossige's symmetric-basis results, any explicit construction in the literature (e.g., Mrose-type) evaluated at that k, and a fresh literature search. If the unrestricted range exceeds 2a_k, report it, but the restricted condition must hold as defined.

partial_wins.statement: A certified exact value of A006638(48): an independently re-runnable exhaustive search (Kohonen-style prefix and suffix enumeration, or a checked UNSAT certificate) proving that no restricted basis with k = 48 has range above some R, together with a basis of range R (expected R = 764).

An exhaustive determination of the most efficient preamble PA(s, a_s) for s = 27 or s = 28 in the Challis-Robinson sense (extending their Table 2), with the search independently re-runnable, and the resulting linear range formula for the derived symmetric bases stated and checked on at least one explicit basis.

targets.verification_method: Compute A+A with a bitset of size 2a_k+1 and check coverage of 0..2a_k, in two independent implementations; also report the full range n_2(A). Compare 2a_k with the Table 3 formula for that k (calibrate by reproducing 734 at k = 47 from Kohonen's listed bases and 588 at k = 42). For p1, rerun the exhaustive search on the verifier's side, and calibrate by reproducing A006638(41..47).
angles: Table 3 keeps only the best formula from the most efficient preamble for each s. Near the row crossovers (k = 52, 56, 58, 62, 67, 80), try other preambles, near-optimal PAs, or two-period ambles; one of them may beat the tabulated line at a single k.
Try non-symmetric restricted bases built from a symmetric skeleton with a modified middle 'amble' (period-changing ambles), searched by SAT over the middle segment.
Kohonen's element-wise lower bounds depend on the exact unrestricted values A001212 (known to k = 24); better bounds there speed up the exhaustive p1 search.
For p2, extend Challis's look-up-table preamble search to s = 27 or 28 and check whether the derived linear formula beats Table 3 anywhere in 48..82.
pitfalls: Restricted means range exactly 2a_k. A basis with larger unrestricted range but 2a_k smaller is not a restricted record.
Off-by-one in k: k counts the positive elements (A006638(1) = 2 with A = {0,1}).
Challis-Robinson Table 2 originally had errors for s = 16 and s = 24 (non-symmetricizable preambles), corrected in the 2010 paper; use the corrected tables.

The unrestricted numbers n(2,k) (A001212, exact only to k = 24; Friedman's Math Magic postage-stamp page 0403 shows k = 25 as '?') belong to the bank entry friedman-mathmagic-archive-records; do not claim them here.

targets.name: Free polyominoes, polyhexes and polyiamonds: close the gap to the fixed counts (A000105 beyond n = 59, A000228 beyond 36, A000577 beyond 52)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (symmetric-animal transfer matrices or enumeration of half-animals; big-integer or multi-prime arithmetic)
targets.statement: Three classic polyform tables have free counts (up to rotation and reflection) that lag far behind the fixed counts (up to translation). Polyominoes: fixed A001168 is known to n = 70 (b-file by Gill Barequet and Gil Ben-Shachar, ALENEX 2024; n <= 56 Iwan Jensen), but free A000105 stops at n = 59 (Toshihiro Shirakawa, arXiv 2510.22446, 2025; terms to 50 also John Mason). Polyhexes: fixed A001207 is known to n = 46 (Voege and Guttmann 2003, b-file by Vaclav Kotesovec) but free A000228 stops at n = 36 (John Mason and Robert A. Russell). Polyiamonds: fixed A001420 is known to n = 75 (Guttmann's 2009 book table, b-file by Kotesovec) but free A000577 stops at n = 52 (John Mason). By Burnside, free = (fixed + symmetric corrections)/|G|, and only the counts of animals with a nontrivial symmetry are missing; those grow roughly like the square root of the fixed counts. For polyominoes we checked (2026-10-30) that the identity fixed = 8 asym + 4(axial + diagonal + C2) + 2(two-axes + two-diagonals + C4) + D8 reproduces A000105 exactly for n = 20, 40, 59 from the b-files, and that at n = 60 every class count is already published (A006746 to 60, A006748 to 66, A056877 to 81, A056878 to 87, A144553 to 95, A142886 to 203) except the exactly-C2 class A006747 (to 59, Mason/Shirakawa). So A000105(60) follows from one new number: the count of fixed polyominoes of 60 cells invariant under a half-turn. All OEIS pages checked live 2026-10-30, no pending drafts.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact value of the first unknown term of A000105 (n = 60 as of 2026-10-30), A000228 (n = 37) or A000577 (n = 53), with the N re-read from the live b-file immediately before claiming. The value must come with every published symmetry-class count it relies on and every new class count it introduces (for A000105(60): the half-turn-invariant count and the resulting A006747(60), A006749(60)). It must satisfy the Burnside identity exactly against the published fixed count (A001168, A001207 or A001420). The same code must reproduce all published free terms and class terms for at least the 15 largest published n. A new class count must also be confirmed by a second, independent method (a different algorithm or decomposition) that agrees exactly.
