partial_wins.statement: The next unknown term of a published polyomino symmetry-class sequence other than A006747/A006749: A006746 (axial, b-file to 60), A006748 (diagonal, to 66), A056877 (two axes, to 81), A056878 (two diagonals, to 87), A144553 (C4, to 95) or A142886 (D8, to 203). The index is re-read from the live b-file. The same reproduction and two-method rules apply. A006747(60) is not a partial: it determines A000105(60), which is the full win.

The next unknown term of any published polyhex or polyiamond symmetry-class sequence that the free count A000228 or A000577 needs, at the first n beyond the free table. The same reproduction and two-method rules apply.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic (< 1 hour): recompute the Burnside identity from the claimant's class counts and the published fixed count, and check divisibility (the result must be an exact integer). Rerun the claimant's symmetric-class program for small n against the OEIS class sequences, and for the new n modulo one fresh prime if it uses modular arithmetic. Optional: an independent half-animal enumerator for n up to 40.
angles: A half-turn-symmetric polyomino of 2m or 2m+1 cells is determined by a 'half' attached to its centre (cell, edge midpoint or vertex). Count the halves with a Jensen-style transfer matrix on a half-plane with a twisted (glued) boundary row, as Barequet, Moffie, Ribo and Rote did for twisted cylinders.
Redelmeier-type enumeration restricted to symmetric animals grows like lambda^(n/2), about 4^30 at n = 60: large but within reach for a multithreaded counter, and a second method for cross-checking.
Use the published fixed counts as a free consistency test: a wrong class count almost always breaks integrality of the Burnside quotient.
pitfalls: A006747 counts polyominoes with exactly the C2 symmetry. A program that counts all half-turn-invariant polyominoes must subtract the two-axes, two-diagonals, C4 and D8 classes, each with the right weight.

Polyhex and polyiamond free counts use the 12-element dihedral group of the hexagonal or triangular lattice. Polyiamonds have cell-centred symmetries for both triangle orientations. Reproduce the small published class counts before trusting the code.

targets.name: Fixed polyominoes: the exact count of 71-cell polyominoes (next term of OEIS A001168 after Barequet and Ben-Shachar's n = 70)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (Jensen's transfer-matrix method; states and run time grow about 2^(n/2) per width, with n = 70 needing a large parallel run)
targets.statement: A001168 counts polyominoes up to translation. Iwan Jensen's transfer-matrix algorithm (2001, 2003 cluster version) gave terms to n = 56. Gill Barequet and Gil Ben-Shachar ('Counting Polyominoes, Revisited', ALENEX 2024) pushed this to n = 70. Vuong Bui (arXiv 2211.14909) quotes a(69) and a(70), and the b-file (0..70) is theirs. The count is the primary input for series analysis of Klarner's constant (about 4.0626) and for the free-polyomino table. The OEIS page was checked live 2026-10-30 (last edit 2026-10-19, links only; no pending draft): a(71) is not listed.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact integer a(71) of A001168, or the next unknown term if the live b-file, re-fetched immediately before claiming, has grown. It must come from two runs that agree exactly. The runs must differ in modulus set or arithmetic AND in decomposition (for example different width splits, or row vs column sweeps). The same code must reproduce every published term for n <= 70 exactly. Sanity check: a(71)/a(70) must lie strictly between a(70)/a(69) = 4.00512... and 4.0626.

partial_wins.statement: An independent reproduction of a(57)..a(70) by a program written from scratch (not Jensen's or Barequet and Ben-Shachar's code) that agrees exactly with the b-file, with source and run logs. It must also give a(71) modulo at least one 61-bit prime, computed by two different decompositions that agree.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: rerun the claimant's program for n <= 50 and compare with the b-file; rerun the n = 71 computation modulo one fresh prime for a subset of width classes and compare residues; check ratio consistency.
pitfalls: Fixed (A001168), one-sided and free (A000105) counts differ; this target is fixed counts only.
Width-split runs must cover every bounding-box shape exactly once (Jensen counts width <= length and doubles the non-square cases); off-by-one in the square case is a classic error.

targets.name: Polycubes: the number of 23-cell polycubes (next term of OEIS A001931 fixed and A000162 / A038119 free, open since Phillip Thompson's n = 22 in 2024)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (or many laptop-weeks: about 2.4e18 fixed polycubes at n = 23 with a Redelmeier-type counter; symmetric classes are far cheaper)
targets.statement: Fixed polycubes are face-connected sets of n unit cubes up to translation: simple-cubic lattice animals, OEIS A001931. Free polycubes are A000162 (rotations only) and A038119 (rotations and reflections). Earlier terms came from Redelmeier, Lunnon, Mertens (1990), Aleksandrowicz and Barequet (2006), and Luther and Mertens (2011). Stanley Dodds computed a(20) in Aug 2023 with a streamlined Redelmeier implementation in C#, now on OEIS with comments by Guenter Rote. Phillip Thompson's Rust port of Dodds's algorithm gave a(21) and a(22) = 306405169166373418 (Feb 2024; the n = 22 run took about 10 days on a 64-thread machine). The free counts reach n = 22 too: A000162 from Dodds and Thompson, A038119 extended by John Mason (2024). John Mason's per-symmetry-class sequences (A376964-A377131, Oct 2024) reach n = 22 for most classes and further for a few (e.g., class A, A376965, to n = 24). OEIS checked live 2026-10-30: all three sequences end at n = 22 (data field only, no separate b-file), all three carry keyword 'more', and there are no pending drafts. The higher-dimensional lattice-animal entry of the bank covers d >= 4; this target is the 3D cubic lattice only.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact value of a(23) of A001931 (fixed), or of A000162 or A038119 at n = 23 (free, which also needs the symmetric-polycube counts at 23), with N re-read from the live b-files before claiming. The value must be computed by two independent programs, or by one program plus an independent check of a stated partition of the count (for example by the first growth steps or by bounding-box class) recomputed separately, and they must agree exactly. The same code must reproduce every published term for n <= 22.

partial_wins.statement: The number of 23-cell polycubes with a nontrivial rotational symmetry (the correction term needed to pass from A001931(23) to A000162(23)), by two methods that agree and reproduce the published symmetric data for n <= 22.
An exact count of 23-cell fixed polycubes inside a stated bounded box class (for example all with bounding-box height at most 3), computed by two methods, presented as a certified lower bound.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: rerun the claimant's code for n <= 18 (minutes) against the b-file; recompute several randomly chosen subtrees of the Redelmeier search (or bounding-box classes) for n = 23 and compare subtotals; check the growth ratio a(23)/a(22) against the trend (about 7.8).
pitfalls: A000162 identifies rotations only (mirror pairs counted twice); A038119 also identifies reflections. Do not mix them.

64-bit overflow: a(23) is about 2.4e18, within a factor of 4 of the signed 64-bit limit (about 9.2e18). Any weighted subtotal (symmetry multipliers, Burnside weights such as 24 or 48 times a class count) can overflow; use 128-bit or checked accumulators.
Stephen Pursey (2026) corrected some published polycube-with-cavity counts; check that the sub-counts you rely on are the corrected ones.

targets.name: Meanders and semi-meanders: the next exact term of OEIS A005316 (open meanders, known to n = 58) or A000682 (semi-meanders, known to n = 49)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (Jensen-type transfer matrix over arch configurations with modular arithmetic; memory is the bottleneck)
targets.statement: Arnold's meander numbers count ways a river can cross a road n times (A005316), with closed meanders A005315(n) = A005316(2n-1). Iwan Jensen's transfer-matrix method gave A005316 to n = 44 and semi-meanders A000682 to n = 45. Andrew Howroyd's C# software extended A005316 to n = 55 (and A005315 to 28). In 2026 Alexy Khrabrov ('Counting Arnold's Meanders with Verified Algorithms', with Lean 4, Rust and OxCaml programs) contributed the A005316 b-file to n = 58. Hunter Hogan (mapFolding, Oct 2026) extended A000682 to n = 49, and his repository lists A000682(50) as a planned computation (estimated at hours with 64 GB of memory). OEIS checked live 2026-10-30: no pending drafts. The field is active, so recheck before and after a run.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact value of A005316(59) or A000682(50) (or the first index beyond each live b-file re-fetched immediately before claiming), computed by two runs that agree exactly. The runs must use different moduli sets or exact arithmetic AND a different decomposition or program. The same code must reproduce every published term of the sequence. Terms that follow from published ones by identities do not count (see pitfalls).

partial_wins.statement: An independent from-scratch reproduction of A005316(56..58) (Khrabrov) or A000682(46..49) (Hogan), by a program not derived from Jensen's, Howroyd's, Khrabrov's or Hogan's code. It must agree exactly with the b-file, with source and logs, using two runs with different moduli.

A new complete row of a published meander refinement table at the first unknown order, two runs agreeing. Examples: A008828 (closed meander systems by number of components, Howroyd's b-file through row 20), or semi-meanders by winding.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: rerun the claimant's program modulo one fresh 61-bit prime for the claimed n and compare the residue; rerun for all n <= 40 against the b-files; check that a(n)/a(n-2) continues the slowly rising trend of the published ratios (about 10.93 for A005316 at n = 58 and 11.27 for A000682 at n = 49, approaching the limit of about 12.26 from below).
pitfalls: A005315 (closed meanders) lags the A005316 b-file. Since A005315(n) = A005316(2n-1), A005315(29) = A005316(57) is already known though not in A005315's b-file. Adding it is bookkeeping, not a win.

Stamp foldings follow from semi-meanders. A000136(n) = n*A000682(n), A001010(2m) = 2*A000682(m+1), A001010(2m-1) = 2*A007822(m) (A007822 is known to m = 26), and A001011(n) = (A001010(n) + A000136(n))/4. So A000136(46..49) and A001011(46..49) already follow from published terms and are not wins; likewise A077014(56..58) follows from A005316.
Offsets differ: A005316 starts at 0, A000682 and A000136 at 1.

targets.name: Knight's tour enumeration: the number of closed tours on the 10 x 10 board (A001230(5)) or open tours on the 9 x 9 board (A165134(9))
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (frontier/transfer-matrix over two-column knight frontiers with path-connectivity states; the 9 x 10 closed partial is laptop-days to cluster)
targets.statement: Closed tours on 8 x 8: 13,267,364,410,532 undirected. Loebbing and Wegener (1996) used BDDs, and Brendan McKay corrected their value (1997). Open tours (directed Hamiltonian paths) on 8 x 8: 19,591,828,170,979,904 (Alex Chernov, 2014, A165134). Frontier methods have since moved on narrow boards. Donald Knuth extended closed tours on 8 x n to n = 32 (A193055 b-file, 2025). Closed tours on 9 x 2n for n <= 4 come from Knuth's Prefascicle 8a and his Christmas lecture 'Adventures with Knight's Tours' (Dec 2025), entered as A391999 by Peter Luschny: 9 x 6 = 3,374,967,940 and 9 x 8 = 7,112,881,119,092,574. Luschny counted undirected Hamiltonian paths on 9 x n up to n = 8 (A391009, Dec 2025). The square boards beyond 8 x 8 remain open. OEIS checked live 2026-10-30: A001230 stops at 8 x 8, A165134 at 8 x 8, A391999 at 9 x 8 and A391009 at 9 x 8, with no pending drafts.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact number of undirected closed knight's tours on the 10 x 10 board (A001230(5)), or of directed Hamiltonian paths in the 9 x 9 knight graph (A165134(9), which is 2 x A391009(9)). It must be computed by two independent runs (different program or decomposition, and different moduli or exact arithmetic) that agree exactly. The code must reproduce A001230(4), A165134(8), and all published terms of A193055 (8 x n) or A391009 (9 x n) for the widths it supports. The live OEIS entries, re-fetched before claiming, must still lack the value.

partial_wins.statement: A391999(5): the number of undirected closed knight's tours on the 9 x 10 board, two runs agreeing, with the code reproducing A391999(3), A391999(4) and the A193055 terms for 8 x n, n <= 20.
A193055(33): the number of closed knight's tours on the 8 x 33 board (Knuth's b-file ends at 32), two runs agreeing, with the code reproducing every A193055 term.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: rerun the claimant's frontier program on the published boards (8 x 8 closed, 8 x 8 open, 9 x 8 closed) and compare; rerun the claimed board modulo one fresh prime; for a 10 x 10 claim also check divisibility by the 8 board symmetries' orbit structure (count of tours fixed by each symmetry computed separately must make the Burnside quotient an integer).
pitfalls: Directed vs undirected and open vs closed conventions differ across these sequences (A165134 counts directed paths; A391009 undirected; A001230 undirected cycles). Factor-2 errors are common.
Loebbing and Wegener's first 8 x 8 figure was wrong; reproduce McKay's value before trusting any new code.
Knuth's December 2025 lecture may contain values not yet in OEIS; check the lecture materials and any 2026 OEIS additions before claiming.

targets.name: Gray codes: the number of Hamiltonian paths in the 6-cube (A091299(6), open since 2005)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (or laptop-weeks): meet-in-the-middle over the bipartite halves in the style of Haanpaa and Ostergard
targets.statement: A091299 counts directed Hamiltonian paths (not necessarily cyclic Gray codes) in the n-cube: 2, 8, 144, 91392, 187499658240. The value for n = 5 is from Janez Brank (2005), and A003043 (paths with a marked start) has 5859364320 for n = 5. For Hamiltonian cycles the 6-cube is done: A066037(6) = 35,838,213,722,570,883,870,720 (Harri Haanpaa and Patric Ostergard, 'Counting Hamiltonian cycles in bipartite graphs', Math. Comp. 2014, correcting Deza-Shklyar 2010). The 6-cube path counts A091299(6) and A003043(6) are still missing, and so is the 7-cube cycle count A066037(7), which is the famous moonshot behind this one. OEIS checked live 2026-10-30: A091299 (last edit 2026-10-27, links only) and A003043 both end at n = 5 with keyword 'more', no pending drafts.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact value of A091299(6), the number of directed Hamiltonian paths in Q6 (equivalently A003043(6) = A091299(6)/64, the factor 2^n checked against n = 5), computed by two independent methods or decompositions that agree exactly. The code must reproduce A091299(1..5), and run in cycle mode it must reproduce A066037(6) of Haanpaa and Ostergard. OEIS re-fetched before claiming must still lack the value.

partial_wins.statement: N3 or N5: the number of (undirected) Hamiltonian paths in Q6 between a fixed vertex and a fixed vertex at distance 3 (N3) or distance 5 (N5). It must come from two methods that agree, and the code must also reproduce the analogous Q5 class counts and N1 = 2*A066037(6)/6 = 11946071240856961290240 (paths with adjacent ends, known from the cycle count). The decomposition is A091299(6) = 64*(6*N1 + 20*N3 + 6*N5).
An independent recomputation of A066037(6) by an algorithm different from Haanpaa and Ostergard's, agreeing exactly, with source and logs.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: check the endpoint decomposition A091299(n) = 2^n * sum over odd d of C(n,d)*N_d, against the Q5 data and with N1 = 2*A066037(n)/n. Recompute one class with the claimant's code modulo a fresh prime. Rerun the code for Q5 paths and Q6 cycles.
pitfalls: A091299 counts directed paths with a distinguished start; A003043 marks the start node differently. Recheck the factor against n = 5 (187499658240 vs 5859364320 differ by 32 = 2^5, the number of start nodes).
The Deza-Shklyar 6-cube cycle value was wrong; use Haanpaa-Ostergard's corrected value as the cycle-mode check.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Perfect matchings of the 8-cube: the exact count A005271(8)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (exact count far beyond direct methods; the modular partial is laptop-days)
targets.statement: This counts perfect matchings of the n-cube Q_n, a problem in Propp's 'Enumeration of matchings: problems and progress' (Problem 19) and his 'Twenty open problems in enumeration of matchings'. The counts are 1, 2, 9, 272, 589185, 16332454526976 for n = 1..6. D. H. Wiedemann first found n = 6 (unpublished), and Per Hakan Lundow published it (1996). For n = 7 the count is 391,689,748,492,473,664,721,077,609,089 (Patric Ostergard and Ville Pettersson, 'Enumerating Perfect Matchings in n-Cubes', Order 30 (2013), using classification under the cube's symmetry group). Q8 has 256 vertices and its count is unknown. OEIS checked live 2026-10-30: A005271 ends at n = 7, with keyword 'more' and no pending draft.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact integer A005271(8), the number of perfect matchings of Q8, computed by two independent methods (different algorithm or decomposition, and different moduli or exact arithmetic) that agree exactly. The code must reproduce A005271(1..7), including Ostergard-Pettersson's n = 7 value. The live OEIS entry must still lack it.

partial_wins.statement: The exact number of perfect matchings of the folded 8-cube (Q7 plus its antipodal matching; 128 vertices, 8-regular, bipartite). This equals the number of perfect matchings of Q8 invariant under the antipodal map. It must come from two independent methods that agree. The code must also reproduce the analogous counts for folded 4-, 5- and 6-cubes computed by brute force, plus A005271(1..7) in plain-cube mode. Literature check: the value must not already be published.

A005271(8) modulo a prime p >= 3 obtained by any method other than computing the full count (for example by counting matchings fixed by a Sylow p-subgroup of Aut(Q8), for p in {3, 5, 7}). A second independent implementation must agree, and the method must reproduce A005271(7) mod p.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: run the claimant's modular permanent code on Q6 and Q7 and compare with the known counts reduced mod 2^k or p; for the full count, check that the residues mod several fresh primes or 2^k computed independently match.
pitfalls: Perfect matchings of Q8 equal the permanent of the bipartite 128 x 128 biadjacency matrix, not its determinant. Q8 is not planar, so Kasteleyn's method does not apply.

Burnside on a p-subgroup P gives A005271(8) = (number of P-fixed matchings) mod p. For a residue claim, state the subgroup used and report the fixed-point count itself. A residue already given in the literature does not count.

A005271(n) has the parity of n (Lovasz, in Propp's progress report), and residues modulo powers of 2 follow from fixed points of the coordinate reflections. That is why p2 asks for p >= 3; a power-of-2 residue is not a partial win.

targets.name: Unlabeled regular graph counts: the next unknown term for cubic, quintic, sextic or 7-regular graphs (A002851, A006821, A006822, A014377), or quartic beyond order 50
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (Burnside over vertex permutations: count labeled k-regular graphs fixed by each cycle type; exp(O(sqrt n)) per degree)
targets.statement: Counts of connected unlabeled k-regular graphs rose in two steps. Generation came first: Meringer's GENREG, run by Jason Kimberley for processor-years at Newcastle (2009-2011). Counting without generation followed: Andrew Howroyd, Mar-May 2020, gave quartic to n = 28, quintic to 28, sextic to 24 and 7-regular to 24. Cubic connected graphs A002851 are known to 40 vertices (Robinson and Wormald, 'Numbers of cubic graphs', J. Graph Theory 1983). In September 2026 Yue Cheng and Zhipeng Xu (arXiv 2609.31407, 'Exact counting of unlabeled quartic graphs by permutation-cycle aggregation', code on Zenodo) gave quartic counts for orders 29..50. They checked them only via the identity-permutation (labeled) part, and they report no counts for degrees 3, 5, 6 or 7. OEIS checked live 2026-10-30: A002851 ends at 2n = 40, A006820 at n = 28 (Cheng-Xu not yet in the b-file), A006821 at 2n = 28, A006822 at n = 24, A014377 at 2n = 24. No pending drafts.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a new exact term of A002851, A006821, A006822 or A014377 at the first order beyond the live b-file, or a connected quartic count at order 51 or more (beyond Cheng-Xu's published table). The term must be computed by two independent methods or implementations that agree exactly, for example a Burnside/cycle-index count and Howroyd-style labeled counting fixed by permutations implemented separately. The same code must reproduce every published term of that sequence and the disconnected version (A005638, A033301, ...) via the inverse Euler transform.

partial_wins.statement: An independent recomputation of Cheng and Xu's connected quartic counts at orders 29..50, including the nonidentity-permutation contributions they did not cross-check, with a second implementation agreeing. Any disagreement with their table must be resolved and reported.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: rerun the claimant's code for all published orders and compare; check the identity-permutation contribution against independently computed labeled regular graph counts (A002829 cubic, A005815 quartic, ...); recompute the new term modulo a fresh prime if the method is modular.
pitfalls: Cheng-Xu's quartic orders 29..50 are already published (arXiv 2609.31407) though not yet in OEIS; claiming them is not a win, only p1 if independently recomputed.
Cubic, quintic and 7-regular sequences are indexed by 2n (half the order); quartic and sextic by n.
Connected vs all graphs: convert with the inverse Euler transform and check both against OEIS.

Cheng-Xu's recurrence and their PARI/GP code (Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.22961966) work for any fixed degree. Running their code for degree 3, 5, 6 or 7 gives one method only; the second method must be implemented separately.

targets.name: Hamiltonian cycles on the 28 x 28 grid: the next term of OEIS A003763 (known to 26 x 26 since Pettersson 2014)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (frontier transfer matrix with on the order of 1e11 non-crossing connectivity states at width 28, i.e. terabytes per modulus, over several primes)
targets.statement: A003763 counts undirected Hamiltonian cycles on the 2n x 2n grid graph (closed rook tours). Earlier terms came from Schmalz, Hite and Klein, from Ponitz and Tittmann, from Herman Jamke (n = 8), from Jesper Jacobsen (n = 9, 10; 2007) and from Artem Karavaev (up to n = 11). Ville Pettersson ('Enumerating Hamiltonian Cycles', Electron. J. Combin. 21(4), P4.7, 2014) gave a(12) and a(13), the 24 x 24 and 26 x 26 boards. The b-file (Sloane) ends at n = 13. The counts up to symmetry, A209077, reach only n = 10 (Ed Wynn, arXiv 1402.0545, 2014). OEIS checked live 2026-10-30 shows no newer term or pending draft. a(13) has 101 digits. a(14), the 28 x 28 board, has about 118 digits and needs a width-28 frontier.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact value of A003763(14), the number of Hamiltonian cycles of the 28 x 28 grid graph (or the next unknown index if the live b-file has grown), computed by two runs that agree exactly. The runs must differ in moduli set or exact arithmetic AND in decomposition (row vs column order, or a different state encoding). The same code must reproduce A003763(1..13).

partial_wins.statement: A209077(11): the Hamiltonian cycles of the 22 x 22 grid counted up to the 8 symmetries. A209077 is known only to n = 10 (Ed Wynn), although A003763 reaches n = 13, and the new term needs the symmetric-cycle counts. Two runs must agree and reproduce A209077(1..10).
The number of Hamiltonian cycles of the 26 x 28 grid, two runs agreeing, reproducing all published m x n values the code covers.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: rerun the claimant's code modulo one fresh 61-bit prime for the 28 x 28 board and compare; rerun for 2n <= 20 against the b-file.
pitfalls: Odd boards have no Hamiltonian cycle; A003763 indexes the side 2n.
Partial-win sequence numbers (A209077 and others) must be checked live for their current extent before claiming; if one is already extended, the partial is the next unknown term.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - The tenth Dedekind number D(10) (OEIS A000372(10)) or inequivalent monotone Boolean functions of 10 variables (A003182(10))
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (D(9) took FPGA supercomputing; D(10) is many orders of magnitude beyond)
targets.statement: Dedekind numbers count monotone Boolean functions (antichains of subsets) of n variables. D(8) came from Wiedemann (1991). D(9) = 286386577668298411128469151667598498812366 was computed independently in 2023 by Christian Jaekel (J. Comput. Algebra) and by Lennart Van Hirtum, Patrick De Causmaecker et al. (FPGA supercomputing, arXiv 2304.03039). Inequivalent monotone functions A003182 reached n = 9 through Bartlomiej Pawelski (2023). Alex Fihman, Lennart Van Hirtum and Christian Plessl (arXiv 2607.08446, July 2026) estimate D(10) to about 4 significant digits; no exact value exists. OEIS checked live 2026-10-30: A000372 and A003182 end at n = 9, keyword 'more', no pending drafts.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact integer D(10) = A000372(10), or the exact A003182(10). It must be computed by two independent methods that agree exactly: a different decomposition (for example interval-based vs pair-matching formula) and different arithmetic. The code must reproduce D(0..9), respectively A003182(0..9). The value must be consistent with every published congruence (Pawelski-Szepietowski). As a sanity check, it is also compared with Fihman-Van Hirtum-Plessl's 4-digit estimate.

partial_wins.statement: D(10) modulo a prime or prime power not determined by published congruences (Pawelski-Szepietowski, arXiv 2302.04615). Two independent implementations must agree and must also reproduce D(9) modulo the same number.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: rerun the claimant's code at n = 7, 8 (minutes) and n = 9 modulo a small prime; recompute the claimed residue for n = 10 with an independent implementation; for a full claim compare several modular residues from independent runs.
pitfalls: The parity and some other residues of D(n) follow from known congruences; a residue implied by Pawelski-Szepietowski is not a new partial.
A000372 counts all monotone functions, including the two constants; A003182 counts orbits under variable permutations.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - The 28-queens count Q(28) (OEIS A000170(28), open since the Q27 project in 2016)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (Q(27) took about a year on FPGAs in 2015-16 and 28.4 days on eight RTX 5090 GPUs in 2025; Yao-Li project Q(28) at about 11 months on 8 GPUs or about 50 days on 64)
targets.statement: Q(n) counts placements of n nonattacking queens on an n x n board. Q(25) took about 53 CPU-years (INRIA ProActive, 2005, confirmed by Yuh-Pyng Shieh's NTU project). Q(26) came from Queens@TUD (2009). Q(27) = 234,907,967,154,122,528 came from the Q27 project of Thomas B. Preusser and Matthias R. Engelhardt (FPGAs, 2016; 'Putting Queens in Carry Chains, No. 27', J. Signal Process. Syst. 2017). Guangchao Yao and Yali Li (arXiv 2511.12009, Nov 2025, PPoPP 2026) confirmed Q(27) independently in 28.4 days on eight RTX 5090 GPUs. They project Q(28) at about 11 months on that machine (about 50 days on 64 GPUs) and report no value. Michael Simkin (2021) gave the asymptotics, and Hugo Nielsen (arXiv 2601.05856, 2026) proved 4 | Q(n) for n >= 6. Related tables: point-symmetric solutions A032522 are known to n = 40 (W. Schubert), quarter-turn-symmetric solutions A033148 to n = 67 in the b-file (plus a(69) in a comment), and toroidal solutions A051906 to n = 34. QuantumBFS/quantum.harness issue #34 (June 2026, a summer-school challenge list, no prize) also names Q(28) as open; nothing has been posted there. OEIS checked live 2026-10-30: A000170 and A002562 (up to symmetry) end at n = 27, no pending drafts.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact value Q(28) = A000170(28), computed by two independent runs that agree exactly. They must use different search decompositions (for example different first-row or symmetry splits) or different programs. The symmetry-class identity A002562(n) = (A000170(n) + A032522(n) + 2*A033148(n))/8 holds for every published n = 4..27. With the published A032522(28) = 1250901440 and A033148(28) = 32896 it gives A002562(28) = (Q(28) + 1250967232)/8, which must come out an exact integer, and it is reported. So Q(28) must be divisible by 8, which is stronger than Nielsen's 4 | Q(n). The program must reproduce Q(n) for n <= 23 and the Q27 project's published sub-counts where available. OEIS re-fetched before claiming must still lack Q(28).

partial_wins.statement: The next unknown term of A032522 (point-symmetric n-queens solutions, known to n = 40, so a(41)) or A033148(68) (rotationally symmetric solutions; the b-file ends at n = 67 and a(69) is already given in a comment, so it does not count), two runs agreeing, reproducing all published terms.
A051906(35): the number of n-queens solutions on the 35 x 35 toroidal board (first unknown; nonzero since gcd(35, 6) = 1), two runs agreeing, reproducing A051906 and A007705 published terms.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: rerun the program for n <= 20; recompute a random sample of the claimed split subtotals for n = 28 independently; check that Q(28) is divisible by 8 and that (Q(28) + 1250967232)/8 is an integer (the symmetry-class identity with the published A032522(28) and A033148(28)).
pitfalls: Distributed n-queens projects have reported wrong values before (A140393 records the NQueens@Home a(24) discrepancy); per-subproblem checksums and duplicate runs are essential.
A002562 counts solutions up to the 8 board symmetries; symmetric solutions need separate counts to convert.

targets.name: Covering arrays CA(N;t,k,v), t = 2..6, v = 2..25: fewer rows than the best known in the living covering-array table
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (exhaustive check is C(k,t) column sets x N rows; arrays with k in the thousands need a C or GPU checker, chunked)
targets.statement: A covering array CA(N;t,k,v) is an N x k array over v symbols in which every choice of t columns shows all v^t tuples in some row; CAN(t,k,v) is the least such N. Charles Colbourn's covering array tables (t = 2..6, v = 2..25) were the reference for two decades but are now behind an ASU sign-in wall (Cloudflare Access, checked 2026-10-30). Ulrike Groemping preserved their November 2024 status (ugroempi/CAs, ColbournTables.md). Christopher Smolen's living table (chrispbsmolen/ca-tools, generated 2026-10-29) uses that snapshot as a baseline and adds checked arrays: 14,450 rows, 648 verified in full, 152 sizes cited from Torres-Jimenez and Izquierdo-Marquez 2024 (Mathematics 12, 1908, order-seven CPHFs), 3 disputed rungs. 110 verified rows are already below the 2024 snapshot. They come from the CAs package data (Torres-Jimenez binary arrays, ordered-design constructions), from Smolen's own Paley-doubling and cyclic-CPHF arrays, and from Mickael Bergeron's strength-3 Raaphorst-Moura-Stevens extension (MichelBacon/covering-arrays-rms-extension, 78 entries for v = 5..19). Rows also come from Shokri, Moura and Stevens (arXiv:2510.13122v3, Oct 2026, strength 4) and from the Dwyer database and NIST library arrays. Numaro's July 2026 report claims 40 improvements but lists only eight cells (largest CA(14928;3,8,24)); all eight are matched or beaten in the live table. Smolen notes that improvements are not yet pushed through recursive constructions, so many derived rows are probably stale. The table takes new arrays by pull request and changes daily.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit N x k array over v symbols (2 <= t <= 6, 2 <= v <= 25, k > t) in which every t-subset of columns contains all v^t tuples, checked exhaustively. N must be STRICTLY SMALLER (direction: min) than the best known N at k in the live table, re-fetched at verification time from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chrispbsmolen/ca-tools/main/table/ca_table.csv. The stair-step rule applies: the best known N at k is the least N over CITED or VERIFIED rows with at least k columns. SCREENED rows do not count. A CITED row that has a DISPUTED twin still counts. N must also be strictly below the frozen Colbourn value (ugroempi/CAs ColbournTables.md) and below every value found for that (t,k,v) in the MichelBacon/covering-arrays-rms-extension improvements.csv, the Numaro list, and any 2024-2026 arXiv or journal paper found by search (for example arXiv:2510.13122v3). N >= v^t always; going below a published exact CAN means a bug. Making a pull request to the table is a human action and is not part of the win.

partial_wins.statement: First explicit witness: for a live-table row at strength t >= 3 that is CITED only (no VERIFIED or SCREENED array on file at that (t,v,k,N) or at any row that dominates it), an explicit array of exactly that N and at least that k, verified exhaustively, with its construction named.

Settle a disputed rung: an explicit, exhaustively verified array at the size of one of the three CITED rows that the table marks DISPUTED (CA(762;3,128,6), CA(43220;3,2162,20), CA(48531;3,2312,21)), or an independently written construction showing those sizes are attained.

targets.verification_method: Write an independent checker in C or numpy; do not reuse ca_verify.c. Parse the array, map symbols to 0..v-1 (reject don't-care entries unless the claim fills them), and assert the shape is N x k. For every t-subset of columns, encode each row's tuple as an integer in [0, v^t) and confirm that all v^t codes appear. Bitsets over v^t and chunking over column subsets parallelise well. Re-download ca_table.csv at check time and compute the stair-step best N at k for the claimed (t,v), using CITED and VERIFIED tiers. Then check the Groemping frozen table, the Bergeron improvements.csv and a fresh arXiv search for the same (t,k,v). Record the SHA-256 of the checked file. Claim only if N is strictly below all of them.
angles: Propagate the new verified rows: run standard recursive constructions (Roux-type and Chateauneuf-Kreher doubling, products, fusion, column extension, CPHF composition) on the 110 post-2024 ingredients. The table's propagation engine is not connected to submissions, so derived rows are probably stale.

Generalise Bergeron's Raaphorst-Moura-Stevens extension (add m columns to the orthogoval-plane CA(2q^3-1;3,q^2+q+1,q)) to strength 4 with the Shokri-Moura-Stevens truncated-Mobius-plane arrays as the base.

Search cyclic covering perfect hash families CPHF(n;k,v,t) over GF(q) with prescribed multipliers (Smolen's route for t = 5, 6). Each CPHF row expands to q^t - q CA rows, so one saved CPHF row saves many CA rows.
Post-optimise stored arrays: delete rows and repair the uncovered tuples with simulated annealing or SAT, focusing on (t,v) blocks whose rows are all CITED and old.
pitfalls: The ASU Colbourn pages are login-walled, so do not compare against the Feb 2025 Wayback crawl alone; the live table and the frozen copy are the baselines.
Use the stair-step rule: an entry (k,N) covers every smaller k, so a 'new' row can already be dominated by a row with more columns.
SCREENED arrays (random column windows only) do not count as best known, and neither do claims checked only on samples.
The table and the CAs package are edited several times a day (four pushes on 2026-10-29), so re-fetch right before claiming.
Arrays may be stored with symbols 1..v or with don't-care entries; normalise before checking. Mixed-alphabet arrays and t >= 7 are outside this table.

targets.name: Crossing number of the hypercube Q_n: a drawing with fewer crossings than Yang-Wang-Wang-Zhou's records (n = 5..13), or a certified lower bound for cr(Q_5)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (n = 5..9); laptop-days for n = 10..13 (up to 8192 vertices)
targets.statement: Erdős and Guy (1973) conjectured cr(Q_n) = (5/32)4^n - floor((n^2+1)/2) 2^(n-2), the count of the Eggleton-Guy construction. Faria, de Figueiredo, Sýkora and Vrt'o (JGT 2008) published a proof that this is an upper bound; Yang et al. claim that proof has an error. Yang, Wang, Wang and Zhou (J. Graph Theory 100(3) (2022) 389-434, doi 10.1002/jgt.22787; arXiv 1201.4700 v5, 22 Dec 2021) give drawings with fewer crossings for every n >= 7, disproving the conjectured equality. Their Table 2 lists 56, 352, 1744, 8128, 35424, 149888, 619456, 2529024 and 10238848 crossings for n = 5..13, against Erdős-Guy values 56, 352, 1760, 8192, 35712, 151040, 624128, 2547712, 10311680. Their concluding remarks say the drawing is not optimal for n >= 11. The only exact values are cr(Q_n) = 0 for n <= 3 and cr(Q_4) = cr(C_4 x C_4) = 8 (Dean-Richter 1995). The best general lower bound, Sýkora-Vrt'o's 4^n/20 - (n+1)2^(n-2), is trivial for small n. Counting the ten Q_4 subcubes of Q_5 gives cr(Q_5) >= 27 (our arithmetic: each subcube needs 8 crossings, and two distinct edges of Q_5 lie in at most 3 common Q_4 subcubes, so cr(Q_5) >= ceil(80/3) = 27). The Clancy-Haythorpe-Newcombe survey (arXiv 1901.05155 v5, Dec 2021) verified Yang et al.'s Q_7 drawing, reports finding its own Q_7 drawings below 1760 without giving a count, and states that cr(Q_n) is undetermined for n >= 5. Credit: Eggleton-Guy, Erdős-Guy, Madej, Faria-de Figueiredo-Sýkora-Vrt'o, Sýkora-Vrt'o, Yang-Wang-Wang-Zhou, Clancy-Haythorpe-Newcombe.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit drawing of Q_n for some 5 <= n <= 13, given as a planarization (crossings as degree-4 dummy vertices), certified planar by two independent testers, with STRICTLY FEWER dummy vertices (direction: min) than the best known value at verification time. That value is the minimum of Yang et al. Table 2 (arXiv 1201.4700, latest version), any count in the Clancy-Haythorpe-Newcombe survey or the authors' later papers, and any value found by a fresh literature search. A drawing of Q_5 below 56 or of Q_6 below 352 would also disprove the Erdős-Guy value at those n.

partial_wins.statement: An independently checkable certificate (formal proof, or a certified ILP/SAT crossing-number lower bound with a re-derived encoding) that cr(Q_5) >= L, for an L strictly above 27 (the Q_4-subcube counting bound) and above any lower bound found by a fresh literature search (state both).

A drawing of Q_n for some n with 14 <= n <= 16, planarization certified planar, with fewer crossings than Yang et al.'s Theorem 1.1 formula evaluated at that n (the formula includes the lambda_n term for n >= 13).

targets.verification_method: Rebuild Q_n from binary labels. Check that the planarization's dummy-vertex paths reproduce exactly the n 2^(n-1) cube edges, that each dummy has degree 4 on two distinct edge paths, and that the graph is planar (networkx plus Boost/OGDF, with an Euler face count on the embedding). A planar planarization with k dummies proves cr(Q_n) <= k. Compare k with the table. For p1, check the formal proof, or regenerate the encoding and check its proof log.
angles: Start from Yang et al.'s recursive construction (their 'enclosed cycles' adjustment) and apply it at the places they say remain for n >= 11.
Crossing-minimisation heuristics (OGDF planarization with edge reinsertion, QuickCross star insertion) seeded with the record drawing, run on n = 7..10.
Exploit symmetry: restrict to drawings invariant under a subgroup of Aut(Q_n), which shrinks the search.
pitfalls: Clancy et al. state that they found their own Q_7 drawings below 1760. Find their counts before claiming a Q_7 record below 1744.
Counting crossings from straight-line coordinates assumes a rectilinear drawing; submit a planarization so that the count is exact.
Edges crossing more than once, or adjacent edges crossing, are allowed in the certificate (they only inflate the count), but count every dummy vertex.
The Q_4-subcube count already gives cr(Q_5) >= 27 by hand; a p1 bound of 27 or less is not a win.

On 2026-10-30 the status source (arXiv v5 and the published JGT version), the survey, and Balko's Harary-Hill exposition (arXiv 2610.34444) were re-read. Web, Crossref, Semantic Scholar (papers citing Yang et al.) and DataCite searches for 2024-2026 hypercube crossing-number work found nothing that improves Table 2 or the lower bounds. arXiv 2603.04665 treats plane substructures and the maximum rectilinear crossing number, not cr(Q_n). Search again before claiming.

targets.name: Harary-Kainen-Schwenk conjecture: is cr(C_8 x C_8) = 48? (smallest open toroidal grid)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exact ILP/SAT lower-bound search); pure thought for a structural proof
targets.statement: Harary, Kainen and Schwenk (1973) conjectured that the Cartesian product of cycles has cr(C_m x C_n) = (m-2)n for 3 <= m <= n. It is proved for m <= 7: Ringeisen-Beineke for m = 3, Beineke-Ringeisen and Dean-Richter for m = 4, Richter-Thomassen and Klešč-Richter-Stobert for m = 5, Anderson-Richter-Rodney and Richter-Salazar for m = 6, Anderson et al. and Adamsson-Richter for m = 7. Glebsky and Salazar (JGT 2004) proved it for all n >= m(m+1). Adamsson and Richter sketched that m = 8 follows for every n once cr(C_8 x C_8) = 48 is shown. As of the Clancy-Haythorpe-Newcombe dynamic survey (arXiv 1901.05155 v5, Dec 2021), cr(C_8 x C_8) is open. The standard drawing gives 48. The best published lower bound that applies seems to be Shahrokhi et al. (1998), cr(C_m x C_n) >= 3mn/5 for n <= 5(m-1)/4, which gives 39. Our own arithmetic: deleting the 8 edges of any one of the 16 C_8-cycles leaves a subdivision of C_7 x C_8 (crossing number 40), and each crossing of a good drawing is lost in at least one of the 16 deletions, so 15 cr >= 16 * 40 and cr(C_8 x C_8) >= 43. An unrefereed Zenodo preprint (Q. Gu, 'The Crossing Number of C_8 x C_8', concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22162314, issued 2026-08-29, prepared with ChatGPT and stated not to be peer reviewed) claims cr(C_8 x C_8) = 48 by a reduction of a hypothetical 47-crossing drawing to weighted subcubic intersection graphs. On 2026-10-30 its version record returned HTTP 410 Gone. No refereed or machine-checked proof is known. Credit: Harary-Kainen-Schwenk, Richter, Salazar, Adamsson, Glebsky, Anderson, Klešč, Shahrokhi et al., and the survey authors.
targets.success_criterion: Either (A) a planarization of a drawing of C_8 x C_8 with at most 47 crossings, certified planar by two independent testers, which disproves the conjecture at its smallest open case (and Gu's 2026 preprint claim); or (B) a proof that cr(C_8 x C_8) >= 48, formalised in a proof assistant or given as an exact crossing-number certificate (for example an ILP/SAT encoding over planarizations or Kuratowski constraints, with a checked proof log and an independently re-derived encoding). A human-readable argument alone, including a re-statement of Gu's preprint, does not count for (B). Before claiming, re-fetch the Clancy-Haythorpe-Newcombe survey (https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.05155, latest version), check the status of Gu's Zenodo preprint (doi 10.5281/zenodo.22162314) and search for papers after 2021 to confirm that no refereed or machine-checked proof has appeared.

partial_wins.statement: A certified lower bound cr(C_8 x C_8) >= L for some L >= 44 (strictly above 43, the bound from counting the 16 cycle deletions to C_7 x C_8) and strictly above any bound found by a fresh literature search, to the certificate standards of (B): a formal proof, or an exact ILP/SAT crossing-number certificate with a checked DRAT/LRAT/VeriPB log and an independently re-derived encoding.
A certified lower bound cr(C_8 x C_8) >= 46, to the same certificate standards as (B).

targets.verification_method: (A) Check that the planarization's edge paths reproduce the 128 edges of C_8 x C_8 and that the graph is planar (two testers plus an Euler check), then count dummies. (B, p1, p2) Regenerate the encoding from the written reduction, check the DRAT/LRAT/VeriPB log, and reproduce known values (cr(C_6 x C_6) = 24, cr(C_7 x C_7) = 35) with the same pipeline as a sanity test.
angles: The m <= 7 proofs rest on case analyses of how the 'tight' cycles cross; encode those lemmas as constraints to prune an exact ILP for C_8 x C_8.
Use the 16-fold rotational symmetry of the torus grid to break symmetry in a SAT search for a 47-crossing planarization.
pitfalls: C_m x C_n here is the Cartesian product (the toroidal grid), not the strong or direct product.
Exact crossing-number ILP solvers are reliable only with proof logging; a bare 'optimal' from a MIP solver is not a certificate.
The cycle-deletion count already gives cr(C_8 x C_8) >= 43 by hand from cr(C_7 x C_8) = 40; bounds of 43 or less are not wins.

Gu's August 2026 Zenodo preprint claims the full value 48 (unrefereed, AI-assisted; its record returned HTTP 410 Gone on 2026-10-30 and could not be read). A (B) win must be a formal or certified proof, not a restatement of that argument; check whether a revised or refereed version has appeared.

On 2026-10-30 the survey (v5, 2021), Balko's Harary-Hill exposition (arXiv 2610.34444) and web, Crossref and DataCite searches were checked; apart from Gu's preprint nothing on C_8 x C_n after 2021 was found. Search again before attacking.

targets.name: Guy-Hill conjecture for the complement of a cycle: determine cr(complement of C_11) (conjectured 36)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exact crossing-number search on 11 vertices, 44 edges)
targets.statement: Guy and Hill (1973) gave drawings of the complement of the n-cycle with (n-3)^2(n-5)^2/64 crossings for odd n and n(n-4)(n-6)^2/64 for even n, and conjectured that these are optimal. They proved equality for n <= 10, and showed that equality at an odd n implies equality at n+1. The Clancy-Haythorpe-Newcombe dynamic survey (arXiv 1901.05155 v5, Dec 2021) still lists n >= 11 as open. Guy and Hill's general lower bound is trivial unless n > 20. The smallest open case is n = 11: an 8-regular graph on 11 vertices with 44 edges and conjectured value 36. Proving 36 would also settle n = 12 (conjectured 54). Our own arithmetic: deleting any vertex leaves K_10 minus a 10-vertex path, which contains the complement of C_10 (crossing number 15). Each crossing involves 4 vertices and so survives in 7 of the 11 deletions, which gives cr(complement of C_11) >= ceil(11*15/7) = 24. The October 2026 Harary-Hill proof (OpenAI; exposition by Balko, arXiv 2610.34444) has corollaries for K_2k - M, K_2k - e, K_2k x P_t, K_m x C_even and Sierpiński graphs, but none for complements of cycles. The OpenAI 2026 manuscript catalogue has no such item either. Credit: Guy and Hill, and the survey authors.
targets.success_criterion: Either (A) a planarization of a drawing of the complement of C_11 with at most 35 crossings, certified planar by two independent testers, which refutes the conjecture; or (B) a certified proof that cr(complement of C_11) >= 36: a formal proof, or an exact crossing-number certificate (ILP/SAT over planarizations or Kuratowski constraints with a checked DRAT/LRAT/VeriPB log and an independently re-derived encoding). Before claiming, re-fetch https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.05155 (latest version) and search the literature after 2021, including Harary-Hill follow-ups, to confirm the case is still open.

partial_wins.statement: A certified lower bound cr(complement of C_11) >= L for some L >= 25, strictly above the vertex-deletion counting bound 24 and strictly above any bound found by a fresh literature search (state it), to the certificate standards of (B).
A certified lower bound cr(complement of C_11) >= 30, to the certificate standards of (B).

targets.verification_method: Rebuild the complement of C_11 (vertices 0..10, i ~ j iff j - i is not +-1 mod 11). Check that the planarization's edge paths reproduce the 44 edges and that the graph is planar (two testers plus an Euler check), then count dummies. For lower bounds, regenerate the encoding and check the proof log; validate the pipeline by reproducing Guy-Hill's n = 9 and n = 10 values (9 and 15).
angles: The complement of C_11 has a dihedral symmetry of order 22; use it to break symmetry in an exact ILP/SAT search.
The new Harary-Hill proof technique may adapt to near-complete graphs; check whether its counting argument gives 36 directly.
pitfalls: The two formulas differ by parity of n; n = 11 uses the odd formula (8^2 * 6^2 / 64 = 36).
The complement of C_11 is 8-regular (44 edges); check your graph construction against this.

On 2026-10-30 the survey (v5, 2021), Balko's exposition (Corollaries 7-11: none for cycle complements) and web, arXiv, Crossref and DataCite searches for 2022-2026 work were checked; no value or improved bound for n = 11 was found. Exact crossing-number tools (Chimani-Wiedera-style ILP proof systems) could in principle already have computed this small case unpublished; search again, including Graph Drawing proceedings, before attacking.

targets.name: Smallest cubic graphs with crossing number 12-15: beat an upper bound in OEIS A110507 (a(12) <= 30, a(13) <= 30, a(14) <= 36, a(15) <= 40)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exact crossing numbers of 28-38-vertex cubic graphs); needs cluster for partial p2
targets.statement: OEIS A110507 gives the order of the smallest cubic graph with crossing number n: 4, 6, 10, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 28 for n = 0..11. Pegg and Exoo (2009) did the early work. Clancy, Haythorpe, Newcombe and Pegg (arXiv 1804.10336, Graphs Combin. 2020) showed by explicit drawings that no cubic graph on 26 vertices has crossing number 10 or more. This gave a(10) = 28 (a 28-vertex graph with crossing number 10) and a(11) = 28 (the Coxeter graph, crossing number 11). The same paper gives a 30-vertex cubic graph with crossing number 12 and conjectures that it is minimal. For n >= 12 only upper bounds are known: a(12) <= 30 (CNG 12A = CNG 10A plus an edge insertion), a(13) <= 30 (the Tutte 8-cage / Levi graph), a(14) <= 36 (GP(18,5)) and a(15) <= 40 (GP(20,8)). Weisstein's MathWorld table and OEIS A110507 mark these with '?'. A307450 records the number of extremal graphs, with only lower bounds for n >= 9. Weisstein's A390643 counts connected cubic graphs on 2n vertices by crossing number, with rows through 22 vertices (row 11 added Feb 2026). Goal: a smaller cubic graph with crossing number exactly n for some n in 12..15. Credit: Pegg, Exoo, Clancy, Haythorpe, Newcombe, Weisstein.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit connected simple cubic graph G on v vertices with v STRICTLY LESS than the A110507 upper bound for some n in {12, 13, 14, 15} at verification time (30, 30, 36, 40 on 2026-10-30), together with (i) a planarization of a drawing with exactly n crossings, certified planar by two independent testers, and (ii) a certificate that cr(G) >= n (formal proof, or an exact crossing-number ILP/SAT certificate with a checked proof log and an independently re-derived encoding). Re-fetch https://oeis.org/A110507 and https://mathworld.wolfram.com/SmallestCubicCrossingNumberGraph.html immediately before claiming, and check that no newer paper lowers the bound.

partial_wins.statement: A cubic graph on 28 vertices other than the Coxeter graph (non-isomorphic by canonical labelling) with crossing number exactly 11, certified by a drawing and a lower-bound certificate, which raises A307450's lower bound for n = 11 (currently 1).
The next row of OEIS A390643: the number of connected cubic graphs on 24 vertices with each crossing number k, computed with certified exact crossing numbers and summing to A002851(12).

targets.verification_method: Check that G is simple, connected and 3-regular, and compute its canonical form (nauty) to compare with known graphs. Check the planarization (edge paths reproduce E(G), planar by two testers plus an Euler check, dummy count = n). Check the lower bound by regenerating the encoding and verifying the DRAT/LRAT/VeriPB log, after reproducing a(11) = 28 (Coxeter graph cr = 11) with the same pipeline.
angles: Search symmetric cubic graphs (generalised Petersen, I-graphs, cubic Cayley and voltage graphs) on 28-34 vertices for high crossing numbers, since the records so far are symmetric graphs.
Edge-insertion and excision moves on the Coxeter graph and the Levi graph (the CNG 9B/10A/12A constructions), screened by fast heuristic upper bounds, then exact lower bounds.
pitfalls: The graph must have crossing number exactly n; a graph with crossing number above n does not bound a(n).
An upper-bound drawing alone is not enough; a lower-bound certificate is required for the claimed crossing number.
MathWorld notes that CNG 8D, 8E and 9A were mislabelled in Pegg-Exoo (2009); check claimed crossing numbers of old examples independently.

targets.name: Smallest open resolvable Steiner 2-designs: a resolvable S(2,5,45) (also v = 345, 465, 645) or a resolvable S(2,6,66)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exact-cover / SAT searches under prescribed automorphism groups)
targets.statement: A resolvable BIBD(v,k,1) (RBIBD) is a Steiner 2-design S(2,k,v) whose blocks can be split into (v-1)/(k-1) parallel classes, each partitioning the point set. For k = 5 the necessary condition is v = 5 (mod 20), and an RBIBD(v,5,1) is known for every such v except possibly v in {45, 345, 465, 645} (R. J. R. Abel, G. Ge and J. Yin, Handbook of Combinatorial Designs 2nd ed.; restated in M. Meszka's lectures, Famnit Lectures 3, 2014). D. Dumicic Danilovic (Bull. ICA 84 (2018) 53-64) states that (45,5,1) is the smallest parameter set for which existence of a resolvable BIBD is still open. Dinitz's Handbook new-results page for Part II (last edited 2019) records no change for k = 5, lambda = 1. V. Krcadinac's Steiner 2-design page (last modified 2026-02-17) lists at least 1072 non-isomorphic S(2,5,45) (Crnkovic, Dumicic Danilovic, Rukavina, Simac; Mezofi and Nagy; and others). The page does not discuss their resolvability, but a reviewer's own exact-cover check of its design file on 2026-10-30 found none resolvable: 870 have no parallel class, and no design has more than 2 pairwise disjoint parallel classes (most parallel classes in one design: 19). Resolvable (45,5,2)-BIBDs are known (Buratti, Yan and Wang 2010; 22 found by Dumicic Danilovic 2018). The same page states that the three known S(2,6,66), those with an automorphism of order 13, are not resolvable and that it is not known whether a resolvable S(2,6,66) exists. A resolvable S(2,5,45) has 99 blocks in 11 parallel classes of 9; a resolvable S(2,6,66) has 143 blocks in 13 classes of 11. Existence of S(2,6,v) itself is the separate target steiner-2-designs-block-6-undecided; S(2,6,66) exists, so only resolvability is asked here.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit S(2,k,v) for (v,k) in {(45,5), (345,5), (465,5), (645,5), (66,6)}, together with a partition of its blocks into (v-1)/(k-1) parallel classes. Every block must be a k-subset of the v points, every pair of points must lie in exactly one block, and each class must consist of v/k pairwise disjoint blocks covering all points. Two independent programs must verify it. It must also be re-confirmed at claim time that the case is still open: no resolvable design for those parameters on Krcadinac's Steiner 2-design page (https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~krcko/results/steiner.html), on the Handbook new-results pages, or in a fresh literature search.

partial_wins.statement: A machine-checked non-existence proof for a resolvable S(2,5,45) (or a resolvable S(2,6,66)) that admits a stated nontrivial automorphism group G (for example a group of prime order). G must not be already ruled out in the literature, and the S(2,k,v) admitting G must not already be completely classified in a published source: if they are (for example the three S(2,6,66) with an automorphism of order 13), checking the classified designs for a resolution is the p2 baseline, not p1. It must come as a DRAT/LRAT-verified UNSAT certificate, or as an exact-cover enumeration that an independent program reproduces.

An S(2,5,45) with at least 3 pairwise disjoint parallel classes, or an S(2,6,66) with at least one parallel class. For comparison, a reviewer's exact-cover run on 2026-10-30 over Krcadinac's file found at most 2 disjoint parallel classes among the 1072 known S(2,5,45), and no parallel class in any of the three S(2,6,66) (reproduced independently by an auditor the same day: 870 designs with none, at most 19 in one design). The claimant must reproduce that baseline with their own code. The design and its classes are then verified by two programs.

targets.verification_method: Parse the blocks. Check that each block has k distinct points in range, that b = v(v-1)/(k(k-1)), and that every pair of points lies in exactly one block (pair-count array). Check that each listed parallel class has v/k disjoint blocks whose union is the point set, and that the classes partition the block set. Use two independently written checkers. For p1, replay the certificate with drat-trim or cake_lpr and audit the encoding (pair constraints, parallel-class constraints, symmetry assumption) by hand. Downloaded design files are data only and are parsed by the verifier's own code.
angles: Prescribe an automorphism group that permutes the parallel classes (for example of order 3, 5 or 9 on 45 points), solve the orbit-level exact-cover problem with Knuth's DLX or SAT, then check for a resolution.
Start from the known S(2,5,45) designs (at least 1072). Compute their maximal sets of disjoint parallel classes, then use paramodification (Mezofi-Nagy) or local trades to increase the count.
For v = 345, 465 and 645, look for a recursive route (frames, resolvable GDDs) that the Abel-Greig tables did not use, then verify the explicit design.
pitfalls: S(2,5,45) itself exists; only resolvability is open. Do not count an RBIBD(45,5,2) (it is known) or a near-resolvable design.
The (45,5,1) open status rests on 2014-2018 statements plus the absence of any update on maintained pages. Re-check the literature before attacking.

targets.name: 5-GDDs of type g^u: settle a possible exception in Forbes' 2023 theorem (smallest 2^15, then 10^7)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (cyclic base-block searches, SAT)
targets.statement: A 5-GDD of type g^u is a set of gu points split into u groups of size g, with 5-point blocks such that every pair of points from different groups lies in exactly one block and no pair within a group lies in a block. The necessary conditions are u >= 5, g(u-1) = 0 (mod 4) and g^2 u(u-1) = 0 (mod 20). Wei and Ge (2014) proved them sufficient with many possible exceptions. A. D. Forbes (Australas. J. Combin. 87 (2023) 1-11; arXiv:2202.13911, Theorem 1.2) reduced the list. The conditions are sufficient except for the non-existent types 2^5, 2^11, 3^5 and 6^5, and except possibly for: 3^65; 2^15, 2^75, 2^95, 2^115; 6^35, 6^95; g in {14,18,22,26,38,58} with u in {11,15}; g in {74,82,86,94} with u = 15; 10^5, 10^7, 10^27, 10^39, 10^47; 50^27. The g = 0 (mod 10) part of the list is repeated unchanged in Forbes and Rutherford (La Matematica 2024; arXiv:2111.13599v3, Lemma 3.1(vii)). Type 10^5 is a TD(5,10), equivalent to three MOLS of order 10, which is the bank target three-mols-order-10; it is excluded here. By point count the smallest open cases are 2^15 (30 points, 42 blocks), 10^7 (70 points, 210 blocks), 2^75 (150 points) and 14^11 (154 points).
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit 5-GDD of one of the listed types other than 10^5: a point set of size gu, a partition into u groups of size g, and a list of 5-subsets such that every pair from distinct groups lies in exactly one block and no block contains two points of one group. Two independent programs must verify it. The type must still be a possible exception at claim time. Check the latest Forbes papers via his arXiv author page and ORCID record, and run a fresh literature search for that type.

partial_wins.statement: A machine-checked non-existence proof for a listed type (for example 2^15), delivered as a DRAT/LRAT-verified UNSAT certificate from an encoding a skeptic audits, or as an exhaustive search independently reproduced.

A certified exhaustive search showing that no 5-GDD of type 2^15 or 10^7 admits a stated automorphism group of order at least 3 (for example the cyclic group generated by x -> x+g on a cyclic point labelling), for a group not already excluded in the literature, with a DRAT/LRAT certificate or a reproduced enumeration.

targets.verification_method: Check the point count, the group partition (all sizes g) and that every block has 5 distinct points meeting each group at most once. Count pair coverage over all cross-group pairs (exactly 1) and confirm that the block count is (C(gu,2) - u C(g,2))/10. When base blocks and a development rule are given, expand them with the verifier's own code. This reproduces Forbes' published 6^15 example (378 blocks), which was checked this way on 2026-10-30.
angles: Forbes' constructions are cyclic: points Z_{gu} with groups as residue classes, developed under x -> x + d. Search base blocks for 2^15 and 10^7 with SAT or DLX under the same ansatz, and also under non-cyclic groups.
Recursive routes: a 5-GDD of type 10^7 would follow from suitable 5-DGDDs or frames. Check whether ingredients published after 2023 now cover a listed type.
pitfalls: 10^5 is three MOLS of order 10: excluded, see three-mols-order-10.
2^5, 2^11, 3^5 and 6^5 are proven not to exist; do not attack them.

targets.name: Quasi-symmetric 2-designs: construct one for an open feasible parameter set with v <= 78 (smallest 2-(33,15,35), x=6, y=9)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (Kramer-Mesner with prescribed automorphism groups)
targets.statement: A quasi-symmetric 2-(v,k,lambda) design (QSD) has no repeated blocks, and any two blocks meet in x or y points (x < y). Neumaier's table of feasible parameters was updated by M. S. Shrikhande (Handbook of Combinatorial Designs, 2007) and others. V. Krcadinac's 2016/17 lecture notes 'Kvazisimetricni dizajni' give Table 1: 94 feasible (v,k,lambda,x,y) with v <= 78, leaving out strongly resolvable designs, Steiner 2-designs and biplane residuals. Each row lists the number of known QSDs (Nqsd) and of block-graph strongly regular graphs (Nsrg). His live page (quasisym.html, last modified 2024-11-03) lists the parameter sets with v <= 70, plus three extra rows, for which a QSD is known. No QSD is known for the rows marked '?' in Table 1, for example (33,15,35,6,9), (39,12,22,3,6), (41,9,9,1,3), (41,20,57,8,11), (42,18,51,6,9), (42,21,60,9,12), (43,16,40,4,7), (45,15,42,3,6), (45,18,34,6,9), (45,21,70,9,13), (46,16,72,4,7), (49,13,13,1,4) and (52,16,20,4,7). Six '?' rows are now settled as impossible and are excluded: (35,14,13,5,8), since its block graph srg(85,14,3,2) does not exist (Brouwer's table, Shpectorov-Zhao); (46,16,8,4,6), since srg(69,20,7,5) does not exist (Brouwer's table, Koval + AI); (56,15,42,3,6), since srg(616,205,90,57) is marked non-existent (Koval + AI); (76,26,52,6,10), since srg(456,325,236,220) is marked non-existent; (37,9,8,1,3), by Harada, Munemasa and Tonchev (J. Combin. Des. 25 (2017)); and (56,12,9,0,3), by Munemasa and Tonchev (J. Combin. Des. 28 (2020) 745-752, via ternary codes of biplanes on 56 points). Block graphs were checked against Brouwer's live table on 2026-10-30.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the incidence matrix of a 2-(v,k,lambda) design with no repeated blocks whose pairwise block intersections all lie in {x,y}, with both values occurring. The design must match a row of Krcadinac's Table 1 marked Nqsd '?', other than the six excluded rows (35,14,13,5,8), (37,9,8,1,3), (46,16,8,4,6), (56,12,9,0,3), (56,15,42,3,6) and (76,26,52,6,10). Two independent programs must verify it. At claim time the row must still be unsettled: absent from the live quasisym.html, its block graph srg(b,a,c,d) not marked '-' in Brouwer's live table, and no existence or non-existence result found by a fresh literature search. The complementary design counts for the same row.

partial_wins.statement: A machine-checked non-existence proof for a non-excluded '?' row (for example via the self-orthogonal code or block-graph route plus an exhaustive search), with a DRAT/LRAT or exact-ILP certificate a skeptic re-runs.

A certified exhaustive search showing that no QSD with a non-excluded '?' row's parameters admits a stated automorphism group of prime order p >= 3, for a (row, group) pair not already excluded in the literature, reproduced by an independent program.

targets.verification_method: Check that every t-subset count matches (each pair of points in exactly lambda blocks), that b = v r / k with r = lambda(v-1)/(k-1), that the blocks are distinct, and that every pairwise block intersection lies in {x,y}. Optionally build the block graph (adjacency = intersection y) and confirm it is srg(b,a,c,d) as in Table 1. Compare the row with Krcadinac's Table 1 and the live quasisym.html, and look up the block graph in Brouwer's table.
angles: Kramer-Mesner with tactical decompositions (Krcadinac-Vlahovic) under prescribed groups: this method produced the 2-(56,16,18) and many 2-(28,12,11) QSDs.

For x = 1, y = 3 rows (for example (41,9,9)), the binary code spanned by the blocks is self-orthogonal-like. Search through doubly even codes of the right length, as was done for (49,9,6) via self-dual [50,25,10] codes.
pitfalls: Feasibility tables omit designs with repeated blocks; a design with repeated blocks does not count.
Always check the block graph in Brouwer's live SRG table: a '-' there settles the QSD row as impossible.

Table 1 (2016/17) is older than some non-existence proofs that do not show up in Brouwer's table: (56,12,9,0,3) is still '?' there and its block graph srg(210,176,148,144) is '?', but Munemasa-Tonchev (JCD 2020) proved non-existence.

Published partial results limit p2: for (41,9,9,1,3), Munemasa-Tonchev (AAECC 33 (2022) 855-866) prove that no cyclic QSD exists and that any automorphism of prime order p < 41 has p <= 5, so only p = 3 and p = 5 remain; Krcadinac-Vlahovic Kruc (Adv. Math. Commun. 15 (2021)) exclude (56,20,19,5,8) for certain prescribed automorphism groups. Check these before claiming a (row, group) pair.

targets.name: Strongly regular configurations: construct a (v_k; lambda, mu) configuration marked '?' in the Abreu-Funk-Krcadinac-Labbate table (smallest (41_5; 9,10))
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (SAT / prescribed-automorphism searches)
targets.statement: A symmetric configuration (v_k) has v points and v lines, k points on each line and k lines through each point, and any two points on at most one line. It is a strongly regular configuration (v_k; lambda, mu) if its point (collinearity) graph is strongly regular with parameters (v, k(k-1), lambda, mu). M. Abreu, M. Funk, V. Krcadinac and D. Labbate (Des. Codes Cryptogr. 90 (2022) 1881-1897; arXiv:2104.04880) tabulated feasible parameters of proper, primitive strongly regular configurations. Krcadinac's online table (srconf.html, last modified 2024-11-03) gives 41 rows and marks existence unknown ('?') for (41_5;9,10), (61_6;14,15), (81_8;37,42), (85_6;11,10), (85_7;20,21), (99_7;21,15), (105_9;51,45), (113_8;27,28), (121_6;11,6), (121_9;43,42), (121_10;65,72), (125_9;45,36), (136_6;15,4), (136_9;36,40), (145_9;35,36), (153_8;19,21), (169_9;31,30), (169_12;101,110), (171_11;73,66), (175_6;5,5), (181_10;44,45), (196_10;40,42), (196_13;122,132) and (196_13;125,120). Two of these are excluded. Brouwer's SRG table marks srg(99,42,21,15) as non-existent (Koval + AI), so (99_7;21,15) cannot exist. (136_6;15,4) cannot exist either: srg(136,30,15,4) is unique, the triangular graph T(17), and as in the paper's rook-graph argument (Theorem 5.2) the lines inside each 16-clique of T(17) would form an S(2,6,16), which violates Fisher's inequality (b = 8 < 16). For the smallest open row, (41_5;9,10), the point graph would have the parameters of the Paley graph P(41).
targets.success_criterion: Success means a list of v lines, each a k-subset of v points, for a row marked '?' in the live table (https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~krcko/results/srconf.html), other than (99_7;21,15) and (136_6;15,4). Every point must lie on exactly k lines, any two points must share at most one line, and the collinearity graph must be strongly regular with parameters (v, k(k-1), lambda, mu). Two independent programs must verify it. At claim time the row must still be '?', the point-graph srg must not be marked '-' in Brouwer's live table, and a fresh literature search must find no construction or non-existence proof.

partial_wins.statement: A machine-checked non-existence proof for a '?' row other than (99_7;21,15) and (136_6;15,4), with a DRAT/LRAT or exact-ILP certificate (or, where every srg with the point-graph parameters is known, an exhaustive clique search over all of them) that an independent checker re-verifies.

For a row whose count of known configurations in the live table is a lower bound (not boldface), a new strongly regular configuration not isomorphic to any in the table's linked files, certified by canonical forms (nauty/Traces on the point-line incidence graph).

targets.verification_method: Parse the lines. Check v lines of size k, point degrees k and pairwise line intersections of at most 1 (a partial linear space). Build the collinearity graph and check that it is k(k-1)-regular, with exactly lambda common neighbours for adjacent pairs and mu for non-adjacent pairs. For p2, compare canonical forms of incidence graphs against the table's linked files, parsed as data.
angles: Start from the known strongly regular graphs with the right parameters (for example Paley(41), Paley(61), Paley(113)). Look for a partition of their edge sets into v cliques of size k with each vertex in k cliques: a clique-partition problem suited to SAT.
Cyclic ansatz: for prime v, search for a k-subset of Z_v whose development is a configuration (a planar-difference-set condition) with the required collinearity graph.
pitfalls: Rows whose point-graph SRG is marked non-existent in Brouwer's table are settled; (99_7;21,15) is the current example.
(136_6;15,4) is ruled out by hand (unique point graph T(17), and Fisher's inequality inside each 16-clique). It is not open and does not count for p1.
When the point graph is unique (for example srg(105,72,51,45) and srg(125,72,45,36) are marked '!'), a full clique search may settle the row quickly. Check the literature before claiming it as new.

targets.name: Small simple t-designs of unknown existence: 3-(20,5,2), 3-(21,7,15), 4-(16,8,15), 4-(18,9,14), 4-(19,9,21), 5-(16,7,5), 5-(17,8,20), 2-(55,10,3) and kin
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (Kramer-Mesner with prescribed automorphism groups)
targets.statement: For given t, v and k, admissible indices of t-(v,k,lambda) designs are multiples m * lambda_min, and simple designs (no repeated blocks) can exist only up to lambda_max = C(v-t,k-t). V. Krcadinac (J. Combin. Des. 26 (2018) 193-200, arXiv:1706.01682) and Krcadinac and Pavcevic constructed many designs with prescribed automorphism groups. These improve Table 4.46 of the Handbook of Combinatorial Designs (Khosrovshahi-Laue, t >= 3) and the Mathon-Rosa BIBD table (Table 1.35). His online table (newdesigns.html, last modified 2024-11-03) still marks the following as unknown: 2-(55,10,lambda) for lambda = 3, 6, 7 (lambda = 1, 2 impossible); 3-(20,5,2); 3-(21,7,15); 4-(16,8,lambda) for lambda = 15, 30; 4-(18,9,lambda) for lambda = 14, 28; 4-(19,9,lambda) for lambda = 21, 42; 5-(16,7,5); 5-(17,8,20). In each row the higher multiples are known to exist. Block counts are b = lambda C(v,t)/C(k,t): 2-(55,10,3) has 99 blocks (a Mathon-Rosa open entry, r = 18); 3-(20,5,2) has 228; 4-(18,9,14) has 340; 4-(16,8,15) has 390; 3-(21,7,15) has 570; 4-(19,9,21) has 646; 5-(16,7,5) has 1040; 5-(17,8,20) has 2210. 4-(15,5,1) = S(4,5,15) is known not to exist. Steiner 3-designs are covered by the bank target small-steiner-3-designs-open and are excluded here.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit simple t-(v,k,lambda) design for a (t,v,k,lambda) listed as '?' in the live table (https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~krcko/results/newdesigns.html): b distinct k-subsets of a v-set such that every t-subset lies in exactly lambda blocks. Two independent programs must verify it. At claim time the entry must still be '?' and a fresh literature search must find no construction or non-existence proof. The supplementary design (all k-subsets not in the design, with index lambda_max - lambda) counts for the same row.

partial_wins.statement: A machine-checked non-existence proof for a listed (t,v,k,lambda), for example 3-(20,5,2) or 5-(16,7,5), with a DRAT/LRAT or exact-ILP certificate that an independent checker re-verifies.

A non-simple t-(v,k,lambda) design (repeated blocks allowed, every t-subset in exactly lambda blocks counted with multiplicity) for a listed row, verified by two programs, provided a fresh literature search finds no earlier non-simple example.

targets.verification_method: Check b = lambda C(v,t)/C(k,t), that the blocks are k-subsets of range v, and (for the main win) that they are distinct. Count, for every t-subset, the blocks containing it (C(20,3) = 1140 up to C(17,5) = 6188 subsets: instant). Two independent checkers. Kramer-Mesner claims must expand the orbit representatives with the verifier's own group code before checking.
angles: Kramer-Mesner: pick a group G acting on v points, form the t-orbit vs k-orbit incidence matrix, and solve A x = lambda * 1 over {0,1} with an ILP, lattice basis reduction (Wassermann) or SAT. Krcadinac used nonabelian groups for the existing rows.
Derived and residual links: a 5-(17,8,20) design derives to 4-(16,7,20) designs. Check whether known 4-designs extend.
pitfalls: The table is about simple designs; a design with repeated blocks is only p2.
Index multiples: the open entries are the smallest multiples m listed as '?'; larger m are already known.

targets.name: Pentagonal geometries: construct PENT(4,r) for r in {8,12,16,28,32,36,44,48,56,64,72} or PENT(5,r) for r in {11,16,66,96,116}
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (SAT on 29-50 point cases)
targets.statement: A pentagonal geometry PENT(k,r) (Ball, Bamberg, Devillers and Stokes) is a partial linear space with k points on each line and r lines through each point, in which for every point x the points not collinear with x form a line (the opposite line of x). It has rk - r + k + 1 points and (rk - r + k + 1)r/k lines, so k must divide r(r-1). For k = 4, A. D. Forbes, T. S. Griggs and K. Stokes (Australas. J. Combin. 82 (2022); arXiv:2007.10810, Theorem 4.2 with Theorem 4.1) proved that PENT(4,r) exists for all r = 0 or 1 (mod 4) except r = 4 and 5, and except possibly r in {8, 12, 16, 28, 32, 36, 44, 48, 56, 64, 72}. For k = 5 and r = 1 (mod 5), Forbes and C. G. Rutherford (La Matematica 2024; arXiv:2111.13599v3, Theorem 5.1, a small improvement on T. S. Griggs and K. Stokes, Springer Proc. Math. Stat. 159 (2016), Theorem 12) proved existence except r = 6 and possibly r in {11, 16, 66, 96, 116}. The smallest open case, PENT(4,8), has 29 points and 58 lines; PENT(4,12) has 41 points and 123 lines; PENT(5,11) has 50 points and 110 lines. PENT(k,k) exists only for k = 2, 3, 7 and possibly 57; that case is tied to a Moore graph of degree 57 and is excluded here.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit PENT(k,r) for (k,r) in {(4,8), (4,12), (4,16), (4,28), (4,32), (4,36), (4,44), (4,48), (4,56), (4,64), (4,72), (5,11), (5,16), (5,66), (5,96), (5,116)}. It must have v = rk - r + k + 1 points and vr/k lines, each a k-subset; every point must lie on exactly r lines and any two points on at most one line. For every point x, the set of points other than x not collinear with x must be exactly one of the lines. Two independent programs must verify it. At claim time the case must still be listed as a possible exception, checked by a fresh literature search for PENT(4,r) and PENT(5,r), including Forbes' ORCID and arXiv lists.

partial_wins.statement: A machine-checked non-existence proof for one listed case (PENT(4,8) on 29 points is the natural first target), with a DRAT/LRAT certificate from an audited encoding, re-verified independently.

A type-A PENT(5,r) (connected deficiency graph of girth at least 5) for some admissible r not in the published lists of known type-A PENT(5,r) (r in {20,25,30,35,40} from Forbes 2021 and {21,26,31,36,41,45} from Forbes-Rutherford 2024), verified by two programs including the girth and connectivity of the non-collinearity graph.

targets.verification_method: Parse the lines. Check the point and line counts, line sizes, point degrees r and pairwise line intersections of at most 1. For each point x, compute the set of points not collinear with x and confirm it equals a line of the geometry. For p2, also compute the deficiency (non-collinearity) graph and check that it is connected with girth at least 5. Two independent checkers.
angles: Forbes' examples are cyclic: points Z_v, lines developed from base lines under x -> x + d. Search PENT(4,8) on Z_29 and PENT(4,12) on Z_41 with SAT, then try non-cyclic groups.

The deficiency graph is a disjoint union of K_{k,k} pieces (opposite line pairs) and a k-regular graph of girth at least 5. Enumerate candidate deficiency graphs first, then complete the remaining pairs to a linear structure.
pitfalls: PENT(4,4), PENT(4,5) and PENT(5,6) are proven not to exist; they are not open.

targets.name: Graph-design spectra: decompose K_16 into 12 copies of a 6-vertex 10-edge graph, K_21 into 7 icosahedra, or settle another listed possible exception
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (SAT / exact cover on K_16 and K_21; larger orders by cyclic base blocks)
targets.statement: A G-design of order n is a decomposition of the edges of K_n into copies of a graph G. The design spectrum of G is the set of n for which one exists; Bryant and McCourt's G-designs site summarises results (last modified 2020). Recent papers leave explicit possible exceptions. (a) A. D. Forbes and T. S. Griggs (Contrib. Discrete Math. 17(2) (2022), Theorem 1.1(i); arXiv:2004.08963) show that designs exist for graphs n3, n6 and n10 (6 vertices, 10 edges) iff n = 0, 1, 5, 16 (mod 20), except n = 5 and possibly n = 16. Edge sets: n3 = {53,52,51,43,42,41,61,32,31,21}, n6 = {62,63,61,52,53,51,42,43,41,21}, n10 = {43,42,45,41,61,32,35,31,25,21}. The same order is impossible for n8 and n13. (b) Forbes and Griggs (Australas. J. Combin. 52 (2012) 215-228) show that icosahedron designs exist iff v = 1, 16, 21, 36 (mod 60), except possibly v in {21, 141, 156, 201, 261, 276}. Forbes and Rutherford (Australas. J. Combin. 91 (2025) 84-103; arXiv:2401.02846) still describe these 6 cases as unresolved.
