Makarov's 37/76 construction is stated without full proof; do not use it as a baseline.
An induced forest must be induced: a chosen vertex set whose induced subgraph contains a cycle does not count, even if a spanning forest exists.
The field moved fast in August 2026; check for later preprints before claiming.

targets.name: Smallest hypohamiltonian graphs with extra properties: a planar one below Tsai's 34 vertices, a planar one of order 35, a planar cubic one below 70, or a first one of girth 8
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days for planar generation (plantri) with Grinberg-type filters; a certificate check takes minutes
targets.statement: A graph is hypohamiltonian if it is non-hamiltonian but every vertex-deleted subgraph is hamiltonian. The order of the smallest planar hypohamiltonian graph is unknown. Cheng-Chen Tsai ('Small planar hypohamiltonian graphs', J. Graph Theory 108 (2025) 799-807, arXiv:2403.18384) found two on 34 vertices, beating the 25 graphs on 40 vertices of Jooyandeh, McKay, Ostergard, Pettersson and Zamfirescu (J. Graph Theory 84 (2017), arXiv:1302.2698), and settled order 41. Durias, Guerrero, Jaiyen, Kaplan, Lapine, Peralta and Shrivastav ('Local modifications in planar hypohamiltonian graphs', arXiv:2610.21210, 15 Oct 2026) proved existence for every order n >= 36, built over 100 examples below 40 vertices and conjecture that 34 is the minimum, so 35 is the only open order from 34 up. Lower bounds: 23 in general (Goedgebeur and Zamfirescu, Ars Math. Contemp. 13 (2017), arXiv:1602.07171; restated in arXiv:2311.10593 and arXiv:2610.21210), 27 without triangles, and exactly 45 for girth 5. The smallest known planar hypohamiltonian graph with a triangle has 216 vertices (arXiv:2610.21210, via Thomassen's construction and Wiener's 31-vertex almost hypohamiltonian graph). Cubic planar: 54 <= h <= 70 (Table 1 of arXiv:1602.07171; 70-vertex graphs of Araya and Wiener and of Jooyandeh and McKay, still cited as smallest by Tsai 2025); cubic planar of girth 5: exactly 76 (McKay). No hypohamiltonian graph of girth 8 or more is known (at least 36 vertices; at least 50 if cubic). Target: a planar hypohamiltonian graph on at most 33 vertices.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit simple planar graph G on N vertices with (1) a planar embedding (rotation system) confirmed by an independent planarity test, (2) for every vertex v an explicit Hamiltonian cycle of G - v, (3) non-hamiltonicity of G proved by a DRAT/LRAT-checked UNSAT proof of an independently generated Hamiltonian-cycle CNF, or by two independent exact Hamiltonicity solvers that agree, and (4) N STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than 34 and than the smallest planar hypohamiltonian graph reported at claim time in the latest version of arXiv:2610.21210, on House of Graphs and in a fresh arXiv/Scholar search for 'planar hypohamiltonian'. N below the proved lower bound 23 (27 for a triangle-free graph) means the checker is wrong.

partial_wins.statement: A planar hypohamiltonian graph on exactly 35 vertices, certified as in the main criterion: the only order >= 34 still open after Tsai (2025) and arXiv:2610.21210. It must be the first one published, per a fresh search at claim time.
A cubic planar hypohamiltonian graph on fewer than 70 vertices, certified as in the main criterion (lower bound 54).
A planar hypohamiltonian graph containing a triangle on fewer than 216 vertices, certified as in the main criterion.

A hypohamiltonian graph of girth at least 8, of any order and not necessarily planar, with girth computed exactly and hypohamiltonicity certified as in the main criterion (none known; at least 36 vertices, at least 50 if cubic).

targets.verification_method: Check simplicity, planarity (two implementations) and the embedding. For each v, check that the supplied cycle visits all vertices of G - v once and uses only edges. Prove G non-hamiltonian with your own CNF (successor or position encoding with subtour elimination), proof-checked, and cross-check with a second exact method (backtracking with pruning, or concorde on a TSP reformulation). Compute girth by BFS.
angles: Shrinking local modifications: arXiv:2610.21210 grows graphs with plus-two, plus-three and plus-four patch replacements. Look for replacements of a patch H by a smaller H' with the same cycle-fragment endpoints, starting from Tsai's 34-vertex graphs and Wiener's 31-vertex almost hypohamiltonian graph.

Exhaustive plantri generation of triangle-free planar graphs on 27-33 vertices with only 4- and 5-faces, pruned by Grinberg-type face counts and the requirement of at least four cubic vertices, as outlined in Section 4 of arXiv:2610.21210.
For p2, apply cubicity-preserving local replacements to the 70-vertex cubic planar graphs of Araya-Wiener and Jooyandeh-McKay.
For p4, screen girth-8 cubic graphs with large automorphism groups (voltage lifts, Cayley graphs) for non-hamiltonicity first, then test every vertex-deleted subgraph.
pitfalls: Hypohamiltonian requires EVERY vertex-deleted subgraph to be hamiltonian; checking a few vertices is not enough.
A planar hypohamiltonian graph has girth at most 5; the girth-8 partial concerns non-planar graphs.
The record moved from 40 (2017) to 34 (Tsai 2025), and which orders are covered changed again in October 2026 (arXiv:2610.21210): re-check arXiv and House of Graphs the day you claim.
Hypotraceable, almost hypohamiltonian and K2-hypohamiltonian graphs are different families with separate records.

targets.name: Smallest snark of girth 7: find one below 298 vertices (none exist up to 42), or a cyclically 7-edge-connected snark
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days for structured constructions (superposition, dot products, lifts) with a SAT 3-edge-colouring test; a certificate check takes seconds
targets.statement: A snark is a cubic, cyclically 4-edge-connected graph of girth at least 5 with no proper 3-edge-colouring. Jaeger and Swart (1980) conjectured that every snark has girth at most 6; Martin Kochol disproved this in 1996 with snarks of arbitrarily large girth (superposition). Gunnar Brinkmann and Jan Goedgebeur ('Generation of cubic graphs and snarks with large girth', J. Graph Theory 86 (2017) 255-272, arXiv:1512.05944) note that the smallest snark of girth 7 is still unknown. The smallest girth-7 snark obtained by Kochol's method has 298 vertices, and their exhaustive generation shows there is no snark of girth at least 7 on 42 or fewer vertices, so 44 <= order <= 298. They also generated all snarks of girth at least 6 up to 38 vertices (39 on 38 vertices). The other Jaeger-Swart conjecture, that there are no cyclically 7-edge-connected snarks, is still cited as open, e.g. by Goedgebeur, Macajova and Skoviera (Ars Math. Contemp. 16 (2019), arXiv:1712.07867). Target: an explicit snark of girth >= 7 on fewer than 298 vertices.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit simple cubic graph G on N vertices with (1) girth >= 7 computed exactly, (2) cyclic edge-connectivity >= 4 computed exactly (a girth-7 non-3-edge-colourable cubic graph can still have a cyclic 2- or 3-edge-cut, which disqualifies it), (3) no proper 3-edge-colouring, proved by a DRAT/LRAT-checked UNSAT proof of an independently generated CNF, and (4) N STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than 298 and than the smallest girth->=7 snark found at claim time in a fresh arXiv/Scholar search ('snark girth 7') and on House of Graphs. N <= 42 means the checker is wrong.

partial_wins.statement: A cyclically 7-edge-connected snark of any order (cubic, not 3-edge-colourable with a checked UNSAT proof, cyclic edge-connectivity computed exactly), refuting the Jaeger-Swart conjecture.
A snark of girth at least 7 on at most 298 vertices that is non-isomorphic to the published Kochol-type example, if that example is downloadable for comparison; not claimable otherwise.

targets.verification_method: Check cubicity and simplicity. Compute girth by BFS from every vertex and cross-check with networkx.girth. Compute cyclic edge-connectivity by an exact method (for small cuts, enumerate edge sets of size < k and test whether two components both contain cycles, or use a max-flow based algorithm cross-checked by brute force). Encode 3-edge-colouring (one variable per edge and colour, exactly one colour per edge, distinct colours at each vertex), fix the colours of the three edges at one vertex, and check the UNSAT proof with drat-trim.
angles: Kochol superposition with smaller 'supervertices' and 'superedges' of girth >= 7; optimise the gadget sizes rather than using the generic construction.
Dot products and 4-joins of girth-6 snarks along carefully chosen edges, then check girth; or voltage lifts of small snarks, whose girth is computable on the base graph.
Search cubic graphs of girth 7 with large automorphism groups (Cayley graphs of groups of order 44-200) and test 3-edge-colourability with SAT.
pitfalls: Girth-7 cubic graphs that are not snarks are plentiful; the hard part is non-3-edge-colourability, which needs a checked proof.
Weak snarks (girth 4) and graphs with small cyclic cuts do not count.

The 298-vertex value comes from Kochol's generic construction as reported in the 2017 paper. Brinkmann and Van Overberghe's 2026 generator (arXiv:2603.17789, March 2026 preprint) lists girth->=5 snarks only up to 38 vertices, so the lower bound 44 is unchanged. Search for newer constructions before claiming.

targets.name: Permutation snarks: a first one of order 6 mod 8 (at least 54 vertices) or a first one of girth at least 6
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days for cycle-permutation searches with SAT colouring tests; a certificate check takes seconds
targets.statement: A cycle permutation graph is a cubic graph with a 2-factor of two chordless cycles (each of length n/2); a permutation snark is one that is not 3-edge-colourable. Such snarks have order 2 mod 4, and Macajova and Skoviera showed that they exist for every n = 2 mod 8 with n >= 10 (cyclically 5-edge-connected ones for n >= 34). No permutation snark of order 6 mod 8 is known. This was posed by Brinkmann, Goedgebeur, Hagglund and Markstrom (JCTB 2013, Problem 1) and revisited in Macajova and Skoviera, 'Are there any permutation snarks on 6 (mod 8) vertices?' (Procedia Comput. Sci. 273, 2025). Jan Goedgebeur, Jarne Renders and Steven Van Overberghe ('Generation of Cycle Permutation Graphs and Permutation Snarks', arXiv:2411.12606, v4 May 2026; conference version SOFSEM 2025, LNCS 15538) generated all permutation snarks up to order 46. They proved that a smallest one of order 6 mod 8, if it exists, has at least 54 vertices and (Macajova-Skoviera) is cyclically 5-edge-connected. Although cycle permutation graphs can have arbitrarily large girth (Shawe-Taylor and Pisanski), no permutation snark of girth >= 6 is known. A smallest one has at least 50 vertices, at least 56 for girth 7, 62 for girth 8 and 72 for girth 9. Target: a permutation snark of order n = 6 mod 8.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit simple cubic graph G on n vertices, n = 6 (mod 8), together with an explicit 2-factor consisting of two induced (chordless) cycles of length n/2 each, such that G has no proper 3-edge-colouring, proved by a DRAT/LRAT-checked UNSAT proof of an independently generated CNF. It must be the first such graph: a fresh arXiv/Scholar search ('permutation snark') at claim time must show no earlier published example. n < 54 means the checker is wrong.

partial_wins.statement: A permutation snark (any order) of girth at least 6, with the two-chordless-cycle 2-factor given explicitly, girth computed exactly and non-3-edge-colourability certified by a checked UNSAT proof (none known; at least 50 vertices).

targets.verification_method: Check cubicity and simplicity; check that the two given cycles are vertex-disjoint, cover all vertices, have length n/2, and that each induces a cycle (no chords). Check n mod 8. Compute girth by BFS. Encode 3-edge-colouring independently, break symmetry at one vertex, solve with proof logging and verify with drat-trim.
angles: A cycle permutation graph is determined by a permutation of Z_{n/2}; search structured permutations (affine maps, products of rotations) for n = 54, 62, 70 with a fast parity pre-filter and a SAT test.
Use the Goedgebeur-Renders-Van Overberghe generator and filter code (GitHub, cited in the paper) to explore beyond order 46 restricted to cyclically 5-edge-connected candidates.
For p1, start from girth-6 cycle permutation graphs with large automorphism groups.
pitfalls: Permutation snarks cannot have order 0 mod 4; an order-0-mod-4 non-colourable claim is a bug.
The two cycles must be chordless and of equal length; a hamiltonian or other 2-factor does not make G a cycle permutation graph.
Many experts suspect order-6-mod-8 permutation snarks may not exist; budget accordingly.

targets.name: Quaternary Hadamard matrices BH(n,4): settle an open even order below 2000 (smallest 334, then 438, 446, 478)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (bordered and plug-in arrays, multiplier-orbit searches, SAT/CP-SAT; checking takes laptop-seconds)
targets.statement: A quaternary (Butson) Hadamard matrix BH(n,4) is an n x n matrix with entries in {1,-1,i,-i} and H H* = nI. Seberry conjectured that one exists at every even order (Problem 8 of Egan, Kotsireas, London and O Cathain, arXiv:2610.27175, 2026); this implies the Hadamard conjecture, since a BH(n,4) gives a real Hadamard matrix of order 2n (Turyn). V. Zaitsev's page 'Quaternary Hadamard matrices' (with H. Kharaghani, A. Mohammadian and B. Tayfeh-Rezaie; last updated 14 October 2026, re-fetched 2026-10-30) lists 115 even orders below 2000 with no known BH(n,4): 334, 358, 418, 438, 446, 478, 498, 502, 506, 550, ... 1990. Recent progress: F. Szollosi settled 94 (arXiv:2603.09572); Kharaghani, Mohammadian, Tayfeh-Rezaie and Zaitsev found 118, 130, 134, 206 and 266 from near-Williamson matrices (arXiv:2605.08661); the page authors added many more. K. Kumar (github.com/vatskishan03/Hadamard, complex-hadamard/, October 2026) gives BH(n,4) at six orders still on Zaitsev's list: 358, 418, 498 (character-bordered and Paley plug-in arrays) and 1286, 1718, 1910 (quaternary conference matrices), leaving 109 open orders below 2000, the smallest 334, 438, 446, 478, 502, 506, 550. Kumar's README states 334 is the smallest open quaternary order and reports exhaustive structured searches that failed there. A BH(1198,4) would also give the smallest open real Hadamard order 2396.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit n x n matrix with entries in {1,-1,i,-i} (stored as exponents 0..3 of i) with H H* = nI checked exactly over Z[i] by two independent programs, for an even n < 2000 that is on the live unknown list of https://www.cs.uleth.ca/~zaitsevv/quaternary.html (re-fetched immediately before claiming) and is not settled by any other public source at claim time: not in the complex-hadamard/ folder or README of github.com/vatskishan03/Hadamard, not in the latest version of arXiv:2610.27175 or arXiv:2605.08661, and not found by a same-day arXiv/GitHub search for BH(n,4) at that order (direction: none; existence target). A non-existence proof for one listed order also counts if it is machine-checked (Lean, Isabelle or Coq) or its computational part (exhaustive search with logs, or a DRAT/LRAT certificate for a CNF the skeptic regenerates) is re-run by the skeptic to the same result.

partial_wins.statement: A certified exclusion, not previously published, of BH(334,4) within a precisely stated structured class (for example a stated bordered or block-circulant array with a stated multiplier group, beyond the classes Kumar's search/NOTES.md already reports as excluded), with a DRAT/LRAT or CP-SAT certificate or an exhaustive search the skeptic re-runs to the same empty result.

targets.verification_method: Read the matrix as exponents e_rj in Z_4. For each pair of rows r != s count c_m = #{j : e_rj - e_sj = m mod 4}; the Hermitian inner product is (c0 - c2) + i(c1 - c3), so orthogonality holds exactly when c0 = c2 and c1 = c3. Check all pairs with two independent programs (no floating point). Optionally build the real Hadamard matrix of order 2n by Turyn's map and verify H H^T = 2nI. Then confirm the order is on Zaitsev's live list and absent from Kumar's complex-hadamard folder and the papers named.
angles: Szollosi's modified Kharaghani-Seberry block array over circulants of order n/2 (how BH(94,4) was found); for n = 2p with p prime try multiplier-invariant circulants.

Near-Williamson quadruples (A circulant, B, C, D symmetric circulant) of odd order w give BH(2w,4); arXiv:2605.08661 v2 (Sep 2026) classifies them for odd w <= 47 and shows existence for every odd w <= 69.
Character-bordered arrays over abelian groups of order n/2 (Kumar's route to 358 and 498) and quaternary conference matrices of order (n+2)/2 or similar plug-ins.
pitfalls: Zaitsev's list (14 Oct 2026) lags: 358, 418, 498, 1286, 1718 and 1910 are on it but have explicit matrices in Kumar's repository.
Use the conjugate transpose: H H^T = nI over the complex numbers is the wrong test.
A quaternary conference matrix or a real Hadamard matrix of order 2n is not itself a BH(n,4).

targets.name: Butson Hadamard catalogue n <= 21, q <= 17: settle an unknown cell (BH(15,12), BH(16,15), BH(17,12), BH(17,15), BH(19,15))
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (orderly generation, SAT over Z_q exponents, structured circulant/core searches; checking takes laptop-seconds)
targets.statement: A Butson Hadamard matrix BH(n,q) is an n x n matrix whose entries are q-th roots of unity with H H* = nI. The online catalogue of Lampio, Ostergard and Szollosi (electronic supplement to Orderly generation of Butson Hadamard matrices, Math. Comp. 89 (2020) 313-331), the Aalto wiki page 'Matrices up to monomial equivalence' (created by F. Szollosi, last updated by P. Lampio on 17 November 2025, re-fetched 2026-10-30), gives for 2 <= n <= 21 and 2 <= q <= 17 the exact number of BH(n,q) up to monomial equivalence, 'E' (existence known) or 'U' (existence unknown); cells excluded by the Lam-Leung theorem are white (0). Czifra, Matolcsi and Szollosi (arXiv:2511.11230, J. Algebraic Combin. 64 (2026) Paper 29) filled the cell BH(18,14), which the page now shows as E. Five cells remain U: BH(15,12), BH(16,15), BH(17,12), BH(17,15) and BH(19,15). None of these is reachable from a smaller root of unity: for example BH(15,3) and BH(15,6) do not exist (catalogue zeros). Ong and Schmidt's Gauss-sum family (arXiv:2609.22754) only gives square orders q^2 with root order lcm(6, d), so it does not touch these cells. Settle one U cell by an explicit matrix or a certified non-existence proof.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for one (n,q) marked 'U' on the live page https://wiki.aalto.fi/display/Butson/Matrices+up+to+monomial+equivalence (re-fetched immediately before claiming), either (a) an explicit n x n matrix of exponents in Z_q whose rows are pairwise orthogonal, checked exactly in Q(zeta_q) by two independent programs, or (b) a non-existence proof whose computational part (exhaustive orderly generation with logs, or a DRAT/LRAT-checked UNSAT certificate on a CNF the skeptic regenerates) the skeptic re-runs; and a same-day arXiv search finds no earlier settlement of that cell (direction: none; existence target).

partial_wins.statement: An exact count up to monomial equivalence for a catalogue cell currently marked 'E' (existence known, count unknown), such as BH(13,12) or BH(14,8), produced by an orderly-generation or canonical-form enumeration that an independent implementation reproduces to the same count.

An explicit BH(26,22) or BH(30,26), instances p = 11, 13 of Conjecture 1 of arXiv:2511.11230 (BH(2p+4,2p) exists for every prime p), after the claimant shows that no such matrix is published, checked exactly as in the main criterion.

targets.verification_method: Store exponents e_rj in Z_q. For each pair of rows r != s form P(x) = sum_m c_m x^m where c_m = #{j : e_rj - e_sj = m mod q}; orthogonality holds exactly when P(x) is divisible by the cyclotomic polynomial Phi_q(x) over Q (integer polynomial remainder zero). Check all pairs with two independent programs; no floating point. For non-existence, regenerate the CNF or rerun the enumeration from the claimant's code and verify the certificate with drat-trim or cake_lpr.
angles: Lam-Leung vanishing-sum structure: for q = 12 or 15 each row inner product is a vanishing sum of q-th roots of unity, which decomposes into rotated regular 2-, 3- or 5-gons; enumerate admissible row types first.
Positive-definite-function criterion of arXiv:2511.11230 as a pruning test or a route to non-existence.
Core or 2-circulant ansatz for n = 16, 17, 19 (prime orders admit circulant cores with a border).
pitfalls: Cells are counted up to monomial equivalence; a non-existence claim must cover all matrices, not one normal form family, unless the reduction is proved.
Numerical orthogonality is not a proof; use exact cyclotomic arithmetic.
The page uses 'U' for unknown and 'E' for known existence; BH(18,14) changed from open to E in late 2025.

targets.name: Symmetric Hadamard matrices: an order 4v where none is known (smallest 428 = 4*107, then 476, 652, 668, 716)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (propus difference families, multiplier-orbit searches, plug-in constructions; checking takes laptop-seconds)
targets.statement: A Hadamard matrix H is symmetric if H = H^T; they are conjectured to exist at every order 4v. D. Z. Dokovic (arXiv:2101.05429 v2, Jan 2022) listed the odd v < 200 still undecided after the propus-array work of Balonin, Dokovic and Kotsireas: 65, 89, 93, 101, 107, 119, 133, 149, 153, 163, 167, 179, 183, 189, 193; he settled 93 (order 372, arXiv:2301.02751) and 189, 473 and 1139 (arXiv:2508.17141, 2025). The unpublished Dokovic-Seberry census of 28 May 2025 lists 595 odd v < 2500 as undecided; Kishan (GitHub vatskishan03; repository 'New Hadamard matrices', github.com/vatskishan03/Hadamard) transcribed it (search/data/symmetric_census_undecided.txt) and in October 2026 posted symmetric Hadamard matrices for 102 census values (symmetric/ folder), including the orders 260, 356, 404, 532, 596, 612, 732, 772 and 876 (v = 65, 89, 101, 133, 149, 153, 183, 193, 219), leaving 490. The smallest remaining values are v = 107, 119, 163, 167, 179, 209, 213, 223, 239, 245, i.e. orders 428, 476, 652, 668, 716, 836, 852, 892, 956, 980. Hadamard matrices of these orders exist (668 and 716 since the 2026 matrices of Alpoge, Voinov and Reynolds-Haertle), but no symmetric one is reported in the sources read.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit 4v x 4v matrix H with entries +-1, H = H^T and H H^T = 4vI, both checked exactly by two independent programs, for v in {107, 119, 163, 167, 179} (orders 428, 476, 652, 668, 716), still listed in the live search/data/symmetric_census_undecided.txt of github.com/vatskishan03/Hadamard, with no symmetric matrix of that order in the repository's symmetric/ folder (re-listed immediately before claiming), and with no symmetric Hadamard matrix of that order found by a same-day arXiv search (direction: none; existence target).

partial_wins.statement: The same for any other odd v < 2500 on the census list, other than 189, 473 and 1139, that is still undecided at claim time (490 values at this check, for example v = 209, 213, 223, 239, 245, 247), verified as in the main criterion.

targets.verification_method: Check every entry is +-1, H equals its transpose entrywise, and H H^T = 4vI in integer arithmetic, with two independent checkers. If the claim is a propus difference family (v; k1, k2, k2, k4; lambda) with X2 = X3 and X1, X4 symmetric, expand it into the propus array with the verifier's own code and check the full matrix. Confirm the order is absent from Kishan's symmetric/ folder and from arXiv.
angles: Propus array: four circulants A, B, B, D of order v with A, D symmetric (Seberry-Balonin); search difference families invariant under a multiplier subgroup of (Z/vZ)*.
Miyamoto's lemma and Yamada-Kiyasu in symmetric quaternary form (Kishan's main routes) from symmetric conference or skew inputs of order about 2v.
For v = 107, 163, 167, 179 (primes), look for structures over Z_v with subgroup-orbit blocks.
pitfalls: A Hadamard or skew-Hadamard matrix of the same order is not enough: Kishan's repository has skew 476, and Alpoge et al. matrices of 668 and 716 are not reported symmetric.
The census itself warns it may miss orders; Kishan found 9 census values settled by older published theorems, so check Spence's and Seberry-Balonin's corollaries before claiming novelty.
A matrix only equivalent to a symmetric one must be presented in symmetric form.

targets.name: Regular Hadamard matrix (Menon design) of order 4u^2 with u = 47 (order 8836), the first unknown order
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (structured searches with a prescribed automorphism group; checking takes laptop-seconds)
targets.statement: A Hadamard matrix is regular if all its row and column sums are equal; this forces order n = 4u^2 and row sum +-2u, and is equivalent to a Menon design, a symmetric (4u^2, 2u^2 - u, u^2 - u) design. Whether every even square is the order of a regular Hadamard matrix is open (Kharaghani conjectured that it is; Wikipedia's 'Regular Hadamard matrix' lists the question as unsolved). D. Crnkovic (A series of regular Hadamard matrices, Des. Codes Cryptogr. 39 (2006) 247-251) gave a regular Hadamard matrix of order 4p^2 whenever p and 2p - 1 are prime powers and p = 3 mod 4, which covers p = 7, 31 and 79 (2p - 1 = 13, 61, 157) but not p = 47 (93 = 3*31); Leung, Ma and Schmidt (J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 113 (2006) 822-838) cover some primes p = 7 mod 16, and 47 = 15 mod 16. Shi, Li, Cheng, Crnkovic, Krotov and Sole (Self-dual Hadamard bent sequences, arXiv:2203.16439 v2, June 2022) state that the first unknown order seems to be 4u^2 with u = 47, i.e. 8836. That 2022 sentence is the newest explicit status statement found; no later construction was found in this check. Abelian Menon difference sets of order 4p^2 with p > 3 prime do not exist (McFarland), so a solution cannot be developed over an abelian group; Kronecker products of smaller regular matrices give only even u, and the Bush-type family of Muzychuk and Xiang only u = m^2.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit 8836 x 8836 matrix H with entries +-1, H H^T = 8836 I, and every row sum and every column sum equal to the same value 94 or -94, all checked exactly by two independent programs (equivalently the 0/1 incidence matrix of a symmetric (8836, 4371, 2162) or (8836, 4465, 2256) design, checked by computing N N^T = (k - lambda) I + lambda J and N J = kJ), where a same-day arXiv and web search finds no earlier regular Hadamard matrix or Menon design of order 8836 (direction: none; existence target).

partial_wins.statement: A certified exclusion, not previously published, of regular Hadamard matrices of order 8836 within a precisely stated class (for example those invariant under a stated group of order at least 47 acting semiregularly, or group-developed over a stated non-abelian group of order 8836), with code and logs the skeptic re-runs to the same empty result or a DRAT/LRAT certificate.

targets.verification_method: Check entries +-1, compute H H^T exactly (or verify the design equations for the 0/1 matrix), and check all 2*8836 row and column sums equal the same value +-94, with two independent programs. If the claim is given as a group-developed or orbit-matrix description, expand it to the full matrix with the verifier's own code first.
angles: Orbit-matrix method (Crnkovic and coauthors): prescribe an automorphism group, solve for the orbit matrix, then refine to the full design.
Product and Kronecker-type constructions from regular Hadamard or Bush-type matrices of smaller orders, or from symmetric designs with Hadamard parameters over non-abelian groups of order 8836.
Look for constructions combining a Hadamard matrix of order 188 = 4*47 with a 47-ary structure, as in families giving 4p^2 for special primes p.
pitfalls: The status source is from 2022 ('seems to be'); search carefully for a 2022-2026 construction before claiming.
Row sums must all be equal (not just constant up to sign per row); normalising a Hadamard matrix by row negations destroys regularity.
Do not confuse with regular Hadamard matrices of order 196 or 4*47 = 188; the order is 4*47^2.

targets.name: Bush-type Hadamard matrices of order 4n^2 with n odd: the first open case n = 7 (order 196)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (block-structured SAT/ILP and orbit-matrix searches; checking takes laptop-seconds)
targets.statement: A Bush-type Hadamard matrix of order 4n^2 is a Hadamard matrix H = [H_ij] partitioned into 2n x 2n blocks of size 2n with H_ii = J (all ones) and H_ij J = J H_ij = 0 for i != j. They exist at order 16n^2 whenever a Hadamard matrix of order 4n exists, but the odd-n case is hard: Bush-type matrices of order 4n^2 with n odd are known only for n = 3 (order 36, Janko 2001), n = 5 (order 100, Janko, Kharaghani and Tonchev 2001) and n = 9 (order 324, Janko, Kharaghani and Tonchev 2001), plus the infinite family of order 4m^4 for every odd m (Muzychuk and Xiang, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 134 (2006), arXiv:math/0501026). H. Kharaghani (On the Siamese twin designs) named order 196 = 4*7^2 as the smallest order for which existence is unknown and conjectured existence for all odd n; Crnkovic and Svob (Switching for 2-designs, arXiv:2108.02529 v2, 2022) restate that only n = 3, 5, 9 and the 4m^4 family are known, and no later arXiv paper on Bush-type matrices of these orders was found. Open odd n therefore include 7, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21, 23 (orders 196, 484, 676, 900, 1156, 1444, 1764, 2116; n = 25 is covered by the 4m^4 family). A Bush-type matrix is regular, yields symmetric designs with Hadamard parameters, infinite families of symmetric designs when 2n - 1 or 2n + 1 is a prime power (Kharaghani), and self-dual bent sequences.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit 196 x 196 matrix with entries +-1 and H H^T = 196 I, partitioned into 14 x 14 blocks of size 14 with every diagonal block equal to J_14 and every off-diagonal block having all row sums and all column sums zero, checked exactly by two independent programs, where a same-day arXiv and web search finds no earlier Bush-type Hadamard matrix of order 196 (direction: none; existence target). A rigorous non-existence proof for order 196 (exhaustive search with a DRAT/LRAT certificate the skeptic re-checks) also counts.

partial_wins.statement: A Bush-type Hadamard matrix of order 4n^2 for some odd n in {11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21, 23} (orders 484 to 2116), not previously published, checked as in the main criterion with blocks of size 2n.

A certified exclusion, not previously published, of Bush-type Hadamard matrices of order 196 within a stated structured class (for example block-negacyclic as in Janko-Kharaghani, or invariant under a stated automorphism group), with code and logs the skeptic re-runs to the same empty result or a DRAT/LRAT certificate.

targets.verification_method: Check entries +-1 and H H^T = 4n^2 I exactly; check each diagonal 2n x 2n block is all ones and each off-diagonal block has zero row and column sums. Use two independent checkers. If a block-circulant or orbit description is given, expand it with the verifier's own code first.
angles: Block negacyclic or block circulant structure over Z_14 as in Janko-Kharaghani's order-36 example; reduce to a search over 13 block types.
Orbit matrices under a prescribed automorphism group of order 7 or 13, then SAT completion (Crnkovic-Svob style).
Switching (arXiv:2108.02529) only transforms existing Bush-type matrices; it can be used to diversify a found one, not to find the first.
pitfalls: The newest explicit status statement found is from 2022; re-search before claiming.
Regular Hadamard matrices of order 196 are known (from symmetric (196, 91, 42) designs) but they are not Bush-type unless the block conditions hold.
The symmetric Bush-type question is a different, murkier problem: sources conflict on whether any symmetric example with n odd is known.

targets.name: Ito's conjecture at t = 47: a negaperiodic Golay pair of length 94 (equivalently quasi-Williamson matrices of order 47)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (spectral-filtered meet-in-the-middle and SAT over Z[y]/(y^94 + 1); checking takes laptop-seconds)
targets.statement: Two +-1 sequences a, b of length v form a negaperiodic Golay (NG) pair if NAF_a(s) + NAF_b(s) = 0 for 1 <= s <= v - 1, where NAF_a(s) = sum_i a_i a_{i+s} with the sign of a term flipped when i + s wraps past v. NG pairs (Ito's 'associated pairs') give Hadamard matrices [[A, B], [-B^T, A^T]] of order 2v with A, B negacyclic. N. Ito conjectured that the dicyclic group of order 8t is a Hadamard group for every t; Balonin and Dokovic (Negaperiodic Golay pairs and Hadamard matrices, arXiv:1508.00640, 2015) showed this is equivalent to NG pairs existing at every even length, and for odd t to quasi-Williamson matrices of order t (four circulants in a Williamson-like array; Williamson matrices are the symmetric special case). Ito listed NG pairs of length 2t for every odd t <= 45; B. Schmidt (Des. Codes Cryptogr. 17 (1999) 61-68) proved the conjecture for t <= 46 and some infinite families. Balonin and Dokovic pose as an open problem whether NG pairs of length 94 (quasi-Williamson matrices of order 47) exist, and list the odd t <= 125 still open: 47, 59, 65, 67, 73, 81, 89, 93, 101, 103, 107, 109, 113, 119. K. Kumar's NOTES.md (github.com/vatskishan03/Hadamard, October 2026) states that the conjecture is verified for t <= 46 only and that this list has been open since 1999, recalls that Williamson matrices of orders 47 and 59 do not exist, and reports empty multiplier-invariant searches for NG pairs of lengths 94, 134, 186, 214 and 254 and for quasi-Williamson matrices of the listed orders. The near-Williamson matrices of order 47 of arXiv:2605.08661 are not quasi-Williamson matrices and do not by themselves settle t = 47. Neither does F. Szollosi's complex Hadamard matrix of order 94 (arXiv:2603.09572, March 2026): its circulant blocks of order 47 have two symmetric blocks, but one block enters as the back-circulant DR, and neither of his two published quadruples satisfies the quasi-Williamson condition AB^T + CD^T = BA^T + DC^T under any ordering, reversal, sign change or cyclic shift of the blocks (checked at audit, 2026-10-30).
targets.success_criterion: Success means two +-1 sequences a, b of length 94 whose negaperiodic autocorrelations sum to zero at every shift s = 1..93, checked exactly by two independent programs, together with the Hadamard matrix [[A, B], [-B^T, A^T]] of order 188 built from the negacyclic matrices A, B and verified to satisfy H H^T = 188 I, where a same-day arXiv search finds no earlier NG pair of length 94 or quasi-Williamson matrices of order 47 (direction: none; existence target). A rigorous non-existence proof (exhaustive search with a DRAT/LRAT certificate) also counts and would refute Ito's conjecture.

partial_wins.statement: An NG pair of length 2t for t in {59, 65, 67, 73, 81, 89, 93, 101, 103, 107, 109, 113, 119} (the Balonin-Dokovic open list), after checking that no NG pair, quasi-Williamson matrices or Williamson matrices of order t have been published, checked as in the main criterion (with H H^T = 4tI for the order-4t matrix).

A certified exclusion, not previously published, of NG pairs of length 94 within a precisely stated structured class not already reported as searched in Kumar's NOTES.md (which reports as empty the multiplier-invariant NG structures with at most 6 orbits, notes there is none between 6 and 48 orbits, and reports as empty the quasi-Williamson quadruples of order 47 constant on the orbits of an odd-order multiplier group), for example the 48-orbit multiplier structure or a stated compression pattern, with a DRAT/LRAT certificate or an exhaustive search the skeptic re-runs to the same empty result.

targets.verification_method: Compute NAF exactly in integers: NAF_a(s) = sum_{i=0}^{v-1-s} a_i a_{i+s} - sum_{i=v-s}^{v-1} a_i a_{i+s-v}, and require NAF_a(s) + NAF_b(s) = 0 for every s >= 1. Then build the negacyclic matrices (row k is the first row shifted k places with wrapped entries negated), assemble the 2N-type array and check H H^T = 2vI. Use two independent programs.
angles: Work in Z[y]/(y^94 + 1) ~ Z[i] tensor Z[Z_47]: the power-spectrum condition |a(zeta)|^2 + |b(zeta)|^2 = 188 at the odd 188th roots of unity is a strong filter for meet-in-the-middle joins.
Use the bijection to quasi-Williamson matrices of order 47 (four blocks with a skew/symmetric pattern) and search there with SAT+CAS.
Turyn-type multiplication: an NG pair of length 2t times a Golay pair of length g gives length 2tg, so lengths in the open list cannot be reached from smaller ones; a direct search is needed.
pitfalls: Negaperiodic is not periodic or aperiodic: Golay pairs are both PG and NG pairs, but periodic Golay pairs (separate bank entries) are not NG pairs.
Williamson matrices of order 47 do not exist (Holzmann-Kharaghani-Tayfeh-Rezaie), so Schmidt's route through Williamson orders does not apply.
Kumar reports that multiplier-invariant structures for v = 94 jump from 6 to 48 orbits; small-orbit searches are already empty.

A Hadamard matrix of order 188 or a complex Hadamard matrix of order 94 is not the target: the near-Williamson (arXiv:2605.08661) and Szollosi (arXiv:2603.09572) quadruples of order 47 give those but are not quasi-Williamson matrices, so they yield no NG pair of length 94.

targets.name: 128-modular Hadamard matrix at an order with no known Hadamard matrix (smallest 2396), or a first explicit 64-modular one there
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days to needs cluster (modular Golay quadruple searches of length ~600; checking takes laptop-seconds)
targets.statement: An m-modular Hadamard matrix of order n (Marrero and Butson) is an n x n +-1 matrix with H H^T = nI mod m. Any m-modular Hadamard matrix of order n < m is a true Hadamard matrix, so the Hadamard conjecture is equivalent to the m-modular conjecture for infinitely many m. The m-modular conjecture is settled for m = 5 (Lee and Szollosi), 12 (Marrero-Butson) and 32 (Eliahou and Kervaire, 2001, via modular Golay quadruples in the Goethals-Seidel array), and asymptotically for m = 7, 11 (Kuperberg). S. Eliahou (A 64-modular Hadamard matrix of order 668, Australas. J. Combin. 93(2) (2025) 422-427) reached m = 64 at 668 and announced the classes l = 1, 3, 5 mod 16 and l = 7 mod 32. His published follow-up (An update on modular Hadamard matrices, J. Algebraic Combin. 64 (2026), article 1, 12 June 2026) constructs 64-modular Hadamard matrices at all orders 4l with l = 3 mod 16 or l = 7 mod 32 and names 892 as the smallest open 64-modular order. The 2026 survey of Egan, Kotsireas, London and O Cathain (arXiv:2610.27175, Section 5.4) reports that he announced m = 64 at all orders (personal communication) and poses Problem 10: does a 128-modular Hadamard matrix exist at every order divisible by 4? At orders with a known Hadamard matrix the answer is trivially yes. Doubling (H -> [[H, H], [H, -H]]) turns a 64-modular matrix of order n into a 128-modular one of order 2n, and a 32-modular one into a 64-modular one. So the open cases are the 86 orders up to 10000 with no known Hadamard matrix on the Hadamard Matrix Explorer (math74.com), smallest 2396 = 4*599, then 2676, 2876, 2956, 3004, minus 5912 = 2*2956, which doubling settles because 2956 = 4*739 has l = 3 mod 16. For 2396, l = 599 (7 mod 16, 23 mod 32) is in neither published class.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit n x n +-1 matrix H (or a 128-modular Golay quadruple of length n/4 that the verifier expands through the Goethals-Seidel array) with every off-diagonal entry of H H^T divisible by 128, checked exactly by two independent programs, for an order n listed on the live page https://www.math74.com/Hadamard/unknown.html (re-fetched immediately before claiming), not settled as a true Hadamard order by any public source at claim time, and not twice an order with a published 64-modular Hadamard matrix (this excludes 5912 = 2*2956), with no 128-modular (or stronger) Hadamard matrix of that order found by a same-day arXiv search (direction: none; existence target).

partial_wins.statement: An explicit 64-modular Hadamard matrix (or 64-modular Golay quadruple) of an order n = 4l on the live unknown-orders list with l odd, l not 3 mod 16 and l not 7 mod 32 (the classes published in Eliahou's J. Algebraic Combin. 2026 paper; for example 2396, 2676, 2876, 3004, or 4676 and 5892 with l = 1 or 5 mod 16, which were announced but not published), provided no explicit 64-modular matrix of that order is public at claim time, checked as in the main criterion with modulus 64. Orders 8p (l even, such as 4792, 5752, 5912) do not count: doubling a 32-modular matrix of order 4p already gives one.

targets.verification_method: Compute all pairwise row inner products of H in integer arithmetic and check each off-diagonal value is 0 mod 128 (mod 64 for p1). If a quadruple (A, B, C, D) is given, check sum of aperiodic (or periodic) autocorrelations at every shift 1..l-1 is 0 mod m, then build the Goethals-Seidel array with the verifier's own code and check H H^T directly. Two independent programs.
angles: Modular Golay quadruples: four +-1 sequences of length l whose autocorrelation sums vanish mod m at every shift (Eliahou-Kervaire); local search with an exact mod-m objective is cheaper than exact Golay quadruples.
Periodic version: four circulants with periodic autocorrelation sums = 0 mod 128 also feed the Goethals-Seidel array; multiplier-orbit restrictions shrink the space for prime l = 599.
Combine a 64-modular base with corrections on a few positions to clear the remaining residues mod 128.
pitfalls: At any order where a true Hadamard matrix is known the problem is trivial; check the order is on the live unknown list, which shrinks as orders fall.
HH^T = nI mod m requires off-diagonal inner products divisible by m; inner products of +-1 rows of even length are even, so do not count parity as progress.

Eliahou's published 64-modular classes are l = 3 mod 16 and l = 7 mod 32 (J. Algebraic Combin. 2026); his l = 1 and 5 mod 16 classes (announced in the 2025 AJC note) and his all-orders result (personal communication in arXiv:2610.27175) are not public as matrices. Cite only what is published when claiming p1, and check for a newer Eliahou paper first.

Doubling: [[H, H], [H, -H]] maps an m-modular matrix of order n to a 2m-modular one of order 2n. A 128-modular matrix at 2n is not new when a 64-modular one of order n is published (5912 = 2*2956), and a 64-modular one at an order 8p is not new because 32-modular matrices exist at every order 4p.

targets.name: Dominant transversals: a Latin square of order 11 (or 15, 19, ...) with a transversal that meets every other transversal (Ghafari-Wanless Question 1)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (enumerating all transversals of an order-11 square takes seconds; the search over squares is the cost)
targets.statement: A transversal of a Latin square of order n is a set of n cells, one in each row, column and symbol. Afsane Ghafari and Ian M. Wanless (arXiv:2607.17547, 20 Jul 2026, 'Latin squares whose transversals intersect in unusual ways') call a transversal dominant if it intersects every other transversal of the square. They prove (Theorem 4/13) that a Latin square with a dominant transversal exists for every n > 4 with n not 3 mod 4 and n != 6; for n = 7 the Egan-Wanless enumeration finds exactly 19 species with one, while orders 2, 3, 4 and 6 have none. Their Question 1 asks whether one exists for every n >= 7. All 36,007 order-9 species with a dominant transversal get it from a subsquare of order 4 via a parity argument that cannot work when n is 3 mod 4, and the authors report failing to find examples of orders 11 and 15. So the smallest open case is n = 11, then 15, 19, 23, ... Wanless's data page (users.monash.edu.au/~iwanless/data/transversals/) lists examples only for orders 5, 7, 8, 9.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit Latin square L of order n with n = 3 mod 4 and n >= 11, plus one transversal T of L, such that T shares at least one cell with every other transversal of L. Both facts are confirmed by two independently written programs that each enumerate ALL transversals of L. Before claiming, re-fetch arXiv:2607.17547 (latest version) and the Wanless data page, and search arXiv for any later paper settling the same order. If an example of that order has been published since, the claim fails.

partial_wins.statement: A Latin square of order 11 or 15 with a transversal T that is disjoint from exactly one other transversal of L (all other transversals meet T), confirmed by two independent full enumerations of the transversals.

An exhaustive search, run by two independent programs that agree, showing that no Latin square of order 11 with a stated nontrivial autotopism (for example a given cycle-structure class not already excluded by Theorems 11-12 of arXiv:2607.17547) has a dominant transversal, with the full list of squares checked published.

targets.verification_method: Check L is Latin. Enumerate every transversal (a DLX or bitmask backtrack; order 11 has at most a few tens of thousands). Check T is among them. Check T has nonempty intersection, as cell sets, with every other transversal. Use two independent programs and compare the transversal counts. (The lane's own checker reproduced the paper's order-7 and order-8 examples: 24 transversals with 3 dominant; 3 with 4 pinned cells; 31 with 9 dominant.)
angles: Seek squares of order 11 with very few transversals (e.g. near Wanless's 778-transversal square) and test each transversal for dominance; fewer transversals make dominance cheaper to reach.
Generalise the parity argument of the paper (equation (15)) to a Z_m-valued labelling that works modulo another prime; the order-9 data says the Z_2 trick alone is exhausted.
pitfalls: The order 7 case is already settled (19 species); n = 7 does not count.
Cayley tables of groups and diagonally cyclic squares have no dominant transversal (Theorems 11 and 12 of the paper); do not search them.

A square with a pinned entry makes every transversal dominant. That is allowed, and the paper's order-5 and order-7 examples have pinned entries, but confirm the pinned entry with both full enumerations.
Dominance must be checked against ALL transversals of L, never a sample.

targets.name: Latin squares of even order 10..26, or odd order, whose transversals pairwise intersect yet share no common cell (Ghafari-Wanless Conjecture 3 small orders)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (finding transversals is cheap; certifying that NO two are disjoint needs a full enumeration of the square's transversals)
targets.statement: Ghafari and Wanless (arXiv:2607.17547, 20 Jul 2026), answering a question of Nick Wormald, construct for every even n >= 28 except n = 30 a Latin square of order n with no two disjoint transversals. They prove (Theorem 6) that for n = 28 and every even n with 32 <= n <= 10000 the square also has no pinned entry (no cell lies in every transversal). Their Conjecture 3 says such a square exists for all even n >= 28. It is false for n <= 8 (Egan-Wanless enumeration). The authors write that it may also hold for some n < 28, and that it would be most interesting to know whether it can hold for any odd n. Their own construction fails at small orders: G_18 and H_16 have disjoint transversals and H_32 has none. The order 30 that the paper leaves out was settled publicly on 21 Sep 2026 in GitHub issue the-omega-institute/trureturing#9291. That issue gives an explicit square obtained from Z_30 by four cyclic trades, a Delta-sum proof that every transversal contains two of three marked entries, and three transversals with no common entry; an audit on 2026-10-30 rebuilt the square and re-checked the witnesses and the proof's finite steps. Small open orders: even n in {10, 12, ..., 26}. Odd n >= 11 is also open. n = 9 appears ruled out by the order-9 data on Wanless's page, where the square with the fewest disjoint transversals still has 3. Even n > 10000 is open too, but out of reach of the enumeration-based check below.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit Latin square L of order n, with n in {10,12,14,16,18,20,22,24,26} or n odd >= 11. L must satisfy all three of: (a) it has at least two transversals; (b) every two transversals share at least one cell; (c) no cell lies in every transversal. Each property is confirmed by two independently written programs that enumerate all transversals of L, or for (c) by exhibiting, for each cell, a transversal that avoids it. Before claiming, re-fetch arXiv:2607.17547 and search arXiv and public repositories (including the-omega-institute/trureturing issues) for a later construction at that order. An order already settled there, or n = 30 (settled in trureturing#9291), is not a win.

partial_wins.statement: An exhaustive search over an explicitly stated, enumerable family of Latin squares of one of the open orders, run by two independent programs that agree. Example families: every square obtained from the Cayley table of Z_n or of Z_2 x Z_(n/2) by at most two cycle switches, or every square of order 10 with a stated nontrivial autotopism. The search either finds a square with properties (a)-(c), which is then a full win, or shows that none in the family has them. It publishes the family's definition, the list of squares checked and, for each square, a witness of failure: two disjoint transversals, a pinned cell, or a certificate that it has fewer than two transversals.

targets.verification_method: Check L is Latin. Enumerate all transversals with two independent programs that agree on the count. Check that every pair intersects, using bitset cell masks. Check that the intersection of all transversals is empty, or verify one avoiding transversal per cell. Confirm that the order is not covered by the paper.
angles: Adapt the paper's section-3 construction (a perturbed group-based square whose transversals are forced through a small region) to orders below 28, then repair with local trades while monitoring the transversal set.
Squares of even order with few transversals (turn-squares of Z_2 x Z_m) are natural seeds.
pitfalls: A square with NO transversals satisfies (b) and (c) vacuously; it does not count, which is why (a) is required.
For order 26 the full transversal enumeration may be large; budget for it before claiming (b).

n = 30 is already done (the-omega-institute/trureturing#9291, 21 Sep 2026). That square forces pairwise intersection with a Delta-sum argument (the sum of L(r,c) - r - c over a transversal is fixed mod n) rather than a full enumeration; such a proof is welcome, but the two-program checks of the criterion are still required.
An odd-order win with n = 3 mod 4 also makes every transversal of L dominant, so it is also a win for the bank entry dominant-transversal-order-3-mod-4.

targets.name: The last open case of the r-self-orthogonal Latin square spectrum: a 193-SOLS of order 14
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (SAT or local search on a 14x14 square)
targets.statement: Superimposing a Latin square A of order n on its transpose gives the n^2 ordered pairs (A[i][j], A[j][i]). A is r-self-orthogonal (an r-SOLS(n)) if exactly r of these pairs are distinct. Xu and Chang (Discrete Math. 2006) and Hantao Zhang ('25 new r-self-orthogonal Latin squares', Discrete Math. 313 (2013) 1746-1753) proved that an r-SOLS(n) exists iff n <= r <= n^2 and r is not n+1 or n^2-1, apart from 26 genuine exceptions with n <= 7 and one possible exception, (n, r) = (14, 14^2 - 3) = (14, 193). Sergey Bereg (arXiv:2311.00992 v3, Feb 2024; COCOA 2023) calls finding a 193-self-orthogonal Latin square of order 14 the only case left to complete the spectrum, and reports that values of r close to n^2 are the hard ones. No later construction or non-existence proof was found in arXiv listings through Oct 2026.
targets.success_criterion: EITHER (existence) an explicit 14x14 Latin square A over {0..13} such that the set {(A[i][j], A[j][i]) : 0 <= i,j < 14} has exactly 193 elements, checked by two independent programs; OR (non-existence) a proof that none exists, delivered as a DRAT/LRAT-verified UNSAT certificate of a CNF that the verifier regenerates from a published encoding, with any symmetry-breaking justified in writing. Before claiming, re-check Bereg's arXiv:2311.00992 and search arXiv and the literature for a construction of a 193-SOLS(14) published since.

partial_wins.statement: A DRAT/LRAT-verified proof that no 193-SOLS(14) exists under a stated structural restriction that is not already in the literature (for example A idempotent, or A invariant under a given automorphism such as x -> x+2 mod 14 on rows, columns and symbols), with the CNF regenerated by the verifier.

targets.verification_method: Check each row and column of A is a permutation of 0..13. Count the distinct ordered pairs (A[i][j], A[j][i]) over all 196 cells and require exactly 193. For non-existence, regenerate the CNF from the published encoder and check the certificate with drat-trim or cake_lpr.
angles: Count bookkeeping: diagonal cells give pairs (a,a), and the pairs (x,y) and (y,x) come from mirror cells, so 193 = 196 - 3 forces a very rigid repeat pattern; enumerate the possible repeat patterns first, then SAT-solve each.
Start from a SOLS(14) (r = 196) and apply small trades that create exactly three repeats.
pitfalls: r = n^2 - 1 = 195 is impossible and r = 194 is known to exist; do not confuse the target with them.
Pairs are ordered: (A[i][j], A[j][i]) and (A[j][i], A[i][j]) are different pairs unless equal.

targets.name: MOLS table: more mutually orthogonal Latin squares of some order n < 500 than the current lower bound (e.g. 4 MOLS of order 22)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (difference-matrix / permutation-code searches; SAT for small orders)
targets.statement: N(n) is the largest number of mutually orthogonal Latin squares (MOLS) of order n. The current table of lower bounds for n < 500 is Table 1 of Alice Miller, R. Julian R. Abel, Ivaylo Valkov and Douglas Fraser, 'Implementing the MOLS table for n up to 500', Symmetry 16 (2024) 1678 (CC BY). It updates the Abel-Colbourn-Dinitz Handbook table (2007) with N(14) >= 4 (Todorov), N(18) >= 5 and N(60) >= 5 (Abel), N(35) >= 6, N(48) >= 10, N(63) >= 8 (Janiszczak-Staszewski, J. Combin. Des. 2019), and N(54) >= 8, N(96) >= 10, N(108) >= 9 (Abel-Janiszczak-Staszewski, arXiv:2412.00480), plus the new N(486) >= 8. Selected current lower bounds, as n:N(n) >= value: 14:4, 15:4, 18:5, 20:4, 21:5, 22:3, 24:7, 26:4, 28:5, 30:4, 33:5, 34:4, 35:6, 36:8, 38:4, 39:5, 40:7, 42:5, 44:5, 45:6, 46:4, 50:6, 51:5, 52:5, 54:8, 55:6, 56:7, 57:7, 58:5, 60:5, 62:5. The paper notes that 22 is the only n other than 4 for which three MOLS are known but four are not. Orders 10 and 12 are covered by other bank entries.
targets.success_criterion: Success means k MOLS of order n (equivalently a TD(k+2,n), or an (n,k+1,1) difference matrix, which gives k MOLS) with k STRICTLY GREATER than the order-n entry of Table 1 of Miller-Abel-Valkov-Fraser (Symmetry 2024, 16, 1678). The order must satisfy 2 < n <= 499, must not be a prime power, and must not be 6 (N(6) = 1 is proven), 10 or 12. The squares must be verified by two independent checkers. Before claiming, re-fetch the Glasgow eprint and arXiv:2412.00480, and search arXiv for any 2025-2026 improvement at that n. A value already matched in print is not a win.

partial_wins.statement: k MOLS of order n for one of the orders 567, 622, 635, 754, 756, 764, 766, 774, 778, 802, 810, 822, 826, 894, 906, 916, 920 or 936, with k strictly greater than the value Miller et al. give in their Theorem 4 (8 for 567 and 936, 10 for the others), verified by two independent checkers.

targets.verification_method: For each square, check rows and columns are permutations of 0..n-1. For each pair of squares, check all n^2 ordered symbol pairs are distinct. For a difference matrix over a group G, check that every pair of rows has every element of G exactly once as a difference, then expand to MOLS and run the MOLS check. Use two independent programs.
angles: Order 22: Miller et al. suggest the method of Todorov (used for 4 MOLS(14) and 3 MOLS(22)) with a special (22,6,2) difference matrix; a targeted SAT/exact-cover search over that structure is the classic attack.
Separable permutation codes and difference matrices with a large automorphism group (the Janiszczak-Staszewski method) produced most recent records; try them at 20, 26, 30, 34, 38.
pitfalls: Prime powers already have N(n) = n-1; they are not targets.
Orders 10 and 12 belong to the bank entries three-mols-order-10 and erdos-723-projective-plane-order-12; claims there count only there.
(n,k,1) difference matrices give k-1 MOLS, not k; off-by-one errors are common.
The Handbook table is stale; compare against Miller et al. Table 1 and newer papers.

targets.name: Maximum number of transversals T(n): a Latin square of order 10 with more than Parker's 5504, or a new record for n = 11..20
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (counting transversals of an order-20 square takes minutes to hours)
targets.statement: T(n), the maximum number of transversals in a Latin square of order n (OEIS A090741), is known only for n <= 9 (McKay, McLeod and Wanless, Des. Codes Cryptogr. 40 (2006); Bedford; Parker). For n = 10 the best known is 5504 transversals, in a turn-square of E. T. Parker. McKay et al. report that none of the several billion order-10 squares met in an earlier search, which included every square with a nontrivial symmetry, had more. Their upper bound is T(10) <= 75000. Ian Wanless's data page lists provisional winners: n=10: 5504, 11: 37851, 12: 198144, 13: 1030367, 14: 3477504, 15: 36362925, 16: 244744192, 17: 1606008513, 18: 6434611200 (two turn-squares of Z_9 x Z_2), 19: 87656896891, 20: 697292390400. For odd n >= 11 these are the cyclic-group counts (OEIS A006717). E. I. Vatutin's A287644 comments (diagonal Latin squares) match them where they give a value. The cyclic square is optimal for n = 3, 5 and 7 but not for n = 9, where Z_3 x Z_3 (2241) beats Z_9 (2025), so the cyclic records at larger odd orders need not be optimal.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit Latin square of order n, 10 <= n <= 20, whose number of transversals is STRICTLY GREATER than the larger of the provisional winner on Wanless's data page and any larger value in OEIS A090741 or A287644 (comments and example files), re-fetched immediately before claiming. Also counted: for odd n in {21, 23}, a square with more transversals than the cyclic Latin square of that order (A006717((n-1)/2): 5778121715415 and 452794797220965). The McKay-McLeod-Wanless group table shows these beat every other group table of those orders. Counts must agree across two independently written programs.

partial_wins.statement: For some n in {10, ..., 20} other than 18 (which already has two inequivalent record squares), a Latin square whose transversal count equals the provisional winner on Wanless's data page exactly. It must not be in the same main class (species) as the square in that page's file for n, or as any square in the OEIS A090741 or A287644 example files. Show this with canonical forms under paratopy computed by two independent programs.
An independent recount that fails to reproduce a listed provisional-winner count (an error in the table), with both programs and the square.

targets.verification_method: Check the square is Latin. Count transversals with two independent exact counters (for example DLX exact cover, and row-by-row backtracking with column and symbol bitmasks). For p1, compute canonical forms under the full paratopy group (rows, columns, symbols and conjugates) using, for example, a nauty graph encoding.
angles: Even orders: perturb group tables of Z_2 x Z_m, Z_2^2 x Z_m or other groups with few cycle switches or turns, as the order-18 record was found; count transversals incrementally after each switch.
Simulated annealing on the transversal count using fast incremental counting restricted to the rows that changed.
pitfalls: The order-18 turn-squares are described incorrectly in the McKay-McLeod-Wanless paper; use the count 6434611200 and the files on Wanless's page.
These OEIS A-numbers are covered here, not by the generic OEIS 'more' entry.
Do not count diagonal transversals (Vatutin's A287648) by mistake.

targets.name: Fewest transversals in a Latin square of odd order: beat 778 (n=11), 11744 (n=13), 165289 (n=15) or a larger-order record (OEIS A091323)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (exact transversal counts up to order 21)
targets.statement: For odd n, let t(n) be the minimum number of transversals in a Latin square of order n (OEIS A091323, indexed by (n-1)/2). Ryser conjectured t(n) >= 1. Exact values are known for n <= 9 (1, 3, 3, 3, 68; McKay, McLeod and Wanless 2006). The live upper bounds have moved repeatedly in 2024-2026: Vatutin (2024-2025), Dennis Yurichev (Sep 2025), and Richard Bean on 20 Sep 2026, giving order 11: 778 (Ian Wanless's square), 13: 11744, 15: 165289, 17: 4384292, 19: 118899160, 21: 3887083600 (Bean's examples in a091323_6.txt, partly from a coloured-block construction). Zur Luria (arXiv:2609.08624, Sep 2026) proves t(n) <= ((1+o(1)) 2n/(3e^2))^n for n = 3 mod 6, improving Dai-Divoux-Kelly, so small-order records are far from settled.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit Latin square of odd order n, 11 <= n <= 21, with STRICTLY FEWER transversals than the upper bound for that order in the live OEIS A091323 entry (comments and links, re-fetched immediately before claiming; values on 2026-10-30: 778, 11744, 165289, 4384292, 118899160, 3887083600). The count must agree between two independently written programs. A square with zero transversals would disprove Ryser's conjecture: it is claimed only after a third independent check and a fresh literature search.

partial_wins.statement: A Latin square of order 11 with exactly 778 transversals that is not in the same main class as Wanless's square, shown by canonical forms under paratopy.
An independent recount that fails to reproduce a count listed in A091323 or its example files (an error), with both programs and the square.

targets.verification_method: Check the square is Latin. Count transversals with two independent exact counters (DLX, and bitmask backtracking). Compare the count with the live A091323 bound for that order.
angles: Luria's 3x3 block construction for n = 3 mod 6 (transversals confined to the diagonal blocks or avoiding them) and Bean's coloured construction are both explicit; optimise the blocks by local search at n = 15 and 21.
Hill-climb with cycle switches, scoring by an exact or sampled transversal count.
pitfalls: Even orders are trivial (Z_2m has no transversals); only odd n counts.
Diagonal Latin squares have their own sequence (A287645), covered by diagonal-latin-square-spectra-vatutin.
The bounds moved in Sep 2026; always re-fetch A091323 before claiming.

targets.name: Largest critical sets lcs(n) of Latin squares: a critical set larger than the A063437 records for n = 8..17 (Bean's 2026 searches, n = 9..15 and 17)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (uniqueness-of-completion checks by SAT/DLX for n <= 17)
targets.statement: A critical set of a Latin square L is a partial Latin square that L is the unique completion of, and that is minimal: deleting any filled cell allows a second completion. The smallest size scs(n) = floor(n^2/4) has just been proved (Richard Bean, arXiv:2610.18199, Oct 2026). The largest size lcs(n) (OEIS A063437) is known only for n <= 7, with lcs(7) = 25 (Bean, Mar 2026). The proven upper bound is lcs(n) <= n^2 - 3n + 3 (Bean and Mahmoodian, Discrete Math. 267 (2003)). Bean conjectures, in the README of github.com/RichardBean/LatinSquares, that lcs(n) <= n^2 - 3^(log2 n). The records at n = 8 (37) and n = 16 (175) meet that bound. They are the older critical sets of size 4^k - 3^k in the elementary abelian 2-group table of order 2^k (Stinson and van Rees). Lower bounds at the other orders improved sharply in 2026 through Bean's searches (OEIS comment, 13 May 2026, examples in a063437_1.txt, which has none for n = 8 or 16): lcs(9) >= 46, lcs(10) >= 59, lcs(11) >= 74, lcs(12) >= 90, lcs(13) >= 105, lcs(14) >= 126, lcs(15) >= 147, lcs(17) >= 198. Earlier records came from Stinson-van Rees (1982) and Bean's thesis (arXiv:2606.12996).
targets.success_criterion: Success means a partial Latin square P of order n, 8 <= n <= 17, with |P| STRICTLY GREATER than the live A063437 lower bound for n. Re-fetch A063437 immediately before claiming; on 2026-10-30 the bounds were 37, 46, 59, 74, 90, 105, 126, 147, 175, 198 for n = 8..17. P must satisfy: (a) P has exactly one completion to a Latin square, shown by a completion plus a DRAT-verified UNSAT proof or an exact-cover count of 1; and (b) for every filled cell e of P, P minus e has at least two completions, shown by an explicit second Latin square containing P minus e. Checked by two independent programs. At n = 8 and n = 16 the record equals Bean's conjectured bound n^2 - 3^(log2 n), which is not proven, so a win there also refutes that conjecture.

partial_wins.statement: Answer Bean's question of how many of the 147 main classes of order 7 contain a critical set of size 25 (his thesis found 113). The answer needs two independent exhaustive programs that agree, the list of classes and one size-25 critical set for each, each set checked as in the verification method.

targets.verification_method: Check P is a partial Latin square. Find its completion L. Prove uniqueness by adding the clause 'differs from L' to a Latin-square CNF with P fixed, then checking the solver's UNSAT certificate with drat-trim, or by a DLX count of 1 from two programs. For each cell of P, check the supplied alternative completion is Latin, contains P minus that cell, and differs from L.
angles: Bean's 2026 records came from perturbation and chunk-shuffle local search on fixed squares; vary the underlying square (intercalate-rich squares host large critical sets).
Grow a critical set greedily, adding cells while uniqueness fails, then prune; use an incremental SAT solver with assumptions for the many uniqueness queries.
pitfalls: A defining set that is not minimal is not a critical set; check condition (b) for every cell.
scs(n) is now proved; only the largest critical set is a target here.
Records moved in May 2026; re-fetch A063437 and Bean's repository.

targets.name: Most intercalates (2x2 subsquares) in a Latin square of order n = 10..28: beat the A092237 / A307164 records
targets.compute_profile: laptop-minutes to laptop-hours (counting intercalates is O(n^3))
targets.statement: An intercalate is a 2x2 Latin subsquare. OEIS A092237 gives the maximum number of intercalates in a Latin square of order n. Any two rows hold at most n/2 intercalates for even n, and at most (n-3)/2 for odd n, because the permutation taking one row to the other is a derangement of odd order. So a(n) <= n^2(n-1)/4 for even n and a(n) <= n(n-1)(n-3)/4 for odd n (Heinrich and Wallis; A092237 FORMULA, Sep 2026). a(n) is known for n <= 9 (Richard Bean, 2004), for powers of 2, where the elementary abelian 2-group table meets the even bound, and for n = 2^k - 1, where a known construction meets the odd bound (630 at n = 15). Lower bounds for the other orders 10..28 come from Bean (thesis 2001) and Eduard I. Vatutin (2023-2025, proving list a092237_2.txt): a(10) >= 125, a(11) >= 172, a(12) >= 324, a(13) >= 216, a(14) >= 391, a(17) >= 736, a(18) >= 729, a(19) >= 472, a(20) >= 1500, a(21) >= 1026, a(22) >= 1497, a(23) >= 985 (proving list; the comment still says 983), a(24) >= 2736, a(25) >= 1888, a(26) >= 2197, a(28) >= 2940. The diagonal-square sequence A307164 also gives lower bounds, and at n = 27 it is higher: a diagonal Latin square of order 27 with 1372 intercalates, against A092237's listed 648. So the real record at 27 is at least 1372.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit Latin square of order n, 10 <= n <= 28 with n not 15 or 16, whose number of intercalates is STRICTLY GREATER than the largest bound listed for that n in A092237 (comments and the a092237_2.txt proving-list headers) and A307164 (comments and its proving-list headers). Re-fetch all of them immediately before claiming. The 2026-10-30 values are above; the n = 23 bar is 985 and the n = 27 bar is 1372. The count must agree between two independent programs. Order 16 is excluded because 960 meets the proven bound n^2(n-1)/4. Order 15 is excluded because 630 meets the proven odd-order bound n(n-1)(n-3)/4.

partial_wins.statement: A diagonal Latin square (both diagonals are transversals) of order n, 10 <= n <= 28 with n not 15 or 16, with more intercalates than the live A307164 bound for that n. The 2026-10-30 values for n = 10..28 are 109, 172, 324, 216, 391, -, -, 736, 547, 457, 1500, 785, 887, 899, 2160, 1888, 1525, 1372, 2892.

targets.verification_method: Check the square is Latin (and, for p1, that the main diagonal and the antidiagonal each have n distinct symbols). Count intercalates: for each pair of rows r < r' and each column c, let c' be the column where row r' has the symbol L[r][c]; count when L[r'][c] = L[r][c'] and c < c'. Use two independent programs.
angles: Direct products and near-products of 2-group tables with small Latin squares (Bean's thesis Chapter 5 bounds for orders 2^a m and 2^a m + 1).
Local search with intercalate-preserving cycle switches; the count updates incrementally.
pitfalls: A092237 understates n = 27 (648) relative to A307164 (1372). Always take the max of both.
The odd-order bound is n(n-1)(n-3)/4: the permutation taking one row to another is a derangement of odd order, so it has at most (n-3)/2 transpositions. No claim may exceed it.
OEIS comments lag the proving lists: a092237_2.txt gives a(23) >= 985 while the comment says 983. Use the larger value.

An audit recount (2026-10-30, two independent counters) does not reproduce two posted witnesses. The order-17 square in both a092237_2.txt and a307164_5.txt has 272 intercalates, not the 736 in its header. The order-20 square in a307164_5.txt has 1100, not 1500 (A092237's order-20 square does give 1500). The bars stay at the listed 736 and 1500. Recount any posted square before building on it.

targets.name: Diagonal Latin squares (Vatutin's proving lists): fewer transversals, fewer or more diagonal transversals, or fewer intercalates than the best known for n = 10..28
targets.compute_profile: laptop-minutes to laptop-hours
targets.statement: A diagonal Latin square (DLS) has both main diagonals as transversals. A diagonal transversal is a transversal with exactly one cell on each main diagonal. Eduard I. Vatutin, with the Gerasim@Home/RakeSearch volunteers Natalia Makarova, Tomas Brada and Harry White, keeps proving lists of best-known DLS in OEIS. Live bounds on 2026-10-30, taking the better of each entry's comment and its best-known-examples file: min transversals in a DLS (A287645; file a287645_21.txt): n=10 <= 128, 11 <= 778, 12 <= 192, 13 <= 26132, 14 <= 2224, 15 <= 170369, 16 <= 7465984 (the comment, updated 18 Sep 2026, still gives 40806 and 25720 for n = 13 and 14). Min diagonal transversals (A287647): 10 <= 3, 11 <= 43, 13 <= 4756, 14 <= 1446, 15 <= 15510, 16 <= 898988, 17 <= 12058840, 18 <= 82577875, 19 <= 592174879, 20 <= 4488686380 (n = 12 is exactly 0). Max diagonal transversals (A287648): 10 >= 890, 11 >= 4828, 12 >= 30192, 13 >= 131106, 14 >= 490218, 15 >= 4620434, 16 >= 32172800, 17 >= 204995269, 18 >= 281593874, 19 >= 11254190082, 20 >= 90010806304, 21 >= 51162162017, 22 >= 3227747329246. Min transversals in an orthogonal DLS (A357514): 10 <= 652, 11 <= 2091, 12 <= 6240, 13 <= 80380 (the last only in a357514_1.txt). Min intercalates in a DLS (A307163): 16 <= 2, 18 <= 9, 21 <= 11, 22 <= 9, 24 <= 2, 26 <= 29, 27 <= 35, 28 <= 33. Every listed bound is open except the exact cells: A287647(12) = 0, and the A307163 cells already equal to 0 (n = 10..15, 17, 19, 20, 23, 25).
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit diagonal Latin square (for A357514, a DLS together with an orthogonal DLS mate) of order n that STRICTLY improves one listed cell in the right direction: fewer for A287645, A287647, A357514 and A307163, more for A287648. The comparison is against the better of the live OEIS comment and the headers of its 'best known examples' file, re-fetched immediately before claiming. The relevant count must agree between two independent programs. Cells with exact known values (such as A287647(12) = 0, or A307163 at orders where it is 0) cannot be improved and do not count.

partial_wins.statement: An independent recount that fails to reproduce a count in one of Vatutin's proving lists (an error in the table), with both programs and the square.

targets.verification_method: Check the square is Latin and that both diagonals contain n distinct symbols; for A357514 also check that the mate is a DLS and is orthogonal (all n^2 pairs distinct). Count transversals, diagonal transversals (with exactly one cell on the main diagonal and exactly one on the antidiagonal; for odd n the centre cell can serve as both) or intercalates with two independent programs, and compare with the live entry.
angles: Many records are found by 'diagonalising' (Vatutin et al., RuSCDays 2023) good Latin squares from the general tables: permute rows and columns of a square with few or many transversals until both diagonals are transversals.
Use the cheap counters (intercalates, diagonal transversals) as a fast filter in local search.
pitfalls: The diagonal-transversal definition is strict: exactly one cell on each main diagonal (a transversal through the centre of an odd square meets both at once).
Maximum transversals in DLS (A287644) coincide with the general table; that cell belongs to latin-max-transversals-n10-20.
A091323 (general odd-order minimum) is a lower bound for A287645 at odd n; a DLS beating A091323 also wins latin-min-transversals-odd-orders.

OEIS comments lag the examples files: on 2026-10-30, a287645_21.txt had 26132 (n = 13) and 2224 (n = 14) against the comment's 40806 and 25720, and a357514_1.txt had an n = 13 bound that the comment lacks. Always read the file headers too.

targets.name: Quantum Latin squares: realise an 'uncertain' cardinality for order 7, 9, 11 or 23 (Zhang-Lv-Cao Table 6)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (exact-arithmetic constructions; numerical search for seeds)
targets.statement: A quantum Latin square QLS(v) is a v x v array of unit vectors in C^v whose every row and every column is an orthonormal basis. Its cardinality c is the number of distinct vectors up to a global phase (Paczos et al.), so v <= c <= v^2, and c = v+1 never occurs. Yuyuan Zhang, Mingzhen Lv and Haitao Cao (arXiv:2607.19969 v2, 23 Jul 2026) prove that every c in [v, v^2] except v+1 is attained for all v >= 8 except v = 9, 11, 23. With known results for v <= 5 and order 6 now closed (Zhipeng Xu, arXiv:2607.11800, and Das-Kumar, arXiv:2608.12607, cardinality 29), the open orders are 7, 9, 11 and 23. Their Table 6 lists the uncertain cardinalities: v=7: 24-27, 29-42 and 45; v=9: 34, 60-62, 65-71, 73, 74; v=11: 13-19, 21, 48, 50, 54-115 (except 105, 111, 112) and 119; v=23: 528. Table 6 lists 105, 111 and 112 for v = 11 as both attainable and uncertain, so treat those three as attainable.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit QLS(v) for v in {7, 9, 11, 23} whose cardinality c lies in the uncertain set of Table 6 of arXiv:2607.19969 (latest version, re-fetched immediately before claiming), with c not settled by any later paper (search arXiv for 'quantum Latin square' cardinality at that order). Entries must be given exactly: algebraic numbers in a stated number field, for example cyclotomic or quadratic surds. Two independent exact-arithmetic programs must confirm that every row and every column is an orthonormal basis and that exactly c distinct rays occur.

partial_wins.statement: A numerical QLS(v) for an uncertain (v, c) with entries to at least 30 significant digits, every row and column orthonormal to residual below 1e-25, and the c rays pairwise separated (1 - | < u,w > | > 1e-6 for distinct rays, below 1e-25 for identified ones), without an exact certificate. This is a PROMISING result, not CONFIRMED.

targets.verification_method: Parse the exact entries. For each row and each column, check <u_i, u_j> = delta_ij exactly. Two unit vectors are the same ray iff | < u,w > | = 1; group the v^2 entries into rays exactly and count them. Use two independent CAS or exact-arithmetic implementations (for example SymPy and PARI/GP or Sage).
angles: Schur-product and direct-sum constructions from dephased Butson Hadamard matrices (Xu's method for order 6) carry over to 9 = 3x3 and to the prime orders with BH(p,p).
Order 23 asks only for c = 528 = v^2 - 1; the order-6 value 35 = 6^2 - 1 was realised by a mixed Butson construction, a template to adapt.
pitfalls: Floating-point orthogonality is not a certificate; exact entries are required for a full win.
Vectors equal up to a global phase are the same ray; count rays, not vectors.
Order 6 is closed; do not target it.

targets.name: Digital (t,m,s)-nets: a smaller quality parameter t than MinT's best known digital net (bases 2-9)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (exact rank checks over F_b take seconds; the search is the cost)
targets.statement: A digital (t,m,s)-net over F_b is given by s generator matrices C_1..C_s in F_b^{m x m}; its quality t is the least t such that for every (d_1..d_s) with d_i >= 0 and d_1+...+d_s = m-t the first d_i rows of the C_i together have rank m-t. Smaller t means better equidistribution. MinT, the database of Rudolf Schurer and Wolfgang Ch. Schmid (University of Salzburg; footer: database last updated 2024-09-05, but its history page lists no new methods after 2008-03-11; reachable over http only on 2026-10-30), lists for each base b and (m,s) the best known digital t and the digital lower bound. On 2026-10-30, for m <= 25 and s <= 30, base 2 has 301 cells where the constructive digital t exceeds the digital lower bound, base 3 has 355 and base 4 has 347. Smallest base-2 gaps: (m,s) = (8,11), best t = 4 (s-reduction of a digital (4,8,17)-net from net-embeddable BCH codes), bound t >= 3; (9,10) 4 vs 3; (10,8) and (10,9) 4 vs 3. Smallest base-3 gap: (6,8), t = 2 (Niederreiter-Xing sequence, genus 2) vs bound 1. Records come from Niederreiter-Xing sequences (Pirsic implementation), Sobol' and Niederreiter sequences, Edel's net-embedding search, BCH-code nets (Ling-Ozbudak; Helleseth-Klove-Levenshtein), shift nets (Schmid), the (u,u+v) construction and propagation rules. Cells where a digital net is only known to exist (MinT 'Digital' below 'Constructive and digital'), in the same range: 4 in base 2 ((23,13), (24,13), (25,13), (24,30), from a manYPoints curve), 11 in base 3, 61 in base 4, 23 in base 5, 301 in base 7 (e.g. (6,22): digital t = 2 from a Gilbert-Varshamov OOA embedding, constructive t = 3), 54 in base 8 and none in base 9.
