targets.success_criterion: Success means explicit generator matrices C_1..C_s in F_b^{m x m} (b in MinT's list 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9; for b = 4, 8, 9 the field model, e.g. F_4 = F_2[x]/(x^2+x+1), is stated) such that: (1) they form a digital (t,m,s)-net, i.e. for every composition (d_1..d_s) of m-t into s non-negative parts the first d_i rows of the C_i together have rank m-t over F_b, checked exhaustively; (2) t is STRICTLY SMALLER (direction: min) than the 'Constructive and digital' value on the live MinT query page http://mint.sbg.ac.at/query.php?b= < b > &m= < m > &s= < s > &p=smt at verification time; (3) t is at least MinT's digital lower bound on that page (below it means a bug); (4) no paper, preprint or public table of any date already gives a digital (t,m,s)-net over F_b with that t (MinT lists no new methods after 2008, so the literature since then must be checked). Two independent rank checkers must agree.

partial_wins.statement: A first explicit construction: generator matrices of a digital (t,m,s)-net over F_b (b = 3, 4 or 5) for a cell where MinT's 'Digital' (existence) value is strictly below its 'Constructive and digital' value (e.g. base 3, (m,s) = (16,23): existence t = 8, constructive t = 9), reaching the existence value, verified as in the main criterion.

A raised digital lower bound: a re-runnable exhaustive classification (with a DRAT proof checked by drat-trim, or two independent search programs that agree) showing that no digital (t,m,s)-net over F_b exists for t equal to MinT's live digital lower bound in a gap cell, e.g. no digital (3,8,11)-net over F_2.

targets.verification_method: Write an independent checker: for each composition (d_1..d_s) of k = m-t with 0 <= d_i <= k, stack the first d_i rows of each C_i and compute the rank over F_b by Gaussian elimination (bitsets for b = 2, table arithmetic for prime powers). The number of compositions is C(k+s-1, s-1), at most a few million for the tabulated range. Confirm that rank = k for all of them. Fetch the live MinT cell over http and compare with both the constructive digital value and the digital bound. Search arXiv and MathSciNet-indexed journals for newer net constructions with the same (b,m,s).
angles: Search for digital nets with a prescribed automorphism (cyclic or quasi-cyclic generator matrices, shift-net structure), so a few first rows define all matrices and the rank checks reduce by symmetry.
Use the duality with linear ordered codes (NRT codes): search for a dual NRT code of large NRT distance, then convert, as Edel's net-embedding search did.
Run an exact SAT or CP-SAT model only on the first m-t rows of each C_i; deeper rows do not affect t.
After any win, apply MinT's propagation rules (s-reduction, m-reduction, base change) to fill neighbouring cells.
pitfalls: MinT answers on http://mint.sbg.ac.at only; https was refused on 2026-10-30.
MinT table URLs need the range parameters minx, maxx, miny and maxy (as in status_source); without them MinT returns 'ERROR: Argument dx is missing'. The per-cell query.php pages need none.
MinT's history page lists no new methods after 2008-03-11 (database footer 2024-09-05), so check the literature since 2008 before claiming, not only since 2024.
Base 2 cells have been searched intensively; the lane check's 60 s randomized search found nothing for the (3,8,11) cell.
For prime-power bases, arithmetic must be in F_q, not in Z_q.

targets.name: Linear ordered orthogonal arrays of depth 2-8: higher strength than MinT's best known (MinT 'Advanced' tables)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-minutes to laptop-hours
targets.statement: A linear OOA(b^m, s, F_b, T, k) of depth T is an m x (sT) matrix over F_b whose columns form s blocks of T columns, such that for every (d_1..d_s) with 0 <= d_i <= T and d_1+...+d_s = k the first d_i columns of each block are linearly independent. Depth T = 1 gives orthogonal arrays (duals of linear codes, covered by codetables-binary-linear); depth T >= k gives digital nets. Its dual is a linear NRT (Rosenbloom-Tsfasman ordered) code. OOAs of intermediate depth feed net constructions such as the (u,u+v) rule. MinT's advanced interface (Schurer and Schmid, University of Salzburg; database footer 2024-09-05, no new methods listed after 2008-03-11) tabulates the best known strength k = m - t and lower bounds on t for depths 2..8. On 2026-10-30, base 2 depth 2 has 182 cells with constructive linear t above the linear lower bound for m <= 20, s <= 30, and depth 3 has 198. The smallest depth-2 gaps were (m,s) = (6,6), best t = 2 from an extended algebraic-geometric NRT code (genus 2), bound t >= 1, and (8,7) and (8,8), t = 3 vs 2. Short randomized depth-first searches in this lane and in an independent skeptic recheck (2026-10-30, under two minutes each, confirmed by exhaustive rank checks) found linear depth-2 OOAs over F_2 with t = 1 at (6,6) and t = 2 at (8,7) and (8,8), each meeting the bound. So the depth-2 tables are soft, and those three cells are taken. Cells (8,11), (9,7), (9,10), (9,15), (10,7), (10,9), (10,10) and (10,12) resisted 40-100 s each. An independent audit search (2026-10-30) reproduced the three easy cells in under a second each and also failed on (8,11), (9,7) and (10,7) within 60 s.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit m x (sT) matrix over F_b (b in MinT's list; field model stated for prime powers), with columns grouped into s blocks of T, whose strength k (every left-justified selection (d_1..d_s), 0 <= d_i <= T, sum k, has full column rank k, checked exhaustively) is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than m minus the 'Constructive and linear' t on the live MinT query page http://mint.sbg.ac.at/query.php?i=x&b= < b > &s= < s > &m= < m > &p=smt&de= < T > , for some depth 2 <= T <= 8 with k > T, and at most m minus that page's linear lower bound on t. With k <= T the array is a digital net; such cells belong to mint-digital-nets-lower-t and do not count here. The cells (b,T,m,s) = (2,2,6,6), (2,2,8,7) and (2,2,8,8), already reached in the 2026-10-30 lane and skeptic checks, do not count. No paper, preprint or public table of any date may already give a linear OOA (or, dually, a linear NRT code) with that strength for the cell (MinT lists no new methods after 2008).

partial_wins.statement: A raised lower bound: a re-runnable exhaustive proof (two independent programs that agree, or a DRAT proof checked with drat-trim) that no linear OOA(b^m, s, F_b, T, k) exists for k = m minus MinT's live linear lower bound on t, for some depth 2 <= T <= 8 gap cell with k > T, so the linear bound on t rises by one. It counts only if no paper or preprint already proves that bound (check the RT-metric literature since 2008, e.g. Wang, Li and Heng, IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 71 (2025) 6844-6856).

An exact rational dual certificate for the Martin-Stinson linear-programming bound for OOAs (association scheme of the ordered Hamming space), verified in exact arithmetic, that excludes an arbitrary (not necessarily linear) OOA(b^m, s, S_b, T, k) in a cell where MinT's arbitrary lower bound on t is smaller than the value the certificate gives.

targets.verification_method: Independent checker: enumerate all left-justified selections (d_1..d_s) with d_i <= T and sum k, and compute rank over F_b; confirm all have rank k, and that k is compared with the live MinT advanced-table cell (fetched over http) for the same base, depth, m and s. For p1, re-run both exhaustive programs. For p2, check dual feasibility and the objective in exact rational arithmetic.
angles: Depth-first search block by block, keeping for every vector of F_b^m the least selection cost that reaches it; a new block is rejected as soon as it closes a dependency of cost <= k. This settled the two smallest depth-2 cells in seconds.
Try depth 2 and 3 in bases 3 and 4, which nobody seems to have searched.
Seed searches from NRT codes: shorten or puncture known AG NRT codes and repair with local search.
pitfalls: Strength must be checked for left-justified selections only (prefixes of each block), not arbitrary subsets.
MinT's t is the log of the index: strength k = m - t.
MinT answers only on http; table URLs need minx, maxx, miny and maxy (as in status_source) or MinT returns 'ERROR: Argument dx is missing'. Read the query page for the exact depth T you claim.

MinT lists no new methods after 2008; search the NRT-code and OOA literature since then before claiming, e.g. LFSR-based OOA constructions (Castoldi, Moura, Panario and Stevens, arXiv:2208.00333) and new RT-metric bounds and optimal linear matrix codes (Wang, Li and Heng, IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 2025).
A strength k <= T makes the array a digital net: that is a different target (mint-digital-nets-lower-t).

targets.name: MOONSHOT - A (t,m,s)-net that beats every digital net: t below MinT's proven digital lower bound, e.g. a (2,8,7)-net in base 2
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (SAT or exact search over 2^m-point sets)
targets.statement: A (t,m,s)-net in base b is a set of b^m points in [0,1)^s such that every elementary box of volume b^(t-m) contains exactly b^t points. In MinT (Schurer and Schmid, University of Salzburg; database last updated 2024-09-05), on 2026-10-30 the best known arbitrary t equals the best digital t in every cell checked (bases 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8, m <= 25, s <= 30). So no non-digital net is known to beat digital nets anywhere in these tables. Yet in 49 base-2 cells, 110 base-3 cells and 105 base-4 cells the general lower bound on t is strictly below the proven digital lower bound, so only a non-digital net can improve them. Base-2 examples: (m,s) = (8,7): no digital (2,8,7)-net (Schmid-Wolf bound on the embedded linear OOA), but the general bound is only t >= 2 (generalized Rao bound); (9,7) has the same gap; (7,12) and (7,13): no digital (3,7,12)-net (Fontaine-Peterson bound on the embedded linear OA), general bound t >= 3 from the LP bound for OOAs, and a non-linear OA(2^7,12,2,4) does exist (Nordstrom-Robinson/Kerdock); (8,12), (8,18) to (8,20). Base-4 examples: (1,4,18) to (1,4,21) and (1,5,12).
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit set of b^m points, each coordinate written as an integer a in [0, b^m) standing for a/b^m, that is a (t,m,s)-net in base b (every elementary box of volume b^(t-m) contains exactly b^t points, checked exhaustively), with t STRICTLY SMALLER (direction: min) than MinT's live digital lower bound for (b,m,s) (http://mint.sbg.ac.at/query.php?b= < b > &m= < m > &s= < s > &p=smt, 'Lower bound on t (digital)') and at least MinT's general lower bound on the same page (below it means a bug). Such a set is necessarily non-digital. No paper, preprint or public table of any date may already contain a net with these parameters (MinT lists no new methods after 2008).

partial_wins.statement: A closed cell: an exact certificate that no (t,m,s)-net in base b exists for t equal to MinT's general lower bound in one of the cells where it is below the digital bound (e.g. no (2,8,7)-net in base 2). The certificate is an exact rational dual solution of the linear-programming bound for the embedded OOA, verified in exact arithmetic, or a DRAT proof of unsatisfiability checked with drat-trim. MinT's general lower bound then rises.

targets.verification_method: For each composition (d_1..d_s) of k = m - t with d_i >= 0, map every point to the box index (floor(a_i / b^(m-d_i)))_i and check that each of the b^k boxes holds exactly b^t points. For (2,8,7) this is 924 compositions of 6 over 256 points. Check also that there are exactly b^m points. Read the digital and general bounds from the live MinT query page over http. For p1, re-verify the LP dual or the DRAT proof independently.
angles: Start from non-linear objects that already beat linear ones: Nordstrom-Robinson, Kerdock and Preparata OAs and Z4-linear codes, and look for an ordering of digits that gives the extra depth a net needs.

Encode the (2,8,7) net as SAT: 256 points x 7 coordinates x 6 digits (only the first m-t = 6 digits of each coordinate matter), with cardinality constraints per box; break symmetry by fixing the first coordinate to the van der Corput order.
For base 4, Z4-linear (Gray-map) constructions are the natural non-digital candidates.
pitfalls: A digital net can never win here: the digital bounds are proofs.
MinT's query page shows two different lines, 'Lower bound on t (digital)' and 'Lower bound on t'; compare with the right one.
Check the general lower bound, too: a claimed t below it means a checker bug.

targets.name: (t,s)-sequences in base 2 or 3: close a MinT gap between the best known t and the lower bound (smallest: is there a (4,8)-sequence in base 2?)
targets.compute_profile: pure thought plus laptop-hours (exact LP certificates or exhaustive digital searches)
targets.statement: A (t,s)-sequence in base b is an infinite sequence in [0,1)^s whose aligned blocks of b^m points form (t,m,s)-nets for every m. Smaller t is better. MinT (Schurer and Schmid, University of Salzburg; database last updated 2024-09-05) lists, on 2026-10-30, these gaps in base 2: s = 8, best digital t = 5 (Niederreiter-Xing, genus 5), lower bound t >= 4; s = 9, 6 vs 5; s = 10, 8 vs 6; s = 11, 9 vs 7; s = 12, constructive 11, a digital 10 known to exist (Niederreiter-Xing on a manYPoints curve of genus 10 with 13 rational places), bound 7. Base 3: s = 8, 3 vs 2; s = 10, 4 vs 3; s = 12, 5 vs 4; s = 13, 6 vs 4. A (t,s)-sequence gives a (t,m,s+1)-net for every m, so MinT's bounds come from finite cases. For example, no (3,m,8)-net exists for large m because m-reduction gives a (3,16,8)-net, whose embedded OOA(2^16, 8, S_2, 4, 13) violates the linear-programming bound for OOAs (Martin-Stinson). Explicit sequence records come from Niederreiter and Xing's function-field constructions, implemented by Pirsic.
targets.success_criterion: Either of two outcomes is a win. (A) Lower bound: an exact certificate that no (t,m,s+1)-net in base b exists for some m, with b in {2,3}, t equal to MinT's live lower bound for (t,s)-sequences (http://mint.sbg.ac.at/query.php?b= < b > &m=seq&s= < s > &p=mst, 'Lower bound on t'), where that bound is STRICTLY BELOW the best known t (direction: raise the bound). The certificate is an exact rational dual solution of the LP bound for an OOA(b^m, s+1, S_b, T, m-t) of any depth T, verified in exact arithmetic. MinT's lower bound for that s then rises. (B) Construction: a digital (t,s)-sequence over F_b, b in {2,3}, with t STRICTLY BELOW (direction: min) the smallest t listed on that MinT page (constructive or existence-only), defined by a finite algebraic recipe for its generator matrices and accompanied either by a machine-checked proof (Lean, Coq or Isabelle) of its t-value or by an instance of a published theorem whose hypotheses (genus, number and degrees of places of an explicit function field) are verified by two independent computer algebra systems. Neither outcome may already appear in any paper or preprint of any date (MinT lists no new methods after 2008, so the literature since then counts).

partial_wins.statement: A digital-only bound: a re-runnable exhaustive proof (DRAT checked with drat-trim, or two independent programs that agree) that no digital (4,m,9)-net over F_2 exists for some m (MinT's digital net bound for s = 9 is 4, e.g. at m = 13, 14, 20 and 25). This proves that no digital (4,8)-sequence over F_2 exists. It counts only if no paper or preprint already proves that the least t of a digital 8-dimensional sequence over F_2 is 5.

A constructive digital (10,12)-sequence over F_2, matching MinT's existence value (constructive value 11): an explicit genus-10 function field over F_2 with at least 13 rational places (genus and place count confirmed by two computer algebra systems), plus generator matrices built from it by the Niederreiter-Xing construction, with the exact t-value of the induced digital (t,m,13)-nets confirmed to be at most 10 for every m <= 30. It counts only if no explicit such function field and no generator matrices of a digital (10,12)-sequence over F_2 are already published (check the references of the manYPoints entry for q = 2, g = 10 and Pirsic's Niederreiter-Xing matrix files).

targets.verification_method: For (A), rebuild the OOA LP (Martin-Stinson ordered Hamming scheme, or MinT's cited LP for OOAs) for the stated parameters and check the dual certificate in exact rationals. For (B), re-run the proof checker or both CAS computations, then sample-check the t-value of the generated nets for m <= 30 with an independent rank checker. Read the live MinT 'Seq' cell over http before claiming.
angles: MinT's sequence bounds use the OOA LP only up to depth 4; LP bounds at depth 5-8, or for larger m, may be sharper.
For p1, the digital (4,13,9)-net search only involves the first 9 rows of nine 13 x 13 matrices over F_2; exploit the column-operation symmetry.
Constructions using places of higher degree (Niederreiter-Xing construction III) can beat the rational-place bound N_2(g).
pitfalls: Sequences have their own MinT query pages (m=seq). The page with m=inf and a given s is the (t,infinity,s)-net, which corresponds to the (t,s-1)-sequence; do not mix up the offsets.
Finite checks of nets from a sequence prove nothing about all m; a construction needs a proof.
Curves from manYPoints: lowering N_q(g) is the separate target manypoints-curves-finite-fields-lower-bounds.

MinT lists no new methods after 2008; check the literature since then (e.g. duality theory for digital sequences) before claiming. Table URLs need their range parameters or MinT returns 'Argument dx is missing'.

Pirsic's legacy Niederreiter-Xing page (sites.google.com/site/isabelpirsic/nxlegacy) redirected to a Google login on 2026-10-30. Nuyens' QMC generators page (people.cs.kuleuven.be/~dirk.nuyens/qmc-generators/) says it mirrors those matrices (nxmats.tgz). Check both before claiming p2.

targets.name: Binary orthogonal arrays with 2^m runs beyond every linear OA: higher strength than MinT's best known (smallest: OA(256, 20, 2, 4))
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: An orthogonal array OA(2^m, s, 2, k) is a 2^m x s binary array in which every k columns contain each binary k-tuple equally often. Linear OAs are duals of linear codes (covered by codetables-binary-linear). Non-linear ones can be stronger: the Nordstrom-Robinson, Kerdock, Preparata and Delsarte-Goethals codes give, e.g., OA(2^8,16,2,5) and OA(2^7,15,2,4), which no linear OA matches. MinT's orthogonal-array table (Schurer and Schmid, University of Salzburg; database footer 2024-09-05, no new methods listed after 2008-03-11) lists the best known strength and upper bounds for OAs with 2^m runs. On 2026-10-30, for m <= 25 and s <= 40, 131 base-2 cells have a best known strength below the general upper bound while already equal to the linear upper bound, so only a non-linear array can improve them. Smallest (by m): (m,s) = (8,20), best k = 3, bound 4; (9,21) 4 vs 5; (9,24)-(9,29) 3 vs 4; (10,25)-(10,30) 4 vs 5; (10,34)-(10,40) 3 vs 4; (11,35)-(11,40) 4 vs 5; (12,25), (12,26) 5 vs 6; (13,26), (13,27) 6 vs 7; (13,28)-(13,34) 5 vs 6; (14,18)-(14,20) 7 vs 8. For arrays without repeated rows this is equivalent to a binary code of length s and size 2^m whose dual distance (Delsarte) is at least k+1.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit 2^m x s array over {0,1} such that every set of k columns contains each of the 2^k binary k-tuples exactly 2^(m-k) times (checked exhaustively, or via all Walsh-Fourier coefficients of weight 1..k vanishing, in exact integer arithmetic), with k STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than both MinT's live best known strength for (m,s) on http://mint.sbg.ac.at/query.php?i=o&b=2&m= < m > &s= < s > &p=smk&de=1 (or the table in status_source) and that page's 'Upper bound on k (linear)'. The array is then necessarily non-linear; cells where a linear array could still win belong to codetables-binary-linear. k must also be at most MinT's general upper bound (above it means a bug). No paper, preprint or public table of any date may already reach that strength for (m,s) (MinT lists no new methods after 2008).

partial_wins.statement: A lowered upper bound: a re-checkable exact certificate proving that no OA(2^m, s, 2, k) exists for k equal to MinT's live upper bound in one of the 131 gap cells, so that the upper bound drops to the best known strength. The certificate is either an LP or SDP dual solution (Delsarte LP with added constraints, or a semidefinite bound) verified in exact rational arithmetic, or a re-runnable exhaustive classification (DRAT proof checked by drat-trim, or two independent programs that agree). It counts only if no paper or preprint already proves that nonexistence (check, e.g., the Bulutoglu-Margot integer-programming classifications and the Boyvalenkov et al. and Kiss-Nagy nonexistence papers).

targets.verification_method: Independent checker: for every k-subset of columns, count the 2^k patterns over all 2^m rows and require 2^(m-k) each; for s = 20, k = 4 this is 4845 subsets of 256 rows. Alternatively compute the Walsh transform of the row multiset and require zero coefficients at all weights 1..k. Read the live MinT cell over http for both the best known value and the bound.
angles: Search Z4-linear codes (Gray images) and their shortenings: the known non-linear winners are all of this kind.
Union-of-cosets constructions: take a linear OA of strength k-1 and choose cosets of a subcode so that the strength-k Fourier coefficients cancel; solve as an exact cover or SAT.
Lengthen known non-linear OAs (Kerdock K(4), Delsarte-Goethals) by appending columns and repairing with local search on the Walsh spectrum.
pitfalls: A linear array cannot win in these cells: the linear upper bound is a proof.
MinT counts runs as exactly 2^m; arrays with other run sizes belong to other tables.
Do not confuse strength (dual distance minus one) with minimum distance.

targets.name: Finite point sets with record-low L-infinity star discrepancy in [0,1]^2 (n = 22..1020) or [0,1]^3 (n = 9..5000)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (exact 2D evaluation is O(n^2); 3D up to a few thousand points is feasible)
targets.statement: The star discrepancy D*(P) of n points is the largest gap between the fraction of points in an anchored box [0,q) (or [0,q]) and its volume. Optimal sets are known only for n <= 21 in 2D and n <= 8 in 3D (Clement, Doerr, Klamroth, Paquete, arXiv:2311.17463). Beyond that, the best published values are spread over several recent papers. Clement-Doerr-Klamroth-Paquete's permutation-based sets (arXiv:2407.11533, PNAS 2025; point files at github.com/frclement/LowDiscPermu): Table 1 gives 2D n = 180: 0.00901, n = 260: 0.00640, n = 420: 0.00412. The text reports 0.02709 (Fig. 3 caption 0.027088) for n = 50, 0.014444 for n = 100, '0.01' for n = 150 and 0.007718 for n = 200. Table 2 covers 3D up to n = 50. Rusch, Kirk, Bronstein, Lemieux and Rus's Message-Passing Monte Carlo (arXiv:2405.15059): 2D n = 20..1020 in steps of 40, e.g. n = 1020: 0.00303. Sadikov's OpenEvolve sets (arXiv:2510.03650 and its repository): 2D n = 500: 0.00509, n = 1020: 0.00245; 3D n = 9..16. Chen, Clement, Doerr and Kirk's L2 subset selection (arXiv:2511.02706): 3D and 2D tables for n = 50..2000. Clement et al.'s projected gradient descent post-processing (arXiv:2511.10496): 2D and 3D tables, not records at its tabulated 2D sizes. FlowBoost (Berczi, Hashemi, Kluver, arXiv:2601.18005): 2D n = 60: 0.029440, not a record. Ait Abderrahim, Doerr, Durand (arXiv:2604.00786 v2): 3D n = 20..5000, e.g. n = 50: 0.04979 after post-processing, n = 500: 0.01115, n = 5000: 0.00210. Several 'new best' claims are beaten by other papers (e.g. Sadikov's 2D n = 100 value 0.01504 versus 0.014444), so the record for a size is the minimum over all sources. The ALGO lab benchmark page cited by FlowBoost (algo.dei.uc.pt/star) did not resolve on 2026-10-30.
targets.success_criterion: Success means n explicit points in [0,1)^d, d in {2,3}, with coordinates given as exact decimals or rationals, whose star discrepancy D*, computed exactly in rational arithmetic by two independent implementations, is STRICTLY SMALLER (direction: min) than the smallest value published for that exact (d,n) in any paper, preprint or public results repository of any date, by more than half a unit in the last printed digit of that value. A value printed with fewer than four significant digits (e.g. the '0.01' for 2D n = 150 in arXiv:2407.11533) is read as if padded with zeros to four significant digits (0.01000, so the bar is 0.009995). A posted point file counts at its exact D* as computed by the verifier, if that is lower. Sources include at least arXiv:2407.11533 (including values stated in its text, and its PNAS 2025 version), github.com/frclement/LowDiscPermu, arXiv:2405.15059, 2510.03650 and its repository, 2511.02706, 2511.10496, 2601.18005, 2604.00786, and anything newer. Here 22 <= n <= 1020 for d = 2 and 9 <= n <= 5000 for d = 3, and some source must give a value for that (d,n). Sizes with a proven optimum (n <= 21 in 2D, n <= 8 in 3D) do not count.

partial_wins.statement: A new proven optimum: the exact optimal star discrepancy for 2D with n = 22 or for 3D with n = 9, with an optimal point set and an optimality certificate (the Clement et al. MILP model solved to proven optimality and re-solved to the same optimum by a second, independent solver), extending the known optimal range.

targets.verification_method: 2D: sort the points and evaluate, for every grid corner q built from the point coordinates and 1, both the open-box excess vol(q) - |P in [0,q)|/n and the closed-box excess |P in [0,q]|/n - vol(q), in exact fractions; D* is the maximum. 3D: use the Dobkin-Eppstein-Mitchell algorithm or an O(n^3 log n) sweep, cross-checked against a brute-force O(n^4) evaluation for n <= 200. Then look up the minimum published value for (d,n) across all listed sources and newer arXiv papers.
angles: Clement et al.'s permutation trick: fix the relative order of a good set and solve the LP for the optimal coordinates; apply it to the best sets of the other papers.
Local search on the exact discrepancy with moves that only touch the critical boxes, followed by the permutation LP as a final polish.
pitfalls: Many papers compare only with a subset of the others; take the minimum over all sources for each n.
Floating-point discrepancy codes misreport ties at critical boxes; final numbers must come from exact arithmetic.
Records exist only at the sizes the papers tabulate; a size with no published value is not a record.
Posted point files are not the whole record: arXiv:2407.11533 states lower values in its text (n = 50: 0.027088, n = 100: 0.014444) than in its Table 1 or its posted files.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Regular tetrahedra: a packing of congruent regular tetrahedra denser than the Chen-Engel-Glotzer dimer double lattice 4000/4671 = 0.856347...
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (periodic hard-polyhedron compression of small cells, then exact certification in minutes)
targets.statement: What is the largest fraction of R^3 that congruent non-overlapping regular tetrahedra can fill? This is part of Hilbert's 18th problem (Aristotle wrongly thought tetrahedra tile space). After a 2006-2010 race (Conway-Torquato about 0.72; Chen 2008 0.7786; Torquato-Jiao 2009 0.823; Haji-Akbari et al. 2009, a quasicrystal approximant of 0.8503; Kallus-Elser-Gravel 2010, 100/117 = 0.854700 with 4 tetrahedra per cell; Torquato-Jiao, analytic dimer constructions up to 12250/14319 = 0.855506), Elizabeth Chen, Michael Engel and Sharon Glotzer (Discrete Comput. Geom. 44 (2010) 253-280, arXiv:1001.0586) gave a three-parameter family of double-dimer packings (triangular bipyramids, 4 tetrahedra per cell) of density exactly 4000/4671 = 0.85634767715692571... This is still the densest known packing on the Wikipedia 'Tetrahedron packing' page (fetched 2026-10-30). The best rigorous upper bound is only 1 - 2.6e-25 (Gravel, Elser and Kallus, DCG 2011, arXiv:1008.2830). The densest lattice packing is 18/49 (Hoylman 1970). Jin, Lu and Li (Sci. Rep. 2015) showed that for slightly ROUNDED tetrahedra a quasicrystal approximant beats the dimer lattice; this does not apply to sharp regular tetrahedra. Web searches on 2026-10-30 found no denser packing of regular tetrahedra and no upper bound below 1 - 2.6e-25 (Dostert, Guzman, de Oliveira Filho and Vallentin, arXiv:1510.02331, bound translative packings only).
targets.success_criterion: Success means a periodic packing: a lattice basis L (3 vectors) and k tetrahedra, each given by 4 vertices with exact rational coordinates (or exact algebraic numbers) such that every tetrahedron is EXACTLY regular, with all six edge lengths equal to a common value a, checked exactly. (1) Interiors are pairwise disjoint over all tetrahedron pairs, including lattice translates within the circumradius cutoff. This is certified exactly by a separating plane per pair (supplied or found by LP) with all vertices of one body weakly on each side. (2) The density k*(a^3/(6*sqrt2))/|det L|, computed exactly, is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than 4000/4671 and than any denser value published by verification time. Rational approximations that are not exactly regular do not count. Instead, shrink each tetrahedron about its centroid by a certified factor and report the density after shrinking.

partial_wins.statement: A new periodic packing of regular tetrahedra whose primitive cell holds a number of tetrahedra other than 4 (so it is not in the Kallus-Elser-Gravel, Torquato-Jiao or Chen-Engel-Glotzer dimer families), with certified density STRICTLY GREATER than 100/117 = 0.854700... (Kallus-Elser-Gravel), certified as in the main criterion.

A rigorous upper bound on the packing density of regular tetrahedra strictly below 1 - 2.6e-25 (Gravel-Elser-Kallus 2011). The proof must be machine-checked or come as a re-runnable exact or interval-arithmetic computation that the skeptic re-executes, with a written reduction that matches it.

targets.verification_method: Independent script in exact arithmetic (sympy or fractions over Q(sqrt2) after a rational change of basis, or an interval library). Check that all 6 edge lengths squared are equal and exact for each body. Enumerate lattice images within 2*circumradius. For every pair, solve a small LP for a separating plane, then re-check it exactly against the 8 vertices. Compute |det L| exactly and the density, then compare with 4000/4671 using exact rational comparison. Calibrate by rebuilding the Chen-Engel-Glotzer packing from arXiv:1001.0586 Theorem 1 and recovering 4000/4671 exactly.
angles: Search periodic cells with 8-16 tetrahedra under exact regularity, using event-driven or ASC (adaptive shrinking cell) compression. Chen-Engel-Glotzer's 3-parameter optimum is a local maximum within dimer families only.

Combine dimer (bipyramid) units with other face-sharing clusters (pentagonal dipyramids, icosahedral fragments) in larger cells. Quasicrystal approximants became competitive for rounded tetrahedra (Jin-Lu-Li 2015).
pitfalls: Floating-point overlap tests: near-face-to-face contacts make tiny overlaps look like touching, so certify with exact separating planes.
Slightly irregular 'tetrahedra' from rational rounding are not regular: shrink them, never stretch them.
The Haji-Akbari 0.8503 quasicrystal and the 100/117 = 0.8547 KEG packing are below the record; do not compare against them.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Archimedean solids without central symmetry: beat 207/208 for truncated tetrahedra (Jiao-Torquato), or the lattice records 0.787699 / 0.788640 for the chiral snub cube and snub dodecahedron
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (floppy-box or adaptive-shrinking-cell Monte Carlo, small cells; exact check in minutes)
targets.statement: Three Archimedean solids lack a centre of symmetry: the truncated tetrahedron and the two chiral snubs. Torquato and Jiao (Phys. Rev. E 80, 041104 (2009), arXiv:0909.0940, Table IV) list the optimal Bravais-lattice densities of the Archimedean solids from Betke and Henk (Comput. Geom. 16 (2000), arXiv:math/9909172). These include the snub cube at 0.787699 and the snub dodecahedron at 0.788640. That paper wrongly calls the truncated tetrahedron the only non-centrally-symmetric Archimedean solid. Because the snubs lack central symmetry, non-lattice packings that use several rotated copies might be denser, as Torquato and Jiao conjecture is generic for shapes without central symmetry. Only proper motions are allowed: the point inversion x -> -x turns a chiral snub into its mirror image, which is not allowed here. Truncated tetrahedra: Conway and Torquato (PNAS 103 (2006) 10612) reached 23/24, de Graaf, van Roij and Dijkstra (PRL 107, 155501 (2011), arXiv:1107.0603) found a 0.988 dimer lattice, and Jiao and Torquato (J. Chem. Phys. 135, 151101 (2011), arXiv:1107.2300v4) built an analytic packing of density 207/208 = 0.995192... whose holes are small regular tetrahedra. Damasceno, Engel and Glotzer (ACS Nano 2012, arXiv:1109.1323) also reach 207/208 for this shape. It is believed optimal but this is not proven. De Graaf et al. state that their floppy-box runs reproduced the Archimedean literature values from below. Searches and fetches on 2026-10-30 found no later record for these three shapes. The de Graaf supplementary table (APS, returned 401) and the Damasceno-Engel-Glotzer Science 2012 supplement were not read.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a periodic packing (lattice basis plus k congruent copies, each a rigid motion of one fixed solid with exact or certified vertex coordinates; for the snubs, mirror images are NOT allowed, since they are not congruent by a proper motion, only rotations and translations) such that (1) interiors are pairwise disjoint, certified exactly or by interval arithmetic with explicit separating planes for every pair within the circumradius cutoff, and (2) the density k*vol/|det L| is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the bar for that solid: 207/208 for the truncated tetrahedron, 0.787699 for the snub cube, 0.788640 for the snub dodecahedron. The bar is the max of these and any denser value published by verification time, including the de Graaf et al. 2011 supplementary table if the verifier can read it. Margin: 1e-6 above the 6-decimal table values for the snubs.

partial_wins.statement: A non-lattice periodic packing of snub cubes or snub dodecahedra (k >= 2 per primitive cell, proper rotations only) whose certified density equals or exceeds that solid's Betke-Henk lattice density minus 1e-4. This is evidence on the Torquato-Jiao generic non-lattice conjecture for chiral shapes.

An exact re-derivation of a lattice density for either snub that differs from the Table IV value of arXiv:0909.0940 in the 6th decimal or earlier, with the lattice certified as a packing and as locally optimal: a certified table correction.

targets.verification_method: Build the solid from exact vertex formulas (snub cube via the tribonacci constant, snub dodecahedron via the root of its cubic; use 50-digit interval enclosures). Apply the claimed rotations as rational quaternions, normalized exactly, or as interval matrices. Check pairwise non-overlap with separating planes verified in interval arithmetic, and compute volume and |det L| as intervals. Accept only if the lower end of the density interval exceeds the bar. Calibrate on the Betke-Henk lattice from Appendix A of arXiv:0909.0940 (recover 0.787699 and 0.788640) and on the 207/208 construction of arXiv:1107.2300.
angles: For the snubs, try 2-particle cells pairing a copy with a copy turned by a proper rotation (e.g. 180 degrees about an axis that is not a symmetry axis of the solid), as in the dimer packings of tetrahedra. The point inversion x -> -x is not a proper motion and gives the mirror image of a chiral snub, so it is not allowed.
pitfalls: The snub cube and snub dodecahedron are chiral: their mirror images are not congruent by proper motions. Packings that mix enantiomers are a different problem.
Torquato-Jiao's text calls the snubs centrally symmetric; they are not. Do not cite their conjecture as covering them.
207/208 leaves only tiny tetrahedral holes. Beating it is far less likely than the snub cases.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Torquato-Jiao conjecture: a non-lattice packing of a centrally symmetric Platonic or Archimedean solid denser than its optimal lattice packing
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (multi-particle periodic compression; exact certification in minutes)
targets.statement: Torquato and Jiao (Nature 460, 876 (2009), arXiv:0908.4107; full version Phys. Rev. E 80, 041104, arXiv:0909.0940) conjectured that the densest packings of the centrally symmetric Platonic and Archimedean solids are their optimal Bravais lattice packings, an analogue of Kepler's conjecture. The lattice optima come from Minkowski (octahedron 18/19), Betke and Henk (Comput. Geom. 16 (2000) 157-186, arXiv:math/9909172) and Hoylman. Non-tiling cases with their Table III/IV lattice densities: icosahedron 0.836357, dodecahedron 0.904508 = (5+sqrt5)/8, octahedron 18/19 = 0.947368, truncated icosahedron 0.784987, rhombicosidodecahedron 0.804708, truncated icosidodecahedron 0.827213, truncated cuboctahedron 0.849373, icosidodecahedron 0.864720, rhombicuboctahedron 0.875805, truncated dodecahedron 0.897787, cuboctahedron 45/49 = 0.918367, truncated cube 0.973747. Wikipedia's Packing problems page (fetched 2026-10-30) still says simulations only 'suggest' these lattices are optimal. For octahedra the best rigorous upper bound is 1 - 1.4e-12 (Gravel-Elser-Kallus 2011). Jiao, Stillinger and Torquato (PRE 79, 041309 (2009), arXiv:0902.1504) made the same lattice-optimality conjecture for superballs |x|^2p+|y|^2p+|z|^2p <= 1, p >= 1/2, with candidate lattices O0/O1 (1/2 <= p <= 1) and C0/C1 (p >= 1). Ni, Gantapara, de Graaf, van Roij and Dijkstra (Soft Matter 8 (2012), arXiv:1111.4357) then found Bravais crystals denser than O0 and O1 for 1/2 < p < 1 (bct 0.7661 against 0.7656 at p = 0.85; deformed bcc 0.832839 against 0.824976 at p = 0.7). Those candidate lattices are therefore not optimal, but no non-lattice superball packing is known to beat the best lattice. De Graaf et al. (2011) report the same lattice behaviour for centrally symmetric Johnson and Catalan solids. No counterexample is known.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a periodic, non-Bravais packing (lattice basis L plus k >= 2 congruent copies per primitive cell, proper rigid motions, exact or 50-digit interval vertex coordinates) of one of the twelve centrally symmetric non-tiling solids listed in the statement, such that pairwise interiors are disjoint (certified by a separating plane for each pair within the circumradius cutoff, checked in exact or interval arithmetic) and the certified lower end of the density interval k*vol/|det L| is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than that solid's optimal lattice density (exact value for 18/19, 45/49 and (5+sqrt5)/8; otherwise the Betke-Henk value recomputed exactly by the verifier from arXiv:math/9909172 or Appendix A of arXiv:0909.0940, and at least 1e-6 above the 6-decimal value).

partial_wins.statement: Superballs: for some exactly stated p >= 1/2, p != 1, a periodic packing of the superball |x|^2p+|y|^2p+|z|^2p <= 1 whose certified density strictly exceeds both the best Jiao-Stillinger-Torquato candidate lattice at that p (O0/O1 for 1/2 <= p <= 1, C0/C1 for p >= 1, arXiv:0902.1504, recomputed by the verifier) and every published packing at that p. For 1/2 < p < 1 that includes the denser Bravais crystals of Ni et al. (arXiv:1111.4357), which already beat O0/O1 (e.g. 0.832839 at p = 0.7), so beating O0/O1 alone is not a win.

A rigorous upper bound on the density of regular octahedron packings strictly below 1 - 1.4e-12 (Gravel-Elser-Kallus, arXiv:1008.2830), delivered as a re-runnable exact or interval computation with a written reduction that the skeptic re-executes.

targets.verification_method: Exact vertex formulas in Q(sqrt2, sqrt5) or 50-digit intervals. Rotations are interval matrices from rational quaternions. For each pair, check a separating plane against all vertices in interval arithmetic. Density uses exact volumes and an interval determinant. Calibrate by reproducing each Betke-Henk lattice from Appendix A of arXiv:0909.0940 and checking that it is a packing with the tabulated density. For superballs, overlap needs a certified test, e.g. a separating plane checked against support functions in interval arithmetic.
pitfalls: A Bravais lattice re-expressed with a supercell (k copies, identical orientations, lattice-related positions) is not a new packing. Require at least two distinct orientations or a non-lattice translate set.
The cube and truncated octahedron tile space (density 1) and are excluded.
Six-decimal table values are rounded: recompute the lattice optimum exactly before claiming a 1e-6 win.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Congruent ellipsoids: a periodic packing denser than the Donev-Stillinger-Chaikin-Torquato SM2 crystal (0.770732, aspect ratios >= sqrt3)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (event-driven or Monte Carlo compression of small periodic cells; certification in minutes)
targets.statement: Densest packing of congruent ellipsoids (semi-axes a, b, c) in R^3. An affine image of FCC, the densest lattice packing, gives only 0.7405. Bezdek and Kuperberg (1991) built non-lattice packings of elongated ellipsoids of density 0.7533, and Wills (1991) raised this to 0.7585. Donev, Stillinger, Chaikin and Torquato (Phys. Rev. Lett. 92, 255506 (2004), arXiv:cond-mat/0403286) found crystals with two ellipsoids per cell in different orientations, a family later named SM2 by Pfleiderer and Schilling (2007). SM2 beats the best lattice packing for a wide range of aspect ratios near the sphere and reaches 0.770732 for prolate and oblate spheroids with aspect ratio at least sqrt3 (or at most 1/sqrt3). The axis perpendicular to the layers can be rescaled without changing the density, so SM2 crystals of triaxial ellipsoids whose in-layer axes have ratio sqrt3 reach the same 0.770732. Jin, Jiao, Liu, Yuan and Li (Phys. Rev. E 95, 033003 (2017), arXiv:1608.07697) found a 24-particle square-triangle (SQ-TR) crystal. It beats SM2 for self-dual ellipsoids a:b:c = alpha:sqrt(alpha):1 with alpha in (1.365, 1.5625), with a maximum of about 0.75806 at alpha = 93/64, still below 0.770732. So 0.770732 is the densest known value for congruent ellipsoids of any shape. No upper bound close to it is known. Web and arXiv searches on 2026-10-30 found no denser packing published from 2017 to 2026.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a periodic packing of congruent ellipsoids with exactly stated semi-axes (rational a >= b >= c) given by a rational lattice basis L and k ellipsoids, each with a rational centre and an orientation given by a rational quaternion. (1) Every pair within the cutoff 2a, including lattice images, has disjoint interiors, certified by a Perram-Wertheim witness: a rational lambda in (0,1) with contact function F(lambda) >= 1 + 1e-12, evaluated in exact rational arithmetic (F >= 1 for any lambda implies non-overlap). (2) The density k*(4/3)*pi*abc/|det L|, with pi enclosed by an interval, is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than 0.770732 + 1e-6 and than any denser value published by verification time.

partial_wins.statement: A periodic congruent-ellipsoid packing with at least 3 ellipsoids per primitive cell in at least 3 distinct orientations and density >= 0.770732 - 1e-4, certified as in the main criterion. Two-orientation crystals do not count: SM2 crystals of spheroids, and their stretches along the layer normal (which include triaxial ellipsoids), already reach 0.770732.

targets.verification_method: Pure rational arithmetic. Build each ellipsoid matrix A_i = R_i diag(1/a^2,1/b^2,1/c^2) R_i^T from a rational quaternion, normalizing by |q|^2 exactly. Use F(lambda) = lambda(1-lambda) r^T [ (1-lambda) A_i^{-1} + lambda A_j^{-1} ]^{-1} r with r the centre difference. Check the supplied witness lambda exactly; any value F >= 1 certifies non-overlap. Enumerate lattice images with |r| < 2a. Compute |det L| exactly and compare the density lower bound with the bar. Calibrate by rebuilding SM2 at aspect ratio sqrt3 (rational approximation, slightly shrunk) and recovering about 0.7707.
pitfalls: Perram-Wertheim contact tests in floating point can pass for overlapping pairs at near contact; only an exact rational witness counts.
Affine images of sphere packings never exceed 0.7405; any 'win' that is affine to FCC is a checker bug.
Stretching an SM2 crystal along its layer normal gives triaxial ellipsoids at exactly the SM2 density; this is a known construction, not a new packing.
The SQ-TR crystal (Jin et al. 2017) beats SM2 only for self-dual ellipsoids with alpha in (1.365, 1.5625), and stays below 0.770732; it is a shape-specific record, not the overall one.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Regular heptagons in the plane: a packing of congruent regular heptagons denser than the Kuperberg double lattice (0.8926906861...)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (small periodic cells; exact certification in seconds)
targets.statement: The densest packings of congruent regular polygons in the plane: even n-gons are centrally symmetric, and for those the lattice optimum is the packing optimum (L. Fejes Toth). Pentagons were settled by Hales and Kusner (arXiv:1602.07220, 2016): the pentagonal ice-ray double lattice with density (5-sqrt5)/3 is optimal. The regular heptagon is the next open case. Its densest double-lattice packing (G. Kuperberg and W. Kuperberg 1990, who showed that the densest double lattice of a convex disk K has density A(K)/(2*Delta(K)), with Delta the least area of an inscribed half-length parallelogram) has density (2/97)(-111+492u-356u^2) with u = cos(pi/7), i.e. 0.892690686126508075767... (Kallus, 'Pessimal packing shapes', Geom. Topol. 19 (2015), arXiv:1305.0289). Kallus proves the heptagon is a local minimum of the double-lattice density and conjectures it is the global pessimum. He notes that whether the heptagon's packing density delta equals its double-lattice density delta_L* is open. No better heptagon packing or proof was found in the sources checked on 2026-10-30. Numerically, the same A/(2*Delta) formula gives 0.9010300784 for the regular 9-gon and 0.9076648819 for the 11-gon, and it reproduces (5-sqrt5)/3 for the pentagon.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a periodic packing of congruent regular heptagons: a lattice basis L and k heptagons, each given by a centre and a rotation angle, with vertices enclosed in 50-digit intervals or given exactly in Q(cos(pi/7), sin(pi/7)), such that (1) all pairs, including lattice images within 2*circumradius, have disjoint interiors, certified by a separating line per pair in interval or exact arithmetic, and (2) the certified lower bound of the density k*A/|det L| is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than (2/97)(-111+492u-356u^2) = 0.8926906861265080757..., u = cos(pi/7), and than any denser heptagon packing published by verification time.

partial_wins.statement: Same certification for the regular 9-gon or 11-gon: a periodic packing whose certified density strictly exceeds that polygon's own Kuperberg double-lattice density, which the verifier recomputes with A/(2*Delta) (numerically, 2026-10-30: 0.9010300784 for n = 9, 0.9076648819 for n = 11), and any published value.

A counterexample to Kallus's conjecture: a convex polygon with rational vertices whose double-lattice density A/(2*Delta) is certified (exact minimisation over the finitely many combinatorial types of inscribed half-length parallelograms) to be strictly below 0.8926906861265.

targets.verification_method: Use interval arithmetic (mpmath iv or arb) at 50 digits. Construct the vertices, check separating lines for all neighbouring pairs, and compute the area and |det L| as intervals. For the bar, recompute Kallus's closed form, and for p1 compute Delta by minimising the half-length parallelogram area over directions: the area is piecewise algebraic in the direction, so minimise per edge-pair piece and certify with intervals. The heptagon check must reproduce 0.892690686126508 (an independent float computation matches it to 1e-15), and the pentagon must give (5-sqrt5)/3.
pitfalls: A double lattice re-expressed in a larger cell is not new: require a density strictly above the bar, not a re-parametrisation.
Floating-point separating-line checks can accept overlaps at contacts; use interval arithmetic.

targets.name: Thinnest coverings by n equal circles: cover the unit square (Nurmela-Ostergard table, n <= 30) or a disk (Tan, n = 21..25) with smaller circles
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Find n equal circles of the smallest radius r that together cover a given region. Square: Nurmela and Ostergard ('Covering a square with up to 30 equal circles', HUT TCS Research Report A62, June 2000) list the best known r(n) for the unit square to 20 digits, n = 1..30, e.g. r(10) = 0.21823351279308384300, r(30) = 0.12203686881944873607. Erich Friedman's 'Circles Covering Squares' page (unit circles, side s = 1/r) shows n <= 12 with the same values, credits Nagy (1974), Melissen (1997), Melissen-Schuur (1997), Tarnai-Gaspar (1995) and Nurmela-Ostergard (2000), and marks n = 3, 4, 5, 7 proved. Disk: Friedman's 'Circles Covering Circles' (unit circles covering the largest circle of radius R) lists n <= 25, found by Melissen (1997) and Jeremy Tan (2018), with proofs credited to Bezdek, G. Fejes Toth and, for n = 11..20, VoxEquinox (2026). The values for n = 21..25 (3.804+, 3.948+, 4.000+, 4.076+, sqrt6+sqrt3) are unproved. Equilateral triangle: Friedman's 'Circles Covering Triangles' shows n <= 9 (Melissen, Schuur 1997), and Nurmela (Experiment. Math. 9 (2000)) extends this to 36. Friedman's polygon-covering pages (squares or triangles covering squares, circles or triangles) were updated 25-Sep-2026 with records by A. Mukhamedov and Ryan Chi (Sep 2026), T. Green, D. Cantrell, M. Morandi and D. Paterson.
targets.success_criterion: Success means n circle centres (rational) and a radius r for one region and n such that the union of the closed disks covers the region, certified by interval arithmetic (see verification), and r is STRICTLY SMALLER (direction: min) than the bar. Square, any n in 6..30 except 7: bar = the Nurmela-Ostergard A62 value for that n, or anything smaller published later, with margin r <= bar - 1e-10. Disk (unit radius R = 1 equivalently: n unit circles covering a circle of radius R* strictly larger), n in 21..25: R* must be at least Friedman's displayed truncated value + 0.001, since the page shows only 3 decimals with '+' and Tan's exact values are not posted, and must beat any later source. Cells marked proved on the live pages cannot be won.

partial_wins.statement: Triangle: n unit circles covering an equilateral triangle of side strictly larger, by at least 0.001 over the displayed value, than Friedman's live 'Circles Covering Triangles' value for n = 7 or 8 (Schuur 1997), certified as in the main criterion, and strictly larger than Nurmela's value for that n (Experiment. Math. 9 (2000) 241-250). If the verifier cannot obtain Nurmela 2000, the claim stays PROMISING until someone checks it.

A polygon-covering record: n unit squares or unit equilateral triangles covering a square, circle or triangle strictly larger than the value on the live Friedman page (squcosqu, sqcovcir, squcotri, tricosqu, tricovcir, tricovtri) for a listed n, beating the displayed value by at least one unit in its last shown decimal, with covering certified by exact or interval arithmetic.

targets.verification_method: Covering certificate: the closed region K is covered by disks D_i iff every 'critical point' is covered, where the critical points are the corners of K, every intersection of a circle with the boundary of K, and every pairwise circle intersection point lying in K. Each must lie in some other closed disk, and the cells must be non-empty. Run this in interval arithmetic at 50 digits with circles of the claimed r. Cross-check by adaptive quadtree subdivision: every box must sit inside some disk, proved by an interval test of the farthest corner. Compare r with the A62 value (from www.tcs.hut.fi/old/reports/A62.ps.gz) or with the live Friedman page, after converting between unit-square r and unit-circle s = 1/r.
angles: Coverings are rigid 'bar frameworks' (equidistant graphs): optimise r by minimising the uncovered area with BFGS from random starts, as Nurmela-Ostergard did, then polish the structure with Newton's method on the active critical points.
For the disk, n = 21..25, start from hexagonal patches with one or two rotated outer rings.
pitfalls: Friedman's covering pages for circles (2005 and 2019 stamps) lag the literature: the square page stops at n = 12 and the triangle page at n = 9, while Nurmela-Ostergard (square, n <= 30) and Nurmela (triangle, n <= 36) go further. Always compare with the literature tables.
Normalisation: A62 gives r for the unit square; Friedman gives the side s for unit circles (s = 1/r). The disk page fixes unit circles and maximises R.
Grid sampling does not prove coverage: tiny uncovered slivers near triple points are typical. Use the critical-point plus interval certificate.
Friedman's covering pages are part of his Packing Center; the bank entry friedman-packing-records covers packings only (its criterion requires disjoint interiors), not coverings.

targets.name: Stanley-Wilf limit of 1324: a certified upper bound below Brignall's 13.167248 (shuffle-automaton certificates)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (thousands of states and tens of thousands of exact polynomial inequalities; the weight search is numerical optimisation, the check is exact arithmetic)
targets.statement: The growth rate gr(Av(1324)) = lim |Av_n(1324)|^(1/n) is the last unknown Stanley-Wilf limit of a length-4 pattern. Upper bounds: 16 (Claesson-Jelinek-Steingrimsson 2012), about 13.93 and 13.74 (Miklos Bona 2012, 2014), 13.5 (David Bevan, Robert Brignall, Andrew Elvey Price, Jay Pantone 2020, via dominoes) and, since 1 Oct 2026, 13.167248 (Robert Brignall, 'Shuffle automata and the growth of 1324-avoiding permutations', arXiv:2610.02535 v1, the only version on 2026-10-30). Brignall bounds gr(Av(1324)) <= lambda * mu(x, y) whenever a weighted shuffle automaton for the BR-avoiding shuffles of domino words admits a lambda-good positive state weighting (Proposition 4.4, from Corollary 4.3 and Proposition 4.2); mu(x, y) is the domino growth rate, the reciprocal of the root of a cubic functional equation (Theorem 3.4). His 3-lookahead automaton (384 states, 1536 inequalities, weights in 139 polynomials of a root t ~ 1.1584233 of 3T^5 + 10T^4 - T^3 - 11T^2 - 6T - 1) gives (1+t)(19+8t)/(4t) ~ 13.1672476; the finite inequalities are Lean-checked in github.com/rbrignall/1324-lookahead. His concluding remarks report unverified larger runs: a 5-lookahead automaton near 13.1498 (6144 states, 24,576 inequalities) and an enlarged-alphabet 3-lookahead near 13.143 (over 13,000 states). Neither has been certified. The best numerical estimate of the true value is 11.600 +- 0.003 (Conway-Guttmann-Zinn-Justin 2018); the best claimed lower bound, 10.412263 (Charles Norton, arXiv:2608.20292 v3, after two withdrawn claims), is not part of this target.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a rigorous upper bound U < 13.167248 (strictly smaller, direction: min) on gr(Av(1324)), delivered as either (a) a certificate inside Brignall's framework of arXiv:2610.02535: an explicit finite weighted shuffle automaton (for example the k-lookahead automaton of Section 5 for some k >= 4, or the enlarged-alphabet variant of the concluding remarks) shown to meet the hypotheses of Corollary 4.3, explicit parameters x, y, lambda (exact algebraic numbers with isolating intervals), an explicit positive state weighting, and a checker in exact rational or certified interval arithmetic (or Lean) that verifies positivity and every lambda-good inequality, together with a certified enclosure of lambda * mu(x, y) below 13.167248; or (b) a kernel-checked formal proof (Lean, Rocq or Isabelle, with no sorry or extra axioms) of any bound below 13.167248. Floating-point checks, unverified optimiser output, or a bound conditional on the Claesson-Jelinek-Steingrimsson conjecture do not count. Before claiming, re-check arXiv:2610.02535 for a later version and search arXiv for a newer bound.

partial_wins.statement: An independent exact re-verification of Brignall's 3-lookahead certificate outside Lean (all 384 weights positive and all 1536 inequalities at the root t of m(T)), plus a Sturm-sequence or interval certificate that m(T) has exactly one root in (1.158423, 1.158424), with the automaton regenerated from the paper's definitions rather than copied from the repository CSV.

A certified bound from a 4-lookahead automaton (the next case after Brignall's 3-lookahead; arXiv:2610.02535 reports no k = 4 value), checked in exact arithmetic as in (a), whose certified value of lambda * mu(x, y) is at most 13.1673 (no worse than Brignall's 13.1672476 to four decimals), together with its exact closed form; a value below 13.167248 is the full win.

targets.verification_method: Run the claimant's checker in a clean environment: regenerate the automaton from the definitions in arXiv:2610.02535 Sections 4-5 (states, active transitions, run weights x^-i y^-r), confirm it reproduces Brignall's 384-state 3-lookahead case and his 13.1672476 bound, then check every inequality sum over active transitions tau(e) kappa(q_e) <= lambda kappa(q) exactly (rational arithmetic in Q(t) with a root-isolating interval, or a Lean build with an axiom audit). Separately compute mu(x, y) as 1/rho where rho is the unique zero of Phi(z; x, y) in (0, 1/2) using certified root isolation, and confirm lambda * mu < 13.167248. Any step that relies on numerical optimisation must only produce the weights; acceptance depends only on the exact check.
angles: Start from Brignall's own pointers: the 5-lookahead (~13.1498) and enlarged-alphabet (~13.143) runs only need certification; set up exact LP feasibility for the weights at a fixed rational lambda slightly above the target, then round to rationals and re-check.

Treat the lambda-good weighting as a Perron-eigenvector problem: lambda is at least the spectral radius of the weighted transfer matrix, so power iteration gives near-optimal weights quickly; certification then needs only rational rounding with slack.
Use rational x, y and a rational lambda instead of algebraic parameters: a slightly worse but fully rational certificate is far easier to check and still counts if below 13.167248.
pitfalls: The bound is lambda * mu(x, y), not lambda alone; changing x and y changes both the run weights and the domino growth rate, so mu must be recomputed with a certified root of the domino equation at those parameters.

Brignall notes that the naive and six-state automata give exactly 13.5 with no gain; a new automaton must still be in bijection with BR-avoiding shuffles (Corollary 4.3 hypothesis), which a checker of inequalities alone does not test.
The 13.1498 and 13.143 values in the concluding remarks were reported as unverified ChatGPT-assisted computations; reproducing them numerically is not a win.
Norton's lower-bound preprint has withdrawn earlier versions; do not use any lower bound as a sanity check beyond 10.271 (Bevan et al. 2020).

targets.name: 1324-avoiding permutations: the exact count |Av_51(1324)| (first term beyond Conway-Guttmann-Zinn-Justin's n = 50)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (the n = 50 run used about 4.2 TB of distributed memory, 168 cores x 20 GB, and memory grows about 4x per +2 in n) unless a new algorithm changes the scaling
targets.statement: The number of permutations of length n avoiding 1324 (OEIS A061552) has no known formula or useful functional equation. Exact counts: early terms by Darko Marinov (2001) and Vincent Vatter (2005), Michael Albert et al. (to n = 25), Fredrik Johansson and Brian Nakamura (to 31, 2014), Andrew Conway and Anthony Guttmann (to 36, 2015) and Andrew Conway, Anthony Guttmann and Paul Zinn-Justin ('1324-avoiding permutations revisited', Adv. Appl. Math. 2018, arXiv:1709.01248) to n = 50. CGZ's transfer-matrix algorithm has states counted by sums of Catalan numbers up to n/2, ran five times modulo different primes and combined the results by the Chinese remainder theorem; 'the only limit to obtaining additional terms is computer memory'. The OEIS b-file (David Bevan; terms 37-50 credited to Bjarki Agust Gudmundsson) stops at n = 50 on 2026-10-30, and an arXiv search the same day found no exact count beyond n = 50 (2024-2026 work on Av(1324) concerns inversions, involutions, growth bounds and griddings).
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact integer |Av_n(1324)| for some n >= 51 (strictly beyond the largest n in the live A061552 b-file and in every paper found by an arXiv search, re-checked immediately before claiming), computed by two independent runs that agree exactly (two different algorithms, or one algorithm run modulo enough distinct primes with a second, independently written implementation for at least one modulus), where the same code reproduces every published term a(0..50) exactly. The value must also pass the ratio-analysis sanity check in verification_method.

partial_wins.statement: a(51) modulo a stated prime p >= 2^31, computed by two independently written programs that agree and that both reproduce a(n) mod p for all n <= 50 from the published b-file.

A documented implementation of an algorithm different from CGZ's transfer matrix (for example the insertion-encoding, functional-equation or Combinatorial Exploration route) that reproduces all of a(0..50) exactly; reproduction only, but a prerequisite for the two-run rule.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: run the claimant's code on small n (<= 30) and compare against the b-file; check the agreement of both independent runs for the new term; if moduli are used, check the CRT reconstruction and that the product of moduli exceeds an upper bound for a(51) (for example 16^51). Sanity: the ratio a(51)/a(50) must sit on the extrapolated ratio curve of CGZ (mu ~ 11.60, with the stretched-exponential correction mu^n mu1^sqrt(n) n^g); a mismatch in the fourth significant figure is a red flag.
angles: Import from statistical-physics series work: CGZ already use modular arithmetic and CRT; a memory-lean variant that streams the transfer matrix from disk (sorted external memory) trades RAM for SSD and may bring n = 51 to one large workstation.
Exploit symmetry: 1324 is fixed by reverse-complement and inverse, so states can be folded by the symmetry group before storage.
Start with a(51) mod a single 61-bit prime (p1); that already needs only one run's memory.
pitfalls: Off-by-one in the index: the OEIS offset is 0 (a(0) = 1); the CGZ paper lists terms by length n.
The data field of the OEIS entry stops at n = 25; the b-file holds n <= 50.
Integer size: a(50) is about 1.5 * 10^42; use 64-bit or 128-bit residues and arbitrary precision only at the CRT step.
A computation of 1324-avoiding involutions (A230554) or of 1324-avoiders with few inversions is a different sequence.

targets.name: Claesson-Jelinek-Steingrimsson conjecture: 1324-avoiders with k inversions never decrease from length n to n+1 (counterexample, or the first full table at n = 18)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (Meng enumerated all 4.6 * 10^11 members of Av_17(1324) in about 18 hours on four cores; Av_18(1324) is about 7.5 times larger, and inversion-pruned enumeration covers low-k regions quickly)
targets.statement: Let a(n, k) be the number of 1324-avoiding permutations of length n with exactly k inversions. Anders Claesson, Vit Jelinek and Einar Steingrimsson (2012) conjectured a(n, k) <= a(n+1, k) for all n, k; the conjecture implies gr(Av(1324)) <= e^(pi sqrt(2/3)) ~ 13.002. Svante Linusson and Emil Verkama (arXiv:2408.15075) proved it for k <= 2n - 7; Lingsen Meng (arXiv:2609.06717 v2, 9 Sep 2026) extended the proof, computer-assisted, to all n and k <= 2n + 6, with regions growing like sqrt(n) for huge n, and states that the unrestricted conjecture is open. Claesson, Linusson, Ulfarsson and Verkama (arXiv:2604.01143, 2026) proved inversion monotonicity for some subclasses. Direct tables: Claesson et al. 2012 for n <= 15; Ruth Hoffmann, Ozgur Akgun and Christopher Jefferson (arXiv:2311.17581) the full table for n = 16; Meng (Section 8 and archival supplement of 2609.06717) a full enumeration of all 458,374,397,312 members of Av_17(1324), about 18 hours on four cores, reproducing the whole table for n <= 17, plus an inversion-pruned table of a(n, k) for n <= 26, k <= 55 and residual runs to n = 30, k <= 63; he checked a(n+1, k) >= a(n, k) directly for n <= 25, k <= 2n + 3. So the inequality is verified for every k only through the step 16 -> 17; from n = 17 on it is unchecked for k > max(55, 2n + 6) up to C(n, 2), which is where a counterexample would have to live.
targets.success_criterion: Success means explicit n, k with a(n, k) > a(n+1, k), both values exact and computed by two independently written programs that agree and that reproduce the published tables exactly: the full rows for n <= 17 (Hoffmann-Akgun-Jefferson to n = 16, Meng's n = 17) and Meng's n <= 26, k <= 55 table. Alternatively, a kernel-checked formal proof (Lean, Rocq or Isabelle, no sorry or extra axioms) of the full conjecture. Re-check arXiv for later versions of 2609.06717 and new results before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: The complete row a(18, k) for every k = 0..153, computed by two independent programs that agree, that reproduce the full n = 17 row of Meng's supplement, and whose row sum equals A061552(18) in the OEIS b-file; this certifies the conjecture at the step n = 17 -> 18 for every k (or refutes it, which is the full win).

Exact a(n, k) for every n <= 30 and every k <= 70, extending Meng's archived table (n <= 26, k <= 55) and his k <= 63 runs, with every inequality a(n, k) <= a(n+1, k) for n <= 29 and k <= 70 checked; two independent programs as above.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic reruns both programs on n <= 13 (minutes) against brute force over all permutations, checks agreement with the Hoffmann-Akgun-Jefferson n <= 16 tables and Meng's n = 17 row and n <= 26, k <= 55 table, checks each full row sums to A061552(n), then compares the claimed (n, k) entries. A full rerun at n = 18 may take days; agreement of two independent implementations is then the main evidence.
angles: Add an inversion-count dimension to a known 1324 counting algorithm (Conway-Guttmann transfer matrix, or Johansson-Nakamura functional equations): states multiply by at most C(n,2)+1 but no permutation is generated.
Use the symmetries inverse and reverse-complement (both preserve 1324-avoidance and inversion count) to cut generation work by up to 4x.

Complement (pi_i -> n+1-pi_i) maps 1324-avoiders with k inversions to 4231-avoiders with C(n,2)-k inversions, so the open high-k part of the 1324 table equals the low-k part of the 4231 table, where generation from few inversions is cheap.
pitfalls: Complement maps 1324-avoiders to 4231-avoiders and k inversions to C(n,2) - k inversions; it is a bijection between different tables, not a symmetry of a(n, k). Inverse and reverse-complement are true symmetries of a(n, k).
The stabilisation a(n, k) = a(k+2, k) for n > k + 2 (Hoffmann et al. Conjecture 2) means low-k columns carry no new information; the open region is large k.

The full n = 17 row is already in Meng's supplement (2609.06717, Section 8), so the first new full row is n = 18, with about 3.4 * 10^12 avoiders for generate-and-filter enumeration; budget accordingly.

targets.name: Pattern-avoiding involutions: the next exact count of involutions avoiding 1324 (n = 35) or 4231 (n = 41)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (Bean-Guttmann-Pantone's Mosaic adaptation ran for several weeks on 60 CPU cores with 300 GB of RAM to reach n = 34 and n = 40; one more term needs comparable resources or a faster algorithm)
targets.statement: Among the involutions avoiding a single pattern of length 4, the classes avoiding 1324 (OEIS A230554) and 4231 (A230556) are the only ones with no known generating function. Of the eight Wilf classes, four had been settled earlier: 1234 by Ira Gessel, 2413 by Robert Brignall, Sophie Huczynska and Vincent Vatter, and 1342 and 2341 by Miklos Bona, Cheyne Homberger, Jay Pantone and Vincent Vatter (2016). Christian Bean, Anthony J. Guttmann and Jay Pantone ('Enumerating Pattern-Avoiding Involutions using Combinatorial Exploration', arXiv:2609.04352, 3 Sep 2026) found algebraic generating functions for 2431 and 3421. By adapting the Mosaic method (a forthcoming counting algorithm of Bean and Pantone), they extended the 1324 count to n = 34 and the 4231 count to n = 40 (ancillary files inv-1324-up-to-34.txt and inv-4231-up-to-40.txt); that computation took several weeks on 60 CPU cores with 300 GB of RAM. On 2026-10-30 the OEIS entries A230554 and A230556 list terms only to n = 20 (last edited 14 Sep 2026; both carry keyword 'more' and cite the 2026 paper), and arXiv v1 is the only version.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an exact count of involutions of length n avoiding 1324 for some n >= 35, or avoiding 4231 for some n >= 41 (strictly beyond the paper's ancillary files and the live OEIS b-files, re-checked before claiming), computed by two independently written programs that agree and that both reproduce every term of the corresponding ancillary file exactly.

partial_wins.statement: An independently written program, using a different method from the Mosaic adaptation (for example a transfer matrix on arc diagrams, or Combinatorial Exploration with an involution-aware strategy), that reproduces all terms in both ancillary files (1324 to n = 34, 4231 to n = 40); reproduction only.

targets.verification_method: Brute force over all involutions for n <= 12 (about 140,000 involutions at n = 12) must match both programs; then compare both programs' outputs with the ancillary files term by term and with each other for the new term. Ratio check: successive ratios should continue the smooth trend used in the paper's asymptotic analysis.
angles: An involution is a matching plus fixed points; encode it as an arc diagram and run a left-to-right transfer method whose state records just enough of the open arcs to detect 1324 (an import of the CGZ transfer matrix to involutions).
4231 is reached to n = 40 but 1324 only to n = 34: the 1324 case is harder, so a new idea helps most there.
pitfalls: Reversal does not preserve involutions; 1324 and 4231 involution counts differ from n = 7 on (126 vs 128), so do not transfer terms between the two sequences.
The ancillary files index by length n starting at n = 1; the OEIS entries start at n = 0.

a(40) for 4231 is 241,382,018,779,553,682 (about 2.4 * 10^17): it still fits in signed 64-bit, but the next terms (ratio about 3) and intermediate sums in a transfer method soon overflow; use 128-bit or arbitrary precision.

targets.name: Packing densities of 2413, 1342 and 1324: beat a Sliacan-Stromquist or Presutti-Stromquist bound with an explicit permuton or a flag-algebra certificate
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours for lower bounds (optimising a few dozen layer/part sizes with exact or interval evaluation); laptop-days for flag-algebra upper bounds at N = 8
targets.statement: The packing density p(S) of a pattern S of length k is the limit over n of the maximum fraction of k-point subsets of a length-n permutation that form a copy of S. For 4-point patterns, 1234, 1432, 2143 and 1243 are solved; three remain open. Current bounds (Jakub Sliacan and Walter Stromquist, 'Improving bounds on packing densities of 4-point permutations', DMTCS 19(2), 2018, Table 3): 0.244054321 < p(1324) < 0.244054540 (lower bound from the layered permuton Gamma with 132-maximiser tails, whose own density is 0.2440543210...; the upper bound is 0.244054549 in Theorem 2 by Flagmatic, sharpened in the same paper to 0.244054540 by the Permpack certificate cert1324permpack.js); 0.198836597 < p(1342) < 0.198837286342 (lower from a 7-part construction Pi whose part sizes are in cert1342lb.txt, and whose own density is 0.198836597...; upper by flag algebras); p(2413) lower bound ~ 0.104724 from the Presutti-Stromquist measure (C. B. Presutti and W. Stromquist, 2010, conjectured optimal) and upper bound 0.10478046354353523761779 (Sliacan-Stromquist, flag algebras at N = 7, in the same range as Balogh et al. 2015). The upper-bound certificates and Sage scripts are public in github.com/jsliacan/permpack. An arXiv search and a citation check of arXiv:1704.02959 on 2026-10-30 found no later paper improving any of these bounds.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a strictly better bound for p(2413): either a lower bound strictly above 0.1047245 (this exceeds the density of the Presutti-Stromquist 2010 construction, listed as ~0.104724 in Sliacan-Stromquist Table 3, whatever its later digits), given by an explicitly specified permuton whose 2413-density is evaluated exactly or with certified interval arithmetic, or an upper bound strictly below 0.10478046354353523761779, given by a flag-algebra certificate (rational positive-semidefinite matrices or their rational Cholesky factors) that an exact-arithmetic checker verifies. Floating-point SDP output alone does not count. Re-check arXiv and the permpack repository for newer bounds before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: A lower bound for p(1324) strictly above 0.244054322 (above the density 0.2440543210... of the Sliacan-Stromquist permuton Gamma itself, so a sharper evaluation of Gamma does not count), from an explicit layered permuton (finite list of layer sizes, possibly with stated recursive or geometric tails) whose 1324-density is evaluated exactly or by certified interval arithmetic.

A lower bound for p(1342) strictly above 0.198836598 (above the density 0.198836597... of the Sliacan-Stromquist construction Pi with the cert1342lb.txt part sizes, so a sharper evaluation of Pi does not count), from an explicit permuton with certified density evaluation.

An upper bound for p(1324) strictly below 0.244054540 (the Permpack certificate cert1324permpack.js) or for p(1342) strictly below 0.198837286342, from an exactly verified rational flag-algebra certificate.

targets.verification_method: Lower bounds: the skeptic writes an independent evaluator of pattern density in a permuton built from blocks (sums, skew sums, inflations of monotone or recursive parts): for block structures this is a finite polynomial (or a convergent series with an explicit tail bound) in the part sizes; evaluate it in exact rationals or interval arithmetic, and cross-check by sampling random 4-point subsets from a large finite approximation (statistical sanity only). Reproduce the Sliacan-Stromquist values for Gamma (1324) and Pi (1342) first. Upper bounds: run an exact checker (permpack's exactify output or a fresh one) confirming the certificate's matrices are PSD over the rationals and that the resulting bound is below the record; reproduce cert2413.js first.
angles: For 1324 (layered, so a layered maximiser exists by Price 1997), the authors fixed the tails to 132-maximisers and optimised only two parameters; optimising more layers with free sizes is a smooth finite-dimensional problem. An audit run on 2026-10-30 (float64, not certified) reached about 0.2440545239 with symmetric layered permutons having a few free layer sizes per side and a free geometric tail ratio, well above Gamma's 0.2440543210 and about 1.6e-8 below the 0.244054540 upper bound; the work for p1 is to certify such a value.

For 1342 the authors say the extremal construction might use a different layer formation than their Pi; search over small block structures (inflations of 2-4 point skeletons with recursive parts) numerically, then certify.
For 2413 upper bounds, move flag algebras to N = 8 with symmetry reduction; the authors stopped at N = 7 for cost reasons.
pitfalls: A finite permutation with high pattern density is NOT a lower bound for p(S): maximum densities decrease with n. Lower bounds need a permuton (or an explicit sequence whose density limit is computed).
For 1324 the bounds are 0.24405432 vs 0.24405454: margins are 10^-7, so float64 evaluation of a polynomial with cancellation is not trustworthy; use exact or interval arithmetic.
The flagmatic (digraph) certificate for 1324 relies on Lemma 1 of the paper (an equivalent digraph problem); a new upper bound by that route must state and use the same reduction.

The published lower bounds are truncations of the densities of Gamma and Pi (0.2440543210... and 0.198836597...). Evaluating Gamma more precisely already gives a number above 0.244054321; that is not an improvement, which is why p1 and p2 set their bars just above the constructions' own densities.

targets.name: Permutations sortable by two stacks in series: the exact count for n = 20 (first term beyond Elvey Price-Guttmann)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (a(19) ~ 4.35 * 10^15, so the count must come from a structural/transfer method, not from testing permutations one by one)
targets.statement: Knuth asked how many permutations of length n can be sorted by two stacks in series; unlike one stack (Catalan), two stacks in parallel (solved by Albert and Bousquet-Melou) or a deque (counted to n = 100 in A182216), no formula or functional equation is known, and recognition is polynomial (Pierrot-Rossin 2013). Andrew Elvey Price and Anthony J. Guttmann ('Permutations sortable by two stacks in series', Adv. Appl. Math. 2017, arXiv:1510.08663) counted them exactly for all n < 20, giving OEIS A263929 (a(19) = 4,351,269,802,153,188), approximated 19 further coefficients numerically, and estimated the growth rate mu ~ 12.45 +- 0.15. On 2026-10-30 A263929 still ends at n = 19 and carries keyword 'more', and an arXiv search for 'two stacks in series' found no later exact enumeration.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact number of permutations of length n that are sortable by two stacks in series (Knuth's model: input -> stack 1 -> stack 2 -> output, output increasing), for some n >= 20 strictly beyond the live A263929 entry and b-file, computed by two independently written programs (different algorithms) that agree and that both reproduce a(1..19) exactly.

partial_wins.statement: A documented independent algorithm (not a per-permutation sortability test) that reproduces all of a(1..19) and reports its running-time growth, making n = 20 a clear projection; reproduction only.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: brute force over all permutations for n <= 11 with a direct two-stack sortability test (an exhaustive search over stack operations, or the Pierrot-Rossin algorithm) must match both programs; then compare both programs with A263929 for n <= 19 and with each other at the new n. Sanity: a(20)/a(19) should be close to the trend of the paper's approximate coefficients (a(19)/a(18) ~ 10.9).
angles: Elvey Price and Guttmann count via a decomposition of operation sequences; a transfer matrix over the joint stack contents, with canonical forms to merge equivalent operation words, is the classical route.
Each sortable permutation has many sorting words; count canonical sorting words (for example by a fixed greedy rule) to avoid overcounting.
