pitfalls: Different 'two stacks in series' models exist (West's 2-stack-sortable, which applies the stack-sorting map twice, is A000139 and solved); this target is the general Knuth model.
Counting operation sequences instead of permutations overcounts; each permutation must be counted once.
The 19 approximate coefficients in the paper are not exact and do not set a record.

targets.name: Superpatterns: the shortest permutation containing all 5040 patterns of length 7 (OEIS A342474(7)), or the next row of A373778
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours for upper-bound searches (annealing over length-22 permutations, C(22,7) = 170,544 subsets per evaluation); laptop-days or more for an exhaustive lower-bound proof
targets.statement: A k-superpattern is a permutation containing every permutation of length k as a pattern (not necessarily contiguous). Its minimum length (OEIS A342474) is known only for k <= 6: 1, 3, 5, 9, 13, 17. Michael Engen and Vincent Vatter ('Containing all permutations', Amer. Math. Monthly 2021) gave the best general construction, length ceil((k^2+1)/2), and reported that Arnar Arnarson found a 6-superpattern of length 17 and computations show none is shorter. Asymptotically the bounds are 1.000076 k^2/e^2 (Zachary Chroman, Matthew Kwan, Mihir Singhal 2021) and about k^2/2. For k = 7 the published upper bound is 25, and A342474 (keyword 'more') has no a(7) on 2026-10-30. A V3R1T4S bank check on 2026-10-30 found, by about six minutes of simulated annealing, a 7-superpattern of length 23, 3 10 20 14 6 17 23 13 2 8 18 12 5 21 16 1 19 7 11 9 22 4 15 (independently re-verified: all 5040 patterns occur among its C(23,7) = 245,157 subsequences), and two 25-minute runs at length 22 reached at best 5030 of 5040 patterns, so 23 is the baseline here. The related triangle A373778 (Thomas Scheuerle 2024; maximum number of distinct length-k patterns in a length-n permutation, with T(n,k) = k! exactly when n >= A342474(k)) is known for rows n <= 12.
targets.success_criterion: Success means determining A342474(7) exactly: an explicit 7-superpattern of length L (L <= 23 is already known, see statement) together with a re-runnable exhaustive computer proof that no permutation of length L - 1 contains all 5040 patterns of length 7, where the proof's search code is independent of any heuristic and its pruning rules are each justified in writing. Before claiming, re-check A342474, A373778 and arXiv for a published value.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit permutation of length at most 22 containing all 5040 permutations of length 7 as patterns (strictly shorter than the length-23 baseline in the statement and the published bound 25).

A re-runnable exhaustive proof that no permutation of length L contains all 5040 patterns of length 7, for some stated L >= 15 (the counting bound C(L,7) >= 7! only rules out L <= 14); the larger L, the stronger, and L = a(7) - 1 is the full win.

Row n = 13 of OEIS A373778 (the maximum, over all permutations of length 13, of the number of distinct length-k patterns, for every k = 1..13), computed exhaustively by two independent programs that both reproduce rows 1..12.

targets.verification_method: For an explicit superpattern: check it is a permutation of 1..L, enumerate all C(L,7) subsets, map each to its pattern, and confirm 5040 distinct patterns (seconds). For an impossibility proof: rerun the claimant's search, audit each pruning rule (symmetry under the 8-element dihedral group of the square, Erdos-Szekeres-type necessary conditions, extension arguments) on small cases, and confirm it reproduces 'no 6-superpattern of length 16' (Engen-Vatter) and the k <= 5 values before trusting it at k = 7. For p3, brute force rows n <= 10 and compare with the OEIS data.
angles: The good small superpatterns look like rank orders of {i * phi mod 1} (Scheuerle's A371822 rows match A194832 up to cyclic shift); seed searches with golden-ratio and other low-discrepancy permutations.
For lower bounds, use a SAT/ILP formulation with symmetry breaking that shows every length-L permutation misses some 7-pattern, rather than enumerating L! permutations.
Use inductive constraints from 6-superpatterns: the length-17 6-superpatterns can be enumerated and constrain how a short 7-superpattern can look after deleting a point.
pitfalls: Patterns here are classical (any subsequence), not consecutive; the substring version is the superpermutation problem, a different bank entry.
Annealing scores near 5039/5040 at length 22 do not show 22 is impossible; only an exhaustive proof does.
Symmetry reduction by reverse, complement and inverse is valid because the set of all k-permutations is closed under them.

targets.name: Shortest word containing every permutation of 1..n as a subsequence (Karp's problem, OEIS A062714): settle n = 10, or circular n = 7
targets.compute_profile: laptop-minutes to check a candidate word (10! subsequence tests); laptop-days or more for exhaustive optimality proofs
targets.statement: Karp's problem (Chvatal-Klarner-Knuth 1972, problem 36) asks for the minimum length a(n) of a word over {1..n} containing every permutation of 1..n as a (not necessarily contiguous) subsequence. Known values (A062714): 1, 3, 7, 12, 19, 28, 39 (Malcolm Newey 1973 for n <= 7), a(8) = 52 (proved by Oliver Tan, 'Conjecture on Supersequence Lower Bound related to Connell Sequence', arXiv:2501.11386, Jan 2025, refuting Newey's conjectured 51 from A337300; it also follows from Vitaliy Garnashevich's 2020 lexicographically least optimal word in A136094, and Pontus von Bromssen entered it in A062714 in Aug 2025) and a(9) = 66 (Vitaliy Garnashevich, Oct 2025; A136094 lists lexicographically least optimal words to n = 9). Upper bounds: n^2 - 2n + 4 (Newey; Koutas-Hu), ceil(n^2 - 7n/3 + 19/3) for n >= 7 (Sasa Radomirovic 2012), and families approaching n^2 - (5/2 - eps)n for infinitely many n (Oliver Tan 2022); the lower bound is n^2 - C n^(7/4 + eps) (Kleitman-Kwiatkowski 1976), and deciding whether a word contains all permutations is coNP-complete (Uznanski 2015). For n = 10, Radomirovic's bound is 83 and Newey's conjectured formula A337300 gives 81. A062714 carries keyword 'more' with no a(10) on 2026-10-30. The circular variant (word on a circle, A373728, Lecouturier-Zmiaikou 2012) is known to n = 6 (2, 4, 8, 12, 17 for n = 2..6; entry by Michel Marcus, June 2024, keyword 'more') and open at n = 7.
targets.success_criterion: Success means determining a(10) of A062714 exactly: an explicit word over {1..10} of length L containing all 3,628,800 permutations as subsequences, plus a re-runnable exhaustive computer proof that no word of length L - 1 does, whose method reproduces a(8) = 52 and a(9) = 66. Alternatively, determining the circular value A373728 at n = 7 in the same way (explicit circular word and a proof that nothing shorter works, reproducing the known value 17 at n = 6). Re-check A062714, A136094, A373728 and arXiv before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit word over {1..10} of length at most 82 containing every permutation of 1..10 as a subsequence (strictly below Radomirovic's 83, the best published construction at n = 10), after checking A062714, A136094 and the papers cited there for a shorter published word.
An explicit word over {1..11} of length at most 101 containing every permutation of 1..11 as a subsequence (strictly below Radomirovic's ceil(121 - 77/3 + 19/3) = 102), after the same check.

An explicit circular word for n = 7 of length at most 24 containing every permutation of 1..7 as a subsequence read around the circle from some starting point (strictly below the Lecouturier-Zmiaikou bound a(n) < n^2/2 + n/4 - 1, which gives at most 25 at n = 7), after checking A373728 and its links for a shorter published word.

targets.verification_method: For an explicit word: for every permutation of 1..n, run greedy left-to-right subsequence matching (for circular words, try every starting position) and assert all succeed; 10! x 82 steps is under a minute in C. For a lower-bound proof: rerun the claimant's exhaustive search, confirm it reproduces a(8) = 52 and a(9) = 66 (or circular a(6) = 17), and audit every pruning rule on small n.
angles: Lift the optimal n = 9 words of A136094: Radomirovic's and Tan's constructions insert a new letter into a good shorter word; try all insertion schedules of the letter 10 into length-66 optimal words.
Local search with an incremental checker: track, for each permutation prefix, the earliest matching position, so a one-letter edit only re-checks affected permutations.
pitfalls: Subsequence, not substring: the substring version is the superpermutation problem, a different bank entry.
Newey's conjectured values A337300 are wrong from n = 8 on (51 vs 52); do not use them as known lengths.
The words in A136094 are lexicographically least optimal words; other optimal words exist and may lift better.

targets.name: Ramsey numbers with K_k - e: close a gap in Radziszowski's Table IIIa/IIIb (e.g. R(K4-e,K8-e) 30-32, R(K6,K5-e) 43-51, R(K8,K4-e) 36-39)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (lower bounds by local search or circulant SAT on 30-100 vertices); needs cluster for most upper bounds
targets.statement: R(G,H) is the least N such that every graph on N vertices contains G or its complement contains H. Radziszowski's dynamic survey DS1 (revision #18, 24 Apr 2026), Tables IIIa/IIIb, lists the known values and bounds when G and H are complete graphs or K_k minus one edge, and not both complete. Open ranges on 2026-10-30 include: R(K3,K11-e) 42-45, R(K3,K12-e) 49-53, R(K3,K13-e) 55-62, R(K3,K14-e) 61-71, R(K3,K15-e) 69-80; R(K4-e,K8-e) 30-32, R(K4-e,K9-e) 36-45, R(K4-e,K10-e) 43-57; R(K4,K7-e) 37-49, R(K4,K8-e) 52-71; R(K5-e,K8-e) 66-91; R(K5,K6-e) 43-59, R(K5,K7-e) 65-102; R(K6-e,K6-e) 45-70; R(K6,K5-e) 43-51; R(K7,K5-e) 65-79; R(K8,K4-e) 36-39, R(K9,K4-e) 41-53, R(K10,K4-e) 49-68. Since the survey, William Wesley (arXiv:2606.17021, Jun 2026) settled R(K4-e,K7) = 28. Credit: lower bounds mostly Goedgebeur and Van Overberghe (DAM 2022; constructions at github.com/Steven-VO/circulant-Ramsey), Exoo, McNamara, Radziszowski; upper bounds by Boza (BZ1-BZ4, recomputed in 2026 after Angeltveit's R(K5,K5-e) = 30), Lidicky-Pfender (flag algebras), Goedgebeur-Radziszowski and Angeltveit-McKay.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) an explicit graph G on N vertices (adjacency matrix or graph6) such that G contains no copy of the first graph and the complement contains no copy of the second (K_k or K_k - e as in the cell), checked exhaustively by two independent programs, with N+1 STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the lower bound for that cell in the live DS1 (https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/view/DS1, latest revision) and in any newer paper found by a fresh arXiv search for that exact cell; or (b) an upper bound STRICTLY BELOW (direction: min) the DS1 upper bound, backed by a machine-checkable certificate: a DRAT/LRAT/FRAT UNSAT proof of a stated encoding that a referee can regenerate, plus a machine-checked or fully written reduction, or an exact-rational flag-algebra certificate that an independent script verifies. Off-by-one: a graph on N vertices proves R >= N+1.

partial_wins.statement: A new lower bound for a cell that DS1 item 3.1.e lists outside Tables IIIa/IIIb (R(K4-e,K16-e) >= 82, R(K4,K12-e) >= 128, R(K14-e,K14-e) >= 2987): an explicit verified graph whose order plus one strictly exceeds the listed bound and every newer published bound.

An exact value: a cell of Table IIIa/IIIb settled by a verified lower-bound graph matching a verified (certificate-backed) upper bound, where both are new or one is new and the other is already published.

targets.verification_method: For a lower bound: parse the graph, confirm symmetry and order N, then search exhaustively for every forbidden subgraph in G and in its complement with (i) a bitset clique enumerator that, for K_k - e, looks for a K_{k-2} inside the common neighbourhood of every edge and non-edge as appropriate, and (ii) a SAT/CP encoding that must return UNSAT; both must agree. For an upper bound: rerun the stated encoding, check the proof with drat-trim or cake_lpr, and audit the reduction. Re-fetch DS1 and grep arXiv for the cell (e.g. "K_4-e", "K_8-e") before claiming.
angles: Block-circulant (2- and 3-block polycirculant) graphs, the method behind most Van Overberghe bounds, searched with SAT over connection sets.
Strongly regular graphs from Brouwer's table: Van Overberghe got R(K5-e,K6-e) = 37 and R(K5-e,K7-e) = 65 from Schlafli, NO-(6,2) and VO-(6,2); try induced subgraphs of other srgs.
One-vertex extension of known critical graphs with SAT for the new neighbourhood.
pitfalls: R(K4-e,K7) is now 28 (Wesley 2026); DS1 still shows 28-29.
Several upper bounds are trivially implied by Table Ib (classical numbers); improving them may need a new R(k,l) upper bound first.
K_k - e versus K_k: check which side of the cell avoids which graph; the table is not symmetric in rows and columns.

targets.name: Ramsey numbers of small complete bipartite graphs R(K_{m,n}, K_{p,q}): close a gap in DS1 Tables IVb/IVc (R(K3,5,K3,4) 25-29, R(K2,10,K2,7) 29-31, R(K2,2,K2,19) 28-29, R(K4,4,K4,4) 33-49)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours for lower bounds (graphs on 20-65 vertices); laptop-days to needs cluster for upper bounds
targets.statement: Here edges of K_N are 2-coloured and complete bipartite graphs are avoided (not the bipartite Ramsey numbers of coloured K_{n,n}). DS1 revision #18 (24 Apr 2026), Section 3.3, Tables IVb and IVc, lists these open cases: R(K3,4, K3,3) 19-20; R(K3,5, K2,4) 19-20; R(K3,5, K2,5) 21-23; R(K3,5, K3,3) 21-24; R(K3,5, K3,4) 25-29; R(K2,5, K2,8) 22-23; R(K2,6, K2,10) 27-29; R(K2,7, K2,10) 29-31; R(K2,m, K2,11) for m = 3..6, where Table IVc prints only the lower bounds 22, 25, 28, 29 but DS1 item 3.3.2(j) (R(K2,n-s, K2,n) <= 4n-2s-3 for s >= 2, n >= s+2) gives the upper bounds 25, 27, 29, 31, so the gaps are 22-25, 25-27, 28-29 and 29-31 (for m = 7 the same item gives <= 33, equal to the printed lower bound 33, so R(K2,7, K2,11) = 33 is already determined and is not part of this target); R(K2,2, K2,19) 28-29 (item 3.3.1.f); and 33 <= R(K4,4, K4,4) <= 49 (item 3.3.1.i). The diagonal case DS1 calls the first open one, 65 <= R(K2,17, K2,17) <= 66 (item 3.3.1.h), is in fact settled. By Exoo-Harborth-Mengersen it equals 66 iff an srg(65,32,15,16) exists, and Gritsenko constructed one (arXiv:2102.05432, 2021), so it is not part of this target. No 2026 arXiv paper found changes the listed cells. Credit: Lortz and Mengersen, Harborth and Mengersen, Exoo-Harborth-Mengersen, Shao and coauthors, Dybizbanski, Goedgebeur and Van Overberghe, and Lidicky-Pfender (flag-algebra upper bounds).
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) an explicit graph G on N vertices such that G contains no K_{m,n} and its complement contains no K_{p,q} (as subgraphs, not necessarily induced), checked by two independent exact programs, with N+1 STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the lower bound for that cell in the live DS1 and any newer paper found by a fresh search; or (b) an upper bound STRICTLY BELOW (direction: min) the DS1 upper bound, backed by a DRAT/LRAT UNSAT certificate of a stated encoding (with any symmetry breaking proved sound) or an exact-rational flag-algebra certificate, re-verifiable by a referee. Off-by-one: a graph on N vertices proves R >= N+1.

partial_wins.statement: An unpublished (asterisked) DS1 entry, such as R(K3,5,K2,3) = 17* (Table IVb) or R(K2,9,K2,5) = 25* (Table IVc), confirmed by a fully verified lower-bound graph and a DRAT/LRAT UNSAT certificate for the upper bound.

targets.verification_method: K_{s,t}-freeness: for every s-subset S of vertices (or every pair when s = 2), count common neighbours and require fewer than t; do the same in the complement. Implement once with bitsets and once as a SAT/CP query that must be UNSAT. For upper bounds check the proof with drat-trim or cake_lpr and re-derive the encoding from the stated parameters.
angles: Polycirculant SAT search as in Goedgebeur-Van Overberghe.

Strongly regular graphs: R(K2,n,K2,n) = 4n-2 iff an srg(4n-3,2n-2,n-2,n-1) exists (Exoo-Harborth-Mengersen). Before searching an off-diagonal cell, check srg witnesses from Brouwer's table: an srg with at most t-1 common neighbours per pair avoids K_{2,t}.
pitfalls: R(K2,17,K2,17) = 66 is settled. DS1 3.3.1.h still prints 65-66, but EHM2's criterion and Gritsenko's srg(65,32,15,16) give 66. Likewise Verma's srg(85,42,20,21) (arXiv:2610.08893) gives R(K2,22,K2,22) = 86. Diagonal R(K2,n,K2,n) cells are not part of this target.
Upper and lower table entries are stacked in the PDF; read the cell from the survey text, not a layout dump.

Table IVc's row n = 11 shows only lower bounds, but upper bounds are not missing: DS1 item 3.3.2(j) gives R(K2,n-s, K2,n) <= 4n-2s-3, which reproduces the table's upper bounds where both exist (e.g. 31 for R(K2,7,K2,10), 35 for R(K2,8,K2,11)) and closes R(K2,7,K2,11) = 33. Compare any new upper bound with it.

targets.name: Quadrilateral versus star (and wheel): settle an open value of R(C4, K_{1,n}) such as n = 39 (46-47) or n = 51-54, 71, 72
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (SAT with symmetry breaking on C4-free graphs of 46-82 vertices)
targets.statement: f(n) = R(C4, K_{1,n}) is the least N such that every graph on N vertices contains a 4-cycle or its complement contains a vertex of degree at least n; for n >= 6 it also equals R(C4, W_{n+1}) (Zhang-Broersma-Chen; Chen-Zhang-Zhang 2025 survey). DS1 revision #18 (Apr 2026) Table IVa gives every value for n <= 41 except 46 <= f(39) <= 47. Luis Boza (arXiv:2409.12770 v2, 12 Jun 2026) settled the eight earlier open values for n <= 38 (f(27) = 33, f(28..33) = n+7, f(37) = 44, plus f(67) = 76) and tabulated f(n) for n <= 82. His table still has ranges at n = 51 (59-60), 52 (60-61), 53 (61-62), 54 (62-63), 71 (80-81) and 72 (81-82), and partly blank entries at n = 39, 42, 44, 46, 56 and 69 (the published TeX omits one side). Monotonicity (f(n) <= f(n+1)), Parsons' bound f(n) <= n + ceil(sqrt(n-1)) + 1 and the neighbouring table values give 49 <= f(42) <= 50, 51 <= f(44) <= 52, 53 <= f(46) <= 54, 64 <= f(56) <= 65 and 78 <= f(69) <= 79, so the open n <= 82 are 39, 42, 44, 46, 51-54, 56, 69, 71 and 72. Credit: Parsons (polarity graphs), Boza, Wu-Sun-Radziszowski, Wu-Sun-Zhang-Radziszowski, Zhang-Chen-Cheng, Dybizbanski-Dzido, Tse, Noviani-Baskoro.
targets.success_criterion: For one open n: either (a) an explicit C4-free graph G on N vertices whose complement has maximum degree at most n-1 (equivalently min degree of G at least N-n), proving f(n) >= N+1, with N+1 STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best lower bound in DS1 Table IVa, Boza's table (arXiv:2409.12770, latest version) and any newer paper; or (b) a proof that no such graph exists on N vertices, giving f(n) <= N STRICTLY BELOW (direction: min) the best published upper bound, certified by a DRAT/LRAT UNSAT proof of a stated encoding (any degree or symmetry reductions proved sound and checkable) that a referee regenerates and checks. Bounds implied by monotonicity f(n) <= f(n+1) and by Parsons' f(n) <= n + ceil(sqrt(n-1)) + 1 (the ranges listed in the statement) count as published. A matching pair settles f(n).

partial_wins.statement: Settle f(39): either a C4-free graph on 46 vertices with minimum degree at least 7, or a certified UNSAT proof that none exists (giving f(39) = 47 or 46 respectively).

Settle one of the cells that Boza's table leaves one-sided: f(42) (49-50), f(44) (51-52), f(46) (53-54), f(56) (64-65) or f(69) (78-79), with a verified graph or a certified UNSAT proof as in the main criterion.

targets.verification_method: C4-freeness: compute A^2 and check that every off-diagonal entry is at most 1 (two independent implementations: numpy matrix product and a common-neighbour bitset count). Check min degree. For UNSAT claims, check the proof with drat-trim or cake_lpr and re-derive the CNF from the stated parameters; reject unproved symmetry-breaking constraints.
angles: Lower bounds near q^2+q+1 come from Erdos-Renyi polarity graphs ER_q with vertices deleted or added; f(51..54) sit just above q = 7 (57 vertices).
Afzaly-McKay's ex(n,C4) tables bound the edge count: a graph on N vertices with min degree N-n needs N(N-n)/2 edges, which must not exceed ex(N,C4).
pitfalls: Boza's table in the arXiv TeX has missing glyphs (e.g. '/46' at n = 39); take bounds from the text, DS1 and the cited papers, not the rendered cell.
Wheel indexing differs between papers (W_n with n or n+1 vertices).

targets.name: Cycles versus complete graphs: close R(C4,K11) 40-43, R(C4,K12) 43-51 or R(C5,K9) 33-36
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours for lower bounds; needs cluster or flag algebras for upper bounds
targets.statement: R(C_n, K_m) is the least N such that every graph on N vertices contains an n-cycle or an independent set of size m. DS1 revision #18 (Apr 2026), Table Vb, lists the small open cases 40 <= R(C4,K11) <= 43 (Van Overberghe; Boza-Radziszowski), 43 <= R(C4,K12) <= 51 (Boza-Radziszowski 2025) and 33 <= R(C5,K9) <= 36 (Lidicky-Pfender). The Erdos-Faudree-Rousseau-Schelp conjecture R(C_n,K_m) = (n-1)(m-1)+1 for n >= m >= 3 (except n = m = 3) is still open for many small cells marked 'conj.' in the table, for example R(C9,K9) = 65 (proved for n >= 4m+2 by Nikiforov, for n >= m(m-2) by Schiermeyer, and for large n by Keevash-Long-Skokan). Erdos also asked for a proof that R(C4,K_m) < m^(2-eps). No 2026 arXiv paper found changes these cells.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) an explicit graph G on N vertices with no C_n (as a subgraph) and independence number less than m, checked by two independent exact programs, with N+1 STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the DS1 lower bound for that cell and any newer published bound; or (b) an upper bound STRICTLY BELOW (direction: min) the DS1 upper bound for R(C4,K11), R(C4,K12) or R(C5,K9), backed by an exact-rational flag-algebra certificate or a DRAT/LRAT UNSAT certificate with a sound, checkable reduction. Off-by-one: a graph on N vertices proves R >= N+1.

partial_wins.statement: A machine-checked proof (Lean/Isabelle, or SAT certificates over a formalised reduction) of the conjectured value for one 'conj.' cell of Table Vb with m <= 9, such as R(C9,K9) <= 65, where no published proof exists.

An end-to-end certified re-verification of a published Table Vb upper bound that has no public checkable certificate, such as R(C4,K10) <= 36 [LaLR]: DRAT/LRAT proofs of a stated encoding with a checkable reduction (or an exact-rational flag-algebra certificate), released with a re-run script.

targets.verification_method: C4: check that A^2 off-diagonal entries are at most 1. C5: for each vertex v and each pair of neighbours, test for a path of length 3 avoiding v (exact search), cross-checked by a SAT encoding. Independence number: exact maximum clique of the complement with two solvers (bitset branch-and-bound and a SAT/MaxSAT query). For certificates: drat-trim/cake_lpr or an exact rational SDP checker.
pitfalls: R(C3,K_m) is the classical R(3,m), covered by the small-ramsey-lower-bounds target; stay with n >= 4.

Off-by-one: R(C4,K11) >= 40 is witnessed by a 39-vertex graph. A record needs a C4-free graph on 40 vertices with independence number at most 10 (R(C4,K11) >= 41). For R(C4,K12) it needs one on 43 vertices with independence number at most 11.

targets.name: Wheels and fans: close a gap in DS1 Table VIII (R(W7,W8) 19-21, R(W8,W8) 22-25, R(W4,W8) 22-26, ...) or R(F4,F4) 18-24
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours for lower bounds (block-circulant SAT on 18-30 vertices); flag algebras or SAT for upper bounds
targets.statement: W_n = K_1 + C_{n-1} is the wheel on n vertices and F_n = K_1 + nK_2 the fan of n triangles. DS1 revision #18 (Apr 2026) Table VIII gives R(W_m,W_n) for m <= n <= 10. Open cells: R(W4,W8) 22-26, R(W6,W8) 22-26, R(W7,W8) 19-21, R(W8,W8) 22-25, and lower-only cells R(W4,W9) >= 25, R(W5,W10) >= 21, R(W6,W9) >= 25, R(W7,W9) >= 19, R(W7,W10) >= 21, R(W8,W9) >= 25, R(W9,W9) >= 21, R(W10,W10) >= 28. For fans, Table X shows only R(F4,F4) <= 28. But Lin and Li's R(F_n,F_n) <= 6n (DS1 item 5.7.b) already gives 24, and Zhang and Chen (arXiv:2604.13850, Theorem 3) give R(F4,F4) >= 18, so 18 <= R(F4,F4) <= 24. Jiang and Shao proved R(F3,F4) = 17 (arXiv:2610.26109). Recent general bounds (Li-Kashima-Mao 2026, DeBiasio-Wimbish 2026, Zhang-Chen 2026) move no two-sided wheel cell. For the lower-only diagonal cells they give the only upper bounds, e.g. R(W9,W9) <= 36 and R(W10,W10) <= 50 (Zhang-Chen; Li-Kashima-Mao give 37 and 54). Bereg (Mathematics 14 (2026) 2310) reports three new off-diagonal wheel lower bounds. Credit: Van Overberghe, Lidicky-Pfender, Lidicky-McKinley-Pfender-Van Overberghe (R(W5,W7) = 15, R(W5,W9) = 18), Wesley, Faudree-McKay, Hendry, Harborth-Mengersen, Lin-Li, Zhang-Chen, Jiang-Shao, Bereg.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) an explicit graph G on N vertices with no W_m (resp. F_m) and whose complement has no W_n (resp. F_n), subgraphs not necessarily induced, checked by two independent exact programs, with N+1 STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the lower bound in the live DS1 tables and any newer paper; or (b) an upper bound STRICTLY BELOW (direction: min) the DS1 upper bound for a cell with one, certified by an exact-rational flag-algebra certificate or a DRAT/LRAT UNSAT proof with a checkable reduction. Off-by-one: a graph on N vertices proves R >= N+1.

partial_wins.statement: A first upper bound below the general-formula bound for one lower-only cell of Table VIII (e.g. R(W9,W9) or R(W10,W10)), certified as in (b), strictly below every bound in DS1, Li-Kashima-Mao (arXiv:2605.22116), Zhang-Chen (arXiv:2604.13850), DeBiasio-Wimbish (arXiv:2604.11937) and any newer paper.
R(F4,F4) improved on either side: a verified graph on 18 or more vertices with no F4 in it or its complement (giving >= 19), or a certified proof that R(F4,F4) <= 23.

targets.verification_method: W_n-freeness: for each vertex v, test whether G[N(v)] contains a cycle C_{n-1} (exact DFS over the neighbourhood, at most 10 vertices deep), cross-checked by a SAT encoding. F_n-freeness: for each v, compute the maximum matching of G[N(v)] (blossom algorithm, e.g. networkx) and require it to be below n. Run on G and the complement; check certificates with drat-trim or an exact SDP checker.
pitfalls: Some papers define W_n = K_1 + C_n with n+1 vertices; DS1 uses n vertices.
R(F3,F4) = 17 is now settled (Jiang-Shao 2026); DS1 still shows that cell blank.
DS1 Table X still prints R(F4,F4) <= 28 with no lower bound; the live range is 18-24 (Lin-Li upper bound 6n, Zhang-Chen lower bound 18).

Bereg, Computational Lower Bounds for Wheel Ramsey Numbers, Mathematics 14(13) (2026) 2310, gives three new off-diagonal wheel lower bounds with explicit certificate graphs (reported to be at n = 11, outside Table VIII); read it before claiming any wheel cell.

targets.name: Book Ramsey numbers off the n-1,n diagonal: close a gap in DS1 Table IXa (R(B4,B7) 22-23, R(B4,B9) 27-28, R(B5,B9) 28-30, R(B7,B11) 37-38) or a lower-only cell of Table VII (books versus cycles)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (2-block polycirculant SAT/IP on 22-45 vertices); upper bounds via flag algebras
targets.statement: B_n = K_2 + nK_1 is the book of n triangles on a common edge. DS1 revision #18 (Apr 2026) Table IXa lists R(B_m,B_n) for m <= 10, n <= 11. After the 2026 papers, the open cells with printed bounds are: - R(B4,B7) 22-23 (lower bound by monotonicity from R(B4,B6) = 22) - R(B4,B9) 27-28 (lower bound from srg(26,10,3,4) via item 5.3.l, upper bound from Rousseau-Sheehan, item 5.3.k) - R(B5,B9) 28-30 (lower bound Van Overberghe, upper bound from item 5.3.k) - R(B7,B11) 37-38 Blank cells of the table (for example R(B4,B8), R(B4,B10), R(B5,B8), R(B5,B10), R(B6,B9)) are open too, with bounds implied by monotonicity (item 5.3.a) and items 5.3.k/l, for example 27 <= R(B4,B10) <= 30 and 28 <= R(B5,B10) <= 32. The cells R(B5,B7) = 25, R(B7,B9) = 33 and R(B8,B10) = 37, still lower-only in DS1, are settled by Dai-Lin's R(B_{n-2},B_n) <= 4n-3 for n >= 3, n != 6 (arXiv:2606.07214) and Kalfus-Lidicky (arXiv:2606.05629). Together with DS1 5.3.j this settles R(B_{n-2},B_n) = 4n-3 for all n <= 21 except n = 6, where R(B4,B6) = 22. The diagonal is closed for n <= 21: srg(65,32,15,16) (Gritsenko 2021) and srg(85,42,20,21) (Verma, arXiv:2610.08893) give R(B16,B16) = 66 and R(B21,B21) = 86. Table VII (books versus cycles) has lower-only cells R(B8,C9) >= 23, R(B9,C9) >= 25, R(B9,C10) >= 26, R(B10,C10) >= 28. This target excludes the nearly diagonal numbers R(B_{n-1},B_n), a live Epoch AI FrontierMath problem. Credit: Rousseau-Sheehan, Wesley, Van Overberghe, Lidicky-Pfender, Lidicky-McKinley-Pfender-Van Overberghe, Shao-Xu-Bao-Pan, Dai-Lin, Kalfus-Lidicky.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) an explicit graph G on N vertices with no B_m and whose complement has no B_n (or no C_k for Table VII cells), verified by two independent programs, with N+1 STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best lower bound for that cell in the live DS1, Wesley (arXiv:2410.03625), Dai-Lin (arXiv:2606.07214), Chung-Wesley (arXiv:2610.36522) and any newer paper; or (b) an upper bound STRICTLY BELOW (direction: min) the best published upper bound for that cell, certified by an exact-rational flag-algebra certificate or a DRAT/LRAT UNSAT proof with a checkable reduction. Published bounds include those implied by DS1 5.3.a (monotonicity), 5.3.k and 5.3.l (strongly regular graphs) and by Dai-Lin's R(B_{n-2},B_n) <= 4n-3. Cells of the form R(B_{n-1},B_n) do not count here, nor do settled cells (R(B_{n-2},B_n) for n <= 21, including R(B5,B7), R(B7,B9) and R(B8,B10); R(B_n,B_n) for n <= 21). Off-by-one: a graph on N vertices proves R >= N+1.

partial_wins.statement: Settle a lower-only cell of Table VII (R(B8,C9), R(B9,C9), R(B9,C10) or R(B10,C10)): either a certified proof (as in (b)) that the listed lower bound is the exact value, e.g. R(B9,C9) <= 25, or a verified graph raising its lower bound.

A new exact value R(B_{n-2},B_n) = 4n-3 for some n >= 22 not covered by Wesley (arXiv:2410.03625), Dai-Lin (arXiv:2606.07214) or any newer paper: an explicit verified graph on 4n-4 vertices with no B_{n-2} and no B_n in its complement (the matching upper bound is Dai-Lin's theorem).

targets.verification_method: B_n-freeness: for every edge uv of G count common neighbours and require fewer than n; for the complement do the same over non-edges with common non-neighbours. Implement twice (matrix product A^2 restricted to edges, and explicit set intersection). For C_k use an exact cycle search cross-checked by SAT. Certificates via drat-trim/cake_lpr or an exact SDP checker.
pitfalls: R(B_{n-1},B_n) = 4n-1 (smallest open n = 64, Chung-Wesley arXiv:2610.36522) is a live Epoch AI problem with its own verifier; it is held, not part of this target.

DS1 (Apr 2026) still shows R(B5,B7) >= 25, R(B7,B9) >= 33, R(B8,B10) >= 37 and 4n+1 <= R(B_n,B_n) <= 4n+2 for n <= 21. All of these are settled (Dai-Lin, Kalfus-Lidicky, and the srgs of Gritsenko and Verma).
Lower bounds from strongly regular graphs: an srg(v,k,lambda,mu) avoids B_{lambda+1} and its complement avoids B_{v-2k+mu-1}. Check Brouwer's table before claiming a 'new' construction.
Text extraction of DS1 Table IXa misplaces columns: the '27-28' and ' > = 28' entries sit in column n = 9 (R(B4,B9), R(B5,B9)), not n = 10. Read the rendered PDF.

For p2: Dai-Lin's lemma gives R(B_{n-2},B_n) = 4n-3 whenever a symmetric Hadamard matrix of order 2n-2 with constant diagonal exists (the order must be 4u^2, so n = 2u^2+1). Any n for which such a matrix is already in the literature counts as covered.

targets.name: Multicolour Ramsey numbers of short cycles: close R5(C4) 27-29, R6(C4) 34-38, R4(C6) 18-20, R(C3,C3,C4,C4) 30-36, R(C4,C4,K4) 20-21 or a similar DS1 cell
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours for lower bounds (colourings of K_17..K_87); needs cluster or flag algebras for upper bounds
targets.statement: R(G1,...,Gk) is the least N such that every k-colouring of the edges of K_N has a colour-i copy of G_i for some i. DS1 revision #18 (Apr 2026), Sections 6.3.2-6.3.3, lists: 27 <= R5(C4) <= 29 (lower Lazebnik-Woldar), 34 <= R6(C4) <= 38 (Exoo; Boza), 33 <= R4(C5) <= 77 (flag algebras, Lidicky-Pfender), 18 <= R4(C6) <= 20 (Sun et al.; Zhang-Sun-Wu), 24 <= R(C3,C4,C4,C4) <= 27, 30 <= R(C3,C3,C4,C4) <= 36, 49 <= R(C3,C3,C3,C4) <= 57, 18 <= R(C4,C6,C6,C6) <= 20, 18 <= R(C4,C4,C6,C6) <= 20, 20 <= R(C4,C4,K4) <= 21, 27 <= R(C3,C4,K4) <= 29, 52 <= R(C4,K4,K4) <= 66, 34 <= R(C4,C4,C4,K4) <= 48, 49 <= R(C3,C4,C4,K4) <= 75, 87 <= R(C4,C4,K4,K4) <= 177. In three colours, Dzido's conjecture R3(C10) = 20 and the Bondy-Erdos case R3(C9) = 33 are the first open cases. Credit: Dybizbanski-Dzido, Xu-Radziszowski, Boza-Radziszowski, Lazebnik-Woldar, Exoo, Wesley (arXiv:2509.03784), Lidicky-Pfender, Sun Yongqi and coauthors, Zhang-Sun-Wu.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) an explicit k-colouring of the edges of K_N (an N x N symmetric colour matrix) with no colour-i copy of G_i for every i, checked by two independent exact programs, with N+1 STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the lower bound for that cell in the live DS1 and any newer paper; or (b) an upper bound STRICTLY BELOW (direction: min) the DS1 upper bound, certified by an exact-rational flag-algebra certificate or a DRAT/LRAT UNSAT proof with a checkable reduction. Off-by-one: a colouring of K_N proves R >= N+1.

partial_wins.statement: A certified proof of R3(C10) <= 20 or R3(C9) <= 33 (each matching the known lower bound and settling a first open case of the Dzido or Bondy-Erdos conjecture).
Any upper-bound improvement by at least 1 for R5(C4), R6(C4) or R4(C6) with a re-checkable certificate.

targets.verification_method: For each colour class, test for the forbidden graph exactly: C4 via common-neighbour counts (A_i^2 off-diagonal at most 1), C_k for k >= 5 via exact cycle search, K4 via clique enumeration; cross-check each with a SAT query that must be UNSAT. Confirm the matrix is symmetric, complete and uses only k colours. Certificates via drat-trim/cake_lpr or an exact SDP checker.
pitfalls: Multicolour classical numbers with only complete graphs (R(3,3,3,3) and the like) belong to the small-ramsey-lower-bounds and classical-upper-bound targets, not this one.
R4(C4) = 18 and R5(C6) = 26 are settled.

targets.name: Small hypergraph Ramsey numbers: beat R(4,5;3) >= 35, R(4,6;3) >= 63, R(5,5;3) >= 88, R(4,4,4;3) >= 79 or R(5,5;4) >= 35, or settle R(K4-t,K5;3) in 14-16
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (cyclic or SAT colourings of triples on 35-90 points; checking needs at most C(89,5) ~ 4.2e7 subsets)
targets.statement: R(s,t;3) is the least N such that every red/blue colouring of the triples of an N-set contains s points with all triples red or t points with all triples blue (similarly for 4-uniform and three colours). The only known nontrivial value is R(4,4;3) = 13 (McKay-Radziszowski 1991). DS1 revision #18 (Apr 2026) Section 7.1 lists the lower bounds R(4,5;3) >= 35 (Dybizbanski 2018), R(4,6;3) >= 63, R(5,5;3) >= 88, R(4,4,4;3) >= 79 (Dybizbanski's addendum, cyclic colourings), R(5,5;4) >= 35 (Exoo 2021), and 14 <= R(K4-t,K5;3) <= 16 (Exoo; Lidicky-Pfender), where K4-t is K4^(3) minus one triple. Dybizbanski's page notes that only cyclic colourings were searched and no negative results exist. No 2026 arXiv paper found improves these small cells (recent work is asymptotic: Conlon-He-Nie-Post, Gishboliner-Hajebi-Li). Credit: Dybizbanski, Exoo, McKay-Radziszowski, Lidicky-Pfender, Budden-Hiller-Rosenberg.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit colouring of all r-subsets (r = 3 or 4) of {0..N-1} (a file listing each subset and colour, or a rule plus the expanded file) such that no s-set is monochromatic in colour 1 and no t-set in colour 2 (no u-set in colour 3 for R(4,4,4;3)), verified by exhaustive enumeration of all s-, t- and u-subsets with two independent programs, with N+1 STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the lower bound in the live DS1, Dybizbanski's page and any newer paper. Off-by-one: a colouring on N points proves R >= N+1.

partial_wins.statement: R(K4-t,K5;3) improved: a verified colouring of the triples of a 14-point set with no red K4-t and no blue K5^(3) (giving >= 15), or a certified (DRAT/LRAT or exact flag-algebra) proof that R(K4-t,K5;3) <= 15.

A new lower bound for R(4,7;3) or R(5,6;3), witnessed by an explicit verified colouring. It must be strictly above every value stated for that number in DS1 or any newer paper, and above the trivial bounds R(4,7;3) >= 64 and R(5,6;3) >= 89 (from adding one point whose triples all get colour 2). The claim must state the comparison value and its source. Multicolour numbers with a 5 in the last colour, such as R(4,4,5;3), do not count: the lexicographic product behind DS1 7.1.a (Bruce-Budden-Hiller) already gives R(4,4,5;3) >= (13-1)^2+1 = 145.

targets.verification_method: Load the colouring into a dictionary keyed by sorted r-tuples and check it covers all C(N,r) subsets exactly once. For each s-subset test whether all its r-subsets are colour 1 (and likewise for t, u); use itertools in one implementation and a bitmask/numba sweep in another. For cyclic colourings also verify the expanded file, not only the orbit representatives.
angles: Go beyond cyclic symmetry: colourings invariant under x -> x+d and x -> -x, or under an affine group AGL(1,p), then SAT over orbit colours.
Seed from Dybizbanski's published 34-point colouring (colouring.txt on his page) and run SAT on a one-point extension.
pitfalls: Do not run downloaded verifier code (verif.cpp); write your own checker.
Bounds derived by recurrences in DS1 7.1.f (e.g. R(5,6;4) >= 67) are not explicit colourings; p2 needs an explicit object.
Lexicographic products (Bruce-Budden-Hiller, DS1 7.1.a) give R(s,t,5;3) >= (R(s,t;3)-1)^2+1 for free. Compare any multicolour claim against these implied bounds, not only against printed values.

targets.name: Octahedron Ramsey number: is R(K_{2,2,2}, K_{2,2,2}) 30 or 31?
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (a 30-vertex witness search, or an UNSAT proof on 30 vertices with symmetry breaking)
targets.statement: The octahedron K_{2,2,2} is the complete 3-partite graph with parts of size 2 (6 vertices, 12 edges). DS1 revision #18 (Apr 2026), item 5.13, gives 30 <= R(K_{2,2,2}, K_{2,2,2}) <= 31: the lower bound is from Harborth and Krause's distance colourings, the upper bound from Lidicky and Pfender's flag-algebra method (SIAM J. Discrete Math. 2021, arXiv:1704.03592). The value is one bit away: a 2-colouring of K_30 with no monochromatic octahedron gives 31, a proof that none exists gives 30. No 2026 paper found by an arXiv title search touches this cell.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) an explicit graph G on 30 vertices such that neither G nor its complement contains K_{2,2,2} as a subgraph, verified by two independent exact programs, proving R = 31; or (b) a proof that every graph on 30 vertices contains K_{2,2,2} in it or its complement, proving R = 30, certified by a DRAT/LRAT/FRAT UNSAT proof of a stated CNF (any symmetry breaking must be proved sound, e.g. via SAT modulo symmetries with a checkable certificate) that a referee regenerates and checks. Either settles the number (the current gap is 30-31, so both directions are strict improvements).

partial_wins.statement: A complete, certified classification showing that no circulant, 2-block or 3-block polycirculant graph on 30 vertices works (exhaustive search with a re-runnable script and an UNSAT certificate per symmetry class), not already reported by Harborth-Krause, Lidicky-Pfender, Lidicky-McKinley-Pfender-Van Overberghe or any newer paper.

A DRAT/LRAT-certified proof, on a CNF the verifier regenerates, that no graph on 30 vertices with G and its complement both octahedron-free has every degree in {14, 15} (so any witness for R = 31 must be irregular). An explicit such graph would instead be the full win.

targets.verification_method: K_{2,2,2}-freeness: G contains an octahedron as a subgraph iff some 6 vertices split into three disjoint pairs with all 12 cross-pair edges present (edges inside a pair are irrelevant). Implement once by brute force over all C(30,6) = 593,775 six-subsets and their 15 pairings into three pairs, and once as a SAT query that must be UNSAT. Run both on G and on its complement. UNSAT claims: regenerate the CNF, check the proof with drat-trim or cake_lpr, and audit any symmetry breaking for soundness.
pitfalls: The octahedron is not induced-forbidden: any 6 vertices with all 12 cross-part edges count, whatever happens inside the parts.

targets.name: Small vertex and edge Folkman numbers: improve a bound in the Hassan-Radziszowski-Van Overberghe 2026 tables
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (witness graphs on 15-65 vertices; arrowing checked by small SAT instances)
targets.statement: G -> (a1,...,ak)^v means every k-colouring of the vertices of G has a colour-i K_{a_i}; ^e is the edge version. The Folkman number F(a1,...,ak; H) is the least order of an H-free graph with that property. Hassan, Radziszowski and Van Overberghe (arXiv:2605.16542, May 2026; code at github.com/Steven-VO/vertexFolkman, witnesses on House of Graphs) tabulate a_i in {2,3}, k <= 4, H in {K_n, J_n = K_n - e, n = 4,5,6} plus C4 and W5. Open entries: Fv(2,2,3;J4) 20-36, Fv(3,3;J4) 24-45 (Table 1 prints 23, but Section 4.5 proves >= 24), Fv(2,3,3;K4) 20-24 (Bikov-Nenov), Fv(2,3,3;J5) 15-18, Fv(3,3,3;K4) <= 51, Fv(3,3,3;J5) <= 32, Fv(3,3,3;K5) <= 21, Fe(3,3;J5) <= 43, Fv(3,3;C4) 30-63, Fe(3,3;W5) <= 64, Fv(2,3,3,3;K5) <= 32, Fv(3,3,3,3;K6) <= 30. Fv(3,3;K5) = 8, which Tong Niu re-proved (arXiv:2605.05526), already follows from Luczak-Urbanski's Lemma 1 and is not open. Excluded: the edge Folkman number Fe(3,3;4) (21-786), which carries a Graham prize (erdosproblems.com/582), and the existence of Fe(3,3; complement of P2 u P3), which bounds it. Credit: Hassan, Radziszowski, Van Overberghe, Bikov, Nenov, Coles-Radziszowski, Deng-Liang-Shao-Xu.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) an explicit graph G (graph6 or edge list) on N vertices that is H-free and arrows the stated tuple, with N STRICTLY BELOW (direction: min) the upper bound in arXiv:2605.16542 (latest version), Bikov's papers and any newer source; H-freeness checked exhaustively, arrowing certified by a DRAT/LRAT UNSAT proof that no vertex (resp. edge) colouring avoids every colour-i K_{a_i}; or (b) for an entry with a printed lower bound (Fv(2,2,3;J4), Fv(3,3;J4), Fv(2,3,3;K4), Fv(2,3,3;J5), Fv(3,3;C4)), a lower bound STRICTLY ABOVE (direction: max) the published one (for Fv(3,3;J4) that is the 24 of Section 4.5, not the 23 printed in Table 1), i.e. a proof that no H-free graph on N vertices arrows the tuple, by a re-runnable exhaustive generation (e.g. nauty geng with stated filters) plus per-graph SAT certificates, or a single checkable certificate. Lower bounds for upper-bound-only entries count only under p1. The witnesses for Fe(3,3;4) and Fe(3,3; complement of P2 u P3) are out of scope.

partial_wins.statement: A certified lower bound (as in (b)) for an upper-bound-only entry, strictly above both the monotonicity bound and the deletion-inequality bound in pitfalls, and above any bound found by a fresh search: Fv(3,3,3;K5) >= 16 (monotonicity from Fv(3,3,3;J6) = 15 and the deletion inequality both give 15), Fv(3,3,3;J5) >= 19 (the deletion inequality gives 18), Fv(3,3,3;K4) >= 25 (the deletion inequality gives 24), or Fe(3,3;J5) >= 16 (it is >= Fe(3,3;K5) = 15).
An exact value: an entry of Tables 1-2 of arXiv:2605.16542 settled by a new certified witness meeting a known or new certified lower bound.

targets.verification_method: H-freeness: exhaustive subgraph search for K_n / J_n (clique enumeration with one missing edge allowed), C4 (A^2 off-diagonal at most 1) or W5 (C4 in a neighbourhood), cross-checked by SAT. Arrowing: encode one Boolean (or one-hot) variable per vertex (edge) colour and one clause per K_{a_i} forbidding colour i on all of it; solve with CaDiCaL/kissat, require UNSAT and check the DRAT proof with drat-trim. Lower bounds: re-run the stated generation and check each certificate.
angles: Semi-polycirculant generation gave most 2026 bounds; vary block structures, or search Cayley graphs of non-abelian groups.
Locally linear graphs gave Fv(3,3;J4) >= 24 (all maximal locally linear graphs on 23 vertices checked); extending that enumeration to 24 vertices would give 25.
pitfalls: Fe(3,3;4) has a $100 Graham prize attached (erdosproblems.com/582) and is held separately; any graph found here that is K4-free and edge-arrows (3,3) must be reported to the human, not posted.
Vertex versus edge arrowing are different: Fv(3,3;C4) and Fe(3,3;W5) are linked by Fe(3,3;W5) <= Fv(3,3;C4)+1.
Table 1 prints Fv(3,3;J4) >= 23, but Section 4.5 of the same paper proves >= 24; a lower-bound claim must reach 25.

Deletion inequality: if G -> (3,3,3)^v and S is an independent set, then G - S -> (2,3,3)^v (give S the colour of the independent class; two independent sets together contain no triangle), so |G| >= Fv(2,3,3;H) + alpha(G). With R(4,4) = 18, R(4,5) = 25 and R(3,5) = 14 this already gives Fv(3,3,3;K4) >= 24, Fv(3,3,3;J5) >= 18 and Fv(3,3,3;K5) >= 15; a lower bound at or below these is not new.

targets.name: Five-colour bipartite Ramsey number b5(2) (26-28): a rectangle-free 5-colouring of the 26 x 26 grid, or a proof that none exists
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days to needs cluster (SAT on 676 cells x 5 colours with symmetry assumptions)
targets.statement: The bipartite Ramsey number b_k(2) is the least b such that every k-colouring of the edges of K_{b,b} has a monochromatic C4; equivalently every k-colouring of the b x b grid has a monochromatic rectangle (four cells at the corners of an axis-parallel rectangle). Known: b2(2) = 5 (Beineke-Schwenk), b3(2) = 11 (Exoo 1991), b4(2) = 19 (Dybizbanski-Dzido-Radziszowski, Ars Combin. 2015; the 4-colouring of the 18 x 18 grid was also found by Steinbach and Posthoff in 2012, and the two colourings are isomorphic). For five colours 26 <= b5(2) <= 28 (Dybizbanski-Dzido-Radziszowski, arXiv:1303.5475, Theorem 10). The lower bound is the affine construction over GF(5): rows and columns are indexed by GF(5) x GF(5), and cell ((a,b),(a',b')) gets colour a*a' - b - b'. The upper bound is the Zarankiewicz bound z(28;2) <= 156, since 5 * 156 < 784. They conjectured b5(2) = 28 (Conjecture 11); Collins-Riasanovsky-Wallace-Radziszowski (2016) call it the smallest open case for five colours. Fenner-Gasarch-Glover-Purewal (arXiv:1005.3750) show the 25 x 30 grid is 5-colourable. Liu, Chew and Heule (arXiv:2012.12582, AAAI 2021) tried SAT with internal 'shift pattern' symmetries on the 26 x 26 grid without success; their closest attempts left 2 or 3 unsatisfied clauses. An arXiv check (to 30 Oct 2026) found no later settlement. DS1 does not cover bipartite Ramsey numbers, so no maintained table tracks this value.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) an explicit 5-colouring of the 26 x 26 grid (a 26 x 26 matrix over {0..4}) with no monochromatic rectangle, verified by two independent programs, proving b5(2) >= 27 STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the current 26; or (b) a proof that every 5-colouring of the 27 x 27 grid has a monochromatic rectangle, proving b5(2) <= 27 STRICTLY BELOW (direction: min) the current 28, certified by a DRAT/LRAT UNSAT proof of a stated CNF with only provably sound symmetry breaking, re-checkable by a referee. A rectangle-free 5-colouring of the 27 x 27 grid would settle b5(2) = 28.

partial_wins.statement: A certified UNSAT proof (drat-trim/LRAT) that no rectangle-free 5-colouring of the 26 x 26 grid exists within a precisely stated symmetry class not already excluded in arXiv:2012.12582 (for example colourings invariant under a stated cyclic shift of rows and columns).
An explicit 5-colouring of the 26 x 26 grid with exactly one monochromatic rectangle, or of the grid minus one cell with none, verified exhaustively (a near-miss object no published source reports).

targets.verification_method: For each colour c and each pair of rows (r1, r2), count the columns where both rows have colour c; a count of 2 or more is a rectangle. That is 5 x C(26,2) x 26 operations; implement with numpy bit operations and with plain loops. Check the matrix shape and colour range. For (b), regenerate the CNF and check the proof with drat-trim or cake_lpr.
pitfalls: Status checked only by arXiv searches and the papers above (no maintained table exists); re-check Gasarch-style grid-colouring literature before claiming.

Each colour class must be a C4-free bipartite graph, so 5 z(n;2) >= n^2 is necessary. z(n;2) is known exactly for all n <= 31 (Collins et al. 2016, Table 3, from DDR and Afzaly-McKay): z(26;2) = 138, z(27;2) = 147, z(28;2) = 156. The counting slack is 690 - 676 = 14 cells for 26 x 26 and 735 - 729 = 6 for 27 x 27, so in a 27 x 27 colouring every colour class has at least 141 edges, close to extremal; 5 * 156 = 780 < 784 is the upper bound 28.

Liu-Chew-Heule already exclude 26 x 26 colourings in which the whole grid splits into shift-pattern subgrids (sizes 2, 13 or 26) and several 25 x 25-plus-border patterns; a p1 class must be one they did not exclude.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Classical Ramsey upper bounds with machine-checkable certificates: R(3,3,3,3) <= 60, R(3,10) <= 40, R(4,6) <= 39, R(5,5) <= 45, R(3,3,5) <= 56, R(3,4,4) <= 76
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (SAT cube-and-conquer over gluing or neighbourhood classifications; proofs of terabyte scale are possible)
targets.statement: Upper bounds for classical Ramsey numbers R(k1,...,kr) (no monochromatic K_{k_i} in colour i) move rarely and only by massive certified computation. Current values: R(3,3,3,3) <= 61 by Milos Tatarevic (arXiv:2610.36648, 27 Oct 2026; Lean-formalised reductions plus SAT refutations with two solvers), improving 62 of Fettes-Kramer-Radziszowski (2004); lower bound 51 (Chung). R(3,10) <= 41 (Angeltveit, E-JC 2025), lower 40. Angeltveit-McKay's 2019-2024 bounds R(4,6) <= 40, R(5,5) <= 46 (DS1 Table Ib). Three colours: R(3,3,5) <= 57, R(3,4,4) <= 77 (from the recurrence 6.1.a), R(3,3,6) <= 91, R(3,4,5) <= 157, R(4,4,4) <= 229 (Boza, arXiv:2603.10851), R(3,3,3,4) <= 149. R(3,3,4) = 30 (Codish-Frank-Itzhakov-Miller 2016) is settled. Source of the table: DS1 revision #18 (Apr 2026), Tables Ia/Ib and Section 6.1, plus the Tatarevic preprint. This target covers upper bounds only; explicit lower-bound constructions belong to small-ramsey-lower-bounds.
targets.success_criterion: An upper bound STRICTLY BELOW (direction: min) the best published upper bound for one of R(3,3,3,3), R(3,10), R(4,6), R(5,5), R(3,3,5), R(3,4,4), R(3,3,6), R(3,4,5), R(4,4,4) or R(3,3,3,4) at verification time (DS1 latest revision, arXiv:2610.36648, arXiv:2603.10851 and a fresh arXiv search), backed by a certificate a stranger's computer can check end to end: every combinatorial reduction machine-checked (Lean/Isabelle/HOL4) or reduced to finite statements, and every finite case refuted by a DRAT/LRAT/FRAT proof that verifies with drat-trim, cake_lpr or an equivalent checker, or by an exact-rational LP/SDP certificate. A computation without checkable certificates is at most PROMISING.

partial_wins.statement: An independent, fully certified re-verification of a published bound whose main computation currently lacks public checkable certificates, released with the proofs and a re-run script: e.g. R(3,3,3,3) <= 61 (Tatarevic's 56,723 K61 refutations are two-solver UNSAT answers without DRAT/LRAT logs; only the 55 classification pairs are LRAT-certified), R(4,6) <= 40, R(5,5) <= 46 or R(3,10) <= 41.

A certified upper bound strictly below the current recurrence (6.1.a) value for a multicolour number not in the main list and not improved in any published source, such as R(3,3,4,4) <= 449 (recurrence value 450) or R(3,3,3,3,3) <= 301 (the recurrence with R(3,3,3,3) <= 61 gives 302; DS1 shows 307).

targets.verification_method: Rebuild every CNF from the stated reduction with an independent generator, check the reduction's formal proof in its proof assistant, check each SAT refutation with drat-trim/cake_lpr (LRAT preferred), and confirm the cases cover the whole space (hash the case list). For LP/SDP certificates, verify feasibility and the bound in exact rational arithmetic.
pitfalls: DS1 (Apr 2026) still shows R(3,3,3,3) <= 62; the live bound is 61 (Tatarevic, Oct 2026).
With R(3,3,3,3) <= 61 the recurrence 6.1.a gives R(3,3,3,3,3) <= 302, not DS1's 307; recompute every recurrence-derived bound before calling one new.
Upper bounds implied only by recurrences from smaller improved bounds count only if the smaller bound itself is new and certified.

targets.name: Sloane's 1973 question: an extremal doubly-even self-dual binary [72,36,16] code
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster for any serious search; verifying a claimed code takes laptop-minutes to laptop-hours (2^36 codewords, or Brouwer-Zimmermann)
targets.statement: A doubly-even self-dual binary code of length n has minimum weight d <= 4*floor(n/24)+4 (Mallows-Sloane; Rains for all self-dual codes). For n = 24m a self-dual code meeting the bound must be doubly even (Rains), and the codewords of each fixed weight hold 5-designs (Assmus-Mattson). At lengths 24m the only known extremal codes are the extended Golay code (24) and the extended quadratic residue code (48). N. J. A. Sloane asked in 1973 whether a [72,36,16] self-dual code exists. It is still open. A long series of papers restricts Aut(C) of such a code. Conway-Pless, Bouyuklieva, O'Brien-Willems and others treat prime orders. Feulner and Nebe (arXiv:1110.6012) exclude Z7, Z3xZ3 and D10. Borello, Dalla Volta and Nebe (arXiv:1303.4899) exclude S3, A4 and D8. Borello (arXiv:1304.7162) excludes the elementary abelian group of order 8, which gives |Aut(C)| <= 5. Yorgov and Yorgov (arXiv:1310.2570, IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 60 (2014) 3302-3307) exclude Z4. So Aut(C) is trivial, C2, C3, C2xC2 or C5. Bouyuklieva, Willems and Yankov (2014) note that no extremal code of length 24m other than those of lengths 24 and 48 is known. The reviewer knows of no construction or non-existence proof since then. Re-check arXiv before claiming.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a 36 x 72 binary generator matrix G with these properties, each checked by two independently written programs. (1) rank(G) = 36 over GF(2). (2) G G^T = 0 over GF(2), so the code is self-dual. (3) Every row of G has weight divisible by 4, which together with (2) makes the code doubly even. (4) There are no codewords of weight 4, 8 or 12, so the exact minimum weight is 16, shown by exhaustive enumeration of all 2^36 - 1 nonzero codewords or by an exact Brouwer-Zimmermann computation, never by sampling. (5) The weight distribution equals the unique extremal Gleason weight enumerator (A_16 = 249849). A non-existence proof is also a full win if it comes as an independently re-runnable certificate (exhaustive search with checkable proof logs) that a skeptic re-runs.

partial_wins.statement: A re-runnable non-existence certificate excluding, for an extremal [72,36,16] code, one automorphism case that the literature still allows at claim time. Examples are Aut(C) containing C2xC2, an automorphism of order 5, or an automorphism of order 3 of the cycle type still allowed. The certificate is published search code that a skeptic re-runs, or SAT runs with DRAT/LRAT proofs, together with a written reduction. A fresh literature search must show that the case was not already excluded.

targets.verification_method: Check rank, G G^T = 0 and row weights mod 4 with bit-packed GF(2) arithmetic. Enumerate all 2^36 codewords with a Gray-code walk over 72-bit words using XOR and popcount, a few minutes in C. Confirm that A_4 = A_8 = A_12 = 0 and that the distribution matches the extremal enumerator from Gleason's theorem. A second independent implementation (e.g. a Brouwer-Zimmermann minimum-distance routine) must agree. Then search arXiv for a newer claim.
angles: Restrict to codes with an automorphism of order 3 or 5 of the cycle types still allowed: the code splits into a fixed subcode and an F2[x]/(Phi_p) module, which shrinks the search enormously.
Use the 5-design structure on the minimum-weight words as a pruning test during search.
Build from known [72,36,12]/[72,36,14] self-dual codes via neighbours, using exact low-weight counts as the fitness function.
pitfalls: Singly-even (Type I) [72,36,14] or [72,36,16] claims are not this problem. The code must be doubly even, and Type I codes cannot reach 16 at n = 72.
The literature already excludes many automorphism groups. A search restricted to an excluded group can only rediscover non-existence.
Minimum weight estimated by random codeword sampling proves nothing.

Dougherty, Karadeniz and Yildiz (arXiv:1303.4920, 2013) claim that Aut(C) has no involution, which would leave only orders 1, 3 and 5. Later papers (Borello 2013, Yorgov-Yorgov 2014) still list C2 and C2xC2 as open, so a p1 claim for an involution case must say how it relates to that claim.

targets.name: Extremal doubly-even self-dual binary codes at lengths 96, 120 and 128 (beyond the famous 72)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster for a search; checking a claimed [96,48,20] code takes laptop-hours, and a [120,60,24] or [128,64,24] code laptop-days, with an exact Brouwer-Zimmermann minimum-weight routine
targets.statement: A doubly-even self-dual binary code of length n (8 | n) has d <= 4*floor(n/24)+4 and is extremal when it meets this bound, so d = 20 needs n >= 96. Harada (arXiv:1902.08739, Adv. Math. Commun. 14 (2020) 89-96) records the status. Existence of an extremal code is unknown at length 96 (d = 20) and at lengths 120 and 128 (d = 24). At 104 the extended quadratic residue code is the only known extremal code. At 112 the first extremal code was found by Harada (2008), and the 2019 note shows at least three inequivalent ones exist. Doubly-even self-dual codes with d = 20 are known at 120 and at 128, so the open step there is d = 24. At 120 the first was found by Gaborit, Nedeloaia and Wassermann (2005), 25 more by Yorgova and Wassermann (2008), and more by Harada. At 128 one comes from Gaborit's table of Type II codes, and Harada gave more. Automorphism restrictions are known. For a [96,48,20] code only the primes 2, 3 and 5 can divide |Aut(C)|, and Bouyuklieva, Willems and Yankov exclude an automorphism of order 15. De la Cruz (arXiv:1302.0033) shows that only 2, 3, 5, 7, 19, 23 and 29 can divide |Aut(C)| of a [120,60,24] code. Length 72 is a separate bank entry (extremal-doubly-even-self-dual-72). The reviewer knows of no construction at 96, 120 or 128. Re-check arXiv before claiming.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a generator matrix of a binary doubly-even self-dual [96,48,20], [120,60,24] or [128,64,24] code. Two independent programs must confirm all of the following. (1) Full rank n/2 over GF(2). (2) G G^T = 0. (3) All row weights are divisible by 4. (4) The exact minimum weight equals the extremal value, with no codeword of any smaller weight divisible by 4, shown by an exact minimum-distance algorithm and never by sampling. (5) The length still has no published extremal code at claim time.

partial_wins.statement: A second extremal doubly-even self-dual [104,52,20] code, proved inequivalent to the extended quadratic residue code of length 104 by an invariant such as the automorphism group order or the number of codewords of weight 20 through a fixed coordinate set, provided that a fresh literature search shows no second [104,52,20] code has been published since Harada (arXiv:1902.08739).

targets.verification_method: Check rank, self-orthogonality and doubly-evenness with bit-packed GF(2) code. Compute the minimum weight with two independent exact implementations, for example a Brouwer-Zimmermann routine with several disjoint information sets plus a separate enumeration of low-weight codewords via the extremal weight enumerator (A_20 for 96 follows from Gleason's theorem), and require agreement. For p1, compute the inequivalence invariant independently.
angles: Quasi-cyclic and double-circulant searches with an allowed automorphism of prime order (19, 23 or 29 at length 120), as Harada and Gulliver did at 112.
Neighbour walks from the known d = 20 codes at 120 and 128, scoring the exact count of weight-20 codewords and pushing it to zero.
pitfalls: A d = 20 code at length 120 or 128 is not extremal. Extremal there means d = 24.
Singly-even codes do not count.
Re-check the literature before claiming p1: Harada's 2019 note is the latest status statement found, and later double-circulant papers may have produced more [104,52,20] codes.

targets.name: Ternary self-dual codes: raise the largest known minimum weight at length 84, 108 or 120
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days for structured (four-negacirculant, bordered double circulant) searches and for exact minimum weight at length 84; exact verification at lengths 108 and 120 may need cluster unless a large automorphism group is used
targets.statement: A ternary self-dual code of length n exists iff 4 | n and has d <= 3*floor(n/12)+3 (Mallows-Sloane). Extremal codes cannot exist at n = 72, 96, 120 or any n >= 144, because the extremal weight enumerator has a negative coefficient (see Rains-Sloane). Araya and Harada (arXiv:2212.01080, Des. Codes Cryptogr. 91 (2023) 1813-1843, Table 1) list the current largest minimum weight d3(12m). It is 12, 15, 18 and 18 for m = 3..6 and 24 for m = 8, all settled. The open cells are d3(84) = 21 or 24, d3(108) = 27 or 30 and d3(120) = 24, 27 or 30. At 84 the extended QR code QR84 and the Pless symmetry code P84 give 21. At 108 two near-extremal codes are known. For m >= 7 the only ternary near-extremal self-dual codes Araya-Harada list are QR84, P84, P96 and those two codes of length 108. QR84 and P84 have 2368488 and 1259520 codewords of weight 21. Harada's later note on near-extremal codes of lengths 36, 48 and 60 (arXiv:2412.04795v2, 3 Jul 2025) leaves these values unchanged.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a generator matrix over GF(3) of a ternary self-dual code with one of the parameters [84,42,24], [108,54,30], [120,60,27] or [120,60,30]. (1) Rank n/2 over GF(3). (2) G G^T = 0 mod 3. (3) The exact minimum Hamming weight is at least the stated value and strictly above the lower bound in Araya-Harada Table 1, computed exactly by two independent minimum-distance implementations and never by sampling. (4) A fresh search shows no earlier publication of a ternary self-dual code with that length and minimum weight.

partial_wins.statement: A ternary self-dual [84,42,21] code whose exact number of weight-21 codewords differs from 2368488 (QR84) and 1259520 (P84), which proves it inequivalent to both. A fresh search must show that no such code has been published since Araya-Harada (2023). Rank, G G^T = 0 mod 3 and minimum weight are checked as in the main criterion, and two independent implementations compute the weight-21 count exactly.

targets.verification_method: Check rank and G G^T = 0 with exact mod-3 arithmetic. Compute the minimum weight with a Brouwer-Zimmermann algorithm over GF(3) using several information sets, cross-checked by a second independent implementation, or confirm that the low-weight counts match the coefficients forced by Gleason's theorem for ternary self-dual codes. Then compare against Araya-Harada Table 1 and search arXiv for newer values.
angles: Four-negacirculant and bordered double-negacirculant constructions, which Harada and coauthors classified up to length 60 and which hold most known extremal ternary codes.
Neighbours of QR84, P84 and the Pless symmetry codes, scored by the exact number of weight-21 codewords.
pitfalls: Lengths 72, 96 and 120 cannot reach the extremal bound (d = 21, 27, 33); the open values listed above are below it.
Ternary self-dual means Euclidean self-dual over GF(3) with G G^T = 0 mod 3, not mod 2.

targets.name: Quaternary Hermitian self-dual codes: an extremal [32,16,12] code, or a better minimum weight at length 42, 48, 54 or 60
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days for quasi-twisted / four-circulant searches over GF(4); exact minimum weight of a [32,16] GF(4) code takes laptop-minutes
targets.statement: A Hermitian self-dual code over GF(4) of length n has d <= 2*floor(n/6)+2 (extremal when equal). Harada (arXiv:2401.15265, Jan 2024) notes that the largest minimum weight d(n) is determined only for n <= 30. At length 32 the currently known largest minimum weight is 10, against the extremal value 12. Kalra and Prakash (arXiv:2501.10163, v3 Mar 2026, Theorem 4) prove that no extremal Hermitian self-dual code of length 12m exists. At x = 1, y = i/sqrt(3) the weight enumerator equals c_{2m}(-16/27)^{2m}, which their magic-state argument shows is non-negative, while the extremal enumerator has c_{2m} < 0. This rules out [36,18,14], [48,24,18] and [60,30,22] and recovers the known non-existence at 12 and 24, so d(36) = 12, attained by the known [36,18,12] codes. Araya and Harada (arXiv:2212.01080, DCC 2023, Table 2) give dH4(6m) as 12, 14 or 16 at 42 and 16, 18 or 20 at 54. With Kalra-Prakash the ranges at 48 and 60 shrink to 14 or 16 and to 16, 18 or 20. Araya-Harada state that existence of a near-extremal code (d = 2*floor(n/6)) is unknown at lengths 42 to 60. Harada's 2024 modified four mu-circulant search gives the same lower bounds and the first Hermitian self-dual [56,28,16] codes. Kim and Lee (IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 59 (2013)) classified extremal codes of lengths 30 and 32 that have an automorphism of odd prime order and showed that an extremal [32,16,12] code has none.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a generator matrix over GF(4) = {0,1,w,w^2} of a Hermitian self-dual code with one of the parameters [32,16,12], [42,21, > =14], [48,24,16], [54,27, > =18] or [60,30, > =18]. (1) Rank n/2. (2) G conj(G)^T = 0, where conj squares each entry. (3) The exact minimum weight is verified by two independent implementations and is strictly above the lower bound stated in the sources above. (4) A fresh literature search shows no earlier code with those parameters.

partial_wins.statement: A quaternary Hermitian self-dual code of length 40, 44, 52 or 56 whose exact minimum weight, verified by two independent implementations, is strictly greater than the largest known value in Table 8 of Harada (arXiv:2401.15265), which is 12 at 40, 12 at 44, 14 at 52 and 16 at 56 (upper bounds 14, 16, 18, 20). It must also beat any code of that length published later.

targets.verification_method: Implement GF(4) arithmetic with exact tables. Check rank and that the Hermitian Gram matrix G conj(G)^T is zero. Compute the minimum weight by full enumeration when 4^(n/2) is small enough, or by a Brouwer-Zimmermann algorithm over GF(4), with a second independent check. For n = 32, enumerating the 4^16 codewords (or one per scalar multiple) takes minutes. For any claimed extremal length-12m code, evaluate its weight enumerator at y^2 = -1/3 first: Kalra-Prakash show it cannot exist.
angles: Search beyond the modified four mu-circulant family, which Harada exhausted at 32 without beating 10: try bordered constructions, quasi-twisted codes, or automorphisms of order 2 or 4 (Kim-Lee exclude odd prime orders for an extremal [32,16,12] code).
Neighbour walks from the known [32,16,10] codes, minimising the number of weight-10 codewords.
pitfalls: Hermitian self-duality uses conjugation (x -> x^2). Euclidean self-dual GF(4) codes are a different family.
Additive self-dual GF(4) codes (quantum codes) are not linear Hermitian self-dual codes and do not count.
No extremal Hermitian self-dual code of length 12m exists (Kalra-Prakash, arXiv:2501.10163, Theorem 4): [36,18,14], [48,24,18] and [60,30,22] are impossible, and d(36) = 12 is settled.
Kim-Lee (2013): an extremal [32,16,12] code has no automorphism of odd prime order, so searches built on an order-3, 5, 7, ... automorphism at length 32 cannot succeed.

targets.name: Near-extremal self-dual codes with new weight enumerators: realize an admissible ternary (lengths 36-72) or quaternary Hermitian (lengths 24-36) enumerator not yet known to exist
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours: negacirculant and neighbour searches plus exact counting of minimum-weight codewords
targets.statement: For a near-extremal ternary self-dual code of length 12m (d = 3m) the weight enumerator depends on the number alpha of minimum-weight codewords. Araya and Harada (arXiv:2212.01080, Des. Codes Cryptogr. 91 (2023) 1813-1843) derived restrictions on admissible alpha for m = 3, 4, 5, 6 (lengths 36, 48, 60, 72) and listed the alpha values known to be realized (their Question 1). They did the same for near-extremal quaternary Hermitian self-dual codes of length 6m, with an explicit Question 2: settle the remaining admissible alpha for m = 4, 5, 6 (lengths 24, 30, 36). Rukavina and Tonchev (J. Combin. Des. 32 (2024) 606-624; Ex. Countex. 5 (2024) 100130) and Pender (Discrete Math. 347 (2024) 113968) added ternary values at lengths 36 and 48. Harada (arXiv:2412.04795v2, 3 Jul 2025; Discrete Math. 349 (2026) 114675) collected those lists, realized many new ternary alpha values at lengths 36, 48 and 60 with a negacirculant construction, and corrected the length-72 list of Araya-Harada Proposition 4.2; his extensive negacirculant search found no near-extremal code of length 72. At length 36 the values still open are alpha = 8 beta with beta in {1..5, 84, 86..89, 92, 94..111}. Harada's 2024 Hermitian paper (arXiv:2401.15265) adds no new near-extremal Hermitian values (its [24,12,8] and [36,18,12] codes have alpha = 513, 594, 837 and 19548, 20844). Weight enumerators and code data are posted at http://yuki.cs.inf.shizuoka.ac.jp/WE/ and https://www.math.is.tohoku.ac.jp/~mharada/F3-9nega/. A 2026-10-30 arXiv search found no later paper. Many admissible values remain unrealized; each new value is a separate cell. A related bank entry asks for larger minimum weights; this one fixes the minimum weight and asks for new enumerators.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit ternary self-dual code of length 36, 48, 60 or 72 with minimum weight exactly 3m, or a quaternary Hermitian self-dual code of length 24, 30 or 36 with minimum weight exactly 2m. Its weight enumerator parameter(s), computed exactly, must be admissible by Araya-Harada (2023) and must differ from every value listed as realized in Araya-Harada (2023), Rukavina-Tonchev (2024), Pender (2024), Harada (arXiv:2412.04795v2 = Discrete Math. 349 (2026) 114675) and any later paper found by a fresh search. Equivalent codes count once; each new parameter value counts as one cell.

partial_wins.statement: A re-runnable non-existence certificate for an admissible weight enumerator listed as open by Araya-Harada (2023) or Harada (2025), for example a classification of all codes with that many minimum-weight codewords under a stated structural restriction proved to be without loss of generality.

targets.verification_method: Check self-duality: G G^T = 0 mod 3 for ternary codes, G conj(G)^T = 0 over GF(4) for Hermitian codes. Compute the exact number of codewords of minimum weight and confirm that no smaller weight occurs, with two independent implementations (for ternary length 60, enumerate weight-15 codewords exactly via information-set splitting). Derive alpha (and beta where the enumerator has two parameters) and compare with the published realized lists.
angles: Harada's negacirculant method (arXiv:2412.04795) found new values quickly at lengths 36, 48 and 60, but his extensive search with it found no near-extremal code of length 72. At 72 try other structures (four-negacirculant, bordered double circulant, codes with an automorphism of odd prime order); for Hermitian length 30 try an omega-circulant or negacirculant analogue.
Neighbour walks: each neighbour step changes alpha by a computable amount, so steer towards unrealized values.
pitfalls: alpha must lie in the admissible set. Values excluded by Araya-Harada's restrictions cannot be realized.
The length-72 ternary list in Araya-Harada Proposition 4.2 was corrected by Harada (2025); use the corrected list.

targets.name: Spherical t-designs on S^2 with fewer points: beat the smallest known N for a degree t (Hardin-Sloane, Graef-Potts and Womersley tables)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (numerical design search plus high-precision polishing; N up to ~5000)
targets.statement: A spherical t-design is a set of N points on S^2 whose equal-weight average integrates every polynomial of degree <= t exactly. The smallest N for each t is unknown beyond small cases. Live records (checked 2026-10-30): (1) R. H. Hardin and N. J. A. Sloane (neilsloane.com/sphdesigns/, DCG 1996, last modified Oct 02 2002) conjecture tau(N), the largest t for an N-point design, for N <= 100, giving minimal N = 12, 24, 24, 36, 48, 60, 70, 84, 94 for t = 5..13; their library /sphdesigns/dim3/ also has des.3.N.t files up to a 240-point 21-design; (2) Manuel Graef's putatively optimal Chebyshev-type rules (TU Chemnitz quadrature page, dated 18 Nov 2016; Graef-Potts, Numer. Math. 2011) for t = 1..42 (except 4 and 6), even t = 44..90, t = 94, 98, 100, 114, 124 and high-degree files for t = 100..1000, e.g. t = 14: 108, 20: 216, 30: 480, 40: 840, 60: 1860, 100: 5100; (3) Rob Womersley's efficient designs (UNSW, index updated 4-Feb-2017): sf for all t <= 180 with N = ceil((t+1)^2/2)+1 for even t and t >= 17 (e.g. t = 92: 4326), and symmetric ss for odd t <= 325 with N = 2 ceil((t^2+t+4)/4) for t >= 17 (e.g. t = 43: 948, 99: 4952). Womersley says these need not be smallest. The record N(t) is the minimum over all these files of designs with strength >= t, e.g. 13: 94, 15: 120, 43: 948, 92: 4326, 96: 4706. Henry Cohn now hosts the Hardin-Sloane table (cohn.mit.edu/sloane, same tau values). A 2026-10-30 literature search found no smaller designs: the AlphaEvolve survey (Georgiev, Gomez-Serrano, Tao, Wagner, arXiv:2511.02864, section 17) reports uncertified numerical (error < 1e-8) 19-designs with 198-204 points and 21-designs with 234-236 points, which improve only on the Hardin-Sloane library files (204, 240) and do not beat Graef's 192 and 234; Xu and Xu (arXiv:2609.15016) prove existence with 54t^2 points, far above the records. Search again before attacking and before claiming.
targets.success_criterion: Success means either (a) for some t in 13..100, an N-point t-design on S^2 with N STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the record N(t) = minimum over the Hardin-Sloane tau table and /sphdesigns/dim3/ library, Graef's Chebyshev-type S^2 files (S2designs and S2designs_high) and Womersley's sf and ss tables of the N of any design with strength >= t, all re-fetched immediately before claiming, or (b) for some N <= 100, an N-point design of strength tau(N)+1 (disproving the Hardin-Sloane conjecture at that N). The design is verified from coordinates given to >= 32 significant digits: after normalization in >= 40-digit arithmetic (mpmath or Arb), S_l = (4 pi/(2l+1)) sum_k |(1/N) sum_j Y_lk(x_j)|^2 (equal to (1/N^2) sum_{i,j} P_l(x_i . x_j)) is < 1e-40 for every l = 1..t, computed from the Weyl sums (the pair-sum form needs >= 60 digits because of cancellation). N must also exceed the Delsarte-Goethals-Seidel bound ((e+1)^2 for t = 2e, (e+1)(e+2) for t = 2e+1) and must not be matched by any design the skeptic finds in the literature for strength >= t.

partial_wins.statement: For some t in 101..325, an N-point t-design with N strictly below the same merged record N(t), verified in double precision with every S_l <= 1e-26 for l = 1..t (the standard of Womersley's posted files), coordinates to >= 16 digits.

A computer-assisted existence proof (interval Newton or Krawczyk in Arb, in a symmetry-reduced system, own code that the skeptic reruns) of a t-design with N equal to the record N(t) for some t >= 14 for which the skeptic finds no published existence proof at that N (Hardin-Sloane's V1/V2 proofs cover only a few small cases; Chen-Frommer-Lang's interval proofs use N = (t+1)^2).

targets.verification_method: Checker: fetch neilsloane.com/sphdesigns/ (tau table), Graef's page (S2designs/N < t > _M < N > _*.dat links) and Womersley's sf.html and ss.html (file names sfTTT.NNNNN, ssTTT.NNNNN) and build N(t) = min N over all entries of strength >= t. Load claimed points in mpmath at 40 digits, normalize, compute Weyl sums sum_j Y_lk(x_j) by the stable Legendre recurrence for l <= t (cost N (t+1)^2; minutes for N <= 1000, about an hour at N = 5000), and S_l = 4 pi/(2l+1) sum_k |sum_j Y_lk(x_j)/N|^2; assert max S_l < 1e-40. Check N < N(t). Run the checker on one posted file per source as a parser sanity test.
angles: Graef's records use rotation-group symmetry (Sobolev's theorem): only invariant harmonics need vanish, so a T-, O- or I-invariant ansatz with N = sum of orbit sizes reduces the equations sharply; try orbit mixes Graef did not list, especially at even t > 60 where only Womersley's sf formula is posted (e.g. t = 92, 96, 102-112) and Graef's pattern sits 2-6 points lower.

Minimize Womersley's potential A_{t,N} (sum of a positive-definite polynomial kernel) with L-BFGS at N = record-1, record-2 from many starts; polish survivors with Levenberg-Marquardt in double-double, then mpmath.
For odd t, antipodal designs need only even-degree harmonics; Womersley's ss family is the record at most odd t >= 43, so a symmetric search with 2 fewer points is the most direct test.
pitfalls: A double-precision residual of 1e-16 does not prove a design when N < (t+1)^2/2 (more equations than unknowns): the 1e-40 standard at >= 30 digits is required for a full win.
The record at t is the minimum over designs of strength >= t, so a 14-design with 108 points also bounds t = 13 and lower.
Graef's regular files start with a header (number of columns, number of points) followed by Cartesian rows; his high-degree S2designs_high files instead give spherical angles (phi, theta).
t <= 12 entries are Hardin-Sloane conjectures backed by extensive search; attacking them is a moonshot.

targets.name: Positive-weight quadrature on the sphere S^2: exact to degree t with fewer nodes than Graef's and Lebedev-Laikov's rules
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (orbit-structured nonlinear least squares, then high-precision polishing)
targets.statement: Find M nodes on S^2 and positive weights such that the rule integrates every polynomial of degree <= t exactly, with M as small as possible (Gauss-type rules; equal weights give designs, a separate bank entry). Live tables (checked 2026-10-30): Manuel Graef's putatively optimal Gauss-type S^2 rules (TU Chemnitz quadrature page, dated 18 Nov 2016; files S2quads/N < t > _M < M > _ < group > .dat, coordinates and weights to 11 digits) for t = 1..30, 32, 34..39 and 44, e.g. t = 13: 64, 20: 148, 30: 322, 35: 422, 39: 522, 44: 672; and the Lebedev-Laikov octahedral rules (degrees 3..131, list at people.sc.fsu.edu/~jburkardt), e.g. 31: 350, 35: 434, 41: 590, 47: 770, 131: 5810. Not every posted rule is positive: Graef's files for t = 18 (M = 122), 24 (M = 210) and 38 (M = 508) and the Lebedev rules of degree 13, 25 and 27 contain negative weights (checked 2026-10-30), so they are not positive-rule records. The record M(t) is the minimum over the positive rules in both tables and the spherical-design records of rules exact to degree >= t.
