Where Graef has no positive rule of degree t the record comes from a neighbour: t = 18 (130, Graef degree 19), 24 (220, Graef degree 25), 31 (350, Lebedev), 33 (410, from degree 34), 38 (522, Graef degree 39), 40 and 41 (590, Lebedev 41), 42 and 43 (672, from degree 44). Graef's rules for t = 1, 2, 3, 5 (M = 2, 4, 6, 12) attain the Delsarte-Goethals-Seidel bound and are optimal. The McLaren efficiency (t+1)^2/(3M) of Graef's odd-degree rules with t >= 13 is 1.02-1.04, so the gaps look improvable. The Encyclopaedia of Cubature Formulas (bank target ecf-cubature-fewer-points) tabulates the solid ball, not the sphere surface. Other published S^2 rules (Ahrens-Beylkin 2009 icosahedral rules, whose efficiency is generally below 1, e.g. 192 nodes for degree 23; A. S. Popov) must be checked for every claim. A 2026-10-30 literature search found no 2024-2026 paper with positive S^2 rules on fewer nodes; search again before attacking and before claiming.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a rule (M nodes on S^2, M positive weights) exact to degree t for some t at which Graef's Gauss-type table has a positive rule, other than t = 1, 2, 3, 5 (t = 4, 6..17, 19..23, 25..30, 32, 34..37, 39, 44), with M STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than Graef's M(t), than every positive Lebedev-Laikov rule of degree >= t, and than every spherical-design record of strength >= t, all re-fetched before claiming, and not matched by any published rule the skeptic finds (check Ahrens-Beylkin 2009, Proc. R. Soc. A, and A. S. Popov's 1994-2008 papers). Verification from nodes and weights given to >= 32 digits, in >= 40-digit arithmetic with weights normalized to sum 1: all weights > 0, |sum w - 1| < 1e-30, and for every l = 1..t, (4 pi/(2l+1)) sum_k |sum_j w_j Y_lk(x_j)|^2 < 1e-40, computed from the weighted Weyl sums (the pair-sum form sum_{i,j} w_i w_j P_l(x_i . x_j) needs >= 60 digits). M must exceed the Delsarte-Goethals-Seidel bound for positive rules ((e+1)^2 for t = 2e, (e+1)(e+2) for t = 2e+1), else it is a bug.

partial_wins.statement: A positive rule exact to degree t for a gap degree t in {18, 24, 31, 33, 38, 40, 41, 42, 43} (no positive Graef rule of that exact degree) with M strictly below the merged positive record M(t) defined in the statement (18: 130, 24: 220, 31: 350, 33: 410, 38: 522, 40-41: 590, 42-43: 672, re-fetched) and not matched by any published rule the skeptic finds (Ahrens-Beylkin, Popov), same high-precision checks.

A positive rule exact to degree t for some t in 45..131 with M strictly below every Lebedev-Laikov rule of degree >= t, every design record of strength >= t and every published rule the skeptic finds (Ahrens-Beylkin 2009 icosahedral rules, Popov), AND McLaren efficiency (t+1)^2/(3M) > 1.0; same checks.

A positive-weight quadrature on SO(3) exact for all Wigner D-functions of degree <= N with fewer nodes than Graef's SO(3) Gauss-type table (N = 1..9, 11, 14: M = 4, 11, 23, 43, 60, 116, 168, 240, 300, 504, 960) and than any published SO(3) rule the skeptic finds, verified with the same residual standard on D-functions.

targets.verification_method: Checker (minutes): build M(t) from Graef's page (S2quads and S2designs links), the Burkardt Lebedev list and the design tables, keeping only rules whose posted weights are all > 0 (this drops Graef's t = 18, 24, 38 files and Lebedev's degree-13, 25, 27 rules). Load the claimed rule at 40 digits; normalize nodes and weights; assert positivity; compute Weyl sums sum_j w_j Y_lk(x_j) for l <= t by recurrence and the quadratic residuals; assert < 1e-40. Sanity: the same code on Graef's N044_M672_Ico.dat must give residuals ~1e-16 in double (11-digit data).
angles: Gap degrees first (p1): Graef's neighbours at t = 30/32 (C4, T) and 34/35 (C4, C5) suggest the group and orbit structure to try at t = 31 and 33; solve the invariant moment equations with Levenberg-Marquardt from many orbit-mix choices.
Node elimination (Xiao-Gimbutas style): start from a rule of degree t with M nodes, remove the smallest-weight node or orbit and re-solve; repeat while it converges.
Caratheodory-Tchakaloff compression: an LP/NNLS on a dense candidate grid yields a positive rule with at most (t+1)^2 nodes, a start for nonlinear node elimination.
pitfalls: A rule with a tiny negative weight is not a positive rule.
Exactness to 1e-16 in double is not exactness when the system is overdetermined; use the 30-digit standard.
Do not compare Lebedev rules by order alone: a rule of degree t also counts for every lower degree.

Graef's posted Gauss-type files for t = 18, 24 and 38 and the Lebedev rules of degree 13, 25 and 27 have negative weights. They are not positive-rule records; a rule that beats only them is a gap-degree claim (p1).

targets.name: Maximum-determinant (Fekete-type interpolation) points on S^2: a larger log det than Womersley's table for some degree n <= 100
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (n <= 40) to laptop-days (n near 100; (n+1)^2 x (n+1)^2 Gram matrices up to 10201 x 10201)
targets.statement: For polynomial degree n choose d_n = (n+1)^2 points x_1..x_dn on S^2 to maximize log det G, where G_ij = sum_{l=0}^n (2l+1)/(4 pi) P_l(x_i . x_j) is the reproducing-kernel Gram matrix of polynomials of degree <= n (maximum determinant, or extremal, systems; good interpolation and cubature nodes). Rob Womersley's MaxDet page (UNSW, updated 03-Jun-2020; with Ian Sloan, Adv. Comput. Math. 2001, 2004) lists n = 1..200 with f = log det G to 2 decimals, bounds log(d_n!/(4 pi)^d_n) <= f <= d_n log(d_n/(4 pi)), the gradient norm, and files S2Pts/MD/mdNNN.NNNNN (x, y, z and cubature weight per row, 16 digits). Only n = 1 (regular tetrahedron) is a proven global maximum; Womersley notes many local maxima and that background searches update the table when better systems are found. Rows n <= 100 are converged (gradient 1e-15 to 3e-10); rows n = 101..200 have gradient 4.9e-4 to 1e-2. Checked 2026-10-30: md010.00121 recomputes to f = 266.3178 (table 266.32). Example values: n = 20: 1535.65, n = 50: 13648.51, n = 100: 67416.72. Womersley's older extremal tables (17-Oct-2007 and 16-Jan-2003 pages) have no row above the 2020 values. A 2026-10-30 literature search found no later improvement; search again before claiming.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for some n in 2..100, (n+1)^2 points on the unit sphere (coordinates to >= 16 digits) whose log det G* (Cholesky in double after normalizing; confirmed in mpmath at 30 digits for n <= 20) is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than both (i) the table value f(n) on the live MaxDet1.html plus 0.005 (the 2-decimal rounding), and (ii) the log det of Womersley's posted md file for n after the skeptic polishes it by gradient ascent to gradient norm < 1e-10, by at least 1e-6 in each case, re-fetched immediately before claiming. The claimed set must be a numerical local maximum (gradient norm < 1e-8) so the value is well defined.

partial_wins.statement: For some n in 101..150 (rows whose posted gradient norm is 4.9e-4 or more), a point set whose log det exceeds the polished posted md file's value by at least 0.01; this beats the table only in its unconverged region, so it is a partial win.
A table-integrity finding: an n whose posted md file recomputes to a log det differing from the table's f by more than 0.01, reported with both values.

targets.verification_method: Checker: fetch MaxDet1.html and parse f(n); download S2Pts/MD/md < n > . < d_n > ; build G from the Legendre recurrence; slogdet via Cholesky (assert positive definite); polish posted points by projected gradient ascent (the gradient of log det G is the row-wise kernel derivative weighted by G^-1); compute the claimed set's log det the same way; assert both margins. About 2 minutes for n = 100 on 16 GB RAM.
angles: Many restarts with diverse seeds (spiral, Thomson minima, efficient designs with (n+1)^2 points, icosadeltahedral sets) followed by L-BFGS on log det; low-n rows (n = 14..46) date from 2002-2006 and may have been searched less than the 2019-2020 rows.
Defect engineering as in Thomson searches: relocate the 12 disclination-like defects of the Voronoi structure and re-optimize.
Use the gradient formula with a G^-1 update (Sherman-Morrison) for single-point moves to make basin hopping cheap.
pitfalls: The table has 2 decimals; always compare against the recomputed and polished posted file, not the printed number.
log det depends on the kernel normalization; use exactly G_ij = sum (2l+1)/(4 pi) P_l, which reproduces Womersley's values.
n >= 101 rows are unconverged; polishing alone raises them, which is why they are only p1.

targets.name: Spherical t-designs on S^3 (including SO(3) Chebyshev rules) with fewer points: beat the smallest known N for a degree t
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (N up to ~12000 points in R^4; high-precision polishing is the bottleneck)
targets.statement: A spherical t-design on S^3 (unit sphere in R^4) is a set of N points whose average integrates every polynomial of degree <= t exactly. Live tables (checked 2026-10-30): (1) Rob Womersley's efficient S^3 designs (UNSW S3SD.html, updated 09-Oct-2017; Womersley 2018, Springer volume for Ian Sloan's 80th): sdf for t = 1..20 (e.g. t = 4: 20, 8: 97, 12: 275, 16: 597, 20: 1106), symmetric sds for odd t <= 31 (e.g. 13: 308, 21: 1184, 25: 1954, 31: 3642) and regular sets sdr (e.g. the 24-cell 5-design and the 120-point 600-cell 11-design); (2) Manuel Graef's Chebyshev-type rules on SO(3) (TU Chemnitz quadrature page, dated 18 Nov 2016) for degrees N = 1..9, 11, 13, 14, 15, 17, 19, 23 with M rotations, which give antipodal S^3 designs of strength 2N+1 with 2M points via unit quaternions +-q (e.g. N = 7, M = 168: a 336-point 15-design). The record N(t) is the minimum over both tables of designs of strength >= t: 12: 275, 13: 308, 14-15: 336, 16: 597, 17: 624, 18-19: 720, 20: 1106, 21: 1184, 22-23: 1344, 24-25: 1954, 26-27: 2352, 28-29: 2520, 30-31: 3552, 32-35: 5040, 36-39: 6600, 40-47: 11760. Above t = 31 the record comes only from sparse SO(3) entries, so t = 32..47 look improvable. Small t (<= 11) involve proven or near-proven cases (8-point cross-polytope, 24-cell, 600-cell; Boyvalenkov-Danev) and Hardin-Sloane-Cara's 4-d tables, so full wins start at t = 12. Checked 2026-10-30: Graef's N07_M168 rotations converted to +-q give a 336-point 15-design (residuals about 1e-17 in double), and a literature search found no 2024-2026 paper with smaller S^3 designs; search again before attacking and before claiming.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for some t in 12..47, an N-point t-design on S^3 with N STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the record N(t) (minimum over Womersley's sdf/sds/sdr files on S3SD.html and Graef's SO(3) Chebyshev entries converted to 2M points of strength 2N+1, re-fetched before claiming), not matched by any design the skeptic finds in the literature, and above the Delsarte-Goethals-Seidel bound. Verified from coordinates given to >= 32 digits: after normalization, S_l = (1/N^2) sum_{i,j} U_l(x_i . x_j)/(l+1) < 1e-40 for every l = 1..t (U_l = C_l^(1), Chebyshev of the second kind; these sums are >= 0 and vanish exactly for a design), computed in >= 60-digit arithmetic (Arb or python-flint) because the pair sum cancels from O(1) terms, or from S^3 harmonic Weyl sums in >= 40-digit arithmetic.

partial_wins.statement: For some t in 32..47, an N-point t-design with N strictly below the record N(t), verified only in double precision with every S_l <= 1e-26 (the standard of the posted files), coordinates to >= 16 digits.

An antipodal (x and -x both present) t-design on S^3 for some odd t in 13..47 with fewer points than every antipodal entry (Womersley sds, sdr, Graef SO(3) conversions) of strength >= t, under the full high-precision checks, even if a smaller non-antipodal design exists.
For some t in 21..31, a t-design with N strictly below the record N(t), verified in double precision as in p1 (a stepping stone toward a full win at the same t).

targets.verification_method: Checker: build N(t) from S3SD.html (file names sd[frs]TTT.NNNNN) and Graef's SO3designs/N < k > _M < m > _*.dat links (strength 2k+1, size 2m). Load claimed points at 40 digits, normalize, compute S_l via S^3 harmonic Weyl sums or the pair sum with the Chebyshev-U recurrence (pair sum cost N^2 t: use Arb or python-flint for N > 2000); assert max S_l < 1e-40. Sanity: convert Graef's N07_M168 rotations to quaternions +-q and confirm a 15-design with S_l ~ 1e-16 in double.
angles: t = 32..35: Womersley's sdf growth (about 1.2 t^3/9 points) predicts roughly 4400 points for t = 32, below the 5040 record; minimize the positive-definite potential A_{t,N} with L-BFGS in double, then polish with double-double Gauss-Newton and confirm in Arb.

Group orbits: unions of orbits of the binary icosahedral group (order 120) acting on both sides of S^3 (pairs G1 x G2 as in Graef's SO(3) tables) reduce the equations by Sobolev's theorem; try group pairs Graef did not list.
Antipodal symmetry halves the work for odd t: only even-degree harmonics need vanish.
pitfalls: Gegenbauer normalization: for S^3 use C_l^(1) = U_l (Chebyshev second kind), divided by U_l(1) = l+1.
SO(3) rotation matrices map to quaternions only up to sign; include both q and -q (2M points).
The record at t is the minimum over designs of strength >= t; for example the 600-cell (120 points) is an 11-design and so bounds t = 10 as well.
Some small cases are proven minimal or unique (e.g. the 8-point cross-polytope 3-design; Boyvalenkov and Danev on the 120-point 11-design); check the literature before attacking t <= 11.

targets.name: Mondrian Art Problem: a smaller defect than the best known for some n = 67..96 (OEIS A276523), or the exact a(67)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (local search or SAT per n; exact optimality proofs are laptop-days)
targets.statement: Split an n x n square into at least two integer-sided rectangles, no two congruent (1x2 and 2x4 may both appear, two 1x2 may not). The defect is the largest rectangle area minus the smallest, and a(n) = OEIS A276523(n) is the least defect. Ed Pegg Jr posed it in 2016 as Gordon Hamilton's Mondrian Art Puzzle. Robert Gerbicz computed the optimal values for n = 3..57 and Michel Gaillard for 58..65. DATA now runs to a(66) = 14 (Mia Muessig). On 2025-11-19 Muessig posted best-known tilings for n = 67..96 (file a276523_2.txt). They are marked optimal ('=') for n = 68-70, 72-75, 78 and 83-85 and are only upper bounds ('<=') for 67 (16), 71 (18), 76 (18), 77 (17), 79 (16), 80 (18), 81 (17), 82 (18), 86 (18), 87 (22), 88 (18), 89 (19), 90 (20), 91 (17), 92 (20), 93 (22), 94 (20), 95 (20) and 96 (24). On 2026-10-30 all 31 tilings in that file were re-checked with an independently written checker: each is a valid partition with exactly the stated defect. García-Colín, Leemans, Müßig and Roldán (arXiv:2311.02385, 2023) showed that no perfect (defect 0) partition exists for n <= 1000. Garrison, Seiler and Semchankau (arXiv:2609.01998, 2026) proved an O(n^{5/6}) upper bound but give no per-n values. Pegg's conjectured upper bound ceil(n/log n)+3 is OEIS A278970. The soft cells are 87, 93 and 96, whose values sit well above their neighbours.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit partition of an n x n square, with n one of 67, 71, 76, 77, 79, 80, 81, 82 or 86..96 (any n whose live A276523 entry still marks the value as only best known), into k >= 2 axis-parallel integer-sided rectangles that are pairwise non-congruent (no two share the same unordered side pair), tile the square exactly and have defect (max area - min area) STRICTLY less than the best-known value for that n in the live A276523 entry, its linked a276523_2.txt and records/values.txt of https://github.com/PhoenixSmaug/mondrian-heuristic (Muessig and Garrison's best-value table for every n up to 3000; on 2026-10-30 it agrees with the OEIS values for 67..96). All three must be re-fetched immediately before claiming, and the OEIS history (including pending drafts) checked for a newer value. The partition is given as a list of rectangles (x, y, w, h) or as an n x n letter grid in Muessig's format.

partial_wins.statement: The exact value of a(67) (best known 16): an exhaustive search proving that no valid partition of the 67 x 67 square has defect <= 15 (or a better tiling, which is a full win), done by two independently written programs that both reproduce every DATA value a(3)..a(66) of A276523.

An extension of the García-Colín–Leemans–Müßig–Roldán result: a computer proof by two independent programs that no perfect (defect 0) Mondrian partition exists for every n <= N, with N >= 1100. It is labelled as a bounded result.
A perfect (defect 0) Mondrian partition of an n x n square for some n > 1000. Nobody has proved it impossible. Verified exactly.

targets.verification_method: Parse the grid or rectangle list. Check that it covers n x n exactly with no overlap (each letter's cells form a full w x h block), that the unordered dimension pairs are pairwise distinct and that k >= 2. Compute max area minus min area and compare with the live value for n. This takes milliseconds. For p1/p2, rerun both programs, check that they reproduce the b-file, and compare their logs.
angles: Fix the rectangle multiset first: choose a window of allowed areas [A, A+d] and enumerate the distinct dimension pairs with area in the window and sides <= n. Their total area must reach n^2 with distinct shapes. Then run an exact-cover / SAT packing of the square (Gerbicz's and Muessig's approach).
Exploit near-symmetric layouts: many optimal tilings for large n are 'pinwheel plus strips'. Search over guillotine and pinwheel skeletons first, then refine with CP-SAT.
From VLSI floorplanning: represent candidate tilings as sequence pairs and anneal over them, with an exact feasibility check per window.
pitfalls: Congruent means the same unordered dimensions. Similar rectangles are allowed, and rotated copies of one shape are NOT allowed.
Muessig's comment and the a(66)..a(96) file supersede the older 2024 best-known list (also in the comments). Compare with the newest one.
Values marked '=' or '*' (68-70, 72-75, 78, 83-85) are proven optimal and cannot be beaten.
A single 1-rectangle 'tiling' is excluded (k >= 2).

The Muessig-Garrison hierarchical heuristic (github.com/PhoenixSmaug/mondrian-heuristic, October 2026 census at 240 s per n) is tuned for large n: at every open n in 67..96 it lands 3 to 12 above the best known (23 vs 16 at n = 67), so running it unchanged will not win here.

targets.name: Mrs Perkins's quilt: a coprime squared square with at most n squares and a larger side than the best known (OEIS A089047/A089046, n >= 19)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (search over squared-rectangle building blocks); exact proofs laptop-days
targets.statement: Mrs Perkins's quilt: tile a k x k square with integer squares whose sides have gcd 1, using as few squares as possible. A005670(k) is that minimum, and Ed Wynn's exhaustive generation (arXiv:1308.5420, 2013) proved it correct for k <= 120. The inverse sequences give the largest square side reachable with at most n squares (A089047) and the least side forcing at least n squares (A089046). Wynn proved A089047 through a(18) = 91. The rest are best known only: A089047(19..33) = 126, 158, 216, 276, 386, 488, 675, 866, 1179, 1544, 2136, 2739, 3755, 4988, 6443. Ed Pegg Jr (2017-07-06) added further best-known terms for n = 34..39 as an OEIS comment: 8568, 11357, 14877, 19594, 26697, 34632. He calls the tables 'almost certainly correct up to 5000', and N. J. A. Sloane deleted DATA terms above 5000. Pegg's July 2017 update on Stuart Anderson's squaring.net extends the best-known quilts to every side up to 40,000. It was built from the squaring.net SPSS and SISS collections (Duijvestijn, Skinner, Anderson, Pegg, Johnson, Milla, Williams and others) by recursive 'builds' from about 65 million prime quilts. Pegg calls that list very reliable only up to 33 squares and says the records are fragile. He expected about 10 solutions up to size 10000 to change once the complete SPSS/SISS collections to order 37 were processed. Jim Williams completed the SPSS enumeration to order 37 in 2020. Earlier contributors include Richard K. Guy, Lance Gay and Geoffrey Morley. J. H. Conway and G. B. Trustrum showed that the answer grows like log k. The weakest records are those for n >= 34 and sides above about 5000.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit dissection of a k x k square into m integer-sided squares with gcd of all sides = 1 and 2 <= m <= n, for some n with 19 <= n <= 39, where k is STRICTLY greater than the best-known value of A089047(n) (DATA for n <= 33, Pegg's listed further terms for n = 34..39), both re-fetched live immediately before claiming. Squares need not be distinct. The dissection is given as a list of (x, y, s) or a Bouwkamp code. It must not already appear in squaring.net's Mrs Perkins's Quilts list or the OEIS history.

partial_wins.statement: For some side k with 121 <= k <= 40000, a coprime dissection of the k x k square into fewer squares than the count on Pegg's best-known list (squaring.net MrsPerkinssQuilts.txt.zip, July 2017), verified exactly.

An extension of Wynn's proved range: exact A005670(k) for every k from 121 up to some K >= 130, by an exhaustive search run with two independent programs that both reproduce Wynn's b-file for k <= 120.
A proof (exhaustive, two independent programs, with checkable logs) that A089047(19) = 126 is optimal, i.e. that no coprime quilt with at most 19 squares has side > 126.

targets.verification_method: Check exact coverage of the k x k grid by the listed squares (an integer sweep or cell count with no overlap), that gcd of the sides is 1, and that the number of squares is <= n. Compare k with the live A089047 entry. This takes milliseconds.
angles: Large good quilts glue a near-square imperfect squared rectangle to one big square. Search over squared rectangles of order <= n-1 with aspect close to 1 (Bouwkamp codes from plantri-generated c-nets) and complete each to a square.
Run Pegg's construction in reverse: start from his best quilts for n = 33..39 and try local Bouwkamp-code mutations that keep the square shape while growing the side.
From electrical network theory: the side equals a spanning-tree-count determinant. Optimise the network's complexity over planar graphs with n+1 edges using Kirchhoff's theorem.
pitfalls: gcd = 1 is required: scaling a smaller quilt is not allowed.
Values for k <= 120 (A005670) are proven, so a quilt with side <= 120 cannot be a win.
A089046 and A089047 are inverse sequences with different directions. Use the stated criterion (larger side with at most n squares).
Pegg's further terms are in comments, not DATA. Re-read the live entry: terms may have been added or corrected.

targets.name: Squared-rectangle census: the next complete count of perfect squared rectangles (order 27), squared squares (order 38) or compound perfect squares (order 40)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (planar-graph generation plus electrical-network solving over ~10^11 graphs); an independent recount of a 2024 term is laptop-days
targets.statement: Squared rectangles correspond to planar electrical networks (Brooks, Smith, Stone and Tutte, 1940), and their complete enumeration by order is one of the classic computer censuses. Live state: simple perfect squared rectangles (squares included) OEIS A002839 to order 26 (2,994,833,854), with a(25) and a(26) contributed by Stuart E. Anderson in 2024. Simple imperfect squared rectangles A002881 also run to order 26 (153,812,801). Simple perfect squared squares A006983 are complete to order 37 (17,086,918; orders 33-37 by Jim Williams, finalised July 2020). squaring.net says the collection for orders 38+ is only partial (about 4.65 x 10^7 SPSSs are estimated in order 38), and Ed Pegg Jr wrote in 2020 that order 38 'is expected to be too large to analyze for at least a few years'. Compound perfect squared squares A217155 are complete to order 39 (62,894,424, Williams, 2018). Earlier orders are due to Duijvestijn, Bouwkamp, Federico, Gambini, Skinner, Pegg, Johnson, Milla and Anderson. Brinkmann and McKay's plantri is the usual graph generator.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact next term of one of: A002839 a(27), A002881 a(27), A006983 a(38) or A217155 a(40), as defined in the live OEIS entry and re-fetched immediately before claiming (the first index not in DATA or the b-file). It must be computed by two independently written pipelines that differ in graph generation (e.g. plantri c-nets vs a custom generator) or in the network solver. The pipelines must agree exactly and must both reproduce every published term of that sequence up to order 24 (A002839/A002881) or order 33 (A006983/A217155). The full list of Bouwkamp codes found must be published (compressed) so that any subset can be checked. The term must not appear in the entry's history (including pending drafts) or on squaring.net.

partial_wins.statement: An independent recount of A002839 a(25) or a(26), or of A002881 a(25) or a(26) (single-source 2024 terms), with a method different from Anderson's. It either confirms the value exactly or finds a discrepancy and explains it with explicit Bouwkamp codes (missing, duplicate or non-simple tilings).
An independent recount of A006983 a(36) or a(37) (Williams's 2020 values, 6,674,067 and 17,086,918), confirming or refuting them in the same way.

targets.verification_method: Spot-check a random sample of the published Bouwkamp codes: decode, verify exact tiling, perfection (or imperfection) and simplicity (no proper sub-rectangle is squared), and canonical form (no two codes equivalent under the rectangle's symmetries). Rerun both pipelines on small orders against OEIS. The full term needs the claimant's cluster logs plus a rerun by a second party.
angles: Generate 3-connected planar graphs by edge count with plantri (-pc3m3 style) on a cluster and solve each Kirchhoff system exactly with fraction-free Bareiss or Cholesky over integers. Filter perfection early with modular arithmetic.
For squared squares only: use the duality and 'c-net' restrictions of Williams's method to prune graphs that cannot give square boundaries.
Count squares versus non-squares separately and cross-check against the A217156/A181735 symmetry conventions.
pitfalls: Conventions differ: A002839 includes squared squares from order 21, squaring.net's SPSR page counts non-squares only, A217156 counts PSS up to symmetries of the square, and A181735 also mods out sub-rectangle symmetries. Use the target sequence's own definition.
Historic counts were revised several times (duplicates, leftover compound tilings). Reproduce the published terms before trusting a new one.
Simplicity testing must catch every squared sub-rectangle, not only those that touch the boundary.

targets.name: Perfect squared squares: smaller side than the best known for an order 38..59 (OEIS A217148 table and squaring.net listings), or a nicer or more odd-sided record square
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (targeted planar-network search; no exhaustive census needed)
targets.statement: A perfect squared square (PSS) tiles a square with integer squares of pairwise distinct sizes, and its order is the number of squares. The smallest side for each order is known exactly for orders 21..37 (OEIS A217148 for all PSS, A129947 for simple ones). These values come from complete enumerations by Duijvestijn, Gambini, Skinner, Anderson, Pegg, Johnson, Milla and, for orders 33..37, Jim Williams (2014-2020). For orders 38..59 only upper bounds are known. A217148 lists them (Williams for 38 and 40-44, Ian Gambini's 1999 thesis for 39 and 45-47, the rest as tabulated): 38: 352, 39: 360, 40: 328, 41: 336, 42: 360, 43: 413, 44: 425, 45: 543, 46: 601, 47: 691, 48: 550, 49: 583, 50: 644, 51: 636, 52: 584, 53: 685, 54: 657, 55: 631, 56: 751, 57: 742, 58: 780, 59: 958. The table dates from 2013 and is stale in places. squaring.net's per-order SPSS tablecode files hold Bernard Moss's 2020 squares of order 58 with side 628 and of order 59 with side 887 (tilings re-checked 2026-10-30), below the table's 780 and 958. For orders 45-57 the smallest listed SPSS is above the table value. The non-monotone values (40 < 38, 52 < 50) show how soft the larger ones are. Stuart Anderson's 'Special' PSS page (squaring.net, items up to September 2026) also records other properties. The nicest SPSS (smallest ratio of largest to smallest element) is 2456/333 = 7.375 (order 36, side 7743, Williams 2020), and no PSS of order <= 37 does better. Among the completely enumerated SPSS orders (up to 37), the fewest even-sided elements is 6 (three SPSSs: two of order 26, one of order 34). The page asks whether 3 or 2 is possible, as it is for rectangles.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit perfect squared square (Bouwkamp code or (x, y, s) list) of order n, with 38 <= n <= 59, all n squares of pairwise distinct integer sizes and tiling exactly, whose side is STRICTLY less than the best known side for that n. The best known side is the smaller of the upper bound in the live A217148 table (re-fetched immediately before claiming) and the smallest PSS of that order in squaring.net's listings: the 'Special' PSS page, the per-order SPSS and CPSS pages and Bouwkamp-code/tablecode downloads, and Bernard Moss's 2018-2020 collections for orders 37-116. As of 2026-10-30 this makes the bar 628 for order 58 and 887 for order 59 (Moss 2020), not the table's 780 and 958. Simple or compound both count. The side must also be smaller than any value in a later OEIS edit.

partial_wins.statement: A perfect squared square of any order whose largest-to-smallest element ratio is strictly less than 2456/333 (the niceness record on squaring.net's 'Special' PSS page, Jim Williams 2020), verified exactly.

A perfect squared square of any order with at most 5 even-sided (reduced) elements. The fewest recorded on squaring.net is 6 (three SPSSs up to order 37), and the page asks whether 3 or 2 is possible. Verified exactly.

targets.verification_method: Decode the Bouwkamp code, check exact coverage of the s x s square, check pairwise distinct sizes and count the order. Compare the side with A217148's table entry, compute the ratio or the even-element count exactly. This takes milliseconds.
angles: Small sides need c-nets with small spanning-tree count. Generate planar graphs of the right order with low complexity (few spanning trees) and solve only those.
Build compound squares by gluing two small perfect squared rectangles with complementary aspect and a few connecting squares (Moroń/Willcocks style), then search the gluing space.
For the even-element question: work mod 2 on the Kirchhoff currents to precompute which c-nets can give few even elements before solving exactly.
pitfalls: A217148 (all PSS) and A129947 (simple only) differ in DATA at order 33 (233 vs 223), and their 38..59 tables differ from order 48 on. Use A217148's table for this target.
Bouwkamp codes give sizes in reduced form. A PSS whose element sizes share a factor must be divided down before comparing sides.

The table entries are upper bounds from different people, and squaring.net holds millions of post-2013 squares (Moss's transforms for orders 48-85, Anderson's substituted CPSSs for orders 41-60). Check those listings and the OEIS history for a smaller side before claiming.

targets.name: Ways to cut an n x n square into integer squares: the next term a(26) of OEIS A045846, or new terms of the inequivalent count A224239
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days for A224239 terms via Burnside; A045846 a(26) is laptop-days to needs cluster
targets.statement: OEIS A045846 (Erich Friedman) counts the ways to cut an n x n square into integer-sided squares of any sizes. Steve Butler computed terms to n = 20 (see 'Counting tilings by taking walks in a graph', with Ekstrand and Osborne), and Andrew Gozzard and Max Ward's b-file runs to n = 25 (a(25) ~ 5.48e81, 82 digits). The latest edit (2026-10-23) only changed a link, and no a(26) is recorded. The companion A224239 counts dissections up to rotation and reflection. Brendan J. Dee extended its b-file to n = 19 in 2026 (earlier terms Don Reble 2013 and Ed Wynn 2013), so it lags A045846 by six terms. By Burnside's lemma, A224239(n) = (A045846(n) + fixed counts under the seven non-trivial symmetries of the square)/8, and dissections fixed by a symmetry are much cheaper to count. The rectangular table A219924 (Alois P. Heinz, b-file antidiagonals 0..30) counts the k x n versions. This target is distinct from the bank's square-grid-lattice-gas entry, which covers only 1x1 and 2x2 tiles (A063443).
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact integer A045846(26), where 26 is the first index absent from the live DATA and b-file, re-fetched immediately before claiming; if the b-file has grown, the next absent index instead. It must be computed by two independently written programs (e.g. a profile/skyline transfer-matrix DP and a different decomposition or modular-CRT run) that agree exactly and both reproduce every b-file term a(0)..a(25). The value must not appear in the entry's history or pending drafts.

partial_wins.statement: New terms of A224239 (inequivalent dissections) beyond the live b-file (currently a(19)): at least a(20), obtained from A045846(n) plus independently computed counts of dissections fixed by each symmetry of the square. Two programs must agree and reproduce a(1)..a(19).
A new antidiagonal of A219924 (k x n rectangles tiled by integer squares) beyond Heinz's b-file (antidiagonals 0..30), with two agreeing programs that reproduce the existing antidiagonals.

targets.verification_method: Rerun both programs on a skeptic machine for n <= 20 against the b-file, then check the claimed a(26) modulo one or two fresh primes with a modular version of either program. Check that the Burnside identities hold exactly (integrality of A224239 terms) for p1.
angles: Skyline (profile) DP: the state is the height profile of the partially filled square, and placing the largest square at the lowest-leftmost gap keeps the state space canonical. Memoise with hashing and do the arithmetic modulo several 62-bit primes with CRT.
For the symmetric counts in p1: a dissection fixed by a reflection is determined by one half plus a compatible diagonal or axis strip. Count with the same DP on the quotient region.
Meet-in-the-middle across the horizontal midline: count top and bottom halves per boundary profile and pair them.
pitfalls: A045846 counts all dissections, including the trivial n^2 unit squares and the single n x n square (a(1) = 1). Reproduce the small terms first.
The 'changed' keyword and Dee's 2026 activity on A224239 mean that new terms may already be in a pending draft. Check the history page before claiming.
CRT with too few primes silently gives a residue. a(26) has about 90 digits, so use enough moduli with a wide margin.

targets.name: Fewest squares tiling a rectangle: a counterexample to h(dn,dm) = h(n,m) beyond the 388 x 388 table, or new exact rows of OEIS A219158
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exact minimum-square tiling search per rectangle)
targets.statement: h(n,m) is the minimum number of integer-sided squares that tile an n x m rectangle (Kenyon, 'Tiling a rectangle with the fewest squares', JCTA 1996; Walters 2009). Bertram Felgenhauer's page computes h exactly for all rectangles up to 388 x 388. Results are by Felgenhauer to 300 (2013), Ed Pegg Jr to 160, and Massimo Ortolano to 388, with rows 323 and 352 corrected on 2017-08-26. A 2025-06-08 change was cosmetic. Ortolano's OEIS b-file A219158 (rows 1..388, corrected by Qizheng He) records the same table. The page lists the conjecture h(dn,dm) = h(n,m) (scaling never helps) and says it is 'likely to be false', citing MathOverflow question 116382. Inside the 388 table no scaled pair violates it (re-checked 2026-10-30 on all 48,490 pairs), so a counterexample with exact h(n,m) needs a scaled rectangle with a side above 388. On MathOverflow, Pegg (2017) reported that his search of rectangles with maximum side <= 760 left a single possible counterexample (2 x 697x611 in 16 squares vs a 17-square 697x611). He collected 4944 more 'possible counterexamples' (scaled tilings beating the best known unscaled tiling, where the unscaled minimum is unproven) in a Wolfram demonstration. On 2026-09-29 a MathOverflow answer by jvvk tiled 697x611 with 14 squares, which rules that case out. A related conjecture, h(n+m,m) = h(n,m)+1 for n >= m, is already refuted on the page (h(112,53) = h(59,53) = 11). For squares, Sascha Kurz observed that A018835(n) = min over prime divisors p of A018835(p) up to n = 104.
targets.success_criterion: Success means integers d >= 2 and n, m <= 388 with max(dn, dm) > 388, plus an explicit tiling of the dn x dm rectangle by integer squares (list of (x, y, s)) that uses STRICTLY fewer squares than h(n,m) as given in the live Felgenhauer table / A219158 b-file. h(n,m) must also be independently re-derived by the claimant's own exact search, because the counterexample depends on it being a true minimum. The table, MathOverflow question 116382 and Pegg's 'Possible Counterexamples to the Minimal Squaring Conjecture' demonstration must be re-fetched before claiming, and the pair must not already be reported or refuted there. Expect the d = 2, max side <= 760 range to have been swept heuristically already.

partial_wins.statement: A complete new row of exact values h(389, m) for all m = 1..389 (or the next row missing from the live table), computed by two independently written exact programs that agree and that reproduce a random sample of at least 1,000 entries of the existing table, including rows 323 and 352.
A computer-checked proof that h(dn,dm) = h(n,m) for all d >= 2 with dn, dm <= D and n, m <= 388, for some D >= 600, labelled as a bounded result. It needs two agreeing programs.

targets.verification_method: Check the tiling's exact coverage of dn x dm and count its squares (milliseconds). Look up h(n,m) in the live table and recompute it with an independent exact search (Felgenhauer-style valley search or a SAT model with a cardinality bound proving that h(n,m)-1 squares fail), with the DRAT proof checked if SAT is used.
angles: Search for n x m where the optimal tiling is 'basic' (no guillotine cut) and highly irregular, like 13 x 11. Scaling by d lets squares of non-multiple sizes appear, so search dn x dm tilings in which some squares are not multiples of d.
Upper-bound heuristics first: build dn x dm tilings from imperfect squared rectangles of low order with the right aspect ratio (from squaring.net catalogues) and compare their counts with h(n,m).
A cheap filter: the table gives h(n,m) for all n, m <= 388, so scan candidate (n, m, d) with dn just above 388 by the number of squares in the best known tiling.
pitfalls: Felgenhauer warns that his list had wrong rows between 2016-06-14 and 2017-08-26. Use the current list, and spot-check against your own exact computation.
Within the 388 table, scaled pairs are already present and show no counterexample, so a win must leave the table range.
Do not run the downloadable young.cc/Young.hs. Write your own search (bank rule: no downloaded code).

targets.name: Polyomino oddities (Sillke figures): settle a '?' or 'Unsolved' cell, or beat a minimal known tile count on George Sicherman's oddity tables
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (SAT/DLX over symmetric figures)
targets.statement: A polyomino oddity is a figure with binary symmetry or better made from an odd number of congruent copies of one polyomino (rotations and reflections allowed). Oddities are also called Sillke figures after Torsten Sillke, with early work by Livio Zucca. George Sicherman's Polyform Curiosities pages keep the minimal known oddities per polyomino and per symmetry type, with many entries by Mike Reid and one improved by Roger Phillips. The hexomino table (35 hexominoes x 7 symmetries: lateral on cell or edge, diagonal, rotary, double lateral on cell or edge, double diagonal on vertex; page 'last revised 2017-09-20', file modified 2026-03-18) gives counts from 1 to 49 tiles, 'None' for cells proven impossible by colouring and 13 cells still marked '?'. The heptomino page (revised 2024-10-02) has 'Unsolved' lists for lateral, diagonal and birotary symmetry. The pentomino page (revised 2026-09-20) lists minimal known counts up to 73 tiles and leaves 8 cells blank because no oddity is known: T and U for double diagonal, double rotary and full symmetry, and V for double lateral and full symmetry. (Composite solutions using pairs of pentominoes do not count.) The large counts (e.g. 27, 33 and 49 tiles for some hexominoes) are probably not optimal. This target is distinct from the bank's compatibility target: it concerns one polyomino and a symmetric figure, not common figures of two polyforms.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a polyomino P and a symmetry class S taken from one of Sicherman's single-polyomino oddity tables (Polyomino Oddities http://sicherman.net/oddities/index.html, Pentomino Oddities, Hexomino Oddities or Heptomino Oddities; not the one-sided, pair, composite, semi-oddity or polyking tables), plus an explicit figure F (set of grid cells) with symmetry S exactly as Sicherman defines it (e.g. lateral on cell = a mirror axis through cell centres) and an explicit tiling of F by k copies of P (reflections allowed), with k odd. One of three must hold on the live page: it shows '?' or 'Unsolved' for (P, S); the (P, S) cell of the pentomino table is blank (no known oddity; as of 2026-10-30 these are T and U for double diagonal, double rotary and full symmetry, and V for double lateral and full symmetry); or k is STRICTLY less than the listed minimal known count. Holeless-variant tables count separately and require F to be holeless. The pages must be re-fetched before claiming. Cells marked 'None' or 'Impossible' are excluded.

partial_wins.statement: A smaller holeless variant: a holeless oddity with strictly fewer tiles than the listed holeless minimum for some (P, S) in a holeless-variant table.

For a '?' or 'Unsolved' cell, a SAT/DLX proof (with DRAT certificate) that no oddity with symmetry S exists using at most k tiles inside a bounding box of side L, for stated k >= 15 and L, labelled as a bounded result.

targets.verification_method: Canonicalise each tile of the tiling under the 8 grid isometries and check that it equals P, that tiles are disjoint and cover F exactly, and that k is odd. Check that F equals its image under the symmetry S (with the right axis or centre type) and that the complement is connected for holeless variants. Compare k with the live table. This takes milliseconds.
angles: Model a symmetric figure as its fundamental domain: tiles either lie in an orbit of size |G| or are fixed by part of the group, so an odd total forces tiles that sit on axes. Enumerate those first, then SAT-pack the orbits.
Grow from the known minimal rectangles and from oddities of related polyominoes (sub- and super-shapes) as seeds for local search.
Colouring arguments from the page's impossibility proofs work as fast filters: only search (P, S) pairs that pass every parity test.
pitfalls: The symmetry types are subtle: axis through cell centres versus along edges, rotation centre on a cell, edge or vertex. A figure with the wrong axis type does not count for that column.
Each hexomino row is identified by a picture. Match P's exact shape from the page image, and do not rely on row order.
'None' means proven impossible by colouring. A claimed solution there is a checker bug.

targets.name: Holeless tetrad from a symmetric polyomino with at most 33 cells (record: 34-ominoes, Rubin and Scherer)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (SAT search over symmetric polyominoes of 12..33 cells)
targets.statement: A tetrad is a figure made of four congruent shapes, each sharing a boundary of positive length with each of the other three. Walter Trump studied polyomino tetrads from 1970-71 and presented his notebooks on trump.de in 2020. Michael R. W. Buckley named them in 1975. George Sicherman's 'Polyomino and Polynar Tetrads' page (revised 2020-01-14, file last modified 2025-12-11) records the minima. The smallest polyomino tetrads use octominoes. The smallest symmetric polyomino tetrad uses a 9-omino. The smallest tetrads for tiles with mirror or with birotary symmetry use 13-ominoes, and Juris Čerņenoks found the smallest for tiles with diagonal symmetry (19-ominoes). So any tetrad of a symmetric tile needs at least 13 cells. The smallest holeless tetrad (union with no hole) is Trump's 11-omino. For symmetric polyominoes, the smallest holeless tetrad known was found independently by Frank Rubin and Karl Scherer and uses 34-ominoes, improving Trump's and Scherer's earlier 48-omino. Sicherman calls it only the smallest known, and Trump's page lists symmetric tiles as a planned topic with no newer record. The range 13..33 cells is open.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a polyomino P with at most 33 cells that has a non-trivial symmetry (mirror or rotation, as on Sicherman's page), and four copies of P (each congruent to P, reflections allowed) with disjoint interiors, such that every pair of copies shares a boundary segment of positive length (not only a corner) and the union of the four has no holes (its complement in the plane is connected). The live Sicherman tetrad page must be re-fetched before claiming and must still list 34 as the smallest known.

partial_wins.statement: An exhaustive, two-method (DLX or SAT with DRAT-checked UNSAT) proof that no symmetric polyomino with at most m cells forms a holeless tetrad, for some m >= 16, labelled as a bounded result.

A holeless tetrad from a polyomino with mirror symmetry and one from a polyomino with birotary symmetry, each with at most 34 cells and each different from the Rubin-Scherer example, so that both symmetry classes have a recorded holeless witness.

targets.verification_method: Check that P is edge-connected and equals one of its non-trivial isometric images. Check that each copy is an isometry of P, that copies are disjoint, that each pair shares at least one unit edge, and that the complement of the union is connected (flood fill on a padded grid). This takes milliseconds.
angles: A holeless tetrad has one tile that touches the other three and one that is partly enclosed. Search over the 'central' configuration (three tiles around a fourth) with SAT on a bounded grid, with P symmetric by construction (variables only on a fundamental half).
Start from Trump's asymmetric 11-omino holeless tetrad and from the 13-omino symmetric tetrads with holes. Try symmetrising or plugging the holes by growing P.
Iterative deepening on cell count: for each size, SAT jointly over the shape of P (with symmetry constraints) and four placements.
pitfalls: Corner contact alone does not count as sharing a boundary.
'Holeless' refers to the union of the four tiles, not to P itself. Use the page's definition.
Check the symmetry type the page counts as 'symmetric' (mirror or rotary). A P with only translational coincidences is not symmetric.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - The binary q-analog of the Fano plane S_2[2,3,7] (fallback: a (7,4;3)_2 subspace code with more than 333 planes)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (exhaustive or symmetry-reduced ILP/SAT); partial wins laptop-days
targets.statement: A binary q-Fano plane is a set of planes (3-dim subspaces) of F_2^7 such that every line (2-dim subspace) lies in exactly one of them; it would have 381 planes. It is the smallest admissible q-Steiner system S_2[2,3,7] and its existence is the best-known open problem on q-analogs of designs. Equivalently A_2(7,4;3)=381, where A_2(7,4;3) is the largest set of planes in F_2^7 pairwise meeting in at most a point; Kurz's survey (arXiv 2112.11766, v3 2025-12-20, Section 6) calls it the smallest unknown binary value and gives 333 <= A_2(7,4;3) <= 381, and either A_2(7,4;3) <= 378 or = 381 (Nakic and Storme: a 380-plane code extends to 381; the rest via divisible codes). The 333 code is by Heinlein, Kiermaier, Kurz and Wassermann (arXiv 1708.06224), who also show any code with >= 334 planes has automorphism group of order <= 12. Braun, Kiermaier and Nakic (arXiv 1501.07790) showed a q-Fano plane is rigid or has a cyclic automorphism group of order 2, 3 or 4, and Kiermaier, Kurz and Wassermann (arXiv 1605.03853) brought this down to order <= 2. Thomas (1996), Heden and Sissokho (2016) and Kiermaier (arXiv 2105.00365) proved that non-alpha points must exist.
targets.success_criterion: Full win (either direction): (a) an explicit list of 381 planes of F_2^7 (each as a 3x7 binary generator matrix of rank 3) such that every one of the 2667 lines of F_2^7 is contained in exactly one listed plane; or (b) a machine-checked proof that no such set exists: a Lean/Isabelle/Coq proof, or a complete exhaustive search with a verifiable certificate (e.g. DRAT/LRAT proof checked by an independent checker for a published SAT encoding, plus an independent check of every symmetry-reduction step). Compared against the status in arXiv 2112.11766 (open, current lower bound 333).

partial_wins.statement: A set of at least 334 planes of F_2^7, pairwise intersecting in at most a 1-dimensional subspace (i.e. every line in at most one plane), strictly beating A_2(7,4;3) >= 333.

Settle the research problem in arXiv 2112.11766 Section 6 in either direction: 240 planes in PG(6,2) admitting an automorphism pi of order 5, all disjoint from the plane F of pi-fixed points (an order-5 element of GL(7,2) fixes exactly a 3-dim subspace, 7 points), no two meeting in a line, and covering each of the 120 points outside F exactly 14 times (explicit planes plus the matrix of pi), or an exhaustive certificate that none exist. The survey text says '15 times', which is arithmetically impossible (240*7 = 1680 = 120*14); 14 is the count forced in a q-Fano plane by the stated complementary set (F plus 140 planes meeting F in a point).

For the relaxation in arXiv 2112.11766 Section 6 (45 planes of F_2^6 with every 5-space containing exactly five, every point in exactly five, each line and each solid in at most one), an explicit set with strictly more alpha'-points in total than the stated lower bound 19, or in one fixed 5-space strictly more than 15.

targets.verification_method: Represent each plane by its reduced row echelon form; enumerate its 7 lines; count how often each of the 2667 lines of F_2^7 is covered (exactly once for a full win, at most once for p1, with all planes distinct and of rank 3). For p2/p3 check every stated incidence condition by brute force over all subspaces of PG(6,2)/PG(5,2). For a nonexistence claim, re-run the certificate checker and independently audit the encoding and symmetry breaking. Re-fetch arXiv 2112.11766 and its citing literature before claiming.
angles: Prescribe automorphism groups allowed by the 333-paper classification (order <= 12 for >= 334 planes; the group G_{12,1} = Z3 x| Z4 named in the survey) and solve the Kramer-Mesner style ILP with a modern solver.
For p1, start from the 333 code (Klein four-group) and run large-neighbourhood search: remove k planes, re-solve the exact cover-at-most-once ILP on the freed lines.
Use the derived structure: through each point the planes induce a line spread of PG(5,2); constrain by non-alpha-point results.
pitfalls: A 380-plane code would already extend to 381, and codes of size 379 or 380 are ruled out unless 381 exists, so heuristic searches stalling near 333 are normal.
Do not confuse with the ternary case or with partial q-Fano planes; the win is about q=2, n=7, k=3.
arXiv 1709.05145 (Bamberg, Ihringer, Lansdown, Royle) claimed a trivial automorphism group but was withdrawn after a computational mistake; the proven bound is order <= 2.
The Bayreuth table site was unreachable on 2026-10-30; use the survey and arXiv for status.

targets.name: Constant dimension subspace codes A_q(n,d;k): beat a best known lower bound in the Bayreuth subspace code tables (q = 2..9, n <= 19)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (structured constructions or ILP with prescribed automorphisms; binary small n may need laptop-days)
targets.statement: A_q(n,d;k) is the largest number of k-dimensional subspaces of F_q^n with pairwise subspace distance d_S(U,W) = 2k - 2 dim(U cap W) >= d. Heinlein, Kiermaier, Kurz and Wassermann maintain online tables of lower and upper bounds (subspacecodes.uni-bayreuth.de, manual arXiv 1601.02864) for 2 <= q <= 9 and n <= 19. The field is very active: Li and Fu (arXiv 2502.12518, 63 new lower bounds; arXiv 2507.07842), Wang, Yao and Fu (arXiv 2508.01258, at least 65), Wang, Gao, Mesnager and Fu (arXiv 2508.03196), Xu and Li (arXiv 2510.27071, A_q(n,8;6) for 16 <= n <= 19) and Fu, Gao, Mesnager and Wang (arXiv 2609.24239, 2026) improved many cells in 2025-2026 via inserting, multilevel and parallel linkage constructions and new optimal Ferrers diagram rank-metric codes. Kurz's survey (arXiv 2112.11766, v3 2025-12-20, Sections 5 and 7) gives the best known small binary values: A_2(8,4;3) >= 1331 (Zhou, Chen, Zhang, Shi and He 2021; 1326 earlier by prescribed automorphisms), A_2(8,4;4) >= 4802 (Zhou et al., extending the 4801 code of Braun, Ostergard and Wassermann; anticode bound 6477), A_2(9,4;3) >= 5986 (Braun, Ostergard, Wassermann), A_2(9,4;4) >= 37265 and A_2(10,6;4) >= 4173; for q = 3, 754 <= A_3(6,4;3) <= 784 (formula (7.1) and Theorem 8.4). The cell A_2(7,4;3) = A_2(7,4;4) is a separate bank entry (binary-q-fano-plane-s2-2-3-7) and partial spread cells (d = 2k) belong to partial-spreads-smallest-open-cases; both are excluded here.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit set of M k-dimensional subspaces of F_q^n (each given by a k x n generator matrix of rank k over F_q; q a prime power <= 9, n <= 19, d < 2k, and (q,n,d,k) neither (2,7,4,3) nor (2,7,4,4)) whose pairwise intersections all have dimension <= k - d/2, with M STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the larger of: the lower bound shown for that cell (equivalently its dual cell k -> n-k) on subspacecodes.uni-bayreuth.de at verification time (if the live site is unreachable, the newest web.archive.org snapshot of that cell's table page, with its date recorded in the claim), and every value for that cell in arXiv 2112.11766, 2502.12518, 2507.07842, 2508.01258, 2508.03196, 2510.27071, 2609.24239 or any newer paper. M must not exceed the tabulated upper bound (that would mean a bug).

partial_wins.statement: An improvement in one of the named small cells, which are the most studied: A_2(8,4;3) >= 1332, A_2(8,4;4) >= 4803, A_2(9,4;3) >= 5987 or A_3(6,4;3) >= 755, in each case also strictly above any newer value for that cell, checked as in the full criterion.

An exact rational certificate (LP or SDP dual, verified in rational arithmetic) proving A_q(n,d;k) <= U with U strictly below the tabulated upper bound for some cell in the scope of the full criterion.

targets.verification_method: Bring each generator matrix to reduced row echelon form over F_q (q prime: integers mod q; q = 4, 8, 9: an explicit field table), assert rank k and distinctness, and for every pair compute dim(U cap W) = 2k - rank([U;W]) <= k - d/2. Use bitsets for q = 2; check all pairs, no sampling. Re-read the Bayreuth cell and the cited papers' tables on the day.
angles: Combine the 2025 inserting/multilevel/parallel-linkage constructions with better small ingredient codes (FDRM codes from ILP) in cells those papers did not touch.
For binary small n, prescribe automorphism groups (Singer subgroups and normalizers) and solve the reduced ILP (Braun-Ostergard-Wassermann method).
pitfalls: The Bayreuth site (and all of mathe2.uni-bayreuth.de) was unreachable on 2026-10-30, so the status_source is the survey. Wayback snapshots (2025-2026) of the table pages still work, but they lag the literature: the 2025-10-06 snapshot still shows 1326 and 4801 for A_2(8,4;3) and A_2(8,4;4), and the 2025-2026 arXiv papers may exceed any snapshot.

The survey quotes two values for A_2(8,4;3): 1326 (Section 7, prescribed automorphisms) and 1331 (Section 5, Zhou et al. 2021); 2025 papers still use the 1326 code as an ingredient. The record to beat is 1331.
A_q(n,d;k) = A_q(n,d;n-k): check the dual cell too.
Many 2025 papers state sizes as formulas in q; evaluate them for the exact q before comparing.

targets.name: Mixed dimension binary subspace codes A_2(n,d), n = 6..8: improve a bound in Kurz's Table 8.1 (A_2(6,3) 108-117, A_2(7,3) 614-776, A_2(8,5) 263-326, ...)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (max independent set on 2825 / 29212 / 417199 subspaces)
targets.statement: A_2(n,d) is the largest set of subspaces of F_2^n of any dimensions with pairwise subspace distance d_S(U,W) = dim U + dim W - 2 dim(U cap W) >= d. Honold, Kiermaier and Kurz (Adv. Math. Commun. 2016), Heinlein and Kurz (Adv. Math. Commun. 2018) and Heinlein and Ihringer (SDP bounds, 2020) set the current state, summarized in Table 8.1 of Kurz's survey (arXiv 2112.11766, latest version 2025-12-20), which poses improving it as a research problem. Open cells: 108 <= A_2(6,3) <= 117, 614 <= A_2(7,3) <= 776, 334 <= A_2(7,4) <= 388, 5687 <= A_2(8,3) <= 9191, 4803 <= A_2(8,4) <= 6479, 263 <= A_2(8,5) <= 326. All other cells with n <= 8 are determined (e.g. A_2(6,4) = 77, A_2(7,5) = 34, A_2(8,6) = 257).
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) an explicit set of M subspaces of F_2^n (n in {6,7,8}; each subspace as a binary generator matrix of full row rank, dimensions 0..n allowed) with pairwise subspace distance >= d and M STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the lower bound for (n,d) in Table 8.1 of arXiv 2112.11766 and any newer published value; or (b) a verifiable proof that A_2(n,d) <= U with U strictly below the Table 8.1 upper bound: an exact rational LP/SDP dual certificate or a VIPR-format ILP certificate checked by an independent checker.

partial_wins.statement: Raise the smallest open lower bound: a mixed dimension code in F_2^6 with 109 or more subspaces and minimum subspace distance >= 3.
Raise A_2(8,5) above 263 or A_2(7,3) above 614 with an explicit code.

targets.verification_method: Reduce each generator matrix to RREF over F_2, assert distinctness, and for every pair compute d_S = rank(U) + rank(W) - 2(rank(U)+rank(W)-rank([U;W])) >= d. For upper bounds, re-check the dual certificate in exact rational arithmetic or run an independent VIPR checker. Re-read the survey and search for newer values before claiming.
angles: Model as maximum independent set on the conflict graph of all subspaces (2825 vertices for n=6) and run modern MIS solvers (KaMIS, ARW-ILS) with symmetry (Singer cycle) restrictions.
For A_2(7,4) and A_2(8,4), note that the lower bounds come from constant dimension codes plus extra codewords; mix dimensions k and k+1 explicitly.
pitfalls: A_2(7,4) >= 334 comes from the 333-plane code; an improvement there likely needs a better A_2(7,4;3) code (separate bank entry), so it is the hardest cell.
Table 8.1 uses the subspace distance, not the injection distance.

targets.name: Maximum partial spreads: settle 129 <= A_2(11,8;4) <= 132 or 244 <= A_3(8,6;3) <= 248
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (ILP with prescribed automorphisms or exhaustive structure search)
targets.statement: A partial k-spread in F_q^n is a set of k-dimensional subspaces pairwise intersecting trivially; A_q(n,2k;k) is its maximum size. For q = 2 all values with n < 11 are known and the smallest undecided binary case is 129 <= A_2(11,8;4) <= 132 (stated by Heinlein, Kiermaier, Kurz and Wassermann, arXiv 1708.06224; the bound is the t = 2 case of the family 2^4 l + 1 <= A_2(4t+3,8;4) <= 2^4 l + 4 from Kurz, Packing vector spaces into vector spaces, 2017, restated in Kurz's survey arXiv 2112.11766, v3 2025-12-20, Section 4.3). For q = 3 the smallest open case is 244 <= A_3(8,6;3) <= 248 (Honold, Kiermaier and Kurz 2018; restated by Kurz, arXiv 2302.08939, and the survey says A_q(8,6;3) is known only for q = 2). If 248 planes exist the 56 uncovered points must form the Hill cap.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) an explicit partial spread beating a lower bound: at least 130 four-dimensional subspaces of F_2^11 pairwise intersecting in {0}, or at least 245 three-dimensional subspaces of F_3^8 pairwise intersecting in {0} (direction: max, strictly above 129 resp. 244); or (b) a machine-checkable proof lowering an upper bound (A_2(11,8;4) <= 131 or A_3(8,6;3) <= 247), e.g. an exhaustive search certificate (DRAT/LRAT or VIPR) with an independently audited encoding, or a formal proof.

partial_wins.statement: An improved lower bound for any other open partial spread value listed in Section 4.3 of arXiv 2112.11766 (for example A_2(6t+4,12;6) or A_2(6t+5,12;6) for the smallest t = 2, currently 1025 <= A_2(16,12;6) <= 1032 and 2049 <= A_2(17,12;6) <= 2066): an explicit partial spread strictly larger than the stated lower bound q^k l + 1 for that family and parameter t, and strictly larger than the Bayreuth table cell (live, or its newest web.archive.org snapshot if the site is unreachable) and any newer published value, verified as in the full criterion.

targets.verification_method: For each subspace compute its full point set (15 points for q=2,k=4; 13 for q=3,k=3), assert rank k, and check that all point sets are pairwise disjoint. Upper-bound claims: re-run the certificate checker and audit the encoding. Re-read the survey's Section 4.3 and recent literature before claiming.
angles: Holes of a partial k-spread form a q^(k-1)-divisible point set: enumerate admissible hole sets (e.g. 2^3-divisible sets of 2047-15M points for A_2(11,8;4)) and solve the packing problem on their complement.
Prescribe Singer-subgroup or normalizer automorphisms to shrink the ILP.
pitfalls: Lower bound 129 = 2^4*8+1 comes from the standard Echelon-Ferrers type construction; plain greedy or random searches usually land well below it.
For A_3(8,6;3) the trivial bound is 252; 248 comes from divisible-code arguments, so do not report 248..252 as an improvement.

targets.name: Doubling construction for mixed dimension subspace codes: decide whether A_q(2k+1,2k-1) = 2q^(k+1)+2 for (q,k) = (3,3) or (2,4)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (SAT/ILP on the 82+82 or 33+33 structure)
targets.statement: Honold, Kiermaier and Kurz (Adv. Math. Commun. 2016) proved A_q(2k+1,2k-1) is 2q^(k+1)+1 or 2q^(k+1)+2 for mixed dimension subspace codes in F_q^(2k+1), and that the larger value needs a doubling construction: q^(k+1)+1 k-subspaces forming a maximum partial k-spread and q^(k+1)+1 (k+1)-subspaces forming the dual of one, with every k-subspace meeting every (k+1)-subspace in at most a point. It exists for k = 2 and for k = 3, q = 2 (A_2(7,5) = 34; the optimal codes were classified by Honold, Kiermaier and Kurz). Kurz's survey (arXiv 2112.11766, latest version 2025-12-20, Section 8) poses it as a research problem: does a doubling construction exist for k >= 4 or for k = 3 and q >= 3? The survey notes that a proven non-existence is also of interest, as it would improve an upper bound for A_q(2k,2k-2;k).
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) an explicit doubling construction for (q,k) = (3,3) or (2,4) (or any other open pair: k >= 4, or k = 3 and q >= 3): 2q^(k+1)+2 subspaces of F_q^(2k+1) (164 subspaces of F_3^7: 82 of dimension 3 and 82 of dimension 4; or 66 subspaces of F_2^9: 33 of dimension 4 and 33 of dimension 5) with pairwise subspace distance >= 2k-1; or (b) a verifiable certificate that none exists for that (q,k) (exhaustive search with DRAT/LRAT or VIPR certificate and an audited encoding, or a formal proof). Compared against the open status in arXiv 2112.11766.

partial_wins.statement: For (q,k) = (3,3) or (2,4) and a stated nontrivial subgroup G of GL(2k+1,q): explicit G-invariant examples of BOTH halves separately (a G-invariant partial k-spread of size q^(k+1)+1 and a G-invariant set of q^(k+1)+1 (k+1)-spaces pairwise meeting in at most a point), together with a verifiable exhaustive certificate (re-runnable search plus DRAT/LRAT or VIPR certificate, encoding audited) that no G-invariant doubling construction exists; or an explicit G-invariant doubling construction, which is the full win.

targets.verification_method: RREF each generator matrix over F_q, check dimensions and distinctness, and for every pair compute d_S = dim U + dim W - 2 dim(U cap W) >= 2k-1 (equivalently: k-spaces pairwise trivial, (k+1)-spaces pairwise meeting in <= 1 dimension, mixed pairs meeting in <= 1 dimension). Re-read the survey and newer papers before claiming.
angles: Fix the k-part as a known maximum partial spread (lifted MRD plus one) and search for a compatible dual partial spread by SAT with symmetry from the spread's stabilizer.
Generalize the explicit q = 2, k = 3 doubling codes classified by Honold-Kiermaier-Kurz.
pitfalls: Both halves must be maximum (q^(k+1)+1 members); 2q^(k+1)+1 is always attainable and is not a win.
Check every mixed pair, not only within each dimension.

targets.name: Equidistant subspace codes: more than 40 four-dimensional subspaces of F_2^8 pairwise meeting in exactly a point (B_2(8,1;4))
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: B_q(n,t;k) is the maximum number of k-subspaces of F_q^n whose pairwise intersections all have dimension exactly t (t-intersecting equidistant codes). Sunflowers (all pairs meeting in the same t-space) give at most A_2(7,6;3) = 17 for (q,n,t,k) = (2,8,1,4), and by Etzion and Raviv (Discrete Appl. Math.) any such code with at least 211 members is a sunflower, so B_2(8,1;4) <= 210. Bartoli and Pavese proved B_2(6,1;3) = 20. Kurz's survey (arXiv 2112.11766, latest version 2025-12-20, Section 9.1) lifts Boston's 5-dimensional binary 4x4 equidistant rank-metric code (rank distance 3) to get B_2(8,1;4) >= 32, adds 8 more codewords by computer to get B_2(8,1;4) >= 40, and poses determining B_2(8,1;4) as a research problem. Similarly B_2(10,1;5) >= 64 from a 6-dimensional 5x5 code.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit set of M >= 41 four-dimensional subspaces of F_2^8 (each a 4x8 binary generator matrix of rank 4) such that every pair intersects in a subspace of dimension exactly 1, with M STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than 40, the value in arXiv 2112.11766 Section 9.1 (and greater than any newer published value).

partial_wins.statement: An explicit set of at least 65 five-dimensional subspaces of F_2^10 pairwise intersecting in exactly a 1-dimensional subspace, beating the B_2(10,1;5) >= 64 noted in arXiv 2112.11766.

An exact upper bound certificate proving B_2(8,1;4) <= U for some U < 210, checkable by an independent program (e.g. an exhaustive search over a stated symmetry-reduced case split with a DRAT/VIPR certificate).

targets.verification_method: For every pair compute dim(U cap W) = 8 - rank([U;W]) over F_2 and assert it equals 1; assert all matrices have rank 4 and the subspaces are distinct (compare RREFs). The check is a few thousand rank computations.
angles: Start from lifted linear 4x4 equidistant rank-metric codes (several inequivalent ones exist) and extend with max-clique search on the compatibility graph of the 200787 solids.
Drop the lifting structure: search for G-invariant codes under subgroups of GL(8,2).
pitfalls: Exactly one dimension: pairs meeting trivially are not allowed (that would be distance 8).
The survey says these lifted bounds had not appeared elsewhere; check Boston's paper and newer arXiv work for larger codes before claiming.

targets.name: Full flag codes over F_2: beat A^f_2(5,2) >= 3120 (upper bound 3255) or A^f_2(6,6) >= 224
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (max independent set on 9765 vertices)
targets.statement: A full flag in F_q^n is a chain V_1 < V_2 < ... < V_(n-1) with dim V_i = i; the Grassmann distance of two full flags is the sum over i of dim V_i - dim(V_i cap V'_i). A^f_q(n,d) is the largest set of full flags with pairwise Grassmann distance >= d. Kurz (Bounds for flag codes, Des. Codes Cryptogr. 2021, arXiv 2005.04768) determined A^f_2(n,d) for all n <= 5 except 3120 <= A^f_2(5,2) <= 3255 (lower bound by ILP with a prescribed cyclic group of order 15; the CPLEX run was stopped with the group-restricted bound at 3178) and gave 224 <= A^f_2(6,6) <= 567 and upper bounds for n = 6, 7. Kurz's survey (arXiv 2112.11766, latest version 2025-12-20, Section 9.2, Table 9.1) still lists 3120-3255 and asks for improved bounds.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit set of M full flags of F_2^5 (each given by an ordered basis b1..b4 with V_i = span(b1..bi)) with pairwise Grassmann distance >= 2 and M >= 3121 (direction: max, strictly above 3120 in Table 9.1 of arXiv 2112.11766 and any newer published value).

partial_wins.statement: A set of at least 225 full flags of F_2^6 with pairwise Grassmann distance >= 6, beating A^f_2(6,6) >= 224 in arXiv 2005.04768 (and any newer published value).
A proof that A^f_2(5,2) <= U for some U <= 3254, given as a VIPR-format ILP certificate or exact LP/SDP certificate verified by an independent checker.

targets.verification_method: Two full flags of F_2^5 are at Grassmann distance 1 exactly when they differ in one position only; so for distance >= 2 check, for each of the 4 positions, that no two flags agree in the other 3 subspaces (bucket flags by the 4 partial flags obtained by deleting one subspace). Assert each basis is independent and flags are distinct. For n = 6, compute all pairwise Grassmann distances directly.
angles: The conflict graph has 9765 vertices and 13020 triangles-as-cliques (each partial flag missing one subspace has 3 completions); run KaMIS or ILS-based MIS solvers, then re-optimize with the order-15 group or groups listed in arXiv 2005.04768 as still promising.
Finish Kurz's aborted ILP: with G of order 15 the bound was 3178 after 9 hours.
pitfalls: The paper has a typo 3225 in two sentences (Example 3.14 discussion and its summary '3120 <= A^f_2(5,2) <= 3225'); Table 5, Proposition 6.1 and survey Table 9.1 give the upper bound 3255 = 9765/3.
Grassmann distance uses injection distance (half the subspace distance).

targets.name: Designs in finite classical polar spaces: a new realizable 2-(r,k,lambda)_Q design (or the first one in a Hermitian polar space)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (Kramer-Mesner with prescribed groups, e.g. solvediophant or ILP)
targets.statement: A t-(r,k,lambda)_Q design is a set of k-dimensional totally isotropic/singular subspaces (blocks) of a polar space Q of rank r over F_q such that every t-dimensional subspace of Q lies in exactly lambda blocks. Kiermaier, Schmidt and Wassermann (Designs in finite classical polar spaces, arXiv 2403.11188, v3 2025-10-01) give admissibility conditions (step Delta_lambda, lambda_max, Lemma 15 bound) and Table 3: the known realizable lambda for q = 2, 3 in Omega^-(2r+2,q), Omega(2r+1,q), Omega^+(2r,q) and Sp(2r,q), over 140 new parameter sets, with data on Zenodo (doi 10.5281/zenodo.13353388). Earlier designs are due to De Bruyn and Vanhove and to Bamberg and Lansdown. No designs with t >= 2 have been found in Hermitian polar spaces. For example in Omega^-(10,2) with k = 4 only lambda in {9,11,12,14,15,16,18,19,21} are known (lambda = 1 impossible).
targets.success_criterion: An explicit 2-(r,k,lambda)_Q design (block list as generator matrices plus the form defining Q) for one of the (Q, q, r, k) rows of Table 3 of arXiv 2403.11188 (q in {2,3}), with lambda a multiple of that row's Delta_lambda, 1 <= lambda <= floor(lambda_max/2), lambda not in the row's 'does not exist' column, and neither lambda nor lambda_max - lambda listed as realizable in that row (including italic and asterisked entries), in the Zenodo dataset doi 10.5281/zenodo.13353388, or in any newer paper. Direction: a new realizable parameter set in a row of Table 3 (for example Omega^-(10,2), k = 4, lambda in {2,...,8,10,13,17,20,22}).

partial_wins.statement: The first 2-design (t = 2, non-trivial: 1 <= lambda < lambda_max, with parameters admissible by the integrality conditions of arXiv 2403.11188) in any Hermitian polar space H(2r-1,q^2) or H(2r,q^2) with r >= 3, verified as in the full criterion; the paper reports none found.

An exhaustive non-existence certificate (complete search with a checkable certificate, encoding audited) for an admissible parameter set in a row of Table 3 of arXiv 2403.11188 that is not yet listed as realizable or as 'does not exist'.

targets.verification_method: Build the form and check it is non-degenerate. In the orthogonal cases (Omega^-, Omega, Omega^+) check that every block is totally singular for the quadratic form: in characteristic 2 vanishing of the bilinear form alone is not enough. In Sp(2r,q) check that every block is totally isotropic for the alternating form. Check that each block has dimension k and that the blocks are distinct after reduced-echelon canonicalisation. Enumerate all t-dimensional totally singular/isotropic subspaces of Q, checking their number against the paper's counting formulas, and count incident blocks, asserting each count equals lambda. Confirm the parameter set is absent from Table 3, the Zenodo data and the complement. Re-read arXiv 2403.11188 (latest version) before claiming.
angles: Prescribe cyclic subgroups of the polar space's isometry group and their normalizers, as the authors did, but try larger or non-cyclic groups and a modern ILP/SAT backend.
Use Theorem 9 of the paper (derived/reduced designs) to turn a new design into further new parameter sets.
pitfalls: Some table entries (in italics) come from Theorem 9 and are already realized even though they were not found by search. Italics are lost in text extraction, so read the rendered PDF.
lambda and lambda_max - lambda are equivalent; Latin-Greek halvings give trivial-looking cases marked with an asterisk.
For even q, Omega(2r+1,q) and Sp(2r,q) are the same polar space (Table 3 lists Sp(2r,2) as 'see Omega(2r+1,2)'); a design counts once, not under both names.
Over GF(2), totally isotropic for the bilinear form is not the same as totally singular for the quadratic form; blocks of an orthogonal design must be totally singular.

targets.name: Turán's tetrahedron problem (Erdős #500): a certified upper bound on pi(K4^(3)) below 0.55733, or a K4^(3)-free construction above 5/9
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (7-vertex 3-graph flag-algebra programs: the K4^(3)-free program at n = 7 has 1,295,600 constraints and the Lidický-Volec solver used 174 GB RAM, where CSDP would need about 12.5 TB; exact certificate checking takes laptop-hours to laptop-days, and the Jeong et al. Lean build took about 12.5 hours with up to 37 GiB of memory)
targets.statement: pi(K4^(3)) is the limit of ex(n,K4^(3))/C(n,3), the largest edge density of a 3-uniform hypergraph with no 4 vertices spanning all four triples. Turán (1941) conjectured 5/9, attained by his 3-part construction; Erdős offered $500 (Erdős problem #500, whose page, last edited 2025-10-05, still quotes only Razborov's 2010 flag-algebra bound). Baber's flag-algebra bound 0.5615 was the best published value until 2026. Jeong, Park, Im, Lee and Yang (arXiv:2609.27495, v2 2 Oct 2026) proved pi(K4^(3)) <= 14993367693127837/26880000000000000 < 0.557789 with an exact 7-vertex certificate and a complete Lean 4 proof (github.com/taeyool/tetrahedron-turan). Lidický and Volec (arXiv:2610.33850, 24 Oct 2026) report 0.557522 via LP cutting planes, with certificates evaluated in MPFI/MPFR interval arithmetic (lidicky.name/pub/lpsdp/); their Table 2 also lists 0.55733 from Fujisawa, Kiem, Pokutta and Spiegel as a 2025 private communication, with no public certificate found. The lower bound 5/9 = 0.5556 is unchanged. The target is a certified upper bound below every claimed value (0.55733), or a construction refuting Turán's conjecture.
targets.success_criterion: Success means EITHER (a) a flag-algebra (or other) proof that pi(K4^(3)) <= U with U STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than 0.55733 and than every upper bound found in a fresh check of arXiv:2610.33850 (latest version), arXiv:2609.27495 (latest version), erdosproblems.com/500 and any paper citing them at claim time; the proof must come as a certificate (list of forbidden-free n-vertex 3-graphs, flag density coefficients, PSD matrices with exact rational or rigorous interval entries) that an independent checker re-verifies, or as a complete Lean 4 proof that compiles; OR (b) an explicit K4^(3)-free 3-graph family, given by a finite pattern (with optional recursion inside named parts) plus a written proof of K4^(3)-freeness, whose limiting edge density is computed exactly and is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than 5/9. Numerical SDP output without a rigorous rounding is not a win.

partial_wins.statement: A publicly released, independently re-checkable certificate (exact rational or rigorous interval arithmetic) proving pi(K4^(3)) <= U for some U strictly below 0.557522, the best published certified bound (Lidický-Volec, arXiv:2610.33850), even if U is not below the unpublished 0.55733.

A complete Lean 4 proof of pi(K4^(3)) <= U for some U strictly below 0.557789, the value formalised by Jeong et al. (arXiv:2609.27495), for example a formalisation of the Lidický-Volec 0.557522 certificate. The proof must compile from a clean checkout with no sorry, and #print axioms on the main theorem may show only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, plus Lean.ofReduceBool and Lean.trustCompiler if native_decide is used (as in Jeong et al.).

targets.verification_method: For a flag-algebra certificate: independently enumerate all K4^(3)-free 3-graphs on the certificate's n vertices up to isomorphism (count must match), recompute every flag product coefficient and edge density, check each matrix is positive semidefinite in exact rational arithmetic (LDL^T) or with rigorous interval Cholesky, and confirm that the combination bounds the edge density by U on every n-vertex graph. Use a checker not written by the claimant (e.g. a fresh Python/Sage implementation, cross-checked with Flagmatic or the lpsdp verifier). For Lean, compile the project from a clean checkout and grep for sorry/axiom. For a construction, brute-force K4^(3)-freeness of the pattern under all maps of 4 vertices into parts, re-derive the density symbolically, and check the written argument for the recursive parts. Re-fetch arXiv:2610.33850 and arXiv:2609.27495 for newer versions.
angles: Lidický-Volec say they stopped their cutting-plane runs when progress slowed, without reaching optimality; longer runs or better LP/SDP hybrids on 7-vertex flags are the obvious route.
Combine the Jeong et al. degree-stationarity (Razborov differential) constraints with the Lidický-Volec cutting-plane solver.
Start from the published certificates at lidicky.name/pub/lpsdp/ and github.com/taeyool/tetrahedron-turan rather than from scratch.
pitfalls: erdosproblems.com/500 still lists only Razborov's 2010 bound; it is stale. The live values are in arXiv:2610.33850 Table 2 and arXiv:2609.27495 v2.

The abstract of arXiv:2610.33850 rounds the tetrahedron bound to 0.55753, but Table 2 gives 0.557522; p1 is measured against 0.557522 (or against the value the published certificate actually evaluates to, if that is smaller).
The footnote to Table 2 of arXiv:2610.33850 quotes the Lean bound 0.557808 from Jeong et al. v1; their v2 lowered it to 14993367693127837/26880000000000000 < 0.557789, which is the p2 bar.
0.55733 (Fujisawa-Kiem-Pokutta-Spiegel) is unpublished but counts as the value to beat for the full win.
