Excluded here: 11 Collatz-type encodings (Yolcu_21 collatz/mahler/farkas/michel/silva/barina, Zantema_04/syracuse, Yamada_21/collatz), whose termination is an open mathematical problem.
targets.success_criterion: For one of the 136 eligible benchmarks (the 147 above minus the 11 Collatz-type files), taken from the TPDB version used by termCOMP 2026 and still unsolved (no YES/NO in the VBS column) in the latest termCOMP table for its category at claim time: a termination (YES) or nontermination (NO) proof in CPF format that the current CeTA release reports as CERTIFIED for that exact problem file. Uncertified tool output, or a proof for a modified system, does not win.

partial_wins.statement: An uncertified proof for one eligible benchmark that is independently checkable: for NO, an explicit looping (or nonloop pattern) witness verified by a short independent script; for YES, explicit interpretations or orderings whose constraints are verified by an independent script.
A CeTA-certified proof for one of the 51 SRS Relative or 14 TRS Relative benchmarks unsolved in termCOMP 2026.

A certified or independently checkable proof for one of the 65 TRS_Innermost benchmarks, or one of the 15 Integer_Transition_Systems benchmarks other than the 3 Collatz-type files (From_AProVE_2014/Collatz.jar-obl-8, From_AProVE_2014/Velroyen08-collatz.jar-obl-8, From_T2/collatz.t2_fixed), with no YES/NO in termCOMP 2026.

targets.verification_method: Fetch https://termcomp.github.io/Y2026/SRS_Standard.html or TRS_Standard.html and confirm the VBS cell for the benchmark is not YES/NO; check the 2023-2025 tables. Download the problem from TPDB (link in the table), run CeTA on the problem and the CPF proof; accept only CERTIFIED. For p1, re-run the witness check. Minutes.
angles: SAT-based search for larger matrix or arctic interpretations (dimension 5-8, wider coefficients) on the one-rule SRS, with long time limits; matchbox and MnM certify such proofs.
For nontermination, search for nonloops (pattern rules) rather than loops; CeTA can certify some nonloop proofs.
Hydras and Ackermann-type systems need ordinal or semantic labelling methods; check CeTA support before investing.
pitfalls: The Collatz-type files encode open problems (Collatz, Mahler 3/2) and are excluded.
TPDB file names and versions change; use the file linked from the 2026 table.
A proof CeTA rejects because it uses an unsupported technique is not a win, even if correct; p1 covers independently checked uncertified proofs.

targets.name: Hex 10x10: solve a second opening move (only the central f5/e6 pair is solved, since 2013)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (the one solved 10x10 opening, f5, took about 64 days of Scalable Parallel DFPN search in 2012-2013; the hardest 9x9 opening, a6, took 111 days); an edge opening with a short refutation could fall in laptop-days with a modern neural-guided solver
targets.statement: Hex on an n x n rhombus (Black connects top-bottom, White left-right, no draws possible; first-player win by strategy stealing, played here without the swap rule). Computer solutions of single opening moves: all 8x8 openings by Henderson, Arneson and Hayward (IJCAI 2009); all 9x9 openings by Jakub Pawlewicz and Ryan Hayward's Scalable Parallel DFPN in Benzene (finished April 2012, published Computers and Games 2013; the hardest opening, a6, took 111 days); and on 10x10 exactly one opening, the centremost f5 (Black wins, 63 days), which by the board's 180-degree symmetry also settles e6. Hayward's Hex page (last modified January 2022) records 'Mar 2013: Solver shows centre wins on 10x10' and no later 10x10 result. Wikipedia's Hex article says one (the most central) 10x10 opening was solved in 2013. Xinyue Chen's 2025 University of Alberta MSc thesis still summarizes the state as all 9x9 first moves and 2 winning 10x10 first moves [PH13]. Randall, Mueller, Wei and Hayward's Expected Work Search (IJCAI 2024) says Hex has been solved up to the 10x10 board and reports no new 10x10 opening. The 10x10 board has 100 opening cells in 50 classes under 180-degree rotation. No class other than {f5, e6} has a published computer solution. Published general results on inferior edge cells may already settle some first-row openings, so check before claiming one. Task: determine the outcome (Black stone on the opening cell, White to move, no swap) of any other 10x10 opening. Status checked 2026-10-30 on Hayward's Hex page, the Wikipedia Hex article and the 2025 thesis.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: for an opening cell X on the 10x10 Hex board, not in the 180-degree symmetry class {f5, e6} and not reported solved by Hayward's group or in the literature at verification time, a solution tree proving the outcome of the position 'Black stone on X, White to move' (no swap). Every node where the winning side moves names one move; every node where the losing side moves lists all legal moves, except moves removed by inferior-cell or fill-in rules only if each such rule is a published theorem (cite it) and the checker re-applies it from its stated pattern. Each leaf must be a completed connection or a virtual connection (a second-player connection strategy on a stated carrier) that the checker proves by exhaustive search on that carrier. The tree must be accepted by a checker written independently of the solver that produced it (sharing no code with Benzene or the solver used), with its own move generator and connection test.

partial_wins.statement: An independent re-verification of the 2013 10x10 f5 result, or of the 9x9 opening a6 (the hardest of the 2012 batch, 111 days), by a solver sharing no code with Benzene, with the solution tree accepted by an independent checker as in the success criterion.

The outcome of a 10x10 Hex position after two moves (an opening X other than f5/e6, then a White reply Y), certified as in the success criterion. Y must be the reply ranked first for White after X by a named, publicly available engine build (for example MoHex from Benzene, or KataHex) at stated settings, with the engine run log published so the verifier can reproduce the ranking.

targets.verification_method: Rebuild the checker from source and test it on small boards (all 1-move openings on 6x6 and 7x7, whose values are published). Then walk the submitted tree: at each losing-side node regenerate all legal moves and subtract only cells covered by a cited, re-verified pruning pattern; at each winning-side node check the named move is legal; verify every virtual-connection leaf by exhaustive search over its carrier; check that the root position is the claimed opening and that no swap move is used. Compare the outcome with an independent strong engine as a sanity check (an engine evaluation is not proof).
angles: Corner and edge openings on large boards are widely believed to lose for Black. Proving a loss needs one White reply plus a full tree, and some obtuse-corner or edge-adjacent openings may have short refutations built from edge templates.

Gao, Mueller and Hayward's focused DFPN with a convolutional net (IJCAI 2017) and Expected Work Search (IJCAI 2024) both cut proof effort; a modern GPU-trained policy can order moves inside a parallel DFPN.
Reuse Benzene's fill-in, inferior-cell and virtual-connection machinery for search, but export the tree in a plain format for an independent checker.
pitfalls: The 2013 paper counts one solved 10x10 opening (f5); later summaries say two, because e6 is its 180-degree image. Do not count e6 as new.
Swap-rule Hex is a different question. The criterion is the no-swap value of the stated opening.
Pruning by mustplay, dead cells and captured cells is sound only for the theorems that prove it; a home-made pattern without proof invalidates the tree.

Some first-row and edge openings may already be settled for all board sizes by published inferior-cell or edge-template theorems (Henderson and Hayward's papers, the book Hex, Inside and Out). Check before claiming an edge opening.
Hayward's Hex page was last modified in January 2022; also check recent Alberta theses and papers before claiming.

targets.name: Connect Four on a board with width + height = 17 (9x8, 10x7, 11x6, 12x5, 13x4): the first unsolved sizes
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (Steininger reports 7x9 took about 16 hours on his machine; for w + h >= 17 he uses 64-bit table entries and recommends 32 GB or more of memory); 9x8 and 10x7 may need weeks or a large-memory server
targets.statement: Connect Four on a board w columns wide and h rows high (stones drop to the lowest free cell; four in a row horizontally, vertically or diagonally wins; a full board is a draw). James D. Allen and Victor Allis solved the 7x6 game in October 1988. John Tromp solved every size with w + h <= 15 (2006) and 8x8 (late 2015, second-player win). Christophe Steininger's solver (github.com/ChristopheSteininger/c4) solved every size with w + h = 16 and some larger ones. His README tables (width x height) give outcomes and last-move numbers for widths 4-12 and heights 4-13, reaching 12x4, 11x5, 10x6, 9x7, 8x8, 8x9, 7x10, 6x11, 6x12, 5x13 and 4x13; every board 4 or 5 columns wide up to height 13 is a draw. Wikipedia's 'Solved game' article credits him with all w + h = 16 boards (May 22, 2024). Of the w + h = 17 boards, 4x13, 5x12, 6x11, 7x10 and 8x9 are solved. 9x8, 10x7, 11x6 and 12x5 are blank in his table, and 13x4 lies outside it (the table stops at width 12); 9x9, 8x10, 7x11, 7x12 and 6x13 are blank too. In issue #2 on his repository (opened May 2025) a user asked about 9x8. Steininger replied (29 May 2025) with the settings he uses for w + h >= 17 boards: 64-bit table entries, WORK_BITS = 0, and a Chinese-remainder trick to store positions exactly. He asked to see the 9x8 book if it was produced; no result was reported there. Task: determine the perfect-play outcome (first-player win, draw, or second-player win) of one of these sizes. Status checked 2026-10-30 on the repository README and issue #2.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: the perfect-play outcome of Connect Four from the empty board for one board size (width x height) with width + height >= 17 and both dimensions >= 4. The outcome must not be given in the results table of github.com/ChristopheSteininger/c4 at verification time (a blank cell, or a size outside the table such as 13x4), nor in Tromp's table or any other published source. It is established by two independent computations that agree: (1) the submitter's solver run, with its source, settings and log published, and (2) a second solver that shares no search or transposition-table code with the first (for example Steininger's c4 with WORK_BITS = 0 and a 64-bit entry as he recommends, Pascal Pons' solver, or Tromp's Fhourstones, adapted to the board size). Each solver must first reproduce at least three published neighbouring results from Steininger's table (for example 12x4, 11x5 and 8x8) and the published last-move numbers for them. A result does not count if it depends on a transposition table with unverified hash collisions (fewer bits stored than the position needs, without a Chinese-remainder or equivalent exact-recovery scheme).

partial_wins.statement: An independent confirmation of one of Steininger's w + h = 17 results (4x13, 5x12, 6x11, 7x10 or 8x9, width x height), so far computed only by his solver, by a solver sharing no search or transposition-table code with his, with the same outcome and last-move number.

An independent confirmation of a w + h = 16 result from Steininger's table that Tromp never computed (for example 9x7, 10x6 or 7x9), by a solver sharing no code with Steininger's, with the same outcome and last-move number.

targets.verification_method: Build both solvers from published source; run each on the claimed size and on the three control sizes; compare outcomes and last-move numbers. Check that the transposition-table entry stores enough bits to recover the position exactly (or that collisions are detected), and that multithreaded writes are atomic. Optionally replay the principal variation in a third, trivial move generator to confirm the claimed game end.
angles: Narrow-tall and wide-short boards are cheapest: 13x4 has 52 cells, and the height-4 row of the table is all second-player wins from width 8 on, a pattern to test first.
Steininger's issue #2 reply explains the settings he uses for w + h >= 17 (64-bit entries, WORK_BITS = 0, a larger NUM_TABLE_ENTRIES) and the Chinese-remainder trick for storing positions exactly.
An opening book of all positions to depth d, each solved and stored, doubles as a checkable certificate: a second solver can re-solve a random sample of book positions.
pitfalls: Width x height order: Steininger's and Tromp's tables put width across and height down; 9x8 means 9 columns and 8 rows.
Tromp's own table is older and stops at w + h = 15 plus 8x8; do not mistake its blanks for open cells.
Bit-packing 81 cells (9x8) into a 64-bit entry is only exact with the Chinese-remainder scheme; naive hashing silently corrupts results.
Steininger's 128-bit-entry workaround is unsafe with multiple threads (his own warning in issue #2).

targets.name: Go on small rectangular boards: an exact first-player score for a blank or ' > =6' cell of van der Werf's m x n table (3x10, 2x12, 4x8, 5x7, 6x6, ...)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days for the 24-33-point boards (2x12, 3x10, 3x11); 4x8, 5x7 and 6x6 probably need a cluster or a much stronger solver
targets.statement: Go solved on small boards: Erik van der Werf's program Migos solved 5x5 (October 2002, first player wins all 25 points from the centre; all openings by December 2002), and in 2008-2009 an improved Migos solved rectangular boards up to 30 intersections, checked against earlier human analyses by Ted Drange (van der Werf and Winands, 'Solving Go for Rectangular Boards', ICGA Journal 32(2), 2009). Van der Werf's table of first-player scores for m x n boards (m, n <= 12) has exact values for every board up to 30 points except two: 3x10 is given only as ' > =6' and 2x12 is blank; 3x11, 3x12, 4x8 and longer, 5x7 and longer, and 6x6 and larger are blank too. In 2024 Randall, Mueller, Wei and Hayward (Expected Work Search, IJCAI 2024) solved empty 5x5 under positional superko, the first full-board solve under that rule, and cite only the van der Werf work as prior board solutions. Wikipedia's 'Solved game' article lists 7x7 as weakly solved in 2015 from professional players' analysis (its source says the work is still under research); neither 6x6 nor 7x7 has a published computer proof. Task: determine the exact first-player score (area scoring, no komi, as in the table) for one blank or bounded cell. Status checked 2026-10-30 on van der Werf's mxngo page and in the 2024 EWS paper.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: the exact first-player score with perfect play on an m x n board (m <= n) whose cell is blank or ' > =6' in van der Werf's table at verification time, and not published elsewhere. The ruleset must be stated in full and labelled: either the Migos rules of van der Werf and Winands 2009 (their formalization of the Chinese rules: area scoring, basic ko plus Migos's long-cycle rule, no superko, specified in van der Werf's 2004 thesis), or positional superko with area scoring and no komi. Proof is one of two routes. (a) Two solution trees: one for 'first player scores at least S' and one for 'second player holds the first player to at most S'. Each is accepted by a checker that shares no code with the solver, regenerates every move of the side that must answer everything, applies the stated ko/superko rule with full game history (no transposition merging that ignores history under superko), and scores terminal positions itself. (b) Agreement of two independent solvers. Each first reproduces at least five published cells of the table under the Migos rules (including 5x5 = 25, 4x7 = 28 and 5x6 = 4), then solves the claimed board under the stated ruleset.

partial_wins.statement: A new proven bound for 3x10 or 2x12 under the Migos rules: one solution tree as in route (a), accepted by an independent checker, proving either that the first player scores at least S with S > 6 on 3x10 (any S on 2x12), or that the second player holds the first player to at most S.

An independent recomputation, under positional superko, of at least five cells of the table with 20 or more intersections (for example 4x5, 4x6, 3x9, 2x10, 5x6), with any disagreement with the Migos (basic-ko, long-cycle-rule) values documented position by position.

targets.verification_method: Rebuild the checker or second solver, run it on the control cells and confirm the published values, then check the submitted proof trees (or rerun the second solver) on the claimed board under the stated rules. Spot-check the principal variation by hand: a final position, its area count, and the ko history used.
angles: Migos used iterative-deepening alpha-beta with static recognition of unconditionally alive blocks and territory (Benson-style) to cut the tree; EWS adds win-rate guidance to proof-number search.
Thin boards (2 and 3 rows) are nearly one-dimensional; their values in the table show patterns (2xn: 8, 10, 12, ... then 4, 6) that suggest where to look and which first moves to try.
For a score proof, solve 'score >= S' and 'score >= S+1' as separate win/loss problems with a threshold-aware solver.
pitfalls: Ruleset changes values and cost: van der Werf's results use the Migos rules (a formalization of the Chinese rules with basic ko and a long-cycle rule, no superko; the EWS paper calls them Japanese-style), and the EWS paper reports that situational superko raised Migos's 4x4 solving time from 14.8 seconds to 1.1 hours. State the rules and compare only like with like.
The page's table is easy to misread when scraped; cells are m rows x n columns, symmetric, and ' > =6' is a bound, not a value.
Graph-history interaction: under superko, transposition tables keyed on board alone give wrong proofs.
Engine evaluations (KataGo) and professional analyses of 6x6 or 7x7 are not proofs.

targets.name: Domineering on the 12x12 board (largest solved square board is 11x11, Uiterwijk 2016)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (each square board from 8x8 to 11x11 was a new record solve; 12x12 has 144 cells and a far larger tree); a named-move refutation (partial win p2) may fit laptop-days
targets.statement: Domineering (Stop-Gate, Crosscram): two players alternately place dominoes on a grid, one player vertically and the other horizontally; the player unable to move loses. On square boards the two roles are symmetric, so the question is whether the first or second player wins. Solved: 8x8 by Breuker, Uiterwijk and van den Herik (2000), 9x9 soon after, 10x10 by Nathan Bullock (MSc thesis, 2002, using combinatorial-game-theory evaluation of regions), 11x11 by Jos Uiterwijk ('11x11 Domineering Is Solved: The First Player Wins', Computers and Games 2016). Wikipedia's Domineering article (edited October 2025) states that the game is a first-player win on 2x2, 3x3, 4x4 and 6x6-11x11, a second-player win on 1x1 and 5x5, and lists no larger square board. Task: determine the outcome of 12x12 Domineering. Status checked 2026-10-30 on the Wikipedia article; Bullock's table of rectangular values (webdocs.cs.ualberta.ca/~games/domineering/updated.html, cited there) now redirects to a University of Alberta directory page and was not readable.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: the outcome (first-player win or second-player win) of Domineering on the empty 12x12 board, while it is not reported solved on Wikipedia's Domineering article or in the literature at verification time, shown by a solution tree for the winning side (one named move at that side's nodes, every legal move of the opponent at the other side's nodes) whose leaves are either terminal positions or positions decided by a cited, proven rule (for example safe-move counting or a combinatorial-game value of independent regions computed by the checker itself), accepted by a checker that shares no code with the solver. Alternatively, agreement of two independent solvers that each first reproduce the published outcomes for 8x8, 9x9 and 10x10.

partial_wins.statement: An independent confirmation of the 11x11 first-player win (Uiterwijk 2016) by a solver or checker that shares no code with Uiterwijk's, with the winning first move and the solution tree or a second-solver agreement as in the success criterion.
A proof, certified as in the success criterion, that one named first move on the empty 12x12 board loses (the opponent then has a winning strategy).

targets.verification_method: Check leaves with an independent implementation: recompute region decompositions and their combinatorial-game values (or safe-move counts) from scratch, regenerate all opponent moves at every AND node, and verify that the root is the empty 12x12 board with the stated player to move. Run the control boards first.
angles: Bullock's solver split the board into independent regions once dominoes partition it and used precomputed combinatorial-game values for small regions; Uiterwijk's 11x11 run relied on safe-move counting and knowledge-based move ordering.
Partial results on 12xn and nx12 rectangles (one side moving first) are natural stepping stones and give move ordering for 12x12.
pitfalls: Which player moves first matters on rectangles but not on squares; on rectangles state who places vertical dominoes and who moves first.
Bullock's rectangular-board table is offline at its old address; do not assume a rectangle is open or solved without another source.
Safe-move counting rules have conditions; a leaf decided by a misapplied rule invalidates the tree.
The Springer page of Uiterwijk's 2016 paper sits behind a login redirect; read the status from Wikipedia and confirm in the ICGA/CG literature before claiming.

targets.name: Kalah(6,6) under standard capture rules: the exact perfect-play margin (proven only 'first player wins by at least 4')
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (Rawlings' empty-capture solve of Kalah(6,6) took searches totalling 106 days and 55 trillion nodes, with endgame databases for all 38.9 billion positions of 34 or fewer seeds; the standard-rule analysis has been 'ongoing' since 2015)
targets.statement: Kalah(6,6): 6 houses per side, 6 seeds per house (72 seeds). Standard rules: sow counter-clockwise including your own store but not the opponent's; a last seed in your store gives another move; a last seed in an empty house of your own captures it together with the opposite house's seeds only if that opposite house is non-empty; when one side's houses are empty the game ends and the other player takes the seeds left on their side. Irving, Donkers and Uiterwijk (2000) solved Kalah for all sizes up to 6 houses and 6 seeds except (6,6); Anders Carstensen (2011) proved (6,6) a first-player win under four rule sets, without the margin. Mark Rawlings (2015) found the exact margins of Kalah(6,4) (win by 8) and Kalah(6,5) (win by 10) under standard rules, and of (6,6) under the empty-capture variant (win by 2). For standard Kalah(6,6), Wikipedia's Kalah article (section restored October 2025) gives only: first move 1-2 proven win by at least 2, 1-3 proven win by at least 4, 1-6 and 6 proven losses by at least 2, 2 'trending towards a win', and 1-4, 1-5, 3, 4 and 5 probable ties from very deep searches but unproven; it says further analysis is ongoing. So the game value is known to be at least +4 for the first player, and the article states no upper bound. Task: determine the exact value. Status checked 2026-10-30 on the Wikipedia article.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: the exact perfect-play final store difference of Kalah(6,6) under the standard rules stated above (no capture when the opposite house is empty). The difference is first player minus second player, with seeds left in a side's houses at the end going to that side's owner. It counts only while Wikipedia's Kalah article still lists it as unproven and no other published source gives it. It must be established by two independent exact solvers that share no search, move-generation or endgame-database code. Each solver first reproduces the published empty-capture values of Irving, Donkers and Uiterwijk, Kalah(6,4) = +10 and Kalah(6,5) = +12. Each also reports its standard-rule values for Kalah(6,4) and Kalah(6,5); Wikipedia gives +8 and +10, and any disagreement must be documented with a principal variation. For Kalah(6,6) each run gives the exact value V of a best first move and a proven upper bound of at most V for every other of the 10 distinct first moves (1-2 to 1-6 and 2 to 6). The two runs must agree on V. Endgame databases used by either solver must be built by that solver's own code.

partial_wins.statement: The exact value of one first move listed as unproven (1-4, 1-5, 2, 3, 4 or 5), or of 1-2 or 1-3 (bounded only from below), confirmed by two independent solvers as in the success criterion.
The first independent confirmation of Rawlings' empty-capture result for Kalah(6,6) (win by 2, with his per-move table) by a solver sharing no code with his.

targets.verification_method: Build both solvers; run the control games; compare per-move values for Kalah(6,6) standard rules. Check the rules implementation on hand-made positions (a capture with an empty opposite house must not capture; extra move on store landing; end-of-game seed assignment). Replay the published principal variations in a third, trivial move generator.
angles: Seed-count endgame databases (all positions with at most k seeds on the board) make the lower part of the tree free; Rawlings' went to 34 seeds, and modern RAM allows more.
MTD(f) with a null-window solver and enhanced transposition cutoffs; prove 'value >= v' and 'value <= v' as separate searches.
Start with the move-3 or move-5 lines claimed as probable ties: proving a tie needs both bounds, but each is a narrow-window search.
pitfalls: Rule variants abound (empty capture, end-of-game counting, Kalaha vs Kalah); Carstensen's numbered variations and Wikipedia's 'standard' use different names. State the rules exactly.
The Rawlings analysis is unpublished and the Wikipedia section is tagged unreferenced; treat its per-move bounds as claims to re-check, not as given.
'Win by at least 4' is a lower bound from one move; the true value may be higher or the same.

targets.name: m,n,k-games: settle five-in-a-row (k = 5) on 9x9 or another board between 8x8 (draw) and 15x15 (win)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (8x8 needed a dedicated research solve in 2018 by Hsu, Ko, Hsueh and Wu; 9x9 has 81 cells); a narrow board such as (9,5,5) or (9,6,5) may fall in laptop-days
targets.statement: In the m,n,k-game two players alternately place stones on an m x n board, and the first to get k in a row (horizontally, vertically or diagonally) wins. No rules restrict moves (free-style, overlines count). Strategy stealing shows the first player never loses. For k = 5: Wei-Yuan Hsu, Chu-Ling Ko, Chu-Hsuan Hsueh and I-Chen Wu proved (7,7,5) and (8,8,5) draws (ICGA Journal 40(3), 2018), so every board with both sides at most 8 is a draw. L. Victor Allis proved (15,15,5) a first-player win (free-style gomoku, 1994). Nothing is listed in between. Wikipedia's m,n,k-game article was last edited in October 2026; its k = 4 results were updated in November 2025 with Christian Vogt's 2025 report that (6,5,4) is a win. It gives no result for any k = 5 board with a side from 9 to 14. Task: settle (9,9,5), or another unlisted k = 5 board with both sides at least 5 and at least one side from 9 to 14. Status checked 2026-10-30 on the Wikipedia article.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: the outcome (first-player win or draw) of the free-style (m,n,5)-game for (m,n) = (9,9), not settled on Wikipedia's m,n,k-game article or in the literature at verification time, shown by a solution tree accepted by a checker that shares no code with the solver. For a first-player win: one named first-player move at each first-player node, every legal second-player reply at the others, and every leaf a completed five. For a draw: one named second-player reply at each second-player node and every legal first-player move at the others, every leaf a full board or a position where the checker itself proves no line of five remains completable by the first player; threat-space or relevance-zone pruning is allowed only if the checker re-derives each pruning step from its stated rule.

partial_wins.statement: The outcome of another free-style (m,n,5) board with 5 <= m <= n <= 14 and n >= 9 (for example (9,8,5), (9,6,5) or (10,10,5)), not settled on the Wikipedia article or in the literature at verification time, certified as in the success criterion.
An independent re-verification of the (8,8,5) draw by a solver and checker sharing no code with Hsu et al., with a checkable second-player strategy tree.

targets.verification_method: Run the independent checker on the tree: regenerate every move of the side that must answer everything, verify every claimed five or 'dead board' leaf by brute force over all lines, and re-derive each pruning step. Sanity-check the checker on small solved cases ((5,5,4) draw, (6,5,4) win, (9,4,4) win).
angles: Threat-space search and dependency-based search (Allis) find first-player wins quickly when they exist; a draw proof instead needs second-player blocking strategies, where pairing strategies on part of the board and relevance zones shrink the tree.
Narrow boards (m = 5 or 6, n large) behave almost one-dimensionally and may be cheapest; check first that they are not already settled in the 4-in-a-row and 5-in-a-row literature (Uiterwijk).
pitfalls: Free-style rules only: gomoku's exactly-five rule, renju restrictions or swap openings define different games.
Wikipedia's silence on a board is not proof it is open; search the ICGA Journal and Computers and Games proceedings before claiming.
k = 6 and k = 7 on the infinite board are famous open questions, but no finite certificate settles them; they are out of scope here.

targets.name: Cram: compute a missing nimber in Beling's normal-play table (5x13, 6x11, 7x10, ...) or a missing misère value (5x8, 5x9, 6x7, 6x8, 6x9)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (Beling reports that for most boards in his table, for example 13x4, his solver needed no more than a few minutes; the open cells are the next sizes up and may take far longer)
targets.statement: Cram is the impartial version of Domineering: players alternately place a domino in either orientation on an m x n grid. Under normal play the player who cannot move loses; under misère play that player wins. Even x even boards are second-player wins and even x odd boards first-player wins by symmetry, so the open questions are nimbers (Grundy values) and misère values. Normal play: Martin Schneider (2009) computed boards up to 3x9, 4x5 and 5x7. Julien Lemoine and Simon Viennot's Glop (2010-2013) reached 3x20, 4x9, 5x9, 6x7 and 7x7. Jos Uiterwijk (ACG 2019) showed 11x5 has nimber 0. Piotr Beling's Rust solver igsolve (github.com/beling/impartial-games) extended the table to 7x9, 8x7, 9x6, 10x5, 11x4, 12x5 and 15x4 (13x4 first computed by Thomas Plick). Beling's table (heights 4-7, widths 4-15) still shows '?' for 13x5, 14x5, 15x5, 11x6, 13x6, 15x6 and 7x10 through 7x15. Misère play: Schneider and Glop reached 3x15, 4x9, 5x7 and 6x6 (2009-2011). Wikipedia's Cram article lists the misère values of 5x8, 5x9, 6x7, 6x8 and 6x9 as '?', and Beling's README says misère support is only planned. Task: compute one missing value. Status checked 2026-10-30 on Beling's README, the Glop records page and the Wikipedia article.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: for a board shown as '?' in Beling's normal-play table or in Wikipedia's misère Cram table at verification time (and not published elsewhere), its exact normal-play nimber or misère Grundy value (Conway's definition: the unique n such that G + *n is a misère second-player win), computed by two independent programs that agree, where each program first reproduces at least five published neighbouring values from the same table (for example 7x9 = 1, 9x6 = 1, 12x5 = 3 for normal play; 5x7 = 1, 6x6 = 1, 4x9 = 1 for misère). For normal play one program may be Beling's igsolve if the other shares no code with it. Each run publishes its source, its command line and the number of positions stored.

partial_wins.statement: The normal-play outcome only (zero or non-zero nimber) of an odd x odd '?' board (5x13, 5x15, 7x11, 7x13 or 7x15), confirmed by two independent programs as in the success criterion.

An extension of a published three-row sequence by at least two new terms: normal-play nimbers of 3xn beyond n = 20, or misère values of 3xn beyond n = 15 (conjectured period 3). Each new term must be confirmed by two independent programs, and none may be given at verification time on the Glop records page, Wikipedia's Cram article, Beling's README or any OEIS entry.

targets.verification_method: Build both programs; reproduce the control cells; run both on the claimed board and compare values. For a normal-play nimber v, a third check is cheap to state: G + *v must be a second-player win and G + *u a first-player win for every u < v. For misère, confirm that the definition used is Conway's misère Grundy value, not the normal nimber of the misère game.
angles: Beling and Rogalski's pruning (Artificial Intelligence 283, 2020) and Lemoine-Viennot's component splitting with nimber databases are the state of the art for normal play; both rely on Sprague-Grundy sums that are invalid in misère play.
For misère, Glop's reduced canonical trees (from its Sprouts work) are the known sound decomposition; a fresh misère solver for Cram is the gap Beling's README names as planned.
pitfalls: Normal and misère values must never be mixed; nimber addition does not hold in misère play.
Width x height symmetry: an m x n board equals n x m; check both spellings before calling a cell open.
Even x even and even x odd outcomes are known by symmetry; only the nimber (or misère value) is open there.
The Glop records page lists Cram values only up to 2013 and has no '?' cells; Beling's README and Wikipedia's tables are the places that mark open cells.

targets.name: Chess from the opening position: the next term of the per-ply counts (distinct positions at ply 12, checkmates at ply 14, perft(16))
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster for perft(16) and checkmates at ply 14 (GPU-weeks); distinct positions at ply 12 is laptop-weeks with tens of TB of disk, or a small cluster
targets.statement: Four OEIS sequences count what can happen in the first n plies of chess. A048987 counts move sequences (perft), known to n = 15: perft(14) = 61885021521585529237 and perft(15) = 2015099950053364471960 (Ankan Banerjee, GPU perft, talkchess 2016 and 2017; perft(14) also Peter Osterlund). A083276 counts distinct positions (placement, side to move, castling rights, an en passant square only when an e.p. capture is legal), known to n = 11: a(11) = 726155461002 (Peter Osterlund 2013, verified by Francois Labelle 2017). A089957 counts uniquely realizable positions, also to n = 11: a(11) = 1994236773. A079485 counts games ending in checkmate at exactly ply n, known to n = 13: a(13) = 346742245764219 (Labelle, 2017). Earlier terms are by Richard Bean, Paul Byrne, Steven Edwards, Arkadiusz Wesolowski and Labelle. Checked 2026-10-30: OEIS A048987 (edited June 2026) stops at a(15), A083276 and A089957 at a(11), and A079485 at a(13). The Chessprogramming wiki Perft Results page has only a Monte Carlo estimate of perft(16) (Ajedrecista, CCC, Feb 2024). Wikipedia's Shannon number table leaves positions blank after ply 11 and checkmates after ply 13. Labelle's page on statistics of chess positions (last updated 2017) gives more per-ply tables: checkmate diagrams to ply 13, mirror-symmetric diagrams to ply 15, at-home diagrams to ply 16.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: an exact value, absent from the OEIS entry and from any published source at verification time, for at least one of A083276 a(12), A089957 a(12), A079485 a(14) or A048987 a(16), under the exact definitions of the OEIS entries (A083276 follows Labelle's definition 2: en passant is recorded only when an e.p. capture is legal; A079485 counts games, not distinct positions). The claim must include (1) per-first-move or per-ply-k subtotals (a 'divide'), (2) code that reproduces every known term of the same sequence exactly, and (3) agreement with a second run by an independently written move generator or counting method, on all subtotals or on a random 2% of them. A finished full second run counts the same.

partial_wins.statement: An independent recomputation of perft(15) = 2015099950053364471960 (the Chessprogramming wiki credits only Ankan Banerjee's 2017 GPU run), with a per-first-move divide, by code that shares nothing with Banerjee's perft_gpu.

The next row of one of Labelle's per-ply diagram tables (checkmate diagrams at ply 14, mirror-symmetric diagrams at ply 16, or at-home diagrams at ply 17) under his definitions, with code that reproduces every earlier row of that table exactly and a second independent check as in the success criterion.

targets.verification_method: Rebuild the claimant's counter and an independent one (for example python-chess's legal move generator for small depths, plus a fast bitboard generator) and confirm both reproduce every known term of the claimed sequence exactly (A048987 a(0..15), A083276 a(0..11), A089957 a(0..11) or A079485 a(0..13)), or for p2 every earlier row of the claimed Labelle table. Then recompute a random 2% of the claimed subtotals (each subtotal is the count below one position at a fixed split depth) with the independent generator and check that the subtotals sum to the claimed total. For distinct-position counts, check the dedup key (placement, side to move, castling rights, legal-e.p. square only) and test it on known transpositions.
angles: Distinct positions: a level-by-level BFS over position sets partitioned by material and pawn structure (pawn moves and captures are irreversible, so partitions are small and independent), with sorted external-memory dedup per partition.
Checkmates at ply 14: perft with a transposition table keyed by position plus remaining depth, counting mates at the leaves; the counts depend only on the position, so transpositions can be merged.
Use the colour-and-board mirror only where it is valid: chess positions with castling rights are not left-right symmetric.
pitfalls: Counting positions with the FEN en passant field set after every double pawn push gives a different, larger sequence; A083276 records e.p. only when the capture is legal.
A079485 counts games, not distinct mate positions; Labelle's 'checkmate diagrams' table is a different quantity.
Perft(16) Monte Carlo estimates are not values.
A value posted on talkchess.com or elsewhere but not yet in the OEIS counts as published: check before claiming.

targets.name: Number of legal chess positions: a provable upper bound well below Tromp's 8.7279e45 ranking
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (exact combinatorial counting); validation runs on sampled positions are laptop-minutes
targets.statement: John Tromp's ChessPositionRanking (GitHub) defines an invertible ranking of 'urpositions', a computable superset of all legal chess positions (placement, side to move, castling rights, en passant). Its size is the best known rigorous upper bound on the number of legal positions. The README still gives N = 8726713169886222032347729969256422370854716254. On 2026-08-11 Michael Spece (GitHub MichaelSpece) reported a legal en-passant position that the ranking misses (issue #927, which Tromp accepted as the winning $256 bug report) and a related multiplicity error (#928). In a #927 comment of 2026-09-09 Tromp gave a fix that raises the size to 8727878536878208144190883427864082859392620550 (about 8.7279e45, 1.00013 times the old N). A commit 'fix incorrect ep counts bug' to src/CountChess.hs followed on 2026-09-29, and both issues were still open on 2026-10-30. Earlier bounds: Chinchalkar 1.77894e46 (1996), Allis 5e52 (1994). Tromp and Peter Osterlund (Texel proof-game engine) estimate the true count from 2 million random urpositions at (4.822 +- 0.028) x 10^44 (95% confidence), so the bound is about 18 times too large. The README notes that the ranking allows adjacent kings and that excluding them would gain only about 10%. In the initial classification of the 1M sample, 492,045 urpositions have both kings in check and 173,401 have the side not to move in check. Tromp writes that there is no hope of ever determining the exact number. Checked 2026-10-30: README, issues #927/#928 and the commit history read; no smaller rigorous bound found.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: an exact integer U <= 4.0 x 10^45, together with (a) a precise definition of a set S of positions and the exact count |S| = U, computed by released counting code and recomputed exactly by an independently written counter, and (b) a written proof that every legal chess position (Labelle/Tromp definition: placement, side to move, castling rights, e.p. square only when an e.p. capture is legal) lies in S, where every excluded class is excluded by a stated, proven necessary condition for legality, and S has a membership test that accepts every certified-legal position in the validation set below. The bound must be strictly below the smallest rigorous bound published at verification time (8727878536878208144190883427864082859392620550 as of 2026-10-30).

partial_wins.statement: Any rigorous upper bound strictly below 8727878536878208144190883427864082859392620550 (for example by also excluding adjacent kings), meeting conditions (a) and (b) of the success criterion.

An independent exact recomputation of the post-fix size 8727878536878208144190883427864082859392620550 (or a demonstrated arithmetic error in it) by counting code that shares nothing with CountChess.hs. Legal but unrankable positions or wrong multiplicities fall under Tromp's bug bounties (held), not here.

A new estimate of the number of legal positions with a 95% half-width below 1.0e42 (current 2.75e42), from a sample whose seed was fixed in advance and published, where each legal sample position has a replayable proof game and each illegal one a reproducible illegality certificate; any unresolved position is counted as legal for the upper end and illegal for the lower end.

targets.verification_method: Run both counters and compare the exact integers. Check each exclusion rule's legality proof. Run the membership test on (i) the 112,754 legal urpositions with proof games in Tromp's Texel.out.* files, (ii) one million positions from random legal games (random moves, 1% stop chance per move, as in the README), including en-passant and castling edge cases such as the #927/#928 FENs. Every position must be accepted. For p3, replay every proof game with an independent legal-move generator, and recompute the estimator with Tromp's estimate.pl formula.
angles: Exclude 'side not to move is in check' exactly: for a fixed king square and attacker set, count arrangements with blocked rays by inclusion-exclusion over attacking lines; it removes the two largest illegal classes (66% of urpositions).
Adjacent kings: condition the placement on the pair of king squares (3612 legal king pairs instead of 4032).
pitfalls: The README number is the pre-fix ranking, which missed legal en-passant positions; quote the post-fix value or a newer one.
En passant, castling and promotions (up to 12 with 4 captures) are where supersets silently lose legal positions; test them explicitly.
Tromp offers bug bounties on the ranking itself; those are a separate setter challenge (see held), not this target.

targets.name: Legal chess diagrams without promotion: beat Gourion's upper bound of 3.7422e37
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (Gourion's 25-men cases took up to 1.6 hours each in MatLab on a desktop)
targets.statement: A diagram is the contents of the 64 squares (no side to move, castling or e.p.). How many diagrams can be reached in a legal game with no promotion? Shannon's rough count was 64!/(32!(8!)^2(2!)^6), about 4.63e42. Stefan Steinerberger (Int. J. Game Theory 44, 2015) proved an upper bound of about 1.53e40 (2e40 in Gourion's abstract). Tromp's ChessPositionRanking README improves this to 2891398339895958031893456691621753206624 (about 2.9e39) by limiting unopposed pawns. Daniel Gourion (ICGA Journal, DOI 10.3233/ICG-220210, 2022; arXiv:2112.09386v2, revised 16 January 2025) reached 3.7422... x 10^37, using a graph on capture quadruplets and classes of legal pawn arrangements; his MatLab code is at github.com/DanielGourion/ChessDiagrams. He conjectures the true count lies between 1e37 and 3.5e37, probably close to 3e37. He names two possible gains: forbidding adjacent kings also for 24 or more men (about 10%; he already does so for 23 or fewer), and better bishop counting (his method loses up to 13% in the worst case). Checked 2026-10-30: arXiv v2 (2025) is the latest version, and Wikipedia's Shannon number article still gives 4e37 (Steinerberger, Gourion) as the upper bound for positions without promotion.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: an exact integer or rigorous decimal upper bound U <= 3.5 x 10^37 on the number of legal chess diagrams reachable without promotion (Gourion's definition), with (a) released counting code whose result an independently written counter reproduces exactly, and (b) a proof that every excluded diagram is illegal without promotion. A membership test of the counted superset must accept every diagram in the validation set described under verification_method. The bound must also be strictly below the smallest bound published at verification time (Gourion's 3.7422... x 10^37 as of 2026-10-30).

partial_wins.statement: An independent recomputation of Gourion's per-men upper bounds for 24 to 32 men (his Table 4, for example 4.93e32 at 32 men and 1.08e37 at 26 men) to the printed digits, by code that shares nothing with his MatLab repository, or a demonstration of an error in one of them.

A sampled estimate of the number of legal diagrams without promotion with a 95% confidence half-width below 10% of the estimate, from a published-seed sample of an exactly rankable superset, where legal sample diagrams carry replayable promotion-free proof games and unresolved ones are counted both ways.

Any rigorous upper bound strictly below 3.7422 x 10^37 (for example by removing illegal pawn-arrangement classes of the kind Gourion describes in his section 5.1), meeting conditions (a) and (b) of the success criterion and the membership test, and below any smaller bound published at verification time.

targets.verification_method: Recompute the claimed bound with both counters and compare. Check the illegality proof of each added exclusion. Generate one million diagrams from random promotion-free legal games, plus every diagram along those games, and confirm the claimant's superset membership test accepts all of them. For p2, replay each proof game with an independent move generator, check that no promotion occurs, and recompute the estimator.
angles: Extend the adjacent-kings exclusion to 24 or more men by conditioning on the king pair before placing the other pieces.
Use exact counting of bishops on each colour per class instead of Gourion's worst-case bishop handling.
pitfalls: 'Without promotion' means reachable by a game with no promotion. Counting all diagrams that merely contain no extra pieces is a different set.
Diagrams are not positions: do not compare with Tromp's position counts.

targets.name: Number of unique legal chess positions with 9 pieces (next term of OEIS A318266, Kryukov's NULP)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days with a combinatorial (inclusion-exclusion) counter; brute-force enumeration of about 1e18 positions needs a cluster
targets.statement: Kirill Kryukov's NULP project counts chess positions with n pieces (kings included). A position is a placement, side to move, castling rights and en-passant rights. It is illegal if a side does not have exactly one king, a pawn stands on its last rank or behind its second rank, or the side to move can capture the enemy king. Positions are counted once per equivalence class under these transformations: swapping the colours of all pieces together with the top-bottom mirror of the board (and of e.p. squares), swapping castling rights and side to move (always); the left-right mirror (only for positions without castling rights); and, for pawnless positions without castling rights, also the top-bottom mirror alone and the a8-h1 diagonal reflection. Values for 2 to 8 pieces: 462, 368079, 125246598, 25912594054, 3787154440416, 423836835667331, 38176306877748245 (8 pieces: Kryukov, 27 December 2013; split by castling and en-passant rights, 14 April 2014). These are OEIS A318266 (entry by Cyril Banderier, 2018). Kryukov's page invites confirmations or corrections of any of his results. Checked 2026-10-30: the NULP page (updated 2025-03-05) and OEIS A318266 both stop at 8 pieces, and no 9-piece count is listed.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: the exact 9-piece NULP under Kryukov's published definitions of legality, uniqueness, castling and en passant, computed by a counter that also reproduces all of Kryukov's 2- to 8-piece totals exactly, the 8-piece split by castling and e.p. rights (38043599567172213 / 68239052958566 / 64406325285316 / 61932332150), and his per-endgame 8-piece values for at least 100 randomly chosen endgames. A second, independently written counter must give the same 9-piece total and the same per-endgame breakdown. The 9-piece value must be absent from the NULP page and OEIS A318266 at verification time.

partial_wins.statement: The first independent confirmation of the full 8-piece table (total, all four castling/e.p. columns, and every per-endgame value in Kryukov's linked text files), or a documented correction that Kryukov's own definitions support.
The exact 9-piece NULP restricted to pawnless endgames (or to endgames with pawns), agreed by two independent counters that also reproduce the matching 8-piece subtotals.

targets.verification_method: Run both counters. Reproduce 2- to 8-piece values and the per-endgame files, then compare the 9-piece per-endgame breakdowns line by line. For small endgames (up to 5 pieces), brute-force enumerate positions with python-chess and canonicalize under the stated symmetries to cross-check the combinatorial method.
angles: Count all placements per material, then subtract those where the side to move attacks the enemy king, by inclusion-exclusion over attackers, with slider rays required empty. Burnside's lemma handles the symmetry quotient without enumeration.
pitfalls: Kryukov's symmetry rules differ for pawnless positions without castling rights; positions fixed by a symmetry (pieces on the long diagonal) must be counted once.
Kryukov counts e.p. positions under his own e.p.-right definition; reproduce his 8-piece E column before trusting the 9-piece one.

targets.name: Legal Go positions: 20x20 (OEIS A094777 a(20)) and the first unknown cells of Tromp's rectangular m x n tables
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days for the rectangular partial cells (m <= 13); needs cluster with tens of TB of disk for m >= 14 and for 20x20 (19x19 took most of 2015 on servers)
targets.statement: A Go position (any point empty, black or white) is legal if every group has a liberty. John Tromp, with Gunnar Farneback (early dynamic-programming code) and Michal Koucky (most of the computation for n = 14 to 16), counted legal positions exactly on n x n boards for n <= 19. L(19,19), about 2.0817e170, was finished on 2016-01-20. The method is a transfer-matrix count modulo many primes, combined by the Chinese remainder theorem. Tromp's site also has tables of L(m,n) for each m <= 19. For m <= 8 they list linear recurrences, so every n is known. For larger m the tables end at: m = 9: n = 208, m = 10: 187, m = 11: 170, m = 12: 156, m = 13: 42, m = 14 to 18: 19, m = 19: 20. The asymptotic form is L(m,n) ~ 0.8506399258457 x 0.965535059338374^(m+n) x 2.9757341920433572493^(mn). Checked 2026-10-30: OEIS A094777 has terms to n = 19, and the legal.html table pages (served with Last-Modified 2026-09-24) end where listed above. No 20x20 value is published.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: the exact value of L(20,20) = A094777(20), the number of legal positions on the 20 x 20 board, absent from OEIS A094777 and Tromp's legal.html at verification time. The claiming code must reproduce A094777(1..16) exactly, and the same 20-wide run must output L(20,n) for n = 1..13 and n = 19 that match Tromp's published L(n,20) values (tables L1 to L13 and L19) reduced modulo every prime the run used. It must be confirmed by an independent check: residues modulo at least three fresh primes (not used in the claim), computed by an independently written transfer-matrix program, must match the claimed integer.

partial_wins.statement: A new exact cell L(m,n) for 9 <= m <= 13 with n one or more beyond the last entry of Tromp's Lm.html table (for example L(13,43)), computed by code that reproduces that table up to its last entry and A094777(1..13) exactly, and confirmed by residues modulo at least three fresh primes from an independently written transfer-matrix program that match the claimed integer.

A new exact cell L(m,20) for 14 <= m <= 18, or L(19,21), computed by code whose same run reproduces Tromp's published L(m,1..19) (or L(19,1..20)) and which reproduces A094777(1..13) exactly, and confirmed by residues modulo at least three fresh primes from an independently written transfer-matrix program that match the claimed integer.

targets.verification_method: Compile an independent transfer-matrix counter (border states tracking colours and group connectivity, with pending-liberty flags). Reproduce A094777(1..13) in full and Tromp's L9 to L13 tables up to their ends. Then compute the claimed value modulo three random 61-bit primes and compare with the claimed integer reduced mod those primes. Sanity check: the ratio to the asymptotic formula should be 1 to many digits for large boards.
pitfalls: For m <= 8 the cells follow from published recurrences and do not count as new.
L(m,n) = L(n,m): a cell is new only if neither orientation is listed.

targets.name: Othello from the start: games after 22 plies (OEIS A124004) and distinct positions after 14 plies (A124005)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days for A124005 a(14) (about 2.5e10 positions, external-memory dedup); needs cluster for A124004 a(22): about 12 times the work of a(21), which took about 1000 hours on a desktop with two GTX 1080 Ti, so GPU-months even on several modern GPUs unless the method improves
targets.statement: A124004 counts Othello (Reversi) games from the standard start after n plies (perft). It is known to n = 21: a(21) = 4228388321175157140 (Dominic Hofer, February 2021, ReversiPerftCUDA). a(20) is Hofer's (January 2021), a(19) Hofer's (2014), a(15) to a(18) Paul Byrne's (2008); Alain Brobecker started the sequence. A124005 counts distinct positions after n plies, known to n = 13: a(13) = 3772081046 (Hofer, 2019). Checked 2026-10-30: both OEIS entries stop there, and the documentation in Hofer's repository (docs/A124004.md) lists terms only to a(21).
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: an exact new term A124004 a(22) or A124005 a(14), absent from OEIS and from any published source (forum posts and code repositories included) at verification time, from code that reproduces every known term of the same sequence, published with subtotals over a fixed split ply (for example one per symmetry-reduced position at ply 7) and confirmed by an independently written move generator on all subtotals or on a random 2% of them, or by a full second run.

partial_wins.statement: A124005 a(15), meeting the same validation, after or together with a(14).

A fully independent verification of A124004 a(21) (credited to one GPU code), with per-position subtotals over Hofer's published 10,649 symmetry-reduced ply-7 positions that sum to 4228388321175157140.

targets.verification_method: Reproduce A124004 a(0..21) and A124005 a(0..13) with the independent generator. Recompute a random 2% of claimed subtotals and check their sum and symmetry multiplicities. For distinct positions, check that positions are keyed by board plus side to move.
pitfalls: Pass and end-of-game conventions (whether a forced pass is a ply, and whether finished games are still counted at later plies) must match the OEIS definitions; reproducing all known terms is the test.
Distinct positions must include the side to move.

targets.name: English checkers from the start: the number of move sequences of 30 plies (OEIS A133046 a(30))
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster, or several weeks on one workstation with a transposition-hashed perft (a(30) is about 3.6e20; a(29) was reached in 2020)
targets.statement: A133046 counts distinct move sequences of n plies from the standard 12-versus-12 English checkers (draughts) position, with forced captures; duplicate king captures (the same pieces captured in different directions) are counted separately. Values to a(28) = 16377718018836900735 come from Aart Bik (a(12)-a(20) in 2009; a(21)-a(28) from distributed runs completed in September 2012; ICGA Journal, December 2012), whose page also gives per-first-move divides for depths 18 to 28. Rein Halbersma was first to compute a(22); Murray Cash confirmed a(23) and a(24), and Paul Byrne confirmed a(23) to a(28). a(29) = 76309690522352444005 was added by Murray Cash on 2020-11-20, and the entry credits no independent confirmation. Checked 2026-10-30: OEIS A133046 (last edited December 2024) ends at a(29), and Bik's page ends at depth 28.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: the exact value of A133046 a(30), absent from OEIS and from any published source (forum posts included) at verification time, from a perft that reproduces a(0..29) exactly (including Bik's per-move divides for depths 18 to 28), published with subtotals over a fixed split ply and confirmed by an independently written checkers move generator on all subtotals or on a random 2% of them, or by a full second run.

partial_wins.statement: An independent confirmation of a(29) = 76309690522352444005 (or proof of an error) with a per-first-move divide, by code that shares nothing with Murray Cash's program.

targets.verification_method: Reproduce a(0..28) and Bik's divides with the independent generator. Recompute a random 2% of the claimed subtotals at the split ply and check their sum.
pitfalls: Duplicate captures (a king capturing the same pieces in different directions) are counted separately, per the OEIS comment and Bik's generator; reproduce Bik's divides exactly before running deep.
The rules are English/American checkers (men capture forward only, no flying kings), not international draughts.

targets.name: Komlos discrepancy constant C_24: a finite matrix with unit-norm columns whose discrepancy beats Kunisky's 1 + sqrt(2)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (an exact discrepancy check is 2^n sign vectors for n nonzero columns, so n <= 30 takes minutes with bit-parallel Gray-code code; the search over real matrices is the expensive part)
targets.statement: Tao's optimization-constants repository, constant 24: for a real matrix A let disc(A) = min over x in {-1,1}^n of ||Ax||_inf. K_n is the supremum of disc(A) over n x n real matrices whose columns all have Euclidean norm at most 1, and C_24 = sup_n K_n. Zero rows and zero columns do not change disc, so any m x n matrix can be padded to a square one. The Komlos conjecture, that C_24 is finite, was proved in September 2026 by S. Guo, E. X. Fang and J. Lu (arXiv:2609.11189). S. R. Karingula and S. Lovett (arXiv:2609.20979) gave an elementary proof with C_24 <= 36, formalised in Lean by G. Dahia. E. Akbas and S. Sra (arXiv:2609.27172v2) claim 6.9013 (starred as unverified on the page). The lower side has not moved since D. Kunisky (SIAM J. Discrete Math. 37(2) 2023, arXiv:2111.02974) showed C_24 >= 1 + sqrt(2) ~ 2.41421. His bound is a limit: it uses a family of matrices built by scaling clause-variable matrices of unsatisfiable Boolean formulas through a second-order cone program, and their discrepancy approaches 1 + sqrt(2). Guo-Fang-Lu describe it the same way. The page asks whether C_24 = 1 + sqrt(2). On 2026-10-30 the live page (constants/24a, last changed 2026-10-22) still lists 1 + sqrt(2) as the best lower bound, and no open pull request touches constant 24. A single explicit finite matrix with discrepancy strictly above 1 + sqrt(2) would be the first improvement since 2021 and would refute the natural guess that the constant equals 1 + sqrt(2).
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit real matrix A with m rows and n nonzero columns, saved as a file. Its entries must be rationals, or exact elements of a stated real quadratic field. Every column must have squared Euclidean norm <= 1, checked exactly. Its exact discrepancy d = min over all 2^n sign vectors x of max_i |(Ax)_i| must be computed by exhaustive enumeration in exact arithmetic by two independently written programs that agree. d must be STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than 1 + sqrt(2), checked exactly as d > 1 and (d - 1)^2 > 2. It must also be strictly greater than the largest lower bound on the live page https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/24a.html, in any open pull request touching constants/24a.md at https://github.com/teorth/optimizationproblems/pulls, and in any paper or preprint found by a fresh literature check (arXiv, and works citing Kunisky arXiv:2111.02974), all re-fetched immediately before claiming. Proposing the bound to the repository is an action for a human.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit matrix with at most 15 nonzero columns, rational entries and every column of squared Euclidean norm <= 1 (checked exactly), whose exact discrepancy (exhaustive over all 2^n sign vectors in exact arithmetic, two independent programs) is at least 2. For reference: Kunisky's tree matrices (arXiv:2111.02974, Theorem 1.1, K(2^k) >= 2^{-k/2} + sum_{a=1..k} 2^{-a/2}) first certify a value above 2 at 16 columns (K(16) >= 2.0607). The only smaller example reported there is D. Spielman's unpublished 15-column matrix with discrepancy in [2.005, 2.006].

An explicit matrix with at most 15 nonzero columns, under the same exactness rules as p1, whose exact discrepancy is strictly greater than 2.006, the upper end of the interval reported for Spielman's unpublished 15-column example in Kunisky (arXiv:2111.02974, Section 1).

targets.verification_method: Parse the matrix as exact rationals (Python Fraction or integers after clearing a common denominator) and check sum_i a_ij^2 <= 1 for every column j. Enumerate sign vectors in Gray-code order, fixing x_1 = +1 by symmetry and updating Ax incrementally. Record the minimum over x of the maximum absolute row sum. Recompute it with a second program in another language or by another method, for example an exact branch-and-bound whose optimum is re-checked by direct evaluation. Compare exactly: d > 1 and (d-1)^2 > 2. Re-fetch the 24a page and its open PRs.
angles: Start from Kunisky's construction: take the clause-variable sign matrix of an unsatisfiable CNF, then choose the row and column scalings by a second-order cone program. His family approaches 1 + sqrt(2) from below. Try formulas with richer structure (Tseitin formulas on expanders, pigeonhole, random unsatisfiable 3-CNF near threshold) and re-optimise the scaling for each.

Use an LP or SOCP inside local search: fix the set of sign vectors that each row is responsible for covering, maximise the common margin over the entries subject to the column-norm constraints, recompute the exact discrepancy, and reassign. This is the same max-min game used for Spencer's C_10c records.

Nikolov showed that the vector-colouring relaxation is at most 1 for Komlos instances, so a good matrix must exploit integrality. Search for matrices whose SDP value is low but whose sign discrepancy is high, as integrality-gap instances.
pitfalls: Floating-point entries: a column norm of 1.0000001 or a rounded discrepancy voids the claim. Use exact rationals throughout.
The constraint is on columns (the vectors being signed), not rows. Normalising rows gives a different problem (Spencer-type).
Sampling sign vectors overestimates the discrepancy. Every one of the 2^n vectors must be checked.
Kunisky's bound is a supremum. A finite matrix that matches 1 + sqrt(2) to many digits but not strictly is not a win.

Kunisky's Theorem 4.1 (arXiv:2111.02974, Section 4): any matrix obtained by scaling the clause-variable matrix of a formula with a read-once resolution refutation (every tree / MU(1) formula among them) has certified value strictly below 1 + sqrt(2), and his Conjecture 4.4 says the same for every unsatisfiable-matrix certificate. Re-optimising tree formulas cannot win; use formulas without read-once refutations, or matrices whose discrepancy is not certified by unsatisfiability alone.
The page and its pull requests move. Compare against the live maximum, not the number in this entry.

targets.name: Matrices filled with 1..n^2 (Pfoertner's OEIS family): beat a best-known maximal determinant or extremal permanent
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (exact det/permanent of a 7x7 to 10x10 integer matrix takes microseconds to milliseconds; the work is local search over arrangements, which parallelises trivially)
targets.statement: A family of OEIS entries, curated mostly by Hugo Pfoertner, asks for the extreme value of the determinant or permanent of an n x n matrix whose entries are a fixed multiset arranged freely. Exact values are known only for small n. Above that, the entries record lower bounds (for maxima) or upper bounds (for minima) together with the people who found them. Open cells as of 2026-10-30, from the live entries: (a) A085000, max det using 1..n^2 once each: a(8) >= 440970981670289 and a(9) >= 346260899916111296 (Benjamin R. Buhrow, 2019), and a(10) >= 356948996371054862392 (Richard Gosiorovsky, 2021). The Gasper-Pfoertner-Sigg upper bounds (JIPAM 2009) are 441077015225642, 346335386150480625 and 357017114947987625629. (b) A180128, max det using the first n^2 primes: a(8) >= 154671943501236284416 (Gosiorovsky, 2021), with upper bound 154715716383037989022 (A180127). (c) A350566, max permanent using 1..n^2: a(7) >= 38677691168324 (Pontus von Broemssen, 2025-03-20; earlier 38677620556961 by Robert Israel). (d) A350565, min permanent using 1..n^2: a(7) <= 4755379618016 (von Broemssen, 2025-08-30). (e) A358487, max permanent using 0..n^2-1: a(7) >= 29821721685800 (von Broemssen, 2025-09-03). (f) A301371, max det of the multiset {1^n, ..., n^n}: a(10) has no listed value. The best known arrangement is the noncirculant Latin square of A309985 with determinant 36860608125 (Arthur Queiroz M., 2026-08-06), and the upper bound is A328031(10) = 37180409223. The matrices given in A350565, A350566 and A358487 were recomputed for this entry (exact Ryser permanent) and match the stated values. Each cell is a separate record. The A301371 cell is the free-arrangement problem, not the Latin-square sequence A309985.
targets.success_criterion: Success means one explicit n x n integer matrix whose entries are exactly the multiset of the chosen cell, checked by sorting. Its exact determinant (absolute value) or permanent must be computed by two independent programs that agree. The value must be STRICTLY BETTER than the best bound for that cell at verification time: strictly greater for the maximisation cells A085000(8), A085000(9), A085000(10), A180128(8), A350566(7), A358487(7) and A301371(10), strictly smaller for A350565(7). The best bound is the best value in the live OEIS entry (data, comments, b-file, links and pending edits in https://oeis.org/Annnnnn/history), in Pfoertner's linked pages, and in any paper or preprint found by a fresh check, all re-fetched immediately before claiming. A maximum claim above a stated upper bound (Gasper-Pfoertner-Sigg, A180127, A328031) indicates a bug and is not accepted. One cell per claim. Submitting to the OEIS is an action for a human.

partial_wins.statement: For A350858(7) or A350859(7) (min or max permanent of a 7 x 7 matrix filled with the first 49 primes), for which no bound is published: an explicit matrix whose exact permanent beats the reference value obtained by putting the primes into the rank pattern of the A350565(7) (for the minimum) or A350566(7) (for the maximum) record matrix. The k-th smallest entry is replaced by the k-th prime. The verifier recomputes this reference value.

targets.verification_method: Check that the entries are a permutation of the required multiset. Compute det by fraction-free Bareiss elimination on Python integers and cross-check with sympy or PARI. Compute the permanent by Ryser's formula with Gray-code updates and cross-check with Glynn's formula or a direct expansion (7! = 5040 terms). Compare against the live entry's comments and history. For the maximisation cells, confirm the value does not exceed the published upper bound.
angles: For the determinant cells, the Gasper-Pfoertner-Sigg bound is attained only by matrices whose rows have equal sums and equal sums of squares and are nearly orthogonal after centring. Search near that structure: start from the known record matrices and use pair-swap simulated annealing with exact incremental determinant updates (rank-2 Sherman-Morrison on a float shadow, exact recheck of the finalists).

For the maximum permanents, the 7 x 7 records are near-'sorted' block patterns (large entries concentrated on one permutation and its neighbours). Try parametrised families (staircase or anti-diagonal sortings, products of sorted vectors) and polish with 2-swaps and 3-cycles.

For the A301371(10) cell, A309985 and A301371(9) show that free arrangements beat Latin squares at n = 9 (Oleg Vlasii's 2019 matrix). Start from the 36860608125 Latin square and allow non-Latin swaps.
pitfalls: Use exact integers: 10 x 10 determinants of this size exceed 2^64, and floats give spurious records.
The A085000 comment bounds for n = 8 and 9 superseded the published 2009 bounds. Compare against the best value anywhere in the entry and its history, not against the first number you see.
A301371 counts the multiset {1^n,...,n^n} (each value n times), not 1..n^2. A309985 (Latin squares only) is a different sequence and a separate record.
The minimum-permanent cell has direction min.
Do not run the FORTRAN or other programs linked from the entries. Write your own checkers.

targets.name: Latin Tableau Conjecture (Chow et al.): a Young diagram with no Latin tableau of type delta, or a certified extension of the 12 x 12 verification
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (13 x 13 box: about 10.4 million partitions, roughly half up to conjugation; each needs a max-flow and a small SAT/ILP colouring)
targets.statement: A Latin tableau of shape lambda is a colouring of the boxes of the Young diagram of lambda with no colour repeated in any row or column. Its type mu lists the colour multiplicities in decreasing order. Let alpha_k be the maximum number of boxes that can be coloured with k colours under this rule, and let delta_k = alpha_k - alpha_{k-1} (the chromatic difference sequence). If a tableau of type mu exists, delta must dominate mu. The Latin Tableau Conjecture, posed by T. Y. Chow et al. in their work on the wide partition conjecture (a generalisation of Rota's basis conjecture), says this necessary condition is also sufficient. A positive answer implies the wide partition conjecture for free matroids. T. Y. Chow and M. G. Tiefenbruck (Electronic J. Combin. 32(2) (2025) P2.48, published 2025-06-20) reduce the conjecture to the existence of a Latin tableau of shape lambda and type exactly delta. Equivalently, the rook-type graph on the boxes of lambda is CDS-colourable; this is the form in the formal-conjectures file Paper/LatinTableau.lean, tagged research open as of 2026-10-30. They prove that a tableau can always match the first four parts of delta, and they report a computer check of every partition lambda that fits inside a 12 x 12 square. They have computed characterisations up to r = 7 terms without publishing proofs. A single partition lambda admitting no Latin tableau of type delta(lambda) would disprove the conjecture.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a partition lambda together with: (i) its sequence delta(lambda), computed exactly by two independent programs; (ii) a proof that no Latin tableau of shape lambda and type delta(lambda) exists, given as a CNF encoding whose correctness is argued in a short note, plus a DRAT/LRAT unsatisfiability proof accepted by a verified checker (cake_lpr or an equivalent formally verified checker); (iii) the check that the conjecture is still open, i.e. the formal-conjectures file is still tagged research open and no newer paper settles it, re-fetched before claiming. Equivalently, a lambda whose box graph is not CDS-colourable, certified the same way. Notifying the authors is an action for a human.

partial_wins.statement: A reproducible verification of the conjecture for every partition lambda inside a 13 x 13 square (one row or column longer than the published 12 x 12 range). It must ship, for each lambda, or for one of lambda and its conjugate with the symmetry argued, an explicit Latin tableau of type delta(lambda) as a witness file, so that the verifier checks witnesses rather than trusting a search. The partition count must match binomial(26,13) = 10,400,600 including the empty partition.

targets.verification_method: Compute alpha_k by maximum flow: cells are edges of the bipartite row-column graph, and a subgraph of maximum degree k splits into k matchings (Koenig), so alpha_k is the largest number of cells with at most k per row and per column. Compute delta, then check each supplied tableau (no repeated colour in any row or column, colour counts sorted equal to delta). For a counterexample, regenerate the CNF from lambda and delta with your own encoder, check that it equals the supplied CNF up to variable renaming or re-derive the UNSAT proof, and run a verified LRAT checker. Re-run small cases against the paper's examples (Figure 1: shape (4,2,1), type (2,2,2,1)).
angles: The paper proves that the first four parts of delta can always be realised, so a counterexample must fail at part 5 or later. Restrict the search to shapes whose normalised CDS (delta-bar_2, ..., delta-bar_7) falls into the long case lists the authors computed but did not publish, and test those shapes far beyond 12 x 12.

Encode 'type exactly delta' with cardinality constraints, one colour class per colour of size delta_i, each a partial transversal, and use an incremental SAT solver across neighbouring shapes (adding a box changes delta locally).

Conjugation (transposing lambda, which maps Latin tableaux to Latin tableaux and preserves delta) halves the work, and Proposition 5 means only type delta itself needs testing for each shape. Shapes with many equal parts (rectangles with staircase additions) are the hardest for greedy colourings, so stress-test those first.
pitfalls: Domination of mu by delta is necessary. A shape with no tableau of some arbitrary type mu is not a counterexample unless delta dominates that mu. Test type delta itself.
alpha_k must be computed exactly by flow or matching, not by a greedy colouring, which underestimates delta and creates false counterexamples.
A SAT solver's UNSAT answer without a checked proof is not a certificate.
The 12 x 12 range is already covered, so search outside it.

Two recent papers prove cases of the different wide partition conjecture (Latin tableaux of shape lambda and type lambda), not this conjecture: Daugherty et al., arXiv:2610.29291 (Oct 2026), and Allsop-Kotlar-Wanless, arXiv:2511.10548. An Academia.edu upload titled 'A constructive AI proof of the Latin Tableau Conjecture with applications' claims a proof. It is unrefereed and could not be read on 2026-10-30 (HTTP 403). If a valid proof exists, no counterexample exists and only p1 remains winnable, so check its status before a long counterexample search.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Gerstenhaber problem: three commuting d x d matrices generating an algebra of dimension > d (or reducibility of C(3,d) for some 11 <= d <= 28)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (checking a candidate is exact linear algebra on d^2-dimensional vectors; the search space is the hard part)
targets.statement: Gerstenhaber (Annals of Math. 1961) proved that two commuting d x d matrices over a field generate a unital algebra of dimension at most d. Whether the same holds for three pairwise commuting matrices has been open for over 60 years (the Gerstenhaber problem). It fails for four or more: E13, E14, E23, E24 in M_4 generate a 5-dimensional algebra. Known positive cases, as summarised by R. Cherny, M. Satriano and Y. Song (arXiv:2402.16334, 2024): the variety C(3,d) of commuting triples is irreducible for d <= 10 (K. Sivic 2012), so the bound holds there. The bound also holds when one matrix has nullity at most 3 (Guralnick-Sethuraman, Sivic), when one matrix squares to zero (Holbrook-Omladic 2001), for one-generated modules, and for several combinatorial gluing classes (Rajchgot-Satriano; Cherny-Satriano-Song). C(3,d) is reducible for d >= 29 (Holbrook-Omladic 2001; Ngo-Sivic 2014), so the generic-point argument breaks there, but no counterexample is known. Holbrook and O'Meara (arXiv:2006.08588) published a computing strategy aimed at finding one. The formal-conjectures file Other/GerstenhaberThreeMatrices.lean tags the triple case research open (last changed 2026-10-14).
targets.success_criterion: Success means three explicit d x d matrices A, B, C with entries in Q or in a stated prime field F_p, such that AB = BA, AC = CA and BC = CB hold exactly, and the unital algebra K[A,B,C] they generate has dimension STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than d. The dimension is computed by two independent exact programs as the rank of the span of all monomials A^i B^j C^k, iterating the degree until the span stops growing. The problem must still be open, i.e. the formal-conjectures file is still tagged research open and no newer paper settles it, re-checked before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: A certificate that C(3,d) is reducible for some d with 11 <= d <= 28: an explicit polynomial parametrisation (over Q) of a family of pairwise commuting triples, verified to commute identically by symbolic expansion, whose Jacobian matrix has exact rank greater than d^2 + 2d (the dimension of the component of simultaneously diagonalisable triples) at a stated rational point. The claim must also show, by a check of the literature cited in arXiv:2402.16334 and newer papers, that reducibility at that d was not already published.

targets.verification_method: Load the matrices exactly (Fractions or integers mod p) and check the three commutators are zero. Vectorise I and every monomial of degree <= t, compute the rank exactly (fraction-free elimination over Q, or Gaussian elimination mod p), and increase t until the rank stabilises; a second independent implementation, for example sympy against a hand-written modular rank, must agree.
