For p1, expand the commutators of the parametrised family symbolically to confirm they vanish identically, then compute the exact rank of the Jacobian at the stated point.
angles: Search only where the known theorems leave room: d >= 11, all three matrices nilpotent (reduction to the local case), each of nullity >= 4, none squaring to zero, and modules needing at least two generators.

Use the combinatorial model of Cherny-Satriano-Song and Rajchgot-Satriano: glue monomial quotients S/I and S/J along an isomorphism of submodules and compute the dimension of the resulting algebra combinatorially. Enumerate gluing data far beyond the classes they settle.

Use the dimension count as a guide: components of C(3,d) other than the main one (known to exist for d >= 29) are where a counterexample could live. Constructions of extra components (Holbrook-Omladic, Ngo-Sivic) give explicit families to test at their generic points.
pitfalls: For d <= 10 the bound is a theorem (irreducibility of C(3,d)), so do not search there.
The dimension is that of the unital algebra (include I), computed over the field of the entries. Mixing fields or floating-point ranks gives false counts.
Generic (diagonalisable) triples always satisfy the bound. Random rational triples will never be counterexamples, so the search must be structured.
Four commuting matrices are known to violate the bound and do not count.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Marcus-de Oliveira determinantal conjecture: normal A, B with det(A + B) outside the convex hull of the n! eigenvalue products
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (an exact check is n! products plus one determinant over Q(i); n = 4..7 is instant)
targets.statement: The determinantal conjecture of M. Marcus (1972) and G. N. de Oliveira (1982): if A and B are n x n normal complex matrices with eigenvalues a_1..a_n and b_1..b_n, then det(A + B) lies in the convex hull of the n! points prod_i (a_i + b_sigma(i)), sigma in S_n. Without loss of generality A = diag(a) and B = U diag(b) U* with U unitary, so the conjecture is a statement about how det(diag(a) + U diag(b) U*) varies over the unitary group. Fiedler (1971) proved the case where both matrices are Hermitian, where the hull is an interval. The case n = 2 is classical, and further special classes are treated in the literature (for example essentially Hermitian pairs). The general conjecture is open: the formal-conjectures file Wikipedia/DeterminantalConjecture.lean, which formalises exactly this statement with A = U1 D1 U1* and B = U2 D2 U2*, is tagged research open as of 2026-10-30, and the Wikipedia article lists it as a conjecture. A single explicit pair of normal matrices with det(A + B) strictly outside the hull would disprove it.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an integer n, eigenvalue vectors a, b with entries in Q(i), and an exactly unitary matrix U with entries in Q(i), with U U* = I checked exactly (rational unitaries come, for example, from the Cayley transform of a skew-Hermitian matrix over Q(i)). With A = diag(a) and B = U diag(b) U*, the value D = det(A + B) must be computed exactly by two independent programs. The claim must also give a separating certificate: w in Q(i) with Re(conj(w) D) STRICTLY GREATER than max over all sigma in S_n of Re(conj(w) prod_i (a_i + b_sigma(i))), checked exactly over all n! permutations. The conjecture must still be open, i.e. the formal-conjectures file is still tagged research open and no newer paper settles it, re-checked before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: A Lean 4 proof, compiling against the pinned toolchain of google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, of the file's statement determinantal_conjecture specialised to n = Fin 2. The statement must be unchanged apart from fixing the index type. The proof may use no sorry, no native_decide and no new axioms (#print axioms shows a subset of propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound), and the n = 2 case must not already carry a formal proof in the repository or an open pull request there.

targets.verification_method: Represent Gaussian rationals exactly (pairs of Fractions). Check U U* = I entrywise, form B = U diag(b) U*, and compute det(diag(a) + B) by exact fraction-free elimination, cross-checked by a Leibniz or Laplace expansion for n <= 7. Enumerate all n! permutations, form the products, and check the separating inequality exactly. Optionally confirm by an exact rational LP that D is outside the hull.
angles: Search with an adversarial optimiser: for fixed eigenvalues, maximise the signed distance of det(diag(a) + U diag(b) U*) outside the hull over U, using Riemannian gradient steps on U(n) in float. Then round promising U to an exact rational unitary via the Cayley transform and recheck exactly.
Choose eigenvalues far from collinear (for example vertices of regular polygons with different radii) for n = 4..6, since Hermitian or nearly collinear spectra are covered by Fiedler-type arguments.
The hull has at most n! vertices, but many products coincide for symmetric spectra. Use spectra with few hull vertices so that the hull is thin and det(A + B) has room to escape.
pitfalls: Floating-point: a determinant just outside the hull by 1e-12 is noise. Only an exact U, exact D and exact separating certificate count.
U must be exactly unitary. A rounded unitary changes the spectrum of B, which is then not normal with eigenvalues b.
Both-Hermitian pairs are covered by Fiedler (1971), and n = 2 is classical. Check the literature for the other settled classes before searching.
The point must be strictly outside the hull. Landing on the boundary is consistent with the conjecture.

targets.name: de Bruijn-Newman constant: a certified upper bound below every claim on Tao's C_21 page (refereed record 0.2; unrefereed claims down to 0.107964910079)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (interval-arithmetic barrier and finite-region checks; pushing the verified RH height would need a cluster)
targets.statement: Tao's optimization-constants repository, constant 21: the de Bruijn-Newman constant Lambda is the threshold such that H_t(z) = integral_0^inf e^{t u^2} Phi(u) cos(zu) du has only real zeros exactly when t >= Lambda. RH is equivalent to Lambda = 0, and Brad Rodgers and Terence Tao (Forum Math. Pi 2020) proved Lambda >= 0. Refereed upper bounds: 1/2 (de Bruijn 1950), < 1/2 (Ki, Kim and Lee 2009), 0.22 (D.H.J. Polymath 2019, arXiv 1904.12438) and 0.2 (Dave Platt and Tim Trudgian 2021, arXiv 2004.09765, from RH verified to 3e12). Since 2026 the live page has carried unrefereed, asterisked certificate packages: 0.1965 and 0.1875 (Mosaic Intelligence), 0.172422 (Daniel Martin Kornaus, Zenodo 22658444), and 0.16 and 0.1595 (Mosaic Intelligence). The README cell reads '0.2 (0.1595*)'. Open pull request #291 (updated 30 Oct 2026) proposes six more asterisked rows: 0.163297, 0.149396, 0.116398 and 0.107964910079 (Raymond, Zenodo), 0.13963 (Hakimoglu-Brown, arXiv 2610.12803) and 0.148612 (Planat, arXiv 2610.18214). Three of them import an unrefereed theorem from an OpenAI preprint (zeta has no zeros with Re s > 7/8). The page says none of its post-2021 rows has been independently replayed. The PR reports that Planat reproduced the finite comparisons behind 0.149396 and 0.116398 (arXiv:2609.37164v2 Section 8; arXiv:2610.18214 Appendix A), and notes that a numerical replay does not validate the analytic foundation. Two kinds of work are useful and checkable: a bound below all claims that rests only on refereed inputs, and an independent replay that confirms or refutes a claimed package.
targets.success_criterion: Main win: an unconditional bound Lambda <= t* with t* STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the smallest upper bound on https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/21a.html, in every open pull request touching constants/21a.md (currently 0.107964910079 in PR #291), and in any paper, preprint or Zenodo deposit found by a fresh check, all re-fetched immediately before claiming. The bound must come with (a) a written argument naming each input theorem by its exact published statement, every input being refereed (no unrefereed imported theorem, no RH beyond a verified height, no GRH or other hypothesis); and (b) a supplied program that certifies every numerical inequality in interval or exact arithmetic (barrier winding number, finite-region zero exclusion, tail and error bounds). A skeptic reruns (b) and finds no failure.

partial_wins.statement: An independent from-scratch interval-arithmetic replay of the finite certificate of one asterisked row on the live page or in PR #291 for which no replay has been reported. This excludes 0.149396 and 0.116398, which Planat reports reproducing. Examples are Mosaic Intelligence 0.1875 and Kornaus 0.172422. The replay must use code that shares nothing with the claimant's bundle. It ends either in agreement with every stated certified inequality, or in a concrete parameter point (t, x, y) where a claimed certified inequality fails, with a rerunnable script that shows the failure.

A rerunnable interval-arithmetic replay bundle, written independently of the Polymath 15 code (github.com/km-git-acc/dbn_upper_bound), reproducing the refereed 0.2 bound of Platt-Trudgian (or Polymath's 0.22) from the published parameters, taking RH up to 3e12 (Platt-Trudgian) as the only cited input and certifying every other numerical step (barrier, finite-region and tail estimates).

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: check the provenance of every cited input (journal version, exact statement). Rerun the certificate program with python-flint/arb or Arb at two working precisions. Spot-check the effective approximation of H_t (the Polymath A + B - C form with error terms) against direct quadrature at 20 random points. Recompute the final arithmetic from the certified parameters. For p1, rerun the claimant's replay and any reported failing point with an independent evaluator.
angles: Start from the refereed Polymath-15 barrier framework and optimise its parameters (t0, y0, barrier location X) with certified evaluation; the framework's limits show what new analytic input any lower bound needs.
Rigorous-numerics import: the argument principle on a rectangle needs a certified lower bound on |H_t| along the contour; use Taylor models in t and x rather than dense meshes.
Formal-methods import: a Lean statement of the barrier lemma with numerics discharged by an external certificate would end the refereed-versus-asterisk ambiguity.
pitfalls: Comparing against the README cell '0.2 (0.1595*)' instead of the smallest claim in open PR #291 (0.107964910079 as of 2026-10-30).
Importing an unrefereed theorem (the 7/8 zero-free claim, or an asterisked package used as a starting row) makes the bound conditional; under this criterion it does not count.
Floating-point winding numbers on a coarse mesh can miss zeros; every contour step needs a certified lower bound on |H_t|.
Lambda >= 0 is proven, so a computation suggesting Lambda <= 0 points to a bug.

targets.name: Bloch's constant B (C_57a): a certified lower bound above Wikstrom's sqrt(3)/4 + 0.0153 = 0.448312701 (claimed upper bound 0.471861652113, Zhang 2026)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (interval-arithmetic verification of a refined Bonk-type argument)
targets.statement: Tao's optimization-constants repository, constant 57a. Bloch's constant B is the infimum, over holomorphic f on the unit disc with f'(0) = 1, of the radius of the largest disc onto which some subdomain is mapped univalently. Ahlfors and Grunsky (Math. Z. 1937) proved B <= A_AG = (1/sqrt(1+sqrt 3)) Gamma(1/3)Gamma(11/12)/Gamma(1/4) = 0.4718616534... and conjectured equality. Teng Zhang (arXiv 2610.16808, 12 Oct 2026, unrefereed; Lean 4 formalization generated with Codex at github.com/zhangteng2000/Bloch-constant) claims to disprove that conjecture. Shearing cylinders of a genus-two translation surface tiled by equilateral triangles gives normalized f with B <= b(f) < A_AG exp(-113569/(4*10^13)) < 0.471861652113 < A_AG - 1.3e-9 (Proposition 8.4; the integrals are interval-enclosed in Lemma 8.3). Lower bounds: sqrt(3)/4 = 0.4330 (Ahlfors), sqrt(3)/4 + 1e-14 (Mario Bonk 1990), sqrt(3)/4 + 2e-4 (Huaihui Chen and Paul Gauthier, J. Anal. Math. 1996) and sqrt(3)/4 + 3e-4 (Xiong Chengji 1998). Frank Wikstrom (arXiv 2608.17660, 18 Aug 2026, unrefereed) refined Bonk's method with 'computer-assisted estimates rigorously verified using interval arithmetic' and proved B >= sqrt(3)/4 + 0.0153 = 0.448312701.... The live page still lists Chen-Gauthier and the Ahlfors-Grunsky bound. Open PR #223 (opened 12 Oct 2026; on 26 Oct the maintainer asked for it to be rebased and split) proposes adding Wikstrom's row, and no pull request yet adds Zhang's bound. The interval [0.448312701, 0.471861652113] is open. Known relation: B <= B_l <= L <= B_u (locally univalent Bloch, Landau and univalent Bloch constants; L and B_u are separate entries).
targets.success_criterion: Main win: a lower bound B >= b* with b* STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the largest lower bound on https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/57a.html, in any open pull request touching constants/57a.md (currently 0.448312701 from Wikstrom via PR #223), and in any later paper an arXiv search finds, all re-checked immediately before claiming. It needs a complete written proof whose analytic steps follow published lemmas cited precisely (for example Bonk's distortion theorem) and whose every numerical inequality is certified by a supplied interval-arithmetic program. Alternative main win: an upper bound B <= u* with u* STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the smallest upper bound on the 57a page, in any open pull request, or in any later paper. That bound is currently 0.471861652113, from Zhang (arXiv 2610.16808, Proposition 8.4). The win must give an explicit normalized f and a complete proof that every univalent disc in f(D) has radius at most u*. Every numerical step must be certified by a supplied interval-arithmetic program, or the whole proof kernel-checked (Lean, Rocq or Isabelle, no sorry or extra axioms). Refuting the Ahlfors-Grunsky conjecture alone no longer counts, since Zhang already claims it.

partial_wins.statement: An independent interval-arithmetic replay of every numerical inequality in Wikstrom's arXiv 2608.17660 proof, written from the paper without the author's code. It ends in either confirmation or a specific inequality and parameter value where the claimed bound fails, with a rerunnable script.

An independent interval-arithmetic replay of Zhang's numerical enclosure (arXiv 2610.16808, Lemma 8.3: q_C in (-370/10^6, -337/10^6)) and of the scalar comparisons in Proposition 8.4, written from the paper without the author's code or Lean files. It ends in confirmation or a specific failing step, with a rerunnable script.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: map every analytic step to the published lemma it cites, then rerun the interval program at two working precisions (for example Arb at 30 and 60 digits). Every box or case in the cover must be closed, and the union of boxes must cover the full parameter domain, which is checked by a separate covering script. Expected: hours.
angles: Wikstrom's jump from +3e-4 to +0.0153 came from making Bonk's estimates computer-assisted; tighten the same chain with finer case splits and higher-order distortion estimates.

Optimisation import: write the extremal problem over the low Taylor coefficients of a Bloch function as a semidefinite or moment relaxation, as Wikstrom did for Landau's constant, and certify the dual.
pitfalls: The Ahlfors-Grunsky value 0.4718616534... is no longer the upper-bound comparator: Zhang (arXiv 2610.16808, unrefereed) claims B < 0.471861652113, so an explicit f that merely beats the Ahlfors-Grunsky value is not a record.
The page table still shows Chen-Gauthier (sqrt(3)/4 + 2e-4); beating that alone is not a record, since the comparator is Wikstrom's 0.448312701.
Confusing Bloch's constant (univalent subdisc) with Landau's constant (any disc in the image) or the locally univalent constant B_l.
Floating-point LP or SDP solutions are discovery tools, not certificates; the dual must be re-verified in rigorous arithmetic.

targets.name: Landau's constant L (C_57b): a certified lower bound above Wikstrom's 0.51 (covering radius 0.51003; upper bound 0.5433)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (LP or SDP relaxations plus an Arb box covering)
targets.statement: Tao's optimization-constants repository, constant 57b. Landau's constant L is the infimum, over holomorphic f on the unit disc with f'(0) = 1, of the radius of the largest disc contained in f(D). Rademacher (1943) proved L <= Gamma(1/3)Gamma(5/6)/Gamma(1/6) = 0.5433... and conjectured equality. The live page lists L > 1/2 + 1e-335 (Yanagihara 1995). Frank Wikstrom (arXiv 2609.23236, 19 Sep 2026, unrefereed) proved B_l > 0.51 and L > 0.51, where B_l is the locally univalent Bloch constant and B_l <= L, improving the 1/2 + 2e-8 of Chen and Shiba. He works with g = log f', where the Bloch condition becomes a one-sided linear constraint on Re g, and uses positive Toeplitz moment matrices as a finite relaxation for the low logarithmic coefficients. Floating-point LP dual vectors are re-verified by an independent Arb program at 80 digits over 1,179 boxes; the smallest certified radius in the final covering is 0.51003. Open PR #223 proposes the 0.51 row. Chain: B <= B_l <= L <= B_u.
targets.success_criterion: Main win: a lower bound L >= l* (or B_l >= l*, which implies the same for L) with l* STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than 0.51003 and than every lower bound on https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/57b.html, in open pull requests touching constants/57b.md, and in any later paper an arXiv search finds, all re-checked immediately before claiming. Proof standard: a written reduction (the relaxation and why it is valid) plus dual certificates and a box covering that a supplied rigorous-arithmetic program verifies. Alternative main win, refuting Rademacher's conjecture: an explicit f with f'(0) = 1 and a rigorous certificate that every disc contained in f(D) has radius at most rho for an explicit rho STRICTLY LESS than the exact Rademacher value Gamma(1/3)Gamma(5/6)/Gamma(1/6) = 0.5432589653429767... (Rademacher's own extremal function attains this value and does not count).

partial_wins.statement: An independent replay of Wikstrom's 2609.23236 certificate: rebuild the relaxation from the paper, re-derive dual vectors and re-verify a box covering of the normalised coefficient body in rigorous arithmetic, confirming L > 0.51 or exhibiting a box where the certificate fails.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: check the relaxation's validity argument (the Toeplitz positivity follows from the cited Herglotz/Caratheodory representation). Rerun the certifier at two precisions and confirm that the boxes cover the full normalised coefficient body (separate covering check). Check that each box's dual certificate gives a radius of at least the claimed l*. Expected: hours.
angles: Raise the truncation order of the moment relaxation and add higher-order Toeplitz or Hankel constraints; the 0.51003 margin suggests the relaxation, not the method, is the bottleneck.
Polynomial-optimisation import: Lasserre hierarchy with rational rounding of SDP duals (as in flag-algebra certificates) gives exact certificates without box splitting.
Adaptive box refinement driven by the dual gap, as in branch-and-bound global optimisation.
pitfalls: The live page still shows 1/2 + 1e-335; the comparator is Wikstrom's 0.51 (covering radius 0.51003).
Bounds for the Bloch constant B do not transfer upward: B <= L, so a lower bound on B says nothing new about L, while a lower bound on B_l does bound L.
Truncating to finitely many coefficients needs a rigorous tail bound; dropping it gives an invalid bound.

targets.name: Univalent Bloch-Landau constant B_u (C_57c): a slit domain with certified inradius/conformal-radius ratio below van Staden's 0.65628589
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Tao's optimization-constants repository, constant 57c. B_u is the infimum, over univalent f on the unit disc with f'(0) = 1, of the inradius of f(D). Equivalently, any simply connected domain Omega and point w0 give the upper bound inradius(Omega) / conformal radius(Omega, w0). Lower bound: 0.5708858 (Brian Skinner 2009). Upper bounds from explicit slit discs: 0.658 (Robinson 1935), 0.65647 (Goodman 1945), 0.6564155 (Beller-Hummel 1985), 0.6563937 (Tom Carroll and Joaquim Ortega-Cerda 2009, theta-function formula), 0.656319277272* (Ortega-Cerda and Bharti Pridhnani 2010, numerical, no rigorous error analysis) and 0.65628589* (Wynand van Staden, preprints.org 202610.1936, 20 Oct 2026, unrefereed, merged into the page via PR #245 on 26 Oct 2026). Van Staden's domain is a disc of radius 5.001117628756668 minus 24 curved slits, invariant under rotation by 2pi/3 and complex conjugation (five base slits and their images). His computer-assisted proof certifies inradius <= 1 + 1e-9 by an exact covering and conformal radius >= 1.523726208329 by an Arb comparison function; code and certificates are at github.com/WynandVStaden/bloch-landau-slit-discs. The README cell reads '0.6563937 (0.65628589*)'. Every explicit domain is a checkable object, and the slit design space (more generations, curved slits, harmonic-symmetry arcs) is barely explored.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit simply connected domain Omega (finitely many slits or arcs with exact or rational parameters) and a point w0, with (a) a certificate that inradius(Omega) <= rho (every point of Omega lies within rho of the complement, by exact or interval covering) and (b) a rigorous lower bound R on the conformal radius of Omega at w0 (interval arithmetic or a comparison-domain argument). The ratio rho/R must be STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the smallest upper bound on https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/57c.html and in any open pull request touching constants/57c.md (currently 0.65628589*), both re-fetched immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: A rigorous certificate (in the sense of the main criterion) for the Ortega-Cerda-Pridhnani 2010 domain, turning the numerical 0.656319277272 into a proven upper bound, or showing that its true certified ratio is larger than stated.

An independent re-certification of van Staden's 0.65628589 domain with a conformal-radius lower bound computed by a different method from his comparison function (for example a boundary-integral or Schwarz-Christoffel-type map with a posteriori error bounds), confirming the bound or locating a failure.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: rebuild Omega from the stated parameters; rerun the inradius covering in exact or interval arithmetic and check that the covering discs reach every point of Omega. Recompute the conformal-radius lower bound with an independent method at two precisions, for example a numerical conformal map checked against van Staden's comparison function, and compare the ratio to the live record. Expected: under an hour.
angles: Shape-optimisation import: parameterise slit shapes by splines and optimise the ratio with adjoint gradients of the conformal radius (computed by a fast boundary-integral solver), then certify the best design.
Extend the harmonic-symmetry construction of Carroll and Ortega-Cerda with further generations of arcs, as the Polya-Tchebotarov connection suggests.
pitfalls: The inradius must be bounded for the whole domain, not only near the slits; long thin channels between slits can hide a larger inscribed disc.
Numerical conformal radii without error bounds are estimates (the 2010 value is starred for exactly this reason).
The conformal radius is taken at the chosen point w0; changing w0 without recomputing invalidates the certificate.

targets.name: Bohr radius of the bidisc K_2 (C_59): an explicit Schur function beating the 0.302825279492 upper bound, or a certified lower bound above Knese's 0.3006
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Tao's optimization-constants repository, constant 59. K_2 is the largest r such that sum |f_{jk}| r^{j+k} <= 1 for every analytic f mapping the bidisc D^2 into D (the Schur class). Bohr proved K_1 = 1/3, and the exact value of K_d is unknown for every d > 1. Bounds on the live page: 1/(3 sqrt 2) <= K_2 <= 1/3 (Harold Boas and Dmitry Khavinson, PAMS 1997). Greg Knese (PAMS Ser. B 12 (2025), arXiv 2410.21693) proved K_2 >= 0.3006. Upper bounds: 0.3177 (Baran, Pikul, Woerdeman and Wojtylak, JFA 2026), 0.3174541 (Sebastian Griego 2026, a degree-(250,250) rational-inner Fejer certificate) and 0.302825279492 (Shivam Patel, 26 Aug 2026). Patel's f = (SQ - P)/(SQ + P) is built from U = (1+z)(1-w), V = 1+zw, P = LU + iTV, Q = LV + iTU with integer L, T, S. Two independent exact computations of the 841 coefficients with j, k <= 28 give a majorant above 1 + 1e-26 at r = 0.302825279492; the Python and Lean proof package is Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.22341928. The open gap [0.3006, 0.30283] is small, and the upper-bound side needs only an explicit object with an exact check.
targets.success_criterion: Main win (upper): an explicit f with exact rational or Gaussian-rational parameters, a certificate that |f| <= 1 on D^2 (an exact algebraic argument, or interval verification on the torus plus the maximum principle with poles excluded from the closed bidisc), and an exact finite partial sum of |f_{jk}| r^{j+k} exceeding 1 at a rational r STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the smallest upper bound on https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/59a.html and in any open pull request touching constants/59a.md, re-fetched immediately before claiming. Alternative main win (lower): a proof that K_2 >= l with l STRICTLY GREATER than the page's best lower bound (0.3006), with all numerics certified by a supplied program.

partial_wins.statement: An independent replay of Patel's certificate in a second language or CAS (exact integer arithmetic): recompute all 841 coefficients and the majorant at r = 302825279492/10^12, and verify the Schur-class property, confirming the bound or exhibiting the step that fails.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: recompute the Taylor coefficients of f exactly (rational or Gaussian-integer arithmetic, two implementations) and the partial majorant at the claimed r. Verify the Schur-class certificate: denominator nonvanishing on the closed bidisc and |f| <= 1, by exact positivity or interval subdivision of the torus. Expected: minutes.
angles: Patel's family is a Cayley transform of a two-variable rational function with a few integer parameters; search richer families (more factors in U and V, higher degree) with the exact majorant as objective.
Rational inner functions on the bidisc have a stable-polynomial description (Agler, Knese), so optimise over stable polynomials p and f = z^n w^m conj(p(1/conj z, 1/conj w))/p.
For the lower bound, Knese's three-radii method plus a computer-assisted coefficient-body estimate (as in Wikstrom's Landau work) may push past 0.3006.
pitfalls: Patel's note is also posted on mathdb.com, which returned HTTP 403 at check time. If that site attaches a live bounty to the problem, the target belongs with setter challenges; re-check before attacking.
A partial sum over a finite coefficient box is a valid lower estimate of the majorant only because all terms are nonnegative; truncating the Schur-class proof the same way is not valid.
Floating-point coefficient sums near 1 + 1e-26 are meaningless; use exact arithmetic.

targets.name: Gauss-Kuzmin-Wirsing constant (C_83): more than Nisoli's 175 certified decimals of |lambda_2|
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Tao's optimization-constants repository, constant 83. The Gauss-Kuzmin-Wirsing operator (Lf)(x) = sum_k (x+k)^-2 f(1/(x+k)) is the transfer operator of the Gauss map. Its subdominant eigenvalue lambda_2 is negative, and C_83 = |lambda_2| = 0.30366300289873265859744812190155623... sets the rate in the Gauss-Kuzmin theorem. Certified bounds: 0.30366299 to 0.30366327 (Dieter Mayer and Gert Roepstorff 1987, Temple inequalities), then a 175-digit enclosure by Isaia Nisoli (arXiv 2602.19435, v2 1 Mar 2026). Nisoli's a posteriori finite-rank method certifies the first 50 nonzero eigenvalues to at least 90 rigorous digits, with eigenvectors and Riesz projectors; code is at github.com/orkolorko/GKWExperiments.jl. Non-certified values are much longer: Wirsing 1974 (20 digits), Flajolet-Vallee (about 30), Keith Briggs 2003 (385 digits; OEIS A038517 b-file has 382 terms) and Giedrius Alkauskas 2012 (over 480 digits). The certified record therefore lags the numerical one by a factor of almost three, and the operator is compact on Hardy spaces of discs around [0,1], so rigorous enclosures converge geometrically.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a rigorous enclosure of lambda_2 with radius below 10^-D, D STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the certified digit count on https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/83a.html and in any open pull request touching constants/83a.md (currently 175, Nisoli 2026), re-fetched immediately before claiming. The enclosure's centre must agree with Nisoli's 175-digit centre to within the two radii. The certificate is a program in rigorous arithmetic (Arb, python-flint, IntervalArithmetic.jl or exact rationals) that bounds the discretisation error on a stated function space and certifies isolation of lambda_2 (for example by a resolvent bound on a contour), and a skeptic reruns it.

partial_wins.statement: A rigorous enclosure of some other eigenvalue lambda_k (3 <= k <= 51) of the GKW operator with at least 150 certified decimals, beating Nisoli's at-least-90-digit guarantee for that eigenvalue.

A non-certified computation of lambda_2 to at least 600 decimals by two independent methods (for example Babenko-Mayer power-series matrices and Briggs-style Chebyshev collocation at sizes differing by at least 2%) agreeing on all 600, with the first 175 matching Nisoli's centre.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: rerun the certifier at two working precisions. Check that the stated function space (for example H^inf of a disc containing [0,1]) makes L compact and that the truncation bound is applied as proved. Confirm that the isolating contour encloses exactly one eigenvalue. Compare the leading digits with Nisoli's centre and OEIS A038517. Expected: under an hour at 200-300 digits.
angles: Use the Mayer representation of L as an integral operator on a Hardy space of the disc |z - 1| < 3/2, where matrix truncation errors are explicit and decay geometrically.

Numerical-analysis import: Kato-Temple and Lehmann-Goerisch bounds give two-sided eigenvalue enclosures from a Rayleigh quotient and a residual norm, often more digits for the same matrix size than resolvent methods.
pitfalls: Counting digits of agreement between two non-rigorous runs is not certification; the main win requires a proved error bound.
lambda_2 is negative and C_83 = |lambda_2|; sign slips produce nonsense comparisons.
The OEIS data field shows 105 digits and the b-file 382, but the record to beat is the certified 175.

targets.name: Brun's constant (C_81): an unconditional upper bound below Platt-Trudgian's 2.288513
targets.compute_profile: pure thought (explicit sieve estimates), plus laptop-hours of certified numerics
targets.statement: Tao's optimization-constants repository, constant 81: Brun's constant B is the sum of the reciprocals of the twin primes. Unconditional bounds on the live page: 1.840503 < B < 2.288513 (Dave Platt and Tim Trudgian, arXiv 1803.01925, 'Improved bounds on Brun's constant'; their abstract calls this about a 13% improvement on the previous best published result, the upper side moving from the Crandall-Pomerance bound 2.347). Lower bounds are partial sums from twin-prime enumeration; Thomas Nicely's enumerations gave 1.8318... (the much-quoted B ~ 1.902 is an extrapolation, not a bound). Under GRH, Dominic Klyve's unpublished thesis bound of 2.1754 was superseded by Lachlan Dunn (Bull. Aust. Math. Soc. 113 (2025), arXiv 2504.15658): B < 2.1594. The README carries the unconditional 2.288513. An unconditional upper bound needs an explicit sieve upper bound for twin primes up to x, with fully explicit constants, combined with computed twin-prime counts up to a large height. Both ingredients have improved since 2018 (explicit Brun-Titchmarsh and Selberg-sieve constants, larger verified twin-prime counts), but the bound has not been updated.
targets.success_criterion: Main win: an unconditional upper bound B < U with U STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the smallest unconditional upper bound on https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/81a.html and in any open pull request touching constants/81a.md (currently 2.288513), both re-fetched immediately before claiming. It needs a complete written proof citing each explicit input by its exact published statement (refereed sieve inequalities, published twin-prime counts or a supplied re-verifiable enumeration), and a supplied interval-arithmetic program that evaluates every numerical step (integrals, sums, optimisation of the sieve parameter) with outward rounding. Conditional results (GRH) do not count for the main win.

partial_wins.statement: Under GRH, a bound B < U' with U' strictly below Dunn's 2.1594, at the same proof and certification standard.
An interval-arithmetic replay that reproduces Platt-Trudgian's 2.288513 from their published inputs and parameters, as a rerunnable bundle, or locates an error in their numerics.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: check each cited explicit inequality against its source (statement, range of validity, constants). Rerun the interval program at two precisions. Spot-check any twin-prime counts used against published tables and, for heights up to 1e12, by an independent segmented-sieve count. Expected: hours to read, minutes to rerun.
angles: Replace the Brun-type sieve in the Crandall-Pomerance and Platt-Trudgian argument with the explicit Selberg-sieve upper bound for twin primes (Riesel-Vaughan style constants), optimised in the switching height.
Use the largest published twin-prime counts (pi_2(x) to 1e18 or beyond, from Oliveira e Silva's computations) for the head of the sum, so the sieve only bounds a shorter tail.
pitfalls: Mixing conditional (GRH) and unconditional bounds: 2.1594 is conditional and does not count as the unconditional record.
The 1.902 'value' of B is an extrapolation; using it anywhere in a proof invalidates the proof.
Nicely's original twin-prime pages return 404 (the trnicely.net domain was taken over by an unrelated site); cite archived or published counts.

targets.name: Masser-Gramain constant delta: a certified bracket narrower than Melquiond-Nowak-Zimmermann's 1.819776 < delta < 1.819833 (2013)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days
targets.statement: Let r_k be the smallest radius of a closed disc (any centre) containing at least k Gaussian integers. The Masser-Gramain constant is delta = lim_{n -> inf} (sum_{k=2}^{n} 1/(pi r_k^2) - log n), a two-dimensional analogue of Euler's constant. It arose in the Gelfond-Polya problem for entire functions taking Gaussian-integer values on Z[i]: Masser (1980) proved a sufficient growth threshold expressed through delta, and Gramain (1981) determined the best constant (OEIS A086056); MathWorld gives both. Gramain conjectured delta = 1.822825249...; OEIS A086058 lists 102 digits of this conjectured value. Gramain and Weber (Math. Comp. 1985, corrected 1987) proved 1.811447299 < delta < 1.897327117. Guillaume Melquiond, W. Georg Nowak and Paul Zimmermann (Math. Comp. 82 (2013) 1235-1246) proved 1.819776 < delta < 1.819833, disproving Gramain's conjecture, so delta is known to only four decimals. MathWorld (Masser-Gramain Constant), OEIS A086058 and Zimmermann's publication list show no later improvement (checked 2026-10-30). The HAL copy hal-00644166 showed a bot check (BLOCKED) and the AMS page returned 403. Each r_k^2 is an exact rational (the circumradius of two or three lattice points), so the head of the sum is exactly computable; the difficulty is a rigorous tail estimate from lattice-point counting in discs.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a rigorous bracket a < delta < b with a > 1.819776 or b < 1.819833 (direction: narrower, strictly improving at least one end), and no wider at the other end than the published bounds or any later published bounds found by search immediately before claiming. The certificate has (i) exact r_k^2 for all k <= N, each with a witness disc and an exact minimality proof, computed by two independent implementations, and (ii) an explicit tail bound for k > N with a written proof (or exact citation of a published explicit estimate with its constants), evaluated in interval arithmetic by a supplied program.

partial_wins.statement: A published dataset of exact r_k^2 for all k <= 10^6 with witness discs, produced by two independently written programs that agree on every entry, together with the resulting exact head sums S(n) = sum_{k=2}^{n} 1/(pi r_k^2) - log n in interval arithmetic for n = 10^3, 10^4, 10^5, 10^6.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: recompute r_k^2 for a random sample of 1,000 k <= N, and for all k <= 2,000, by brute-force enumeration of candidate circles through two or three lattice points. Check monotonicity and the 'at least k' convention. Rerun the interval tail evaluation and check that its inputs match the cited theorem's hypotheses. Expected: hours.
angles: Computational-geometry import: r_k is the k-th order minimum enclosing circle problem on a lattice; incremental algorithms over candidate centres (circumcentres and midpoints) make k up to 10^7 feasible.

Analytic-number-theory import: the tail is governed by the lattice-point discrepancy in discs (the Gauss circle problem); use the best explicit discrepancy bounds with explicit constants rather than asymptotic exponents.
pitfalls: The disc centre need not be a Gaussian integer; restricting centres to lattice or half-lattice points overestimates r_k.
OEIS A086058 lists Gramain's disproved conjectured value 1.82282..., not delta; do not use it as a comparator.
'At least k points' versus 'exactly k points' changes the sequence.
A 2024-2026 literature search could not be completed when this entry was written (search budget exhausted); re-check for newer bounds before attacking.

targets.name: Bernstein's constant beta = lim 2n E_2n(|x|): more than the 50 decimals of Varga and Carpenter (1985)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days
targets.statement: Let E_m(|x|) be the error of the best uniform approximation of |x| on [-1,1] by real polynomials of degree at most m. Bernstein (Acta Math. 1913/14) proved that beta = lim_{n -> inf} 2n E_{2n}(|x|) exists, showed 0.278 < beta < 0.286, and conjectured beta = 1/(2 sqrt(pi)) = 0.28209.... Richard S. Varga and Amos J. Carpenter (Constr. Approx. 1 (1985) 333-348; Mat. Sb. 1986, English Math. USSR Sb. 57 (1987)) disproved the conjecture with high-precision Remez computations and Richardson extrapolation. Their value 0.2801694990238691330364364912306720000424821398... is the source of the 50 decimals in OEIS A073001 (keyword 'more'; b-file n = 0..49). For the value, MathWorld cites only Varga-Carpenter (1987) and Varga's SIAM book (1990), and Wikipedia quotes 12 digits. An unexplained OEIS extension to a(106) was proposed in Aug 2026 and reverted by the editors within a week, so the published record is still 50 decimals. No closed form is known. Because E_{2n}(|x|) = E_n(sqrt t) on [0,1] and 2n E_{2n} has an asymptotic expansion in 1/n^2 (exploited by Varga-Carpenter), today's multiprecision Remez codes should reach far larger n and many more digits on a laptop.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a decimal value of beta with D decimals, D >= 60 and STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the digit count of OEIS A073001 re-fetched live and of any published value found by a literature search re-run immediately before claiming. Conditions: (a) two independent determinations agree on all D decimals (for example Richardson or Levin-type extrapolation from two disjoint ranges of n, or two different Remez implementations); (b) the first 50 decimals match A073001, or any disagreement is confined to its last few decimals and is explained in the write-up and backed by the certified E_{2n} brackets; (c) the digits are stable when the largest n used is increased by at least 20%. Each E_{2n} used must be certified to the working precision by an equioscillation (de la Vallee Poussin) bracket.

partial_wins.statement: A table of E_{2n}(|x|) for all n <= 200, each with a certified two-sided de la Vallee Poussin bracket of relative width below 10^-60, posted with the alternation points and coefficients so that every row can be rechecked independently.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: for 10 random rows, recheck the de la Vallee Poussin lower bound (alternating signs and sizes at the stated points) and the upper bound (the maximum of |p(x) - |x|| over [-1,1], by interval subdivision) in multiprecision interval arithmetic. Rerun both extrapolations and compare digits. Expected: hours.
angles: Work with sqrt(t) on [0,1] (half the degree) and a barycentric Remez in Chebfun-style multiprecision; reuse the previous n's alternation set as the starting guess.
Sequence-acceleration import: fit the known 1/n^2 expansion by least squares with many terms and validate on held-out n, as in high-precision extrapolation of lattice series.
pitfalls: Agreement of two extrapolations from overlapping n ranges is not independent; use disjoint ranges.
Remez iterates that have not equioscillated to full precision inflate E_{2n}; certify each value with an equioscillation bracket.
E_n for odd n equals E_{n-1} for the even function |x|; indexing slips shift the limit by a factor of 2.

The A073001 history shows digits a(50)-a(106) proposed in Aug 2026 without a method and then reverted. Matching them is not verification, and OEIS editors reject unexplained machine-computed digits, so a claim must include its method and certificates.

targets.name: Hausdorff dimension of the Apollonian gasket: more than Vytnova-Wormell's 128 rigorous decimals
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (the 128-decimal run took about 90 hours on 30 cores; public Julia code)
targets.statement: The residual set of the Apollonian circle packing has Hausdorff dimension delta_A = 1.3056867... (OEIS A052483). No closed form is known. delta_A also governs circle counting: the number of circles of curvature at most x grows like c x^delta_A (Kontorovich-Oh). The value was estimated by Boyd, McMullen (1998), Manna-Herrmann (1991) and Thomas-Dhar (1994), and extended by Bai and Finch (Fractals 2018, 30 non-rigorous decimals). Polina Vytnova and Caroline Wormell ('Hausdorff dimension of the Apollonian gasket', arXiv 2406.04922, Invent. Math. 239 (2025) 909-946) developed an efficient method for parabolic limit sets with rigorously justified error bounds and computed delta_A to 128 decimal places (Theorem 1.1 prints 129 digits with radius 10^-129). Their run used precision 2^-447 and took about 90 hours on 30 cores. Their Julia code is public (github.com/wormell/apollonian), and they estimate that doubling the digit count costs about 100 times more computing. OEIS A052483 lists 110 terms from their work (extension of Nov 2023). The parabolic fixed points make the transfer-operator problem harder than for uniformly hyperbolic Cantor sets, so this is a strong benchmark for certified dimension computation, and the authors expect the method to extend.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a rigorous enclosure of delta_A of radius at most 10^-(D+1), the convention of Vytnova-Wormell's Theorem 1.1 (128 decimals, radius 10^-129), with D STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than 128 and than any certified digit count found in a literature/OEIS search re-run immediately before claiming. A 129-decimal win therefore needs radius at most 10^-130. The enclosure must be consistent with Vytnova-Wormell's 128 decimals. The certificate is a program in rigorous arithmetic (Arb or similar) plus a written account of the error bounds (transfer-operator discretisation, treatment of the parabolic cusps, and the bisection in the dimension parameter) that a skeptic reruns and checks.

partial_wins.statement: A non-rigorous computation of delta_A to at least 200 decimals by two independent methods (for example a Vytnova-Wormell-style discretisation and a periodic-orbit or cycle-expansion method), agreeing on all 200, with the first 128 matching Vytnova-Wormell.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: rerun the certified program at two precisions and check that the enclosure of the leading eigenvalue of the transfer operator brackets 1 on either side of the dimension interval. Check the parabolic-cusp error terms against the written argument. Compare the leading 128 decimals with the published value. Expected: hours.
angles: Induce on the cusps: replace the parabolic maps by their first-return (infinite-alphabet, uniformly expanding) system, whose transfer operator has explicitly summable tails (zeta-type sums), then use Chebyshev or Lagrange collocation with a posteriori bounds.
Reuse certified-spectral techniques for the Gauss map (Nisoli 2026) on the induced operator.
pitfalls: Digits of agreement between two non-rigorous runs do not count for the main win.
Different 'Apollonian' sets (the gasket, the strip packing, packings with other root quadruples) share the dimension only when they are Moebius-equivalent; state which limit set is computed.
The OEIS lists 110 terms but the record to beat is 128 certified decimals; Theorem 1.1 prints a 129th digit only inside its radius 10^-129, so that digit is not certified.
Rerunning the public Vytnova-Wormell code at higher precision is allowed, but cost grows roughly like (digits)^6.5; even a few extra digits need a multi-core server for days, not a laptop.

targets.name: Viswanath's random Fibonacci constant 1.1319882487943...: a rigorous enclosure to 17 or more decimals
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days
targets.statement: For t_{n+1} = +-t_n +- t_{n-1} with independent fair random signs, Divakar Viswanath (Math. Comp. 69 (2000) 1131-1155) proved |t_n|^{1/n} -> 1.13198824... almost surely. His method uses Furstenberg's formula with an invariant measure built on the Stern-Brocot tree, evaluated in floating point with a rounding-error analysis. J. B. Oliveira and L. H. de Figueiredo (Reliable Computing 8 (2002) 131-138) gave an interval computation that left the 9th decimal as 7, 8 or 9, certifying 1.13198824. This is recorded in a 2006 OEIS comment by R. J. Mathar, removed from the entry in Oct 2017 but visible in its history. Zai-Qiao Bai (J. Phys. A 40 (2007), cycle expansion) gave further non-rigorous digits, and OEIS A078416 (keywords hard, more) lists 14 digits, 1.1319882487943. Jerome Raulin proposed three more (...061, from Viswanath's program with 2^32 subdivisions, 128-bit floats and Wynn-epsilon extrapolation) in Oct 2017; N. J. A. Sloane deleted them on 25 Feb 2018 'as there seems to be some doubt about them'. So only about 8 decimals are backed by a rigorous enclosure and the published non-rigorous record is 13 to 16 decimals. The constant is the top Lyapunov exponent of an i.i.d. product of two 2x2 matrices; after removing non-increasing segments the problem maps to products of nonnegative matrices (Bai 2011), a setting where Fredholm-determinant and cycle-expansion methods with explicit error bounds (Pollicott 2010, Jurga and Morris 2019) now certify dozens of digits for positive matrices.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a rigorous interval enclosure of Viswanath's constant of radius below 10^-D with D >= 17 decimals (settling the disputed digits 061 of 1.1319882487943061), D STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the number of decimals in OEIS A078416 re-fetched live and in any published value found by search immediately before claiming, and consistent with the 13 decimals 1.1319882487943 of A078416. The certificate is a program in rigorous arithmetic (Arb, python-flint, IntervalArithmetic.jl or exact rationals) plus a written proof of every truncation bound it uses (Stern-Brocot depth, cycle-expansion or Fredholm-determinant tail), which a skeptic reruns.

partial_wins.statement: A rigorous interval enclosure of Viswanath's constant contained in [1.1319882487943, 1.1319882487944], certifying all 13 decimals of OEIS A078416.
A rigorous interval enclosure of radius below 10^-10 (at least 10 certified decimals), beating the roughly 8 decimals of Viswanath (2000) and Oliveira-de Figueiredo (2002).

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: rerun the interval program at two working precisions and check that each truncation error bound is proved in the write-up or cited from a published theorem with matching hypotheses (in particular any reduction from signed to nonnegative matrices). Check that the final enclosure contains 1.1319882487943 and has the claimed radius. Sanity check by Monte Carlo (10^9 steps) that the growth rate agrees to about 4 decimals. Expected: hours.
angles: Dynamical-zeta import: the Lyapunov exponent of an i.i.d. product of finitely many positive matrices has a Fredholm-determinant expansion with explicit error bounds (Pollicott 2010; Jurga and Morris 2019); first reduce the signed random Fibonacci product to nonnegative matrices by removing non-increasing segments (Bai 2011), then check the contraction hypotheses.

Interval import: Viswanath's Stern-Brocot formula is already a convergent sum with explicit structure; redo it in ball arithmetic with a proved tail bound at deeper truncation, as Oliveira and de Figueiredo did at lower depth.
pitfalls: Monte Carlo growth rates converge like N^-1/2 and can only sanity-check digits, never supply them.
Raulin's 16-decimal value was removed from OEIS for doubt; matching it is not verification.

The Embree-Trefethen threshold 0.70258 (OEIS A118288) belongs to the generalised recurrence t_{n+1} = +-t_n +- x t_{n-1}; growth rates of that family were computed by Y. Lan (J. Stat. Phys. 142 (2011)) and Zhang-Lan (2013), behind a login wall at review time, so it is not part of this target.
The reduction to nonnegative matrices changes the step count; convert the per-step exponent back correctly before comparing with 1.13198824.

targets.name: Lander-Parkin-Selfridge at k = 5: a solution of a^5 + b^5 = c^5 + d^5 (5.2.2) or a^5 + b^5 + c^5 = d^5 (5.1.3)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (the search-extension partial wins are laptop-days to cluster scale)
targets.statement: The Lander-Parkin-Selfridge (LPS) conjecture (Math. Comp. 21 (1967)) says that a nontrivial equal sum of k-th powers x1^k+...+xm^k = y1^k+...+yn^k in positive integers needs m+n >= k. It holds for k <= 4 (Fermat's Last Theorem for exponents 3 and 4), so the first open exponent is k = 5. There the only possible counterexample types are 5.2.2 (a^5+b^5 = c^5+d^5, also called Taxicab(5,2,2), OEIS A046881(5)) and 5.1.3 (a^5+b^5+c^5 = d^5). Neither has a known solution (Wikipedia 'Lander, Parkin, and Selfridge conjecture', edited 2026-09-14; MathWorld 'Diophantine Equation--5th Powers', updated 2026-10-29; Wikipedia 'Generalized taxicab number', edited 2026-09-06; OEIS A046881). Search frontiers for 5.2.2: MathWorld, citing Guy (UPINT, 1994, p. 140), still quotes 1.02e26, but larger bounds are published. Randy Ekl (Math. Comp. 67 (1998) 1309-1315, Table 9) gives 4.01e30. Stuart Gascoigne's exhaustive search (September 2002, reported on Christian Boyer's multimagie.com 'Squares of cubes' page) found no sum below 3.26e32. Julien Courties (OEIS A046881 comment, Nov 2020) gives a(5) > 1e33, the largest bound found on 2026-10-30. Jaroslaw Wroblewski (2006) searched only special forms, up to 2.43e37. Bill Butler's unreviewed long-double search to 3.6e28 (durangobill.com) is superseded. For 5.1.3, MathWorld cites Lander et al. (1967) for 'no solutions known' and states no search bound. Ekl 1998 extends search limits for many k.m.n types; its table could not be read on 2026-10-30 because the AMS site showed a bot check. Credit: Lander, Parkin, Selfridge, Guy, Ekl, Gascoigne, Courties, Wroblewski, Butler, and Meyrignac's EulerNet. The 5.1.4 case is a separate bank entry.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED for positive integers a, b, c, d with a^5 + b^5 = c^5 + d^5 and {a,b} != {c,d} as multisets, or positive integers a, b, c, d with a^5 + b^5 + c^5 = d^5. Both sides are checked exactly with Python big integers. The win also needs that neither the Wikipedia LPS article nor MathWorld's 5th-powers page lists a solution of that type at verification time. Either one disproves the LPS conjecture. Solutions using zero or negative terms, and solutions of the 5.1.4 or 5.2.3 types (Lander-Parkin, Scher-Seidl, Frye, Braun), do not count.

partial_wins.statement: 5.2.2 frontier: an exhaustive sorted-sums (Bernstein-style) enumeration in exact integer arithmetic, proving that there is no nontrivial a^5+b^5 = c^5+d^5 with a^5+b^5 <= B. The verifier reimplements it independently on randomly chosen windows, with matching per-window counts and hashed full logs. B must be strictly greater than 1e33 (Julien Courties, OEIS A046881, Nov 2020, the largest bound found on 2026-10-30; earlier exhaustive bounds: Gascoigne 2002, 3.26e32; Ekl 1998, 4.01e30). B must also exceed any larger bound published at verification time (re-check OEIS A046881, Boyer's multimagie.com Squares of Cubes page and EulerNet).

5.1.3 frontier: an exhaustive search, reimplemented and spot-rerun as in p1, proving that a^5+b^5+c^5 = d^5 has no positive solution with d <= B. B must be strictly greater than the largest 5.1.3 bound in the literature, which the claimant cites and the verifier confirms. That includes Ekl 1998 (Math. Comp. 67, search-limit tables) and EulerNet; MathWorld states no numeric 5.1.3 bound on 2026-10-30.

targets.verification_method: Exact big-integer evaluation and a multiset comparison, under 1 second. For the partial wins, the verifier reimplements the merge of sorted a^5+b^5 streams (or the 5.1.3 kernel) with exact integer arithmetic, not long doubles, reruns sampled windows, compares counts and log hashes, and audits that the windows cover the claimed range.
angles: Use modular sieving: fifth powers mod 11 are 0 or +-1, and mod 25, 31, 41 they are similarly sparse. Combine this with Bernstein's heap-based sorted-sums method in exact 128-bit or multiprecision arithmetic to pass Butler's range without floating-point error.

5.2.2 as a curve problem: for a fixed ratio s = a+b and t = c+d, the equation becomes a plane quartic condition. Search for rational points on the genus-1 or genus-2 quotients that Browning's paucity arguments use, rather than scanning by brute force.
pitfalls: MathWorld's 1.02e26 and Butler's long-double 3.6e28 are far below the published exhaustive 5.2.2 bounds (Ekl 4.01e30, Gascoigne 3.26e32, Courties 1e33, all cited in OEIS A046881). A search that passes only Butler's or MathWorld's figure is not a partial win.
Moving a negative term across turns signed 5.1.4 or 5.2.3 solutions (for example Braun's 2026 one) into look-alike equations. Those are not 5.2.2 or 5.1.3 solutions in positive integers.

targets.name: A number that is a sum of two fourth powers in three different ways (Taxicab(4,2,3))
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (sorted-sums enumeration beyond 1e28)
targets.statement: Euler knew 635318657 = 59^4+158^4 = 133^4+134^4, and Leech (1957) proved it is the smallest number that is a sum of two positive fourth powers in two ways (OEIS A003824). No number is known that is a sum of two fourth powers in three ways. Guy (UPINT D1, quoted in OEIS A230561) writes that no one knows of three such equal sums. Search frontiers: Donovan Johnson found none <= 1e21 (OEIS A230561, 2014). Bill Butler lists all 1,413 primitive two-way solutions below 1e28, and Martin Fuller built the A003824 b-file from that list. Butler reports that his search to 1e28 found no three-way solution (unreviewed; he notes the program could be faulty). D. J. Bernstein's sorted-sums method (Math. Comp. 70 (2001)) produced the first 516 primitive solutions. Target: a three-way representation. Credit: Euler, Leech, Bernstein, Butler, D. Johnson, M. Fuller, D. W. Wilson, and the A003824/A230561 editors.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED for a positive integer N and three pairwise distinct unordered pairs {a,b} of positive integers with a^4 + b^4 = N for each pair, checked exactly with Python big integers. The win also needs that OEIS A230561, A003824 and MathWorld's 4th-powers page list no such N at verification time. Since none is known, any such N, primitive or not, is the first known example. Representations that use zero or negative fourth powers or differences do not count.

partial_wins.statement: Frontier extension: an exhaustive enumeration of ALL N = a^4+b^4 <= B (primitive or not) with at least two representations as a sum of two positive fourth powers. The verifier independently reimplements it on sampled windows, with identical per-window lists and hashed logs. It must certify that no N <= B has three or more representations, for a B strictly greater than 1e28 (Butler's bound, the largest claimed on 2026-10-30) and than any larger bound published at verification time. Its primitive sublist below 1e28 must agree with the A003824 b-file (1,413 terms), or the verifier must confirm any disagreement.

targets.verification_method: Three exact big-integer evaluations and a check that the pairs are distinct, under 1 second. For p1, the verifier reruns sampled windows with an independent sorted-sums or hash-join implementation in exact integer arithmetic, compares the lists with the A003824 b-file and audits coverage.
angles: For gcd(a,b) = 1, every odd prime factor of a^4+b^4 is 1 mod 8 (because -1 is then a fourth power mod p), and a^4+b^4 is 1 or 2 mod 16 (Fuller's note on A003824). A three-way N is g^4 times numbers of this shape, so build candidates multiplicatively from primes 1 mod 8 and test them, instead of scanning all sums.

Euler's and Gerardin's parametric 4.2.2 families: look for a parameter value where two different parametric families give the same N, using resultants and rational-point searches on the resulting curves instead of brute force.
pitfalls: Multiples g^4*N of a two-way N are not new two-way solutions. They give a third pair only if g^4*N also has an unrelated representation, so check every candidate exactly and do not filter non-primitive N away.
Floating-point sums lose exactness above about 1e16 for doubles (2^53) and about 1e19 for x87 long doubles. Use exact integers.

targets.name: Equal sums of like powers for k = 7..32: a k.m.n solution with fewer terms than Meyrignac's EulerNet records
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (high-k cells); needs cluster for k = 7..10
targets.statement: For a k.m.n equation x1^k+...+xm^k = y1^k+...+yn^k (positive integers, primitive, no term on both sides), Jean-Charles Meyrignac's EulerNet site (euler.free.fr, with database.txt, latest entry 2021) keeps the smallest known n for each (k, m) and the smallest known total m+n for each k. The record totals for k = 7..17 are 8, 8, 10, 11, 14, 14, 17, 18, 21, 23, 28, and for k = 18..32 they are 28, 32, 34, 39, 41, 44, 48, 52, 52, 61, 63, 67, 69, 72, 75. Recent moves include Duncan Moore's 10.5.6 (2020, the k = 10 record), Ian Stopher's 6.1.7 (2021), many cells by Scott I. Chase and Laurent Lucas (2011-2015), and new 7.2.7 and 7.3.6 solutions by J. Glickman on MathWorld (2026). LPS predicts m+n >= k, and for k = 8 the record already equals k (8.4.4 by Kuosa, 8.3.5 by Chase). MathWorld lists many cells as unknown, for example 7.1.6, 7.2.5, 7.3.4, 8.1.7, 8.2.6 and 9.4.5. Credit: Meyrignac, Wroblewski, Chase, Lucas, Childers, Yura, Alm, Kuosa, Ekl, Dodrill, Resta, Moore, Glickman, Lander-Parkin-Selfridge. Cases with k <= 6 are covered by other bank entries.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED for some 7 <= k <= 32 and positive integers x1..xm, y1..yn with sum x_i^k = sum y_j^k exactly (Python big integers), gcd of all terms 1, and no value on both sides. m+n must be STRICTLY SMALLER (direction: min) than three values at verification time: the 'LOWEST NUMBER OF TERMS' value for k on http://euler.free.fr/; every m+n for k in http://euler.free.fr/database.txt; and every m+n on MathWorld's 'Diophantine Equation--kth Powers' page for k where such a page exists (7th to 10th powers on 2026-10-30). The values above on 2026-10-30 are context only. For k = 8 such a solution has m+n <= 7 and disproves the LPS conjecture.

partial_wins.statement: Cell record: for some 7 <= k <= 32 and some m in the 'KNOWN LOWER BOUNDS' table on euler.free.fr, a primitive nontrivial solution of type (k, m, n) with m <= n (sides swapped if needed). n must be strictly smaller than the table's value for (k, m) and than any (k, m, n') in database.txt or on the MathWorld page for k (where one exists) at verification time. Cells whose table value already equals m cannot be improved this way.

New type at the record total: for some 7 <= k <= 32, a primitive nontrivial solution of type (k, m, n) with m+n equal to the current record total for k, where no solution of that exact type appears in database.txt or on the MathWorld page for k at verification time (for example 8.1.7, 8.2.6, 9.1.9, 9.3.7, 10.4.7, 10.3.8).

targets.verification_method: Exact big-integer evaluation of both sides, a gcd check, a check that no value is on both sides, and a lookup against the euler.free.fr table, database.txt and the MathWorld page for k. Under 1 second.
angles: Wroblewski's congruence method: choose a modulus M where k-th powers take few residues (for example M = 2^a 3^b p with p-1 | k), fix congruence classes for all but two terms, then meet in the middle. His published congruence-solution files (math.uni.wroc.pl/~jwr/eslp) are the natural starting point.

For high k (20..32), the gaps between neighbouring cells in the table are irregular, which suggests the cells were explored unevenly. Target the cells whose n is much larger than for the neighbouring m.
pitfalls: MathWorld's 9th and 10th power pages lag euler.free.fr (for example, 10.5.6 by Duncan Moore 2020 is not on MathWorld, and 9.2.8 and 10.1.12 by Wroblewski are in database.txt while MathWorld says none are known). Check all three sources.
Non-primitive solutions, solutions with a common term on both sides, and permuted repeats are not new.

database.txt lists bases only, in the form (k,m,n) a+b+...=c+d+..., and writes x*c for c copies of the base x (for example 17*2 is two terms 17^k, not 34^k). Count terms with multiplicity when comparing m+n, and parse it exactly before calling a type new.

targets.name: Diophantine D(n)-quintuples: a quintuple with -255 < n < 256 (beat Dujella's n1 <= 256 or n2 >= -255)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days
targets.statement: A set of m positive integers has property D(n) if a_i*a_j + n is a perfect square for all i < j. Andrej Dujella's survey page (section 3.2 of the Diophantine m-tuples page, which cites results up to Bonciocat-Cipu-Mignotte 2022) asks for the least positive n1 and the greatest negative n2 for which a D(n)-quintuple exists. It records n1 <= 256 and n2 >= -255, from {1, 33, 105, 320, 18240} and {5, 21, 64, 285, 6720} (property D(256)) and {8, 32, 77, 203, 528} (property D(-255)), all checked by us. Some cases are proven impossible: no D(1)-quintuple (He-Togbe-Ziegler 2019), no D(4)-quintuple (Bliznac Trebjesanin-Filipin 2019), no D(-1)- or D(-4)-quadruple (Bonciocat-Cipu-Mignotte 2022), and no D(n)-quadruple for n = 2 mod 4 (Brown; Gupta-Singh; Mohanty-Ramasamy 1985). Our own exhaustive checks (2026-10-30) found no D(n)-quintuple with all elements <= 100000 for 0 < |n| < 256 (the same search recovers exactly the three record sets above). Target: a D(n)-quintuple with -255 < n < 256. Credit: Dujella and coauthors, Filipin, Fuchs, He, Togbe, Ziegler, Bonciocat, Cipu, Mignotte.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED for five distinct positive integers a1..a5 and an integer n with n != 0 and -255 < n < 256, such that a_i*a_j + n is a perfect square (math.isqrt) for all 10 pairs. It must also strictly beat (direction: smaller |n| on that sign side) the n1/n2 bounds stated on https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~duje/dn.html at verification time (n1 <= 256, n2 >= -255 on 2026-10-30, context only). Claims for n = 1, n = 4, n = -1, n = -4 or n = 2 mod 4 contradict published theorems and are bugs.

partial_wins.statement: Search certificate: for every n with 0 < |n| < 256 that no theorem above excludes, an exhaustive search proving that there is no D(n)-quintuple with all elements <= B. B must be at least 10^8 and strictly greater than any bound published for this question. The verifier reimplements it independently, for example by extending D(n)-triples through the standard Pell-system bound, and reruns randomly chosen n, comparing the per-n counts of D(n)-quadruples found.

A new record-side example: a D(256)- or D(-255)-quintuple of distinct positive integers that is not, as a set, any of the three on dn.html and not in the papers dn.html cites for them (its references [62] and [68]), as checked by the verifier at verification time.

targets.verification_method: Ten exact isqrt checks plus the range and exclusion checks, under 1 second. For p1, independent reimplementation and sampled per-n reruns with count and hash comparison.
angles: Extend D(n)-quadruples instead of searching blindly. For a quadruple {a,b,c,d}, the fifth element e satisfies four simultaneous conditions a*e+n = square and so on. Use the regular-extension formulas and the elliptic curve y^2 = (ax+n)(bx+n)(cx+n) to find rational points that happen to be integers.
Scale rational D(1)-quintuples (Dujella-Kazalicki-Mikic-Szikszai) with small common denominator q. Multiplying by q gives integer D(q^2)-quintuples, so q <= 15 would beat n1 = 256.
pitfalls: The definition on dn.html uses positive integers. Quintuples with negative or zero elements (allowed in some papers) are not the same record.
Repeated elements are not allowed. Quintuples of the form k*S for a D(n/k^2)-quintuple S are fine but must still have |n| inside the range.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - a D(n)-quadruple for n in {-3, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20} (disprove Dujella's conjecture)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster
targets.statement: A D(n)-quadruple is four distinct positive integers with ab + n a perfect square for all six pairs. No such quadruple exists for n = 2 mod 4 (Brown; Gupta-Singh; Mohanty-Ramasamy 1985). Dujella (1993) proved that one exists for every other n outside S = {-4, -3, -1, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20}, and conjectured that none exists for n in S. Bonciocat, Cipu and Mignotte (2022) settled n = -1, which also gives n = -4. Filipin and Jurasic (Glasnik Mat. 57 (2022)) ruled out polynomial D(-3)-quadruples, which leaves the integer case open. Dujella's survey page (live 2026-10-30) still lists the conjecture as open for n in {-3, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20}. Our own check found no D(n)-quadruple with elements <= 3000 for these six n. Credit: Dujella, Filipin, Fuchs, Jurasic, Bonciocat, Cipu, Mignotte and the 1985 authors.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED for four distinct positive integers a < b < c < d and n in {-3, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20} with xy + n a perfect square (math.isqrt) for all six pairs. https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~duje/dn.html must still list that n as conjectured impossible (not proven) at verification time, and a same-day check of the references on Dujella's ref.html must find no published proof that no D(n)-quadruple exists for that n. A claimed D(-1)- or D(-4)-quadruple contradicts a published theorem and is a bug.

partial_wins.statement: Search certificate: for one n in {-3, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20}, an exhaustive search proving that no D(n)-quadruple has largest element <= B, independently reimplemented by the verifier. B must be at least 10^10 and strictly greater than the largest such bound published (the claimant cites it and the verifier confirms). It must ship hashed logs of all D(n)-triples examined, and the verifier reruns sampled ranges.

targets.verification_method: Six exact isqrt checks, under 1 second. For p1, an independent reimplementation reruns sampled triple ranges and compares counts and log hashes.

targets.name: Fermat-Catalan: an eleventh solution of a^m + b^n = c^k with 1/m + 1/n + 1/k < 1 (one exponent equal to 2)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster
targets.statement: The Fermat-Catalan conjecture says that a^m + b^n = c^k with a, b, c coprime positive integers and 1/m + 1/n + 1/k < 1 has only finitely many solutions, counted as distinct triples (a^m, b^n, c^k). Wikipedia (edited 2026-06-04, 'as of 2024') lists ten known solutions: 1^m+2^3=3^2, 2^5+7^2=3^4, 7^3+13^2=2^9, 2^7+17^3=71^2, 3^5+11^4=122^2, 33^8+1549034^2=15613^3, 1414^3+2213459^2=65^7, 9262^3+15312283^2=113^7, 17^7+76271^3=21063928^2, 43^8+96222^3=30042907^2. We rechecked all ten, and each one has an exponent 2. The larger ones come from the 1993 Fermat-day computer search at Utrecht (cited in Beukers, Duke Math. J. 91 (1998)). Adam Sikora (arXiv 2410.21552, 2024) verified that these are the only coprime solutions with min exponent d <= 113 and all three powers below M_d, where M_2 = 2^71, M_3 = 2^80, M_4 = 2^100 and M_d = 2^113 for d >= 5. Darmon-Granville proved finiteness for each fixed signature. Many signatures are fully solved (Poonen-Schaefer-Stoll for (2,3,7); Bruin; Chen; Ellenberg; and others). Target: a new solution. This target covers only solutions with an exponent equal to 2. A solution with all exponents >= 3 would be a Beal counterexample, which is a live-prize matter (see held). Credit: Beukers, Zagier, Darmon, Granville, Sikora, Poonen, Schaefer, Stoll, Bruin.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED for positive integers a, b, c with gcd(a,b,c) = 1 and positive integers m, n, k with 1/m + 1/n + 1/k < 1 (exact rational comparison) and min(m,n,k) = 2, such that a^m + b^n = c^k exactly in Python big integers. The triple (a^m, b^n, c^k), up to swapping the two summands, must not be among the solutions listed on https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%E2%80%93Catalan_conjecture at verification time (ten on 2026-10-30). By Mihailescu's theorem, no new solution has a, b or c equal to 1. A solution with m, n, k all >= 3 is outside this target: report it to the human (Beal Prize) and make no claim here.

partial_wins.statement: Search certificate: an exhaustive search, independently reimplemented by the verifier, proving that the ten known solutions are the only coprime ones with max(a^m, b^n, c^k) <= B over all admissible signatures with an exponent 2. B must be strictly greater than 2^71 = 2361183241434822606848 (Sikora 2024, the largest such bound found on 2026-10-30) and than any larger bound published at verification time. The run ships hashed logs, and the verifier reruns sampled ranges (enumerating x^p - y^q = +-z^2 style differences against a squares test).

targets.verification_method: Exact big-integer evaluation, a gcd check, exact rational comparison of 1/m+1/n+1/k with 1, and a set comparison with the ten listed triples. Under 1 second. For p1, independent reimplementation and sampled reruns.
angles: Fix a signature (2, 3, k) or (2, 4, k) not yet solved in the literature and search via the associated Frey-curve twists or Thue equations, which turn the search into finitely many low-degree equations that can be searched much further than brute force.
pitfalls: Signatures already solved completely (for example (2,3,7), (2,3,8), (2,3,9), (2,4,5)) cannot give new solutions. A claimed solution there is a bug.
Non-coprime triples, such as scalings like 2^3 + 2^3 = 2^4, never count.
Brute force with all powers below 2^71 repeats Sikora's 2024 search and cannot find anything new.

targets.name: Goormaghtigh conjecture: a third number that is a repunit ( > = 3 digits) in two bases
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster
targets.statement: Goormaghtigh (1917) asked about (x^m - 1)/(x - 1) = (y^n - 1)/(y - 1) with x > y > 1 and n > m > 2, that is, numbers that are repunits with at least three digits in two different bases. The only known solutions are 31 = 111_5 = 11111_2 and 8191 = 111_90 = 1111111111111_2. The conjecture that there are no others is open (Wikipedia, edited 2026-10-26; Grantham 2026). Known partial results: Makowski-Schinzel (no others with both bases <= 10, or with the larger exponent n <= 5); Davenport-Lewis-Schinzel (finitely many for fixed exponents); Nesterenko-Shorey and Bugeaud-Shorey (effective bounds in restricted cases with gcd(m-1, n-1) > 1; Bugeaud-Shorey needs gcd(m-1, n-1) large relative to (n-1)/(m-1)); Yuan (2005, m = 3 with odd n); He-Togbe (2008, at most one solution for fixed bases). Bennett-Garbuz-Marten (Publ. Math. Debrecen 96 (2020); Theorems 3, 4 and 6) proved there are no others with both bases <= 10^5, none with gcd(m-1, n-1) > 1 and n <= 50, none with n = m+1 for 3 <= m <= 17, and none with (n-1)/(m-1) = 3. Jon Grantham (arXiv 2410.03677, Integers 24 (2024) A98; v3 2026-10-17 corrects the computation and supplies code, data and a Lean 4 development) proved there is no other prime value (a 'Goormaghtigh prime') below 10^700. Bennett-Gherga-Kreso (Trans. AMS 373 (2020)) settle further small-exponent cases used by Grantham. Credit: Goormaghtigh, Makowski, Schinzel, Yuan, He, Togbe, Shorey, Bugeaud, Bennett, Garbuz, Marten, Gherga, Kreso, Grantham.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED for integers x > y > 1 and n > m > 2 with (x^m - 1)/(x - 1) = (y^n - 1)/(y - 1) exactly (Python big integers), where the common value is neither 31 nor 8191, and no third solution is listed on https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goormaghtigh_conjecture at verification time. Solutions with an exponent 2 (repunits 11_x) are outside the problem and do not count.

partial_wins.statement: Goormaghtigh-prime frontier: a computation proving that there is no Goormaghtigh prime other than 31 and 8191 below 10^E, for E strictly greater than 700 (Grantham, arXiv 2410.03677 v3) or than any larger bound published at verification time. The only non-computational steps allowed are citations of published theorems by exact statement number. Code, data and survivor logs must be published, and the verifier reruns the computation independently (fully, or on sampled intervals plus a coverage check).

Base-range extension: a computation proving that the two known solutions are the only ones with both bases <= Y, for Y strictly greater than 10^5 (Bennett-Garbuz-Marten 2020, Theorem 3) and than any larger published range. It must use a published explicit exponent bound (for example He-Togbe's Lemma 2.3, as used in BGM Section 2) plus exhaustive sieving and Baker-Davenport reduction. Every step is rerunnable by the verifier in PARI/GP or Sage, and nothing is left unproved apart from citations of published theorems.

targets.verification_method: Exact big-integer evaluation of both repunits and the inequalities, under 1 second. For the partial wins, the verifier reruns the claimant's code and an independent reimplementation on sampled ranges, checks that the ranges are covered, and checks that every cited theorem is applied within its stated hypotheses.

targets.name: Mordell curves y^2 = x^3 + k: a smaller |k| of given rank 7..16 than the OEIS upper bounds, or rank >= 18
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (descent and point search per candidate k); needs cluster for rank >= 18
targets.statement: OEIS A031507 (k > 0), A031508 (curves y^2 = x^3 - k) and A373795 (smallest |k|) give the smallest k for which y^2 = x^3 + k has rank n. Exact values are known only for n <= 6 (A031507: 1, 2, 15, 113, 2089, 66265, 1358556; Gebel-Petho-Zimmer 1998, Womack 2003). Upper bounds from Tom Womack's thesis (2003, Table 3.3) are: A031507 a(7) <= 47550317, a(8) <= 1632201497, a(9) <= 185418133372, a(10) <= 68513487607153; A031508 a(7) <= 56877643, a(8) <= 2520963512, a(9) <= 463066403167, a(10) <= 56736325657288, a(11) <= 46111487743732324, a(12) <= 6533891544658786928. Noam Elkies (ANTS-XVI, 2024) gave a(16) <= 1160221354461565256631205207888 (recorded in both A031507 and A031508) and showed that some k has rank >= 17, the largest Mordell-curve rank recorded in these OEIS entries. The entries carry the keyword 'more'; their latest dated comments are from June-July 2024. Curves for k and -27k are 3-isogenous and have the same rank (Elkies). Target: beat a listed bound, or reach rank 18. Credit: Gebel, Petho, Zimmer, Quer, Womack, Elkies, Klagsbrun, Cremona, and the OEIS editors (Hasler, Aranda, Sloane, Sondow).
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED for a nonzero integer k and a rank r of one of two kinds. (A) 7 <= r <= 16, a rank-r upper bound is listed for k's sign in OEIS A031507 (k > 0) or A031508 (k < 0, as |k|) at verification time, and |k| is STRICTLY SMALLER (direction: min) than that bound and than any rank-r example of the same sign found in a same-day literature check (Womack 2003 Table 3.3, Elkies ANTS-XVI 2024, and later work). (B) r >= 18, any k, provided OEIS A031507, A031508 and A373795 and a same-day literature check show no Mordell curve of rank >= 18. In both cases the rank needs r points on y^2 = x^3 + k with nonzero canonical-height regulator (PARI ellheightmatrix, determinant > 0 at >= 38 digits, stable at 2x precision). For (A) it also needs an upper bound rank <= r from a 2-descent or 3-isogeny Selmer computation (PARI ellrank, or Magma TwoDescent/ThreeIsogenyDescent) that the verifier reproduces; the claim states whether that bound assumes GRH (PARI class groups do unless certified).

partial_wins.statement: Rank-at-least record: as in (A), but the rank is certified only as >= r (r independent points, no matching upper bound), for some 7 <= r <= 16 with a listed OEIS bound for k's sign, with |k| strictly smaller than that bound and than any rank-r example of that sign found in the same-day literature check of (A).

Rank-17 example: an explicit k with 17 independent points (nonzero regulator as in the main criterion). If an explicit rank->=17 Mordell k is published (Elkies, ANTS-XVI, 2024, or later, as cited in OEIS A031507/A373795 or found by the verifier), |k| must be strictly smaller than the smallest such published |k|. If none is published explicitly, any such k counts.

targets.verification_method: PARI/GP: ellinit([0,0,0,0,k]), check that each point lies on the curve, compute ellheightmatrix and its determinant at high precision, and run ellrank (or Magma descent) for the upper bound. Compare |k| with the bound listed in OEIS on the day as exact digit strings. Minutes per claim.
angles: Quer's method: a high 3-rank of the class group of Q(sqrt(-3k)) forces a large 3-Selmer group. Search k with large 3-class rank (via class-group computations in PARI) and then hunt points with ellrank. This is how ranks 12+ were reached.
Elkies-style lattice search: choose k as a value of a polynomial for which y^2 = x^3 + k(t) has many sections, then specialise t.
Use the k <-> -27k isogeny. A good k divisible by 27 gives a candidate -k/27 on the other sign with smaller |k|.
pitfalls: Rank lower bounds from points need the regulator to be clearly nonzero. Dependent points, for example torsion multiples, are common mistakes.
2-descent upper bounds can exceed the true rank because of Sha[2]. For full win (A) the upper bound must actually equal r, otherwise it only counts as p1.
