targets.name: MOONSHOT - an integer above 7373170279850 that is not a sum of four nonnegative cubes (Deshouillers-Hennecart-Landreau)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster
targets.statement: Deshouillers, Hennecart and Landreau ('7373170279850', Math. Comp. 69 (2000), 421-439, appendix by Purnaba) conjectured, on numerical and probabilistic evidence, that every integer greater than 7373170279850 is a sum of four nonnegative cubes, and that exactly 113936676 positive integers are not. The conjecture is recorded as open in OEIS A022566 (numbers that are not the sum of 4 nonnegative cubes, keyword 'fini'; conjecture comment by Felix Frohlich, 2019-06-01) and A181381 (comment by Martin Fuller, 2026-10-11); OEIS A003327 (sums of 4 positive cubes) carries a related comment (Greathouse and Noe, 2017) that every number above 7373170279850 is a sum of 4 positive cubes. It would give G(3) = 4 for Waring's problem for cubes, far beyond current methods (G(3) <= 7 is the proved bound), so it is believed but unproven. A counterexample would be a striking computational find. Credit: Deshouillers, Hennecart, Landreau, Purnaba, and the OEIS editors (Noe, Frohlich, Greathouse, Fuller).
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED for an integer N > 7373170279850 such that N != a^3 + b^3 + c^3 + d^3 for all integers 0 <= a <= b <= c <= d. This is proved by a complete, independently rerunnable enumeration: for every a <= b with a^3 + b^3 <= N, the remainder N - a^3 - b^3 is shown not to be a sum of two nonnegative cubes, using exact integer cube-root tests or a sorted two-cube table. The verifier runs its own implementation. OEIS A022566 must still state the conjecture as open at verification time.

partial_wins.statement: Verified range extension: an exhaustive computation, independently reimplemented on sampled windows, certifying that every integer in (7373170279850, B] is a sum of four nonnegative cubes. B must be strictly greater than the largest range reported verified in Deshouillers-Hennecart-Landreau 2000 or later literature (the claimant cites it and the verifier confirms), with hashed per-window logs.

targets.verification_method: For a single N, an exact enumeration of a <= b with a^3 + b^3 <= N and a two-cube representability test on the remainder (about N^(2/3)/2 cases, minutes to hours for N near 10^14 to 10^16). For p1, sampled windows are rerun with an independent sieve over four-cube sums.
pitfalls: Numbers at or below 7373170279850 that are not sums of four cubes are expected and known; they are not counterexamples.
The DHL paper's verified range sits behind an AMS bot check (BLOCKED on 2026-10-30). Read it through a library copy before claiming p1.

targets.name: Near-repdigit factor tables (Kamada): factor a composite on the 'hoped to be factored' lists
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (GNFS on a C145-C160 with CADO-NFS on 8+ cores; SNFS difficulty ~210 for the SNFS list)
targets.statement: Makoto Kamada's STUDIO KAMADA site (stdkmd.net/nrr) keeps factor tables of near-repdigit-related numbers: repunits, near-repdigits such as AA...AB, plateau-and-depression and quasi-repdigit numbers, and near-repdigit palindromes. Its page 'Composite numbers that are hoped to be factored' (wanted.htm, Last-Modified 2026-10-27) has three lists. (1) 100 composites from the top 100 smallest SNFS polynomials, C153-C204, SNFS difficulty 211.00-213.15 (94 'Free to factor' and 6 'Reserved' on 2026-10-30). (2) 1,000 composites suited to GNFS, C145-C192 (992 free); the first is the C145 cofactor of (791*10^264-8)/9 = 8788...88, ECM to t45. (3) 94 composites with no known prime factor, C268-C476, ECM to t55-t65, for example (53*10^267-71)/9 = 5888...881. Each row shows digits, the expression, the ECM level done and whether it is 'Free to factor', 'Reserved' or 'Submitted'. The site credits hundreds of contributors, among them NFS@Home, Greg Childers, Ryan Propper, Serge Batalov and yoyo@home; its July 2026 news credits Propper and Batalov with the near-repdigit prime 6*10^4000494-1.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a composite N listed on https://stdkmd.net/nrr/wanted.htm (re-fetched immediately before the claim, with a row status other than 'Submitted') and a prime p, proven prime, with 1 < p < N and N mod p = 0, provided p does not appear for that number in Kamada's factor tables or the 'Contributed factorization results' pages at verification time (direction: max on the count of known factors).

partial_wins.statement: Complete factorisation of a composite from the 'suitable for GNFS' list into proven primes, with every factor checked by multiplication against the listed composite.
First prime factor of a composite from the 'no prime factor is known' list (C268 and up), proven prime and dividing the listed number.

targets.verification_method: Recompute N from its listed expression and confirm it equals the listed composite, confirm N mod p = 0, prove p (and any cofactor claimed prime) with PARI isprime / ECPP (Primo) for large values, and grep p against Kamada's table page for that expression and the contributed-results pages.
angles: Run GNFS with CADO-NFS on the smallest 'Free to factor' C145-C150 entries; they need about a day or two on a modern 16-thread desktop.
For SNFS-list entries, build the SNFS polynomial straight from the expression (k*10^n+m) and sieve with CADO-NFS or msieve/ggnfs.
Extra ECM at t50-t55 on the 'no prime factor known' list before committing to NFS.
pitfalls: Rows marked 'Reserved' are being worked on by someone else, and 'Submitted' rows are already done; pick 'Free to factor' rows and re-check the status column before and after the run.

The listed composite is a cofactor after small factors are removed; recompute it from the expression (note the /9 or /3 denominators shown as fractions on the page) and the table rather than trusting copied digits.
The tables cover several families with similar names (AA..AB vs ABB..B); match the expression exactly.

targets.name: Fibonacci and Lucas numbers F_n, L_n (n < 10,000): a new factor of a listed composite cofactor
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (GMP-ECM or P-1 on the large cofactors; NFS on the C200-C280 holes needs cluster)
targets.statement: The Fibonacci and Lucas factorization tables at mersennus.net/fibonacci carry on the Brillhart-Montgomery-Silverman tables (Math. Comp. 1988). They list known factors of F_n and L_n for n < 10,000, mark composite cofactors with (C), and publish every remaining composite in composite2000.gz ... composite10000.gz, along with 'holes' files. On 2026-10-30 every F_n and L_n with n <= 1000 is fully factored. The first holes are F1423 (C276) and L1423 (C232); fibholes.txt lists 3,641 incomplete F_n and lucholes.txt 7,604 incomplete Lucas entries (7,224 distinct L_n; the Aurifeuillian parts L_nA and L_nB are listed separately). The history page shows steady progress through 2026: L1673 C203 split by NFS (K. Askine et al., 2026-10-21), B. Kelly's ECM factors of L2507, L2581 and L2728, many P-1/ECM factors by H. Bock of C700-C1350 cofactors (2026-02 to 2026-10), and results from NFS@Home, G. Childers, S. Batalov and yoyo@home. The status page for 1000 < n < 2000 says B. Kelly ran 20158 ECM curves at B1=110M and 8000 at B1=260M on every composite, and A. Kruppa ran P-1 (B1=1G, B2=1T) and P+1 on them. Blair Kelly and Hartmut Bock are the most frequent contributors on the references page.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for an index n < 10000 and a prime p, proven prime, that divides a composite cofactor of F_n or L_n listed in the matching composite*.gz file linked from https://mersennus.net/fibonacci/composite.html, re-fetched immediately before the claim, with p absent from the big tables (fibonacci.txt / lucas.txt) and from history.html at verification time (direction: max on the count of known factors).

partial_wins.statement: Hole filled: a complete proven-prime factorisation of every remaining cofactor of some F_n or L_n listed in fibholes.txt or lucholes.txt, so that the number would leave the holes list.
A proper prime factor of the first-hole composites (F1423 C276 or L1423 C232) as listed at verification time.

targets.verification_method: Compute F_n or L_n exactly (Python big integers or PARI fibonacci()), divide out the factors in the big table, confirm the remaining cofactor matches the composite file entry, check divisibility by p, and prove p prime (PARI isprime or ECPP). For p1, prove every remaining part prime.
angles: ECM with small B1 (1e6-11e6) across the thousands of C700-C2000 cofactors for n > 4000; these got far less ECM than the n <= 2000 range, and H. Bock's 2026 harvest shows factors of 30-45 digits are still there.

Use the known shape of primitive factors: a primitive prime p (p != 5) of F_n or L_n satisfies p = +-1 mod n for odd n, so put n into the P-1 stage-1 exponent to catch p = 1 mod n and run P+1 for p = -1 mod n.
Use the status pages to pick composites with the least ECM effort recorded.
pitfalls: Factors already listed in the big tables or history do not count; known algebraic factors of F_n and L_n (from divisors of n) are not new factors.
The site's server rejects some non-browser clients; fetch honestly and record BLOCKED if it refuses.
A probable-prime factor must be proven before the claim counts.

targets.name: Odd perfect number proof tree: factor a 'most wanted roadblock' composite on Ochem's lists
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (ECM over the list; NFS for the smaller C193-C230 entries needs cluster)
targets.statement: Pascal Ochem and Michael Rao proved bounds on any odd perfect number N with a factor-chain proof tree like the one of Brent, Cohen and te Riele: N > 10^1500 (since pushed to N > 10^2200), Omega(N) >= 101 (since pushed to >= 115) and Omega(N) >= 2 omega(N) + 51. The tree stalls at 'roadblocks', composite factors c of sigma(p^e) that nobody has factored; each roadblock forces an expensive detour. Ochem's page publishes mwrb2200.txt, 'the most difficult composites for the proof of N > 10^2200' (format 'p q-1 composite weight', so c divides sigma(p^(q-1)); 1,629 composites from 193 to 1,099 digits; Last-Modified 2026-09-01; weights up to 63,862,958, 16 of them at least 1,000,000). The top line, '11 330' C344 (weight 63,862,958), is the Cunningham number 11,331- = (11^331-1)/10, which 'Lu' split as p136 * p209 by SNFS in 2026 (Cunningham update page149.txt, #6886); it was still listed on 2026-10-30, so the largest open weight is 25,238,981 (127 192 C404) and 15 open composites have weight at least 1,000,000. It also publishes complete composite files t570 ... t2300 (2/2025) and the known-factor file checkfacts.txt (12/2022). The page says every composite that gets factored, even partially, is removed from the list within a few days. The page source (partly commented out) acknowledges earlier factorizations by Tom Womack and Ryan Propper and NFS reservations by Warut Roonguthai and Frank Schickel; the page points helpers to the mersenneforum OPN threads. This continues the old oddperfect.org roadblock lists, now offline (archived).
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a line 'p q-1 c w' of https://www.lirmm.fr/~ochem/opn/mwrb2200.txt (re-fetched immediately before the claim) and a prime f, proven prime, with 1 < f < c and c mod f = 0, where c divides sigma(p^(q-1)) = (p^q - 1)/(p - 1), provided f is not in checkfacts.txt and, when p <= 12, c has not already been split in the Cunningham main tables or on any Cunningham update page (page149.txt or later, linked from https://homes.cerias.purdue.edu/~ssw/cun/index.html) at verification time; the line '11 330' C344 (Cunningham 11,331-, split on page149.txt #6886) does not count (direction: max on the count of roadblock composites split).

partial_wins.statement: A proven prime factor of any composite in one of the tXXXX.txt files (t570 ... t2300) linked from https://www.lirmm.fr/~ochem/opn/ that is not in checkfacts.txt at verification time and, when p <= 12, is not already in the Cunningham main tables or on a Cunningham update page (page149.txt or later).

A proven prime factor of one of the composites in mwrb2200.txt whose weight (fourth column) is at least 1,000,000 (16 listed, C305-C572, on 2026-10-30; 15 open, since '11 330' C344 was already split as Cunningham 11,331- on page149.txt), dividing the listed composite, which must still be listed and must not be already split in the Cunningham tables or update pages at verification time.

targets.verification_method: Recompute sigma(p^(q-1)) = (p^q-1)/(p-1) exactly, confirm c divides it and equals the listed composite, check c mod f = 0, prove f prime (PARI isprime / ECPP). For p1 also grep f in checkfacts.txt.
angles: Sort by weight per digit: high-weight composites under 230 digits give the most proof-tree pruning per unit of NFS effort.
Note that the second column is q-1, the exponent in sigma(p^(q-1)), so q is the exponent of p^q - 1: run SNFS on (p^q-1)/(p-1) with the cyclotomic polynomial for q when p is small.
Cross-check with Cunningham tables: when p is 2..12 the number is a Cunningham cofactor and may already be factored there.
pitfalls: The file's second column is q-1, not q; a wrong exponent gives a different number.

checkfacts.txt (12/2022) is older than the t-files; also check the mersenneforum OPN threads before claiming novelty for p1 (the forum shows a Cloudflare bot check to scripts; record BLOCKED and leave the forum check to a human).
A factor of sigma(p^(q-1)) outside c (already known and divided out) does not count.

mwrb2200.txt can lag: on 2026-10-30 its top line '11 330' C344 was still listed although it is Cunningham 11,331-, split on page149.txt. For p = 3, 5, 7, 11 always rebuild the Cunningham number and check its main table and update pages first.

targets.name: Cunningham project: a new factor of a composite cofactor of b^n +- 1 (b = 2..12), above all from the wanted lists
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster for NFS on C216+; ECM attempts run at laptop-days but are a lottery
targets.statement: The Cunningham project, run by Samuel S. Wagstaff Jr. (Purdue), keeps the tables of factorizations of b^n +- 1 for b = 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12 (with Aurifeuillian L/M parts). The 'Wanted' lists issued 2026-01-04 (want148.txt) give Ten Most Wanted, Twenty More Wanted and Smaller-but-Needed composites. Many have since been factored on the update page page149.txt (Last-Modified 2026-10-23), nearly all by NFS@Home with SNFS (2,1129+, 3,703-, 6,431+-, 7,397+, 12,311-, 12,313-, ...) and by 'Lu' (2,1207-, 11,331-, and 2,1277- C385 = p106 * p117 * p163, which completes the factorization of M1277). Still unfactored from the lists on 2026-10-30: 2,1139+ C248, 10,353- C328, 10,346+ C300, 5,503- C260, 2,1213- C297, 2,1217- C248, 2,2266L C255, ..., and all six Smaller-but-Needed: 2,1421+ C216, 10,407- C216, 2,1415+ and 2,1415- (C217 and C219; want148 and Appendix C assign the two sizes oppositely), 7,917L C217, 11,371- C217. Appendix C (appc126.txt, as of 2026-01-05; appc.txt is the bare 'Numbers to factor' list) gives every composite cofactor; the smallest is C216. Reservations are in who.txt. Champions (champ.txt): ECM record P83 by R. Propper (7,337+); SNFS record C355 (2,1193-) by J. Bos, T. Kleinjung and A. K. Lenstra; GNFS record C221 by NFS@Home.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a composite cofactor C listed in Appendix C or the 'Numbers to factor' list linked from https://homes.cerias.purdue.edu/~ssw/cun/index.html (appc126.txt and appc.txt on 2026-10-30; re-fetched immediately before the claim) and a prime p, proven prime, with 1 < p < C and C mod p = 0, provided p is not on any update page issued since that Appendix C (page149.txt and any later page linked from the index) at verification time and p divides the part of C that is still composite after dividing out every factor on those update pages (the prime cofactor left by a split reported there, printed only as pNNN, does not count) (direction: max on the count of known factors).

partial_wins.statement: The factor is for a composite on the current Wanted lists (Ten Most Wanted, Twenty More Wanted or Smaller-but-Needed, the want*.txt file linked from the index page), not yet reported on the update page.

Complete proven-prime factorisation of a composite listed as one of the 'first five holes' of any table in champ.txt that is not already completely factored on page149.txt or any later update page at verification time (on 2026-10-30, 2,1207-, 2,1129+, 3,703-, 3,709+, 6,431-, 6,431+, 6,436+, 7,397+, 7,398+, 7,401+, 11,331-, 12,311-, 12,313- and 12,319- were already done).

targets.verification_method: Rebuild b^n +- 1 (or the L/M Aurifeuillian part) exactly, divide out the factors in the main table and on every update page issued since (page149.txt and later), confirm the remaining composite part is the Appendix C entry or a still-composite cofactor of it, check divisibility by p, and prove p (and any cofactor claimed prime) with PARI isprime / ECPP.
angles: ECM at B1=850M-2.9G on the unreserved Smaller-but-Needed C216-C219, which are the cheapest composites in the whole table.
SNFS by cyclotomic polynomial: for 2,1421+ the primitive part comes from Phi_2842(2); pick a degree-6 or degree-8 polynomial and estimate the sieving with CADO-NFS before committing.
pitfalls: Check who.txt: many wanted numbers are reserved by NFS@Home or individuals.
File names roll over (want148, appc126, page149 become want149, appc127, page150); always follow the index page.
Appendix C is only reissued with each edition, so a composite already split on page149 still appears there; check the update pages.
Rebuild sizes from b^n +- 1 yourself: want148 and Appendix C disagree on which of 2,1415+ and 2,1415- is the C217.
M1277 (2,1277-) was fully factored in 2026 (page149); it is no longer open.

targets.name: Homogeneous Cunningham numbers a^n +- b^n: a new factor of one of the 565 listed composites
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (ECM on C250-C309; SNFS on the C201-C230 entries)
targets.statement: The Homogeneous Cunningham tables factor a^n +- b^n for 1 < b < a <= 12 with gcd(a,b) = 1, up to 1024 bits, with Aurifeuillian parts. Bob Silverman created them; Paul Leyland made them public in 2006 and maintained them; Paul Leyland and Jon Becker extended them in 2016; Jon Becker has maintained them since October 2018 at unshlump.com/hcn. On 2026-10-30 the page says there are 565 composites in the tables, the smallest about C201. UPDATE.txt records steady progress through 2026: NFS@Home and G. Childers by SNFS/GNFS, for example 6+5 410 C207 on 2026-09-27 and 11-9 269 C240 on 2026-09-24, and yoyo@home by ECM, for example 5-3 461 C262 on 2026-09-05. A reservations page and an ECMNET server are linked from the main page.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a composite C marked as composite in one of the a+-b tables linked from https://www.unshlump.com/hcn (re-fetched immediately before the claim) and a prime p, proven prime, with 1 < p < C and C mod p = 0, where p is absent from that table and from UPDATE.txt at verification time (direction: max on the count of known factors).

partial_wins.statement: Complete proven-prime factorisation of a listed composite, so that a^n +- b^n (or its Aurifeuillian part) becomes fully factored.
A proven prime factor of at least 50 digits of a listed composite of at least 250 digits (an ECM-scale find on the tables' hardest tier).

targets.verification_method: Rebuild a^n +- b^n exactly, divide out the listed factors and algebraic parts, confirm the remaining cofactor is composite and has the digit count the table shows for it (the tables print composites only as C < digits > ), check divisibility, prove primes with PARI isprime / ECPP, and grep UPDATE.txt.
angles: SNFS with the homogeneous polynomial: a^n - b^n gives a degree-d polynomial in (a^(n/d), b^(n/d)), which is as easy as an ordinary Cunningham number of the same size.
Pick composites whose SNFS difficulty is far below their table neighbours (n with many small divisors).
pitfalls: Check the reservations page before sieving.
The 9^n +- 4^n tables are omitted because they are subsets of 3^n +- 2^n; do not count a factor twice.
Aurifeuillian L/M parts are separate entries; say which part p divides.

targets.name: Generalized Cullen and Woodall numbers n*a^n +- 1 (a <= 12, n <= 1000): factor a listed composite cofactor
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (ECM on the large cofactors; NFS on the C188-C220 entries needs cluster)
targets.statement: Paul Leyland's GCW factorization tables (brnikat.com/nums/cullen_woodall) give factorizations of the Cullen numbers C(n) = n*2^n+1, the Woodall numbers W(n) = n*2^n-1 and their generalisations GC(a,n) = n*a^n+1 and GW(a,n) = n*a^n-1 for bases a = 2..12 and n <= 1000. The page, last updated 2026-10-28, says 24,845 factors have been found since the tables went public in September 2000 and 11,643 GCW numbers are fully factored. It also publishes comps.gz with the 10,369 remaining composite cofactors in numerical order; on 2026-10-30 the smallest is C188 (for example 2,934- and 5,440+) and the largest is above C1000. Progress tables credit the many contributors, and an ECMNET server is loaded with these numbers. Algebraic and Aurifeuillian factorizations are documented in algebraic.txt.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a composite C listed in https://brnikat.com/nums/cullen_woodall/comps.gz (re-fetched immediately before the claim) and a prime p, proven prime, with 1 < p < C and C mod p = 0, where p is absent from the table file for that base and sign at verification time (direction: max on the count of known factors).

partial_wins.statement: Complete proven-prime factorisation of a listed composite, so that its GCW number becomes fully factored.
A proven prime factor of a composite of at most 220 digits in comps.gz (the smallest, most-ECMed tier).

targets.verification_method: Compute n*a^n +- 1 exactly, divide out the table's factors, confirm the cofactor equals the comps.gz entry, check divisibility, and prove primes with PARI isprime / ECPP.
angles: Low-B1 ECM sweeps over the C500-C1100 cofactors, which have had the least work per digit.
SNFS for n*a^n +- 1: when n = a^k*m, write it as m*a^(n+k) +- 1 and use a sextic in a^((n+k)/6).
pitfalls: Read contributor_info.html for reservations and the submission format.
Known algebraic factors (algebraic.txt) are not new factors.
The comps.gz snapshot can trail the tables by a little; check the base table too.

targets.name: Fermat numbers F_m = 2^(2^m)+1: a new prime factor not in Keller's table, above all for F12-F33
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (sieve k*2^n+1 and test divisibility of F_m; ECM on F12-F19 cofactors needs cluster for any real chance)
targets.statement: Wilfrid Keller's 'Fermat factoring status' page (prothsearch.com, last modified 2025-12-05) lists every known prime factor k*2^n+1 of a Fermat number F_m, plus the completely factored cases (F5-F11) and the composite cofactors that remain: F12 = 114689*...*C1133, F13 ... C2391, F14 ... C4880, and so on up to F19 ... C157770. F20 and F24 are known composite but have no known factor. The two newest factors on the page: Gary Gostin's 36812439837*2^3144+1 | F3135 (2025-11-27) and 1085*2^3943263+1 | F3943261 by Sascha Beat Dinkel and PrimeGrid (2025-12-03). Earlier ones include Valter Cavecchia (F5798447, 2025-01-14), Propper and Batalov (F414677, 2025-01-10) and Lelio de Paula (F7220, 2024-12-07). The page also lists the known search limits. Searches are coordinated by FermatSearch, PrimeGrid and GIMPS ECM.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for m with 12 <= m <= 33 and a prime p = k*2^n+1 (n >= m+2), proven prime, such that F_m mod p = 0 and p is not listed for F_m on http://www.prothsearch.com/fermat.html (re-fetched immediately before the claim) (direction: max on the count of known Fermat factors).

partial_wins.statement: A proven prime p = k*2^n+1 dividing F_m for some m >= 34 that is not on Keller's page at verification time, outside the k- and n-ranges the page lists as fully searched.
A first known factor of a composite Fermat number with no known factor (for example F20 or F24), which is also a full win.

targets.verification_method: Prove p prime (Proth's theorem: find a with a^((p-1)/2) = -1 mod p). Then check 2^(2^m) = -1 mod p by m modular squarings (for huge m, by computing 2^(2^m) mod p with exponent arithmetic mod p-1). Look up p in Keller's table.
angles: For p1, sieve k*2^n+1 over a (k, n) window just past the page's search limits, then run Proth tests plus the Fermat-divisor check (pfgw -gxo style, or your own GMP code).
For F12-F14, stage-1 ECM with very large B1 on the C1133/C2391 cofactors; GIMPS and FermatSearch keep the effort records.
pitfalls: FermatSearch reserves k-ranges; a found factor in someone else's reserved range is still checkable but should be coordinated by a human.
A k*2^n+1 prime that divides F_m for one m divides no other Fermat number; check which m with the squaring chain, not by guessing m = n-2.

targets.name: Open aliquot sequences below 5,000,000: terminate one (reach a prime) or close it into a cycle
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (YAFU/CADO-NFS on C100-C140 cofactors along a downdriver run)
targets.statement: An aliquot sequence iterates s(n) = sigma(n) - n. The Catalan-Dickson conjecture says every sequence terminates (reaches a prime and then 1) or becomes periodic; Guy and Selfridge conjectured that many grow without bound. The MersenneForum aliquot table (rechenkraft.net/aliquot/AllSeq.html, made by Dubslow with ChristianB, hosted by Rechenkraft.net and fed from FactorDB) lists every open sequence with starting value below 5,000,000: 46,322 sequences on 2026-10-30 (reservations current as of 02:10 UTC), from 276 to 4,999,980, with 2,947 reserved. For each it gives the current index, the size, the known factors and the size of the composite blocking the next step, the driver or guide (Clifford Stern's classes), the reservation and the last progress. All 64 sequences in the 'Downdriver!' state (where terms tend to shrink) are reserved (59 by yafu@home, 5 by Batalov). The smallest blocking composites (C61-C64) sit on unreserved sequences, most of them carrying the 2^2*7 driver (two of the C64s carry the 2^4*31 guide). Earlier work includes Wolfgang Creyaufmueller's tables (aliquot.de) and the extensions by Paul Zimmermann, Christophe Clavier and many mersenneforum contributors.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a sequence listed as open in https://www.rechenkraft.net/aliquot/AllSeq.txt (re-fetched immediately before the claim), other than the Lehmer five (276, 552, 564, 660, 966). The claim is a chain of terms starting from the sequence's term at the index the live table lists. The table shows only that term's known factors and the size of its blocking composite; the full term is the FactorDB entry whose id AllSeq.json gives. Each term in the chain has a complete proven-prime factorisation, and each next term equals sigma minus the term. The chain must end at a prime (the sequence terminates) or at a term already in a known aliquot cycle, including perfect numbers and amicable pairs (direction: max on the count of resolved sequences).

partial_wins.statement: An unreserved sequence advanced by at least 20 indices beyond the live table's index, with every term fully factored into proven primes.
A merge: a chain from a listed sequence's last term reaching a term that a different listed open sequence also reaches, shown by complete factorised chains for both.

targets.verification_method: Recompute sigma from each factorisation with Python big integers, check each step s(t_i) = t_{i+1}, prove every prime factor (BPSW below 2^64, PARI isprime / ECPP above), confirm the start matches the table's last term at its index, and confirm the final prime (or the cycle member against Moews' list).
angles: Advance the unreserved sequences with the smallest blocking composites (C61-C100 in the 2026-10-30 snapshot) with YAFU or aliqueit; each step takes minutes to hours on a laptop, and a driver change can start a downward run toward termination.
Rank by Stern's class and the absence of a 3 in the factorisation; the table has checkboxes for exactly this.
pitfalls: rechenkraft.net (the status source) and FactorDB have intermittently refused automated clients (on 2026-10-30 some fetches were refused and others succeeded); fetch honestly and record BLOCKED instead of working around it.

The table lists the known factors and the size of the blocking composite (for example C61), not the term itself; take the full term from FactorDB by the id in AllSeq.json and check its index and factors against the table.
Reserved sequences (including every 'Downdriver!' one on 2026-10-30) are being run by someone else; coordinate through a human on the reservation thread.
A term lower in the table than the live index (stale cache) leads to duplicated work; always start from the live last term.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - the Lehmer five: decide the fate of the aliquot sequence of 276, 552, 564, 660 or 966
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (GNFS on C179-C210 blocking composites at every step)
targets.statement: 276 is the smallest number whose aliquot sequence (iterate s(n) = sigma(n) - n) is not known to terminate or become periodic. Together with 552, 564, 660 and 966 it forms the 'Lehmer five', the open main sequences below 1000. In the MersenneForum aliquot table (rechenkraft.net/aliquot) snapshot of 2026-10-30 they stand at: 276 at index 2162, 215 digits, 2*3^3*41*89*C210; 552 at index 1249, 211 digits, 2^3*P31*C179; 564 at index 3575, 209 digits, 2^2*3*5*137*C205; 660 at index 1187, 211 digits, 2^2*7*71*433*547048291*C196; 966 at index 1149, 209 digits, 2^4*13*31*67^2*C201. All five are reserved by the mersenneforum group. OEIS A008892 holds the 276 trajectory (b-file to index 2157 by Tyler Busby) and still calls its fate open. Paul Zimmermann carried 276 to index 2051 (C201) by 2017. Earlier work is due to D. H. Lehmer, Wolfgang Creyaufmueller, Christophe Clavier, Paul Zimmermann and many mersenneforum contributors.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for one of 276, 552, 564, 660, 966: a chain of terms starting from the last term listed for it in https://www.rechenkraft.net/aliquot/AllSeq.txt (re-fetched immediately before the claim), each with a complete proven-prime factorisation and each next term equal to sigma minus the term, that ends at a prime (termination) or at a member of a known aliquot cycle, perfect number or amicable pair.

partial_wins.statement: Next step: a complete proven-prime factorisation of the blocking composite of one of the five as listed at verification time, giving the next term at index + 1.
One of the five advanced by at least 10 indices beyond the live table's index, every term fully factored into proven primes.

targets.verification_method: Recompute every step from the factorisations with big-integer arithmetic, prove every prime (ECPP for large ones), check that the start equals the table's last term at its index, and check the end (a prime, or membership in a cycle on Moews' list).
angles: Heavy ECM (t65+) on each new blocking composite before committing to GNFS.
Watch for a driver escape: 552 currently carries the 2^3 guide, and losing it changes the expected trend.
pitfalls: All five are reserved by the mersenneforum group; any work should be coordinated by a human.

rechenkraft.net and FactorDB, the community stores for these sequences, refused automated clients during the 2026-10-30 check; do not bypass them, and cross-check the start term with the OEIS A008892 b-file and Zimmermann's page.
A single wrong factorisation corrupts every later term; prove every prime.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - home prime HP(49) = HP(77): factor the c251 at step 119 and continue to a prime
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (GNFS on a c251 is at the edge of public records; ECM is a lottery)
targets.statement: The home prime HP(n) is the prime reached by repeatedly replacing n with the concatenation of its prime factors in increasing order, with repetition. HP(49) = HP(77) (77 is step 1 of 49's trajectory) is the only open case below 100. Patrick De Geest's World!Of Numbers page (topic1.htm; server Last-Modified 2026-07-18, page footer December 12, 2022) records the history: Warut Roonguthai to step 55; Paul Leyland's MPQS and ECM breaks (steps 56 and 74); Alex Kruppa, Nicolas Daminelli, David Cleaver (WraithX) and others through step 117. HP49(119) = 73 * 16249 * c251; David Cleaver ran about 2*t60 of ECM on the c251, and Tom Dean's 2022 CADO-NFS attempt failed after six weeks, with no reported result since. OEIS A056938 has the trajectory as a b-file to step 119 (257 digits), and the 251-digit cofactor is composite.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for the complete continuation of the HP(49) trajectory from HP49(119) (as given in the OEIS A056938 b-file and on https://www.worldofnumbers.com/topic1.htm, re-fetched immediately before the claim). Each step must carry a complete proven-prime factorisation, and each next step must be the decimal concatenation of the previous step's prime factors in non-decreasing order with repetition. The chain ends at a proven prime, which is HP(49).

partial_wins.statement: Complete proven-prime factorisation of the c251 cofactor of HP49(119) (= HP49(119)/(73*16249)), giving HP49(120).
A proven prime proper factor of that c251 (even if the cofactor stays composite).

targets.verification_method: Take HP49(119) from the b-file, check 73 * 16249 * c251 = HP49(119), check divisibility and prove primes with ECPP, form each concatenation exactly, and prove the final prime with ECPP (Primo or CM).
angles: ECM at B1 = 3e9 and up is the only laptop-scale route; it pays off only if the c251 has a factor of at most about 80 digits.
pitfalls: The OEIS comment text says 117 steps while the b-file runs to step 119; use the b-file and the World!Of Numbers page.
Order matters: concatenate the prime factors in increasing order with repetition, never with exponents (that is A195264).

Tom Dean's 2022 note on the page says 'a c251 is being attempted at nfs@home'. That was C251_127_108, an XYYXF SNFS number (factored p107 * p145 by Jon Becker), not HP49; on 2026-10-30 the NFS@Home status page lists no HP49 number. FactorDB refused automated fetches that day, so check FactorDB and mersenneforum by hand for any result on this c251 before claiming novelty.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Euclid-Mullin sequence: the 52nd term (least prime factor of a 335-digit number)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (GNFS on a C335 is far beyond public records; ECM is the realistic route)
targets.statement: The Euclid-Mullin sequence (OEIS A000945) has a(1) = 2, and a(n+1) is the least prime factor of 1 + a(1)*...*a(n). Mullin (1963) asked whether it contains every prime, which is still open; 41 is the smallest prime absent from the known terms a(1)..a(51), and Booker and Irvine (2016) studied the related Euclid-Mullin graph. Wagstaff (1993) computed it through a(43). The 180-digit product+1 behind a(44) was factored by GNFS in March 2010 (mersenneforum). Ryan Propper found a(48), a 75-digit factor of a 256-digit number, by ECM in September 2012, and the OEIS b-file (Propper; first 47 terms by T. D. Noe) now runs through a(51) = 211. a(52) is the least prime factor of 1 + a(1)*...*a(51), a composite of 335 digits (checked: it fails a base-3 Fermat test and has no factor below 2*10^5). OEIS still flags this as hard (keywords nonn, nice, hard).
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a prime p, proven prime, that divides N = 1 + a(1)*...*a(51) (terms taken from the OEIS A000945 b-file, re-fetched immediately before the claim), together with a proof that p is the least prime factor of N. Acceptable proofs: N/p proven prime with N/p > p, or a complete proven-prime factorisation of N.

partial_wins.statement: Any proven prime proper factor of N (the least or not), with its cofactor's status stated (prime, composite, or split further).

targets.verification_method: Rebuild N from the b-file with big integers (it has 335 digits), check N mod p = 0, prove every prime with ECPP, and when the factorisation is complete take the minimum factor. Then check the OEIS entry still ends at a(51).
angles: Deep ECM (B1 >= 3e9) is the realistic route, as for a(48) in 2012; its value rests on how much ECM has already been done, which FactorDB's 'Status of EM51' records but which blocked automated fetches on 2026-10-30.
pitfalls: Finding a factor is not enough for a(52): the least prime factor needs the full factorisation (or a prime cofactor).
OEIS's FactorDB link may hold new partial results; check it by hand before claiming novelty.

targets.name: Imperial FLT project: fill an unclaimed Prop-valued sorry (de Smit-Lenstra representability, compact exponent-p groups, quaternion base change)

A separate complete Lean proof of FLT exists (anthropics/fermats-last-theorem, Apache-2.0, unmaintained); this target is the Imperial declarations with their own definitions. Target: prove one.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a patch that replaces exactly one Prop-valued `sorry` (a theorem, lemma or Prop-valued instance, never a sorry inside a def or structure) in a declaration on live FLT main, re-fetched immediately before claiming. At that moment the declaration must not be touched by any open FLT pull request, must not be named in an assigned or claimed issue, and must not already be proved in the repository under another name (as the PGL2 Defs/Proofs pair is). Its statement must not depend on a sorried definition (isCorepresentable_narrowSLiftFunctor and B4_proof do on 2026-10-30). The instance IsQuaternionAlgebra E (E ⊗[F] D) is excluded while issue #631 is open. The statement must be unchanged (diff-checked). The project must compile with `lake build` at the pinned lean-toolchain and lake-manifest. `#print axioms` on the declaration must show only a subset of {propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound}: no sorryAx, no knownin1980s, Mazur_statement or Odlyzko_statement, no new axiom, no native_decide. No PR is opened and no issue is claimed. The claim is for the checked patch.

partial_wins.statement: Group.subsingleton_of_pow_prime_eq_one (or its additive version, which @[to_additive] generates) proved sorry-free in the FLT repo with the statement unchanged, using only Mathlib and FLT lemmas that are already sorry-free.

A sorry-free Lean proof, in a separate file that compiles against FLT main, of de Smit-Lenstra Prop. 2.3(1) for one explicit finite group G (e.g. G cyclic of prime order), stated through the FLT `deformationFunctor` API: the special case is corepresentable.

targets.verification_method: Clone the FLT repository at the stated commit, fetch the Mathlib cache, apply the patch and run lake build; then print the axioms of the declaration and require only the standard ones. Search the diff for sorry, admit, axiom, native_decide, implemented_by and extern, and compare the statement with the original. Check the project's open pull requests and issues for the same declaration, so the claim is not already taken.
angles: p1: a nontrivial compact Hausdorff abelian group has a nontrivial continuous character. The docstring says YaelDillies/mean-fourier is building this, so check whether it has landed in Mathlib or mean-fourier before building it again. An alternative route is to show that a compact Hausdorff group of exponent p is totally disconnected via the open-subgroup structure of compact groups.

Representability: Schlessinger's criteria or the de Smit-Lenstra explicit construction (a quotient of a power series ring by the universal relations); check what the FLT Deformations folder already provides.

anthropics/fermats-last-theorem (Apache-2.0, a complete FLT proof on a different route) contains elliptic-curve and representation-theory lemmas that may port. Credit it, and check that the definitions match before porting.
pitfalls: A sorry inside a def or structure field can be 'filled' with junk that type-checks, or sits under a definition other theorems use. These never count.
Some sorried statements in Defs files are proved as copies elsewhere (PGL2/Proofs.lean). Filling a duplicate is not a new result.
The project moves quickly and AI-assisted PRs appear weekly. Re-list open PRs and claims just before claiming.
`knownin1980s` is an axiom: a proof that uses it does not count.

`#print axioms` also collects axioms from the definitions in the statement. Before starting, run it on the still-sorried declaration: anything beyond sorryAx and the three standard axioms comes from the statement and cannot be removed. cyclic_base_change imports AutomorphicForm/QuaternionAlgebra/Basic.lean, where the instance isFiniteRelIndex_Δ is proved by knownin1980s; check that it does not reach the Hecke algebra in the statement.

targets.name: Brownian Motion Lean project: close an unclaimed sorry (uniform integrability of stopped submartingales, UI martingale convergence, reflection principle)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The Brownian Motion project (RemyDegenne/brownian-motion, Lean v4.35.0 at master 497e5e2, 2026-10-27) builds Brownian motion and stochastic integration in Lean against a blueprint. Tasks are claimed by commenting on issues (bot-assigned). On 2026-10-30 it has 21 sorries in 10 files. In progress or claimed: Komlos.lean (PRs #442, #358; #430 assigned to Aaron1011), DoobMeyer, QuadraticVariation and SquareIntegrable (PR #487), DoobLp (PR #498), and Submartingale.stoppedValue_min_ae_le_condExp in OptionalSampling.lean (blueprint lem:optionalSamplingSubmartingale, issue #263 claimed by YanYablonovskiy). LocalMartingale.isStable_submartingale is also off-limits: its blueprint proof uses that claimed lemma. Unclaimed with no open PR: Submartingale.uniformIntegrable_stoppedValue (issue #262, unassigned since CoolRmal disclaimed), Martingale.ae_tendsto_limitProcess, Martingale.condExp_limitProcess_ae_eq and its stopping-time version Martingale.condExp_limitProcess_ae_eq' (UniformIntegrable.lean), and the reflection principle IsBrownianReal.reflection (Gaussian/IteratedLogarithm.lean, needs the strong Markov property). Two statements are false as written. IsStandardGaussian.tail claims P(X ≥ x) ~ exp(-x²/2)/x, but the true asymptotic carries a factor 1/√(2π); the ratio is 0.3951 at x = 10. hasIntegrableSup_const in ClassD.lean asks that a constant be integrable for an arbitrary measure P (there is no IsFiniteMeasure in scope), which fails for P = volume on ℝ and c ≠ 0. Credit: Rémy Degenne and the project's contributors.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a patch that replaces the `sorry` in one of Submartingale.uniformIntegrable_stoppedValue, Martingale.ae_tendsto_limitProcess, Martingale.condExp_limitProcess_ae_eq, Martingale.condExp_limitProcess_ae_eq' or IsBrownianReal.reflection on live brownian-motion master, re-fetched immediately before claiming. At that moment the declaration must not be in a file touched by an open PR and must not be the subject of an assigned or claimed issue. The statement must be unchanged (diff-checked). `lake build` must succeed at the pinned toolchain and manifest, and `#print axioms` on the declaration must show only propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound (no sorryAx, no new axiom, no native_decide). IsStandardGaussian.tail and hasIntegrableSup_const are false as stated and can never be the full win. stoppedValue_min_ae_le_condExp and isStable_submartingale are excluded while issue #263 is claimed.

partial_wins.statement: hasStronglyMeasurableSupProcess_const proved sorry-free with the statement unchanged, together with a kernel-checked Lean counterexample to hasIntegrableSup_const as stated (e.g. Ω = ℝ, P = volume, c = 1) and a sorry-free proof of the same lemma with [IsFiniteMeasure P] added.

A kernel-checked Lean proof, compiling against the project, of the negation of IsStandardGaussian.tail as stated (exhibit Ω, P, X with HasLaw X (gaussianReal 0 1) P for which the IsEquivalent fails), together with a sorry-free proof of the corrected statement with the factor 1/√(2π).

targets.verification_method: Clone main, `lake exe cache get`, apply the patch, `lake build`, `#print axioms`, grep for forbidden tokens, diff the statement. Check open PR file lists and the project board for claims.
angles: Uniform integrability of stopped values at bounded stopping times: dominate by the conditional expectation of the value at the bound (the discrete case is in Mathlib) and pass through the right-continuous approximation used elsewhere in the repo.
Corrected Gaussian tail: Mills-ratio bounds x/(1+x^2) φ(x) <= Q(x) <= φ(x)/x by integrating by parts, which gives IsEquivalent with φ(x)/x.

The optional-sampling lemma for submartingales (issue #263) is claimed, and isStable_submartingale depends on it. Do not prove it inline to get around the claim.
The Komlos sorries are claimed and have PRs, and lean-pool has a separate Komlos project. Do not port it into claimed tasks.
Claims are made by commenting on issues. Agents never comment, so a claimed issue stays off-limits.

targets.name: IEANTN (explicit analytic number theory network): a Comparator-verified solution for an unclaimed node (e.g. the cotangent zeta-value expansion)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: IEANTN (teorth/IEANTN, the Integrated Explicit Analytic Number Theory Network maintained by Terence Tao and contributors; main ec66e38, 2026-10-18, Lean v4.34.0-rc2) records explicit analytic number theory as a graph of nodes. Each node's Challenge.lean states conditional theorems with deliberate sorries. A node becomes Lean-backed when a separate Solutions/ < Family > . < version> project proves the challenge and Comparator accepts it. STATE.md (generated) lists 63 node versions and 132 conclusions: 47 lean-comparator (17 of those receipts are stale after a Mathlib bump), 45 literature, 32 numerical, 4 none-yet, 3 bridged, 1 asserted. Tasks are claimed by commenting 'claim' on an issue (a bot assigns it and moves the card on github.com/users/teorth/projects/3); CONTRIBUTING.md calls claiming a courtesy, not a lock. Unclaimed awaiting-solution nodes on 2026-10-30 include CotangentSeries.v1, cot_series_zeta_values: π cot πz = 1/z − 2 Σ ζ(2n) z^{2n−1} as a HasSum for 0 < |z| < 1. Mathlib lacks this: it has Euler's partial fractions (cot_series_rep) and riemannZeta_two_mul_nat, but not the expansion at the origin. The node has no linked issue and no open PR. Another is GammaAsymptotics.v1, digamma_sub_log_isBigO (ψ(w) − log w = O(1/|w|) on Re w ≥ 1). Its linked issue #64 is closed, though it still lists teorth as assignee. The node itself records that its recurrence route does not prove it and that a Binet or Gauss integral representation is needed. The sibling GammaAsymptotics.v2 strip version is already lean-comparator. Claimed nodes are excluded: BKLNW (#50, xinjiegit), FKS (#52, marcosadriano27), Buthe (#56, AlstonTZ), DudekPlatt (#63, elmismisimoxhunca). On #111 (closed 2026-09-26) Tao wrote that other matters have limited his time on the project; 13 PRs are open, none touching these two nodes. Target: supply a Solution for an unclaimed node version.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a Lake project under Solutions/ < Family > . < version> for one node version. Re-fetch live IEANTN main immediately before claiming. At that point the node version must have no Solutions directory, no lean-comparator receipt, no open issue that is assigned to or claimed for it (a closed issue, such as #64, does not count), and no open PR that touches it. leanprover/comparator must accept it against the node's generated Challenge.lean: same statements, only propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound, and the node's imports used only as the hypotheses the scaffold provides. Excluded: nodes in the RosserSchoenfeld families (they overlap the PNT+ bank entry), the claimed BKLNW, FKS, Buthe and DudekPlatt families while their issues are open and assigned, and statements that are the headline problem of an active lean-eval problem. No PR is opened.

partial_wins.statement: CotangentSeries.v1 challenge_cot_series_zeta_values proved and accepted by Comparator, provided Mathlib at the pinned revision does not already contain the expansion.

For a node version that meets every exclusion and claim condition of the success criterion and whose evidence is `literature`, a Comparator-accepted proof of at least one of its conclusions as a conditional theorem from the node's declared imports, with the other conclusions of that node left open.

targets.verification_method: Clone IEANTN at the stated commit, build the core (`lake build`; one sorry warning per conclusion is expected), build the Solution project, and run Comparator against the challenge as docs/SOLUTIONS.md and CONTRIBUTING.md describe. Check the board and open PRs for claims.
angles: Cotangent: start from Mathlib's cot_series_rep (Euler's partial fractions), expand each 1/(z±n) geometrically for |z| < 1 and swap the double sum (summable by comparison with Σ |z|^{2k}/n^{2k}), then identify Σ_n n^{-2k} with riemannZeta (2k).
pitfalls: Audit the challenge statement against the source before proving, as SOLUTIONS.md insists. On FKS2 such an audit found four wrong statements.
An upstream development that 'does' a theorem may thread numerics as deliberate sorries. Comparator rejects that.
Mathlib moves; if the cotangent expansion has landed upstream, p1 is a cleanup, not a win.

targets.name: Clay Class Field Theory project: Herbrand quotient of local units and unramified cohomology vanishing
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: kbuzzard/ClassFieldTheory, the repository of the 2025 Clay summer school Formalizing Class Field Theory, is an ongoing project led by Kevin Buzzard to formalise local and global class field theory, with a blueprint (main d48e8a0, 2026-10-29, Lean v4.36.0-rc2). Open PRs cover Tate cohomology shifting (#193, plp127, UpDown.lean) and inflation-restriction (#190 by Whysoserioushah, #68 by Paul-Lez). The Corestriction sorries are inside comments, and the instances in IsNonarchimedeanLocalField/Instances.lean (imported only by the root ClassFieldTheory.lean) have sorry-free replacements in Actions.lean; its lemma valuation_ringEquiv (every ring automorphism of a local field preserves the valuation) has no counterpart there. Live sorries outside those, on 2026-10-30: Rep.herbrandQuotient_isNonarchimedeanLocalField_integer_units in IsNonarchimedeanLocalField/HerbrandQuotient.lean (the Herbrand quotient of the integral units of a cyclic extension of local fields is 1, marked 'hard work' with a blueprint link); the instance Subsingleton (groupCohomology (Rep.units Gal(L/K) 𝒪[L]) q) for unramified L/K and q > 0 in UnramifiedCohomology.lean; and Algebra.unramifiedLocus_eq_univ_iff' and Algebra.isOpen_unramifiedLocus' in IsNonarchimedeanLocalField/Basic.lean (universe-polymorphic versions of Mathlib lemmas). Target: prove one.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a patch replacing one live `sorry` (not one inside a comment, and not in a file touched by an open PR) on ClassFieldTheory main, re-fetched immediately before claiming, with the statement unchanged (diff-checked). `lake build` must succeed at the pinned toolchain and manifest, and `#print axioms` on the declaration must show only propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound (no sorryAx, no native_decide, no new axiom). Declarations in Instances.lean whose sorry-free version already exists in Actions.lean do not count.

partial_wins.statement: Algebra.unramifiedLocus_eq_univ_iff' or Algebra.isOpen_unramifiedLocus' proved sorry-free with the statement unchanged (deriving them from the Mathlib versions is fine).
The unramified-cohomology Subsingleton instance proved sorry-free for q = 1 only, stated as a separate lemma with the same hypotheses.

targets.verification_method: Clone main, `lake exe cache get`, apply the patch, `lake build`, `#print axioms`, grep for forbidden tokens, diff the statement, and check the open PR file lists.
angles: Herbrand quotient of units: take a finite-index open subgroup of the units that is cohomologically trivial (via the exponential or an induced module from a normal basis), then use multiplicativity of the Herbrand quotient in short exact sequences and h(finite) = 1, which the repo already has in Cohomology/FiniteCyclic/HerbrandQuotient.

Existing formalisations to study or port, with credit, after checking the definitions match: TauCeti/NumberTheory/LocalField/UnitFiltration/HerbrandQuotient.lean (TauCeti project) and anthropics/fermats-last-theorem Theorems/Thm_M4aLocalCFT_unitsDecomp_herbrandQuotient_eq_one.lean (Apache-2.0).

Unramified case: filter the units by 1 + 𝔪^n. The graded pieces are residue-field modules with trivial cohomology by Hilbert 90 and the additive normal basis theorem over finite fields. Pass to the limit by completeness.
pitfalls: Several 'sorry' hits in a plain grep are inside comments (Corestriction.lean). They are not tasks.
The instances in Instances.lean are superseded by the sorry-free Actions.lean. Proving those old copies is not a win (valuation_ringEquiv, which Actions.lean does not cover, still counts).

Cohomology/TrivialityCriterion.lean uses δDownResIsoTate, a sorried definition in Cohomology/Functors/UpDown.lean (open PR #193). A proof routed through the triviality criterion carries sorryAx until that sorry is filled upstream, so check `#print axioms` early.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - LeanAPAP: formal proof of the Kelley-Meka bound for 3AP-free sets of integers (corrected form of theorem `int`)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days
targets.statement: Kelley and Meka (2023, arXiv 2302.05537) proved that a 3AP-free A ⊆ {1..N} has |A| ≤ N/exp(c (log N)^{1/12}). Bloom and Sisask (arXiv 2302.07211) improved the exponent to 1/9. YaelDillies/LeanAPAP (Yaël Dillies and Bhavik Mehta; master b200197, 2026-10-22, Lean v4.36.0-rc1) formalises the finite-field analogue: theorem `ff` in APAP/FiniteField.lean, with open PR #19 adding Comparator CI for it. The integer case is a bare `sorry` in APAP/Integer.lean, and as written it is false: `theorem int : ∃ c > 0, ∃ C > 0, ∀ ⦃A : Finset ℕ⦄ ⦃N : ℕ⦄, A ⊆ range N → ThreeAPFree (α := ℕ) A → #A ≤ N / exp (c * log N ^ (12⁻¹ : ℝ))` never uses C, and N = 2, A = {0, 1} gives 2 ≤ 2/exp(c (log 2)^{1/12}) < 2 for every c > 0. The intended statement has C in front of N. Issue #25 (closed 2026-09-28) reported this counterexample together with a quantifier-order bug; the fix moved the constants in front and added C but left C out of the bound. The maintainer notes that development now happens mostly in YaelDillies/mean-fourier, which has no integer theorem either. The missing mathematics is the Bohr-set version of the almost-periodicity and density-increment steps. Prerequisites are also unproved, among them Bohr set regularity (`BohrSet.regularity` in APAP/Prereqs/Bohr/Regular.lean, also a sorry in mean-fourier); the NewMarcinkiewiczZygmund sorries are in open PR #20. No Lean proof of the integer bound is in LeanAPAP, mean-fourier or Mathlib.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a sorry-free Lean theorem compiling against live LeanAPAP master (re-fetched immediately before claiming) at its pinned toolchain and manifest, with `open Finset Real` as in APAP/Integer.lean and statement exactly `∃ c > 0, ∃ C > 0, ∀ ⦃A : Finset ℕ⦄ ⦃N : ℕ⦄, A ⊆ range N → ThreeAPFree (α := ℕ) A → (#A : ℝ) ≤ C * N / exp (c * log N ^ (12⁻¹ : ℝ))` (statement diff-checked). `#print axioms` on it must show only a subset of {propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound}, with no native_decide and no new axiom. Proving `int` as currently written is impossible, because it is false.

partial_wins.statement: BohrSet.regularity in APAP/Prereqs/Bohr/Regular.lean proved sorry-free with the statement unchanged.

A sorry-free Lean theorem compiling against LeanAPAP of the same shape as the success statement (∃ c > 0, ∃ C > 0, (#A : ℝ) ≤ C * N / exp (c * log N ^ e)) with a fixed exponent e with 0 < e < 1/12, or the same bound with exponent 1/12 for 3AP-free subsets of ZMod N with N prime, stated as a separate theorem.

targets.verification_method: Clone LeanAPAP master, `lake exe cache get`, apply the patch, `lake build`, `#print axioms int` (or the partial-win theorem), grep for forbidden tokens, diff the statement.
angles: Follow Bloom-Sisask section by section. The finite-field proof `ff` is a template: subspaces become regular Bohr sets, and almost periodicity is already formalised.
An easier route to a weaker statement for p2 is to embed {1..N} in Z/pZ with p ≈ 2N and run the finite-group density increment.
pitfalls: `int` as written is false at N = 2 (C is unused). A kernel-checked disproof is easy, already exists (linked from issue #25), and is not a win. Prove the corrected statement.
Natural-number subtraction and `log` of 0 and 1 make small N degenerate; the constant C must absorb them.
If upstream corrects `int` to a different form before the claim, the claim is still judged against the statement fixed in the success criterion.

APAP/Prereqs/DummyPositivity.lean holds sorried dummy lemmas behind unsound `positivity` extensions (APAP/Prereqs/Convolution/Order.lean, imported by FiniteField). A proof that calls `positivity` on convolution terms can silently depend on sorryAx. Run `#print axioms` early and often, not only at the end.

targets.name: LeanCamCombi: formal proof of the van den Berg-Kesten-Reimer inequality (card_certificator_le)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The van den Berg-Kesten inequality says that disjoint occurrence of two events is at most as likely as their joint product. It was conjectured for all events by van den Berg and Kesten (1985) and proved by D. Reimer (2000). YaelDillies/LeanCamCombi (Yaël Dillies; master bc7d1c9, 2026-10-29, Lean v4.36.0-rc2) defines the certificator 𝒜 □ ℬ of two set families in CamCombi/PlainCombi/VanDenBergKesten.lean (a ∈ 𝒜 □ ℬ iff some complementary pair x, y witnesses membership of a in 𝒜 through a ⊓ x and in ℬ through a ⊓ y). It states the uniform-measure inequality `lemma card_certificator_le : 2 ^ Fintype.card α * #(𝒜 □ ℬ) ≤ #𝒜 * #ℬ := sorry`, tracked as issue #34 (open since 2025-01-22, unassigned, no linked PR). No Lean proof was found in Mathlib, lean-pool (project list scanned 2026-10-30) or lean-eval's problem list. The upper-set/lower-set case already follows from Mathlib's Harris-Kleitman inequality.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a sorry-free proof of `Finset.card_certificator_le` exactly as stated on live LeanCamCombi master, re-fetched immediately before claiming (the statement and the certificator definition are diff-checked). Issue #34 must still be open with no PR proving the lemma. The proof must compile with `lake build` at the pinned toolchain and manifest, and `#print axioms` must show only propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound (no native_decide, no new axiom).

partial_wins.statement: The inequality for up-sets: if 𝒜 and ℬ are both upper sets, 2^n · #(𝒜 □ ℬ) ≤ #𝒜 · #ℬ (the original van den Berg-Kesten case; IsUpperSet.certificator_eq_disjSups in the file rewrites 𝒜 □ ℬ as 𝒜 ○ ℬ), proved sorry-free as a separate lemma.

targets.verification_method: Clone master, `lake exe cache get`, apply the patch, `lake build`, `#print axioms Finset.card_certificator_le`, grep for forbidden tokens, diff the statement and definition, and check issue #34 and open PRs.
angles: Reimer's proof (2000) rests on his 'butterfly' lemma about the Boolean cube. Expositions include Borgs-Chayes-Randall's review of the BKR inequality and the account in Bollobás-Riordan, Percolation. Formalise the butterfly lemma first, then the reduction.
p1: van den Berg-Kesten's original argument for increasing events, by induction on the number of coordinates (split off one coordinate and compare the conditional families).
pitfalls: The Lean statement is for the uniform measure on subsets of a finite type. Weighted product versions are not required, and a proof for them may not specialise trivially.
Check that IsCompl in the definition matches disjoint witness sets (it does by monotonicity). Do not change the definition.
The case of an upper set and a lower set is not a win: it follows in two lines from IsUpperSet.certificator_eq_inter and Mathlib's IsUpperSet.card_inter_le_finset.

targets.name: Physlib semiformal result FXNL5: the restricted Lorentz group SO+(1,d) is connected
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Physlib (leanprover-community/physlib, formerly HepLean/PhysLean, founded by Joseph Tooby-Smith; master a4f5411, 2026-10-30) lists its open formal items on its auto-generated TODO page. Its one Lean-stated 'semiformal result' is tag FXNL5 in Physlib/Relativity/LorentzGroup/Restricted/Basic.lean: `semiformal_result "FXNL5" restricted_isConnected {d : ℕ} : IsConnected (restricted d : Set (LorentzGroup d))`. Here `restricted d` is the subgroup of proper (det 1) and orthochronous (Λ₀₀ ≥ 0) Lorentz transformations. A conditional lemma in the same file, restricted_eq_identity_component_of_isConnected, already derives `restricted d = connectedComponent 1` from it. Much of the route is already formalised and sorry-free. Restricted/FromBoostRotation.lean has the homeomorphism `toBoostRotation : restricted d ≃ₜ Lorentz.Velocity d × Matrix.specialOrthogonalGroup (Fin d) ℝ` and `exists_boost_mul_rotation`, and `Lorentz.Velocity.isPathConnected` shows the velocity factor is path-connected. What is missing is connectedness of SO(d) = Matrix.specialOrthogonalGroup (Fin d) ℝ, which Mathlib (pinned 56a0058) does not have, plus the transfer from the subtype to the set. None of physlib's 69 open PRs on 2026-10-30 touches Relativity/LorentzGroup (the only Lorentz-titled one, #968, refactors the Lorentzian metric elsewhere).
targets.success_criterion: Success means a sorry-free Lean proof of `IsConnected (LorentzGroup.restricted d : Set (LorentzGroup d))` for all d : ℕ. It must use physlib's definitions as they stand on live main (re-fetched immediately before claiming; statement diff-checked) and be stated as a theorem replacing the semiformal_result. It must compile with `lake build` at physlib's pinned toolchain, and `#print axioms` must show only propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound (no native_decide, no new axiom). The FXNL5 entry must still be open on the TODO page or in the source at claim time.

partial_wins.statement: The case d = 2, `IsConnected (LorentzGroup.restricted 2 : Set (LorentzGroup 2))`, proved sorry-free as a separate theorem against physlib's definitions.
The case d = 3, `IsConnected (LorentzGroup.restricted 3 : Set (LorentzGroup 3))`, proved sorry-free as a separate theorem against physlib's definitions.

targets.verification_method: Clone physlib main, `lake exe cache get`, replace the semiformal_result with the theorem, `lake build`, `#print axioms`, diff the statement, and check the physlib TODO page and open PRs.
angles: Use toBoostRotation: restricted d is homeomorphic to Velocity d × SO(d), and Velocity d is already path-connected, so it suffices to prove Matrix.specialOrthogonalGroup (Fin d) ℝ connected and push connectedness through the homeomorphism and the subtype coercion.

For SO(d): induct on d using Givens (plane) rotations, which join any element to 1 one coordinate plane at a time; or use the fibration SO(d) → S^{d-1}, A ↦ A e₁, with fibre SO(d-1). For d = 2, SO(2) is the continuous image of the circle under the rotation-matrix map.
pitfalls: d = 0 is a degenerate case (restricted 0 is trivial). Make sure the proof covers it rather than adding a hypothesis.
Physlib refactors often. Re-check the definitions of IsProper and IsOrthochronous, and the statement of toBoostRotation, on master before claiming.
The boost-times-rotation decomposition (exists_boost_mul_rotation) and the case d = 1 (SO(1) is a single point) already follow from existing physlib code and are not wins on their own.

targets.name: Andrews-Curtis: an AC-trivialisation of AK(3), or of one of the last two open length-14 Miller-Schupp classes
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (search over balanced presentations; RL or breadth-first search with supermoves)
targets.statement: The Andrews-Curtis conjecture says every balanced presentation of the trivial group reduces to <x,y|x,y> by AC moves: inverting a relator, multiplying one relator by another, and conjugating a relator by a generator. AK(n) = <x,y | x^n = y^(n+1), xyx = yxy> (Akbulut and Kirby, 1985) has total relator length 2n+7. AK(3), of length 13, is the shortest potential counterexample: balanced trivial-group presentations of length <= 12 are AC-trivial (Miasnikov-Myasnikov), and those of length 13 are AC-trivial or AC-equivalent to AK(3) (Havas-Ramsay), as summarised by Carreras (2026). Shehper, Medina-Mardones, Fagan, Lewandowski, Gruen, Qiu, Kucharski, Wang and Gukov (arXiv 2408.15332, v2 Feb 2025) showed AK(3) is stably AC-trivial (re-derived by Lisitsa, arXiv 2501.18601); the unstable question is open. Their Miller-Schupp study (MS(n,w) = <x,y | x^-1 y^n x = y^(n+1), x = w > ) left six hard length-14 presentations, four of which they asserted without proof to be AC-equivalent to AK(3). Carreras (arXiv 2607.23611, v1 July 2026) gave the first explicit certificates for the two MS(3) ones, MS(3, y x^2 y) and MS(3, y^-1 x^2 y^-1). He also linked the two MS(2) holdouts, MS(2, y x^2 y x^-2) and MS(2, y x^2 y^-1 x^-2), to the uncertified MS(2, x^-2 y^-1 x^2 y) and MS(2, x^-2 y^-1 x^2 y^-1) via the automorphism y -> y^-1, and related the classical candidate <x,y | x^-1 y^2 x = y^3, y^-1 x^2 y = x^3> to them. None of these MS(2) presentations is certified AC-trivial or AC-equivalent to AK(3). Fagan et al. (ICML 2026, arXiv 2606.21611) released the AC-19 and AC-1M datasets of solved instances.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit finite sequence of elementary AC moves (r_i -> r_i^-1; r_i -> r_i r_j with i != j; r_i -> g^±1 r_i g^∓1 for a generator g; free reduction allowed) that starts at AK(3) = <x,y | x^3 y^-4, xyx y^-1 x^-1 y^-1> and ends at <x,y | x, y> (up to relabelling and inverting relators). An independent free-group replayer must check it. A machine-checked proof (Lean, Coq or Isabelle) that AK(3) is NOT AC-trivial also counts. A trivialisation of AK(3) through stabilisation (adding generators) does not count, because that is already known.

partial_wins.statement: An elementary AC-move certificate that takes any of MS(2, y x^2 y x^-2), MS(2, y x^2 y^-1 x^-2), MS(2, x^-2 y^-1 x^2 y) or MS(2, x^-2 y^-1 x^2 y^-1) (Carreras 2026 notation) to the trivial presentation <x,y | x, y > .
An elementary AC-move certificate that one of those four MS(2) presentations is AC-equivalent to AK(3), certifying the Shehper et al. assertion for the MS(2) branch of the length-14 collapse.
An elementary AC-move trivialisation of AK(4) = <x,y | x^4 = y^5, xyx = yxy> or of any AK(n) with n >= 4.

targets.verification_method: Replay the move list with a small free-group word library: apply each move, freely reduce, and confirm the final pair is (x, y) up to inversion and order, or reaches the stated target presentation up to cyclic permutation and inversion of relators. Carreras's paper ships a dependency-free Python replayer that can serve as a second implementation. Also confirm the starting presentation is exactly AK(3) (or the named MS presentation).
angles: Start from Carreras's MS(3) certificates (13 and 66 packaged moves) as entry points into the AK(3) class. His exhaustive GS-substitution-graph searches show any GS path from MS(2, x^-2 y^-1 x^2 y) or MS(2, x^-2 y^-1 x^2 y^-1) to AK(3) must reach total relator length 27 or more, so search above that bottleneck or use multiplications the GS generator omits.
Use the AC-1M 'hard but solvable' data to train a policy with supermoves, then run it on the AK(3) class with a large length cap.
pitfalls: A stable trivialisation (extra generators) is already known and does not count.
Carreras's 19 and 27 bottleneck results apply only to his GS substitution graph and to specific representatives. They are not AC-distance lower bounds and prove nothing about non-triviality.
Carreras's preprint is v1 and not peer reviewed; re-run its certificates with an independent replayer before building on them.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - The exact number of groups of order 2048
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (counting about 1.77e15 2-groups mostly without listing them; new theory needed)
targets.statement: gnu(n), the number of groups of order n up to isomorphism (OEIS A000001), is known for every n < 2048. A000679 (groups of order 2^n) stops at a(10) = 49,487,367,289 (a(9) and a(10) by Eamonn O'Brien; a(10) corrected by David Burrell in 2022). gnu(2048) is unknown. Eick and O'Brien's methods give 1,774,274,116,992,170 groups of order 2^11 with exponent-2 class 2, which is a strict lower bound. Conway, Dietrich and O'Brien ('Counting groups: gnus, moas and other exotica', Math. Intelligencer 2008) expect the true value to agree with it in the first three digits. Eick, Horn and Hulpke ('Constructing groups of small order: recent results and open problems', 2018) treat orders divisible by 2^10 as infeasible to enumerate. Max Horn's table (groups.quendi.de, data of 2023-12-12, site updated 2026-09-14) still lists 2048 as unknown.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact integer gnu(2048), which must be STRICTLY GREATER than 1,774,274,116,992,170. It must be produced by public, re-runnable code (for example a p-group generation or enumeration method in GAP or Magma, with the split by 2-class and rank reported) and reproduced either by an independent second method or by an independent re-run on separate hardware. The method must reproduce gnu(512) = 10,494,213 and gnu(1024) = 49,487,367,289 as a sanity check.

partial_wins.statement: The exact number of groups of order 2048 with exponent-2 class exactly 3, from re-runnable code that, run at order 512, reproduces the exponent-2 class-3 count obtained directly from the SmallGroups library (PClassPGroup over the 10,494,213 groups of order 512).

targets.verification_method: Re-run the released code (GAP or Magma) on independent hardware. Check that the per-class or per-rank breakdown sums to the total, that the class-2 part equals 1,774,274,116,992,170, and that the same code gives the known values for orders 2^n with n <= 10.
pitfalls: The 2002/2008 value 49,487,365,422 for order 1024 is wrong; the corrected value is 49,487,367,289 (Burrell 2022). Use the corrected value as the sanity check.
Counting a group twice across p-classes, or mixing exponent-2 class with nilpotency class, gives a wrong total.

targets.name: Number of groups of order n: settle an order up to 20,000 that is still unknown in Max Horn's table (smallest: 3072, 4096, 4608, 5120, 6144, 6400, 6912, 7168)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (GAP GrpConst / Frattini-extension or Eick-Horn-Hulpke counting methods; some orders need cluster)
targets.statement: Max Horn's table of gnu(n) for n <= 50,000 (groups.quendi.de; data from the SmallGroups library of Besche, Eick and O'Brien, GrpConst, Archer's Zphi method, and Burrell 2023) shows 134 orders as unknown. Up to 20,000 it shows 37 unknown orders: 2048, 3072, 4096, 4608, 5120, 6144, 6400, 6912, 7168, 7680, 8192, 8748, 9216, 10240, 10368, 10752, 11264, 11520, 12288, 12544, 12800, 13122, 13312, 13824, 14336, 15360, 16000, 16128, 16384, 16896, 17408, 17496, 17920, 18432, 19200, 19456 and 19968. The raw data file gap/grps.json marks one more, 19683 = 3^9, as unknown, but the page fills it in with Burrell's count 5,937,876,645 (Comm. Algebra 51 (2023)). Eick, Horn and Hulpke (2018) sort the hard cases into orders divisible by 2^10 or 3^9, orders with 2^9 p as a proper divisor (p in {3,5,7}), and orders divisible by 2^8 p^2. Their 'exceptional' orders 8748 = 2^2 3^7, 10368 = 2^7 3^4, 13122 = 2 3^8, 16000 = 2^7 5^3 and 17496 = 2^3 3^7 have known nilpotent counts but unknown solvable counts (18816 has since been filled in the table). 2048 is a separate moonshot entry in this bank.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact value gnu(n) for at least one order n <= 20,000, other than 2048 and 19683, that groups.quendi.de lists as unknown at verification time. It must come from public, re-runnable GAP/Magma code and be reproduced by a second independent method or an independent re-run, as Eick-Horn-Hulpke did for their 1,875 doubly checked orders. The nilpotent part must match the known count where one is published (for example 18,620 for 8748, 34,920 for 10368, 1,396,077 for 13122, 11,640 for 16000, 46,550 for 17496).

partial_wins.statement: The exact gnu(n) for an order 20,000 < n <= 50,000 listed as unknown on groups.quendi.de, with the same reproducibility standard.

For one of the exceptional orders 8748, 10368, 13122, 16000 or 17496 (all solvable by Burnside's p^a q^b theorem): the exact number of groups of that order that have a normal Sylow subgroup, reproduced by two independent methods (for example orbit counting of Hom(Q, Aut(P)) and an explicit GAP construction).

targets.verification_method: Re-run the released scripts on independent hardware. Check that the counts split into nilpotent, solvable non-nilpotent and non-solvable parts that match the table's known parts, and that the same pipeline reproduces several neighbouring known orders from the table (for example 2304 = 15,756,130 and 1536 = 408,641,062).
pitfalls: The table's JSON (gap/grps.json) stores [non-solvable, solvable, ...] per order, so the total is the sum of the first two fields; a -1 in the second field means unknown. For prime-power orders the page ignores the JSON and uses its own nilpotent-count table in js/code.js, so read the rendered page, not only the JSON.
19683 shows as -1 in the JSON but the page lists it as known (5,937,876,645, Burrell 2023); do not claim it.

targets.name: Smallest order with exactly 33 groups (OEIS A046057 a(33), the first unknown moa)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (GAP: Holder formula, CubeFree package and GrpConst over roughly 100k orders)
targets.statement: moa(k) is the smallest order m with exactly k groups of order m (Conway, Dietrich and O'Brien (CDO), Math. Intelligencer 2008; OEIS A046057, data a(1..32), a(32) = 630). a(33) is unknown; OEIS still gives only a(33) > 30500 (M. A. Asiru, 2017), and CDO's Table 2 guesses 163293. Two facts tighten this, both re-runnable from public data (checked 2026-10-30). First, Max Horn's table at groups.quendi.de has no known order n <= 50,000 with gnu(n) = 33, and every order <= 50,000 that the table leaves unknown has a proper divisor d with gnu(d) >= 1181. Since gnu(n) >= gnu(d) for d | n (take G x C_(n/d)), a(33) > 50,000. Second, Hölder's formula gives gnu(163293) = 33 with 163293 = 3*13*53*79, the smallest squarefree order with 33 groups. So 50,000 < a(33) <= 163,293. CDO report computing gnu(n) with the CubeFree package for the cubefree n in [2048, 163293] whose lower bounds were at most 30. The main remaining work is the non-cubefree orders in range (7,686 are not ruled out by the divisor bound alone), plus any cubefree orders that computation did not cover. Later unknown terms include a(65), a(82), a(95) and a(107): no order <= 50,000 has 65, 82, 95 or 107 groups.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact value of a(33), with: (i) an order m and a re-runnable certificate that gnu(m) = 33, and (ii) a re-runnable certificate that gnu(n) != 33 for every n < m. For (ii), an exact count, or a lower bound > 33 from a divisor or an explicit list of 34 pairwise non-isomorphic groups, is enough for each n. The value must be <= 163,293, which already has 33 groups, and > 50,000. Either a(33) = 163,293 or a smaller order beats the CDO guess; both count.

partial_wins.statement: A re-runnable certificate that gnu(n) != 33 for every n <= 100,000 (giving a(33) > 100,000).
An order m < 163,293 with gnu(m) = 33, certified by two independent methods (for example GrpConst or a Frattini-extension count cross-checked against CubeFree or SmallGroups-style enumeration).

targets.verification_method: Re-run the released script: squarefree orders by Hölder's formula, cubefree orders by GAP CubeFree, the rest by GrpConst or SmallGroups. Divisor lower bounds are taken from the table values and checked by recomputation. Spot-check the pipeline against Horn's table for n <= 50,000 and the known moa values a(22) = 6321 and a(31) = 11774.
pitfalls: Horn's JSON stores [non-solvable, solvable] counts per order; the total is their sum.
gnu(n) >= gnu(d) for d | n relies on Krull-Remak-Schmidt cancellation (G x C_m determines G); do not use it with other constructions without proof.

targets.name: Lovász conjecture, smallest open order: is every connected Cayley graph on a group of order 144 Hamiltonian?
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (GAP enumeration of irredundant generating sets up to automorphism for the 197 groups of order 144, plus LKH or a SAT search per graph)
targets.statement: A special case of the Lovász conjecture asks whether every connected Cayley graph on a finite group (order > 2) has a Hamiltonian cycle. Morris and Wilk ('Cayley graphs of order kp are hamiltonian for k < 48', Art Discrete Appl. Math. 3 (2020), arXiv 1805.00149) proved it, with computer help, for all orders kp with k < 48. Their Corollary 1.2 deduces that every connected Cayley graph on a group of order < 144 is Hamiltonian. Earlier work covers prime-power orders (Witte 1986), kpq (k < 6), pqr, kp^2 (k < 5) and kp^3 (k < 3) (Kutnar, Marušič, Morris, Morris and Šparl 2012), 16p, 27p and 30p. Later work adds 8pq (Abedi, Morris, Rezaee and Salarian 2025) and pqrs (Lehner, Maghsoudi and Miraftab, arXiv 2607.14440, 2026). No result we found covers order 144 = 2^4 3^2. By our reading, the next orders up to 300 outside all published families are 162, 192, 216, 240, 270, 288 and 300. A Hamiltonian-path version of the question for symmetric generating sets is Kourovka Notebook 20.32 (posed by E. Rapaport Strasser, submitted by B. Green; 21st ed., arXiv 1401.0300v49).
targets.success_criterion: Success means a complete certificate for order 144: for each of the 197 groups SmallGroup(144,i), a list of irredundant generating sets that represents every irredundant generating set up to automorphisms of the group and inversion of generators, and for each listed set either a Hamiltonian cycle in the undirected Cayley graph, given as a sequence of generators, or a proof of non-Hamiltonicity. A non-Hamiltonian example would be a counterexample, which also counts if machine-checked by exhaustive search. Supersets of generating sets need no separate check.

partial_wins.statement: The same complete certificate restricted to irredundant generating sets of size 2, for all 197 groups of order 144.
The same complete certificate for all irredundant generating sets of size at most 3, for all 197 groups of order 144.

targets.verification_method: For each cycle, multiply the generator sequence in the group (GAP or a permutation representation): the 144 partial products must be distinct and the full product must be the identity. Completeness: an independent GAP run recomputes the irredundant generating sets up to Aut(G) and inversion (as IrredUndirGenSetsUpToAut does in Morris-Wilk's ancillary code) and checks that each is covered.
angles: Reuse Morris-Wilk's GAP ancillary code (HamiltonianCycles.gap, LKH.gap, IsHamiltonianCycle.gap) as a reference; write your own checker.
