Many groups of order 144 fall under structural theorems (abelian, cyclic commutator subgroup of prime-power order, commutator subgroup of order 2p, and so on); a direct computer search over all of them is still the cleanest certificate.
pitfalls: Equivalence must use automorphisms of G plus inversion of individual generators; cutting the list down with a coarser equivalence leaves gaps.
A Hamiltonian path is not enough; the cycle must close.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Burnside group B(2,5): finite or infinite? (with Kourovka 11.48, Kostrikin's fifth-power question)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (coset enumeration or rewriting on candidate presentations), or pure thought
targets.statement: B(2,5) = F(x,y)/F^5 is the free 2-generator group of exponent 5. Whether it is finite is the smallest open case of the Burnside problem (Wikipedia, 'Burnside problem'). B(m,n) is finite for n = 2, 3, 4, 6 (Burnside, Sanov, M. Hall). It is infinite for odd n >= 665 (Novikov-Adian, improved by Adian) and for all n >= 8000 (Ivanov for large even n, then Lysenok). Kostrikin's solution of the restricted Burnside problem for prime exponent, with the Havas-Wall-Wamsley computation (1974), shows that the largest finite quotient R(2,5) has order 5^34. So B(2,5) is finite exactly when it equals R(2,5). Kourovka Notebook problem 11.48 (A. I. Kostrikin, still open in the 21st edition, arXiv 1401.0300v49, 20 Oct 2026) asks whether the commutator [x,y,y,y,y,y,y] is a product of fifth powers in the free group <x,y > . If it is not, B(2,5) is infinite.
targets.success_criterion: Success means either (a) a finite set W of words in x, y with a machine-verifiable proof (coset-enumeration certificate, confluent rewriting system, or a formal proof in Lean, Coq or Isabelle) that G = <x,y | w^5, w in W> is finite. B(2,5) = G/G^5 is a quotient of G, so it is then finite and equal to R(2,5). As a consistency check, the certificate must also show that G/G^5 has order 5^34 (G itself may be larger). Or (b) a machine-checked formal proof that B(2,5) is infinite, for example a formally verified negative answer to Kourovka 11.48.

partial_wins.statement: A positive answer to Kourovka 11.48: an explicit list of words u_1..u_k in the free group on x, y such that u_1^5 u_2^5 ... u_k^5 freely reduces to the left-normed commutator [x,y,y,y,y,y,y], using the Kourovka convention [a,b] = a^-1 b^-1 a b and [a,b,c] = [[a,b],c].

targets.verification_method: For p1: freely reduce the product and compare it with the commutator word computed by a second implementation. For (a): replay the coset table or rewriting system (ACE, KBMAG or a formal-proof kernel) and confirm the order 5^34 (it should match the nilpotent quotient R(2,5) of class 12). For (b): run the proof assistant's checker.
pitfalls: Showing that some finite quotient has order 5^34 says nothing about B(2,5); only finiteness of a presentation that uses fifth powers alone counts.
Commutator conventions differ ([a,b] = a b a^-1 b^-1 in some texts); state and use the Kourovka one.

targets.name: Kourovka 20.36 (Havas-Newman): define B(3,4) with fewer than a million fourth powers
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days to needs cluster (the 2-quotient half takes minutes in ANU pq; the finiteness certificate is the hard part, since a coset enumeration needs a subgroup whose own order is proved and indices beyond about 10^9 cosets are out of laptop reach)
targets.statement: The free Burnside group B(3,4) has order 2^69 (Bayes, Kautsky and Wamsley, 1974). Their proof uses Sanov's theorem, and Sanov's argument for B(3,4) uses more than 2^32 fourth powers. Havas and Newman (1980) showed that B(3,4) needs at least 105 relations. Kourovka Notebook problem 20.36 (G. Havas and M. F. Newman), still open in the 21st edition (arXiv 1401.0300v49, 20 Oct 2026), asks: (a) can B(3,4) be defined with fewer than a million fourth powers; (b) with fewer than a thousand; (c) what is the smallest number of fourth powers that define it?
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit set S of fewer than 1,000,000 words in a, b, c together with a machine-verifiable proof that G = <a,b,c | w^4, w in S> is finite of order exactly 2^69, and hence equal to B(3,4). B(3,4) is a quotient of G, so |G| >= 2^69 is automatic and the proof must show |G| <= 2^69. An accepted proof is a 2-quotient (p-quotient with p = 2) computation showing the largest 2-quotient of G has order 2^69 (class 7, with the class-8 quotient equal to the class-7 one), plus a coset-enumeration or rewriting certificate that a referee can replay showing |G| <= 2^69. For example, the certificate can give the index [G:H] of a subgroup H together with a proof that |H| <= 2^69 / [G:H]. Fewer than 1,000 fourth powers (part b) is a stronger full win.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit set of fewer than 100,000,000 fourth powers with a full certificate that it defines a group of order exactly 2^69, which beats the more than 2^32 relations in Sanov's argument.

targets.verification_method: Re-run ANU NQ or GAP's pq on the presentation to confirm the 2-quotient of order 2^69 (class 7), then replay the coset-enumeration certificate (ACE) for finiteness. Independently confirm that every relator is a fourth power of a stated word and count them.
pitfalls: A stable 2-quotient alone does not prove finiteness; a separate finiteness certificate is required.

The 2-quotient half is routine and is not progress on 20.36. The ANU p-Quotient Program enforces exponent 4 by imposing explicit fourth powers, and Newman and O'Brien report 1016 fourth powers giving the 2-quotient of B(4,4), so a standard run yields a small set of fourth powers for B(3,4) with a stable 2-quotient of order 2^69. The whole difficulty is finiteness.
Relators must be literally fourth powers w^4, not arbitrary consequences of the exponent law.

targets.name: Kourovka 16.46 (Conder): does the index-8 subgroup K of an amalgam acting on the 3-valent tree have a non-trivial finite quotient?
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (low-index subgroups, homomorphism searches into simple groups)
targets.statement: Among the finitely presented groups that act arc-transitively on the 3-valent tree with finite vertex stabiliser are G3 and G4 (Djokovic-Miller types), each containing PSL(2,Z) = <h,a | h^3, a^2> with finite index. Their free product with <h,a> amalgamated has a normal subgroup K of index 8 with presentation K = <A,B,C,D,E,F | A^3, B^3, C^2, D^2, E^2, F^2, (AC)^3, (AD)^3, (AE)^3, (AF)^3, (BC)^3, (BD)^3, (BE)^3, (BF)^3, (ABA^-1C)^2, (ABA^-1D)^2, (A^-1BAE)^2, (A^-1BAF)^2, (BAB^-1C)^2, (B^-1ABD)^2, (BAB^-1E)^2, (B^-1ABF)^2 > . Kourovka Notebook problem 16.46 (M. Conder), still open with no comment in the 21st edition (arXiv 1401.0300v49, 20 Oct 2026), asks whether K has a non-trivial finite quotient. Our quick hand check: K's abelianisation is trivial, so any finite quotient is non-abelian.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit non-trivial homomorphism from K to a finite group: images of A, B, C, D, E, F as permutations in some S_n (or matrices over a finite field), not all the identity, that satisfy all 22 relators exactly. A machine-checked proof that K has no non-trivial finite quotient also counts.

partial_wins.statement: A re-runnable exhaustive low-index-subgroups certificate (for example GAP LowIndexSubgroupsFpGroup, cross-checked by an independent implementation) that K has no proper subgroup of index at most 30, published with code and run log.

targets.verification_method: Substitute the permutation or matrix images into each of the 22 relators and check that each gives the identity, and that at least one generator image is non-trivial. Re-type the presentation from the Kourovka PDF independently, because a transcription error makes the check meaningless.
pitfalls: Problems marked ♯ in the Notebook have unverified AI solutions and those marked ∗ are solved; 16.46 has neither mark as of v49, but re-check the latest version.
Check relator orientation (A^-1 B A versus A B A^-1) against the PDF; the two are not interchangeable.

targets.name: Kourovka 20.21 (Verret/Conder): isomorphic normal subgroups K and L of index 12 with G/K = C12 and G/L = A4
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (GAP search over SmallGroups and extensions, filtering groups with both a C12 and an A4 quotient)
targets.statement: Kourovka Notebook problem 20.21 (posed by G. Verret, submitted by M. Conder, 20th issue 2022), still unanswered in the 21st edition (arXiv 1401.0300v49, 20 Oct 2026): does there exist a finite group G with two normal subgroups K and L, each of index 12, such that K is isomorphic to L but G/K is cyclic of order 12 while G/L is the alternating group A4? A positive answer is a finite object that anyone can check.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit finite group G (as a permutation group or a pc-presentation), explicit generators of normal subgroups K and L, and an explicit isomorphism K -> L, such that a GAP or Magma check confirms: K and L are normal in G, |G:K| = |G:L| = 12, the map is an isomorphism, G/K is cyclic of order 12, and G/L is isomorphic to A4. A machine-checked proof that no such G exists also counts.

partial_wins.statement: A re-runnable exhaustive certificate that no such G exists with |G| <= 1000, covering every order divisible by 12 in the SmallGroups library (pre-filtering to groups with both a C12 quotient and an A4 quotient is allowed), with the code and the run log.

targets.verification_method: Load G in GAP; check IsNormal for K and L, the indices, IdGroup or StructureDescription of G/K and G/L (C12 versus A4), and that the given generator map extends to an isomorphism K -> L (GroupHomomorphismByImages plus IsBijective).
pitfalls: K and L must be isomorphic as abstract groups, not conjugate or equal; a map that is not a homomorphism fails.
Re-check the latest Notebook version: AI-proposed solutions are being posted (♯ marks), and only ∗ marks mean confirmed.

targets.name: Diameter of the Cayley graph of S_n with generators (1,2) and the two n-cycle rotations (LRX): prove n(n-1)/2, or compute a(16) exactly
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (an n = 16 BFS over 16! = 2.1e13 states needs about 5 TB at 2 bits per state); the main proof is pure thought plus Lean
targets.statement: OEIS A186783 gives the diameter of the Cayley graph of S_n generated by the transposition (1,2) and the rotations (1,2,...,n)^{±1} (the 'LRX' graph). The OEIS data run to n = 13: 0, 1, 2, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 45, 55, 66, 78. These come from Bartoletti, Hardin, Li and Bieron, with a(13) by Ben Whitmore in 2018. The conjecture a(n) = n(n-1)/2 for n > 3 (Alexandersson 2020, in the OEIS entry) is open for general n. Antiufeev (arXiv 2601.08715, v3 June 2026) proved a(n) >= n(n-1)/2, so the open part is the matching upper bound. The best proven upper bound is n(n-1)/2 + 3n (Chervov, Soibelman, Lytkin et al., 'CayleyPy RL', arXiv 2502.18663, 2025). That paper also reports full BFS traversals of the LRX graphs for n <= 15 confirming that the longest element has length n(n-1)/2, so the conjecture is computationally settled through n = 15 (not yet in the OEIS data). It also conjectures that the unique longest element is (2,1,n,n-1,...,3), a conjecture Dmitry Kamenetsky recorded in the OEIS. The same paper gives an explicit word of length n(n-1)/2 for that element for every n, and its diffusion-distance pipelines and a Kaggle challenge (n = 2..200) found no shorter word. Those bound only that element's distance, not the diameter.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a machine-checked proof (Lean, Coq or Isabelle) that the LRX diameter is at most n(n-1)/2, and hence equals n(n-1)/2, for all n >= 4. A counterexample also counts: an n >= 16 and a permutation whose distance exceeds n(n-1)/2, certified by an exhaustive BFS that the skeptic re-runs, or by a machine-checked distance lower-bound proof.

partial_wins.statement: The exact value a(16) from a complete, re-runnable BFS of the 16! vertices (layer sizes published and summing to 16!), provided no published source already reports it.
A machine-checked proof of an upper bound n(n-1)/2 + c*n for all n with c < 3, improving the 2025 bound n(n-1)/2 + 3n.
A machine-checked proof (Lean, Coq or Isabelle) of the known lower bound a(n) >= n(n-1)/2 for all n > 3 (Antiufeev 2026), as the first half of a formal proof of the conjecture.

targets.verification_method: For BFS claims: re-run the released BFS (bit-packed visited set) on independent hardware and compare the layer sizes, which must sum to n!, and the final depth. For proofs: run the proof assistant's checker on the released file.
pitfalls: a(14) and a(15) are already settled by the full BFS reported in arXiv 2502.18663 (n <= 15), even though the OEIS data stop at n = 13; do not claim them.
Word lengths found by beam search, diffusion distance, Kaggle solutions or GAP for one element are upper bounds for that element, not the diameter.
The CayleyPy group runs large GPU BFS computations; check their latest papers and OEIS before claiming a(16).

targets.name: Chvatal-Sankoff constant (C_31a): a certified bound on the expected LCS of two random binary strings beating 0.792665992 <= gamma_2 <= 0.821963
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (Lueker-type automata at the frontier need 10^8 to 10^11 states; the binary upper side now needs a cluster or a new idea, the k-ary partial wins fit a big laptop)
targets.statement: gamma_2 = lim E[LCS(X,Y)]/n for independent uniform binary strings X, Y of length n (Chvatal-Sankoff 1975). The exact value is unknown; simulations suggest about 0.812. Rigorous upper bounds: Lueker (JACM 2009) 0.826280 with his history-length-h automaton at h = 8; L. Jack (2026) 0.825101 (h = 9) and 0.824120 (h = 10), merged on Tao's page 31a and independently replayed by C. Toledo and Jeetu SK (teorth/optimizationproblems PR #249, open); T. S. Tomar (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.23610945, v5, 24 Oct 2026) pushed Lueker's method to h = 13 (1.66e11 states after symmetry), gamma_2 <= 0.821963, with h <= 12 kernel-checked in Lean 4 and h = 13 as compiled code. Rigorous lower bounds: Dancik 1994 0.773911, Lueker 2009 0.788071, Heineman-Miller-Reichman-Salls-Sarkozy-Soiffer (arXiv:2407.10925, 2024) 0.792665992. The 0.79970 'lower bound' of Archivara Agent (2026) is a Monte Carlo/Hoeffding estimate, not a proof, and Tao's page labels it so. For larger alphabets Jack (Oct 2026; PR #272, open) reports 0.686509 <= gamma_3 < 0.737495 and 0.617356 <= gamma_4 < 0.679701. Open as of 2026-10-30.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED requires a rigorous bound on gamma_2 strictly better than the best rigorous bound found at verification time on that side (direction: upper bound min, lower bound max), taken over Tao's live page https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/31a.html, the open PRs at https://github.com/teorth/optimizationproblems/pulls touching 31a/31b/91, the latest version of Tomar's Zenodo record, and any newer arXiv or Zenodo claim; on 2026-10-30 these bars are 0.821963 (upper) and 0.792665992 (lower). Probabilistic (Monte Carlo/Hoeffding) bounds never count as bars or as wins. The bound must come with a certificate a skeptic re-runs: for Lueker-type upper bounds the automaton (or the code that generates it), z, and a positive vector v with A_z v <= lambda v checked with outward rounding, giving gamma_2 <= 2 log(2z)/log(lambda); for lower bounds the finite-length computation with exact or outward-rounded arithmetic. Improvements must be at least 1e-6 absolute.

partial_wins.statement: For one alphabet size k with 3 <= k <= 15 (two strings), a certified bound on gamma_k strictly better than the best rigorous value at verification time on that side, counting Jack's Oct 2026 values (repository leandrejack-afk/chvatal-sankoff-bound and PR #272), Rosenfeld (arXiv:2407.18113) and Heineman et al. (arXiv:2407.10925).

An independent, code-disjoint replay of Tomar's h = 11, 12 or 13 certificate (re-deriving the automaton from Lueker 2009 and certifying lambda with outward rounding), or a concrete error in it, recorded with logs; this is credited only while no independent replay of that h is listed on Tao's page or in an open PR.

targets.verification_method: Rebuild the automaton from Lueker 2009 independently, reproduce Lueker's Table II for h <= 8 and Jack's h = 9 value as calibration, then check the claimed positive vector entrywise in directed rounding (or exact rationals) and recompute 2 log(2z)/log(lambda) with interval arithmetic. For lower bounds, rerun the published computation with exact integers. Compare against the bars freshly fetched from the sources named in the criterion.
angles: Lower side: Lueker's lower-bound method with the Heineman et al. memory scheme, plus Jack's symmetry reduction (one stored value per class under alphabet permutation and swapping), which has not been applied to k = 2 at larger n.
Upper side: instead of raising h uniformly, refine only the automaton states with large eigenvector weight (adaptive histories), keeping a valid domination certificate.
Store the eigenvector in compressed form and certify A_z v <= lambda v by streaming, as Jack's verify_cert_stream does.
pitfalls: Tao's main table can lag the constant pages and the PR queue: Tomar's 0.821963 was not on the 31a page on 2026-10-30.
Float power iteration gives a number, not a certificate: the domination A_z v <= lambda v must be checked with directed rounding.
The Monte Carlo 0.79970 row is not a rigorous lower bound; beating it proves nothing.

targets.name: Average edit distance of two random binary strings (C_91): a certified bound beating 0.216276 <= alpha_2 <= 0.315514
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days for the lower side (transfer-matrix certificates); the upper side's Lueker-type automata needed 100 GB RAM at h = 17 (Rosenfeld) and grow about 4x per extra h, so h >= 18 needs a large-memory server or symmetry reduction
targets.statement: alpha_2 = lim e_n/n, where e_n is the expected Levenshtein distance (insertions, deletions, substitutions) between two independent uniform binary strings of length n; the limit exists by subadditivity and alpha_2 <= e_n/n for every n. Upper bounds: Bilardi-Schimd (Information 17 (2026) 685, arXiv:2211.07644) give exact e_n up to n = 24, so alpha_2 <= 0.36932, and M. Rosenfeld (arXiv:2407.18113, 2024) adapted Lueker's automaton method (h = 17) to get 0.315514. Lower bounds: alpha_2 >= 1 - gamma_2 gives 0.178037 from Tomar's gamma_2 <= 0.821963 (2026); Bilardi-Schimd 0.170552; L. Jack (Oct 2026, repository leandrejack-afk/chvatal-sankoff-bound, commit 574220e) 0.216276 from a first-moment count of canonical optimal alignments with an exact rational certificate, proposed as new constant C_91 in teorth/optimizationproblems PR #273 (open, 26 Oct 2026); Jack also gives 0.424710 for k = 4. Monte Carlo at n = 2^15 suggests alpha_2 ~ 0.27496 (Bilardi-Schimd). The gap 0.216-0.316 is wide. Open as of 2026-10-30.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED requires a rigorous bound on alpha_2 strictly better than the best rigorous bound at verification time on that side (direction: upper min, lower max), over PR #273 / the 91a page of teorth/optimizationproblems if merged, Jack's repository, Rosenfeld (arXiv:2407.18113 and later versions), Bilardi-Schimd, and any newer arXiv/Zenodo claim; on 2026-10-30 the bars are 0.315514 (upper) and 0.216276 (lower). The improvement must be at least 1e-6 and come with a re-runnable certificate: for an upper bound the automaton, parameter and positive vector checked with outward rounding (or an exact e_n with e_n/n below the bar); for a lower bound an exact rational or outward-rounded transfer-matrix certificate plus a written proof of the counting argument. Monte Carlo estimates never count.

partial_wins.statement: For an alphabet of size 4, a certified bound on the expected normalized edit distance strictly better (on either side) than the best rigorous value at verification time, counting Jack's 0.424710 lower bound and Rosenfeld's and Bilardi-Schimd's tables.

The exact rational value of e_25 (binary, n = 25), one length past Bilardi-Schimd's exact table, computed by two independent programs that agree and that reproduce the published e_n for n <= 24, provided no exact e_25 is published at verification time.

targets.verification_method: Recompute the certificate independently: for transfer-matrix lower bounds, verify the matrix entries from the stated canonical-alignment rules by exhaustive enumeration on small n, then check A v < v (or the stated inequality) in exact rationals; for upper bounds re-run the automaton check with directed rounding. Calibrate by reproducing Rosenfeld's 0.315514 and Jack's 0.216276 with the same code.
angles: Lower side: add more local rules to the canonical-alignment normal form (each rule cuts the first-moment count) and re-solve the transfer matrix.
Upper side: Rosenfeld's h = 17 automaton with symmetry reduction under bit complement and string swap, as Jack did for the LCS case, to reach h = 18-20.
pitfalls: alpha_2 >= 1 - gamma_2 lower bounds move whenever gamma_2's upper bound moves; recompute the bar from the best gamma_2 bound before claiming.
The constant is for Levenshtein distance with unit costs; LCS-only (indel) distance is 2(1 - gamma_2), a different constant.

targets.name: Turan's pure power-sum constant (C_42, Erdos #519): a certified upper bound below 0.6873358063 or an explicit lower bound above 1/2
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (step-profile optimisation plus Arb/exact-rational certificate checks)
targets.statement: R_n = min over z_1..z_n in C with max|z_i| = 1 of max_{1<=k<=n} |sum_i z_i^k|, and C_42 = limsup R_n (Tao's optimization constants, page 42a; C_42 is the optimal constant for Erdos problem #519, which asked only whether some absolute c > 0 works and was settled by Atkinson). Lower bounds: Atkinson 1/6 (1961) and pi/8 (1969), Biro 1/2, and Biro (Indag. Math. 11 (2000) 343-358) a computable but uncomputed constant c > 1/2. Upper bounds: Biro 5/6, Harcos 0.69368 (computer search, reported by Biro), and in 2026 asymptotic step-profile certificates: S. Griego 0.6906538 (repo sebastian-griego/turan-c42-certificate v1.0.0), A. Rohrig 0.688983 (PR #184, open), R. Pinho 0.6888863712 = 215276991/312500000 (22 Oct 2026), and D. Koshta 0.6873358063 = 6873358063/10^10 (23 Oct 2026, repo DennisKoshta/c42-turan-power-sum-certificate, commit 8e1797e; first-block cut-off 41/200, 64 middle blocks, Arb at 384/640 bits). All 2026 bounds are unrefereed, asterisked, and give no explicit finite threshold N. Cheer-Goldston (Math. Comp. 1996) computations suggest values near 0.7 for moderate n. Open as of 2026-10-30.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED requires either (i) an upper bound C_42 <= U with U STRICTLY BELOW (direction: min) the smallest upper bound at verification time on https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/42a.html and in open PRs of teorth/optimizationproblems (0.6873358063 on 2026-10-30), by at least 1e-8, given as an exact rational profile in a written asymptotic reduction (Griego's two-block reduction or a new one with full proof) whose finite hypotheses are verified by two independent checkers (exact rationals and Arb/interval arithmetic); or (ii) a lower bound C_42 >= L from a complete proof whose numerical steps are interval-certified, with L STRICTLY ABOVE (direction: max) both the best explicit lower bound listed at verification time (1/2 on 2026-10-30) and the explicit value of Biro's computable constant c from Indag. Math. 11 (2000) 343-358, once that value has been published or established under p1. Merely evaluating Biro's own constant counts only as p1, not as (ii).

partial_wins.statement: An explicit, interval-certified numerical value for Biro's computable constant c > 1/2 (Indag. Math. 11 (2000) 343-358), following his proof step by step, provided no explicit value is listed on the 42a page at verification time.

An explicit finite threshold N_0, with a proof whose numerical steps are interval-certified, such that R_n <= 0.6906538 (Griego's 2026 bound) for every n >= N_0 (none of the 2026 asymptotic certificates states a threshold).

targets.verification_method: Re-derive the reduction's finite inequality from the written argument, then evaluate it on the submitted rational profile with exact rationals and independently with python-flint/Arb at >= 384 bits; both must clear the bound with a strictly positive margin. Calibrate by re-running Koshta's and Pinho's published certificates with the same checker.
angles: Free the block boundaries in Koshta's profile (non-uniform middle blocks) and optimise the cut-off jointly with the block heights by LP in the rational profile parameters.
For the lower side, Biro's 2000 argument is constructive: implement its constant first (p1), then look for the step that loses the most.
pitfalls: The 2026 bounds are asymptotic reductions with no explicit N; a numerically small max |s_k| for one finite n is not an upper bound on the limsup.
Several AI agents are improving this constant weekly; re-fetch the 42a page and the PR list right before claiming.

targets.name: Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley TSP constant (C_12): a certified bound beating 0.6421 <= beta_2 <= 0.861715646305
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (the current record's integer computation takes about 76 minutes in C on 8 threads at k = 9)
targets.statement: For n uniform random points in the unit square, the shortest tour length L_n satisfies L_n/sqrt(n) -> beta_2 almost surely (Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley 1959); Held-Karp experiments suggest beta_2 is about 0.71 (Johnson-McGeoch-Rothberg 1996). Upper bounds: 0.92117 (BHH 1959), Steinerberger (2015) 0.92117 - (9/16)e-6, Carlsson-Yu (computer-aided; 2023 preprint < 0.90304, INFORMS J. Comput. 2025 version cited as 0.90380 by later papers), Gaudio-Guan (arXiv:2602.11250, Feb 2026) 0.90367 with band crossovers, Z. Dong and J. Cao (arXiv:2610.02809, 2 Oct 2026) 0.8810 with blocks of six consecutive points in strips, and D. O'Keefe (2026, github.com/devinokeefe/travelling-sales-person-constant-bounds, commit f5d1842; unrefereed) beta_2 <= 0.861715646305 = 5A/(6^10 2^32 9 11) with A = 4430997795015293889, from blocks of ten points in strips of height 2.2/sqrt(n) and the Edmundson-Madansky inequality, checked by Python, C and Rust programs. Lower bounds: 0.625 (BHH), 0.6277 (Gaudio-Jaillet, ORL 2020), and 0.6421 (Dong-Cao 2026, not yet on Tao's page 12a, which still lists 0.6277). Dong-Cao's importance-sampling bounds 0.6536 and 0.8749 hold only with probability 1 - 2e-4 and are not proofs. Open as of 2026-10-30.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED requires a rigorous bound on beta_2 strictly better than the best rigorous bound at verification time on that side (direction: upper min, lower max), over Tao's page https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/12a.html, its open PRs, arXiv:2610.02809 (latest version), O'Keefe's repository and any newer arXiv claim; on 2026-10-30 the bars are 0.861715646305 (upper) and 0.6421 (lower). The bound must come from a written proof whose final step is a deterministic computation (exact integer/rational arithmetic, or interval arithmetic rounded in the safe direction) that two independent programs reproduce. Bounds holding only with high probability over random sampling do not count.

partial_wins.statement: An exact, independent verification at k = 9 of the cell-sum identities that O'Keefe's README says were checked only for smaller k (or an explicit counterexample to one of them), with code that shares nothing with his checkers.

An independent, code-disjoint deterministic replay of Dong-Cao's lower bound beta_2 >= 0.6421 (arXiv:2610.02809), rebuilt from the paper's description with exact or safely rounded arithmetic and reproducing the printed value, or a concrete error in it, recorded with logs; credited only while no independent replay of that bound is listed on Tao's page 12a or in an open PR at verification time.

targets.verification_method: Re-derive the integer quantity from the paper's theorem, run two independent implementations (e.g. C and Python) on the published spec, and check that the bound is below the claimed rational threshold with no floating point in the final comparison. Calibrate by reproducing O'Keefe's k = 5..9 table (A_0 values) and Dong-Cao's 0.8810.
angles: Run O'Keefe's construction at k = 10 or 11 with the strip height re-optimised; his README table drops by 0.003 to 0.006 per step in k.
Lower side: combine nearest-neighbour and second-nearest-neighbour exclusion with a finite LP over local configurations, as Gaudio-Jaillet and Dong-Cao do, and certify the LP dual exactly.
pitfalls: Tao's page 12a lagged on 2026-10-30: it listed 0.6277 as the lower bound although Dong-Cao claim 0.6421, and printed O'Keefe's bound as 0.8618 (exact value 0.861715646305).
Dong-Cao's 0.6536 and 0.8749 are probabilistic; beating them with another sampled estimate proves nothing.

targets.name: Robbins' problem (full-information expected rank): a certified bound beating 1.908 <= V <= 2.32614
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (dynamic programming over truncated-loss states with interval arithmetic, or rigorous evaluation of history-dependent stopping rules)
targets.statement: X_1, ..., X_n are i.i.d. Uniform[0,1], observed one at a time; you must stop on exactly one, with no recall, and you lose its absolute rank among all n. V(n) is the minimal expected rank over all stopping rules, V(n) is nondecreasing, and V = lim V(n) (Robbins' problem, the 'fourth secretary problem'). The optimal rule depends on the whole history (Bruss-Ferguson 1996; Gnedin 2007) and V is unknown. Lower bound 1.908: Bruss and Ferguson (J. Appl. Prob. 30 (1993) 616-626), from the loss truncated at rank 5 (V >= V_n(5)). Upper bounds come from explicit rules: memoryless threshold rules give 2.3318 (Assaf and Samuel-Cahn, Adv. Appl. Prob. 28 (1996)), Bruss and Swan (2009) 2.33183 in continuous time, and Meier and Sogner (J. Appl. Prob. 54 (2017) 331-336) state an expected rank of 2.32614 for a rank-plus-threshold rule in Gnedin's Poisson embedding, the smallest published value. Goldenshluger and Malinovsky (arXiv:2610.33701, 24 Oct 2026) report that rule's value as 2.33044, and Brice, Bruss, Majumdar and Raskin (arXiv:2608.27419, Aug 2026) still quote 2.3318 and 1.908. Exact V(n) is known only for n <= 4 (Dendievel and Swan 2016, V(4) ~ 1.4932). For 5 <= n <= 100 Brice et al. give MDP-abstraction upper approximations (V(5) about 1.57128), and Goldenshluger-Malinovsky give uncertified DP approximations for n <= 10 (V(5) ~ 1.5707); neither gives certified values or new limit bounds. Open as of 2026-10-30.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED requires either (i) a fully specified stopping rule (it may depend on the whole history) together with a rigorous enclosure, by interval arithmetic or exact computation plus a written error analysis, of lim sup_n of its expected rank (or of its value in Gnedin's Poisson embedding, with the transfer to V proved or cited), whose upper end is STRICTLY BELOW (direction: min) the smallest upper bound published at verification time (2.32614, Meier-Sogner 2017, on 2026-10-30, used as the bar even though Goldenshluger-Malinovsky 2026 report that rule's value as 2.33044) by at least 1e-4; or (ii) a rigorous lower bound V >= L with L STRICTLY ABOVE (direction: max) the best published lower bound at verification time (1.908 on 2026-10-30) by at least 1e-4, from a finite computation (e.g. V >= V(n) >= truncated-loss values) whose every rounding is in the safe direction and whose reduction is proved. Simulation estimates, and finite-n values that are not bounds on the limit, never count.

partial_wins.statement: A rigorous enclosure of V(5) of width at most 1e-4, both ends certified with directed rounding, together with the optimal rule's description, computed by two independent programs, provided no certified V(5) of that width is published at verification time (Brice et al., arXiv:2608.27419, report 1.57128 and Goldenshluger-Malinovsky, arXiv:2610.33701, report 1.5707, both uncertified).

targets.verification_method: For upper bounds, re-derive the expected-rank integral for the submitted rule from its definition, evaluate it with interval arithmetic (and spot-check by Monte Carlo at large n as a sanity test only), and check the n -> infinity limit argument. For lower bounds, re-run the truncated-loss DP with directed rounding and check the inequality chain V >= V(n) >= bound. Calibrate by reproducing Bruss-Ferguson's 1.908 and the memoryless value 2.3318.
angles: Rules that depend on the current value and the number of earlier values below a moving threshold (one extra statistic beyond memoryless) can be evaluated by a two-dimensional integral recursion.
Lower side: Bruss-Ferguson truncate the loss at a fixed rank; modern hardware allows larger truncation levels and larger n in the same DP, provided every step is interval-certified.
pitfalls: The published upper values disagree: Meier-Sogner's abstract says 2.32614, Goldenshluger-Malinovsky (2026) report the same rule as 2.33044, Brice-Bruss et al. (2026) quote only 2.3318, and Wikipedia quotes 2.329. The bar is the smallest, 2.32614; re-read Meier-Sogner's paper and check newer citations of it and of Bruss-Ferguson 1993 before claiming.

The expected-rank value of a rule must be its n -> infinity limit (or a bound valid for all n); a value at one finite n is not an upper bound on V, while a certified lower bound on any V(n) is a lower bound on V.
The 2026 MDP and DP tables (Brice et al., Goldenshluger-Malinovsky) are approximations without certified error bounds; reproducing them is calibration, not a win.
Do not confuse with the Chow-Robbins S_n/n game or the no-information expected-rank problem (solved: 3.8695, Chow et al. 1964).

targets.name: Mahler's problem for Littlewood polynomials: beat the skew-symmetric record Mahler measure at an even degree 32-60 in Mossinghoff's tables
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (local search over +-1 coefficient vectors with root-finding; exhaustive extensions need laptop-days)
targets.statement: For a Littlewood polynomial f (all coefficients +-1) of degree d, Mahler's problem asks how large M(f)/sqrt(d+1) can be (is it bounded by 1 - epsilon? Borwein's book, Problem P10). M. Mossinghoff's Mahler-Measure-Database lists the largest Mahler measures of all Littlewood polynomials of each degree d <= 30 (LargeLittlewood.txt, 23 Jun 2026, extending Borwein-Mossinghoff 2008) and of skew-symmetric ones for each even d <= 60 (LargeSkewSymmLittlewood.txt, 18 Jul 2026). For even d in 32..60 only the skew-symmetric maximum is known, so it is the best known value at that degree; at d <= 30 a non-skew polynomial beats the skew maximum at d = 8, 16, 18, 24 and 30 (e.g. d = 30: 5.367254 vs 5.315882). The largest known normalized value is 0.98636 at d = 12 (the Barker polynomial of length 13). For large degree Erdelyi (2020) showed Rudin-Shapiro polynomials reach sqrt(2/e) = 0.8578, and Mossinghoff (arXiv:2405.08281v2, Oct 2025) set the asymptotic record above 0.951 with Turyn polynomials (Fekete shifted by about p/4), suggesting generalized Turyn polynomials may do better. All 1280 table entries were recomputed on 2026-10-30 with no mismatch. Open as of 2026-10-30.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED requires either (i) a Littlewood polynomial f of even degree d, 32 <= d <= 60, with certified M(f) STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the largest value listed for that d in LargeSkewSymmLittlewood.txt (re-downloaded from https://github.com/mossinghoff/Mahler-Measure-Database at verification time) and than any value for that d in other files of the database or in newer literature (d = 60: 7.524118801007 on 2026-10-30); or (ii) a Littlewood polynomial of any degree d >= 13 with certified M(f)/sqrt(d+1) > 0.98636599 (the Barker-13 value). M(f) must be certified by rigorous root isolation (Arb/acb_poly) or by two independent high-precision methods agreeing to 20 digits. Improvements must exceed the listed value by more than 1e-9.

partial_wins.statement: An exhaustive, independently reproducible computation of the largest Mahler measure (with the top-25 list in the database's format) over all Littlewood polynomials of degree 31, provided the database does not list degree 31 at verification time; the same code must reproduce LargeLittlewood.txt for d <= 30 as a regression.
The same exhaustive extension for skew-symmetric Littlewood polynomials of degree 62, reproducing LargeSkewSymmLittlewood.txt for d <= 60, provided degree 62 is not listed at verification time.

For some degree d with 61 <= d <= 200, a Littlewood polynomial with certified M(f)/sqrt(d+1) > 0.971124, the largest normalized value in LargeSkewSymmLittlewood.txt for d >= 32 (at d = 52), provided no larger value at degree >= 61 is published at verification time.

targets.verification_method: Parse the +- string, compute all roots with python-flint acb_poly at >= 200 bits, take M(f) = product of max(1,|root|) as a certified ball, and compare with the freshly downloaded table for that degree after canonicalisation (f(x), f(-x), reversal and sign give the same M). Calibrate by recomputing the table entries (a numpy check on 2026-10-30 matched all 1280 entries to 1e-8).
angles: Seed local search (single and double flips, maximising log M via the sum of log|roots| outside the circle) with the skew-symmetric record polynomials and with truncated or periodically extended Turyn polynomials (Jedwab-Katz-Schmidt parameters t ~ 0.221p, d ~ 1.058p).
log M(f) is the mean of log|f| on the unit circle (Jensen), so flips can be scored quickly with an FFT on a fine grid before exact certification.
pitfalls: Jensen-formula estimates on a grid are not certificates; near-unimodular roots make log|f| singular, so certify with root isolation.
The general table stops at d = 30 and the skew table at even d = 60; at odd d >= 31 there is no listed value to beat, which is why only even d in 32..60 count for (i).

targets.name: MOONSHOT - L1 Poincare constant of the Hamming cube (C_11a): a function on {-1,1}^n with ratio above sqrt(pi/2)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours per candidate, but only at large n: exact multinomial sums for functions of a few block sums with n in the hundreds to thousands. Tables over 2^n points cannot win, because ILvHV's per-dimension dual bound keeps every function on n variables at or below C_dual,n, which is about 1.06 for n <= 7 and is extrapolated to reach sqrt(pi/2) only near n = 60.
targets.statement: C_11a is the smallest constant with E|f - Ef| <= C E|grad f| for all n and all f: {-1,1}^n -> R, with D_j f(x) = (f(x) - f(x^(j)))/2 and |grad f| the Euclidean norm of (D_j f) under the uniform measure (Tao's page 11a). Ben Efraim and Lust-Piquard (PTRF 2008) proved C_11a <= pi/2; Ivanisvili, Li, van Handel and Volberg (arXiv:1811.05584) proved it is strictly smaller, and Ivanisvili-Stone (arXiv:2407.04835, 2024) made the gap explicit, about 1.3e-4. The lower bound sqrt(pi/2) = 1.2533141 comes from Pisier's sharp Gaussian inequality via the central limit theorem. ILvHV write that it is still not clear whether C_11a > sqrt(pi/2); their computations of a dual constant suggest low dimensions approach sqrt(pi/2) only slowly (perhaps near n = 60). A check on 2026-10-30 found symmetric functions g(sum x_i) of erf/tanh shape reaching only about 1.134 at n = 1001, so a win needs genuinely new structure. Open as of 2026-10-30.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED requires an explicit function f: {-1,1}^n -> Q (any n; given as a table, or as a formula in the coordinates that a checker can evaluate exactly, such as a function of a few block sums) for which E|f - Ef| / E|grad f| is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than sqrt(pi/2) = 1.2533141373155..., computed with exact rationals and certified square-root enclosures (interval arithmetic with outward rounding) so that the certified lower end of the ratio exceeds sqrt(pi/2), and strictly greater than any larger lower bound listed on https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/11a.html at verification time. This would show C_11a > sqrt(pi/2).
targets.verification_method: Evaluate f on all 2^n points (or via exact multinomial sums for block-structured f), compute E|f - Ef| exactly in rationals, enclose each |grad f|(x) = sqrt(sum_j D_j f(x)^2) by outward-rounded intervals, sum, and compare the certified lower end of the ratio with sqrt(pi/2). Calibrate on n = 1 (f = x gives ratio 1) and on majority functions.
angles: Functions of two or three block sums (e.g. g(S_A, S_B)) keep exact evaluation cheap at large n while leaving room for non-Gaussian behaviour; symmetric g(S/sqrt n) of erf shape approach sqrt(pi/2) only from below (about 1.039 at n=101, 1.134 at n=1001, 1.193 at n=10001).

Use ILvHV's dual problem as a filter: ratio(f) <= C_dual,n = sup over |g| <= 1 of the sup-norm of the integral of grad P_t g, which in Fourier terms is sum over S containing j of g^(S)/|S| chi_S. Before searching for f at dimension n, look for a g whose dual value at n exceeds sqrt(pi/2); without one, no f at that n can win.
pitfalls: The gradient uses D_j f = (f(x) - f(x^(j)))/2, not the unhalved difference; a factor 2 error flips the comparison.
Ratios computed in floating point near sqrt(pi/2) are not certificates; the comparison must be certified.

Small n cannot win. ILvHV (arXiv:1811.05584, sections 2 and 12) show that E|f-Ef|/E|grad f| <= C_dual,n in each dimension. They find C_dual,n constant for n = 2..7 (optimizer min(x1,x2), value 3*sqrt(2)/4, about 1.0607) and growing slowly after that, reaching sqrt(pi/2) only near n = 60-70 by extrapolation. Exhaustive or gradient-free search over 2^n-point tables at n <= 26 is a dead end for the win.

Two- and three-valued symmetric functions stay uniformly below sqrt(pi/2) (ILvHV sections 9-10), and Boolean-valued functions satisfy a sharp L1 Poincare inequality (Durcik-Ivanisvili-Roos-Xie, arXiv:2602.20462, 2026); a winning f must take many values.

targets.name: Pancake numbers: settle P(20), the diameter of the 20-pancake graph (OEIS A058986), now known to lie in {22, 23, 24}
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (exhaustive proof); laptop-hours for a single-stack lower-bound certificate
targets.statement: The pancake number P(n) is the largest number of prefix reversals (flips) needed to sort any stack of n distinct pancakes; equivalently the diameter of the pancake graph on S_n. OEIS A058986 (re-fetched 2026-10-30, revision 185, edited 2026-09-16) lists exact values only for n = 1..19, ending P(18) = 20 and P(19) = 22. Both were proved by Josef Cibulka (arXiv 2009, Theoret. Comput. Sci. 2011), who extended the method of Kounoike, Kaneko and Shinano (n = 14, 15, 2005) and Asai, Kounoike, Shinano and Kaneko (n = 16, 17, PC cluster, 2006): he showed that no 18-stack needs 21 flips, and the two Heydari-Sudborough (1997) stacks of order 19 give P(19) >= 22. His code and data are public. Simon Singh's 2013 blog post later stated the two values, which is how they entered the OEIS entry, and Gerold Jäger and Marcin Peczarski re-confirmed P(19) by branch and bound (OEIS comment, 2020). For n = 20 nothing is listed. J. K. McLean's argument in the entry gives P(20) <= P(19) + 2 = 24, and putting a largest pancake under a hard 19-stack gives P(20) >= 22, so P(20) is 22, 23 or 24. Kazuyuki Amano (IEICE Trans. Inf. & Syst. E108-D(3), 2025) showed that Heydari and Sudborough's stack, built for the (15/14)n lower bound, can be sorted in ceil((15/14)n + 2) flips, so that construction is essentially tight and is not a known source of 20-stacks needing 23 flips. Cibulka's page lists at least 410 stacks of 19 pancakes needing 22 flips (OEIS A067607), but a Cibulka-style proof for n = 20 would have to start from all 19-stacks needing 21 or 22 flips, a set nobody has computed. Deciding P(20), or even showing that one 20-stack needs 23 flips, is new.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) P(20) = 22: a complete, independently re-runnable certificate that every permutation of 20 elements can be sorted in at most 22 prefix reversals (for example a symmetry- and inverse-reduced exhaustive search with released code, logs and per-class counts); or (b) P(20) >= 23: an explicit 20-element stack together with an exhaustive-search certificate (re-runnable within a stated time budget, admissible pruning only) that it cannot be sorted in 22 flips, plus a sorting sequence showing its exact distance; if its distance is 24 that settles P(20) = 24. The value or bound must be strictly new versus the live OEIS A058986 entry and its references re-fetched immediately before claiming, and a novelty check must find no later publication giving P(20).

partial_wins.statement: The exact value of A067607(18), the number of 18-pancake stacks needing exactly 20 flips (the live entry gives only a(18) >= 12,357,059, from Cibulka's webpage), with a reproducible enumeration and released code, provided the live entry still lists no exact a(18) at claim time.

The exact value of A067607(19), the number of 19-pancake stacks needing exactly 22 flips (the live entry gives only a(19) >= 410), with the complete list released and every listed stack's distance certified by an exact solver with a proved-admissible bound, provided the live entry still lists no exact a(19) at claim time.

targets.verification_method: For a stack claim: apply the flips with a ten-line checker; rerun the released exact solver (IDA* or bidirectional search with a gap-type heuristic proved admissible) and confirm it exhausts depth 22 with no solution, matching node counts. For an upper-bound certificate: rerun the released exhaustive search on a sample of classes and check the reduction argument (inverse and symmetry classes) on paper.
angles: Start from Heydari and Sudborough's hard stacks and Amano's 2024 analysis; search their 20-element extensions for one whose exact distance is 23.
The gap heuristic (number of non-adjacent neighbours) is admissible and very strong on random stacks; hard stacks are the ones with few gaps, so target that region with exact search.
For the upper bound, combine the inverse map (a stack and its inverse have equal distance) with the reduction that only stacks needing many flips after the largest pancake is placed need deep search.
pitfalls: Do not confuse P(n) with the burnt pancake numbers (A078941, A078942) or with sorting by unrestricted reversals.
A heuristic that is not proved admissible makes any 'needs 23' claim worthless.
Credit P(18) = 20 and P(19) = 22 to Cibulka (2011), not to Simon Singh's blog post, which gave no proof.

When this entry was checked no literature search beyond the OEIS entries, Cibulka's paper and his webpage could be run; re-check arXiv and the live A058986 for 2024-2026 work on P(20) before claiming.

targets.name: Burnt pancake graph diameter g(18) (OEIS A078941): decide 29 or 30
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster for a full proof; laptop-hours for single-stack certificates
targets.statement: g(n) is the largest number of flips needed to sort any stack of n burnt pancakes (signed prefix reversals), the diameter of the burnt pancake graph, OEIS A078941. It differs from T(n) = A078942, the distance of the single stack -I_n = [-1,...,-n] (the bank's burnt-pancake-even-n-exact-flips entry): T(n) <= g(n), and they differ at n = 15, where Josef Cibulka found two stacks (J_15 and Y_15) needing 25 flips against T(15) = 24. A078941 (re-fetched 2026-10-30) lists g(1..17) = 1, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 23, 25, 26, 28. The values up to n = 10 are from Cohen and Blum (1995), g(11) and g(12) are credited to Korf (2008), and g(13)-g(17) are from Cibulka (2009, 2011), added to the entry by Pontus von Brömssen in August 2026. No value is listed for n = 18. The lower side is fixed by T(18) = 29 (A078942, and Cibulka's 2011 table citing Cohen and Blum), so g(18) >= 29, and g(n+1) <= g(n) + 2 (Cohen and Blum) gives g(18) <= 30. So g(18) is 29 or 30. Cibulka also checked that no J_n or Y_n with n <= 20 other than n = 15 beats -I_n, and Bruno Bouzy (SoCS 2016) grew hard stacks one pancake at a time (changing one orientation or adding +n or -n at the bottom, then solving exactly by IDA*) and found none at n = 18 needing more than 29 flips (his hardest were -I_18, Y_18, H_18,4 and J_18). So a stack needing 30 flips, if one exists, is not of these forms. Cibulka settled g(17) = 28 by the bound g(16) + 2 rather than by listing the 17-stacks that need 28 flips. Those stacks are the candidate base for n = 18 under his contraction method (Lemma 10). Deciding g(18) either way is new.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) an explicit signed stack of 18 burnt pancakes with a re-runnable exact-search certificate that it cannot be sorted in 29 flips (an admissible lower bound whose admissibility proof is given, and matching node counts on rerun), plus a 30-flip sorting sequence, which settles g(18) = 30; or (b) a complete, independently re-runnable certificate that every signed 18-stack sorts within 29 flips (for example Cibulka's candidate-set method extended from the 17-stacks needing 28 flips, with released code, logs and per-depth counts), which settles g(18) = 29. The value must be new versus the live OEIS A078941 entry and its references at claim time, and a novelty check must find no later publication giving g(18).

partial_wins.statement: An independent recomputation of g(16) = 26 (no signed 16-stack needs 27 flips) with released code different from Cibulka's, together with the exact number of 16-stacks needing 26 flips, which Cibulka's published tables (counts up to n = 15) do not give.

The complete set, with its size, of signed 17-stacks needing exactly 28 flips, each certified by an exact solver with a proved-admissible bound and released with code, if this set is not published at claim time.

targets.verification_method: Apply the claimed flips with a short checker that reverses the prefix and negates signs. Rerun the released exact solver (with an admissible heuristic whose admissibility proof is given) to confirm that no shorter sequence exists, comparing node counts. For an upper-bound claim, rerun the released exhaustive search and check its symmetry and inverse reductions.
angles: Cibulka's Lemma 10 lets adjacent pancakes be contracted, so every 18-stack needing 30 flips arises from a 17-stack needing at least 28 flips. Computing that set first is the natural route to either answer.

Bidirectional search with a signed-gap heuristic decides the exact flip distance of a single 18-stack on a laptop; use it to screen structured candidates beyond those already tried (-I_18, J_18, Y_18 and Bouzy's H_18,M family and one-step extensions of hard 17-stacks).
pitfalls: T(n) (A078942) and g(n) (A078941) are different sequences; a result about -I_18 belongs to the other bank entry, and T(18) = 29 is already known.
A stack needing 29 flips is not a result: g(18) >= 29 is already known.
Flip conventions (whether flipping the top pancake alone counts) change values; reproduce g(1..12) first.

targets.name: Rectangular sliding-tile puzzles: the first unknown God's numbers of the m x n table (OEIS A151944): 3x6, 2x9, 4x5
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster for an exact diameter (about 3.2e15 states for 3x6 and 2x9); laptop-hours for certified lower bounds
targets.statement: OEIS A151944 tabulates T(m,n), the maximal number of single-tile moves needed to solve the m x n sliding-tile puzzle. The entry (re-fetched 2026-10-30, last edited 2024-06-08) gives data through the seventh antidiagonal plus 1 x 8 = 7 and 2 x 7 = 108, and its example array adds 2 x 8 = 140: the 1 x n and 2 x n values to 2 x 8 (140), 3 x 3 = 31, 3 x 4 = 53, 3 x 5 = 84 and 4 x 4 = 80, from complete breadth-first searches by Richard Korf (JACM 2008, with corrections by Tomas Rokicki, 2011), Anton Kulchitsky and others. The 2 x n row A151943 also ends at n = 8, and Ben Whitmore (2021) gave T(2,n) >= 2n^2 - n. No value is listed for 3 x 6 (equivalently 6 x 3), 2 x 9 or 4 x 5, the first open cells. The square n x n cases are A087725 (the 5 x 5 case is the bank's slide-24-puzzle-lower-bound entry and is excluded here).
targets.success_criterion: For at least one cell of A151944 with m, n >= 2, m != n and no value in the live entry at claim time (3 x 6, 2 x 9 and 4 x 5 being the first): the exact God's number, certified by a complete search whose per-depth position counts sum to (mn)!/2 and which an independent skeptic can rerun or check against a second implementation, together with an explicit antipodal position and its optimal solution. The value must not appear in A151944, A151943 or a later publication found at claim time.

partial_wins.statement: A 2 x 9 position with a certified optimal solution length strictly greater than 153 = 2*9^2 - 9 (Whitmore's general lower bound), certified by an exact IDA* or bidirectional search with an admissible heuristic, giving a new lower bound for T(2,9).

A 3 x 6 position with a certified optimal solution length strictly greater than 84 = T(3,5), giving the first published certified lower bound for T(3,6) above that value, or strictly greater than the best lower bound published for T(3,6) at claim time if one exists.

A rigorous upper bound for T(3,6), T(2,9) or T(4,5) from a phase decomposition in which every phase diameter is computed by complete BFS and the skeptic reproduces each one, strictly below every upper bound for that cell published at claim time and strictly below the naive two-phase bound (the BFS diameter of solving one end column or row, plus the known value of the remaining smaller puzzle: T(2,8) = 140 for 2 x 9, T(3,5) = 84 for 3 x 6, T(4,4) = 80 or T(3,5) = 84 for 4 x 5), which the claim must also compute and report.

targets.verification_method: Check solvability parity, apply the optimal solution, and rerun the optimal solver with independently built pattern databases to confirm no shorter solution. For an exact diameter, rerun the disk-based BFS (or compare against a second implementation) and check the per-depth counts and their total.
angles: Search for hard positions (reflections of the goal, blank-far configurations) and certify them with additive pattern databases; T(2,n) antipodes for n <= 8 show a regular structure worth extrapolating.
Korf's two-bit BFS with the blank position as the outer index keeps memory per slice small; 3 x 6 needs about 0.8 PB of bits in all, so think about symmetry and frontier search before trying.
pitfalls: Single-tile metric only; multi-tile metric values are different.
The goal configuration (blank in a corner) and the orientation (3 x 6 versus 6 x 3 are the same puzzle) must match the OEIS convention.
Kulchitsky's 3 x 4 antipode list in the OEIS file has a known error (noted in the entry).

targets.name: Rubik's Cube, half-turn metric: the exact number of positions at distance 16 (next term of OEIS A080601), or new distance-20 positions
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster for the distance-16 count; laptop-hours per optimal solve for distance-20 hunting
targets.statement: God's number for the 3x3x3 Rubik's Cube in the half-turn metric is 20 (Tomas Rokicki, Herbert Kociemba, Morley Davidson and John Dethridge, 2010), but the full distance distribution is not known. cube20.org (re-fetched 2026-10-30) gives exact counts for distances 0 to 15, the last being 91,365,146,187,124,313 (Rokicki, independently confirmed), and only estimates beyond: about 1.1e18 at 16, 1.2e19 at 17, 2.9e19 at 18, 1.5e18 at 19 and about 490 million at 20. OEIS A080601 (re-fetched the same day) also ends at n = 15, with terms by Jerry Bryan, Rokicki, Kociemba, Thomas Scheunemann, Davidson and Dethridge. The distance-20 list on cube20.org/distance20s holds 102,772,698 known positions as of 25 July 2025 and Rokicki says he is still finding new ones sporadically, so the list is known to be incomplete. The bank's rubiks-cube-qtm-distance-25-26 entry covers the quarter-turn metric; this entry is HTM only.
targets.success_criterion: The exact number of 3x3x3 positions at HTM distance exactly 16 (the next term of A080601), computed by a complete coset enumeration whose per-coset counts are released and reproduced independently, and consistent with the exact counts for distances 0 to 15 and the group order 43,252,003,274,489,856,000. It must be strictly new versus the live A080601 entry and cube20.org at claim time.

partial_wins.statement: A 3x3x3 position whose HTM distance is certified to be exactly 20 by an optimal solver (no solution of length 19 or less, plus a 20-move solution), and which is not in the current htm4.txt list on cube20.org/distance20s, up to the 48 cube symmetries and inversion, checked at claim time. Several new positions count as one partial win per batch.

The exact number of positions at HTM distance 20 within a stated complete set of cosets of Kociemba's subgroup H = <U, D, R2, L2, F2, B2 > , computed by optimal coset solving with released code and per-coset counts and reproduced on a sample by the skeptic, where the solved cosets contain at least one distance-20 position that is not in the current htm4.txt list (up to symmetry and inversion), so the count is not already implied by that list. Cosets with no distance-20 positions, or whose distance-20 positions all appear in htm4.txt, do not count. Families defined by a nontrivial symmetry or antisymmetry do not qualify, since cube20.org/symmetry already gives the distance of every such position.

targets.verification_method: For p1, run an independent optimal solver (for example Kociemba's Cube Explorer optimal mode or a twsearch-based solver) to confirm distance 20, and canonicalize under symmetry and inversion to check absence from htm4.txt. For the main win, rerun a random sample of cosets and check that the per-coset counts sum to the claimed total and match the exact lower-distance counts.
angles: Neighbours of known distance-20 positions and positions with symmetry are rich in new distance-20 positions; Rokicki's own hunting uses such seeds.
For exact counts, the Kociemba subgroup coset method with the prepass trick (described in the SIAM paper) gives per-coset distance tables.
pitfalls: Half-turn metric only; QTM counts are A080602 and belong to the other bank entry.
Positions equal up to symmetry or inversion are not new; canonicalize before comparing with the list.
A heuristic two-phase solver gives upper bounds only; distance 20 needs a proof that 19 moves fail.

targets.name: Peg solitaire on the 9x9 square board: a central-game solution shorter than Alain Maye's 34 moves
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days
targets.statement: On the 81-hole 9x9 square board (orthogonal jumps), the central game starts with only the centre hole empty and must finish with one peg in the centre. A move is one or more consecutive jumps by the same peg. George Bell's peg solitaire site (re-fetched 2026-10-30, page last modified 23 October 2026, 9x9 subpage dated 2015) calls the shortest central-game solution 'currently an open question'. The shortest known solution, 34 moves, was found by hand by Alain Maye in 2004. Bell gives a lower bound of 24 moves, generalizing Robin Merson's 1962 argument for the 6x6 board, and expects the minimum to be around 30 by analogy with the 10x8 board. The odd side length makes the techniques used to settle the 8x8 and 10x8 boards much weaker here. Bell also poses as challenges reaching the board's symmetric 32-loops from single-vacancy starts.
targets.success_criterion: A legal central-game solution on the 9x9 board (centre vacancy to one peg in the centre, orthogonal jumps only) using at most 33 moves, where a move is a maximal run of consecutive jumps by the same peg, verified by a simulator that replays every jump and counts moves. It must be strictly shorter than the best solution on Bell's page at claim time (34 moves as of 2026-10-30).

partial_wins.statement: A single-vacancy-to-single-survivor solution on the 9x9 board that finishes with a 33-sweep or a 32-loop ending at a5 (or a symmetric equivalent), or a machine-checked proof that neither can be reached from any single-vacancy start. Bell's 9x9 page leaves both unresolved; this counts only if the page still lists the question as open at claim time.
A rigorous lower bound of 25 or more moves for the 9x9 central game, either as a written proof whose case analysis is machine-checked, or as an exhaustive-search certificate re-runnable by a skeptic.

targets.verification_method: A short simulator on the 9x9 grid applies each jump (a peg jumps an orthogonally adjacent peg into an empty hole two steps away, removing the jumped peg), checks legality, counts moves as maximal runs of jumps by the same peg, and confirms the start and final states.
angles: Bidirectional or backward search from the finish with pattern-based pruning (Barker and Korf 2012) settled smaller boards; combine it with long-sweep endings, since the board supports sweeps of up to 34 jumps.
Beam search over positions ranked by Bell's position-class and resource counts is a cheap way to look for 30-33 move solutions.
pitfalls: Count moves, not jumps: every central-game solution has 79 jumps, far more than 34 moves.
Diagonal jumps are not allowed on this board.
The finish must be in the centre hole, not anywhere.
Bell proves that no 32-sweep ending at e5 can be reached from a single-vacancy start, so do not target it.

targets.name: Triangular peg solitaire: shorter single-vacancy solutions on Triangle(11) and Triangle(12) (OEIS A127500 bounds 19..28 and 21..29)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: On the triangular board of side n (T(n) = n(n+1)/2 holes, jumps along the three lattice directions), A127500(n) is the length of the shortest solution to any problem that starts with one peg missing and ends with one peg, a move being one or more consecutive jumps by the same peg. George Bell computed the values for n = 4..10: 5, 9, 9, 12, 13, 16, 18. Triangle(10) needs 18 moves, and showing that no 17-move solution exists was the hard part. His page on large triangular boards (last modified 2007) and OEIS A127500 (re-fetched 2026-10-30, unchanged since 2015) give 19 <= a(11) <= 28 and 21 <= a(12) <= 29. The upper bounds are explicit solutions: 28 moves from a4 to a1 on Triangle(11) and 29 moves from e11 to a3 on Triangle(12). Bell writes that a(11) is believed to be 20, 21 or 22, so the known solutions are far from optimal, and his main triangular page (updated 27 April 2025) reports nothing better. A single shorter solution on either board is a strict improvement.
targets.success_criterion: A legal solution on Triangle(11) in at most 27 moves, or on Triangle(12) in at most 28 moves, starting from a single vacancy and ending with a single peg, verified by a simulator; or an exact value of a(11) or a(12) with a re-runnable exhaustive certificate. The result must be strictly better than the bounds in the live OEIS A127500 entry and Bell's triangular page at claim time.

partial_wins.statement: Each further strict improvement of the best known upper bound for a(11) or a(12) beyond the first counts as a partial win once published with its solution.
A lower bound a(11) >= 20 or a(12) >= 22, from an exhaustive search certificate or a machine-checked counting argument.

targets.verification_method: Simulate the solution on a triangular-lattice board: check every jump (along one of the three lattice directions over an adjacent peg into an empty hole), count maximal same-peg runs as moves, and confirm a single starting vacancy and a single final peg.
angles: Bell's solutions for Triangle(9) and Triangle(10) end with long sweeps; design endings with long sweeps for side 11 and 12 and search backward from them.
The problem allows any starting vacancy and any finishing hole, which gives many targets for bidirectional search.
pitfalls: Count moves, not jumps.
Bell's later work may contain better unpublished solutions; check his triangular page and paper versions before claiming.
Triangular boards of some sides have parity or position-class restrictions on which vacancy/finish pairs are solvable; use a solvable pair.

targets.name: Sokoban maximum moves: a board with n floor squares and k boxes whose shortest solution beats the DeStefano-qqwref archive
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Which Sokoban levels with n floor squares (spaces) have the longest shortest solution, measured in player steps? Erich Friedman posed the problem (Problem of the Month, March 2000); Brendan Owen, Philippe Fondanaiche, Trevor Green, John Hoffman and others contributed. Zachary DeStefano and qqwref maintain the Sokoban Max Moves Archive (re-fetched 2026-10-30), a table of best-known move counts for 3 to 32 spaces and 1 to 8 boxes, with proven column maxima in bold and best guesses in italics, and they invite new results. OEIS A195667 (longest game with n spaces, any number of boxes) lists exact values for n = 3..20, ending a(20) = 146 (a(18)-a(20) by DeStefano, 2021); A195668 is the 1-box case. Most archive cells beyond about 20 spaces are best-known values, not proven maxima, so better boards are expected.
targets.success_criterion: A Sokoban level (walls, floor squares, player, boxes, goals; standard rules: the player pushes one box at a time and cannot pull) with exactly n floor squares and k boxes, for a cell (n, k) that the live archive shows in italics (a best guess) at claim time. Its minimum number of player steps to solve, certified by a complete BFS over the level's state space, must be strictly greater than the archive's value for that cell. Cells shown in bold (proven column maxima) or in plain type (computed values) are settled and do not count. Alternatively, an exact column maximum not yet listed (A195667(21) or later), certified by an exhaustive enumeration of all boards with that many spaces that a skeptic can rerun, and not already listed in OEIS or marked proven on the archive.

partial_wins.statement: Each further italic archive cell (n, k) beaten in the same way counts as one more partial win.
A proof by exhaustive search that an italic (best-guess) archive value is optimal for its cell, with released enumeration code.

targets.verification_method: Parse the level in standard .sok format, count floor squares and boxes, and run an independent BFS over (player region, box set) states to compute the exact minimum number of steps; compare with the archive's value for that cell. For exhaustive claims, rerun the released enumeration of polyomino boards with that number of spaces.
angles: The archive lists proved structural facts (maximal boards have at least two cycles, no bent arms); use them to prune a search over polyomino shapes, then optimize box and goal placement with exact BFS.
Hill-climb over board shapes with an exact BFS evaluator; small boards make each evaluation fast.
pitfalls: The archive counts player steps (moves), not pushes; Friedman's page also discusses pushes separately.
Spaces means all non-wall squares, including those under the player, boxes and goals.
The archive's rows start at different space counts; align columns carefully before comparing values.

targets.name: Generalized repunits (b^p-1)/(b-1): a first (probable) prime for one of the 26 bases b <= 1024 with none known (smallest: b = 185)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days per base for most bases (just above the published limits candidates have roughly 55 000 to 155 000 digits; one gwnum-based PRP test takes minutes to an hour); b = 185 above p = 350 000 means candidates of about 800 000 digits, which is cluster scale
targets.statement: For a base b that is not a perfect power, the generalized repunit conjecture predicts infinitely many primes (b^p-1)/(b-1) with p prime. Several bases still have no known prime or PRP at all. Richard Fischer's table (GenRepu.txt, 30.09.2026) shows every base <= 200 except 185 has one, and that (185^p-1)/184 is composite for all p < 350000. The public Google Docs table 'Smallest odd prime p such that (b^p-1)/(b-1) and (b^p+1)/(b+1) is prime for bases 2<=b<=1024' (linked from Wikipedia's Repunit article; the OEIS A084740 links credit Eric Chen with these base tables) lists 41 positive bases with no known PRP. Its search limits are 66337 for b=185, 63659 for 269, 63421 for 281, 50000 for 301-400, 30000 for 401-512 and 19001 for 513-1024. That list is stale. Norman Luhn's live table of generalized repunit PRPs with at least 1000 digits (TableRepunitGen, updated 29 Oct 2026) now has PRPs for 15 of those bases, found by Michael Stocker (2020), Jinyuan Wang (2023-24), Serge Batalov and Tom Wu. Examples: b=485 at p=99523 and b=1005 at p=89087. On 2026-10-30 these 26 bases have no known PRP: 185, 269, 281, 380, 384, 385, 396, 452, 465, 511, 574, 598, 601, 631, 632, 636, 711, 759, 771, 795, 866, 881, 938, 951, 956, 1015.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a base b from the 26 listed in the statement and a prime p such that N = (b^p-1)/(b-1) is a probable prime. N must pass a strong Fermat test to base 3 and a BPSW test (strong base 2 plus strong Lucas), rerun independently. At claim time b must still have no entry on Luhn's live TableRepunitGen (https://pzktupel.de/Primetables/TableRepunitGen.php, re-fetched), in Fischer's GenRepu.txt or in the OEIS A084740 data or b-file. p must be larger than every published search limit for b: 350000 for b=185 (Fischer), otherwise the Google Doc limit. A primality proof is not required: every source table accepts PRPs. Each base that leaves the no-PRP list counts (direction: min on the number of bases <= 1024 with no known PRP, 26 on 2026-10-30).

partial_wins.statement: Search-range certificate for one listed base: every prime p from that base's published limit up to at least 1.5 times the limit sieved and PRP-tested with no hit. The sieve file, the factors that remove each candidate and the PRP residues are saved, so a verifier can recheck the factors of a random 2% of removed candidates and retest a random 2% of the survivors.

targets.verification_method: Recompute N exactly and confirm that p is prime and b is on the list. Run PFGW (Fermat base 3) and PARI/GP ispseudoprime (BPSW) on the verifier's own install. Check that b is absent from the live Luhn, Fischer and OEIS sources and that p exceeds the published limit. Spot-check sieve factors: any prime factor q of N satisfies q = 1 (mod 2p).
angles: Sieve all 26 bases together over prime exponents. Any factor q of (b^p-1)/(b-1) is 1 mod 2p, so trial factoring by 2kp+1 is cheap and removes most candidates.

Rank bases by expected primes per CPU-hour. The heuristic count of primes per base between exponents x and y is about e^gamma*ln(y/x)/ln(b), so small b near 300-400 with low published limits pay best.
Use gwnum-based PRP testing with Gerbicz error checks (PRST or PFGW) so that a hardware fault never yields a false PRP at 100 000+ digits.
pitfalls: The Google Doc's no-prime list is out of date: 15 of its positive bases have PRPs in Luhn's table. Always check Luhn's table first.
Published search limits are lower bounds. Jinyuan Wang, Michael Stocker and others searched well past the Doc's limits without always publishing them, so a 'new' PRP may already be known unreported.
Perfect-power bases (and composite p) give algebraic factors and can never count.

Base 598 was on both of the Doc's lists, but the negative-base form is solved ((598^32077+1)/599, Jinyuan Wang, May 2024). Only (598^p-1)/597 is still open, and it is a different number from the base -598 repunit.

targets.name: Generalized Wagstaff / negative-base repunits (b^p+1)/(b+1): a first (probable) prime for one of the 41 bases b <= 1024 with none known (smallest: b = 97)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days per base (candidates of roughly 40 000 to 300 000 digits; b = 97 needs exponents above 800 000, so that base alone is cluster scale)
targets.statement: (b^p+1)/(b+1) is the base -b repunit. The conjecture predicts infinitely many primes for every b that is not a perfect odd power (b = m^r with r odd > 1) and not of the form 4k^4; those excluded bases have algebraic factorisations. OEIS A084742 records that a(97) > 800000 (Wang Runsen, May 2023), and Richard Fischer's GenRepuP.txt (05.10.2026) also gives ( > 800000) for b = 97. The Google Docs base table linked from Wikipedia's Repunit article lists 54 bases <= 1024 with no known PRP. Its limits are 59863 for 97, 59509 for 103, 59021 for 113, 50000 for 161-400, 30000 for 401-512 and 17327 for 513-1024. That list is stale: Norman Luhn's live generalized Wagstaff table (TableWagstaffGen, 1385 entries of at least 1000 digits, updated 26 Oct 2026) has PRPs found by Jinyuan Wang in 2024 for 13 of them (445, 498, 557, 592, 598, 624, 717, 730, 873, 923, 944, 996, 1004). On 2026-10-30 these 41 bases have no known PRP: 97, 103, 113, 186, 187, 220, 304, 306, 309, 335, 414, 416, 428, 433, 459, 486, 539, 550, 587, 597, 617, 637, 659, 665, 671, 677, 696, 726, 740, 754, 766, 790, 851, 890, 914, 929, 943, 965, 984, 985, 1005.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a base b from the 41 listed in the statement and a prime p such that N = (b^p+1)/(b+1) passes a strong Fermat test to base 3 and a BPSW test, rerun independently. At claim time b must still have no entry on Luhn's live TableWagstaffGen (https://pzktupel.de/Primetables/TableWagstaffGen.php, re-fetched), in Fischer's GenRepuP.txt or in OEIS A084742. p must exceed every published limit for b: 800000 for b=97, otherwise the Google Doc limit. A PRP suffices, as in all the source tables. Each base that leaves the list counts (direction: min on the count of bases <= 1024 with no known PRP, 41 on 2026-10-30).

partial_wins.statement: Search-range certificate for one listed base other than 97: every prime p from the published limit up to at least 1.5 times the limit sieved and PRP-tested with no hit. The sieve file and PRP residues are saved so a verifier can retest a random 2% of survivors and recheck the removing factors of a random 2% of removed candidates.

targets.verification_method: Recompute N, confirm that p is prime and b is listed. Run PFGW Fermat base 3 and PARI/GP ispseudoprime on the verifier's own install. Confirm b is absent from Luhn's live table, Fischer's file and OEIS A084742, and that p exceeds the stated limit. Any prime factor q of N satisfies q = 1 (mod 2p).
angles: Skip b = 97 (above 800 000, about 1.6 million digits per candidate). The bases 161-512 at limits of 30 000-50 000 are the cheapest per expected prime.
Sieve many bases at once using q = 1 mod 2p, then PRP-test in increasing p so each base stops at its first hit.
pitfalls: The Doc lists 97, 103 and 113 with limits near 60 000, but Fischer and OEIS give 800 000 for 97. Use the maximum over all sources.
13 bases on the Doc's list already have PRPs (Jinyuan Wang 2024). Check Luhn's table first.
Bases of the form 4k^4 (324, 1024) and odd perfect powers have algebraic factorisations and are excluded.
Do not confuse (b^p+1)/(b+1) with the positive-base repunit target.

targets.name: Prove a listed PRP prime in Luhn's generalized repunit, generalized Wagstaff or generalized Mersenne tables (at least 10 000 digits)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (ECPP of a 10 000-digit number takes a few CPU-days with CM or Primo; the 3 500-6 000-digit entries take hours)
targets.statement: Norman Luhn's tables list every known (probable) prime of at least 1000 digits of three forms, each marked Prime or PRP from its factordb or PrimePages status. (b^n-1)/(b-1) has 3873 entries, 3069 of them PRP (updated 29 Oct 2026). (b^n+1)/(b+1) has 1385 entries, 767 PRP (26 Oct 2026). b^n-(b-1)^n has 4335 entries, 1750 PRP (29 Oct 2026). The smallest PRPs are recent finds by Richard Fischer: 638^1237-637^1237 (3470 digits, Jul 2026), (506^1433+1)/507 (3873 digits, Jul 2026) and (1004^1951-1)/1003 (5854 digits, Aug 2026). Among the smallest PRPs of at least 10 000 digits are (4813^2719-1)/4812 (10009 digits, Bernardo Boncompagni, 2010), (172^4483+1)/173 (10020 digits, 2000) and 19365^2333-19364^2333 (10001 digits, Lelio R Paula, 2008). The base-3 repunits (3^49681-1)/2 (23704 digits) and (3^57917-1)/2 (27634 digits) have been PRPs since Henri Lifchitz found them in 2003. The largest proven entries reach 141416 digits ((124750^27751-1)/124749, Tom Wu, CM). Credit goes to Luhn (tables), Fischer, Andy Steward, Tom Wu, Boncompagni, Lifchitz and the provers.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a number with at least 10 000 digits that is marked PRP on one of the three live Luhn tables (TableRepunitGen.php, TableWagstaffGen.php, TableMersenneGen.php, re-fetched immediately before the claim). The claim needs a complete primality certificate for exactly that number that an independent verifier checks as valid: a Primo certificate, a CM or PARI/GP ECPP certificate, or an N-1/N+1 (Pocklington/BLS/Coppersmith-Howgrave-Graham) proof whose factored part has every prime factor proven. Each newly proven entry counts (direction: min on the number of PRP entries of at least 10 000 digits).

partial_wins.statement: A verified primality certificate for any entry marked PRP on one of the three live tables, of any size (the smallest is 3470 digits).

targets.verification_method: Rebuild N from the expression and compare it with the certificate's N. Check Primo certificates with an independent Primo-certificate verifier, PARI/GP certificates with primecertisvalid, and CM certificates with CM's checker. For N-1/N+1 proofs rerun PFGW -tp/-tm with the factor helper file, or Broadhurst's chgcertd.gp for CHG, on the verifier's own install. Confirm the entry is still PRP on the live table.
angles: For (b^n-1)/(b-1) with n prime, N-1 = b(b^(n-1)-1)/(b-1) splits into cyclotomic pieces Phi_d(b), d | n-1. Pick entries where n-1 is smooth and the small Phi_d(b) are fully factored (Cunningham-style tables). Then a BLS (1/3) or CHG (about 30%) proof replaces ECPP.
For b^n-(b-1)^n and Wagstaff-type entries, N-1 or N+1 rarely factor well, so plan on ECPP: CM (Enge's FastECPP) scales better than Primo above 10 000 digits.
Sort the 1666 generalized repunit PRPs of 10 000-20 000 digits by size and start with the smallest.
pitfalls: Luhn takes the status from factordb, which can lag: someone else may already have uploaded a certificate. Check factordb (in a browser) before spending CPU-days. Uploading a certificate to factordb is an action for the human.
A certificate for (b^n-1) or b^n+1 instead of the divided form, or for the wrong n, is worthless. Compare N digit by digit.
A PRP test, however strong, is not a proof.
The proven-versus-PRP marks also cover numbers of 1000-3470 digits found earlier. Only entries currently marked PRP count.

targets.name: Leyland primes: prove the smallest unproven Leyland PRP (x^y+y^x: 13 749 digits; x^y-y^x: 10 483 digits)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (ECPP of a 10 000-14 000-digit number with no useful N-1/N+1 structure; CM or Primo)
targets.statement: Leyland numbers of the first kind are x^y+y^x with 1 < x < y, and of the second kind x^y-y^x. Their N-1 and N+1 do not factor usefully, so large ones can only be proven by ECPP. Norman Luhn's tables number every known Leyland (probable) prime and mark each Prime or PRP. The first-kind table (updated 06 Oct 2026) has 2853 entries, 416 proven. Every first-kind Leyland prime below 13 749 digits is proven, up to the 379th, 471^5140+5140^471 (13740 digits).
