The 380th, 2133^4130+4130^2133 (13749 digits, found by Paul Leyland in May 2002), is the smallest still only PRP. The second-kind table (27 Oct 2026) has 3675 entries, 726 proven. The first 692 are proven, and the 693rd, 1635^3262-3262^1635 (10483 digits, Norbert Schneider, 2011), is the smallest PRP. The largest proven first-kind entry is 5^104824+104824^5 (73269 digits): Andrey Kulsha found it as a PRP in 2010, and its ECPP proof (Feb 2023) is #3 on the PrimePages ECPP top-20. Credit goes to Paul Leyland, Andrey Kulsha, Norbert Schneider, Henri Lifchitz, Mark Rodenkirch, Hans Havermann (OEIS A094133) and Luhn.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a complete, independently verified primality certificate (Primo, CM or PARI/GP ECPP) for the Leyland number that is the smallest-digit entry still marked PRP on the live Luhn table of its kind (https://pzktupel.de/Primetables/TableLeyland1.php or TableLeyland2.php, re-fetched immediately before the claim; on 2026-10-30 these are 2133^4130+4130^2133 and 1635^3262-3262^1635). This advances the contiguous proven range of that kind (direction: max on the number of smallest Leyland primes all proven: 379 for the first kind, 692 for the second).

partial_wins.statement: A verified certificate for any other entry marked PRP on either live Leyland table with fewer than 20 000 digits (117 first-kind and 348 second-kind PRPs above the current boundary entries and below 20 000 digits on 2026-10-30).
A verified certificate for any entry marked PRP on either live Leyland table with at least 20 000 digits.

targets.verification_method: Recompute N = x^y +/- y^x and compare it with the certificate's N. Verify the certificate with an independent checker (PARI/GP primecertisvalid, CM's checker, or a Primo-certificate verifier) on the verifier's own install. Confirm on the live table that the entry is marked PRP and is the smallest PRP of its kind for the full win.
angles: CM (FastECPP) on all cores: at about 10 000-14 000 digits expect a few to a few tens of CPU-days.

Do the second-kind boundary entry first: at 10 483 digits it is about 3 times cheaper than the 13 749-digit first-kind one, since ECPP cost grows roughly with the fourth power of the digit count ((13749/10483)^4 = 2.96).
pitfalls: Proofs here go in size order, which suggests an organised effort. Look for a reservation thread on mersenneforum and avoid duplicating a claimed number.
Luhn mirrors factordb status. A certificate may already be uploaded but not yet reflected, so check factordb in a browser before starting.
x^y-y^x with y > x is a different list from x^y+y^x. The boundary entries differ.
Over-reliance on Primo's own 'verified' message: the verifier should use an independent checker.

targets.name: Near-repdigit-related sequences with no known prime (Kamada): 298...89, 25...567, 45...529, 54...427, 454...41
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (candidates of 50 000 to 200 000 digits; PFGW PRP tests of minutes each)
targets.statement: Makoto Kamada (STUDIO KAMADA) tracks primes in more than 4600 near-repdigit-related decimal sequences. The 'Number of prime numbers in each near-repdigit-related sequence' table was last updated on 2 Aug 2026. Most sequences without a prime are either provably prime-free (covering sets or algebraic factors, marked 'not exist') or are of the form k*10^n+-1, which is Riesel/Sierpinski base-10 territory. Exactly five other sequences are marked '(not found)', with no known (probable) prime. 298w9 = (269*10^(w+1)+1)/9 (2989, 29889, ...) has been searched to n <= 100000. Four have been searched to n <= 50000: 25w67 = (23*10^(w+2)+103)/9, 45w29 = (41*10^(w+2)-239)/9, 54w27 = (49*10^(w+2)-157)/9 and 454w1 = (409*10^(w+1)-31)/9. Here n is Kamada's index (n = w+1 or w+2), so the term has about n digits. None of the five is in Kamada's list of reserved ranges (which on 2026-10-30 holds 31w, 919w and 949w only).
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for one of the five sequences and an integer w such that the term (formula as listed) has index n strictly above the searched range on the live table (https://stdkmd.net/nrr/prime/prime_sequences.htm, re-fetched; the sequence must still show count 0 and '(not found)'), and the term passes a strong Fermat test to base 3 and a BPSW test, rerun independently. A PRP suffices: Kamada's lists record PRPs and proofs separately. Each sequence that gets its first (probable) prime counts (direction: min on the number of such sequences, 5 on 2026-10-30).

partial_wins.statement: Range certificate: one of the five sequences sieved and PRP-tested with no hit from its listed limit to at least twice that limit (n <= 100000 for the four 50000 sequences, n <= 200000 for 298w9). The sieve file and PRP residues are saved for a verifier's 2% random retest.

targets.verification_method: Recompute the term from the formula for the claimed w and check the n index. Run PFGW Fermat base 3 plus PARI/GP ispseudoprime on the verifier's own install. For p1, retest a random 2% of the sieve survivors and recheck the removing factors of a random 2% of the removed candidates.
angles: Each sequence is (a*10^m + c)/9, so 9*term = a*10^m + c is a k*b^n+c form. Sieve 9*term with srsieve2/mtsieve (k*10^m+c), then PRP-test the survivors divided by 9.
Before searching, compute small-prime periods to see why these five are so sparse (near-covering sets), and rank the five by expected primes per CPU-hour from their sieve survival rates.
pitfalls: Index n is not w: check the n = w+1 or n = w+2 convention for each sequence.
Kamada's 'pr' status flags are not complete proof records. They do not matter here: a PRP is the win.
The many k*10^n+-1 sequences with no prime on the same page (for example 4421*10^n-1) mostly duplicate the Conjectures 'R Us base-10 Riesel/Sierpinski work and are not part of this target.

targets.name: MOONSHOT: an ECPP proof of a famous probable prime: Wagstaff (2^267017+1)/3, Lucas L(344293) or Fibonacci F(397379)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (tens of CPU-years: the 109 297-digit repunit proof took about 220 CPU-years)
targets.statement: ECPP is the only general proof method for numbers without useful N+-1 structure. The record is R(109297) (109297 digits), proven by Andreas Enge and Paul Underwood with Enge's CM software (May 2025), after R(86453) (May 2023) and R(49081) (Mar 2022). Enge's write-up puts the next repunit, R(270343), about 37 times further out of reach. Other famous families have a smallest unproven PRP of 70 000-85 000 digits. The PrimePages Wagstaff record table lists proven (2^p+1)/3 up to p = 141079 (Oct 2025), and (2^267017+1)/3 (80380 digits) is the smallest Wagstaff PRP without a proof. The Lucas-number table's largest proven is L(202667) (Nov 2023), and the next Lucas index in OEIS A001606 is 344293 (71953 digits). The Fibonacci table's largest proven is F(201107) (Sep 2023), and F(397379) (83047 digits, in OEIS A001605 since 2003) is the next PRP. On 2026-10-30 the 20th entry of the PrimePages ECPP top-20 has 45428 digits.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a complete ECPP (or other) primality certificate, checked by an independent verifier, for one of (2^267017+1)/3, L(344293) or F(397379), provided that number is not yet listed as proven on the live PrimePages Wagstaff, Lucas Number or Fibonacci Number top-20 pages (https://t5k.org/top20/page.php?id=67, id=48, id=39) or the ECPP top-20 (id=27) at claim time.

partial_wins.statement: A verified ECPP certificate for any number not already listed that has more digits than the 20th entry of the live PrimePages ECPP top-20 (45428 digits on 2026-10-30), so that it would enter that table.

targets.verification_method: Rebuild N from its definition (Wagstaff formula, or the Lucas/Fibonacci recurrence by fast doubling). Verify the certificate with an independent implementation (PARI/GP primecertisvalid for PARI-format certificates, or CM's checker). For the R(86453) record, verification took about 190 CPU-days (almost two days of real time on many cores), so budget accordingly. Confirm the number is not yet in the live tables.
angles: Use FastECPP (CM) with a gwnum-linked arithmetic backend, as Underwood did for R(109297). Phase 1 (the curve chain) and phase 2 (CM curve construction) can run in parallel on different machines.
Pick the smallest candidate: L(344293) at 71953 digits needs roughly 0.6 times the work of the 80380-digit Wagstaff number, since ECPP cost grows roughly with the fourth power of the digit count.
pitfalls: Enge and others publish these runs only at the end. A 21-month effort may already be under way, so ask around (a human action) before committing a cluster.
A probable-prime test or a partial certificate chain is not a proof.
Primes of 45 000+ digits that are provable by N-1/N+1 tests do not enter the ECPP table.

targets.name: Numerical semigroups: the next exact count by genus (n_81, OEIS A007323) or by Frobenius number (N_133, OEIS A124506)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (n_81: about 1.6 x the 231,300 core-hours Bras-Amoros and Torra spent on n_80; N_133 is far cheaper but still roughly double N_131, which took almost 115 hours in their cluster runs)
targets.statement: n_g counts the numerical semigroups of genus g (OEIS A007323). N_F counts those with Frobenius number F (A124506). Maria Bras-Amoros and Vicenc Torra (arXiv 2607.23111, v3 10 Sep 2026) ran the seeds algorithm on genus- and Frobenius-leaf-discriminating trees, which are pruned so that their leaves are exactly the objects counted. They obtained n_78, n_79 and n_80 = 199583757387067387, using 231,300 core-hours on the Kebnekaise and Tetralith clusters. They also got N_F for every F <= 132 (N_132 = 92876546429911575576; N_131 took about 115 hours) and irreducible-semigroup counts up to F = 132. They prove a closed formula for the semigroups with m >= (F+1)/3, so only small-multiplicity nodes need exploring. Earlier records: Fromentin and Hivert (to 70, github hivert/NumericMonoid), Fernandez-Gonzalez and Bras-Amoros (71-72), Delgado, Eliahou and Fromentin (73-75, 2023), and Bras-Amoros's unleaved tree (76-77, 2025). Martin Fuller computed A124506 terms 40-100. Both OEIS b-files, re-fetched 2026-10-30, stop at g = 80 and F = 132. A new term also extends the checked range of Bras-Amoros's conjectured Fibonacci-like growth n_g >= n_{g-1} + n_{g-2}. The same holds for monotonicity n_{g+1} >= n_g, which Zhai proved only for large g.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact value of A007323(81) or A124506(133), or a later term: the first index beyond the live b-file, re-fetched immediately before claiming. Two independent methods or independently written codes must agree exactly, for example a seeds/leaf-discriminating-tree count against a Kunz-coordinate or Fromentin-Hivert decomposition count. The code must reproduce every published term for g <= 60 (resp. F <= 110) and the Bras-Amoros-Torra per-multiplicity decomposition wherever they publish it. The per-work-unit counts (split by multiplicity and first jumps) must be published so a skeptic can recompute random units. A literature search must find no earlier value.

partial_wins.statement: The number of irreducible numerical semigroups with Frobenius number 133 (OEIS A158206; Bras-Amoros and Torra 2026 report them through F = 132). Because 133 is odd, these are exactly the symmetric numerical semigroups with F = 133 (genus 67). The value must come from code that reproduces the published A158206 values for a contiguous range of F ending at 132, and a second, independently written code using a different method (for example a direct enumeration of symmetric semigroups through Kunz coordinates or Apery sets) must agree exactly.

An independent recomputation of n_78, n_79 or n_80 by a different algorithm and code, agreeing exactly with Bras-Amoros and Torra's value (each of these terms has a single published computation). A confirmed discrepancy would be a major finding and needs a third run.

targets.verification_method: Rerun the claimant's code for small g/F (seconds to minutes) and compare with the b-files. Recompute a random sample of the published work units (multiplicity / first-jumps splits) with independent code and check that the partial sums match. Sum the units and compare with the claim. Check the Bras-Amoros-Torra closed formula for the m >= (F+1)/3 part independently.
angles: Count the m >= (F+1)/3 part by the Bras-Amoros-Torra formula and enumerate only the small-multiplicity remainder; the Frobenius tree explores about 0.03% of the full tree.
Use Fromentin-Hivert's SIMD decomposition representation with 192/256-bit gap masks (the 64-bit limit is what stopped earlier codes).
Kunz-coordinate counting (Bernardini; Kaplan) for fixed multiplicity as an independent second method on low-multiplicity slices.
pitfalls: Offsets: A007323 starts at g = 0, while A124506 starts at F = 1 and counts by Frobenius number, not genus.
Bitset width: genus above 64 overflows 64-bit gap masks silently.
Cluster-scale runs need checkpointed, independently checkable work units; an unsplit single total cannot be spot-checked.

targets.name: Wilf's conjecture on numerical semigroups: extend the computer verification beyond genus 100, or find a counterexample
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (the genus-100 run used up to 1500 cores for two weeks); smarter trimming may bring a few extra genera within laptop-days
targets.statement: Wilf's conjecture (1978) says that every numerical semigroup S with conductor c, embedding dimension e and genus g satisfies e(c - g) >= c. Manuel Delgado, Shalom Eliahou and Jean Fromentin (arXiv 2310.07742, 2023; published in J. Algebra) verified it for every semigroup of genus g <= 100; the previous record was g <= 66 (Maria Bras-Amorós, 2023), after g <= 65 (Bras-Amorós and Rodríguez, 2021), g <= 60 (Fromentin and Hivert, 2016) and g <= 50 (Bras-Amorós). They combined three things: Eliahou's 2020 theorem settling the case e >= m/3; trimming the tree of numerical semigroups of subtrees that cannot hold a counterexample (the trimmed tree T_100(3) has about 4.5e15 nodes, with per-genus counts t_g published in Section 5.1); and a parallel exploration on up to 1500 cores of the CALCULCO platform over two weeks in summer 2023 (code: github.com/jfromentin/trim_tree_semigroups). For semigroups with m dividing c they reached g <= 120. Later results add sufficient conditions but do not extend the exhaustive range. Delgado, Kumar and Marion (arXiv 2501.04417, v3 1 Oct 2026) show that Wilf holds when |S n (m, 2m)| >= sqrt(2m) and for almost all semigroups with large maximum primitive. Delgado's 2026 IMNS overview still names the genus-100 verification as the strongest published result, and reports that all semigroups with Frobenius number <= 111 or maximum primitive <= 100 are Wilf. Bras-Amoros and Torra (arXiv 2607.23111, v3 10 Sep 2026) count semigroups up to genus 80 with a seeds-based tree but do not extend the Wilf verification. The conjecture is open and no counterexample is known.
targets.success_criterion: Success means EITHER (a) an explicit numerical semigroup, given by minimal generators, with e(c - g) < c, confirmed by two independent exact checkers (for example GAP NumericalSgps and an independent Apery-set computation); OR (b) a computer verification that every numerical semigroup of genus g <= G satisfies Wilf's inequality, for some G >= 101. Option (b) requires: published code; every trimming rule justified by a cited theorem whose statement is reproduced; per-genus node counts from a run of the same code with G = 100 (the trimmed tree T_G(3) depends on G), truncated at some genus >= 66, that exactly reproduce Delgado-Eliahou-Fromentin's published t_g table for T_100(3) (Section 5.1 of arXiv 2310.07742) up to that genus; and an independent re-run of at least a random 5% of the work units with separately written code, agreeing exactly. In both cases a literature search immediately before claiming must find no earlier counterexample or published verification beyond genus 100.

partial_wins.statement: Verification of Wilf's conjecture for all numerical semigroups with m dividing c up to genus G >= 121 (Delgado-Eliahou-Fromentin reached 120), to the same evidence standard as option (b).
An independent re-verification of the genus <= 100 result with code written from scratch, reproducing the published per-genus counts of the trimmed tree.

targets.verification_method: Counterexample: compute the Apery set, the conductor, the genus and the minimal generators exactly, then check the inequality (seconds). Verification run: rebuild the trimmed tree to small genus and compare node counts with the published table; recompute random work units with independent code; check each pruning rule against the cited theorem.
angles: Add the new Delgado-Kumar-Marion sufficient condition (|S n (m,2m)| >= sqrt(2m)) as an extra pruning rule; it was proved after the 2023 run.
Port the Bras-Amoros-Torra seeds/leaf-discriminating tree (which descends only three levels above the leaves) to the Wilf-trimmed tree.
pitfalls: Embedding dimension means the number of minimal generators, not of all small elements.
A pruning rule needs a theorem behind it; a heuristic prune voids the verification.
Gaps can be as large as 2g - 1, so 64-bit gap masks overflow from genus 33 on; codes in the Fromentin-Hivert style need wider (for example SIMD) representations.

targets.name: Semigroups of order 10 up to isomorphism (OEIS A027851(10)), equivalently the self-converse semigroups of order 10, or the labeled count A023814(10)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster for the full win (likely a large constraint-solver run on the non-nilpotent order-10 semigroups); the monoid, band and inverse-semigroup partial wins look laptop-days
targets.statement: Andreas Distler, Chris Jefferson, Tom Kelsey and Lars Kotthoff (CP 2012) counted the semigroups of order 10 up to isomorphism or anti-isomorphism: A001423(10) = 12,418,001,077,381,302,684. They combined a constraint search for the semigroups that are not nilpotent of degree 3 with Distler and Mitchell's formulas for the degree-3 nilpotent ones (EJC 19(2) P51, 2012). Those formulas count up to equality, up to isomorphism, and up to isomorphism or anti-isomorphism. The count up to isomorphism alone, A027851(10) = 2*A001423(10) - A029851(10), is still missing because nobody has counted the self-converse semigroups of order 10 (A029851 stops at a(9) = 623,492,664, Distler 2011). The labeled count (associative operations on a 10-set, A023814) also stops at n = 9; it came from Distler and Kelsey's automorphism-group census (arXiv 1301.6023). For monoids, A058133(10) = 52,991,253,973,742 is known up to iso or anti-iso (Distler-Kelsey 2009). Self-converse monoids A058132 reached n = 9 only in Sep 2026 (Ben Spitz), and A058129 (monoids up to isomorphism) stops at a(9) = 3,685,886,630 (Cruttwell and Leblanc, added 2025). Related census entries: bands A058112 are known to n = 9 (Andrew Howroyd 2022), and inverse semigroups A001428 to n = 15 (Martin Malandro, Semigroup Forum 2019). All entries were re-fetched 2026-10-30.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact value of A027851(10) (equivalently A029851(10)) or of A023814(10), re-fetched live and still missing immediately before claiming. The degree-3-nilpotent part must come from the Distler-Mitchell formulas, evaluated by two independent implementations that reproduce their published small values. The remaining part must come from a published search code that reproduces A029851(n) (resp. A023814(n)) for every n <= 9. A second independent method or code must agree on the non-nilpotent part, for example a constraint search for semigroups admitting an anti-automorphism versus a filter over a full enumeration. A literature search must find no earlier value.

partial_wins.statement: A058129(10), the number of monoids of order 10 up to isomorphism, obtained via A058132(10) = 2*A058133(10) - A058129(10). The pipeline must reproduce A058129(n), A058132(n) and A058133(n) for n <= 9 and A058133(10) = 52,991,253,973,742.
A058112(10), the number of bands (idempotent semigroups) of order 10, by code reproducing a(n) for n <= 9 and a second independent method agreeing.
A001428(16), the number of inverse semigroups of order 16 up to isomorphism or anti-isomorphism, by code reproducing Malandro's values for n <= 15 and a second independent method agreeing.

targets.verification_method: Re-evaluate the Distler-Mitchell formulas independently. Rerun the search code for n <= 9 against OEIS. For the new term, recompute a random sample of the search's work units (for example by fixed idempotent structure or minimal ideal) with independent code and compare the partial sums.
angles: Search directly for order-10 semigroups together with an anti-automorphism (an involutive or finite-order bijection reversing products) as part of the constraint model; this space is far smaller than all non-nilpotent semigroups.
Monoids with trivial group of units correspond to semigroups of order n-1 with an identity adjoined, so A058129(10) needs new search work only for monoids with nontrivial units.
pitfalls: Up to isomorphism (A027851) and up to iso or anti-iso (A001423) are different counts; check which one each formula gives.
OEIS offsets: these entries start at n = 0 except A001428, which starts at n = 1.
Nilpotent semigroups of degree 3 dominate the totals; a bug in the formula part swamps everything else.

targets.name: Count the rings of order 32: the smallest unknown value of OEIS A027623 (only a(32) > 18,590 is known)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days
targets.statement: A027623 counts the rings with n elements: associative and distributive, not necessarily unital or commutative. It is known for every n <= 31 and for 33..63, but a(32) is unknown. Christof Noebauer ('The Numbers of Small Rings', 2000) computed a(16) = 390 and reported only a(32) > 18,590. Commutative rings of order 32 (A037289) likewise have only a(32) > 876. Unital rings of order 32 are known (A037291(32) = 208; commutative unital A127707(32) = 109, as corrected by Bernard Schott in 2022). The count is multiplicative over prime powers and every smaller order is known, so a(32) is the smallest open value. A027623 and A037234 (re-fetched 2026-10-30) still say a(32) is unknown. The rings split by additive group: Z32, Z16+Z2, Z8+Z4, Z8+Z2^2, Z4^2+Z2, Z4+Z2^3 and Z2^5. The last case is the classification of 5-dimensional associative algebras over F_2 without identity, where nilpotent algebras dominate. For nonassociative rings (A037292, a(8) = 801288), the data stop at n = 15; a comment gives values up to n = 24, but a(16) is unknown.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact value of A027623(32). It needs a complete list of representatives (additive group plus structure constants), with a checker confirming each is an associative ring; pairwise non-isomorphism certified by canonical forms; and completeness certified independently: for each additive group A, the sum over representatives R of |Aut(A)|/|Aut(R)| must equal the number of associative bilinear products on A, counted by a separate program. The same code must reproduce A027623(8) = 52, A027623(16) = 390, A027623(27) = 59 and A037289(16) = 162. A027623 must be re-fetched live, and a literature search must find no earlier value.

partial_wins.statement: A037289(32), the number of commutative rings of order 32 (only > 876 known), with the same representative-list and orbit-counting certificate, reproducing A037289(16) = 162.

A037292(16), the number of nonassociative rings of order 16 (the first missing value of A037292, whose comment lists every other n <= 24), by orbit counting of bilinear maps under Aut(A) for each abelian group A of order 16, with a second independent method agreeing and the code reproducing a(4) = 55, a(8) = 801288 and the listed values for n = 17..24.

targets.verification_method: Check the ring axioms on every listed table (seconds). Recompute canonical forms to confirm non-isomorphism. Independently count the associative bilinear products on each additive group (for example by SAT model counting or a structured enumeration) and check the orbit-stabilizer identity.
angles: Unital rings of order 32 are known; any ring embeds into its Dorroh extension or splits off a unital summand, so count by the annihilator/nilpotent structure and reuse the unital classification.
For the Z2^5 case, build nilpotent F_2-algebras by central extensions (the p-group generation analogue, as de Graaf does for nilpotent Lie algebras).
pitfalls: A027623 includes non-unital and noncommutative rings, A037291 only unital ones, and A037289 only commutative ones; do not mix them.
Rings on Z8+Z4 need products respecting the orders of the generators; an unconstrained bilinear map over Z may not descend.
Noebauer's original files (ftp at algebra.uni-linz.ac.at) are offline; take the small values from OEIS.

targets.name: Racks and quandles: count those of order 14 (OEIS A181770/A181769), or the connected quandles of order 48 (A181771)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days for the kei and representative-list partial wins; racks or quandles of order 14, and connected quandles of order 48 over the full degree-48 transitive-group library, likely need a cluster
targets.statement: Racks and quandles are set-theoretic solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation, and quandles give knot invariants. Petr Vojtechovsky and Seung Yeop Yang (Math. Comp. 88 (2019) 2523-2540, arXiv 1911.04991) enumerated racks and quandles of order n <= 13 up to isomorphism: 25,794,670,618 racks and 469,250,886 quandles of order 13. Their method combined conjugacy classes of subgroups of small symmetric groups, the Joyce-Blackburn representation, and the Jedlicka-Pilitowska-Stanovsky-Zamojska-Dzienio enumeration of 2-reductive racks and quandles. They list representatives only for racks of order <= 11 and quandles of order <= 12; larger orders were counted only, and their Problem 6.1 asks for order 14. Kei (involutory quandles, A178432) are known to order 12 (6,926,801; Choiwah Chow, 2023). Connected quandles (A181771) are known for every order <= 47, from the libraries of transitive permutation groups: order < 36 by Leandro Vendramin (arXiv 1105.5341) and order < 48 by Alexander Hulpke, David Stanovsky and Petr Vojtechovsky (J. Pure Appl. Algebra 220 (2016) 735-758), with the library in Vendramin's Rig package. The transitive groups of degree 48 were classified later (Holt, Royle and Tracey, 2022). OEIS A181769, A181770, A178432 and A181771, re-fetched 2026-10-30, carry 'more' and stop at those orders.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact value of A181769(14), A181770(14) or A181771(48), re-fetched live and still missing immediately before claiming. Two independent methods or codes must agree exactly, and the code must reproduce every published term of that sequence. For A181771(48), every connected quandle class must come from a transitive group of degree 48 with an explicit construction, plus a non-isomorphism check. A literature search (Vojtechovsky, Vendramin, Stanovsky and coauthors, arXiv 2019-2026) must find no earlier value.

partial_wins.statement: A178432(13), the number of kei (involutory quandles) of order 13, by code reproducing a(n) for n <= 12 and a second independent method agreeing.

An explicit representative list (canonical Cayley tables) of all racks of order 12 (836,395,102) or all quandles of order 13 (469,250,886), which Vojtechovsky and Yang counted but did not list. A checker must confirm the axioms, pairwise non-isomorphism by canonical form, and a total equal to the published count.

targets.verification_method: Check the axioms on any table in milliseconds. Rerun the counting code for small n against OEIS. For a new count, split by an isomorphism invariant (orbit structure of the displacement or operator group) and recompute random parts with independent code.
angles: Extend the Vojtechovsky-Yang subgroup-of-S_n method to n = 14: count conjugacy classes of subgroups of S_14 with the needed properties rather than listing every rack.
For connected quandles of order 48, a connected quandle's inner automorphism group acts transitively, so filter the degree-48 transitive groups by Vendramin's criterion before constructing.
pitfalls: Racks vs quandles vs kei vs connected quandles are four different sequences with different offsets (A181771 starts at n = 1).
Iso-classes of racks are not counted by orbits of the labeled count under S_n without care for automorphisms.
The degree-48 transitive-group data is large; check that the whole library was processed.

targets.name: Finite lattices: the next count of unlabeled lattices (A006966, n = 21), semimodular (A229202, n = 26), modular (A006981, n = 36) or distributive lattices (A006982, n = 61)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (distributive and modular terms likely laptop-hours to days with Kohonen's vertical 2-sum recurrence; general lattices at n = 21 likely needs cluster)
targets.statement: Unlabeled lattices on n elements (A006966; also semilattices of order n-1) are known to n = 20, with a(20) = 23,003,059,864,006. That term comes from Volker Gebhardt and Stephen Tawn's orderly layer-by-layer algorithm (J. Algebra 545 (2020) 213-236, arXiv 1609.08255); a(19) is Nathan Lawless's. Jukka Kohonen extended semimodular lattices (A229202) to n = 25 (2017) and modular lattices (A006981) to n = 35 (2021). He also extended distributive lattices (A006982 b-file) to n = 60, with a(60) = 758,556,959,660,012, by counting vertical 2-sums of vertically indecomposable lattices (Order 2021, arXiv 2007.03232). That work builds on Jipsen and Lawless (modular lattices, 2013) and Erne, Heitzig and Reinhold (distributive lattices to 49, EJC 2002). All four OEIS entries and their b-files, re-fetched 2026-10-30, stop at those n.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact next term of A006966 (n = 21), A229202 (n = 26), A006981 (n = 36) or A006982 (n = 61), re-fetched live immediately before claiming. Two independent methods or codes must agree exactly, for example an orderly generation of indecomposables plus the vertical 2-sum recurrence against a direct orderly generation, or two different work partitions with independent kernels. The code must reproduce every published term of that sequence, and a literature search must find no earlier value.

partial_wins.statement: The number of vertically indecomposable modular lattices on 36 elements or distributive lattices on 61 elements, extending Kohonen's classification (to 35 and 60 elements) and reproducing his published counts.
An independent confirmation of A006966(20) = 23,003,059,864,006 by a different algorithm and code (the value rests on one published computation).

targets.verification_method: Rerun the claimant's code for small n against the b-files. Recompute the vertical 2-sum recurrence from independently generated indecomposables. Spot-check random work units of the orderly generation with independent code.
angles: Birkhoff duality: distributive lattices with n elements correspond to posets with exactly n down-sets, so generate posets by down-set count rather than lattices.
Kohonen's recurrence needs only the vertically indecomposable lattices; their growth rate (about 1.725^n for distributive) is far below the totals.
pitfalls: Unlabeled vs labeled lattices; A006966 counts lattices with top and bottom included in n.
The vertical 2-sum has symmetry cases that create one or two lattices; mishandling them is the classic error (Kohonen corrected A006981(24) in 2017).

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Posets and topologies: unlabeled counts on 17 points (A000112, A001930) or labeled counts on 20 points (A001035, A000798)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (Ayala's P(19) swept all 6.8e13 posets on 15 points; P(20) or unlabeled 17-point counts need a sweep over the 4.5e15 posets on 16 points or an equivalent shortcut)
targets.statement: Unlabeled posets (A000112) and unlabeled topologies or quasi-orders (A001930) have been known to n = 16 since Gunnar Brinkmann and Brendan McKay (Order 19 (2002) 147-179): there are 4,483,130,665,195,087 posets on 16 points. The labeled counts moved in 2026. Rafael Ayala (arXiv 2606.31526, 30 Jun 2026; code at github.com/Rafael-Ayala/posets-and-topologies-19) obtained P(19) = A001035(19) = 646099441937791106493755218560442089979 and, by the Stirling transform, A000798(19). He used the Erne-Stege moment reduction: the 16-point moment G(16,3) was harvested by inserting one element into each of the 68,275,077,901,156 unlabeled 15-point posets. He also reported G(16,4), an input for P(20). The b-files, re-fetched 2026-10-30, stop at n = 16 for the unlabeled sequences and n = 19 for the labeled ones.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact value of A000112(17), A001930(17), A001035(20) or A000798(20), re-fetched live and still missing immediately before claiming. Two independent methods or codes must agree exactly. The pipeline must reproduce all published terms, and for the moment route also Ayala's G(16,k) values. Per-shard residues modulo several primes must be published so a skeptic can recompute random shards. A literature search must find no earlier value.

partial_wins.statement: An independent confirmation of A001035(19) (Ayala 2026, a single computation), using a different code and either a different route (for example direct counting over 16-point posets) or an independently written moment kernel, agreeing on G(16,3) and P(19).

targets.verification_method: Rerun the shard pipeline on a random sample of shards with independent code and compare the residues. Check the CRT reconstruction and the Erne-Stege assembly. Check the modular periodicity of A001035 as a sanity test.
angles: P(20) needs only one new 17-point moment, which can be harvested from the 16-point posets by one-point insertion; the work splits naturally into shards.
pitfalls: Labeled vs unlabeled, and posets (T0) vs quasi-orders (all topologies): four different sequences.
Moments must be accumulated modulo several primes; 128-bit sums overflow at these sizes.

targets.name: Scholz-Brauer conjecture: an addition chain for 2^n - 1 of length n - 1 + l(n) at one of the six unrepaired non-Hansen numbers (33167549, 33247629, 33573479, 33580601, 33626279, 44177985)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (constraint search over the optimal chains of n); verification takes minutes
targets.statement: The Scholz-Brauer conjecture (Scholz 1937, Brauer 1939; Knuth, TAOCP vol. 2, section 4.6.3) says l(2^n - 1) <= n - 1 + l(n), where l is the length of a shortest addition chain. It holds whenever n has an optimal star chain (Brauer) or an optimal l^0 chain (Hansen). Neill Clift found the smallest non-Hansen number, 5784689 (August 2005), so the conjecture holds for n < 5784689. Clift's Star and l^0 page lists the first 40 non-Hansen numbers. It colours those for which a chain of length n - 1 + l(n) for 2^n - 1 is known: built by hand (red), by Gecode edge labelling (green), by the 'spawn' construction (purple; Repair page, September 2026 update, credited there to Claude Fable 5.1), or as a continuation 2m of a repaired m (blue). Six entries are uncoloured: 33167549, 33247629, 33573479, 33580601, 33626279 and 44177985. The Repair page says a CP-SAT model of the spawn template, run over all their optimal chains, proves that these six cannot be repaired that way. The template uses elements 2^s(2^v - 1) plus at most two spawned powers of two. Related: Flammenkamp's page reports that on 1 July 2024 Clift showed equality can fail, first with n = 30978119. Clift's smallest example so far (ExactScholz2 page) gives l(2^1541527 - 1) <= 1541551 < l(1541527) + 1541526 = 1541552. Clift's Scholz-Brauer page also gives a 'monster', 32428466573: he proves that the derivative graph of its chain cannot be labelled, and all its chains appear to share that structure.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for an explicit addition chain for 2^n - 1, with n one of the non-Hansen numbers still uncoloured on http://www.additionchains.com/StarL0.html (re-fetched before the claim; on 2026-10-30 these are 33167549, 33247629, 33573479, 33580601, 33626279 and 44177985). The chain must be written in Clift's run format: comma-separated items, where 'a,...,b' is a doubling run a, 2a, ..., b = 2^d*a contributing d + 1 elements. Every element after the initial 1 must equal the sum of two earlier elements, checked with exact integers. The chain must end at 2^n - 1, and its length (elements after the initial 1) must be AT MOST n - 1 + l(n). Here l(n) is the true shortest-chain length from Clift's complete table (all n <= 2^39, Flammenkamp's page), confirmed by the verifier's own optimal-chain run on n. Direction: min on the number of uncoloured entries. A chain for 2m when m is already repaired does not count.

partial_wins.statement: A smaller strict-inequality example: an n < 1541527 together with an explicit chain for 2^n - 1 of length at most n + l(n) - 2 (strictly below n - 1 + l(n)), verified as in the full win, with l(n) taken from Clift's table and rechecked by the verifier.

The monster: an explicit chain for 2^32428466573 - 1 of length at most 32428466572 + l(32428466573), with l(32428466573) from Clift's table (the number is below 2^39). Verified with an exact run-length (bit-interval) representation of the elements.

targets.verification_method: Parse the run format and keep each element exactly. Store runs by odd part and exponent range so that membership of any 2^j*s is O(1). For each non-run element, and for each run start, find an earlier pair summing to it. Count the elements and compare with n - 1 + l(n) (or n + l(n) - 2 for p1). Python big integers are fine up to about 10^8 bits. Use Clift's published 5784689 chain (length 5784715, Repair page) and his 1541527 chain (length 1541551, ExactScholz2 page) as regression tests: the checker must accept both with exactly those lengths. Read l(n) from Clift's add39 data (linked from Flammenkamp's page) and recheck it with an independent optimal-chain program the verifier writes. Re-fetch StarL0.html and Repair.html to confirm that n is still unrepaired.
angles: Widen the Repair-page CP-SAT model: elements 2^s(2^v - 1) with free offsets, plus three or more spawned powers of two (2^m - 1) + 1 = 2^m. The page shows two spawns cannot fix the six.
Mix templates: let some elements be general sums such as 2^a(2^b - 1) + 2^c(2^e - 1), not only Mersenne-shaped blocks, and solve the edge labelling of the derivative graph as a SAT problem.

Use the exact-equality machinery in reverse: Clift's 1541527 construction saves a step through an 'impossible' building-block set from a 2^47 - 1 chain. Saved steps elsewhere could pay for a non-Hansen gap.
Search all optimal chains of n (Clift's nmc program counts them) for one whose derivative graph needs only a small, local repair.
pitfalls: Counting: a run 'a,...,b' adds d + 1 elements, and the initial 1 is not counted. Off-by-one errors here fake a win.
l(n) must be the true optimum. Using a longer chain for n makes the target bound easier and the claim wrong.
Continuations (2m of a repaired m, coloured blue) are trivial and do not count.
Disproving the conjecture would need a proven lower bound on l(2^n - 1); no chain can do that, and nothing here asks for it.

targets.name: Shortest addition chains: compute c(48), the smallest n with l(n) = 48, or d(46) (Clift's c(r)/d(r) tables)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (extending the complete l(n) table from 2^39 towards 2^40, terabyte-scale storage); spot verification is laptop-hours
targets.statement: Let l(n) be the length of a shortest addition chain for n, c(r) the smallest n with l(n) = r (OEIS A003064), and d(r) the number of n with l(n) = r. Knuth, Flammenkamp, Bleichenbacher and Neill Clift built these tables. Clift computed l(n) for every n <= 2^39 (September 2022). He found c(47) = 498691112447 in January 2021, and his c(r)/d(r) page gives d(r) up to d(45) = 243724383149 (September 2022). The OEIS b-file for A003064, taken from Flammenkamp's page in 2021, stops at a(46) = 257661019487. c(47) is known but missing there, so it is not a new term. Flammenkamp's page holds the history and the downloadable l(n) data: add39.4ln.bz2, 51662 MB, covers n <= 2^39. Because the table is complete to 2^39 and lists no n with l(n) = 48, c(48) > 2^39. The ratio c(47)/c(46) is about 1.94, so c(48) is very likely below 2^40. Clift notes that finding chains for c(r) is easy; proving that no shorter chain exists is what takes the time.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for c(48): an integer N with (a) a certificate that l(N) >= 48, given by an exhaustive shortest-chain search that the verifier reruns with its own independently written program, and an explicit chain of length 48; and (b) for every m < N, an explicit chain of length <= 47. Part (b) may be a published extension of Clift's complete l(n) table from 2^39 up to N, with chains for spot checks. Two independently written programs must agree on N. N must not appear on http://additionchains.com/crdr.html, on Flammenkamp's page or in OEIS A003064 (each re-fetched before the claim). Direction: extend the table (first unknown index).

partial_wins.statement: d(46): the exact number of n with l(n) = 46, computed by two independently written methods that agree (for example small-step enumeration and a table count), and absent from the live crdr.html and Flammenkamp pages.

A rigorous lower bound c(48) > X with X > 2^39: a published extension of the complete l(n) table beyond 2^39 to X, with no n <= X having l(n) = 48. A second independent program must reproduce randomly chosen blocks exactly.

targets.verification_method: For N: run an independent optimal-chain prover (for example Clift's published ac2fastfg techniques reimplemented) to confirm that no chain of length 47 exists. Check the 48-step chain. Download the claimant's table extension and check chains for random m < N, and for every m in the top 10^7 below N, against the claimed l(m) <= 47. Compare d-counts by recounting the table and the enumeration. Re-fetch crdr.html and A003064.
angles: Clift's crouton/dual pruning plus the generalized Thurber bounds (Calculating.html) for single-n lower-bound proofs.

Small-step enumerations (Clift's SmallStepEnumeration pages publish the convex-set enumerations for s <= 5; Flammenkamp's page records Clift's s = 6 work to November 2023) settle most n quickly. Only n not matched by an enumeration need the full search.
c(r) values follow Flammenkamp's observation that the record holders for the number of small steps are among the c(r).
pitfalls: c(47) = 498691112447 is already known (Clift, January 2021) even though OEIS's b-file stops at a(46).
A chain of length 48 for N proves nothing about minimality. Both l(N) >= 48 and l(m) <= 47 for all m < N are needed.
Flammenkamp's 1997 data had four errors above 2.5*10^6 that Clift found in 2004. Independent recomputation matters.

targets.name: Shortest Lucas (differential addition) chains: compute C_L(51), the smallest n whose shortest Lucas chain has length 51 (OEIS A104892)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days to a week (extend the complete L(n) table from 2^33 to about 1.1*10^10, with SIMD pruning); verification laptop-hours
targets.statement: A Lucas chain (Montgomery's differential addition chain) is an addition chain 1 = a_0 < ... < a_r = n in which each a_i = a_j + a_k also satisfies a_j - a_k = 0 or a_j - a_k = a_d for some earlier element. L(n) is the length of the shortest one. Daniel Bleichenbacher (thesis, ETH 1996) computed L(n) for n <= 432199 and C_L(r), the smallest n with L(n) = r. Neill Clift used Fibonacci-type element bounds and the factor method L(nm) <= L(n) + L(m) to compute L(n) for all n <= 2^33 (data addl33.bin.gz on his Lucas page). That gave C_L(r) up to r = 50: C_L(48) = 2680042177, C_L(49) = 4243717559, C_L(50) = 6698246557. OEIS A104892 credits terms from a(30) onwards to Clift (October 19, 2024). C_L(50) < 2^33 < C_L(51). Successive ratios are about 1.58, so C_L(51) is about 1.06*10^10, just past Clift's range. Bernstein, Cottaar and Lange (2024) also searched for differential addition chains.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for an integer N with (a) an explicit Lucas chain of length 51 for N, every step checked for the difference condition; (b) a certificate that L(N) >= 51, given by an exhaustive search the verifier reruns with its own program; and (c) L(m) <= 50 for every m < N, shown by an extension of Clift's complete L(n) table from 2^33 to N that a second, independently written program reproduces (hash of the table, plus spot-check chains). N must not appear in https://oeis.org/A104892 or on http://additionchains.com/Lucas.html (re-fetched before the claim). Direction: extend the table (first unknown index r = 51).

partial_wins.statement: A rigorous lower bound C_L(51) > X for some X >= 9*10^9: a published complete L(n) table to X, matching Clift's addl33 data exactly on n <= 2^33, in which no n has L(n) = 51. A second, independently written program must reproduce randomly chosen blocks above 2^33 exactly.

targets.verification_method: Check that every element is a sum of two earlier elements whose difference is 0 or an earlier element. Rerun the exhaustive lower-bound search for N with an independent implementation using Fibonacci element bounds. Recompute random blocks of the table with factor-method propagation followed by single-doubling search. Diff against addl33 on the overlap.
angles: Clift's layered method: get all L(n) = r + 1 targets from the L = r database through the factor method, then search only chains with a single doubling step under the Fibonacci bound a_i >= ceil((n - F_{r-i+1})/F_{r-i+2}) + 1.
Pack 8 64-bit lanes into 512-bit SIMD registers as Clift did, and handle overflow explicitly (his first 2^32 run lost results to an overflow bug).
pitfalls: Differential condition: a_j - a_k must itself be in the chain (or be 0). Ordinary addition chains are shorter and do not count.
Clift's addl33 file is indexed from zero: byte n holds L(n) and byte 0 is a dummy. Treating the first byte as L(1) shifts every value by one index.
Overflow in vectorised pruning silently stops the search at the last level (Clift's own reported bug).

targets.name: Integer complexity Conjecture A: ||2^a 3^b 5^c|| = 2a + 3b + 5c for c < 6 (Selfridge's ||2^a|| = 2a); a counterexample, or a proof beyond Altman's a <= 48
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (defect-based exact algorithms); verification of a counterexample is instant
targets.statement: The integer complexity ||n|| (Mahler and Popken 1953; Guy 1986) is the fewest 1s needed to write n using +, * and parentheses (OEIS A005245). Selfridge asked whether ||2^a|| < 2a for some a. Iraids, Balodis, Cernenoks, Opmanis, Opmanis and Podnieks (arXiv:1203.6462, 2012, Hypothesis 5) conjectured the general form. Konyagin and Oganesyan call it Conjecture A (arXiv:2603.20876v2, April 2026, where it is still open): for nonnegative a, b, c with a + b + c > 0 and c < 6, ||2^a 3^b 5^c|| = 2a + 3b + 5c. Iraids et al. verified it for all 2^a 3^b 5^c < 10^12 while computing ||n|| for n <= 10^12. Harry Altman (Integers 18 (2018) A45; arXiv:1606.03635) built on the defect delta(n) = ||n|| - 3 log_3 n and the Altman-Zelinsky theory of low-defect numbers. He gave an algorithm that decides when 2^k is stable and proved the case c = 0 for all a <= 48 and every b, by showing that 2^48 is stable with ||2^48|| = 96 (about 20 hours on his laptop). His Haskell implementation is public. Konyagin and Oganesyan (2026) cite a <= 48 as the current state. Other work: Arias de Reyna and van de Lune (algorithms, 2014), Cordwell et al. (2017), Qizheng He (2023), Zelinsky (upper bounds, 2022). A counterexample with b = c = 0 would also answer Selfridge's question.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for either (a) an explicit expression built only from the literal 1, +, * and parentheses that evaluates exactly to 2^a 3^b 5^c (a + b + c > 0, 0 <= c <= 5) using STRICTLY FEWER than 2a + 3b + 5c ones (direction: min on the ones count), or (b) a Lean 4 (Mathlib) proof of Conjecture A for all such a, b, c, with no sorry and only standard axioms. The expression is checked by parsing it, counting the 1s and evaluating it with exact integers.

partial_wins.statement: A computer-assisted proof that ||2^a 3^b|| = 2a + 3b for all a <= A and all b, with A >= 49 (strictly beyond Altman's a <= 48). The program must be published, the verifier must rerun it, a second independently written implementation must agree on the case list, and both must reproduce Altman's a <= 48 as a regression.

A computer-assisted proof, independently reimplemented as in p1, that ||2^a 3^b 5^c|| = 2a + 3b + 5c for some fixed c in 1..5, all b and all a <= 10. This lies beyond the box 2^a 3^b 5^c < 10^12 checked by Iraids et al.

targets.verification_method: For an expression: parse it with a restricted grammar (only '1', '+', '*', parentheses), count the 1s, and evaluate it with Python integers. For p1/p2: rerun the published program, diff its output with the second implementation, and confirm the a <= 48 regression. Check the arithmetic of the defect bounds with exact rationals or interval arithmetic, not floats.
angles: Altman's defect algorithm: numbers with defect below a bound s are covered by finitely many 'low-defect polynomials'. Extending a is a matter of pushing s up efficiently (memoisation, better pruning).
Search for counterexamples near the top of the defect spectrum: an expression for 2^a 3^b using a big sum term, of the shape 2^x 3^y (2^u 3^v + 1), is the only kind that could beat the product form.
pitfalls: Writing 11 or 111 by putting 1s side by side is not allowed; only + and * of 1s.
Floating-point log_3 in defect comparisons gives wrong cases at the boundary; use exact arithmetic.
c >= 6 is excluded on purpose: 5^6 has a cheaper representation, so the conjecture is stated only for c < 6.

targets.name: Integer complexity: the smallest number of complexity 90, A005520(90), beyond the 10^12 computation of Iraids et al.
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (expressions with at most 89 ones for every n from 10^12 to about 1.3*10^12, plus exact lower bounds for a few candidates) up to needs cluster (a full exact table to N); verification laptop-hours for spot checks
targets.statement: A005520(k) is the smallest n with integer complexity ||n|| = k (fewest 1s using + and *). The b-file by Janis Iraids runs to k = 89: a(87) = 424847520719, a(88) = 630371064959, a(89) = 872573642639 (a(68)-a(89) from Iraids, April 2011). It comes from the computation of ||n|| for all n <= 10^12 by Iraids, Balodis, Cernenoks, Opmanis, Opmanis and Podnieks (arXiv:1203.6462; Iraids' online calculator covers n < 10^12). Earlier terms are credited to David W. Wilson, John W. Layman and Piotr Fabian. Since ||n + 1|| <= ||n|| + 1 and no n <= 10^12 has complexity 90, a(90) is the least n with ||n|| >= 90. It is above 10^12 (successive ratios suggest about 1.2-1.3*10^12) and unknown. Ed Pegg Jr. noted that the terms are -1 mod 120. The entry says this holds from a(45) = 590399 through a(89), and that all terms from a(54) to a(89) are prime (Iraids). Faster algorithms exist: Arias de Reyna and van de Lune (2014), Cordwell et al. (2017), and Qizheng He (2023: O(N polylog N) for all n <= N, and O(n^0.6154) for a single n). The entry (last edited 2025-11-26) has no 'more' keyword and lists no a(90).
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for an integer N = a(90) with (a) a certificate that ||N|| = 90: an explicit 90-one expression plus an exact lower-bound proof (for example the Arias de Reyna-van de Lune algorithm or a defect-based certificate) that the verifier reruns, and (b) a proof that ||m|| <= 89 for every m < N: an explicit expression with at most 89 ones for every m, or a published table extension from 10^12 to N reproduced by a second, independently written program. N must be absent from the live https://oeis.org/A005520 data, b-file and history (re-fetched before the claim). Direction: extend the table (first unknown index 90).

partial_wins.statement: A rigorous lower bound a(90) > X with X >= 1.1*10^12: an exhaustive, independently reproduced computation showing ||n|| <= 89 for all n <= X (explicit expressions with at most 89 ones, or an exact table, for every n in (10^12, X]).

An upper bound a(90) <= M with M < 2*10^12: an explicit integer M with a certificate that ||M|| >= 90, given by an exact single-number lower-bound computation (for example He's 2023 algorithm) that the verifier reruns with an independently written implementation. Because ||n + 1|| <= ||n|| + 1, this proves a(90) <= M.

targets.verification_method: Evaluate the claimed expressions with exact integers and count the 1s. Rerun the lower-bound algorithm for ||N|| >= 90 with an independent implementation. For the 'all smaller m' part, recompute randomly chosen blocks of the claimed table with a second program and diff the hashes. Check that the extension agrees with Iraids' data below 10^12 on sampled n.
angles: Only candidates of the conjectured shape (primes, -1 mod 120) need exact lower bounds first. The rest of the proof is a sieve showing every smaller m has an expression with at most 89 ones, and most m need only a small additive correction to a product form.
A segmented sieve: a sum term n = a + b with b small covers almost everything, and products need only divisors up to sqrt(n). Stream the table in blocks with a cache of small-complexity values.
pitfalls: Juxtaposing 1s is forbidden.
Finding the first prime with ||p|| = 90 is not enough; every m < N must be covered.
Off-by-one in the offset: A005520 has offset 1, with a(1) = 1.

targets.name: Hofstadter's Q-sequence: does it die? Find an n where Q(n) is undefined, or push the existence frontier past 3*10^10
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (memory of a few hundred GB to go past 3*10^10, since Q(n) refers back to about n/2)
targets.statement: Hofstadter's Q-sequence (Goedel, Escher, Bach, 1979; OEIS A005185) is Q(1) = Q(2) = 1 and Q(n) = Q(n - Q(n-1)) + Q(n - Q(n-2)). Its growth is chaotic and its rate unknown. It is not even known whether Q(n) is defined for all n: the sequence 'dies' at the first n where n - Q(n-1) < 1 or n - Q(n-2) < 1. Roman Pearce computed that Q(n) exists for n <= 10^10 (2014). M. Eric Carr extended this to n <= 3*10^10 (OEIS comment, July 2, 2023). The entry lists no larger frontier on 2026-10-30. Erdős Problem #422 (erdosproblems.com, no prize listed) asks the related question whether Q misses infinitely many integers, and notes that Q is not even known to be well-defined. Related sequences (Golomb, Conolly, the Hofstadter-Conway $10,000 sequence) are well understood; Q itself is not.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for an index N such that Q(1..N-1) are defined and N - Q(N-1) < 1 or N - Q(N-2) < 1. Two independently written programs (different languages or memory layouts) must both reach N and agree on Q(N-1) and Q(N-2), and on checkpoint values Q(k*10^9) for every k up to N/10^9. Alternatively, a Lean proof (no sorry, standard axioms) that Q is defined for all n. Checked against the live https://oeis.org/A005185.

partial_wins.statement: Frontier extension: a computation showing that Q(n) is defined for all n <= M, with M at least TWICE the largest bound stated in the live A005185 entry (M >= 6*10^10 on 2026-10-30). It must publish Q(k*10^9) for every k <= M/10^9 and a hash of the whole sequence, reproduced exactly by a second, independently written program.

targets.verification_method: Rerun both programs (or a third, the verifier's own) to the claimed N or M, keeping Q values in 5-byte or bit-packed storage. Compare all checkpoints. For a death claim, print Q(N-2) and Q(N-1) and check the failing index condition by hand. Re-fetch A005185 for any newer frontier.
angles: Q(n) - n/2 stays small in relative terms, so Q(n) is about n/2. Store the offsets Q(n) - floor(n/2) in a compact signed format and keep only the window [n/2 - c, n] in RAM, streaming older blocks to disk.
Pinn's generation structure (the sequence splits into 'generations' of doubling length) gives natural checkpoints and a way to parallelise the verification of later generations.
pitfalls: A death claim from a buggy indexing convention (1-based versus 0-based) is the most likely false positive. Reproduce Q(1..100) from the OEIS DATA first.
32-bit overflow in Q values or indices beyond 2^32 corrupts results silently.
Reaching 3*10^10 again is a regression test, not a result.

targets.name: Conway's subprime Fibonacci sequences: a seventh non-trivial cycle, or an exhaustive check of starting pairs beyond 10^6
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (about 2.4*10^12 coprime starting pairs for N = 2*10^6, with memoised node tables); a new cycle verifies in milliseconds
targets.statement: John Conway's subprime Fibonacci rule: from a pair (x, y) of positive integers, the next term is s = x + y if s is prime, and otherwise s divided by its least prime factor. Richard K. Guy, Tanya Khovanova and Julian Salazar ('Conway's subprime Fibonacci sequences', arXiv:1207.5099, v2 2014) studied these orbits, which behave pseudo-randomly, much like 3x+1 trajectories. A start (a, a) gives the trivial cycle a, a, a, .... Coprime pairs stay coprime, so their sequences are non-trivial, and every non-trivial sequence eventually has coprime consecutive terms. Six non-trivial cycles are known: lengths 10, 11, 18, 19, 56 and 136, through the nodes (127, 509), (37, 199), (48, 13), (23, 27), (119, 109) and (47, 23), with largest terms 827, 607, 97, 191, 5693 and 347. The paper checked every starting pair with both terms at most 10^6 and found no other non-trivial cycle. It conjectures that no orbit grows without bound. Conway's sequence from (1, 1), A214674, enters the 18-cycle at (48, 13). OEIS A214897 and A214898 (Wouter Meeussen) list the lengths 1, 10, 11, 18, 19, 56, 136 (the 1 is a trivial cycle) and largest elements. Their comment still says 'checked to [10^5, 10^5]', and A214898 gives 239 for the 18-cycle, but 239 lies on A214674's pre-period and the cycle's largest term is 97 (rechecked with an independent program that reproduces the paper's Table 1). Tables A282812-A282814 give per-start data for small pairs.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a coprime starting pair (x, y) of positive integers and an explicit non-trivial cycle: a cyclic list of terms t_1..t_L with consecutive terms coprime, such that the rule maps each pair (t_i, t_{i+1}) to (t_{i+1}, t_{i+2}), with indices taken mod L. Every step must be checked with exact arithmetic and proven primality. The cycle's set of terms must differ from each of the six known non-trivial cycles, those generated from the nodes (127, 509), (37, 199), (48, 13), (23, 27), (119, 109) and (47, 23), and the orbit of (x, y) must be shown to reach it. Trivial cycles a, a, a, ... never count. Re-fetch https://oeis.org/A214897 and the arXiv paper before the claim. Direction: max on the number of known non-trivial cycles.

partial_wins.statement: An exhaustive certificate that every coprime starting pair in [1, N] x [1, N] with N >= 2*10^6 (beyond the 10^6 of Guy, Khovanova and Salazar) enters one of the six known non-trivial cycles. It must give per-cycle counts, which a second, independently written program reproduces exactly, along with the longest pre-period and the largest term seen.

targets.verification_method: Iterate the rule from the given pair with Python integers. Compute least prime factors by trial division or a sieve, and check primality with a deterministic Miller-Rabin test below 3.3*10^24 (or with ECPP). Confirm that the cycle closes, that it is not trivial, and that its term set differs from the six known cycles, regenerated from their nodes. First reproduce the paper's Table 1 for a, b <= 10^3 (cycle lengths 1/10/11/18/19/56/136 with counts 10022/33/390/467014/30490/21990/470061) and A214674 entering the 18-cycle at (48, 13). For p1, rerun both programs and diff the per-cycle counts.
angles: Memoise orbit outcomes over visited pairs (a hash or Bloom set of pairs known to reach each loop) so that a new start stops as soon as it hits a known pair.
Look for loops directly rather than from starts: search cycles of the pair map over pairs with a large prime term, since every known loop's largest element is prime.
pitfalls: Trivial cycles: any start (a, a) loops on a forever, and non-coprime starts can end in such cycles. They are not new cycles.

A rotation of a known cycle, or the same cycle entered from another pair, is not new. Compare term sets with the six cycles regenerated from their nodes, not with A214898's maxima (its 18-cycle entry, 239, is wrong; the maximum is 97).
Primality errors (Fermat-only tests) can create fake cycles; use deterministic tests.

targets.name: Generalized Collatz maps: a cycle missing from the known lists (Lagarias 3x+k for k < 20000, 3x-k, and the three known 5x+1 cycles)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (parity-vector / cycle-equation search); verification is instant
targets.statement: For odd k with gcd(k, 6) = 1, Lagarias' 3x+k map is T_k(x) = x/2 if x is even and (3x + k)/2 if x is odd. A cycle is primitive if its elements are coprime to k. Lagarias (1990) conjectured that every such k has at least one primitive cycle and only finitely many. E. G. Belaga and M. Mignotte tabulated the cycles (2000, 2006). Geoffrey H. Morley's OEIS A226607 (b-file rows 1..6667) lists the smallest elements of 42757 primitive cycles for k < 20000, found by following every trajectory that starts below 10^8; A226613 gives the counts. He adds that for k < 158195 no start below 10^8 reaches a primitive cycle whose minimal element exceeds 28306063. So a cycle whose elements all exceed 10^8 cannot have been seen by these searches. For the 3x-k map, Morley's A226630 and A226629 list the k with primitive cycles and the conjectured counts. For the 5x+1 map (x -> 5x+1 if x is odd, x/2 if even) only three cycles are known: the cycles through 1, 13 and 17 (A393125, M. F. Hasler, February 2026). Kontorovich and Lagarias predict that most 5x+1 orbits diverge.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for an explicit cycle: distinct positive integers x_1..x_L with T(x_i) = x_{i+1} and T(x_L) = x_1, checked with exact integers. T is T_k for some 1 < k < 20000 with gcd(k, 6) = 1, and every element is coprime to k (primitive). The cycle's minimal element must NOT be among the entries of row n = floor(k/3) + 1 of https://oeis.org/A226607. The b-file b226607.txt stores rows 1..6667 flattened; row n begins after the first A226613(1) + ... + A226613(n-1) entries and has A226613(n) entries, taken from b226613.txt. Re-fetch both before the claim. Direction: max on the number of known cycles. k = 1 (the Collatz problem itself) is out of scope.

partial_wins.statement: A primitive T_k cycle for some 20000 <= k < 158195 (gcd(k, 6) = 1) whose minimal element exceeds 10^8, beyond the reach of every search described in A226607.

A primitive cycle of the 3x-k map T(x) = x/2 or (3x - k)/2, with k at most the largest entry of the A226630 b-file. Either k is absent from A226630, or the cycle is beyond the count A226629 gives for that k (cycles listed by smallest element; the claimant reproduces Morley's cycles for that k first).

A fourth cycle of the 5x+1 map x -> 5x+1 (x odd), x/2 (x even) on positive integers, different from the three cycles listed in A393125. Merely resolving a '?' entry of A393125 does not count here, since that entry carries keyword 'more' and belongs to the OEIS-more target.

targets.verification_method: Iterate the map over the claimed cycle with Python integers. Check closure, that the elements are distinct and coprime to k (for primitivity), and the minimal element. Compare with the A226607 row for k (or the A226630/A226629 data, or the A393125 list) fetched live. Reproduce a few listed cycles for the same k to confirm the map convention.
angles: Cycle equation (Bohm-Sontacchi): a parity vector with O odd steps and L total steps gives x_1 = k*N/(2^L - 3^O), where N is a fixed sum of 3^i 2^j terms. Enumerate the (L, O) with D = 2^L - 3^O dividing k*N, so that cycles with huge elements (> 10^8) appear directly, with no trajectory search.
Divisors of the 'Collatz numbers' 2^L - 3^O (Belaga-Mignotte Table 2 gives their factorizations) say which k can carry cycles of a given shape.
For 5x+1 use the same equation with 2^L - 5^O < 0 handled by sign; a positive cycle needs 2^L > 5^O, which forces L/O > log2(5), long and sparse in odd steps.
pitfalls: Non-primitive cycles (all elements multiples of a divisor of k) are scaled copies of cycles of a smaller k and do not count.
Use exactly T_k(x) = (3x + k)/2 on odd x (the shortcut form). Row lengths differ under the unshortened map, but cycle sets do not.
Rows of A226607 are indexed by floor(k/3) + 1 over all odd k coprime to 6; misreading the row index is the easiest false 'new' cycle.

targets.name: Busy Beaver for FRACTRAN: beat a BBf(22..24) champion, decide BBf(23)'s or BBf(24)'s holdouts, or settle a Fenrir cryptid
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours for enumeration and simple deciders; Lean proof checking per holdout in minutes
targets.statement: BBf(n) is the longest run, starting from 2, of a halting FRACTRAN program of size n. A rule a/b has size Omega(a) + Omega(b) (prime factors with multiplicity), and a program's size is its number of rules plus the sum of rule sizes. The bbchallenge wiki's Fractran page (last edited 2026-10-28) lists exact values through n = 21: BBf(20) = 746 (champion [7/15, 22/3, 6/77, 5/2, 9/5], Jason Yuen, 2025-11-13) and BBf(21) = 31,957,632 (champion [7/15, 4/3, 27/14, 5/2, 9/5], Jason Yuen, 2025-11-16; the last 140 holdouts proved non-halting with Lean proofs prompted from Claude Opus 4.6, March 2026). Beyond that it lists lower bounds: BBf(22) > 1.146 x 10^62 (Shawn Ligocki and Jason Yuen), BBf(23) > 4.393 x 10^124 (Ligocki, 2026-06-01), BBf(24) > 9.000 x 10^14448 (Yuen, 2026-09-09). Size 22 is decided except for the three Fenrir cryptids (sz22_3.txt; Jason Yuen and Claude Opus 4.6, 2026-03-22; non-halting if and only if a Hydra-type walk never stops). The holdout lists are kept in Jason Yuen's int-y1/BBFractran repository, whose README is newer than the wiki: size 23 has 13 holdouts (sz23_13.txt, official since 2026-10-16: Fenrir, 11 Hydra-like cryptids and #601), and size 24 has 3,580 (sz24_3580.txt, 2026-10-27, after Lean-verified progress certificates; the wiki still shows an older 231,432). The README's TODO names a size-24 program, [2/15, 1/6, 441/2, 11/3, 25/7, 6/11], that should beat the BBf(24) champion if it halts. The wiki lists it as 'Energy Vampire' (Jason Yuen and Claude Opus 5.5; Beaver Math Olympiad problem 12, still unsolved): a Hydra-type pseudo-random walk, Hydra(8, 3, [0, 3, 6], [-1, 0, 1], (1, 1)), that is expected to halt on probabilistic grounds, though it is unknown whether it does in practice.
targets.success_criterion: Success means one of: (a) a FRACTRAN program of size n, 22 <= n <= 24 (size convention of https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Fractran), that halts from 2 after STRICTLY more steps than the lower bound listed for n on that page, re-fetched live before claiming, with the step count established by exact simulation or by an accelerated simulation whose rules are proved (a Lean or Coq proof, or exactly re-derived macro rules); (b) all holdouts of sz23_13.txt or of the current size-24 holdout list decided, each non-halter with a Lean (or Coq) proof that compiles and each halter with an exact step count, so that BBf(23) or BBf(24) becomes exact; or (c) one Fenrir program from sz22_3.txt decided: a halting step count or a compiled non-halting proof.

partial_wins.statement: Compiled Lean proofs of non-halting for at least 100 programs on the current BBf(24) holdout list (sz24_3580.txt or its successor) that the repository does not already mark as proved.
Criterion (a) for n = 24: a size-24 program halting from 2 after more than 9.000 x 10^14448 steps, with a proved step count.
An independent re-enumeration of all programs of size at most 21, with its own deciders, that reproduces BBf(20) = 746 and BBf(21) = 31,957,632 and leaves no holdout without a certificate.

targets.verification_method: Simulate with exponent vectors: at each step apply the first fraction whose denominator divides the current number, counting rule applications until none applies (the BBf(21) champion halts after 31,957,632 steps, a calibration that was reproduced). Recompute program sizes from the fractions. Compile Lean proofs with the stated toolchain and check that their theorem statements name the exact program. For huge step counts, re-derive every acceleration rule by hand or with a proof assistant.
angles: FRACTRAN programs are vector addition systems with priorities; borrow VASS techniques (linear invariants, the 'Masked Linear Invariant' and 'Power Limit' deciders already used at sizes 18-21, Presburger acceleration with the FAST tool) to close most size-24 holdouts automatically.
Group the size-24 holdouts into equivalence classes (the repository has an unofficial 2,245-class grouping) and prove one representative per class.
For new champions, look for programs that simulate fast-growing Collatz-like maps, as the size-22 to 24 champions do.
pitfalls: Fenrir and the size-23 Hydra-like cryptids are as hard as the Hydra problem (see the bb33-bb25-cryptid-adjacent target); do not expect them to fall to generic deciders.
Step counting: a step is one rule application; reaching a number no fraction applies to ends the run without an extra step.
Rule order matters (first applicable fraction wins), so reordering a program gives a different program.
The wiki and the repository README disagree on current holdout counts (the wiki is older); use the newest README list, quote its file name, and note that the size-21 errata show lists get corrected.

The README's TODO candidate [2/15, 1/6, 441/2, 11/3, 25/7, 6/11] is public. It is the wiki's 'Energy Vampire' (BMO problem 12), and whether it halts at all is open, so a plain simulation may never end. Showing that it halts satisfies (a) and p2 only with a proved step count, and the claim must credit the README and the wiki for the candidate.

targets.name: Busy Beaver for 2-tag systems: settle BB_PT(8) (7 holdouts) or beat a size 8-11 champion
targets.compute_profile: laptop-minutes to laptop-hours
targets.statement: A 2-tag system has an alphabet {0, 1, ...} and one production word w_a per symbol: while the tape has at least 2 symbols, read the first symbol a, delete the first 2 symbols and append w_a. Size is |A| + sum of |w_a|. BB_PT(S) is the most steps any size-S 2-tag system takes before halting when started on 00. The bbchallenge wiki's Post Tag System page (last edited 2026-09-16) lists exact values through size 7 (BB_PT(7) = 10, champion 0111_1) and lower bounds above: BB_PT(8) >= 19 (111_20_, 7 holdouts), BB_PT(9) >= 49 (11_021_2, 154 holdouts), BB_PT(10) >= 779 (112_1_002, 1,933 holdouts), BB_PT(11) >= 196,841 (120221_0_2, 11,759 holdouts). It also lists a size-11 Collatz-like cryptid, 11111_20_1, constructed by realsheepthe. Search tools: Shawn Ligocki's Rust enumerator (sligocki/etc, post_tag) and AzertyWasTaken's Busy-Beaver repository.
targets.success_criterion: Success means (a) a 2-tag system of size S, 8 <= S <= 11 (size and step conventions of https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Post_Tag_System), that halts from 00 after STRICTLY more steps than the bound listed for S on that page, re-fetched live before claiming, verified by direct simulation; or (b) an exact value of BB_PT(S) for some S in 8..11 that the page still lists with ' > =': every size-S system either halts (with its step count) or carries a checkable non-halting certificate (cycle, translated cycle, or another proof re-checked by an independent decider or a proof assistant), and the largest halting count is reported.

partial_wins.statement: Exact BB_PT(8): all size-8 systems classified, the 7 wiki holdouts each with a non-halting certificate (or a new champion).
Exact BB_PT(9), with all size-9 holdouts certified.
A new champion at size 10 or 11 (criterion (a)).

targets.verification_method: Independent simulator: queue starting 00, at each step read the first symbol, delete two, append its word, stop when fewer than two symbols remain, counting steps (calibration: 0111_1 halts after 10 steps, 111_20_ after 19, 120221_0_2 after 196,841; all reproduced). For exact values, re-enumerate all systems of size S with independent code, check the count, and re-run each non-halting certificate.
angles: Most holdouts are growing queues; certify them with translated-cycler or 'immortal substring' style arguments (a substring that regenerates itself), as in AzertyWasTaken's decider list.
Collatz-like holdouts can often be reduced to a closed-form recurrence on block counts, like the cryptid 11111_20_1.
pitfalls: Two conventions are in use: the wiki counts size as |A| + sum |w_a| and does not count an extra halting step, while AzertyWasTaken's results.md counts size as sum |w_a| and counts the halting step (its 'BBPT(5) = 19' is a different function). Use the wiki convention.
Systems that differ only by renaming non-initial symbols are equivalent; say how duplicates were handled in an exhaustive count.

targets.name: Busy Beaver for cyclic tag systems: settle BBCT(8) or beat a size 8-14 champion
targets.compute_profile: laptop-minutes to laptop-hours
targets.statement: A cyclic tag system is a list of binary production words used in rotation: the string starts as 1 with the head on the first word; each step deletes the first bit, appends the current word if that bit was 1, and moves the head to the next word, cyclically; it halts when the string is empty. Size is the total length of the words plus their number. BBCT(n) is the longest halting run of a size-n system. Cyclic tag is the model Matthew Cook used for the universality of rule 110. The bbchallenge wiki's Cyclic Tag page (last edited 2026-10-11) gives exact values through n = 7 (BBCT(7) = 13, champion 0110__) and lower bounds: BBCT(8) >= 28 (101_10_), 9 >= 717 (1011_00_), 10 >= 1,626,862 (1001_1_00), 11 >= 1,859,166 (10_10010_0), 12 >= 6,328 (0111__010_0), 13 >= 5,217,735 (001110_1_0_0), 14 >= 154,171,565 (01011__0_0100). AzertyWasTaken's repository (documentation, deciders, holdout lists) reported 1 holdout at size 8, 17 at size 9 and 133 at size 10 when its table was written.
targets.success_criterion: Success means (a) a cyclic tag system of size n, 8 <= n <= 14 (conventions of https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Cyclic_Tag), that halts after STRICTLY more steps than the bound listed for n on that page, re-fetched live before claiming, verified by direct simulation; or (b) an exact BBCT(n) for some n in 8..14 that the page still lists with ' > =', with every size-n system either halting (step count given) or carrying a checkable non-halting certificate re-checked by an independent decider.

partial_wins.statement: Exact BBCT(8), with every non-halting size-8 system certified.
A size-12 system halting after more than 6,328 steps (verified by direct simulation).
Exact BBCT(9), or a new champion at any size from 9 to 14.

targets.verification_method: Independent simulator with the stated rules (calibration: 010_ halts after 7 steps, 010_0 after 8, 0110__ after 13, 101_10_ after 28; all reproduced). For exact values, enumerate all word lists of the given size, confirm the count, and re-check every certificate (exact cycles of (head, string) states; translated cycles, where the string's suffix repeats at the same head position while the prefix grows).
angles: Seed the size-12 search with the size-10 and size-11 champions plus an extra empty or one-bit word, then search the neighbourhood.
Certify growing holdouts by finding a period of the head together with a repeating block structure (translated-cycler style).
pitfalls: The repository's results.md is older than the wiki (for example it lists BBCT(10) >= 209 where the wiki lists >= 1,626,862), and its spec.md halts at fewer than two symbols, not at the empty string; the wiki's definitions and table are the authority.
Empty words count toward size through the word count (each '_' separator closes a word); size 8 means total word length plus number of words equals 8.

BBCT is not obviously monotone in n, because adding a word changes the rotation. A skeptic's exhaustive run of all 177,147 size-12 systems to 3,000,000 steps (cutting off strings above 200,000 bits) found no halter above 6,328, so a size-12 record needs a long-running system, not a quick search.

targets.name: Busy Beaver for Wang tiles: exact BBWT(5), or n Wang tiles that tile a larger largest square than the n = 5..10 records
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (SAT on d x d grids; exhaustive n = 5 enumeration up to colour renaming)
targets.statement: For a finite set of Wang tiles (unit squares with coloured edges, no rotation or reflection, touching edges must match), its score is the largest d such that the set tiles a d x d square, or 0 if there is no largest d (so every set that tiles the plane scores 0). BBWT(n) is the largest score over all sets of n tiles. The bbchallenge wiki's Wang Tiles page (last edited 2026-10-03) lists BBWT(1..4) = 1, 2, 3, 4 and only lower bounds above: BBWT(5) >= 6, BBWT(6) >= 8, BBWT(7) >= 11, BBWT(8) >= 14, BBWT(9) >= 17, BBWT(10) >= 212 (no tile set given for n = 10). The n = 5 champion is [1,0,2,0] [2,0,3,0] [3,0,4,0] [4,6,1,5] [4,5,2,6] (notation [top,right,bottom,left]). Exact values are finite computations up to n = 10 because Jeandel and Rao proved that every set of at most 10 Wang tiles that tiles the plane also tiles it periodically, so every set either has a periodic (torus) tiling or fails at some finite square size.
targets.success_criterion: Success means (a) a set of n Wang tiles, 5 <= n <= 10, with a score STRICTLY greater than the lower bound listed for n on https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Wang_Tiles, re-fetched live before claiming, certified by an explicit d x d tiling and a DRAT (or LRAT) proof, checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr, that no (d+1) x (d+1) tiling exists (free boundary, matching only between adjacent tiles); or (b) an exact BBWT(5) (or BBWT(6)) while the page lists ' > =': an enumeration of all n-tile sets up to colour renaming and tile order in which each set gets either a periodic tiling certificate (a k x l torus tiling) or an UNSAT certificate at its score + 1, the maximum matching the reported value.

partial_wins.statement: Exact BBWT(5) with all certificates (expected 6 if the listed champion is optimal).
A tile set beating the listed bound for one n in 6..9 (criterion (a)).
A 10-tile set with a certified score STRICTLY greater than 212 (criterion (a) for n = 10; the page lists 212 without a tile set), with the explicit tiling and the DRAT/LRAT certificate published.

targets.verification_method: Check the d x d tiling edge by edge. Encode (d+1) x (d+1) as SAT (one tile per cell, horizontal and vertical edge matching) with independent code and check the UNSAT proof with drat-trim; a tiling of a larger square restricts to every smaller one, so UNSAT at d+1 bounds the score. For exhaustive claims, re-generate canonical tile sets independently, confirm the count, and re-check each torus tiling and UNSAT certificate.
