Calibration: the listed n = 5 champion tiles 6 x 6 and not 7 x 7 (reproduced by backtracking).
angles: The listed champions are counters: a column of 'clock' tiles plus a few tiles that force a contradiction after a fixed number of rows. Search for counter gadgets with longer forced periods.
For n = 10, encode tile sets from small Turing machines or the Jeandel-Rao construction pruned to 10 tiles, which tile large but finite regions.
pitfalls: The page does not define the boundary condition; this target assumes free boundary (outer edges unconstrained). State the convention used.
A set that tiles the plane scores 0, not infinity; long-tiling sets must be shown NOT to tile the plane (UNSAT at d+1).
Tile sets are unordered and colours are names: count canonical forms in exhaustive claims.

targets.name: Busy Beaver for reversible Turing machines: decide BBrev(6)'s 388 holdouts or beat the 537,556-step champion
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (bbchallenge-style deciders on 388 machines)
targets.statement: BBrev(n, m) is the longest run of a halting n-state, m-symbol Turing machine that is reversible in Bennett's sense, using Bruce Smith's 'microscopic reversibility' condition for one-tape quintuple machines: for every state, all transitions into it move in the same direction and write different symbols. The bbchallenge wiki's Reversible Turing Machine page (last edited 2026-07-16) lists exact values BBrev(2) = 6, BBrev(3) = 17, BBrev(4) = 48 (Matthew House and Shawn Ligocki) and BBrev(5) = 388 (champion 1RB0RD_1RC0RB_1RD1RZ_1LE1LA_0LE0LA, Shawn Ligocki and Matthew House), and lower bounds BBrev(6) >= 537,556 (1RB1LD_1LC1RE_0LD0LC_0RE0RF_0RA1RZ_1RF1RA, Ligocki), with 388 holdouts in BBrev6_holdouts_388.txt, and a BBrev(7) lower bound from an early enumeration.
targets.success_criterion: Success means (a) a reversible (per the page's condition) 6-state 2-symbol machine in bbchallenge text format that halts from a blank tape after STRICTLY more than the BBrev(6) bound listed on https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Reversible_Turing_Machine, re-fetched live before claiming, verified by direct or proved-accelerated simulation; or (b) an exact BBrev(6) while the page still shows ' > =': every machine on the current holdout list decided. Each non-halter carries a certificate an independent decider re-checks (cycler, translated cycler, finite automata reduction, backward reasoning, or a Coq/Lean proof). Each holdout that reaches an undefined ('---') transition is reported with the step at which it does so, and is then expanded into all of its reversible tree-normal-form completions (halting there, or each reversible new transition), every one of which is decided the same way, with each halter's step count given.

partial_wins.statement: Non-halting certificates, re-checked by an independent decider, for at least 300 of the 388 machines in BBrev6_holdouts_388.txt, with the remaining list published.
Exact BBrev(6) (criterion (b)).
A reversible 7-state 2-symbol machine beating the BBrev(7) lower bound listed on the page, with a proved step count.

targets.verification_method: Check the reversibility condition mechanically for every state. Simulate with an independent TM simulator using the bbchallenge step convention (calibration reproduced: BBrev(5) champion halts after 388 steps, BBrev(6) champion after 537,556). For holdout claims, re-run independent deciders on each certificate and confirm that the decided set equals the published holdout list.
angles: Run the BB(5) decider stack (Coq-BB5 deciders: cyclers, translated cyclers, backward reasoning, FAR) on the 388 machines first; reversibility makes backward reasoning especially strong, because each configuration has at most one predecessor.
For new champions, search reversible machines built from known 6-state counters, or enumerate in tree normal form with the reversibility constraint pruning early.
pitfalls: The holdout file contains undefined transitions ('---'); a machine can halt by reaching one. Count steps the way the page's champions do.
Reversibility is a constraint on the whole transition table including transitions added later in tree normal form; check it on the completed machine.

targets.name: Lazy Beaver: compute a missing LB(n, m) value (LB(7,2), LB(5,3), LB(4,4), LB(3,5) or LB(2,7))
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days to needs cluster (all tree-normal-form machines of the domain run to the answer's step count)
targets.statement: The Lazy Beaver LB(n, m), defined by Scott Aaronson in his 2020 survey, is the smallest k > 0 such that no n-state, m-symbol Turing machine halts in exactly k steps from a blank tape. Unlike the Busy Beaver it is computable: deciding it only needs every machine simulated for k steps. The bbchallenge wiki's Lazy Beaver page (last edited 2026-10-09) lists values computed by Terry and Shawn Ligocki in 2021: LB(2..6, 2) = 7, 22, 72, 427, 8,407; LB(2,3) = 23, LB(3,3) = 351, LB(4,3) = 189,270; LB(2,4) = 93, LB(3,4) = 242,789; LB(2,5) = 956; LB(2,6) = 33,851. OEIS A337805 (Zachary Vance, 2020; a(6) added by Tijn Caspar de Leeuw, 2026-02-04) has LB(n,2) through n = 6. The cells LB(7,2), LB(5,3), LB(4,4), LB(3,5) and LB(2,7) are empty.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an exact value for one cell that is empty on https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Lazy_Beaver and in OEIS A337805 when re-fetched before claiming: a number k, a list of witness machines halting in exactly j steps for every j < k, and a complete tree-normal-form enumeration of the domain, run by code that can be audited, showing that no machine halts in exactly k steps (every machine either halts at some other step count or is still running after k steps). The step convention must match the listed values, and the enumeration must reproduce at least one listed value in a neighbouring cell.

partial_wins.statement: An independent re-computation of LB(6,2) = 8,407 or LB(2,6) = 33,851 with published code, or a demonstration that a listed value is wrong.

targets.verification_method: Re-run every witness machine and confirm it halts in exactly the stated number of steps. Re-run the enumeration with an independently written tree-normal-form generator, check the machine counts per depth, and confirm that no machine halts at step k. Calibrate on small cells (LB(2,2) = 7, LB(3,2) = 22, LB(2,3) = 23).
angles: Enumerate in tree normal form with a step cap equal to the current candidate k. Most branches halt or are pruned early, and machines still running at k need no further work.
Grow the witness set incrementally. A sorted bitmap of achieved halting times, updated as the enumeration runs, gives the answer as its first gap.
Cells with n*m = 14 (LB(7,2) and LB(2,7)) have the smallest raw machine domains among the empty cells. LB(5,3) and LB(3,5) have 15 transitions and LB(4,4) has 16.
pitfalls: Halting-step conventions differ (whether the halting transition counts), so calibrate on the listed values first.

Checked 2026-10-30: no value beyond the wiki table turned up on Shawn Ligocki's blog (sligocki.com) or in web search. The googology wiki page was unreadable (HTTP 402) and the Busy Beaver Discord needs a login, so neither was checked. Re-check both, the second as a human step, before claiming.
Tree normal form must not drop machines that halt in exactly k steps through symmetric variants. Prove that the reduction preserves halting times.

targets.name: Tiny Tag busy beaver: the first exact value beyond n = 10 (all 2,048 length-11 strings classified)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-minutes to laptop-hours
targets.statement: Tiny Tag (bbchallenge wiki page created 2025-12-02 by Discord user Jack, last edited 2026-08-11) is a self-describing cyclic tag system: the runs of an initial binary string b (maximal blocks of equal bits) become the production rules p_1..p_k, used cyclically; each step deletes the first bit and, if it was 1, appends the current rule, then advances the rule pointer; it halts when the string is empty. f(n) is the largest finite number of steps taken by any length-n string. The page lists f(1..10) = 1, 5, 9, 13, 15, 334, 404, 670, 12,584, 2,180,995 (the last for 0100011110), says values beyond n = 10 are 'not currently known', and gives a deliberately weak bound f(48) >> 971,038 from eight copies of 010111. Determining f(11) means classifying 2,048 strings, each halting or proved non-halting.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an exact f(n) for some n >= 11 while https://wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Tiny_Tag (re-fetched before claiming) lists no exact value for it: every one of the 2^n strings either halts (step count by direct simulation) or carries a non-halting certificate re-checked by an independent program (an exact repeated (pointer, string) state, or a translated-cycle or block-growth proof checked symbolically), and the maximum halting step count is reported with its string.

partial_wins.statement: Exact f(11), with all non-halting length-11 strings certified.
Exact f(12).

A classification of the 2,048 length-11 strings in which every string either halts (with its step count) or carries a re-checked non-halting certificate, except at most 20 strings, which are published as an explicit holdout list.

targets.verification_method: Independent simulator from the page's definition (calibration reproduced: f(1..10) champions halt after 1, 5, 9, 13, 15, 334, 404, 670, 12,584 and 2,180,995 steps). Re-check every non-halting certificate, and confirm the classified strings number exactly 2^n.
angles: Most non-halting strings grow linearly: detect a fixed pointer phase in which the string's suffix repeats with a growing prefix, and prove it symbolically.
Complementary symmetry: the rules depend only on run lengths and the first bit, so strings with the same run structure can share analysis.
pitfalls: The rules are the runs of the INITIAL string and never change; the pointer advances on every step, including steps that delete a 0.
A quick 2e7-step run (made while this entry was written, not published) left several hundred length-11 strings running; most are probably growers, but each needs a certificate.
The page is young and has few contributors; re-fetch it, and check its history, before claiming.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Post's 1921 tag problem (00, 1101; delete 3): a word that never halts or cycles, or a proof that none exists
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster for exhaustive extensions; pure thought for the full problem
targets.statement: Emil Post's tag system deletes the first 3 symbols of a binary word and appends 00 if the first symbol was 0, or 1101 if it was 1. Post found it 'hopeless' in 1921, and Minsky (1967) wrote that he and Post found it intractable. It is unknown whether every initial word eventually halts (length below 3) or enters a cycle. Shigeru Watanabe described the basic cycle families in 1963, and Liesbeth De Mol studied the system in a series of papers following her 2007 thesis. In March 2021 Stephen Wolfram reported that all initial words up to (uncompressed) length 84, about 2 x 10^25 words, end in a cycle or halt. The longest transient he found is 643,158,954,877 steps (compressed initial word 28:264107671:2, ending in a cycle of length 10). No word is known to grow forever.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED only for (a) an initial binary word with a machine-checked proof (Lean, Isabelle or Coq) that its evolution under (delete 3; 0 -> 00, 1 -> 1101) never reaches a word shorter than 3 and never repeats a word, or (b) a machine-checked proof that every initial word eventually halts or repeats. Long simulations without a proof never count.

partial_wins.statement: An exhaustive verification, by code that can be audited and was independently re-run, that every initial word of length 85 (or every length from 85 to some L) halts or enters a cycle, with the maximum transient and its word reported, provided no publication found at claim time already covers that length.
An initial word whose transient exceeds 643,158,954,877 steps before it halts or enters a cycle, verified by an independent simulator run to the cycle, with the cycle length reported.

targets.verification_method: Simulate exactly with an independent implementation (calibration reproduced: 100100100000100000 reaches a cycle of length 28 after 2,141 steps). For transient claims, run to the first repeated word and report the step at which the cycle starts and its length. For exhaustive claims, re-run a random sample plus all words with the longest transients on an independent simulator, and audit the compression or symmetry reductions used. For proofs, compile the formal development and check the theorem statement against the rule.
angles: Only every third symbol is read, so the word splits into three interleaved phases; Wolfram's compressed representation works on the read phase and makes exhaustive search far cheaper.
Treat the evolution as a Collatz-like map on block counts and search for a self-similar 'highway' family with a provable invariant, which would give a candidate for (a).
pitfalls: The status rests on a 2021 article; the web search budget ran out while this entry was checked, so later extensions (De Mol, Wolfram, or others) were not ruled out. Search before claiming p1 or p2.
Lengths in Wolfram's tables are often compressed lengths (28 compressed corresponds to 84 uncompressed); state which one you use.
Halting means the word becomes shorter than 3 symbols; an empty word is not the only halting state.

targets.name: Generalized Wilson primes: the first prime of order n for the 24 orders n < 100 with none known (OEIS A128666)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (an all-primes Wilson-quotient remainder tree to 1e10 or more; checking a claim takes seconds)
targets.statement: A prime p >= n is a generalized Wilson prime of order n when p^2 divides (n-1)!(p-n)! - (-1)^n. Order 1 gives the Wilson primes. Equivalently, the Wilson quotient w_p is congruent to the harmonic number H(n-1) mod p. OEIS A128666 (Alexander Adamchuk 2007; terms added by Max Alekseyev 2012; edited by M. F. Hasler 2015; last revision #30, 2025-02-16; keywords hard, more) lists the least such prime for each order. Its comments give values for most n <= 100, including large ones such as a(72) = 14273449 and a(18) = 13151527. They also state that no prime below 1.4*10^7 is known for n in {8, 12, 14, 22, 23, 25, 29, 31, 38, 46, 48, 50, 52, 66, 77, 79, 82, 84, 87, 89, 91, 95, 96, 98, 99}. That list is out of date for n = 31, because the same entry gives a(31) = 20981, which a lane checker confirmed on 2026-10-30. So 24 orders below 100 have no known prime, and no search past 1.4e7 is reported anywhere. The Costa-Gerbicz-Harvey remainder-tree method computes (p-1)! mod p^2 for all p up to 2e13. Every order then follows at no extra cost, because (p-n)! = (p-1)!/((p-1)(p-2)...(p-n+1)) mod p^2. Heuristically, each order expects about ln(ln X / ln 1.4e7) primes up to X: about 0.33 per order at X = 1e10, or roughly 8 hits over the 24 open orders.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for each pair (n, p) where n is in the open set {8, 12, 14, 22, 23, 25, 29, 38, 46, 48, 50, 52, 66, 77, 79, 82, 84, 87, 89, 91, 95, 96, 98, 99} and p is a proven prime with ((n-1)! * (p-n)! - (-1)^n) mod p^2 == 0. The claim must also show, from a complete logged search, that no prime below p satisfies the condition for that order, which settles a(n). The order must still have no value in the DATA, comments or b-file of https://oeis.org/A128666, re-fetched immediately before the claim. A prime of order n that is not shown to be the least counts as partial win p1. Each order settled counts once. Direction: minimize the number of unsettled orders below 100.

partial_wins.statement: A proven prime p > 1.4e7 that is a generalized Wilson prime of an open order n (congruence checked exactly), with the minimality search not yet complete. This gives an upper bound on a(n).

Search certificate: all primes up to at least 1e9 tested for all 24 open orders, with the Wilson residues (p-1)! mod p^2 published in hashed blocks. The run must reproduce every known a(n) <= 1e9 from the A128666 comments (for example a(18) = 13151527 and a(72) = 14273449) and survive a random 0.1% recomputation by the verifier.

First prime p > 1.4e7 for an order n in 100 < n <= 200 that has no generalized Wilson prime below 1.4e7 and no value given anywhere in A128666, shown to be the least by a logged search over all primes from n to p. (Most orders in this range have small least primes, for example a(101) = 149 and a(102) = 2903, found in seconds; those do not count.)

targets.verification_method: Prove p prime (BPSW plus PARI isprime). Compute (n-1)! mod p^2 directly, and compute (p-n)! mod p^2 independently, either by a direct product for p up to about 1e8 or as (p-1)! times the inverse of prod_{j=1}^{n-1}(p-j), with (p-1)! from a fast factorial (PARI or FLINT), and check the congruence. For minimality, rerun the claimant's search on random sub-ranges and reproduce all known small a(n). A naive O(p) checker reproduces every listed a(n) < 60000 in minutes; a(31) = 20981 was independently re-confirmed on 2026-10-30.
angles: Implement the Costa-Gerbicz-Harvey accumulating remainder tree for (p-1)! mod p^2 over all primes in a block, then test all open orders in O(n) per prime from the one Wilson residue.
Use the equivalent test w_p == H(n-1) (mod p), with H(n-1) mod p precomputed for n <= 200, so each prime needs one Wilson quotient mod p plus a table lookup.
Run blocks in order of increasing p so the first hit for each order is its least prime, and keep a block log for minimality.
pitfalls: The A128666 comment's 'not known' list wrongly includes n = 31; a(31) = 20981 is already in the same entry.
p must be at least n; for p < n the expression is undefined.
An upper bound (some prime of order n) is not a(n) unless every smaller prime was tested.
Floating point or 64-bit overflow in mod p^2 products: use 128-bit or Montgomery arithmetic.

targets.name: Wieferich primes to other bases: a new p with b^(p-1) == 1 (mod p^2) beyond Richard Fischer's searched limits (incl. Mirimanoff base 3)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (per base or batch of bases; composite bases come almost free from prime-base residues)
targets.statement: A base-b Wieferich prime is a prime p with b^(p-1) == 1 (mod p^2). Base 2 is a separate target, wieferich-base-2-beyond-2-64. Richard Fischer (fermatquotient.com, building on Wilfrid Keller and Joerg Richstein's tables) maintains two tables. The first, FermQ_Sort.txt, covers bases 2 to 1052. Its stated limits: bases whose largest prime factor is at most 149 are searched to 2.00e14, the other bases to 7.4e13, and bases 3, 5 and 7 beyond 1.2e15. Its latest record is base 770 with p = 194092950328757 (2024-11-01), and News.txt was dated 2025-09-01. The second, FermQ_Sorg.txt, covers bases 2 to 10125, all searched to 4.8e12, and was updated 2026-10-21. Its statistics table matches the heuristic ln-ln count well (549 hits observed against 552.2 expected for 1e12 to 4.8e12). Base 3 (the Mirimanoff primes, OEIS A014127) has only 11 and 1006003 known; OEIS cites Dorais-Klyve's search to 9.7e14, and Fischer gives more than 1.2e15. Extending all 10000 bases from 4.8e12 to 1e13 should yield about 10000*ln(ln 1e13/ln 4.8e12), roughly 250 new pairs. A new pair can be checked with one modular exponentiation.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for each pair (b, p): an integer base 3 <= b <= 10125 that is not a perfect power (a pair for b = a^k with p not dividing k is the same pair as for a), and a proven prime p not dividing b with pow(b, p-1, p^2) == 1. The p must also be STRICTLY GREATER than that base's searched limit stated in the live FermQ_Sort.txt (for b <= 1052) or FermQ_Sorg.txt (for 1053 <= b <= 10125), and absent from that base's row in both files and from OEIS (the base-b Wieferich sequence, if one exists). All of these are re-fetched immediately before the claim. Each new pair counts once. Direction: maximize the number of new pairs. A new Mirimanoff prime (b = 3, p > 1.2e15) or a new double Wieferich pair (with p^(b-1) == 1 mod b^2 as well, absent from SwitchFermQ.txt) is flagged as a headline result.

partial_wins.statement: New pair for a base 10125 < b < 65537 that is not a perfect power, with p above 1e12, b^(p-1) == 1 mod p^2 checked exactly, and absent from both Fischer tables and OEIS.

Range certificate: one base b <= 1052 extended contiguously from its stated limit by at least 20%, with Fermat quotients q_p(b) mod p published in hashed blocks and surviving a random 1% recomputation by the verifier.

targets.verification_method: Prove p prime (BPSW plus PARI isprime). Check pow(b, p-1, p*p) == 1 with Python big integers. Read the base's row and the stated limit lines in the live Fischer file (latin-1 text) and check that p is greater and absent. For double pairs, also check pow(p, b-1, b*b) == 1.
angles: For each prime p, compute q_p(r) mod p for the 1229 prime bases r <= 10125, then get every composite base's quotient additively (q_p(ab) = q_p(a) + q_p(b) mod p). This tests all 10000 bases at the cost of the prime bases.
Montgomery arithmetic modulo p^2 with p < 2^50 fits in 128-bit words; a GPU segmented sieve feeds primes.
Prioritise the bases 1053-10125 range at 4.8e12, where yield per CPU-hour is highest.
pitfalls: The two Fischer tables have different limits: a p between 4.8e12 and 7.4e13 for a base <= 1052 is already searched.
Perfect-power bases (4, 8, 9, 16, 25, ...) repeat their root's pairs and are excluded; a pair for a power of 2 is a base-2 Wieferich prime, which is the separate target wieferich-base-2-beyond-2-64.
Base 65537 appears in FermQ_Sort.txt with its own limit (1.2e14 on 2026-10-30).
p dividing b is trivially excluded.
The files are latin-1 German text; read the limit lines carefully ('durchsucht bis').

targets.name: Lerch primes: a sixth one beyond 2*10^8 (OEIS A197632)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (extending the 2026 search by a factor of 2 is several times its cost; claims check in minutes)
targets.statement: An odd prime p is a Lerch prime if p divides the Lerch quotient l_p = (sum_{a=1}^{p-1} q_p(a) - w_p)/p, where q_p(a) is the Fermat quotient and w_p the Wilson quotient. Equivalently, sum_{a=1}^{p-1} a^(p-1) - (p-1)! == p (mod p^3). Lerch (1905) showed this congruence holds mod p^2 for every odd prime. Jonathan Sondow named these primes (2011). OEIS A197632 (revision 93, 2026-08-30; keywords hard, more) lists 3, 103, 839, 2237 and 42447347. Veljko Vranic added the fifth term on 2026-08-21 and the comment 'a(6) > 2*10^8 if it exists' on 2026-08-30. His repository github.com/veljkovranic/lerch reports an exhaustive test of every prime up to 200,000,000 with a primitive-root recurrence for Fermat quotients, three independent rechecks of hits (Rust mod p^2/p^3, CPython, FLINT Bernoulli), and invites outside reproduction. The lane checker confirmed the four small terms below 3000. Rene Gy showed a prime is both Lerch and Wilson iff (p-1)! == -1 (mod p^3).
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a proven prime p > 2*10^8 (direction: the first new term above the bound stated in the live entry) such that (sum_{a=1}^{p-1} pow(a, p-1, p^3) - (p-1)! - p) mod p^3 == 0, computed exactly and checked by two independently written programs. p must be absent from the DATA, comments and b-file of https://oeis.org/A197632 and from the veljkovranic/lerch repository (both re-fetched immediately before the claim), and p must be greater than any searched bound they state at that time. Being a(6) also requires a logged complete search from the stated bound to p; without that it is still a new Lerch prime and counts as the full win.

partial_wins.statement: Search extension certificate: every prime from 2e8 to at least 4e8 tested, with per-block hashes of l_p mod p published, reproducing all five known terms, and surviving a random 0.5% recomputation by the verifier with a different algorithm.

Independent reproduction of Vranic's 2e8 search with code sharing nothing with his repository, with block hashes that agree (or a demonstrated discrepancy: a prime below 2e8 where the two disagree, settled by a direct mod p^3 computation).

targets.verification_method: Prove p prime. Compute S = sum a^(p-1) mod p^3 directly (O(p) modular powers, or via a primitive root g so that a^(p-1) runs over g^(k(p-1))), and (p-1)! mod p^3 with a fast factorial (FLINT or PARI). Check S - (p-1)! - p == 0 mod p^3. Cross-check with Lerch's formula in the form sum q_p(a) == w_p mod p^2.
angles: Faulhaber's formula gives sum_{a < p} a^(p-1) == p*B_{p-1} (mod p^3) for p > 3, which reduces the test to p*B_{p-1} - (p-1)! == p (mod p^3). Derive this rigorously before relying on it, then look for multi-prime remainder-tree methods for both pieces.
Amortised remainder trees for (p-1)! mod p^3 (an extension of Costa-Gerbicz-Harvey) remove the O(p) factorial cost per prime.
pitfalls: Vranic may have extended the search since 2026-08-30: re-read the repository's VERIFIED_INTERVALS.md before claiming.
The congruence holds mod p^2 for every odd prime, so a mod p^2 test accepts every prime and proves nothing; the test must be done mod p^3.
Overflow: p^3 exceeds 2^64 for p > 2.6e6.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Kurepa's left factorial conjecture: an odd prime p dividing !p = 0!+1!+...+(p-1)!, beyond 2^40
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (the full 2^40 search was a major run; a contiguous range extension is laptop-days)
targets.statement: Duro Kurepa (1971) conjectured that gcd(!n, n!) = 2 for all n >= 2, where !n = sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k!. This is equivalent to: no odd prime p divides !p. Vladica Andrejic and Milos Tatarevic (Math. Comp. 85, 2016) searched all primes below 2^34 and found none, though heuristics suggest a counterexample probably exists. Their generalised k = 5 variant has the counterexample p = 9632267. Andrejic, Alin Bostan and Tatarevic ('Improved algorithms for left factorial residues', Information Processing Letters 167, 2021; arXiv 1904.09196 v3) computed !p mod p for all primes p < 2^40 and found no odd p dividing !p. Claimed proofs exist and are not accepted: Barsky-Benzaghou (2004, withdrawn in 2011) and V. M. Abramov (arXiv 2209.12677, 2022, withdrawn by the author). No 2024-2026 extension was found on 2026-10-30. Heuristically, the expected count in [2^40, 2^41] is about ln(41/40), roughly 0.025.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for an explicit odd prime p (proven prime) with sum_{k=0}^{p-1} k! == 0 (mod p), computed exactly by two independent methods. Since the 2021 search covered all p < 2^40 (= 1099511627776), any genuine counterexample should exceed it; a p below 2^40 is reported as a discrepancy with that search and still counts if it checks out. Direction: existence of one counterexample. A proof of the conjecture also counts as the full win, but only as a Lean 4 proof with no sorry and a clean axiom audit.

partial_wins.statement: Range extension certificate: all primes in [2^40, 2^40 + 10^10] with residues !p mod p published in hashed blocks and every prime with |!p mod p| < 100 (symmetric residue) listed. The certificate must survive a random 0.1% recomputation by the verifier using a different algorithm (a single-prime O(sqrt(p) log p) method).

Independent reproduction: !p mod p computed, with code sharing nothing with the authors', for all 24 primes in Table 1 of arXiv 1904.09196 (primes in (2^34, 2^40) with |!p mod p| < 100) and for p = 6855730873 (residue 2, from arXiv 1409.0800), all matching the published values, or an exactly demonstrated discrepancy.

targets.verification_method: Prove p prime. Compute !p mod p for that single p with an O(sqrt(p) log p) fast algorithm (matrix-product / polynomial multipoint evaluation of the recurrence (s, f) -> (s + f, f*k)), and independently by a straight O(p) loop if p is small enough. Check the residue is 0.
angles: Port the 2021 amortised remainder-tree idea: !p mod p is a product of 2x2 matrices [[k,0],[1,1]] evaluated mod p, computed for many primes at once.
GPU batch over consecutive primes with 64-bit Montgomery arithmetic (p < 2^42 fits).
pitfalls: Claimed full proofs (Barsky-Benzaghou 2004, withdrawn 2011; Abramov, arXiv 2209.12677, withdrawn 2022) are not accepted.
The k-generalised left factorial counterexample (p = 9632267) is not a Kurepa counterexample.
!p sums k! for k = 0..p-1 (includes 0! = 1).

targets.name: MOONSHOT - a third Wieferich prime (p^2 | 2^(p-1) - 1) beyond 2^64
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (primes above 2^64 need 128-bit moduli; a small range certificate is laptop-days)
targets.statement: A Wieferich prime satisfies 2^(p-1) == 1 (mod p^2). Only 1093 (Meissner 1913) and 3511 (Beeger 1922) are known (OEIS A001220). Search history: Crandall-Dilcher-Pomerance (1997); Knauer-Richstein (2005); Dorais-Klyve to 6.7e15 (2011). Wieferich@Home (2007-2016) and PrimeGrid's PRPNet search (to about 4.97e17) were not double-checked; PrimeGrid suspended its search as unreliable in May 2017. PrimeGrid's BOINC Wieferich and Wall-Sun-Sun project (2020-2022) reached the software limit 2^64 = 18446744073709551616 and closed in December 2022 (end notice: forum thread 10037, 2022-11-14). OEIS (Charles R Greathouse IV, 2024-09-24) records that PrimeGrid completed the search to 2^64 with no plans to continue. Wikipedia ('As of 2026') says any third Wieferich prime exceeds 2^64. Heuristically the expected count in [2^64, 2^65] is ln(65/64), about 0.016, so this is a long shot. A hit would be checked instantly.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a proven prime p > 2^64 (direction: existence) with pow(2, p-1, p^2) == 1, checked with exact big-integer arithmetic. p must not already be reported on the status sources (OEIS A001220 and the Wikipedia Wieferich prime page, re-fetched immediately before the claim). A p below 2^64 contradicts PrimeGrid's completed search and is reported as a discrepancy, which is partial win p2, not a win.

partial_wins.statement: Range certificate above 2^64: every prime in [2^64, 2^64 + 10^14] tested, with q_p(2) mod p published in hashed blocks and every near-Wieferich prime (2^((p-1)/2) == ±1 + A*p mod p^2 with |A| <= 1000) listed. Survives a random 0.5% recomputation by the verifier.

A verified error in the prior search: a prime p < 2^64 with pow(2, p-1, p^2) == 1, or a near-Wieferich prime with |A| <= 100 below 2^64 that contradicts a published PrimeGrid near-Wieferich list, demonstrated exactly.

targets.verification_method: BPSW plus an ECPP/PARI primality proof for p (a 20-digit number takes milliseconds). Check pow(2, p-1, p*p) == 1 in Python. For range certificates, recompute random primes' Fermat quotients with independent code (gmpy2) and compare block hashes.
angles: 128-bit p means a 256-bit modulus p^2: use Montgomery multiplication with four 64-bit limbs, or work mod p via Fermat-quotient tricks (2^(p-1) mod p^2 from 2^((p-1)/2) computations).
Combine with the Wall-Sun-Sun test in the same sieve pass, as PrimeGrid did.
pitfalls: PrimeGrid's 2^64 result is the bound; older 'not double-checked' claims (4.97e17) are superseded.
Wieferich primes are a different question from base-2 Wieferich pseudoprimes (composites); only primes count here.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - a Wall-Sun-Sun (Fibonacci-Wieferich) prime: p^2 | F_(p - (p/5)), beyond 2^64
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (Lucas-sequence doubling mod p^2 with p > 2^64; a small range certificate is laptop-days)
targets.statement: A Wall-Sun-Sun prime is a prime p with F_(p - (p/5)) == 0 (mod p^2), where (p/5) is the Legendre symbol. It is also called a Fibonacci-Wieferich prime. None is known. Before Wiles, Sun and Sun showed that a failure of the first case of Fermat's Last Theorem for p would force p to be a Wall-Sun-Sun prime. Search history: McIntosh and Roettger (Math. Comp. 2007) to 2e14; Dorais and Klyve to 9.7e14; PrimeGrid's first project (2011-2017, suspended as unreliable). PrimeGrid's combined Wieferich and Wall-Sun-Sun BOINC project ran from November 2020 to its close in December 2022 and reached the software limit 2^64 without a find (Wikipedia, page last edited August 2026). Heuristically about one prime per ln-ln unit is expected, and none was found below 2^64. Generalised k-Wall-Sun-Sun primes for other Lucas sequences have known small examples and do not count here.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a proven prime p > 2^64 (direction: existence) with F_(p - (p/5)) mod p^2 == 0, where F is the Fibonacci sequence (F_0 = 0, F_1 = 1), computed by fast doubling with exact big integers. p must not be reported on the Wikipedia Wall-Sun-Sun prime page at verification time. A p < 2^64 contradicts PrimeGrid's search and is reported as a discrepancy (partial win p2).

partial_wins.statement: Range certificate above 2^64: every prime in [2^64, 2^64 + 10^14] tested, with F_(p-(p/5))/p mod p published in hashed blocks and every near-Wall-Sun-Sun prime (|A| <= 1000 in PrimeGrid's classification) listed. Survives a random 0.5% recomputation by the verifier.
A verified error in the prior search: a prime p < 2^64 with p^2 | F_(p-(p/5)), shown exactly.

targets.verification_method: Prove p prime. Compute the Legendre symbol (p/5), then F_n mod p^2 by fast doubling in Python big integers, and check zero. Cross-check with the Lucas-sequence matrix power [[1,1],[1,0]]^n mod p^2 in independent code.
angles: Share the prime sieve and 256-bit Montgomery machinery with the Wieferich base-2 search: one pass tests both conditions.
Use the Lucas V-sequence doubling (V_2n = V_n^2 - 2Q^n), which needs fewer multiplications than Fibonacci doubling.
pitfalls: This is the same problem as 'Fibonacci-Wieferich prime'; do not double count.
Use p - (p/5), not p - 1, as the index; p = 5 is excluded.
Primes for other Lucas sequences (Pell, k-Wall-Sun-Sun) are different problems.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - a fourth Wilson prime (p^2 | (p-1)! + 1) beyond 2*10^13
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (amortised remainder trees over all primes; a range certificate past 2e13 is laptop-days to weeks)
targets.statement: A Wilson prime satisfies (p-1)! == -1 (mod p^2). Only 5, 13 (Mathews 1892) and 563 (Goldberg 1953, on SEAC) are known (OEIS A007540, revision 2026-05-25). Search history: Crandall-Dilcher-Pomerance to 5e8 (1997); the Ibercivis and mersenneforum distributed searches (Tapio Rajala's status page, last updated 2011, shows ranges done to 4e11); Edgar Costa, Robert Gerbicz and David Harvey ('A search for Wilson primes', Math. Comp. 83 (2014) 3071-3091; arXiv 1209.3436) to 2e13 with new amortised algorithms. The OEIS entry and Wikipedia (edited 2026-08-21) both give 'next term > 2*10^13', and no later search was found on 2026-10-30. Near-Wilson primes ((p-1)! == -1 + B*p mod p^2 with |B| <= 100) are tabulated from 1e6 to about 4e11 on Wikipedia. Heuristically, the expected number of Wilson primes in [2e13, 4e13] is about ln(ln 4e13 / ln 2e13), roughly 0.02.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a proven prime p > 2*10^13 (direction: existence) with ((p-1)! + 1) mod p^2 == 0, computed by two independent fast-factorial implementations, and p absent from OEIS A007540 and the Wikipedia page at verification time. A p below 2e13 contradicts the Costa-Gerbicz-Harvey search and is reported as a discrepancy (partial win p2).

partial_wins.statement: Range certificate: every prime in [2e13, 2e13 + 1e11] tested, with Wilson quotients w_p mod p published in hashed blocks and all near-Wilson primes with |B| <= 100 listed. Survives a random spot-check of 1000 primes recomputed by the verifier with an independent single-prime fast factorial.
A verified error in the prior record: a prime below 2e13 that is a Wilson prime, or a near-Wilson prime with |B| <= 100 between 1e6 and 4e11 missing from the published table, demonstrated exactly.

targets.verification_method: Prove p prime. Compute (p-1)! mod p^2 for that single p with a sqrt(p)-time fast factorial (FLINT or PARI) and independently via the Wilson quotient and Lerch/Glaisher relations if available; check the result equals p^2 - 1.
angles: Reimplement the Costa-Gerbicz-Harvey accumulating remainder tree. The same residues also settle generalized Wilson orders (see target generalized-wilson-primes-open-orders), so run both together.
GPU-friendly polynomial product trees with NTT over 64-bit primes and CRT.
pitfalls: Rajala's distributed-search page (last updated 2011) is stale; the 2e13 bound is Costa-Gerbicz-Harvey.
Near-Wilson primes (B != 0) are not Wilson primes.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - a third Wolstenholme prime (p | B_(p-3) numerator, i.e. C(2p-1,p-1) == 1 mod p^4) beyond 10^11
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (GPU-scale; per-prime cost grows linearly in p; a single claim checks in under an hour)
targets.statement: A Wolstenholme prime is a prime p with binomial(2p-1, p-1) == 1 (mod p^4). Equivalently, p divides the numerator of the Bernoulli number B_(p-3), so (p, p-3) is an irregular pair. Only 16843 (Selfridge-Pollack 1964) and 2124679 (Buhler-Crandall-Ernvall-Metsankyla, 1993) are known (OEIS A088164, revision 2026-04-05). Search history: McIntosh (1995) to 2e8; Trevisan-Weber (2001) to 2.5e8; McIntosh-Roettger (2007) to 1e9; McIntosh later to 1e10. Andrew R. Booker, Shehzad Hathi, Michael J. Mossinghoff and Timothy S. Trudgian ('Wolstenholme and Vandiver primes', Ramanujan J. 58 (2022) 913-941; arXiv 2101.11157 v2, 2022-03-27) raised the bound tenfold and found none below 1e11, using new congruences for Bernoulli numbers mod p and GPU searches. The OEIS comment still cites the 6e10 bound of the paper's first version (Hathi-Mossinghoff-Trudgian 2021); Wikipedia (edited 2026-08-21) gives 1e11. No search past 1e11 was found on 2026-10-30. The log log heuristic expects about one Wolstenholme prime between 1e9 and 1e24, so about 0.8 between 1e11 and 1e24.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a proven prime p > 10^11 (direction: existence) with binomial(2p-1, p-1) mod p^4 == 1, or equivalently B_(p-3) == 0 (mod p). Both forms must be checked by independent programs. p must be absent from OEIS A088164 and the Wikipedia page at verification time. A p below 1e11 contradicts the 2022 search and is reported as a discrepancy (partial win p2).

partial_wins.statement: Block certificate: the first 10^5 consecutive primes above 1e11 tested, with B_(p-3) mod p published for each, and a random 20 of them recomputed by the verifier with an independent single-prime Bernoulli-mod-p algorithm (Harvey's bernmm-style method), all matching.
A verified error in the prior search: a Wolstenholme prime below 1e11, demonstrated exactly.

targets.verification_method: Prove p prime. Compute B_(p-3) mod p for the single p with an O(p log p) algorithm (Harvey's method or FLINT), and independently compute binomial(2p-1, p-1) mod p^4 via a fast factorial mod p^4 (product trees). Both must agree.
angles: Start from the 2022 paper's congruences for B_(p-3) mod p, which shorten the sum per prime, and port them to GPU with 64-bit Montgomery arithmetic.
Share the pass with the Vandiver-prime test (target vandiver-euler-prime-beyond-1e11), as the 2022 paper did.
pitfalls: The OEIS comment's 6e10 bound is older than the 2022 published 1e11.
Composite n with binomial(2n-1, n-1) == 1 mod n^4 is a separate open question (converse of Wolstenholme's theorem) and does not count here.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - a ninth Vandiver (Euler) prime, p | E_(p-3), beyond 10^11 (OEIS A198245)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (GPU-scale per-prime Euler-number residues; a single claim checks in under an hour)
targets.statement: A Vandiver prime (also called an Euler prime) is a prime p that divides the Euler number E_(p-3). Zhi-Wei Sun found 149 and 241 (2010) and Romeo Mestrovic found 2946901 (2011). OEIS A198245 (revision 67, 2026-06-28; keyword more) lists eight terms and credits the next five, 16467631, 17613227, 327784727, 426369739 and 1062232319, to Hiroaki Yamanouchi (2017, with a(9) > 2e9); Booker et al. say 16467631 and 17613227 were already reported by John B. Cosgrave and Karl Dilcher (Acta Arith. 161, 2013). Andrew R. Booker, Shehzad Hathi, Michael J. Mossinghoff and Timothy S. Trudgian ('Wolstenholme and Vandiver primes', Ramanujan J. 58 (2022); arXiv 2101.11157 v2) increased the search range twentyfold and found no others below 1e11. No later extension was found on 2026-10-30. Heuristically, about one Vandiver prime is expected per factor-e increase of ln p, so the expected count in [1e11, 1e12] is ln(27.6/25.3), roughly 0.09.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for a proven prime p > 10^11 (direction: existence) with E_(p-3) == 0 (mod p), computed by two independent programs. p must be absent from OEIS A198245 (DATA, comments, b-file) re-fetched immediately before the claim. A p below 1e11 not in the list contradicts the 2022 search and is reported as a discrepancy (partial win p2).

partial_wins.statement: Block certificate: the first 10^5 consecutive primes above 1e11 tested, with E_(p-3) mod p published, and a random 20 recomputed by the verifier with an independent algorithm, all matching.
A verified error in the prior search: a Vandiver prime below 1e11 not among the eight listed, demonstrated exactly.

targets.verification_method: Prove p prime. Compute E_(p-3) mod p for the single p through its relation to Bernoulli-type sums (for example via sums of Legendre-like characters or the generalized Bernoulli number B_(p-2, chi_4)), using two independent methods. Reproduce the eight known terms as a regression first.
angles: E_(p-3) mod p is a twisted Bernoulli number B_(p-2, chi_4) up to a unit, so Harvey-style multimodular methods for Bernoulli numbers apply.
Run in the same GPU pass as the Wolstenholme test.
pitfalls: OEIS notes an inconsistency: Hathi et al. list 2124679 (the second Wolstenholme prime) in a Vandiver context; it is not an accepted term.
A different 'Euler primes' sequence (A196230) exists; use A198245.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Erdős–Straus conjecture (Erdős #242): 4/n with no 3-term Egyptian fraction, or verification beyond 10^18
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days for a range-extension partial win; needs cluster for a large extension
targets.statement: The Erdős–Straus conjecture (Erdős problem #242) says that for every n > 2 there are positive integers x < y < z with 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z. It suffices to treat primes n, and Mordell's identities cover every prime except those in six classes mod 840 (1, 121, 169, 289, 361, 529). Verification history: Oblath to 1e5; Yamamoto to 1e7; Swett to 1e14; Salez to 1e17 (arXiv 1406.6307, 2014); Spiridon Mihnea and Bogdan C. Dumitru to 1e18 (arXiv 2509.00128, 2025-08-29), extending Salez's modular-filter sieve with S_29 to a set R_8 of 2,101,514 residue classes. Problem page #242 (last edited 2026-05-07) cites the 1e18 bound and still lists the problem as open. Its forum thread rejects several 2025-2026 'proofs': a ResearchGate paper, arXiv 2508.07367, the Bradford preprint arXiv 2602.11774, and a Lean 'full CRT coverage' claim. A counterexample is believed not to exist; the realistic win is a certified extension.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (full win) for an integer n > 10^18 with a complete proof that no positive integers x, y, z solve 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z (finite exhaustive case analysis, machine-checked or independently re-run in full). This is a moonshot. A full proof of the conjecture counts only as a Lean proof with no sorry and a clean axiom audit. Range extensions are partial wins only and must start from the bound stated on https://www.erdosproblems.com/242 and in arXiv 2509.00128 at verification time (1e18 on 2026-10-30; direction: larger verified bound).

partial_wins.statement: Certified extension: every prime p in (1e18, 1e18 + 1e16] that lies in a residue class not covered by the published identities and filters is given an explicit (x, y, z), and the code that proves the remaining classes are covered is released. The verifier checks 4xyz == n(xy + yz + zx) exactly for a random 10^6 of the listed primes and re-runs the class-coverage proof.

Independent reproduction of the 1e17 to 1e18 range (Mihnea-Dumitru) with code sharing nothing with theirs, publishing per-block hashes of the hard primes and their solutions, or a demonstrated error in their filter (a prime in a class they excluded as covered for which their identity fails).

targets.verification_method: For listed solutions, check 4*x*y*z == n*(x*y + y*z + z*x) with exact integers. For coverage, re-derive each modular identity symbolically (SymPy) and check that the union of covered classes plus the explicitly solved primes is the whole range. Spot-check random primes with an independent solver.
angles: Add one more prime filter (S_31) to the Salez/Mihnea-Dumitru sieve so the surviving class density drops, then sieve primes only in surviving classes.
For survivors, use the divisor criterion: a solution with x = ceil(n/4) + t exists iff some divisor condition on (4x - n) holds; search small t first.
pitfalls: Many 'proofs' circulate; the problem page and its forum thread reject all of them so far.
Periodicity arguments do not prove a residue class is covered (Bloom on the #242 forum).
The generalized Erdős–Straus–Schinzel versions (5/n, k/n) are different problems.

targets.name: 16 x 16 Sudoku with 54 or fewer clues: beat the 55-clue record (OEIS A198297, 15 <= a(4) <= 55)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (one uniqueness check by SAT takes seconds; the cost is the search)
targets.statement: OEIS A198297(n) is the fewest givens in a uniquely solvable n^2 x n^2 Sudoku. a(3) = 17 (McGuire, Tugemann and Civario, Exp. Math. 2014). For 16 x 16 with 4 x 4 boxes the entry states 15 <= a(4) <= 55. The lower bound is the trivial n^2 - 1 bound (David Radcliffe, 2019); the entry carries keywords hard and more and was last edited in January 2026 with the bound unchanged. The 55-clue record was posted by 'ton' on the New Sudoku Players' Forum (thread 'Minimum givens on larger puzzles', 1 Apr 2015, citing a Japanese puzzle book) and transcribed by m_b_metcalf. It improved T_Shirakawa's 56 (May 2011) and gsf's 77 (2006). No smaller puzzle has been posted since: the thread's last post is from June 2024, and the separate thread 'minimum number of clues 16x16 and higher' ends in 2017 pointing to the 55. We re-verified the 55-clue puzzle printed in A198297 on 2026-10-30 with two independent SAT checks: unique solution, and minimal. ton's empirical formula floor(N^2/4) - (h-1)(w-1) gives exactly 55 here. His records also meet it for 3x4, 3x5 and 4x5 boxes, so 54 would beat both the record and the community's heuristic. Target: a 16 x 16 puzzle with at most 54 clues and a unique solution, or a certified proof that a(4) = 55.
targets.success_criterion: Success means either (a) a 16 x 16 array of givens (values 1..16; standard rows, columns and 4 x 4 boxes) with at most 54 givens (STRICTLY fewer than 55; direction: min) that has exactly one completion; or (b) a machine-checked proof that no 16 x 16 puzzle with at most 54 givens has a unique completion. Uniqueness in (a) must be shown either by a solution plus a DRAT/LRAT-checked UNSAT proof (drat-trim or cake_lpr) for 'givens AND NOT that solution', or by two independent exact solvers (e.g. DLX and a CDCL SAT solver) each reporting exactly one solution. In both cases, re-fetch OEIS A198297 (https://oeis.org/A198297 and https://oeis.org/history?seq=A198297) and the last page of http://forum.enjoysudoku.com/minimum-givens-on-larger-puzzles-t4801.html immediately before claiming; they must still show 55 as the best known.

partial_wins.statement: A uniquely solvable, minimal 16 x 16 puzzle with exactly 55 clues that provably differs from every 55-clue puzzle posted in A198297 or the 'Minimum givens on larger puzzles' thread (on 2026-10-30 only ton's). Proof of difference: its sorted per-digit clue counts, or its sorted per-box clue counts, differ from each known 55's. Both are invariant under Sudoku symmetries and relabelling.

A certified proof that a(4) >= 16, i.e. that no 16 x 16 puzzle with 15 givens has a unique completion. It needs a DRAT/LRAT certificate, or an exhaustive search reproduced by two independent implementations.

targets.verification_method: Parse the 256 cells and count the givens. Encode the puzzle as CNF (4096 variables). Get one model, block it, and check UNSAT with a proof log (about 3 s with pysat/CaDiCaL for the 55-clue example). Cross-check with a DLX solver. For p1, recompute the two invariants. For (b), check the proof with drat-trim or cake_lpr, and check that the encoding reproduces a(2) = 4 and known 9 x 9 facts.
angles: Neighbourhood search {-k+m} around ton's 55 (remove k clues, add m) as was done for 9 x 9 17s and 39s, using a fast 16 x 16 SAT/bitset uniqueness test.

Pick solution grids with many automorphisms or few unavoidable sets, as with the 9 x 9 'MC grid' studies; hitting-set enumeration over unavoidable sets (McGuire et al.) for a fixed grid finds its minimum-clue puzzles.
Start from the qiuyanzhe / hkociemba constructions (about floor(N^2/4) = 64 clues) and reduce.
pitfalls: Only 4 x 4 boxes count here; other box shapes are the separate rectangular-box target.
Hex formats (0-F vs 1-G vs 1-16) cause off-by-one transcription errors; ton's 55 was hard to read even for forum veterans.
Lass (2012) and Cooper-Kirkpatrick (Discrete Math 2014) study critical sets of generalized Sudoku; check them before claiming any lower bound.

targets.name: Fewest clues for Sudoku with other box shapes: beat ton's records (10x10 2x5: 22, 12x12 2x6: 32, 12x12 3x4: 30, 15x15 3x5: 48, 20x20 4x5: 88, 25x25 5x5: 146)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (SAT uniqueness checks take seconds to a minute even at 25 x 25)
targets.statement: For N x N Sudoku with h x w boxes, the fewest givens of a uniquely solvable puzzle is known only up to 9 x 9. OEIS A372224 (Gomez de la Vega and Karamchedu, 2024) tabulates the smallest critical set with A033676(n) x A033677(n) boxes for n <= 9 (a(6) = 8, a(8) = 14, a(9) = 17), so its a(10) (2 x 5 boxes) and a(12) (3 x 4 boxes) are open. For prime n the board is a Latin square; Richard Bean's October 2026 preprint (arXiv:2610.18199, not yet refereed) proves the minimum floor(n^2/4) there. The best-known values are in the New Sudoku Players' Forum thread 'Minimum givens on larger puzzles'. All are by 'ton': 10x10 (2x5) 22, 12x12 (2x6) 32, 12x12 (3x4) 30 and 15x15 (3x5) 48 (1 Apr 2017); 25x25 (5x5) 146 (1 Apr 2019); 20x20 (4x5) 88 (1 Apr 2024, after 91 in 2019 and 89 in 2021). Mathimagics (2019) and coloin keep summary tables there, now stale for 4x5. ton's heuristic floor(N^2/4) - (h-1)(w-1) is met exactly for 3x4, 3x5 and 4x5 boxes but not for 2x5 (21), 2x6 (31) or 5x5 (140). The thread's last post is from June 2024. We re-verified all six records on 2026-10-30 by SAT: each is unique and minimal. 16 x 16 (4x4) is a separate bank target. Target: strictly fewer clues for one listed shape, or a certified optimality proof.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for one listed shape (N, h x w) in {(10, 2x5), (12, 2x6), (12, 3x4), (15, 3x5), (20, 4x5), (25, 5x5)} with h rows and w columns per box, either (a) a puzzle with STRICTLY fewer givens than the live record (direction: min) and exactly one completion, shown by a solution plus a DRAT/LRAT-checked UNSAT proof after blocking it, or by two independent exact solvers each reporting one solution; or (b) a machine-checked proof that the live record is optimal. Case (b) would settle A372224 a(10) = 22 or a(12) = 30. Re-fetch the forum thread (all pages, http://forum.enjoysudoku.com/minimum-givens-on-larger-puzzles-t4801.html) and https://oeis.org/A372224 immediately before claiming; the claim must beat the best value shown there and in any later post.

partial_wins.statement: A certified lower bound above the trivial N - 1 for one listed shape, e.g. a DRAT-checked or two-implementation exhaustive proof that no 10 x 10 (2 x 5) puzzle with 11 or fewer givens is uniquely solvable.

A first record for a box shape absent from the thread on 2026-10-30: a unique, minimal puzzle with STRICTLY fewer than floor(N^2/4) givens (the value of the generic qiuyanzhe/hkociemba construction), i.e. 14 x 14 (2x7) with <= 48, 18 x 18 (3x6) with <= 80, or 24 x 24 (4x6) with <= 143 givens.

targets.verification_method: Generic CNF encoder for N x N with h x w boxes. One model, block it, UNSAT. Minimality is optional for (a) but required for p2: each single removal must give a second model. Our pysat checker verified ton's 25 x 25 record in under 60 s. Cross-check with an independent DLX.
angles: The shapes where records sit above ton's formula (2x5 at 22 vs 21, 2x6 at 32 vs 31, 5x5 at 146 vs 140) are the natural first attacks.
Neighbourhood search {-k+m} from ton's puzzles with a fast SAT oracle; or SAT-based search with cardinality constraints on a fixed solution grid (minimum hitting set of unavoidable sets).
pitfalls: 2x6 and 3x4 boxes on 12 x 12 are different problems; A372224 uses the A033676 x A033677 shape (2x5 for 10, 3x4 for 12).
For prime N the board is a Latin square, and Bean's October 2026 preprint proves the minimum floor(N^2/4): nothing to win there.
The thread mixes 'h x w' and 'w x h' notation; state rows x columns per box explicitly.
The summary tables in the thread (coloin, Mathimagics 2019) still show 91 for 4x5; the live record is ton's 88 of April 2024.

targets.name: Most clues in a minimal 9 x 9 Sudoku: a minimal puzzle with 41 clues (only two 40-clue minimal puzzles are known)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days
targets.statement: A minimal (irreducible) Sudoku has a unique solution, and deleting any clue gives a puzzle with several solutions. The minimum, 17, is settled (McGuire-Tugemann-Civario 2014). The maximum is open. Mladen Dobrichev ('dobrichev') found the only two known 40-clue minimal puzzles during the programmers-forum project on the 40+ clue space, where he and 'blue' made the main progress. He also collected 2,650 minimal 39-clue puzzles (batches to July 2015) and posted one more on 7 Aug 2025. The search is documented in eleven's thread 'High clue tamagotchis' (New Sudoku Players' Forum, 2010-2025), building on Havard's and others' earlier 'Max number of clues' threads. On 29 Jun 2025 eleven confirmed that the two 40s are still the only known ones and that nobody has searched seriously since; he rates the chances of a 41 as close to zero. Nobody has published a proof that 40 is the maximum. Mathimagics' 2019 table lists GNC = 40 for 3x3 boxes and leaves it unknown for every larger size. We re-verified both 40s on 2026-10-30 by SAT. Both are unique and minimal, with the same solution grid. Target: a minimal 41-clue puzzle, or a proof that none exists.
targets.success_criterion: Success means either (a) a 9 x 9 Sudoku with at least 41 givens (STRICTLY more than 40; direction: max) that has exactly one completion and is minimal: for every given, deleting it leaves at least two completions, shown by an explicit second solution. Both properties must be confirmed by two independent exact solvers. Or (b) a machine-checked proof that no minimal 9 x 9 puzzle has 41 or more givens, establishing 40 as the maximum. Re-fetch the last pages of http://forum.enjoysudoku.com/high-clue-tamagotchis-t30020.html immediately before claiming: they must show no 41.

partial_wins.statement: A third minimal 40-clue puzzle that is not equivalent to either known 40 under the Sudoku symmetry group (3,359,232 geometric maps x 9! relabellings), shown by comparing minlex canonical forms.
A minimal 39-clue puzzle that is not equivalent to any of the 2,651 known 39s: dobrichev's list, reposted by ghfick on 8 Aug 2025 in the thread, plus dobrichev's 7 Aug 2025 puzzle.

A reproducible exhaustive proof, agreed by two independent programs, that the solution grid of the two known 40s (576821349812934567934576182741358296358692471629147853463715928185269734297483615) has no minimal puzzle with 41 or more clues.

targets.verification_method: Check that the givens are consistent. Run a SAT or DLX count capped at 2 for uniqueness, then one count per deleted given for minimality (81 checks, well under a second). Canonicalize to minlex (gsf-style or Serg's canonicalizer) to compare with the known 40s and 39s.
angles: Dobrichev's sudoku35plus tool describes the seed-and-strip approach (subgrids with up to 40 givens, then strip to minimal); the forum says nobody has searched seriously since the 40s were found.
High-clue minimal puzzles concentrate clues in a few boxes with many 'pinned' cells; search the space of minimal sub-puzzles of grids with many unavoidable 4-sets.
pitfalls: 'Minimal' means no single clue is redundant; it does not mean the minimum number of clues for its grid.
A valid but non-minimal 41-clue puzzle is trivial (any 41 cells of a grid); only minimal ones count.
The original 40+ thread was lost in a forum crash; check dobrichev's and blue's later posts before calling a 39 or 40 new.

Mathimagics (Apr 2019) mentions 1,261,278 puzzles extracted from Mladen's data, so larger unposted collections of high-clue puzzles may exist; p2 is judged only against the 2,651 posted 39s, and a claimant must say where a 'new' 39 came from.

targets.name: Sudoku-X with 11 clues: beat the 12-clue minimum (known since 2007; 558,981 12-clue puzzles known, 552,952 public)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days
targets.statement: Sudoku-X is 9 x 9 Sudoku in which both main diagonals must also contain 1-9. The diagonals destroy many unavoidable sets, so Sudoku-X needs fewer clues than the 17 of plain Sudoku. Since November 2005 the best was 13. In July 2007 Ruud (SudoCue) found 12-clue Sudoku-X puzzles by neighbourhood search (forum thread '13-clue Sudoku X', 2005-2024). His 'Minimum Sudoku-X Collection' page says the search continues, doubts an 11 will ever be found, and offers a zip of 552,952 12-clue puzzles. That zip is the community list. From August 2018 Mathimagics, Leren and ton grew Ruud's 7,193 puzzles (7,180 after duplicates were removed) to 552,950 in the New Sudoku Players' Forum thread 'SudokuX (Diagonal Sudoku)', and Ruud added 2 in January 2022. Leren and ton kept searching. They had 558,389 known 12s by 10 Dec 2023 and 558,981 by 24 Nov 2024 (Leren, same thread). The roughly 6,000 newer puzzles are not posted. No 11-clue Sudoku-X has been found. Leren (Sept and Nov 2024) listed 67 'almosts': 11-clue sets with exactly two Sudoku-X solutions, only four of them using 8 distinct digits. m_b_metcalf (2022-2024) keeps analysing the collection (symmetric patterns, ratings up to ED 10.6). Mathimagics counted 9! x 153,255,603,504 Sudoku-X grids, and blue (Aug 2018) reduced this to 1,596,582,158 essentially different ones. Equivalence: 96 geometric maps (8 rotations and reflections x the joint r4 < ->r6, c4 < ->c6 swap x 6 joint permutations of the row/column pairs {1,9}, {2,8}, {3,7}), times relabelling. The trivial lower bound is 8. We re-verified two 12-clue examples on 2026-10-30 by SAT: unique and minimal as Sudoku-X, and not unique as plain Sudoku. All 67 almosts have exactly two Sudoku-X solutions. Target: an 11-clue Sudoku-X, or a proof that 12 is the minimum.
targets.success_criterion: Success means either (a) a 9 x 9 array with at most 11 givens (STRICTLY fewer than 12; direction: min) with exactly one completion satisfying rows, columns, 3 x 3 boxes and both main diagonals, confirmed by two independent exact solvers or by a solution plus a DRAT-checked UNSAT proof; or (b) a machine-checked proof that every Sudoku-X with at most 11 givens has zero or several completions, e.g. a certified exhaustive search over essentially different Sudoku-X grids. Re-fetch https://www.sudocue.net/minx.php and the last pages of http://forum.enjoysudoku.com/sudokux-diagonal-sudoku-t34959.html and http://forum.enjoysudoku.com/13-clue-sudoku-x-t2715.html immediately before claiming: none may report an 11-clue puzzle or a proof.

partial_wins.statement: A new 'almost': a set of 11 givens with exactly two Sudoku-X completions, confirmed by two independent exact solvers. It must not be equivalent to any of the 67 almosts Leren posted on 27 Sept 2024 in the thread 'Symmetric 12-clue x-sudokus' (http://forum.enjoysudoku.com/symmetric-12-clue-x-sudokus-t43405.html) under the 96-element Sudoku-X geometric group and relabelling, compared by canonical form.
A reproducible exhaustive proof, agreed by two independent programs, that none of the solution grids underlying the SudoCue 12-clue collection has an 11-clue Sudoku-X puzzle.

targets.verification_method: CNF or DLX with 29 constraint groups (9 rows, 9 columns, 9 boxes, 2 diagonals). Count solutions up to 2 and check minimality per given. For p1, count up to 3 and require exactly 2. Then canonicalize under the 96 geometric maps (check that your enumeration of Sudoku maps preserving the diagonal pair finds exactly 96) and relabelling, and compare with Leren's 67 posted almosts. For p2, the grids come from solving the downloaded SudoCue zip.
angles: Grow from Leren's 67 'almosts' (11 clues, two solutions): try all one-cell moves and relabellings, then test uniqueness.

Port the McGuire hitting-set method: with 1,596,582,158 essentially different Sudoku-X grids (blue, Aug 2018) and only 11 clues to place per grid, an exhaustive search looks cluster-scale rather than out of reach.
pitfalls: Ruud's early collections contained invalid puzzles and duplicates from a canonicalization bug: swapping rows 4 and 6 alone is not a Sudoku-X symmetry, it must go with columns 4 and 6.
Diagonal conventions differ between sites; both main diagonals must hold 1-9.
Sudoku-DG/SudokuP, Windoku-X and other combined variants are different problems.

The SudoCue zip (552,952) is not the full list. Leren and ton knew 558,981 12-clue puzzles on 24 Nov 2024, and the extra ones are unpublished, so a 12 missing from the zip is not evidence that it is new. That is why it is not a partial win.
Most almosts use only 7 distinct digits, so they are two-solution sets for a trivial reason (swap the two missing digits). Only the 4 with 8 distinct digits are close to an 11.

targets.name: Uniquely solvable nonograms: count the 7 x 7 case (OEIS A242876 a(7)) or a new n x m cell beyond n*m = 44 (A384764)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (7 x 7 is 2^49 grids, 32 times the largest size done; the n*m = 45..48 cells are laptop-hours to laptop-days)
targets.statement: A nonogram's clues are the run lengths of filled cells in each row and column. A242876(n) counts the n x n binary grids that are the unique solution of their clues: 1, 2, 14, 384, 52362, 25309575, 49745060669 for n = 0..6 (Charles R Greathouse IV and Sophia Greathouse 2014; a(5) Mark E. Shoulson 2014; a(6) = 49745060669 by Bertram Felgenhauer, June 2025, correcting the value 49866168063 entered by Karl W. Heuer in January 2015). Batenburg and Kosters (ICGA J. 2012) gave the erroneous 49745060370, 299 below Felgenhauer's value; a parity argument by olligobber (May 2026, cited in the OEIS history) shows a(6) is odd. Felgenhauer's 'Counting Nonograms' page and OEIS A384764 (b-file to antidiagonal n+m = 13) give n x m counts up to n*m = 44 (June 2025): m = 3 to n = 14, m = 4 to n = 11, m = 5 to n = 8, m = 6 to n = 7. The 7 x 7 value and the cells 3x15, 5x9 (n*m = 45), 4x12, 3x16 and 6x8 (48) are unknown. Related: A391619 (line-solvable grids, Andrei Zabolotskii 2026, with olligobber's LocalNonogram, whose README estimates over 12 years for 7 x 7 with that code) and the yesnogram counts A385861/A385862 (Karl W. Heuer 2025, from Felgenhauer's table). We reproduced the 2x2, 3x3, 4x4, 2x6 and 3x5 counts with our own brute force. Target: A242876 a(7).
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact value of A242876 a(7): the number of 7 x 7 binary grids whose (row clues, column clues) pair is shared by no other 7 x 7 grid. It must be computed by two independently written programs (different algorithms or languages) that agree, and both must reproduce every entry of Felgenhauer's table with n*m <= 42. The value must not appear in A242876 DATA, its history page (https://oeis.org/history?seq=A242876, including pending drafts) or https://int-e.eu/nono/, all re-fetched live immediately before claiming. No OEIS submission is part of the win.

partial_wins.statement: A new A384764 cell with n*m >= 45 and min(n, m) >= 3 (e.g. 5x9, 3x15, 4x12 or 6x8). It must be absent from the live int-e.eu/nono table, the A384764 b-file and A383345, and computed by two independent programs that reproduce the n*m <= 42 table.
A391619 a(7): the number of 7 x 7 nonograms solvable by iterated single-line reasoning, by two independent programs that reproduce a(0..6).
A new yesnogram count (A385861 a(7), or an A385862 cell with n*m >= 45 and min(n, m) >= 3) by two independent programs that reproduce Felgenhauer's yesnogram table.

targets.verification_method: Rerun both programs. Check the n x m vs m x n symmetry. Check the parity of the result against olligobber's parity argument where it applies. Check the partial sums by column-signature class. Brute force verifies the small cases in seconds.
angles: Felgenhauer's method groups grids by column signature (F(n+2) classes per column) so only row signatures are stored per class. 7 x 7 needs chunked parallel enumeration with on-disk sorting or hashing per class.
A transfer-matrix or meet-in-the-middle count over row signatures, using the reflection and transposition symmetries to cut the work by up to 8.
pitfalls: The count is of grids with a unique clue signature (equivalently clue sets with exactly one solution), not of all clue sets.
Empty rows have the empty clue; mishandling them changes every count.
The 2012 Batenburg-Kosters 6 x 6 value is wrong; validate against Felgenhauer's table, not the paper.

targets.name: KnotInfo stick numbers: a polygon with fewer edges than the best known for a prime knot up to 13 crossings, or a 9-stick realisation of a knot listed [9,10]
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (simulated annealing over polygons; checks take seconds)
targets.statement: The stick number (KnotInfo field polygon_index) of a knot K is the fewest straight edges in a closed polygon of type K. KnotInfo (Charles Livingston and Allison Moore, knotinfo.org) lists it for all prime knots up to 13 crossings. The data through 9 crossings comes from Cromwell, Calvo, Negami and Randell. Calvo's classification of the knots with at most 8 sticks gives the lower bound 9 for every other knot. The upper bounds for all knots through 13 crossings come from Cantarella, Rechnitzer, Schumacher and Shonkwiler, 'New upper bounds for stick numbers' (arXiv:2508.18263, JKTR 35 (2026) 2650008). They found low-stick polygons by simulated annealing with moves that preserve knot type, building on Eddy and Shonkwiler's random sampling (arXiv:1909.00917). In database_knotinfo 2026.10.5, 12,910 of the 12,965 prime knots have interval-valued stick numbers. Of these, 513 are [9,10], including every 8-crossing knot except 8_16-8_21 and most 9-crossing knots, e.g. 8_1, 9_1, 9_10. The rest include 1,134 12-crossing knots at [9,11], 6,107 13-crossing knots at [9,12] and 877 at [9,13]. Can an explicit polygon close an interval, or beat a listed upper bound?
targets.success_criterion: For a prime knot K whose polygon_index is an interval [a,b] in the live KnotInfo database (https://knotinfo.org/, or the database_knotinfo mirror when that is not older than the site), re-fetched immediately before claiming: a closed polygon with n vertices, given as exact rational coordinates. It must be in general position: no three consecutive vertices collinear, and non-adjacent edges disjoint, both checked in exact arithmetic. Its knot type, read off a regular projection as a PD code, must be identified as K (or its mirror) by SnapPy and Regina. n must equal a, which closes the interval (e.g. a 9-stick polygon for a knot listed [9,10]).

partial_wins.statement: For any interval-valued knot, a polygon verified the same way with n STRICTLY LESS than the listed upper bound b and than the bound in arXiv:2508.18263's table (direction: min), even if n > a.

A demonstrated table inconsistency: a polygon whose verified knot type contradicts a KnotInfo entry, e.g. an n-stick realisation of a knot whose listed lower bound exceeds n, with the coordinates saved.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic loads the rational coordinates, checks general position exactly, projects along a generic rational direction to get a PD code, and identifies the knot with SnapPy (identify(), plus a verified isometry for hyperbolic knots) and Regina. The edge count is the vertex count. Minutes.
angles: Conventional: start from the arXiv:2508.18263 polygons and run annealing at the target edge count with crankshaft and pivot moves, rejecting moves that change knot type (fast checks with HOMFLY or a hyperbolic volume).
Conventional: search for 9-stick knots with the Eddy-Shonkwiler confined-polygon sampler, targeted with importance weights at the remaining [9,10] types.
Cross-domain import (protein folding / molecular conformations): treat edges as rigid bonds and run parallel tempering on vertex positions.
pitfalls: Floating-point coordinates can hide a self-intersection. Rationalise them and recheck exactly before identifying the knot.
Knots listed [9,10] have survived heavy 9-gon sampling by Eddy and Shonkwiler and by Cantarella et al. Expect long odds there, and record negative runs.
Check arXiv:2508.18263 and any newer preprint for the current upper bound. KnotInfo may lag behind a paper.

targets.name: Superbridge index: a polygon realising superbridge index 3 for one of Jeon-Jin's nine candidates (5_2, 6_1, ..., 8_9), or 4 for a 9-10 crossing knot listed [4,5]
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: For a knot embedding K in R^3 and a direction v, b_v counts the local maxima of the height v.x on K. The superbridge index sb(K) is the minimum over embeddings of the maximum of b_v over all v (Kuiper, 1987). KnotInfo (Livingston and Moore) lists sb, with bounds from Randell (sb <= stick/2), Kuiper's torus-knot values, and Clayton Shonkwiler's computations (arXiv:2009.13648, 2112.10902, 2206.06950) and Eddy-Shonkwiler (arXiv:1909.00917). Jeon and Jin showed there are only finitely many 3-superbridge knots and narrowed the candidates (JKTR 2001, 2002). Shonkwiler (arXiv:2009.13648) removed 8_7 from their list, and Jeon and Jin conjecture that only 3_1 and 4_1 have sb = 3. In database_knotinfo 2026.10.5, nine knots are still listed [3,4]: 5_2, 6_1, 6_2, 6_3, 7_2, 7_3, 7_4, 8_4 and 8_9. Twelve 9-crossing knots (e.g. 9_2, 9_10, 9_38) and 164 of the 165 10-crossing knots are [4,5]. Shonkwiler proved that every prime knot through 10 crossings has sb <= 5. Lower bounds come from sb > bridge index (Kuiper) and from Jeon-Jin (sb >= 4 for every knot other than 3_1, 4_1 and the nine). Adams et al. (arXiv:2008.06483) proved sb <= 3b - 1, so every 2-bridge knot has sb <= 5 even where KnotInfo shows no entry. Is any of the nine a 3-superbridge knot, or does any [4,5] knot have a 4-superbridge polygon?
targets.success_criterion: For a knot K whose super_bridge_index is an interval [a,b] in live KnotInfo (https://knotinfo.org/, or the database_knotinfo mirror when that is not older than the site), re-fetched immediately before claiming: a closed polygon with exact rational coordinates, in general position (checked exactly), whose knot type SnapPy and Regina identify as K. Its superbridge number max_v b_v must be computed exactly and equal a. For a [3,4] knot, every direction v must have at most 3 local maxima. To compute it, enumerate the cells of the arrangement of great circles {v : v.e_i = 0} over the edge vectors e_i, and count, at a rational interior point of each cell, the vertices that are strict local maxima.

partial_wins.statement: For a prime 11- or 12-crossing knot with no KnotInfo super_bridge_index entry, a polygon verified as above (exact general position, SnapPy/Regina identification) whose superbridge number, computed exactly by cell enumeration, is at most 5 (direction: min). The knot must also satisfy three conditions. Its KnotInfo bridge_index is at least 3, since for 2-bridge knots sb <= 5 already follows from Adams et al.'s sb <= 3b - 1. Its KnotInfo polygon_index upper bound is 12, so Randell's sb <= stick/2 gives only 6. It has no value in the appendices of arXiv:2206.06950. In database_knotinfo 2026.10.5 that leaves 737 knots: 12 at 11 crossings and 725 at 12. For a 4-bridge knot this pins sb = 5.

For an 11- or 12-crossing knot with no KnotInfo superbridge entry, a verified polygon whose superbridge number, computed exactly by cell enumeration, is 4. This pins sb = 4, because Jeon and Jin's theorem gives sb >= 4 for every knot other than 3_1, 4_1 and the nine candidates. By Kuiper (sb > b), such a knot must have bridge index 2 or 3.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic checks general position exactly, identifies the knot type with SnapPy/Regina, and independently computes max_v b_v by exact cell enumeration of the great-circle arrangement, counting local maxima at one rational interior point per 2-cell. Under an hour.
angles: Conventional: optimise many-stick polygons (not minimal-stick ones) with the objective max_v b_v, as in Shonkwiler's non-minimal realisations (arXiv:2206.06950).
Cross-domain import (computational geometry / robust optimisation): minimise the worst case over the sphere of directions with a minimax solver over the arrangement cells.
pitfalls: b_v must be maximised over ALL directions, including near-degenerate ones. Sampling random v underestimates sb, so enumerate cells exactly.
Jeon and Jin's finiteness work constrains 3-superbridge knots heavily. The nine [3,4] cases may all be 4, so record negative runs honestly.
Only the knot type matters, but identify it with a verified tool, never by matching invariants alone.

targets.name: KnotInfo bridge index: settle one of the 536 13-crossing knots listed [3,4] by a 3-bridge diagram or a rank-4 Coxeter quotient
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The bridge index br(K) is the minimum number of local maxima of K (Schubert). KnotInfo (Livingston and Moore) lists it for all prime knots up to 13 crossings. Chad Musick did 11 crossings (arXiv:1208.4233). Blair, Kjuchukova, Velazquez and Villanueva did 12 crossings via the Wirtinger number (arXiv:1705.03108, Comm. Anal. Geom. 28 (2020)). Ella Pfaff did 13 crossings by combining upper bounds from that work and from Blair-Kjuchukova-Pfaff, 'The plain sphere number of a link' (arXiv:2504.10517, Pacific J. Math. 342 (2026)), with lower bounds from Blair-Kjuchukova-Morrison, 'Coxeter quotients of knot groups through 16 crossings' (Exp. Math. 34 (2025), arXiv:2208.09032). Those lower bounds use Baader-Blair-Kjuchukova: if the knot group surjects onto a Coxeter group of rank r with meridians mapped to reflections, then the meridional rank (and hence br) is at least r. In database_knotinfo 2026.10.5, every knot through 12 crossings is determined, but 536 13-crossing knots are still [3,4]. On 2026-10-20/21 Deep Bhattacharjee (github.com/creelie/conjecture-to-choose, Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.23521967; unrefereed, AI-assisted) posted certificates that 243 of the 536 have br = 4. Each certificate is a representation of the knot group into GL(4, F_q) that sends meridians to pseudo-reflections with no common nonzero fixed vector: transvections in Sp(4,F_3) for 67 knots, in Sp(4,F_5) for 161, and reflections in O(4,F_5) for 15. So fewer than four meridians cannot generate the group. An independent re-check on 2026-10-30 confirmed all 243 certificates against the KnotInfo PD codes. The other 293 knots (data/still_open.json in that repository) remain [3,4]. Those searches found no such representation over Sp(4,F_q) for q in {3,4,5,7,8,9,11}, over O(4,F_q) for q in {3,5,7}, or by pseudo-reflections in GL(4,F_2) and GL(4,F_3). They also found no 3-bridge diagram among 300 random diagrams per knot. Can a certificate settle one of the 293?
targets.success_criterion: The target is a 13-crossing knot K that meets two conditions, both re-fetched immediately before claiming: (i) its bridge_index is [3,4] in live KnotInfo (https://knotinfo.org/, or the database_knotinfo mirror when that is not older than the site); (ii) it is not settled by data/certificates.json in github.com/creelie/conjecture-to-choose, or by any other public source found in a fresh search. Today that leaves the 293 knots in that repository's data/still_open.json. A win is one of two certificates for K. (a) br = 3: a PD code D, verified as K by SnapPy/Regina identification, plus three seed strands from which the Wirtinger colouring process of Blair-Kjuchukova-Velazquez-Villanueva (arXiv:1705.03108) colours every strand of D. This shows the Wirtinger number of D is at most 3, hence br(K) <= 3. A 6-strand braid whose plat closure is verified as K also counts. (b) br = 4: an assignment to each Wirtinger generator of a verified diagram of K that satisfies every Wirtinger relation and is one of two kinds. (b1) Each generator goes to a reflection (a word conjugating a standard generator) in an explicit Coxeter group W of rank 4; the relations are checked by a word-problem solver for Coxeter groups, and the images generate W. (b2) Each generator goes to an invertible 4x4 matrix A over an explicit finite field with rank(A - I) = 1 (a pseudo-reflection), and the matrices (A - I) of all generators, stacked, have rank 4, so no nonzero vector is fixed by the image. Either gives meridional rank >= 4, and the known upper bound then gives br = 4.

partial_wins.statement: Settle 10 or more of the knots that count under the main criterion, each with a certificate (a) or (b), in one reproducible run.

A demonstrated inconsistency, with all inputs saved: a certificate (a) for a knot listed 4 in KnotInfo, or for one of the 243 knots certified br = 4 in creelie/conjecture-to-choose; or a certificate (b) for a knot listed 3.

targets.verification_method: (a) The skeptic re-identifies D as K with SnapPy/Regina and reruns the Wirtinger colouring from the three seeds, or builds the plat closure and identifies it. (b1) The skeptic checks every Wirtinger relation in W with a Coxeter-group word-problem routine (for example the Tits/Brink-Howlett solution, or the geometric representation over exact algebraic numbers) and checks that the images generate W. (b2) Working over F_q, the skeptic checks: the matrices are constant along arcs; one orientation convention holds at every crossing (x_c = x_o^e x_a x_o^-e); each matrix is invertible with rank(A - I) = 1; and the stacked (A - I) have rank 4. In every case, also confirm that K is not among the knots already certified in creelie/conjecture-to-choose data/certificates.json. Minutes per knot.
angles: Conventional: randomised Reidemeister exploration, recomputing the Wirtinger number on each new diagram, since non-minimal diagrams can have a lower Wirtinger number. The 300 random diagrams per knot already tried are a small sample, and many of the 293 may well be 3-bridge.
Conventional: search for 3-bridge plat presentations (6-strand braids) by matching HOMFLY or Alexander data, then identify the closure with SnapPy.

Conventional: for br = 4, search rank-4 Coxeter quotients beyond the finite and small dihedral targets of arXiv:2208.09032, or 4-dimensional pseudo-reflection representations over fields not yet tried (larger q, extension fields beyond F_4, F_8, F_9, or orthogonal forms over other q).
