Only dimension 4 is useful: a fixed-point-free pseudo-reflection representation in dimension d forces meridional rank >= d, and br <= 4 is already known.
pitfalls: The Wirtinger colouring rule must be the published one (a strand is coloured when it is the understrand at a crossing whose overstrand and other understrand are coloured). A looser rule gives false upper bounds.

A Coxeter quotient certifies rank r only if the meridians go to reflections and the target has Coxeter rank r. A surjection onto a group that merely needs 4 generators is not enough. Likewise a matrix certificate needs every generator to be a pseudo-reflection and no common fixed vector.

243 of the 536 KnotInfo [3,4] knots are already br = 4 by the creelie/conjecture-to-choose certificates (independently re-checked on 2026-10-30). KnotInfo had not taken them in at database_knotinfo 2026.10.5, so a [3,4] entry in KnotInfo alone does not mean a knot is open.

That repository's verifier and search programs are third-party code. Its certificates are plain JSON (PD code, prime q, one 4x4 matrix per edge, four seed edges) and can be re-checked with an independent program.
Check for newer preprints by Blair, Kjuchukova and coauthors, and for later releases of creelie/conjecture-to-choose (its Zenodo record already has newer versions), which may settle more of the 293.

targets.name: KnotInfo Turaev genus: a Turaev-genus-1 diagram for one of the 25 non-alternating knots (11n_118 and 24 at 12 crossings) listed [1,2]
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: For a diagram D with c crossings whose all-A and all-B smoothings have s_A and s_B circles, the Turaev surface has genus g_T(D) = (2 + c - s_A - s_B)/2. The Turaev genus of K is the minimum over diagrams, and it is 0 exactly for alternating knots. KnotInfo (Livingston and Moore) records it from several sources: Abe-Kishimoto (arXiv:0808.0573) for non-alternating knots under 12 crossings (except 11n_95 and 11n_118), Jablan's 154 almost-alternating 12-crossing knots (arXiv:1404.4967), Howie's unpublished bound of 2 for the rest, and Dasbach-Lowrance's genus-2 results (arXiv:1604.03501), with lower bounds from Khovanov and knot Floer width (Manturov, Lowrance). In database_knotinfo 2026.10.5, 25 knots are [1,2]: 11n_118 and 12n_285, 12n_318, 12n_328, 12n_358, 12n_370, 12n_371, 12n_407, 12n_426, 12n_439, 12n_443, 12n_451, 12n_462, 12n_487, 12n_488, 12n_591, 12n_730, 12n_749, 12n_750, 12n_801, 12n_807, 12n_809, 12n_830, 12n_835 and 12n_838. Non-alternating knots have g_T >= 1, so a Turaev-genus-1 diagram of any of them closes it at 1.
targets.success_criterion: For a knot K whose turaev_genus is [1,2] in live KnotInfo (https://knotinfo.org/, or the database_knotinfo mirror when that is not older than the site), re-fetched immediately before claiming: a PD code D (of any crossing number) that SnapPy and Regina identify as K (mirror allowed), with g_T(D) = (2 + c(D) - s_A(D) - s_B(D))/2 = 1, where s_A and s_B are the numbers of circles in the all-A and all-B Kauffman states, computed by the skeptic.

partial_wins.statement: For one of the 25 knots, a reproducible computation showing that it meets the hypotheses of a published theorem implying Turaev genus >= 2: for example Khovanov width at least 4 (g_T >= w_Kh - 2, Manturov / Champanerkar-Kofman-Stoltzfus), knot Floer width at least 3 (g_T >= w_HF - 1, Lowrance arXiv:0709.0720), or a Turaev-genus-one obstruction from Dasbach-Lowrance (arXiv:1604.03501). It counts only if neither KnotInfo nor any paper the skeptic finds has already applied that theorem to K, and it must name the theorem and save every input, with each invariant recomputed from a verified diagram.

An almost-alternating diagram (one crossing change from alternating) verified as one of the 25 knots. This implies g_T = 1 and is reported separately because almost-alternating status is of independent interest.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic identifies D as K with SnapPy/Regina and counts the all-A and all-B state circles in D directly from the PD code. Seconds.
angles: Conventional: random Reidemeister and flype walks that increase the crossing number, evaluating g_T(D) on each diagram (minimisers need not be minimal-crossing).
Conventional: build almost-alternating and Turaev-genus-1 diagrams from Dasbach-Lowrance's classification of Turaev genus one diagrams, and match them by HOMFLY before identifying.
pitfalls: The KnotInfo description text says Jablan's work leaves 37 knots without values (before Dasbach-Lowrance's genus-2 results), while the 2026.10.5 data has 25 [1,2] entries. Go by the live data entry.
Identify the diagram with SnapPy/Regina, not by Jones or HOMFLY alone (12-crossing knots share polynomials).
Some of these knots may genuinely have g_T = 2. Check for 2024-2026 preprints on Turaev genus of 12-crossing knots before claiming.

targets.name: KnotInfo crosscap numbers: a nonorientable spanning surface beating the best upper bound for an 11- or 12-crossing knot (573 intervals)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The crosscap number C(K) is the smallest first Betti number of a nonorientable surface in S^3 bounded by K. KnotInfo (Charles Livingston and Allison Moore, knotinfo.org) records it from several sources. Upper bounds include Seifert-algorithm bounds (C(K) <= 2g(K)+1) and state surfaces. Results and bounds come from Murakami-Yasuhara, Teragaito, Hirasawa-Teragaito (2-bridge knots, arXiv:math/0504446), Burton-Ozlen (normal surfaces and integer programming, arXiv:1107.2382), Adams-Kindred (arXiv:1205.5520), Kindred (all alternating knots through 13 crossings, arXiv:1905.11367), Kalfagianni-Lee (Jones-polynomial bounds, arXiv:1408.4493), Ito-Takimura, and Jaco, Rubinstein, Spreer and Tillmann, 'Slope norm and an algorithm to compute the crosscap number' (arXiv:2108.07599, Algebr. Geom. Topol. 24 (2024) 4307-4351). JRST determined 196 previously unknown crosscap numbers (all five open 10-crossing knots, 45 of 96 open 11-crossing knots and 146 of 668 open 12-crossing knots), and all 196 values are installed in the database, although the description page still calls this preliminary work on 195 knots. In database_knotinfo 2026.10.5 every knot through 10 crossings is determined, and the 573 entries still left as intervals after JRST are 51 at 11 crossings and 522 at 12, mostly [2,5] (298) and [2,4] (263). For these, can an explicit nonorientable spanning surface close the interval or lower the upper bound?
targets.success_criterion: For a knot K whose crosscap_number is an interval [a,b] in live KnotInfo (https://knotinfo.org/, or the database_knotinfo mirror when that is not older than the site), re-fetched immediately before claiming, and whose crosscap number is not determined in any source the skeptic finds after arXiv:2108.07599 (AGT 24 (2024), already installed): a certified nonorientable spanning surface of K with first Betti number k = a, which closes the interval. Accepted certificates: (i) a PD code D, verified as K by SnapPy/Regina, and a Kauffman state s of D whose state surface is nonorientable, with k = c(D) - |s| + 1, where |s| is the number of state circles; or (ii) a Regina triangulation of the exterior of K with real torus boundary and a boundary edge representing the meridian (meridian filling certified as S^3 by Regina and the exterior identified as K), with a connected nonorientable normal surface whose single boundary curve meets the meridian once, and k = 1 - Euler characteristic.

partial_wins.statement: For a knot eligible as in the main criterion, a certificate (i) or (ii) with a < k < b, i.e. k STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the listed upper bound b and than every published upper bound for K, lowering the bound without closing the interval.
A demonstrated KnotInfo inconsistency: a verified certificate with k below a listed lower bound, or a listed exact value contradicted by such a certificate, with inputs saved.

targets.verification_method: (i) Skeptic identifies D with SnapPy/Regina, rebuilds the state surface from s and counts the state circles. Skeptic checks one-sidedness directly. A band joining a state circle to itself already gives a Mobius band. Otherwise propagate a normal orientation over the disks and half-twisted bands, taking nesting of the state circles into account, or rebuild the surface in Regina. (ii) Skeptic loads the triangulation in Regina, checks the meridian edge by filling along it and recognising S^3, identifies the exterior as K, and verifies the normal surface: connectedness, nonorientability, Euler characteristic, and that its boundary meets the meridian once. Minutes.
angles: Conventional: enumerate all 2^c states on many non-minimal diagrams of K (state surfaces of non-minimal diagrams can beat minimal ones).
Conventional: Regina normal-surface enumeration in small ideal triangulations of the exterior, in the spirit of Burton-Ozlen and JRST.
pitfalls: A state surface can be orientable. Check one-sidedness explicitly, since an orientable surface bounds the genus, not the crosscap number.

Jaco-Rubinstein-Spreer-Tillmann's 196 values (AGT 2024) are already in the database even though the description page calls them preliminary. The remaining intervals are knots where their normal-surface algorithm was inconclusive or too large (around 30 tetrahedra), so plain Q-fundamental enumeration in the Burton-Ozlen triangulations is unlikely to settle them.
The relation C(K) <= 2g(K)+1 already gives an upper bound. Make sure yours is strictly below every listed or published bound.

targets.name: KnotInfo smooth 4D crosscap numbers: a nonorientable band certificate beating an upper bound for an 11-13 crossing knot (3,525 intervals)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The smooth 4D crosscap number gamma_4(K), the nonorientable 4-genus, is the smallest first Betti number of a smooth nonorientable surface in B^4 bounded by K (gamma_4 = 1 for slice knots). KnotInfo (Livingston and Moore) gives upper bounds from nonorientable band moves to slice knots, immersed disks and crossing changes. Lower bounds come from Yasuhara's Arf/signature criterion, Gilmer-Livingston and Ozsvath-Stipsicz-Szabo's unoriented knot Floer upsilon. Values are complete through 10 crossings (Jabuka-Kelly for 8-9, Ghanbarian arXiv:2011.03480 for 10). Fairchild treated non-alternating 11-crossing knots (arXiv:2403.00996). Lee and Sabloff extended the data to 11-crossing alternating knots and to 12 and 13 crossings, with an algorithmic Mobius-band search through 14 crossings ('An algorithmic search for knots bounding Mobius bands in B^4', arXiv:2607.23582, July 2026). In database_knotinfo 2026.10.5, 3,525 entries are intervals: 59 at 11 crossings, 455 at 12 and 3,011 at 13. Most are [2,3] (1,751), [1,2] (991) or [1,3] (773).
targets.success_criterion: For a knot K whose smooth_4d_crosscap_number is an interval [a,b] in live KnotInfo (https://knotinfo.org/, or the database_knotinfo mirror when that is not older than the site), re-fetched immediately before claiming: a PD code D verified as K by SnapPy/Regina and a sequence of k band moves D = K_0 -> K_1 -> ... -> K_k. Each move must be a nonorientable (one-component to one-component) band move, the final knot K_k must be certified smoothly slice, and k must be STRICTLY LESS than b (direction: min). K_k counts as slice when Regina certifies the unknot, KnotInfo lists smooth_four_genus 0, or a ribbon certificate is given as band moves to a Regina-certified unlink. k = a closes the interval; for [1,2] entries this means one band to a slice knot, i.e. K bounds a Mobius band.

partial_wins.statement: For a prime knot with 14 crossings that Lee-Sabloff (arXiv:2607.23582) do not list as bounding a Mobius band in B^4, and that is not obstructed by Yasuhara's criterion or any other obstruction they report: a certified Mobius band, i.e. one nonorientable band move from a diagram identified as the knot by SnapPy/Regina to a knot certified smoothly slice as in the main criterion.
A demonstrated KnotInfo inconsistency: a certificate with k below a listed lower bound, with every intermediate knot identified and inputs saved.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic replays each band move on the PD code, checks that every step stays a knot (one component), identifies K_0 and K_k with SnapPy/Regina, and checks the slice certificate for K_k. Under 30 minutes.
angles: Conventional: exhaustive short nonorientable bands between arcs of many diagrams of K, keeping only results whose HOMFLY matches a slice knot, then identifying them.
Conventional: crossing changes to knots of known gamma_4 combined with the immersed-disk construction KnotInfo describes.
Cross-domain import (reaction-network search): breadth-first search over band moves with canonical PD hashing.
pitfalls: An oriented (coherent) band produces a 2-component link. Only one-component bands add a crosscap; mixing the two needs separate bookkeeping, so this criterion uses only nonorientable bands.
Lee-Sabloff's July 2026 search is the frontier. The remaining [1,2] knots survived it, so check their data before claiming.
Yasuhara's criterion rules out gamma_4 = 1 for some knots. A claimed Mobius band for one of them signals a bookkeeping error.

targets.name: Knot mosaics: the first mosaic, or a 7-mosaic, for one of the 854 11- and 12-crossing knots with no known mosaic in KnotInfo
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: A knot mosaic (Lomonaco-Kauffman) is an n x n grid of tiles from 11 standard square tiles (blank, arcs and crossings) whose arcs join into a knot diagram. The mosaic number of K is the smallest n with an n-mosaic of K, and the tile number is the fewest non-blank tiles. KnotInfo (Livingston and Moore) stores the pair [mosaic number, tile number] from Aaron Heap and coauthors (Heap-Knowles, Heap-LaCourt, and 'Tabulating knot mosaics: crossing number 10 or less', in preparation) and from Lee, Hong, Lee and Oh. Heap's Knot Mosaic Space site (geneseo.edu/knotmosaics) tabulates mosaics through 10 crossings. In database_knotinfo 2026.10.5, every knot through 10 crossings and most 11-12 crossing knots have exact pairs, mostly [7,31] or [7,29]. But 29 eleven-crossing knots (e.g. 11a_17, 11a_101, 11n_119, 11n_184) and 825 twelve-crossing knots (e.g. 12a_1, 12a_2) are listed [[7,infty), [32,infty)]: no mosaic is recorded at all. Can an explicit mosaic give them a finite value, or close the mosaic number at 7?
targets.success_criterion: For a knot K listed '[ [7,infty) , [32,infty) ]' in KnotInfo's mosaic_tile_number field (live site or the database_knotinfo mirror when not older), re-fetched immediately before claiming, and not shown with a mosaic on Heap's Knot Mosaic Space site (https://www.geneseo.edu/knotmosaics): a 7 x 7 mosaic, given as a matrix of the 11 standard tile codes. It must be suitably connected, with every arc endpoint matched on each tile edge, and its diagram, converted to a PD code, must be identified as K (mirror allowed) by SnapPy and Regina. This closes the mosaic number at 7.

partial_wins.statement: An 8 x 8 mosaic, checked as in the main criterion (tile-edge matching, a single closed component, SnapPy/Regina identification of the PD code), verified as one of the 854 knots. This bounds its mosaic number by 8 and gives its first finite tile-number upper bound.
A mosaic of any size verified as one of the 854 knots with exactly 32 non-blank tiles, which closes the tile number at its listed lower bound 32.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic checks tile-edge matching and that the arcs form a single closed component, converts the mosaic to a PD code, and identifies it with SnapPy/Regina. Seconds.
angles: Conventional: convert KnotInfo grid diagrams (arc index 11-14) into mosaics and compress them with mosaic moves.
Conventional: enumerate space-efficient 7-mosaics (Heap-LaCourt) with fast HOMFLY filtering, keeping those that match a target knot.
pitfalls: Do not run the code from Heap's GitHub repository. It is for reading the published method only; write your own checker.

Heap's pipeline defines 7-mosaic layouts with 27, 29, 31, 32, 34, 36, 37, 39 and 41 non-blank tiles, and KnotInfo's [32,infty) tile bound reflects that the 27-, 29- and 31-tile layouts did not produce these knots. A 7-mosaic for one of them must use at least 32 non-blank tiles. Some may need 8 or more; report 8-mosaics under p1.
KnotInfo stores mosaic and tile numbers as a pair, not as an interval. Read the field format carefully.

targets.name: KnotInfo Nakanishi index: prove the Alexander module cyclic (index 1) for one of the 229 11- and 12-crossing knots listed [1;2]
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The Nakanishi index m(K) is the minimum size of a square presentation matrix of the Alexander module H_1 of the infinite cyclic cover, a module over Lambda = Z[t,t^-1]; m(K) = 1 exactly when the module is cyclic. KnotInfo (Charles Livingston and Allison Moore, knotinfo.org) records values from several sources: Nakanishi's computations via Kawauchi's book, Kearton-Wilson, Borodzik and Friedl's program Knotorious, 82 values by Castellano-Macias and Owad (arXiv:1908.01693), 77 [1,2] entries set to 1 by Ana Wright via algebraic unknotting number, and three 12-crossing knots (12a_504, 12a_642, 12n_278) settled by Tetsuya Ito (Arch. Math. 2025, arXiv:2501.15821). In database_knotinfo 2026.10.5, 229 entries are still '[1; 2]': 42 at 11 crossings and 187 at 12. For all of them the second Alexander polynomial is 1. In every case checked, the first elementary ideal of V - tV^T is the whole ring, so the module is cyclic after localising at every maximal ideal, and no residue-field rank count can show m = 2. Proving m = 1 needs an explicit global generator, which has a finite certificate: unimodular row and column operations over Lambda, allowing an identity block, that bring a presentation matrix to diag(1, ..., 1, Delta). Can such a certificate be found for one of the 229?
targets.success_criterion: For a knot K whose nakanishi_index is '[1; 2]' in live KnotInfo (https://knotinfo.org/, or the database_knotinfo mirror when that is not older than the site), re-fetched immediately before claiming, and not settled in any paper the skeptic finds: let V be KnotInfo's seifert_matrix of K (n x n) and A = V - tV^T. A certificate that the Alexander module is cyclic: an integer k >= 0 and square matrices P and Q of size n + k over Z[t,t^-1], with det P and det Q units (+-t^j) checked by exact polynomial arithmetic, such that P * (A block-diagonal I_k) * Q = diag(1, ..., 1, f), where f is +-t^j times the Alexander polynomial of K. This sets m(K) = 1.

partial_wins.statement: Settle 10 or more of the 229 entries at m = 1, each with the certificate above, in one reproducible run.
A certificate as above for a knot that KnotInfo lists with Nakanishi index exactly 2, with inputs saved, demonstrating a table error.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic rebuilds A from the KnotInfo Seifert matrix and checks that det A reproduces the listed Alexander polynomial up to units. Skeptic then multiplies P (A + I_k block) Q exactly in Z[t,t^-1] and checks the diagonal form, and that det P and det Q are units. Seconds.
angles: Conventional: randomised unimodular row and column operations over Lambda (Euclid on entries with a unit leading or trailing coefficient), stabilising with an identity block when stuck.
Conventional: search for a generator vector x with H_1 = Lambda x using Grobner bases over Z[t,t^-1], then extend it to the unimodular certificate.
Conventional: an algebraic unknotting number of 1 (Fogel, Murakami) implies a cyclic module, so search for single 'algebraic crossing changes' of the Seifert form, as Ana Wright did with Knotorious.
pitfalls: E_1 = Lambda (local cyclicity) does not prove cyclicity over Lambda, which is not a PID. That is exactly why these entries are open, so the certificate must be an explicit global diagonalisation.
Rank counts of A over residue fields F_p[t]/(g) cannot certify m = 2 for these knots, because their first elementary ideal is the unit ideal. Do not claim 2 that way.
Use the KnotInfo Seifert matrix and check that it reproduces the listed Alexander polynomial before building A.
Check Ito (Arch. Math. 2025, arXiv:2501.15821) and any later preprint for knots already settled but not installed.

targets.name: KnotInfo concordance genus: a certified concordance to a lower-genus knot for one of the 208 11- and 12-crossing knots listed as intervals (incl. the Conway knot 11n_34 at [1,3])
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days
targets.statement: The smooth concordance genus g_c(K) is the minimum Seifert genus of a knot smoothly concordant to K (Livingston). Lower bounds come from Alexander-polynomial factorisation (Casson's argument), signatures and Heegaard Floer invariants. Upper bounds come from exhibiting a concordant knot of lower genus. KnotInfo (Livingston and Moore) compiles results from Livingston (arXiv:math/0107141, arXiv:0807.0765), Kearney ('The concordance genus of 11-crossing knots', arXiv:1208.5059, extending McAtee), and Lamm's slice results. The KnotInfo page lists 20 unknown 11-crossing cases. In database_knotinfo 2026.10.5, 208 entries are intervals: 19 at 11 crossings (e.g. 11a_6 [2,3], 11a_72 [2,4], 11n_34 [1,3], 11n_145 [1,3]) and 189 at 12. The Conway knot 11n_34 is topologically slice but not smoothly slice (Piccirillo), so its smooth g_c is 1, 2 or 3.
targets.success_criterion: For a knot K whose smooth_concordance_genus is an interval [a,b] in live KnotInfo (https://knotinfo.org/, or the database_knotinfo mirror when that is not older than the site), re-fetched immediately before claiming: a knot J with Seifert genus g STRICTLY LESS than b (direction: min), and a concordance between K and J. The genus of J is certified by KnotInfo's three_genus for J or by an explicit Seifert surface (a diagram plus Seifert's algorithm, with g = (c - s + 1)/2). The concordance is certified by a ribbon disk for K # -J (mirror and reverse of J), given as n band moves on a verified diagram of K # -J that produce an (n+1)-component link that Regina certifies as the unlink. g = a closes the interval.

partial_wins.statement: A certified ribbon concordance in the same form between two different knots that both have interval-valued KnotInfo concordance genus. A future value for one then fixes or bounds the other.
For 11n_34 specifically, a certified concordance to a genus-2 knot, lowering its upper bound from 3 to 2, reported separately because of the Conway knot's prominence.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic builds K # -J, replays the band moves in SnapPy, identifies the result as the unlink with Regina (split and trivial components), and checks the genus of J. Under an hour.
angles: Conventional: genus-reducing band moves on K (an oriented band to a 2-component link, then a second band back to a knot) searched for results of lower genus with the same algebraic concordance class.
Conventional: search for ribbon disks of K # -J for candidates J with matching Alexander-polynomial factorisation, using Herald-Kirk-Livingston style band searches.
pitfalls: Orientation and mirror conventions: concordance from K to J means K # -J is slice, where -J is the reversed mirror. Getting this wrong gives false certificates.
The KnotInfo text has small inconsistencies (11a_57, 11a_102 and 11n_69 appear as both unknown and resolved). Go by the live data entry.
Unlink recognition must certify split and trivial components.

targets.name: Cosmetic crossing conjecture: a certified non-nugatory crossing change that preserves the knot type (KnotInfo lists 1,216 knots up to 13 crossings as open)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days
targets.statement: A crossing change is cosmetic if the new diagram represents the same oriented knot, and nugatory if some 2-sphere meets the knot only at the two points of the crossing. Nugatory crossing changes are always cosmetic. The cosmetic crossing conjecture (Kirby problem list 1.58) says they are the only cosmetic ones. It is proven for 2-bridge knots (Torisu), fibered knots (Kalfagianni), genus-one knots with nontrivial Alexander polynomial (Ito, after Balm-Friedl-Kalfagianni-Powell), Whitehead doubles of prime non-cable knots (Balm-Kalfagianni) and special alternating knots (Boninger, after Lidman-Moore). For alternating (more generally Khovanov-thin) knots, Lidman-Moore (a condition on the homology of the branched double cover) and Boninger (an Alexander polynomial condition) give obstructions that together settle alternating knots with square-free determinant; Ito gives a further obstruction via the Casson-Walker invariant. KnotInfo (Livingston and Moore) marks a knot U when the conjecture is open for it, and cites Lidman-Moore for 10_128 and Ito for 10_67. In database_knotinfo 2026.10.5, 1,216 prime knots are U: 4 at 10 crossings (10_87, 10_98, 10_129, 10_147), 38 at 11, 172 at 12 and 1,002 at 13.
targets.success_criterion: A PD code D of a knot K and a crossing x of D with two properties, both certified by the skeptic's own computation. (1) The diagram D' obtained by changing x represents the same oriented knot as D. For hyperbolic K this means SnapPy verified hyperbolic structures plus an orientation-preserving isometry of the exteriors that preserves the meridian and longitude; for any K, Regina knot recognition with orientation and mirror handled. (2) x is not nugatory: the link K union C, where C is the crossing circle around x, is non-split, certified for example by SnapPy verify_hyperbolicity on its exterior, or by a Regina proof that the exterior is irreducible. A crossing circle that bounds a disk disjoint from K would make K union C split.

partial_wins.statement: For one of the four 10-crossing U knots (10_87, 10_98, 10_129, 10_147), or any U knot, a reproducible computation showing that it satisfies the hypotheses of a published theorem ruling out cosmetic crossings (name the theorem, e.g. a Lidman-Moore, Boninger or Ito criterion). It counts only if KnotInfo has not applied that theorem, and every invariant must be recomputed from a verified diagram.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic rebuilds D and D', certifies the knot-type equality with SnapPy (verified isometry with peripheral data and orientation) and Regina, builds the crossing-circle link K union C, and certifies non-splitness by verified hyperbolicity or irreducibility. Under an hour.
angles: Conventional: for each U knot and many diagrams, change each crossing and compare hyperbolic invariants (volume, Chern-Simons, cusp shape) before attempting a verified isometry.

Conventional: search the crossing-circle exteriors K union C directly. A cosmetic crossing gives a pair of fillings of the same 2-cusped manifold yielding isotopic knots, a SnapPy-searchable condition.
pitfalls: Orientation matters. K and its reverse or mirror can have isometric exteriors, so an isometry that reverses orientation or the meridian is not a cosmetic crossing.
Many diagram crossings are visibly nugatory. Certify non-splitness of K union C, not just the absence of an obvious sphere.
Expect the conjecture to hold. Record negative searches honestly, and never claim from matching invariants alone.

targets.name: Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv constants s(C_n^r) for even n that is not a power of two: beat s(C_6^4) >= 85, s(C_6^5) >= 177, s(C_10^4) >= 153 or s(C_6^3) >= 41
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (checking a candidate takes seconds; the search for one takes hours)
targets.statement: For a finite abelian group G of exponent n, the Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv constant s(G) is the least l such that every sequence of l elements of G (repetition allowed) has a subsequence of exactly n terms summing to 0. eta(G) is the least l that guarantees a zero-sum subsequence of length 1..n. Harborth (1973) showed s(C_n^r) >= 2^r(n-1)+1 by repeating each vertex of {0,1}^r n-1 times, with equality when n is a power of two. For even n that is not a power of two, Guoqing Wang and Xiangneng Zeng (arXiv:2610.25271, v2 25 Oct 2026) showed this bound is not sharp in every rank r >= 4. They add 2^(r-3)(m-1), where m is the odd part of n, which disproves the Property C problem of Gao-Hou-Schmid-Thangadurai and the Property D conjecture of Gao-Geroldinger. Christian Elsholtz (arXiv:2610.35819, v2 27 Oct 2026; Table 1 and Theorems 1.3/1.4, computer-checked certificates) raised the excess to (m-1)2^(r-3)floor(r/4) in general, and further for n = 2 mod 4. Current lower bounds include s(C_6^4) >= 85, s(C_6^5) >= 177, s(C_6^6) >= 353, s(C_10^4) >= 153, s(C_10^5) >= 321, s(C_12^4) >= 181 and eta(C_6^5) >= 172. In rank 3 only Harborth's 8n-7 is known: s(C_6^3) >= 41 and s(C_10^3) >= 73. Elsholtz reports that a search for n = 6 and 10 found no rank-3 sequence reaching the subgroup value 17q-9 (n = 2q, one light block beyond Harborth's 16q-8), and that the weak form of Property D is open. Find an explicit sequence that beats a current lower bound.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit sequence S over C_n^r, given as a list of r-tuples over Z_n with multiplicities, where n is even and not a power of two, 3 <= r <= 7 and n^r <= 10^7. No subsequence of exactly n terms of S may sum to 0, verified by two independent programs. |S|+1 must be STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best known lower bound for s(C_n^r) at verification time. That bound is the maximum over the formulas and tables of the latest versions of arXiv:2610.35819 and arXiv:2610.25271 (re-fetched immediately before claiming), any certificates the authors have released, and a fresh arXiv search over the last 24 months for 'Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv' and 'Property D'. Bounds that those sources obtain through product or inductive formulas count toward this bar. Off-by-one: a sequence of length L proves s >= L+1, so C_6^4 needs L >= 85 and C_6^3 needs L >= 41. The claim itself must be an explicit sequence checked as above; a bound derived only by plugging known blocks into a product or inductive formula is not a win.

partial_wins.statement: Short zero-sums (eta): an explicit sequence over C_n^r (n even, not a power of two, 4 <= r <= 7, n^r <= 10^7) of length L with no zero-sum subsequence of length 1..n, where L+1 strictly exceeds the best known lower bound for eta(C_n^r) in the same sources (for example, beat eta(C_6^5) >= 172), verified by two programs.

Rank-3 weak Property D: a sequence over C_6^3 of length 40 (or over C_10^3 of length 72) with no zero-sum subsequence of exactly n terms in which no element occurs n-1 times, verified by two programs. If s(C_6^3) = 41, this refutes the weak form of Property D, which arXiv:2610.35819 lists as open.

targets.verification_method: Encode the group elements as integers. Run a DP over subsequence size: R_0 = {0}, and for each term g, for j from n-1 down to 0, set R_{j+1} |= R_j + g. The claim fails if and only if 0 is in R_n. The cost is O(|S| * n * n^r) bitset operations, about 10^7 for C_6^5. For the second implementation, group the terms by distinct element and use a count-limited generating function over multiplicities, or meet-in-the-middle. Run both on Harborth's construction, which must pass, and on that construction plus any one extra element, which must fail. For p1, test every length 1..n. Check that every coordinate lies in Z_n and that |S| is the claimed length. Then re-fetch arXiv:2610.35819 and 2610.25271.
angles: Elsholtz's constructions combine 'heavy' points (multiplicity n-1, on {0,1}^r) with 'light' blocks carrying the odd part m. Search for new light blocks in rank 5 with light density 1/4 for n = 0 mod 4, which Elsholtz asks for explicitly.

Formulate an ILP or SAT instance over multiplicities on a fixed support (for example {0,1}^r plus a few extra points). The no-n-term-zero-sum condition is checked lazily: solve, test with the DP, add a cut for the zero-sum found, and repeat.
Use symmetry: GL_r(Z_n) and translations (when n divides the length shift) preserve the property, so search over orbit representatives of supports.
For rank 3 with n = 6, start from Harborth's 40-term sequence and try to swap one heavy term for a light pair (the rank-3 subgroup-bound gap 17q-9 that Elsholtz mentions).
pitfalls: The records are days old, from two preprints revised within the last week. Re-fetch both and read the latest version before taking any number as the baseline.
Off-by-one: a sequence of length L proves s >= L+1. Matching a bound is not a record.
s needs zero-sums of EXACTLY n terms; eta allows any length 1..n. Do not mix the checkers up.
A sequence over C_n^r is a multiset. Any element with multiplicity n gives an immediate zero-sum, so multiplicities must be at most n-1.
The C_n^r results for n a power of two are exact (Harborth equality). Do not attack n = 2, 4 or 8.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv constant for odd n: refute s(C_n^3) = 9n-8 (smallest open n = 7) or beat 20n-19 in rank 4
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days
targets.statement: s(G) is the least l such that every sequence of l elements of G has an n-term zero-sum subsequence, where n = exp(G). For odd n, Elsholtz (2004) proved s(C_n^3) >= 9n-8, Edel, Elsholtz, Geroldinger, Kubertin and Rackham (Q. J. Math. 2007) proved s(C_n^4) >= 20n-19, and Edel (Des. Codes Cryptogr. 47 (2008) 125-134) gave s(C_n^5) >= 42n-41 and s(C_n^6) >= 96n-95, the bounds quoted in arXiv:2610.35819. All these bounds come from point sets in {0,1,2}^r, each point taken n-1 times. The standing conjecture for odd n is s(C_n^3) = 9n-8 (Fan-Gao-Zhong, arXiv:1010.5101, J. Number Theory 2011; their Conjecture 4.2 states s(C_n^r) = a_3(r)(n-1)+1 in every rank, with cap sizes a_3(r) = 9, 20, 45, 112 for r = 3..6). It is proven for n = 3 (19) and n = 5 (37, Gao-Hou-Schmid-Thangadurai, Integers 2007), and so for every n = 3^a 5^b via s(C_mn^r) <= (s(C_m^r)-1)n + s(C_n^r). Fan-Gao-Zhong also prove it for n = 3^a 5^b 7^c 11^d 13^e when the 3^a 5^b factor is astronomically large, using a computer check that C_7^3, C_11^3 and C_13^3 have Property D0 with respect to 9: every sequence g T^(n-1) with |T| = 9 has an n-term zero-sum. In rank 4, s(C_3^4) = 41 = 20*3-19, and hence s(C_{3^a}^4) = 20*3^a-19. In October 2026 Wang-Zeng (arXiv:2610.25271) and Elsholtz (arXiv:2610.35819) broke the analogous Harborth bound for even non-power-of-two n in ranks >= 4. Elsholtz notes that for odd exponents no counterexample to Property C or D is known, and that Property D for C_15^3 is open. The smallest odd n for which s(C_n^3) is undetermined is n = 7 (9n-8 = 55). Find an odd n and an explicit sequence that beats one of these bounds.
targets.success_criterion: Success means one of the following, verified by two independent programs. (a) An explicit sequence over C_n^3 of length 9n-8 with no zero-sum subsequence of exactly n terms, where n is odd and not of the form 3^a 5^b (for n = 7, length 55). (b) An explicit sequence over C_n^4 of length 20n-19 with no n-term zero-sum, where n is odd, n >= 5, n is not a power of 3 and n^4 <= 10^7 (for n = 5, length 81). In both cases |S|+1 must be STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best known lower bound for that (n, r) at verification time. That bound is 9n-8 or 20n-19 unless the latest arXiv:2610.35819, Edel et al. 2007, Edel 2008 or a fresh arXiv search shows a larger value for that n. The cell must not be one where s is proven equal to the bound, since that would contradict a theorem: n = 3^a 5^b in rank 3, the Fan-Gao-Zhong 2011 cases, or n = 3^a in rank 4. Check this first.

partial_wins.statement: Ranks 5 and 6: an explicit sequence over C_n^r with no n-term zero-sum, where n is odd, n >= 5, 3 does not divide n, r is 5 or 6 and n^r <= 10^7 (for example C_5^5, C_7^5, C_5^6). Its length L must satisfy L+1 strictly greater than the best known lower bound for that cell. That bound is the general 42n-41 or 96n-95 (Edel, Des. Codes Cryptogr. 2008, quoted in arXiv:2610.35819), or any larger value for that specific n in Edel 2008, Edel et al. 2007 or a fresh search. Multiples of 3 are excluded because the caps behind s(C_3^5) = 91 and s(C_3^6) = 225 can give larger bars there.

Property D for C_15^3, listed open in arXiv:2610.35819 (Remark 10(5)). The win is a sequence over C_15^3 of length 126 = s(C_15^3)-1 (s(C_15^3) = 127 is proven), verified by two programs, with no 15-term zero-sum subsequence and not of the form T^14: some element must occur between 1 and 13 times. Report the full multiplicity profile. If in addition no element occurs 14 times, the sequence also disproves the weak form of Property D (arXiv:2610.35819, Section 8).

targets.verification_method: Use a DP over subsequence size: R_0 = {0}, and for each term g, for j from n-1 down to 0, set R_{j+1} |= R_j + g. The claim is valid if and only if 0 is not in R_n. This costs O(|S| n^(r+1)), which is trivial for C_7^3 (55 * 7 * 343). For the second implementation, use a generating function grouped by distinct elements with multiplicity caps. Test both on the cap-based constructions: 9 points, each taken n-1 times, in rank 3 must pass, and adding any element must fail. For p2, also compute the multiplicity profile and confirm that some multiplicity is not 14. Then re-fetch arXiv:2610.35819 and search for new rank-3 to rank-6 values for that n.
angles: Port the even-n mechanism (light terms replacing heavy multiplicity, Wang-Zeng blocks) to odd n. Elsholtz reports that heavy-to-light swaps fail for n = 9, 15, 21, 25 in rank 3. Record which supports were excluded before searching.
For n = 7, move beyond {0,1,2}^3 supports: search over supports with entries in Z_7 using a lazy-cut ILP (solve, find a 7-term zero-sum with the DP, add a cut, repeat).

For rank 5 with n = 5 or 7, try to lift 45-point caps from F_3^5 (which give s(C_3^5) = 91) to supports valid for general odd n. Elsholtz reports that 42-point-support searches with q = 5, 7 failed in a related setting.
pitfalls: For n = 3^a 5^b in rank 3 (and n = 3^a in rank 4) the bound is proven, so no sequence of length 9n-8 (resp. 20n-19) exists there. Choose n = 7, 11, 13, ... (rank 3) or n = 5, 7, 11, ... (rank 4).

Fan-Gao-Zhong (1010.5101, Lemma 2.5) checked by computer that for n = 7, 11 and 13 every sequence g T^(n-1) with |T| = 9 over C_n^3 has an n-term zero-sum. A length-(9n-8) candidate therefore cannot be nine heavy (multiplicity n-1) terms plus one extra element.
Off-by-one: a sequence of length L proves s >= L+1.
Do not confuse s (exactly n terms) with eta (1..n terms) or with the Davenport constant (any length).
Property D versus its weak form: a length-(s-1) sequence that is not T^(n-1) disproves Property D. Only one with no term of multiplicity n-1 disproves the weak form.
Expect failure: no counterexample is known for any odd exponent. Report search coverage honestly as a negative result.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Davenport constant in rank 3: a group C_n1 + C_n2 + C_n3 with D(G) > D*(G)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (a certificate checks in milliseconds)
targets.statement: The Davenport constant D(G) of a finite abelian group G = C_n1 + ... + C_nr (n1 | ... | nr) is the least l such that every sequence of l elements has a nonempty zero-sum subsequence, and D(G) >= D*(G) = 1 + sum(n_i - 1). Olson (1969) proved equality for rank <= 2 and for p-groups. Equality is also known for some rank-3 families: C_3+C_3+C_3d (Bhowmik-Schlage-Puchta), C_4+C_4+C_4d, C_6+C_6+C_6d, C_{3*2^t}+C_{3*2^u}+C_{3*2^v}, C_{2p^a}+C_{2p^b}+C_{2p^c}, C_2+C_2m+C_2mn for all m and n (Girard-Schmid, J. Number Theory 197 (2019), Theorem 2.7, completed by Reiher's proof of Property B), and G1 + C_{p^k n} with G1 a p-group and p^k >= D*(G1). Most of this list is in Agarwal-Chen-Garg (MIT PRIMES 2024, section 2), which still carries an older restriction for C_2+C_2n+C_2n (no prime p >= 11 dividing n). Biswas-Mazumdar (arXiv:2402.09999) treat C_p^(d-1)+C_pq, conditionally when gcd(p,q) = 1, and cite A. Sheikh's 2017 University of London thesis for C_p+C_p+C_2p. In rank >= 4 there are infinitely many groups with D(G) > D*(G) (Geroldinger-Schneider and later work). For rank 3 it is conjectured that D(G) = D*(G) always. Benjamin Girard and Alain Plagne (arXiv:2510.20412 v1, Oct 2025) call this conjecture 'wide open'. One zero-sum-free sequence of length D*(G) over any rank-3 group would refute it.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit sequence over a group G of rank exactly 3 (n1 | n2 | n3, n1 >= 2) of length D*(G) = n1+n2+n3-2 with no nonempty zero-sum subsequence, verified by two independent programs. This proves D(G) >= D*(G)+1, STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than D*(G). Before claiming, check G against every family where D(G) = D*(G) is proven: the PRIMES 2024 list, Girard-Schmid (arXiv:1806.07636, all C_2+C_2m+C_2mn), arXiv:2402.09999 and the Sheikh thesis it cites, the Gao-Geroldinger survey, and a fresh arXiv search. A hit on a proven family means the checker has a bug.

partial_wins.statement: A certified determination D(G) = D*(G) for a rank-3 group G that no published result covers at verification time (check the PRIMES 2024 list, Girard-Schmid arXiv:1806.07636, arXiv:2402.09999 and the Sheikh thesis it cites, the surveys and a fresh arXiv search; a candidate to examine first is C_5+C_5+C_10, after confirming that Sheikh's work on C_p+C_p+C_2p does not already cover it; C_2+C_2m+C_2mn groups such as C_2+C_22+C_22 are settled). This needs an exhaustive search, with independently re-runnable code and two implementations that agree, showing that no zero-sum-free sequence of length D*(G) exists.

targets.verification_method: Keep a bitset R over G of the sums of nonempty subsequences seen so far. For each term g, set R = R | (R + g) | {g}. The sequence is zero-sum-free if and only if 0 never enters R. The cost is O(L |G|). For the second implementation, use explicit subset enumeration for L <= 25, or a Smith-normal-form-independent encoding of G as Z_n1 x Z_n2 x Z_n3. Check that n1 | n2 | n3 (or convert to invariant factors), that the rank is 3, and that the length is exactly D*(G).
angles: The rank->=4 counterexamples (Geroldinger-Schneider) use groups C_n^{(k-1)n+rho} + C_kn whose rank grows with n. Look for a 'rank-compressed' analogue: groups with two coprime-mixed factors, such as C_m + C_mn + C_mnk with gcd conditions, where the projection argument could fail.
Search groups of moderate order (<= 2000) not covered by known theorems with SAT or ILP plus lazy cuts: the variables are the sequence terms, and each zero-sum found adds a cut.
Use the inverse structure: extremal zero-sum-free sequences in the known cases have a rigid form (Property B-like). Search for long zero-sum-free sequences that avoid that structure.
pitfalls: Convert to invariant factors first. C_2+C_3+C_6 has rank 2 (it is C_6+C_6), and D* must use the n1 | n2 | n3 decomposition.
Zero-sum-free means no NONEMPTY subsequence of any length sums to 0. The empty sequence does not count, and single terms equal to 0 are already zero-sums.
Most small rank-3 groups are covered by theorems; check the list before spending compute.
The PRIMES 2024 list is out of date for C_2+C_2n+C_2n: Girard-Schmid (2019, Theorem 2.7) settle every C_2+C_2m+C_2mn, including C_2+C_22+C_22.

targets.name: Generalized off-diagonal Schur numbers S(3; s,t,u): refute Ahmed–Schaal's S = stu - tu - u - 1 or settle a new cell with a certificate
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Let L(t) be the equation x_1 + ... + x_{t-1} = x_t. The generalized off-diagonal Schur number S(3; s,t,u) is the least N such that every 3-colouring of [1,N] has a solution of L(s) in colour 1, L(t) in colour 2 or L(u) in colour 3, with all variables taken from that colour class. This is the smallest-failing-N convention of Song-Mao. The diagonal case S(3;k,k,k) = k^3-k^2-k-1 was proven by Boza, Marín, Revuelta and Sanz (2019), matching Znám's lower bound. Tanbir Ahmed and Daniel Schaal (2015/16) computed small values, proved a general lower bound that gives S(3;s,t,u) >= stu-tu-u-1, and made two conjectures: (1) S(3;3,t,u) > 2tu-u-1, and (2) S(3;s,t,u) = stu-tu-u-1 for 4 <= s <= t <= u. Yanyan Song and Yaping Mao (arXiv:2604.11030, Apr 2026) proved (1) and rederived the lower bound in (2) (Proposition 3.1). They report SAT-computed values in Table 3, for example S(3;3,3,8) = 59, S(3;3,4,8) = 67, S(3;4,4,8) = 87, S(3;4,5,8) = 111 and S(3;4,6,7) = 118. Every published cell with s >= 4 agrees with stu-tu-u-1. Equality in Conjecture 2 is open, and so is every value outside the published tables.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a 3-colouring c of {1..N} with N = stu-tu-u-1, for some 4 <= s <= t <= u not all equal. Colour class 1 must contain no solution of x_1+...+x_{s-1} = x_s, class 2 none of L(t) and class 3 none of L(u), with variables from the class, repetition allowed unless the latest arXiv:2604.11030 uses a different convention. Two independent programs must verify it. This shows S(3;s,t,u) > stu-tu-u-1 (STRICTLY GREATER, direction: max) and refutes Conjecture 2 as stated in the latest arXiv:2604.11030. Re-fetch that paper and search arXiv for newer results immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: The exact value of S(3;s,t,u) for a triple with 4 <= s <= t <= u, s < u, u <= 12, that is not in the Ahmed-Schaal tables, Song-Mao Tables 2-3 or any later source found by a fresh search. It needs a valid colouring of [1, M-1] and a DRAT or LRAT certificate, checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr, that [1, M] has no valid colouring, using an encoding independent of the solver's preprocessing.
The same for s = 3, where no closed form is conjectured: the exact value of S(3;3,t,u) for some 3 <= t <= u <= 14 not in those tables, with a colouring and a checked UNSAT certificate.

targets.verification_method: For each colour class C and its equation length k, compute the set of sums of exactly k-1 elements of C with repetition. Use a bitset DP: P_1 = C, P_{j+1} = (P_j + C) truncated at N. The class is valid if P_{k-1} and C are disjoint. The cost is O(k N^2 / 64). For the second implementation, enumerate solutions directly for small N, or use a DP over multisets. Check that the colouring has exactly N entries and that colours are matched to equations consistently. For p1 and p2, check the UNSAT proof with drat-trim or cake_lpr and audit the CNF generator against the definition.
angles: Song-Mao's lower bound colourings are block or interval constructions. Use SAT with the block colouring fixed on most of [1, N-1] and a free window near the boundaries, then try to extend to N.

For the UNSAT side, use symmetry breaking: 1 must take a colour whose equation is not solvable with x = 1 alone. Use interval-structure lemmas from Ahmed-Schaal to fix early cells, then use cube-and-conquer.
Look at unbalanced triples (s = 4, u large), where the gap between stu-tu-u-1 and Song-Mao's Ramsey-type upper bound is largest.
pitfalls: Convention: S here is the least N at which every colouring fails, so a valid colouring of [1, N-1] only proves S >= N.
Generalized Schur numbers allow repeated variables (x_1 = x_2 allowed); weak versions require distinct variables. Use the paper's convention.
The diagonal case s = t = u is proven exact, so no counterexample exists there.
Assigning equations to colours: S(3;s,t,u) is symmetric under permuting (s,t,u) together with the colours. Do not double count a known cell under a permutation.

targets.name: Three-colour Rado numbers R_3(ax + by = cz): refute an Ahmed–Zaman–Bright conjecture or settle a cell beyond the SAT tables
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The k-colour Rado number R_k(E) is the least n such that every k-colouring of [1,n] has a monochromatic solution of E in positive integers (infinite if no such n exists). Yuan Chang, Jesús De Loera and William Wesley (ISSAC 2022, arXiv:2210.03262) used SAT to compute R_3(ax+by=cz) for all small coefficients (1 <= a,b,c <= 5 per their abstract, <= 6 as cited later), R_3(ax-ay=bz) for a,b <= 15 and R_3(ax+ay=bz) for a,b <= 10. They also proved Myers' conjecture R_3(x-y=(m-2)z) = m^3-m^2-m-1. Tanbir Ahmed, Lamina Zaman and Curtis Bright (arXiv:2505.12085 v3, Oct 2025; SC-square 2025) tabulated R_3(ax+by=bz) for 1 <= b <= 15, 1 <= a <= 30 and R_3(ax+ay=bz) for 1 <= a <= 15, 1 <= b <= 25, and proved lower bounds with symbolic sets. They conjecture: (1.1) R_3(ax+by=bz) = a^3+a^2+(2b+1)a+1 for coprime a > b >= 3 with a^2+a+b > b^2+ba, where the lower bound is their Theorem 1.3; and (1.2) R_3(ax+ay=bz) = a^3 b for odd a coprime to b with 3 <= a < b <= 2a-1. For odd a >= 7 they prove only R_3(ax+ay=(a+1)z) >= a^3(a+1). Values outside these tables are open, as are both conjectures.
targets.success_criterion: Success means refuting Conjecture 1.1 or 1.2 of the latest arXiv:2505.12085 for an admissible (a,b), with one of two certificates. (i) A 3-colouring of [1, V], where V is the conjectured value, with no monochromatic solution in positive integers (variables need not be distinct), verified by two independent programs. This proves R_3 > V (direction: max). (ii) For Conjecture 1.2 only, at an (a,b) where the lower bound R_3 >= a^3 b is not proven (it is proven for b = a+1 with odd a >= 7, Theorem 1.4): a DRAT or LRAT certificate, checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr, that every 3-colouring of [1, V-1] has a monochromatic solution. This proves R_3 < V (direction: min). Re-fetch arXiv:2505.12085 and search for newer Rado-number papers immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: A new exact value R_3(ax+by=cz) for positive a,b,c <= 30 with gcd(a,b,c) = 1, a+b != c and R_3 finite, for a triple that appears, up to swapping a and b, in none of the tables of arXiv:2210.03262, arXiv:2505.12085 or later papers found by a fresh search. (With repetition allowed, a+b = c gives the monochromatic solution x = y = z, so R = 1 trivially; such cells do not count.) It needs a valid colouring of [1, R-1] and a checked DRAT or LRAT UNSAT certificate for [1, R].

A new exact four-colour Rado number R_4(ax+by=cz) with a,b,c <= 6 and gcd(a,b,c) = 1, for an equation with a = c or b = c (so R_4 is finite by Rado's theorem; the other columns-condition case a+b = c is trivial, R = 1 via x = y = z), excluding x+y=z (Schur, R_4 = 45) and counting (a,b,c) and (b,a,c) as one equation, with no published value found by a fresh search. It needs a valid colouring of [1, R-1] and a checked UNSAT certificate for [1, R].

targets.verification_method: Colouring check: for every pair (x, y) in [1,N]^2 with a x + b y divisible by c and z = (a x + b y)/c in [1, N], assert that x, y and z do not all share a colour. This is O(N^2), about 10^10 for N = 10^5, so use C. For the second implementation, loop over (x, z) and solve for y. UNSAT side: regenerate the CNF from the definition with an independently written generator, check the solver's proof with drat-trim or cake_lpr, and confirm that the CNF has exactly one at-least-one-colour clause per integer.
angles: Ahmed-Zaman-Bright's symbolic-set colourings are unions of intervals scaled by powers of a. Search the parametric family one level richer (more intervals per colour) with a solver, for (a,b) near the boundary a^2+a+b = b^2+ba of Conjecture 1.1.
For Conjecture 1.2, test even a and the edge b = 2a-1 first, where Observation 2.3 says patterns break down.
Incremental SAT: fix the best colouring of [1, V-1] except a sliding window and try to extend to V.
pitfalls: Convention: R_k is the least n at which every colouring fails, so a valid colouring of [1, N] proves R > N.
Equations with degree of regularity < 3 have R_3 = infinity. Check Rado's conditions and the dor results in arXiv:2210.03262 before computing.
Do not require x, y, z to be distinct; the standard Rado number allows x = y.

With repetition allowed, every equation with a+b = c has the solution x = y = z, so its Rado number is 1; such cells are not new values. Scaled triples (common factor) and a <-> b swaps are the same equation.
Theorem 1.4 of arXiv:2505.12085 proves R_3(ax+ay=(a+1)z) >= a^3(a+1) for odd a >= 7, so an UNSAT refutation of Conjecture 1.2 cannot exist at b = a+1 there.
The abstract of arXiv:2210.03262 says exact values for 1 <= a,b,c <= 5, while later citations say <= 6. Check the actual tables before calling a cell new.

targets.name: Tensor rank of the 3x3 determinant as a 9x9x9 tensor: 17 or 18? (Shitov's Question 11.1)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (numerical CP searches over C with ALS / Levenberg-Marquardt and symmetry ansatzes, then exactification; the exact check takes seconds)
targets.statement: Let det3 = sum over sigma in S3 of sgn(sigma) x_{1,sigma(1)} x_{2,sigma(2)} x_{3,sigma(3)}, a cubic in the 9 entries of a generic 3x3 matrix, and let T in C^9 (x) C^9 (x) C^9 be its symmetric tensor: T[a,b,c] = sgn(sigma) when {a,b,c} = {(1,sigma(1)),(2,sigma(2)),(3,sigma(3))} as a set of three distinct indices, else 0 (36 nonzero entries, each flattening has rank 9). Conner, Harper and Landsberg (Forum Math. Pi 11 (2023) e17, arXiv:1911.07981) proved its border rank is 17, so rank >= 17. Conner, Gesmundo, Landsberg and Ventura (Comput. Complexity 31 (2022), arXiv:1909.04785) gave an 18-term expression, so rank <= 18. Shitov (viXra:2010.0193, 2020) proved that the Waring (symmetric) rank and the partially symmetric rank are both exactly 18, and left open as his Question 11.1 whether the tensor rank is 17 or 18. A rank of 17 would be a 9x9x9 counterexample to Comon's conjecture (rank = symmetric rank); the smallest known order-3 counterexample is Lovitz's 27x27x27 tensor with rank 55 and symmetric rank 56 (arXiv:2609.28292, Sep 2026), whose survey table lists no smaller one. Earlier history: Waring rank lower bounds 14 (Landsberg-Teitler), 15 (Boij-Teitler 2020). This is NOT the 3x3x3 'determinant tensor' of Krishna-Makam (rank 5), and NOT the Waring rank (settled at 18).
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit list of 17 triples (u_i, v_i, w_i) of vectors in K^9, where K is Q or a number field given by an explicit minimal polynomial, such that sum_{i=1..17} u_i (x) v_i (x) w_i equals T exactly (all 729 entries, in exact arithmetic), with T built as in the statement (any nonzero rescaling of T is fine; the variable order x_{11},x_{12},...,x_{33} must be stated). Direction: min; the bar is the known upper bound 18, so 17 terms is required. Before claiming, re-read Shitov's paper and Lovitz arXiv:2609.28292 and search arXiv for any later paper settling the rank; a published proof that the rank is 18 makes the target closed, not winnable.

partial_wins.statement: An exact 17-term decomposition of T over a finite field F_p with p >= 5, checked entrywise mod p (the border-rank lower bound 17 is a statement over C, so this does not settle Question 11.1, but it is a concrete lead for Hensel lifting).

A numerical 17-term decomposition over C with relative Frobenius residual <= 1e-40 after Newton refinement in 60-digit arithmetic, with every factor vector of Euclidean norm <= 100 after balancing the three factors of each term, so that it is not a border-rank degeneration; the residual and norms are recomputed independently with mpmath.

targets.verification_method: Build T from the definition (36 entries of +-1; check nnz = 36 and flattening ranks 9). For the full win, expand the 17 triples with exact arithmetic (SymPy or Sage over Q or the stated number field) and compare all 729 entries with T; confirm the number of terms by counting triples, never from a file name. For p1 do the same mod p. For p2 recompute the residual with mpmath at 60 digits and the per-term balanced norms. Re-fetch the status sources. Seconds to minutes on a laptop.
angles: The symmetry group of det3 (X -> AXB with det(AB)=1, transpose, and the S3 permuting the three tensor factors) is large; search for 17-term decompositions invariant under a finite subgroup (for example a Z3 that cycles the tensor factors combined with a matrix symmetry), which shrinks the unknowns a lot.
Start from the CHL border-rank-17 family and the CGLV 18-term expression and look for a degeneration-free 17-term limit point.
Search over small finite fields first (SAT or Groebner over F_7, F_13), then Hensel-lift a solution to Q_p and recognise algebraic numbers (LLL).
pitfalls: Shitov proved that the symmetric rank and the partially symmetric rank (sums of terms a (x) a (x) b, symmetric in one fixed pair of modes) are both 18. So no 17-term decomposition can have all its terms symmetric, or all its terms symmetric in the same pair of modes, and ansatzes of that form cannot succeed. Decompositions where only some terms are symmetric are still allowed.
Border rank is 17, so numerical optimisers reach small residuals with diverging factor norms; such sequences are border decompositions, not rank 17. Check norms (p2) and exactify.
Different 'det3 tensors' exist: the 3x3x3 alternating tensor has rank 5 (Krishna-Makam); this target is the 9x9x9 tensor of the cubic polynomial.
Shitov's paper is a viXra preprint; the 17-or-18 range for tensor rank rests on CHL and CGLV alone and does not depend on it.

targets.name: Determinantal complexity of the 4x4 permanent: a determinantal expression smaller than Grenet's 15 x 15
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (structured search over affine matrices with SAT/Groebner on small patterns; the exact check takes minutes)
targets.statement: A determinantal expression of size m for a polynomial f in variables x_1..x_k is an affine linear map L into m x m matrices with det(L(x)) = f(x) identically; dc(f) is the least such m. Valiant's permanent-versus-determinant conjecture says dc(per_n) grows superpolynomially. Small cases: Grenet (2011) turned a 2^n-vertex algebraic branching program into expressions of size 2^n - 1 for every n (characteristic other than 2), with entries in {x_ij} and the constants -1, 0, 1, so dc(per_4) <= 15. Huttenhain and Ikenmeyer (arXiv:1410.8202, Theorem 1.3 and Lemma 6.2) note that swapping two rows fixes the sign, so size 2^n - 1 is reached with the constants 0 and 1 alone. Mignon and Ressayre (2004) proved dc(per_n) >= n^2/2 in characteristic 0 (Cai, Chen and Li extended a quadratic bound to characteristic other than 2). Alper, Bogart and Velasco (Found. Comput. Math., arXiv:1505.02205) proved dc(f) >= codim Sing(f) + 1 when that codimension is at least 5 and deduced dc(per_3) = 7 and dc(per_4) >= 9 (characteristic other than 2), noting that 8 <= dc(per_4) <= 15 was the state before their work. Yabe (arXiv:1504.00151, not refereed) claims dc(per_n) >= (n-1)^2 + 1 over the reals, which would give >= 10 for expressions over Q. Huttenhain and Ikenmeyer (Linear Algebra Appl. 504 (2016)) showed 7 is also optimal for per_3 with entries in {0, 1, variables} and wrote that the binary case for per_4 is out of reach of their enumeration. Landsberg and Ressayre proved Grenet's expressions optimal among determinantal representations that respect left multiplication by permutation and diagonal matrices (roughly half the symmetry group of the permanent), so a smaller expression for n = 4 must break that symmetry. A check on 2026-10-30 of papers citing Alper-Bogart-Velasco and Huttenhain-Ikenmeyer found no improvement: 9 <= dc(per_4) <= 15 (at least 10 over the reals if Yabe's bound holds).
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit m x m matrix L(x) with m <= 14 whose entries are affine linear forms over Q (or a number field given by an explicit minimal polynomial) in the 16 variables x_ij, such that det L(x) = per_4(x) as polynomials, verified by exact symbolic expansion (direction: min; the bar is Grenet's 15). Before claiming, search arXiv and the GCT literature for any published determinantal expression of per_4 of size below 15; a smaller published size becomes the bar.

partial_wins.statement: An expression of size <= 14 for per_4 over a finite field F_p with p >= 3, with det L(x) = per_4(x) verified as polynomials over F_p.
An expression of size <= 2^n - 2 for per_n for some n >= 5 (for n = 5, size <= 30) over Q, verified exactly.

targets.verification_method: Parse L as a matrix of affine forms. Screen with random evaluations: compare det L(x) with per_4(x) at 50 random integer points mod several 61-bit primes. Then confirm exactly: compute det L(x) symbolically (Bareiss or Berkowitz in SymPy/Sage/Singular over Q[x_11..x_44], or over F_p[x] for p1), expand, and compare with the 24-term per_4. Calibrate on Grenet's 15 x 15 construction, which must pass. Report m from the matrix. Minutes.
angles: Grenet's matrices are adjacency matrices of layered graphs over subsets; search non-equivariant graph shapes (ABP-like digraphs with fewer vertices, allowing constants other than 0 and 1) with SAT over F_3 first.
Huttenhain-Ikenmeyer enumerated bipartite graphs for per_3; extend their enumeration with pruning to size 13-14 patterns for per_4.
pitfalls: Characteristic 2 is trivial (per = det there); claims must be in characteristic 0 for the full win and odd characteristic for p1.
Random evaluation is only a screen; the claim needs an exact symbolic identity.

Grenet's 15 x 15 matrix for n = 4 uses the constant -1; swapping two rows gives a 15 x 15 matrix with constants 0 and 1 only (Huttenhain-Ikenmeyer, Lemma 6.2). The bar is 15 either way; Grenet's 16 x 16 0/1 variant is not the calibration target.
Over Q or any real field, Yabe's claimed bound (n-1)^2 + 1 rules out sizes below 10 for per_4; do not spend search on m <= 9.
Representations that respect left multiplication by permutation and diagonal matrices cannot beat Grenet (Landsberg-Ressayre); ansatzes with that symmetry waste time.

targets.name: Spherical coverings: N points on the sphere with a smaller covering radius than the Hardin-Sloane-Smith table (N = 4..130, kept by Henry Cohn)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Place N points on the unit sphere S^2 so that the covering radius (the largest angular distance from any point of the sphere to the nearest of the N points) is as small as possible. R. H. Hardin, N. J. A. Sloane and W. D. Smith computed putatively optimal coverings for N = 4..130 in 1994 (neilsloane.com/coverings, page last modified 2015, point files cover.3. < N > .txt) and coverings with icosahedral symmetry for N = 2+10(i^2+ij+j^2) from 72 up to 78032 (1994-2000, 267 rows). Henry Cohn now maintains these tables (cohn.mit.edu/sloane, radii rounded UP to 7 decimals, so his last digit can be 1e-7 above Sloane's; files cov3-N.txt in data set hdl.handle.net/1721.1/147004) and asks for improvements. The general table carries no credited change since 1994. Recomputing the posted files for N = 20, 77, 100 and 130 on 2026-10-30 reproduced the table (e.g. N = 130: 11.3165625 degrees). Only a few small N are proven optimal: at least N <= 7 and N = 12 (L. Fejes Toth, Schutte), and survey literature also reports small cases such as N = 10 and 14 as settled, so this target counts only N >= 15. Tarnai and Gaspar studied rigidity; Rathbun (arXiv:2008.04441) gave algebraic forms for some putatively optimal N. The AlphaEvolve survey (Georgiev, Gomez-Serrano, Tao, Wagner, arXiv:2511.02864) did not try coverings. Minimax objectives are non-smooth, and the 1994 searches for N near 100-130 were short, so the upper rows are plausible targets.
targets.success_criterion: Success means N unit vectors ( > = 20 significant digits) for some N in 15..130 listed in the live general table at https://cohn.mit.edu/sloane (re-fetched immediately before claiming), whose covering radius R*, computed exactly as stated in verification_method, is STRICTLY SMALLER (direction: min) than the table's covering radius for N by at least 1e-7 degrees (Cohn's values are rounded up; Sloane's page https://neilsloane.com/coverings/ rounds to nearest and can be 1e-7 lower, so compare against the smaller of the two). Also, no published value for N found in an arXiv / Google Scholar check ('covering' 'sphere' 'equal circles' / 'spherical caps' plus N) is lower than R*. N <= 14 is excluded because several small cases are proven optimal.

partial_wins.statement: A configuration of any symmetry with covering radius at least 1e-7 degrees smaller than the SMALLEST icosahedral-table value listed for that N (cohn.mit.edu/sloane, icov3 rows) for some listed N with 132 <= N <= 2000 (66 such rows covering 60 distinct N on 2026-10-30; N = 492, 912, 1332, 1472, 1692 and 1962 each have two rows with different (i, j), and the smaller radius is the bar), same exact checker. Rows with N <= 130 do not count, because the general table already matches or beats the icosahedral rows there (e.g. N = 92: 13.4878634 vs 13.6762972).

A table-integrity finding: at least one N in 4..130 where the posted cover.3.N.txt (or Cohn's cov3-N.txt), run through the exact checker, does not reproduce the tabulated radius to within 1e-7 degrees, reported with both values.

targets.verification_method: Checker (seconds per N): normalise the points in mpmath (50 digits). Take the convex hull (scipy for the combinatorics). Assert the origin is strictly inside. For each facet, compute the unit outward normal and the angular circumradius arccos(n . a). Assert the empty-cap (Delaunay) property: every other point p satisfies n . p <= n . a + 1e-30. R* is the maximum angular circumradius. Run the same checker on Sloane's posted cover.3.N.txt to reproduce the table first (verified 2026-10-30 for N = 20, 77, 100, 130). Compare R* with the live table value minus 1e-7.
angles: Smooth the minimax objective: minimise the log-sum-exp of the facet circumradii (or an L_p norm with p rising to infinity), then finish with an exact active-set Newton step on the equal-radius facets, as done for Tammes polishing.
Seed from Tammes and Thomson optima at the same N (spherical-codes.org, Deeter tables). Good coverings are often near-uniform minimum-energy configurations with defect motifs moved around.
Use the icosahedral rows as seeds for N slightly above or below 2+10(i^2+ij+j^2) by inserting or deleting points near the 12 disclinations and re-optimising without symmetry.
pitfalls: Directions: the table gives covering radii in degrees, rounded UP. Smaller wins. Do not confuse it with the packing (Tammes) table, where larger minimal angles win.
A wrong hull (degenerate co-circular facets) gives a wrong radius. Always run the empty-cap check in high precision.

neilsloane.com serves point files only to a browser-like User-Agent (plain curl gets HTTP 403). MIT DSpace returned HTTP 429 to scripted requests on 2026-10-30, so fetch the data set slowly or use the Sloane files.

targets.name: Fejes Toth problem: N points on the unit sphere whose convex hull has larger volume than the best known (Hardin-Sloane-Smith and Deeter tables, N = 10..130 except 12)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Maximise the volume of the convex hull of N points on the unit sphere S^2 (the Fejes Toth problem, 1964). Berman and Hanes (1970) solved N <= 8. Fejes Toth's inequality V <= (N-2)/6 * cot(w) * (3 - cot^2 w), w = pi N/(6(N-2)), is attained by the regular icosahedron, so N = 12 is settled (bound = table value 2.536150710120). S. Hoehner and J. Ledford (arXiv:2608.04392, Aug 2026) proved N = 9: the maximum is 3*sqrt(2*sqrt(3)-3) = 2.043750115900, the table value. Mutoh (2003) gave numerical candidates for N <= 30. Horvath and Langi (arXiv:1402.6496) solved d+2 points in d dimensions, and d+3 when d is odd. Hardin, Sloane and Smith tabulated putatively optimal arrangements for N = 4..130 in 1994 (neilsloane.com/maxvolumes, 12 decimals, files maxvol.3. < N > .txt) and icosahedral-symmetric ones for N = 72..78032 (neilsloane.com/icosahedral.codes, 12 decimals). Henry Cohn now maintains these tables (cohn.mit.edu/sloane, 7 decimals rounded DOWN, 267 icosahedral rows, data set hdl.handle.net/1721.1/147004) and invites improvements. W. Deeter's table (deetour.net/oppp/maxvols/maxvol-summary.html, N = 4..492, 12 decimals, coordinates maxvol. < N > .txt, last modified 26 Feb 2018, linked from OEIS A081314), built by optimising duals of roundest polyhedra, is strictly better than Sloane and Cohn at N = 62 (3.825221379534 vs 3.825219246599) and N = 124 (4.005307382615 vs 4.005226779889) and agrees with Sloane to 12 decimals at every other N <= 130. An auditor's checker reproduced both Deeter values from his files on 2026-10-30, and BFGS polishing of Sloane's files for 62 and 124 gains nothing (different basins). The AlphaEvolve survey (Georgiev, Gomez-Serrano, Tao, Wagner, arXiv:2511.02864, Nov 2025) calls Sloane's table 'the most up to date database'; it matched the first ~60 rows to all 13 digits, improved none, and did not try the remaining ~70 rows. On 2026-10-30 the posted Sloane files for N = 9, 12, 20, 61, 77, 100 and 130 reproduced the table to 12 decimals (N = 130: 4.013655508770), and BFGS polishing changed none by more than 2e-15. Any gains are therefore in other basins, most likely for N = 61..130. Credit: Berman, Hanes, Fejes Toth, Mutoh, Hardin, Sloane, Smith, Deeter, Cohn, Hoehner, Ledford.
targets.success_criterion: Success means N unit vectors ( > = 20 significant digits) for some N in 10..130 other than N = 12 (N <= 9 and N = 12 are proven optimal and can never count), such that the convex-hull volume V*, computed in mpmath at 40 digits after normalisation, is STRICTLY LARGER (direction: max) than the best known value for N by at least 1e-10, where the best known value is the maximum of the 12-decimal value at https://neilsloane.com/maxvolumes/index.html, the 12-decimal value at https://deetour.net/oppp/maxvols/maxvol-summary.html and the 7-decimal value at https://cohn.mit.edu/sloane (all re-fetched immediately before claiming; at N = 62 and N = 124 Deeter's value is the bar). It must also be a different basin: polishing the posted Sloane file maxvol.3. < N > .txt and Deeter's maxvol. < N > .txt with the same routine stays below V* - 1e-10. And no published value for N found in an arXiv / Google Scholar check ('maximal volume' 'inscribed' polyhedra N) or among the links of OEIS A081314 is larger, and no paper proves the posted value for N optimal.

partial_wins.statement: For an N with 132 <= N <= 2000 listed in the icosahedral maximal-volume table, a configuration of any symmetry whose hull volume, with the same checker, beats by at least 1e-10 the larger of the 12-decimal icosahedral value at https://neilsloane.com/icosahedral.codes/index.html and, for N <= 492, Deeter's 12-decimal value at https://deetour.net/oppp/maxvols/maxvol-summary.html, and is not a re-polish of a posted file (polishing the posted ivol.3. < N > .*.txt and Deeter's maxvol. < N > .txt stays below V* - 1e-10). Cohn's 7-decimal icosahedral values are rounded down and are not the bar: re-posting Sloane's own file already beats them by up to 1e-7. At N = 492 Deeter's 4.142251571462 already beats the icosahedral 4.142250389453, so Deeter's value is the bar there. Rows with N <= 130 do not count.

A table-integrity finding in the 127 general rows (N = 4..130): at least one N whose posted Sloane file maxvol.3.N.txt or Deeter file maxvol.N.txt does not reproduce its own table's 12-decimal value to 1e-11, or polishes more than 1e-10 higher (an under-converged row, reported as such and not counted as a record). The known Sloane-versus-Deeter gaps at N = 62 and 124 are different basins and do not count.

targets.verification_method: Checker (seconds): normalise in mpmath. Get the hull facets from scipy. Assert all N points are hull vertices and the origin is inside. V* = sum over facets of |det(a,b,c)|/6 in mpmath at 40 digits. Compare with all three live tables (Sloane 12-decimal, Deeter 12-decimal, Cohn 7-decimal) and take their maximum as the bar. Run the same polish (BFGS on the normalised coordinates, then a high-precision Newton step) on Sloane's and Deeter's files for N and confirm the distinct-basin margin. Sanity-check against the Fejes Toth bound. Verified 2026-10-30 on Sloane's files for N = 9, 12, 20, 61, 77, 100, 130 and Deeter's files for N = 62, 124, 492.
angles: The Berman-Hanes necessary condition (each vertex is the normalised sum of its neighbours' cross products) gives a fixed-point iteration that converges fast inside a hull topology. Combine it with topology moves (edge flips, which switch between degree-5/6 vertex patterns) as a basin-hopping step.
For N = 61..130, AlphaEvolve did not even try. Seed from Thomson and covering optima at the same N, since maximal-volume polyhedra are close to uniform.
Deeter's route (take duals of near-roundest circumscribed polyhedra, then optimise for volume) found better basins than Hardin-Sloane-Smith at N = 62 and 124; apply it systematically to the other N.
pitfalls: The bar is the maximum of three tables. Deeter's table is higher than Sloane's and Cohn's at N = 62 and 124; Sloane's 12-decimal values are sharper than Cohn's 7-decimal values, which are rounded down, so beating only Cohn by rounding is not a win.

N <= 9 (Berman-Hanes 1970; Hoehner-Ledford 2026 for N = 9) and N = 12 (Fejes Toth's bound, attained by the icosahedron) are proven, so a 'win' there is a bug. Re-check arXiv for new optimality proofs before claiming.
neilsloane.com point files need a browser-like User-Agent (plain curl gets 403).
Do not confuse with Deeter's roundest-polyhedra (minimal circumscribed) tables on the same site; only the maxvol summary is the bar.

targets.name: Minimal-energy clusters of hard spheres: N unit spheres in R^3 (N <= 99) or R^4 (N <= 32) with smaller second moment than the Sloane-Hardin-Duff-Conway table
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Arrange N non-overlapping unit spheres (centres at mutual distance >= 2) to minimise the second moment sum_i |x_i - c|^2 about their centroid c. This is the hard-sphere limit of cluster energy minimisation, and the minimisers interpolate between close-packed and spherical clusters. N. J. A. Sloane, R. H. Hardin, T. D. S. Duff and J. H. Conway ('Minimal-energy clusters of hard spheres', Discrete Comput. Geom. 14 (1995), 237-259) tabulated putative minima for n = 3, N = 4..99 (96 rows, e.g. N = 13: 47.7012169, N = 99: 1532.2299539) and n = 4, N = 5..32 (28 rows, N = 32: 145.0449556). Henry Cohn now maintains the table (cohn.mit.edu/sloane, 7 decimals rounded UP, files clust-n-N.txt, data set hdl.handle.net/1721.1/147004) and asks for improvements. The small cases are easy to check by hand: N = 4 gives 6 (tetrahedron of edge 2) and N = 6 gives 12 (octahedron). The 1995 searches are three decades old, and the problem has received far less attention than Lennard-Jones or Morse clusters.
targets.success_criterion: Success means N points in R^n (n = 3 or 4; >= 20 significant digits) for an (n, N) row of the live table at https://cohn.mit.edu/sloane (re-fetched immediately before claiming), whose scale-invariant moment M* = (4 / d_min^2) * sum_i |x_i - c|^2 is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the table's moment for (n, N) by at least 1e-6, computed in mpmath at 40 digits with d_min the minimal pairwise distance and c the centroid. Also, no published value for (n, N) found in an arXiv / Google Scholar search ('hard sphere' 'second moment' OR 'moment of inertia' cluster) is lower than M*.

partial_wins.statement: A table-integrity finding: at least one posted clust-n-N.txt that violates d_min >= 2 by more than 1e-7, or whose scale-invariant moment M* does not reproduce the table's moment for (n, N) to within 1e-6, reported with both values.

For some n = 3 row with N >= 20, a configuration whose M* is within 1e-7 of the table value (allowing for 7-decimal rounding) but whose contact graph (pairs with distance <= 2(1 + 1e-9) after rescaling to d_min = 2) is not isomorphic to that of the posted file: a degenerate competing minimum, checked with networkx isomorphism.

targets.verification_method: Checker (seconds): load coordinates, compute d_min and the centroid moment in mpmath, form M* = 4 M / d_min^2 (which rescales any configuration to unit-radius spheres), and compare with the live table. Run the same computation on the posted file for (n, N) to confirm it reproduces the table value.
angles: Treat it as a cluster global optimisation with a hard-core constraint: basin hopping on a steep soft repulsion plus a harmonic trap (moment term), annealing the repulsion exponent to infinity, then a final active-set QP on the contact graph.
Seed from Lennard-Jones, Morse (long-range) and sticky-hard-sphere cluster minima at the same N (CCD), which share compact polytetrahedral and decahedral motifs.
pitfalls: Normalisation: the table uses unit RADIUS (centres >= 2 apart), so N = 4 gives 6.0. Using unit diameter gives values 4 times smaller.
Small overlaps lower the moment. Always use the scale-invariant M*, never the raw moment with a tolerance.

targets.name: Grassmannian packings: N subspaces of R^m (m <= 16) with larger minimal squared chordal distance than Cohn's table
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Choose N n-dimensional subspaces of R^m that maximise the minimal squared chordal distance d^2 = n - ||U_i^T U_j||_F^2, which is the sum of the squared sines of the principal angles. The table was started by J. H. Conway, R. H. Hardin and N. J. A. Sloane (Experiment. Math. 5 (1996), 139-159) and Sloane's 1997 web table. Henry Cohn now maintains it at cohn.mit.edu/grassmannian with 10-decimal distances rounded DOWN, upper bounds (simplex/orthoplex, rounded up), notes crediting each construction, and all configurations in the data set hdl.handle.net/1721.1/147005 (files m-n-N.txt). On 2026-10-30 it had 3,511 rows for m = 3..16 and n = 1..6, 1,163 of them starred (the bound is met, so they cannot be improved). Another 15 unstarred rows are noted 'optimal packing' with a proof of optimality (e.g. (3,1,8), Mixon-Parshall), so they cannot be improved either. It is actively contested: the notes credit 'Henry Cohn' with 15 rows in 2023, 75 in 2024, 528 in 2025 and 50 in 2026, plus constructions by Fickus, Jasper, Mixon, Ganzhinov and others. 1,562 unstarred rows still cite only the original Conway-Hardin-Sloane paper [9] or Sloane's 1997 table [29]. Eight rows are flagged 'unclear whether bound is tight', e.g. (6,3,17): 1.5937499963 vs bound 1.59375. The n = 1 rows are real projective line packings. Complex line packings are a separate bank target (game-of-sloanes-complex-line-packings).
targets.success_criterion: Success means N matrices U_i (m x n, >= 20 significant digits) for an UNSTARRED (m, n, N) row of the live table at https://cohn.mit.edu/grassmannian (re-fetched immediately before claiming) whose note does not say 'optimal packing' or 'proof of optimality', such that after orthonormalising each U_i in mpmath at 50 digits, the minimum over i < j of n - ||U_i^T U_j||_F^2 is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the table's squared chordal distance for (m, n, N) by at least 1e-9. It must also not exceed the row's listed bound by more than 1e-10 (a larger value means a bug). And no value for (m, n, N) published after the table's last change, found in an arXiv search (Grassmannian / line packing / fusion frame with m, n, N), is larger.

partial_wins.statement: An improvement by at least 1e-9 (same checker and exclusions) on an unstarred row whose note cites only [9] (Conway-Hardin-Sloane 1996) or [29] (Sloane's 1997 table), i.e. a value never improved since the 1990s (1,562 such rows on 2026-10-30).

For one of the eight rows marked 'unclear whether bound is tight' ((6,3,17), (7,2,18), (7,3,23), (10,2,28), (10,5,56), (11,4,69), (12,2,35), (15,2,46)), a packing attaining the bound with a rigorous certificate: exact algebraic coordinates, or an interval Newton proof that an exact solution lies within 1e-30 of the given point.
