targets.verification_method: Checker (seconds): parse the vectors (the first n lines span subspace 1, and so on), orthonormalise each block by QR in mpmath, compute all pairwise n - ||U_i^T U_j||_F^2, and take the minimum. Compare it with the live row (10 decimals, rounded down) and its bound. Reproduce the posted file for the row first.
angles: Rows with empty notes in m = 11..16 were often run only once in 1996 (Sloane's page says so). Run multistart alternating projection (Dhillon-Heath-Strohmer-Tropp) followed by a smooth max-min polish (log-sum-exp of the distances, then an active-set Newton step).
For n >= 2, build candidates from complex or quaternionic line packings (Game of Sloanes, Hoggar) viewed as real planes, which the table already credits for several tight rows.
pitfalls: Starred rows meet the bound. No improvement is possible there.
The distance is the squared chordal distance (n minus the sum of squared cosines), not the chordal distance or the smallest principal angle. Mixing them up gives meaningless 'records'.
MIT DSpace returned HTTP 429 to scripted requests on 2026-10-30. Download the tar file once, slowly.

targets.name: Harmonic energy on spheres in 4 to 32 dimensions: lower the best known energy in the Ballinger-Blekherman-Cohn-Giansiracusa-Kelly-Schurmann table
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Place N points on the unit sphere S^{n-1} in R^n to minimise the harmonic energy sum_{i < j} |x_i - x_j|^{-(n-2)}. For n = 3 this is the Thomson problem (a separate bank target, excluded here). Henry Cohn's live table (cohn.mit.edu/harmonic-energy) lists the best energies known for 3 <= n <= 32 and n+1 <= N <= 64, plus larger cases up to N = 336 (1,682 rows, 10 decimals). Each row also gives the minimal-angle cosine, the design strength and the number of distinct distances. The data come from Brandon Ballinger, Grigoriy Blekherman, Henry Cohn, Noah Giansiracusa, Elizabeth Kelly and Achill Schurmann (Experiment. Math. 18 (2009), 257-283, arXiv:math/0611451) and their 2021 update with coordinates (hdl.handle.net/1721.1/130937). The page asks for improvements. A companion page (cohn.mit.edu/harmonic-optima) lists the proven universal optima, which cannot be beaten (e.g. 24 points in R^4 are not among them, but 120 in R^4, 16 in R^5 and 27 in R^6 are), and conjectured optima such as 40 points in R^10 and 64 in R^14. Sanity checks on 2026-10-30 reproduced (n,N) = (4,10): 22.5, (4,24): 167 and (5,12): 23.6035593670 with plain BFGS multistart. Rows for n >= 4 with large N and irregular structure (many distinct distances, design strength 0) are the natural targets.
targets.success_criterion: Success means N unit vectors in R^n (n in 4..32; >= 20 significant digits) for an (N, n) pair listed at https://cohn.mit.edu/harmonic-energy (re-fetched immediately before claiming), whose energy E* = sum_{i < j} |x_i - x_j|^{-(n-2)}, computed in mpmath at 40 digits after normalisation, is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the SMALLEST table energy for that (N, n) by at least max(1e-9, 1e-12 * E). The (N, n) must not be a proven optimum: not a simplex (N = n+1), not a cross polytope (N = 2n), not a universal optimum listed on https://cohn.mit.edu/harmonic-optima, and not proven optimal for harmonic energy in any paper found in an arXiv check. It must be a different basin: polishing the 2021 data set's coordinates for (N, n) with the same routine stays above E* + max(1e-9, 1e-12 * E). And no lower published value is found in an arXiv search.

partial_wins.statement: An improvement (same rules) for a row with n >= 4 and N >= 65 (the 'larger cases' beyond the full grid).
An audit of the 2021 data set: (N, n) rows where the posted coordinates do not reproduce the table energy to 1e-9, or polish more than 1e-9 lower (under-converged, reported as such, not a record).

targets.verification_method: Checker (seconds to minutes): normalise in mpmath, compute E* exactly, and compare with the live table minimum for (N, n). Polish the data-set configuration and the claim with the same L-BFGS plus mpmath Newton routine, and compare the basins. Check the harmonic-optima page for proven rows.
angles: Large-N rows in moderate dimensions (n = 4..8, N = 65..256) were run with limited restarts in 2009. Use symmetry-seeded starts (orbits of root systems, the 600-cell and E8 subsets) and basin hopping.
Rows with 'Distances' in the hundreds or thousands are unstructured local minima, likely far from optimal. Rows with few distances are probably sharp.
pitfalls: The exponent is n - 2, which depends on the dimension. Using 1/r in higher dimensions is a different problem.
Some (N, n) pairs appear twice in the table with equal energies (different configurations). Use the minimum.
n = 3 rows are the Thomson problem: they belong to thomson-problem-live-tables and do not count here.

targets.name: Largest small polygons: a convex n-gon of diameter 1 with larger area than Bingane-Mossinghoff's P_n* for some even n = 14..120
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: A polygon is small if its diameter is 1. For odd n the regular n-gon has maximal area (Reinhardt 1922). For even n the optimum is known only for n = 4, 6 (Graham 1975), 8 (Audet, Hansen, Messine and Xiong 2002), 10 and 12 (Henrion and Messine 2013). Foster and Szabo (2007) proved Graham's conjecture on the diameter graph of an optimal polygon, a cycle of n-1 diameters plus a pendant edge. Uniqueness and axial symmetry of the optimum are open. Christian Bingane and Michael J. Mossinghoff ('Small polygons with large area', J. Global Optim. 88(4) (2024) 1035-1050, arXiv:2204.04547, Table 4) computed P_n*, the best axially symmetric small n-gon in the Foster-Szabo skeleton, for n = 14, 16, ..., 24, 30, 40, ..., 120. Their values match or slightly exceed the earlier literature (Mossinghoff 2006, Pinter et al. 2021, Bingane 2021) and are the current records, e.g. A(P_14*) = 0.7675310111, A(P_16*) = 0.7718613220, A(P_120*) = 0.7851717941. Code and coordinates are in OPTIGON (github.com/cbingane/optigon). Mulansky and Potschka (Math. Program. 2025) settle the analogous perimeter problem numerically to 90 digits under a symmetry conjecture, but leave area untouched. A plain SLSQP multistart run on 2026-10-30 reproduced A(P_14*) to 10 digits, so the records are sharp under symmetry. A win most likely needs an asymmetric polygon, which would refute the symmetry expectation, or a better symmetric basin for large n.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the n vertices ( > = 25 significant digits, in cyclic order) of a convex polygon, for an even n listed in Table 4 of arXiv:2204.04547 with n >= 14, such that, in mpmath at 50 digits: every pairwise vertex distance is <= 1 (after rescaling by the computed diameter, the area is divided by diam^2); the polygon is strictly convex and simple (all consecutive cross products > 0 and total turning exactly 2 pi); and the shoelace area is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than A(P_n*) in Table 4 by at least 1e-9. Also, no larger value for n is found in an arXiv / Google Scholar check ('small polygon' 'maximal area' n), including any OPTIGON update.

partial_wins.statement: For some listed even n >= 14, a strictly convex small n-gon that is a numerically certified local maximiser of area (KKT residual < 1e-20 in mpmath for the diameter-constrained problem, with a positive-definite reduced Hessian of the Lagrangian) and has no axis of symmetry (no reflection maps the vertex set to itself within 1e-6), with area within 1e-7 of A(P_n*): a competing asymmetric basin, not a perturbation of P_n*.

For an even n in 26..118 not listed in Table 4, a certified small n-gon (same checker as the full win) whose area beats, by at least 1e-9, the optimum of the paper's symmetric problem (16) at that n, as computed by the skeptic with OPTIGON's AMPL model max_area/ampl_max_area_diameter.mod (param n set to that n, Ipopt, its built-in initial angles plus at least 20 random starts) and reported to 12 digits. Reported as beating the symmetric optimum, not a published record.

targets.verification_method: Checker (seconds): mpmath at 50 digits. Compute the diameter as the maximum over all vertex pairs and rescale. Check strict convexity via cross products and the turning number via the sum of exterior angles. Compute the shoelace area and compare with Table 4 (10 decimals). Reproduce A(P_n*) from Table 3 angles or OPTIGON for the same n first.
pitfalls: Shoelace area of a non-simple polygon (winding twice) silently doubles: an unconstrained optimiser on 14 vertices 'found' area 1.39 > pi/4 on 2026-10-30. Always check convexity and turning number.
Diameter <= 1 must hold for ALL vertex pairs, not only the diameter-graph edges, and in high precision. Use the scale-invariant area / diam^2.
Odd n and n <= 12 are solved, so a 'win' there is a bug. Perimeter and width records are different problems and do not count here.

targets.name: M4 competition (100,000 series): an honestly out-of-sample point forecast with overall OWA below N-BEATS's 0.795
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (100,000 series; about 270 MB of CSV in Dataset/Train and Dataset/Test; deep ensembles benefit from a GPU, statistical combinations run on CPU)
targets.statement: The M4 competition (Spyros Makridakis, Evangelos Spiliotis and Vassilios Assimakopoulos, 2018; IJF 2020) asked for point forecasts and 95% prediction intervals for 100,000 series (23,000 yearly, 24,000 quarterly, 48,000 monthly, 359 weekly, 4,227 daily, 414 hourly) at fixed horizons 6/8/18/13/14/48. The organisers' repository Mcompetitions/M4-methods holds the train and test sets, M4-info.csv, the point forecasts of all 49 valid submissions and the R code that computes sMAPE, MASE and OWA (the mean of sMAPE and MASE, each divided by the Naive2 value, over all series). In its Evaluation and Ranks sheet the winner, Slawek Smyl's ES-RNN hybrid (Uber), scores sMAPE 11.374 and OWA 0.821, and Montero-Manso, Talagala, Hyndman and Athanasopoulos (FFORMA) score 0.838. After the competition, N-BEATS (Boris Oreshkin, Dmitri Carpov, Nicolas Chapados, Yoshua Bengio; ICLR 2020, arXiv:1905.10437 Table 1) reported OWA 0.795 (sMAPE 11.135) for its N-BEATS-I+G ensemble. That is the lowest overall M4 OWA this entry could pin to a primary source. By frequency, N-BEATS leads on Yearly, Quarterly and Monthly (Table 12). On the Others subset (weekly, daily and hourly combined), submission 237 (Pawlikowski, Chorowska and Yanchuk, ProLogistica Soft) scores about 0.742 when recomputed from the organisers' per-frequency sheet, below N-BEATS's 0.822. For intervals, the winner's overall MSIS is 12.23 (Montero-Manso et al. 14.334). Open task: a forecast pipeline that never sees the test set and scores an overall OWA below 0.795.
targets.success_criterion: Saved point forecasts for all 100,000 M4 series at the official horizons whose overall OWA, computed with the organisers' evaluation code from https://github.com/Mcompetitions/M4-methods (Naive2 normaliser, MASE seasonal period from M4-info.csv), is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than 0.795 (N-BEATS-I+G, arXiv:1905.10437 Table 1) and than any lower overall M4 OWA the skeptic finds in a credible post-2020 paper for a method with test-free training. LEAK RULE: forecasts come from a frozen, hashed script that the skeptic reruns in a fresh environment where only Dataset/Train and M4-info.csv exist (no test files on disk); every model, hyperparameter and ensemble choice is fixed on a holdout carved from the end of each training series; any pretrained component must have published training-data documentation excluding all M4 series (time-series foundation models trained on Monash/LOTSA-type corpora are excluded unless proven otherwise).

partial_wins.statement: Overall OWA strictly below 0.821 (Smyl, M4 winner) under the full-win leak rule, with a pipeline that the skeptic reruns end to end in under 24 hours on one 8-core CPU machine with no GPU.

Under the full-win leak rule, with forecasts submitted for all 100,000 series, an OWA on one frequency subset that is strictly below the lowest known value for that subset: Yearly 0.758, Quarterly 0.800 or Monthly 0.819 (N-BEATS, arXiv:1905.10437 Table 12), or Others (weekly, daily and hourly combined) below the value of submission 237 (ProLogistica Soft), about 0.742. For Others, the claimant recomputes submission 237's exact value with the organisers' code from its released point forecasts and must beat that value.
95% prediction intervals for all 100,000 series under the full-win leak rule, with overall MSIS (organisers' code) strictly below Smyl's 12.23 and overall empirical coverage between 94% and 96%.

targets.verification_method: Clone Mcompetitions/M4-methods, hash the Train/Test CSVs, rerun the frozen script in a container without the Test folder, then score the saved forecasts with the organisers' R evaluation code; as a scorer check, score submission-118 (Smyl) and confirm OWA 0.821 and sMAPE 11.374. Read the script for any test-file access or test-informed constants, and check pretrained models' data cards. Re-read the record in arXiv:1905.10437 and search for later lower overall OWAs before accepting.
angles: Forecast combination in the FFORMA / Theta tradition, weighted by features learned on training-only holdouts, stacked with a global deep model.
Per-frequency specialists: M4's yearly and quarterly subsets dominate the series count, so gains there move overall OWA most.
Ensembling over loss functions and lookback lengths, the main source of N-BEATS's gain, is cheap to reproduce with smaller networks.
pitfalls: Test leakage through pretraining: many public time-series corpora contain the full M4 series, including the test horizon.
OWA in M4 is computed from aggregate sMAPE and MASE relative to Naive2 over all series, not as a mean of per-series OWAs; use the organisers' code.
N-BEATS's per-frequency table compares only four M4 entries; always check all 49 released submissions before claiming a subset win.
The 2026-10-30 checks fetched the primary sources but could not complete a 2024-2026 literature search; a claimant must search for, and beat, any lower credible overall OWA before claiming.

targets.name: M5 accuracy competition (Walmart unit sales): beat the winning private WRMSSE 0.52044 with a frozen, test-blind pipeline
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (about 450 MB of CSV, 30,490 bottom-level series; LightGBM-style models need 16-32 GB RAM)
targets.statement: The M5 competition (Spyros Makridakis, Evangelos Spiliotis and Vassilios Assimakopoulos with Walmart and Kaggle, 2020; IJF 2022) asked for 28-day forecasts of 42,840 hierarchical series of Walmart unit sales (3,049 products in 10 stores in 3 states, 12 aggregation levels) for days d_1942 to d_1969. The accuracy track was scored by WRMSSE: RMSSE per series, weighted by dollar sales over the last 28 training days and averaged over the 12 levels. The organisers' Scores and Ranks.xlsx (Mcompetitions/M5-methods) gives the private scores: YJ_STU (Yeonjun In) 0.52044, Matthias 0.52816, mf 0.53572, monsaraida 0.53583. Their public Google Drive folder releases sales_train_evaluation.csv (d_1 to d_1941), sales_test_evaluation.csv (the 28 scored days), calendar.csv, sell_prices.csv, weights_evaluation.csv and the R scorer (Estimate WRMSSE.R), so the private leaderboard can be recomputed exactly. Open task: a pipeline that never reads the test days and scores below 0.52044.
targets.success_criterion: Saved 28-day point forecasts for all 30,490 bottom-level series (aggregated to all 12 levels as the organisers' scorer does) whose WRMSSE on d_1942-d_1969, computed with the organisers' Estimate WRMSSE.R and weights_evaluation.csv, is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than 0.52044 (YJ_STU, Accuracy-Top50 (AL) sheet of https://github.com/Mcompetitions/M5-methods Scores and Ranks.xlsx) and than any lower WRMSSE that a paper or public write-up reports for a test-blind method on the same task: all 42,840 series, days d_1942-d_1969, the organisers' weights and scorer. Numbers computed with other scorers, on subsets or other windows, or without the full 12-level hierarchy (for example the 0.092-0.661 'WRMSSE' values in arXiv:2506.13036) are not comparable and are not records. LEAK RULE: a frozen, hashed script that the skeptic reruns in a fresh environment containing only sales_train_evaluation.csv, calendar.csv and sell_prices.csv (sales_test_evaluation.csv absent); all tuning, including any global multiplier, done on folds that end by d_1941; any pretrained component documented as never trained on M5 data.

partial_wins.statement: Scorer check plus a modest win: reproduce YJ_STU's 0.52044 from the organisers' released submission files, then score strictly below 0.53572 (3rd place, mf) under the full-win leak rule.

Under the full-win leak rule, a mean WRMSSE over the three bottom levels strictly below YJ_STU's 0.92622 (mean of L10 0.965581, L11 0.928931 and L12 0.884160 in the Accuracy-Top50 (AL) sheet), with overall WRMSSE no higher than 0.53.

targets.verification_method: Download the organisers' Dataset folder, hash the files, run the frozen script in a container without sales_test_evaluation.csv, then score with Estimate WRMSSE.R; first confirm the scorer reproduces 0.52044 on YJ_STU's released accuracy submission. Read the code for constants tuned on the test days (multipliers, day-of-week fixes).
angles: Store-by-department LightGBM with Tweedie loss, the winning family, plus recursive and direct horizon blends chosen on several late training folds.
Hierarchical reconciliation (MinT or top-down from level 9) because WRMSSE averages all 12 levels equally.
pitfalls: Post-deadline Kaggle notebooks often tune a 'magic multiplier' or the final days against the leaked evaluation labels; any constant chosen on d_1942-d_1969 voids the claim.
Using sales_train_validation.csv weights instead of weights_evaluation.csv changes the score.

Some papers print M5 'WRMSSE' values far below 0.52 that are not comparable. arXiv:2506.13036 (a 2025 forecast-then-optimize survey) reports 0.092 for TimeSpeaks and 0.157 for NLinear without exogenous features, plainly a different computation. A literature search on 2026-10-30 (arXiv, IJF, Kaggle write-ups, Nixtla's M5 evaluation) found no test-blind score below 0.52044 on the official task; re-check before claiming.

targets.name: M5 uncertainty competition: beat the winning private WSPL 0.15420 for nine-quantile Walmart sales forecasts
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (same 450 MB M5 data; quantile models at 12 levels)
targets.statement: The uncertainty track of M5 (Makridakis, Spiliotis, Assimakopoulos, Chen, Gaba, Tsetlin and Winkler; IJF 2022) asked for the 0.005, 0.025, 0.165, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.835, 0.975 and 0.995 quantiles of 28-day Walmart unit sales for all 42,840 series at 12 aggregation levels, scored by WSPL, the weighted scaled pinball loss. In the organisers' Scores and Ranks.xlsx (Uncertainty-Top50 sheets) the winner Everyday Low SPLices (described by Lainder and Wolfinger, IJF 2022) scores 0.15420, GoodsForecast - Nick Mamonov 0.15891, Ouranos 0.15893 and Marisaka Mozz 0.15958. The same public Drive folder as the accuracy track holds the evaluation-period truth, weights and the organisers' R evaluation code, and the uncertainty submissions folder holds the top-50 quantile files. Open task: a test-blind pipeline with WSPL below 0.15420.
targets.success_criterion: Saved quantile forecasts at the nine official levels for all 42,840 series and 28 days d_1942-d_1969 whose WSPL, computed with the organisers' uncertainty evaluation code and weights from the M5 Drive folder, is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than 0.15420 (Everyday Low SPLices, Uncertainty-Top50 (AL) sheet of Scores and Ranks.xlsx at https://github.com/Mcompetitions/M5-methods) and than any lower WSPL the skeptic finds in a credible paper for a test-blind method. LEAK RULE: a frozen, hashed script rerun in a fresh environment containing only sales_train_evaluation.csv, calendar.csv and sell_prices.csv; all tuning on folds ending by d_1941; no pretrained component trained on M5 data.

partial_wins.statement: Reproduce 0.15420 from the winner's released quantile file with the organisers' code, then score strictly below 0.15891 (2nd place) under the full-win leak rule.
Under the full-win leak rule, a mean scaled pinball loss over levels 10-12 strictly below the winner's (L10 0.28385, L11 0.27006, L12 0.26504; mean 0.27298) with overall WSPL no higher than 0.160.

targets.verification_method: As for the accuracy track: hash the released data, rerun the frozen script without the test file, score with the organisers' R code after confirming it reproduces 0.15420 on the winner's submission, and audit for test-tuned constants.
angles: Quantile gradient boosting per level with augmentation over many training windows, then isotonic or conformal recalibration fitted on late training folds.
Coherent quantiles across levels via sample-path simulation from a bottom-level count model.
pitfalls: The extreme quantiles (0.005, 0.995) dominate errors on intermittent bottom-level series; calibrating them on the test days is leakage.
No 2024-2026 literature sweep could be run on 2026-10-30; check for lower published WSPL first.

targets.name: M3 competition (3,003 series): an out-of-sample average sMAPE below the best published 12.37
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (3,003 short series, a few MB)
targets.statement: The M3 competition (Spyros Makridakis and Michele Hibon, IJF 2000) has 3,003 series: 645 yearly (horizon 6), 756 quarterly (8), 1,428 monthly (18) and 174 other (8). The Theta method of Vassilios Assimakopoulos and Konstantinos Nikolopoulos won it with average sMAPE 13.01 (M3 definition, averaged over all series and horizons as in arXiv:1905.10437 equation 5). Later published results, as tabulated in arXiv:1905.10437 Table 14, are DOTM (Fiorucci et al. 2016) 12.90, EXP (Spiliotis et al. 2019) 12.71 and N-BEATS-I+G (Oreshkin, Carpov, Chapados, Bengio, ICLR 2020) 12.37. That is the lowest average this entry could pin to a primary source. Smyl, Bergmeir, Dokumentov, Long, Wibowo and Schmidt (arXiv:2309.13950, 2024) report {L,S}GT with a per-series mean sMAPE of 12.29. That is a different averaging (Theta scores 12.76 under it), and their subsets give about 12.76 under the horizon-weighted average used here. Their LGT holds the best yearly value, 15.18. The best listed values on the other subsets are Quarterly 8.84 and Monthly 13.11 (N-BEATS-I+G) and Other 4.19 (N-BEATS-G). The data with the held-out test values are distributed in Rob Hyndman's Mcomp R package on CRAN. Open task: beat 12.37 without touching the test values.
targets.success_criterion: Saved forecasts for all 3,003 M3 series at the official horizons whose average sMAPE, computed with the M3 definition (200/H times the sum of |y - f| / (y + f)) averaged over all series and horizons as in arXiv:1905.10437 Appendix C.2, against the test values in the CRAN Mcomp package, is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than 12.37 and than any lower credible published M3 average the skeptic finds. LEAK RULE: a frozen, hashed script rerun in a fresh environment that has only the training parts of the series (the $xx test component stripped); all choices fixed on holdouts carved from the training parts; no pretrained component whose documented training data include any M3 series.

partial_wins.statement: Under the full-win leak rule, an average sMAPE (horizon-weighted as in arXiv:1905.10437 equation 5) strictly below 12.71 (EXP) with a method containing no neural network.

Under the full-win leak rule, with all 3,003 series forecast, a subset sMAPE strictly below the best known value for Yearly (15.18, LGT, arXiv:2309.13950 Table 4), Quarterly (8.84), Monthly (13.11) or Other (4.19) (arXiv:1905.10437 Table 14).

targets.verification_method: Install Mcomp from CRAN, export M3 train and test parts, rerun the frozen script with test parts removed, score with an independent sMAPE script, and as a scorer check confirm it gives Theta's 13.01 (horizon-weighted, equation 5) on the original M3 THETA forecasts shipped in Mcomp's M3Forecast object. A fresh forecast::thetaf run is a different implementation and will not reproduce 13.01 exactly.
angles: Combinations of Theta variants, damped ETS and a small global network, with weights chosen on the last training horizon of each series.
pitfalls: M3 full series, including test values, sit in Monash, LOTSA and many other pretraining corpora.
The forecasters.org M3 page sat behind a bot check on 2026-10-30; use the CRAN package.
No 2024-2026 literature sweep could be run on 2026-10-30; check for lower published averages first.

targets.name: Tourism forecasting competition (1,311 series): an out-of-sample average MAPE below N-BEATS-G's 18.47
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (1,311 series, under 1 MB)
targets.statement: The 2010 tourism forecasting competition (George Athanasopoulos, Rob Hyndman, Haiyan Song and Doris Wu, IJF 2011) has 1,311 series: 518 yearly (horizon 4), 427 quarterly (8) and 366 monthly (24). Its Kaggle follow-up (Athanasopoulos and Hyndman 2011) ran in two parts. Team SaliMali (Phil Brierley) won the quarterly/monthly part. Team LeeCBaker (Lee C. Baker; see Baker and Howard 2011) is the best Kaggle team with results on all three subsets: overall MAPE 19.35 in the comparison of arXiv:1905.10437 Table 15, where the best statistical benchmark is ForecastPro at 19.84. N-BEATS-G (Oreshkin, Carpov, Chapados, Bengio, ICLR 2020) reports 18.47, the lowest overall average (horizon-weighted, Table 15 equation 6) this entry could pin to a primary source. The best listed values per subset are Yearly 21.44 (N-BEATS-I+G), Quarterly 14.71 (N-BEATS-G) and Monthly 19.17 (N-BEATS-G). The data with test values are in Peter Ellis's Tcomp R package on CRAN. Open task: beat 18.47 without touching the test values.
targets.success_criterion: Saved forecasts for all 1,311 series at the official horizons whose average MAPE over all series and horizons (as in arXiv:1905.10437 Appendix C.3) against the Tcomp test values is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than 18.47 and than any lower credible published overall tourism MAPE the skeptic finds. LEAK RULE: a frozen, hashed script rerun in a fresh environment holding only the training parts (Tcomp's $xx stripped); all choices fixed on holdouts carved from the training parts; no pretrained component whose documented training data include tourism competition series.

partial_wins.statement: Under the full-win leak rule, an overall MAPE strictly below 19.35 (LeeCBaker, winner of the Kaggle yearly part and the best Kaggle team with results on all three subsets) with a method containing no neural network.
Under the full-win leak rule and with all 1,311 series forecast, a subset MAPE strictly below Yearly 21.44, Quarterly 14.71 or Monthly 19.17.

targets.verification_method: Install Tcomp from CRAN, export train and test parts, rerun the frozen script without the test parts, recompute MAPE independently (horizon-weighted, arXiv:1905.10437 equation 6), and as a scorer check reproduce the published SNaive average 21.25 with forecast::snaive (a fresh forecast::thetaf run should land near, not exactly on, the published Theta 20.88).
angles: The margin over the Kaggle winner is under one MAPE point, and yearly series dominate the series count: damped-trend combinations with shrinkage toward the cross-series mean trend are a cheap start.
pitfalls: Monash's tourism_yearly/quarterly/monthly files and LOTSA-type corpora contain the full series including the test horizon.
The Kaggle competition itself was scored by MASE; this target uses the MAPE comparison of the N-BEATS paper, so do not mix the two.
No 2024-2026 literature sweep could be run on 2026-10-30; check for lower published values first.

targets.name: Genomic Benchmarks (Gresova et al.): beat the best published test accuracy on Human Enhancers Cohn, Human OCR Ensembl or Drosophila Enhancers Stark
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (small CNN/SSM from scratch on sequences of 200-4,700 bp; a fine-tuned 100M+ model needs a GPU for hours)
targets.statement: Genomic Benchmarks (Katarina Gresova, Vlastimil Martinek, David Cechak, Petr Simecek and Panagiotis Alexiou, BMC Genomic Data 2023; github.com/ML-Bioinfo-CEITEC/genomic_benchmarks) is a pip-installable set of nine DNA sequence-classification datasets with fixed train/test splits: human, mouse and Drosophila enhancers, open chromatin, promoters, regulatory classes and two demo tasks. The README still calls HyenaDNA the SOTA, and the experiments page lists HyenaDNA at Cohn 74.2 and OCR 80.9, but later papers have moved these cells. Best published accuracies found on 2026-10-30: Human Enhancers Cohn 0.763 (GENERator 1.2B, Wei Wu and co-authors, arXiv:2502.07272v5 Table S5, 10-fold CV), then DNABERT-2 0.759 on the official split (MxDNA paper, Lifeng Qiao and co-authors, arXiv:2412.13716) and Caduceus-PS 8M 0.749 (GENERator table). Human OCR Ensembl 0.828 (Caduceus-Ph 470k, Yair Schiff and co-authors, arXiv:2403.03234), with Caduceus-PS 0.826 (GENERator table) and DNA-xLSTM-PH 0.826 (arXiv:2411.04165). Drosophila Enhancers Stark 0.827 (Caduceus-Ph as run in GENERator Table S5; the Caduceus, JanusDNA, ConvNova and Omni-DNA papers omit this dataset). Of the six other datasets, five sit at 0.92-0.98 and mouse enhancers (0.87, high variance) is very small. Models from 0.4M to 1.2B parameters land within about two points of each other on Cohn and OCR, which suggests that label noise or the sequence-only signal is the limit, not scale. Protocols differ (official split with seeds versus cross-validation over the training data), so the criterion uses the official test split and takes the highest published number under any protocol as the bar.
targets.success_criterion: Predictions for every sequence of the official test split (genomic_benchmarks package, dataset version 0) of human_enhancers_cohn, human_ocr_ensembl or drosophila_enhancers_stark, from a model trained only on that dataset's official train split (pretrained weights allowed if the corpus is declared; no test labels anywhere), whose test accuracy, recomputed by the skeptic as the mean over at least three training seeds, is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the best published accuracy for that dataset by at least 0.01 absolute. Bars as of 2026-10-30: Cohn 0.763, OCR Ensembl 0.828, Drosophila Stark 0.827, so a win needs at least 0.773, 0.838 or 0.837. The bar must also exceed any later published value found by a novelty check immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: With a model of at most 10M parameters trained from scratch (no pretraining), beat the best published accuracy of any model under 10M parameters on human_enhancers_cohn (0.749, Caduceus-PS 8M, arXiv:2502.07272 Table S5) or human_ocr_ensembl (0.828, Caduceus-Ph 470k, arXiv:2403.03234) by at least 0.01, mean of three seeds on the official test split.
Beat the best published accuracy on any one of the three named datasets by at least 0.005 (mean of three seeds, every seed above the bar) on the official test split.

A reproducible audit of human_enhancers_cohn and human_ocr_ensembl listing every train/test sequence pair at 90% or higher identity (or exact reverse-complement duplicates), with counts, and the accuracy of a stated model on the test split with those sequences removed.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic installs genomic_benchmarks, downloads the dataset's version-0 split, checks that the prediction file covers each test sequence exactly once, computes accuracy per seed, reruns one seed of the attacker's training script, and checks the training data for test sequences (exact and reverse complement). Under an hour for small models.
angles: Ensemble both strands: reverse-complement averaging at inference is free, and Caduceus-PS shows that RC equivariance helps on OCR.
Human Enhancers Cohn shows the narrowest spread across model sizes; model label noise explicitly (noise-robust loss, co-teaching) instead of adding parameters.
Use k-mer and GC/CpG composition features with gradient-boosted trees as a strong cheap baseline and stack them with a CNN.
Cross-domain import (tabular ML): calibrate with a held-out slice of the training split and select by a paired test across seeds, not by one lucky seed.
pitfalls: Several papers (Caduceus, GENERator, JanusDNA) report cross-validation over the training data instead of accuracy on the official test split; numbers across protocols are not strictly comparable, so the criterion fixes the official test split.
The README still names HyenaDNA as SOTA; that is stale, so do not use it as the bar.
Large genomic models pretrained on the human reference saw the test regions unlabelled; this is allowed but must be declared.
drosophila_enhancers_stark is missing from most papers' tables (its bar comes from GENERator's rerun of Caduceus-Ph), so check that any bar quoted is for that dataset.

targets.name: BEACON RNA benchmark: beat the best listed score on an unsaturated task (CRISPR off-target, structure-score imputation, splice sites, APA, RNA switches)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (most tasks are short RNA sequences with 10^3-10^5 training examples; fine-tuning a 100M RNA language model wants a GPU)
targets.statement: BEACON (Yuchen Ren, Zhiyuan Chen, Lifeng Qiao, Hongtai Jing, Yuchen Cai, Sheng Xu, Peng Ye, Xinzhu Ma, Siqi Sun, Hongliang Yan, Dong Yuan, Wanli Ouyang and Xihui Liu, NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks, arXiv:2406.10391; code and data at github.com/terry-r123/RNABenchmark, Apache-2.0) fixes 13 RNA tasks with train/validation/test splits and a common evaluation harness. It benchmarks CNN, ResNet and LSTM baselines and 14 RNA language-model variants (RNA-FM, RNABERT, RNA-MSM, three SpliceBERT, two UTR-LM, four UTRBERT, BEACON-B and BEACON-B512) over three seeds. Several tasks are far from saturated (best values in the main table, x100 where applicable): CRISPR off-target Spearman 11.50 (ResNet; the paper's literature column lists 12.6); structure-score imputation from icSHAPE R^2 42.36 (RNA-FM); splice-site ACC@K 50.55 (SpliceBERT-MS510) on 100-nt inputs (the centre 100 nt of 5,000-nt blocks, BEACON Table 1 and A.2.5) from genes on SpliceAI's test chromosomes 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9; programmable RNA switch R^2 57.72 (SpliceBERT-MS1024); alternative polyadenylation isoform R^2 72.71 (UTRBERT-4mer). This target leaves out BEACON's secondary-structure task (bpRNA), its mean-ribosome-loading task (several models in the table already exceed the literature value and RiNALMo reports a higher R^2 on a similar Optimus test set, so the table bar is not current) and its mRNA-vaccine degradation task.
targets.success_criterion: Predictions for every test example of a BEACON task among CRISPR off-target (CRI-Off), structure-score imputation (SSI), splice-site prediction (SPL), programmable RNA switches (PRS) or APA isoform (APA), from a model trained only on that task's BEACON train split (validation for selection; pretrained weights allowed if declared and free of the task's test labels), whose metric, computed by the skeptic with the BEACON repository's evaluation code as the mean over at least three seeds, is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the bar by at least 1.0 point on the x100 scale (2.0 for CRI-Off). Bars as of 2026-10-30 (max of the main table and the paper's literature column, to be re-read from arXiv:2406.10391v2 before claiming): CRI-Off 12.6, SSI 42.36, SPL 50.55, PRS 57.72, APA 72.71. The bar must also exceed any later published value on the same split found by a novelty check.

partial_wins.statement: Beat the bar by at least 0.5 points on any one of the five named tasks (mean of three seeds, every seed above the bar), computed with BEACON's code.

One frozen recipe (same architecture and training schedule) that beats BEACON-B's published Table 3 score on at least 8 of the 11 BEACON tasks other than secondary structure (SSP) and vaccine degradation (VDP), mean of three seeds.
CRISPR off-target: Spearman STRICTLY HIGHER than 12.6 by any margin with a model of at most 5M parameters, mean of three seeds.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones the BEACON repository, downloads the task data from its linked Google Drive, checks prediction coverage of the test split, runs the repository's metric code, reruns one seed of the attacker's training, and checks that no test sequence (exact, or at 90% or higher identity for SPL and SSI) is in training. Under an hour per task.
angles: CRISPR off-target: the signal is mismatch position and type between guide and site; explicit pairwise alignment features beat a language model fed concatenated sequences in most published comparisons.
Structure-score imputation is masked-value regression; a model that predicts base-pairing probabilities (ViennaRNA) as an extra input channel is a cheap physics prior.
Cross-domain import (recommender systems): for APA isoform usage, treat the two polyA sites as items and learn a pairwise preference, not two independent regressions.
pitfalls: Text extraction of the main table can misalign the 'literature SOTA' row; re-read the table from the PDF before quoting a bar.
SPL uses short windows and ACC@K on BEACON's own subset; it is not SpliceAI's full-transcript top-k accuracy, so the two cannot be compared.
SpliceBERT and other models pretrained on genomes saw the test regions unlabelled; this is allowed but must be declared.
Do not tune on the test split; BEACON provides a validation split for every task.

targets.name: scTab cross-tissue cell-type annotation: beat macro F1 0.8441 on the CELLxGENE donor-held-out test split (164 cell types)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster or a GPU workstation (22.2M cells; the processed train/val/test archive is 164 GB; inference on the 3.45M test cells fits on one GPU)
targets.statement: scTab (Felix Fischer, David S. Fischer, Roman Mukhin, Andrey Isaev, Evan Biederstedt, Alexandra-Chloe Villani and Fabian J. Theis, Nature Communications 15, 6611, 2024; github.com/theislab/scTab) turned the CELLxGENE census (version 2023-05-15) into a fixed annotation benchmark: 22.2 million human 10x cells from 5,052 donors and 56 tissues, 164 Cell Ontology labels, with test and validation holdouts defined by donor (15,240,192 train, 3,500,032 validation, 3,448,832 test cells), so classifiers must generalise to unseen people. A prediction counts as correct if it equals the author's label or is a descendant of it in the Cell Ontology (docs/classification-evaluation-metrics.md). The processed train/val/test archive (164 GB), a 0.5 GB minimal subset and all checkpoints (8.1 GB) are posted. Macro F1 on the donor-held-out test set in the scTab paper: scTab 0.8295 +/- 0.0007 (default size), 0.8323 +/- 0.0010 for the largest scTab variant (16.2M parameters, Fig. 2f), XGBoost 0.8127, MLP 0.7971, optimised logistic regression 0.7848, CIForm 0.766, fine-tuned scGPT 0.749, CellTypist 0.7304 and a linear probe on scGPT embeddings 0.7301; on 31 coarse labels scTab reaches 0.897. The best published value on this split found on 2026-10-30 is later: S. Cultrera di Montesano, D. D'Ascenzo, S. Raghavan, A. P. Amini, P. S. Winter and L. Crawford (Nature Computational Science 6, 243-249, 2026; github.com/microsoft/hce-classification) retrained TabNet with scTab's hyperparameters and standard cross-entropy on the same donor split and evaluation rule and report in-distribution macro F1 0.8441 (mean of four runs: 0.8453, 0.8449, 0.8430, 0.8431; Source Data Fig. 1d), with MLP 0.8213 and linear 0.7972; their hierarchical cross-entropy loss is evaluated only out of distribution. Single-cell foundation models fine-tuned on this split have so far not beaten a tabular nonlinear model, so the bar is a clean, testable claim. Credit: Fischer, Fischer, Mukhin, Isaev, Biederstedt, Villani, Theis; Cultrera di Montesano, D'Ascenzo, Raghavan, Amini, Winter, Crawford.
targets.success_criterion: Cell-type predictions for every cell of the scTab test partition (merlin_cxg_2023_05_15_sf-log1p, test split as released), from a model trained only on the scTab training partition (validation for selection; pretrained single-cell models allowed only if their pretraining corpus is declared, and never with test-cell labels), whose macro F1 over the 164 labels, computed by the skeptic with scTab's evaluation code (docs/classification-evaluation-metrics.md, notebooks/model_evaluation, including its descendant-counts-correct rule), is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than 0.8441 (TabNet with standard cross-entropy, mean of four runs, Cultrera di Montesano et al., Nature Computational Science 6:243-249, 2026, Source Data Fig. 1d) by at least 0.01 (that is, at least 0.8541), as the mean over at least three seeds, and higher than any later published value on this split found by a novelty check immediately before claiming (including the scTab paper's 0.8323, Cultrera di Montesano et al. 2026 and any follow-up from github.com/microsoft/hce-classification, and Richter et al., Nature Machine Intelligence 2025 / bioRxiv 2024.02.16.580624, which uses the scTab data).

partial_wins.statement: Macro F1 STRICTLY HIGHER than 0.8441 by any margin on the scTab test partition, mean of three seeds with every seed above 0.8441.

A frozen single-cell foundation-model embedding (scGPT, Geneformer or another declared model) with at most a two-layer head trained on the scTab train partition that beats XGBoost's 0.8127 macro F1 on the test partition.
On the paper's 31 coarse labels (its published mapping), macro F1 STRICTLY HIGHER than 0.897 by at least 0.01, mean of three seeds.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the released test partition, checks that predictions cover every test cell once with labels from the 164-label vocabulary, computes macro F1 with scTab's code, reruns inference from the attacker's checkpoint, and checks the attacker's data loader reads only the train and validation partitions. Hours on one GPU for inference.
angles: Hierarchical classification over the Cell Ontology (predict the parent, then refine) can lift macro F1 on rare fine subtypes, where most of the error sits.
Cross-domain import (long-tail vision): logit adjustment or class-balanced losses for the many rare cell types, which macro F1 weights equally.
Ensembling scTab with XGBoost, whose errors may differ, is a cheap first experiment, using the released checkpoints.
pitfalls: CELLxGENE-pretrained foundation models may have seen the test donors' expression unlabelled; declare it, and never use their labels.

Label granularity differs across studies (B cell versus naive B cell); the benchmark's mapping is fixed, and remapping labels is not allowed. scTab's metric counts a prediction of a descendant of the author's label as correct; scores computed without that rule are not comparable.
The minimal 0.5 GB subset is for debugging; scores on it are not comparable with the full test partition.
The scTab paper's 0.8323 is no longer the best published value: a plain TabNet retrained in Cultrera di Montesano et al. (2026) already reaches 0.8441 on the same split, so beating 0.8323 is not new.

On 2026-10-30 pklab.med.harvard.edu answered scripted downloads with an Imperva/Incapsula bot-check page. Do not get around it: download in a browser as a human step, or rebuild the split from CELLxGENE census 2023-05-15 (LTS) with notebooks/store_creation/01_create_train_val_test_splits.ipynb and check the 15,240,192 / 3,500,032 / 3,448,832 cell counts.

targets.name: Plants Genomic Benchmark (AgroNT): beat the published R^2 for plant gene expression on held-out gene families or for promoter and terminator strength
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours for promoter and terminator strength (170 bp, tens of thousands of sequences); needs a GPU for gene expression (6 kb inputs, 10^4-10^5 genes x tissues)
targets.statement: The Plants Genomic Benchmark (PGB) was released with AgroNT (Javier Mendoza-Revilla, Evan Trop, ..., Thomas Pierrot and Marie Lopez, InstaDeep; Communications Biology 7, 835, 2024) at huggingface.co/datasets/InstaDeepAI/plant-genomic-benchmark, with fixed splits and the numeric data behind every figure. Values (as R^2, from the paper and its Figures folder): promoter strength (plant STARR-seq of Jores et al. 2021), AgroNT in the maize protoplast system 0.62 (A. thaliana promoters), 0.68 (S. bicolor), 0.71 (Z. mays), and in the tobacco leaf system 0.62, 0.74, 0.75, against the Jores CNN at 0.57-0.73. Terminator strength (Gorjifard et al.): AgroNT 0.65-0.77 against the Gorjifard CNN at 0.64-0.77; they tie in two tobacco cells (0.77 for A. thaliana, 0.76 for Z. mays), and the CNN is higher in one cell (Z. mays terminators in the maize system, 0.67 against 0.65; Figures/Fig3_panelf.txt). Tissue-specific gene expression from promoter-proximal 6 kb (5 kb upstream, 1 kb downstream of the TSS), on test genes from held-out gene families: squared Pearson between predicted and observed across all held-out gene x tissue values, recomputed from Figures/Fig5_panela.txt: A. thaliana 0.617, Z. mays 0.621, S. lycopersicum 0.552, G. max 0.533, O. sativa 0.419. For Z. mays only, AgroNT trained on windows shifted downstream reached up to 0.662 (1 kb upstream, 5 kb downstream; Figures/Fig6_panelb.txt), so that is the Z. mays bar. The paper calls tissue-specific expression an open challenge; AgroNT is a 1B-parameter model, so a smaller model that matches it is also informative.
targets.success_criterion: Predictions for every test example of a PGB task (promoter_strength, terminator_strength, or gene_exp for one species), from a model trained only on that task's PGB train split (validation for selection; pretrained weights allowed if declared; for gene_exp, extra genomic context around the same genes is allowed if declared, but no gene from a test gene family may enter training), whose metric, computed by the skeptic on the PGB test split (R^2 as in the paper; for gene expression, squared Pearson over all test gene x tissue values), is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the best published value for that cell (AgroNT, or the Jores or Gorjifard CNN where higher) by at least 0.02 and higher than any later published value on the same split found by a novelty check. Bars as of 2026-10-30: promoter maize system 0.62 / 0.68 / 0.71 and tobacco 0.62 / 0.74 / 0.75; terminator maize 0.69 / 0.68 (GC) / 0.67 (Z. mays, Gorjifard CNN) and tobacco 0.77 / 0.67 / 0.76; gene expression A. thaliana 0.617, Z. mays 0.662 (Fig. 6b), S. lycopersicum 0.552, G. max 0.533, O. sativa 0.419.

partial_wins.statement: Gene expression: beat AgroNT's O. sativa value (0.419) by at least 0.03 squared Pearson on the PGB test split with a model of at most 100M parameters.
Promoter strength: one recipe that beats AgroNT on all six promoter cells (both systems, three species) at once, mean of three seeds.
Terminator strength: beat both AgroNT and the Gorjifard CNN by at least 0.02 R^2 on any terminator cell.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the task's raw files from the Hugging Face dataset (without running its loading script), checks prediction coverage of the test split, computes R^2 or squared Pearson, compares with the Figures/*.txt values (Fig3_panele, Fig3_panelf, Fig5_panela), reruns one seed, and checks that no test gene family or test sequence is in training. Under an hour for strength tasks.
angles: Promoter strength is short-sequence MPRA regression; DREAM-challenge style CNN/RNN recipes (LegNet, DREAM-RNN) are strong and cheap.
Gene expression: the paper's own window scan (Fig. 6) shows that more downstream context helps; try 3' UTR and gene-body features as well.
Cross-domain import (multi-task learning): predict all tissues jointly with a low-rank output head, since tissue profiles are strongly correlated.
pitfalls: The dataset's loading script is code; read the raw files directly instead of executing it.
Gene-expression test genes are held out by gene family; any training gene from the same family breaks the design.
Gene-expression R^2 is pooled over genes x tissues; a per-tissue mean gives different numbers, so state which one, and compare like with like.
Promoter-strength labels differ by assay system (maize protoplast versus tobacco leaf); do not mix the two bars.

targets.name: SteinLib PUC and I640: a cheaper Steiner tree for one of the 32 unsolved instances (hypercube, code-covering, bipartite, incidence graphs)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days per instance (graphs of 640 to 4,096 vertices and up to 28,512 edges; checking a tree takes milliseconds)
targets.statement: SteinLib (Thorsten Koch, Alexander Martin, Stefan Voss, with Daniel Rehfeldt; ZIB) is the standard library for the Steiner tree problem in graphs. Its PUC set (Rosseti, de Aragao, Ribeiro, Uchoa and Werneck, 2001) holds hypercube (hc), code-covering (cc) and bipartite (bip) graphs, with unit (u) or perturbed (p) edge costs, built to defeat reductions. Re-fetched 2026-10-30, the PUC page (last update 2015-02-11) prints 29 of its 50 values in italics (optimum unknown) and the I640 page italicises i640-311 to -315. The pages are stale. hc9p was proved optimal at 30242 by Shinano, Rehfeldt and Koch (ZIB Report 18-58, CPAIOR 2019, up to 24,576 cores). The same report (Section 5.2, Table 2) lowers hc11p to 119297, with a dual bound of 117,468.85 after runs on up to 43,000 cores. i640-313 was proved optimal at 35535 by Fischetti, Leitner, Ljubic, Luipersbeck, Monaci, Resch, Salvagnin and Sinnl ('Thinning out Steiner trees', Math. Prog. Comp. 2017), so 32 instances remain open. Later work lowered many bars: the DIMACS-11 bounds file (2014-09-12); Fischetti et al. (hc12u 2256, hc11u 1144, bip52u 233, bipa2u 337, cc10-2p 35257, i640-312 35768, i640-315 35720); Braunstein and Muntoni (arXiv:1607.03866: cc11-2p 63405, cc12-2p 121056, bipa2p 35285, hc11p 119456 (beaten by the 119297 of ZIB Report 18-58), and the challenge best 236042 for hc12p by team 'polito'); and Rehfeldt and Koch, 'Implications, conflicts, and reductions for Steiner trees' (Math. Prog. 197, 2023, Table 13: hc10p 59777, dual bounds such as hc10u >= 567.89 and bip52u >= 230.58, every listed PUC instance still unsolved after 54,340 s). The bars below are the minimum over these sources.
targets.success_criterion: A Steiner tree (edge list of the SteinLib .stp graph, edges matched by endpoints) that connects every terminal, is a tree, uses only graph edges, and costs STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the bar for that instance: bip52p 24526, bip52u 233, bip62p 22843, bip62u 219, bipa2p 35285, bipa2u 337, cc10-2p 35257, cc10-2u 342, cc11-2p 63405, cc11-2u 612, cc12-2p 121056, cc12-2u 1172, cc3-10p 12772, cc3-10u 125, cc3-11p 15582, cc3-11u 153, cc3-12p 18826, cc3-12u 185, cc7-3p 56799, cc7-3u 549, cc9-2p 17199, hc9u 292, hc10p 59777, hc10u 575, hc11p 119297, hc11u 1144, hc12p 236042, hc12u 2256, i640-311 35766, i640-312 35768, i640-314 35532, i640-315 35720. The tree must also beat any value in a later publication found at claim time. hc9p (30242) and i640-313 (35535) are proved optimal and cannot be won. A proof of optimality for a listed instance also counts if it can be checked without trusting the solver, for example a VIPR certificate from exact SCIP checked by viprchk. A solver log alone does not count.

partial_wins.statement: A certified lower bound for one listed instance strictly above the best published dual bound for it. That is the bound in Rehfeldt and Koch (Math. Prog. 2023, Table 13), or for hc11p the higher 117,468.85 in ZIB Report 18-58 (Table 2), or any higher bound found at claim time. For unit-cost instances the bound must exceed that dual bound rounded up, e.g. at least 569 for hc10u or 232 for bip52u. It must come with a certificate checked independently, such as an exact-arithmetic branch-and-bound certificate (VIPR) or an exact rational dual of a stated valid relaxation, rebuilt from the .stp file by the checker.

targets.verification_method: Download the instance from steinlib.zib.de and parse the SECTION Graph and Terminals blocks. Rebuild the edge set and check the following: each claimed edge exists, with its cost taken from the file (for parallel edges use the cheapest); the chosen edges form a connected acyclic subgraph containing every terminal; the costs sum exactly in integers. This takes milliseconds. Then re-read the SteinLib page, the DIMACS-11 bounds files, the four papers named above and ZIB Report 18-58, and search the literature after 2023 for lower values before claiming.
angles: The hc and cc graphs are highly symmetric, as hypercubes and Hamming-type graphs. Use automorphisms to seed and repair trees, and orbital fixing in exact search.

For unit-cost instances a tree with k edges has k+1 vertices, so the problem is choosing a small connected vertex set: use node-based models (Fischetti et al.) and set-covering heuristics, which produced most hc/bip improvements.
Combine reduction-based presolve (SCIP-Jack) with long multistart local search (key-path exchange, vertex insertion/elimination) and path relinking; run many seeds in parallel.
pitfalls: SteinLib's own pages have not changed since 2015 and are beaten by later papers on most open PUC and I640 instances (e.g. i640-313: page 35758, proved optimum 35535). Beating the page value is not a win; use the compiled bars and re-check the literature.
hc9p is proved optimal at 30242 (ZIB Report 18-58) and i640-313 at 35535 (Fischetti et al. 2017); neither is a target even though both pages still print them in italics.

hc11p: ZIB Report 18-58 (Section 5.2, Table 2) reports 119,297. Tables quoting 119,456 (Braunstein-Muntoni), 119,492 (DIMACS file, SteinLib page) or 119,854 (Rehfeldt-Koch Table 13 primal column) are stale.
Variants with the same base names (e.g. hc10p2, cc3-12nu, bip52nu) are prize-collecting or node-weighted instances from the DIMACS challenge, not the SPG instances here; several papers tabulate both.
The cc and bip graph files list some edges twice in some formats (|A| = 2|E| in solver tables); count each undirected edge once.

targets.name: Gset Max-Cut: a larger cut than the best published for a non-toroidal Gset graph (G60 14190, G61 5799, G63 27047, G64 8753, G70 9595, ...)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (GPU or many-core local search on graphs of 800 to 10,000 vertices; checking a cut takes milliseconds)
targets.statement: Gset (C. Helmberg and F. Rendl, generated with G. Rinaldi's rudy; hosted by Yinyu Ye at Stanford) has 71 Max-Cut graphs with 800 to 20,000 vertices: random graphs, 'planar' graphs (unions of two planar graphs, not themselves planar) and toroidal grids, with +1 or +-1 weights. It is still the main heuristic Max-Cut benchmark. Its records come from breakout local search (Benlic and Hao 2013), global equilibrium search teams (Shylo, Glover and Sergienko 2015), MOH (Ma and Hao 2017), the large-population island algorithm (Goudet, Goeffon and Hao, Comput. Oper. Res. 168, 2024), population annealing (Khan and Shukla, arXiv:2510.21105, Oct 2025: G63 27047, the first gain over 27045 in about ten years) and Cosm (Zick, Shukla and Marakov, arXiv:2605.30355v4, 11 Oct 2026). Cosm set a new G64 record of 8753 (previous 8752) and reached the best-known 14190 (G60), 5799 (G61) and 9595 (G70). The toroidal graphs are closed. Ikuta, Imai and Yano (RIMS Kokyuroku 1941, 2015, in Japanese) solved every toroidal instance with up to 10,000 vertices to optimality with CPLEX 12.6, all except G77 and G81. Cosm reports Gurobi certificates for G72, G77 and G81 (G81 = 14060). Glass and Feder (arXiv:2606.28478, Jun 2026) obtain planar-relaxation upper bounds matching the known cuts of G11, G48, G49, G57, G65, G72, G77 and G81, and a new matching 4872 for G62; their bounds leave small gaps elsewhere (e.g. G66 6364 vs 6366, G67 6950 vs 6952), but those instances were already solved in 2015. The random and two-planar instances have no published upper bounds near their records.
targets.success_criterion: A +-1 (or 0/1) assignment to the vertices of a Gset graph that is not toroidal (not G11-G13, G32-G34, G48-G50, G57, G62, G65-G67, G72, G77 or G81), whose cut value sum_{ij in E, x_i != x_j} w_ij, recomputed from the Stanford Gset file, is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the highest cut published for that graph at claim time. Bars confirmed on 2026-10-30: G60 14190, G61 5799, G63 27047, G64 8753, G70 9595. For every other instance the bar is the maximum over the BLS, GES, MOH and Goudet et al. 2024 tables, Cosm (arXiv:2605.30355v4), Khan and Shukla (arXiv:2510.21105) and any later publication found by a literature search.
targets.verification_method: Download the graph from https://web.stanford.edu/~yyye/yyye/Gset/ (first line n m; then lines i j w, 1-based). Read the partition (one label per vertex), check it has exactly n entries, and recompute the cut in integers. This takes milliseconds. Reproduce the bar by re-reading the cited tables (Cosm Supplementary Table S5 gives G60/G61/G64/G70/G72/G77/G81), and search for anything newer before claiming.
angles: Physics heuristics dominate the recent records: population annealing with non-local moves (G63), switched collective dynamics (Cosm), parallel tempering. Run them long and wide on a GPU.
Memetic search with large populations and backbone-preserving crossover (Goudet et al. 2024) produced six records; combine it with the strongest one-flip/two-flip tabu as the local improver.
G64 has a very heterogeneous degree distribution (maximum degree 589). Treat hub vertices as a small exact subproblem (enumerate or branch on hubs, optimise the rest by local search).
pitfalls: There is no single maintained Gset leaderboard; best-known values are scattered across papers and some tables lag (e.g. GES tables list G70 at 9591 and MOH at 9544, against 9595). Always compare with the maximum over all sources.

Toroidal instances are solved: CPLEX optimality for all up to 10,000 vertices (Ikuta et al. 2015), Gurobi certificates for G72, G77 and G81 (Cosm), and matching planar bounds (Glass and Feder 2026). A 'record' there is a bug.
G81 and other +-1-weight graphs: the cut is a signed sum, not a count of crossing edges; Ising energy and cut differ by an affine map. Recompute the cut from the edge list.
QPLIB contains some Max-Cut instances under other names; this entry is only for the Gset files.

Ikuta et al. 2015 (RIMS Kokyuroku 1941, pp. 49-56) is in Japanese and tabulates CPLEX lower and upper bounds for all Gset graphs; include it when compiling bars and when checking whether a two-planar instance is already proved optimal.

targets.name: Gset Max-k-Cut (k = 3, 4): a better k-partition than the best published for a Gset graph
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (local search on graphs of 800 to 20,000 vertices; checking a partition takes milliseconds)
targets.statement: Max-k-Cut asks for a partition of the vertices into k parts that maximises the total weight of edges joining different parts; on Gset it is benchmarked mainly for k = 3 and 4. Ma and Hao's multiple search operator heuristic (MOH, Ann. Oper. Res. 248, 2017) tabulated k = 2, 3, 4 and 8 on Gset. In 2026 three works raised several bars: Garvardt, Gruettemeier, Komusiewicz and Morawietz (Parameterized local search for Max c-Cut, Ann. Oper. Res., 2026); Shao and Yang's PEAF (J. Intell. Algorithms Sci. Comput., 2026; arXiv:2607.17158); and Khan, Redding and Shukla's population-dynamics method (PAMC, arXiv:2606.25203). Shao and Wu (East Asian J. Appl. Math. 15, 2025) report a Gurobi value of 16670 for G81 with k = 4. Yaocheng Chen's certificate release (github.com/yaochengchen/gset-maxkcut_by_PdSB, v2.0.0, 15 Oct 2026) publishes explicit partitions with verifiers. It improves G81 k=3 to 16510, G22 k=4 to 18787 and G55 k=3 to 12437 (re-checked for this entry from the Stanford G55 file). It matches G1-G5 at k=3 (15165, 15172, 15173, 15184, 15193) and at k=4 (16804, 16810, 16806, 16814, 16816), G22 k=3 (17169) and G43 (8573, 9377). G55 at k=4, G70 at k = 3, 4 and G48-G50 at k = 3, 4 (6000, PAMC table) have every edge cut, so they are optimal and closed.
targets.success_criterion: A labelling of the vertices of a Gset graph with labels 0..k-1, k in {3, 4}, whose k-cut value sum_{ij in E, label_i != label_j} w_ij, recomputed from the Stanford Gset file, is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the highest published value for that (graph, k) at claim time. Confirmed bars on 2026-10-30 include G81: 16510 (k=3) and 16670 (k=4); G22: 17169 and 18787; G55 k=3: 12437; G43: 8573 and 9377; and G1-G5 as in the statement. For other pairs the bar is the maximum over MOH 2017, Shao and Wu 2025 (EAJAM 15), Garvardt et al. 2026, PEAF (arXiv:2607.17158), PAMC (arXiv:2606.25203), the Chen release and any later publication. Pairs whose bar equals the total positive edge weight (all such edges cut, such as G55 k=4, G70 k=3,4 and G48-G50 k=3,4) cannot be won.

partial_wins.statement: For k = 5 on one of G1-G5, a partition strictly better than the values in Chen's release (17706, 17710, 17705, 17710, 17711), which themselves beat PEAF 2026 Table 21 on G1-G4.

targets.verification_method: Download G < i> from https://web.stanford.edu/~yyye/yyye/Gset/, read one label per vertex (n lines), check that labels lie in 0..k-1, and recompute the k-cut in integers (signed for +-1 graphs such as G81). This takes milliseconds. The Chen release's verify.py is a reference, but write your own checker. Re-read the listed papers and search for newer Max-k-Cut results before claiming.
angles: Start from the best Max-Cut solutions and split each side (k = 4) or use 3-colouring-like tabu search; then run label-move and swap tabu search with long-term memory (MOH-style).

Low-degree sparse graphs (G55, G60, G70, G81) are near the all-edges-cut ceiling: the gap is the number of monochromatic edges. Attack them as a graph-colouring-defect minimisation (minimise monochromatic edges) with colouring heuristics such as TabuCol and partialcol.
Potts-machine and population annealing dynamics (PAMC) carry over directly from Max-Cut.
pitfalls: Many papers report Max-k-Cut on Gset with different k or with balanced-partition constraints (graph k-partitioning). Only unconstrained Max-k-Cut with k = 3 or 4 counts here.
Some instances are trivially optimal when every edge can be cut (bar = total edge weight); check the total before attacking.
Chen's release is recent and partly self-reported against a literature check of 15 Oct 2026; its G81 k=4 value (16666) is below the Gurobi value 16670 in Shao and Wu 2025.

targets.name: QOBLIB node-disjoint Steiner tree packing (multi-layer switchbox routing): a cheaper packing for an instance without a proved optimum
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (multi-layer grid graphs up to 100 x 100 per layer and 5 layers; the 14 best-known instances are at most 70 x 70; the official checker runs in seconds)
targets.statement: QOBLIB's problem class 04 (ZIB-AOPT/QOBLIB, after Hoang and Koch, 'Steiner tree packing revisited', Math. Methods Oper. Res. 76, 2012) asks for node-disjoint Steiner trees connecting several terminal nets in a multi-layer grid graph with holes (switchbox wire routing), minimising total edge cost. There are 190 generated instances (grids up to 100 x 100, 1 to 5 layers), all feasible by construction, and every instance directory also ships the generator's seed solution (sol.txt). On 2026-10-30 the auto-generated best-known table lists 43 instances: 29 marked optimal and 14 marked best known, all from the curated reference. The 14 are stp_s020_l2_t3_h3_rs97531 363, s020_l2_t4_h0_rs24098 189, s020_l3_t4_h0_rs24098 344, s020_l4_t3_h3_rs37235 390, s020_l4_t4_h0_rs24098 228, s020_l5_t3_h3_rs24098 296, s020_l5_t4_h0_rs24098 242, s030_l3_t4_h0_rs24098 304, s030_l4_t4_h0_rs97531 480, s050_l2_t3_h1_rs97531 834, s050_l2_t4_h1_rs97531 756, s050_l3_t6_h2_rs97531 343, s060_l3_t4_h1_rs123 321 and s070_l4_t6_h0_rs97531 375. The other 147 have no table value, but they are not untouched: better packings live in two public places. In issue #2 (opened 2026-02-24) a commenter signing as RoutingEnthusiast posted checker-valid packings for all 190 instances (attachment 'solutons.tar.gz', 2026-03-06, offered for free re-use), including cost 475 for stp_s030_l3_t5_h1_rs24098 whose table row says 'optimal' at 476, cost 374 for stp_s070_l4_t6_h0_rs97531, and values strictly below both pull requests on 52 of the 147. And two open pull requests give checker-validated packings for all 147 and also reach 374 on stp_s070_l4_t6_h0_rs97531: #62 (Marcin Kaminski, 4colors, 2026-09-08) and #88 (Manan Gupta / mnn31, negotiated congestion, 2026-10-09); maintainer Maximilian Schicker has asked both to meet QOBLIB's AI policy before merging. In issue #2 (2026-03-09) and again in issue #55 he called the checker the source of truth and put the '476 optimal' row down to a log-parsing error.
targets.success_criterion: A packing in the QOBLIB 04-steiner solution format ('node1 node2 net_id' per selected edge) for one instance in 04-steiner/instances, accepted by the official checker (04-steiner/check: every net's terminals connected, each net's edges forming a connected subgraph, node-disjoint across nets). Its total cost must be STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the minimum, over every public value for that instance, of: the table value in 04-steiner/solutions/README.md; the cost of the instance's own sol.txt; every value in merged or open QOBLIB submissions and pull requests (today #62 and #88); and every checker-valid packing posted in a QOBLIB issue thread, in particular the solution set attached to issue #2 on 2026-03-06. All of these must be re-read, and the competing solution files re-scored with your own checker, at claim time. An instance whose optimum is proved can only be won by showing that proof wrong.

partial_wins.statement: Certified optimality for one of the 14 'best known' instances, or for one of the 147 with no table value: a packing plus a lower-bound certificate checked independently of the solver (e.g. an exact-arithmetic VIPR certificate for the shipped multicommodity-flow ILP, checked by viprchk), with the model rebuilt from arcs.dat/terms.dat/roots.dat.

A certified optimum for stp_s030_l3_t5_h1_rs24098, whose 'optimal' 476 label is contradicted by checker-accepted packings of cost 475 (posted in issue #2 on 2026-03-06, restated in issue #55, and resubmitted in PR #62): a packing of cost at most 475 confirmed by your own independently written checker, plus a lower-bound certificate checked independently of the solver (e.g. VIPR checked by viprchk) for the model rebuilt from the instance files.

targets.verification_method: Read arcs.dat (undirected 'tail head cost'), terms.dat (terminal, net id) and param.dat. Check that the solution's node sets are pairwise disjoint and that each net's chosen edges exist in arcs.dat and connect all of its terminals. Sum the costs. Run both the official Rust checker and an independently written one. Then re-read the BKV table in 04-steiner/solutions/README.md, the instance's sol.txt, the open pull requests and the packings attached to the QOBLIB issue threads, and re-score each competing file with the same checker. A checker written during vetting accepted the issue-#2 packings for stp_s060_l5_t6_h2_rs37235 at 1402 and stp_s030_l3_t5_h1_rs24098 at 475.
angles: Negotiated-congestion (PathFinder) routing gives feasible packings fast; improve them with rip-up-and-reroute where each net is re-solved as an exact Steiner tree problem (e.g. SCIP-Jack) on the graph minus the other nets' nodes.
The shipped multicommodity-flow ILP plus a strong heuristic incumbent may close the 20x20 instances; use the layered grid symmetry and via costs for cuts.
Large-neighbourhood search: free a window of the grid across all layers and re-solve it exactly with the ILP.
pitfalls: Public better values are not only in pull requests: the packings attached to issue #2 on 2026-03-06 beat the best open-PR value on 52 of the 147 instances and already reach 374 on stp_s070_l4_t6_h0_rs97531. Score them yourself before claiming a first or improved value.
Values in open pull requests are not yet on the auto-generated table; check the PRs, or your 'first value' may already be beaten.
Every instance directory ships the generator's seed solution sol.txt; its cost is a public value too, and for many instances it is worse than the heuristics above, but never assume it.
A row marked 'optimal' may be wrong (stp_s030_l3_t5_h1_rs24098 at 476 versus checker-accepted 475); do not trust status flags without a certificate.
Node-disjointness includes Steiner (non-terminal) nodes; edge-disjoint packings are a different, easier problem.

targets.name: Single-deletion-correcting binary codes of length 12: is the Varshamov-Tenengolts code (316 words) optimal? (bounds 316-320)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days to needs cluster (exact independent-set or ILP search on a 4,096-vertex graph with symmetry; checking a code takes milliseconds)
targets.statement: A binary code of length n corrects one deletion when no two codewords share a subsequence of length n-1. Equivalently, it is an independent set in Sloane's graph 1dc.2^n. The Varshamov-Tenengolts code VT_0(n) has A000016(n+1) words: 30, 52, 94, 172, 316 for n = 8..12. It has long been conjectured optimal (Levenshtein; N. J. A. Sloane, 'On single-deletion-correcting codes', 2002). Optimality is proved for n <= 10 (n = 10 by Brian Borchers in 2005 with Lovasz-theta branch and bound, recorded on Sloane's challenge page). For n = 11, Kazuhisa Nakasho, Manabu Hagiwara, Austin Anderson and J. B. Nation proved that 172 is optimal (arXiv:2309.14736, 2023), by integer linear programming with added linear constraints. For n = 12 their method could not go below the upper bound of 320 from Albert No (Entropy 21:1202, 2019), so the maximum size M(12) lies in 316..320 (their Table 1). Sloane's challenge page (oeis.org/A265032/a265032.html, last updated Dec 2015) still lists 1dc.2048 as 'most wanted' and has no 4,096-vertex graph. No later result was found on 2026-10-30.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) RECORD: an explicit set of at least 317 distinct binary words of length 12 whose single-deletion balls are pairwise disjoint (checked for all pairs), which would show VT_0(12) is not optimal; or (b) CLOSURE: a proof that M(12) = 316 with a certificate checkable without trusting the search. That means a VeriPB proof log for a maximum-independent-set or ILP formulation verified by VeriPB (preferably CakePB), or an exact-arithmetic branch-and-bound certificate (VIPR, checked by viprchk), together with a short argument that the encoding is correct and that any symmetry breaking is valid. Direction: (a) max size, (b) upper bound equal to 316.

partial_wins.statement: A certified upper bound of 319, 318 or 317 on M(12), below No's 320. This means an exact rational certificate of an LP/ILP relaxation or a verified proof log as in (b), rebuilt by the checker from the definition.

targets.verification_method: For a code: compute every word's deletion ball (the set of length-11 subsequences) and check that the balls are pairwise disjoint. Rebuild the 1dc-type graph on 4,096 words from the definition and confirm independence. For a bound: run VeriPB/CakePB on the proof log, or viprchk on the VIPR file. Rebuild the model from the definition, not from the claimant's files. Before claiming, re-read arXiv:2309.14736 (and later versions) and search for later work on single-deletion code bounds.
angles: Use the symmetries of the deletion metric (reversal and complement, which generate a group of order 4) to break symmetry, and split the words by weight and by number of runs. Deletion balls of words with r runs have size r, which gives strong weighted clique-cover constraints.

Nakasho et al. needed extra valid inequalities to close n = 11; derive families of clique inequalities from shared subsequences (each length-11 string's preimage set is a clique) and add Lovasz-theta or SDP cuts.
A closure via proof-logged search (Glasgow solver with VeriPB) on a reduced, symmetry-broken model is more checkable than a commercial-solver log.
pitfalls: Sloane's challenge page is stale: it still lists 1dc.2048 (n = 11) as open, but 172 was proved optimal in arXiv:2309.14736.

Codes correcting one insertion are the same as single-deletion codes, but codes correcting a deletion OR a substitution, multiple deletions (see the bank's multiple-deletion entry) or deletions over larger alphabets are different problems.
A Gurobi or CPLEX 'optimal' log is not a certificate; the closure needs an independently checked proof.

targets.name: Binary codes correcting one adjacent transposition at length 12: first unknown terms of OEIS A057608 and A057657 (Sloane's 1tc/1et graphs)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (exact maximum independent set on 13 weight components with up to 924 vertices each; checking takes milliseconds)
targets.statement: A binary code of length n corrects one adjacent transposition when the sets {x, and x with one pair of adjacent unequal bits swapped} of distinct codewords are disjoint. A057657 also allows swapping the end bits ('end-around' transposition). Transpositions preserve weight, so the conflict graph (Sloane's 1tc.2^n and 1et.2^n graphs) splits into n+1 components by Hamming weight. The maximum code size is the sum of the per-weight maxima, given in triangles A085684 (1tc) and A085685 (1et). OEIS A057608 gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 12, 20, 38, 63, 110, 196, 352 for n = 0..11; n = 11 was proved by Brian Borchers in 2009 with SDP branch and bound, after two weeks on the middle components. A057657 gives ..., 100, 171, 316 for n = 9, 10, 11 (Butenko, Pardalos, Sergienko, Shylo and Stetsyuk for the lower bounds; Borchers 2005 and 2009 for optimality, the latter with Gurobi). The weight-2 case without end-around is solved for all n (Gomez Soto, Leanos, Rios-Castro and Rivera 2018, OEIS A085680; 15 at n = 12). The end-around weight-2 component is a different graph (A085685 T(11,2) = 11 against A085684 T(11,2) = 13). Gomez Soto et al. state that A057608 is known only for n <= 11. The OEIS entries (A057608 last edited 2018, A057657 Jan 2026) list no term for n = 12. A checker written for this entry reproduces A057608, A057657 and rows 0-8 of both triangles. At n = 12 the components have C(12,k) vertices: 220, 495, 792 and 924 for k = 3..6.
targets.success_criterion: For A057608 (1tc) or A057657 (1et) at n = 12: for every weight k = 0..12, an explicit code of length 12 and weight k plus a certificate that no larger one exists. The certificate is a VeriPB proof log of a maximum-independent-set/clique run verified by VeriPB (preferably CakePB), or an exact-arithmetic ILP certificate (VIPR, checked by viprchk), each for a model rebuilt from the definition. Together these give the exact value a(12), the first unknown term. Components of weight 0, 1, 11 and 12 are trivial. For A057608 the weight-2 and weight-10 components follow from A085680 (15 each). For A057657 the end-around weight-2 and weight-10 components are not covered by A085680 and need their own code and certificate (they are small, 66 vertices).

partial_wins.statement: The exact value, with an explicit code and a certificate as above, of T(12,k) in A085684 or A085685 for one weight k with 3 <= k <= 9.
The exact value, with code and certificate, of the central component T(12,6) of either triangle: 924 words of weight 6, the hardest component.

targets.verification_method: Rebuild the conflict graph from the definition: two words conflict iff their transposition balls intersect, with the end-around swap of positions 1 and n included only for A057657. Check that the code is an independent set and count it. Run VeriPB/CakePB or viprchk on the certificates. Cross-check the builder by reproducing A085684/A085685 rows for n <= 10 and Sloane's 1tc/1et files for n <= 11. Then re-read the OEIS entries and search for later results.
angles: Reversal (and complement, which maps weight k to 12-k) are symmetries; break them with orbital branching, and use weight k vs 12-k equality so only k <= 6 needs solving.
Modern exact clique/MIS solvers with proof logging (Glasgow subgraph solver with VeriPB) are much faster than the 2009 SDP code that needed two weeks for the n = 11 middle components.
Seed lower bounds with structured constructions (cyclic-shift orbits, run-length classes) and local search, then prove optimality with the exact solver given the incumbent.
pitfalls: Adjacent transposition only: swapping non-adjacent bits, or the deletion metric, gives different graphs. Build the graph from the definition and match it against Sloane's 1tc/1et files for n <= 11.
A085684's data currently stop at row 10 even though a(11) = 352 is known; row 11 per weight is on Sloane's page (1,4,13,32,55,71,71,55,32,13,4,1). Re-deriving it is not new.
A solver log is not a certificate; each component needs its own checkable bound.

targets.name: SWOT KaRIn noise-filtering data challenge 2022a: beat the leaderboard's best vorticity or current RMSE on cycle 13
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (dc_inputs.tar.gz is 1.69 GB: 270 passes of cycle 13)
targets.statement: Ocean data challenge 2022a (Datlas, IMT Atlantique and CLS, CMEMS SLICING project; experiment design by Anaelle Treboutte and Pierre Prandi, CLS) asks for filters that remove spatially uncorrelated KaRIn instrumental noise from simulated SWOT swath sea-surface height. Ground truth: the eNATL60 NEMO simulation. Evaluation inputs (ssh_karin) and noise-free targets (ssh_true) cover one orbital cycle (cycle 13, 270 passes); targets may be used only for evaluation, never for filtering or tuning. Scores: mean RMSE over the whole domain, in coastal areas ( < 200 km) and in offshore low- and high-variability regions, plus the wavelength where SNR = 1, each for SSH, geostrophic current and relative vorticity (derivatives amplify residual noise). README leaderboard (unchanged since Dec 2022, re-checked 2026-10-30). CNN (U-Net of Treboutte, Carli, Ballarotta, Carpentier, Faugere and Dibarboure, Remote Sensing 15, 2183, 2023; CLS & Datlas notebook): SSH global RMSE 0.002 m, lambda(SNR1) 10.5 km; geostrophic current global 0.055 m/s, coastal 0.068 m/s, lambda 9.4 km; relative vorticity global 0.637, coastal 0.881, offshore low/high variability 0.475/0.303, lambda 15.4 km. GOMEZ_V2 (spatially variable Gomez-Navarro-type filter): current coastal 0.065 (best in that column), vorticity global 0.65. Baselines: NO FILTER, MEDIAN, GOMEZ (Gomez-Navarro et al. 2018, 2020). Open task: a filter that beats the best leaderboard value on a headline score without losing elsewhere.
targets.success_criterion: Filtered SSH files for all 270 cycle-13 passes, evaluated with the repository's own unmodified benchmark code (src/benchmark.py as in notebook/demo_benchmark_CNN.ipynb). The filter must be produced without using ssh_true, or any eNATL60 (or derived) SSH for the cycle-13 dates, in any fitting, tuning, checkpoint or selection step. Every tunable parameter is fixed by a procedure in the released code that reads only ssh_karin or independent training data the claimant generates or downloads, and that data must not cover the cycle-13 period. The results must give a relative-vorticity mu(RMSE global) of at most 0.636, strictly below the CNN's printed 0.637 by at least one unit in the last printed digit. In the same evaluation, SSH lambda(SNR1) must be at most 10.5 km and geostrophic-current mu(RMSE global) at most 0.055 m/s.
