Re-fetch the README leaderboard immediately before claiming and compare with its best row for each column (direction: min for all three). The result must also beat the best value for the same metric reported by any paper that scores all 270 cycle-13 passes with this repository's benchmark. Treboutte et al. 2023 was checked explicitly. Cutolo et al. 2025 (arXiv 2503.21303) uses a left/right-swath split and its own U-Net baseline, so it is not comparable, but re-check it and any newer paper for tabulated benchmark scores.

partial_wins.statement: Geostrophic-current mu(RMSE coastal) of at most 0.064 m/s (below the best printed 0.065, GOMEZ_V2), with geostrophic-current mu(RMSE global) of at most 0.056.

A filter using no training data at all other than the cycle-13 ssh_karin inputs (for example a self-supervised or analytic filter) that is at least as good as GOMEZ_V2 on all four relative-vorticity RMSE columns (0.65, 0.882, 0.504, 0.321) and strictly better on at least one.
Relative-vorticity lambda(SNR1) of at most 15.3 km (below the CNN's 15.4) with relative-vorticity mu(RMSE global) of at most 0.65.

targets.verification_method: The skeptic downloads dc_inputs.tar.gz from the MEOM THREDDS server. It gives the claimed filter a copy of the 270 input files with the ssh_true variable removed, and runs the filter end to end from a clean environment, including any training or parameter selection. It then runs the repository's benchmark code on the outputs against the original files and compares the printed table with the README leaderboard. This takes under an hour on CPU for analytic filters, plus any training time.
angles: Self-supervised blind-spot denoising (Noise2Self / Noise2Void): the target noise is spatially uncorrelated, which is exactly what these methods assume, and they need no clean targets.
Physics prior: penalise the Laplacian of the filtered SSH (vorticity) in a variational filter, with a regularisation weight that varies with local variance (the GOMEZ_V2 idea).
Cross-domain import (image processing): BM3D or non-local means tuned only on noise statistics estimated from the inputs themselves.
pitfalls: Only the cycle-13 evaluation archive is public. The THREDDS folder holds just dc_inputs.tar.gz (1.69 GB, 270 passes with ssh_karin and ssh_true), and the README's 'Extra training data' section is empty. The CNN was trained on 2009 eNATL60-BLB002 swaths that are not posted (docs/setup_CNN.md). Plan on self-supervised or analytic filters, or on training data you simulate yourself (for example with CNES swot_simulator) from fields that do not overlap the cycle-13 dates.

ssh_true is eNATL60 SSH on the swath. Any eNATL60 or derived SSH covering the cycle-13 dates is the target in disguise and may not be used. Cycle-13 ssh_true may not pick hyperparameters, checkpoints or the stopping epoch either.

Leaderboard RMSE values are printed to 3 decimals (SSH 0.002 m ties several methods; GOMEZ_V2 is printed to 2 or 4 decimals in places), so SSH RMSE cannot separate entries. Use the vorticity and current columns.

The leaderboard has not changed since Dec 2022 (last commit Sep 2023, a data-link change). A search on 2026-10-30 found one later paper using the cycle-13 data: Cutolo, Granero-Belinchon, Thiraux, Wang and Fablet (SIMPGEN, arXiv 2503.21303, 2025). It trains on the left swaths, tests on the right swaths against its own U-Net, and reports RMSE only by scale in figures. No paper with full benchmark-table scores below the leaderboard was found. Search again before claiming.
The 2022a leaderboard is separate from the 2024b SWOT denoising challenge (real SWOT data, no numeric leaderboard) and from the SSH mapping challenges (2020a, 2021a), which are existing bank entries.

targets.name: CAMELYON16 lymph-node metastasis detection: beat the best lesion-level FROC on the public 129-slide test reference
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (or one GPU workstation for days; about 750 GB of whole-slide images: 220.7 GB test, 532 GB training, on the public camelyon-dataset S3 bucket)
targets.statement: CAMELYON16 (Babak Ehteshami Bejnordi, Mitko Veta, Jeroen van der Laak, Geert Litjens and colleagues, JAMA 2017; Computational Pathology Group, Radboud UMC, with UMC Utrecht) asks for detection of breast-cancer metastases in H&E whole-slide images of sentinel lymph nodes. The full data set is open under CC0 on the AWS Registry of Open Data (s3://camelyon-dataset/CAMELYON16, no account needed): 270 training slides (111 tumour, 159 normal) and 129 test slides (49 tumour, 80 normal; test_049 was removed as a duplicate). The bucket holds test images, test masks, lesion XML annotations, evaluation/reference.csv (labels for all 399 slides) and the organisers' evaluate.py, so both official metrics can be recomputed offline: the lesion-level FROC score (mean sensitivity at 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2, 4 and 8 false positives per slide; isolated tumour cells excluded) and the slide-level ROC AUC. The challenge results page (closed November 2016) is topped on both boards by Harvard Medical School and MIT, Method 2 (updated) (Dayong Wang, Aditya Khosla, Rishab Gargeya, Humayun Irshad, Andrew Beck): AUC 0.9935 and FROC 0.8074. After the challenge, Liu et al. (Google, arXiv:1703.02442, Table 1) report a test FROC of 0.885 for an ensemble of three models (95% CI 0.843 to 0.922), with 92.4% sensitivity at 8 FP and AUC 0.977. Both the leaderboard values and Liu et al.'s were computed on the original 130 test slides. Slide-level AUC is close to saturation; the lesion-level FROC is the less saturated number.
targets.success_criterion: A detection CSV (p, x, y at level 0) for each of the 129 official test slides and a slide-level probability per slide, from a model trained only on the 270 CAMELYON16 training slides and their annotations (public pretrained backbones allowed if declared; pathology foundation models and any CAMELYON17 data are a separate comparison class, reported separately), frozen before any test scoring. The win is a FROC score, computed by the skeptic with the official CAMELYON16/evaluation/evaluate.py against the public test masks and reference.csv, that is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) by at least 0.005 than the maximum of three values. The first is 0.8074 (challenge leaderboard, re-fetched live immediately before claiming). The second is 0.885 (Liu et al., arXiv:1703.02442, Table 1, ensemble-of-3, on 130 test slides). The third is any other FROC on the official CAMELYON16 test set found by the NOVELTY check. The win threshold is therefore at least 0.890.

partial_wins.statement: FROC strictly above the maximum of the challenge leaderboard's 0.8074 and any FROC on the official test set found by the NOVELTY check for a model meeting the same budget (trained in under 48 hours on one GPU, with released code and weights), on the 129-slide test reference, computed with the official evaluate.py.

Slide-level ROC AUC strictly above 0.9935 on the 129 test slides (labels from evaluation/reference.csv), from the same frozen model and comparison class, and above any same-class AUC on the official test set found by the NOVELTY check. Report it with a 1,000-sample bootstrap 95% interval.

Using only slide-level labels for training (no lesion annotations), a slide-level AUC strictly above every weakly-supervised (multiple-instance learning) AUC on the official test set found by the NOVELTY check for the same feature-extractor class (ImageNet-pretrained or pathology foundation model, stated).

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads CAMELYON16/images/test_*.tif, masks, annotations and evaluation/ from s3://camelyon-dataset with --no-sign-request, checks MD5s against checksums.md5, runs the official evaluate.py on the claimed detection CSVs for all 129 slides, and computes slide AUC from the claimed probabilities against reference.csv. Audits training code for any read of test files before scoring and re-runs inference from released weights on a sample of test slides. Hours for scoring, days for re-inference.
angles: Hard-negative mining on normal tissue that mimics tumour (germinal centres, histiocytes) is what lifted post-challenge FROC; budget training time for it.
Multi-resolution context: pair a 40x patch classifier with a lower-magnification context branch, then turn the heatmap into detections with non-maximum suppression tuned on held-out training slides.
Cross-domain import (astronomy source extraction): treat the probability heatmap like a sky image and use blob detection with a local-background model to place detection points.
pitfalls: The leaderboard was computed on 130 test slides; test_049 has since been removed as a duplicate, so the reference now has 129. State the count and recompute any baseline you compare against on 129.

Some published FROCs also exclude test_114 (e.g. the evaluation script of NCRF, Li and Ping 2018), but test_114 is in reference.csv as a macro-metastasis slide. Compare like with like, and score claims on all 129 slides.
Test annotations, masks and labels are public: choosing thresholds, epochs or the NMS radius by test FROC is leakage. Use a split of the training slides.
PatchCamelyon (existing bank entry pcam-patchcamelyon-from-scratch-accuracy) is built from CAMELYON16 slides; using PCam test patches for training leaks test slides.
Twenty training tumour slides are not exhaustively annotated (README list); treating their unannotated area as negative teaches false negatives.
Pathology foundation models may have been pretrained on CAMELYON16 test slides; such claims must be flagged and reported in their own class.
evaluate.py depends on ASAP's multiresolutionimageinterface and reads the masks at a fixed level; detections must be in level-0 coordinates.
A research benchmark on curated slides; a higher FROC is not evidence of clinical readiness and must not be framed as diagnostic advice.

targets.name: MoNuSeg 2018 multi-organ nucleus segmentation: beat the best published AJI (0.7063; challenge best 0.6907) on the public 14-image test set
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (30 training and 14 test 1000x1000 H&E tiles; a small GPU or Apple MPS helps)
targets.statement: MoNuSeg (Multi-Organ Nucleus Segmentation, MICCAI 2018; Neeraj Kumar, Ruchika Verma, Amit Sethi and colleagues; post-challenge paper Kumar et al., IEEE TMI 2020) asks for instance segmentation of nuclei in H&E tiles from TCGA covering several organs. The training set has 30 images with about 22,000 annotated nuclear boundaries; the test set (with about 7,000 annotated nuclei, including organs absent from training) is now public with annotations on the challenge Data page under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Ranking is the mean Aggregated Jaccard Index (AJI, Algorithm 1 of Kumar et al. 2017) over the 14 test images; challenge rules exclude external training data. The final results page is topped by CUHK&IMSIGHT at 0.6907, then BUPT.J.LI 0.6868, pku.hzq 0.6852, Yunzhi 0.6788 and Navid Alemi 0.6779. The best published AJI on the official 14-image test set from a model without external annotated data that we found is 0.7063: a ResUNet-101 with instance-aware self-supervised pretraining on MoNuSeg images (Xinpeng Xie, Jiawei Chen, Yuexiang Li, Linlin Shen, Kai Ma and Yefeng Zheng, MICCAI 2020, arXiv:2007.11186), above all five leaders. Results from models trained on pooled external annotated sets (e.g. 0.8042 from MoNuSeg+CPM-17+CoNSeP training, Furkan Atlan and Emrah Hancer, Turk. J. Elec. Eng. & Comp. Sci. 2025) are a different class. The organisers' evaluation code (AJI per image, mask generation from XML) is at github.com/ruchikaverma-iitg/MoNuSeg. Many later papers report Dice or IoU on MoNuSeg, AJI from cross-validation on the 30 training images, or AJI on the older 16/14 split of Kumar et al. 2017, which are different benchmarks.
targets.success_criterion: Instance label maps (one unique positive integer per nucleus, 0 background) for all 14 official MoNuSeg 2018 test images, from a model trained only on the 30 official training images (public ImageNet-pretrained backbones allowed if declared; self-supervised pretraining allowed on the 30 training images only; no other annotated nuclei data; pathology foundation models reported as a separate class), frozen before any test scoring, whose mean AJI over the 14 images, computed by the skeptic with the organisers' AJI code against masks generated from the released test XML annotations, is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max), by at least 0.005, than every AJI on the official 14-image 2018 test set from a model without external annotated nuclei data: the results page (0.6907, re-fetched live immediately before claiming), Xie et al. 2020 (0.7063, arXiv:2007.11186), and any higher such value found by the NOVELTY check. On 2026-10-30 this means a mean of at least 0.7113 over 3 training seeds. Values from models trained with external annotated data or pathology foundation models do not set this bar and are reported separately.

partial_wins.statement: Mean AJI strictly above 0.6868 (the second-place entry) on the 14 test images, 3-seed mean, from a model under 5M parameters trained on a laptop in under 6 hours.

A reproducible scoring note: AJI of a released baseline (e.g. HoVer-Net or Cellpose retrained on the 30 training images) on the official test set, computed with both the organisers' MATLAB code and a Python port, agreeing to 1e-4, with the port released.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the training and test data from the MoNuSeg Data page, generates instance masks from the test XML with the organisers' code, scores the claimed label maps with Aggregated_Jaccard_Index_v1_0.m (or a port checked against it), retrains one seed from the released script, and audits that no test file is read before final scoring. Minutes for scoring, hours for a retrain.
angles: Boundary-aware targets (distance maps or horizontal/vertical gradient maps as in HoVer-Net) separate touching nuclei, which is what AJI punishes most.
Stain augmentation from the training tiles only, since the test organs and sites differ.
Cross-domain import (cell biology): Cellpose-style flow fields trained only on the 30 tiles.
pitfalls: AJI, AJI+ and PQ differ; Kumar et al.'s 2017 16/14 split (used by HoVer-Net) is not the 2018 challenge test set. Compare only mean AJI on the 14 official test images.
Test annotations are public: picking epochs or post-processing thresholds by test AJI is leakage.
Masks must be generated from the XML the same way the organisers did (he_to_binary_mask_final.m); a different rasterisation of overlapping nuclei shifts AJI.
External annotated nuclei sets (Kumar, CPM, PanNuke, Lizard, MoNuSAC) overlap TCGA sources and break the challenge's no-external-data rule; report separately.
A research benchmark; it says nothing about clinical diagnosis.

targets.name: MoNuSAC 2020 nucleus segmentation and classification: beat TIA-Lab's challenge-best PQ 0.6119 on the public test set
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (a few GB of H&E regions; a small GPU or Apple MPS helps)
targets.statement: MoNuSAC 2020 (Multi-organ Nuclei Segmentation And Classification, ISBI 2020; Ruchika Verma, Neeraj Kumar, Amit Sethi and colleagues; post-challenge paper Verma et al., IEEE TMI 2021) asks for instance segmentation and classification of four nucleus types (epithelial, lymphocyte, neutrophil, macrophage) in H&E regions from several organs and hospitals. The testing data set, images and annotations, is now public on the challenge Data page (Google Drive), together with organiser code for mask generation and the PQ metric (github.com/ruchikaverma-iitg/MoNuSAC, PQ_metric.ipynb). The ranking metric is the weighted average of class-specific Panoptic Quality (definition in section V of the challenge document). The final leaderboard is topped by TIA-Lab (Warwick) at 0.6119, then SJTU_426 0.5793, IVG 0.5084, LSL000UD 0.4969 and Sharif HooshPardaz 0.4808; a post-challenge leaderboard lists six more teams (Amirreza Mahbod, IIAI, Sharif_HooshPardaz, Trnal, Cp&ig, Onward) without scores on the page. The gap between first and second place suggests the task is far from saturated.
targets.success_criterion: Per-class instance masks for every official MoNuSAC 2020 test image, from a model trained only on the official training set (public ImageNet-pretrained backbones allowed if declared; no other annotated nuclei data; pathology foundation models reported as a separate class), frozen before any test scoring. The masks' final average PQ is computed by the skeptic with the organisers' PQ_metric code, against masks generated from the released test XML annotations, with ambiguous regions excluded as the organisers do. It must be STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max), by at least 0.005 and as the mean over 3 training seeds, than two values. The first is 0.6119 (TIA-Lab, final leaderboard on the results page, re-fetched live immediately before claiming). The second is any weighted-average PQ on the official test set, computed with the organisers' metric, found by the NOVELTY check. That includes any scored post-challenge entry reported in Verma et al., IEEE TMI 2021.

partial_wins.statement: Final average PQ strictly above 0.5793 (second place) on the official test set, 3-seed mean, with a model trained on a laptop in under 8 hours.

Final average PQ strictly above 0.6119 (the challenge-best TIA-Lab entry) on the official test set, computed with the organisers' PQ_metric code, 3-seed mean, without the NOVELTY margin, with released code and weights.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the MoNuSAC test data and annotations from the Data page, generates n-ary masks with the organisers' notebook, scores the claimed masks with PQ_metric.ipynb logic, retrains one seed, and audits that no test file is read before final scoring. Minutes for scoring, hours for a retrain.
angles: The rare classes dominate the weighted average; class-balanced sampling and copy-paste augmentation of rare nuclei.
Cross-domain import (panoptic segmentation for street scenes): Mask2Former-style query heads with a nucleus-scale pixel decoder.
pitfalls: The colour-coded ground-truth images on the Data page are illustrative only (the page says so); generate masks from the XML annotations.
Test annotations are public: tuning on the test set is leakage.
Many papers evaluate MoNuSAC on their own splits or with unweighted PQ; only the official test set and the organisers' PQ compare.
A research benchmark; not clinical diagnosis.

targets.name: PanNuke pan-cancer nucleus segmentation and classification: beat the best published three-split mPQ (0.5123, PromptNucSeg-H)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (three 700 MB folds of 256x256 patches; one GPU for days is more realistic for transformer models)
targets.statement: PanNuke (Jevgenij Gamper, Navid Alemi Koohbanani, Ksenija Benes, Simon Graham, Mostafa Jahanifar, Syed Ali Khurram, Ayesha Azam, Katherine Hewitt, Nasir Rajpoot; ECDP 2019 and arXiv:2003.10778) is a semi-automatically generated pan-cancer set of H&E patches from 19 tissue types with five nucleus classes (neoplastic, inflammatory, connective, dead, epithelial). It is released by Warwick TIA as three folds (fold_1.zip etc., direct download, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) with three fixed train/validation/test splits, and scored with the official PanNuke-metrics code: mPQ (PQ averaged over classes and tissues) and bPQ (all nuclei as one class, averaged over tissues), averaged over the three splits. The extension paper's HoVer-Net baseline is about 0.46 mPQ; CellViT (Fabian Hörst, Jens Kleesiek and colleagues, Medical Image Analysis 2024) reports 0.4980 mPQ; LKCell (Ziwei Cui, Jingfeng Yao, Lunbin Zeng, Juan Yang, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang; arXiv:2407.18054) reports 0.5080 and CellVTA (arXiv:2504.00784) 0.506. PromptNucSeg (Zhongyi Shui, Yunlong Zhang, Kai Yao, Chenglu Zhu, Sunyi Zheng, Jingxiong Li, Honglin Li, Yuxuan Sun, Ruizhe Guo, Lin Yang; arXiv:2311.15939v4, Table 1), a prompt-driven SAM-based method, reports 0.5123 mPQ and 0.6924 bPQ for PromptNucSeg-H on the same three splits, the best value we could pin. Our 2024-2026 literature sweep was limited, so the NOVELTY check carries weight here.
targets.success_criterion: Predictions (instance maps and class maps in the PanNuke-metrics format) on the test fold of each of the three official splits (split 1: train fold 1, validate fold 2, test fold 3; split 2: train 2, validate 1, test 3; split 3: train 3, validate 2, test 1, as on the Warwick page). Each split's model is trained only on its train fold and selected only on its validation fold. Public pretrained backbones are allowed if declared; no other annotated nuclei data. The mPQ averaged over the three splits, computed by the skeptic with TissueImageAnalytics/PanNuke-metrics, must be STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max), by at least 0.005, than two values. The first is 0.5123 (PromptNucSeg-H, arXiv:2311.15939v4 Table 1, re-checked live immediately before claiming). The second is every three-split PanNuke mPQ found by the NOVELTY check (LKCell's 0.5080, CellVTA's 0.506 and later work included). bPQ must not be below 0.6924 or the best published bPQ found, whichever is higher. Where a released PromptNucSeg or LKCell checkpoint exists, the skeptic also scores it with the same code, and the claim must beat that reproduced value too.

partial_wins.statement: Three-split mPQ strictly above 0.4980 (CellViT-SAM-H as reported by Hörst et al. 2024) with a model under 50M parameters, released code and weights, computed with the official metrics code.

A model under 5M parameters trained on a laptop whose three-split mPQ and bPQ, computed with the official metrics code, are strictly above 0.4629 and 0.6596 (HoVer-Net as tabulated from the PanNuke extension paper).

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the three folds from the Warwick PanNuke page, runs the released inference on each split's test fold, and scores with PanNuke-metrics run.py; checks fold assignments against the page's three split definitions and audits that test folds are never read in training or selection. Hours.
angles: The dead-cell class is tiny and drags mPQ down; targeted oversampling and loss reweighting for it.
Tissue-conditioned heads: the metric averages over 19 tissues, so per-tissue calibration helps rare tissues.
pitfalls: Some papers report a single split or the best split; only the three-split mean with the official folds compares.

Published numbers for the same model differ by evaluation protocol (CellVTA, arXiv:2504.00784, reports CellViT SAM-L at 0.492 and HoVer-Net at 0.443, against 0.4980 and 0.4629 elsewhere). Score the claim and any reproducible baseline with the same official code before comparing.
Labels are semi-automatic and noisy; tiny mPQ gains can be seed noise, so report seed variance.
Pathology foundation models are often pretrained on TCGA, the same source as PanNuke images; declare such backbones.
Selecting on the test fold is leakage; each split has its own validation fold, and fold 3 is the test fold of two splits.

targets.name: 0-1 multidimensional knapsack: beat a best known value on an OR-Library 30.500 (Chu-Beasley) or MK_GK (Glover-Kochenberger) instance
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (a 500 x 30 instance file is about 70 KB; record runs used 2 h per seed with a MIP solver inside an evolutionary loop)
targets.statement: The 0-1 multidimensional knapsack problem (MKP): pick a subset of n items maximising total profit subject to m capacity constraints. The standard benchmark is Chu and Beasley's OR-Library set (J. Heuristics 4, 1998; files mknapcb1..9, 270 instances). Xu, Li and Yin (FEPSS; arXiv 2210.03918v3, May 2024; Applied Soft Computing 164, 111934, 2024) report that the small classes are proven optimal but (250,30), (500,10) and (500,30) are still open. The hardest class, mknapcb9 = 30.500 (n=500, m=30; instances 500-30-0..29 in file order, tightness 0.25/0.50/0.75 in blocks of ten), carries best known values built up by Vasquez and Vimont, Boussier et al., Mansini and Speranza (CORAL), Lai, Hao, Glover and Lu (TPTEA, 2018) and FEPSS, which raised 500-30-3, -4, -11 and -18. The best published values (maximum of the BK column and every fbest column in Tables 2 and 5 of arXiv 2210.03918v3) for 500-30-0..29 are: 116056 114810 116741 115370 116553 115741 114181 114403 115419 117116 | 218104 214660 215978 217910 215689 215919 215907 216542 217364 214739 | 301675 300055 305087 302032 304462 297012 303364 307007 303199 300596. The 11 MK_GK instances (n up to 2500, m up to 100; hosted by Jin-Kao Hao's group) have best published values gk01..gk11: 3766 3958 5656 5767 7561 7680 19221 18808 58091 57296 95239 (FEPSS raised gk07-gk11). No 30.500 instance is reported proven optimal.
targets.success_criterion: A 0/1 vector x of length 500 for one instance 500-30-j (the j-th of the 30 problems in https://people.brunel.ac.uk/~mastjjb/jeb/orlib/files/mknapcb9.txt, counting from 0 in file order) that satisfies every one of the 30 constraints sum_i r(k,i) x_i <= b(k) in exact integer arithmetic and whose profit sum_i p(i) x_i is strictly greater than the value listed for 500-30-j in this entry's statement, and also strictly greater than every value for that instance in any 2024-2026 paper or preprint found in a literature check made at claim time (the check and what it found are written down). Feasibility and profit are recomputed by an independent checker from the downloaded file, whose sha256 is recorded. Nothing is submitted anywhere; the write-up goes to the human.

partial_wins.statement: The same for one MK_GK instance gk01..gk11 from https://leria-info.univ-angers.fr/~jinkao.hao/mkp/MK_GK_Instances.zip: a feasible 0/1 vector (exact integer check) whose profit is strictly greater than the gk value listed in the statement and than any 2024-2026 published value found in the claim-time literature check.

A proof that the listed value of some 500-30-j is optimal, as a VIPR certificate produced by exact SCIP on an MPS model regenerated from mknapcb9.txt and accepted by viprchk, together with a feasible vector attaining the listed value.

targets.verification_method: Download mknapcb9.txt and parse it (first token K=30; then per problem: n m opt, n profits, m rows of n weights, m capacities; a parser written during vetting consumed the file exactly and found 30 problems of n=500, m=30). Read the claimed vector, check every constraint and recompute the profit with integer arithmetic, compare with the statement's value and with the claim-time literature check. Seconds. FEPSS posts code (github.com/jetou/FEPSS) but no solution vectors, so there is no posted vector to reproduce; the checker is validated on the OR-Library file format instead.
angles: Fix the cardinality sum x_i = K for each plausible K and run a reduced-cost-guided tabu or LNS per K (the Vasquez-Vimont idea), solving freed sub-problems exactly with CP-SAT or HiGHS.
Core-problem approach: fix items with extreme LP reduced costs and solve the core exactly with long time limits; target the tightness-0.25 block (500-30-0..9), where FEPSS and TPTEA disagree most.
pitfalls: The BK column of FEPSS Table 5 is not the latest value for four instances: Table 2 (the time-limit study) reports 116553 for 500-30-4 and 214660 for 500-30-11, above Table 5. Use the statement's maxima.
The OR-Library mkcbres file holds 1998 GA values, far below the current records; do not compare against it.
Instance numbering: 500-30-j is the j-th problem in file order (0-based); the file header 'opt' field is 0 (unknown) and carries no information.
MK_GK files use a different layout from the OR-Library files; check the parser against the n and m printed in FEPSS Table 6.

targets.name: Social Golfer Problem (CSPLib 010): more rounds than the 2026 Miller-Valkov-Abel table for a (v,k) cell with at most 10 groups per round
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (SAT/CP or design-theoretic search; schedules are a few kilobytes)
targets.statement: Social Golfer Problem (CSPLib prob010, proposed by Warwick Harvey): schedule v = m*k players into rounds of m groups of size k so that no two players share a group twice, for as many rounds as possible. Miller, Valkov and Abel (Symmetry 18(2):269, 2026, doi 10.3390/sym18020269; open copy Glasgow eprint 377866) gather design constructions (RBIBD, RGDD, RTD, URD, RITD, MOLR, starter blocks) into tables of the best currently known round count r against the counting bound MAX for all (v,k) with k > =4, k|v and k^2<=v<=150, building on CP and SAT work by Harvey and Winterer, Triska and Musliu and others. k=3 is fully maximal and k=4 is maximal in all but nine cases. Cells with at most 10 groups per round (m1<=10, Tables 4-5) where r < MAX and v is not k^2: (30,5) 6 of 7 (classic 6-5-7), (35,5) 7/8, (40,5) 8/9, (45,5) 9/10*, (50,5) 9/12, (42,6) 7/8, (48,6) 8/9, (54,6) 9/10, (60,6) 7/11, (56,7) 8/9, (63,7) 9/10, (70,7) 7/11, (72,8) 9/10, (80,8) 5/11, (90,9) 5/11. The authors state that non-maximal cells may be improved. A naive randomized greedy written during vetting stays well below r on all of these cells (for example 4 rounds for (30,5), 3 for (70,7)).
targets.success_criterion: For one (v,k) in the list in the statement, an explicit schedule of r+1 or more rounds (r = the round count printed for that cell in Tables 4-5 of doi 10.3390/sym18020269), each round a partition of players 0..v-1 into v/k groups of exactly k, in which no unordered pair of players appears together in more than one group over all rounds. The round count must also be strictly greater than any value for that cell in 2024-2026 literature found in a claim-time check (cite it). An independent checker reads the schedule and verifies the partition and pair conditions. Nothing is submitted anywhere; the write-up goes to the human.

partial_wins.statement: Close a listed cell at its current r: a SAT encoding (regenerated by the skeptic from a written description) of 'v players, k per group, r+1 rounds' with a DRAT or LRAT proof of unsatisfiability that drat-trim or cake_lpr accepts, together with any symmetry-breaking constraints justified in the write-up.

For a listed cell, an (r+1)-round schedule (each round a partition into groups of exactly k) in which exactly one unordered pair of players meets twice and every other pair at most once (the minimum-repeat variant in the CSPLib prob010 specification).

targets.verification_method: A 20-line checker (written and self-tested during vetting on the 5-round AG(2,4) schedule for (16,4)) reads one round per line, groups separated by '|', and asserts that each round is a partition of 0..v-1 into groups of size k and that no pair repeats; it prints the round count. Compare with the printed r for the cell, re-read from the Glasgow eprint PDF. Seconds.
angles: Start from the paper's construction for the cell (for example the URD(30,5,2) rounds for (30,5) or the ownSG starter blocks for (60,6) in Appendix A) and look for an extra parallel class with a SAT or exact-cover solver over the unused pairs, or impose a cyclic automorphism of order v/k or v-1 to shrink the search.
Use symmetric SAT encodings (Triska-Musliu) with incremental round addition and solution-based restarts.
pitfalls: Cells with v = k^2 are excluded: there r = N(k)+2 for the number N(k) of MOLS, so (36,6) is proven at 3, (100,10) is the separate three-MOLS-of-order-10 moonshot and (144,12) needs six MOLS of order 12.

Cells with more than 10 groups per round (rest of Tables 5-6) are left out on purpose: during vetting a 60-second naive greedy found 7 rounds for (140,7), where the table prints 5, so those large cells do not reflect a serious search.

MAX is a counting bound; an asterisk marks cells with a sharper bound. A cell may have a true maximum below MAX, so check the Handbook of Combinatorial Designs (resolvable packings, RGDD nonexistence) before a long run.

For (45,5) the paper's MAX of 10* rests on treating RBIBD(45,5) as nonexistent; a resolvable S(2,5,45) is in fact an open case (the separate bank target rbibd-45-5-1-smallest-open-resolvable). A 10-round schedule wins this cell; an 11-round one would be that resolvable design and belongs to that target too.
CSPLib's prob010 page still says the 32-golfer problem is open; it is not (10 rounds, Aguado 2004). Do not use it as a status source.

targets.name: PESPlib periodic timetabling: lower the best known weighted slack of a railway instance R1L1..R4L4
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (instances have 2,600-8,400 events and 6,400-18,000 activities; files are a few hundred KB)
targets.statement: The Periodic Event Scheduling Problem (Serafini and Ukovich 1989): given events and activities (i,j) with bounds [L,U] and weights w, choose periodic event times (period T=60) so that each activity duration D, with D congruent to pi_j - pi_i mod T, lies in [L,U], minimising the weighted slack sum w(D-L). PESPlib, created by Marc Goerigk and now hosted with TimPassLib, keeps 22 instances and a dated record history. Records have been improved by Goerigk, Liebchen, Paetzold, Matos and Albino, Lindner, Roth, Bortoletto, Masing, Ebert, Gleixner, Heidemann and, in August 2026, Ramos, who lowered every instance. Current best values (live 2026-10-30): R1L1 29,824,049; R1L2 30,055,723; R1L3 28,339,653; R1L4 25,877,852; R2L1 39,943,601; R2L2 38,783,647; R2L3 36,765,606; R2L4 31,497,313; R3L1 42,089,847; R3L2 43,281,389; R3L3 37,654,146; R3L4 31,553,558; R4L1 46,345,944; R4L2 46,062,018; R4L3 43,245,224; R4L4 35,799,285 (railway set 01); BL1 6,134,104; BL2 6,282,830; BL3 6,337,431; BL4 5,775,151 (bus set 02); R1L1v 42,391,128; R4L4v 60,097,211 (variant set 03). The best lower bounds are far lower (for example 20,230,655 for R1L1; the page notes that lower bounds are not verified), so every instance is open.
targets.success_criterion: A solution file ('activity; duration' lines) for one railway instance R1L1..R4L4 from https://timpasslib.aalto.fi/data/pesplib/set-01.tar.gz such that every duration lies within its activity's [L,U], the durations are periodic (event times pi in Z_60 exist with pi_j - pi_i congruent to D mod 60 for every activity, checked by propagating along a spanning forest and testing all activities), and the weighted slack sum w(D-L) is strictly below the best objective shown for that instance on https://timpasslib.aalto.fi/pesplib.html, re-fetched immediately before claiming. An independent checker must first reproduce the posted best objective from the posted .sol file. Nothing is submitted (the page takes submissions by email); the write-up goes to the human.

partial_wins.statement: The same checks for one bus instance BL1..BL4 (set-02.tar.gz): a feasible periodic solution with weighted slack strictly below the live best objective for that instance.
The same checks for one variant instance R1L1v or R4L4v (set-03.tar.gz): a feasible periodic solution with weighted slack strictly below the live best objective for that instance.

targets.verification_method: Parse the instance ('N; O; T; L; U; W') and the solution ('N; D'). Check that the activity sets match and that L<=D<=U, build event times by BFS over the activity graph with pi_j = pi_i + D mod 60, assert that every activity satisfies (pi_j - pi_i - D) mod 60 = 0, and sum w(D-L). A 40-line Python checker written during vetting reproduced the posted R1L1 record file R1L1-29824049.sol exactly (objective 29,824,049) in seconds. Re-fetch pesplib.html with curl and parse the last (lowest) objective listed for the instance.
angles: Start from the posted record .sol files and improve them with the modulo network simplex plus cycle-based MIP neighbourhoods (fix most periodic offsets, re-optimise a subnetwork with CP-SAT or HiGHS), the approach of the Lindner and Masing line of work.
Concurrent heuristics: combine modulo network simplex, maximum-cut style moves and sub-MIPs over fundamental cycles, restarting from different spanning trees.
pitfalls: Each instance row on the page lists its history; the best value is the lowest (last) entry, not the first.
Lower bounds on the page are marked 'not verified'; do not claim a bound improvement as a win.
The PESPlib-derived instances inside TimPassLib (R1L1 etc.) have different activity sets and objectives; they belong to the separate TimPassLib entry.

targets.name: TimPassLib: a periodic timetable with lower total passenger travel time than the best known for an open integrated timetabling-and-routing instance
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (instances from 32 to 21,328 events; evaluating one timetable is a series of shortest-path runs, seconds)
targets.statement: Integrated periodic timetabling and passenger routing: choose event times in {0..T-1} that satisfy the periodic bounds of every activity (drive, wait, change, sync, headway), then route every OD demand along shortest paths through drive, wait and change activities, a change costing its duration plus the instance's change penalty; minimise total passenger travel time. TimPassLib (Schiewe, Goerigk and Lindner, Operations Research Forum 4:64, 2023) maintains 27 instances with dated best solutions and lower bounds. Records have been set by Schiewe, Schöbel, Goerigk, Lindner, van Lieshout, Loebel and, on 31 Aug 2026, Ramos. Only toy and toy_2 are solved optimally. Current best totals (live 2026-10-30): Hamburg 140,850,920 (bound 139,892,927); Schweiz_Fernverkehr 61,855,004; Stuttgart 48,210,542,340; regional 1,827,124; grid 48,827; long-distance 66,981,422; metro 11,990,908; Erding_NDP_S020 12,228,304; Erding_NDP_S021 12,235,729; R1L1 538,536,289; R1L2 537,742,639; R1L3 537,105,340; R1L4 532,591,640; R2L1 670,939,152; R2L2 669,302,510; R2L3 667,292,632; R2L4 659,596,899; R3L1 686,543,137; R3L2 685,694,233; R3L3 683,258,276; R3L4 672,473,277; R4L1 745,524,467; R4L2 747,493,422; R4L3 742,094,966; R4L4 731,939,240.
targets.success_criterion: A Timetable.csv ('event_id; time' with times in 0..T-1) for Hamburg, Schweiz_Fernverkehr, Stuttgart or one of R1L1..R4L4 from https://timpasslib.aalto.fi/data/ < instance > .zip such that every activity's periodic duration ((pi_j - pi_i - L) mod T) + L is at most U, and whose total passenger travel time, recomputed by an independent evaluator (sum over OD pairs of customers times the shortest path from any departure event at the origin to any arrival event at the destination over drive, wait and change activities, each change adding ean_change_penalty from Config.csv), is strictly below the best total shown for that instance on https://timpasslib.aalto.fi/solutions.html, re-fetched immediately before claiming. The evaluator must first reproduce the posted best total from the posted best Timetable for that instance. Nothing is submitted; the write-up goes to the human.

partial_wins.statement: The same checks and strict improvement for one of the smaller open instances regional, grid, long-distance, metro, Erding_NDP_S020 or Erding_NDP_S021.

For one open instance, a feasible timetable whose total ties the live best total exactly and whose periodic activity durations ((pi_j - pi_i - L) mod T) + L differ from those of the posted best timetable on at least 5% of the drive, wait and change activities (an independent alternative record, not a global time shift of the posted one; checked by direct comparison of the two duration vectors).

targets.verification_method: Read Config.csv (period_length, ean_change_penalty), Events.csv, Activities.csv, OD.csv and the timetable. Check periodic feasibility of all activities, then run Dijkstra from the set of departure events at each origin station over drive/wait/change arcs (duration, plus the penalty on change arcs) and take the cheapest arrival event at each destination; total = sum customers x distance. A 60-line Python evaluator written during vetting reproduced the posted toy optimum (21,466) and the posted Hamburg record (140,850,920) exactly. Re-fetch solutions.html and take the first (lowest) total listed for the instance.
angles: Alternate: fix passenger routes from the incumbent, solve the resulting PESP with weights = passengers per arc (modulo network simplex or sub-MIP), re-route by shortest paths, repeat; then perturb with local event shifts evaluated exactly.
On small open instances (grid, metro, regional) a full MIP with route variables restricted to k-shortest paths per OD pair may reach or beat the records.
pitfalls: Periods differ by instance (Hamburg uses T=10); read period_length from Config.csv.
Sync and headway activities must be feasible but cannot carry passengers; including them in routing gives a total that is too low.
Solutions are listed best-first on solutions.html; bounds are listed separately and are not wins.

targets.name: QOBLIB network design (Bienstock-Gunluk demands): a 2-in/2-out digraph and routing with lower maximum edge load for an open instance network11..network24
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (n = 11..24 nodes; scoring a topology is one min-congestion multicommodity-flow LP)
targets.statement: QOBLIB problem class 08 (Network Design, Bienstock and Gunluk, Math. Programming 68, 1995): for the first n rows and columns of a fixed 24 x 24 demand matrix, build a simple digraph on n nodes with in-degree and out-degree exactly 2 and route every demand t_ij from i to j so as to minimise the maximum aggregate flow on any arc (objective z in thousandths of a unit). QOBLIB (ZIB-AOPT, maintained on GitHub with an auto-generated best-known table) lists network05..network10 as optimal and network11..network24 as best known only. A parallel-tempering submission (Manan Gupta, PR #45, dated 2026-08-18, merged 2026-10-19) lowered eleven of them (network13..network23), matched the reference value on network11 and was worse on network12 and network24; the auto-generated table credits it for twelve rows because it also re-attributed the network11 tie. Table best known z on 2026-10-30: network11 238334, network12 276474, network13 300620, network14 343091, network15 370870, network16 397908, network17 437000, network18 473375, network19 492924, network20 528528, network21 569273, network22 618135, network23 659369, network24 663688; network12 and network24 are still held by the curated reference solutions, the other twelve rows by the 2026-08-18 submission. Two open pull requests already go below the table and are not on it: #61 (Marcin Kaminski, 4colors, 2026-09-08) gives network20 520929 and network22 616578, and #98 (Manan Gupta, 2026-10-25) gives network20 522657 and network23 648241. Maintainer Maximilian Schicker has asked the open pull requests to meet QOBLIB's AI policy before merging.
targets.success_criterion: A solution file in the QOBLIB Gurobi-style format (x#i#j arc indicators, f#k#i#j flow of commodity k on arc (i,j) in thousandths) for one instance networkNN with NN in 11..24 such that an independent checker confirms: every node has exactly 2 outgoing and 2 incoming arcs with no loops; flow is non-negative and only on chosen arcs; for each source k, net outflow at k equals 1000 times the sum of t_kj and net inflow at each j equals 1000 t_kj (t from the first NN rows and columns of 08-network/instances/demand.txt); and the maximum aggregate arc flow is STRICTLY BELOW (direction: min) the minimum, for that instance, of the Best Known value in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ZIB-AOPT/QOBLIB/main/08-network/solutions/README.md and the objective of every solution file in a merged or open QOBLIB submission or pull request (today #61 and #98), all re-fetched and re-scored immediately before claiming. The checker must first validate the posted best solution for that instance and the best open-pull-request solution. Nothing is submitted; the write-up goes to the human.

partial_wins.statement: Prove the listed value of one instance network11..network24 optimal: a VIPR certificate from exact SCIP on the QOBLIB integer model that viprchk accepts, or another machine-checkable certificate whose checker the skeptic can build.

For one open instance, a checker-valid solution whose maximum load equals the listed best known value exactly and whose arc set differs from the posted best solution's arc set (an alternative record topology).

targets.verification_method: Parse demand.txt (24 rows of '|i | t_i1, ..., t_i24|'), take the leading n x n block, read x and f from the claimed file, check degrees, arc support, per-commodity conservation and recompute the max arc load. A 90-line Python checker written during vetting validated the posted network11.bst.sol (max load 238334 = z) and network20.bst.sol (528528 = z). Then re-read the solutions README and score the solution files attached to the open pull requests with the same checker. Seconds.
angles: Search over topologies only (a 2-in/2-out digraph is a union of two derangements) with degree-preserving 2- and 3-exchanges, scoring each topology by the exact min-congestion LP; then restore integral thousandths by re-solving with integer flows.
Seed from the posted best topology for n and from good topologies for n-1 and n+1 (add or remove a node and repair degrees).
pitfalls: Flows are integers in thousandths of a unit; a fractional LP routing must be rounded to an integral routing that still meets the claimed z.

The table is not the whole record: open pull requests #61 and #98 already hold values below it on network20, network22 and network23, and they are not on the auto-generated table. Score the PR solution files yourself before claiming.

network12 and network24 are still held by the curated reference solutions, the other twelve table rows by the 2026-08-18 submission; re-fetch the README, which is regenerated by CI on every accepted submission.

targets.name: IWLS 2026 Programming Contest: an AIG off the virtual-best delay/area Pareto frontier for one of the 100 released truth tables (ex200-ex299)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours per benchmark (ABC/mockturtle/SAT-based resynthesis on 16-input-scale truth tables); exhaustive verification takes seconds
targets.statement: The IWLS 2026 Programming Contest (chairs Alan Mishchenko, UC Berkeley, and Attila Jurecska, Siemens EDA) asked for and-inverter graphs (AIGs) for 100 completely specified multi-output Boolean functions given as truth tables ex200..ex299 (ex200, for instance, has 16 inputs and 16 outputs). Unlike earlier years it scored a delay/area trade-off: area = number of two-input AND nodes, delay = AND logic levels (ABC print_stats 'and' and 'lev'). Scoring finished in May 2026 (scoring report dated 2026-05-24). The organisers released the truth tables, the 10,553 submitted AIGs from 12 teams (10,537 functionally correct), and, per benchmark, the virtual-best-solver (VBS) Pareto frontier formed from the union of all teams' Pareto points (results/pareto_tables, VBS AIGs in virtual_best_solver.tar.gz). Examples of VBS frontier end points (level, ANDs): ex200 (13, 7617) ... (70, 1055); ex211 (8, 251) ... (26, 154); ex265 (6, 48) ... (13, 37); ex299 (17, 153970) ... (116, 15410). Top three: JetBrains / NUP / EPFL / MBZUAI, NTHU / CUHK, Freiburg. The contest is over and the data are public, so the frontier is a fixed record table; OPEN as of 2026-10-30 (last commit 2026-06-20, no post-contest frontier updates found). The contest description says a few benchmarks may duplicate functions from earlier IWLS contests, whose released best circuits also count as bars. Cirbo (SPbSAT/cirbo, release 1.1.0 of 2026-10-13) ships ex215 circuits for metaheuristic experiments.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a binary AIGER file for some benchmark exNNN (200 <= NNN <= 299) that (1) is functionally equivalent to exNNN.truth on all input vectors, and (2) has a (level L, AND count A) point that is STRICTLY BETTER than the VBS frontier in results/pareto_tables/exNNN.txt: A is strictly smaller than the minimum VBS area over all listed levels <= L (direction: min area at a given delay; if no VBS point has level <= L, any correct AIG at level L is a new frontier point). Equivalently the point is neither dominated by nor equal to any VBS point. L and A are recomputed by the verifier (AND nodes; levels = longest input-to-output path counted in AND nodes, inverters free), never taken from the filename. The point must also not be dominated by or equal to any other published AIG for the same function known at claim time: post-contest papers, the Cirbo repository, contest-repo updates, and released circuits of earlier IWLS contests whose truth table is identical. Each benchmark is a separate cell; one non-dominated point is a full win.

partial_wins.statement: A fully automatic, released synthesis script that, run from exNNN.truth alone (no submitted or VBS circuits as input), produces a functionally equivalent AIG whose AND count at some level L is at most 1.01 times the minimum VBS area over levels <= L, for at least 10 of the 100 benchmarks; the skeptic re-runs the script and checks every output.

targets.verification_method: Parse the AIGER file with an independent reader, simulate all 2^n input vectors bit-parallel and compare every output with the truth-table columns of exNNN.truth (cross-check with ABC: read_truth -xf exNNN.truth; st; &get; &cec -t cand.aig, as in the contest's evaluation_notes.md). Recompute AND count and AND-level depth (ABC read_aiger; print_stats). Compare (L, A) against every row of results/pareto_tables/exNNN.txt and any newer published point.
angles: Start from the VBS AIGs (virtual_best_solver.tar.gz) and apply resubstitution, SAT-based window resynthesis and depth-aware rewriting at a fixed level budget.
Target benchmarks whose frontier has few points or large area jumps between adjacent levels (e.g. ex210, ex275, ex285-ex294).
Balance a minimum-area circuit to a lower level and re-minimise area under that level constraint.
pitfalls: Levels count AND nodes only; inverters are free. Use the verifier's recomputed level, not the filename's LLL field.
A point equal to a VBS point, or dominated by any VBS point at a lower level, is not a record: the comparison is against the minimum area over all levels <= L.
Benchmark descriptions are undisclosed and may be reused in future IWLS contests; publish circuits openly but do not assume a benchmark's identity.
Check the repository and recent papers for post-contest improvements before claiming.

targets.name: Small symmetric Boolean functions over the full binary basis: smaller circuits for SUM_n (sideways sum), MAJ_n, SORT_n, or exact values such as Knuth's MOD3 n = 6 cases
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (SAT-based exact synthesis and local subcircuit improvement); verification laptop-minutes
targets.statement: Circuit size over B2 (two-input gates computing any of the 16 binary functions; equivalently XAIG with free negations) is the classical measure of TAOCP 7.1.2. SUM_n outputs the binary representation of x1+...+xn and underlies every symmetric function. Best known B2 sizes (Kulikov-Pechenev-Slezkin, MFCS 2022, Table 3; circuit files in alexanderskulikov/circuit_improvement/circuits/sum; Cirbo, AAAI 2025, Table 3; Goncharov-Kulikov-Levtsov, arXiv:2509.13966): SUM_2..SUM_5 = 2, 5, 9, 11 (optimal); SUM_6 <= 16, SUM_7 <= 19, SUM_8 <= 25, SUM_9 <= 27, SUM_10 <= 31 (sum10_size31.ckt, verified exhaustively by this review), SUM_11 <= 34, SUM_15 <= 51, SUM_16 <= 59, SUM_31 <= 119. AIG basis (AND only, free inverters; Cirbo): SUM_5, 7, 9, 11, 15 <= 17, 28, 41, 52, 77. Asymptotically 2.5n - O(1) <= size(SUM_n) <= 4.5n + o(n) (Stockmeyer; Demenkov-Kojevnikov-Kulikov-Yaroslavtsev), and size(SUM_n) <= size(SUM_k) n/(k - ceil(log2(k+1))) + o(n), so a SUM_15 with 49 gates, a SUM_7 with 17 or a SUM_31 with 116 would beat 4.5n. Cirbo lists XAIG MAJ_7, 9, 11, 13, 15 <= 17, 24, 31, 45, 48 and SORT_12..16 <= 58, 62, 68, 73, 82. Knuth (TAOCP 7.2.2.2, answer to ex. 480) found size(MOD3^r_n) for 3 <= n <= 5, proved size(MOD3^0_6) = 12 and conjectured size(MOD3^r_n) = 3n - 5 - [(n+r) = 0 mod 3]; Kulikov et al. proved the matching upper bound, so MOD3^1_6 and MOD3^2_6 have 13-gate circuits and are conjectured optimal, a case Knuth called 'tantalizingly close' to solver limits. OPEN as of 2026-10-30 (repository last changed 2026-03; Cirbo 1.1.0 of 2026-10-13).
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit circuit, as a straight-line program over two-input gates with each gate's 4-bit truth table, that computes the stated multi-output function exactly on all 2^n inputs and has STRICTLY FEWER gates (direction: min) than the value listed in the statement for that function and basis: SUM_n in B2 for n in {6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 15, 16, 31}, or in the AIG basis for n in {5, 7, 9, 11, 15}. For SUM_n the outputs are the ceil(log2(n+1)) bits of x1+...+xn. Gate count is the number of two-input gates; inputs and constants are free; in the AIG basis only AND gates count and negations are free. A candidate must also beat every smaller circuit for the same function and basis published at claim time: re-check the three primary papers, the circuit_improvement circuits folder, what the current Cirbo generators produce, and any IWLS 2023-2026 contest circuit whose truth table equals the function.

partial_wins.statement: A B2 circuit with strictly fewer gates than listed for XAIG MAJ_n (n in {7, 9, 11, 13, 15}; output [x1+...+xn > n/2]) or SORT_n (n in 12..16; outputs the sorted input bits), verified exhaustively, and also smaller than any circuit for the same function in the circuit_improvement maj/sort folders and the IWLS 2023-2026 contest results.

An exact value for MOD3^1_6 or MOD3^2_6 (output [x1+...+x6 = r mod 3]): either a SAT proof (CNF from an independently re-implemented circuit-existence encoding that allows unused gates, plus a DRAT/LRAT certificate checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr) that no B2 circuit with at most 12 gates computes it (settling it at 13), or a circuit with at most 12 gates (disproving Knuth's conjecture at n = 6), provided no later source has settled that case.

A certified lower bound: a checked UNSAT proof (same certificate standard as p2) that no B2 circuit with at most 15 gates computes SUM_6, making the listed 16 optimal, provided no published proof exists.

targets.verification_method: Evaluate the straight-line program on all 2^n inputs (n <= 31: bit-sliced over 2^31 inputs is minutes in C; for n <= 16 trivial) and compare with the defined function; count gates and confirm each gate's basis membership. For lower bounds, rebuild the CNF encoding independently (Kojevnikov-Kulikov-Yaroslavtsev style), check the certificate with drat-trim or cake_lpr, and review the symmetry-breaking constraints for soundness.
angles: Local SAT improvement of 7-gate windows (Kulikov's circuit_improvement) seeded with MDFA-based SUM circuits from the STACS 2026 generator.
Search for new constant-size blocks on the (p, p xor q) encoding beyond MDFA; any SUM_k block beating the 4.5(k - ceil(log2(k+1))) threshold improves the asymptotic bound.
For MOD3_6 use strong symmetry breaking (topological gate order, normal gates) and incremental SAT with proof logging.
pitfalls: B2 sizes and AIG sizes are different tables; do not compare across bases.
Count only two-input gates; a circuit that relies on free fan-in-3 gates or unary gates that the basis does not include is invalid.
An UNSAT result is only as good as its encoding: symmetry breaking that is not sound for multi-output functions has produced wrong 'optimality' claims; have the encoding re-derived independently.
Knuth's TAOCP Volume 4B (2022) answer to 7.2.2.2-480 and its errata may contain newer MOD3 values; check before claiming p2.

targets.name: Minimum-comparison sorting: settle S(23) in {75, 76} or S(24) in {80, 81} (OEIS A036604), or raise the n = 28 lower bound
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (Stober-Weiss needed 89 h on 48 threads with 768 GB RAM for n = 18; n = 23 is harder); certificate replay similar
targets.statement: S(n) is the minimum worst-case number of pairwise comparisons that suffices to sort n distinct elements (Knuth TAOCP 5.3.1; OEIS A036604). The information-theoretic bound gives S(n) >= ceil(log2 n!), and Ford-Johnson merge insertion gives the upper bound F(n) (A001768); Peczarski (IPL 2007) showed no split-and-merge algorithm beats it for n < 47, and whether any algorithm beats it for some n < 47 is open. S(n) is known for n <= 22: Wells (n = 12), Kasai-Sawato-Iwata and independently Peczarski (13), Peczarski (14, 22), Cheng-Liu-Wang-Liu (15, 19), and Florian Stober and Armin Weiss (ALENEX 2023, arXiv:2206.05597), who proved S(16) = 46, S(17) = 50, S(18) = 54 with a bidirectional poset search and also showed that 28 elements cannot be sorted with 98 comparisons. Open cells (information bound, or the Stober-Weiss bound for n = 28, to F(n)): S(23) in {75, 76}, S(24) in {80, 81}, S(25) in {84, 85, 86}, S(26) in {89, 90, 91}, S(27) in {94, 95, 96}, S(28) in {99, 100, 101}. Stober and Weiss wrote that for n >= 23 the value of S(n) is still a wide open question and that S(23) and S(24) look computable with improved methods. OPEN as of 2026-10-30: OEIS A036604 (last edited 5 Nov 2025) lists terms only to n = 22; their code repository (CodeCrafter47/sortinglowerbounds) was last changed Feb 2024.
targets.success_criterion: Success means one of: (a) a proof that 23 elements cannot be sorted with 75 comparisons (so S(23) = 76) or that 24 elements cannot be sorted with 80 (S(24) = 81), delivered as an exhaustive-search result with released code and a certificate (the set of posets shown unsortable with their remaining budgets) that an independent re-implementation re-derives; or (b) an explicit comparison strategy sorting 23 elements in 75 comparisons or 24 in 80 (STRICTLY BETTER than Ford-Johnson, direction: min), given as a decision table over poset isomorphism classes and checked to reach a total order on every branch within the budget. Either must improve on OEIS A036604 and the literature at claim time.

partial_wins.statement: A checked proof that 28 elements cannot be sorted with 99 comparisons (S(28) >= 100), improving the Stober-Weiss bound of 99.

For n in {25, 26, 27}, a checked proof that n elements cannot be sorted with ceil(log2 n!) comparisons (84, 89 or 94), provided no published source (including those cited by OEIS A036604 and Peczarski's Algorithmica 2004 table) already shows it.

targets.verification_method: For lower bounds: re-run the search with an independently written poset-sortability checker (canonical forms via nauty or brute force, forward plus backward search), confirm that the root poset is unsortable within C comparisons, and cross-check sample entries of the certificate. For an upper bound: replay the strategy, for every reachable poset class apply the stated comparison, and verify by memoised recursion that both outcomes lead to total orders within the remaining budget.
angles: Extend the Stober-Weiss bidirectional search with stronger poset canonisation and disk-backed storage; their n = 28, C = 98 run took 10 h at efficiency 0.96, while C = 99 halves the efficiency and needs a much larger search.
Exploit duality (a poset and its dual are equally sortable) and the efficiency threshold n!/2^C to prune.
For upper bounds, seed from Ford-Johnson and search locally for a first comparison sequence that leaves more balanced posets.
pitfalls: S(n) is the worst-case count for adaptive algorithms, not comparator networks (A003075) and not selection (V_t(n)).
An unsortability proof must cover all comparison choices at every poset; heuristic pruning that is not provably safe invalidates it.
Known values n <= 22 are proven; a result contradicting them means a bug.

targets.name: Online bin stretching: a computer-certified adversary tree beating the best lower bound for some m in 3..12 (41/30, 19/14, 15/11 cells), with randomized and upper-bound cells as partial wins
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (minimax game-tree search with DP feasibility caching; LRCB reached 15/11 for m = 6-8 on desktop hardware, harder cells may need a cluster as in Bohm's parallel runs; Rocq certification of a large tree takes hours and several GB)
targets.statement: Online bin stretching (Azar and Regev 1998): items arrive one at a time and are known to fit into m bins of size 1. Each item is placed irrevocably, and the stretching factor is the largest final load. s*(m) is the best stretching factor of a deterministic algorithm. Lower bounds come from adversary trees found by computer and certified in Coq/Rocq. Bohm's binstretch README (state as of 2023-06-29) lists m = 2: 4/3, tight. m = 3: 41/30, unpublished (Bohm) but Coq-verified; the published value is 112/82 (Bohm and Simon, TCS 2022). m = 4, 5: 19/14 (Bohm and Simon). m = 6, 7, 8: 15/11 (Lhomme, Romane, Catusse and Brauner, arXiv:2207.04931), Coq-verified. m = 9-12: 19/14, unpublished and unverified. m >= 13: 4/3. Upper bounds: 11/8 for m = 3 (Bohm, Sgall, van Stee and Vesely). 31/22, 23/16 and 19/13 for m = 4, 5, 6 (Lieskovsky, arXiv:2201.12393, by computer search). 3/2 for all m. 139/93 < 1.495 for large m (Bohm, Lieskovsky, Schmitt, Sgall and van Stee, APPROX 2024). Lhomme, Catusse and Brauner (arXiv:2506.17271, 2025) prove that these computational searches converge. Randomized algorithms (Lhomme, Catusse and Brauner, arXiv:2405.19071): m = 2 lies in [7/6, 5/4]; lower bounds are 19/16 for m = 3 and 11/9 for m = 4, by LP over the finite game. Credit: the authors named above.
targets.success_criterion: A full win is an adversary tree establishing Lower_bound m t g (all items integer, the whole input packable into m bins of capacity g at every node, every algorithm forced to a load of at least t) for some m in 3..12. It must be certified by the Rocq/Coq development of github.com/bs24/LB_BinStretching, or by an independent exact checker that shares no code with the search and reproduces the published witnesses first. It must hold with t/g strictly greater than the best lower bound for that m at claim time (higher is better). Current bars: m = 3: 41/30. m = 4 or 5: 19/14. m = 6, 7 or 8: 15/11. m = 9 to 12: 19/14. Each bar is the larger of the published value and the value in Bohm's README; re-check the README, arXiv and the Lhomme and Bohm repositories before claiming. Every cell lies strictly below a proven upper bound (m = 3: 11/8; m = 4, 5, 6: 31/22, 23/16, 19/13; otherwise 3/2), so no cell asks to beat a proven optimum. The gaps are open, and the true value may still equal the current lower bound. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: The first certified (Rocq/Coq-checked) adversary tree proving 19/14 for some m in 9..12, where the README lists the bound as unpublished and unverified, or any certified lower bound strictly above 4/3 for some m >= 13.

Deterministic upper bound: an explicit algorithm strategy for m = 3, 4, 5 or 6 in Lieskovsky's computer-search framework (a finite strategy over item classes plus 'good situations' that cover all continuations). An independent checker must certify that its stretching factor is strictly below 11/8, 31/22, 23/16 or 19/13 respectively.

Randomized bounds: an exact rational LP certificate (primal and dual) on a finite discretised game giving a lower bound on the randomized stretching factor strictly above 7/6 (m = 2), 19/16 (m = 3) or 11/9 (m = 4). Or a randomized algorithm for m = 2 with a certified stretching factor strictly below 5/4.

targets.verification_method: Deterministic lower bounds: convert the tree from DOT to Rocq with the LB_BinStretching converter and run 'cd Rocq && ./testnewtree.sh m t g'. Calibrate first on the shipped witnesses (4..8 19 14, 3 112 82). An independent checker must at every adversary node check that the items sent so far fit offline into m bins of capacity g (exact bin-packing feasibility by DP or ILP). At every algorithm node it must check that all placements are covered, and that each leaf has a bin of load at least t. Randomized: rebuild the finite game at the stated granularity, solve the sequence-form LP in exact rationals, and check the dual certificate. Upper bounds: replay the algorithm strategy against every adversary move, including the class-interval and good-situation arguments, with exact arithmetic.
angles: Granularity is the lever. LRCB proved 15/11 for m = 6-8 but not for m = 4, 5. Try 15/11 = 30/22 or intermediate fractions such as 26/19 or 41/30 for m = 4 and 5 at larger g, using LRCB's pruning propagation (precomputed always-winning packings for the algorithm) and Bohm's parallel caching.
For m = 9-12 the unverified 19/14 trees may already exist in Bohm's runs. Rebuilding one with the tree-proof variant of LRCB's bound_finder and certifying it is the cheapest win (p1).
The randomized m = 2 gap [7/6, 5/4] is small, and the LP game is tiny at moderate granularity. Push g upward and exploit symmetry (bin relabelling) to shrink the LP.
pitfalls: The README's m = 3 value 41/30 is unpublished. Compare against it, not against the published 112/82.
The 9-12 bin 19/14 bound is listed as unverified. A certified 19/14 there is p1, not a full win.
An adversary node is legal only if the whole input so far fits into m bins of capacity g. Skipping the offline feasibility check yields bogus trees.
Never compare randomized and deterministic values, and do not treat online makespan scheduling without the known-OPT promise as the same problem.

targets.name: Classic online bin packing: a deterministic lower bound above Balogh-Bekesi-Dosa-Epstein-Levin's 1.54278, or an algorithm at most 1.57821 (Advanced Harmonic, retuned by Martin in 2026 to 1.5782147)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exact LPs over packing patterns and weight-function checks; the hard part is designing the adversary or algorithm, not the computation)
targets.statement: In online bin packing, items of rational size in (0,1] arrive one by one and must be packed irrevocably into unit bins. The measure is the asymptotic competitive ratio of deterministic algorithms. Lower bounds follow Yao (1980), Brown and Liang (1.53635) and van Vliet (1.5401474). Balogh, Bekesi and Galambos (TCS 2012) found a better batched sequence of identical items, giving 248/161 ~ 1.5403726. Balogh, Bekesi, Dosa, Epstein and Levin (BBDEL; arXiv:1807.05554, Algorithmica 2021) used branching inputs, fully adaptive item sizes and a weight-based analysis. Their bound is R >= (1363 - sqrt(1387369))/120 ~ 1.5427809 (their Theorem 9). The same five authors designed Advanced Harmonic (AH; arXiv:1707.01728, ESA 2018), proved at most 1.57829. It was the first algorithm below 1.58, the barrier that had held Super Harmonic-type algorithms such as Seiden's Harmonic++ (1.58889). In October 2026 Karyamsetty Martin (arXiv:2610.32367, unrefereed) re-certified AH as an exact optimisation over its dual parameters. Re-tuning its proportion parameters gave the certified exact rational 1.5782147437..., with code and certificates public. That paper also reports that natural batch extensions of the BBDEL adversary do not raise the lower bound. The optimal ratio therefore lies in [1.5427809..., 1.5782147...]. Credit: the authors named above.
targets.success_criterion: Either of the following counts. (a) Lower bound: a complete proof that every deterministic online algorithm has asymptotic competitive ratio at least R, with R STRICTLY GREATER than (1363 - sqrt(1387369))/120 ~ 1.5427809 (BBDEL Thm 9), the comparison made exactly. The proof must be a machine-checked formal proof, or a written proof whose numerical content consists of finitely many explicit inequalities and LPs. Those must come with exact rational dual certificates and be re-checked by an independent program. (b) Upper bound: an online algorithm with asymptotic competitive ratio at most R', with R' <= 1.57821 (exact rational comparison). That is a margin of about 4.7e-6 below 1.5782147437..., the exact rational of Martin (arXiv:2610.32367, Thm 3.2). That paper reports that resuming its own coordinate descent still accepts smaller moves, so re-running its public harness for longer is not a win. If Martin's certificate fails independent re-verification, the bar reverts to AH's published certificate 1.5782895555... (cited as 1.57829) with the same margin, i.e. R' <= 1.57828. The analysis must reduce to finitely many weighting-function and knapsack checks, in the style of the Super Harmonic or AH analyses, verified by an independent program in exact arithmetic. In both cases re-check arXiv and recent SODA/ESA/ICALP/Algorithmica papers for newer bounds before claiming. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: A non-branching input in the Brown-Liang-van Vliet framework: a fixed list of item sizes presented in batches of identical items, where the adversary only chooses where to stop. Its exact LP value must be strictly greater than 248/161, the Balogh-Bekesi-Galambos record for this class. It is verified by an exact rational LP with a dual certificate.

targets.verification_method: For (a) and p1, write the van Vliet LP: variables are the numbers of bins the algorithm opens with each packing pattern of the batched sizes; constraints are item counts and, for each stopping point, ALG <= R * OPT_LP with OPT computed exactly. Solve it in exact rationals (SoPlex exact or QSopt_ex) and check the dual. Calibrate on the Brown-Liang sequence (1.53635), van Vliet (1.5401474) and BBG (248/161) first. For branching and adaptive proofs, check every case inequality of the written proof with exact arithmetic. For (b), enumerate the finitely many knapsack instances of the weighting system exactly and confirm that the maximum weight is at most R'. Calibrate on Harmonic++ (1.58889) and on the AH certificate (1.57829).
angles: BBDEL's gain over 248/161 came from branching plus full adaptivity (Theorem 1 of arXiv:1807.05554, borrowed from the cardinality-constrained work). Searching over branching trees of batched sizes with LP leaves is a finite search in which every leaf is an exact LP.
For p1, search sequences of the form 1/k_i + eps in a larger space than the greedy Sylvester-like one (BBG showed greedy is not optimal), and score each with the exact LP.
pitfalls: The lower-bound side concerns all deterministic algorithms. Lower bounds for restricted classes (Harmonic-type algorithms: 1.58333 of Ramanan et al.; the Heydrich-van Stee fixed-fraction floor, 1.5762 in the full version per Martin) or for randomized algorithms (best 1.5403) are different cells.
Asymptotic, not absolute, ratio. The absolute ratio is settled at 5/3 and is not this target.

Martin's 2026 bar is unrefereed. Re-run its public certificate before treating it as the incumbent. A further retune inside AH's own proportion family is what that paper already optimised to a local optimum; tiny descent gains from its harness fall inside the 1.57821 margin and do not count.
Floating-point LP solutions are not certificates; give exact rational duals.

targets.name: Randomized list update (partial cost model): a lower bound above Ambuhl's 1.50115, or a 5-item algorithm certified below COMB's 1.6
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (game trees over list states: 5! = 120 states for five items, 720 for six; exact rational LPs)
targets.statement: In list update an online algorithm keeps a list of n items. Accessing the item in position i costs i - 1 in the partial cost model. The accessed item may move forward for free; other swaps cost 1. Randomized algorithms face an oblivious adversary. The optimal randomized competitive ratio is open. The best algorithm is COMB (Albers, von Stengel and Werchner 1995), which runs BIT with probability 4/5 and TIMESTAMP with probability 1/5 and is 1.6-competitive. With two items a lower bound of 1.5 is easy. Ambuhl, Gartner and von Stengel (TCS 268, 2001) proved 1.50084 for five-item lists by game trees and a modified Teia argument. Ambuhl's ETH thesis (2002) improved this to 1.50115. Their TALG 2013 paper (arXiv:1002.2440) states the ratio lies between 1.50115 and 1.6, with the true value unknown. It also proves that no projective algorithm beats 1.6. A non-projective partial-order algorithm is 1.5-competitive for lists of up to four items. Extending that approach to five items 'is not straightforward', and no non-projective algorithm is known to beat 1.6 there.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) a lower bound c >= 1.5012 on the randomized competitive ratio in the partial cost model (higher is better; the margin covers rounding of 1.50115). It is given as an explicit Yao-type certificate: a finite list length n, a finite family of request phases with rational probabilities (or a game tree as in Ambuhl-Gartner-von Stengel), and an exact rational computation. The computation shows that every deterministic online algorithm, from every list state, pays in expectation at least c times the offline optimum per phase, up to an additive constant that vanishes over repeated phases. A claim below 1.5012 counts only by an exact comparison with Ambuhl's certificate. Or (b) a randomized online algorithm, possibly non-projective, with a machine-checkable proof that it is c'-competitive for all list lengths with c' < 1.6. Re-check arXiv and recent ICALP/ESA/SODA papers for newer list update bounds before claiming. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: Lists of exactly five items: a randomized (necessarily non-projective) online algorithm whose competitive ratio in the partial cost model is certified strictly below 1.6. The certificate is finite and exact, for example a potential-function LP over (list state, algorithm memory state, OPT list state) with a rational solution.

targets.verification_method: For (a), enumerate list states (n! permutations) and compute exactly, by DP over each phase's request sequences, the minimum expected online cost against the adversary's distribution and OPT's cost with paid exchanges. Check the per-phase inequality and the amortisation argument. Calibrate on the two-item 1.5 bound and on reproducing 1.50084 for five items. For p1 and (b), verify the potential-function inequalities for every transition in exact rational arithmetic, including paid exchanges by OPT. Calibrate on COMB (1.6) and on the four-item 1.5-competitive algorithm.
angles: The 1.50084 to 1.50115 gain came from better game trees on five items. Six-item lists (720 states) are now cheap; a larger tree search with LP-optimised phase distributions is the direct route.
For p1, the four-item 1.5 algorithm uses partial orders as memory. Search small memory automata for five items with an LP whose feasibility certifies competitiveness.
pitfalls: Partial and full cost models differ (access cost i - 1 vs i); in the full cost model the best randomized lower bound is Teia's 1.5 and needs long lists. Do not mix them.
AGvS's 1.6 lower bound for projective algorithms is not a bound for all algorithms. Only non-projective algorithms can win (b) or p1.
Oblivious adversary only; adaptive adversaries give deterministic-like bounds.

Other list update models are different cells: the uniform-cost model, where every swap costs 1 (Basiak, Bienkowski, Bohm, Chrobak, Jez, Sgall and Tatarczuk, arXiv:2503.17264: 3.3904); the paid-exchange model P^d (Albers and Janke, STACS 2020); and iid request models.

targets.name: Steiner tree bidirected cut relaxation: an explicit instance with integrality gap above Vicari's 6/5 (hypergraphic 8/7 and BCR+ 36/31 as partial wins)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (instance search; each candidate needs one exact LP and one exact Steiner tree computation, minutes for graphs with up to about 60 vertices and 15 terminals)
targets.statement: For the Steiner tree problem in graphs, the bidirected cut relaxation (BCR) directs edges both ways from a root terminal. It asks for capacity at least 1 into every vertex set that contains a terminal but not the root. Its integrality gap is famously open. Byrka, Grandoni and Traub (arXiv:2407.19905, FOCS 2024) proved the first upper bound below 2: 1.9988. The same paper cites 6/5 as the best lower bound, proved by Vicari (arXiv:2002.07912) with simplex-based instances whose gaps tend to at least 6/5. That improved the 36/31 ~ 1.161 of Byrka, Grandoni, Rothvoss and Sanita, which came from Skutella-type set-cover instances. Vicari's Table 1 also records two more lower bounds: the hypergraphic relaxation HYP has gap at least 8/7 (Skutella's instance; Konemann, Pritchard and Tan) and at most ln 4 ~ 1.386 (Goemans, Olver, Rothvoss and Zenklusen). BCR with Steiner-vertex flow-balance constraints (BCR+) has gap against the integral optimum at least 36/31. Vicari's 6/5 is a limit over a family, so a single finite instance above 6/5 would be new.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit finite instance: an undirected graph, a terminal set R and nonnegative rational edge costs, with OPT_STP / OPT_BCR strictly greater than 6/5 (higher is better). It must also be strictly greater than any lower bound published at claim time; re-check arXiv. The certificate has two parts. (i) A feasible BCR solution, rational directed capacities for a stated root terminal, of cost L, so that OPT_BCR <= L. Feasibility is checked by exact max-flow from the root to every terminal. (ii) A certified lower bound U on the minimum Steiner tree cost: exact enumeration (Dreyfus-Wagner DP, or MST over every Steiner-vertex subset), or an ILP solve with a VIPR-style certificate. The verifier checks U/L > 6/5. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit instance with OPT_STP / OPT_HYP strictly greater than 8/7, the best known lower bound for the hypergraphic relaxation (upper bound ln 4). The upper bound on OPT_HYP is a rational feasible solution of the full-component LP, with every partition or subtour constraint checked exhaustively (feasible for small terminal counts).

An explicit instance with OPT_STP / OPT_BCR+ strictly greater than 36/31, where BCR+ adds the Steiner-vertex flow-balance (in-degree <= out-degree) constraints, certified as in the main criterion with the extra constraints checked.

targets.verification_method: About 200 lines of Python with exact rationals (fractions) plus networkx max-flow on rational capacities. Check that the stated directed solution satisfies x_uv >= 0, and that root-to-terminal max-flow is at least 1 for every terminal; this is equivalent to all BCR cut constraints. Compute L. Compute the Steiner optimum by Dreyfus-Wagner over terminals (O(3^|R| n)) or brute force over Steiner subsets, with an independent second implementation. Calibrate on Skutella's 8/7 instance and on a small Vicari simplex instance, and confirm that BCR is exact on series-parallel graphs and on spanning-tree instances. For p1, enumerate full components exactly for |R| <= 10 and check the HYP subtour form.
angles: Vicari's instances embed Steiner instances into simplices through the dual formulations of Chakrabarty, Devanur and Vazirani. Larger simplex dimensions and non-uniform cost profiles are the obvious knobs. Search their parameters with exact LP scoring.

Cast the search as a bilevel problem: fix a graph template and optimise edge costs to maximise OPT_STP subject to the LP value being at most 1, using cutting planes on the Steiner trees that achieve the optimum.
pitfalls: Vicari's 6/5 is a limit. A finite instance just below 6/5 is not a win.
Do not confuse BCR (directed) with the undirected cut relaxation (gap exactly 2) or with HYP; each has its own bar.
Floating-point LP values are not certificates; give the rational primal solution.

targets.name: 2D irregular strip packing (nesting, ESICUP and Gardeyn instances): a shorter strip than a record in sparrow's live records folder
