targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (multi-core helps; the records came from 20-minute 16-core runs and longer record hunts)
targets.statement: Irregular strip packing (nesting): place every copy of a set of polygons, using only each item's allowed rotations, without overlap in a strip of fixed height, and make the strip as short as possible. The classic benchmarks (albano, blaz1 = shapes2, dagli, fu, jakobs1/2, mao, marques, shapes0/1, shirts, swim, trousers) come from 1980s-2000s papers and are kept in the ESICUP datasets repository (github.com/ESICUP/datasets, moved from euro-online.org in 2025). For about ten years the best layouts came from Leung et al. 2012, Elkeran 2013, Wang et al. 2017 and Sato et al. 2019. Jeroen Gardeyn, Greet Vanden Berghe and Tony Wauters (KU Leuven) then released the open-source sparrow heuristic (arXiv:2509.13329, v4 6 Oct 2026), which beats or ties every previous best density (swim 75.94% to 79.83%, shirts 88.96% to 90.92%), plus ten real-world instances gardeyn0-9. The repository's data/records folder keeps the best layouts as exact SVGs and is maintained: on 2026-10-06 the maintainer merged refinements by Touko Ursin (Helios One; PR #175) that shortened gardeyn0/2/4/5/6 and shapes0. Record lengths (strip height) on 2026-10-30: albano 9692.056 (4900), blaz1 25.049 (15.0015), dagli 56.087 (60), jakobs1 10.980 (40.004), mao 1696.802 (2550), marques 75.176 (104), shapes0 56.996 (40.004), shirts 59.393 (40), swim 5541.653 (5752), trousers 235.172 (79), gardeyn0 48629.967 (20000), gardeyn1 16181.270 (20000), gardeyn2 47305.935 (10000), gardeyn3 60397.832 (20000), gardeyn4 4724.856 (1500), gardeyn5 4301.942 (2000), gardeyn6 17037.131 (3990), gardeyn7 5067.831 (1524), gardeyn8 48718.980 (20000), gardeyn9 65.793 (44). fu, jakobs2 and shapes1 are left out: there sparrow only ties the older literature. The paper claims no optimality and expects large gains on gardeyn4, 5 and 7.
targets.success_criterion: For one of the 20 instances listed in the statement (not fu, jakobs2 or shapes1), a layout that places every item copy listed in https://github.com/JeroenGar/sparrow/tree/main/data/input/ < name > .json (same polygons, same demands, only the rotations that file allows, no mirroring) inside a strip whose height equals that file's strip_height, with every item inside the strip and pairwise disjoint item interiors (touching allowed). Its strip length must be STRICTLY SHORTER (direction: min) than the container width of data/records/final_best_ < name > .svg, read from the container path 'M0,0 L < w > ,0' (not the rounded footer text), re-fetched immediately before claiming; if the file has been replaced since 2026-10-30, the new value is the bar. If any published layout for that instance, at a strip height no greater than that strip_height, is shorter still, the claim must beat it too. Feasibility is judged by an independent exact checker, not by the generating heuristic.

partial_wins.statement: For blaz1, jakobs1 or shapes0, a layout in the ORIGINAL ESICUP strip height (15, 40, 40 respectively) whose length is at most the live record length in data/records (whose records use sparrow's 0.01%-inflated height), passing the exact checker. The stored records are only claimed at the inflated height (the shapes0 one is stated to be invalid at height 40), so this would be a new best at the original height.

For any gardeyn0-gardeyn9 instance, a layout that passes the exact checker and is within 0.5% of the live record length, found from scratch (no published layout used as a start) by code other than sparrow, released with the command and seed so that a rerun reproduces it.

For any of albano, dagli, mao, marques, shirts, swim or trousers, a layout that passes the exact checker and is within 0.1% of the live record length, found from scratch (no published layout used as a start) by code other than sparrow, released with the command and seed so that a rerun reproduces it.

targets.verification_method: Parse the claimed layout (sparrow-format SVG or JSON: item id, rotation, translation) and rebuild each placed polygon from data/input/ < name > .json. Check the item multiset against the demands and each rotation against the allowed set. Check containment in [0, L] x [0, strip_height] and pairwise interior-disjointness in exact rational arithmetic (Python fractions on the decimal coordinates exactly as written, after rotating by the allowed multiples of 90 degrees, which are exact; segment-intersection and point-in-polygon tests; touching boundaries allowed, positive-area overlap not). Compare L with the container-path width of the live final_best_ < name > .svg. For p2/p3, rerun the released code with the stated seed and check its output the same way. A few hundred lines of independent code; seconds per layout.
angles: Start from the published record SVGs and run long compaction or overlap-minimisation searches (sparrow's own strategy splits the work into a series of feasibility problems at shrinking lengths). The gardeyn instances have hundreds of items and the newest records, so they are the likeliest to have slack.
Exact feasibility at a fixed length for small instances (shapes, jakobs, blaz1) via no-fit-polygon MIP or dotted-board models, to test whether the record length can be pushed down by a provable step.

Cross-domain import from rigid-body physics (gravity-and-shake compaction with collision resolution) and from the strip-packing 'squeaky wheel' and guided local search literature (Egeblad-Nielsen-Odgaard, Umetani et al.).

Separation: sparrow keeps a tiny positive gap between items, but exact touching is allowed in the classical problem, so closing those gaps under an exact checker can shave length on high-density instances.
pitfalls: Strip-height inflation: sparrow's input files raise the ESICUP height by 0.01% for blaz1, fu, jakobs1, jakobs2, shapes0 and shapes1 (e.g. 40.004 instead of 40). Densities printed in the SVGs use the inflated height, the paper's Table 3 uses the original one (89.247% vs 89.26% for jakobs1). Compare strip lengths at a stated height, never densities across conventions.
Footer rounding: the SVG footer prints 3 decimals (jakobs2 shows 22.000 while the container is 22.000465). Use the container path value.

fu, jakobs2 and shapes1 are excluded: sparrow only ties Elkeran 2013 / Sato 2019 there, those older layouts at the original height may already be shorter than the inflated-height records, and these small integer-coordinate instances may be at or near optimal.

Rounding: the record coordinates are written at full f64 precision and the refined layouts sit about 1e-6 apart; re-serialising with fewer digits (or reading as f32) creates tiny overlaps that a tolerant floating-point or buffered Shapely test will miss. Check exactly.
Rotations vary by instance (shapes0 allows only 0, several only 0/180); a forbidden orientation or a reflected item is infeasible.
Literature versions of some instances (swim, shirts, trousers) differ slightly in vertex data. Use the polygons in sparrow's data/input, which the records refer to, and say so.
The records folder changes (six records replaced on 2026-10-06 by an outside contributor). Re-fetch before claiming.

targets.name: FLIP GB1 fitness landscape: beat the PLMFit scoreboard Spearman on the one-vs-rest or three-vs-rest split
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (8,733 rows, 8,705 of them test under one-vs-rest; sequences are 265 aa with only four positions varying, so one-hot features or frozen small-ESM2 embeddings train on CPU in minutes)
targets.statement: FLIP (Dallago, Mou, Johnston, Wittmann, Bhattacharya, Goldman, Madani and Yang, NeurIPS 2021 Datasets & Benchmarks) is a set of protein-fitness benchmarks with fixed, published train/test splits and a traffic-light marker saying which splits may be used for performance comparison. Its GB1 landscape comes from Wu, Dai, Olson, Lloyd-Smith and Sun (eLife 2016;5:e16965), a combinatorially complete assay of the four sites V39, D40, G41 and V54 of protein G domain B1. The 8,733 released rows carry the fitness value and the split columns, and every sequence is the 265-residue construct inferred from PDB 5LDE chain A with those four positions substituted, not the 56-residue domain alone. Green splits are one_vs_rest (train = wild type plus all single mutants), two_vs_rest, three_vs_rest and low_vs_high; 'sampled' is orange and must not be used for comparisons. PLMFit (Bikias, Stamkopoulos and Reddy, Briefings in Bioinformatics 26(4):bbaf381, 2025; github.com/LSSI-ETH/plmfit) publishes a scoreboard of the best setups it found. As of 2026-10-30 that scoreboard lists Spearman 0.4571 for GB1 one-vs-rest (ProGen2-small, frozen feature extraction) and 0.8791 for three-vs-rest (ProGen2-medium with adapters). The paper's Table 1 gives train/test counts 29/8,704 and 2,968/5,765. Both released files (FLIP splits.zip and plmfit's gb1_data_full.csv) instead hold 28/8,705 (one-vs-rest) and 2,990/5,743 (three-vs-rest). Of those training rows, 3 and 299 are flagged for validation (FLIP's validation column; plmfit labels them 'validation', leaving 25 and 2,691 'train'). No scoreboard value exists for two_vs_rest or low_vs_high. FLIP's repository received a FLIPv2 release in 2026-03 with new baseline code (ESM-C, Dayhoff, CARP and ESM2 zero-shot); the GB1 split files are unchanged. One-vs-rest is the unsolved cell: extrapolating from singles to doubles, triples and quadruples leaves most of the rank order unexplained, and the data are small enough to run on a laptop CPU.
targets.success_criterion: Predictions for every test row of one named FLIP GB1 split that HAS a PLMFit scoreboard value - one_vs_rest or three_vs_rest, both green - from a model fit only on that split's train rows (public pretraining corpora allowed if declared; nothing derived from the test rows). The Spearman correlation, recomputed by the skeptic with scipy.stats.spearmanr against the split's target/score column, must be STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) by at least 0.02 than the value listed for that split at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LSSI-ETH/plmfit/main/README.md (0.4571 one-vs-rest, 0.8791 three-vs-rest as of 2026-10-30; re-fetched live immediately before claiming). It must also be higher than any published value for the same split and test set found by the NOVELTY check, from any year from the 2021 FLIP paper's own baselines onward, including later FLIP releases such as the 2026 FLIPv2 baselines and 2024-2026 papers. Report the mean and standard deviation over at least three seeds, with a bootstrap 95% interval over test sequences that excludes the published bar. Split membership must be taken unchanged from one named released file (one_vs_rest.csv or three_vs_rest.csv in FLIP splits/gb1/splits.zip, or data/gb1/gb1_data_full.csv in the plmfit repo). Name that file in the claim and report the train/test/validation counts it contains. two_vs_rest and low_vs_high have no scoreboard value and cannot be claimed as a record (see p3).

partial_wins.statement: Beat the listed one-vs-rest Spearman (0.4571) by >= 0.02 with a model of at most 10M parameters, or with no pretrained language model at all, under the same split.

Exceed the listed three-vs-rest Spearman (0.8791) under the same split by less than the full 0.02 margin: a three-seed mean strictly above 0.8791 whose bootstrap 95% interval over test sequences excludes 0.8791, with the full prediction file published.

Publish reference numbers for the two FLIP GB1 green splits that currently have no scoreboard entry (two_vs_rest and low_vs_high) from a released, reproducible pipeline, with seeds and bootstrap intervals - infrastructure, reported as a baseline and not a record.

An ablation, reproducible from released code, isolating how much of the one-vs-rest score is explained by additive single-mutant effects alone (a site-wise linear model) versus epistatic terms, with the residual error analysed per mutation count.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads splits.zip from github.com/J-SNACKKB/FLIP/tree/main/splits/gb1 (or gb1_data_full.csv from the plmfit repo), uses the exact file the claim names, checks that the submitted predictions cover each test sequence exactly once and that the train/test membership matches the published split column, recomputes Spearman with scipy, reruns the attacker's training script from the released seeds to reproduce the number within its stated standard deviation, audits the code for any read of test targets, and re-fetches the PLMFit scoreboard. Under an hour.
angles: With 28 training sequences (25 if the 3 validation-flagged rows are held out), regularisation is everything: a site-wise additive model with shrinkage, or Gaussian-process regression on a mutation kernel, may beat any fine-tuned language model.

Cross-domain import (statistical genetics): treat the four mutated sites as loci and fit an additive-plus-pairwise epistasis model with sparsity priors, the standard approach for genotype-phenotype maps.
Zero-shot ensembling: average rank predictions from several frozen likelihood models (ESM-2 sizes, ProGen2) and calibrate the ensemble on the 28 training points only.
Data augmentation by symmetry: all four sites are interchangeable in the encoding, so train on site-permuted copies to regularise the pairwise terms.
Monotone calibration: the metric is rank-based, so fit the model for ranking (pairwise ranking loss) instead of squared error.
pitfalls: The 'sampled' split is marked orange in FLIP and must never be used for a performance claim; the PLMFit scoreboard's AAV-sampled entry shows how tempting the easy splits are.
Only one_vs_rest and three_vs_rest carry a GB1 scoreboard value; quoting a number from another split, or from another dataset's row, is a false record.

The released sequences are the full 265-residue 5LDE construct, not the 56-residue GB1 domain; the wild type was inferred from 5LDE chain A and the original dataset never contains it, so any pipeline that trims sequences, drops special characters or mismatches lengths changes the test set.

Counts differ between sources. The PLMFit paper's Table 1 says 29/8,704 (one-vs-rest) and 2,968/5,765 (three-vs-rest). FLIP's split files and plmfit's gb1_data_full.csv both hold 28/8,705 and 2,990/5,743, with 3 and 299 of the training rows flagged validation (FLIP's validation column, plmfit's 'validation' label, leaving 25 and 2,691 'train'). A claim must name its file and report the counts it used.
low_vs_high exists in FLIP's splits.zip but is not a column in plmfit's gb1_data_full.csv; a pipeline that assumes the two files carry the same columns will silently score the wrong rows.

Scoreboard values come from ProGen2 models (ProGen2-small is 151M parameters, ProGen2-medium 764M); a claim must state parameter count and compute, and must not compare a tuned model against the scoreboard entry for a different split.
Rank metrics on thousands of near-identical variants are noisy; a single seed above the bar is not a win, hence three seeds plus a bootstrap.

The GB1 four-site landscape also appears inside other benchmark suites (for example ProteinGym's SPG1_STRSG_Wu_2016, a larger variant set). A claim must be made on the named FLIP or plmfit split file, not on a reimplementation with different filtering, and numbers from those suites are not comparable bars.

targets.name: FLIP AAV capsid fitness: beat the PLMFit scoreboard Spearman on the one-vs-rest (one_vs_many) split
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (82,583 sequences; the mutated region is 28 aa so one-hot or small-embedding models are cheap, full-length embeddings are not)
targets.statement: The FLIP AAV landscape (Dallago and co-authors, NeurIPS 2021 Datasets & Benchmarks) is built from Bryant, Bashir, Sinai, Jain, Ogden, Riley, Church, Colwell and Kelsic's deep diversification of the adeno-associated virus 2 capsid protein (UniProt P03135, 735 aa), a non-pathogenic, replication-defective gene-therapy vector: mutations are introduced in the 28-residue region 561-588 and the target is the measured packaging/viability score, averaged over synonymous variants. FLIP defines green splits des_mut, mut_des, one_vs_many, two_vs_many, seven_vs_many and low_vs_high, where 'des' are designed or library variants and 'mut' are machine-learning-designed ones; the 'sampled' split is marked orange and may not be used for comparisons. The split columns ship in FLIP's splits/aav/full_data.csv.zip (284,009 rows, of which the 82,583 'des' rows carry the one_vs_many labels) and in splits.zip; the plmfit repository ships only a subsample, data/aav/aav_data_sample.csv, not a full CSV. PLMFit (Bikias, Stamkopoulos and Reddy, Briefings in Bioinformatics 26(4):bbaf381, 2025) keeps a public scoreboard. As of 2026-10-30 it lists Spearman 0.8315 for AAV one-vs-rest (1,170 training sequences at Levenshtein distance <= 1 from the reference region, 81,413 test sequences further away; ProGen2-xlarge with LoRA) and 0.9320 for the orange sampled split. The hard, honest cell is the extrapolation one: train on near-reference variants, predict the distant library, where the paper reports feature extraction averaging about 0.44 against a roughly 0.565 baseline while fine-tuning methods reach about 0.75 on average.
targets.success_criterion: Predictions for every test row of the FLIP AAV one_vs_many split (PLMFit's 'one-vs-rest': 1,170 train, 81,413 test), from a model fit only on that split's train rows plus declared public pretraining corpora, such that the Spearman correlation recomputed by the skeptic with scipy.stats.spearmanr against the split's score column is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the scoreboard value for that split at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LSSI-ETH/plmfit/main/README.md (0.8315 as of 2026-10-30; re-fetched live immediately before claiming) by at least 0.01, AND higher than any value for the same split found by the NOVELTY check over 2024-2026 literature, with three seeds (mean and standard deviation) and a bootstrap 95% interval over test sequences excluding the bar. The same Spearman must also be reported on the 81,272 test sequences that survive plmfit's own deduplication (see pitfalls), since that is the set the scoreboard value was measured on. Claims on the orange 'sampled' split do not count, and claims on a green split with no scoreboard entry belong in p3.

partial_wins.statement: Match the listed 0.8315 to within 0.01 using a model of at most 150M parameters (the scoreboard leader has 6.4B), with compute and parameter count reported.
Beat the attacker's own reproduced feature-extraction baseline on one_vs_many by >= 0.05 Spearman while using only CPU, with the baseline and the new pipeline both published.
Publish reproducible reference Spearman values for the FLIP AAV green splits with no scoreboard entry (des_mut, mut_des, two_vs_many, seven_vs_many, low_vs_high), reported as baselines, not records.

A released analysis of where the error concentrates (by Levenshtein distance from the reference region, by insertion/deletion presence, by stop codons) that identifies one systematic failure mode and shows a fix improving the overall Spearman.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads full_data.csv.zip and splits.zip from github.com/J-SNACKKB/FLIP/tree/main/splits/aav (the plmfit repo ships only aav_data_sample.csv, which is NOT the benchmark), checks the prediction file covers each row with one_vs_many_split == 'test' exactly once with the published split membership (1,170 train / 81,413 test), recomputes Spearman against the 'score' column, reruns the attacker's script from released seeds, audits for any use of test scores or of the orange sampled split, and re-fetches the scoreboard. An hour or two plus training time.
angles: Only 28 residues vary: encode the mutated region explicitly (one-hot plus insertion/deletion flags) rather than embedding the whole 735-residue capsid, which removes most of the compute and most of the noise.
Cross-domain import (sequence alignment): the mutation mask encodes insertions and deletions, so a model over aligned region strings with gap tokens may generalise better than a fixed-width encoder.
Rank-only objectives: Spearman rewards ordering, so train with a listwise or pairwise ranking loss on the 1,170 training points.
Semi-supervised use of the unlabelled test sequences' identities (transductive feature normalisation) is legitimate as long as no test score is read - declare it explicitly.
Distance-aware calibration: fit a per-Levenshtein-distance monotone recalibration on held-out training folds to counter the systematic shift away from the reference region.
pitfalls: The orange 'sampled' split (0.9320 on the scoreboard) is not a valid comparison target; quoting it as the bar would make this look saturated when it is not.

The plmfit repository ships data/aav/aav_data_sample.csv, a 10,000-row subsample, and no aav_data_full.csv; scoring on the sample is not scoring on the benchmark the scoreboard value came from. Use FLIP's full_data.csv.zip or splits.zip.

plmfit's own parser (data/aav/data_parse.py) keeps the 'des' rows, drops any sequence containing '*' and then drops duplicate full sequences, which leaves 81,272 of the 81,413 one_vs_many test sequences and 985 train plus 110 validation of the 1,170 train rows; 0.8315 was measured on that set, so a claim at the 0.01 margin must report both numbers. The parser also rescales the target to 0-1, which leaves Spearman unchanged.

Sequences contain special characters ('*' for deletions, lower case for insertions in the mutation mask); naive tokenisation silently corrupts the test set, and full_aa_sequence lengths run from 734 to 749 because of deletions and insertions (28 des rows are 734 long; the paper's Table 1 gives the same range).
Scores are averaged over synonymous variants in the released file; recomputing targets from the raw study data changes the benchmark.
The scoreboard leader is a 6.4B-parameter model fine-tuned with LoRA; a CPU-only claim must still clear the same bar, not a self-chosen weaker baseline.
Any model pretrained on data that already contains this library's measured variants (for example a checkpoint fine-tuned on AAV fitness data) breaks the extrapolation design and must be declared.

targets.name: FLIP meltome mixed split: beat the PLMFit scoreboard Spearman for melting temperature from sequence
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (24,817 train / 3,134 test full-length proteins; CPU embedding of long sequences dominates, small-ESM2 features are feasible)
targets.statement: The FLIP meltome landscape (Dallago and co-authors, NeurIPS 2021 Datasets & Benchmarks) turns the Meltome Atlas of Jarzab, Kurzawa, Hopf and co-authors (Nature Methods 17:495-503, 2020) into a sequence-to-melting-temperature regression. Sequences were clustered at 20% identity with MMseqs2 and the clusters split 80/20, so the green 'mixed' split trains on cluster members and tests on cluster representatives (the 'full' and 'clustered' variants are marked red and must not be used); 'human' (8,148/1,945) and 'human_cell' (5,792/1,366) are green restrictions of the same construction. This is thermostability prediction across the tree of life with no homology shortcut, and it stays far from saturated: the PLMFit scoreboard (Bikias, Stamkopoulos and Reddy, Briefings in Bioinformatics 26(4):bbaf381, 2025) lists Spearman 0.7232 for meltome mixed as of 2026-10-30, reached with ProGen2-xlarge and LoRA. FLIP's mixed_split.csv (27,951 rows) carries 24,817 training and 3,134 test proteins, the counts the paper's Table 1 reports, but PLMFit's pipeline loads data/meltome/meltome_data_full.csv, which its own data_parse.py builds from that same file by dropping sequences containing '*', dropping duplicate sequences and keeping only lengths <= 750: 19,003 rows, 14,781 train / 1,651 validation / 2,571 test, and the 20-750 length range Table 1 also quotes. The 2,571 test proteins are a subset of the 3,134 (the 563 that are missing are longer than 750 aa), so the 0.7232 is a 2,571-protein number and a claim here has to report both sets. The paper reports that on this task fine-tuning can improve on the baseline methods by up to 117.82% where frozen feature extraction does not. No entry exists on that scoreboard for the green human or human_cell splits.
targets.success_criterion: Predicted melting temperatures for the FLIP meltome 'mixed' split, from a model fit only on rows that split marks train or validation (plus declared public pretraining corpora with no melting-point supervision), scored on BOTH released test sets and clearing the bar on each: (a) the 2,571 rows with mixed == 'test' in plmfit's data/meltome/meltome_data_full.csv at https://github.com/LSSI-ETH/plmfit/tree/main/data/meltome, which is the set the scoreboard value was measured on, and (b) all 3,134 rows with set == 'test' in mixed_split.csv inside splits.zip at https://github.com/J-SNACKKB/FLIP/tree/main/splits/meltome (24,817 train / 3,134 test). On each set the Spearman correlation recomputed by the skeptic with scipy.stats.spearmanr against that file's target column ('score' in the plmfit file, 'target' in FLIP's) must be STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the scoreboard value at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LSSI-ETH/plmfit/main/README.md (0.7232 as of 2026-10-30; re-fetched live immediately before claiming) by at least 0.02, AND higher than any value for the same split found by the NOVELTY check over 2024-2026 literature, reported over at least three seeds with a bootstrap 95% interval over test proteins that excludes the bar. Red splits ('full', 'clustered') do not count.

partial_wins.statement: Beat 0.7232 by >= 0.02 on the mixed split using only CPU and a model of at most 150M parameters, with wall-clock time reported.
Publish reproducible reference Spearman values for the green 'human' and 'human_cell' splits (no scoreboard entry today) with seeds and bootstrap intervals, reported as baselines rather than records.
A released error analysis over the test clusters showing which organisms or length ranges carry the error, plus a fix that demonstrably improves the mixed-split Spearman.

A leakage audit of the mixed split: show, from the released cluster file, whether any test representative has a training member above a stated identity threshold, and report the Spearman restricted to the clean subset.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads splits.zip and meltome_PIDE20_clusters.tsv from github.com/J-SNACKKB/FLIP/tree/main/splits/meltome, uses mixed_split.csv unchanged, checks the prediction file covers each test protein exactly once with the published 'set' column and that the counts are 24,817/3,134, recomputes Spearman, reruns the attacker's pipeline from released seeds, audits for use of the red splits or of test targets and for any melting-point-supervised pretrained checkpoint, and re-fetches the scoreboard. An hour or two plus training time.
angles: Melting temperature correlates strongly with organism growth temperature and with composition (charged-residue fraction, IVYWREL); a well-regularised model on cheap global features plus small embeddings is a serious baseline that costs minutes.

Cross-domain import (domain adaptation): the mixed split puts cluster representatives in test, so importance weighting or domain-adversarial training against cluster identity targets exactly the shift being measured.
Length and run-level batch effects exist in the atlas; model the run as a random effect on the training side only.
Pool per-residue embeddings with attentive statistics pooling (from speaker recognition) instead of mean pooling, which loses the local signals that set stability.
Multi-task training with the green human and human_cell splits as auxiliary targets, which share the construction but differ in distribution.
pitfalls: The 'full' and 'clustered' splits are red in FLIP: performance on them is not comparable and must not be quoted as the bar. splits.zip in fact ships only mixed_split.csv, human.csv and human_cell.csv.

plmfit's data/meltome/meltome_data_full.csv is the file its loader actually reads, and data_parse.py builds it from mixed_split.csv by dropping sequences containing '*', dropping duplicate sequences and keeping lengths <= 750 (not 1,000 aa, as the plmfit data README says): 19,003 rows, 14,781 train / 1,651 validation / 2,571 test. Its test set is FLIP's 3,134 minus the 563 proteins longer than 750 aa, and 5,449 rows of the whole split exceed that length. Scoring one set against the other's bar silently changes the comparison, which is why both are required.

Melting points in the atlas can be null and the proteinId/runName pair is not always unique; FLIP's 24,817 training rows hold only 20,206 distinct sequences (and no training sequence appears in the test set), so dropping or deduplicating rows differently from the released split changes the benchmark.
Any pretrained model that saw melting-point labels (for example a thermostability-fine-tuned checkpoint) breaks the comparison and must be declared.
Full-length embeddings for 28,000 proteins on CPU can take days; a claim should report compute honestly rather than silently truncating sequences, since truncation changes the test inputs.
Scoreboard numbers come from a 6.4B-parameter model; comparing a small model against a different, self-chosen baseline is not a record.

targets.name: Trastuzumab CDR-H3 variant binding (PLMFit herH3 one-vs-rest): beat the scoreboard MCC of 0.3898
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (174 training sequences, 36,386 test; the variable region is 10 aa, so CPU-only models suffice)
targets.statement: Mason, Friedensohn, Weber and co-authors, with Reddy, measured antigen binding for a deep mutational library of the CDR-H3 loop of the therapeutic antibody trastuzumab (data released at github.com/dahjan/DMS_opt), a standard testbed for predicting which CDR variants keep binding their target. PLMFit (Bikias, Stamkopoulos and Reddy, Briefings in Bioinformatics 26(4):bbaf381, 2025) ships this landscape as the herH3 dataset - data/herH3/herH3_data_full.csv, 36,560 rows of 449-aa heavy chains with a binary_score column, a one_vs_rest column and ten varying positions (99-108) - and keeps a public scoreboard of the best setups found. As of 2026-10-30 the scoreboard's Trastuzumab one-vs-rest entry is the lowest value it lists: MCC 0.3898 with ProGen2-xlarge and a memory-reduced LoRA, from 174 training rows (173 train plus 1 validation, the single mutants) predicting 36,386 held-out variants, well below the 0.5545 MCC the same framework reaches on its other binary task. The split is an extrapolation design (train on the smallest edit distance, test on everything further away), the labels are binary binder/non-binder, the data and split column are public in the repository, and the sequences differ in only ten positions, so the whole experiment is a laptop job.
targets.success_criterion: Binary predictions (or scores thresholded by a rule fixed on training data only) for every row with one_vs_rest == 'test' in data/herH3/herH3_data_full.csv of github.com/LSSI-ETH/plmfit (36,386 rows), from a model fit only on that split's 173 train and 1 validation rows plus declared public pretraining corpora, such that the Matthews correlation coefficient recomputed by the skeptic with sklearn.metrics.matthews_corrcoef against the file's binary_score column is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the value listed for 'Trastuzumab - one-vs-rest' at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LSSI-ETH/plmfit/main/README.md (0.3898 as of 2026-10-30; re-fetched live immediately before claiming) by at least 0.02, AND higher than any value for the same split found by the NOVELTY check over 2024-2026 literature, reported as mean and standard deviation over at least three seeds with a bootstrap 95% interval over test sequences that excludes the bar. The threshold rule must be published and fixed without any read of test labels.

partial_wins.statement: Beat 0.3898 by >= 0.02 with a model of at most 10M parameters, or with no pretrained language model at all, under the same split and threshold rule.
Report AUROC and average precision for the same split with a published prediction file - threshold-free numbers that nobody has posted for this cell - as a baseline rather than a record.

A released ablation showing how much of the achievable MCC comes from position-wise amino-acid preferences learned from the 174 training sequences versus pairwise interactions within the 10-residue loop.

A threshold-selection audit: show that the claimed MCC is stable under a threshold chosen only by cross-validation on the training rows, and report how much MCC a test-set-optimal threshold would have added.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones github.com/LSSI-ETH/plmfit, reads herH3/herH3_data_full.csv, checks the prediction file covers each test row exactly once with the published split membership, recomputes MCC with scikit-learn, reruns the attacker's script from released seeds, audits the code for any read of test labels and for any threshold tuned on test, and re-fetches the scoreboard. Well under an hour.
angles: 174 labelled sequences over 10 positions: a position-specific scoring matrix with shrinkage, or logistic regression on one-hot plus pairwise features with heavy regularisation, is the honest first baseline and may already be competitive.

MCC is threshold-sensitive and the classes are imbalanced; choose the threshold by nested cross-validation on the training rows and report the rule, since much of the gap to the leader may be calibration rather than ranking.
Cross-domain import (few-shot classification): prototype or nearest-centroid classifiers in a frozen embedding space are strong when training data are this scarce.
Zero-shot antibody likelihoods from several frozen models, combined by rank averaging and calibrated on the 174 training points.
Augment by sampling labelled variants' neighbourhoods under a mutation model to regularise the pairwise terms without touching the test set.
pitfalls: This is binding of an antibody variant library, not developability: FLAb-style properties and ProteinGym substitution scores are different problems and their numbers are not comparable bars.
The split is extrapolation by edit distance; shuffling the rows into a random split inflates MCC enormously and is not the benchmark.
MCC can be gamed by tuning the decision threshold on the test labels; the threshold rule must be fixed on training data and published.
Pretrained checkpoints fine-tuned on this very library (several antibody-specific models were trained on public DMS data) break the design and must be declared.
The scoreboard cell is reported for one setup only; the NOVELTY check must look for higher published MCC on the same split before any claim.

targets.name: Single-point folding stability ddG: beat the published Pearson on the leak-controlled S461 blind set (and the Megascale split record)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours for S461 inference and for training on the public ddG sets; laptop-days if the Megascale split is used for training
targets.statement: Predicting the change in folding free energy on a single point mutation is a long-standing benchmark with maintained public test sets. ProtDDG-Bench (Capriotti, Montanucci and Fariselli, 2023; protddg-bench.github.io and github.com/protddg-bench/protddg-bench) distributes the standard sets with fixed folds: VB1432 (1,432 variants) and S2648 (2,648) with matched 10-fold splits, Ssym (684 rows - 342 mutations and their reverses, although the repository's own README calls it 634), Broom (605), Myoglobin (134), P53 (42), PTMUL (914 multiple-site variants) and the KORPM directory, which holds s461-korpm and ssym-korpm test files plus 10-fold splits of KORPM's 2,371 training mutations. S461 is the 461-mutation subset (48 proteins) of Pancotti and co-authors' S669 blind set, built by Hernandez, Chacon and co-authors to remove erroneous entries and interaction-mediated mutations. As of 2026-10-30 the highest S461 Pearson verifiable from a primary source is 0.69, and three published methods sit on it: JanusDDG (Barducci, Rossi, Codice, Rollo, Repetto, Pancotti, Iannibelli, Sanavia and Fariselli, Communications Biology 9:494, 3 February 2026), which is sequence-only, enforces antisymmetry exactly (forward/reverse Pearson -1.00) and reaches balanced accuracy 0.75 on the stabilising/destabilising call; GeoDDG-Seq (Xu, Liu and Gong, Nature Computational Science, 2024) at Pearson 0.69 with Spearman 0.68; and DVE-stability (Briefings in Bioinformatics, 2025) at Pearson 0.69 with Spearman 0.67, the last two read from DVE-stability's Supplementary Table S1. For context, the structure-based predictors tabulated by OrgNet+ (Bioinformatics 2026) top out near 0.63 on S461 and OrgNet+ itself reaches 0.58. On the separate Megascale benchmark of Tsuboyama and co-authors, using the ThermoMPNN 8:1:1 split of Dieckhaus, Brocidiacono, Randolph and Kuhlman (PNAS 121:e2314853121), SPURS (Li and Luo, Nature Communications 17:891, 20 December 2025) reports median per-protein Spearman 0.83 against ThermoMPNN's 0.77 over 28,312 mutants in 28 proteins, while its own S461 numbers are Spearman 0.66 and Pearson 0.64.
targets.success_criterion: Predicted ddG for every variant of the S461 test file s461-korpm.csv (or .tsv) in the KORPM directory of github.com/protddg-bench/protddg-bench, taken unchanged and in the released order, from a model trained only on declared public data that contains no S461 variant (same protein and position counts as leakage unless the attacker publishes the clustering showing otherwise), such that the Pearson correlation recomputed by the skeptic against the released experimental values is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than 0.69 - the S461 Pearson reported by JanusDDG at https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC13056967/fullTextXML, re-fetched live immediately before claiming - by at least 0.02, AND higher than any newer published S461 value found by the NOVELTY check (including values that appear only in figures or supplementary tables, with the source stated), with a bootstrap 95% interval over variants excluding 0.69, with RMSE reported, and with the antisymmetry check on ssym-korpm reported (Pearson between forward and reverse predictions, target -1).

partial_wins.statement: Beat the Megascale-split value instead: median per-protein Spearman strictly above 0.83 - the value SPURS reports, against ThermoMPNN's 0.77 - on the ThermoMPNN 8:1:1 test split of the Tsuboyama megascale data, with the per-protein table published, the split files taken unchanged from the ThermoMPNN repository, and a NOVELTY check against 2026 hybrid models that report gains on this same split.
Beat 0.69 on S461 with a sequence-only model of at most 150M parameters that needs no experimental structure at inference time, with runtime reported.

Publish a reproducible 10-fold result on the matched VB1432/S2648 folds distributed by ProtDDG-Bench (training on one set's complement, testing on the other's fold) that beats the attacker's own reproduced baseline by >= 0.03 Pearson, with all fold files unchanged.
Exact antisymmetry with no loss of accuracy: Ssym forward/reverse Pearson of -1.00 together with an S461 Pearson at least equal to 0.69, demonstrated from published prediction files.
A multiple-mutation result on the PTMUL set from ProtDDG-Bench that beats the attacker's own reproduced single-mutation-additive baseline by >= 0.05 Pearson, with the prediction file published.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic clones github.com/protddg-bench/protddg-bench, takes the S461 (and Ssym) test files unchanged, checks the prediction file covers each variant exactly once in the released order, recomputes Pearson, Spearman, RMSE and the antisymmetry correlation, bootstraps over variants, audits the declared training data for S461 proteins and positions (by sequence clustering, not only by PDB id), reruns the attacker's inference from released weights or code, and re-fetches the JanusDDG and SPURS papers for the current bars. An hour or two.
angles: Transfer learning from the megascale dataset to the small classical sets is what moved the field (ThermoMPNN); the remaining headroom on S461 may come from better regularisation of that transfer rather than from a bigger encoder.

Enforce antisymmetry architecturally (predict from the mutation and its reverse with a sign-flipping head) instead of penalising it in the loss - the published leaders do this and it also removes a whole class of evaluation artefacts.

Cross-domain import (physics-informed learning): combine a cheap empirical energy term (hydrophobic burial, hydrogen-bond counts from the structure) with the learned term as an additive, interpretable model.
Ensemble sequence-only and structure-based predictors with a weighting fitted on the training folds only; the two families fail on different mutation classes.
Report and exploit the reverse-mutation data: Ssym's reverse entries are free training signal for symmetry without new experiments.
pitfalls: S669/S461 leakage is the classic trap: most published training sets (S2648, VB1432, FireProt, megascale) overlap S461 proteins. A claim must publish the clustering that shows the training data is clean, not just a PDB-id comparison.

0.69 is the best S461 Pearson verifiable from a primary source on 2026-10-30 and it is a three-way tie (JanusDDG, GeoDDG-Seq, DVE-stability), not a proven ceiling. Several 2025-2026 papers report S461 PCCs only in supplementary tables (for example Pythia with mass-balance correction in Protein Science 2025, stated in the text only as above DDGun3D's 0.62, and DVE-stability in Briefings in Bioinformatics 2025), so the bar may already have moved where a text search cannot see it.

A June 2026 preprint (arXiv 2606.08100, Shivram, Chivukula, Gupta and Chowdhury) reports S461 Spearman 0.711 +- 0.006 by retraining the SPURS backbone with balanced-MSE, Siamese antisymmetry and OOD-margin losses against its own 0.653 baseline, and publishes no S461 Pearson. A Pearson claim anywhere near 0.69-0.71 must engage with that result and state its metric explicitly.

Different papers report different metrics on these sets (overall Pearson, per-protein mean, Spearman, balanced accuracy, direct versus reverse, with or without conformational-ensemble augmentation); mixing protocols produces false records. State the metric and the exact file.
Predictors that are only antisymmetric on average can score well on S669 while failing Ssym; report both.

The Megascale split and the S461 blind set are different problems with different bars; a win must be claimed on one of them explicitly, and 2026 papers (SA-MPNN, UniStab, StrucNS) report Megascale-family numbers on subsets that are not this split.
ddG sign conventions differ between datasets (destabilising positive or negative); a sign error turns a strong model into a negative correlation.
This field publishes fast, so the NOVELTY check must be done immediately before claiming and must say where each competing number was read.

targets.name: SKEMPI 2.0 binding ddG: beat the published external-validation Pearson on the fixed S1131 and M1707 test sets
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (7,085 mutations with public complex structures; CPU-trainable graph and descriptor models)
targets.statement: SKEMPI 2.0 (Jankauskaite, Jimenez-Garcia, Dapkunas, Fernandez-Recio and Moal, Bioinformatics 35:462-469, 2019; life.bsc.es/pid/skempi2) is the reference database of experimentally measured changes in protein-protein binding energetics on mutation: 7,085 mutations, each with a solved complex structure, downloadable without registration together with cleaned PDB files. The community evaluates on fixed derived subsets: S1131 (non-redundant interface single-point mutations), S4169 and its reverse-augmented S8338, and M1707 (multiple mutations), either under split-by-structure cross-validation or as fixed blind test sets with training on the complementary SKEMPI subsets C5062 and C4856. IGMI (Wu, Xu, Xin, Zhang, Liu, Zhu, Wei, Zhao, Yu and Feng, Bioinformatics 42(4):btag150, published online 27 March 2026; github.com/ShiweiWu-545/IGMI with a Zenodo archive) reports the current published highs: in the blind external-validation setting Pearson 0.74 on S1131 and 0.91 on M1707, and under split-by-structure cross-validation 0.79 on S1131, 0.69 on S4169 and 0.77 with RMSE 2.08 on M1707, against GeoPPI at 0.57, 0.50 and 0.73, MutaBind2 at 0.71 and FoldX at 0.51 on M1707. Interface ddG prediction on structurally disjoint complexes is still far from solved, and all the data and splits are public.
targets.success_criterion: Predicted binding ddG for every mutation in the fixed external-validation test sets (S1131 and M1707) distributed with the IGMI release, from a model trained only on the complementary SKEMPI 2.0 subsets published with that release (C5062 for S1131, C4856 for M1707) plus declared public structural pretraining that contains no binding ddG labels, such that the Pearson correlation recomputed by the skeptic is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the published external-validation values - 0.74 on S1131 and 0.91 on M1707, from Bioinformatics 42(4):btag150 at https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC13070472/fullTextXML, re-fetched live immediately before claiming - by at least 0.02 on the set being claimed, AND higher than any newer published value on the same set found by the NOVELTY check, with RMSE reported and a bootstrap 95% interval over mutations that excludes the published value.

partial_wins.statement: Beat the published split-by-structure cross-validation Pearson on S4169 (0.69, against GeoPPI 0.50) by >= 0.02 using the released split files unchanged, with per-fold numbers published.
Beat the published split-by-structure M1707 result on BOTH metrics (Pearson > 0.77 and RMSE < 2.08 kcal/mol) with the released splits, for multiple-mutation prediction.

A reproduction artefact: an end-to-end pipeline, published with code and manifest, that reproduces a documented baseline's S1131 external-validation Pearson to within 0.03 from the public SKEMPI 2.0 download - reported as a reproduction, not a record.
A sequence-only model (no complex structure at inference) that beats GeoPPI's published S1131 and S4169 numbers (0.57 and 0.50) under the same protocol, with prediction files published.

A released leakage audit of the chosen split: for every test mutation, the maximum interface similarity to any training complex (for example by iAlign or Foldseek), plus the metrics restricted to the least similar half.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads SKEMPI 2.0 from life.bsc.es/pid/skempi2 (free, no registration) and the split files from the IGMI repository or its Zenodo archive, checks the prediction file covers each test mutation exactly once, recomputes Pearson, Spearman and RMSE, bootstraps over mutations, audits training membership against the test sets by complex and by mutation, checks no reverse-mutation twin of a test entry is in training, reruns the attacker's code from released seeds, and re-fetches the IGMI paper. A few hours.
angles: Antisymmetry again: S8338 is S4169 plus reverse mutations, so a sign-flipping architecture gives the right inductive bias for free and prevents the common over-prediction of destabilisation.

Cross-domain import (graph learning with structural priors): featurise only the interface neighbourhood (contacts, burial, conservation) rather than the whole complex; with a few thousand labels, small feature sets regularise better than large ones.
Additive decomposition for M1707: predict single-mutation effects and learn a correction for the interaction between mutations, which gives an interpretable baseline that is hard to beat.
Empirical energy terms (FoldX-style) as features inside a learned model rather than as competitors, with the weighting fitted on the training complexes only.
Use the kinetic data in SKEMPI 2.0 (on-rates and off-rates) as auxiliary supervision for mutations where ddG is unavailable.
pitfalls: Mixing protocols is the main source of false records here: external-validation, split-by-structure and random-split numbers differ by 0.1 or more Pearson on the same data. State which protocol and which file.
Reverse mutations make random splits leaky: a mutation's reverse in training all but gives away the label. Check for reverse twins explicitly.
Homologous complexes across splits (the same interface in a different PDB entry) are the subtler leak; an interface-similarity audit is required for a credible claim.

Several entries in SKEMPI 2.0 have corrected or duplicated measurements (the database's own news page records such fixes); recomputing the subsets from a fresh download can silently change the test set, so use the released split files.
Published highs for IGMI on S8338 are not numerically stated in the paper's text (they appear only in a figure), so a claim must be made on a set whose number can be read literally.
Antibody-antigen subsets of SKEMPI are used by separate antibody-specific benchmarks; comparing against those numbers is a category error.

targets.name: TSPTW makespan (Lopez-Ibanez collection): beat the best-known makespan 917.83 of rc_204.1, the last open makespan cell
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (one 46-node asymmetric instance with 4-decimal travel times; anytime DP, beam search or LNS runs)
targets.statement: Manuel Lopez-Ibanez (with Christian Blum) maintains the canonical TSPTW benchmark collection at lopez-ibanez.eu/tsptw-instances. It has 467 instances, best-known permutations for the travel-time and makespan objectives, and a bounds file per objective (page last modified 30 Dec 2023, re-fetched 2026-10-30). For makespan (the return time to the depot, waiting included), Makespan_Bounds.csv still shows 5 rows with a nonzero gap against the peel-and-bound dual bounds of Isaac Rudich, Quentin Cappart and Louis-Martin Rousseau (JAIR 2023). That count is what remained after Romain Fontaine, Jilles Dibangoye and Christine Solnon (EJOR 2023) closed 7 of 12. Four of those five are now closed. F. J. Soulignac ('Beware of the Classical Benchmark Instances for the Traveling Salesman Problem with Time Windows', arXiv 2512.01064, Computers & Operations Research 2026; code and results.json at github.com/fsoulignac/tsptw-m) solved every classical instance with 50 or more customers exactly. His published optimal routes give n80w180.002 = 633, n80w200.004 = 667, n200w120.002 = 1072 and n200w140.003 = 1083, equal to the posted best-known values; the CSV has not been updated. The one remaining open makespan cell is SolomonPotvinBengio rc_204.1 (Potvin and Bengio 1996, derived from Solomon's RC2 instances; 46 nodes = depot + 45 customers; travel times with 4 decimals). Its best-known makespan is 917.83 (the posted permutation evaluates to 917.8265), from the Beam-ACO and compressed-annealing work of Lopez-Ibanez, Blum, Ohlmann and Thomas (Applied Soft Computing 2013) and later contributors credited on the page. Its Rudich bound is 915.2194. Soulignac's exact solver runs out of memory on it, and he reports that the exact methods of Rudich et al. and Fontaine et al. jointly left it unsolved within an hour. Find a feasible route with makespan below 917.83, or certify that the gap is closed.
targets.success_criterion: A permutation of customers 1..45 of rc_204.1 (depot 0 excluded, as in the site's best-known files). It is evaluated by a standalone checker written from the page's format description: line 1 is n = 46; then the 46 x 46 matrix (row i = travel time i->j, with the service time of i already folded in); then 46 time windows (e_i, l_i), node 0 = depot. Start at the depot at time 0. At each next node j, t = max(t + d[i][j], e_j), and t <= l_j must hold, including on the return to the depot; use exact decimal arithmetic. The checker must report zero violations and a return time at the depot that, rounded to 2 decimals, is at most 917.82. That is strictly below the 'Best Known Solution' 917.83 in the rc_204.1 row of Makespan_Bounds.csv (direction: min). Before any claim, the same checker must reproduce the posted rc_204.1 permutation in SolomonPotvinBengio-best-known-makespan.txt (makespan 917.8265, travel time 917.7523, 0 violations; vetted 2026-10-30). The new value must not fall below the Rudich bound 915.2194, which would mean a checker bug. Right before claiming, re-fetch the CSV and the page, and search the citing works of arXiv 2512.01064 and of Fontaine et al. (EJOR 2023) for newer exact results on rc_204.1; the cell must still be open. The permutation, checker and CSV snapshot are saved together. Nothing is submitted; the write-up goes to the human.

partial_wins.statement: Close the rc_204.1 makespan gap without improving the route. This means a proof that no feasible route has makespan below 917.8265, or a proven lower bound strictly above 915.2194. It must come from an exact solver whose code is released and which the skeptic re-runs to the same result, cross-checked by a second, independently implemented exact method (for example a labelling DP over (visited set, last node) with dominance, against a MIP or decision-diagram bound).

targets.verification_method: The skeptic downloads SolomonPotvinBengio.tar.gz and SolomonPotvinBengio-best-known-makespan.txt from lopez-ibanez.eu/files/TSPTW/. It writes or reuses an independent checker of about 30 lines; the site's check_solution.cpp may be read to confirm the conventions but need not be run. The checker must first reproduce the posted rc_204.1 makespan 917.8265. Then it evaluates the claimed permutation: zero violations, makespan rounded to 2 decimals <= 917.82, and not below 915.2194. Finally the skeptic re-fetches Makespan_Bounds.csv and searches for newer exact results on rc_204.1. This takes seconds on any machine. For p1, the skeptic re-runs the released solver and the second method.
angles: rc_204.1 is small (45 customers), but its windows are loose relative to the horizon, which is why exact informed searches exhaust memory on it. A labelling DP over (visited set, last node, arrival time) is the natural first try, with time-window reachability pruning, dominance and 917.83 as the incumbent. A bidirectional search may help.

Anytime beam search for domain-independent dynamic programming (Kuroiwa and Beck, AAAI 2024), or the Fontaine-Dibangoye-Solnon anytime approach, run for hours with the best-known value as the incumbent.

Large neighbourhood search with CP sequence variables (Delecluse et al. 2022) or decision diagrams (Gillard and Schaus 2022), seeded from the posted permutation. Re-optimise windows of 10-20 consecutive positions exactly for makespan.
GVNS for makespan (Amghar, Cordeau and Gendron) or Beam-ACO with many seeds as a cheap restart loop.
pitfalls: The other four rows that still show a gap in Makespan_Bounds.csv (n80w180.002, n80w200.004, n200w120.002, n200w140.003) are closed. Soulignac's exact solver proves their posted values optimal (results.json in github.com/fsoulignac/tsptw-m), and the CSV is simply not updated. Do not chase them.
The distance matrix already includes the service time of the origin node, so do not add service times again.
Makespan is the arrival time back at the depot, waiting included. A tour that is shorter in travel time can be worse in makespan.
rc_204.1 travel times have 4 decimals. Evaluate in exact decimal arithmetic and compare after rounding to 2 decimals, as the table does (917.8265 is listed as 917.83).

Do not chase the travel-time rows that show a gap in Traveltime_Bounds.csv. Their 'Relaxed Bound' is Baldacci et al.'s reported optimum, which the maintainer says is not reliable on the canonical files.
Use the canonical file from this page, not a recreated Potvin-Bengio instance.

targets.name: Sartori-Buriol real-road PDPTW instances (100-5000 locations): hierarchically beat a best known solution in the live GitHub table
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (instance files carry full OSRM travel-time matrices, up to 5000 x 5000 integers)
targets.statement: Carlo S. Sartori and Luciana S. Buriol (Computers & Operations Research 2020) published 300 pickup-and-delivery-with-time-windows instances built from real addresses and OSRM travel times in Barcelona, Berlin, New York and Porto Alegre. There are 12 sizes (100, 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000 and 5000 locations) with 25 instances each, under CC BY 4.0 on Mendeley Data (doi 10.17632/wr2ct4r22f.2). Sartori maintains the best known solutions, each with a solution file, in github.com/cssartori/pdptw-instances (solutions/README.md and solutions/bks.dat). They are ranked hierarchically: fewer vehicles first, then lower total travel time (integer minutes). The table is live. On 2026-10-30, 270 of the 300 rows had been set by the BigThree team (Dmitriy Yampolskiy, Egor Nikolaev, Daria Savina; Smart Logistics Point) on 01-Oct-2026. One row is by Pengfei He, Zixiang Tian (spelled 'Tain' in the README), Jin-Kao Hao, Yuning Chen and Qinghua Wu (poa-n800-5, 70 vehicles / 4271, 25-Aug-2026). One is by Yuskov, Kulachenko, Kochetov, Vasilyev et al. (nyc-n100-3, 28-Apr-2025). Advantum (Churilov & Galko) holds 1 row (2025), CUHK-SZ with Huawei 2 (2024), Isaiah Reimer (RideCo) 12 (2023) and Sartori & Buriol 13 (2019). The table has no optimality column. All rows with 200 or more locations moved in 2024-2026 except ber-n200-3 (Sartori & Buriol, 2019) and ber-n200-4 (Reimer, 2023). Find a feasible solution that is hierarchically better than the listed BKS on any instance with 200 to 5000 locations, other than ber-n200-3 and ber-n200-4.
targets.success_criterion: A solution file in the repository's format ('Route k : id id ...', depot 0 not listed) for one instance with 200-5000 locations, other than ber-n200-3 and ber-n200-4. It is judged by a standalone checker written from instances/how_to_read.txt, which verifies that: (a) every node 1..SIZE-1 is visited exactly once; (b) each pickup i and its delivery i+(SIZE-1)/2 are on the same route, with the pickup first; (c) the running load never exceeds CAPACITY; (d) on each route, starting at the depot at t=0, for each next node a: t += T[prev][a], t = max(t, etw_a), t <= ltw_a, then t += dur_a, and the return to the depot satisfies t <= the depot's ltw; and (e) cost = the sum of T over all arcs, the return arc included. The result must have strictly fewer routes than the instance's row in solutions/bks.dat, or the same number of routes and a strictly smaller integer cost. The bks.dat row is re-fetched live right before claiming (raw.githubusercontent.com/cssartori/pdptw-instances/master/solutions/bks.dat; 300 rows, sha256 036fd50d... on 2026-10-30). Before any claim, the same checker must reproduce the vehicles and cost in the posted BKS file name ( < instance > . < vehicles > _ < cost > .txt in solutions/files/) for that instance and for poa-n800-5 (70 / 4271, reproduced by the vetter 2026-10-30). The solution, checker, instance sha256 and bks.dat snapshot are saved together. The agent emails and submits nothing; the write-up goes to the human.

partial_wins.statement: For an instance with 1000 or more locations, a feasible solution (same checker) whose total cost is strictly below the bks.dat cost while using more vehicles than the BKS: cost-side progress that is not a hierarchical win.

For an instance with 1000 or more locations, a feasible solution with exactly the BKS vehicle count and cost whose undirected arc set differs from the posted BKS file's arc set in at least 10% of arcs (same checker computes the comparison): an independent alternative optimum candidate.

targets.verification_method: The skeptic downloads the size-group zip from https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/wr2ct4r22f/2 (public, CC BY 4.0) and the posted BKS file from https://github.com/cssartori/pdptw-instances/tree/master/solutions/files. It runs an independent checker (rules (a)-(e) above, written from how_to_read.txt; it need not run the repository's validator.py) on the posted file first, which must reproduce the vehicles and cost in its file name, then on the claimed file. Finally it re-fetches bks.dat and compares the instance's row hierarchically. Minutes per instance; the 5000-location matrices are about 25 million integers.
angles: Seed from the posted BKS file and run pair-aware ALNS (Ropke-Pisinger removal and insertion of whole request pairs) with a route-elimination phase (ejection pool / squeeze); vehicle count is the primary objective, so most value lies in removing one route.
Decomposition for the 2000-5000 location instances (Hiermann & Schiffer 2024, arXiv 2405.00230, built on these instances): split by geography or time, re-optimise sub-problems, re-merge.

Exact polishing at equal vehicle count: fix all but 3-5 neighbouring routes and solve the induced small PDPTW exactly with CP-SAT or set partitioning over enumerated routes; any strict improvement is global.
Travel times are asymmetric road times (OSRM); neighbourhoods that assume symmetry (2-opt reversal) change cost in both directions and must be re-evaluated in full.
pitfalls: The repository's own validator.py checks precedence with a global visited array, so a delivery on a different route from its pickup can pass it. PDPTW requires the same route, so the independent checker must check same-route pairing explicitly.
Ranking is hierarchical (updater.py compares vehicles first, then cost): a lower-cost solution with more vehicles is not better.
The table moves in bursts (270 rows replaced on 2026-10-01). A win against a cached bks.dat may already be stale, so re-fetch the raw file right before claiming.

The 100-location rows (many unchanged since 2019) and the two 200-location rows unchanged since 2019/2023 (ber-n200-3, ber-n200-4) are left out of the win condition. The table carries no optimality information, and long-unbeaten small rows may be optimal.
SIZE counts the depot. Pickups are 1..(SIZE-1)/2, and their deliveries are offset by (SIZE-1)/2. Cost excludes service and waiting time, but both count toward time-window feasibility.

The Mendeley 'Download All' bundle is 1.23 GB as the page reports it (the 14 files in Instances/ sum to 1.32 GB). Range-read only the size-group zip you need from the Instances folder (n800.zip is 13.35 MB; n5000.zip is 506.73 MB); the page lists them only with JavaScript, so the folder ids come from /public-api/datasets/wr2ct4r22f/folders/2.

This target overlaps in problem class with the bank's sintef-lilim-pdptw-bks (Li & Lim instances, SINTEF table). It is a different instance library and table, so do not mix the two tables or their solution formats.

targets.name: Flexible job shop (FJSPLib: Brandimarte mk10, Dauzere-Peres-Paulli, Behnke-Geiger, Hurink): lower the best known makespan of an open instance
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: In the flexible job shop (FJSP) each operation of a job must run, in job order, on one machine chosen from an eligible set with a machine-dependent duration; minimise makespan. FJSPLib, maintained by ScheduleOpt (Diego Olivier Fernandez Pons and colleagues) at github.com/ScheduleOpt/benchmarks, keeps a best-known-bounds archive for 452 instances (solutions/bks.json, with a dated history per bound); the last commits are 2026-10-18 ('New bks, historical bks') and 2026-10-22. On 2026-10-30 the flexible and machine-independent families still open there (LB < UB) are: mk10 (189/193, UB Quintiq); 10 Dauzere-Peres-Paulli instances (e.g. dpp05a 2195/2199 and dpp06a 2164/2169 from Coupvent des Graviers, Kobrosly, Guettier and Cazenave 2025, and dpp07a 2216/2254 from Ding, Lu, Li, Shen, Xu and Glover 2019); 27 Behnke-Geiger instances (e.g. behnke7 117/124 and behnke16 392/412; UBs from OptalCP 2025, LBs from CP-SAT and DOFP2026a); and 15 Hurink instances (abz7/abz8/abz9 rdata, abz7/abz8 edata, abz8_vdata 506/507, la21-la26 and la28-la30 rdata). Earlier bounds come from Mastrolilli-Gambardella 2000, Quintiq's 2013 records, Puget's CP Optimizer 12.6 runs (2013) and Touko Ursin's 2026 issue reports. FJSPLib does not carry every published record. Zhang, Lu, Ding, Su, Li and Gao (AWLS, Engineering 50 (2025) 117-127, Table 7) report smaller makespans on eight of these instances: dpp07a 2249, dpp13a 2227, dpp16a 2224, abz8_rdata 534, abz9_rdata 535, la21_rdata 824, la23_rdata 830 and la30_rdata 1070. Find a feasible schedule for one of these open instances with makespan strictly below its best known upper bound, i.e. the smaller of the FJSPLib value and any published value.
targets.success_criterion: A schedule for one instance whose bks.json entry (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ScheduleOpt/benchmarks/main/flexible-jobshop/solutions/bks.json) has status 'open' and family mk, dpp, behnke, abz or la. Give it as one line per operation (job, operation index, machine, start time). An independent checker reads the FJSPLib text instance (flexible-jobshop/instances/fjsp/ < family folder > / < name > .txt; machines are numbered from 1, e.g. mk01.txt '2 1 5 3 4' = two eligible machines, machine 1 with duration 5 and machine 3 with duration 4). It confirms that every operation is assigned exactly once to an eligible machine with that machine's duration, that the operations of a job run in order without overlap, and that no machine runs two operations at once. The makespan must be strictly below the smallest of three values: (a) the instance's upper_bound in bks.json, (b) its README table value, and (c) any makespan published for that instance in the literature. Re-fetch (a) and (b) live immediately before claiming. Search 2024-2026 FJSP papers for (c); at minimum it includes the AWLS values of Zhang et al., Engineering 50 (2025), Table 7: dpp07a 2249, dpp13a 2227, dpp16a 2224, abz8_rdata 534, abz9_rdata 535, la21_rdata 824, la23_rdata 830 and la30_rdata 1070. yfjs and dafjs (flexible assembly) entries do not count. The agent submits nothing to the maintainers; reporting a new bound through an issue is the human's choice.

partial_wins.statement: A schedule meeting the success-criterion threshold on any open Behnke-Geiger instance (behnke7, behnke11-behnke20, behnke32, behnke34-behnke40, behnke51, behnke53-behnke59; behnke33 and behnke52 closed in October 2026; behnke29 is closed in bks.json), verified by the checker.

A schedule meeting the success-criterion threshold on any open Dauzere-Peres-Paulli instance (dpp05a, dpp06a, dpp07a, dpp10a-dpp13a, dpp16a-dpp18a) or on mk10, verified by the checker. For dpp07a, dpp13a and dpp16a the bar is the AWLS value (2249, 2227, 2224), not bks.json.

A schedule meeting the success-criterion threshold on any open Hurink instance (abz7, abz8, abz9, la21-la26 and la28-la30 rdata; abz7 and abz8 edata; abz8_vdata), verified by the checker. la27_rdata is closed. For abz8_rdata, abz9_rdata, la21_rdata, la23_rdata and la30_rdata the bar is the AWLS value (534, 535, 824, 830, 1070).

targets.verification_method: Fetch the instance text file from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ScheduleOpt/benchmarks/main/flexible-jobshop/instances/fjsp/ < folder > / < name > .txt (first line 'jobs machines [avg]', then per job: number of operations, and per operation the number of eligible machines followed by (machine, duration) pairs with machines numbered from 1). Hurink files sit in HurinkJurischThole1994/ < edata|rdata|sdata|vdata > / < laNN|abzN > .txt. A ~60-line Python checker validates assignment, durations, job precedence and machine no-overlap and recomputes the makespan. Test it first on a schedule for a closed instance (e.g. mk01, proven 40). Then parse bks.json and the README row for the instance and compare. Seconds.
angles: CP with optional intervals per (operation, machine) plus failure-directed search seeded from a good heuristic schedule; OptalCP and CP-SAT set most 2025-2026 bounds, so long multi-worker runs with solution hints are the baseline to beat.
Tabu search on the machine-assignment plus sequencing graph (Mastrolilli-Gambardella neighbourhoods, Ding et al. 2019 two-individual EA) run for hours, seeded with a CP-SAT incumbent.
Large-neighbourhood search: free all operations in a time window or on a machine subset and re-solve exactly with CP-SAT.
Gap-1 instances (abz8_vdata, la26/la28/la29_rdata) are best attacked as satisfiability searches for makespan UB-1.
pitfalls: bks.json lags the literature. AWLS (Zhang et al., Engineering 2025, Table 7) beats it on dpp07a, dpp13a, dpp16a, abz8_rdata, abz9_rdata, la21_rdata, la23_rdata and la30_rdata, and that paper's own text and Tables 6 and 7 disagree on dpp16a (2228, 2226, 2224), so take the smallest, 2224. Search recent FJSP papers for the instance before claiming.
bks.json and the README table can disagree (e.g. dafjs: README says 3 closed/27 open, bks.json lists 30 open); re-read both and use the smaller UB.
The yfjs/dafjs flexible assembly bounds date from Birgin-Ferreira-Ronconi 2015 and may lag the literature; they are excluded from this target.
Some UB dates in bks.json are placeholders (e.g. Quintiq values dated 2026-01-01); credit the solver field, not the date.
Hurink instances exist in four variants (sdata/edata/rdata/vdata) with identical names; a claim must name the variant folder.

Instances close quickly through GitHub issues: behnke33, behnke52, behnke60 and mk13 closed in October 2026 (issues #10-#13). Issue #8 (behnke29) is still open, but bks.json already lists behnke29 as closed at 117. Re-check the issue tracker as well as bks.json before claiming.

targets.name: XHSTT high school timetabling (Post archive): beat a best known solution cost on an open XHSTT-2014 instance
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: XHSTT is the XML standard for (high) school timetabling instances created by Gerhard Post and colleagues. The archive at the University of Twente keeps, per instance, every submitted solution with its cost (infeasibility value, objective value) and lower bounds. The archive is live: on 2026-09-29 Dionisio Chiuratto Agourakis submitted Brazil Instance7 at 44 (with a lower bound of 40), and on 2026-10-06 Wieslaw Dudek submitted 42. The XHSTT-2014 overview (instances and best solutions, last updated 16 Nov 2022) lists these open instances as best/LB: AU-BG-98 126/0 (its instance page lists 128 as the best stored solution), DK-FG-12 1263/412, DK-HG-12 12.2330/7.0 (infeasibility 12, objective 2330), DK-VG-09 2.2323/2.0, ES-SS-08 335/334, NL-KP-03 199/0, NL-KP-05 425/89, NL-KP-09 1620/180, UK-SP-06 2.1410/0.0. Most of these bests are from the UFOP-GOAL team (George Fonseca, Haroldo Santos, Eduardo Carrano; solutions dated Dec 2016, received 17 April 2017). ES-SS-08's best is Matias Sorensen's (Jan 2016), with LB 334 from Simon Kristiansen, Sorensen and Thomas Stidsen. UK-SP-06's best is Wieslaw Dudek's (Oct 2022). Jeffrey Kingston wrote the HSEval evaluator and KHE. Costs compare hierarchically: lower infeasibility first, then lower objective. Find a solution strictly better than the best known for an open instance.
targets.success_criterion: An XHSTT solution file for one instance that is open (best > LB) on https://www.utwente.nl/en/eemcs/dmmp/hstt/archives/XHSTT-2014/overview.html, whose cost, computed by an independent evaluator written from the XHSTT specification that first reproduces the cost of the best solution stored in that instance's own XML file, is hierarchically strictly lower (smaller infeasibility value, or equal infeasibility and smaller objective) than the best value on both the overview and the instance's dataset page, re-fetched live immediately before claiming. A cross-check with Kingston's HSEval is done by the human, not the agent; nothing is submitted to the archive by the agent.

partial_wins.statement: A strictly better feasible solution (infeasibility 0) for NL-KP-03, NL-KP-05, NL-KP-09, DK-FG-12 or AU-BG-98, verified by the independent evaluator.

For DK-HG-12 (best 12.2330, LB 7.0) or UK-SP-06 (best 2.1410, LB 0.0): a solution with lower infeasibility than the best, or equal infeasibility and lower objective. For DK-VG-09 (best 2.2323, LB (2,0)): infeasibility 2 with objective below 2323. Verified by the evaluator.

A strictly better solution for an instance outside XHSTT-2014 whose dataset page shows best > LB (e.g. Brazil Instance7: best 42 by Dudek on 2026-10-06 vs LB 40; Netherlands Kottenpark2008: 0.34586 vs LB 2795), verified by the evaluator.

targets.verification_method: Download the instance XML from its dataset page (e.g. https://www.utwente.nl/en/eemcs/dmmp/hstt/datasets/Netherlands/Kottenpark2009/, file 'instance and solutions'), which embeds the submitted solution groups. Write an evaluator for the constraint types present (AssignTime, AssignResource, SplitEvents, DistributeSplitEvents, PreferTimes, PreferResources, SpreadEvents, LinkEvents, OrderEvents, AvoidClashes, AvoidUnavailableTimes, LimitIdleTimes, ClusterBusyTimes, LimitBusyTimes, with Linear/Quadratic cost functions) from the specification; it must reproduce the stored best solution's (infeasibility, objective) exactly before evaluating the claim. Minutes.
angles: Kottenpark instances (NL-KP-03/05/09) have the largest gaps (199/0, 425/89, 1620/180) and best values from a single 2016 method; a MIP/CP-SAT matheuristic that fixes most of the timetable and re-optimises one class or one day at a time is the natural lever.
Two-phase: first time assignment with CP-SAT (hard constraints only), then resource assignment as a min-cost flow or small MIP.
Kristiansen-Sorensen-Stidsen style integer programming for the Danish (Lectio) instances, where students are explicit resources.
pitfalls: The overview page was last updated 16 Nov 2022 and can disagree with the instance pages (AU-BG-98: overview 126, instance page 128); a claim must beat the better of the two.
Instances were revised (e.g. Australian ones in March 2016, Brazil Instance7 in April 2015); evaluate against the current XHSTT-2014 file, not older archive versions.
Cost is hierarchical: a solution with lower objective but higher infeasibility is worse.
ES-SS-08 has a gap of one (335 vs LB 334), and DK-VG-09's infeasibility cannot drop below its LB of 2. Check the literature for an optimality proof before working on near-closed instances.
Papers may report better values than the archive without submitting them; only archived values are the reference, but note any such published claim in the write-up.

targets.name: Curriculum-based course timetabling (ITC-2007 track 3, UD2): beat the best known penalty on an open comp instance
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days
targets.statement: Curriculum-based course timetabling (CB-CTT; Di Gaspero and Schaerf 2002; ITC-2007 track 3) assigns lectures of courses to periods and rooms subject to conflicts, availabilities and room occupancy, minimising soft penalties for room capacity, minimum working days, isolated curriculum lectures and room stability (formulation UD2, Bonutti, De Cesco, Di Gaspero and Schaerf 2012). OptHub (Intelligent Optimization Lab, University of Udine) is the live successor of the old CB-CTT portal and lists every uploaded solution per instance. On 2026-10-29 the best known UD2 values on the 21 ITC-2007 instances include comp03 64 (Kiefer; matched by Schaerf 2026-02-20), comp05 283 (Luciano Rigolin de Almeida, 2022), comp09 96 (Lu and Hao; matched by Schaerf 2026), comp12 289 (Andrea Schaerf, 2026-02-20), comp15 62 (Alexander Kiefer), comp18 61 (Kiefer), comp21 74 (Antony Phillips). Banbara et al. (teaspoon, Ann. Oper. Res. 2019, Table 4) proved optimality in UD2 for comp02, 04, 06, 07, 08, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16, 17, 19, 20, and comp01 = 5 is known optimal; the seven instances above have no published matching lower bound as far as the vetter found. Find a feasible timetable with a strictly lower UD2 penalty than the OptHub best for one of comp03, comp05, comp09, comp12, comp15, comp18 or comp21.
targets.success_criterion: A solution file (one line per lecture: course room day period) for comp03, comp05, comp09, comp12, comp15, comp18 or comp21, that an independent checker written from the UD2 definition (Bonutti et al. 2012) reports as hard-feasible (all lectures scheduled, no conflicts, availabilities respected, at most one lecture per room and period) with UD2 penalty strictly below the 'Best solution' shown for that instance on https://opthub.uniud.it/problems/timetabling/edutt/ctt/cb-ctt-ud2, re-fetched live immediately before claiming. The checker must first reproduce the OptHub objective of the current best solution file (e.g. 289 for comp12_15.sol, 283 for comp05_melhorado_luciano_almeida.sol). Nothing is uploaded by the agent.

partial_wins.statement: A strictly better UD2 solution for comp05 (283) or comp12 (289), the two instances with the largest penalties, verified by the checker.
A strictly better UD2 solution for comp03, comp09, comp15, comp18 or comp21, verified by the checker.
A strictly better UD2 solution for an erlangen2011_2 to erlangen2014_1 instance (best 4,441 to 8,813 on OptHub), verified by the checker.

targets.verification_method: Instances: https://opthubstorage.blob.core.windows.net/opthub-data/timetabling/edutt/ctt/cb-ctt-ud2/instances/ectt/ < name > .ectt. Best solution files: linked from each instance page (e.g. https://opthubstorage.blob.core.windows.net/opthub-data/timetabling/edutt/ctt/cb-ctt-ud2/solutions/comp12/comp12_15.sol). The checker computes hard violations and the four UD2 soft costs (RoomCapacity 1 per excess student, MinWorkingDays 5 per missing day, IsolatedLectures 2 each, RoomStability 1 per extra room), must reproduce the OptHub value of the posted best file, then evaluates the claim. Seconds.
angles: Fix-and-reoptimise with a MIP/CP-SAT model of UD2: free all lectures of a few curricula or a few days and re-solve exactly from the best posted file.
Simulated annealing with Kempe-chain and swap moves (the Bellio-Ceschia-Di Gaspero-Schaerf line) tuned per instance, run for days on many seeds.
ASP/MaxSAT (teaspoon-style) with solution hints from the posted best file.
pitfalls: OptHub is a JavaScript app; read it in a browser or via its rendered page, and note the 'Created at' date of imported solutions (2021-12-07) is the import date, not the discovery date.
Other formulations (UD1, UD3-UD5) use different penalties; only UD2 counts here.
comp01 (5) and the UD2 instances proven optimal by Banbara et al. 2019 cannot be improved; check the literature for any later optimality proof of the seven listed instances before investing.

targets.name: ITC-2007 examination timetabling (track 1): beat the best known penalty on one of the 12 competition instances
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: The ITC-2007 examination track (McCollum, McMullan, Burke, Parkes and Qu) asks for an assignment of exams to periods and rooms meeting hard constraints (no student conflicts, room capacity, period lengths, period and room hard constraints) and minimising weighted soft penalties (two in a row, two in a day, period spread, mixed durations, front load, period and room penalties). OptHub (University of Udine) keeps the uploaded solutions. On 2026-10-30 the best known values are set1 3,085, set2 380, set3 7,041, set4 10,448, set5 2,327, set6 25,120, set7 3,225, set8 7,077, set9 898, set10 12,878, set11 22,186, set12 5,095. David Van Bulck holds set1, set4, set7, set9 and set11 (files posted 2022-2023). Yuri Bykov holds set2, set3, set5, set10 and set12 (files posted 2021-12-19).
