targets.name: OGB ogbn-arxiv: beat the top no-external-data test accuracy (0.7611) for arXiv CS subject classification
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (169k nodes, 1.2M edges; CPU training of GNN/MLP+propagation models is feasible)
targets.statement: ogbn-arxiv (Open Graph Benchmark: Weihua Hu, Matthias Fey, Marinka Zitnik, Yuxiao Dong, Hongyu Ren, Bowen Liu, Michele Catasta, Jure Leskovec) is the citation graph of 169,343 arXiv CS papers with 128-dim word2vec features. The task is the 40-way primary subject area with a time split (train before 2018, validation 2018, test 2019+), scored by test accuracy averaged over at least 10 runs, with model selection on validation. The live leaderboard (81 rows, last entry 2026-02-10) is topped by LLM-text entries marked 'Ext. data: Yes' (SimTeG+TAPE+RevGAT, Keyu Duan, 0.7803). Among entries marked 'No', the best are GIANT-XRT+DRGAT (anonymous_zhang, 0.7611 +- 0.0009, 2022-01-17), LGGNN+LabelReuse+C&S (Shichao Ma, OPPO, 0.7570) and AGDN+BoT+self-KD+C&S (Chuxiong Sun, 0.7431). The top two 'No' rows appear to rely on GIANT-XRT text-derived features: the first says so in its name, and the LGGNN row repeats, number for number, a 'Yes' row named GIANT-XRT+LGGNN+LabelReuse+C&S. The best 'No' entry that plausibly uses only the shipped inputs is therefore AGDN+BoT+self-KD+C&S at 0.7431. The best 'No' entry under 1M parameters is UniMP_v2 (Weiyue Su, PGL, 0.7397, 687,377 params; the 'Yes' row SciBERT & EHGCN reaches 0.7461 with 621,944), and the best CPU entry is PCAPass + XGBoost (Krzysztof Sadowski, Intel, 0.7187). No 'No'-marked entry has improved on 0.7611 since January 2022. Can a model that uses only the shipped ogb inputs beat it?
targets.success_criterion: Saved code, seeds and per-run test predictions such that, on the official ogbn-arxiv split loaded via the ogb package and scored with ogb's Evaluator, the mean test accuracy over at least 10 runs (seeds 0-9 or the first 10 runs, all reported; each run's checkpoint chosen by validation accuracy only) is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the highest 'Test Accuracy' among rows with 'Ext. data' = 'No' in the ogbn-arxiv table at https://ogb.stanford.edu/docs/leader_nodeprop/, re-fetched live immediately before claiming (0.7611 on 2026-10-30). Inputs are limited to what the ogb package ships for ogbn-arxiv (graph, 128-dim features, years, training labels): no raw titles or abstracts, no language-model embeddings and no models pretrained on outside data. Validation labels may be used only as the OGB rules allow (hyperparameter tuning).

partial_wins.statement: Mean test accuracy over 10 runs of at least 0.7451, i.e. 0.002 above 0.7431, the best 'No'-marked entry on the live board whose name shows no GIANT-XRT or other text-derived features (AGDN+BoT+self-KD+C&S, Chuxiong Sun, 2021-07-22, on 2026-10-30), and strictly above any higher ogbn-arxiv test accuracy from a shipped-inputs-only model found by the NOVELTY check, under the full-win protocol and input restriction.

A model with fewer than 1,000,000 learned parameters whose 10-run mean test accuracy is strictly above every 'No'-marked entry listed with fewer than 1,000,000 parameters (UniMP_v2, 0.7397 on 2026-10-30), under the same protocol.

targets.verification_method: pip install ogb and load the official split. Re-run the saved script for 2 of the 10 seeds and confirm the per-run numbers. Score all saved test predictions with ogb.nodeproppred.Evaluator('ogbn-arxiv'). Check that the logs show checkpoint selection by validation only, grep the code for any raw-text or external-embedding download, count parameters with sum(p.numel()), and re-fetch the leaderboard.
angles: Label propagation tricks from semi-supervised learning: label reuse, Correct-and-Smooth and self-knowledge-distillation stacked on a strong base model. They are behind most of the top 'No' entries.
Exploit the time split: weight training papers by year, or add year-aware features, since test papers are 2019+ (covariate shift).
Directed-graph propagation (separate in- and out-citation operators, as in DRGAT and magnetic Laplacians) instead of symmetrising the graph.
Gradient-boosted trees on multi-hop propagated features (SIGN-style A^k X and propagated training labels), which run on CPU.
pitfalls: Using raw text or LM embeddings moves the entry to the external-data comparison. The input restriction above is stricter than some 'No' labels on the board: the 0.7611 record itself uses GIANT-XRT features.
Feeding validation labels into label propagation at test time breaks the OGB rule (validation labels only for tuning).
Test-set checkpoint selection or best-of-many-seeds reporting is not the protocol.
Differences of 0.001 are within run-to-run noise; report the standard deviation.

targets.name: OGB ogbn-mag: beat the leaderboard's top test accuracy (0.5801) for heterogeneous-graph paper venue prediction
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (1.9M nodes, 21M edges; precomputed-propagation models need about 32 GB RAM, GPU helpful)
targets.statement: ogbn-mag (Open Graph Benchmark, Hu et al. 2020) is a heterogeneous subgraph of the Microsoft Academic Graph: 736,389 papers (128-dim word2vec features), 1,134,649 authors, 8,740 institutions and 59,965 fields of study, with four relation types. The task is the 349-way venue of each paper with a time split (train before 2018, validation 2018, test 2019+), scored by test accuracy over 10 runs. The leaderboard is still moving. HGAMLP-HOPE (Wei Zhou, HUST, 2026-01-11) leads at 0.5801 +- 0.0012, ahead of gHAWK (Bloom+TransE) (Fatima Farooq, UT Arlington, 2025-12-24) at 0.5797 +- 0.0038, HGAMLP+LP+MS with LINE embeddings (Yuxuan Liang, PKU-Tencent, 2025-05-13) at 0.5794 and LMSPS (Chao Li, HUST, 2024) at 0.5784. All four are marked 'Ext. data: No' and lie within 0.0017 of each other. Can a model beat 0.5801?
targets.success_criterion: Saved code, seeds and per-run test predictions such that, on the official ogbn-mag split (ogb package) scored with ogb's Evaluator, the mean test accuracy over at least 10 runs (seeds 0-9 or the first 10 runs, all reported; checkpoints chosen by validation accuracy only) is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the highest 'Test Accuracy' among 'Ext. data' = 'No' rows of the ogbn-mag table at https://ogb.stanford.edu/docs/leader_nodeprop/, re-fetched live immediately before claiming (0.5801 on 2026-10-30). Only data shipped by ogb for ogbn-mag may be used. Structural embeddings (LINE, TransE, metapath2vec) computed from that graph alone are allowed. Validation labels only for tuning, per the OGB rules.

partial_wins.statement: A model with fewer than 8,000,000 learned parameters (structural embeddings counted as parameters) whose 10-run mean test accuracy is strictly above 0.5773 (RpHGNN+LP+CR (LINE embs), Jun Hu, 7,720,368 params, the best listed entry under 8M on 2026-10-30), under the full-win protocol.

A model with fewer than 5,000,000 learned parameters (structural embeddings counted as parameters) whose 10-run mean test accuracy is strictly above 0.5752 (PSHGCN, Mingguo He, 4,852,434 params, the best listed entry under 5M on 2026-10-30), under the full-win protocol.

targets.verification_method: Load ogbn-mag with ogb. Re-run 2 of the 10 seeds from the saved script, including the embedding precomputation. Score all saved predictions with ogb.nodeproppred.Evaluator('ogbn-mag'), confirm validation-only selection from the logs, count parameters including any learned embedding tables, and re-fetch the leaderboard.
angles: Metapath feature precomputation (SeHGNN/HGAMLP style) plus multi-stage label propagation, then ensembling diverse metapath subsets.
Knowledge-graph embeddings (TransE, RotatE) of the full heterogeneous graph as extra features for authors and fields, which have no features of their own.
Venue priors from author history: the share of each author's training papers per venue is a strong, cheap feature.
pitfalls: Leaderboard differences at the top are smaller than one standard deviation. A claim must beat the mean, and the skeptic reports the spread.
Label-propagation features must use training labels only; validation-paper labels may not be inputs.
Embeddings trained with any test-paper labels leak; the structural embedding objective must be label-free.

targets.name: OGB ogbl-collab: beat the leaderboard's top test Hits@50 (0.7129) for future co-authorship prediction
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (235k nodes, 1.3M edges; heuristics run in minutes on CPU)
targets.statement: ogbl-collab (Open Graph Benchmark, Hu et al. 2020) is a co-authorship graph of 235,868 MAG authors with 128-dim features. Edges until 2017 are for training, 2018 for validation and 2019 for test. Each true 2019 collaboration is ranked against 100,000 random negatives and scored by Hits@50, averaged over at least 10 runs. Uniquely among OGB datasets, validation edges may be used for training and as input once hyperparameters are fixed. The leaderboard (31 rows) is led by HyperFusion (Xinwei Zhang, Tsinghua, 2024-02-24) at 0.7129 +- 0.0018. Next come GIDN@YITU (Zixiao Wang, Yu Zhang, 2022) at 0.7096, PLNLP + SIGN (Liang Yao, Tencent) at 0.7087 and the CPU-trained HOP-REC (Bo-Yu Lin) at 0.7012. A parameter-free heuristic, AA-DC (Daisuke Hirota, 2026-02-07), reaches 0.6802 on CPU. Can a model beat 0.7129?
targets.success_criterion: Saved code, seeds and per-run test scores such that, on the official ogbl-collab split with ogb's Evaluator (Hits@50 against the official test negatives), the mean test Hits@50 over at least 10 runs (seeds 0-9 or the first 10 runs, all reported) is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the highest 'Test Hits@50' among 'Ext. data' = 'No' rows of the ogbl-collab table at https://ogb.stanford.edu/docs/leader_linkprop/, re-fetched live immediately before claiming (0.7129 on 2026-10-30). Hyperparameters must be fixed using validation edges before those edges are added to the training graph, as the OGB rules require. No test edges may be used as input.

partial_wins.statement: A method trained and evaluated entirely on CPU (no GPU) whose 10-run mean test Hits@50 is strictly above 0.7012 (HOP-REC, Bo-Yu Lin, the best CPU-trained entry on the board on 2026-10-30), under the full-win protocol.

A method with no gradient-trained parameters (a deterministic graph heuristic or closed-form score) whose test Hits@50 is strictly above the best zero-parameter entry on the live board (AA-DC, 0.6802 on 2026-10-30).

targets.verification_method: Load ogbl-collab with ogb and re-run the saved script for 2 seeds. Check in the code that hyperparameters are frozen before validation edges join the graph and that test edges never enter the input. Score the saved positive and negative test scores with ogb.linkproppred.Evaluator('ogbl-collab'), and re-fetch the leaderboard.
angles: Time-decayed common-neighbour and Adamic-Adar scores (recent collaborations matter more), blended with a learned model by validation tuning.
Use the edge-year and edge-weight metadata explicitly; many GNN entries discard it.
Recommender-systems methods (HOP-REC is one) and random-walk augmentation, both CPU-friendly.
pitfalls: Adding validation edges before the hyperparameter search is fixed breaks the one exception the rules allow.
Some entries report validation Hits@50 of 1.0 because validation edges were in the training graph; compare on test only.
Duplicate (multi-year) edges inflate degree heuristics; handle the multigraph the same way for validation and test.

targets.name: OGB ogbl-vessel: beat the leaderboard's top test ROC-AUC (0.9838) for mouse-brain vessel link prediction
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (3.5M nodes, 5.3M edges, 3-dim spatial features; 16-32 GB RAM)
targets.statement: ogbl-vessel (contributed to OGB by Johannes C. Paetzold et al., NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks) is the whole-mouse-brain vessel graph. Nodes are bifurcation points with (x, y, z) coordinates in Allen atlas space, and edges are vessels. Edges are split 80/10/10 at random with spatially sampled negatives, scored by test ROC-AUC. GAV (Bastian Wittmann, UZH, 2023-03-28) leads at 0.9838 +- 0.0002 with only 8,194 parameters, then SIEG(SPG) (anonymous, 2023) at 0.9687 and MLP+DiffPredictor (Chuxiong Sun) at 0.9414. Recent parameter-free CPU entries are far below: DRESS (Eduar Castrillo Velilla, 2026-04-22) at 0.7476 and the Homogeneity Index (Mehrdad Rafiepour, 2025) at 0.5460. Can a model beat 0.9838?
targets.success_criterion: Saved code, seeds and per-run test scores such that, on the official ogbl-vessel split with ogb's Evaluator (ROC-AUC on the official test positives and negatives), the mean test ROC-AUC over at least 10 runs (all reported; checkpoints chosen on validation only) is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the highest 'Test ROC-AUC' among 'Ext. data' = 'No' rows of the ogbl-vessel table at https://ogb.stanford.edu/docs/leader_linkprop/, re-fetched live immediately before claiming (0.9838 on 2026-10-30). No validation or test edges may be inputs, and only data shipped by ogb for ogbl-vessel may be used.

partial_wins.statement: A model with fewer than 8,194 learned parameters (fewer than GAV) whose 10-run mean test ROC-AUC is strictly above 0.9687 (SIEG(SPG), the second-ranked entry on 2026-10-30), under the full-win protocol.
A method with no gradient-trained parameters whose test ROC-AUC is strictly above 0.85, beating every parameter-free entry on the live board (best: DRESS, 0.7476 on 2026-10-30).

targets.verification_method: Load ogbl-vessel with ogb and re-run 2 runs from the saved script. Score the saved test scores with ogb.linkproppred.Evaluator('ogbl-vessel'). Check that only training edges form the message-passing graph and that selection used validation, then re-fetch the leaderboard.
angles: Geometry first: edge length, direction and local vessel-tree statistics from the coordinates, fed to gradient-boosted trees, then a small GNN (GAV wins with 8k parameters).
Biological priors from vascular anatomy: bifurcation points have low degree (about 3), so score candidate edges by how they change local degree and angle distributions.
Spatial negatives are close to positives; train with hard, spatially sampled negatives that match the evaluation sampler.
pitfalls: Train with negatives drawn like the official spatially sampled ones. A model trained only on uniformly random negatives separates random pairs easily but scores much lower on the official validation and test negatives.
Only training edges may form the message-passing graph or feed degree and neighbourhood features; computing them on the full edge set leaks validation and test edges.
The score is ROC-AUC averaged over runs; a single lucky run is not the protocol.

targets.name: OGB ogbg-molpcba: beat the leaderboard's top test AP (0.3204) on 128 PubChem bioassays
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (437,929 molecules, 128 tasks; a GPU shortens training, fingerprint forests run on CPU)
targets.statement: ogbg-molpcba (Open Graph Benchmark, Hu et al. 2020, from MoleculeNet's PCBA) asks 128 sparse binary bioactivity questions about each of 437,929 molecules. It uses a fixed scaffold split and is scored by test average precision (AP), averaged over tasks and over at least 10 runs. Among entries without external data, HyperFusion (Xinwei Zhang, Tsinghua, 2024-02-24) leads at 0.3204 +- 0.0001. It is followed by PDF (Mingqi Yang, 2023) at 0.3031, PAS (Xu Wang, 4Paradigm) at 0.3012 and the Nested GIN + virtual node ensemble (Muhan Zhang) at 0.3007. The strongest classic-GNN entry, GatedGCN+ (Yuankai Luo, PolyU, 2025-02-13), reaches 0.2981. Entries pretrained on PCQM4M (HIG 0.3167, Graphormer 0.3140) are marked as using external data. The best CPU entry is MorganFP + Random Forest (Cyrus Maher) at 0.2054. Can a model without external data beat 0.3204?
targets.success_criterion: Saved code, seeds and per-run test predictions such that, on the official ogbg-molpcba scaffold split with ogb's Evaluator, the mean test AP over at least 10 runs (seeds 0-9 or the first 10 runs, all reported; selection by validation AP only) is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the highest 'Test AP' among 'Ext. data' = 'No' rows of the ogbg-molpcba table at https://ogb.stanford.edu/docs/leader_graphprop/, re-fetched live immediately before claiming (0.3204 on 2026-10-30). Fingerprints and descriptors computed from the molecules themselves are allowed. Models pretrained on any outside molecular data are not.

partial_wins.statement: A model with fewer than 4,000,000 learned parameters whose 10-run mean test AP is strictly above 0.3031 (PDF, Mingqi Yang, 3,842,048 params, the best entry under 4M on 2026-10-30), under the full-win protocol and the no-external-data rule.

A method with no neural network (tree ensembles, kernel or linear models on fingerprints and descriptors computed from the molecules themselves), trained entirely on CPU, whose 10-run mean test AP is strictly above 0.2500, beating the board's only non-neural entry (MorganFP+Rand. Forest, Cyrus Maher, 0.2054) by a wide margin, under the full-win protocol and the no-external-data rule. Re-running a listed GNN on CPU does not count.

targets.verification_method: Load ogbg-molpcba with ogb and re-run 2 of the 10 seeds. Score all saved predictions with ogb.graphproppred.Evaluator('ogbg-molpcba'), which ignores NaN labels. Check validation-only selection and that no pretrained checkpoint is loaded, then re-fetch the leaderboard.
angles: Multi-task structure: the 128 assays share chemistry, so task-relationship priors (assay-assay label correlations from training data) can regularise rare tasks.
Self-supervised pretraining on the 437k unlabelled molecules of this dataset only (allowed), then fine-tuning.
Per-task fingerprint gradient boosting blended with a GNN, weighted by validation AP per task.
pitfalls: Pretraining on PCQM4M, ZINC or ChEMBL is external data and moves the entry to the other comparison.
AP averages only over tasks with both classes in the test split; use the evaluator rather than a hand-rolled metric.
HyperFusion's spread is tiny (0.0001); a claim must exceed its mean, not its lower bound.

targets.name: OGB ogbg-ppa: beat the leaderboard's top test accuracy (0.8258) for classifying protein-association graphs by taxonomic group
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (158,100 graphs averaging 243 nodes and 2,266 edges; GPU strongly helpful)
targets.statement: ogbg-ppa (Open Graph Benchmark, Hu et al. 2020, built from STRING protein-protein association networks) contains 158,100 undirected graphs. Each is the neighbourhood of a protein in one of 1,581 species, with 7-dim edge features for association types and no node features. The task is to predict which of 37 taxonomic groups the species belongs to. The split is by species (test species are unseen), and the score is test accuracy over at least 10 runs. GatedGCN+ (Yuankai Luo, Lei Shi, Xiao-Ming Wu, PolyU; ICML 2025 'Can Classic GNNs Be Strong Baselines for Graph-level Tasks?'; 2025-02-13) leads at 0.8258 +- 0.0055. Behind it are PAS+F2GNN (Xu Wang, 4Paradigm, 2022) at 0.8201 and ExpC* + bag of tricks (Hao Zhang, 2021) at 0.8140. Can a model beat 0.8258?
targets.success_criterion: Saved code, seeds and per-run test predictions such that, on the official ogbg-ppa split with ogb's Evaluator, the mean test accuracy over at least 10 runs (all reported; checkpoints chosen by validation accuracy only) is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the highest 'Test Accuracy' among 'Ext. data' = 'No' rows of the ogbg-ppa table at https://ogb.stanford.edu/docs/leader_graphprop/, re-fetched live immediately before claiming (0.8258 on 2026-10-30). No external protein data (sequences, other STRING releases, pretrained protein models).

partial_wins.statement: A model with fewer than 4,000,000 learned parameters whose 10-run mean test accuracy is strictly above 0.8140 (ExpC*+bag of tricks, Hao Zhang, 3,758,642 params, the best entry under 4M on 2026-10-30), under the full-win protocol.
A model with fewer than 1,000,000 learned parameters whose 10-run mean test accuracy is strictly above 0.7500, far above the best sub-1M entry on the board (GCN, 0.6839).

targets.verification_method: Load ogbg-ppa with ogb and re-run 2 seeds from the saved script. Score the saved predictions with ogb.graphproppred.Evaluator('ogbg-ppa'). Check validation-only selection and that nothing is downloaded from outside, count parameters, and re-fetch the leaderboard.
angles: Graph-kernel and spectral features (Weisfeiler-Lehman subtree counts on edge-type-labelled graphs, Laplacian spectra) fed to gradient-boosted trees, as a CPU baseline and an ensemble member.
Message passing that leans on edge features: nodes have no features, so the association-type vectors carry most of the signal.
Ensembles of several seeds of a strong classic GNN with different readouts (mean, attention, virtual node).
pitfalls: Test species are unseen, so tuning on a random split of training graphs overestimates accuracy; use the official validation split.
Standard deviations are about 0.005. A margin of 0.001 over the leader is within noise and should be reported as such.

targets.name: TGB dynamic link prediction (tgbl-wiki-v2, review-v2, coin-v2, comment, flight-v2): beat a leaderboard's top test MRR
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours for tgbl-wiki-v2 and tgbl-review-v2; laptop-days or more for coin, comment and flight (23M-67M edges)
targets.statement: The Temporal Graph Benchmark (Shenyang Huang, Farimah Poursafaei, Jacob Danovitch, Matthias Fey, Weihua Hu, Emanuele Rossi, Jure Leskovec, Michael Bronstein, Guillaume Rabusseau, Reihaneh Rabbany; NeurIPS 2023) scores future-edge prediction on continuous-time graphs. Each true edge is ranked against pre-generated negatives and scored by MRR over 5 runs, in a streaming setting where test edges may update memory but not gradients. Live leaders on 2026-10-30: - tgbl-wiki-v2: TPNet (Xiaodong Lu, Beihang, 2025-08-14) 0.827, then a parameter-free Heuristic(LocalGlobal) by King AI Labs (2026-01-20) 0.821 and HyperEvent (Jian Gao, Xidian) 0.810. - tgbl-review-v2: GraphMixer (TGB team, 2023) 0.521, then CTAN (Alessio Gravina, Pisa, 2025) 0.405. - tgbl-coin-v2: TPNet 0.832, then a heuristic at 0.774. - tgbl-comment: TPNet 0.825, then HyperEvent 0.760. - tgbl-flight-v2: TPNet 0.884, then a heuristic at 0.878. Can a method beat a dataset's top test MRR?
targets.success_criterion: For a named dataset D in {tgbl-wiki-v2, tgbl-review-v2, tgbl-coin-v2, tgbl-comment, tgbl-flight-v2}: saved code and seeds such that, with the official chronological split, the official pre-generated validation and test negatives and the tgb package's Evaluator, the mean test MRR over 5 runs (all reported) is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the highest 'Test MRR' for D at https://tgb.complexdatalab.com/docs/leader_linkprop/, re-fetched live immediately before claiming. Rules (https://tgb.complexdatalab.com/docs/leader_rules/): training edges may be used in any way. Validation edges only for hyperparameter tuning (no gradients) and memory updates. Test edges only for memory updates after each prediction batch, never for gradients or tuning.

partial_wins.statement: For some dataset D, mean test MRR over 5 runs strictly above the second-highest Test MRR for D on the live board, with all training and evaluation of the 5 runs done on CPU only (no GPU), under the full-win protocol, using a method that is not one of D's listed board entries (re-running or re-training a listed method such as TPNet on CPU does not count).

A method with no gradient-trained parameters whose test MRR on some dataset D is strictly above every training-free entry listed for D on the live board (rows named Heuristic(...), EdgeBank(...) or Base3; on 2026-10-30 the best are 0.821 on tgbl-wiki-v2, 0.108 on tgbl-review-v2, 0.774 on tgbl-coin-v2, 0.723 on tgbl-comment and 0.878 on tgbl-flight-v2).

targets.verification_method: pip install the pinned tgb release and load D with its official negative sampler. Re-run 2 of the 5 runs and recompute MRR with tgb's Evaluator. Read the code to confirm that test edges reach the model only after prediction and only through memory or history updates. Re-fetch the leaderboard.
angles: Recency and popularity blends from recommender systems (time-decayed item popularity per source node); such heuristics already sit second on wiki, coin and flight.
tgbl-review-v2 is an outlier where one 2023 model leads by 0.12; study what GraphMixer's link encoder captures and combine it with recency features.
Point-process ideas (Hawkes intensities per node pair) as cheap scorers or features.
pitfalls: Datasets were re-released as v2 with changed negatives; older v1 numbers in papers are not comparable.
Negatives must be the official pre-generated ones; random negatives inflate MRR.
Updating model weights on test edges breaks the streaming rules; only memory or history may change.

targets.name: TGB dynamic node affinity (tgbn-trade, genre, reddit, token): beat NAVIS's top test NDCG@10
targets.compute_profile: laptop-minutes for tgbn-trade (255 nodes); laptop-hours for genre and reddit; laptop-days for token (72M edges)
targets.statement: TGB's dynamic node property prediction track (Huang et al., NeurIPS 2023) asks, at each time step, for a ranking of a node's future interaction affinities (trade partners, music genres, subreddits, tokens), scored by NDCG@10 in a streaming setting. Simple forecasts are strong: Persistent Forecast and Moving Average (TGB team, 2023) beat learned TGN models on every dataset. NAViS (Or Feldman, Ben-Gurion University, 2025-10-20; arXiv 2510.06940), a trained state-space model, now leads all four boards by small margins: - tgbn-trade: 0.863 vs Persistent Forecast 0.855. - tgbn-genre: 0.528 vs Moving Average 0.509. - tgbn-reddit: 0.569 vs Moving Average 0.559. - tgbn-token: 0.513 vs Moving Average 0.508. TGNv2 (Benedict Aaron Tjandra, Oxford, 2024) is third on genre and reddit and fourth on trade and token. Can a method beat NAVIS on a dataset?
targets.success_criterion: For a named dataset D in {tgbn-trade, tgbn-genre, tgbn-reddit, tgbn-token}: saved code and seeds such that, with the official chronological split and the tgb package's node-property Evaluator, the test NDCG@10 (mean over 5 runs if the method is stochastic, all runs reported) is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the highest 'Test NDCG@10' for D at https://tgb.complexdatalab.com/docs/leader_nodeprop/, re-fetched live immediately before claiming. TGB rules apply. Validation data only for tuning and memory. Test labels are revealed in stream order after each prediction and are never used for gradients or tuning.

partial_wins.statement: A method with no gradient-trained parameters (persistence, moving-average, exponential-smoothing or similar forecasts, with any constants tuned on validation only) whose test NDCG@10 on some dataset D is strictly above both TGB-team heuristics for D (on 2026-10-30 the better of Persistent Forecast and Moving Average is 0.855 on tgbn-trade, 0.509 on tgbn-genre, 0.559 on tgbn-reddit and 0.508 on tgbn-token), under the full-win protocol.
One fixed no-gradient method of the p1 kind, with one fixed validation-only tuning procedure, that achieves p1 on all four datasets.

targets.verification_method: Install tgb and re-run the saved script on D (all runs if stochastic). Recompute NDCG@10 with tgb's Evaluator. Read the code to check that each test label is used only after its prediction is made and that no tuning used test scores, then re-fetch the leaderboard.
angles: Forecasting methods from econometrics and demand planning: exponential smoothing with a tuned decay per node, Croston's method for intermittent affinities, and persistence/moving-average blends chosen on validation.
Gravity-model features for tgbn-trade: international trade flows follow partner size and distance.
Learn only a small correction on top of the moving-average forecast (a residual model), which keeps the strong baseline as a floor.
pitfalls: Using the label at time t to predict time t (an off-by-one in the stream) gives impossible scores; check the evaluation loop.
Smoothing constants tuned on test NDCG are test tuning; tune on validation only.
Margins at the top are 0.005-0.02; report exact unrounded scores.

targets.name: TabArena-v0.1: beat the best mean test error of all 94 leaderboard entries on one of the 51 curated tabular datasets
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours per small dataset (up to 2,400 rows, 30 splits); laptop-days for the 9-split datasets up to 150k rows
targets.statement: TabArena-v0.1 (Nick Erickson, Lennart Purucker, Andrej Tschalzev, David Holzmuller, Prateek Mutalik Desai, David Salinas, Frank Hutter and contributors; arXiv 2506.16791) is a living benchmark of 51 curated IID tabular datasets. Each has fixed outer splits (30 for the 17 datasets of up to 2,400 rows, 9 for larger ones), and the metric is 1-AUC (binary), log loss (multiclass) or RMSE (regression). The full leaderboard view (models plus open-source systems, systems with LLMs and closed-source API systems; space updated 2026-10-28) has 94 entries; by Elo, Kumo-Tabular (2025), LimiX-2 (2001) and Chakra-Tab full (1961) lead. On most datasets a foundation model or a 4-hour AutoGluon system has the best mean test error, often by tiny margins. For example, on heloc (1-AUC) LimiX-2 scores 0.196859 against Kumo-Tabular's 0.196863; on Food_Delivery_Time (RMSE) Kumo-Tabular scores 7.19902 against ChimeraBoost (tuned + ensemble) at 7.19924; on hiva_agnostic tuned RandomForest and tuned ExtraTrees tie at the top (log loss 0.173849); on polish_companies_bankruptcy AutoGluon 1.5 (extreme, 4h) leads (0.003449). LimiX-2 is flagged for leakage on blood-transfusion-service-center and diabetes. Can a method beat the best entry's mean test error on a dataset?
targets.success_criterion: For a named TabArena-v0.1 dataset D: saved code, seeds and per-split test predictions for every official outer split of D (TabArena's OpenML task and split definitions), each model fit only on that split's training part. The mean test error over all splits (TabArena's metric for D, computed with TabArena's scorer) must be STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the lowest mean error for D among all entries not flagged for leakage on D in the full entrant view (models, open-source systems, systems with LLMs and closed-source API systems; no imputation). That bar is the POINTS 'e' values in https://huggingface.co/spaces/TabArena/leaderboard/resolve/main/data/entrants_open_llm_api/imputation_no/splits_all/tasks_all/datasets_all/per_dataset_explorer.html (94 entries on 2026-10-30), re-fetched live immediately before claiming; leakage flags are window.TABARENA_LEAKAGE in the same file. No pretrained model whose training data include D or its source may be used.

partial_wins.statement: On a dataset D, mean test error over all splits strictly below the best entry in the Tree-based, Neural Network, Baseline and Other families (no foundation models or systems) in the live full-view per-dataset data, with a model trained from scratch on each split's training data only.

Beat the lowest non-leakage mean error for D over the TabArena-Lite splits (as defined by the tabarena package), as listed in https://huggingface.co/spaces/TabArena/leaderboard/resolve/main/data/entrants_open_llm_api/imputation_no/splits_lite/tasks_all/datasets_all/per_dataset_explorer.html, under the same fitting rules.

targets.verification_method: Install tabarena and rebuild D's outer splits from its OpenML task. Check that the saved predictions align with each split's test indices. Recompute the metric per split with TabArena's scorer and average. Re-run fitting on 2 splits from the saved script. Check that training never touched test rows and that no pretrained model saw D, then re-fetch the full-view (entrants_open_llm_api) per-dataset explorer data and compare against the lowest non-leakage 'e' for D.
angles: Pick datasets where the leader's margin over strong trees is tiny (Food_Delivery_Time, heloc) or where trees lead (hiva_agnostic). Domain features, such as delivery distance from coordinates or monotonic constraints on credit scores, can move the last 0.1%.
Stack locally runnable open-weight tabular foundation models with tuned GBDTs, fitting the blender on inner cross-validation only.
Post-processing matched to the metric: temperature scaling for log-loss datasets, rank-averaging for 1-AUC.
pitfalls: Many datasets have public copies online, so a pretrained model or LLM that saw D is leakage (TabArena flags LimiX-2 on two datasets).
The bar is the mean over all splits, not the best split; 30-split datasets need all 30.

Margins are often below 0.1%, and the explorer's 'e' values are rounded to 6 significant figures; a claim must be strictly below the listed value, and a margin smaller than that rounding should be reported as unresolved.

targets.name: Integer Chebyshev constant of [0,1]: a certified bound beating Niedbala Giraudin's 2026 bracket 0.422228600019 <= t_Z([0,1]) <= 0.422684697505
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (LP over a polynomial library plus interval-arithmetic bisection; the published certificates re-check in seconds to minutes)
targets.statement: The integer Chebyshev constant (integer transfinite diameter) of I = [0,1] is t_Z(I) = lim_n (min over nonzero P in Z[x], deg P <= n, of ||P||_I)^(1/n). By Fekete it is an infimum, so one explicit integer polynomial P gives the upper bound ||P||_[0,1]^(1/deg P). Gelfond and Schnirelman observed that the value 1/e would give an elementary proof of the prime number theorem; the true value is larger. Successive upper bounds came from Borwein-Erdelyi, Habsieger-Salvy, Pritsker (2005), Flammang (2009), Meichsner (2009) and Flammang (2014, 0.422685). The lower bound 0.4213 is Pritsker's (2005). That bracket was the state of the art in Flammang's 2019 survey. David Niedbala Giraudin, 'New bounds for the integer Chebyshev constant of [0,1]', arXiv:2610.00386 (v3, 12 Oct 2026, unrefereed, computations done with Claude), proves 0.422228600019 <= t_Z([0,1]) <= 0.422684697505 (Corollary 3: 0.4222286000 and 0.4226846976). The upper certificate is a product of 92 integer factors with integer exponents. Most come from the Hare-Hodges 23 factors, Hare's Gorshkov-Wirsing tower and Flammang's Table 1. The lower certificate is a discrete measure on 947 cells plus 206 irreducible polynomials, through a new inequality (Theorem 7) that charges for divisibility. Both certificates ship with ancillary verifier scripts. The author claims saturation on neither side: the lower bound still grew when the library went from 70 to 206 polynomials, and no finite library is optimal for the upper one. Qu and Yang (arXiv:2609.39505) independently proved Montgomery's conjecture relating t_Z to leading coefficients of totally real polynomials; this gives no numbers. Push either side of the bracket.
targets.success_criterion: Either of the following. (A) An explicit integer polynomial P (or a list of integer factors Q_j with positive integer exponents e_j, P = prod Q_j^e_j) with ||P||_[0,1]^(1/deg P) STRICTLY BELOW 0.422684697505 (direction: min), proved by rigorous interval arithmetic: a bisection of [0,1] (or of w = x(1-x) in [0,1/4] for factors symmetric under x -> 1-x) in which every subinterval carries an outward-rounded upper bound on sum_j e_j log|Q_j| / deg P. (B) A certified lower bound STRICTLY ABOVE 0.422228600019 (direction: max): a measure and polynomial library satisfying the hypotheses of Theorem 7 of arXiv:2610.00386 (pairwise distinct, primitive, irreducible Q_j; budget B <= 1; inf A, the leading-coefficient term and every G_i bounded rigorously), or a certificate for Pritsker's (2005) method. In both cases the value is compared with the best bound on either side published at verification time (re-read the abstract page, its version history and the 2026 literature). For (B) the skeptic must also re-derive Theorem 7 from the paper, since it is new and unrefereed. Floating-point maxima without rigorous enclosures do not count.

partial_wins.statement: An independent rigorous re-verification of Niedbala Giraudin's shipped upper certificate (0.422684697505) or lower certificate (0.422228600019). It must use interval or exact arithmetic written from the paper's description, not the ancillary scripts. Report a confirmation or a located error. A located error counts as a win only if the skeptic reproduces it.

targets.verification_method: The verifier writes an independent checker with mpmath interval arithmetic (mpmath.iv) or python-flint arb. Upper bound: expand or factor P, confirm integrality and degree, then bisect [0,1] until every subinterval's rigorous enclosure of (1/deg P) * sum e_j log|Q_j(x)| is below log(claimed value). Calibrate on x(1-x), which must give exactly 0.5, and on Giraudin's certificate, which must give <= 0.422684697505. Lower bound: check irreducibility and primitivity (sympy factor_list), that the library is pairwise distinct, the budget B <= 1, and the three quantities of Theorem 7 with outward rounding. Then compare against the live arXiv abstract page for 2610.00386 and any newer paper.
angles: Upper side: enlarge the factor library with new low-height irreducible polynomials with all roots in [0,1] (Gorshkov-Wirsing tower members, transported auxiliary-function factors à la Proposition 6, and greedy LP column generation), then re-solve the semi-infinite LP for the weights and round to integer exponents.
Lower side: column generation on the 206-polynomial library (the paper reports that its value still grew from 70 to 206 polynomials) and adaptive refinement of the 947 cells.
pitfalls: The upper-bound margin over Flammang is only 3e-7: double-precision suprema are not proofs.
Weights c_j must become integer exponents (or rationals with a common denominator) before the result is a single integer polynomial.
A lower bound from one polynomial with all roots in [0,1] proves nothing (Remark 8 of the paper): divisibility must be paid for by the G_i terms.

targets.name: Vertex-minor Ramsey numbers: a 13-vertex graph with no 5-vertex edgeless vertex-minor (R_vm(5) >= 14), or beat Bae's explicit bounds for k = 6..9
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (an exact check of one 13- or 14-vertex graph takes seconds; the search is local or SAT-guided)
targets.statement: A graph H is a vertex-minor of G if H is an induced subgraph of a graph locally equivalent to G (local complementation at v complements the edges inside N(v)). R_vm(k) is the least n such that every n-vertex graph has the edgeless graph E_k as a vertex-minor. Equivalently, every n-vertex graph has beta(G) >= k, where beta(G) is the largest independence number over the local-equivalence orbit of G. Ascoli, B. Frederickson, S. Frederickson, McFarland and Post ('Almost all graphs are vertex-minor universal', arXiv:2602.09049, 2026) proved (1+o(1)) k^2/(2 log2 3) <= R_vm(k) <= 2^k - 1. Ji Ho Bae, 'Vertex-minor Ramsey numbers: exact values and extremal structure', arXiv:2604.13434 (v1, 15 Apr 2026), proves R_vm(4) = 11 by exhaustive classification: exactly six 10-vertex graphs, in five LC classes, avoid E_4. Disjoint unions of these with K_2 and the complement of C_6 give the first explicit lower bounds (Corollary 6.3): R_vm(5) >= 13, R_vm(6) >= 17, R_vm(7) >= 21, R_vm(8) >= 23, R_vm(9) >= 27. The paper conjectures R_vm(5) = 15 (Conjecture C), states R_vm(5) as the next open case, and reports that more than five million 10-vertex graphs still avoid E_5. So no explicit graph on 13 or more vertices with beta <= 4 is known. A single explicit graph raises a bound.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit graph G (graph6 or an edge list) on N vertices and an integer k in 5..9 with beta(G) <= k-1, that is, E_k is NOT a vertex-minor of G, where N is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the largest order of such a graph known at verification time. The values on 2026-10-30 come from Corollary 6.3 of arXiv:2604.13434: N > 12 for k = 5 (giving R_vm(5) >= 14), N > 16 for k = 6, N > 20 for k = 7, N > 22 for k = 8, N > 26 for k = 9. beta(G) <= k-1 must be certified by two independent exact methods (see verification_method). Re-check the arXiv abstract page and any 2026 follow-up for a larger explicit graph before claiming. A graph with N >= 15 for k = 5 contradicting a later proof of R_vm(5) = 15 means a bug.

partial_wins.statement: A connected 12-vertex graph with beta(G) = 4, certified as above. Connectivity is invariant under local complementation, so it is structurally new: the published 12-vertex example is the disjoint union of a 10-vertex extremal graph and K_2.

The exact number of non-isomorphic 10-vertex graphs with beta(G) <= 4 (Bae's 5,464,788 is only an upper bound because of an orbit-search budget), found by two independent exhaustive implementations whose full logs agree.

targets.verification_method: Method 1, Bouchet elimination: E_k is a vertex-minor of G iff for some k-set S the vertices outside S can be eliminated one at a time, each by deletion G-v, by G*v-v or by the pivot G x vw - v, so that the graph left on S is edgeless. E_k is alone in its LC class, so the final graph must be literally edgeless. Try all three options, and all neighbours w for the pivot, for every S. Method 2: BFS over the full labeled LC orbit of G (local complementation at every vertex until closure) and take the maximum independence number. The two must agree. Calibrate both on the complement of C_6 (beta = 2, labeled orbit size 132 by the auditor's own check) and on Bae's 10-vertex extremal graphs (beta = 3, orbit 8712). The lane's own checker reproduced Method 1 = Method 2 on 30 random 7-vertex graphs.
angles: Local search on 13-vertex graphs seeded by Bae's six extremal 10-vertex graphs plus three vertices, scoring the number of k-sets S that admit an edgeless elimination.
Highly symmetric candidates (circulants, Paley-type and other strongly regular graphs and their LC orbits) of order 13-14, whose many automorphisms cut the S-enumeration.
pitfalls: beta is the maximum independence number over the whole LC orbit, not alpha(G) itself.
Pivoting needs the edge vw to exist; skipping the pivot branch under-reports vertex-minors and can fake a win.

targets.name: Erdős #272: more than C(N,2)+1+floor((N-1)/4) subsets of {1..N} with pairwise AP intersections, or the exact t(13)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (maximum-clique search over the 2^N - 1 nonempty subsets; N = 13 means 8191 vertices)
targets.statement: Let t(N) be the largest number of distinct sets A_1..A_t in {1..N} such that every pairwise intersection is a nonempty arithmetic progression (Erdős Problem #272, from Simonovits-Sós and Erdős-Graham). Simonovits and Sós proved t(N) = O(N^2) and conjectured C(N,2)+1. Szabó (Europ. J. Combin. 1999) disproved this with a construction of B(N) = C(N,2)+1+floor((N-1)/4) sets and proved t(N) = N^2/2 + O(N^{5/3}(log N)^3). He conjectured t(N) = C(N,2)+O(N) and that every extremal family has a common element (the kernel conjecture). Stijn Cambie (erdosproblems forum, Aug 2025) verified N <= 9, and for 10 <= N <= 14 found B(N) under the assumption that the family contains a singleton (for N = 13: five such extremal families, all through 7). Zhanfu Yang, arXiv:2607.23004 (v1, 25 Jul 2026), determines t(3..12) = 4, 7, 12, 17, 23, 30, 39, 48, 58, 69 by exhaustive maximum-clique computation; all equal B(N). Yang proves that B(N) is the exact maximum over starred families (those with a common element) for every N, and conjectures t(N) = B(N) for all N, which reduces to Szabó's kernel conjecture (Problem 7.1). Starred families were checked exhaustively for N <= 13 and a structured class for N <= 61. A Lean proof of Szabó's first question in the form t(N) = N^2/2 + O(N) ('Erdős problem 272 - szabo strong') was marked solved on the Conjectures.io bounty pool on 11 Sep 2026; it is unrefereed and gives no exact value. The erdosproblems.com page for #272 shows no resolution of the exact value or the kernel question. Open: t(13) (B(13) = 82), and any N with t(N) > B(N).
targets.success_criterion: An explicit family F of distinct subsets of {1..N}, for some N >= 13, such that every pairwise intersection of members is a nonempty arithmetic progression (singletons count as APs; all checked exhaustively), with |F| STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than B(N) = C(N,2)+1+floor((N-1)/4) and than any larger value published for that N at verification time. Re-check https://www.erdosproblems.com/272, its forum thread and the arXiv page of 2607.23004 first. Such an F refutes Yang's Conjecture 1.3 and, by Yang's Theorem 1.4, must have no common element. A non-starred F larger than B(N) for N <= 12, or a starred F larger than B(N) for any N, contradicts published computation or proof: treat it as a bug and re-verify both sides before any claim.

partial_wins.statement: A complete enumeration, up to isomorphism, of all maximum families (size B(N) = t(N)) for one N in 10..12. It must come from two independently written exhaustive implementations whose outputs agree, and it must report for each family whether its members share a common element. Yang's Problem 7.1 asserts in passing that every maximum family for N <= 12 is starred, but Section 6 describes no such check. A non-starred maximum family would disprove Szabó's kernel conjecture.

A certified value of t(13). Either a family of size 83 or more (which is also the full win), or a proof that no 83-family exists. The proof is an exhaustive search log plus an agreeing independent implementation, or a checked DRAT/LRAT proof for a SAT encoding.

targets.verification_method: An independent script: check distinctness, that every set lies in [N], and for every pair that the intersection is nonempty with constant consecutive gaps. Compute |F| and B(N) exactly, and the common intersection of all members. Calibrate on Szabó's construction (Section 2 of arXiv:2607.23004), which must give B(N) for N = 5..14. For a p2 exhaustive claim, re-run with a separately written clique solver and require agreement on N = 3..12 with 4, 7, 12, 17, 23, 30, 39, 48, 58, 69.
angles: Yang's Section 7 localises a counterexample in one regime: by Theorem 7.5 and Proposition 7.6, for N >= 10^4 and a family larger than B(N) whose members of size >= 4 are all progressions, the triples form a star at some c and the members avoiding c are progressions of more than N/12 elements and difference at most 12. This is proved only under those hypotheses; for small N or non-progression members the structure is unconstrained.
pitfalls: Empty intersections are forbidden (with them allowed, the Graham-Simonovits-Sós answer is different).
The sets must be distinct; the empty set is excluded automatically because every intersection must be nonempty.

targets.name: No three collinear in the n x n x n grid (OEIS A399138): beat a(7) >= 73, a(8) >= 94, a(9) >= 116, a(10) >= 138 or a(11) >= 164
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (CP-SAT or local search inside symmetry strata; a witness is checked in seconds)
targets.statement: a(n) is the largest number of points of {0..n-1}^3 with no three collinear in R^3. Pór and Wood (Algorithmica 2007) proved a(n) = Theta(n^2). The trivial upper bound is 2n^2, since each of the 3n^2 axis-parallel lines holds at most two points. Aleksei Kudriashov, 'Certified computations on no-three-in-line problems...', arXiv:2609.25133 (v1, 20 Sep 2026), determined a(1..6) = 1, 8, 16, 28, 40, 64 with SAT decision procedures. Single-call instances carry drat-trim-checked DRAT proofs; the split n = 6 instances rest on one solver, with certificates regenerated on demand. The sequence became OEIS A399138 in Aug 2026. He gave verified lower bounds a(7) >= 73, found by restricting the search to a cyclic axis symmetry after randomised search stalled at 71. The bounds a(8) >= 94, a(9) >= 116, a(10) >= 138 and a(11) >= 164 came from a CP-SAT sweep over the 33 conjugacy classes of subgroups of the cube group (25-40 minutes per class). He also proved a(p) >= p^2 for every prime p. He calls the randomised bounds weak. Earlier, on SeqFan (June 2026), Ed Pegg and Lucas Brown gave a(1..5) and the bounds a(7) >= 72, a(8) >= 91, and Rob Pratt confirmed a(5) = 40 and a(6) = 64 by integer linear programming; Henry Nance (SeqFan, 24 Oct 2026) independently found 73, 92, 116 and 134 for n = 7..10 with symmetry-restricted CP-SAT, none above Kudriashov's values. The layer pattern of the small optima suggests 2n^2-2n+4 = 88 at n = 7; that exact layer profile is infeasible, but the value 88 is not excluded. A399138 (revision #39, 27 Oct 2026, comment updated by Eric W. Weisstein) lists a(7) >= 73 and a(8) >= 94 with keyword 'more'. MathWorld (updated 29 Oct 2026) gives the same values and notes that they beat a 93-point n = 8 example illustrated by Ed Pegg (2026).
targets.success_criterion: A set S in {0..n-1}^3 for some n in 7..11 with no three points collinear (checked over all C(|S|,3) triples with exact integer cross products), and |S| STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best lower bound for that n at verification time. On 2026-10-30 these were 73 (n=7), 94 (n=8), 116 (n=9), 138 (n=10) and 164 (n=11), from arXiv:2609.25133 and OEIS A399138. Re-read the live OEIS entry, its linked files and the Kudriashov repository first. |S| > 2n^2 is impossible and means a bug.

partial_wins.statement: The exact value a(7) or a(8). Give a witness of size m together with a checked DRAT/LRAT (or cake_lpr-verified) proof that no set of size m+1 with no three collinear exists in [n]^3. The proof file can be published outside git.

A certified upper bound a(7) <= 97, that is, any bound below the trivial 2n^2 = 98, given by a checked unsatisfiability proof without the matching witness. The skeptic first confirms that no published argument already gives a bound below 98 at n = 7.

targets.verification_method: An independent script: confirm the coordinates lie in [0,n-1] and are distinct, and test every triple (p,q,r) by checking that (q-p) x (r-p) is the zero vector in integers. Calibrate on the a(6) = 64 witness from the OEIS a399138.txt file (must pass) and on a corrupted copy with one point moved onto a line (must fail). For p1 and p2, re-encode the CNF from the problem definition and check that it is identical (up to variable renaming) to the one the proof refers to, then run drat-trim or cake_lpr.
angles: Symmetry strata: the best n = 8 witnesses came from order-4 subgroups; medium-size groups (orders 3-6) balance solver reach against richness of solutions.
For n = 11 and 13 compare with the quadratic-form construction (x, y, Q(x,y) mod p) plus extra points in unused fibres.
pitfalls: Collinearity is in R^3, not mod n.
Do not confuse with the planar problem (A000769, already a bank target) or with the no-four-coplanar problem (A280537).

targets.name: Packing vs piercing for axis-parallel rectangles after Wegner's conjecture fell: a finite family with tau > (5/2) nu
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exact nu and tau by ILP for families of a few hundred to a few thousand rectangles)
targets.statement: For a finite family R of closed axis-parallel rectangles in the plane, nu(R) is the largest number of pairwise disjoint members and tau(R) is the fewest points meeting every member. Wegner (1965) conjectured tau <= 2nu - 1, and Gyárfás and Lehel asked whether tau/nu is bounded by a constant. The best general upper bound was O(nu (log log nu)^2) (Correa, Feuilloley, Pérez-Lantero and Soto); Rao, Eom and Kim (arXiv:2610.16703, Oct 2026) improve the factor to log log nu * log log log nu. Earlier lower constructions: Fon-Der-Flaass and Kostochka (ratio 5/3) and Jelínek (tau = 2nu - 4). Ajwani, Gajjala, Raman and Ray, 'Counterexamples to Wegner's Conjecture for Rectangles', arXiv:2606.17854 (v2, 9 Jul 2026), disproved Wegner. Their v2 abstract gives an explicit triangle-free family of 64 rectangles with nu = 16 and tau >= 32, and triangle-free families with tau >= (5/2 - eps) nu for every eps > 0. They also proved that the clique-LP gap is at most 3 on triangle-free families. Aranya Kumar Bal, arXiv:2607.11318 (v2, 14 Jul 2026), gave a hand-checkable 64-rectangle triangle-free counterexample (nu = 16, tau >= 32) and a finite clique-LP gap of at least 73/32 (Ajwani et al.: 17891/8064). He also built recursive families P_r with tau(P_r)/nu(P_r) -> 5/2 and alpha*(P_r)/nu(P_r) -> 5/2. Adding isolated rectangles makes every rational in [1, 5/2) occur both as tau/nu and as an LP gap. Bal states that the global supremum over rectangle families remains open. No finite family with tau/nu >= 5/2 is published.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit finite family of closed axis-parallel rectangles with rational coordinates whose exactly computed ratio tau(R)/nu(R) is STRICTLY GREATER than 5/2 (direction: max) and than any larger finite ratio published at verification time. Re-check the arXiv pages of 2606.17854 and 2607.11318 and any 2026 follow-up first. Both nu and tau must be certified exactly: nu by a maximum independent set of the intersection graph with an optimality proof, and tau by a minimum hitting set over a provably sufficient candidate point set with an optimality proof, each confirmed by two independent exact solvers.

partial_wins.statement: A finite family with tau(R) = (5/2) nu(R) exactly. This attains the published limit, which no finite family is known to reach.

A finite family whose standard clique (point) LP relaxation of maximum independent set has value alpha*(R) >= (5/2) nu(R), computed exactly in rationals. This beats every published finite gap: Bal's 73/32 and the interpolated values below 5/2.
A counterexample to Wegner's conjecture (a family with tau >= 2 nu) with fewer than 64 rectangles, the size of the smallest published examples (Ajwani et al. v2 and Bal).

targets.verification_method: An independent script: parse the rectangles as closed boxes [x1,x2] x [y1,y2] with exact rationals. Build the intersection graph (closed boxes intersect iff their x- and y-intervals both overlap, touching included). For tau, use the candidate points (left x of rectangle i, bottom y of rectangle j) that lie in at least one rectangle: any piercing point can be moved to such a point without leaving any rectangle. Solve both ILPs with two solvers (e.g. CBC via pulp and OR-Tools CP-SAT) to proven optimality. For p2, solve the LP over the same point set in exact rational arithmetic (or verify a rational primal and dual pair). Calibrate on Bal's 64-rectangle family: nu = 16, tau >= 32.
pitfalls: Open versus closed rectangles changes the intersection graph: use closed rectangles, the convention of both papers.
Ratios that only tend to a limit are not a finite family: the win needs one explicit family with exact tau and nu.

targets.name: Slicing the hypercube: fewer hyperplanes than ceil(4n/5) cutting every edge of Q_n (e.g. 5 for Q_7), or new S(n,k) edge records
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (edge-weighted local search over integer hyperplanes; a full check of Q_n for n <= 20 takes seconds)
targets.statement: S(n) is the fewest hyperplanes in R^n such that every edge of the cube Q_n on {-1,1}^n is cut in its interior by one of them. Trivially S(n) <= n. Paterson's construction (reported by O'Neil, 1971) gave S(n) <= ceil(5n/6), and this stood for over fifty years. S(n) = n for n <= 5 and S(6) = 5 (Emamy-Khansary and Ziegler). Lower bounds are sublinear: O'Neil Omega(sqrt n), then Yehuda-Yehudayoff, Klein, and Sauermann-Xu (2025) Omega(n^{13/19} polylog). Sauermann-Xu (2026) show that integer coefficients suffice and give n/(4C) for coefficients bounded by C. Soiffer, Itty, Rosin, Bruell, DiCicco, Sárközy, Offstein and Reichman, 'Improved Upper Bounds for Slicing the Hypercube', arXiv:2602.16807 (v2, 29 Jun 2026), found 8 hyperplanes slicing Q_10 with CPro1-assisted search. By subadditivity S(n) <= ceil(4n/5), or 4n/5 + 1 when n is an odd multiple of 5. Current bounds: S(7) <= 6, S(8) <= 7, S(9) <= 8, S(11) <= 9, S(12) <= 10, S(13) <= 11. The paper says it is open whether S(7) = 5. Its Tables 1-2 give record partial slicings S(n,k), the most edges of Q_n cut by k hyperplanes, for example S(7,5) >= 440 of 448, S(9,7) >= 2298 of 2304 and S(11,8) >= 11240 of 11264. Code and solutions: github.com/DSoiffer/upper-bounds-for-hypercube-slicing.
targets.success_criterion: Integer vectors a_i and rational thresholds b_i (equivalently, all integers after scaling), i = 1..k, for some n >= 7. k must be STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the best upper bound on S(n) at verification time. On 2026-10-30 that bound is ceil(4n/5), or 4n/5 + 1 for odd multiples of 5, from arXiv:2602.16807; S(n) is known exactly for n <= 6. For EVERY edge {u, v} of Q_n some i must have (a_i.u - b_i)(a_i.v - b_i) < 0, checked over all n 2^(n-1) edges in exact arithmetic. For an odd multiple of 5 this means 4n/5 hyperplanes already win (for example 12 for Q_15, removing the '+1' exception). Any construction with k/n < 4/5 also lowers the asymptotic constant. Re-check the arXiv page, the authors' GitHub repository (results.txt, other-constructions) and any 2026 follow-up first.

partial_wins.statement: A new S(n,k) record for n >= 7: k hyperplanes (integer normals, rational thresholds) cutting STRICTLY MORE edges of Q_n, counted exactly with a strict sign change, than the value for that (n,k) in Table 1 (n = 7..11, k = 4..10) or Table 2 (n = k+3, k = 9..12) of arXiv:2602.16807, or than any later published record. The cell's current value must be below the total n 2^(n-1).

targets.verification_method: An independent script: read the integer matrix A (k x n) and vector b, enumerate all 2^n vertices, compute A x - b exactly, and for every edge (flip one coordinate) test for a strict sign change in some row. Count the sliced edges and compare with n 2^(n-1). Calibrate on Paterson's 5 planes for Q_6 and the paper's 8 planes for Q_10 (both must slice everything) and on a corrupted plane (must fail). For n up to about 24 this is a direct loop; beyond that use the paper's reduced-cube symmetry argument only if its correctness is re-derived.
angles: The successful Q_10 solutions fix many coefficients to one common value and the bias to 0.5. Search compositions b = [6,1,1,1,1]-style reduced cubes for Q_11 with 8 planes or Q_7 with 5.
pitfalls: A hyperplane through a vertex does not cut the edge's interior; require strict sign change.
Floating-point coefficients can hide zeros; use integers (Sauermann-Xu: an integer solution exists whenever a real one does).

targets.name: ATOM3D RSR: beat the published Spearman for ranking RNA structural models by RMSD
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (dataset is a few GB; CPU training of a modest model)
targets.statement: ATOM3D (Raphael Townshend, Martin Vogele, Patricia Suriana, Alexander Derry, Alexander Powers, Yianni Laloudakis, Sidhika Balachandar, Bowen Jing, Brandon Anderson, Risi Kondor, Russ Altman and Ron Dror; NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks) includes RSR, RNA structure ranking: for each of the first 21 RNA-Puzzles targets, score FARFAR2 candidate models - generated by Andrew Watkins, Ramya Rangan and Rhiju Das (2020) - by their RMSD to the experimental structure, under a temporal split by competition year (puzzles 1-13 train, 14-17 without 16 validation, 18-21 test), with data and split indices public on Zenodo (record 4961085, doi 10.5281/zenodo.4961085). The paper's full results (Table 8) report mean per-target Spearman 0.264 +/- 0.046 for the 3DCNN and 0.234 +/- 0.006 for the GNN, with global Spearman 0.372 +/- 0.027 and 0.512 +/- 0.049 respectively, against the benchmark's reference row - the Rosetta all-atom energy function of Rebecca Alford and co-authors (2017), scoring the same candidates - at mean per-target 0.173 and global 0.304. The only later row published on this split is the GVP-GNN of Bowen Jing, Stephan Eismann, Pratham Soni and Ron Dror (arXiv:2106.03843), at mean per-target 0.211 +/- 0.142 and global 0.330 +/- 0.054, below both ATOM3D models; later protein-structure work on ATOM3D (for example AtomSurf) does not evaluate RSR at all, so the 2021 rows remain the published state. A mean per-target Spearman near 0.26 means that picking the better of two candidate RNA models is still close to a coin flip inside a target, which is exactly what matters when choosing a model to publish. The task is small enough to train on a laptop from cached features.
targets.success_criterion: A predicted score (or predicted RMSD) for every candidate model in the ATOM3D RSR test split, from a model trained only on the designated training split (temporal: no candidates from a test-year puzzle, and declared pretraining corpora checked for the test puzzles' experimental structures), such that the mean per-target Spearman correlation computed by the skeptic with the ATOM3D evaluation code is STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than 0.264 (3DCNN, arXiv:2012.04035 Table 8, re-fetched live immediately before claiming) by at least 0.03, reported as mean and standard deviation over at least three seeds, with global Spearman and per-target values also reported, and higher than any later published mean per-target Spearman for the same split found by the novelty check.

partial_wins.statement: Global Spearman on the same RSR test split strictly above 0.512 (GNN) by at least 0.03 over three seeds, with the mean per-target value also reported.

A features-only model (no 3D deep network; for example gradient-boosted trees over base-pair, stacking, clash, radius-of-gyration and solvent-exposure features), trained only on the designated training split, whose mean per-target Spearman on the RSR test split matches the published 3DCNN value of 0.264 within 0.02 over three seeds, with the feature list, training script and per-target table published.

A reproducible diagnosis, from the public split alone, of which puzzles carry the error (for example candidate pools whose RMSD range is narrow) plus a controlled experiment showing one named fix raises the mean per-target Spearman, even if it stays below the bar.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the RSR dataset and split indices from Zenodo record 4961085, checks the prediction file covers every test candidate exactly once, computes mean per-target and global Spearman with the ATOM3D code, reruns the attacker's training script from the released seeds to reproduce the numbers within the stated standard deviation, and verifies no test-year puzzle appeared in training or in any declared pretraining corpus. An hour or two plus the attacker's training cost.
angles: Learn to rank rather than to regress: a pairwise ranking loss within each target optimises exactly the per-target Spearman that the task measures, while RMSD regression optimises the global correlation.
Cross-domain import (information retrieval): per-query normalisation and listwise losses (LambdaRank-style) are built for the mean-over-queries metric used here.

Cheap physical features first - base-pair geometry, stacking, radius of gyration, clash counts - and a small gradient-boosted model on them; with 21 targets a large network overfits the puzzle identity.
Report both metrics always: global Spearman is dominated by between-target RMSD scale, so a method can look strong globally while being useless inside a target.
Augment by generating extra candidate pools for training-year puzzles with open RNA modelling tools, keeping the temporal split intact.
pitfalls: The experimental structures of all 21 puzzles are public, so any feature or pretrained model that encodes a test puzzle's own structure breaks the temporal split; declare every corpus.
Papers reporting RNA model-scoring results (for example ARES-style networks) often use their own benchmark, not the ATOM3D RSR split; the comparison must be on this split or it is not a comparison.
Mean per-target and global Spearman are different numbers; quoting the global value against the mean bar is a category error.
Candidate pools come from FARFAR2 only, so a scorer tuned to its artefacts may not transfer; a claim should stop at the benchmark.
The test set has few targets, so seed variance is large: three seeds and a reported standard deviation are the minimum.

targets.name: CryoBench: beat the best published per-image FSC AUC for cryo-EM heterogeneity on a ground-truth dataset
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (GPU; 100k-335k simulated particles per dataset, tens of GB)
targets.statement: CryoBench (Minkyu Jeon, Rishwanth Raghu, Miro Astore, Geoffrey Woollard, Ryan Feathers, Alkin Kaz, Sonya Hanson, Pilar Cossio and Ellen Zhong; NeurIPS 2024 spotlight, arXiv:2408.05526) provides simulated cryo-EM datasets with known ground-truth structures for the heterogeneity problem: IgG-1D (100 Fab rotation states, 100k images), IgG-RL (100 linker-driven conformations, 100k images), Ribosembly (16 bacterial ribosome assembly states, 335,240 images) and Tomotwin-100 (100 distinct cellular complexes, 100k images), with code, per-image FSC and embedding metrics in the repository and data on Zenodo (records 11629428 and 12528292). In the CryoBench tables RECOVAR led IgG-1D at 0.386, IgG-RL at 0.363 and Ribosembly at 0.429 mean per-image FSC AUC, and CryoDRGN led Tomotwin-100 at 0.316, all with poses given. Three later papers have moved those rows. CryoSPIRE (Shayan Shekarforoush, David B. Lindell, Marcus A. Brubaker and David J. Fleet, arXiv:2506.09063) raised IgG-1D to 0.396 and IgG-RL to 0.375 with poses given, while reporting 0.422 on Ribosembly and not evaluating Tomotwin-100. SOLVAR (arXiv:2602.17603) reports 0.388 / 0.369 / 0.431 on the three and 0.333 on Tomotwin-100 at rank 50. CryoHype (arXiv:2512.06332) reports 0.346 on Tomotwin-100 with poses given, against a backprojection upper bound of 0.364. So the current fixed-pose bests are IgG-1D 0.396, IgG-RL 0.375, Ribosembly 0.431 and Tomotwin-100 0.346. Ab initio remains far behind: CryoDRGN-AI 0.351 / 0.329 / 0.341 / 0.072 and 3D Class abinit 0.130 on IgG-1D, with SOLVAR's RELION-initialised pose-optimising run the best published ab initio pipeline at 0.385 / 0.334 / 0.424 / 0.103. On clustering, RECOVAR reaches ARI 0.968 on Ribosembly and CryoDRGN 0.956 on Tomotwin-100, but every ab initio method collapses on Tomotwin-100 (best ARI 0.116, CryoDRGN2), and the authors state that current ab initio reconstruction cannot recover the 100 ground-truth structures. This target covers those four datasets only.
targets.success_criterion: For a declared CryoBench dataset among IgG-1D, IgG-RL, Ribosembly and Tomotwin-100: the reconstructed per-particle volumes (or a generator plus the per-particle latent codes needed to produce them) for the full released dataset, such that the skeptic, running the repository's metrics/fsc code against the released ground-truth volumes, obtains a mean per-image FSC AUC STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the best published value for that dataset - IgG-1D 0.396 and IgG-RL 0.375 (CryoSPIRE, arXiv:2506.09063), Ribosembly 0.431 (SOLVAR, arXiv:2602.17603) and Tomotwin-100 0.346 (CryoHype, arXiv:2512.06332), all re-fetched live immediately before claiming - by at least 0.010, and higher than any later published value for the same dataset and metric found by the novelty check; with the input regime declared (poses given, or ab initio) and compared only against published rows of the same regime, no ground-truth volume, conformational label or ground-truth embedding used at any stage, and code, configs, seeds and latent codes published so the metric recomputes.

partial_wins.statement: In the ab initio regime (poses not supplied, pose estimation part of the attacker's own pipeline), a mean per-image FSC AUC on a declared dataset strictly above the best published ab initio value for it - SOLVAR with RELION initialisation and pose optimisation at 0.385 on IgG-1D, 0.334 on IgG-RL, 0.424 on Ribosembly and 0.103 on Tomotwin-100 (arXiv:2602.17603), above CryoDRGN-AI's 0.351 / 0.329 / 0.341 / 0.072 - by at least 0.010.

On Tomotwin-100, a clustering ARI strictly above 0.116 (best published ab initio, CryoDRGN2) by at least 0.05 in the ab initio regime, or strictly above 0.956 (CryoDRGN, poses given) by at least 0.005 in the fixed-pose regime, computed with the repository's metrics.

A reproduction artefact: reproducing a published CryoBench row (method, dataset, FSC AUC) to within 0.010 with the public code and data, with runtime and hardware reported, published as a reproduction.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the declared dataset from its Zenodo record and the ground-truth volumes, installs cryodrgn and the CryoBench metrics code at the pinned versions, recomputes mean per-image FSC AUC (and ARI/AMI where claimed) from the attacker's volumes or latents, checks that every particle of the released dataset is covered, reads the configs to confirm no ground-truth volume, label or embedding was used and that the pose regime matches the rows compared against, and re-fetches the paper's tables. Scoring is hours of GPU time; the reconstruction is the attacker's cost.
angles: The compositional datasets punish continuous latent models: try a discrete-plus-continuous latent (mixture over states with a per-state deformation) instead of one smooth embedding.
Tomotwin-100 is the clearest failure: 100 unrelated complexes with shared pose estimation, so a pipeline that alternates clustering and per-cluster ab initio refinement may beat joint embedding.

Cross-domain import (mixture modelling and clustering): initialise with a robust covariance/PCA step (the route RECOVAR takes) before any neural model, which fixes the collapse that random initialisation causes.
Spend effort on pose accuracy in the ab initio regime; the paper reports pose error separately and it is the dominant term in the FSC gap.
Report the per-conformation FSC curve, not only its AUC, so a gain concentrated on the easiest states is visible.
pitfalls: Ground-truth volumes, state labels and reference embeddings ship with the datasets; touching them anywhere in the pipeline (even for model selection) invalidates the result.
Fixed-pose and ab initio numbers are not comparable; a fixed-pose result quoted against an ab initio row is not a win, and a pipeline that takes poses from a prior consensus refinement must say so.
On Tomotwin-100 the headroom is small: CryoHype reports a backprojection upper bound of 0.364 against its own 0.346, so a gain there has to be close to that ceiling.
FSC AUC is sensitive to box size, downsampling and masking; use the repository's code unchanged and state the resolution of the images used.
The datasets are simulated, so a gain here is a benchmark result and need not transfer to experimental micrographs; claims must stop at the benchmark.
The paper's Spike-MD dataset is outside this target's scope; results on it do not count toward this win.

targets.name: Motif scaffolding benchmark (24 tasks): more unique in-silico successes than the published best on a task
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (GPU for sampling plus ProteinMPNN/AlphaFold2 self-consistency over thousands of designs)
targets.statement: The standard motif-scaffolding benchmark is the 25-task set curated by Joseph Watson, David Juergens, Nathaniel Bennett and colleagues for RFdiffusion, from six earlier publications. Genie 2 (Yeqing Lin, Minji Lee, Zhao Zhang and Mohammed AlQuraishi, arXiv:2405.15489) evaluates 24 of them (dropping 6VW1, whose motif spans chains) with a fully specified in-silico criterion: a design counts as a success when the self-consistency RMSD is at most 2 A, predicted pLDDT at least 70, predicted aligned error at most 5, and the motif backbone RMSD at most 1 A, and successes are clustered by single-linkage TM-score at 0.6 so only unique scaffolds count. Proteina (Tomas Geffner and co-authors, ICLR 2025, arXiv:2503.00710) re-ran that same criterion, clustering and sample budget (1,000 backbones per task) on the same 24 tasks and published the current record table, four columns wide: Proteina, Genie 2, RFdiffusion and FrameFlow (Jason Yim and co-authors), with 2,094 unique successes in total for Proteina against 1,445 for Genie 2. Per task the best published counts are now 6E6R_long 713, 6E6R_med 417, 1YCR 249, 5TRV_long 179, 6E6R_short 56, 7MRX_85 31, 4ZYP 11 and 5YUI 5 (Proteina); 6EXZ_long 403, 6EXZ_med 110, 1QJG 18 and 5WN9 3 (FrameFlow); 7MRX_128 66 (RFdiffusion); 3IXT 14, 5TPN 8, 7MRX_60 5, 5TRV_med 23 and 5TRV_short 3 (Genie 2); 6EXZ_short 3 (Proteina and FrameFlow); and 1PRW, 5IUS, 1BCF and 2KL8 at 1 each. Ten of the 24 tasks are still at or below 8 unique successes and 4JHW has no unique success in any of the four columns, while the scoring pipeline (ProteinMPNN plus a structure predictor) is public and the win is a file of backbones and sequences. Two later suites must be surveyed but are not this benchmark: MotifBench (arXiv:2502.12479) scores a different 30-problem set, including two 4JHW cases, under its own criterion and clustering; and GPFlow (arXiv:2607.09039) reports much higher counts on several of these tasks (for example 1PRW 42, 1BCF 11, 3IXT 398, 4ZYP 144, and 4JHW still 0) but clusters successes with FoldSeek and merges the length variants of a task, so its numbers are not counts under this criterion. This target is about in-silico benchmark scores only.
targets.success_criterion: For a declared task of the 24-task benchmark: a published set of designed backbones with their designed sequences and the exact sampling configuration (model, N samples, seeds), such that the skeptic, re-running the benchmark's own public self-consistency pipeline (ProteinMPNN sequence design plus the declared structure predictor at a pinned version) and applying the published criterion (scRMSD <= 2 A, pLDDT >= 70, pAE <= 5, motif backbone RMSD <= 1 A, single-linkage TM-score clustering at 0.6), counts a number of unique successes STRICTLY HIGHER (direction: max) than the best published count for that task across the four columns of arXiv:2503.00710 Table 5 (Proteina, Genie 2, RFdiffusion, FrameFlow) and the Genie 2 table of arXiv:2405.15489, both re-fetched live immediately before claiming, and than any later published count for the same task and criterion found by the novelty check, at the same or a smaller sample budget N, with the per-sample metric table published. For 4JHW, at least one unique success under this criterion and the benchmark's own motif specification counts as the full win, provided the novelty check finds no earlier published unique success for 4JHW under this criterion. The motif specification must be the benchmark's own (same residues, same contiguity and length ranges), and no experimental structure of the benchmark's native scaffold may be used as a template.

partial_wins.statement: At least one unique success on 4JHW under the published criterion and the benchmark's own motif specification, verified by the skeptic's re-run of the scoring pipeline, with the novelty check reporting whether any earlier 4JHW success has been published under this, the MotifBench or the FoldSeek-clustered GPFlow criterion.

Strictly more unique successes than the best published count on at least three of the tasks still at or below 8 (1PRW 1, 5IUS 1, 1BCF 1, 2KL8 1, 5TRV_short 3, 6EXZ_short 3, 5WN9 3, 5YUI 5, 7MRX_60 5, 5TPN 8) at the same or a smaller sample budget.

A reproduction artefact: reproducing a published per-task unique-success count to within 20 percent on at least five tasks with public weights and the public scoring pipeline, with the harness and all per-sample metrics published.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic takes the attacker's backbones and sequences, re-runs ProteinMPNN and the declared structure predictor at the pinned versions, recomputes scRMSD, pLDDT, pAE and motif RMSD per design, applies the TM-score 0.6 clustering to count unique successes, checks the motif residues and length ranges against the benchmark specification, confirms the sample budget from the published seeds and configs, and re-fetches the published tables. Hours of GPU time for scoring; sampling is the attacker's cost.
angles: Condition harder on the motif: increase the fraction of conditional training or inference-time guidance strength, which the Genie 2 ablation shows moves the success count substantially.
Diversity is what is scored (unique clusters, not raw successes), so explicitly penalise similarity to already-accepted designs during sampling rather than drawing more independent samples.

Cross-domain import (constrained generation): treat the motif as a hard constraint via projection or twisted sampling at every denoising step instead of a soft loss, which is what made TDS-style samplers work on hard motifs.

The never-solved task is a long, mostly-helical epitope: try scaffolding it inside a larger designed fold with explicit secondary-structure conditioning, and report the per-sample metric distribution to see which threshold fails.
Measure which of the four thresholds fails most often per task; if pAE is the binding constraint, more samples will not help and the fold choice must change.
pitfalls: Scoring details move the count a lot: predictor version, single-sequence vs MSA input, number of ProteinMPNN sequences per backbone and the clustering threshold must all be pinned and re-run by the skeptic.

Counts clustered another way are not counts here: GPFlow clusters with FoldSeek and merges a task's length variants, and MotifBench uses its own criterion, so neither sets the bar for a task on this benchmark.
Loosening or re-defining the motif (fewer residues, wider length ranges) makes the task easier and is not the benchmark; the specification must be the published one.
Unique successes depend on the sample budget, so a count at 10,000 samples is not comparable to a published count at 1,000; the budget must be equal or smaller.
Self-consistency success is an in-silico proxy: a win here says nothing about whether any design folds or functions in reality, and no claim beyond the benchmark is admissible.
Templating from the native scaffold of the motif's source structure is leakage and is excluded by the criterion.

targets.name: CATH 4.2 inverse folding: beat the best published sequence recovery (0.63, Refold) on the standard test split
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (GPU helps; the CATH 4.2 split is a few hundred MB)
targets.statement: The standard table for protein inverse folding is sequence recovery on the CATH 4.2 test split used by GraphTrans, GVP, ProteinMPNN and PiFold. As compiled by Zhangyang Gao, Cheng Tan and Stan Z. Li in Knowledge-Design (arXiv:2305.15151), the published recoveries on the full test set are StructGNN 35.91, GraphTrans 35.82, GCA 37.64, ESM-IF 38.3, GVP 39.47, AlphaDesign 41.31, ProteinMPNN 45.96, PiFold 51.66, LM-Design 55.65 and Knowledge-Design 60.77 percent, with 44.66 on the short subset, 45.45 on the single-chain subset, and TS50 62.79 and TS500 69.19 for the same model. Refold (Yiran Zhu, Changxi Chi, Hongxin Xiang, Wenjie Du, Xiaoqi Wang and Jun Xia, arXiv:2603.14350) reports higher recovery on the same benchmark through the ProteinInvBench framework: 0.63 on the CATH 4.2 full test set and 0.51 on the short subset for Refold (Joint), and 0.61 full for Refold (Frozen); its figures are given to two decimals only and the paper does not name the split file. Credit for the current state belongs to those authors and to the ProteinMPNN (Justas Dauparas and co-authors) and PiFold lines of work the table is built on.
