Ajtai-Komlos-Szemeredi proved an approximate version, and Zhao (EJC 18 (2011) P27) proved it for all sufficiently large n, with no explicit threshold. The problem's status on the site database is 'decidable'. Zeraoulia Rafik (forum proof claim of 14 Jul 2026, updated 16 Jul 2026, with a manuscript and a Zenodo archive of CNF files and DRUP certificates) claims the vertex formulation for every n <= 19. The main new computer case is n = 18: of the 47 trees on 9 vertices, 42 are handled by theory, and the other 5 reduce to four rooted-core configurations whose SAT instances are certified UNSAT; each odd order follows from the even order below it by deleting a high-degree vertex. A moderator reclassified it as a partial proof claim (23 Jul 2026), and it is not verified by the site. In the same thread Johan Land (23 Jul 2026) said he had extended the check to n <= 21, but posted no code or certificates.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: an explicit graph G on n vertices with at least ceil(n/2) vertices of degree >= n/2, and an explicit tree T on at most n/2 vertices that is not a subgraph of G. Non-containment is certified by an exhaustive embedding search (or an UNSAT certificate) that two independent implementations reproduce.

partial_wins.statement: A certified verification for n = 20: every graph satisfying the degree hypothesis contains every tree on at most 10 vertices. Reductions are written out, every SAT case comes with a DRAT/LRAT proof checked by a verified checker, and the tree list matches the 106 unlabelled trees on 10 vertices (OEIS A000055). This counts only if no certified n = 20 verification (code and proofs) is public at verification time; Johan Land's 23 Jul 2026 forum statement, with nothing posted, does not count as one.

The same certified verification for n = 22 (every tree on at most 11 vertices; 235 unlabelled trees on 11 vertices, OEIS A000055). n = 21 alone does not count, since it follows from n = 20 by the odd-order reduction.

targets.verification_method: For a counterexample: check the degree condition, then run two independent subgraph-isomorphism searches (for example a VF2-style search and a SAT encoding) showing T is not in G. For p1/p2: referee the reduction, regenerate the CNF instances from the stated encoding, and check every proof with cake_lpr or drat-trim.
angles: Reuse the edge-minimal-counterexample reduction to a bipartite structure from the n <= 19 manuscript, and encode only the trees that the embedding theorems do not handle.
pitfalls: The n <= 19 result is a proof claim, not yet accepted; read it before building on it.

There are two formulations: the site's vertex version (every tree on at most n/2 vertices) and the stronger classical EFLS/Zhao edge version (every tree with at most n/2 edges), plus Komlos-Sos variants with k. The n <= 19 claim covers only the vertex version; state which one is verified.
Zhao's 'sufficiently large n' gives no explicit threshold, so finite checks cannot close the problem.

targets.name: Erdos #1095 (Ecklund-Erdos-Selfridge function g(k)): g(401) and beyond, or an independent replay of g(378..400)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (GPU wheel sieve; Eastwood's 2026 runs used CUDA), laptop-hours for checking witnesses
targets.statement: g(k) is the least n > k+1 such that every prime factor of C(n,k) is > k (Ecklund-Erdos-Selfridge 1974; Erdos #1095; OEIS A003458). Bounds: g(k) >> exp(c (log k)^2) (Konyagin 1999; Woett formalised this lower-bound proof in Lean, Jun 2026) and g(k) <= exp((1+o(1))k) (Ecklund-Erdos-Selfridge 1974). Exact values come from Scheidler-Williams (1992), Lukes-Scheidler-Williams (1997) and Sorenson-Sorenson-Webster (to k = 377), with the CUDA wheel method of Alexander Eastwood (2026, github.com/AlexanderEastwood/erdos-selfridge; an earlier snapshot is archived at doi 10.5281/zenodo.22057210, which predates the 400-term release) for k = 378..400. The OEIS b-file now covers k = 1..400 (A003458 edited 18 Sep 2026); g(400) = 58305842808280308870124770403739. Eastwood's README says minimality for 378..400 rests on recorded exhaustive block scans with two wheels that share implementation components, not on a fresh independent replay.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: the exact value of g(401) (or of the next k beyond the OEIS b-file at verification time). The witness must satisfy the defining condition, checked with exact big-integer arithmetic and Kummer digit tests for every prime p <= k. Minimality needs an exhaustive scan of all smaller candidates, reproduced by two implementations that share no code.

partial_wins.statement: An independent exhaustive replay of g(378), ..., g(400) by code sharing no components with Eastwood's wheels, matching all 23 values or exhibiting a smaller admissible n for some k.
Exact g(k) for every 401 <= k <= 410 with minimality as in the success criterion.

targets.verification_method: Check the witness by Kummer's theorem: for each prime p <= k, adding k and n-k in base p has no carries, equivalently p does not divide C(n,k). Confirm with an exact binomial computation for small cases. Re-run the minimality scan with an independent sieve and compare survivor lists and hashes.
angles: Use the Sorenson-Sorenson-Webster partial-prime-power wheel: CRT over small prime powers gives admissible residues, then filter the remaining primes by digit constraints.
pitfalls: Admissibility of a witness is easy to check; minimality is the hard part and must be exhaustive.
Values grow irregularly (g(397) has 34 digits, g(400) 32), so a search bound from neighbouring k can be wrong.

targets.name: Erdős #217 (crescent configurations): 9 points in general position whose 8 distances occur 1, 2, ..., 8 times
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exact integer lattice searches; off-lattice needs algebraic-number optimisation)
targets.statement: For which n are there n points in the plane, no three on a line and no four on a circle, determining exactly n-1 distinct distances such that (in some order) the i-th distance occurs exactly i times? Burt, Goldstein, Manski, Miller, Palsson and Suh (arXiv:1509.07220) call these crescent configurations. Known: n=4 (isosceles triangle plus centre), n=5 (Pomerance), n=6 with no equilateral triangle (Palásti 1989), n=7 (Palásti 1987), n=8 (Palásti 1989b). Erdős believed they cannot exist for large n. No n=9 example is known. Burt et al. exhaustively searched a 91-point hexagonal patch of the triangular lattice (none). Forum, sallerk (2026-08-31): exact search shows no 9-point crescent configuration on the triangular lattice with squared diameter <= 400 (1,459 lattice points, ~3.1e12 nodes), and the same code recovers Palásti's n=8 example. Forum, IheartTesla (2026-09-04): relaxing general position, a 9-point triangular-lattice set with multiplicities 1..8 and only C+Q = 3 defects (1 collinear triple, 2 concyclic quadruples); best for n=10 was (C,Q) = (2,2). Status on erdosproblems.com and the teorth database: open.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: exact coordinates (integers, rationals, or elements of an explicitly given number field with exact arithmetic) for 9 points in R^2 such that (i) no three are collinear and no four are concyclic, checked with exact 3x3 and 4x4 determinants; (ii) the squared pairwise distances take exactly 8 distinct values; (iii) the multiset of their multiplicities is exactly {1,2,...,8} (any order of distances is allowed, as in Palásti's n=8 example). The same with n >= 10 points and multiplicities {1,...,n-1} also counts. Alternatively a machine-checked proof that no 9-point crescent configuration exists in the plane.

partial_wins.statement: A 9-point planar set with exact coordinates whose distances have multiplicities exactly {1,...,8} and whose number of collinear triples plus concyclic quadruples (counted as in IheartTesla's 2026-09-04 forum comment) is at most 2, strictly below the best value posted on the #217 thread at verification time (3 on 2026-10-30).
A 10-point planar set with exact coordinates, multiplicities exactly {1,...,9}, and C+Q at most 3, strictly below the best value posted at verification time (4, i.e. (2,2), on 2026-10-30).

A reproducible exhaustive exact search proving that no 9-point crescent configuration lies on the triangular lattice with squared diameter up to at least 800, double the forum's 400, with code that also recovers the known n=4..8 configurations.

targets.verification_method: Recompute all C(9,2)=36 squared distances exactly, tally multiplicities, and test every triple (collinearity determinant) and every quadruple (concyclicity determinant, 126 quadruples) in exact arithmetic with an independent script. For p3, rerun the search at a verifier-chosen rung and check the positive controls (Palásti's n=8 set scaled by sqrt 7 at squared diameter 21).
angles: Off-lattice: fix a combinatorial pattern of which pairs share a distance (from the n=8 Palásti set plus one point) and solve the polynomial system with Gröbner bases or certified Newton, then check genericity exactly.
Other lattices (Z^2, Z[sqrt(-d)]) are not covered by the forum search.
pitfalls: 'In some ordering' matters: Palásti's own n=8 set has multiplicities 1,4,5,6,7,2,3 by increasing distance, so do not require monotone multiplicities.
Floating-point concyclicity tests give false negatives; use exact determinants.
The triangular lattice up to squared diameter 400 is already excluded (sallerk).

targets.name: Erdős #203: an m coprime to 6 with every 2^k 3^l m + 1 composite (a two-dimensional Sierpiński number)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (covering search over prime pools from cyclotomic gcds)
targets.statement: Is there an integer m >= 1 with gcd(m,6) = 1 such that 2^k 3^l m + 1 is composite for all k, l >= 0 (Erdős-Graham [ErGr80, p.27])? Ordinary Sierpiński numbers (one exponent) exist via covering systems; here the covering must work on the two-dimensional torus. For a prime p, the pairs (k,l) with p | 2^k 3^l m + 1 form one coset of a lattice of index |H_p| = | < 2,3> mod p| = lcm(ord_p 2, ord_p 3); a covering set P needs sum 1/|H_p| >= 1. Forum: AnimishSharma (2026-06-21) proves the subgroup formula and the density condition and, computationally, excludes coverings with lcm |H_p| < 5040 among primes p <= 5e7, with best coverage 71-72% at moduli 5040 and 10080; veljjanoski (2026-09-15, code: github.com/veljjanoski/erdos203) builds complete prime pools from gcd(Phi_a(2), Phi_b(3)) (442 primes with |H_p| <= 2000, sum 1/|H_p| = 1.97; 1006 primes with |H_p| <= 5000, sum 2.15) and reaches at best 76.0% exact coverage of the torus at N = 55440 (55 primes); his README also reports sampled (not exact) strip coverages up to 81.3% with the 1006-prime pool. Off the forum, the-omega-institute/trureturing issue #9414 (2026-09-22, an AI-agent project, reviewed only by agents) claims that no prime-only covering exists using primes with |H_p| <= 5000 (all sizes), plus finite-family obstructions at N = 404779703328000. Any solution must itself be an ordinary Sierpiński number (take l = 0); 78557 fails (2*3^2*78557+1 = 1414027 is prime). Status: open on erdosproblems.com and in the teorth database.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: an integer m >= 1 with gcd(m,6)=1, together with a finite set P of primes, such that for EVERY (k,l) in Z_{ > =0}^2 some p in P divides 2^k 3^l m + 1 and 2^k 3^l m + 1 > p. Checked by: for each p, computing a = ord_p(2), b = ord_p(3) and the set of residue pairs (k mod a, l mod b) killed by p; verifying the union covers all of Z_A x Z_B with A = lcm of the a's and B = lcm of the b's; and confirming 2^k 3^l m + 1 != p for the finitely many small (k,l) where equality could occur. A proof that no such m exists is also a full win (pure thought, checkable line by line or in Lean).

partial_wins.statement: An exact, reproducible proof (density computation plus exhaustive search where needed) that no covering set exists with lcm(|H_p| : p in P) < 10080, valid for primes of every size (using that p | gcd(Phi_a(2), Phi_b(3)) bounds the pool). This improves the forum exclusion (lcm < 5040, primes p <= 5e7) and is not implied by the trureturing #9414 claim (all |H_p| <= 5000), because it must also handle primes with 5000 < |H_p| < 10080 that divide the lcm.

targets.verification_method: Independent re-implementation: compute multiplicative orders with exact integer arithmetic, build the killed cosets, and count uncovered cells of the torus (or verify the covering by iterating over a coarser CRT decomposition). For m itself, spot-check thousands of random (k,l) by direct trial division by P. For p2, re-derive the complete prime pool from cyclotomic gcds and recompute the density sums exactly.
angles: Look for nested lattice chains: primes whose (ord_p 2, ord_p 3) pairs divide each other, mimicking the 2|4|8|...|64 chains of 1D Sierpiński coverings; the forum found these are rare at small order, so consider primes of order in the 10^4-10^6 range from factor tables of 2^a - 1 and 3^b - 1.
Partial algebraic factorisations (m a perfect power) can cover a sublattice without primes; the forum tried cubes and 12th powers with no gain, but other shapes are untested.
pitfalls: The density condition sum 1/|H_p| >= 1 is necessary but far from sufficient; plateaus near 1 - exp(-sum) are expected for random choices.
m must be coprime to 6, and the case 2^k 3^l m + 1 = p itself must be excluded.
Erdős-Graham's variant with primes q = 1 mod 4 has the trivial answer m = 1 (Dogmachine); do not confuse the variants.

Torus coverage percentages are not a partial win: sampled strips already reach about 81%, and a trureturing construction attempt (#9414) is reported to fail only at (k,l) = (1,2). Only a complete covering counts.

targets.name: Erdős #273: a covering system with distinct moduli of the form p - 1, p >= 5 prime
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exact covering search; lcm candidates in the 10^7 range)
targets.statement: Is there a covering system all of whose (distinct) moduli are of the form p - 1 with p >= 5 prime (Erdős-Graham [ErGr80, p.24])? Selfridge found one using divisors of 360 when p = 3 (modulus 2) is allowed. Progress (forum and proof-claims): R. Zeraoulia (2026-07-27, doi:10.5281/zenodo.21613011) proved any such covering has lcm L >= 393120; veljjanoski (forum 2026-09-24/28, github.com/veljjanoski/erdos273) pushed this, with two independent exact searches, to L >= 4e6 and then L >= 8e6 (all 420 counting-admissible candidates in [4e6, 8e6) have no covering). A forum comment by ideal_ombrer (2026-07-12) states that the 149 moduli with p <= 877 cannot cover Z alone (BBMST distortion sieve, exact rational check). Greedy plus local search with the full pool leaves 10-14% of residues uncovered at lcm 55440 to 1.66e6. Status: open on erdosproblems.com.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: an explicit finite list of pairs (a_i, m_i) with distinct m_i, each m_i = p_i - 1 for a prime p_i >= 5, such that every integer is congruent to some a_i mod m_i. Checked by enumerating all residues modulo L = lcm(m_i) (or by an exact CRT-structured check when L is large) with two independent programs, and by proving each p_i = m_i + 1 prime. Alternatively a complete proof that no such covering exists (checkable line by line or in Lean).

partial_wins.statement: A reproducible exact proof (two independent searches, as in the forum) that no such covering has lcm L < 1.6e7, strictly above the best bound posted on the #273 thread or proof-claims page at verification time (L >= 8e6 on 2026-10-30).

A system of congruences with distinct moduli p - 1 (p >= 5 prime) whose exactly computed uncovered density modulo its lcm is below 0.08, strictly better than the best value posted on the thread at verification time (about 0.10 on 2026-10-30).

targets.verification_method: Recompute L, the full set of residues mod L, and the coverage with an independent sieve; verify primality of each p_i = m_i + 1. For p1, reproduce the counting test (sum of 1/m over admissible divisors m of L) for every candidate L and rerun the exact search on a verifier-chosen sample of candidates plus all borderline ones.
angles: All moduli are even: a covering splits into two coverings of Z by moduli (p-1)/2, one of which cannot use 2 (forum observation); attack the harder half first.
Use the Balister-Bollobás-Morris-Sahasrabudhe-Tiba distortion method as a filter to discard lcm candidates before search.
pitfalls: Modulus 2 (p = 3) is excluded; with it Selfridge's 360 example already works.
Moduli must be distinct.
Below lcm 8e6 is already excluded; do not re-announce weaker bounds.

targets.name: Erdős #313: a new primary pseudoperfect number (1/p_1 + ... + 1/p_k = 1 - 1/m), beyond the 11 known
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (port-filling / extension search from known terms)
targets.statement: Erdős-Graham [ErGr80, p.40] ask whether 1/p_1 + ... + 1/p_k = 1 - 1/m has infinitely many solutions with distinct primes p_i; necessarily m = p_1...p_k, so solutions are the primary pseudoperfect numbers m (sum over p | m of 1/p plus 1/m = 1), OEIS A054377. As of 2026-10-30, 11 are known: the 8 in the OEIS data (2, 6, 42, 1806, 47058, 2214502422, 52495396602, 5998279018951962402), plus three in OEIS comments: 8490421583559688410706771261086 (long known, formerly in the data), 35979351189199316534587473905773572006 (Pedro Martins and Han M. Wang, Apr 2026; Wang, arXiv:2605.21518 'Port fillings', obtained as N(N+1) from N = 5998279018951962402 with N+1 prime), and a 61-digit term with 10 prime factors, 2318487344461212044808266715505249967391337588451045543300838 (Pedro Martins, OEIS comment 2026-09-27). Max Alekseyev: no other terms below 10^24 (OEIS comment, 2026-08-12). Original definition: Butske, Jaje and Mayernik (2000). The erdosproblems.com page still says '8 known'; the OEIS entry is the up-to-date record. Whether infinitely many exist, or any odd one, is open.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: a squarefree integer N > 1 with its complete factorisation into PROVEN primes (deterministic test below 2^64, ECPP/Pocklington certificates above) such that 1/N + sum_{p | N} 1/p = 1 holds exactly (equivalently 1 + sum_{p|N} N/p = N), and N is not among the 11 numbers above nor in the data, comments or b-file of OEIS A054377 re-fetched at verification time.

partial_wins.statement: A reproducible exhaustive search proving there are no primary pseudoperfect numbers in [10^24, 10^26) other than any listed ones, extending Alekseyev's 10^24 bound, with code an independent verifier reruns.

targets.verification_method: Exact Fraction or integer arithmetic for the defining identity; primality certificates checked with an independent tool (e.g. PARI isprime with certificate, Primo, or a Pocklington check); comparison against the live OEIS entry.
angles: Wang's port-filling framework: known terms arise from a 'port' (pair of primes/cofactor) that can be completed; enumerate ports systematically.
Inheritance: if N is a term and N+1 is prime then N(N+1) is a term; test N+1 for each newly found term.
pitfalls: The erdosproblems.com page is stale ('8 known'); the record is the OEIS entry.
1 is not a primary pseudoperfect number.
Giuga numbers (sum 1/p - 1/N integer) are a different sequence already in the bank (giuga-numbers-new).

targets.name: Erdős #396 and #389: the first n with (n)(n-1)...(n-17) dividing C(2n,n), or a first witness for #389 at n = 36
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days to needs cluster (sieved exhaustive scans near 1e17)
targets.statement: 396 (Erdős-Graham): is it true that for every k there is n with prod_{i=0..k} (n - i) dividing C(2n,n)? OEIS A375077 gives the least such n for k = 1..16; the last three are a(14) = 359503904702190 (Justin Dehorty and Sharvil Kesarwani, Apr 2026, also found by wibble132), a(15) = 2394789405254721 (Kesarwani, Jul 2026) and a(16) = 20021368432952099 (Dehorty, Jul 2026); minimality of a(8)-a(13) is certified (Dehorty, with a Lean-verified small-prime barrier theorem, github.com/jdehorty/erdos396). Heuristically a(k+1)/a(k) is about 1/c_1 = 8.75 (Ford-Konyagin density; Nat Sothanaphan). #389 (Erdős-Straus): for every n is there k with n(n+1)...(n+k-1) | (n+k)...(n+2k-1)? OEIS A375071 (Bhavik Mehta, then Kesarwani, then Leandre Jack) gives the least k exactly for n <= 29 (k_min(28) = 18253129921815, k_min(29) = 18253129921814, Leandre Jack, forum 2026-09-04). Witnesses, not known minimal, exist for n = 30..35 (KentaKitamura 2026-08-01, Kesarwani 2026-08-25; corrected values for n = 34, 35 by Leandre Jack). A #396 witness N for k gives #389 witnesses for n = 2k+2 and 2k+3 via (n,k) -> (n+k-1, n). Both problems are open.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED (either): (A) an integer n with prod_{i=0..17} (n-i) | C(2n,n), i.e. a #396 witness for k = 17 (or for the smallest k with no entry in A375077 at verification time); or (B) a positive integer k with 36*37*...*(35+k) | (36+k)*...*(35+2k), i.e. a first #389 witness for n = 36 (or for the smallest n with no posted witness at verification time). In both cases the witness must not already appear in OEIS A375077/A375071 (data or comments), the #396 or #389 threads, or the Dehorty, Kesarwani (github.com/sharky564/ErdosProblems) or Leandre Jack repositories at verification time. Divisibility is checked prime by prime with Legendre's formula for the factorials involved (exact integer arithmetic), by two independent programs.

partial_wins.statement: A certified minimality proof (exhaustive scan with a provably complete sieve, reproducible) for the least k in #389 for some n in 30..35, i.e. a new exact term of A375071 beyond k_min(29).
A witness for #389 at some n in 30..35 with k strictly smaller than the smallest witness posted on the #389 thread or in A375071 comments at verification time.

targets.verification_method: For each prime p up to 2n (#396) or up to n+2k (#389), compute v_p of both sides via Legendre's formula v_p(N!) = sum floor(N/p^j) and check the inequality; a separate implementation recomputes with Kummer carries. For minimality claims, rerun the scan on verifier-chosen sub-intervals and audit the sieve's completeness argument.
angles: Governor primes: v_p(C(2n,n)) is the number of carries adding n+n in base p (Kummer); candidates must make n, n-1, ..., n-k all smooth relative to sqrt(2n). Sieve by large prime factors first.
Search directly for #389 witnesses at n = 36 using its own structure rather than the #396 transformation, which does not give minimal k.
pitfalls: A375071 is indexed from 0: OEIS index i corresponds to n = i+1 in the site's formulation.
Posted witnesses for n = 34, 35 were wrong at first (they fail at p = 67); verify every posted witness before using it.
Floating-point binomials are useless; work with valuations.

targets.name: Erdős #82 small cases: a graph on 21 vertices with no regular induced subgraph of order >= 6, or on 30 vertices with none of order >= 7
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (SAT/local search over graphs on 20-30 vertices)
targets.statement: Erdős, Fajtlowicz and Staton: let N_{ > =k} be the least n such that every n-vertex graph has a regular induced subgraph on at least k vertices (the page's G(k)); #82 asks to prove F(n)/log n -> infinity, i.e. N_{ > =k} = 2^{o(k)}. Known: N_{ > =3} = 5, N_{ > =4} = 7 (Fajtlowicz-McColgan-Reid-Staton 1995), N_{ > =5} = 17 (Brendan McKay 1997, confirmed by Boris Alexeev 2025), N_{ > =6} >= 21 and N_{ > =7} >= 30 (Paul Dyson and Brendan McKay, 'Ramsey numbers for regular induced subgraphs', arXiv:2604.08215 v3, Theorem 1.2; OEIS A394563). For exact order k (OEIS A394564): N_5 = 21, N_6 >= 28, N_7 >= 71; also N_{6,7} >= 28 and N_{7,8} >= 31 (605,961,088 graphs on 30 vertices with no regular induced subgraph of order 7 or 8). McKay's data page (users.cecs.anu.edu.au/~bdm/data/ramsey.html) posts samples of 1,000,000 graphs on 20 vertices (none of order >= 6) and on 29 vertices (none of order >= 7). Dyson-McKay v3 section 5 report 49,871,540 graphs on 20 vertices and 174,775,920 on 29 vertices, none of which extends by one vertex; more than 6,000 further 29-vertex graphs from a random-restart process were all outside that collection, so they judge it far from complete and call a 30-vertex extension 'a good possibility'. Forum, arieledgardolevy (2026-08-07): a SAT extension test certifies 66 sampled 29-vertex graphs non-extendable to 30. Asymptotically N_{ > =k} >= (1/(2e) - o(1))k^2 (Dyson-McKay v3, Theorem 1.1; the problem page still shows the earlier 9/163, corrected by a forum update of 2026-08-14). Status: open on erdosproblems.com and in the teorth database.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: a graph (graph6) on 21 vertices with no induced regular subgraph on 6 or more vertices (giving N_{ > =6} >= 22), or on 30 vertices with none on 7 or more vertices (N_{ > =7} >= 31), strictly beyond the values in Dyson-McKay and on the #82 thread at verification time. Regular includes empty and complete subgraphs. Alternatively a certified proof (exhaustive search with DRAT/LRAT-checked SAT certificates) that N_{ > =6} = 21.

partial_wins.statement: A graph on 28 vertices with no induced regular subgraph of order exactly 6 (N_6 >= 29), or on 71 vertices with none of order exactly 7 (N_7 >= 72), strictly beyond Dyson-McKay Theorem 1.2 at verification time.
A graph on 31 vertices with no induced regular subgraph of order 7 or 8 (N_{7,8} >= 32), beyond Dyson-McKay's N_{7,8} >= 31.

targets.verification_method: Independent exhaustive check of every vertex subset of the relevant sizes for regularity (with pruning: a subset is regular iff all induced degrees are equal), plus an independent SAT encoding whose UNSAT result is checked with a proof checker. Compare against McKay's posted collections to confirm the graph is new and the bound improves.
angles: One-vertex extension of known extremal graphs is hopeless by clause density (Levy); search for structured graphs (circulants, Cayley graphs, blow-ups of Paley-type graphs) on 21 or 30 vertices directly.
For exact-order N_7 >= 72, random-like constructions with degree constraints from the Dyson-McKay first-moment model are a natural start.
pitfalls: 'Order at least k' (N_{ > =k}) and 'order exactly k' (N_k) are different quantities with different records.
Empty and complete induced subgraphs are regular; a construction must avoid large cliques and independent sets too.
McKay's posted 20- and 29-vertex graphs are samples, not complete collections; non-extension of them proves nothing about exact values.

targets.name: Erdős #302: a certified upper constant below 0.84617 for the largest set in [1,N] with no 1/a = 1/b + 1/c
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (exact gadget optimisation plus density sums; Lean optional)
targets.statement: Let f(N) be the size of the largest A in {1,...,N} with no distinct a, b, c in A satisfying 1/a = 1/b + 1/c (Erdős-Graham). The conjecture f(N) = (1/2+o(1))N is false: Stijn Cambie showed f(N) >= (5/8+o(1))N (odd numbers <= N/4 plus [N/2, N]); SamKorsky (forum 2026-07-05) adds N/(log N)^{0.00415...+o(1)}; a proof claim of Dmitry Khanukov (2026-09-13, github.com/khanukov/erdos302, unrefereed) asserts 5/8 + delta via Della Pietra's #301 work, with an explicit but astronomically small delta = 1/(86400 commonL) in a Lean overlay. Upper bounds: Wouter van Doorn 9/10 (still the value on the problem page); Robert Schuh 373/420 ~ 0.888 (proof claim); Khanukov 140803024/163562355 ~ 0.86085 (proof claim with Lean); Kenta Kitamura (forum 2026-09-25, github.com/KitaKen1/erdos-302-upper-bound, Formal Conjectures PR #6580, merged 2026-09-27) a Lean-verified limsup f(N)/N <= C, an explicit rational C = 0.84617398279640096..., axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only. Exact small values are OEIS A390395 (68 terms in the data section; the b-file by Sharvil Kesarwani, first 658 terms from Chai Wah Wu, runs to n = 731 with a(731) = 606 on 2026-10-30). The method: decompose [1,N] into disjoint dilated gadgets a*T, compute exactly the largest solution-free subset of each finite T, and sum densities.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: a complete proof that f(N) <= (c+o(1))N with an explicit rational or exactly specified c strictly below Kitamura's exact constant C = 303298432907684665348375061155255053723893276661771828230864577892179469/358435072543067896655954874015956559321978063343228205466655134412800000 = 0.84617398279640096... (not merely below the rounded 0.8461739827964010 stated in his Lean theorem), and strictly below any smaller constant posted on the #302 thread or proof-claims page at verification time, where every finite optimisation used is supplied as a certificate (explicit gadget sets, exact maximum solution-free subsets with ILP optimality certificates or exhaustive search) and the density sum is computed in exact rational arithmetic. A Lean proof with a clean axiom audit (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only) is accepted in place of the certificate.

partial_wins.statement: Exact values of A390395(n) for every n from 732 up to at least 800, beyond the OEIS b-file at verification time (n = 1..731 on 2026-10-30), each with a witness set and an optimality certificate (exhaustive branch-and-bound or ILP dual bound) that an independent solver reproduces.

A complete, explicit proof that f(N) >= (c+o(1))N for an explicitly computed rational c >= 5/8 + 1/10000 = 0.6251, strictly above every explicit constant posted on the #302 thread or proof-claims page at verification time (Khanukov's Lean overlay gives only 5/8 + 1/(86400 commonL), astronomically close to 5/8), checkable line by line or in Lean.

targets.verification_method: Recompute each gadget's maximum solution-free subset independently (brute force for small gadgets, a different ILP solver for large ones), check disjointness and coverage of the gadget family, and recompute the limiting density in exact rationals. For Lean, run lake build and #print axioms.
angles: Use gadgets from divisors of larger smooth numbers (Wang's #301 configuration uses divisors of 720); 1/a = 1/b + 1/c iff (b-a)(c-a) = a^2, so solutions in a*T are governed by divisor structure.
Weight gadgets by the dilation density and solve a single LP over many overlapping gadget families.
pitfalls: The thread moves fast (0.86085 to 0.84617 in two weeks); re-check the record before claiming.
301 (sums of k unit fractions) and #327 are different problems.
Non-distinct b = c changes the answer (2/3 threshold, Cambie); distinctness is required.

targets.name: Erdős #23: a triangle-free graph on 5n vertices needing more than n^2 deletions to be bipartite, or a certified extension of Ferudun's n <= 40 range
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (flag-algebra SDP for the bound; exact max-cut for counterexample checks)
targets.statement: Can every triangle-free graph on 5n vertices be made bipartite by deleting at most n^2 edges (Erdős; Erdős-Faudree-Pach-Spencer 1988)? The balanced blow-up of C_5 shows n^2 would be sharp. Balogh, Clemen and Lidický (2021, flag algebras, 'Max cuts in triangle-free graphs', arXiv:2103.14179) prove that deleting at most (2/47)N^2 = 1.0638...n^2 edges suffices for N = 5n vertices, and that N^2/25 suffices for large N when the edge density is at most 0.2486 or at least 0.3197; 1.064n^2 is still the bound on the problem page. Alper Ferudun (arXiv:2606.28041, 26 Jun 2026; computer-assisted, unrefereed, ancillary exact-arithmetic verifier) claims a(5n) = n^2 for every 1 <= n <= 40 (N <= 200): an order-10 flag-algebra certificate bounds the medium density band by 2/25 + delta with an explicit rational delta ~ 4.8558e-5, the tails are transferred to every N by blow-up, and integrality turns beta(G) <= n^2 + (25/2)n^2 delta into beta(G) <= n^2 while (25/2)n^2 delta < 1. n = 41 would need delta < 4.7591e-5, which the paper says its order-10 relaxation does not reach (order 11 is out of reach computationally). The same argument gives beta(G) <= (1/25 + delta/2)N^2 ~ 0.0400243 N^2 for every triangle-free G, far below 2/47, though the paper does not state it as a theorem. OEIS A389646 gives the exact maximum number of deletions needed for N <= 23 vertices (Brendan McKay; a(23) = 20 from a 4,5,4,5,5 blow-up of C_5 plus extra edges); its comment by Ferudun (2026-06-29) records a(5k) = k^2 for k <= 40. Status: open on erdosproblems.com (last edited 2026-01-18, no proof claims).
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: (A) an explicit triangle-free graph G on N = 5n vertices with a certificate that its maximum cut has fewer than e(G) - n^2 edges (exhaustive search or an exact branch-and-bound/ILP log for small N, or a rational SDP or LP dual certificate bounding the max cut), triangle-freeness and the cut bound verified independently (Ferudun's arXiv:2606.28041 claims no such G exists for n <= 40, so a graph with n <= 40 also refutes that certificate and is checked with extra care); or (B) a complete proof that n^2 deletions always suffice (machine-checked flag-algebra certificate plus a rigorous rounding argument, or a line-by-line proof).

partial_wins.statement: A rigorous certificate in exact rational arithmetic (flag-algebra or other, with the PSD and identity checks independently reproduced) that either proves a(5n) = n^2 for every n <= m with m >= 41, beyond Ferudun's n <= 40 (arXiv:2606.28041) and any larger range on the #23 page, thread, OEIS A389646 or arXiv at verification time (on Ferudun's route this means a medium-band delta below 4.7591e-5), or proves that every triangle-free graph on N vertices can be made bipartite by deleting at most c N^2 + o(N^2) edges for an explicit c strictly below 1/25 + delta_F/2 ~ 0.0400243, delta_F being the exact rational of Ferudun's Theorem 3.2, and below any smaller constant posted at verification time.

The exact value A389646(24) (or the next missing term at verification time), with an extremal graph and a reproducible optimality proof (exhaustive enumeration of triangle-free graphs on that many vertices via nauty-type generation, two independent implementations).

targets.verification_method: For (A) recompute max cut exactly with an independent solver (or check the dual certificate in exact arithmetic) and test triangle-freeness. For p1, verify the SDP certificate in exact rationals (positive semidefiniteness via LDL^T over Q) and the flag-algebra identities with independent code.
pitfalls: Asymptotic statements (c N^2 + o(N^2)) do not settle the exact n^2 claim for small n; keep (A) and p1 separate.
Erdős's general odd-girth version (Er92b) is a different statement; only the triangle-free 5n version counts here.
Blow-ups of C_5 are extremal at n^2 exactly; perturbations must beat it strictly.
The problem page still shows only Balogh-Clemen-Lidický's 1.064n^2; the live bar is Ferudun's arXiv:2606.28041 (n <= 40, constant ~0.0400243), so a bound between 1/25 + delta_F/2 and 2/47 is not new.

Ferudun reports that the order-10 per-root-MaxCut envelope is essentially at its ceiling (it cannot reach the 4.7591e-5 needed for n = 41); more solver precision on the same relaxation will not extend the range.

targets.name: Erdős #366: a 2-full n with n+1 3-full (or two consecutive 3-full integers)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (enumerate 3-full numbers to ~1e27 and test neighbours for powerfulness)
targets.statement: Are there 2-full n with n+1 3-full (every prime dividing n divides it at least twice, every prime dividing n+1 at least three times)? Erdős-Graham [ErGr80, p.68] note (8,9) and ask whether it is the only consecutive pair with one 3-full and one 2-full; Ralf Stephan observed 12167 = 23^3, 12168 = 2^3 3^2 13^2 (known to Golomb 1970). Both known pairs have the 3-full number first; no n with n 2-full and n+1 3-full is known. By OEIS A060355 there are no other such pairs below 10^22 (site page, edited 2026-07-16). Erdős also asked whether two consecutive 3-full integers exist (Guy B16); none is known. David Turturean (forum 2026-04-14) notes abc implies finitely many; a proof claim (Theofil Xeff, 2026-07-22) bounds n < 10^16136778163 assuming Baker's explicit abc. Status: open.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: an integer n with complete PROVEN prime factorisations of n and n+1 showing that n is 2-full and n+1 is 3-full (every prime dividing n divides it at least twice, every prime dividing n+1 divides it at least three times). Two consecutive 3-full integers (in either order) also count, since they answer Erdős's weaker question in [Er76d] and Guy B16.

partial_wins.statement: A third consecutive pair in the other direction: n 3-full and n+1 2-full with (n, n+1) not (8, 9) or (12167, 12168), with complete proven factorisations (the site records none other below 10^22).

A reproducible exhaustive search (code plus logs, rerun by the verifier on sampled ranges) proving there is no pair of either type (2-full next to 3-full, in either order) below 10^25 other than (8,9) and (12167,12168), extending the 10^22 bound stated on the #366 page.

targets.verification_method: Factor n and n+1 completely (the 3-full side is enumerable as a^3 b^4 c^5 forms); prove each prime factor prime; check exponents. For p2, recount 3-full numbers up to the bound (asymptotically about 4.66 x^{1/3}) and audit the powerfulness test of each neighbour on verifier-chosen subranges.
angles: Enumerate 3-full m = a^3 b^4 c^5 (b, c squarefree, coprime) up to X; there are only about 4.66 X^{1/3} of them, so X = 1e27 means ~5e9 candidates. Test m-1 and m+1 for powerfulness by trial division to X^{1/5} and exact square/cube/a^2 b^3 tests on the cofactor.
Pell-type families x^2 - D y^3 = +-1 parametrise many candidates.
pitfalls: Direction matters: both known examples are (3-full, 2-full); the title asks for (2-full, 3-full).
A060355 lists consecutive powerful pairs, not 3-full ones; filter it rather than citing it as the answer.

targets.name: SPOCK orbital-stability benchmark (Thadhani et al. 2025 cleaned data): beat SPOCK 2.0's holdout AUC for 10^9-orbit stability of compact three-planet systems
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (labels and initial conditions are a 33 MB Zenodo zip; short REBOUND integrations of ~1.3e5 systems take CPU-hours to a day; the 10^9-orbit labels are supplied)
targets.statement: SPOCK (Tamayo et al. 2020, PNAS 117, 18194, arXiv:2007.06521) predicts whether a compact three-planet system survives 10^9 orbits from features of a short N-body integration; Cranmer et al. 2021 (PNAS, arXiv:2101.04117) added a Bayesian neural-network instability-time regressor (holdout RMSE 1.02 dex; theoretical chaos limit about 0.43 dex). Thadhani, Ba, Rein & Tamayo 2025 (SPOCK 2.0, RNAAS 9, 27, doi:10.3847/2515-5172/adb150) found 10,984 duplicated resonant systems and 124 planet losses mislabelled stable, and released a cleaned set on Zenodo 14327471 (resonant 102,497 and random 24,941 rows with instability_time, shadow_instability_time and Stable labels, plus REBOUND initial conditions; the note quotes 127,428 systems). Training on the first 80% of the resonant rows and testing on the rest, with test systems that go unstable during the short integration excluded, they report AUC 0.9430 for the original 10^4-orbit features and 0.9502 for SPOCK 2.0 (integrating to each system's fastest secular timescale and adding it as a feature); the repository's train_spock.ipynb gets 0.9494 for the released model. The shadow-trajectory labels agree with the primary labels for 98.6% of the last 20% of resonant rows (computed 2026-10-30), so chaos leaves room above 0.95. The SPOCK changelog (v2.1.0; repository pushed 2026-09-23) lists no later stability classifier, and no 2024-2026 work citing SPOCK in OpenAlex or on arXiv reports a higher AUC on this data. Open task: a stability predictor with a strictly higher holdout AUC than SPOCK 2.0 under the same short-integration budget.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (frozen training code, trained model, per-system probabilities). Test set: rows 81,997-102,496 (0-based, file order; the last 20,500 rows) of dataset/resonant/sim_labels.csv in Zenodo record 14327471, minus the systems that go unstable during the short integration of the latest released SPOCK FeatureClassifier (InitialStable = False from its generate_features, run by the skeptic), as in Thadhani et al. 2025 section 2; label = column Stable. Training and tuning use only rows 0-81,996 (the rows the released SPOCK model was trained on); the random dataset is never used for training. Per-system inputs: the initial conditions plus at most one N-body integration no longer than max(10^4 innermost orbits, the system's fastest secular timescale as defined in Thadhani et al. 2025); the instability_time and shadow columns are never inputs. Win: test ROC AUC strictly greater (direction: max) than both 0.9502 and the AUC the skeptic gets from the latest released SPOCK FeatureClassifier on the identical rows, with the paired-bootstrap (2,000 resamples) 95% interval of the difference above zero; and on the random-dataset rows with instability_time >= 1e4 (17,463 systems) an AUC no more than 0.005 below SPOCK's on the same rows. Re-fetch the Zenodo record and the SPOCK changelog immediately before claiming, and beat any value on this split in later papers (ADS/arXiv search for 'SPOCK' and 'Thadhani', last 24 months).

partial_wins.statement: Reproduce SPOCK 2.0 on the defined test set: an AUC within 0.005 of 0.9502 from the bundle's own feature pipeline, trained only on rows 0-81,996 (validates the split and features).

Instability-time regression: on defined test-set rows with instability_time < 9.98e8, a log10-time RMSE strictly below that of the released SPOCK DeepRegressor (Cranmer et al. 2021) median predictions, recomputed by the skeptic on the same rows, under the same input budget.
An AUC >= 0.9502 on the defined test set with a single N-body integration of at most 10^3 innermost orbits per system (ten times shorter than SPOCK's minimum).
On the random-dataset rows with instability_time >= 1e4, an AUC strictly greater than the skeptic's recomputed SPOCK 2.x AUC on the same rows, while training only on resonant rows 0-81,996.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads Zenodo 14327471, checks the CSV hash and row split, reruns the frozen training on rows 0-81,996 with a new seed, recomputes the test AUC and paired bootstrap, and installs the latest SPOCK release to score the identical rows. A few CPU-hours to a day.
angles: Conventional: gradient boosting on SPOCK features plus analytic resonance-overlap and secular quantities (Tamayo et al. 2021 AnalyticalClassifier, Yang & Tamayo 2024 secular timescales).
Sequence models (1D CNN or transformer) on the short-integration orbital-element time series, as in Cranmer et al. 2021, trained as classifiers with calibrated outputs.
Cross-domain import (survival analysis): treat instability time as a right-censored survival target and train a discrete-time hazard model; the censored-at-1e9 structure is exactly survival data.
Cross-domain import (weather ensembles): run two shadow short integrations per system and use their divergence (a finite-time Lyapunov proxy) as a feature.
pitfalls: The original 2020 Zenodo training set contains the duplicates removed in 2025; mixing it in leaks test systems into training.
generate_FC_data.py joins features to sim_labels.csv in file order and train_spock.ipynb takes the first 80% as training: keep that order, or the split no longer matches the released model's.
Scoring all 20,500 rows without removing the systems that go unstable during SPOCK's short integration inflates AUC (those systems are trivially unstable) and is not comparable with 0.9502.
Different REBOUND versions give different chaotic trajectories; record the version and integrator settings in the bundle.
Integrating longer than the allowed budget makes the problem easier and is not a win.

targets.name: 2018 WFIRST/Roman Microlensing Data Challenge: one automated pipeline that recovers more planetary (s, q) solutions than all four entries
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (293 two-band light curves, about 100 MB; binary-lens fits with public codes such as MulensModel, pyLIMA or VBMicrolensing take minutes to hours per event)
targets.statement: The 2018 Microlensing Data Challenge (coordinated by Rachel Street, simulations by Matthew Penny; panel Rachel Akeson, Scott Gaudi, Hyungsuk Tak, Eamonn Kerins) released 293 simulated Roman bulge-survey light curves in W149 and Z087: 93 cataclysmic variables, 74 single lenses (free-floating planets included), 83 stellar binary lenses and 43 bound-planet lenses (github microlensing-data-challenge/data-challenge-1; Zenodo 18041245). The full simulation parameters were released in 2019 (Answers/master_file.txt; Jennifer Yee's summary). Four teams entered (contacts Etienne Bachelet for teams 1 and 2, Geoffrey Bryden for team 3, Clement Ranc and Arnaud Cassan for team 4); the entries were released on Zenodo 21235143 (Street et al., July 2026), and the panel graded them qualitatively, noting that classification of subtle anomalies stayed hard. Scoring the released entries against the truth on 2026-10-30 (low-q set = the 51 events with true q < 0.03; recovered = some listed binary-lens model with |dlog10 q| <= 0.3 and |dlog10 s| <= 0.1, the close/wide s <-> 1/s degeneracy allowed, a listed q > 1 read as 1/q), team 1 recovers 41/51, team 2 32, team 4 12 and team 3 2 (one of them, event 267, listed with q = 3162). Team 1 also lists a q < 0.03 model for 9 events whose truth is not low-q (team 2: 5), recovers 1 of the 3 planets with log10 q < -5 (events 47, 131, 152) and 6 of the 10 low-q events with s > 2, and its first-listed models classify 268/293 events correctly in three classes (variable or flat, single lens, binary lens). The organisers' evaluation code is still being written (commits to June 2026), and no published quantitative ranking exists. Open task: beat every entry with a single frozen pipeline.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle: a fully automated, frozen pipeline (no per-event human choices; every threshold and prior fixed beforehand and tuned only on light curves the claimant simulated independently) that the skeptic runs on the 293 light curves of Zenodo 18041245. It outputs exactly one model per event: a class, plus s and q (q <= 1, the lighter lens over the heavier) for binary lenses. The pipeline never reads the Answers folder or any team entry. Scoring uses master_file.txt (0-based whitespace columns 46 = q, 47 = s, event-type token, last column = light-curve number) and the rules in the statement. Win, direction max for counts: (a) more than 41 of the 51 low-q events recovered by the single output model; (b) at most 9 events with an output q < 0.03 whose truth is not q < 0.03; (c) three-class accuracy of at least 268/293. All three must hold, and the result must also beat any later quantitative results the organisers publish on the same events (github microlensing-data-challenge/evaluation_code and an ADS/arXiv search for the 2018 Microlensing Data Challenge, re-fetched before claiming).

partial_wins.statement: Condition (a) alone (more than 41 of 51 low-q events recovered with one output model per event), with at most 15 false low-q outputs.
Three-class accuracy strictly above 268/293 with one output model per event.
Recover at least 2 of the 3 planets with true log10 q < -5 (events 47, 131, 152) within the tolerances; the best entry recovers 1.
Recover at least 8 of the 10 low-q events with true s > 2 (wide planets); the best entry recovers 6.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the light curves and master_file.txt, checks that the pipeline never opens Answers/ or the entries (sandboxed run), runs it end to end, and scores it and the four Zenodo entries with an independent implementation of the rules. About a day of CPU.
angles: Conventional: a PSPL fit with parallax first, then a residual-anomaly detector that seeds a dense (log s, log q, alpha) grid of binary-lens fits, with finite-source magnification from VBMicrolensing.
Simulation-based inference: train a neural posterior estimator on light curves simulated with the same cadence and noise model, then refine the top modes with chi^2 minimisation.
Cross-domain import (gravitational-wave template banks): build a stochastic template bank in (s, q, alpha, rho) with a mismatch metric to guarantee coverage of caustic-crossing morphologies.
Handle the s <-> 1/s and offset degeneracies explicitly: fit both branches and report the lower-chi^2 one.
pitfalls: The truth file is public: tuning thresholds on the challenge events themselves is test-set contamination; tune on independent simulations.
Team entries list several models per event; the bar counts them generously (any listed model), while the claimant gets one model per event.
In the simulation the binary frame's x-axis points from the centre of mass to the less massive lens at t0 (data-challenge README); alpha conventions differ between codes.
About 8 low-q events are stellar-binary simulations with brown-dwarf companions (ombin, q < 0.03); they count in the low-q set.

targets.name: ExoMiner++ TESS 2-minute TCE vetting benchmark: beat the published 10-fold cross-validated PR-AUC (0.976) on the 57,162 labelled SPOC TCEs with the released folds
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (the released TFRecord inputs are 19 GB; a CNN trains in hours per fold on CPU or an Apple GPU, ten folds; or rebuild inputs from MAST SPOC DV products)
targets.statement: ExoMiner++ (Valizadegan, Martinho, Jenkins, Twicken, Caldwell, Maynard, Wei, Zhong, Yates, Donald, Collins, Latham et al.; AJ 170, 2025, doi:10.3847/1538-3881/ae03a4; code at github nasa/ExoMiner) classifies TESS SPOC 2-minute threshold-crossing events (sectors 1-67) as planet or non-planet. Zenodo 15466292 releases the labelled catalogue: 57,162 TCEs (KP 1,835, CP 1,846, EB 12,738, NTP 39,009, NEB 816, FP 793, NPC 93, BD 32), a fold column 0-9 grouping TCEs by target star (17,206 stars, none split), the out-of-fold score of the TESS+Kepler individual model, and 19 GB of TFRecord inputs. Recomputed on 2026-10-30 with positives = KP or CP and all other labels negative: PR-AUC 0.9704, ROC-AUC 0.9971, precision/recall 0.924/0.927 at 0.5, matching the 'TESS+Kepler, Individual' row of the paper's Table 6 (whose FP-subclass recall, 0.887, is reproduced when NEB and NPC count as FP). The best row (TESS+Kepler with multi-sector score aggregation) reports PR-AUC 0.976, ROC-AUC 0.998, precision/recall 0.933/0.951 and FP-subclass recall 0.896; the TESS-only aggregate row reports PR-AUC 0.967. ExoMiner++ 2.0 (arXiv:2601.14877, January 2026) uses a different 2-minute plus FFI set with 5 folds and reports lower values. The nasa/ExoMiner repository (pushed 2026-10-13) still names ExoMiner++ as its current 2-minute model. Open task: a vetter with a higher cross-validated PR-AUC on the same labels and folds.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle: frozen training code, the ten fold models, and an out-of-fold score for each of the 57,162 TCEs in the labelled-TCE catalogue CSV of Zenodo 15466292 (exominerplusplus_catalog_labeled_tces_s1-s67_tess-spoc-2min_complete_1-14-2025_1039.csv; SHA-256 8c97e5bff6019cd7bd979e7ad21423448d67299bdf47a98f8510d25db4f197b2 as downloaded 2026-10-30). The score of a TCE in fold k comes from a model that never used fold k for training, validation, early stopping or normalisation statistics. Allowed inputs: public TESS photometry and SPOC DV products, Kepler data, and TIC/Gaia stellar parameters. Forbidden: TOI, CTOI or ExoFOP dispositions and comments, TFOPWG or follow-up results, and the catalogue's label and score columns. Win: average-precision PR-AUC over all 57,162 TCEs (positives = KP or CP, every other label negative) strictly greater (direction: max) than 0.9765, so above any value that rounds to the published 0.976, with ROC-AUC >= 0.9975, both recomputed by the skeptic. The result must also beat any value on this labelled set in later papers: re-fetch the Zenodo record and the nasa/ExoMiner repository and search ADS/arXiv for ExoMiner++ citations (last 24 months) before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: Out-of-fold PR-AUC strictly above 0.9704 (the released TESS+Kepler individual-model scores) without multi-sector score aggregation.
Trained on TESS data only (no Kepler examples), an out-of-fold PR-AUC strictly above 0.9675 (above the paper's TESS-only aggregate row, 0.967).

At threshold 0.5, precision >= 0.933 and recall >= 0.951 overall, together with a correctly-rejected (score <= 0.5) fraction of the FP subclass, taken as the FP, NEB and NPC labels together (1,702 TCEs, as in the paper's Table 6), strictly above 0.896 (the paper's best).
PR-AUC >= 0.9704 using only phase-folded flux views and scalar DV statistics (no difference images, centroids or periodograms).

targets.verification_method: Skeptic checks the catalogue hash, verifies that the fold assignment is the released one and that no fold-k TCE is in model k's training data, retrains at least two folds from the frozen code with new seeds, and recomputes PR-AUC and ROC-AUC on all out-of-fold scores. Hours for the metrics, a day or two to retrain folds.
angles: Conventional: retrain the ExoMiner++ architecture with modern augmentation (period-phase jitter, odd-even swaps) and an ensemble over seeds; ensembles alone often add a few thousandths of PR-AUC.
Gradient-boosted trees on SPOC DV scalar statistics stacked with CNN scores; label noise in CP and NTP rewards robust losses.
Cross-domain import (noisy-label learning in medical imaging): co-teaching or confident learning to down-weight TFOPWG labels that are likely wrong, evaluated only on out-of-fold scores.
Multi-sector aggregation: the paper's aggregation adds about 0.006 PR-AUC; learn the aggregation rather than use the longest-run rule.
pitfalls: TOI and ExoFOP dispositions are the source of the labels: any feature derived from them is leakage.
Folds are grouped by target star; re-splitting by TCE leaks multi-sector TCEs of the same star across folds.
The paper's negatives include NEB and NPC TCEs; dropping them raises PR-AUC (0.979 for the released scores) and is not comparable.
PR-AUC differences of a few thousandths are within seed noise; report the spread over at least three seeds.

targets.name: First measured mass (TTV or RV, public data only) for a transiting planet whose NASA Exoplanet Archive mass still comes from a mass-radius relation
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (transit-time extraction from Kepler/TESS light curves plus TTVFast/N-body or Keplerian RV fits; data are MB per system)
targets.statement: On 2026-10-30 the NASA Exoplanet Archive composite table (PSCompPars) lists 6,451 planets; 3,035 of them, all transiting, have pl_bmassprov = 'M-R relationship', meaning no measured mass (2,310 Kepler, 396 K2, 326 TESS discoveries). Of these, 160 carry ttv_flag = 1 and 139 orbit stars brighter than V = 11. Public data can still yield masses: Kepler and TESS transit times (Rowe et al. 2015; Holczer et al. 2016; Hadden & Lithwick 2017 analysed the TTVs of 145 planets in 55 Kepler systems), and public radial velocities (ESO HARPS/ESPRESSO Phase 3 products, Keck KOA HIRES, the HARPS RVBank of Trifonov et al. 2020). The archive's default parameter set can lag the literature, so novelty is judged on all archive rows plus a paper search. Open task: a robust first dynamical mass for such a planet, credited to the archive team (Akeson et al. 2013; Christiansen et al. 2025) for the census.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (planet name, the archive rows as fetched, all transit times or RVs with provenance, model configuration, posterior chains) for a planet whose PSCompPars row has pl_bmassprov = 'M-R relationship' (TAP: select pl_name,pl_bmassprov from pscomppars where pl_bmassprov='M-R relationship') and none of whose rows in the PS table (select pl_name,pl_bmassprov,pl_refname from ps where pl_name='NAME') has a pl_bmassprov other than 'M-R relationship' or empty (so no 'Mass', 'Msini' or 'Msin(i)/sin(i)' row), both re-fetched immediately before claiming, with: (1) mass / sigma >= 3; (2) TTV route: dynamical model preferred over linear ephemerides by delta BIC > 10, at least 4 independent chains with R-hat < 1.01, the mass stable within 1 sigma under two different eccentricity priors, and the perturber identified (a known transiting planet, or a unique non-transiting solution after an alias search); RV route: K detected at the transit period and phase at >= 3 sigma, instrument offsets free, and no activity-indicator peak at that period; (3) no paper found by an ADS/arXiv search on the planet and host names with 'mass', 'TTV' or 'radial velocity' reports a measured mass.

partial_wins.statement: Reproduce at least 10 of the Hadden & Lithwick 2017 TTV masses within 1 sigma with the bundle's pipeline (validation).

For an eligible planet, a 99.7% upper limit on the mass below half of the archive's M-R mass, with the same data-provenance and chain rules, where no paper found by the same search reports an equal or tighter mass upper limit.
A unique non-transiting perturber solution (period, mass, eccentricity) explaining significant TTVs (delta BIC > 20 over linear) of an eligible planet, not in any paper found by the search.
Released transit times, with a significance test against a linear ephemeris, for every eligible planet with ttv_flag = 1 at claim time (160 on 2026-10-30), listing those with p < 1e-4.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic re-fetches the two archive queries, re-extracts a random subset of transit times or re-downloads the RVs, reruns the fit with new seeds and both eccentricity priors, and repeats the literature search. Under an hour per planet.
angles: Conventional: start from the 160 ttv_flag planets, measure transit times from Kepler short cadence plus TESS, and fit pairs near first-order resonance with the Lithwick-Xie-Wu analytic model before full N-body.
Synchronous chopping signals break the mass-eccentricity degeneracy; prioritise pairs with high SNR transits.
Cross-domain import (pulsar timing): a joint timing model with red-noise terms keeps stellar-activity timing noise from inflating TTV significance.
Bright TESS hosts (V < 11) may have public HARPS or HIRES spectra taken for other programmes; query the ESO and KOA archives by coordinates.
pitfalls: The composite table picks one default solution: a measured mass can exist in another PS row or in a paper the archive has not ingested.
TTV masses are degenerate with eccentricity (Lithwick, Xie & Wu 2012); a mass that moves with the eccentricity prior is not a measurement.
Kepler long-cadence smearing biases short-duration transit times; use short cadence where available.
The archive's TAP service sits behind Cloudflare: a query with a subquery returned a block page on 2026-10-30. Keep queries simple and stop if blocked.

targets.name: New planetary-anomaly candidate in public KMTNet 2024-2025 microlensing light curves, absent from the KMTNet planet list and the archives
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (3,348 KMTNet 2025 events plus 3,441 from 2024; pySIS photometry is KB-MB per event; binary-lens grid searches take CPU-hours per anomalous event)
targets.statement: The Korea Microlensing Telescope Network (KASI; Kim et al. 2016, JKAS 49, 37) posts pySIS photometry of every event it finds from its three sites. Under its data policy the data become public on 1 July of the following year, so the 2024 season (3,441 events, public since 2025-07-01) and the 2025 season (3,348 events in listpage.dat, public since 2026-07-01) may now be analysed and published, with the requested acknowledgement. The KMTNet AnomalyFinder series (Zang et al. 2021, 2022; Hwang et al. 2022; Gould et al. 2022; Jung et al. 2022, 2023, and later papers up to paper XIII on the 2021 prime fields, arXiv:2605.17053) searched earlier seasons systematically; 2024-2025 planets so far appear only in individual and small-batch papers. The KMTNet list of microlensing planets (based on exoplanet.eu, updated 2026-04-13) counts 361 microlensing planets, 276 of them with KMTNet data. Open task: a planetary microlensing anomaly (binary lens with q < 0.03) in a 2024 or 2025 KMTNet event that no publication or list reports. A win is a candidate, never 'a planet'.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle: the event name, the KMTNet pySIS files as downloaded (date and SHA-256), the fit code and the results, showing: (1) a 2L1S model with q < 0.03 beats the best 1L1S model (parallax and finite source allowed) by delta chi^2 > 100 after the errors of each site and field are rescaled to chi^2/dof = 1; (2) a 1L2S (binary-source) model is worse than the 2L1S model by delta chi^2 > 15; (3) the anomaly is covered by at least two KMTNet sites, or by at least 10 points from different nights or fields, and is not caused by flagged or outlying frames; (4) the event is in the KMTNet 2024 or 2025 public event list; (5) the event is absent from the KMTNet planet list PDF, the NASA Exoplanet Archive microlensing table and exoplanet.eu, and an ADS/arXiv search on its KMT, OGLE and MOA names finds no planetary interpretation. All of these are re-fetched immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: A candidate meeting every criterion except that delta chi^2 is between 50 and 100, or the anomaly is covered by one site only.

A free-floating-planet candidate: a 1L1S event with tE < 0.5 d and the finite-source size rho measured at >= 3 sigma, not in any published free-floating-planet sample (KMTNet, MOA or OGLE) found by the search.
A complete anomaly scan of the 2025 season: every event fitted, residual-anomaly thresholds stated in advance, and the anomaly list released, with at least one anomaly absent from all publications.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic re-downloads the pySIS files for the event, checks the hashes, reruns the 1L1S, 1L2S and 2L1S fits with an independent code (MulensModel or VBMicrolensing), checks the coverage and frame flags, and repeats the list and literature checks. A few hours per event.
angles: Conventional: an AnomalyFinder-style scan (Zang et al. 2021): fit 1L1S, then search the residuals with a grid of short Gaussian or Paczynski bumps and dips, then run full 2L1S grids on the survivors.
Prioritise high-magnification events, where central caustics make planets most detectable.

Cross-domain import (particle-physics trigger design): set anomaly thresholds by injecting simulated planetary anomalies into real KMTNet baselines and measuring the false-alarm rate on events with no injection.
Cross-check against OGLE EWS and MOA alert photometry where the event has OGLE or MOA counterparts.
pitfalls: pySIS online photometry has systematics (bad seeing, cosmic rays, field-edge effects) that mimic short anomalies; demand multi-site or multi-field confirmation.
Binary-source events (1L2S) produce planet-like bumps; always fit them.
The KMTNet team analyses these seasons too: check the latest arXiv listings, not only the April 2026 planet list.
Policy item 5: data for events found only by other teams are not given out; only events in KMTNet's own public list qualify.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Positronium negative ion Ps- (e- e+ e-): a variational ground-state energy below Frolov's 2023 record -0.26200507023298010777040211998
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (multiprecision linear algebra at 40-60 digits, 3,000-6,000 three-body exponential basis functions)
targets.statement: Ps- is the bound three-body Coulomb system e- e+ e-. All three masses are equal, so there is no mass-ratio convention to pin down. Its only bound state is the 1^1S (L = 0) ground state, with the two electrons in a spin singlet. The nonrelativistic energy in atomic units (hbar = m_e = e = 1) is a classic three-body benchmark, next to helium and H-. The record is held by Alexei M. Frolov (arXiv:2212.03723v7, 2 April 2023, 'the most recent, updated and corrected version'). His Table I uses a three-body exponential expansion in perimetric coordinates under two optimisation strategies. The best value, N = 3842 functions with variant B, is E = -0.26200507023298010777040211998 a.u. The abstract and conclusions call it 'the lowest variational energy ever obtained for this ion'. His previous best variational value (arXiv:1502.01691v3, 2015) was -0.26200507023298010777040051. Frolov's estimate of the limit (Chem. Phys. Lett. 626, 49, 2015, as quoted in arXiv:2405.08818) is -0.2620050702329801077704065(55), about 4e-24 below the 2023 record. The record has not converged: between N = 3800 and N = 3842 it still drops by 1.1e-24, so a larger or better-optimised basis should lower it. Frolov's arXiv listing, checked 2026-10-30, shows later papers on PsH (2024), muonic ions (2025), one-electron diatomic ions (2026) and muonic helium (2026), but none revisits the Ps- energy, and no paper citing 2212.03723 was found. Frolov publishes no wavefunction, so no open certificate for the record exists. The bar is a raw variational eigenvalue (Table I, not an extrapolation), so a strictly lower upper bound is possible in principle.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a published file giving an explicit L = 0 trial function, symmetric under exchange of the two electrons, for the e- e+ e- Hamiltonian H = -1/2 (nabla_1^2 + nabla_2^2 + nabla_3^2) - 1/r31 - 1/r32 + 1/r21, with equal unit masses and the centre of mass removed. The file holds the basis type, every nonlinear parameter as an exact decimal or rational, and the linear coefficients (or the checker may re-solve for them). The checker computes the Rayleigh quotient E_var with interval certification. E_var must be STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than -0.26200507023298010777040211998 by at least 1e-27, i.e. E_var <= -0.26200507023298010777040212098 with the whole error ball below that value. It must also be lower than any later published variational energy for Ps- found by a literature search (arXiv, Google Scholar, Phys. Rev. A, Mol. Phys., Chem. Phys. Lett.) immediately before claiming. Extrapolated or estimated energies, such as Frolov's 2015 estimate -0.2620050702329801077704065(55), do not count.

partial_wins.statement: The first openly published, independently checkable Ps- certificate whose interval-certified Rayleigh quotient is <= -0.262005070232980107770 (agreement with the record to 21 significant digits). No record is claimed.
Basis efficiency: a certified variational energy below Frolov's N = 3800 variant-B value -0.26200507023298010777040100869 using at most 3,000 basis functions (the file's function count is checked).

targets.verification_method: Checker (minutes to a few hours): parse the basis. For exponentials in r21, r31, r32 (or perimetric u1, u2, u3), use the closed-form three-body integrals (the volume element 8 pi^2 r21 r31 r32 dr21 dr31 dr32 reduces every overlap, kinetic and Coulomb matrix element to rational functions of the exponents). Assemble S and H in python-flint arb ball arithmetic at >= 60 digits. Take the Rayleigh quotient c^T H c / c^T S c with the given coefficients, or solve the generalized eigenproblem in arb and certify the lowest root. Check that the upper end of the error ball is below the threshold, and that the function count matches for p2.
angles: Korobov-style randomly tempered exponentials with complex exponents (exp(-a r31 - b r32 - c r21), with a, b and c drawn from several nested intervals) converge to 30+ digits for equal-mass systems with fewer functions than real exponents.

The record still drops about 1.1e-24 per 40 added functions near N = 3800-3842, and Frolov's own estimate of the limit lies about 4e-24 lower. Extending a good tempered basis to 5,000-6,000 functions at 50-digit precision is the straightforward route. The closed-form integrals make the matrices cheap; the cost is the multiprecision eigensolve.

Use the symmetric structure (equal masses, exchange of the two electrons) to halve the matrix size. Do the eigensolve by inverse iteration in multiprecision, preconditioned by a double-double factorisation.
pitfalls: The bar is Frolov's printed Table I raw eigenvalue for N = 3842, variant B. Variant A at N = 3842 is slightly higher (-0.26200507023298010777040206643), so do not use it as the bar.
Double or quad precision is far from enough. The overlap matrices become nearly singular, and only interval or ball-arithmetic results at >= 50 digits count.
Conventions: equal masses m_e, centre-of-mass motion removed, no relativistic, QED or annihilation corrections; values in Rydberg (twice as large in magnitude) appear in the older literature.
H- and helium are other bank entries (helium-ground-state-energy-digits); this target is Ps- only.

targets.name: Muonic molecular ions dd-mu and dt-mu: a lower variational energy for the weakly bound (J,v) = (1,1) states than Frolov's 2025 values (the (2,0) states of dd-mu, dt-mu and tt-mu are partial wins)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (three-body exponential bases with L = 1 or 2 angular parts, quad or multiprecision arithmetic)
targets.statement: Muon-catalysed fusion is driven by the resonant formation of the weakly bound (J, v) = (1,1) states of the muonic molecular ions dd-mu+ and dt-mu+. These states have binding energies of about 1.975 eV and 0.660 eV, and their energies set the formation rates. Alexei M. Frolov (arXiv:2503.17389v1, 17 March 2025) computed the (1,1) states of dd-mu and dt-mu and the rotationally excited (2,0) states of dd-mu, dt-mu and tt-mu. He used three-body exponential expansions with up to 5,500 functions and the masses of his eq. (14): m_mu = 206.7682830 m_e, M_d = 3670.48296788 m_e, M_t = 5496.92153573 m_e. Energies are in muon-atomic units (hbar = m_mu = e = 1). His Table I, best rows: dd-mu (1,1), N = 3842: -0.47368672970969890623. dt-mu (1,1), N = 3842: -0.4819915265298649455. dt-mu (2,0), N = 5500: -0.500118077325475. dd-mu (2,0), N = 3700: -0.4887083249914. tt-mu (2,0), N = 3800: -0.5125686450010. He reports that his (1,1) results are about 1,000 times more accurate than his 2019 values (Phys. Lett. A 389, 1288). The binding energies he quotes (1.97498052811 eV and 0.66032991051 eV for the (1,1) states) can be reproduced from these totals and the muonic-atom energies -1/(2(1 + m_mu/M)). The (2,0) rows are still converging: tt-mu moves by 4e-10 between N = 3700 and 3800, and dd-mu by 3e-11. Earlier work at other mass values includes Korobov's three-body calculations, Kamimura (PRA 38, 621, 1988) and Vinitsky, Ponomarev and coworkers. Energies at different mass ratios are not comparable at these digit levels, so the record is defined for the eq. (14) masses.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit variational wavefunction for the (1,1) state of dd-mu or of dt-mu. It is a three-body Coulomb system with charges (+1, +1, -1) and exactly the masses of arXiv:2503.17389 eq. (14), in muon-atomic units with the centre of mass removed. The state has total angular momentum L = 1, natural parity (-1)^L, and, for dd-mu, the exchange symmetry (-1)^L under d <-> d. The energy must be the SECOND-lowest root of the generalized eigenproblem in that symmetry block (Hylleraas-Undheim-MacDonald: the second root bounds the (1,1) level from above). The checker's certified root must be STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than Frolov's Table I value for that state (-0.47368672970969890623 for dd-mu, -0.4819915265298649455 for dt-mu) by at least 1e-19. It must also be lower than any other published variational value for the identical masses found by a literature search immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: A (2,0) cell: for dd-mu, dt-mu or tt-mu, with the same masses, L = 2, natural parity (exchange-symmetric spatial part for dd-mu and tt-mu), the lowest root of that block certified STRICTLY LOWER than Frolov's Table I value (-0.4887083249914, -0.500118077325475 or -0.5125686450010) by at least 1e-13.

An open, checkable certificate for either (1,1) state whose certified second root lies within 1e-15 of Frolov's Table I value, above or below. It is the first public reproduction, since Frolov releases no wavefunctions.

targets.verification_method: Checker (under an hour for a few thousand functions): build the basis with the declared angular coupling (e.g. Korobov's r1^l1 r2^l2 {Y_l1 x Y_l2}_LM exp(-a r1 - b r2 - c r12) with l1 + l2 = L). Compute the overlap and Hamiltonian matrices with the published closed-form three-body integrals in arb ball arithmetic at >= 40 digits, using the exact eq. (14) mass ratios. Solve the symmetric generalized eigenproblem, certify the required root (second for the (1,1) states, lowest for (2,0)) with an error ball, and compare it with the bar. Then recompute the binding energy with Frolov's factor 5626.451612133 eV per m.a.u. as a consistency check.
angles: Korobov's variational expansion with exponents drawn pseudo-randomly from several intervals (including very small ones for the long-range tail of the weakly bound state) is the standard tool for these states and needs no exotic integrals.
The (1,1) state is very diffuse (a d or t nucleus far from a compact t-mu or d-mu atom): add a sub-basis with small exponents in the nucleus-atom distance, and optimise that sub-basis separately.
The tt-mu and dd-mu (2,0) rows still move at 1e-10 to 1e-11 per 100 functions, so p1 should be within reach with a few thousand well-tempered functions in quad precision.
pitfalls: Masses: use exactly the eq. (14) values (m_mu = 206.7682830, M_d = 3670.48296788, M_t = 5496.92153573 m_e). The paper calls them CODATA 2022 values, but all three are the CODATA 2018 values (CODATA 2022 gives 206.7682827, 3670.482967655 and 5496.92153551). Never substitute a CODATA table lookup: any change in the last digits shifts the energies by far more than the margins, and results for other masses are not comparable.
State identity: the (1,1) energy is the SECOND root in the L = 1 natural-parity block (the (1,0) state lies about 230 eV below it), and a lowest-root bound does not bound it.

Frolov's Table I prints two columns headed dt-mu (2,0). They are one state continued to larger N (4,500-5,500). His text lists the (2,0) binding energies in the order 'dd-mu, dt-mu, tt-mu' as 102.65, 86.49 and 172.70 eV, but recomputation from the totals shows that 102.65 eV belongs to dt-mu and 86.49 eV to dd-mu.
Binding energies in eV depend on the conversion factor; the success test is on the total energy in m.a.u.

Earlier, more mature codes (Korobov's, Kamimura's) were run at other mass sets. Their published numbers are not the bar, but the literature search before claiming must also look for any recalculation at the eq. (14) masses.

targets.name: Collinear H3 benchmark potential energy curve: a lower variational Born-Oppenheimer energy than Ferenc and Matyus (2022) at the van der Waals minimum or at any of their 114 tabulated geometries
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (3-electron explicitly correlated Gaussians, 1,000-2,000 functions, nonlinear optimisation; Ferenc-Matyus used 12 cores for months on the best point)
targets.statement: H + H2 is the simplest chemical reaction, and its Born-Oppenheimer surface underlies reactive-scattering benchmarks. Dávid Ferenc and Edit Mátyus (arXiv:2203.11978, Chem. Phys. Lett. 2022, doi 10.1016/j.cplett.2022.139734) computed the clamped-nuclei, nonrelativistic ground-state (doublet) energy of collinear H3. They used explicitly correlated Gaussians built by fragment initialisation and Powell refinement in their QUANTEN program, and give energies to 9 decimals with sub-ppm precision. The geometry is three collinear protons, with H2 bond length R_H2 and the third proton at distance R from the H2 nuclear midpoint. Table 1: R_H2 = 1.4, R = 6.442 bohr, 1200 ECGs and 3000 Powell cycles: -1.674561687 Eh (extrapolated -1.67456175(3)). At R = 7.142 bohr they give -1.674547750, against -1.67454742100 by Pavanello, Tung and Adamowicz (J. Chem. Phys. 131, 184106, 2009, six months of computation). Table 2: R_H2 = 1.4015 and R = 6.51205 bohr, the MRCI van der Waals minimum of Mielke, Garrett and Peterson (2002): -1.674562264, 74 microhartree below the best MRCI. Their van der Waals well depth is 86.54(3) microhartree. Table 3 (Supplementary Material): 114 points at R_H2 = 1.4 with R = 3.942 to 15.242 bohr in 0.1 steps, each from 5 Powell cycles after basis rescaling. Its lowest point is -1.674561899 at R = 6.542. The gap between their raw values and the CBS extrapolation (about 6e-8 Eh at 6.442) shows that the energies are not converged at the printed digits.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit trial wavefunction for three electrons in the field of three fixed unit-charge protons at the Table 2 geometry. The protons are collinear: two at +-0.70075 bohr along z (R_H2 = 1.4015) and the third at z = 6.51205 bohr from their midpoint. The state is the doublet ground state with spin and permutation symmetry imposed. Its checker-computed energy expectation value must be STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than -1.674562264 Eh by at least 1e-9 Eh, i.e. <= -1.674562265 Eh. It must also be lower than any later published variational value for the identical geometry found by a literature search (arXiv, J. Chem. Phys., Chem. Phys. Lett.) immediately before claiming. Infinite nuclear masses; no relativistic, QED or adiabatic corrections.

partial_wins.statement: Any Table 3 geometry (R_H2 = 1.4 bohr, R in {3.942, 4.042, ..., 15.242} bohr from the H2 midpoint): a variational energy STRICTLY LOWER, by at least 2e-9 Eh, than the lowest value the paper prints for that geometry. That is the Table 3 value, except at R = 6.442, where Table 1's -1.674561687 is lower than Table 3's -1.674561676 and is the bar. At R = 7.142, Table 3's -1.674547764 is lower than Table 1's -1.674547750 and is the bar.

An openly published ECG wavefunction file for the Table 2 geometry (all centres, exponent matrices, linear coefficients and the spin function), built without starting from any basis parameters deposited by Ferenc and Matyus, whose checker-computed energy is <= -1.674562261 Eh, i.e. within 3e-9 Eh of Ferenc-Matyus's -1.674562264 or below it. Reformatting, rescaling or refining their Supplementary Material basis does not count for this partial (it does for p1 and the full win).

targets.verification_method: Checker (minutes for <= 2,000 functions): read the floating ECG basis (centres, exponent matrices, coefficients) and the spin function. Build the overlap, kinetic, electron-nucleus and electron-electron matrices with the standard Boys-Singer closed forms, using the Boys function for the Coulomb terms. Apply the three-electron antisymmetrizer with the doublet spin coupling explicitly (6 permutations). Compute the Rayleigh quotient in float64 with a quad-precision re-check, or solve the generalized eigenproblem, and confirm the overlap matrix is positive definite. Confirm the nuclear positions match the declared geometry to 1e-10 bohr, and compare with the bar.
angles: Start from fragment products (H2 ECG ground state at 1.4 bohr times an H-atom Gaussian expansion), as Ferenc and Matyus did, then spend the budget on full-basis refinement at a single geometry. Their PEC points had only 5 Powell cycles each and are the softest cells.

Stochastic variational method (Suzuki-Varga) with competitive selection over random floating centres along the molecular axis, and analytic energy gradients for the exponents and centres (Adamowicz-style), should beat Powell refinement at equal cost.
The long-range points (R > 10 bohr) depend on describing the dispersion tail; add Gaussians with diffuse correlation factors between the H atom electron and the H2 electrons.
