It must be exhaustively certified as in criterion (2) and must not be acutely triangulated and nearly flat in O'Rourke's sense (that class unfolds). A literature check must find no prior example.

A machine-checked proof (Lean 4, Coq or Isabelle, kernel-checked) that every prismatoid, the convex hull of two convex polygons in parallel planes, has an edge unfolding to a net. The case is listed open in the GFALOP 22.5 update.

targets.verification_method: Check convexity exactly with rational arithmetic. Enumerate or replay the branch-and-bound over spanning trees: unfold each face by exact rational rotations (choose a coordinate frame where unfolding maps are rational, or use exact algebraic arithmetic) and test strong overlap with exact polygon-intersection predicates. Two independent codes must agree on the tree counts. For p2, compile the formal proof and audit the statement against the GFALOP definition.
angles: Lucier (2006/2009) showed steepest-edge unfoldings can overlap for every direction. Use his local-overlap gadgets as building blocks and then kill the non-steepest trees.
Random convex polytopes overlap for almost all trees. Search small, highly curved polytopes with few nets, using SAT or exact enumeration to count nets, and hill-climb on that count.
pitfalls: Weak (boundary) contact is allowed in a net. A certificate must show strong overlap.
Floating-point unfolding gives false overlaps or false nets near touching configurations. Use exact arithmetic.
Most random convex polytopes have some overlapping edge unfoldings; that is not a counterexample. Every spanning tree must fail.

targets.name: Smallest edge-ununfoldable polyhedra in restricted classes: triangulated with fewer than 20 vertices, convex-faced with fewer than 13 faces, or stacked with acute triangles
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (exhaustive spanning-tree certification for polyhedra with fewer than 20 vertices)
targets.statement: Some non-convex but topologically convex polyhedra (1-skeleton isomorphic to that of a convex polyhedron) have no edge unfolding to a net. Records per face class: all faces triangles, 36 faces and 20 vertices (Bern, Demaine, Eppstein, Kuo, Mantler and Snoeyink, CGTA 2003, 'hat' constructions; the same paper gives a 24-face convex-faced example); all faces convex polygons, 13 faces and 13 vertices (Grünbaum). Akitaya, Demaine, Eppstein, Tachi and Uehara (JCDCGGG 2019; CGTA 103, 2022) found ununfoldable topologically convex polyhedra with 7 vertices and 6 faces and with 6 vertices and 7 faces (their faces include non-convex polygons), and listed improving the triangular (36 faces, 20 vertices) and convex-faced (13, 13) records as future work. The GFALOP update 22.4 (3 Sep 2025) adds that it is still open whether 5 or 6 faces/vertices are possible. Demaine, Demaine and Eppstein (CCCG 2020, arXiv 2007.14525) built ununfoldable polyhedra with all faces acute triangles and ununfoldable stacked polyhedra, and left open whether an ununfoldable STACKED polyhedron with all faces ACUTE triangles exists. GFALOP 22.4 lists no smaller triangular or convex-faced examples.
targets.success_criterion: An embedded, topologically convex polyhedron P with exact rational vertex coordinates, plus a complete certificate that every spanning tree of its edges unfolds with strong overlap (two face-interior points coinciding). The certificate is an exhaustive enumeration, or a branch-and-bound over dual spanning trees with exact overlap witnesses, reproduced by two independent exact-arithmetic implementations. P must satisfy one of the following. (A) All faces triangles and strictly fewer than 20 vertices. (B) All faces strictly convex polygons and strictly fewer than 13 faces, or strictly fewer than 13 vertices. (C) P is a stacked polyhedron (tetrahedra glued face to face in a tree pattern, the result embedded) and every face angle is strictly below 90 degrees; any size. Records are those in the status source and the literature at claim time (direction: min).

partial_wins.statement: An exact computer certificate of edge-ununfoldability for a published example, where none has been published before (literature check): explicit rational coordinates realising Bern et al.'s 36-triangle polyhedron or Grünbaum's 13-face polyhedron (matching the published combinatorics and inequalities), with an exhaustive two-implementation check that all spanning trees overlap.

An edge-ununfoldable topologically convex polyhedron with all faces strictly convex, 13 faces and 13 vertices, not combinatorially equivalent to Grünbaum's example, exactly certified as in the success criterion.

targets.verification_method: Check embeddedness (faces meet only in shared edges and vertices) and planarity and convexity of faces in exact arithmetic, and check topological convexity (3-connected planar 1-skeleton). Replay the spanning-tree enumeration or branch-and-bound: unfold along each dual tree with exact maps and test strong overlap with exact predicates. Compare tree counts with the matrix-tree theorem. For (C), check the stacking sequence and every face angle exactly.
angles: Leaves of a cut tree cannot sit at negatively curved vertices, and every negatively curved vertex needs at least 2 cut edges. Concentrating negative curvature cuts the space of admissible trees drastically, as in Akitaya et al.'s 6-vertex example; transplant that idea to triangulations.
Search over triangulated spheres with 10-19 vertices (plantri) and optimise coordinates to maximise forced overlaps, then certify exactly.
pitfalls: A triangulated sphere with V vertices always has 2V - 4 faces, so the triangular record is a vertex count.
Self-intersecting realisations are not polyhedra. Check embeddedness exactly.
Tarasov's examples and the very-ununfoldable families: do a literature check before claiming a record.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Edge-unfolding polycubes (TOPP Problem 64): a genus-0 polycube with no edge unfolding along cube edges
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exhaustive or SAT search; overlap tests are integer-exact on the unit grid)
targets.statement: A polycube is a polyhedron built by gluing unit cubes face to face. Its surface is tiled by unit squares, and all cube edges on the surface (including flat ones) may be cut. TOPP Problem 64 (George Hart and Joseph O'Rourke, 2004) and GFALOP Open Problem 22.4 ask whether some genus-0 polycube has no edge unfolding: a tree of surface cube edges containing every non-flat vertex whose cutting unfolds the surface to one weakly simple polygon. Demaine and O'Rourke's GFALOP update 22.5 (3 Sep 2025) says it remains open. Proven classes: well-separated orthotrees (Damian, Flatland, Meijer and O'Rourke 2005), one-layer polycubes with sparse cubic holes (Liou, Poon and Wei 2014) and with general cubic holes (Minarik 2022), polycubes with orthogonally convex layers (Damian and Meijer 2024), and level-1 Menger polycubes (Richaume, Andres, Largeteau-Skapin and Zrour 2019). Some polycubes have no edge-unzipping (Demaine, Demaine, Eppstein and O'Rourke 2022). Harismendy, da Silva, Largeteau-Skapin and Andres (DMTCS) unfold 'solid polycubes', which keep the shared internal faces; that is a different object and does not settle the question.
targets.success_criterion: (1) A list of unit cubes, face-connected, whose boundary surface is a 2-manifold of genus 0 (Euler characteristic 2; no edge-only or vertex-only contacts). (2) A complete certificate that no cut tree works: no tree T of surface unit edges containing every non-flat surface vertex, such that cutting T leaves a topological disk, unfolds to a set of unit squares occupying pairwise distinct lattice cells. Squares unfold onto Z^2, so overlap is exact integer cell collision. The certificate is either (a) an exhaustive or branch-and-bound search re-run by two independent implementations that agree, or (b) a SAT encoding whose UNSAT is proven by a DRAT or LRAT proof checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr, cross-checked by a second independent encoding. (3) A literature check confirms the problem is still open.

partial_wins.statement: A complete certified census: for every polycube with n <= N cubes, up to rotation and reflection, whose surface is a genus-0 2-manifold, an explicit edge unfolding (cut tree plus lattice net) checked by an independent verifier, for N >= 10. The enumeration before the manifold and genus filter must match OEIS A038119(n) for each n, and N must exceed any published census (literature check required; the largest known to the bank is Langerman and Winslow, JCDCGG 2016, Theorem 3.2: every k-cube with k <= 7 has an edge unfolding).
A genus-0 polycube with no strictly simple edge unfolding: every one of its nets has two boundary edges in contact. Certified exhaustively by the method of criterion (2).

targets.verification_method: Rebuild the surface from the cube list and check manifoldness and genus. For a counterexample, run the submitted search and an independent re-implementation (or check the DRAT or LRAT proof and the second encoding). Overlap is integer cell collision after unfolding, so no floating point is involved. For p1, check each net, its cut tree and its refold, and recount the enumerated free polycubes (up to rotation and reflection) against OEIS A038119 before the manifold and genus filter.
angles: The known positive classes all have layer convexity or tree structure. Search where they fail: polycubes with non-orthogonally-convex layers and deep pockets, analogues of Biedl et al.'s box-with-lids.
A SAT encoding is natural: tree variables on surface edges, plus position variables of squares in a bounded lattice window with at-most-one-square-per-cell constraints.
pitfalls: Higher-genus polycubes are out of scope: a tree cut cannot open them to a disk.
'Solid polycube' results keep internal faces, which is a different notion.
Cuts only along edges of the orthogonal polyhedron (not all cube edges) is a different, already-negative problem: box-with-lids examples exist.

targets.name: Polycube trees and edge-unzipping: a polycube tree with no edge zipper unfolding, or certified unzippings of all small ones (Demaine-Demaine-Eppstein-O'Rourke Question 1)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (Hamiltonian-path enumeration on small surfaces; integer-exact overlap tests)
targets.statement: An edge zipper unfolding (edge-unzipping, Shephard's Hamiltonian unfolding) cuts a polycube surface along a single simple path of cube edges that visits every non-flat vertex and may pass through flat ones, and unfolds it to one weakly simple polygon. Demaine, Demaine, Eppstein and O'Rourke ('Some polycubes have no edge zipper unfolding', CCCG 2020, Geombinatorics XXXI(3) 2022, arXiv 1907.08433) built polycubes with no edge-unzipping by forcing the absence of a suitable Hamiltonian path (parity arguments on the 1-skeleton). They proved (their Lemma 1) that for a single cube and for every polycube tree (cube-adjacency graph a tree) the whole 1-skeleton, flat vertices included, has a Hamiltonian cycle, so their method does not apply to trees. Their closing open problem, Question 1, asks: does every polycube tree have an edge zipper unfolding? O'Rourke's 2019 survey table lists polycube edge-unzipping as negative in general, and the GFALOP update 22.5 (Sep 2025) still cites the 2022 paper as the state of the art.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) a COUNTEREXAMPLE: a polycube tree (unit cubes glued face to face, cube-adjacency graph a tree, boundary a 2-manifold), plus a complete certificate that every simple cut path along surface cube edges containing all non-flat vertices unfolds with two unit squares in the same lattice cell. The certificate is an exhaustive path enumeration reproduced by two independent implementations, or a SAT encoding with a checked DRAT or LRAT UNSAT proof plus an independent second encoding. Or (b) a machine-checked proof (Lean 4, Coq or Isabelle) that every polycube tree has an edge zipper unfolding. In both cases, literature check at claim time.

partial_wins.statement: A certified census: for every polycube tree with n <= N cubes, up to rotation and reflection, an explicit edge-unzipping (cut path plus lattice net) checked by an independent verifier, for N >= 12 and beyond any published census (literature check required).

A genus-0 polycube that is not a tree, whose corner vertices DO admit a Hamiltonian cut path along surface edges, yet has no edge-unzipping because every such path overlaps. Certified exhaustively. Prior negative examples work by ruling out Hamiltonian paths altogether.

targets.verification_method: Rebuild the surface, check the tree property and manifoldness, enumerate the admissible cut paths (or check the DRAT or LRAT proof and the second encoding), and unfold each path on Z^2 with integer arithmetic, testing for cell collisions. For p1, check each net and its refolding, and the completeness of the enumeration of polycube trees of each size.
angles: Long thin polycube trees with many branch points ('crosses' and 'combs') constrain the path most; their paper's P+ cross gadget is a natural seed.
Encode path plus positions in SAT. Because positions are integral, the whole check is finite and exact.
pitfalls: A cut path must include every non-flat vertex; flat vertices are optional. Getting this wrong changes the answer.
Weakly simple nets (touching boundaries) count as unzippings.
The polycube must be a tree in the cube-adjacency sense, not just genus 0.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - A 12-face Szilassi-type polyhedron: an embedded genus-6 polyhedron whose 12 faces pairwise share an edge
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster for full nonexistence (b): about 19,000 core-hours for all 59 maps by the polyhedraproof pilot estimate; laptop-days for exact-coordinate searches (p2) and a few hundred core-hours for one map's SAT refutation (p1)
targets.statement: Only two polyhedra are known in which every two faces share an edge: the tetrahedron and Szilassi's 7-face toroidal polyhedron (1977), the dual of Császár's polyhedron (Wikipedia, citing Arseneva et al., DCG 2024). The next admissible case has 12 faces, 66 edges and 44 vertices on a genus-6 surface, with every face an 11-gon. This assumes, as for Szilassi's polyhedron, that every vertex has degree 3 and every two faces share exactly one edge. Combinatorially it is the dual of one of the 59 neighbourly 12-vertex triangulations of the genus-6 surface (Altshuler, Bokowski and Schuchert 1996; Lutz's list manifold_lex_d2_n12_o1_g6). Wikipedia's Szilassi polyhedron article (edited 22 Sep 2026) lists its geometric realisability as open. Schewe (DCG 2010, arXiv 0801.2582) proved that the vertex version (the K12 analogue of Császár's polyhedron) is not realisable; that proof does not transfer to the face version. CodeParade (HackerPoet, github.com/HackerPoet/NeighborlyPolyhedra) searched all 59 types numerically. His best near-miss, the 'Razorcross' (type 42), has 0 polygon self-crossings and 4 edge-face intersections (or 4 crossings and 0 intersections). A 2026 AI-assisted repository (github.com/Hashirama1337s/szilassi-12, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.23003257, not peer reviewed) claims DRAT-certified proofs that no 12-face example has a non-trivial symmetry; the asymmetric case remains open. Andrei Pirozhkov's polyhedraproof (release 1.0.0, Oct 2026, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.23434449) reduces the question to 59 SAT formulas, one per map, with LRAT proofs checked by cake_lpr. A rehearsal run refuted maps 1 and 2 (by its own account this does not count: one encoding, proofs not kept). It estimates about 19,000 core-hours for all 59 and claims no nonexistence result.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) EXISTENCE: exact rational coordinates for 44 vertices and a face list of 12 planar 11-gons realising the dual of one of the 59 maps, such that each face is a simple planar polygon (exact coplanarity), any two faces meet only in their shared edge and its endpoints (every pair shares exactly one edge), and no edge or face intersects another face's interior (exact segment-polygon tests after triangulating faces). The surface is then a closed embedded orientable genus-6 polyhedron. Or (b) NONEXISTENCE: a certified proof that none of the 59 dual maps is realisable, which settles the trivalent genus-6 case. For example, a chirotope or SAT encoding with DRAT or LRAT UNSAT proofs checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr for every map, plus an independent second encoding and a written proof that the encoding is complete.

partial_wins.statement: A DRAT- or LRAT-checked non-realisability proof for the face version of one of the 59 maps, with no symmetry assumption. Two independent encodings must agree, and a written argument must cover the completeness of the encoding. The map must not already have a published refutation meeting these same conditions (literature check at claim time). The polyhedraproof rehearsal refutations of maps 1 and 2 (Oct 2026; one encoding, proofs not kept) do not meet them.

An exact-coordinate near-miss: 12 planar faces realising one of the 59 dual maps with zero polygon self-crossings and at most 3 edge-face intersections, strictly fewer than the Razorcross's 4 under the same counting (an edge passing through the interior of a non-incident face counts once). Counted by an independent exact checker.

targets.verification_method: For (a) or p2, load the coordinates as rationals and check exact coplanarity of every face, polygon simplicity, adjacency of every face pair, and Euler characteristic -10. Run exact segment-triangle intersection over all edge-face pairs. For (b) or p1, re-run the SAT instances, check the proofs with drat-trim, and audit the encoding against the definition, using Lutz's map list (sha256 as given in the szilassi-12 README).
angles: Polarity: the face problem is a problem about 12 planes, so Schewe's oriented-matroid enumeration applies to the plane arrangement with the order-along-line conditions of the face version. The szilassi-12 README sketches such an encoding.
If the symmetric-case claim holds, search only asymmetric configurations, starting from CodeParade's low-intersection solutions with exact-arithmetic repair.
pitfalls: The 2026 symmetric-nonexistence claim is unreviewed. Re-check it rather than relying on it.
Floating-point near-misses with tiny intersections are not embeddings. Only exact checks count.
CodeParade's counts (crossings c, intersections i) are from his own code. State your counting rule for p2 and apply it to the Razorcross too.
polyhedraproof (Pirozhkov) plans the full 59-map LRAT campaign. Check its release page at claim time: a completed, certified run would settle (b) and change which maps p1 can use.

targets.name: Monostable polyhedron with fewer faces: a homogeneous convex polyhedron that rests stably on only one face, with fewer than Reshetov's 14 faces
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (exact-centroid optimisation over small polyhedra)
targets.statement: A homogeneous convex polyhedron is monostable (unistable, monostatic) if it can rest in stable equilibrium on only one of its faces: the centroid projects orthogonally into the relative interior of exactly one face. Conway, Goldberg, Guy and Knowlton described these shapes in 1969, and Conway showed that no tetrahedron is monostable. Guy and Knowlton independently built a 19-face example, Bezdek an 18-face one (2011), and Reshetov a 14-face one by computer search (IJCGA 24(1), 2014). Lángi (Bull. LMS 2022, arXiv 2008.02090) answered two of Conway's other questions on monostable polyhedra (near-spherical examples, and k-fold rotational symmetry for every k). As of Wikipedia's 'Monostatic polytope' article (edited 19 Oct 2026), 14 is the fewest faces known. The minimum number of faces is not determined: the only proven bound excludes tetrahedra.
targets.success_criterion: A convex polyhedron given by exact rational vertex coordinates (the faces being the facets of their convex hull, computed exactly) with F faces, F STRICTLY LESS than 14 (direction: min) and less than any smaller count published by claim time (literature check). Compute the centroid of the homogeneous solid exactly (rational tetrahedral decomposition). For every face, test exactly whether the orthogonal projection of the centroid onto the face's plane lies in the face's relative interior. Exactly one face must pass, and the centroid must project onto no face's boundary (non-degenerate).

partial_wins.statement: An exact-rational monostable polyhedron with exactly 14 faces and fewer vertices than every published 14-face example (literature check, starting with Reshetov 2014), certified exactly as in the success criterion.

An exactly certified monostable polyhedron with at most 30 faces and an n-fold rotational symmetry axis for some n >= 3, with no such explicit example published before (literature check). Lángi proved such polyhedra exist for every n, but his construction approximates a sphere and is not explicit or small.

targets.verification_method: Rebuild the hull from rational vertices (exact arithmetic) and count facets, merging coplanar triangles. Compute volume and centroid exactly by signed tetrahedra from an interior point. For each facet, project the centroid onto the facet plane and test strict containment with exact orientation predicates. Count stable facets. All in rationals with sympy or fractions; seconds.
angles: Conway-Guy style spirals: a polygonal 'spiral' of faces whose successive tipping leads to one face. Optimise vertex positions with a smooth margin objective (minimum over unstable faces of how far the centroid's projection falls outside the face), then snap to rationals.
Start from Reshetov's 14-face polyhedron and try face-merging moves that keep the stability margin positive.
pitfalls: Mono-unstable and mono-monostatic are different properties, and point-mass (non-homogeneous) models do not count.
Floating-point centroids can misclassify faces with small margins. Certify in exact arithmetic.
The status source is a general reference. Search the literature since 2022 for smaller examples before claiming.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Four mutually unbiased bases in C^6 (only three known), or a checkable proof that none exist
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (numerical search plus certification); a non-existence proof is pure thought or needs cluster for exact certificates
targets.statement: Two orthonormal bases {a_i}, {b_j} of C^d are mutually unbiased (MUB) if | < a_i|b_j > |^2 = 1/d for all i, j. In prime-power dimensions d+1 MUBs exist (Ivanovic; Wootters and Fields). Dimension 6 is the smallest open case: only triples are known, including infinite families of MUB triplets (Jaming, Matolcsi, Mora, Szollosi and Weiner), and no fourth basis has been found. Numerical searches by Butterley and Hall (quant-ph/0701122) and Brierley and Weigert found no four MUBs. Raynal, Lu and Englert (PRA 83, 062303 (2011), arXiv:1103.1025) maximised the average squared distance D^2 = (1/6) sum_{a < b} [1 - (1/(d-1)) sum_{i,j} (| < a_i|b_j > |^2 - 1/d)^2] over four bases; D^2 = 1 exactly for four MUBs, and their numerical global maximum is 0.9983 (closed form (71 - 3((r^2+12r-3)/(14r))^2)/70, r = (21 sqrt3 - 36)^(1/3), = 0.998291692700...), reached by a two-parameter family plus the identity. A lemma of Chen and Yu (arXiv:1610.04875) on product vectors has a wrong proof, which invalidates three later theorems (McNulty and Weigert, Comment, arXiv:2504.13067, 2025). The McNulty-Weigert review (Quantum 10, 2051, 1 April 2026) gives fourteen equivalent formulations and says no more than three MUBs have been found in d = 6 and that a complete set of seven is unresolved. The complete classification of order-6 complex Hadamard matrices by Cardenes Wuttig and Tindall (arXiv:2608.18053, Aug 2026) states that it does not settle the MUB question. Dimension 10 is also open, with three MUBs known.
targets.success_criterion: Success means EITHER (a) four orthonormal bases of C^6 that are pairwise mutually unbiased, given with exact entries (elements of an explicit number field, e.g. cyclotomic or a stated algebraic extension) for which orthonormality and | < a_i|b_j > |^2 = 1/6 for all 6x6 overlaps of every pair of bases are verified exactly, or given to at least 40 significant digits together with a rigorous certificate that an exact solution of the FULL MUB system exists nearby (an interval Newton/Krawczyk certificate counts only for a square, gauge-fixed system, with a proof that the remaining equations follow from it; interval residuals that merely contain zero are not proof); the number of MUBs, 4, is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the 3 known for d = 6 per the McNulty-Weigert 2026 review (re-fetched before claiming, with an arXiv check for newer papers); OR (b) a proof that no four MUBs exist in C^6, either machine-checked (Lean, Isabelle, Coq) or as an exact algebraic certificate (e.g. rational SOS / Positivstellensatz or Groebner certificate) that an independent tool re-verifies.

partial_wins.statement: Four orthonormal bases of C^6 whose ASD (Raynal-Lu-Englert Eq. 2-3), computed in mpmath at 50 digits, exceeds 0.998291692700 by at least 1e-10, contradicting the published global numerical maximum.
A machine-checked or exact-certificate proof that no complete set of seven MUBs exists in C^6 (weaker than excluding four), re-verifiable by independent software.
Four pairwise mutually unbiased bases in C^10, certified as in (a).

targets.verification_method: (a) Load the 24 vectors; check exact orthonormality inside each basis and all 36 overlaps for each of the 6 pairs of bases with exact arithmetic (sympy/flint over the stated field), or re-run the existence certificate with an independent implementation (mpmath.iv or Arb), checking that the certified system is square and gauge-fixed and that the argument that the remaining equations follow is valid. (b) Re-run the proof checker or verify the certificate identity exactly. p1: recompute the ASD at 50 digits from the posted bases after normalisation, having first checked that the code gives distance 1 for every pair of a known MUB triple. Literature check against the 2026 review and arXiv.
angles: Lift the Raynal-Lu-Englert two-parameter family or the Jaming et al. Fourier-family triplets and search for a fourth basis by Riemannian optimisation on U(6), as a stress test of the 0.9983 ceiling.
Polynomial optimisation: the Gribling-Polak symmetry-reduced hierarchy for MUBs and Delsarte-type LP bounds are routes to an exact certificate for (b) or p2.
The 2026 Cardenes Wuttig-Tindall classification of order-6 complex Hadamard matrices gives a complete domain in which to impose the joint compatibility conditions of three Hadamards for (b).
Product-vector constraints can cut the search space, but check each one against the 2025 McNulty-Weigert Comment (arXiv:2504.13067): some theorems built on Chen and Yu's lemma are invalid.
pitfalls: Near-MUBs: numerically optimised bases with overlap residuals around 1e-8 are not MUBs; given the 0.9983 numerical ceiling, a claimed quadruple without a certificate is almost certainly a bug.
Conventions: the ASD averages over the k(k-1)/2 pairs; check the formula on a known MUB triple (each pair gives distance 1) before comparing with 0.99829.
Normalisation and conjugation errors: compute overlaps as conjugate(a).b with unit-normalised vectors.
Unverified solver claims (numerical SDP values without an exact dual certificate) are not proofs for (b) or p2.

targets.name: Three-qubit GHZ nonlocality robustness: a certified Bell violation at white-noise visibility below 0.49143 (Designolle-Vertesi-Pokutta)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (Frank-Wolfe search plus exact local-bound computation; symmetry reduction needed beyond about 16 settings)
targets.statement: For the N-qubit GHZ state mixed with white noise, v|GHZ> < GHZ| + (1-v) I/2^N, the nonlocality robustness v_c is the smallest visibility at which some Bell inequality with finitely many projective measurement settings is violated. For N = 3, Mermin's inequality gives 1/2; Vertesi and Pal (arXiv:1108.1998) found 0.496057 with 5x5x5 settings. Sebastien Designolle, Tamas Vertesi and Sebastian Pokutta (PRA 109, 022205 (2024); arXiv:2310.20677, v3 revised 5 Oct 2026) used symmetry-adapted Frank-Wolfe algorithms (BellPolytopes.jl) with each party measuring a regular m-gon in the XY plane of the Bloch sphere and certified the local bound exactly: N = 3 reaches 0.49143 with m = 22; N = 4: 0.32493 (m = 20); N = 5: 0.20872 (m = 18); N = 6: 0.13422 (16); N = 7: 0.08569 (12); N = 8: 0.05544 (11); N = 9: 0.03521 (10); N = 10: 0.02301 (9) (Table III). With m = 224 they reach 0.49132 for N = 3, but that local bound is out of reach, so it is not a certified value. They also prove the rigorous lower bound v_XY >= 0.49129 for N = 3 when all measurements are restricted to the XY plane, so planar strategies have at most 1.4e-4 left, while strategies using the full Bloch sphere are not bounded that way. These are the best known upper bounds on GHZ nonlocality robustness for 3 to 10 parties.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a tripartite Bell functional with rational coefficients and binary outcomes (m_A, m_B, m_C settings), its EXACT local bound L (maximum over all deterministic local strategies, certified as in verification_method), and projective qubit measurements on the three-qubit GHZ state with value Q_GHZ and white-noise value Q_noise, such that the critical visibility v* = (L - Q_noise)/(Q_GHZ - Q_noise), recomputed in exact or 40-digit interval arithmetic, is STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than 0.49143, the best certified value in arXiv:2310.20677 Table III (re-fetched live before claiming, plus an arXiv check for newer results), by at least 1e-5 (v* <= 0.49142).

partial_wins.statement: The same certified improvement by at least 1e-5 for N in 4..10 parties over the corresponding certified value in arXiv:2310.20677 Table III (0.32493, 0.20872, 0.13422, 0.08569, 0.05544, 0.03521, 0.02301).

An exact certification of the local bound of one of the arXiv:2310.20677 instances listed as out of reach (e.g. N = 3 with m = 32 or more planar settings), turning its uncertified visibility into a certified one below the Table III value for that N.

targets.verification_method: Recompute the quantum value from the posted measurement angles (exact trigonometric or 40-digit). Compute L: for a full-correlation functional, L = max over a in {+-1}^mA, b in {+-1}^mB of sum_k |sum_ij M_ijk a_i b_j|, so brute force over 2^(mA+mB) is laptop-hours when mA + mB <= 32 in C; for larger instances require a symmetry-reduced orbit enumeration whose correctness is independently re-implemented and agrees, or an exact branch-and-bound certificate re-run with an open solver. For functionals with marginal terms enumerate the third party's best response per setting. Compare v* with the live table.
angles: Leave the XY plane: the 0.49129 floor only binds planar measurements, so non-planar symmetric configurations (e.g. polyhedral orbits on the Bloch sphere) are the room left.
Use the paper's orbit-reduction trick to certify local bounds for larger m, as p2 asks.
pitfalls: Heuristic local bounds (a QUBO or Frank-Wolfe value not proven maximal) give an invalid visibility.
Noise model: the state must be mixed with the maximally mixed state I/8; other noise models are not comparable.
Uncertified values in Table VI of the paper (large m) are not the record to beat; the certified Table III values are.
Margins below 1e-5 are within rounding of the published 5-decimal values and are not wins.

targets.name: n-to-1 qubit random access codes with shared randomness: prove the 4-to-1 code (p = 0.741481) optimal, or beat a numerical optimum for n = 4..9
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (rigorous interval branch-and-bound over 2(n-1) measurement angles)
targets.statement: In an n-to-1 quantum random access code (QRAC) with shared randomness (SR), Alice encodes n bits into one qubit and Bob must output any requested bit; p is the worst-case success probability. Andris Ambainis, Debbie Leung, Laura Mancinska and Maris Ozols (arXiv:0810.2937, 2008-2009) showed that with SR the problem reduces to choosing n unit vectors v_i in R^3 (Bob's measurement axes): the optimal encoding is then fixed and p = 1/2 + S/(n 2^(n+1)) with S = sum over x in {+-1}^n of ||sum_i x_i v_i||. They proved p <= 1/2 + 1/(2 sqrt n), tight only for n = 2, 3 (orthogonal axes), and found numerical codes for n = 4..12 (Table 2): 0.741481 (n = 4, exactly 1/2 + (1+sqrt3)/(8 sqrt2)), 0.713578, 0.694046, 0.678638, 0.666633, 0.656893 (n = 9). Their open problem 'Optimality of numerical codes' asks to prove the optimality of any of these for n >= 4. Laura Mancinska and Sigurd Storgaard (arXiv:2106.00155) proved the m-qubit bound p <= 1/2 + (1/2) sqrt(2^(m-1)/n) for SR codes, which for m = 1 is the old bound. Shuo Tan and Syed Jafar (arXiv:2607.10414, v3 23 Oct 2026) settled the binary (n, n-1) and (n, n-2) families and list (2,1), (3,1), (3,2), (4,2) and (6,2) as the only cases solved before them, so the 4-to-1 optimum is open: it lies in [0.741481, 0.75].
targets.success_criterion: Success means EITHER (a) a rigorous, independently re-checkable proof that the optimal n-to-1 QRAC with SR for n = 4 has p <= 0.741481 + 1e-6, i.e. that max over unit vectors v_1..v_4 in R^3 of S/(4*2^5) + 1/2 does not exceed that value (interval-arithmetic branch-and-bound with a posted cover of the parameter domain, an exact SOS certificate, or a machine-checked proof); OR (b) n unit vectors in R^3 for some n in 4..9 whose p, computed in mpmath at 40 digits from the formula above, is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the arXiv:0810.2937 Table 2 value for that n by at least 1e-6 (re-fetch Tan-Jafar arXiv:2607.10414 and search arXiv before claiming, in case a newer value or proof exists).

partial_wins.statement: A rigorous certified upper bound p(4) <= 0.745 for the 4-to-1 QRAC with SR (strictly below the proven 0.75), re-checkable as in (a).
A rigorous optimality proof, as in (a), for n = 5 (0.713578) or n = 6 (0.694046) within 1e-6.

targets.verification_method: (b): recompute p from the posted vectors in mpmath; first check the formula reproduces 0.853553 (n = 2, orthogonal axes) and 0.741481 for the paper's n = 4 code. (a), p1, p2: re-run the posted interval branch-and-bound with an independent implementation (mpmath.iv or Arb), checking that the boxes cover the whole domain (v_1 fixed to (0,0,1) by symmetry, remaining 2(n-1) angles) and that each box's rigorous upper bound is below the claimed value; or re-check the SOS identity in exact rationals.
angles: S is a sum of norms that is Lipschitz in the angles; the sign symmetries x -> -x and permutations of the v_i cut the domain by a large factor before branch-and-bound.
For p1, a relaxation (e.g. bounding each ||sum x_i v_i|| by a quadratic SDP-friendly form) may suffice without full branch-and-bound.
pitfalls: Without shared randomness a 4-to-1 qubit QRAC with p > 1/2 does not exist (Hayashi et al.); do not mix the two settings.
Worst-case p with SR equals the optimal average-case value; compare like with like.

Table 2 cells for n >= 10 are weak records: a quick multistart BFGS run in this lane (2026-10-30) reached 0.6482412 for n = 10 (table 0.648200) and 0.6410553 for n = 11 (table 0.641051), so they are excluded from (b). The same run reproduced n = 4..9 to all 6 decimals, so those are probably global optima and (a) is the realistic win.
Floating-point branch-and-bound is not a proof; bounds must be rigorous (outward rounding).

targets.name: Smallest unsolved quantum random access code: three trits into one qutrit (n = d = D = 3), best 0.69715 vs bounds 0.69853 (projective only) and about 0.699 (general POVMs, floating-point)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (seesaw searches; exact-arithmetic SDP dual certificates for upper bounds)
targets.statement: In a quantum random access code (QRAC) with n variables over a d-letter alphabet encoded into a D-dimensional quantum system, Alice prepares rho_x for x in [d]^n, Bob receives i in [n] and measures a d-outcome POVM {M^i_a}; the average success probability is ASP = (1/(n d^n)) sum_x sum_i Tr(rho_x M^i_{x_i}). Exact optima are known only for a few cases, e.g. (n,d,D) = (2,d,d) with 1/2(1 + 1/sqrt d) and (3,2,2) with 1/2(1 + 1/sqrt3). Mate Farkas, Nikolai Miklin and Armin Tavakoli (Quantum 9, 1643 (2025), arXiv:2312.14142) state that the smallest unsolved case is n = d = D = 3 and that whether MUB measurements are optimal there is unresolved. Their best lower bound is 0.69715 (best of 100 seesaw runs; three MUB measurements with optimal states give about 0.6971), their analytic upper bound (Corollary 1) is 0.71823, and dimension-restricted SDP relaxations (QDimSum) give 0.69853 at level 2+MMM+rhoMM, but only under the assumption of projective measurements. The best numerical bound valid for general POVMs is the almost-qudit SDP of Jef Pauwels, Stefano Pironio, Erik Woodhead and Armin Tavakoli (PRL 129, 250504 (2022), arXiv:2208.07887), plotted but not tabulated in arXiv:2312.14142 Fig. 2 at about 0.699 for D = 3 (read off the plot; floating-point, no exact certificate). Table 2 of arXiv:2312.14142 also lists open seesaw-versus-bound gaps for other n = 3 cells, e.g. (d,D) = (3,4): 0.72567 vs 0.77778, (3,5): 0.76241 vs 0.83024, (4,4): 0.64434 vs 0.66667.
targets.success_criterion: Success means EITHER (a) 27 density matrices on C^3 and three 3-outcome POVMs (positive semidefinite, summing to the identity, given exactly or to 30 digits and verified in exact or interval arithmetic) whose ASP for n = d = D = 3, computed by the formula above at 40 digits, is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than 0.69715, the best value in arXiv:2312.14142 (re-fetched live before claiming, plus an arXiv check for newer results), by at least 1e-5 (ASP >= 0.69716); OR (b) a proven upper bound on the ASP valid for ALL states and POVMs in dimension 3 that is STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than 0.69853, given as an exact (rational or algebraic) dual certificate or a machine-checked proof.

partial_wins.statement: A proven upper bound of at most 0.6990 on the ASP for n = d = D = 3, valid for general POVMs, given as an exactly verified certificate (a rational SDP dual whose feasibility and value are checked in exact arithmetic, for a relaxation that does not assume projective measurements) or as a machine-checked proof. This is the first rigorous POVM-valid bound at the level of the floating-point Pauwels et al. value.
For another n = 3 cell of the arXiv:2312.14142 table with (d,D) in {(3,4), (3,5), (4,4), (4,5), (2,3)}, an explicit strategy beating the tabulated seesaw value by at least 1e-5, verified as in (a).

targets.verification_method: (a) Check each rho_x has unit trace and eigenvalues >= 0 and each POVM element is PSD with sum I (exact or interval arithmetic after rationalising); compute ASP in mpmath. Sanity-check the formula on the known (2,3,3) optimum 1/2(1 + 1/sqrt3) = 0.78868 before comparing. (b) and p1: verify the dual certificate identity exactly (rational SDP dual feasibility and value), confirming that the relaxation used does not assume projective measurements, or re-run the machine-checked proof.
pitfalls: The 0.69853 SDP value assumes projective measurements; using it as a general bound, or comparing a POVM-valid bound against it without saying so, is wrong.
Normalisation: ASP averages over all d^n inputs and n questions.
Seesaw runs stall in local optima (the paper notes this for some cells); the 1e-5 margin guards against rounding of the 5-decimal table, not against bugs.
Do not confuse this with qubit QRACs or the n = 2 family, which are solved.

targets.name: Quantum chromatic number vs rank-1 quantum chromatic number: a graph on at most 20 vertices with chi_q(G) < chi_q^(1)(G) (smallest known: Lalonde's 21-vertex G21)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (graph search, exact quantum colourings, and a rigorous orthogonal-rank lower bound)
targets.statement: In the quantum colouring game a graph G has quantum chromatic number chi_q(G) <= c if there are projectors P_{v,1..c} on C^D for each vertex with sum_i P_{v,i} = I and P_{u,i} P_{v,i} = 0 for every edge uv and colour i. chi_q^(r) restricts to rank-r projectors, and chi_q = min_r chi_q^(r). The orthogonal rank xi(G) is the least dimension of an orthogonal representation. It satisfies xi(G) <= chi_q^(1)(G) <= chi(G), and the two can differ (Scarpa and Severini; Mancinska and Roberson's 13-vertex G13 has xi = 3 and chi_q^(1) = 4). Olivier Lalonde (Electron. J. Combin. 32(1) P1.18, 2025; arXiv:2311.08194) proved the Mancinska-Roberson conjecture that their 14-vertex G14 is the smallest graph with chi_q < chi. He also constructed G21 (21 vertices, 72 edges, graph6 given in the paper) with chi_q = chi_q^(2) = 4 and xi = chi_q^(1) = chi = 5. G21 is the smallest known separation between chi_q and chi_q^(1). The previous one was the 57-vertex magic-square graph Gmsg from Mancinska and Roberson's 2016 paper, with chi_q = 3 and chi_q^(1) = xi = 4. G21 is also the first separation between chi_q^(1) and chi_q^(2). His lower bound xi(G21) > 4 needed a new algorithm, since no general practical method certifies orthogonal rank. In the paper's open problems he suggests looking for graphs on 20 vertices or fewer that separate chi_q and chi_q^(1), or for the smallest such graph. He also notes that no proof is known that all chi_q^(r) are distinct parameters. Lalonde's 'Quantum colorings of spheres' (arXiv:2606.10872, June 2026) gives a 19-vertex G19 with xi = 3 < chi_q = 4, which is the opposite direction and not a chi_q vs chi_q^(1) separation. The abstracts of the 2025-2026 citing papers seen in this check report no smaller separation.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a graph G with at most 20 vertices (STRICTLY FEWER, direction: min, than the 21 of G21 in arXiv:2311.08194; re-check arXiv for newer separations before claiming), together with (i) and (ii). (i) An explicit quantum c-colouring: projectors P_{v,i} in C^D with entries in an explicit number field (e.g. cyclotomic), verified exactly to satisfy P^2 = P = P^dagger, sum_i P_{v,i} = I and P_{u,i}P_{v,i} = 0 on every edge. (ii) A rigorous, independently re-checkable proof that G has no rank-1 quantum c-colouring (chi_q^(1)(G) > c). Proving that G has no orthogonal representation in C^c (xi(G) > c) suffices, since xi <= chi_q^(1). The proof may be an exact algebraic certificate (e.g. a Groebner basis or Nullstellensatz certificate over Q(i) re-verified by independent software), a run of Lalonde's algorithm re-implemented independently that agrees, or a machine-checked proof.

partial_wins.statement: A graph of any size with chi_q^(3)(G) < chi_q^(2)(G), with the colouring verified exactly and the lower bound on chi_q^(2) proven by a re-checkable certificate: the first separation between the rank-2 and rank-3 quantum chromatic numbers.
A graph on at most 100 vertices with chi_q^(1)(G) - chi_q(G) >= 2, with no such graph of at most 100 vertices published before (literature check), certified as in the main criterion.

targets.verification_method: Parse G (graph6). Recompute the vertex and edge counts and the classical chromatic number by SAT. Check every projector identity exactly with sympy or flint over the stated field. Re-verify the lower-bound certificate (on xi or directly on chi_q^(1)) with independent software, e.g. Singular or Macaulay2 for a Groebner or Nullstellensatz certificate, or re-run an independent implementation of the stated algorithm. Confirm that the certificate excludes c-dimensional orthogonal representations, or rank-1 quantum c-colourings, and not a weaker real-only or SDP relaxation. Confirm no graph with fewer vertices is already published.
pitfalls: chi_q < chi is not the target: that separation is settled at 14 vertices (G14). Here the gap must be between chi_q and chi_q^(1).
xi and chi_q^(1) are different parameters (xi <= chi_q^(1)). A graph with xi < chi_q, such as Lalonde's 19-vertex G19 (arXiv:2606.10872: xi = 3, chi_q = 4), goes the wrong way and does not count.

Numerical failure to find a c-dimensional orthogonal representation is evidence, not proof; the criterion needs a certificate. A real-only search or an SDP bound (xi_SDP) below c+1 proves nothing about complex representations.
Floating-point projectors with residual 1e-12 are not a quantum colouring until made exact.

targets.name: Erdős discrepancy, C = 3: a +-1 sequence longer than 130,000 with discrepancy at most 3
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (SAT on a 130k-variable instance; checking a candidate takes seconds)
targets.statement: For a +-1 sequence x_1..x_N, the discrepancy is the maximum over d >= 1 and k with kd <= N of |x_d + x_{2d} + ... + x_{kd}|. Tao (arXiv:1509.05363, 2015) proved that every infinite +-1 sequence has unbounded discrepancy, so for each C the longest length L(C) of a sequence with discrepancy <= C is finite. L(1) = 11. L(2) = 1160 (Boris Konev and Alexei Lisitsa, SAT 2014: a length-1160 sequence plus an UNSAT proof at 1161). For C = 3 only lower bounds are known. Le Bras, Gomes and Selman (arXiv:1407.2510) cite 17,000 as the record before 2014, and they proved that completely multiplicative discrepancy-3 sequences stop at exactly 127,645. Konev and Lisitsa (Artificial Intelligence 224, 2015, arXiv:1405.3097) proved the same for completely multiplicative and multiplicative sequences. They then generated an unrestricted discrepancy-3 sequence of length 130,000 whose first 127,600 terms satisfy the complete-multiplicativity conditions (files at cgi.csc.liv.ac.uk/~konev/edp), listed the unconstrained C = 3 value as ' > 130 000' in their Table 1, and remarked that their solvers struggled to extend it much further. No upper bound for unrestricted sequences is published. The AlphaEvolve survey (Georgiev, Gómez-Serrano, Tao and Wagner, arXiv:2511.02864, 2025) still cites C(3) >= 13,000, which is stale. Re-fetches of the Konev-Lisitsa page and papers on 2026-10-30 show no record above 130,000. Find a longer sequence.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit +-1 sequence x_1..x_N (plain text, one sign per line, 1-indexed) such that every partial sum x_d + x_{2d} + ... + x_{kd}, for every d >= 1 and every k with kd <= N, lies in [-3, 3]. Two independent checkers must confirm this. N must be STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best published length at verification time: the maximum of 130,000 (Konev-Lisitsa page https://cgi.csc.liv.ac.uk/~konev/edp and arXiv:1405.3097), any newer value on that page, and any value found by a fresh search for 'discrepancy 3' sequence records over the last 24 months. A sequence that is completely multiplicative cannot win, because it is capped at 127,645.

partial_wins.statement: A DRAT- or LRAT-checked proof (drat-trim or cake_lpr) that no discrepancy-3 sequence of a stated length N' with 130,000 < N' <= 140,000 agrees with the first 127,600 terms of Konev-Lisitsa's published length-130,000 sequence. The CNF must be generated by the claimant's own encoder and regenerated by the skeptic from a published script. After the fixed prefix is substituted, the CNF must not be refuted by unit propagation alone (the skeptic checks this), so the certificate says more than a forced-sign clash at one index. This certifies that the published prefix is a dead end at N'.

targets.verification_method: Checker A: for each d in 1..N, sum x_{kd} for k = 1..floor(N/d) and track the running maximum of |partial sum|. This is about N ln N, roughly 1.6M additions. Checker B: use independent code in another language, or a numpy cumulative sum over each strided view x[d-1::d]. Both must report a maximum <= 3 and confirm that the length is N and all entries are +-1. For p1, regenerate the CNF from the published encoder and check the proof with drat-trim. Then re-fetch the Konev-Lisitsa page and search arXiv for newer C = 3 records.
angles: Start from the published length-130,000 sequence. Keep the completely multiplicative prefix fixed up to some M < 127,645, free the tail, and grow N with incremental SAT (CaDiCaL/kissat assumptions), freeing a sliding window when it gets stuck.
Relax complete multiplicativity only at large primes: require x_{pq} = x_p x_q for primes p, q < P and leave large primes free. This keeps most of the structure while escaping the 127,645 cap.
Use the Konev-Lisitsa automaton encoding of partial-sum states, which needs only O(N log N) auxiliary variables, rather than cardinality constraints.
Use local search (probSAT) seeded with the published sequence, minimising the number of violated progression sums.
pitfalls: Completely multiplicative and multiplicative sequences are proven to stop at 127,645. A search confined to them cannot win.
Every difference d and every length k counts. Checking only d up to some bound, or only full-length progressions, gives false records.
Off-by-one: the sequence is 1-indexed (x_1 is the first term). A 0-indexed file shifts every progression.
The discrepancy-2 and discrepancy-3 files on the Konev-Lisitsa page are different. Use the unrestricted length-130,000 file as the baseline.

targets.name: Property B: a non-2-colourable 5-uniform hypergraph with at most 50 edges (m(5) <= 51 since 1969)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (search; certifying a candidate takes seconds to minutes)
targets.statement: An n-uniform hypergraph has property B if its vertices can be 2-coloured with no monochromatic edge. m(n), the minimum number of edges in an n-uniform hypergraph without property B, is the Erdős-Hajnal problem (Erdős #901, OEIS A392185). Known values are m(1..4) = 1, 3, 7, 23. For n = 5 the upper bound 51 comes from the Abbott-Hanson-Toft recursive construction, m(5) <= 2^4 + 5 m(3). It is still listed as the current upper bound in Aglave, Amarnath, Shannigrahi and Singh (Australas. J. Combin. 76, 2020, arXiv:1602.00218 v4) and in Table 1 of Grill and Linzmayer (arXiv:2403.05674 v3, Jun 2024). Lower bounds rose from 28 to 29 (Aglave et al.) and then to 32 (Grill-Linzmayer, Theorem 1). OEIS A392185 (Kyle Wood, Jan 2026) still prints 29 <= a(5) <= 51, so its lower bound is stale but its upper bound agrees. Other upper bounds from Aglave et al.'s Table 1 and Section 4 are m(6) <= 147 (Abbott-Moser), m(7) <= 421 (Abbott-Hanson-Toft) and m(8) <= 1212 (Aglave et al., improving Mathews-Panda-Shannigrahi's 1269). No smaller explicit 5-uniform non-2-colourable hypergraph has been published. Find one.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit list of E distinct 5-element subsets of a finite vertex set such that the hypergraph has no proper 2-colouring. This must be certified either by exhaustive enumeration of all 2^v colourings (feasible for v <= about 34) or by an UNSAT result on the CNF (for each edge, one clause forbidding all-colour-1 and one forbidding all-colour-0), with the UNSAT proof checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr. E must be STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than the best published upper bound on m(5) at verification time: 51 per OEIS A392185 (re-fetched before claiming), arXiv:2403.05674 v3 and arXiv:1602.00218 v4, unless a fresh search for 'property B' upper bounds over the last 24 months shows a smaller one. A hypergraph with fewer than 32 edges contradicts Grill-Linzmayer's lower bound and means a bug.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit non-2-colourable 6-uniform hypergraph with at most 146 edges (beating m(6) <= 147), certified the same way.
An explicit non-2-colourable 7-uniform hypergraph with at most 420 edges (beating m(7) <= 421), certified the same way.

An explicit non-2-colourable 8-uniform hypergraph with fewer edges than the best published upper bound on m(8) (1212 in arXiv:1602.00218 v4, or a smaller value found by a fresh search), certified the same way.

targets.verification_method: Parse the edge list. Assert that each edge has exactly n distinct vertices and that the edges are pairwise distinct, and count them. Build the 2-colouring CNF with one's own script. Run CaDiCaL with --lrat or DRAT output and check the proof with drat-trim or cake_lpr. When there are at most about 34 vertices, also enumerate all colourings directly with a bitmask in C. Then re-fetch arXiv:2403.05674 and search for newer bounds.
angles: Search over hypergraphs with a large automorphism group, for example orbits of 5-sets under a cyclic or affine group on v points, with v in the range where the lower-bound arguments force the extremal example (Grill-Linzmayer study m(5, v) for 17 <= v <= 25).
Use local search on hypergraphs to maximise the number of edges a 2-colouring must violate, with a SAT oracle for 2-colourability, adding and removing edges as in Exoo-style Ramsey searches.
Generalise the Abbott-Hanson-Toft and Seymour (m(4) = 23) constructions: replace the Fano-plane ingredient by other small non-2-colourable systems and SAT-search the gluing.
Exploit the lower-bound proofs: they show an extremal 5-uniform example must have about 23 to 25 vertices with nearly regular degrees, which shrinks the search space.
pitfalls: Improving the lower bound (for example to m(5) >= 34) is a different and much harder problem. Only an explicit hypergraph counts here.
Edges must be exactly 5-uniform. Adding a smaller edge, or a repeated edge, makes the claim invalid.
Bounds from recursive formulas are not explicit hypergraphs. Expand any recursive construction fully and certify the explicit object.
An UNSAT verdict without a checked proof is not a certificate.

targets.name: (k,s)-SAT threshold: an unsatisfiable 5-CNF in which every variable occurs at most 7 times, proving f(5) <= 6
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (SAT Modulo Symmetries style search; candidate formulas can be large)
targets.statement: A (k,s)-CNF has clauses of exactly k literals on k distinct variables, and every variable occurs, positively or negatively, in at most s clauses. Kratochvíl, Savický and Tuza showed that there is a threshold f(k) such that every (k, f(k))-CNF is satisfiable while (k, f(k)+1)-SAT is NP-complete. Known values are f(3) = 3 (Tovey) and f(4) = 4. Hoory and Szeider (SAT 2004 and later papers) built unsatisfiable formulas inside the class MU(1), giving f(5) <= 7, f(6) <= 11, f(7) <= 17, f(8) <= 29 and f(9) <= 51. Gebauer, Szabó and Tardos (arXiv:1006.0744) record that Hoory-Szeider determined f1(5..9) = 7, 11, 17, 29, 51 exactly, where f1 is the MU(1)-restricted threshold, and that these remain the best upper bounds. Zhang, Peitl and Szeider (SAT 2024, arXiv:2405.16149 v3) state f(5) is in [5, 7]. They found the smallest unsatisfiable (3,s) and (3,p,q) formulas for all parameters, and cut the smallest known unsatisfiable (4,5)-CNF from Knuth's 257 clauses to 235 by searching outside MU(1). Their conclusion names the exact value of f(5) as open. An unsatisfiable (5,7)-CNF would show f(5) <= 6.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a DIMACS CNF in which every clause has exactly 5 literals on 5 distinct variables, and every variable occurs in at most 7 clauses (counting both polarities), together with a DRAT or LRAT proof of unsatisfiability checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr (or an explicit tree-like resolution certificate that the skeptic checks). The occurrence bound 7 must be STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than 8, the smallest s for which an unsatisfiable (5,s)-CNF is published (Hoory-Szeider; f(5) <= 7 in arXiv:2405.16149 v3), unless a fresh search for '(k,s)-SAT' or 'f(5)' over the last 24 months shows a published unsatisfiable (5,7)-CNF, in which case the target is solved.

partial_wins.statement: An unsatisfiable (4,5)-CNF with at most 234 clauses (beating Zhang-Peitl-Szeider's 235), with clause width exactly 4, at most 5 occurrences per variable, and a checked DRAT/LRAT proof.
An unsatisfiable (6,11)-CNF, proving f(6) <= 10 and beating Hoory-Szeider's f(6) <= 11, certified the same way.
An unsatisfiable (7,17)-, (8,29)- or (9,51)-CNF, beating f(7) <= 17, f(8) <= 29 or f(9) <= 51, certified the same way.

targets.verification_method: Parse the CNF. Assert that every clause has exactly k literals with pairwise distinct variables, and count the occurrences of each variable (both polarities) to confirm the maximum is <= s. Then run drat-trim or cake_lpr on the supplied proof; a second solver run, such as kissat, gives a sanity cross-check. For p1, also count the clauses. Then re-fetch arXiv:2405.16149 and search for newer bounds.
angles: Follow the enforcer route: find a small satisfiable (5,7)-formula that forces a backbone literal false, then join 5 copies with one 5-clause. Search for enforcers with SAT Modulo Symmetries, as Zhang-Peitl-Szeider did for (3,s) and (4,5).

Leave MU(1): since f1(5) = 7 exactly, any improvement must use minimal unsatisfiable formulas of deficiency >= 2. Combine disjunctive splitting with extra axioms, as in Zhang-Peitl-Szeider's (4,5) construction.
Design 5-CNFs from combinatorial designs, for example orbit-closed clause sets under a group action, where occurrence counts are uniform by construction, then test unsatisfiability.
For p1, restart Zhang-Peitl-Szeider's SMS pipeline with new auxiliary axioms. Their artifact is on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.11282310); write your own encoder rather than running downloaded code.
pitfalls: Clauses with fewer than k literals, or with a repeated variable, are not allowed. The width must be exactly k.
Count occurrences of variables, not of literals: x and not-x both count toward s.
Formulas in MU(1) cannot beat f1(5) = 7, so a search restricted to MU(1) is a dead end for the main criterion.
An UNSAT claim without a checked proof does not count, and for large formulas the proof file is the deliverable.

targets.name: Chromatic number of the square of the hypercube: is Q_9^2 13-colourable? (13 <= chi <= 14; n = 10, 11 also open)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (512-vertex SAT instance with heavy symmetry; a proof of non-colourability may need a cluster)
targets.statement: Q_n^2 has vertex set {0,1}^n, with edges between words at Hamming distance 1 or 2. A proper colouring is a partition of the Hamming space into binary codes of minimum distance >= 3, so chi(Q_n^2) >= ceil(2^n / A(n,3)). Kokkala and Östergård (arXiv:1607.01605; Math. Comp. 87, 2018) settled the case they call the smallest open one, chi(Q_8^2) = 13, after 25 years in which only 14-colourings were known (Hougardy 1991, Royle 1993). They note that for n <= 15 the value is unknown for n = 8, 9, 10, 11, with counting bounds 13, 13, 15, 15 (A(n,3) = 20, 40, 72, 144) and the general upper bound 2^ceil(log2(n+1)) = 16 for n = 9, 10, 11. Lauri (arXiv:1605.07613, 2016) found a 14-colouring of Q_9^2, so 13 <= chi(Q_9^2) <= 14. Kokkala-Östergård also showed that none of their classified symmetric 13-colourings of Q_8^2 extends to a 13-colouring of Q_9^2 (each class C = 0D u 1E). A search on 2026-10-30 found no later result settling n = 9.
targets.success_criterion: Success means one of two things. (a) An explicit partition of {0,1}^9 into 13 classes, each with pairwise Hamming distances >= 3, so that 13 is STRICTLY LESS (direction: min) than Lauri's 14. (b) A DRAT or LRAT proof, checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr, that Q_9^2 has no proper 13-colouring, which settles chi(Q_9^2) = 14. For (b), the CNF must be regenerated by the skeptic from a published encoder, and any symmetry breaking must be sound (for example, fixing distinct colours on the 10-clique formed by 0 and the 9 weight-1 words) and justified in writing. Before claiming, re-fetch arXiv:1607.01605 and arXiv:1605.07613 and search for any newer value of chi(Q_9^2).

partial_wins.statement: A DRAT/LRAT-checked proof that no 13-colouring of Q_9^2 is invariant under a stated nontrivial subgroup of Aut(Q_9^2), such as a translation subgroup or a coordinate permutation of order 3, 7 or 9. The case must not already be excluded in arXiv:1607.01605 or arXiv:1605.07613.
An explicit 15-colouring of Q_10^2 or Q_11^2 (classes with pairwise distance >= 3), beating the general upper bound of 16, provided a fresh search shows no published 15-colouring for that n.

targets.verification_method: For a colouring, load 2^n integers, assert that the colours lie in 0..k-1, and for every word x and every y at distance 1 or 2 (n + n(n-1)/2 neighbours) assert that colour(x) != colour(y). This takes under a second. A second checker computes the minimum distance of each class directly. For proofs, regenerate the CNF and run drat-trim. Then do a literature check.
angles: A 13-colouring partitions 512 words into 13 codes of size at most A(9,3) = 40, so at least five classes are optimal (9,40,3) codes and every class has size >= 32. Classify or enumerate these large codes up to equivalence (equivalently even (10,M,4) codes), then solve the partition as exact cover.
Work in the even-weight picture used by Kokkala-Östergård, where Q_9^2 is isomorphic to the halved 10-cube. Prescribe automorphism groups and run exhaustive classification inside each.
Use cube-and-conquer with the 10-clique colour fix plus lexicographic leader constraints for the remaining symmetry, aiming at a checkable UNSAT proof for (b).
Glue a 13-colouring of the even half to one of the odd half via a SAT search over the 1820 class-size profiles that Kokkala-Östergård enumerate.
pitfalls: Distance 1 and distance 2 both count as edges. A partition into distance-2 codes (distance-1 only) solves the wrong problem.
Excluding only symmetric colourings proves nothing about chi. Only an unrestricted UNSAT proof establishes chi(Q_9^2) = 14.
Symmetry breaking beyond fixing a clique must be proven sound, or the UNSAT certificate is invalid.
The Q_8^2 case is already solved (13); do not resubmit it.

targets.name: Pythagorean triples with three colours: a triple-free 3-colouring of {1..N} for N above 25,000,000
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (tens of millions of triples; SAT or local search with a streaming checker)
targets.statement: Erdős and Graham asked whether the positive integers can be finitely coloured with no monochromatic Pythagorean triple a^2 + b^2 = c^2. For two colours the answer is no: Heule, Kullmann and Marek (SAT 2016) proved that {1..7824} admits a triple-free 2-colouring and {1..7825} does not, with a 200 TB proof that was later formally verified. For three colours the question is open, and progress is measured by the longest interval {1..N} with a triple-free 3-colouring. Heule and Kullmann ('The science of brute force', CACM 60(8), 2017) reported a 3-partition of {1..10^7}. A Zenodo preprint by Python Song (record 23329356, v1 12 Oct 2026, not peer reviewed) claims a 3-colouring of {1..25,000,000} that avoids all 62,324,099 triples, with the colouring file data/pyth3col_N25000000.raw.gz and Lean checking code at github.com/Geeksongs/Three-Colour-Pythagorean-Triples-Problem. An independent check on 2026-10-30 decompressed the file (25,000,000 bytes, SHA-256 e1500d6c25b116bdf1cb237bd9954b6f5a90b102fb1a77cb754e8d7be153e7d6). An Euclid-formula enumerator written separately from the preprint's code counted 62,324,099 triples and found none monochromatic. Push N higher.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit colouring c:{1..N} -> {0,1,2} (raw bytes or text, with a SHA-256 hash) such that no Pythagorean triple a < b < c <= N with a^2 + b^2 = c^2, primitive or not, is monochromatic. Two independent triple enumerators must confirm this and agree on the triple count. N must be STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best published value at verification time: the maximum of 25,000,000 (Zenodo 23329356 and its GitHub data), 10^7 (Heule-Kullmann CACM 2017), and anything found by a fresh search for three-colour Pythagorean records over the last 24 months.
targets.verification_method: Enumerator A uses Euclid's formula: for coprime m > n of opposite parity, take the primitive triple (m^2 - n^2, 2mn, m^2 + n^2) and all its multiples with hypotenuse <= N. Enumerator B, for each c <= N and each a with a < c/sqrt(2), tests whether c^2 - a^2 is a perfect square using integer isqrt (slower; run it on a random sample of c plus the full range up to 10^6). Count the triples with A and compare with the count reported by the record holder. Check that no triple is monochromatic. Do not run downloaded code; treat the published colouring as data only.
angles: Only integers that occur in some triple matter. Integers in no triple (Pythagorean-free numbers, such as those all of whose prime factors are 3 mod 4 except for powers of 2) can take any colour, which shrinks the instance a lot.

Use incremental SAT or local search over a sliding window, but make the window large. Keeping the published colouring on {1..20,000,000} fixed already forces a clash at 25,000,365 (see pitfalls), so free several million integers below 25,000,000 together with the new ones.

Use residue- or valuation-based seed colourings, such as colour determined by v_p(n) for small primes p, then repair the conflicts with local search. The Song preprint analyses which such families fail and where.
Decompose by connected components of the triple hypergraph restricted to [1..N]: many components are small and can be solved exactly and independently.
pitfalls: The 25,000,000 record is a single-author, unrefereed preprint. Its colouring passed an independent check on 2026-10-30, but re-verify it yourself (as data) and look for errata before claiming. If it ever fails, the baseline is 10^7.

The published colouring cannot simply be extended. 25,000,030 is the hypotenuse of triples whose two legs are at most 25,000,000 and share a colour, and these pairs cover all three colours, so no colouring that keeps {1..25,000,000} fixed gets past 25,000,029. Keeping only {1..24,000,000} or {1..20,000,000} fixed still forces a clash at 25,000,081 or 25,000,365. A longer interval means recolouring millions of earlier integers, not appending new ones.
Non-primitive triples (multiples of primitive ones) must be included.
Matching N = 25,000,000 is not a record; N must be strictly larger.
Two colours are already settled (7824). A 2-colour claim is not this target.

targets.name: Kotzig's perfect 1-factorisation conjecture: a perfect 1-factorisation of K_64 (or K_66, 70, 76, 78, 88, 96, 100)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exact-cover or SAT search over symmetric starters; checking takes seconds)
targets.statement: A 1-factorisation of K_{2t} partitions its edges into 2t-1 perfect matchings. It is perfect (a P1F) if the union of every two matchings is a Hamilton cycle. Kotzig conjectured in 1963 that K_{2t} has a P1F for every t >= 2. Known results are two infinite families (2t = p+1 and 2t = 2p, p an odd prime) plus sporadic orders found mostly by computer searches for starters with multiplicative symmetry (Dinitz-Stinson quotient-coset starters, Ihrig-Seah-Stinson, and the list kept by Ian Wanless). The smallest orders were settled one at a time, most recently 52 by Wolfe and 56 by David Pike (2019). Tomasz Maciosowski (arXiv:2610.20408, 14 Oct 2026) constructed two non-isomorphic P1Fs of K_92 from starters in Z_91 invariant under a multiplier subgroup of order 3. He states that the open orders up to 100 were 64, 66, 70, 76, 78, 88, 92, 96 and 100, so 64, 66, 70, 76, 78, 88, 96 and 100 remain open, with K_64 the smallest. A 2026 preprint (arXiv:2607.09459) proves an asymptotic version, which leaves every small order open.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit 1-factorisation of K_{2t} for some 2t in {64, 66, 70, 76, 78, 88, 96, 100} that is still listed as open at verification time. It is given as 2t-1 lists of t edges each, or as a starter in a stated group together with its development rule. Verification must show that (i) the matchings partition all C(2t,2) edges, each being a perfect matching, and (ii) for each of the C(2t-1,2) pairs of matchings, the union is a single cycle through all 2t vertices. The result must be new (direction: existence where none is published): re-fetch arXiv:2610.20408 and search for P1F results on that order over the last 24 months. K_64 is the headline cell.

partial_wins.statement: A verified perfect 1-factorisation of K_{2t} for one of the orders that Maciosowski's Section 3 table (arXiv:2610.20408) lists as having no known P1F but an admissible multiplier subgroup: 2t in {248, 260, 342, 404, 428, 452, 470, 512, 560, 590, 638, 672, 680, 704, 722, 764, 782, 872, 890, 932, 950, 962}, provided a fresh literature search shows no published P1F of that order.

targets.verification_method: Expand any starter into explicit matchings. Assert that every edge of K_{2t} appears exactly once and that each matching covers every vertex once. For every pair of matchings, build the union (a 2-regular multigraph) and confirm that it is one cycle of length 2t by walking it. That is C(63,2) = 1953 walks of 64 steps for K_64, which takes milliseconds. Two independent implementations must agree. Then do the literature check.
angles: Maciosowski's U-invariant cyclic starters cannot reach the eight remaining orders up to 100: by his Lemma 2.12, Z*_{2t-1} has no admissible subgroup U != 1 for 2t-1 = 63, 65, 69, 75, 77, 87, 95, 99. So for K_64 and the others, use starters or one-point extensions in non-cyclic groups of order 2t-1 (for 63 the only non-cyclic abelian group is Z_3 x Z_21 = Z_3 x Z_3 x Z_7), or prescribe automorphism groups that act on 2t-2 points with two fixed points.

Use SAT with a lazy Hamiltonicity check: encode the starter (or the symmetric 1-factorisation) as exact cover, and add a blocking clause each time a pair of factors fails to form a single cycle (CEGAR loop).

For p1, apply Maciosowski's method directly: his table gives the largest admissible |U| and the number c of Hamilton-cycle conditions for each order (for example 2t = 248 with |U| = 3 and c = 41, or 2t = 962 with |U| = 15 and c = 32).
Use non-abelian groups of order 2t-1 where they exist, or Ihrig-Seah-Stinson style automorphism prescriptions, to break the obstruction that applies to cyclic multiplier symmetry.
pitfalls: The patterned starter {x, -x} never gives a P1F when 2t-1 is composite (Maciosowski Lemma 2.10), so do not search near it.
Checking only pairs (F_0, F_d) is sound only when the factorisation is induced by a starter. For an arbitrary factorisation, check all pairs.
K_92 is now solved (Oct 2026) and orders up to 56 were already done. Re-check the open list before claiming.
A union consisting of two cycles of total length 2t is not a Hamilton cycle. Walk the cycle; do not just check degrees.

targets.name: Oriented chromatic number of planar graphs by girth: an explicit planar oriented graph beating a lower bound (18..80, 11..40, 7..16, 7..11, 6..7, 5..7, 5..6)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (SAT for k <= 10 colours on a few hundred vertices; larger k is harder)
targets.statement: An oriented k-colouring of an oriented graph (no loops, no 2-cycles) is a homomorphism to an oriented graph on k vertices. Adjacent vertices get distinct colours, and all arcs between two colour classes point the same way. Let chi_o(P_g) be the maximum oriented chromatic number over oriented planar graphs of girth >= g. Table 1 of Das, Nandi and Sen (arXiv:2208.10188 v2, 3 Jul 2026) gives the state of the art. g=3: 18..80 (lower bound Marshall 2015, upper bound Raspaud-Sopena 1994). g=4: 11..40 (lower bound by Ochem 2004 via a computer check, upper bound Ochem-Pinlou 2013). g=5: 7..16 (Marshall 2013; Pinlou 2009). g=6: 7..11 (Marshall 2013; Borodin, Kostochka, Nešetřil, Raspaud, Sopena 1999). g=7: 6..7 (Nešetřil-Raspaud-Sopena 1997; Borodin-Ivanova 2005). g=8,9,10: 5..7. g=11: 5..6 (Ochem-Pinlou 2008). g > =12: 5 (Borodin-Ivanova-Kostochka 2007). The paper says the exact value is unknown for every g in 3..11. Most lower bounds rest on arguments that no small target graph works, not on explicit witness graphs.
targets.success_criterion: Success means, for some g in {3,...,11}, an explicit oriented graph G (arc list) with (i) a planar embedding certified by an independent planarity test (for example networkx check_planarity plus a second implementation), (ii) underlying girth >= g computed by BFS, and (iii) a DRAT/LRAT-checked proof (drat-trim or cake_lpr) that G has no oriented L-colouring, where L is the current lower bound for that g. That makes chi_o(P_g) >= L+1, STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the lower bound in Table 1 of arXiv:2208.10188 (latest version) and in any newer paper found by a fresh search. The CNF is the skeptic's own: colour variables x_{v,c} with exactly-one constraints, and orientation variables y_{c,d} = not y_{d,c}. Each arc u->v gets the clauses not(x_{u,c} and x_{v,c}) and (not x_{u,c} or not x_{v,d} or y_{c,d}). For g = 7 a win settles chi_o(P_7) = 7, and for g = 11 it settles chi_o(P_11) = 6.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit triangle-free planar oriented graph with a checked proof that it has no oriented 10-colouring, giving an explicit witness for chi_o(P_4) >= 11, provided no explicit witness of that size or smaller is published (fresh search).
An explicit planar oriented graph (any girth) with a checked proof that it has no oriented 17-colouring, giving an explicit witness for Marshall's chi_o(P_3) >= 18, under the same proviso.

targets.verification_method: Load the arc list. Check that there are no loops or 2-cycles. Run two planarity tests on the underlying graph and compute its girth by BFS from every vertex. Generate the CNF with an independent script, check the proof with drat-trim, and cross-check that the same CNF with L+1 colours is SAT when the claimant supplies such a colouring (sanity only). Then re-fetch arXiv:2208.10188 and search for newer bounds for that girth.
angles: Start with g = 11 (5 versus 6) and g = 7 (6 versus 7). Build large girth-g planar oriented graphs by iterated gadget gluing: whenever a SAT solver finds an oriented 5- or 6-colouring, add a gadget that kills that colouring's target tournament, and repeat (a CEGAR loop over targets).

The number of tournaments on L vertices is small for L <= 7 (456 non-isomorphic tournaments on 7 vertices). For each, find a planar girth-g oriented graph with no homomorphism to it, then combine them by disjoint union plus connecting paths that preserve girth.

Use the 'minimal bound' viewpoint from Das-Nandi-Sen: show by exhaustive SAT that no oriented graph on L vertices with the required extension properties exists, then extract an explicit graph from the failing cases.
Break colour symmetry by fixing colours on a small oriented clique, which is sound, to speed up the UNSAT proof.
pitfalls: Oriented colouring is not proper colouring of the underlying graph. The arc-consistency condition between colour classes is essential; leaving it out makes every planar graph 4-colourable.
Girth is measured on the underlying undirected graph and must be >= g, so a single short cycle disqualifies the graph.
Planarity must be checked exactly. Drawing coordinates alone are not a certificate.
Upper-bound improvements are theoretical proofs and are not covered by this target.

targets.name: New irregular (or small inner) satellite of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Neptune in public archival images, shown bound by an orbit fit
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (tens of GB of archival CCD frames per planet field per night; shift-and-stack over a grid of rates)
targets.statement: Irregular satellites are still being found in old images. The JPL list of planetary satellites (re-fetched 2026-10-30) gives Jupiter 115, Saturn 293, Uranus 29 and Neptune 16. Most of its 2025-2026 additions came from data taken years earlier: 20 Jupiter moons announced in MPECs 2025-H and 2026-F/G from 2010-2024 images (17 credited to S. S. Sheppard alone, two to Sheppard with D. J. Tholen, one of them also with C. Trujillo, and S/2010 J5 to E. J. Ashton, M. Beaudoin, B. J. Gladman and S. Deen), and 147 Saturn moons announced in MPECs 2025-E153/154/155 and 2026-F14, G68-G72, G74-G75 and M19, found in 2004-2023 data by Sheppard, Jewitt, Kleyna, Ashton, Gladman, Petit, Alexandersen, Fraser, Lawler and Kavelaars (S/2009 S2 credited to the Cassini Imaging Science Team). The other recent additions are S/2025 U1 (El Moutamid, Hedman, Showalter, Tiscareno, de Pater, Lissauer and Souami; 2025 JWST images, CBET 5593) and, from 2024, S/2023 U1 and S/2021 N1 (Sheppard, Tholen, Trujillo and Lykawka; MPEC 2024-D112). Shift-and-stack along trial satellite rates (as in Ashton, Gladman and colleagues' searches) reaches well below the single-frame limit. Deep giant-planet fields from CFHT MegaCam (CADC), Subaru Suprime-Cam/HSC (SMOKA), DECam (NOIRLab Astro Data Archive) and HST/JWST (MAST) are public after their proprietary periods. Open task: a satellite that none of these lists or announcements contain, found in public images and shown by an orbit fit to be bound to its planet.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (frame list with archive URLs, astrometric and photometric calibration against Gaia DR3, stacking code, stacked cutouts, ADES-format astrometry, orbit-fit code and output) where: (1) the object is detected at >= 5 sigma in stacks on >= 3 nights spanning >= 20 days, and the rate of each night's best stack matches the motion predicted by the final orbit to within 0.2 arcsec/hr; (2) an N-body fit (Sun, all giant planets from JPL DE440/Horizons) to all astrometry has RMS <= 0.3 arcsec, and >= 95% of >= 1,000 orbits sampled from the fit covariance (or MCMC) are bound to the planet (planetocentric energy < 0) with apocentre < 0.7 Hill radii; (3) at each epoch no designated satellite lies within 60 arcsec of the object, per JPL Horizons ephemerides for every satellite on https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/sats/discovery.html, and no known asteroid lies within 30 arcsec (IMCCE SkyBoT); (4) the object is not on the JPL discovery page, no MPEC in the MPC archive announces it, and no paper or preprint reports it (all re-fetched immediately before claiming). Reporting to the MPC is a human action and is not part of the win.

partial_wins.statement: The pipeline recovers >= 80% of the designated satellites predicted (Horizons) to lie in the processed frames with V brighter than the stacks' 5-sigma limit minus 0.5 mag, with the recovered list, missed list and limit saved.
A candidate meeting (3) and (4) seen at >= 5 sigma on 2 nights >= 1 day apart, with rates consistent with a bound orbit, but without the 20-day arc of (1).
Archival precovery astrometry (residuals <= 0.3 arcsec against the current JPL orbit) of a satellite announced in 2025-2026 that extends its observed arc, as stated in its MPEC, by >= 1 year.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic re-downloads the listed frames, re-runs the stack at the saved rates, re-measures astrometry against Gaia DR3, refits the orbit with an independent integrator, re-samples the covariance, and queries Horizons and SkyBoT for each epoch. A few hours.
angles: Conventional: shift-and-stack of CFHT or Subaru frames over a rate grid around the planet's motion (Ashton and Gladman style), masking the planet's scattered light with a radial model.
Many archival planet fields were taken for other programmes (rings, outer moons' astrometry, occultation support); SSOIS finds every frame within a few degrees of the planet.
Cross-domain import (radar): treat the rate grid as a matched-filter bank and set the threshold from the empirical false-alarm rate in off-planet control stacks.
pitfalls: The JPL page's own 'last updated' line is stale; the per-satellite MPEC references are the live information.
Discovery teams hold many unannounced candidates; a new announcement can appear at any time, so re-check MPECs before claiming.
