Stacks at the planet's rate also build up slow background TNOs and Hildas/Trojans near the field; the bound-orbit test (2) and SkyBoT check (3) are what separate them.
Scattered light and ghosts near the planet produce coherent stack artefacts; require the detection in independent stacks of different frame subsets.

targets.name: New lunar pit (steep-walled collapse feature) in public LROC NAC images, absent from the LROC Pits Atlas
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (LROC NAC EDR/CDR frames are 100-500 MB each; searches restricted to mare, impact-melt and highland target areas)
targets.statement: Lunar pits are steep-walled collapse pits, some opening into voids, first recognised in SELENE and LROC images (Haruyama et al. 2009; Robinson et al. 2012; Wagner and Robinson 2014). The LROC team (R. V. Wagner, M. S. Robinson and the LROC Science Operations Center, ASU) maintains the LROC Pits Atlas, whose list page on 2026-10-30 has 278 entries, with host feature, coordinates, funnel and inner diameters, azimuth and depth; every entry gives a depth, but 40 depths are only lower bounds (" > ") and 12 entries have no inner diameter. Most are small pits in impact-melt deposits; the mare pits (Mare Tranquillitatis, Marius Hills, Mare Ingenii and others) are candidate cave entrances for exploration. LRO has imaged most of the Moon at 0.5-1.5 m/pixel under several illumination angles, and all NAC images are public through the PDS. Open task: a pit that the atlas does not list, with its depth measured from shadows in two images.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (NAC product IDs, map-projected cutouts, illumination geometry from the PDS labels, shadow measurements and code) where: (1) the feature is seen in >= 2 NAC images whose solar incidence angles differ by >= 10 deg; (2) its inner (steep-walled) opening has a maximum diameter >= 5 m and spans >= 5 pixels in each of those images; (3) in each image the shadow edge falls on the pit floor (not on the far wall), and the depth estimates from the shadow length (depth = shadow length x tan(90 deg - incidence), corrected for local slope from the SLDEM2015 or a NAC DTM where available) agree within 30%, with depth / inner diameter >= 0.3, deeper than fresh simple impact craters of that size (about 0.2); (4) the feature has no raised rim or ejecta blanket (described with a radial brightness profile in each image); (5) no entry on https://lroc.im-ldi.com/atlases/pits/list (re-fetched immediately before claiming) lies within 200 m, and no published pit or cave-candidate list found by search (including Le Corre et al. 2025, Icarus 441, 116675) gives it.

partial_wins.statement: A detector that, on NAC images of >= 30 atlas pits not used to tune it, recovers >= 80% of them with <= 1 false candidate per 10 km^2 of searched area, with all candidates saved.
A candidate meeting (2), (4) and (5) in a single NAC image, with a single-image depth estimate giving depth / diameter >= 0.3.

A depth for an atlas pit whose depth is listed only as a lower bound (" > "), measured as in (3) from two NAC images in which the shadow edge falls on the pit floor, larger than the listed bound, with the result saved.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the NAC products from the PDS, re-projects the cutouts, re-measures the shadow lengths and incidence angles from the labels, recomputes depth and diameter, and checks the live atlas list for entries within 200 m. Under an hour per candidate.
angles: Conventional: search mare and impact-melt regions with a small CNN trained on atlas pits, then confirm with shadow geometry.
Use the incidence-angle diversity: a pit's shadow fraction grows much faster with incidence than a bowl crater's, which is a cheap physical discriminator.
Cross-domain import (karst and sinkhole mapping on Earth): sinkhole detectors trained on lidar and imagery use closed-depression and wall-steepness features that carry over.
pitfalls: Small fresh craters, boulder shadows and image noise can mimic pits at high incidence; the two-image depth agreement in (3) is the main safeguard.
Several atlas entries share host features and have close coordinates; check distance to every entry, not only to entries with the same host name.

Published pits are not all in the atlas: Le Corre et al. (2025, Icarus 441, 116675) report the South Marius Hills Pit and the Bel'kovich A Pit, found with a Mask R-CNN on NAC images, and other machine-learning pit searches have published candidate lists; search for them before claiming.
At high incidence the shadow of a deep pit often ends on the far wall, which gives only a lower bound on depth; use the lower-incidence image or a DTM for the floor.

targets.name: New satellite of a TNO, Centaur, Jupiter Trojan or asteroid resolved in public archival HST, JWST or adaptive-optics images, absent from Johnston's Archive
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (HST WFC3/ACS cutouts are MB each; PSF fitting of a few thousand visits overnight)
targets.statement: W. R. Johnston's Asteroids with Satellites database (last updated 24 October 2026) lists 654 small bodies with companions: 113 NEAs, 36 Mars-crossers, 340 main-belt asteroids, 8 Jupiter Trojans and 157 TNOs; 122 of the TNO systems were found by space-based imaging, mostly HST. Archival discoveries continue: e.g. the satellite of (501214) 2013 TC146, found by B. Proudfoot and W. Grundy in HST images taken on 2017 Dec 13, was announced on 2026 Sep 23 (per its Johnston page), and Johnston's date-ordered list shows new systems reported every few days through September and October 2026. HST snapshot programmes have imaged hundreds of TNOs and Centaurs (Noll, Grundy, Benecchi, Parker and others), and MAST, the JWST archive and the Keck Observatory Archive make them public. Close, faint companions near the PSF core are the ones most often missed. Open task: a companion of a small body, resolved in public images, that Johnston's database does not list.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (MAST/KOA dataset IDs, cutouts, PSF models, fitting code, astrometry and photometry) where: (1) in >= 2 separate visits (or >= 2 HST orbits >= 3 hours apart) a two-source PSF model beats a single-source model by delta chi^2 >= 25 in each visit, with empirical or TinyTim-type PSFs validated on stars in the same images; (2) the secondary moves with the primary: between visits its offset from the primary changes by less than 10% of the primary's own sky motion over the same interval, and at each epoch no Gaia DR3 source and no source in a stack of other-epoch images lies at the secondary's sky position; (3) the flux ratio agrees between visits within 0.5 mag and the separation is < 0.3 Hill radii of the primary at its distance; (4) the primary has no companion in https://www.johnstonsarchive.net/astro/asteroidmoons.html or its date-ordered list (re-fetched immediately before claiming), and no CBET, paper or preprint reports one.

partial_wins.statement: The pipeline recovers >= 90% of the Johnston-listed binaries whose separation in the processed archival images is > 2 pixels, and on >= 50 isolated stars in the same images returns no detection meeting (1), all results saved.
A companion meeting (1), (3) and (4) in a single visit, with a background-source check as in (2) at that epoch.

A first mutual orbit for a listed binary that Johnston's database gives without orbit elements and for which no paper, preprint or CBET found by a fresh search gives an orbit, fitted to >= 5 epochs of relative astrometry with reduced chi^2 <= 2 (the mirror ambiguity stated, not necessarily resolved).

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads the datasets from MAST/KOA, refits single- and two-source PSF models with an independent PSF, recomputes delta chi^2, checks Gaia DR3 and other-epoch images at the secondary's position, and re-reads Johnston's lists. About an hour.
angles: Conventional: forward-model each visit with two PSFs on a grid of separations and flux ratios, as in the HST binary surveys of Noll and Grundy.
Search the shortest separations first: drizzled products blur close pairs, so fit the individual flt/flc frames.
Cross-domain import (exoplanet direct imaging): reference-differential imaging with the other TNOs of the same programme as PSF references.
pitfalls: Cosmic rays and hot pixels in single frames make false companions; require consistency across all frames of a visit.
Elongated primaries (contact binaries) can be fitted by two close PSFs; demand a separation > 1.5 pixels or a resolved gap.
Several discovery teams are mining the same HST archive now; Johnston's date-ordered list shows new systems every week.

targets.name: Physical model of a tumbling (non-principal-axis) asteroid from public lightcurves, beyond the tumbler models in DAMIT
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (ALCDEF lightcurves are KB-MB per object; NPA inversion over a period grid takes hours per object)
targets.statement: Most asteroids spin about their shortest axis; tumblers are in non-principal-axis (NPA) rotation, usually slow rotators whose damping time exceeds their age (Pravec et al. 2005, 2014). The Asteroid Lightcurve Database flags many objects as tumbling or possibly tumbling. Full physical NPA models (shape, the two periods, angular-momentum direction and inertia ratios) are rare. DAMIT (Durech, Sidorin and Kaasalainen 2010; run by J. Durech and V. Sidorin) holds 27,963 models of 18,033 asteroids, but on 2026-10-30 its tumbler section has 8 models of only 5 objects: 2008 TC3, (99942) Apophis, 2012 TC4, (319) Leona and (469219) Kamo'oalewa. Some other tumblers have been modelled from radar or lightcurves, e.g. (4179) Toutatis and (5247) Krylov (Lee et al. 2020). The ALCDEF database (B. D. Warner and collaborators) holds 387,503 lightcurve blocks for 24,819 objects (updated 2026-10-28), and survey photometry adds sparse points. Open task: a physical NPA model for a tumbler that DAMIT and the literature do not have.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (ALCDEF and other photometry with times and errors, Horizons geometry, model code, fitted parameters and residuals) where: (1) a 2D Fourier series in two frequencies (Pravec et al. 2005) of order >= 2 fits the dense lightcurves with chi^2 lower by >= 25 than the best single-period Fourier series with at least as many free parameters (period scanned over the whole plausible range), and the two frequencies are not in a ratio of small integers (up to 1:6) within their errors; (2) a physical NPA model (convex or ellipsoid shape, precession and rotation periods, angular-momentum direction, inertia ratios, epoch angles) reproduces data from >= 2 apparitions or >= 2 viewing geometries >= 20 deg apart with RMS residual <= 1.2 x the photometric noise; (3) the model is stable: >= 80% of 50 fits started from random initial angles converge to the same periods within 1% and pole within 20 deg; (4) the object is not in https://damit.cuni.cz/projects/damit/tumblers and no paper gives a physical NPA model for it (re-checked immediately before claiming).

partial_wins.statement: The pipeline reproduces DAMIT's precession and rotation periods (P_phi, P_psi) of (99942) Apophis or 2012 TC4 within 1% with a physical NPA model fitted to public photometry only, with residuals saved.
A new tumbling detection meeting test (1) for an asteroid with an LCDB period but no tumbling flag, without a physical model.
A physical NPA model meeting (2) and (4) with one apparition only and the stability test (3) passed.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic re-downloads the ALCDEF blocks by object, recomputes geometry from Horizons, refits single- and two-frequency Fourier series, reruns the NPA fit from random starts with independent code, and checks the DAMIT tumbler list. A few hours.
angles: Conventional: start from LCDB objects with tumbling flags and long, dense ALCDEF coverage; 2D Fourier analysis first, physical inversion second.
Add TESS full-frame-image photometry, whose month-long continuous coverage is ideal for slow tumblers.
Cross-domain import (spacecraft attitude determination): tumbling-satellite lightcurve inversion uses the same torque-free Euler equations and has mature estimators (unscented filters).
pitfalls: Slow rotators need long nightly runs; sparse survey data alone rarely constrain an NPA model.
Combining lightcurves from different observers needs careful zero-point handling; ALCDEF blocks often have arbitrary offsets.
A binary asteroid with an unsynchronised secondary also shows two periods; check for mutual-event dips before calling it a tumbler.

targets.name: Significant Yarkovsky drift for a near-Earth asteroid that neither the JPL SBDB nor ESA NEOCC orbit solves for
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (MPC astrometry per object is KB-MB; a full N-body least-squares fit with ephemerides DE440 and SB441-N16 takes minutes)
targets.statement: The Yarkovsky effect makes small asteroids drift in semimajor axis, and it shows up as a transverse acceleration A2 in orbit fits to long astrometric arcs (Chesley et al. 2003; Farnocchia et al. 2013; Greenberg et al. 2020). On 2026-10-30 the JPL Small-Body Database solves for A2 in 671 of 43,028 near-Earth objects (SBDB query API, field A2). ESA's NEO Coordination Centre publishes its own orbit files, which give the Yarkovsky parameter and its signal-to-noise ratio when it is fitted (e.g. (1566) Icarus: SNR 14.7), and none otherwise (e.g. (433) Eros: no non-gravitational parameters). New astrometry, archival precoveries, Gaia DR3 astrometry and radar keep making new detections possible. The NEODyS service (SpaceDys) also publishes Yarkovsky lists, but it serves a bot check to automated clients, so agents cannot check it themselves. Open task: a statistically significant, physically plausible A2 for an NEA that neither JPL nor ESA fits.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (MPC astrometry as fetched from the MPC get-obs API with the fetch date, any added precovery astrometry with images, weighting and outlier-rejection scheme, fit code, covariance) where: (1) the fit includes the Sun, planets, Moon and Pluto from DE440, the 16 SB441-N16 perturbers, general relativity, star-catalogue debiasing (Eggl et al. 2020) and Veres et al. 2017 weights, with outlier rejection at 3 sigma; (2) A2 / sigma(A2) >= 3 and the A2 fit lowers chi^2 by >= 9 relative to the gravity-only fit with the same observations; (3) A2 is physically plausible: the implied |da/dt| is no more than 3 times the maximum expected for the object's size (diameter from H with any albedo 0.05-0.5, scaled as in Farnocchia et al. 2013); (4) the object has no A2 in the SBDB (https://ssd-api.jpl.nasa.gov/sbdb.api?sstr= < designation > &full-prec=true) and no non-gravitational parameters in its ESA NEOCC orbit file, both fetched immediately before claiming, and no paper reports a Yarkovsky detection for it.

partial_wins.statement: The pipeline reproduces the SBDB A2 value within 1 sigma for >= 20 SBDB objects with A2 / sigma >= 5, with all fits saved.
An object meeting (1), (3) and (4) with 2 <= A2 / sigma < 3: a candidate needing more astrometry.
A significant A2 (meeting (1)-(3)) obtained only after adding >= 1 new precovery night measured from public archival images, for an object where the MPC data alone give A2 / sigma < 3.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic re-fetches the astrometry from the MPC API, refits with an independent orbit code (e.g. a REBOUND/ASSIST-based or OrbFit-type fitter) under the same weighting, compares A2 and sigma, and re-fetches the SBDB and NEOCC records. Under an hour per object.
angles: Conventional: rank NEAs by expected Yarkovsky SNR (small H, long arc, many radar or Gaia points) and fit those first.
Archival precoveries from DECam, SDSS or photographic plates (DASCH) lengthen arcs most cheaply.
Cross-domain import (GNSS orbit determination): empirical-acceleration estimation with process noise checks whether a constant A2 is really needed.
pitfalls: Old astrometry with uncorrected star-catalogue biases fakes drifts; debiasing and weighting matter more than anything else.
JPL and ESA sometimes find an A2 but reject it as implausible; check (3) honestly.
NEODyS may already list the object; note this as an open risk and leave the check to a human with a browser rather than getting round its bot check.

targets.name: A new YORP detection: significant change in an asteroid's rotation rate measured from decades of public lightcurves
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (lightcurves KB-MB per object; convex inversion with a linear frequency change over a period grid takes hours)
targets.statement: The YORP effect changes asteroid spin rates through thermal emission, and only lightcurves spanning decades show it. Durech et al. (A&A 2022, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202141844) measured spin-up for (10115) 1992 SK, confirmed (1685) Toro and refined (1620) Geographos (ten detections); Durech et al. (A&A 2024, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202348350) added (2100) Ra-Shalom and (138852) 2000 WN10, bringing the total to twelve, all spinning up, and showed that a reported detection for (85989) 1999 JD6 is not statistically required. Earlier detections include (54509) YORP, (1862) Apollo, (3103) Eger, (25143) Itokawa, (161989) Cacus, (68346) 2001 KZ66 and (101955) Bennu (Lowry, Taylor, Kaasalainen, Durech, Vokrouhlicky, Pravec, Nolan and others). Feng et al. (ApJ 2025, doi:10.3847/1538-4357/addd23) reported a spin-down for (433) Eros of (-5.0 +/- 4.6) x 10^-10 rad/day^2, not significant, and Rodriguez Rodriguez et al. (PSJ 2026, doi:10.3847/PSJ/ae2d11) a possible acceleration of about 2.05 x 10^-8 rad/day^2 for (66146) 1998 TU3. Whether any asteroid is measurably spinning down remains open: theory predicts both signs. Public photometry (ALCDEF, published lightcurves, survey data) now spans 30-70 years for many NEAs and Mars-crossers. Open task: a statistically significant rotation-rate change for an asteroid with no published YORP detection or YORP value.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (all photometry with times and sources, Horizons geometry, inversion code, best models with and without YORP, bootstrap output) where: (1) the data cover >= 3 apparitions spanning >= 10 years, including >= 2 dense lightcurves; (2) a convex-inversion model with a linearly changing rotation rate, dw/dt = nu, beats the best constant-rate model by delta chi^2 >= 25 with the same shape resolution; (3) nu / sigma(nu) >= 3, with sigma(nu) from >= 200 bootstrap resamplings of whole lightcurves; (4) nu stays significant at >= 3 sigma when any single apparition is left out; (5) |nu| <= 1e-5 rad/day^2 (the largest measured value, for (54509) YORP, is about 3.5e-6 rad/day^2); (6) no paper, preprint or DAMIT model reports a YORP value for the object (re-checked immediately before claiming). A significant negative nu (spin-down) meets the same criterion.

partial_wins.statement: The pipeline reproduces a published YORP value (e.g. (1862) Apollo or (1620) Geographos) within 1 sigma from public photometry only, with all inputs saved.
An object meeting (1), (5) and (6) with 2 <= nu / sigma(nu) < 3 and test (4) passed at 2 sigma: a candidate that names the apparitions it needs next.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic re-collects the photometry from the cited sources, re-runs inversion with and without nu from independent starting poles, re-runs the bootstrap and the leave-one-apparition-out test, and searches the literature. A few hours.
angles: Conventional: pick NEAs with dense lightcurves from the 1970s-1990s (published in Icarus, A&A and Minor Planet Bulletin) and recent ALCDEF data.
Gaia DR3 sparse photometry and TESS lightcurves add precise recent epochs that pin the rotation phase.
Cross-domain import (pulsar timing): the YORP fit is a phase-coherent timing solution with a frequency derivative; pulsar-timing tools for phase connection across gaps apply directly.
pitfalls: Rotation-phase counting across long gaps is ambiguous; wrong cycle counts imitate a frequency change. Show the cycle-count solution is unique.
Old photographic or photoelectric timings may be in local or uncorrected time; check light-time correction and time standards.
Only twelve detections are known and the community checks candidates closely; claim nothing without (4).

targets.name: Moonstone lunar benchmark: beat MG-MAE on crater segmentation, mare segmentation or geologic-unit classification on the fixed split
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (the repository's downstream scripts read patch pixels from pretraining/mmap, about 123 GB, and split metadata from benchmark/lunar_patches_v4.h5, about 75 GB: about 200 GB of downloads; one GPU recommended)
targets.statement: Moonstone (Ayush Prasad and Swarnalee Mazumder; ECCV 2026, arXiv:2607.03644) is a 28-channel, 128 pixel/degree global lunar data cube (LRO WAC, LOLA, Diviner, Mini-RF, Chandrayaan-1 M3, GRAIL, Lunar Prospector GRS, Clementine) with a benchmark of 16,200 patches and a fixed 70/15/15 split (11,340 / 2,430 / 2,430), released on Hugging Face (ayushprd/Moonstone, CC BY 4.0) with code (MIT). Labels: 49-class geology and 5-class age from the USGS Unified Geologic Map, mare/highland segmentation, and crater segmentation from the Robbins global crater catalogue (craters > 10 km). Table 3 of the paper gives the best test scores, all from the authors' modality-grouped masked autoencoder fine-tuned (MG-MAE): geology accuracy 56.3%, age accuracy 73.2%, crater mIoU 0.768, mare mIoU 0.936; on the geographic split of Table 6 (train within +/-60 deg latitude, test at 70-80 deg; the code's --geo-split option) geology accuracy is 51.2%. The paper says the Hugging Face dataset hosts the pretrained MG-MAE checkpoint, but on 2026-10-30 no checkpoint file was in the dataset and the GitHub repository had no releases. Two later papers (LunarFM, arXiv:2607.22408; SomBench, arXiv:2609.13277) cite it but report no results on its tasks (full texts checked 2026-10-30). Open task: beat MG-MAE on one of these tasks.
targets.success_criterion: A saved bundle (code, config, seeds, weights or exact recipe, per-patch test predictions) where: (1) the model is trained only on the train and val patches of benchmark/lunar_patches_v4.h5 (the fixed split), using only the input channels of the benchmark patches and no label raster (geologic_units.tif, mare_mask.tif, crater_mask.tif or the Robbins catalogue) as input; any self-supervised pre-training may use the pretraining cube; (2) the metric is computed with the Moonstone repository's evaluation code for the task; (3) the mean over 3 seeds beats the Table 3 value for that task by the stated margin: geology accuracy >= 57.3%, age accuracy >= 74.2%, crater mIoU >= 0.778, or mare mIoU >= 0.943, or, on the geographic split, geology accuracy >= 52.2%; (4) no later paper reports a higher value on the same split (checked immediately before claiming).

partial_wins.statement: A reproduction of the MG-MAE fine-tuned crater mIoU within 0.02 of 0.768 with the released code (pre-training MG-MAE yourself, since no weights are released), all logs saved.

A model without any pre-training (trained from scratch on the train split only), scored as in (2) as a mean over 3 seeds, that beats the paper's vanilla-MAE baseline on one task: crater mIoU > 0.668, geology accuracy > 44.8% or age accuracy > 63.5%.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic downloads benchmark/lunar_patches_v4.h5 and the pretraining/mmap arrays the repository's downstream scripts read, runs the saved model on the test patches with the Moonstone evaluation code, recomputes the metric for each seed, and checks the inputs used. A few hours with a GPU.
angles: Conventional: a U-Net on elevation and slope alone is a strong crater baseline, since craters > 10 km are topographic features.
Use the geographic split as the honest test: random patch splits let neighbouring patches share craters and units across train and test.
Cross-domain import (Earth geology mapping): multi-scale context models used to map geologic units from DEMs and multispectral data.
pitfalls: Composition and cross-modal tasks use channels that are also inputs (lpgrs_feo, lpgrs_tio2, Diviner); they are left out of this target for that reason.
Large craters cross patch boundaries; check that predictions are not scored on padded or NaN-filled regions differently from the paper.

The repository's task scripts (downstream_dataset.py) read patch pixels from the z-scored pretraining/mmap arrays (about 123 GB) and use lunar_patches_v4.h5 only for the split and patch locations, so 'benchmark/*' alone (about 75 GB) does not run them. If you feed the h5 pixels instead, show that they match the mmap inputs patch for patch.

targets.name: Orientable sequences: a binary orientable cycle of order 18-20 longer than the best claimed period, or a k-ary period beating the Mitchell-Wild tables
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (an ILP on the order-n de Bruijn graph with HiGHS or SCIP as in Mitchell 2026, or cycle joining plus local search; a check takes linear time)
targets.statement: An orientable sequence OS_k(n) is a periodic sequence over k symbols in which each length-n window occurs at most once per period in either direction. No window equals the reversal of another window, and no window is a palindrome. Dai, Martin, Robshaw and Wild introduced them in 1993 for position sensing. Chris J. Mitchell, 'Searching for binary orientable sequences' (arXiv:2610.33601 v1, 24 Oct 2026, ILP searches with HiGHS and SCIP), settled the maximum binary period for every n <= 16 (31776 at n = 16; aperiodic length 31810). He reports no maximum for n >= 17. A write-up on Drew Stone's site (drewstone.github.io/research/orientable-sequences, assessed 2026-10-07, merged 2026-10-12; an LLM-run ILP search with no outside review, whose sequence and certificate repository was not public on 2026-10-30) gives the same maxima as Mitchell for n = 9..16. It claims the exact maximum 63578 for n = 17, an OS_2(18) of period 128794 with an uncertified bound of 128796, and an OS_2(19) of period 257650 with an uncertified bound of 257652. The L*_n column of Joe Sawada's debruijnsequence.org orientable page still lists the Gabrić-Sawada periods 63135, 128639, 257272 and 519160 for n = 17..20. The DMRW upper bounds there are U_n = 64662, 129911, 260386 and 521964. The best acyclic lengths on the same page ('Extended from OS') are 63219, 128680, 257340 and 519212, against bounds 65296, 130833, 261650 and 523795. The claimed periods give longer acyclic sequences of length p + n - 1: 63594 (n = 17), 128811 (n = 18) and 257668 (n = 19). For k = 3..8, Mitchell and Wild's Table 7 ('New orientable sequences', arXiv:2507.02526, Acta Inform. 63 (2026) 14) gives the largest known periods with upper bounds for n = 2..8; the bound is met for n <= 3 and for n = 4 with k odd. Mitchell and Wild, arXiv:2603.18646 v2 (14 Aug 2026), Table 3 raised many cells. Examples: k = 3 gives 303 (n = 6), 948 (n = 7) and 3006 (n = 8); k = 4 gives 396, 1744, 7480 and 31000 for n = 5..8.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a binary periodic orientable sequence of order n, 18 <= n <= 20, given as one period of length p, verified exhaustively. The p cyclic windows must be pairwise distinct, and no window may equal the reversal of any window, itself included. The period p must be STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best period claimed for that n at verification time on the debruijnsequence.org orientable page (L*_n column), in the latest version of arXiv:2610.33601, on drewstone.github.io/research/orientable-sequences, and in any newer paper or write-up by Mitchell, Wild, Gabrić, Sawada, Stone or others found by a fresh search. On 2026-10-30 these values were 128794 (n = 18), 257650 (n = 19) and 519160 (n = 20). The period must also be at most the DMRW bound U_n (129911, 260386, 521964); a larger value means a checker bug. n = 17 does not count, because its claimed maximum 63578 meets its claimed upper bound. At n = 18 and 19 the claimed but uncertified upper bounds (128796, 257652) leave at most 2 of headroom; n = 20 has the most room.

partial_wins.statement: A binary aperiodic (acyclic) orientable sequence of order n, 17 <= n <= 20, verified exhaustively (all length-n windows distinct, no window equal to the reversal of any window). It must be strictly longer than the best acyclic length on the debruijnsequence.org orientable page, the length p + n - 1 implied by the best claimed period (including drewstone.github.io/research/orientable-sequences), and any newer source (context 2026-10-30: 63594, 128811, 257668, 519212 for n = 17..20). It must also be at most the bound Û_n (65296, 130833, 261650, 523795).

A k-ary orientable sequence for a cell with 3 <= k <= 8 and 4 <= n <= 8 whose largest known period is still below the Table 7 upper bound of arXiv:2507.02526 (this excludes n = 4 with k odd, where the bound is met). Its period must be strictly greater than the maximum for that cell over Table 7 of arXiv:2507.02526, Table 3 of arXiv:2603.18646 (latest version) and any newer source, and at most the Table 7 upper bound.

The exact maximum binary period for n = 18 or n = 19: an explicit OS_2(n) of period at least the best claimed one (128794 or 257650), together with an ILP upper bound equal to its period, obtained by two different solvers (for example HiGHS and SCIP) on a model the claimant publishes, which a skeptic re-runs. This is labelled computational.

targets.verification_method: Read the period as a string s of length p. Form the p cyclic windows w_i = s[i..i+n-1] (indices mod p), put them in a set W and check |W| = p. Then check that reverse(w) is not in W for every w in W; this also excludes palindromes. Compare p with the live values and with U_n. Calibrate the checker by accepting one of Mitchell's published maximum-period examples (n <= 16) and rejecting a de Bruijn sequence. For k-ary cells, use the same check over k symbols.
angles: Scale Mitchell's ILP: maximise the number of de Bruijn-graph edges in a balanced, connected edge set with at most one edge from each reversal pair. He reports that the optimum was always connected up to n = 16. At n = 18 the model has 2^18 edge variables; symmetry breaking, the parity cuts described on the drewstone.github.io write-up and warm starts from the Gabrić-Sawada cycle may help.
Local improvement: start from the Gabrić-Sawada cycle-joining sequence and use cycle-swap moves (remove a cycle of windows, insert a longer one) while keeping the orientable constraint.
pitfalls: Periodic and aperiodic records are separate tables. For n >= 17, Mitchell's derived aperiodic values p + n - 1 (63151 and so on) are below the debruijnsequence.org 'Extended from OS' values, but the drewstone.github.io periods give longer ones (63594, 128811, 257668).
The bracketed values in Table 3 of arXiv:2603.18646 compare with an older table, not with Table 7 of arXiv:2507.02526. Take the maximum over both tables.
Negative orientable sequences (NOS) are a different object; values such as 318 for NOS_3(6) are not OS records.

The drewstone.github.io claims (63578, 128794, 257650) have no outside review, and their sequences were not public on 2026-10-30. They still set the bar: a sequence that beats only the debruijnsequence.org values is not a win.
The area moved five times in 2026 (Mitchell, Wild, Stone). Re-check arXiv listings for Mitchell and Sawada, and the drewstone.github.io research page, before claiming.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Beckett-Gray codes: does a 9-bit Beckett-Gray code exist? (open for every n >= 9)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster for exhaustive search; laptop-days for heuristic or SAT attempts (a code checks in microseconds)
targets.statement: A Beckett-Gray code is a cyclic n-bit Gray code (a Hamilton cycle of the n-cube starting at 0^n) in which every 1->0 transition clears the 1-bit that has been set longest. The positions of the 1s behave as a first-in first-out queue; 0->1 transitions are unconstrained. The name comes from Samuel Beckett's play Quad (Knuth, TAOCP 4A, Sec. 7.2.1.1). Cooke, North, Dewar and Stevens (arXiv:1608.06001, 2016; published as J. Combin. Math. Combin. Comput. 126 (2025) 195-200, doi:10.61091/jcmcc126-12) found codes by computer for n = 2, 5, 6, 7 and 8, and showed that none exist for n = 3 and 4. They enumerated all codes for n <= 6: 8 non-isomorphic cyclic codes for n = 5 and 94,841 for n = 6. They estimated the n = 7 search tree at about 2^102 nodes and called an exhaustive n = 7 search infeasible. Their 8-bit code was found by simulated annealing plus backtracking. Sawada and Wong (Electron. Notes Discrete Math. 29, 2007) gave a faster algorithm and almost 10,000 cyclic 7-bit codes. Torsten Mütze's survey 'Combinatorial Gray codes - an updated survey' (arXiv:2202.01280 v4, 30 Jul 2024) lists existence for n >= 9 as open Problem P9. A check on 2026-10-30 of the papers citing Cooke et al. and the survey found no resolution.
targets.success_criterion: Success means one of two things. (a) An explicit Beckett-Gray code for some n >= 9: a cyclic sequence of all 2^n distinct n-bit words, starting at 0^n, with consecutive words (including last to first) at Hamming distance 1, in which every 1->0 transition clears the oldest set bit under the FIFO rule simulated from the all-zero start. It must pass two independently written checkers. (b) A rerunnable nonexistence proof for n = 9: an UNSAT certificate (DRAT/LRAT, checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr) of a published SAT encoding whose correctness is argued in a short note.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit 9-bit Beckett-Gray path: all 512 words visited once from 0^9 with single-bit steps and the FIFO clearing rule at every 1->0 step, without the closing step back to 0^9. It counts only if none is published at claim time, and it is verified by the same checker as the full win.

targets.verification_method: Simulate a queue. Start at 0^9 with an empty queue. At each step exactly one bit changes; if it is set (0->1), push its index; if it is cleared (1->0), require that it equals the queue head and pop it. Check that all 2^9 words are distinct and that the last step returns to 0^9 with an empty queue. Calibrate the checker on the published 8-bit code (Knuth or Cooke et al.) and on codes found for n = 5 and 6.
angles: The queue structure makes the state the current word plus the queue order; dynamic programming over (word, queue) with transposition tables, plus symmetry breaking on the first transitions, extends Sawada-Wong-style backtracking.
Try SAT/CP encodings with an explicit queue position per bit, or search for codes invariant under a coordinate rotation of order 3 or 9.
pitfalls: The FIFO rule applies only to 1->0 transitions; 0->1 steps are free. Codes must be cyclic.
Conventions vary on counting symmetric copies (reversal, renaming); state the convention for counts.
Search logs and timeouts are not nonexistence proofs.

targets.name: Felsner-Trotter order-preserving Gray paths: one for n = 11 (open for all n >= 11), or the exact count for n = 8 (OEIS A259839)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days to needs cluster (backtracking or SAT; a path of 2048 subsets checks in milliseconds)
targets.statement: An order-preserving Gray path lists all 2^n subsets of [n] as x_1 = empty set, ..., x_N with consecutive sets differing in one element, such that whenever x_i is obtained from x_j by removing one element (a 1->0 flip), i <= j + 1. Felsner and Trotter posed the problem (Discrete Math. 144, 1995) and built such paths of length 2^(n-1)(1 + o(1)); see also Jackson-Stevens-Hurlbert, Research problems on Gray codes and universal cycles, Problem 483. OEIS A259839 (Torsten Mütze, 2015; revision 27, 30 May 2026) counts these paths up to renaming coordinates: 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 10, 123, 1492723 for n = 0..7. It states that a(n) >= 1 is known for n = 8, 9, 10 (found by Trotter and Mütze independently) and that it is unknown whether a(n) >= 1 for n >= 11. Biró and Howard (Order 26, 2009) built, for all n >= 11, an order-preserving path through every subset of size at most 3. Mütze's survey (arXiv:2202.01280 v4, Problem P6) calls existence for n >= 11 a challenging open problem. Independent backtracking counters reproduced 10 and 123 for n = 5 and 6 (labelled counts 1200 and 88560 divided by n!).
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit order-preserving Gray path for some n >= 11: a list of all 2^n subsets of [n], each exactly once, starting from the empty set, consecutive sets at symmetric-difference size 1, and for every pair A ⊂ B with |B| = |A| + 1 the position of A at most the position of B plus 1. It must be verified by two independent checkers, and it must also satisfy the stronger all-subset-pairs reading (A ⊂ B of any sizes) used in the OEIS comment. Existence is the criterion: none is known at any n >= 11 (context 2026-10-30, OEIS A259839).

partial_wins.statement: The exact value a(8) of OEIS A259839 (order-preserving paths in the 8-cube up to coordinate renaming), computed by two independently written programs that agree, each first reproducing a(5) = 10, a(6) = 123 and a(7) = 1492723. It counts only if a(8) is still absent from the OEIS entry at claim time; the result is labelled computational.

targets.verification_method: Record the position pos[S] of each subset. Check that all 2^n subsets appear, that pos[empty] = 0, and that consecutive sets differ in exactly one element. For every S and every element e of S, check that pos[S minus e] <= pos[S] + 1. Run the all-pairs version (for all A ⊂ B) as a second check; for n = 11 it takes 3^11 pair checks. Calibrate by enumerating n = 5, 6 and reproducing 10 and 123 (labelled counts divided by n!).
angles: The rule forces strong structure: after visiting a set, at most one unvisited lower cover may remain and it must come next. Paths are level-accurate (Felsner-Trotter), which allows level-by-level dynamic programming with pruning.
Extend the n = 10 solution: search for paths whose restriction to sets not containing element 11 resembles a known n = 10 path, then repair with SAT.
pitfalls: The rule says that a set may not come more than one step after any set obtained from it by adding an element: subsets are visited before their supersets, or immediately after them. A monotone or level-accurate path (Savage-Winkler) is not enough.
Counts in A259839 are up to coordinate renaming: divide labelled counts by n!.

targets.name: n-antipodal Gray codes: is there a 10-bit Gray code in which every word's complement is exactly 10 steps away? (Killian-Savage, open for even n >= 10)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (SAT/CP on 1024 positions with heavy symmetry; a code checks instantly)
targets.statement: In a t-antipodal n-bit Gray code (a cyclic listing of all 2^n words with single-bit steps), the complement of every word appears exactly t steps before or after it. Killian and Savage ('Antipodal Gray codes', Discrete Math. 2004) studied t = n, attributing the question to Snevily. They showed that no n-antipodal code exists for odd n >= 5 or for n = 6, and gave a construction when n is a power of 2. They asked whether n-antipodal n-bit codes exist for even n >= 10. Chang, Eu and Yeh (2007) characterised t-antipodal codes for odd n (t = 2^(n-1) - 1 only) and gave codes for other values of t when n is even. Knuth (TAOCP 4A, Ex. 7.2.1.1-49) gives t = 2^(n-1). Mütze's survey (arXiv:2202.01280 v4, 30 Jul 2024, Problem P7) lists even n >= 10 as open. The smallest open case is n = 10. A Semantic Scholar check of papers citing the survey (2026-10-30) found no resolution.
targets.success_criterion: Success means settling n = 10, in one of two ways. (a) An explicit cyclic 10-bit Gray code: all 1024 words, consecutive words (cyclically) differing in one bit, and for every position i the complement of word i at position i + 10 or i - 10 (mod 1024). It must pass two independent checkers. (b) A rerunnable nonexistence proof: an UNSAT certificate (DRAT/LRAT, checked by a verified checker) of a published encoding whose correctness is argued in a short note, or a written proof.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit n-antipodal n-bit Gray code for n = 12 or n = 14 (even, not a power of 2), verified the same way. It counts only if that case is unsettled in the survey and later literature at claim time.

targets.verification_method: Read the 1024 words into a position table. Check that it is a permutation of {0..1023}, that consecutive XORs (including last to first) are powers of 2, and that for each i, word[(i+10) mod 1024] or word[(i-10) mod 1024] equals word[i] XOR 1023. Calibrate on Killian-Savage's 8-antipodal 8-bit construction, and check that a SAT search finds nothing for n = 6.
angles: If the complement of word i sits at position i + n, the n transitions between them flip every coordinate exactly once. The transition sequence is therefore built from length-n windows that are permutations of [n]. Encode the transition sequence in SAT/CP with this window structure, and break symmetry by fixing the first n transitions as 0, 1, ..., n-1.

Look for codes with a cyclic symmetry: the transition sequence invariant under a shift combined with a fixed coordinate permutation (for example a shift by 2n with a rotation of the coordinates). Generalise the structure of the Killian-Savage power-of-2 construction.
pitfalls: The distance must be exactly n in one direction, measured cyclically along the code, not in Hamming distance.
For odd n the answer is known (impossible for t = n when n >= 5); only even n that are not powers of 2 are open.

targets.name: Gray codes with long bit runs: an 8-bit Gray code whose bit runs all have length at least 6, or a proof that r(8) = 5
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (SAT/CP or clever backtracking; naive DFS does not even reproduce r(7) = 5 in 30 s)
targets.statement: For a cyclic n-bit Gray code, the run length of a coordinate is the number of steps between two consecutive flips of that coordinate. Let r(n) be the largest r such that some n-bit Gray code has all run lengths at least r. Knuth (TAOCP 4A, Sec. 7.2.1.1) gives r(n) = 1, 2, 2, 2, 4, 4, 5 for n = 1..7, and his Fig. 34 shows an 8-bit code with all runs at least 5. The value r(8) is unknown. Goddyn and Gvozdjak (Electron. J. Combin. 10, 2003) proved r(n) >= ceil(n - 2.001 log2 n), building on Evdokimov and on Goddyn-Lawrence-Nemeth; that bound gives only 2 for n = 8. Mütze's survey (arXiv:2202.01280 v4, 30 Jul 2024, Problem P8) lists r(n) for n >= 8 as open. Such codes are used in image detectors and structured light. A Semantic Scholar citation check on 2026-10-30 found no paper settling r(8).
targets.success_criterion: Success means settling whether r(8) >= 6. (a) An explicit cyclic 8-bit Gray code (256 distinct words, single-bit steps including last to first) in which, for every coordinate, any two cyclically consecutive flips of that coordinate are at least 6 steps apart. This shows r(8) >= 6 (direction: max; context: best known 5, Knuth Fig. 34). It must pass two independent checkers. (b) A proof that r(8) = 5: an UNSAT certificate (DRAT/LRAT, checked by a verified checker) of a published encoding with a correctness note.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit 8-bit Gray path (all 256 words, single-bit steps, not necessarily closing) in which any two consecutive flips of the same coordinate are at least 6 steps apart. It counts only if none is published at claim time.

targets.verification_method: Compute the transition sequence d_1..d_256 (cyclic) and check that all words are distinct. For each coordinate, list its flip positions and check that every cyclic gap between consecutive flips is >= 6. Calibrate the gap convention by verifying Knuth's 8-bit code (gaps >= 5), finding 5-bit codes with gaps >= 4, and confirming that no 5-bit code has gaps >= 5 (r(5) = 4).
angles: Encode the transition sequence directly: 256 positions over 8 values, with each coordinate absent from any window of 6 consecutive positions containing it (a sliding-window cardinality constraint) and a Hamiltonicity side condition checked lazily or by prefix-XOR distinctness.
Look for codes whose transition sequence is periodic under a coordinate permutation (for example 4 blocks of 64 related by a cyclic relabelling).
pitfalls: Gap conventions: a run of length r means flips at positions i and i + r. Calibrate on r(5) = 4 and r(7) = 5.
The code must be cyclic for the full win; the wrap-around gaps count.

targets.name: Avoiding words in synchronizing automata: an automaton with n >= 8 states and 1-avoiding threshold 2n-2 (largest known example has 7 states), or one above 2n-2
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (random or structured search; the exact threshold of one n-state automaton takes a BFS over at most 2^n subsets)
targets.statement: A word w avoids state q of an automaton (Q, Σ, δ) if q is not in δ(Q, w). The 1-avoiding threshold is the maximum, over avoidable states, of the length of a shortest avoiding word. Kisielewicz, Kowalski and Szykuła ('Experiments with Synchronizing Automata', CIAA 2016, Conjecture 5) conjectured that for strongly connected synchronizing n-state automata the threshold is at most 2n - 2. Marek Szykuła restates this for all synchronizing automata as Conjecture 2 in 'Synchronizing Automata: Open Problems' (EPTCS 451 (2026) 33-47, arXiv:2608.24245, 25 Aug 2026). The survey notes that only two particular examples over a minimal alphabet reach 2n - 2, and that 2n - 3 is the best lower bound for all n >= 6. The classical upper bound is (n-2)(n-1) + 2; the survey's subspace-chain refinement lowers this to order n^2 - n log2 n + O(n). Ferens, Szykuła and Vorel (MFCS 2021) give a binary, strongly connected, synchronizing series reaching 2n - 3 for every n. Their examples meeting 2n - 2 include A5 (threshold 8) and a 7-state binary automaton with threshold 12 (their Fig. 3, 'a largest known automaton meeting this bound'). No binary synchronizing automaton exceeds 2n - 3 for n in {8, ..., 11}. Their Conjecture 13: at most 2n - 3, except finitely many cases (and trivial extensions) equal to 2n - 2.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit synchronizing automaton (complete DFA, any alphabet, given as a transition table) that is not a trivial extension of a smaller-alphabet automaton (no letter acts as the identity or as a copy of another letter), and that satisfies one of two conditions. (a) It has n >= 8 states and 1-avoiding threshold >= 2n - 2; this beats the largest known example meeting 2n - 2 (7 states, direction: max n). A binary automaton needs n >= 12, since binary n = 8..11 are excluded. (b) It has any n >= 2 states and 1-avoiding threshold >= 2n - 1, which refutes Conjecture 2 of arXiv:2608.24245. Synchronization and the threshold must be confirmed by two independent programs.

partial_wins.statement: The exact maximum 2-avoiding threshold of binary synchronizing automata with 11 states, computed by two independent exhaustive programs. Both must first reproduce the published values for n = 3..10 (6, 8, 12, 17, 19, 23, 25, 28; Ferens-Szykuła-Vorel MFCS 2021). It counts only if the value for n = 11 is unpublished at claim time. This is labelled computational.

targets.verification_method: Check that the automaton is synchronizing with the pair-automaton BFS. Then BFS from the full set Q over images δ(Q, w), expanding each image by every letter. For each state q, the shortest avoiding word length is the depth of the first image not containing q. Take the maximum over avoidable q. Calibrate by reproducing threshold 12 on the 7-state automaton of Ferens et al. Fig. 3 and 2n - 3 on their binary series, and by checking that the automaton is not a trivial extension.
angles: Search over ternary and quaternary automata with 8-10 states, which earlier exhaustive binary experiments did not cover. Use hill-climbing on transitions with the exact avoiding threshold as the objective.
Grow the Fig. 3 seven-state automaton: add one state and one letter at a time, keeping strong connectivity, and look for steps that raise the threshold by 2 per added state.
pitfalls: Trivial extensions (adding identity letters or copies of letters) do not count as new examples.
A non-synchronizing automaton can have far larger avoiding thresholds; the conjecture concerns synchronizing automata only.

Exhaustive ranges: KKS 2016 Table 2 checked the 2n - 2 bound (their Conjecture 5, stated for strongly connected automata) for all alphabets at n <= 4, up to 8 letters at n = 5, 4 letters at n = 6, 3 letters at n = 7 and 2 letters at n = 8..10. Ferens et al. add binary n = 11. Ternary and larger alphabets at n >= 8 are unchecked.

targets.name: Shorthand universal tori for permutations of [7]: an R x C torus with 2x3 windows for some R >= 3 (only 2-row tori are known)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (backtracking or SAT over 5040 cells; a torus checks instantly)
targets.statement: A shorthand universal torus is an R x C toroidal array over [n] with R*C = n!. Each (n-1)-permutation of [n] (a permutation with its redundant last value dropped) must appear exactly once as an r x c window read in row-major order, where r*c = n - 1 and windows wrap in both directions. Gerlach, Hartung, Herkenrath, Sawada and Williams, 'Shorthand Universal Tori for Permutations: Existence, Symmetry, and Generation of Twori' (arXiv:2609.27583 v1, 23 Sep 2026), prove that 2-row tori with 2 x m windows exist for every odd n = 2m + 1 (Theorem 1). They settle n = 5 with 2 x 2 windows completely: tori exist for 2x60, 4x30, 6x20 and 8x15, and none exist for 1x120, 3x40, 5x24 and 10x12. Two independent backtracking programs established this, with hand proofs for 3x40 and 5x24. Their final remarks name as the main open problem 'for which values (R,C,r,c) do shorthand universal tori exist'. For n = 7 (2 x 3 windows, or 3 x 2 on the transpose) only R = 2 is settled; no search beyond n = 5 is reported.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit R x C array over {1..7} with R*C = 5040, R dividing 5040 and 3 <= R <= 1680 (so that C >= 3), in which every 2 x 3 window (read row-major, wrapping toroidally) is a 6-permutation of [7] and all 5040 such 6-permutations occur exactly once. Two independent checkers must confirm it. A torus with 3 x 2 windows counts as the transposed case. Existence for any R other than 2 is new as of 2026-10-30: arXiv:2609.27583 and later sources settle no n = 7 case except R = 2.

partial_wins.statement: A rerunnable nonexistence proof for one n = 7 case (R, C) with 2 x 3 windows and R >= 3: a written proof, an UNSAT certificate (DRAT/LRAT, checked by a verified checker) of a published encoding, or two independent exhaustive programs that agree (labelled computational). It counts only if that case is unsettled in the latest version of arXiv:2609.27583 at claim time.
An explicit shorthand universal torus for n = 9 with 2 x 4 windows and R >= 3 rows, verified the same way.

targets.verification_method: For each of the R*C top-left positions, read the window cells (i+a mod R, j+b mod C) for a < 2 and b < 3 in row-major order, check that the six values are distinct, and insert the tuple into a set. Check that the set has 5040 elements. Calibrate on the paper's n = 5 example tori (Figure 3, 2 x 2 windows) and on its 2-row construction (Theorem 1).
angles: Count symbol occurrences per column first, as in the paper's 3 x 40 argument; this decides quickly which R values for n = 7 are blocked by counting, so search effort goes only to the rest.
Stack copies of a 2-row twori with shifted symbol relabellings so that the window rows crossing the seam are also new.
pitfalls: Windows are read row-major, and the omitted last symbol is the one missing from the window.
Some (R, C) may fall to a simple counting argument; a nonexistence proof is only a partial win.

targets.name: Slowly synchronizing binary automata with a sink: beat Ananichev-Vorel's n^2/4 + 2n - 9 reset threshold (n = 16, 28) or the best known value for another n
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (local search over 2-letter automata; the exact reset threshold costs a BFS over 2^n subsets, which is easy at n = 16 and needs a few GB of bitsets at n = 28)
targets.statement: An automaton with zero (a sink) has a state fixed by every letter. With an unbounded alphabet the maximum reset threshold of n-state synchronizing automata with zero is n(n-1)/2 (Rystsov 1977, tight). For binary automata with zero the maximum is unknown. Volkov's living list (arXiv:2508.15655 v4, 13 Jan 2026, item B1) gives the best known lower bound n^2/4 + 2n - 9, attained for n ≡ 4 (mod 12) from n = 16 on by the Ananichev-Vorel series (J. Autom. Lang. Comb. 24 (2019) 153-164). Other series of order n^2/4 are Martyugin's (Inf. Comput. 206, 2008: two letters, n >= 8, ceil(n^2/4 + 3n/2 - 4)) and Pribavkina's (Math. Notes 90, 2011: any fixed number k of letters, even n >= 2k, n^2/4 + n/2 - 1). The general upper bound n(n-1)/2 applies, so the binary-sink question (is it n^2/4 + O(n)?) is wide open. At n = 16 the record value is 87; at n = 28 it is 243.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit binary complete DFA with n states, n in {16, 28}, that has a sink state and is synchronizing, whose exact reset threshold (computed by BFS over subsets) is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than n^2/4 + 2n - 9 (87 for n = 16, 243 for n = 28). It must also exceed every value for that n in any newer source found by a fresh search before claiming (Volkov's list, papers citing Ananichev-Vorel 2019). Two independent programs must confirm the reset threshold.

partial_wins.statement: For some n with 17 <= n <= 30 and n not ≡ 4 (mod 12), a binary synchronizing automaton with a sink whose exact reset threshold is strictly greater than ceil(n^2/4 + 2n - 9), the Ananichev-Vorel formula evaluated at n. It must also exceed every published value for that n and be confirmed by two independent programs.

targets.verification_method: Check that the input is a 2-letter complete DFA with a state z where both letters map z to z. Run BFS from the full set over subset images under both letters until a singleton is reached; the BFS depth is the reset threshold. Use bitset subsets, and canonicalise to avoid revisiting. Run a second, independent implementation (for example the Szykuła-Zyzik algorithm or a SAT-based shortest-reset-word check). Calibrate on Rystsov's automata R_n (n(n-1)/2) and on Martyugin's series at n = 16 (ceil(64 + 24 - 4) = 84).
angles: Start from the Ananichev-Vorel and Martyugin automata and run simulated annealing on single transitions, scoring by exact reset threshold (cheap at n = 16).
Exploit the sink: synchronizing means reaching z, so the threshold is the maximum over states of a 'reach z from a set' process. Incremental BFS under single-transition changes speeds up the search.
pitfalls: The Ananichev-Vorel construction is open as arXiv:1701.07954 (v1 lists Ananichev alone; the JALC 2019 version adds Vorel). An almost-permutation automaton A_n with reset threshold 4n - 13, given a tail of length k that is a multiple of the order 6 of a, has reset threshold rt(A_n) + nk (Lemma 2.1). Rebuild A_10 plus a 6-tail (87 at n = 16) and A_16 plus a 12-tail (243 at n = 28) to calibrate.

For p1, the same tail construction already gives published values for other n just below the bar (for example 211 at n = 26, where the bar is 212; 97 at n = 17, where the bar is 98). A claim must beat both the bar and these values. For small n the exact maxima may already be known from exhaustive searches. The headline cells n = 16 and 28 are beyond exhaustive reach, but check any tables before claiming p1.
The sink state must be fixed by both letters, and the automaton must be complete.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Eulerian synchronizing automata: a reset threshold above floor((n^2-3)/2) (refuting the Szykuła-Vorel conjecture), or binary Eulerian records
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (heuristic search; the exact reset threshold is a BFS over 2^n subsets) to needs cluster (exhaustive extensions)
targets.statement: A complete DFA is Eulerian if its underlying digraph is Eulerian: strongly connected, with every state having in-degree equal to the alphabet size. Kari (Theoret. Comput. Sci. 295, 2003) proved the upper bound n^2 - 3n + 3 for Eulerian synchronizing automata. Szykuła ('Synchronizing Automata: Open Problems', arXiv:2608.24245, Corollary 20) recently improved it slightly, to n^2 - n log2 n + O(n). Szykuła and Vorel (DLT 2016, LNCS 9840; arXiv:1604.02879) gave a 4-letter series with n = 4m + 1 states and reset threshold (n^2-3)/2, and conjectured that floor((n^2-3)/2) is the maximum for n >= 3 (their Conjecture 19, which also asks for (n^2-5)/2 in the binary case). Their exhaustive searches confirmed it for 2 letters with at most 11 states, 4 letters with at most 7, 8 letters with at most 5, and all DFAs with at most 4 states. At n = 7 they also found 2 ternary and 12 quaternary automata meeting the bound. Volkov's living list (arXiv:2508.15655 v4, 13 Jan 2026, item A6) reports all of this. For binary Eulerian automata, Pavel Martyugin (unpublished) proposed a series conjectured to reach (n^2-5)/2 (for odd n in Volkov's list). The 2016 searches found the binary maximum (n^2-5)/2 met uniquely by Martyugin's automata for n in {5, 7, 8, 9, 11} and not reachable for n = 6 and 10. The best published binary lower bound is (n^2 - 3n + 4)/2 (Gusev, Reachability Problems 2011).
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit Eulerian synchronizing complete DFA with n states whose exact reset threshold is STRICTLY GREATER than floor((n^2 - 3)/2), refuting Szykuła-Vorel Conjecture 19. Two independent programs must confirm the Eulerian property and the threshold. It must have at most 30 states, so that exact BFS is feasible.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit binary Eulerian synchronizing automaton with odd n >= 13 states and exact reset threshold >= (n^2 - 5)/2, which makes Martyugin's conjectured value explicit beyond n = 11 and beats the published (n^2 - 3n + 4)/2. It counts only if no such automaton for that n is published at claim time.

An exhaustive verification of the floor((n^2-3)/2) bound for a range not covered in Szykuła-Vorel 2016 or Volkov's list: binary Eulerian automata with 12 or 13 states, or 3- or 4-letter Eulerian automata with 8 states. Two independently written programs must agree and must first reproduce the published small cases; the result is labelled computational.

targets.verification_method: Check completeness, that in-degree equals |Σ| at every state, and strong connectivity. Check synchronization with the pair-automaton test, then compute the exact reset threshold by BFS over subset images from Q (bitsets; 2^n subsets). Run a second implementation independently. Calibrate on the Szykuła-Vorel 4-letter series A_m (n = 4m + 1) at n = 5 ((25-3)/2 = 11) and n = 9 ((81-3)/2 = 39), and on the Černý automaton (not Eulerian; expect the Eulerian check to fail).
angles: Search near the Szykuła-Vorel series with 3 letters or 5-6 letters, where the reported exhaustive ranges stop; Eulerian moves can be done as transition swaps that preserve in-degrees.
For p1, reconstruct Martyugin's series from the n <= 11 extremal automata (found by a quick search on binary Eulerian automata with 5-9 states), then extend the pattern to n = 13 and 15.
pitfalls: Eulerian means in-degree equal to the alphabet size at every state, counted with multiplicity; strong connectivity is required.
Martyugin's series is unpublished; the published binary lower bound is Gusev's (n^2 - 3n + 4)/2.

targets.name: Least quadratic non-residue records: the next term of A000229 (least prime whose least QNR is the 39th prime, 167) or of a sibling prescribed-character sequence
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (CRT/wheel enumeration of candidates with prescribed Legendre symbols; minutes to verify)
targets.statement: Lehmer, Lehmer and Shanks (Math. Comp. 24, 1970) studied integers with prescribed quadratic character modulo the first primes, the extreme cases of the least quadratic non-residue problem. OEIS keeps several such record sequences, and they have been extended very unevenly. On 2026-10-30: A000229 (least m, always a prime q, whose least quadratic non-residue is prime(n)) has b-file terms n = 1..38 from Tomas Oliveira e Silva's tables, ending a(38) = 70864718555231 (least QNR 163). His exhaustive, double-checked run over all primes up to 10^14 (table q_B, the column the b-file comes from) has no entry for 167, so a(39) > 10^14. The sibling b-files bracket it much more tightly. Since 2 must be a QR, q = 1 or 7 mod 8. A002223 (least prime q = 7 mod 8 with the first n primes all QRs; b-file n = 1..57 by Jinyuan Wang, ending a(57) = 3546374752298322551) has a(38) = 317398900373231, whose least QNR is exactly 167, so a(39) <= 317398900373231. A002224 (the same with q = 1 mod 8; b-file n = 1..41 by Michael Hortmann, more terms from Mike Oakes, 2022) has a(38) = a(39) = 112434732901969 with least QNR 173, so any q = 1 mod 8 with least QNR 167 exceeds it. Hence a(39) is either 317398900373231 or the least prime q = 1 mod 8 in (112434732901969, 317398900373231) with least QNR 167, a window nobody has searched for this condition. The same b-files already imply a(40) = 112434732901969 and a(42) = 178936222537081 (= A002224(41), least QNR 181), which OEIS cannot list before a(39); a(41) (least QNR 179) exceeds 1.789 x 10^14 and is open. Further siblings: A002224 ends at a(41) = 178936222537081, A045535 (least negative pseudosquare) at a(50) = 423414931359807911 (Bert Dobbelaere, 2021), A001992 (least prime = 5 mod 8 that is a QNR of every odd prime <= p) at a(55) = 637754768063384837 (b-file by Jinyuan Wang, extended 2026), and the pseudosquares A002189 at L_373 = a(73) = 4235025223080597503519329 (J. Sorenson's 2010 parallel doubly focused sieve, which also showed L_379 > 10^25; b-file by Charles R Greathouse IV from D. J. Bernstein's page). Target: the next term of any of these sequences, with a proof of minimality.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a value q for the next unknown index of A000229 (n = 39), A002223 (n = 58), A002224 (n = 42), A045535 (n = 51), A001992 (n = 56) or A002189 (n = 74). Those indices are re-fetched from the live OEIS b-files immediately before claiming and must still be absent. The claim must satisfy two checks. (1) Property: q has exactly the prescribed character, verified by an independent script (Euler's criterion or the Jacobi symbol for every prime up to the bound), plus a deterministic primality proof where the sequence requires a prime (BPSW plus a Pocklington/ECPP certificate above 3.3e24). (2) Minimality: a complete search shows that no smaller integer has the property. For A000229(39) the search may start from the bracket, so that only primes q = 1 mod 8 in (112434732901969, 317398900373231) need checking, but only if the claimant's enumerator first reproduces A002223(38) = 317398900373231 and A002224(38) = 112434732901969 from 1. Otherwise it starts from 1. The skeptic re-runs that search with a separately written enumerator (a different modulus split, or a plain sieve on a sub-range), and it must find nothing below q. Direction: a new term (index strictly beyond the b-file). No OEIS submission is made by the agent.

partial_wins.statement: A certified lower bound when the next term is not settled: an independently re-run exhaustive search showing either that no prime q = 1 mod 8 in (112434732901969, 2 x 10^14] has least QNR 167 (which narrows A000229(39) to (2 x 10^14, 317398900373231]), or that A002224(42) exceeds 10^16.
An independent re-computation that confirms (or corrects) the last five listed terms of A000229, A002223 or A002224 by a method different from the original sieve.

targets.verification_method: Property check with Python big integers: pow(p, (q-1)/2, q) for each prime p up to the index prime (seconds). Minimality: re-run the claimant's enumeration from scratch using a different split of the CRT modulus (e.g. Bernstein-style doubly focused enumeration against a wheel sieve over residues mod 8*3*5*...*37). Cross-check it on known values: A000229 a(30)..a(38), A002223(38) = 317398900373231 and A002224(38) = 112434732901969.
angles: Doubly focused enumeration (Bernstein; Sorenson 2010): split the prime set into two groups, enumerate residues mod M1 and M2 that satisfy the character conditions, and combine them in sorted order, so the work is about sqrt of the candidate count.

For A000229(39) only q = 1 mod 8 below 317398900373231 is left. For such q, (p/q) = (q/p) by reciprocity, so q needs (q/p) = 1 for the odd primes p < 167 and (q/167) = -1. These are residue conditions mod 8*3*5*...*167, with density about 2^-38 among q = 1 mod 8. Expect a handful of hits in the 2 x 10^14-wide window.
Calibrate on the known terms first: an enumerator that reproduces A000229 a(30)..a(38), A002224(35..41) and A002223(35..38) is trustworthy.

Keep going past the bracket: the same q = 1 mod 8 pass beyond 1.789 x 10^14, plus a q = 7 mod 8 pass beyond A002223(40) = 501108392233679, settles A000229(41) (least QNR 179), and the 1 mod 8 pass also serves A002224(42).
pitfalls: A000229's offset: a(n) is the least prime whose least QNR is prime(n), counting 2 as prime(1); A002189 and A045535 index by odd primes. Off-by-one indices give wrong targets.
Minimality is the hard part: listing a q with the right character is not a term unless no smaller q exists. Partial windows do not count.
Deterministic Miller-Rabin base sets are proven only up to about 3.3e24; above that, give a real primality certificate.
The sibling b-files constrain A000229: a(39) <= A002223(38) = 317398900373231, and a(40) and a(42) are already implied, so they are not new results. A claimed a(39) above 317398900373231 is wrong.
Re-check the b-files on the day: these sequences are being extended by individuals (A001992 and A002223 changed in April 2026).

targets.name: Gilbreath's conjecture: extend the verification beyond Colonna's x = 1.5 x 10^15 (2026)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (sieve the primes to about 2e15 and run about 820 rows of absolute differences over byte arrays; SIMD and multicore)
targets.statement: Gilbreath's conjecture (Proth 1878, Gilbreath 1958): in the triangle of iterated absolute differences of the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ..., every row after the first starts with 1. Odlyzko (1993) verified it for the first pi(10^13) = 3.4 x 10^11 rows, showing that 635 rows suffice: once a row starts with 1 followed only by 0s and 2s over a long enough stretch, all later rows in that range start with 1. The record moved in 2025-2026. Simon Plouffe (arXiv:2510.06688, Oct 2025) verified up to 10^14 independently of Jean-Francois Colonna (collaborating with Jean-Paul Delahaye). Colonna's page (last updated 2026-08-12) lists G(pi(10^14)) = 693, G(pi(2.2 x 10^14)) = 773, G(pi(6.15 x 10^14)) = 800, G(pi(10^15)) = 800, G(pi(1.2125 x 10^15)) = 811, and finally 'Verification up to 1.5x10^15 (03/18/2026)'. It says the computation was interrupted there and could have continued. Colonna also lists 'relative records', local depths in windows far beyond the verified range (for example G = 1935 near 6.02 x 10^27); these are not verifications. Wikipedia (edited 2026-10-20) cites the same 1.5 x 10^15. Target: a verification for a strictly larger x.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the claimant's own computation, starting from p_1 = 2, showing that the leading entry of difference row k is 1 for every k <= pi(X), for some X STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the largest verified bound on Colonna's live page (1.5 x 10^15 on 2026-10-30), in the same convention: X is the bound on the primes, the rows covered are k <= pi(X), and G(pi(X)) is reported. Colonna's and Plouffe's block data are not published, so the whole range from 2 must be covered by the claimant's logs. The claim gives the code, the depth G used, the block and overlap scheme (each block's overlap must exceed its depth so that no row is cut) and pi(X) checked against an independent pi(x) value (primecount). The skeptic re-runs the algorithm with an independently written difference-table routine on at least three randomly chosen blocks, and runs the full computation from scratch if compute allows. Colonna's page and arXiv are re-checked immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: An independent reproduction of Colonna's G values at x = 10^14 (693) and x = 10^15 (800), or a documented discrepancy, with code.

Local Gilbreath depths for every block of a contiguous range of primes from 1.5 x 10^15 to at least 1.6 x 10^15 (block overlaps larger than the depths), with the maximum depth reported and at least three sampled blocks recomputed independently: the extension step toward the next bound.

targets.verification_method: Generate the primes with primesieve and check pi(X) against primecount. Recompute rows 1..G with an independently written loop (numpy uint8 abs-diff or C) on sampled blocks with the stated overlap, and confirm that at row G the leading entry is 1 and the following pi(X) entries are all in {0, 2}. A full re-run takes laptop-days.
angles: Odlyzko's reduction: you never need the full triangle, only the first G rows; once a row is 1 followed by a long run of 0/2 the remaining rows follow. Memory is one byte per prime per block.
Rows beyond the first few fit in bytes after entries shrink, so store differences as uint8 and run abs-diff with SIMD; the cost is about G * pi(X) byte operations (about 5e16 for X = 2e15).
Block decomposition: split the prime list into blocks overlapping by more than G entries, process them independently on all cores, and re-check the overlaps.
Cross-domain import (streaming/GPU stencil codes): the row recurrence is a 1-D stencil, so temporal blocking (several rows per memory pass) cuts memory traffic by the blocking factor.
pitfalls: Convention: Colonna's 1.5 x 10^15 bounds the primes (x), not the number of rows (about pi(1.5 x 10^15) = 4.4 x 10^13 rows), while Odlyzko's 1993 record is usually quoted in rows (3.4 x 10^11); compare in the page's convention.
Block overlaps smaller than the row depth silently corrupt later rows; a verifier must check each block's overlap.
An off-by-one in where the prime list starts (2 or 3) changes the triangle.
Local depths in windows far out (Colonna's 'relative records') grow with the local prime gaps; a large one near a big known gap is easy to produce and is not a verification or a win here.

targets.name: Mertens function oscillations: a certified bound beating Hurst's liminf M(x)/sqrt(x) < -1.837625 or limsup > 1.826054
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (or one multi-core workstation for weeks: Hurst's fplll runs at N = 800, nu = 17,000 took about 35 days each, and he projected 2 months for +-1.90 by the same method); laptop-days for about 15,000 zeta zeros to 5,000+ digits and for partial win p1
targets.statement: Let q(x) = M(x)/sqrt(x) for the Mertens function M(x) = sum_{n<=x} mu(n). Odlyzko and te Riele (1985) disproved the Mertens conjecture by showing limsup q > 1.06 and liminf q < -1.009, using Ingham's theorem and LLL. Ingham's theorem (Hurst, Theorem 4.2) needs no RH: for any real y and any N, liminf q <= h(y,N) <= limsup q, where h(y,N) = 2 sum_{i<=N} a_i f(gamma_i/gamma_N) cos(gamma_i y + psi_i), with a_i = 1/|rho_i zeta'(rho_i)|, psi_i = arg(rho_i zeta'(rho_i)) and f(t) = (1-t)cos(pi t) + sin(pi t)/pi. A y that makes the cosines line up gives a bound, and finding one is a simultaneous Diophantine approximation (lattice) problem. Best and Trudgian (2015) showed limsup |q| >= 1.6383. Greg Hurst (Math. Comp. 87, 2018, arXiv:1610.08551) used fplll with nu = 17,000 and N = 800, about 35 days per run, to find y- = 1.50546e5096 and y+ = -2.58842e5097, giving h(y-,14400) = -1.837625 and h(y+,14400) = 1.826054. He estimated that bounds of +-1.90 / 1.95 / 2.00 need about 2 / 5 / 10 months with the same method. Kim and Nguyen (ANTS XVI, 2024) still cite Hurst's values as the record. They note that pruned lattice enumeration, which sped up their own counterexample search by a factor of millions, 'seems likely' to reach a larger value in much shorter time. Wikipedia (edited 2026-03-15) still lists Hurst's bounds. Target: a strictly better certified bound on either side.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a real y (given exactly, as a rational or a decimal string), an N, and the list of zeros used, such that h(y,N), evaluated in rigorous interval arithmetic (Arb/FLINT ball arithmetic with certified enclosures of gamma_i and zeta'(rho_i)), has an enclosure lying entirely above 1.826054 (limsup side, direction: max) or entirely below -1.837625 (liminf side, direction: min). Before claiming, check that these remain the best published values: re-fetch the Wikipedia Mertens conjecture page, check arXiv for 2024-2026 work citing Hurst or Kim-Nguyen, and beat any newer value. The skeptic recomputes h(y,N) with an independently written evaluator, using zeros computed by separate software (mpmath zetazero at high precision cross-checked against Arb). The zero list must be complete up to gamma_N, which is verified by Turing's method or by matching N(T).

partial_wins.statement: A certified |h(y,N)| >= 1.75 from a y found by the agent's own lattice search (not Hurst's), evaluated in ball arithmetic over a complete zero list, showing the pipeline works end to end.
A certified |h(y,N)| >= 1.81 from the agent's own search, matching Hurst's N = 700 level (-1.81111 / 1.81252), with timings.

targets.verification_method: Compute the first N zeros and zeta'(rho) with python-flint (acb_dirichlet_zeta_zeros plus derivatives) at about 1.2 x log10|y| + 50 digits, confirm completeness with N(T), evaluate the finite sum in ball arithmetic, and check the sign of the enclosure. This takes hours on a laptop for N of about 15,000.
angles: Replace one long LLL run with BKZ plus pruned enumeration around the target vector (the Kim-Nguyen pipeline, code on Zenodo), aimed at maximising h rather than proving |h| > 1.
Order zeros by weight a_i rather than by height (Hurst section 4) and put only the heaviest few hundred in the lattice; evaluate the full sum with N = 15,000 afterwards.

Cross-domain import (phase retrieval / beamforming): maximising a weighted sum of cosines over one real parameter y is the array-steering problem; local refinement of y after the lattice step (Newton on h'(y)) can add a few thousandths.
Kernel choice: Ingham's theorem holds for other admissible kernels; a kernel with a heavier tail at fixed N may raise the achievable value (prove admissibility).
pitfalls: Precision: y is about 10^5097, so gamma_i y mod 2 pi needs gamma_i to about 5,100 or more significant digits; double or 100-digit zeros give garbage.
The bound uses h(y,N) with the f(gamma/gamma_N) taper; dropping the taper or using a raw partial sum of the explicit formula gives values that do not bound limsup q.
A missed or duplicated zero below gamma_N invalidates the certificate; check the count against N(T).
Hurst's exact y-values and zero data were linked only through a Wolfram Cloud notebook (wolfr.am/mertens), which returned 404 on 2026-10-30; do not plan on re-evaluating his y.
Not a counterexample: these bounds do not exhibit any x with |M(x)| > sqrt(x).

targets.name: Smallest Mertens counterexample: a certified bound below exp(3.485 x 10^18) (2026 claim under review), or below Kim-Nguyen's published exp(1.96 x 10^19)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (BKZ-80..90 plus pruned enumeration in dimension about 140; 74,000 zeta zeros at 300 digits take under a core-day)
targets.statement: No explicit x with |M(x)| > sqrt(x) is known. Pintz (1987) made the 1985 disproof effective: with h_P(y) = 2 sum_{gamma < 14000} alpha exp(-1.5e-6 gamma^2) cos(gamma y - psi), any y in [e^7, e^50000] with |h_P(y)| > 1 + e^-40 gives x < exp(y + sqrt(y)) for the smallest counterexample x. Saouter and te Riele (2014) refined this to h_StR(y) = 2 sum_{gamma < 74000} alpha exp(-3e-9 gamma^2) cos(gamma y - psi), where |h_StR(y)| > 1 + 6e-8 suffices for practical y. Bounds: exp(3.21e64) (Odlyzko-te Riele data), exp(1.59e40) (Kotnik-te Riele 2006), exp(1.004e33) (Saouter-te Riele 2014), exp(1.017e29) (Rozmarynowycz-Kim, arXiv:2305.00345). The peer-reviewed record is from Seungki Kim and Phong Q. Nguyen (ANTS XVI, 2024; arXiv:2502.21021): BKZ-88 reduction plus pruned enumeration found y = 19571878850562201959.215107 with h_StR(y) = -1.007, so x < exp(1.96e19). That is far below Kotnik-van de Lune's conjectured location exp(5.15e23), and took 'barely half a day on a single core'. The paper says that 'an even lower bound ... may be attainable' with better parameters, and lists small refinements (perturbing y; the sharper x < exp(y + 2 sqrt(k y)) of Saouter-te Riele Lemma E). Wikipedia (edited 2026-03-15) still cites exp(1.96e19). A public repository, github.com/bzyzz/mertens_bound (last commit 2026-10-22, marked 'not peer-reviewed'), claims x < exp(3484971332733178124), about exp(3.485e18). Its lattice-found point v = 3484971332733132396.538... gives K_2 = 0.9957 at Saouter-te Riele's parameters, below 1. With Gaussian width k = 1.5e-10, summed over all 2,325,572 zeros below T0 = 1.3e6, it gives K_2 = 1.0003052504 +- 2.3e-11, using error terms J1..J6 re-derived for those parameters (E <= 2.4e-11) that no specialist has checked yet. Target: a certified upper bound smaller than that claim, or, by the published criterion alone, smaller than Kim-Nguyen's.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a real y (or v), given exactly, evaluated in rigorous ball arithmetic over the complete zero list below the stated cutoff, that meets one of three criteria. The first is |h_StR(y)| > 1 + 6e-8 (Saouter-te Riele's published parameters). The second is |h_P(y)| > 1 + e^-40 with y in [e^7, e^50000] (Pintz). The third is the bzyzz/mertens_bound criterion at its stated (k, T0, T1) with its error bound E. The claim also gives the resulting bound B on the smallest counterexample, computed by the formula that goes with the criterion used. B must be STRICTLY SMALLER (direction: min) than exp(3484971332733178124), the smallest public claim on 2026-10-30. A claim that uses the bzyzz criterion inherits its unreviewed status and must say so. A claim that uses a new kernel or new error terms gives the full derivation, and the skeptic checks every inequality numerically. A refinement (Saouter-te Riele Lemma E, the |M(x +- n)| argument) counts only when compared with the same refinement applied to the record point. The skeptic re-evaluates h at y with independently computed zeros and re-checks the theorem's hypotheses (range of y, error margin). Before claiming, re-check arXiv, the Wikipedia page and the bzyzz/mertens_bound README for a newer record, and beat it.

partial_wins.statement: An independent certified re-evaluation of Kim-Nguyen's best y values (Tables 1-2) for h_P and h_StR, confirming or correcting their reported values to 3 decimals.
A certified y with |h_StR(y)| > 1 + 6e-8 and y < 1.0e20 that is not in Kim-Nguyen's tables (an independent hit of the same quality).

A bound below the published record by the published criterion alone: a certified y < 19571878850562201959.215107 with |h_StR(y)| > 1 + 6e-8 at Saouter-te Riele's own parameters (k = 3e-9, zeros below 74,000), so that exp(y + sqrt(y)) < exp(y_KN + sqrt(y_KN)) without relying on unreviewed error terms.
