An independent check of the bzyzz/mertens_bound certificate, done with separately written code: either the ball-arithmetic K_2 sum at its point over all zeros below 1.3e6, or a numerical re-derivation of its error terms J1..J6 and the 1/zeta bound. The result either confirms it or documents a concrete error.

targets.verification_method: Compute zeros below 74,000 with Arb at 300 digits, complete by N(T). Evaluate h_StR(y) with an independent ball-arithmetic script and check the enclosure against 1 + 6e-8. Recompute B from the formula. This takes hours.
angles: Start from the Kim-Nguyen Zenodo code: it builds the lattice (3.2) with parameters (N, nu, nu_y, nu_t) and runs enumeration around a target. A wider parameter sweep (they tried only a few N) is the cheapest lever.
Their Figure 3: the best y are not the closest lattice points, so enumerate a ball and rank by the exact h rather than by distance.
Bias the lattice toward small y: weight the y-coordinate more heavily so short vectors correspond to smaller y, since the bound is about exp(y).
Hathi (2023) refined Saouter-te Riele's estimates (cited by Kim-Nguyen as not fully exploited); a sharper explicit lemma with a proof lowers the threshold below 1 + 6e-8 or allows a larger kernel.
pitfalls: The threshold is |h| > 1 plus a small margin, not |h| > 1; check the enclosure, not the midpoint.
Pintz's theorem needs y in [e^7, e^50000]; Saouter-te Riele's h_StR needs its own range conditions (Lemma E). Check them.
Comparing a refined bound for your y with the unrefined headline bound for Kim-Nguyen's y is a fake improvement.
This bound says nothing about limsup |q|; it is the location of the first counterexample.

targets.name: Exact Mertens function values: M(10^24) (A084237) or M(2^76) (A084236), with new terms of A084235 (first k with |M(k)| = 2^n) as partial wins
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (or an 80+ core server for weeks: Helfgott-Thompson's M(2^75) took about 9.7 days and M(10^23) about 18.6 days on 80 cores); laptop-hours for the A084235 partial win (segmented Mobius sieve to about 3.3e11)
targets.statement: Exact values of M(x) = sum_{n<=x} mu(n) at large x come from combinatorial algorithms in the Lagarias-Miller-Odlyzko / Deleglise-Rivat tradition. On 2026-10-30 OEIS A084237 (M(10^n)) ends at M(10^23) = 62467771689. M(10^18)-M(10^22) are from Eugene Kuznetsov's GPU code (2011-2012; a(17)-a(19) independently confirmed by Richard Sladkey). a(21)'s sign correction and a(23) are from Harald Helfgott and Lola Thompson ('Summing mu(n): a faster elementary algorithm', arXiv:2101.08773, time O(x^(3/5)(log x)^(3/5+eps)), the first exponent improvement for an elementary method since 1985). A084236 (M(2^n)) has a b-file to n = 75: terms to 2^73 are from Greg Hurst (Math. Comp. 2018, an O(x^(2/3)) method), and M(2^74) = -6336351930 and M(2^75) = -4000846218 are from Helfgott-Thompson. Their M(10^23) took about 18.6 days on an 80-core machine and M(2^75) about 9.7 days, so M(2^76) (about 7.6e22) is a multi-week server job and M(10^24) more. Neither is in OEIS. A cheap side cell: A084235, the least k with |M(k)| = 2^n, stops at a(17) = 108500046711 (Ashley Jordan and Luke March, 2014). Hurst's published list of prominent extrema for x <= 10^16 suggests a(18) (|M| = 262144) lies between 2.97e11 and 3.31e11 and a(19) between 1.44e12 and 1.65e12; the exact first hits need only a segmented Mobius sieve. Target: a new exact value of M(10^24) or of M(2^n) for some n >= 76.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a new term of A084237 (n = 24) or A084236 (n >= 76), at an index absent from the live OEIS entry and b-file when re-fetched immediately before claiming, computed twice with different algorithm parameters or different code and agreeing exactly. The claim states the exact integer, the code, the run logs, and a consistency check: the same code reproduces M(10^22), M(10^23), M(2^74) and M(2^75). The skeptic reproduces at least one smaller known value with the claimant's code and re-runs the new value if compute allows. Direction: a new term (higher index).

partial_wins.statement: New terms of A084235 beyond a(17): the least k with |M(k)| = 2^18 (expected in (2.97e11, 3.31e11) from Hurst's extrema list) and, for more, 2^19 and 2^20, each from a full segmented Mobius sieve from 1, verified by a second independent run, at indices absent from OEIS on the day of claiming.
An independent re-computation of M(10^22) or M(2^75) by a different code (confirming Kuznetsov or Helfgott-Thompson), documented with timings.

targets.verification_method: For the large values, build Helfgott-Thompson's algorithm (or a Deleglise-Rivat Mertens code) independently, reproduce known values at 10^20..10^23, then run the new x with two parameter settings. For the sieve terms, run a segmented Mobius sieve with a running sum and record the first k where |M| hits 2^18, then re-run on separate hardware.
angles: A084235(18) first: Hurst's extrema list puts it in (2.97e11, 3.31e11), so a segmented sieve of mu with a running sum to 3.31e11 takes well under an hour on 8 cores. Record the first k where |M(k)| = 2^18.
Helfgott-Thompson give pseudo-code and analysis; the space-saving variant (Helfgott 2020) keeps memory near x^(1/5), so M(10^24) runs on a workstation.
Cross-domain import (pi(x) engineering in primecount): reuse Walisch's load balancing and the 'alternative alpha tuning' double-check trick, so the second run uses different internal bounds.
M(2^76) before M(10^24): 2^76 = 7.6e22 is cheaper than the known 10^23 value and gives a calibration point.
pitfalls: Silent hardware errors in multi-week runs: OEIS records a past sign error (a(21)). Always do two runs with different parameters.
Overflow: Helfgott-Thompson's implementation uses 128-bit signed integers and needed a stricter parameter choice at 10^23 to avoid overflow; check the bounds again at 10^24.
A084235 uses |M(k)| = 2^n exactly; since M moves by at most 1 per step the first k with |M| >= 2^n has |M| = 2^n, but mind the offset (corrected March 2026).

Hurst's 10^16 sieve recorded every extremum, so exact A084235 terms up to about n = 25 may exist in his data; the linked notebook (wolfr.am/mertens) returned 404 on 2026-10-30. Re-check OEIS before claiming.

targets.name: Skewes numbers for prime k-tuples: A210439(10), A332493(9), or the sexy-prime (p, p+6) Skewes number
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days for the sexy-prime search (primesieve-style counting with a running Hardy-Littlewood comparison); laptop-minutes to test A210439(10) against Luhn's public 10-tuplet lists up to 10^20 (a win only if a crossing occurs there); needs cluster for 9-tuplets beyond 2^64 and 10-tuplets beyond 10^20
targets.statement: Tóth (CMST 2019, arXiv:1910.02636) defined the Skewes number of an admissible prime k-tuple pattern P as the first prime p at which the count pi_P(p) exceeds the Hardy-Littlewood prediction C_P Li_P(p), with Li_P(x) = int_2^x dt/(log t)^k. Known values: twins 1369391 (Marek Wolf 2011), cousins 5206837, triplets, quadruplets, quintuplets and the 6-tuplet 251331775687 (Tóth 2019), 7-tuplets 7572964186421 and 214159878489239 (Hugo Pfoertner 2020), the three 8-tuplet patterns (Pfoertner and Norman Luhn 2021, up to 750247439134737983). OEIS A210439 (minimal Skewes number over the n-tuplet patterns) got a(9) = 3658988336628289781 from Karl Desfontaines and Hugo Pfoertner on 2026-06-03, using Desfontaines' enumeration of all four 9-tuplet patterns up to 2^64; a(10) is open. A332493 (the latest first sign change among the n-tuplet types) stops at a(8) = 750247439134737983 (2021), so a(9) is open. Wikipedia's Skewes number page (edited 2026-10-28) states that the Skewes number for sexy primes (p, p+6), if it exists, is still unknown. A check for this entry found pi_6(x) < C Li_2(x) at every sexy pair up to 10^10 (deficit about 4,500 there and growing), with C = 4 C_2 = 2.6406. Hardy-Littlewood constants for every pattern are tabulated by Tony Forbes and Norman Luhn. Luhn's public database of the smallest prime k-tuplets (updated 2026-09-27) lists the four 9-tuplet patterns only up to 10^18, below A210439(9), so Desfontaines' 2^64 run is not in it. It lists both 10-tuplet patterns up to 10^20 (about 5.12 million of each). Target: a new Skewes number in any of these three cells.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a prime p and a pattern P such that (1) p starts an instance of P; (2) an exhaustive enumeration of all instances of P up to p (code and counts given) shows pi_P(q) <= C_P Li_P(q) at every instance q < p and pi_P(p) > C_P Li_P(p), with Li_P evaluated by rigorous quadrature (mpmath or Arb) and C_P computed to at least 15 digits; and (3) the value fills a cell absent on the day of claiming: A210439(10), A332493(9), or the (p, p+6) Skewes number, re-checked on OEIS (A210439, A332493) and on Wikipedia/OEIS for the sexy case. The skeptic recounts the instances with an independent sieve: all of them for the sexy case. For 9- and 10-tuplets the recount is cross-checked against Luhn's smallest k-tuplet database where it reaches (9-tuplets to 10^18, 10-tuplets to 10^20), plus random-window recounts beyond it. The skeptic also re-evaluates the comparison near p. A full win for A332493(9) also requires the first crossings of all four 9-tuplet types.

partial_wins.statement: A certified lower bound: an exhaustive verification that no sexy-prime Skewes number exists below 10^14 (pi_6(x) <= C Li_2(x) at every sexy pair up to 10^14), with counts at each power of 10 checked by an independent run.

The first crossing for one of the 9-tuplet types other than p + [0, 2, 6, 8, 12, 18, 20, 26, 30] (the one giving A210439(9)), not recorded in OEIS A210439 or A332493 on the day of claiming, with full enumeration up to it, independently re-verified (a step toward A332493(9)).

targets.verification_method: Recount with a separately written segmented sieve (primesieve for pairs; a wheel sieve over admissible residues mod 2*3*5*7*11*13*17*19*23 for 9- and 10-tuplets). Compute C_P with an independent Euler-product evaluation, and Li_P with mpmath.quad. Compare the running count against the prediction at each instance near the claimed crossing.
angles: Sexy pairs: run primesieve's segmented counting and track D(x) = pi_6(x) - C Li_2(x) at every pair; D drifts like -sqrt(x)/log x with fluctuations, so watch for upward excursions. If none occurs by 10^15 or so, report p1.

For 9- and 10-tuplets, the minimal-span patterns are few (four 9-tuplet types of span 30, two 10-tuplet types of span 32); one wheel sieve over the union of admissible residue classes serves all of them at once.
Use Kourbatov's PARI code (linked from A210439) as an independent reference for the Li_n integral and constants.

Cross-domain import (sequential change detection): D(x) is a slowly drifting random-walk-like process; bound how far ahead a crossing can be from the current value and the local variance, to schedule compute.
pitfalls: Li_P integrates from 2, not 0 or the first instance; the constant C_P must include the correct local factors for each pattern (sexy pairs: 2 C_2 times 2 for the prime 3).
The Skewes number is the FIRST crossing; a crossing found in a window without a complete count from 2 is not a Skewes number.

Patterns versus consecutive-prime tuples: A333586/A333587 use consecutive primes of minimal span. For pairs (p, p+6) Tóth's definition does not require consecutiveness; state which definition is used.
Floating-point Li_P near 10^20 loses digits; use mpmath with at least 30 digits.

targets.name: Primes between consecutive squares and cubes: extend Legendre's conjecture past n = 7.05 x 10^13 or the cube result past n^3 = 1.649 x 10^40
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (the squares record ran for months on 256 Xeon Phi and 192 Xeon cores; the cubes record used about 415,000 core-hours); laptop-days for a verified block in the partial wins
targets.statement: Legendre's conjecture says there is a prime between n^2 and (n+1)^2 for every n. The stronger Oppermann's conjecture asks for primes in both (n^2 - n, n^2) and (n^2, n^2 + n). Proven results reach only primes between n^3 and (n+1)^3 for n >= exp(exp(32.537)) (Ingham; Dudek 2016; Cully-Hugill's thesis). The maximal-gap tables imply Legendre only up to about n = 10^10. Jonathan Sorenson and Jonathan Webster designed an algorithm in O(N log N log log N) time under Cramér's model. It sieves the progression 1 mod mR with a large prime R > n^(2/3), so each prime found is proven by a single Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge test, and it averages fewer than 3 primality tests per interval. arXiv:2401.13753 (Jan 2024) reported Oppermann's conjecture verified to N = 3.33 x 10^13. The published version ('An algorithm and computation to verify Legendre's conjecture up to 7 x 10^13', Res. Number Theory 11, article 4, 2025; code and data at github.com/sorenson64/olc) states N = 7.05 x 10^13 in its abstract (the title rounds it), after about half a year each on four Xeon Phi 7210s (256 cores) and a 192-core Xeon cluster. Johnston, Sorenson, Thomas and Webster ('Primes and almost primes between cubes', arXiv:2601.15564, v2 March 2026) adapted it to cubes and proved a prime in (n^3, (n+1)^3) for all n <= 2.54569 x 10^13, i.e. n^3 <= 1.649 x 10^40. That is a factor 10^5 beyond the n^3 <= 1.42 x 10^35 implied by interval estimates, at about 415,000 core-hours on Butler University clusters and NCI Gadi. Target: a strictly larger verified N for squares (Legendre) or for cubes.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a verification, with a primality proof for every prime used, that each interval (n^2, (n+1)^2) for 7.05 x 10^13 < n <= N_2 contains a prime, with N_2 >= 7.5 x 10^13, or that each (n^3, (n+1)^3) for 2.54569 x 10^13 < n <= N_3 contains a prime, with N_3 >= 2.7 x 10^13 (direction: max; a shorter contiguous extension is partial win p2, not a full win). Below the published bounds the claim may rely on Sorenson-Webster (squares, N = 7.05 x 10^13) and Johnston-Sorenson-Thomas-Webster (cubes); the new range is the claimant's own logged computation from the published bound + 1, with no gap. If a newer bound is published (re-check arXiv and the sorenson64 GitHub repositories immediately before claiming), N must exceed it by at least 7%. The claim publishes code and per-block logs (first and last n, the primes found or their offsets, and the BLS certificate data R and witness). The skeptic re-runs a random sample of at least 1,000 blocks spread over the new range with independently written code (different sieve, primality proved by PARI isprime or an independent Pocklington/BLS check), and a gap in coverage voids the claim. Oppermann's two-sided form counts on the squares side under the same bar.

partial_wins.statement: An independent re-verification, with different code and proved primes, of a contiguous block of at least 10^11 consecutive n inside the already-covered range (squares: [3.33e13, 7.05e13]; cubes: [2e13, 2.54569e13]), confirming the published single computation.

A verified contiguous block of at least 10^11 consecutive n directly above either record (squares from 7.05e13 + 1, or cubes from 2.54569e13 + 1), published with logs, as a contribution toward the next bound.

targets.verification_method: Reimplement the progression sieve and the BLS test in C with GMP (or Python with gmpy2 for sampled blocks). For sampled n, confirm that the reported prime p lies in the interval and that p - 1 has the stated prime factor R > p^(1/3) with a valid BLS witness, or prove p with PARI. Check that the blocks tile the claimed range.
angles: Start from the published MPI/GMP code (olc, cubes); the cube version uses m = the product of the first ten primes and no bit-mask sieve. A GPU port of the sieve-in-progression step is the obvious speed-up.
Squares and cubes share the machinery (Theorem 2.2 of arXiv:2601.15564 covers any exponent alpha > 3/2), so a single code base can attack both frontiers.

Cross-domain import (Monte Carlo variance reduction): Cramér's model predicts the number of candidates needed per interval; adaptive t (intervals per batch) tuned to cache, as the authors suggest, is the main lever.
pitfalls: Probable primes do not count: every prime used must be proved (BLS with R > p^(1/3), or another certificate).
Check the bound conventions: the cube record is stated both as n <= 2.54569e13 and as n^3 <= 1.649e40; compare in the same unit.
The squares record is N = 7.05 x 10^13 (published abstract), not the 7 x 10^13 in the paper's title or the olc README; a new range starting at 7e13 + 1 only re-covers known ground.
Wikipedia's Legendre page (Jan 2026) still quotes only the maximal-gap bound (n^2 = 2e19); the real record is Sorenson-Webster's.

targets.name: The 86th maximal prime gap: the first gap above 1854 (rank 85 confirmed at 1.0141 x 10^20 in May 2026)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (exhaustive gap search above the swept frontier, about 1.37e20 in late October 2026, with mingap filtering; a heuristic estimate puts the next maximal gap near 4.4e20); laptop-days for the partial-win gap hunt with primorial-offset sieving
targets.statement: A maximal prime gap is a gap between consecutive primes larger than every earlier gap (OEIS A005250/A002386). Proving a gap maximal needs an exhaustive search of everything below it. Oliveira e Silva, Herzog and Pardi searched exhaustively to 4 x 10^18 (rank 75, found 2009), and distributed and GPU searches carried it past 2^64. The 'Prime Number Gap Record Rising' table kept by Norman Luhn after Jens Kruse Andersen and Thomas Nicely (pzktupel.de, updated 2026-10-26) lists confirmed ranks 78-85: Steve Cole (2018), Bertil Nyman (found 2014, verified 2018), Craig Loizides (1552 and 1572, verified 2023-2024), Brian Kehrig (1676 at 2.07e19, 2024), Martin Raab and Kehrig (1724 at 6.81e19, Jan 2026), and Robert Smith and Kehrig (rank 85: 1854 at 101412319996363309069, merit 40.25, found 2026-05-08, verified 2026-05-22). Ranges above 1e20 are reserved and swept in the mersenneforum '1e20' prime-gap thread. By 2026-10-30, posts report completed ranges up to about 1.37e20 (for example BriK 1.365-1.37e20, mart_r 1.35-1.355e20) with no gap above 1854, and further reservations such as 1.38-1.39e20. The same table lists unconfirmed candidates: the smallest known start of a gap above 1854 is the 1858 at 39422251630462640179641871 (Loizides 2021, 3.94e25). Legendre's, Andrica's and Firoozbakht's conjectures and the Cramér-Shanks-Granville ratio are checked up to the same exhaustive frontier, so they are not separate targets here.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a pair of consecutive primes (p, p + g) with g > 1854, p > 1.0141e20, every integer strictly between them proved composite and both endpoints proved prime, together with exhaustive coverage of [101412319996363310923, p] (from the end of the rank-85 gap) showing no gap > 1854 there. Coverage can come from the claimant's own double-checked runs or from runs already published as double-checked in the mersenneforum gap-search threads, with every sub-range cited. The claim must match the table's notion of confirmation: rank 86 is shown as confirmed on the live pzktupel page, or the evidence meets the same standard (two independent sweeps of each range). The skeptic re-verifies the gap itself (minutes) and re-sweeps a random sample of at least 1% of the claimant's own coverage with independent code. The page is re-fetched before claiming. Direction: a new confirmed rank.

partial_wins.statement: A prime gap with g >= 1856 whose start p is below 3.9422e25, i.e. below the smallest known start of any gap exceeding 1854 on the live table. This lowers the known upper bound on the start of the 86th maximal gap. Endpoints must be proved prime (ECPP/APR-CL) and interior composites must be checked.
A gap g > 1854 with start below 1e22 (an unconfirmed rank-86 candidate in the plausible window), checked as in p1.

targets.verification_method: For the gap: gmpy2 is_prime on all interior numbers after a wheel sieve, and ECPP (PARI primecertify or ecpp-dj) on the endpoints. For coverage: re-run an independent segmented sieve with mingap filtering on random sub-ranges and compare the lists of gaps >= 1380 with the claimant's logs.
angles: For p1/p2: primorial-offset candidates N = m * P#/d - a with combined sieving (Troisi's combined_sieve) target merits of about 32-33 at 10^24-10^25, which the 1858 record shows is reachable.

For the exhaustive search: Kehrig-style GPU sieving with mingap filtering (report only gaps >= 1380, as the forum reservations do) is orders of magnitude faster than enumerating all primes. Coordinate ranges in the forum thread so the work does not duplicate live reservations.

Cross-domain import (extreme-value statistics): Kourbatov's record-gap heuristics (arXiv:1709.05508 on the nth record gap; the forum's own estimate puts rank 86 near 4.4e20) show where rank 86 is most likely to fall, so compute can go to that window first.
pitfalls: Not the merit table: the Prime Gap List (index entry prime-gap-list-merit-improvement) records the largest merit per gap size; maximality needs exhaustive coverage from below, which a merit record does not give.
Reservations are not coverage; only double-checked, published sweeps count.
Endpoints near 10^20-10^25 must be proved prime; BPSW alone is the forum's 'D' (double-checked, not deterministic) status, not proof.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Goldbach verification beyond 4 x 10^18 (Oliveira e Silva, Herzog and Pardi, 2012/2014)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (the 4e18 run took about 4.6 million work units on university grids and volunteer machines); laptop-days for a 10^13-10^14 block in the partial wins
targets.statement: The strong Goldbach conjecture (every even n > 2 is a sum of two primes) has been verified for all even n <= 4 x 10^18 by Tomas Oliveira e Silva, Siegfried Herzog and Silvio Pardi (Math. Comp. 83, 2014). Their distributed project page (sweet.ua.pt/tos/goldbach.html) gives 4 x 10^18 as the limit 'reached' on 2012-04-04, says the range is double-checked only up to 4 x 10^17 with no further double-checking planned, and credits contributors (DETUA, IEETA, PSU, INFN, Kraken and others) and a top-50 table of minimal Goldbach partitions. The record minimal partition is p = 9781 for n = 3325581707333960528 (Pardi). For each n the algorithm finds the least prime p with n - p prime, using a segmented sieve over intervals with a precomputed small-prime list. It also produces first-occurrence prime gaps. Wikipedia (edited 2026-09-27) still gives 4 x 10^18 with no later verification, and the project page has not moved since 2015. Two unreviewed claims go past it. Gridbach (gridbach.com, a browser volunteer-compute project; Show HN 2025-04-19) claimed 4 x 10^18 + 7 x 10^13. Its server accepts client results without independent checking, and its kernel is now in a private repository. A non-peer-reviewed preprint by Gosar, Das and Pardasani (preprints.org 202503.0949, March 2025) claims checks above 4 x 10^18 using probabilistic primality tests. Neither is a double-checked, published verification, so the accepted frontier has stood at 4 x 10^18 for about 14 years. Target: extend the verified range past 4 x 10^18.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a verification that every even n in (4 x 10^18, X] is a sum of two primes, for some X >= 4.1 x 10^18 (direction: max; a shorter contiguous extension is partial win p2, not a full win). The range below 4 x 10^18 may be taken from Oliveira e Silva, Herzog and Pardi (Math. Comp. 83, 2014); the new range is the claimant's own computation, and unverified volunteer or preprint claims above 4 x 10^18 (Gridbach, preprints.org 202503.0949) may not be relied on. Records are re-checked on the project page, Wikipedia and arXiv immediately before claiming. If a newer bound exists that is published with logs or code and independently double-checked, X must exceed it by at least 10^17; unverified claims do not raise the bar but must be cited. The claim publishes code and per-interval logs: for each interval, the count of even n, the maximum minimal partition p(n) and its location, and a checksum of the p(n) values. The skeptic re-runs at least 1,000 randomly chosen sub-intervals of length 10^9 with independently written code (different sieve, and n - p proved prime by a deterministic test such as Miller-Rabin with the first 12 prime bases, proven deterministic below 3.18 x 10^23) and must reproduce the logs exactly. A coverage gap voids the claim.

partial_wins.statement: An independent double-check of a contiguous block of length at least 10^14 inside (4 x 10^17, 4 x 10^18], which the project lists as single-checked only. It must reproduce the project's published statistics for that block (minimal-partition counts or first occurrences where published) or document a discrepancy.
An independently re-verified contiguous block of length at least 10^15 directly above 4 x 10^18, published with logs, as a step toward the next bound.

targets.verification_method: Re-implement the minimal-partition search: segmented sieve of the interval [n - P, n] (P about 10^4) against a precomputed prime table, so that for each even n the least p with n - p prime is found. Verify the reported p(n) values by recomputation on sampled sub-intervals, compare checksums, and check the tiling of the logs.
angles: Minimal partitions are tiny (below 10^4), so for each n only n - p for small primes p must be tested; sieve the window [n - 10^4, n] once per block of n and reuse it across all even n in the block.
GPU port: the per-n work is uniform and branch-light, unlike 2005-2012 CPU grids.

Cross-domain import (BOINC-style volunteer computing with redundancy): issue every work unit twice to independent hosts and accept only matching checksums. This is the double-check the project lacked above 4e17.
pitfalls: Do not 'win' by constructing one huge n with a large least Goldbach prime (easy with the CRT); records only count inside an exhaustively verified range.
BPSW is not a proof; below 3.3e24 use deterministic Miller-Rabin with a proven base set.
Hardware errors over long runs: insist on two independent runs per interval.

Claims past 4e18 exist but are unverified: Gridbach's volunteer server accepts results without checking them, and the 2025 preprints.org manuscript uses probabilistic tests and is not peer-reviewed. Do not start from their bounds; an independent re-check of their ranges is p2 material.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Riemann hypothesis verified beyond Platt-Trudgian's height 3.0001753328 x 10^12, or a rigorous window above it
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster for a new height record (Platt-Trudgian used rigorous interval arithmetic over about 1.2 x 10^13 zeros); laptop-days for a rigorous window of 10^5-10^6 zeros at large height
targets.statement: Riemann hypothesis verification: show that all zeros of zeta(s) with 0 < Im(s) <= T lie on the critical line and are simple. Rigorous record: David Platt and Tim Trudgian, 'The Riemann hypothesis is true up to 3 x 10^12' (Bull. LMS 2021, arXiv:2004.09765), T = 3.0001753328 x 10^12, using interval arithmetic with Turing's method and an Odlyzko-Schönhage-type multi-evaluation. It also re-checked earlier work. Gourdon and Demichel (2004) computed the first 10^13 zeros, plus 2 x 10^9 zeros near the 10^13-th, ..., 10^24-th zero, but without rigorous error control. Odlyzko computed zeros near index 10^23. The Wikipedia RH page (edited October 2026) states the Platt-Trudgian height as the record. Many explicit results (zero-free regions, explicit prime-counting bounds, Mossinghoff-Trudgian-Yang 2024) start from this height, so a larger T propagates. Target: a rigorous verification to a larger height, or a rigorously certified window of zeros above the record height.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a rigorous computation showing that every zero with 0 < gamma <= T is simple and on the critical line, for some T >= 3.3 x 10^12 (direction: max; at least 10% beyond the record, since a short window adjoining the record height is partial-win territory). The range up to 3.0001753328 x 10^12 may be taken from Platt-Trudgian (Bull. LMS 2021) if the claimant's computation starts at or below that height and applies Turing's method at the junction; everything above is the claimant's own computation. The claim gives the sign changes of Hardy's Z(t) located with interval arithmetic (ball arithmetic with proven error bounds for the Riemann-Siegel or Odlyzko-Schönhage evaluation), a count matching N(T) via Turing's method at each block boundary, and published code and logs. The skeptic recomputes randomly chosen blocks with independent software (Arb/FLINT or a separately written Riemann-Siegel evaluator with rigorous error terms) and checks the Turing-method inequalities. Re-check Wikipedia and arXiv for a newer height record before claiming; if one exists, T must exceed it by at least 10%.

partial_wins.statement: A rigorous window: for some T0 > 3.0001753328 x 10^12, a certificate that all zeros in [T0, T0 + H] (at least 10^5 consecutive zeros) are simple and on the line, with completeness by Turing's method at both ends, reproducible with Arb. Windows already rigorously certified in the literature do not count.
An independent rigorous re-verification of a block of at least 10^8 consecutive zeros below 3 x 10^12, by software different from Platt's, documented with timings.

targets.verification_method: Use FLINT/Arb's rigorous Platt-style local zero isolation (acb_dirichlet_platt_local_hardy_z_zeros or the equivalent) or an independent Riemann-Siegel evaluator with Gabcke's error bounds. Recount the sign changes, verify Turing's bound on S(t) at the window ends, and compare the count with the claimant's.
angles: Arb/FLINT already implements Platt's rigorous method for isolating zeros near a given height; use it for p1 at heights like 10^13 or 10^15 and measure cost per zero.
Gram-block bookkeeping: most of the work is counting sign changes in Gram blocks; only Rosser-rule failures need extra evaluations.

Cross-domain import (FFT-based multi-evaluation, as in radio astronomy channelisers): Odlyzko-Schönhage is a non-uniform FFT; modern GPU NUFFT libraries with rigorous error bounds could make a new height record feasible.
pitfalls: Non-rigorous floating-point zero counts (like Gourdon's 10^13) do not count; every evaluation needs a proven error bound.
Turing's method is required at block boundaries; locating sign changes alone does not exclude off-line zeros.
Do not confuse zero index n with height T: the record is a height, about 1.2 x 10^13 zeros.

targets.name: Prime-counting records: pi(10^30) (A006880), or a new pi(2^n), pi(e^n), pi(10^(n/2)) or 10^n-th prime value beyond Baugh and Walisch
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (or a 64+ core server for weeks to months; pi(10^29) took months); laptop-days only for checking smaller values
targets.statement: Exact values of pi(x) at large x come from combinatorial Meissel-Lehmer methods (Lagarias-Miller-Odlyzko, Deleglise-Rivat, Gourdon) and from analytic methods (Lagarias-Odlyzko; Platt; Büthe-Franke-Jost-Kleinjung, who computed pi(10^25) unconditionally in 2013). Kim Walisch's primecount, run by David Baugh, holds most records, each computed twice with different alpha tuning: pi(10^27) (2015), pi(10^28) (2020), and pi(10^29) = 1520698109714272166094258063 (2022-02-28). In sibling sequences the primecount records page (doc/Records.md, read 2026-10-30) lists pi(2^92) (2020) for A007053, pi(e^62) (2022) for A040014, pi(10^(53/2)) (2016) for A122121, and the 10^25-th prime (2022) for A006988. OEIS A006880's b-file ends at n = 29. pi(10^30) is unknown in OEIS and on the records page. The cheapest open cells are around 2-3 x 10^27: pi(e^63) (2.29e27) and pi(10^(55/2)) (3.16e27); even-indexed A122121 terms duplicate A006880. A double-checked new value in any of these sequences is a record.
targets.success_criterion: Success means a new exact value for an index absent from both the live primecount Records.md and the OEIS entry (A006880 n = 30; A007053 n >= 93; A040014 n >= 63; A122121 odd n >= 55, since even n duplicate A006880; A006988 n >= 26), re-fetched immediately before claiming. It must be computed twice with different internal parameters (primecount --double-check or two different algorithms), agree exactly, and come with logs and the software version. The skeptic re-runs the same and an independent code on smaller sanity points (for example pi(10^24) and pi(10^25)) to rule out a broken build, and checks the new value against the analytic estimate R(x) + O(sqrt(x) log x) under RH as a gross-error test. A full independent re-run is the gold standard if compute allows. Direction: a new term.

partial_wins.statement: Independent confirmation of one existing record (pi(10^28), pi(10^29), pi(2^92) or pi(e^62)) by a different algorithm (an analytic method such as Platt's or Büthe-Franke-Jost-Kleinjung's), agreeing exactly.

targets.verification_method: Build primecount from source; run the claimed x with and without --double-check (on 64+ cores this takes weeks for x near 3e27). Check that the reported values agree, and compare against li(x) - (1/2) li(sqrt(x)) and Riemann's R(x) for plausibility.
angles: primecount 7.x is much faster than the v6.4 backup build used for the records; on a modern 128-core server pi(e^63) is weeks, not months. Use a UPS and tee logs, as the records page advises.
Analytic route for p1: Platt's and Büthe et al.'s Weil-explicit-formula methods use zeta zeros plus a short sieve and are completely independent of Meissel-Lehmer, which makes an ideal cross-check.
Pick the cheapest open cell (e^63, about 2.29e27) before attempting 10^30.
pitfalls: OEIS b-files lag the records page (A122121's b-file ends at n = 52 while Records.md lists 10^(53/2)); check both.
Single runs do not count; Gourdon's 2002 pi(10^23) needed a correction of 14,037,804.
Do not confuse pi(x) at x = 10^n with the number of primes below 10^n (identical here, since 10^n is not prime), or A006988's 10^n-th prime with pi(10^n).

targets.name: ISPD 2024 large-scale global routing benchmarks: a lower official evaluator cost than the best published router
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours for benchmarks 0-4 and 7-11 (up to 3.3M nets, 64 GB RAM helps); the 10.6M and 59.3M-net cases need a large-memory machine (needs cluster for 6 and 13)
targets.statement: The ISPD 2024 contest, GPU/ML-Enhanced Large Scale Global Routing, was organised by Rongjian Liang, Wen-Hao Liu and colleagues at NVIDIA. It set routing as an optimisation problem on a 3D GCell grid graph, given as a .cap resource file and a .net pin-access file. Its benchmarks are Ariane, MemPool tile, group and cluster, NVDLA, BlackParrot and TeraPool, from 0.13M to 59.3M nets, each with a sample (public) and a rank (hidden) version. The contest ended in March 2024; the hidden benchmarks were released on 2024-03-26 and the evaluator is public. Quality is a single cost: wirelength cost + via cost + an exponential overflow penalty, with unit wire, via and per-layer overflow costs read from the .cap file. The best published scores, from Xiao, Lin, Liu, Duan, Ho and Young (InstantGR, IEEE TCAD 45(1), Jan 2026, Table III, official evaluator), are the lower of HeLEM-GR and InstantGR 2.0 for benchmarks 0-13: 0 Ariane_sample 19655065, 1 MemPool-Tile_sample 15094708, 2 NVDLA_sample 47938219, 3 BlackParrot_sample 112149983, 4 MemPool-Group_sample 395530319, 5 MemPool-Cluster_sample 1615066379, 6 TeraPool-Cluster_sample 18468687634 (HeLEM-GR), 7 Ariane_rank 22481586, 8 MemPool-Tile_rank 13736300, 9 NVDLA_rank 42936806, 10 BlackParrot_rank 109588812, 11 MemPool-Group_rank 380869353, 12 MemPool-Cluster_rank 1771528815, 13 TeraPool-Cluster_rank 11970080776. The 2024 contest winner scored, for example, 22602876 on Ariane_rank. GANGR (Nov 2025, arXiv 2511.17665) builds on InstantGR 1.0 and reports scores within about 0.002% of it, none below the values above.
targets.success_criterion: A global-routing solution file in the ISPD 2024 contest output format (GCell coordinates) for one of the 14 benchmarks above, as released by the organisers. The official ISPD 2024 evaluator (the contest's evaluation code, also redistributed as run/evaluator.cpp in cuhk-eda/InstantGR, compiled with g++ -O3 -std=c++17) must run to completion and print both 'Number of open nets : 0' and 'Number of incompleted nets : 0' (every net of the .net file present and connected: the evaluator still prints a cost when nets are missing from the file, so the second line is mandatory), and a total cost (wirelength cost + via cost + overflow cost) strictly below the value listed above for that benchmark. Direction: minimise. Runtime is not part of this criterion. The claim must also be below any later published value on the same benchmark found at claim time.

partial_wins.statement: A valid solution (0 open and 0 incompleted nets) for one of benchmarks 0-5 or 7-13 whose evaluator total cost is strictly below both HeLEM-GR's and InstantGR 1.0's published scores for that benchmark in InstantGR TCAD 2026 Table III (for example below 19716744 on Ariane_sample), but not below InstantGR 2.0's. On benchmark 6 HeLEM-GR's 18468687634 is itself the listed record, so this partial does not apply there.

A valid solution for benchmark 12 (MemPool-Cluster_rank) or 13 (TeraPool-Cluster_rank) whose total cost is strictly below the ISPD 2024 first-place team's score in the same table (1782191834 and 12528609838).

targets.verification_method: Fetch the .cap and .net files for the benchmark (Google Drive links on the ISPD24 contest page; record sha256). Compile the evaluator and run it on the claimed solution. Require 'Number of open nets : 0' and 'Number of incompleted nets : 0', then read 'total cost'. Calibrate by routing the bundled mempool_tile_rank case with InstantGR and checking the WL, via and overflow lines. For an independent re-check, re-implement the cost from evaluator.cpp: on each routing layer and GCell, demand = 2*wires + stacked vias; if capacity c > 0 add exp(0.5*(demand/2 - c)), if c = 0 and demand > 0 add exp(0.75*demand); multiply each layer's sum by that layer's overflow weight from the .cap; add wirelength times the unit length cost and vias times the unit via cost. Also check that every net of the .net file appears once with all pins connected. Compare with Table III of the TCAD paper. Minutes to an hour, depending on size.
angles: Start from the open-source InstantGR solution and run long CPU rip-up-and-reroute with negotiated congestion focused on the remaining overflow, which is often 30-40% of the cost on these cases.

Layer assignment is where HeLEM-GR and InstantGR differ (HeLEM-GR has fewer overflows, InstantGR 2.0 has fewer vias). A post-pass ILP or Lagrangian layer reassignment per 2D route can trade the two under the exact cost.
pitfalls: Benchmarks 0-6 are the *_sample versions and 7-13 the *_rank (hidden) versions, as numbered in InstantGR's Table I. The contest page's alpha/beta leaderboards on public benchmarks do not compare.
The evaluator asserts that there are no open nets, but a net missing from the output file is only counted as 'incompleted' and its cost is silently left out: require both counts to be 0.
Runtime-scaled contest scores are not comparable; use the raw total cost only.

There may be 2026 papers newer than this check; search before claiming. Chiang et al., 'Late Breaking Results: Scalable GPU-Friendly Parallelization for Sweep-Based Maze Routing' (DAC 2025), uses the ISPD'24 benchmarks and was not checked for scores (paywalled). The ISPD 2025 contest benchmarks and its timing-weighted scores are a different problem and do not compare.

targets.name: ICCAD 2022 CAD Contest Problem B (3D placement with D2D vertical connections): a shorter legal 3D placement than the best published
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (2.7k to 221k cells); the evaluator runs in seconds to minutes
targets.statement: ICCAD 2022 CAD Contest Problem B, set by Synopsys Taiwan (K.-S. Hu, I.-J. Lin, Y.-H. Huang, H.-Y. Chi, Y.-H. Wu and C.-F. C. Shen, ICCAD 2022), asks for a partition of a netlist into two face-to-face bonded dies, possibly in different technologies. Each die has its own maximum utilisation and row structure. Hybrid bonding terminals (HBTs) of fixed size and spacing must be placed for every cut net, and the objective is the total HPWL of both dies, counted through the terminals. The contest is over. The public cases (case2, case3, case4), the hidden cases (case2h, case3h, case4h) and the official evaluator are on the contest's Problems page (public Google Drive links). The best published results are from Liao, Zhao, Guo, Lin and Yu ('Analytical Die-to-Die 3-D Placement With Bistratal Wirelength Model and GPU Acceleration', IEEE TCAD 43(6) 2024; arXiv 2310.07424, Table II, official evaluator): case2 1944656, case2h 2462553, case3 30062713, case3h 26727327, case4 267400694 and case4h 289245472. In the same table the contest first place scored 2072075 / 2555461 / 30580336 / 27650329 / 281315669 / 301193374, the second place 274026687 on case4, and the analytical placer MTWA (Chen et al., DAC 2023) 2011447 / 2514597 / 30302643 / 27135602 / 272327370 / 296655075. CoPlace (Fu et al., ASP-DAC 2024) reports 270141472 on case4 and 292195136 on case4h, which is not better.
targets.success_criterion: A placement output in the contest's output format, for one of case2, case2h, case3, case3h, case4 or case4h as released on the ICCAD 2022 contest Problems page. The official Problem B evaluator must report it legal: every cell on a row of its assigned die with no overlap, per-die utilisation within the stated maximum, and terminals of the stated size and spacing inside the die. Its reported total wirelength (score) must be strictly below the value listed for that case from Liao et al. TCAD 2024 Table II. Direction: minimise. It must also be below any later published value for the same case found at claim time.

partial_wins.statement: A legal solution for any of the six cases whose evaluator score is strictly below every other published value for that case (the 1st, 2nd and 3rd place and MTWA columns of Liao et al. TCAD 2024 Table II, and CoPlace ASP-DAC 2024 Table II), but not below Liao et al.'s.
A legal solution for case4h with evaluator score below 301193374 (contest first place) using fewer HBTs than the 47712 of Liao et al.'s published case4h result.

targets.verification_method: Download the case files and the evaluator from the Problems page (record sha256). Run the official evaluator on the claimed output and read its legality report and wirelength. Independently, a short script parses the case and output files, recomputes each net's HPWL on each die through its terminal, and checks for overlaps, row alignment, utilisation and terminal spacing. Calibrate the script against the evaluator on a trivial legal placement before use. Compare with TCAD 2024 Table II. Minutes.
angles: Polish the published-style flow: alternate die reassignment of boundary cells (FM with an HPWL gain) and per-die 2D detailed placement (independent-set matching, global swap), then re-optimise terminal locations exactly per net (median of the two dies' pin boxes).
pitfalls: The evaluator binary and case files were updated several times in 2022 (hidden cases 11/4). Use the final versions and record the file hashes.
Scores are the official evaluator's wirelength, not a self-computed HPWL with different terminal handling. Two dies may use different technologies (cell sizes differ per die).

targets.name: ICCAD 2023 CAD Contest Problem B (3D placement with macros): a lower HPWL + 10 x HBT score than the best published
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (14k to 740k instances, 6 to 34 macros); the evaluator runs in minutes
targets.statement: ICCAD 2023 CAD Contest Problem B, '3D Placement with Macros' (Hu, Chi, Lin, Wu, Chen and Hsieh, Synopsys, ICCAD 2023), extends the 2022 face-to-face 3D placement problem to mixed-size designs with movable, rotatable macros on two dies, mostly in heterogeneous technologies. The official raw score is total D2D HPWL + beta * #HBTs, with beta = 10 in all cases. The contest is over. Cases case2, case2h1, case2h2, case3, case3h, case4 and case4h, the evaluator and the final results are linked from the 2023 Problems page. The contest first place (official) scored 16506066 / 18123044 / 18124483 / 98928220 / 122459408 / 1047716115 / 656528147; the second place was lower on case2 (16287082) and the third on case3h (117889705). Later records come from the CUHK group of Yibo Lin and Bei Yu: Zhao, Liao, Liu, Jiang, Lin and Yu, IEEE TCAD 44(2) 2025 (arXiv 2403.09070, Tables IV-V, CPU and GPU runs); and Liao, Zhao, Liu and Yu, 'Ultrafast Density Gradient Accumulation in 3D Analytical Placement with Divergence Theorem', ICCAD 2025 (paper Tables I-II, slides of Oct 28 2025). The lowest published score per case across them is case2 15443965 (ICCAD'25, GPU), case2h1 16569703 (TCAD'25, GPU), case2h2 16721757 (ICCAD'25, GPU), case3 97388944 (TCAD'25, CPU), case3h 107621590 (ICCAD'25 Table II, vanilla GPU), case4 1035731150 (ICCAD'25 Table II, vanilla GPU) and case4h 630601092 (ICCAD'25, GPU).
targets.success_criterion: A placement output in the contest's output format for one of the seven cases, using the files released on the ICCAD 2023 contest Problems page. The official Problem B evaluator must report it legal (no overlap, macros and cells on legal sites of their die, utilisation limits, terminal size and spacing). Its raw score, HPWL + 10 * #HBTs as reported by the evaluator, must be strictly below the lowest published value listed above for that case. Direction: minimise. It must also be below any later published value found at claim time.

partial_wins.statement: A legal solution whose evaluator raw score is strictly below the TCAD 2025 Table IV (GPU) value for that case (case2 15635352, case2h2 16820960, case3 98206238, case3h 108166770, case4 1037676163, case4h 635259476), but not below the lowest value listed in the statement for that case.
A legal solution for case4 or case4h whose raw score is strictly below the contest first place (1047716115 or 656528147).

targets.verification_method: Download the case files and the evaluator (Google Drive links on the 2023 Problems page; record sha256). Run the evaluator, then read legality and raw score. An independent script recomputes HPWL per die through the HBTs and counts HBTs (score = HPWL + 10 * HBT), checks macro and cell overlap and terminal spacing, and is calibrated first on a trivial legal placement. Compare with the published tables: TCAD 2025 Tables IV-V and ICCAD 2025 paper Tables I-II. Minutes.
angles: The published runs vary by up to 1% between CPU and GPU runs and between seeds of the same placer, so multi-start plus a careful detailed placement and macro-rotation MILP (as in TCAD 2025, Fig. 10) is a natural first lever.
pitfalls: case2h1 and case2h2 are two hidden versions of case2, and hidden case2 had a v1 and a v2 file. Name the exact file and hash.
Use the evaluator's raw score (HPWL + 10*HBT), not the contest's runtime-weighted ranking score.

Not checked at drafting (paywalled): Phan, Song, Huang, Fang, Chen, Hu and Shen, 'Multi-Die Concurrent Global Placement with Macro Flipping-aware Wirelength Model for 3D-ICs' (ISQED 2026), which reports up to 5% HPWL reduction on these benchmarks, and MOMC3D (Huang, Zhao and Liu, IEEE TCAD 2025, ICCAD 2023 case2). Read their tables before claiming; if either lists a lower raw score, that value is the bar.

targets.name: ISPD 2026 contest (post-placement buffering and sizing): a result that dominates the per-design winner on every non-runtime metric
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days per design (OpenROAD global route and OpenSTA on 0.1M to 1M-instance ASAP7 designs; evaluation flows of 10 to 1,700 s)
targets.statement: The ISPD 2026 contest, 'Post-Placement Buffering and Sizing', was organised by Andrew B. Kahng, Sayak Kundu, Yiting Liu and Davit Markarian (UCSD), Zhiang Wang (Fudan) and Seokhyeong Kang and Seonghyeon Park (POSTECH). Starting from a placed, debuffered ASAP7 netlist, a tool may only insert buffers and inverters and resize cells (drive strength and VT). Results must pass a legality check and a logic equivalence check before an open OpenROAD global-routing and OpenSTA flow reports TNS, dynamic and leakage power, cap/slew/fanout violation sums, GR overflow and average displacement. The final leaderboard (results announced 2026-03-18) gives full rows for the top three teams. Per-design top rows with published numbers are: ariane, Team29: TNS -18254.21 ns, dynamic 140.20 mW, leakage 4.80, slew over 46.91, disp 0.02; bsg_chip, Team33: TNS -44875.21, 747.20 mW, cap over 98.01, slew over 40659.66; jpeg_encoder, Team33: TNS -488.89, 93.60 mW, no violations; ariane_h2 (hidden), Team33: TNS -3271.86, 157.14 mW, slew over 993.40. Each contest score mixes in tool runtime, so this target counts quality only. The winners were IRISLab (NTU and NTUST: Huang, Fang Chiang, Kuo, Liang, Jiang), PTSD (NTHU: Pai, Tsai, Chen, Huang, Xu, Wang) and HLFC (NTHU: Fu, Chiu, Hung, Lin, Wang).
targets.success_criterion: An output .v netlist and .def for one of ariane, ariane_v2, bsg_chip, bsg_chip_v2, jpeg_encoder, jpeg_encoder_v2 or ariane_h2, from the public or hidden benchmarks on the contest page. The official evaluation flow in ABKGroup/ISPD26-Contest must report it legal and logically equivalent: scripts/evaluation.tcl as called by the base design's eval.sh (scripts/ariane, scripts/bsg_chip or scripts/jpeg_encoder; for the _v2 and _h2 designs, the same script pointed at that variant's benchmark files), run in the provided Docker image, plus the equiv_check flow. On every one of TNS, dynamic power, leakage power, Cap/Slew/Fanout Over Sum, Max and Total GR overflow, and Avg Disp, it must be no worse than the README's final-leaderboard row of the per-design top team. That team is named in 'Leaderboard per design' and must have a published row: Team29 for ariane, Team33 for the others. TNS must be strictly better (less negative). Runtime is excluded. The README is re-fetched at claim time.

partial_wins.statement: A legal, equivalent result that dominates the 2nd-place (Team31) published row on all non-runtime metrics listed above for one of these designs, with strictly better TNS.

A legal, equivalent result on ariane_h1, bsg_chip_h1 or bsg_chip_h2 that dominates all three published final rows (Teams 33, 31 and 29) on every non-runtime metric with strictly better TNS than the best of them. Team6, the unpublished per-design leader there, may still be better, so this is a partial win only.

targets.verification_method: Clone ABKGroup/ISPD26-Contest (ASAP7 platform, eval scripts, equivalence scripts, Dockerfile). Download the benchmarks from the contest page and record hashes. Run the design's eval.sh in the provided Docker image (or with a locally built OpenROAD of the pinned version) on the claimed .v/.def. Confirm that the legality and equivalence steps pass, then read the reported metrics. Calibrate by running the pre_opt contest.def and the OpenROAD RSZ baseline script, and check that they match the README's pre_opt and RSZ rows. Compare metric by metric with the live README rows. An hour or more per large design.
pitfalls: A contest 'Design Score' includes tool and flow runtime and so depends on hardware. This target is quality-only dominance; never claim a higher contest score.

Only buffer and inverter insertion and sizing (drive strength and VT) are allowed. Any other netlist change fails equivalence; moving macros or I/Os, changing the floorplan or PDN, or placing logic gates in soft blockages fails legality.
The README was last changed on 2026-05-03 and the organisers say next year's evaluation will be stricter. Use the live table and re-fetch it at claim time.

The per-design 'Top Team' is chosen by the runtime-weighted Design Score, so other published rows can be better on single metrics (Team33's ariane TNS -6377.76 beats Team29's); the criterion is dominance of the named row only.

The repo's eval.sh scripts hard-code DESIGN_NAME for the four base designs only; for a _v2 or hidden design, record exactly how the base script was pointed at the variant's files so the skeptic can rerun it.

The ISPD 2027 contest (ABKGroup/ISPD27-Contest, MCMM post-CTS buffering and sizing, prizes, final deadline 2027-03-20) is a different, live setter challenge. A result here is not an ISPD 2027 entry, and agents never register or submit to it; that is a human decision.

targets.name: Fractional chromatic number of the plane: an explicit finite unit-distance graph with fractional chromatic number above 4 (best explicit: about 3.9898)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exact LP/ILP on graphs of 1,000-20,000 vertices; exact algebraic coordinates)
targets.statement: Lower bounds on chi_f(R^2), the fractional chromatic number of the plane's unit-distance graph, come from finite unit-distance graphs G via chi_f(R^2) >= chi_f(G); Matolcsi, Ruzsa, Varga and Zsamboki showed the supremum over finite G equals the geometric fractional chromatic number and the Hall ratio of the plane. Explicit finite graphs climbed slowly: Moser spindle 7/2, Mahan 144/41, Fisher-Ullman 32/9, Cranston-Rabern 76/21 (2017), Bellitto-Pecher-Sedillot 3.899 (607 vertices), and unpublished computations of Jaan Parts about 3.9898 (1057 vertices, Polymath16 comment, 2022). Matolcsi, Ruzsa, Varga and Zsamboki (arXiv 2311.10069) proved chi_f(R^2) >= 4 via a 27-vertex configuration with geometric fractional chromatic number 4, noting no finite subgraph was known to reach 4. Duecz and Varga (arXiv 2606.28157, June 2026) added two vertices (G29, geometric value > 4.0007 by a rational dual) and proved that a finite unit-distance graph with independence ratio below 1/4 exists, answering Erdos's 1987 question and giving chi_f(R^2) > 4; but their finite graph is described as astronomically large and is not written down. The upper side is chi_f(R^2) <= 1/delta_Croft < 4.36 from Croft's 1967 periodic set of density 0.22936... Target: write down an explicit, checkable finite unit-distance graph with chi_f > 4.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit finite graph G with vertex coordinates given exactly (integers or rationals combined with stated square roots, or minimal polynomials with isolating boxes) such that (i) every listed edge has Euclidean length exactly 1, verified by exact symbolic arithmetic (sympy or SageMath, not floating point); (ii) chi_f(G) > 4, certified by rational vertex weights y >= 0 with sum(y) > 4 and max over independent sets I of y(I) <= 1, the latter confirmed by two independent exact maximum-weight-independent-set or ILP solvers (exact rational arithmetic, e.g. SCIP exact or a clique solver on the complement). The uniform-weight special case |V|/alpha(G) > 4, with alpha certified the same way, also suffices (it implies chi_f(G) > 4 but is stronger). Listing fewer than all unit pairs is allowed (it can only lower chi_f). arXiv 2606.28157 and a literature search (OpenAlex citations of it and of arXiv 2311.10069), rerun before claiming, must show no explicit finite example with chi_f > 4 published earlier.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit finite unit-distance graph with certified chi_f(G) >= 3.99, above Parts's approximately 3.9898 (1057 vertices, unpublished, Polymath16 comment of 2022-09-21), verified as in the success criterion.

An explicit finite unit-distance graph with certified chi_f(G) >= 4 exactly (arXiv 2311.10069 and 2606.28157 report no finite subgraph reaching 4 before the existence proof of 2606.28157), verified as in the success criterion.

A finite point configuration whose geometric fractional chromatic number, in the LP framework of arXiv 2311.10069, is certified by a rational dual solution to be at least 4.001. This is above Duecz-Varga's certified 4.0007 for G29 and their unverified estimates of about 4.0009. Checked by rebuilding the LP from exact coordinates and verifying the dual in rational arithmetic.

targets.verification_method: Recompute all edge lengths symbolically; rebuild the independent-set LP/ILP from the edge list; check the rational weights and solve maximum-weight independent set exactly with two solvers. Minutes to hours for a few thousand vertices.
angles: Start from Matolcsi et al.'s G27 and Duecz-Varga's G29: their geometric (weighted, congruence-invariant) LP certificate indicates which vertex classes need many rotated/translated copies; build the finite graph by taking the Minkowski-style closure of G29 under a finite set of rotations in the Moser lattice and solving the plain fractional LP with column generation.

Column generation: the fractional colouring LP has one column per independent set; generate columns by exact max-weight independent set (the pricing problem) and stop when no column has reduced cost below 0, as Cranston-Rabern and Bellitto et al. did.
Graph minimisation (Parts, arXiv 2010.12665): once a large certificate is found, delete vertices while chi_f stays above 4.
pitfalls: Floating-point coordinates are not a proof that distances equal 1; unit-distance graphs in the Moser lattice need exact arithmetic in Q(sqrt3, sqrt11, ...).
The geometric fractional chromatic number of a configuration is not the fractional chromatic number of a finite graph; only p3 accepts it.
Measurable versus ordinary: m1(R^2) < 1/4 (Ambrus et al. 2023) bounds the measurable fractional chromatic number, not chi_f of a finite graph.

targets.name: A Type 2 cubic graph of girth at least 5 (total chromatic number 5), open since Cavicchioli et al. 2003
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days for constructions and checks; needs cluster for exhaustive extensions beyond 32 vertices
targets.statement: A total colouring colours vertices and edges so that adjacent or incident elements differ. Rosenfeld showed every cubic graph has total chromatic number 4 (Type 1) or 5 (Type 2). Cavicchioli et al. (2003) asked for the smallest Type 2 snark of girth at least 5. Brinkmann, Preissmann and Sasaki (DMTCS, 2015) built the first Type 2 snarks (all of girth 4, every even order >= 40), and split the question: Question 2, what is the smallest Type 2 cubic graph of girth at least 5? Their computer search showed all cubic graphs of girth 5 on up to 32 vertices are Type 1, so such a graph needs at least 34 vertices; they note that no Type 2 cubic graph of girth greater than 4 is known, and ask (Question 3) whether some girth forces Type 1. Later work by Sasaki, Dantas, de Figueiredo, Araujo and others (2023-2025, Kochol superpositions) produced more Type 2 snarks, still of girth 4, and describes Type 2 snarks as rare and hard to construct. Target: one explicit Type 2 cubic graph of girth >= 5.
targets.success_criterion: An explicit simple cubic graph G (edge list, graph6) with girth >= 5 (checked by BFS) that has no total 4-colouring, certified by an UNSAT result with a DRAT/LRAT proof checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr for a CNF the skeptic regenerates (variables for colours of vertices and edges; constraints for adjacency and incidence; symmetry breaking only by fixing the colours at one vertex and its three edges), confirmed by a second independent method (e.g. Brinkmann-style strong 4-edge-colouring test, or a second solver and encoding). A literature search (OpenAlex citations of DMTCS 2111), rerun before claiming, must show no Type 2 cubic graph of girth >= 5 published earlier.

partial_wins.statement: A rerunnable exhaustive proof that every connected cubic graph of girth >= 6 on 34 vertices is Type 1, with published generator and checker code and a graph count equal to OEIS A014374 at 34 vertices (93,990,692,595).

A rerunnable exhaustive proof that every connected cubic graph of girth >= 5 on 34 vertices is Type 1 (raising the bound to >= 36), with published generator and checker code, its graph count cross-checked by a second generator (OEIS A014372 lists counts only up to 32 vertices).

targets.verification_method: Girth check; regenerate the total-colouring CNF; check the DRAT/LRAT proof; second method agreement. Seconds to minutes for graphs of a few hundred vertices.
angles: Lemma 1 of Brinkmann et al.: a cubic graph is Type 1 iff it has a strong 4-edge-colouring (a proper 4-edge-colouring in which the two ends of every edge together see all 4 colours); encode only edge colours, which shrinks the SAT instance.

Gadget gluing: their Type 2 snarks are junctions of Type 2 bricks of girth 4; search for girth-5 bricks (cubic semi-graphs with four semi-edges) whose total colourings force the same boundary obstruction.
Search high-girth Cayley and voltage-lift cubic graphs (girth 5-7) with SAT, which scales to thousands of vertices.
pitfalls: Type 2 is about total colouring, not edge colouring (Class 2); snarks are Class 2 but almost all are Type 1.
Girth 4 examples already exist; the girth >= 5 requirement is the whole problem.

targets.name: Chromatic numbers of lattices (Voronoi graphs): settle a 5-dimensional primitive lattice, the Coxeter-Todd lattice K12 or the Barnes-Wall lattice BW16
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (SAT on finite induced subgraphs of Cayley graphs of Z^n; periodic colourings of discrete tori)
targets.statement: The chromatic number chi(L) of a lattice L in R^n is the chromatic number of its Voronoi graph, the Cayley graph on L generated by the strict Voronoi vectors (equivalently, colour the Voronoi tessellation so that cells sharing a facet differ). Dutour Sikiric, Madore, Moustrou and Vallentin (arXiv 1907.09751, J. London Math. Soc. 2021) settled all lattices of dimension 2 and 3, all irreducible root lattices and their duals (with chi(D_n) reduced to the halved cube) and the Leech lattice (4096), and named K12 and BW16 as the next natural cases, expecting the spectral bound to be close. Vallentin, Weissbach and Zimmermann (arXiv 2407.03513, Indag. Math. 2024) determined all 4-dimensional lattices (52 parallelohedra, 16 Voronoi-graph types, maximum 7) by finite-subgraph SAT lower bounds and periodic upper bounds, and report that for dimension 5 their computations 'remained inconclusive', the bounds being far apart; they also ask whether 2^(n-1) colours always suffice for n >= 3. Target: an exact, certified chromatic number for a new lattice.
targets.success_criterion: Exact determination chi(L) = c, not published before, for L either (a) a 5-dimensional lattice whose Voronoi cell is one of the 222 primitive 5-dimensional parallelohedra (explicit Gram matrix) and whose Voronoi graph is not isomorphic to that of A_5^* (the permutohedron; chi(A_5^*) = 6 by arXiv 1907.09751), or (b) K12 or BW16 (explicit Gram matrix from the Nebe-Sloane catalogue). Upper bound: an explicit c-colouring of a discrete torus L/M (M a sublattice given by a basis) checked against every strict Voronoi vector. Lower bound: an explicit finite induced subgraph of the Voronoi graph certified non-(c-1)-colourable by an UNSAT result with a DRAT/LRAT proof checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr for a CNF the skeptic regenerates (as in arXiv 2407.03513), or, for (b) only, a written proof by a clique, the sphere-packing bound (Theorem 4.1 of arXiv 1907.09751) or a spectral bound, every numerical input certified in exact or interval arithmetic. The strict Voronoi vectors must be recomputed independently (Voronoi's criterion: v is strict iff +-v are the only shortest vectors in v + 2L). A literature search (citations of arXiv 2407.03513 and 1907.09751), rerun before claiming, must show the value not published before.

partial_wins.statement: For one primitive 5-dimensional lattice whose Voronoi graph is not isomorphic to that of A_5^*, certified lower and upper bounds (as in the success criterion) differing by exactly 1.

targets.verification_method: Recompute strict Voronoi vectors from the Gram matrix; check the periodic colouring on the torus; regenerate the finite-subgraph CNF and check the proof.
angles: Use sublattice cosets: if M is a sublattice with no strict Voronoi vector in M, then L/M gives a periodic colouring with [L:M] colours; search sublattices with SAT on L/kL for small k.

Lower bounds: grow finite induced subgraphs greedily around a dense clique and use symmetric (automorphism-orbit) encodings; sphere-packing (Theorem 4.1 of 1907.09751) and spectral bounds give targets.
pitfalls: The Voronoi graph uses strict Voronoi vectors (facet vectors), not all vectors of the two shortest norms.
Isomorphic Voronoi graphs from different Gram matrices are the same problem: check combinatorial type before claiming a new lattice.

targets.name: Meunier's s-stable Kneser conjecture: certify chi = n - sk + s for open small cases with odd s (e.g. all of (k, s) = (3, 5), n = 16..21)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (SAT with proof logging on graphs of 100 to 3,000 vertices)
targets.statement: A k-subset S of the cycle Z_n is s-stable if any two of its elements are at cyclic distance at least s; the s-stable Kneser graph KG(n,k)_{s-stab} joins disjoint s-stable k-sets. For n >= sk it is (n - sk + s)-colourable, and Frederic Meunier (2011) conjectured equality, extending Schrijver's s = 2 theorem. Proven: n = sk + 1 (Meunier), s even (Peng-An Chen 2015), s >= 4 with n >= 2s(k-1) + 2 (Jakob Jonsson 2012), k = 2 (Daneshpajouh, Meunier and Mizrahi), and, by Wei-Chia Chen, Alex Parker and Shira Zerbib (arXiv 2607.12912, July 2026), s = 3 with k >= 4 and n >= k^3 + 3k^2, and k = s = 3 (small n by SAT). Still open: odd s with k >= 3 and sk + 2 <= n below these thresholds, e.g. (k,s) = (3,5) for n = 17..21, (3,7) for n = 23..29, (4,5) for n = 22..31, and (4,3) for n = 14..111. Each case is a finite graph: (n,k,s) = (21,3,5) has 196 vertices and conjectured value 11; (20,4,3) has 825 vertices and value 11. Fractional and clique bounds are far below the conjectured values, so the lower bound needs a real certificate.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) every open n for one pair (k,s) with s odd, k >= 3 (e.g. (3,5): n = 17..21; or (3,7): n = 23..29) certified, each by an UNSAT result with a DRAT/LRAT proof checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr for the CNF 'KG(n,k)_{s-stab} is (n-sk+s-1)-colourable' regenerated by the skeptic, plus the explicit (n-sk+s)-colouring; or (b) a counterexample: an explicit proper colouring with fewer than n - sk + s colours for some open triple. Symmetry breaking only by fixing colours on a clique of pairwise disjoint s-stable sets. arXiv 2607.12912 and a citation search, rerun before claiming, must show the cases not already proven.

partial_wins.statement: One open triple with conjectured value n - sk + s >= 10 (e.g. (20,3,5), (21,3,5), (19,4,3)) certified as in the success criterion.
All triples (n, 4, 3) with 14 <= n <= 20 certified as in the success criterion (conjectured values 5..11).
One open triple with odd s >= 5 and k >= 4 (e.g. (n,4,5) with 22 <= n <= 31), or with s = 3, k = 5 and 19 <= n <= 199, certified as in the success criterion.

targets.verification_method: Rebuild the vertex set and edges from (n,k,s); regenerate the CNF; check the proof (minutes to hours); check the explicit colouring.
angles: Use the dihedral symmetry of Z_n: lex-leader symmetry breaking, or fix the colouring on the n rotations of one stable set, and cube-and-conquer.
Topological lower bounds (Z_2-index of box complexes) could give a computer-assisted proof via a certified simplicial computation instead of SAT.
pitfalls: n = sk is trivial (the graph is complete on s vertices); n = sk + 1 (Meunier), s even, k = 2, s >= 4 with n >= 2s(k-1)+2, s = 3 with k >= 4 and n >= k^3+3k^2, and k = s = 3 are already proven.
Use the cyclic distance min(j-i, n+i-j), not the linear distance (that defines a different, 'almost stable' graph, settled by P.-A. Chen in arXiv 1711.06621).

The smallest open cases are easy: a scouting run for this entry (plain CNF, CaDiCaL via PySAT, one fixed vertex) refuted the (n-sk+s-1)-colourings for (n,k,s) = (14..16, 4, 3) and (17..19, 3, 5) in under a minute each, with time growing about 50-fold per step of n; these are not claimed, and the partial wins are set above them. Check the literature for computer verifications of small cases before claiming.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Neumann-Lara conjecture: a planar oriented graph that cannot be split into two acyclic sets, or verification beyond 26 vertices
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days for extending the verification; counterexample search open-ended
targets.statement: Neumann-Lara (1985) conjectured that every planar oriented graph (no digons) has dichromatic number at most 2: its vertices split into two sets each inducing an acyclic digraph. It is the directed analogue of the Four Colour Theorem and remains open; Li and Mohar proved it for digirth at least 4. Knauer and Valicov (arXiv 1712.06143, European J. Combin.) reduced it, by planar duality, to finding in planar cubic 3-connected digraphs a perfect matching without a directed cut; only duals of non-Hamiltonian triangulations matter, and using McKay's lists of non-Hamiltonian planar cubic graphs they verified the conjecture for all planar graphs on at most 26 vertices, all 4-connected planar graphs on at most 27 vertices and 4-connected planar graphs of minimum degree 5 on at most 39 vertices. They also show a counterexample would follow from a planar 3-connected cubic digraph with an 'a-arc', and found none among the girth-4 planar cubic graphs with an a-edge up to 38 vertices. Target: a counterexample, or a larger verified range.
targets.success_criterion: A full win is an explicit planar oriented graph D (arc list plus a planar embedding as a rotation system) such that (i) planarity is confirmed by two independent testers and the rotation system satisfies Euler's formula, (ii) D has no digons, and (iii) D has no vertex 2-partition into acyclic sets, certified by an UNSAT result with a DRAT/LRAT proof checked by drat-trim or cake_lpr for a CNF the skeptic regenerates (acyclicity encoded by, e.g., per-class topological-order variables or one clause per directed cycle when D is small). Knauer-Valicov arXiv 1712.06143 and a citation search, rerun before claiming, must still describe the conjecture as open.

partial_wins.statement: A rerunnable exhaustive verification that the conjecture holds for all planar graphs on 27 vertices (equivalently, by the Knauer-Valicov reduction, for orientations of all triangle-free non-Hamiltonian 3-connected planar cubic graphs on 50 vertices), with published code and the list of cubic graphs produced by two independent generators (e.g. plantri plus a Hamiltonicity filter, and McKay's lists where they reach) agreeing.
Verification for all 4-connected planar graphs on 28 vertices, or for 4-connected planar graphs of minimum degree 5 on 40 vertices, rerunnable as in p1.

targets.verification_method: Planarity and embedding checks; CNF regeneration and proof check for a counterexample; for p1-p2, rerun the published enumeration and compare counts with plantri/McKay data.
angles: Work in the dual: only non-Hamiltonian cyclically 4-edge-connected planar cubic graphs (Holton-McKay style lists) can be duals of minimal counterexamples; for each, decide by SAT whether some orientation makes every perfect matching contain a directed cut.
Eulerian triangulations are named by Knauer-Valicov as the natural open special case: search orientations of Eulerian triangulations first.
pitfalls: Digons (pairs of opposite arcs) are excluded; with digons the statement is false.
A Hamiltonian dual already gives a partition into two induced trees, so random triangulations are useless search space.

targets.name: Normal-play Sprouts: settle the 63-spot game or another open n <= 105 (SPOTS frontier, 2026)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (SPOTS solved its hardest position in 24 days on 512 cores; n = 0 or 3 mod 6 are the hardest classes); a proof checker is laptop-hours
targets.statement: Sprouts (Conway and Paterson, 1967) starts with n spots in the plane. A move joins two spots (or a spot to itself) with a curve that crosses nothing and puts a new spot on it; no spot may have more than 3 lines. In normal play the last player to move wins. Conway, Mollison and Applegate, Jacobson and Sleator (1991) settled n <= 11, Purinton n = 12-14 (2006), and Lemoine and Viennot's Glop (2007-2011) all n <= 44 plus 46, 47 and 53. In 2025-2026 Cizek, Balko and Schmid's massively parallel proof-number solver SPOTS (arXiv:2511.10339, v2 9 Feb 2026, AAAI 2026; code github.com/cizektom/spots) added 42 outcomes: all n <= 62 and the 27 least complex cases with 63 <= n <= 104, 89 known in all. The 32 outcomes from its sequential solver were fully verified with Lemoine and Viennot's procedure; the README says the 10 from the parallel solver could not be fully verified and were only spot-checked on simpler positions. Wikipedia's Sprouts table and Table 2 of the paper (re-read 2026-10-30) still leave 63, 66, 69, 72, 75, 78, 81, 84, 87, 90, 93, 96, 99, 101, 102 and 105 unknown. The Sprouts conjecture (the first player wins exactly when n = 3, 4 or 5 mod 6) predicts wins at 63, 69, ..., 99, 101 and 105 and losses at 66, 72, ..., 102. Lemoine and Viennot's extended conjecture says the n-spot Grundy number is 0 for n = 0, 1, 2 mod 6 and 1 otherwise. Nowakowski's Unsolved Problems column (Games of No Chance 6, 2025, problem C2) still asks for the analysis to be extended. Settle any one open n.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: the normal-play outcome (first-player win or loss) of the n-spot starting position in the plane, for one n that is unknown at verification time in Wikipedia's Sprouts table and in the SPOTS repository and paper (on 2026-10-30: 63, 66, 69, 72, 75, 78, 81, 84, 87, 90, 93, 96, 99, 101, 102, 105), with both of the following. (1) A certificate (a solution tree, or a database of proven Grundy numbers in a documented format as SPOTS publishes) accepted by a checker that shares no code with the solver. The checker regenerates the full child list at every node where all children must be refuted, and recomputes every Grundy-number or land-splitting reduction it uses. (2) The outcome reproduced by a second, independent program (for example Lemoine and Viennot's verifier, or Glop/SPOTS run on the certificate). An outcome that contradicts the Sprouts conjecture is an equally full win.

partial_wins.statement: The first fully independent re-verification of one of the ten outcomes obtained only by parallel SPOTS, which the SPOTS README says could not be fully verified (shaded in Table 2 of arXiv:2511.10339v2; they appear to be the ten entries with proof size 1e9: n = 57, 60, 89, 94, 95, 97, 98, 100, 103, 104). The checker shares no code with SPOTS or Glop, walks the published certificate with its own move generator and agrees with the published outcome; a demonstration that one of these outcomes is wrong also counts.

targets.verification_method: Write an independent Sprouts move generator in Lemoine-Viennot string notation. Test it by reproducing the outcomes for n <= 14 from scratch, and compare child counts of random small positions against Glop or SPOTS. Then walk the certificate: at each node where the player to move must lose, regenerate every child and check that each is a proven win; at each winning node, check that the named child is legal and proven lost. Recompute any Grundy number used to replace a land (normal-play Sprague-Grundy sums are valid). Finally, confirm the outcome with a second program and check that n is still listed as unknown.
angles: Odd n = 5 mod 6 such as 101 needs only one proven-losing child at the root. Try first the child that links one spot to itself and splits the rest into two equal regions, the move that worked for earlier refutations.
Warm-start from the SPOTS Grundy-number databases, so every land already solved for n <= 104 costs nothing.

SPOTS reports that n = 3 mod 6 positions are the most complex. Among the open cases, the 0 mod 6 losses (66, 72, ...) need every root child refuted: order the children by Lemoine-Viennot 'lives' and share a transposition table.
pitfalls: Normal play only: Grundy-number reductions are valid here but not in the misere game (misere-sprouts-21-spots is a separate target).
The Glop records page lags behind SPOTS; use Wikipedia's table and the SPOTS repository as the authority for which n are open.
A single solver run proves nothing, because a move-generator bug gives a wrong outcome. Two independent implementations are required.
Crowding: the SPOTS team is actively extending these results. Re-check arXiv and the repository before and after a run.

targets.name: Grundy's game: certify an eventual period (or that of 0.6111...), beyond Flammenkamp's 2^39 computation
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster for a new range (Flammenkamp's 2012 run took 25 days to reach 2.85e11; his table now reaches 2^39 = 5.5e11); laptop-days for p1 with a sparse-space evaluator
targets.statement: In Grundy's game a move splits one heap into two non-empty heaps of different sizes. Its Sprague-Grundy sequence (OEIS A002188) begins 0,0,0,1,0,2,1,0,2,... Berlekamp, Conway and Guy (Winning Ways) conjectured that it is eventually periodic, and Nowakowski's Unsolved Problems column (Games of No Chance 6, 2025, problem A2) still lists it as unsolved. Dan Hoey reached 1.1e10 (1995-96), and Achim Flammenkamp reached 2^35 (2002) and 284,944,236,543 (2012-11-25). Flammenkamp's octal-games table (last updated 2026-10-28) and its statistics file stat_grundys now give all G(n) for n < 2^39: 1,287 rare values (the sparse set), the last rare one at n = 48,399,022, depth 51,335,130, largest value 297 (first at n = 21,544,358,589), and 42 zeroes, the last at 1,222. No period. The same table lists 0.6111... (remove one token leaving one or two heaps, or remove a whole heap of at least two tokens), computed to 2^43 with 171 rare values, the last at 2,026, also without a period. The bank's octal entry (octal-games-unsettled-periodicity) excludes exactly these two games. Couples-are-forever is not included here, because Flammenkamp shows it is a shifted copy of the octal game .6, which that entry covers. Flammenkamp remarks that if the rare values die out the sequence must become periodic. Because a heap may be split anywhere, the Guy-Smith window for finite octal games does not apply as stated; a residue argument suggests that checking G(n + p) = G(n) for n0 <= n < 2*n0 + 2p would suffice, but whatever window is used must be proved or cited.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: for Grundy's game or for 0.6111..., an explicit preperiod n0 and period p such that G(n + p) = G(n) for every n >= n0, established by both of the following. (1) An exact check of every value over the finite window that the sufficient condition requires, by a program that shares no code with the claimant's. (2) The sufficient condition itself: either a theorem already published in a refereed source, with its hypotheses verified for this game, or a theorem proved in the submission and formalised in Lean 4, Coq or Isabelle. The recomputed sequence must match Flammenkamp's frequency tables (nim/stat_grundys or nim/stat_.6111) up to his max n, and octal.html must still show the game without a period at verification time. A machine-checked proof that either game is never periodic is an equally full win. A long repeated block or a hash match without (2) does not count.
