partial_wins.statement: The first published independent reproduction of Flammenkamp's Grundy's-game statistics up to heap size 2^35 - 1 (the first table of nim/stat_grundys: the count of every value, the 1,287 rare values and their positions), by a program that shares no code with his or with the programs of Tyler Satchel Orden and Udo Sprute that supported his table in 2026, matching exactly; a demonstration that an entry is wrong also counts.

Grundy's game computed exactly up to 2^40, one doubling beyond Flammenkamp's 2^39, reproduced by a second independent program. Publish the full frequency table, the sparse set, the largest value and its first index; the range up to 2^39 must match stat_grundys. A new rare value beyond n = 48,399,022 found on the way is reported as part of this win.

targets.verification_method: Write an evaluator from the definition (G(n) = mex of G(a) xor G(n - a) for 1 <= a < n/2) and test it on OEIS A002188 (b-file to 20,000 and a.txt to 200,000). Then run it with a sparse-space acceleration whose common/rare split is re-derived, not copied, and compare the value counts with nim/stat_grundys. For a period claim, check G(n + p) = G(n) exactly over the stated window and check the cited or formalised sufficient condition line by line. For 0.6111..., use nim/stat_.6111 and nim/sparse_.6111 in the same way.
angles: All the rare values lie below n = 48,399,022, so beyond that point every G(n) is a common value fixed by the xors with the 1,287 rare positions. A proof that no new rare value can appear, plus a shift-register argument of length about last + depth, is the natural route to a sufficient condition.
For 0.6111... the rare set is tiny (171 values, the last at 2,026) and the run already reaches 2^43, so it may be the cheaper of the two to certify once a valid sufficient condition exists.
pitfalls: grundy.html (last updated 2021) still says the computation stopped at 284,944,236,543. octal.html and the stat_grundys header ('total=2^39') are newer and are the authority.
OEIS A002188's data and b-file reach only 200,000 terms; they are a calibration, not the record.
Couples-are-forever and the octal game .6 are the same game shifted (octal.html), so a period for either belongs to the octal entry, not here.
Flammenkamp and others are extending these runs; re-fetch octal.html and the stat file before and after a run.

octal.html credits Tyler Satchel Orden (July 2026) and Udo Sprute (October 2026, a parallel C/OpenMP program) with extending the octal-games sequences, and the 2^39 table of stat_grundys ('total=2^39 bitmask=1') is in a newer output format than the 2^35 table, so it may come from one of those programs: a reproduction for p1 or p2 must share no code with them either.

targets.name: Number of short games born by day 4: tighten Suetsugu's bounds 10^28.2 < |G4| < 4.0e184 (OEIS A065401 a(4))
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (G3 has 1,474 elements; chain decompositions and antichain counts of its order; the exact |G4| would need far cleverer counting)
targets.statement: The short partizan games in canonical form born by day n number 1, 4, 22 and 1474 for n = 0..3 (OEIS A065401). The games born on day n number 1, 3, 18 and 1452 (A065402); a(3) was found by Dean Hickerson and Robert Li in 1974. The day-4 count is unknown. Wolfe and Fraser (Theoret. Comput. Sci. 313, 2004) proved 3.0e12 < |G4| < 10^434. Koki Suetsugu (arXiv:2208.13403, v2 24 Feb 2024; Games of No Chance 6, 2025) improved this to 10^28.2 < |G4| < 4.0e184 by dividing the partial order G3 into 86 chains (its width is 86), counting antichains, and bounding the canonical forms {L | R} built from them. He publishes G3 with its 45-level stratification as a spreadsheet (sites.google.com/site/kokisuetsugu2/games-born-by-day-3). The OEIS entry, re-read 2026-10-30, still has the keyword 'more' and no a(4), and a comment by Zhujun Zhang (May 06 2026) records Suetsugu's bounds as the current ones. Nowakowski's Unsolved Problems column (Games of No Chance 6, 2025, problem E7, Siegel's day-4 question) lists the same bounds as open. Applied one day earlier, to bound |G3| from G2, Suetsugu's methods give 208 <= |G3| <= 451,584 against the true 1,474, so the truth for G4 is probably much nearer 10^28 than 10^184. The lattice of games born by day 4 is known to have 2,949 levels (A065407).
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: either the exact value of |G4|, computed by two independent programs, or a proven bound at least ten times better than Suetsugu's: a lower bound |G4| >= 10^29.2 or an upper bound |G4| <= 4.0e183. A program that shares no code with the claimant's must reproduce every computational ingredient: the 1,474 canonical forms of G3, their partial order, any chain or antichain counts, and any family of day-4 games claimed to be distinct and canonical. Every mathematical step must be written out in full or formalised; a bound from a heuristic or from sampling does not count. The bound must not already be published at verification time (OEIS A065401 and its history, arXiv, Games of No Chance).

partial_wins.statement: Any rigorously proven lower bound above 10^28.2 or upper bound below 4.0e184, under the same reproduction rules as the success criterion.

An independent recomputation of G3 from the definitions, not from Suetsugu's tables or spreadsheet: all 1,474 canonical forms with their full partial order, published as a machine-readable file. It must reproduce A065402 (1, 3, 18, 1452), the 45 levels of the day-3 lattice (A065407) and Suetsugu's width of 86, shown by an 86-element antichain and a division of G3 into 86 chains. Chain divisions are not unique, so the chain lengths need not match his. A demonstration that one of these published numbers is wrong also counts.

targets.verification_method: Generate G_n from G_(n-1): every pair of antichains (L, R) of G_(n-1) gives {L | R}. Reduce each to canonical form (remove dominated options, bypass reversible ones) and compare games with the recursive order (G <= H unless some G^L >= H or some H^R <= G). Check |G1| = 4, |G2| = 22 and |G3| = 1474. Recompute the order on G3, any chains and the antichain counts with exact integer arithmetic, and re-derive the counting lemmas. For an upper bound, check that every canonical day-4 game is counted; for a lower bound, check that the claimed games are canonical and pairwise distinct.
angles: Upper side: |G4| is at most the number of pairs of antichains of G3 that give canonical games. An exact count of the antichains of the 1,474-element poset (or of those with no reversible option) is the obvious first step below 4.0e184.
Lower side: find large sub-posets of G3 in which every pair of antichains gives a distinct canonical game, as Suetsugu did with his stratification, and count them exactly.
pitfalls: The OEIS 'last modified' footer is the site's date, not the entry's; read the entry's history for its last edit.
Counting requires canonical forms: many pairs of antichains give equal games through reversible options, so a count of option pairs is only an upper bound.

targets.name: Toads and Frogs: values of T^a [ ]^b F^a beyond Thanatipanonda's table, or a counterexample to Erickson's Conjecture 5
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days per cell (boards of length 2a + b from 20 to 30; canonical-form evaluation with memoisation)
targets.statement: Toads and Frogs (Richard Guy, Winning Ways) is played on a strip. Left's toads T move one square right into an empty square or jump one frog; Right's frogs F move left in the same way; the player unable to move loses. Jeff Erickson (Games of No Chance, 1996) made six conjectures. Jesse Hull proved the sixth (NP-hardness, 2000), and Doron Zeilberger and Thotsaporn Thanatipanonda proved 1-3 and refuted 4 (T^7 [ ]^7 F^6 > 2). Conjecture 5 says that T^a [ ]^b F^a (a toads, b empty squares, a frogs) is infinitesimal for every (a, b) except (3, 2), whose value is +-1/8; Wikipedia (re-read 2026-10-30) calls it 'the last one still open'. Thanatipanonda tabulated T^a [ ]^b F^a in Figure 2 of arXiv:0804.0640 (v1, 2008) and in Table 3.1 of the published version (Electron. J. Combin. 18 (2011) P67). Rows a <= 4 are given for b <= 20 and are 0 or *, apart from (3,2) and the b = 2 column (an unspecified infinitesimal for a >= 4). Row 5 is known to b = 13 in the arXiv figure (to b = 12 in the published table), row 6 to b = 7, row 7 to b = 5, and rows 8-10 only to b = 5 or 4. The cells (5,11), (6,8), (7,6) and (7,7) are marked only as non-zero in the arXiv figure and left blank in the published table. He adds that T^2 [ ]^b F^2 = 0 for 21 <= b <= 103 except b = 25, 31, ..., 103 (which are *), and that T^3 [ ]^b F^3 = 0 for 21 <= b <= 53 except b = 29 (which is *). He conjectures that T^a [ ]^b F^a = * for a > b > 0 (b not 2), and that it is 0 or * for b >= a > 0. No later table was found (2026 arXiv math.CO titles checked).
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: a position T^a [ ]^b F^a, with a >= 1, b >= 0 and (a, b) not (3, 2), whose value is not infinitesimal (its Left stop or Right stop is non-zero), refuting Erickson's Conjecture 5. The canonical form (or both stops, with a certified game-tree evaluation) must be computed by two independent programs, for example CGSuite and one written by the claimant. The counterexample must not be published at verification time (Wikipedia's Toads and Frogs article, arXiv, Electron. J. Combin.).

partial_wins.statement: The exact canonical value, computed by two independent programs, of one of the four cells that the arXiv v1 Figure 2 marks only as non-zero and the published Table 3.1 leaves blank, (a, b) = (5, 11), (6, 8), (7, 6) or (7, 7), or of any other cell with a <= 10 and b <= 20 that both versions leave blank.

A counterexample to Thanatipanonda's stronger conjectures, computed by two independent programs: a cell T^a [ ]^b F^a with a > b > 0 and b not 2 whose value is not *, or with b >= a > 0 whose value is neither 0 nor *.

targets.verification_method: Implement Toads and Frogs from the rules (moves: one step into an empty square, or a jump over exactly one opposing piece into an empty square) together with a canonical-form engine. Calibrate on Winning Ways values (T[ ][ ]F = 0, TF[ ][ ] = 1, T[ ]F[ ] = 1/2, TFT[ ]F = *, T[ ]TFF = up) and on Figure 2 cells such as (3,2) = +-1/8 and the rows a <= 4. Recompute the claimed cell with a second program (CGSuite has a Toads and Frogs ruleset) and compare the canonical forms, or at least both stops.
angles: The four non-zero cells are the cheapest: boards of length 20 to 23. Thanatipanonda's Java program only compared sums; a full canonical-form evaluation with a transposition table keyed by the strip is the obvious upgrade.
Positions split into independent pieces once toads and frogs are blocked against each other. Evaluate the pieces separately and add their canonical forms.
pitfalls: Thanatipanonda's 'N' in column b = 2 means an infinitesimal he did not write out, not 'unknown'.
'Not equal to 0' in the table is consistent with *. Computing only the outcome class cannot refute Conjecture 5; the stops are needed.
Check the convention: Left owns the toads and moves right; swapping the sides negates every value.

targets.name: Hexadecimal games: certify the (arithmetic) periodicity of one game on Nowakowski's unsolved list (.f6, .7f, .9, .e, .b6, ...)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (three-heap splits cost O(n^2) per value; 1e5 to 1e6 values per game)
targets.statement: Hexadecimal games extend octal codes to the digits 0-f: bit 8 of digit d_k lets a player remove k tokens and leave three non-empty heaps (Winning Ways, pp. 116-117). Their nim-sequences may be arithmetic periodic: G(n + p) = G(n) + s from some n0 on. Nowakowski computed the first 100,000 values of every 1-, 2- and 3-digit game. Richard Austin's Theorem 6.8 (Calgary thesis, 1976) and Howse and Nowakowski's generalisation (Theoret. Comput. Sci. 313, 2004) certify several of them, for example .28 = .29 (period 53, saltus 16, only G(0) exceptional) and .9c (period 36, preperiod 28, saltus 16). Nowakowski's Unsolved Problems column (Games of No Chance 6, 2025, problem A3) lists as unsolved .1x (x in 8,9,c,d,e,f), .2x (a-f), .3x (8-e), .4x (9,b,d,f), .5x, .6x and .7x (8-f), .9x (1-a), .9d, .bx (6,9,d), .dx (1-f) and .fx (4,6,7). It singles out .9 (fractal-like values to 100,000), .e, .7f (a tendency to period 8, saltus 4, with 14 exceptional values to 100,000, the largest G(94,156) = 26,614), .b6 ('looks octal'), .b33b, and .f6 ('period 43, saltus 32, apparent preperiod 604', not certifiable because a theorem condition fails). The lane's own check on 2026-10-30, with two independent programs, reproduced .28 and .9c but found that .f6 keeps G(n + 43) = G(n) + 32 only for 604 <= n <= 1,885 and breaks at G(1,929) = 326 (pattern value 1,253). Even the listed patterns therefore need recomputation.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: for one game that problem A3 of the latest Unsolved Problems column at verification time (Games of No Chance 6, 2025, on 2026-10-30) names as unsolved, an explicit n0, period p and saltus s (s = 0 allowed) with G(n + p) = G(n) + s for every n >= n0, established by both of the following. Eligible games are those in A3's list of 'other unsolved hexadecimal games' (.1x, .2x, .3x, .4x, .5x, .6x, .7x, .9x, .9d, .bx, .dx and .fx with the stated digits x) and the specimens .9, .e, .7f, .b6, .b33b and .f6. Games that A3 reports as regular (.28, .29, .9c, .205200c, .660060008, the .200...0048 family) do not count. (1) An exact check of every value over the finite window that the sufficient condition requires, by a program that shares no code with the claimant's. (2) The sufficient condition: Austin's Theorem 6.8 or the Howse-Nowakowski theorem with every hypothesis verified for this code, or a new theorem proved in the submission and formalised in Lean 4, Coq or Isabelle. A machine-checked proof that an eligible game is not arithmetic periodic is an equally full win. The code convention (bit 1: leave no heap; bit 2: one heap; bit 4: two; bit 8: three non-empty heaps) must be stated and calibrated on .28 and .9c. The result for that game must not already be published at verification time (Games of No Chance volumes, Theoret. Comput. Sci., Integers, Electron. J. Combin., arXiv).

partial_wins.statement: A formalisation in Lean 4, Coq or Isabelle of the Howse-Nowakowski arithmetic-periodicity theorem (or of Austin's Theorem 6.8), together with a verified executable checker that certifies .28 (period 53, saltus 16) and .9c (period 36, preperiod 28, saltus 16) from their nim-sequences.

targets.verification_method: Implement the nim-sequence from the code: for digit d_k and heap n, the options are the xors over all ways to leave n - k tokens in exactly h non-empty heaps, for each bit 2^h of d_k. Cross-check a fast version against brute-force enumeration of all splits for n <= 150 and calibrate on .28 and .9c. Then recompute the claimed game to the end of the window and test G(n + p) = G(n) + s for every n in [n0, window end - p]. Check each hypothesis of the cited theorem, or run the formal proof checker on the submitted formalisation.
angles: Several listed games look octal or sparse (like .b6 and .7f). Adapt Flammenkamp's rare/common sparse-space bookkeeping to three-heap splits to reach 10^7 values cheaply before looking for a period.
Most listed games have a single digit with bit 8 set. A periodicity theorem only needs that digit's three-heap options to be handled, which may admit a cleaner window bound than Howse-Nowakowski's.
pitfalls: The specimen patterns quoted in A3 are not reliable at scale: .f6 breaks its quoted period-43, saltus-32 pattern at n = 1,929 (lane check with two programs, 2026-10-30). Recompute before trusting a quoted preperiod.
Sources write hexadecimal codes with or without a leading digit before the point. In a code d1 d2 d3 here, digit k applies to removing k tokens.
Arithmetic periodicity with rare exceptional values (as in .7f) is not arithmetic periodicity; the certificate must cover every n >= n0.

targets.name: NoGo: a position on a Go board with value 1/16 (only 1, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/8 are known)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (canonical-form search over small partly filled grids)
targets.statement: NoGo (also called 'Anti-Atari Go'; invented independently by Neil McKay) is played on a Go board. Players alternately place stones of their colour (Black = Left), and a placement is illegal if afterwards any group of either colour has no liberty, so nothing is ever captured; the player who cannot move loses. Burke and Hearn (Int. J. Game Theory 48, 2019) showed that NoGo is hard on graphs. McKay, Nowakowski and Angela Siegel found NoGo positions on a Go board with the values 1, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/8. Nowakowski's Unsolved Problems column (Games of No Chance 6, 2025, problem B12) asks whether the denominators of the numbers that occur on the two-dimensional board are bounded, and asks for the nim-dimension of the one- and two-dimensional boards. Disjoint regions walled off by stones add as a sum, so multiples of 1/8 are cheap, but 1/16 cannot arise as a sum of positions of value 1, 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: a legal NoGo position on an m x n rectangular grid whose canonical value, with Black as Left, is a number with denominator at least 16 (for example 1/16), computed exactly by two independent programs. Legal means stones of both colours placed so that every group has at least one liberty; any m and n are allowed. Reachability from the empty board is not required, but the claim must say whether it holds. The value must not be published at verification time (Games of No Chance volumes, arXiv, Sensei's Library AntiAtariGo page).

partial_wins.statement: A legal NoGo position on a general planar graph (NoGo on graphs, same legality rule) whose canonical value is a number with denominator at least 16, computed by two independent programs, while the grid question is still open.

targets.verification_method: Implement NoGo legality (after a placement, every maximal same-colour connected group of both colours must be adjacent to an empty point) and a canonical-form engine. Test them on small cases such as the one-dimensional position . x . . o . = +-1 quoted in GONC6 B12. Recompute the claimed position's canonical form with a second program (for example a CGSuite ruleset script) and compare.
angles: Number values arise when one player has a reservoir of safe moves the other lacks. Look for corridor-shaped empty regions bordered by stones whose options are 0 and 1/8, which gives {0 | 1/8} = 1/16.
Search systematically over small empty regions (up to about 14 empty points) inside a frame of stones, caching canonical forms by region shape and boundary colours.
pitfalls: The one-dimensional nimber question is not part of this target. GONC6 states that the strips x . o . x . o ... are equivalent to the octal game .6 (Officers), whose values reach 16 at heap 381 and 256 at heap 10,344 (Flammenkamp), so large nimbers there follow from the octal game.
Capture never happens in NoGo, so a Go engine's legality code is wrong for it.

targets.name: Nim-dimension of Amazons: a position equal to *8 (only *4 is known)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (canonical-form search over small Amazons regions, which grow explosively)
targets.statement: Carlos Santos defined the nim-dimension of a ruleset: it is n if the ruleset has a position of value *2^(n-1) but none of value *2^n. Toppling Dominoes, Thinning Thickets and Konane have infinite nim-dimension, and Col has nim-dimension 1 (Winning Ways). Nowakowski's Unsolved Problems column (Games of No Chance 6, 2025, problem E17) conjectures that Amazons has nim-dimension 3: only *4 is known, and no position of value *8. In Amazons each player moves one of her amazons like a chess queen through empty squares and then shoots an arrow from its landing square, also like a queen, which burns the square it lands on; the player unable to move loses. Regions separated by burnt squares add as a sum, so *5, *6 and *7 follow from known positions, but *8 does not. Any position of value *k with k >= 8 also gives a *8. The canonical form of *k has *8 among its options for both players, and every option of a canonical form is the value of a position reachable from the original one, so some reachable Amazons position equals *8. The same column conjectures that Clobber has nim-dimension 1, but that is false on small positions (see pitfalls), so Clobber is not part of this target.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: a position of standard Amazons on a rectangular board (amazons of either or both colours, burnt squares allowed) whose canonical value is *k for some k >= 8, computed exactly by two independent programs (for example CGSuite, which implements Amazons, and one written by the claimant). The position must not be published at verification time (Games of No Chance volumes, Theoret. Comput. Sci., arXiv, CGSuite example libraries).
targets.verification_method: Recompute the canonical form of the claimed position with two independent canonical-form engines and check that it equals *k exactly, not just its outcome class. An outcome-only cross-check is that G + *k is a second-player win while G + *j is a first-player win for every j < k. First check the move generator on small published values: a queen move for the amazon, then a queen-move arrow from its landing square that burns a square, where the arrow may cross or land on the square just vacated.
angles: Start from the known *4 and search for small regions whose options include *4, *2, * and 0 for both sides.

Nimbers appear early: an audit search on 2026-10-30 found a *2 on a 3 x 4 board with one amazon of each colour. Enumerate regions of 12 to 20 empty squares inside burnt borders, caching canonical forms by region shape and amazon placement, and keep only positions whose canonical form is a nimber.
pitfalls: This is a counterexample hunt: the conjecture may be true.
A position equal to *8 plus an infinitesimal is not *8; compare canonical forms exactly.

E17's companion conjecture that Clobber has nim-dimension 1 is false on small positions. The one-row position o o x x o x o o x x equals *2 (checked 2026-10-30 with a canonical-form engine and a separate outcome-only search). The column's Amazons claim may be just as stale, so search the Amazons literature first, for example Snatzke's exhaustive searches (Theoret. Comput. Sci. 313, 2004) and the 2 x n Amazons work.
Domineering is left out: its nim-dimension question depends on whether positions with holes count (Drummond-Cole's *2 has holes).

targets.name: Impartial misere quotients: exhibit an element of period 5 (or 8, or any period other than 1, 2, 3, 4, 6)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (quotient computations over many small game trees or heap rules; enumeration of the quotients of order 20 for p1)
targets.statement: Plambeck and Siegel's misere quotient of a set A of impartial games (closed under options and sums) identifies two games G and H when G + X and H + X have the same misere outcome for every X in A. The quotient Q is a commutative monoid with a P-portion. An element x has period p if p is the least positive integer with x^(n+p) = x^n for some n. Nowakowski's Unsolved Problems column (Games of No Chance 6, 2025, problem E12, from Plambeck and Siegel) says that quotients with elements of periods 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and infinity have been found. It conjectures that every period occurs and asks for a quotient with a period-5 element, then period 8 and so on. It also asks for the smallest quotient with a period-4 (or 3 or 6) element, and for Siegel's classification of quotients to be extended beyond order 18. Siegel (arXiv:math/0703070, 2007) counted the quotients of orders 2, 4, ..., 18 as 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 6, 9, 50, 211. Plambeck and Siegel (arXiv:math/0609825, Section A.6) gave a period-6 generator in the order-200 quotient of *(2#210)(2#30)3#21 and a period-4 element in the quotient of *(2#1)(2#0)4310, of order 120, the smallest then known with a period above 2. Simon Rubinstein-Salzedo and Stephen Zhou (arXiv:2603.18244, March 2026) showed that partizan misere quotients can have any finite cardinality except 3 and note that impartial ones have even cardinality. No 2026 arXiv math.CO title reports a new period.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: an explicit impartial game G (a finite game tree in a documented notation, or a heap game with stated rules) and the misere quotient Q of its closure, in which some element x has a period p not in {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}, with p shown to be minimal from the table. Q is given as a presentation with its P-portion and multiplication table (or a finite rewriting system), computed by two independent programs (for example Siegel's MisereSolver and one written by the claimant). The example must not be published at verification time (Games of No Chance volumes, Siegel's Combinatorial Game Theory (AMS, 2013), arXiv).

partial_wins.statement: The number of non-isomorphic misère quotients of order 20, from two independent enumerations that both reproduce Siegel's counts 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 6, 9, 50, 211 for orders 2 to 18. The count must not be published at verification time (check Siegel's Combinatorial Game Theory, AMS, 2013, and arXiv first).

A misère quotient that contains an element of period 4 (or 3 or 6) and has order strictly smaller than the smallest one published at verification time (order 120 in arXiv:math/0609825; check Siegel's 2013 book first), computed by two independent programs.

targets.verification_method: Recompute the quotient of the claimed game's closure with an independent implementation of the Plambeck-Siegel algorithm (outcomes of sums, indistinguishability, reduced bipartite monoid) and check that it is a valid misere quotient. Then compute powers of the claimed element until they repeat and confirm the cycle length. For p1, rerun the enumeration with separate code and compare the counts of isomorphism classes and their representatives.
angles: The period-3 and period-6 elements came from games built by adjoining small options to nimbers (*(2#...)...). A structured search over game trees of the form *(a#b)(c#d)... with a MisereSolver-style engine, filtering for torsion in the quotient, is cheap per tree.
Search heap games too: quaternary codes with 3-4 digits give quotients of moderate size quickly.
pitfalls: Partizan misere quotients (arXiv:2603.18244) are a different object; this target is about impartial ones.
Infinite quotients are common, and a computation that never stabilises is not evidence of anything.
Plambeck's cash prizes (Dawson's Chess, .3102, .3122, .3123, .3312) are separate setter challenges and are not part of this target.

targets.name: Fraenkel's N-heap Wythoff conjectures: prove the three-heap case with smallest heap 11 (Sun-Zeilberger stopped at 10)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (P-position tables for a fixed smallest heap, plus a check of Sun-Zeilberger's eight finite conditions)
targets.statement: In Fraenkel's N-heap Wythoff game a move removes tokens from one heap, or removes (a_1, ..., a_N) from all heaps with 0 <= a_i <= p_i, sum a_i > 0 and a_1 xor ... xor a_N = 0; the last player to move wins (N = 2 is Wythoff's game). Fix the N - 2 smallest heaps K. Fraenkel conjectured (1) that from some m(K) on, the n-th P-position has A_n^N = A_n^(N-1) + n with A_n^(N-1) = mex({A_i^(N-1), A_i^N : i < n} union T) for a small set T, and (2) that A_n^(N-1) = floor(n*phi) + eps_n + a with eps_n in {-1, 0, 1}. Fraenkel and Krieger, and Sun (Discrete Math. 300, 2005), proved that (1) implies (2), along with structural results for N = 3. Xinyu Sun and Doron Zeilberger (Ann. Comb. 8 (2004) 225-238) gave a finite sufficient condition: their Claim 3.5, which asks for integers n2 < n1 beyond a computable N satisfying eight checkable conditions on the P-positions. With it they proved both conjectures for N = 3 when the smallest heap A1 is at most 10, listing T, S, alpha, N1 and N2 for each case in their Table 1. Nowakowski's Unsolved Problems column (Games of No Chance 6, 2025, problem A4) still lists only these cases as proved, and no 2026 arXiv math.CO title extends them.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: both of Fraenkel's conjectures for N = 3 with smallest heap A1 = 11 (or any larger single value, once 11 is done). The proof gives explicit integers n2 < n1 and the derived constants (T, S, alpha, N1, N2, N3 and the set S1(n1) of Claim 3.3) satisfying every hypothesis of Sun and Zeilberger's Claims 3.4 and 3.5. Their Table 1 supplies T, S, alpha, N1 and N2 for the cases i < 11 but not N3, so the claim must also state N3^i and B^i_{N3^i} for every i < 11, recomputed. A program that shares no code with the claimant's must check this by recomputing the P-positions directly from the game rules. A general proof for all A1, formalised in Lean 4, Coq or Isabelle, also counts. The case must not be published as proved at verification time (GONC Unsolved Problems column, arXiv, journals citing Sun-Zeilberger).

partial_wins.statement: An independent recomputation of Sun and Zeilberger's Table 1 (T, S, alpha, N1, N2 for A1 = 0..10) from the game rules, by a program that shares no code with their Maple package, confirming every entry or demonstrating an error.

targets.verification_method: Compute the P-positions (A1, A_n^2, A_n^3) for a fixed A1 by a direct mex/retrograde construction from the rules, not from the conjectured recurrences, and cross-check small cases by brute-force game search. Then evaluate each condition of Claims 3.4 and 3.5 for the claimed n1 and n2. This includes N3^i for every i < 11, and membership in S1(n1) decided by the three rules of Claim 3.3; the third rule checks a window of length p(m) = 2^(floor(log2 m) + 1), which is 16 for m = 11, using the periodicity of (a xor b) - b. Finally compare the constants with the claim.
angles: Sun and Zeilberger's epilogue says a numerical rather than symbolic implementation could improve performance, provided Claim 3.3 (deciding membership in S) is redone without generating functions. The periodicity of (a xor b) - b with period p(m) makes that a finite check. A C program for the P-position table and the eight conditions should then handle A1 = 11..20 quickly.
Their Table 1 shows the thresholds N1 and N2 growing into the hundreds by A1 = 10, so allow n1 in the tens of thousands.
pitfalls: Sun and Zeilberger's notation differs from Fraenkel's: their [a, b, c] is the position with heaps a, a + b and a + b + c, and some signs are reversed. State the convention.
Claim 3.5 needs N1, N2 and N3 for all smaller first heaps, and Table 1 omits N3, so a gap in the chain for some i < 11 invalidates the argument.
A pattern seen in a long table is not a proof; only the eight conditions (or a formal proof) count.

targets.name: Kotzig's Nim: refute a Tan-Ward periodicity conjecture or extend its verified range (G(1,5;n) beyond n = 140, G(3,5;n) beyond 111, ...)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (memoised search over visited sets; the 2014 database was computed in C++ on an 8-core Mac Pro)
targets.statement: Kotzig's Nim (Anton Kotzig, 1946; Winning Ways pp. 515-517) is played on a circle of n locations with a move set M. From the current location a player moves m steps clockwise (m in M) and marks the landing location, which must not already be marked. Location 0 is marked at the start, and the player unable to move loses. Nowakowski's Unsolved Problems column (Games of No Chance 6, 2025, problem A6) asks whether the outcome is eventually periodic in n for every finite M. Xin Lu Tan and Mark Daniel Ward (Integers 14 (2014) G06) proved one primitive theorem and published a database of 185,134 outcomes (all 1 <= m1 < m2 <= 72 with n <= 72, plus longer runs for chosen pairs). They made six conjectures for two-move sets, verified as follows: {1,5} to n <= 140; {2,5} to n <= 114; {3,5} to n <= 111 (P exactly for odd n outside {9, 11, 17}); {4,5} to n <= 109; {4,7} to n <= 115; {5,6} to n <= 112. They also verified Fraenkel et al.'s conjecture for {3,4} (the first player wins for n = +-3 mod 7) to n <= 115. The database (re-read 2026-10-30) still ends at those n, and GONC6 reports no later progress.
targets.success_criterion: CONFIRMED: a board size n beyond the verified range at which the outcome of G(m1, m2; n) contradicts one of Tan and Ward's Conjectures 4.1-4.6 or Fraenkel et al.'s {3, 4} conjecture, computed by two independently written solvers that both reproduce the Tan-Ward database entries for that move set. A proof of one of these conjectures for all n, formalised in Lean 4, Coq or Isabelle, also counts. The result must not be published at verification time (Integers, arXiv, the GONC Unsolved Problems column).

partial_wins.statement: The verified range of one of Conjectures 4.1-4.6 (or of the {3, 4} conjecture) extended by at least 20 consecutive board sizes beyond the published bound (for example G(3, 5; n) for all n <= 131), by two independent solvers that agree and both reproduce the Tan-Ward database for that move set.

targets.verification_method: Rerun the claimed G(m1, m2; n) with two solvers (memoised search on (visited set, current location), or a smarter state encoding), using the convention of Tan and Ward's Section 1: location 0 is marked, Player I moves first, and P means the second player wins. Both solvers must first reproduce kotzigdatabase.txt for that move set. The lane checked such a solver against the database for six move sets and n <= 30 on 2026-10-30.
angles: With two step sizes the game is a walk with at most two choices per move. Prune by symmetry and store only the reachable visited sets, which are far fewer than 2^n for small step sizes.
Conjecture 4.3 ({3,5}) is the simplest to state and its exceptional set {9, 11, 17} is small, which makes it a good first extension.
pitfalls: The two conventions in the literature (an empty board versus location 0 pre-marked) swap N and P; use Tan and Ward's.
The database's http address redirects; use the https URL.
Extending a verified range is only a partial win; it proves nothing about periodicity.

targets.name: Periodic billiard paths in obtuse triangles: extend the 112.3-degree theorem (Tokarsky-Garber-Marinov-Moore 2018)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (the 112-112.3 strip alone took 118,809 codes and 27.8 million interval-checked squares; a cluster helps)
targets.statement: Does every triangle have a periodic billiard path? Acute triangles do (Fagnano's orthic triangle), right triangles do, and rational triangles do (Masur 1986). For obtuse triangles the question is open. Richard Schwartz (Experimental Math. 18 (2009) 137-171, McBilliards) proved by a finite computation that every triangle with largest angle at most 100 degrees has a periodic path. Patrick Hooper and Schwartz (J. Modern Dynamics 2009) handled triangles near the isosceles ones. George Tokarsky, Jacob Garber, Boyan Marinov and Kenneth Moore (arXiv 1808.06667, 2018; only v1) improved Schwartz's method. Their interval-arithmetic prover (GMP/MPFR, no division) covers the (x,y) angle plane with squares, each inside the open region of a stable orbit code (CS, OSO and OSNO codes) or handled by their triple rule. They proved the bound for largest angle up to 112.3 degrees: 2,439 codes for 105-110, 38,132 for 110-112 and 118,809 codes in 27,783,085 squares with 1,115 triples for 112-112.3. Quanta Magazine (15 Feb 2024) still calls 112.3 the state of the art. Checked 2026-10-30: arXiv 1808.06667 has no later version, and a fetch of arXiv 2605.04362 (2026, persistence of billiard orbits) shows no new threshold.
targets.success_criterion: A proof that every triangle whose largest angle is at most theta has a periodic billiard path, for some theta >= 112.4 degrees (strictly beyond 112.3 by at least 0.1 degree; direction: max), and above the best threshold found by an arXiv and Google Scholar search re-run just before claiming. The certificate must contain: a finite list of orbit codes; a cover of the uncovered region {0 < x <= y, 180 - theta <= x + y <= 67.7} (angles in degrees, largest angle z = 180 - x - y) by closed squares with exact rational corners, each square proven inside one stable code's open region by outward-rounded interval evaluation of that code's defining inequalities; and, for any infinite code family used near the thin-triangle edge x -> 0, a parametric proof for all n that is symbolic or interval-checked and posted with the claim.

partial_wins.statement: A certified cover, by the same certificate rules, of every triangle with largest angle in [112.3, 113] degrees and smallest angle at least 1 degree.

A certified cover of any closed region of at least 1 square degree in the (x,y) angle plane where the largest angle is at least 115 degrees, at distance at least 1 degree from the isosceles line x = y. The region must not be covered by any published result found by a literature search.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: (1) check that the squares tile the target region exactly, using rational arithmetic on the corners; (2) for each square, re-evaluate its code's inequalities, sums of +-u_i sin(m_i x + n_i y) > 0 as in Tokarsky et al. section 'The Program and Proof', with MPFR interval arithmetic and an outward-rounded enclosure of pi, and require every lower endpoint > 0; (3) for a random sample of codes, unfold the code at the centre of one of its squares and confirm in exact or high-precision arithmetic that the unfolded path closes; (4) recheck any parametric infinite-family argument. Hours to days, and the work splits into parallel chunks.
angles: Port the Tokarsky et al. prover to a GPU or SIMD interval kernel. The cost is dominated by evaluating sine sums over millions of squares, an embarrassingly parallel workload.

Use adaptive code search: for each uncovered square, run a McBilliards-style search for short stable codes at its centre and keep the codes whose region contains the most uncovered neighbours (greedy set cover).
Near x -> 0, look for one-parameter code families as in Schwartz's and Hooper-Schwartz's infinite patterns, and prove them with symbolic inequalities in n.
pitfalls: Unstable codes (CNS, ONS) cover only line segments, never area: a square cannot be certified by one.
A pixel or sample-point check is not a proof: every square needs an interval lower bound strictly above 0 for every inequality of its code.
Rational triangles and exactly isosceles triangles are already known to have periodic paths, so covering them adds nothing.

targets.name: Chirikov standard map: shrink the rigorous window [0.9716, 0.9718] around the breakup of the golden invariant circle
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (multiprecision FFT-based a posteriori KAM near criticality needs many Fourier modes)
targets.statement: The standard map is y' = y - (k/2 pi) sin(2 pi x), x' = x + y'. Greene's residue criterion and MacKay's renormalization put the breakup of the golden-mean rotational invariant circle (RIC), believed to be the last RIC to break, at k_c = 0.971635406... The rigorous results lag behind: Mather proved there are no RICs for |k| > 4/3; MacKay and Percival (Commun. Math. Phys. 98, 1985; converse KAM) proved none for |k| >= 63/64 = 0.984375; Jungreis (Ergodic Th. Dyn. Sys. 11 (1991) 79-84) proved non-existence at several given parameters, including k = 0.9718. On the existence side, Celletti and Chierchia (J. Stat. Phys. 65, 1991) got the golden circle for every |k| <= 0.838, and Jordi-Lluis Figueras, Alex Haro and Alejandro Luque (arXiv 1601.00084; Found. Comput. Math. 17 (2017) 1123-1193) validated the golden circle at k = 0.9716 with an a posteriori KAM theorem. Salvador Addas-Zanata (arXiv 2610.28449, 20 Oct 2026) restates exactly this state. He notes that existence at a given parameter does not give the whole interval, that non-existence at 0.9718 does not give every larger k, and that the conjecture that the set of k with RICs is [-k_c, k_c] is unproven.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) a computer-assisted proof that an analytic invariant circle with rotation number (sqrt5 - 1)/2 exists at some k >= 0.97161, or (b) a computer-assisted proof that no rotational invariant circle exists at some k <= 0.97179. Direction: the window [0.9716, 0.9718] gets strictly narrower by at least 1e-5 on one side, and the result also beats any later rigorous value found by a literature search re-run just before claiming. All inequalities must be verified in outward-rounded interval arithmetic.

partial_wins.statement: A computer-assisted proof that no rotational invariant circle exists for every k in the whole closed interval [0.9718, 0.98], uniform in the parameter, for example by covering parameter subintervals with interval-valued Jungreis or MacKay-Percival cone-crossing certificates.
The same uniform non-existence for the whole interval [0.9718, 63/64], which together with MacKay-Percival proves that there are no RICs for any k >= 0.9718.

An independent, publicly posted, interval-checked a posteriori KAM certificate for the golden circle at k = 0.9716, written with a code base different from that of Figueras-Haro-Luque. Reproduction only; it validates the tooling for (a).

targets.verification_method: Existence: the certificate gives the Fourier coefficients of the parameterization K(theta) and of the approximate inverse, the analyticity strip and the Diophantine constants of the golden mean. A checker evaluates every hypothesis of the stated a posteriori KAM theorem (Figueras-Haro-Luque form), with rigorous FFT error bounds, in arb or MPFR interval arithmetic; this takes hours. Non-existence: the certificate gives finite orbit segments and cone data; a checker iterates them in interval arithmetic and verifies the cone-crossing condition, for each parameter subinterval in p1 and p2.
angles: Existence: near criticality the needed Fourier dimension grows fast. Use the critical-circle renormalization scaling to choose the grid, and use mixed precision: Newton steps in double, the final validation in multiprecision.

Non-existence just above k_c: periodic orbits with Fibonacci rotation numbers have large residues there, and their stable and unstable manifolds supply the orbit segments for a converse-KAM certificate.
pitfalls: Normalisation: some papers write lambda V(theta) with V = -(1/2 pi) sin(2 pi theta); check that sup|V'| = 1 so that lambda = k.
Existence at the critical value itself is expected to give only a non-analytic critical circle; aim strictly between 0.9716 and 0.971635.
A non-existence claim below 0.971635 contradicts Greene's numerics and almost surely means a bug.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Is the Henon attractor a sink? A certified attracting periodic orbit at exactly (a, b) = (1.4, 0.3), or a sink closer than Galias-Tucker's
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (exhaustive symbol-sequence search at periods > 100 with multiprecision continuation; partial wins need laptop-days)
targets.statement: The Henon map is h(x,y) = (1 + y - a x^2, b x), and its classical parameters are (a,b) = (1.4, 0.3). It is not known whether the attractor seen there is strange or is a stable periodic orbit with an extremely narrow basin. Benedicks-Carleson theory covers only small b, and Anikushin and Romanov (arXiv 2503.11150, 2025) state that chaos of the classical attractor is not rigorously established. Zbigniew Galias and Warwick Tucker (Chaos 24, 013120 (2014)) proved a period-28 sink at (1.4, 0.2999999774905). In Chaos 25, 033102 (2015) they combined the Biham-Wenzel method with continuation and proved (interval Newton) 90,510 sink regions of period <= 41 in [1.3999, 1.4001] x [0.2999, 0.3001]; the closest is a period-41 window at distance < 4.728e-10. Their Theorem 1 gives a period-115 sink at a = 1.39999999999999999999968839903277301984563091568983, b = 0.29999999999999999999944845519288458244332946957783, at Euclidean distance < 6.335e-22 from (1.4, 0.3). They also prove that the period-115 sink exists at a = 1.4 exactly with b = 0.29999999999999999999927578971518934110292052859235 (|b - 0.3| < 7.243e-22). They estimate that a sink at the classical point, if one exists, would be practically impossible to see by simulation.
targets.success_criterion: Main win: a period-p orbit of h at exactly a = 7/5, b = 3/10 with a computer-assisted proof of existence (interval Newton or Krawczyk on the p-periodic system) and of attraction: an interval enclosure of the monodromy matrix M (the product of the p Jacobians, with det M = (-3/10)^p exactly) satisfying |tr M| < 1 + det M, so that both eigenvalues lie strictly inside the unit circle.

partial_wins.statement: A sink certified the same way at rational parameters (a,b) whose exact Euclidean distance to (7/5, 3/10) is strictly less than 6.3347994e-22, the exact distance of Galias-Tucker 2015's Theorem 1 period-115 sink (stated there as < 6.335e-22), and less than any closer published value found by a literature search.

A sink certified the same way with a = 7/5 exactly and rational b with |b - 3/10| strictly less than 7.2421e-22 (closer than Galias-Tucker 2015's a = 1.4 period-115 sink at b = 0.29999999999999999999927578971518934110292052859235), and closer than any a = 1.4 sink found by a literature search.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: from the posted p, the parameters (exact rationals), a point enclosure for each orbit point and the symbol sequence, run an independent interval Newton (or Krawczyk) step on F(z_0..z_{p-1}) = (z_{i+1} - h(z_i)) at precision at least 60 decimals per 100 periods. Then enclose M by interval matrix products and check |tr M| < 1 + det M. For p1 and p2, compute the distance in exact rational arithmetic. Minutes to hours.
angles: Galias-Tucker found that admissible sequences avoid (- - -), (+ + +), (- - +) and 28 longer forbidden blocks; enumerate only pruned sequences and continue each unstable orbit toward the classical point.
pitfalls: Long simulated trajectories that look periodic are not evidence: transients near (1.4, 0.3) last far beyond any feasible simulation.
Floating-point parameters such as 1.4 are not exactly 7/5; certify with exact rationals or tight intervals around them.
Interval wrapping over 100+ iterates explodes: use the multiple-shooting formulation, never a single long composition.

targets.name: Topological entropy of the classical Henon map: a rigorous lower bound above 0.46469, a certified upper bound below ln 2, or periodic-orbit counts beyond period 30
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (interval-verified covering relations or trellis computations; orbit counts at p = 31-34 take laptop-days with pruning)
targets.statement: The Henon map h(x,y) = (1 + y - 1.4 x^2, 0.3 x) has numerical topological entropy (on Henon's trapping region, i.e. on the attractor A) about 0.4649-0.4651: Galias and Tucker (Chaos 25, 033102 (2015)) estimate H_p = (1/p) log(fixed points of h^p), which stabilises around 0.46493 for p up to 50, and D'Alessandro et al. get 0.4651. Rigorous lower bounds: Galias (covering relations, about 2001-2002) 0.4300; Sarah Day, Rafael Frongillo and Rodrigo Trevino (Conley index, SIAM J. Appl. Dyn. Syst. 2008) 0.4320; S. Newhouse, M. Berz, J. Grote and K. Makino (Contemp. Math. 469 (2008) 243-270, a trellis built from verified homoclinic tangles) 0.46469, cited as the lower bound by Anikushin and Romanov (arXiv 2503.11150, 2025). The rigorous upper bound cited there is ln 2 = 0.693147 (Newhouse 1988). Anikushin and Romanov's adapted-metric method gives 'robust' upper estimates of the largest uniform Lyapunov exponent, which bounds h_top from above. These estimates converge down to 0.6542706..., the exponent at the fixed point q+, which is also a lower bound for that exponent (0.6542720 after 10^6 steps). They say the estimates could potentially be made rigorous, but they are not interval-verified. Rigorous counts of all period-p orbits are published only for p <= 30 (Galias, Int. J. Bifurcation Chaos 11 (2001) 2427), as Galias-Tucker 2015 state. Their Table I gives Biham-Wenzel counts P_31..P_34 = 58,656, 90,343, 139,674 and 215,597 that are not rigorous.
targets.success_criterion: Main win: a computer-assisted proof that h_top >= L with L >= 0.46470 (strictly above 0.46469; direction: max) and above any rigorous value found by a literature search re-run just before claiming. The certificate is a finite family of h-sets or boxes with covering relations, or a trellis, all verified in outward-rounded interval arithmetic. It yields an integer transition matrix A whose Perron root is certified >= e^L in exact arithmetic (for example a Collatz-Wielandt test vector), and the claim states the semiconjugacy theorem used.

partial_wins.statement: A rigorous count, with an interval-Newton existence and uniqueness certificate per orbit and a proof that no other period-p orbit exists in the trapping region, of all period-p orbits for some p in 31..34 for which no rigorous count is found by a literature search, compared with the Galias-Tucker 2015 Table I value; any difference must be explained.
A fully interval-verified upper bound h_top < 0.693147 (below ln 2), for example from a rigorous symbolic image (outer box covering) or an interval-checked adapted metric.
A fully interval-verified upper bound h_top < 0.6542706, below the uniform-Lyapunov ceiling of the adapted-metric method. This needs a method other than the largest uniform exponent.

targets.verification_method: Lower bound: re-verify each covering relation with an independent interval library (images of the box edges against the target box's sides), rebuild A, and check the Perron-root certificate exactly; hours. p1: re-run interval Newton on each listed orbit and the exclusion argument for the rest of the trapping region. p2/p3: recompute the outer image graph or the metric inequalities in interval arithmetic and the bound from them.
pitfalls: Periodic-orbit counts alone give an entropy estimate, not a rigorous lower bound; a semiconjugacy or horseshoe argument is required.
The Newhouse et al. trellis paper and Grote's MSU thesis may contain larger values; the thesis was access-limited when this entry was written, so search it before claiming.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Hilbert's 16th problem for quadratic systems: a quadratic vector field with five limit cycles (H(2) >= 4 since Shi 1980)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours per candidate (validated integration); the search itself is open-ended
targets.statement: The second part of Hilbert's 16th problem asks for H(n), the maximal number of limit cycles of planar polynomial vector fields of degree n. Even the finiteness of H(2) was long open. An unrefereed OpenAI draft ('Uniform bounds for planar polynomial limit cycles', dated 24 Sep 2026, released 6 Oct 2026, cited in the closing remark of Qin-Sun) claims that H(d) is finite for every d. Finiteness, even if correct, does not decide whether a quadratic system can have five cycles. Since Chen Lansun and Wang Mingshu (1979) and Shi Songling (Scientia Sinica 23 (1980) 153-158), quadratic systems with four limit cycles in the (3,1) distribution have been known, and no quadratic system with five has ever been found. Bautin proved that at most three small-amplitude cycles bifurcate from one quadratic focus. Table 1 of Chaoyang Qin and Xiaoming Sun (arXiv 2610.12218, 8 Oct 2026) still lists H(2) >= 4 (Shi 1980) as the best explicit lower bound. Wikipedia's Hilbert's sixteenth problem page records the same state, citing Ilyashenko's 2002 survey and the narrow basins that make numerical counting unreliable (Kuznetsov-Kuznetsova-Leonov 2011, Leonov-Kuznetsov 2013).
targets.success_criterion: An explicit quadratic system x' = P(x,y), y' = Q(x,y) (degree <= 2, rational coefficients) with at least 5 limit cycles (direction: more than the current 4), certified in one of two ways. (a) Validated numerics: for each cycle, a transversal segment on which an interval-arithmetic validated Poincaré return map shows the displacement changing sign between two points, with the segments and orbit enclosures showing that the 5 sign changes belong to 5 distinct closed orbits. A sign change excludes a period annulus, so each is a limit cycle by analyticity. (b) A one-parameter family plus an exact-arithmetic check of every hypothesis of a cited bifurcation theorem (Lyapunov constants, Melnikov or Abelian integrals) that yields 5 limit cycles for all small enough parameter values.

partial_wins.statement: A validated-numerics certificate (rule (a)) of four limit cycles in one explicit quadratic system with rational coefficients of absolute value <= 10, all four certified at that single parameter value (no 'for epsilon small enough' argument), such that no validated-numerics certificate of four limit cycles in a quadratic system is found by a literature search.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: re-run the validated integrator (for example CAPD or arb-based Taylor models) from each segment endpoint, confirm the displacement signs and the disjointness of the orbit enclosures, and check that the system has degree 2. For (b), recompute the Lyapunov or Melnikov quantities in exact rational arithmetic and confirm the theorem's rank or zero conditions. Minutes to hours.
pitfalls: Plots and floating-point integration routinely miss or invent nested cycles with tiny basins; only interval-validated return maps or exact bifurcation certificates count.

Known theory restricts the configurations: at most 3 small cycles around one focus (Bautin), and four-cycle examples have the (3,1) distribution; check a candidate's nests against these results before a long computation.

targets.name: Hilbert numbers H(3)..H(8): a planar polynomial vector field with more limit cycles than 13, 28, 37, 53, 74 or 96
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exact symbolic Melnikov or Lyapunov computations for degree 4-8 families)
targets.statement: H(d) is the maximal number of limit cycles of a planar polynomial vector field of degree d. The best explicit lower bounds for small d, from Table 1 of Chaoyang Qin and Xiaoming Sun (arXiv 2610.12218, 8 Oct 2026, whose own result improves only the asymptotic d^2 log d growth), are: H(3) >= 13 (Chengzhi Li, Changjian Liu and Jiazhong Yang, J. Differential Equations 246 (2009) 3609-3619, via Poincaré-Pontryagin-Melnikov perturbation of a cubic Hamiltonian); H(4) >= 28, H(5) >= 37, H(6) >= 53, H(7) >= 74 and H(8) >= 96 (Rafel Prohens and Joan Torregrosa, Nonlinearity 32 (2019) 331-355, perturbations of reversible centers). Torregrosa (São Paulo J. Math. Sci. 19:4, 2025) also confirms 13 as the highest known for cubic systems in a global configuration (other 13-cycle cubic configurations: Liu-Li 2014, Yang-Han-Li-Yu, Zhao).
targets.success_criterion: For some d in 3..8, an explicit degree-d planar polynomial vector field, or family, with at least T(d) + 1 limit cycles, where T = (13, 28, 37, 53, 74, 96) for d = 3..8 (direction: max), also beating any later value found by a literature search re-run just before claiming. Certified either by interval-validated Poincaré return maps (one sign change of the displacement per cycle, with distinct cycles shown) or by exact-arithmetic verification of every hypothesis of a cited bifurcation theorem (Melnikov or Abelian-integral simple zeros, the Lyapunov-constant rank, averaging) giving that many limit cycles for small parameters.

partial_wins.statement: A cubic system with 13 limit cycles in which all 13 are certified simultaneously by validated numerics at one explicit rational parameter value (not only 'for epsilon small enough'), such that no such single-parameter validated certificate of 13 cubic limit cycles is found by a literature search re-run before claiming.

The same explicit-parameter validated certificate for a quartic system with 28 limit cycles, such that no such certificate for 28 quartic limit cycles is found by a literature search re-run before claiming.

targets.verification_method: For bifurcation certificates: recompute the first-order (or higher) Melnikov function or Lyapunov constants in exact rational or algebraic arithmetic (Sage, Singular), check the claimed number of simple zeros with Sturm sequences or the rank condition, and check that the theorem cited applies. For validated certificates: re-run an interval ODE integrator from each segment endpoint. Hours.
pitfalls: Counting limit cycles in different nests requires that the perturbation is small enough for all of them simultaneously; a certificate that treats the nests with separate small parameters proves less.
Zeros of a Melnikov function count only if they are simple, or of certified odd multiplicity, and lie inside the period annulus.

targets.name: Local cyclicity M(n): 13 small-amplitude limit cycles from one cubic equilibrium, or beat M(4) >= 21, M(5) >= 33, M(6) >= 48, M(7) >= 61, M(8) >= 76, M(9) >= 88
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (high-order Lyapunov constants with parallel exact arithmetic, as in Liang-Torregrosa 2015)
targets.statement: M(n) is the maximal number of small-amplitude limit cycles that bifurcate from one elementary monodromic equilibrium (degenerate Hopf bifurcation) of a degree-n planar polynomial vector field; clearly M(n) <= H(n). Bautin proved M(2) = 3. For cubics, Zoladek's 1995 claim of 11 had gaps; 11 was proved by Christopher (2005) and Bondar-Sadovskii (2008), and Zoladek's family was revisited by Gouveia-Torregrosa (2021) and Tian-Yu. Pei Yu and Yun Tian (CNSNS 19 (2014)) found 12 in the CD12 family, with the proof completed by Jaume Gine, Luiz Gouveia and Joan Torregrosa (J. Differential Equations 275 (2021) 309-331), whose technique also gives M(4) >= 21. Gouveia and Torregrosa (JDE 271 (2021) 447-479) proved M(5) >= 33, M(7) >= 61, M(8) >= 76 and M(9) >= 88 (and M(4) >= 20); M(6) >= 48 is due to Bastos, Buzzi and Torregrosa (CPAA 2021). Joan Torregrosa (Sao Paulo J. Math. Sci. 19:4, 2025) found two new cubic families reaching 12 via Cremona transformations and lists 12 (cubic), 21 (quartic), 48 (sextic) and 33, 61, 76, 88 (n = 5, 7, 8, 9) as the best known. Higher orders exist only over the complex numbers: Graf and Kroker (2010) found complex curves of cubic weak foci of orders 12 and 13, and Sadovskii (2020) an explicit complex cubic system with a weak focus of order 14. For Kolmogorov systems, Carvalho, Da Cruz and Gouveia (arXiv 2304.05111, 2023) gave another example with M_K(3) >= 6 and proved M_K(4) >= 13 and M_K(5) >= 22.
targets.success_criterion: For some n in 3..9, a degree-n polynomial family with a center or weak focus at the origin and an exact-arithmetic certificate that at least M + 1 small-amplitude limit cycles bifurcate from it, where M = 12, 21, 33, 48, 61, 76, 88 for n = 3..9 (direction: max), also beating any value found by a literature search re-run just before claiming. The certificate gives the Lyapunov constants, or the higher-order developments in the perturbation parameters, computed in exact rational or algebraic arithmetic, and verifies the rank or degeneracy conditions of a cited theorem (for example Christopher 2005 and Gine-Gouveia-Torregrosa 2021).

partial_wins.statement: Kolmogorov systems: an exact certificate that M_K(3) >= 7, M_K(4) >= 14 or M_K(5) >= 23, beating Carvalho-Da Cruz-Gouveia 2023 and any later value found by a literature search.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: recompute the Lyapunov constants of the posted family in an independent computer algebra system (Sage, Singular, Maple) to the stated order, check the Jacobian rank or higher-order conditions exactly, check that the unperturbed system has a center (by the posted Darboux or reversibility certificate), and check that the perturbation stays within degree n. Hours to a day.
pitfalls: Torregrosa 2025 credits the n = 6 bound of 48 and the n = 5, 7, 8, 9 bounds to Gouveia-Torregrosa 2021 and Bastos-Buzzi-Torregrosa with the citation order swapped; the JDE 271 abstract states n = 4 (20), 5, 7, 8, 9, and its introduction attributes M(6) >= 48 to Bastos-Buzzi-Torregrosa.
A first-order rank argument can fail to give the full count when the center family is more degenerate than predicted (Zoladek's 1995 gap); high-order developments must be checked.
Complex weak foci of high order do not count: the bifurcating cycles must be real.

targets.name: Three-body problem: a computer-assisted proof of KAM (or linear) stability for an equal-mass periodic orbit other than the figure-eight, from the Hristov-Hristova-Tanikawa list of 971
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days per orbit (CAPD-style validated integration of the variational equations)
targets.statement: In the planar equal-mass zero-angular-momentum three-body problem, the figure-eight (Moore 1993, Chenciner-Montgomery 2000) is linearly stable and has been proven KAM-stable by computer (Tomasz Kapela and Carles Simo, Nonlinearity 20 (2007) 1241-1255). Kapela and Simo later gave a general computer-assisted method for KAM stability around arbitrary periodic orbits ('Rigorous KAM results around arbitrary periodic orbits for Hamiltonian systems', arXiv 1105.3235). They applied it to the figure-eight and to two orbits of the rotating-Eight family, which have non-zero angular momentum and are not in the list below. Milovan Suvakov and Veljko Dmitrasinovic (2013) found the linearly stable Bumblebee, Moth I, Moth II and Butterfly III; Dmitrasinovic, Hudomal, Shibayama and Sugita (2018) extended the list to 20, Li and Liao (2017) found hundreds of new periodic orbits, and Danya Rose (thesis) 25 linearly stable collisionless ones. Ivan Hristov, Radoslava Hristova and Kiyotaka Tanikawa (arXiv 2510.22802; New Astronomy 125, July 2026) found 971 initial conditions (685 distinct solutions) of linearly stable collisionless periodic orbits in the Martynova-Orlov-Rubinov domain. They publish 100-digit initial conditions and 40-digit monodromy eigenvalues and stability angles at db2.fmi.uni-sofia.bg/3bodystab971, grouped into four stability regions (Schubart/S 377, Intermediate-Moth 147, Figure-8 346, Broucke 101). All satisfy the order-4 non-resonance condition. They call them candidates for KAM-stable orbits, leave the twist condition to future work and write that it would be excellent to prove KAM stability rigorously as done for the figure-eight. Their stability checks are high-precision floating point, not interval proofs.
targets.success_criterion: A computer-assisted proof (outward-rounded interval arithmetic) of KAM stability for at least one solution in the 971-row list that is not the figure-eight itself. Required: existence of the periodic orbit near the listed initial condition (interval Newton or Krawczyk on a Poincaré-section return map); ellipticity of the reduced monodromy (the nontrivial multipliers certified on the unit circle and distinct); non-resonance of the stability angles to the order the cited KAM theorem needs; and the cited theorem's twist (non-degeneracy) condition certified. For the two stability angles this is a certified non-zero determinant of the 2x2 matrix of first Birkhoff coefficients, or the exact twist quantity the cited theorem uses, as in Kapela-Simó 2007 and arXiv 1105.3235. The solution must not have a published rigorous KAM proof (literature search re-run before claiming).

partial_wins.statement: A computer-assisted proof of existence and linear stability (certified ellipticity of the reduced monodromy) for one listed solution other than the figure-eight, with no prior rigorous linear-stability proof found by a literature search.
The p1 certificate for at least one solution in each of the four stability regions of the list (in the Figure-8 region, a solution other than the figure-eight).

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: check that the certified initial condition lies within 1e-30 of the posted row of the 100-digit (vx, vy, T, T*) data file at db2.fmi.uni-sofia.bg/3bodystab971. Re-run the posted proof script with CAPD or another open-source validated ODE solver. Confirm the Krawczyk inclusion, the interval enclosure of the reduced monodromy eigenvalues on the unit circle, the non-resonance inequalities, and that the twist determinant (or the cited theorem's twist quantity) is certified non-zero. Hours per orbit.
pitfalls: The full monodromy has trivial multipliers equal to 1 from the energy, angular momentum and symmetries; ellipticity must be certified on the reduced (symplectically reduced or section) matrix, or the trivial block must be handled explicitly.
Symmetry type II solutions appear as two rows with the same T*; they are one solution, not two.
Scale-invariant period T* differs from T; use the normalisation of the data file.

targets.name: Hilbert's 16th problem for invariant tori in 3D: more normally hyperbolic limit tori than N_h(2) >= 3, N_h(3) >= 5, N_h(4) >= 7, N_h(5) >= 13
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (exact averaged functions and root isolation; validated numerics for p1)
targets.statement: Douglas Novaes and Pedro Pereira (arXiv 2212.12006, v2 Sept 2024) posed a 3D version of Hilbert's 16th problem: the maximal number of isolated, normally hyperbolic invariant tori of a polynomial vector field of degree m in R^3. Using averaging they showed growth at least m^3/128. Lucas Queiroz Arakaki, Luiz F. S. Gouveia and Douglas Novaes (arXiv 2507.17932, July 2025) studied families near Hopf-zero and nilpotent-zero monodromic singularities and proved N_h(2) >= 3, N_h(3) >= 5, N_h(4) >= 7 and N_h(5) >= 13, which they describe as the best available lower bounds. They extend these to higher degrees by strict monotonicity and a Christopher-Lloyd-type recursion.
targets.success_criterion: For some m in 2..5, an explicit degree-m polynomial vector field family in R^3 with at least N + 1 normally hyperbolic limit tori, where N = 3, 5, 7, 13 for m = 2..5 (direction: max), also beating any value found by a literature search re-run just before claiming. Certified by an exact-arithmetic check of every hypothesis of a cited averaging theorem for invariant tori (Novaes-Pereira 2022 or Arakaki-Gouveia-Novaes 2025 form): the first non-vanishing averaged function is computed exactly, and its N + 1 simple zeros in the admissible domain are isolated by Sturm sequences or interval Newton, with the non-degeneracy conditions the theorem needs.

partial_wins.statement: A validated-numerics certificate (interval Poincaré map on a 2D section, with an invariant-circle validation for the section map) showing 3 normally hyperbolic invariant tori in an explicit quadratic 3D field at one explicit rational parameter value, not only for epsilon small enough.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: recompute the averaged function of the posted family in exact arithmetic (Sage or Mathematica), re-run the Sturm or interval root isolation, check the theorem's hypotheses (smoothness, the transformation to the standard averaging form, Jacobian non-vanishing at each zero), and confirm the degree of the vector field. Hours.
pitfalls: Tori coming from planar limit cycles in a degree-m/2 - 1 subsystem must be counted with the degree bookkeeping of Novaes-Pereira; a degree slip gives a false record.
A young area: re-check arXiv for 2026 papers by Novaes, Gouveia or coauthors before claiming.

targets.name: invrs-gym photonic inverse design: a manufacturable design beating the frozen invrs leaderboard's efficiency-vs-length-scale front
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (JAX; FMMAX RCWA or ceviche FDFD per evaluation; a GPU helps for metalens and Bayer sorter)
targets.statement: invrs-gym (Martin F. Schubert, invrs.io; arXiv 2410.24132) packages photonic inverse design problems behind one JAX interface, using FMMAX (RCWA) and ceviche (FDFD) for the physics and imageruler (NanoComp) to measure the minimum width and spacing of a design. The companion invrs leaderboard (github.com/invrs-io/leaderboard) lists every evaluated solution with eval_metric (higher is better), minimum_width, minimum_spacing and binarization_degree. All invrs-io repositories were archived in late October 2025 (last leaderboard push 2025-10-23), so the table is frozen at commit ed27c5c (PR #85, 2025-10-22). That PR removed the 2025 entries of riarrieta (Arrieta, Romano and Johnson, arXiv 2507.16108) and smartalecH (Alec Hammond, subpixel-smoothed projection); they stay public in git history and count as records here. They were the last additions; none moved the seven main fronts, and nothing was added after the archive. Fronts of metric against L = min(width, spacing) in pixels, recomputed 2026-10-30 (selected points): - metagrating: 0.99603 at L=5, 0.98224 at 7, 0.96441 at 9, 0.96017 at 11, 0.93853 at 15. - metalens: 19.955 at 3, 18.801 at 5, 15.246 at 7, 14.593 at 11, 7.867 at 12. - bayer_sorter: 0.55110 at 8, 0.51050 at 10, 0.49273 at 12. - diffractive_splitter: 0.59640 at 10, 0.53885 at 17. - meta_atom_library: 0.95139 at 10, 0.86868 at 24. - photon_extractor: 13.9314 at 10, 12.0894 at 16. - ceviche_mode_converter: 0.90951 at 6, 0.76166 at 10, 0.61101 at 14, 0.17374 at 16. Credits: Ian Williamson, Ardavan Oskooi, Mo Chen, Rasmus Christiansen, Jiaqi Jiang, You Zhou and the photonics-opt-testbed authors (Chen et al., JOSA B 2024), Martin Schubert, Aaditya Chandrasekhar and Rahul Padhy, Rodrigo Arrieta, Giuseppe Romano, Steven G. Johnson and Alec Hammond.
targets.success_criterion: A design for one of bayer_sorter, ceviche_mode_converter, diffractive_splitter, meta_atom_library, metagrating, metalens or photon_extractor, evaluated with invrs-gym 1.6.2, imageruler 0.3.0 (the leaderboard does not pin it), jax_enable_x64, and the leaderboard's own evaluation path (scripts/eval.py at commit ed27c5c: default challenge, eval_metric, imageruler minimum width and spacing). The design must have binarization_degree exactly 1.0. Let L = min(minimum_width, minimum_spacing); L must not exceed the largest L among that challenge's record entries. The record set is the challenge's leaderboard.txt at ed27c5c plus the lines removed in PR #85. Every record entry whose stored OR re-evaluated length scale is at least L is a competitor. The design's eval_metric must be STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than both the stored and the re-evaluated (same environment) eval_metric of every competitor, by at least 1e-4 x max(1, |that value|). It must also beat any design published after the freeze for the same invrs-gym challenge with length scale at least L, found by a literature search re-run just before claiming (papers or repositories reporting the gym's eval_metric, or releasing a design that can be re-evaluated).

partial_wins.statement: The same rules on ceviche_beam_splitter, ceviche_wdm, ceviche_power_splitter or ceviche_waveguide_bend, whose record sets hold 1-3 entries (fronts: beam splitter -0.45719 at L=11, which also dominates L<=11; wdm 0.05395 at L=4 and 0.04377 at L=11; power splitter 0.009037 at L=8; waveguide bend -1.25043 at L=7): a binarized design that beats every competitor with length scale at least its own.

A script a skeptic reruns that re-evaluates every record entry of one main challenge under invrs-gym 1.6.2 and imageruler 0.3.0 and prints, for each entry, the re-evaluated eval_metric, width and spacing beside the stored values. It counts when the skeptic's rerun matches the script's printed values to 1e-9 relative, and either every entry reproduces (eval_metric within the leaderboard's own RTOL 1e-5, width and spacing exactly) or each mismatch is listed with both numbers.

A binarized design whose length scale is at least 2 pixels larger than the largest record L of a main challenge, with eval_metric strictly above the best record value at that largest L (extends the front to a more manufacturable regime).

targets.verification_method: pip install invrs-gym==1.6.2 imageruler==0.3.0 and the leaderboard package from the archived repo at ed27c5c. Load the claimed .json (totypes json_utils) or .csv density, then run the leaderboard's eval path in float64: challenge.eval_metric plus the imageruler width and spacing. Re-evaluate every competitor record entry (stored or re-evaluated L at least the claim's L, including the PR #85 lines restored from git history) in the same run. Compare using the criterion's tolerance. Minutes to an hour per design on a laptop CPU.
angles: Density topology optimisation with the subpixel-smoothed projection, or hyperparameter-free length-scale constraints (the two removed 2025 methods), aimed at L values where the front drops steeply (metalens L=11-12, mode converter L=14-16).
Level-set or shape-library parameterisations (PhoTOS) that enforce a minimum feature size by construction, followed by a final binarized polish.
Start from the best record design at a smaller L and apply morphological opening and closing to reach the target L. Then re-optimise with the length-scale constraint active.
pitfalls: The leaderboard repository is archived: no pull request can be accepted, and opening one is not part of a win.
eval_metric definitions differ by challenge. Several are min-over-wavelengths or synthetic scores, not average efficiency, so a higher average efficiency is not a win.

Version drift: stored numbers come from older invrs-gym and imageruler versions, and imageruler is not pinned by the leaderboard. Evaluate both the record entries and the claim under the same pinned versions, and beat both the stored and the re-evaluated values.
Designs that are not fully binary, or that only meet the length scale after thresholding outside the evaluator, are not wins.
Entries removed in PR #85 are part of the record set, even though they no longer appear at HEAD; on ceviche_beam_splitter and ceviche_wdm they are the only entries.
Large-L points on some fronts are weak (mode converter: 0.17374 at L=16, negative beyond); check that a claimed L is within the largest record L, otherwise only p3 applies.

targets.name: IEA Wind Task 37 case study 1: a feasible 16-, 36- or 64-turbine circular-farm layout with higher AEP than every published or posted layout
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (one AEP evaluation is about 1 ms; multistart gradient or large-neighbourhood search)
targets.statement: Wind farm layout optimisation (WFLO) case study 1 is from IEA Wind Task 37 (Baker, Stanley, Thomas, Ning and Dykes, AIAA SciTech 2019-0540, BYU FLOW Lab and NREL). Turbines are IEA37 3.35 MW machines (D = 130 m). The wind speed is a constant 9.8 m/s over a 16-bin wind rose, and the wake model is the simplified Bastankhah Gaussian (k = 0.0324555, CT = 8/9) combined by root sum of squares. All hubs must lie within the boundary radius (1300, 2000 or 3000 m for 16, 36 or 64 turbines) and every pair must be at least 2D = 260 m apart. The results folder (IEAWindSystems/iea37-wflo-casestudies; byuflowlab copy archived) posts 36 layouts from 12 participants. Re-checked 2026-10-30 with an independent evaluator that reproduces all 36 posted AEPs. Best values in MWh: - 16 turbines: participant 12 posted 421561.897, 3.518 m outside the boundary (421451.07 once projected inside). Next: DPCRO-SL 419935.7905 (arXiv 2212.00742) and SNOPT+WEC 418924.4064 (Thomas and Ning, participant 4; its file is 4e-12 m outside). An open V3R1T4S claim (PR #578, unreviewed) reports a strictly feasible 424131.9503; it reproduces in an independent evaluator. - 36 turbines: participant 12 posted 882383.304, 4.9 mm outside (882382.78 once projected). Next: Perez-Rua, Stolpe and Cutululis (WES 2023), about 865 GWh; SNOPT+WEC 863676.299 (file 4e-11 m outside). - 64 turbines: participant 12 posted 1526474.802, 4.1 mm outside (1526474.68 once projected). Next: SNOPT+WEC 1513311.194 (file 1.4e-10 m outside). Valotta Rodrigues et al. (WES 2024) use a modified setup and report only normalised values. No later published absolute record was found.
targets.success_criterion: A layout for the 16-, 36- or 64-turbine scenario with every hub at distance at most R from (0,0) and every pair at least 260 m apart, both checked with no tolerance in double precision. Its AEP from the official iea37-aepcalc.py model (16-bin rose, constant 9.8 m/s, iea37-335mw.yaml) must be STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) by at least 0.01 MWh than the posted record, used as posted even though it lies outside the boundary: 421561.8972 (16), 882383.3040 (36) or 1526474.8025 (64), and also strictly greater than every CONFIRMED V3R1T4S known-known for the same scenario at claim time. Re-check the known-knowns and open claims (PR #578 reports 424131.9503 at 16) immediately before claiming; a claim must state which of them it beats.

partial_wins.statement: A feasible 36- or 64-turbine layout with AEP strictly above the best posted non-participant-12 value (SNOPT+WEC: 863676.2993 for 36, 1513311.1936 for 64) by at least 1 MWh, such that under the minimum-total-distance one-to-one matching to the participant-12 layout at least one third of the turbines are more than 50 m from their partner (an independent topology).

A feasible 16-turbine layout strictly above 419935.7905 MWh (DPCRO-SL, the best published value by a non-participant) such that, under the minimum-total-distance one-to-one matching, at least 6 of its 16 turbines are more than 50 m from their partner in the participant-12 layout and in every V3R1T4S known-known or open-claim layout.

An independent standard-library re-implementation of the wake model that reproduces all 36 posted AEP values in iea37-cs1-results to within 1e-4 MWh, plus a feasibility report (boundary excess and minimum spacing, full precision) for every posted layout.

targets.verification_method: Parse xc and yc from the claimed YAML or JSON. Check max sqrt(x^2+y^2) <= R and min pairwise distance >= 260 m exactly. Compute AEP from the wake-model equations (wind-frame rotation by 270 - theta, sigma = k*dx + D/sqrt(8), deficit (1 - sqrt(1 - CT/(8 sigma^2/D^2))) exp(-0.5 (dy/sigma)^2), RSS combination, cubic power curve between 4 and 9.8 m/s, 8760 h). First reproduce par4-opt16 = 418924.406363 and par12-opt36 = 882383.304032. Seconds.
angles: Ruin-and-recreate large-neighbourhood search with SLSQP polishing found the 16-turbine claim. Apply it to 36 and 64 turbines from random starts, not from participant 12.
Wake expansion continuation (inflate k, then anneal to 0.0324555) with exact gradients, many starts.
Ring-structured parameterisations (boundary ring plus inner rings with rotational offsets) searched globally, then freed for local refinement.
pitfalls: Participant 12's files exceed the boundary (3.5 m at 16 turbines, millimetres at 36 and 64), and the SNOPT+WEC files by 1e-12 to 1e-10 m. A layout that only beats a record inside a tolerance is not a win.
Boundary hubs must keep full float precision: rounding to 1e-3 m can push a hub outside R.
The 16-bin wind rose is exploited by every record. No physical or site-realism claim is part of a win.
Do not confuse case study 1 with case studies 3 and 4 (IEA 10 MW, polygon boundaries, a different wind rose).

targets.name: IEA Wind Task 37 case study 4 (Borssele III/IV, 81 x 10 MW): a feasible layout with higher AEP than DEBO's 2,913,220.604 MWh
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (vectorised AEP about 0.1 s for 81 turbines x 360 directions x 20 speeds)
targets.statement: IEA Wind Task 37 case study 4 places 81 IEA37 10 MW turbines (D = 198 m, cut-in 4, rated 11, cut-out 25 m/s). The site is five disjoint polygonal regions adapted from Borssele III and IV by Sebastian Sanchez Perez-Moreno and Erik Quaeghebeur and modified by N. F. Baker. Turbines may be placed inside any region but not between regions, and every pair must be at least 2D = 396 m apart.
