The wake model is the simplified Bastankhah Gaussian (k = 0.0324555, CT = 8/9, root sum of squares) over the 360-direction x 20-speed wind rose iea37-windrose-cs4.yaml. Thomas, Baker, Malisani, Quaeghebeur, Sanchez Perez-Moreno, Jasa, Bay, Tilli, Bieniek, Robinson, Stanley, Holt and Ning compared eight methods ('A comparison of eight optimization methods applied to a wind farm layout optimization problem', Wind Energ. Sci. 8, 865-891, 2023; data on Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.7125349). The best layout came from discrete exploration-based optimization (DEBO): 2,913,220.60417 MWh. Next best: DPA 2,910,537.867, SNOPT+WEC 2,910,115.644, ADREMOG 2,909,489.259; the provided base layout scores 2,851,096.413. An independent re-implementation run on 2026-10-30 reproduces all nine posted layouts to 1e-5 MWh. The DEBO layout lies inside the regions with zero excess and a minimum spacing of 2.058D. Note that debo.yaml's stored 'default' value (2,861,182.5) comes from an older 20-bin rose; the 360-bin value matches the paper's 2913.221 GWh. I found no later absolute record (Valotta Rodrigues et al. 2024 and Perez-Rua et al. 2023 use case study 1).
targets.success_criterion: 81 turbine positions, each inside or on one of the five polygons of iea37-boundary-cs4.yaml (IIIa, IIIb, IVa, IVb, IVc; point-in-polygon with zero tolerance, edges included), with every pair at least 396 m apart (no tolerance). The AEP, computed with the provided_model.py equations from the Zenodo record using the 360-bin iea37-windrose-cs4.yaml and iea37-10mw.yaml, must be STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than 2,913,220.60417 MWh (DEBO, Thomas et al. 2023) by at least 1 MWh.

partial_wins.statement: A feasible layout (same zero-tolerance checks) with AEP strictly above 2,910,537.86749 MWh (DPA, second best) by at least 1 MWh, such that under the minimum-total-distance one-to-one matching to the DEBO layout at least 27 of the 81 turbines are more than 198 m (1D) from their partner (an independent layout, not a perturbed DEBO).

An independent evaluator (not running provided_model.py) that reproduces all nine posted 360-bin AEPs (base, snoptwec, debo, gps, cmaes, gagb, adremog, pg, dpa) to within 1e-3 MWh, plus a per-layout boundary-excess and minimum-spacing report.

targets.verification_method: Load the claimed positions. Run a point-in-polygon test against the five region polygons, with the distance to the nearest edge reported, and a pairwise spacing check. Compute AEP from the wake-model equations over 360 directions x 20 speeds with the per-direction speed probabilities and direction frequencies, x 8760 h / 1e6. First reproduce snoptwec.yaml = 2,910,115.64377 and debo.yaml = 2,913,220.60417. Under a minute.
angles: DEBO-style sequential discrete allocation on a fine candidate grid inside each region, followed by continuous gradient polishing with exact boundary projections.
Region-wise turbine-count reallocation: enumerate how many of the 81 turbines go in each of the five regions, then optimise each split.
Wake expansion continuation with SNOPT or IPOPT from many DEBO-like seeds.
pitfalls: debo.yaml's stored AEP (2,861,182.5) was computed with the older 20-bin wind rose. Always evaluate with the 360-bin file.

Only DEBO and GPS lie inside the regions with zero tolerance. The others sit slightly outside: CMA-ES 0.23 m, DPA 0.087 m, base 0.065 m, GA-GB 0.020 m, SNOPT+WEC 3.8 mm, ADREMOG and ADREMOG+PG about 0.1 mm. Feasibility here is judged with zero tolerance.
Turbines between regions are infeasible even if inside the convex hull of the site.
No later paper publishes an absolute CS4 AEP above DEBO as far as checked, but re-check before claiming; a literature search could not be repeated on 2026-10-30.

targets.name: ESA GTOP / GTOPX interplanetary trajectory benchmarks: beat a best-known Delta-v, mass or mission time (Messenger full 1.9579 km/s, Cassini2 8.3830 km/s, Rosetta 1.34334 km/s, GTOC1, Sagas) by 0.1%
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (millions to billions of objective evaluations; each about 10 microseconds in C)
targets.statement: ESA's Advanced Concepts Team built the GTOP database (2005-2014: Izzo, Vinko, Biscani and others). It poses multiple-gravity-assist spacecraft trajectory design as box-constrained black-box problems (MGA and MGA-1DSM). Martin Schlueter, Neshat, Wahib, Munetomo and Wagner extended it as GTOPX (arXiv 2010.07517; SoftwareX 2021), with one GPL C/C++ source file, gtopx.cpp, and posted best solution vectors. The GTOP pages carry the record histories and have no entry after 2014. Best-known values (GTOPX page and solution files, fetched 2026-10-30, and the GTOPX paper): - Cassini1: 4.9307 km/s (Stickel) - Cassini2: 8.382998066 km/s (Schlueter, Fiala, Gerdts 2009, MIDACO; Danoy et al.'s 2012 8.383091 is higher) - Messenger reduced: 8.629944278 km/s (Biscani, Rucinski, Izzo) - Messenger full: 1.957873052 km/s (Schlueter, Wahib, Maruyama 2014, MXHPC/MIDACO; GTOP rounds to 1.959) - GTOC1: -1,581,950.1318 (Schlueter, Gerdts) - Rosetta: 1.34334419 km/s (GTOPX paper Table 13, local search, refining Vasile and Minisci 2008; the posted rosetta.txt still lists the older 1.343367) - Sagas: 18.187747 years (Vinko, Izzo) - Cassini1-MINLP: 3.5007 (Schlueter, Munetomo) The GTOPX authors believe all values are 'essentially converged', and note that GTOP improvements traditionally need at least 0.1% to count as significant. Neither GTOP nor GTOPX proves any of them optimal. No improvement on these GTOPX values since 2021 was found (a fresh literature search could not be repeated on 2026-10-30).
targets.success_criterion: A decision vector x within the instance's box bounds (and satisfying g(x) >= 0 for constrained instances: Cassini1, GTOC1, Sagas, Cassini1-MINLP), evaluated with gtopx.cpp compiled from the GTOPX source, whose objective f(x) is STRICTLY LOWER (direction: min) than the best-known value by at least 0.1% relative. The values are 4.9307, 8.382998066, 8.629944278, 1.957873052, -1581950.1318, 1.34334419, 18.187747 and 3.5007 for instances 1-8; for GTOC1 (negative objective) the requirement is f(x) < -1581950.1318 x 1.001. In the same build, the record vector must reproduce its value: the posted solutions/ < instance > .txt vector for every instance except Rosetta, and for Rosetta the local-search vector of GTOPX paper Table 13 (f = 1.34334419 to the digits shown).

partial_wins.statement: A strict improvement of at least 1e-5 relative (but under 0.1%) on any of instances 2-8 over the values in the success criterion (Rosetta: 1.34334419), checked the same way.
For Cassini1-MO or Cassini1-MO-MINLP (GTOPX instances 9 and 10), a feasible point that strictly dominates at least one point of the posted paretofront.txt, evaluated with gtopx.cpp.

A from-scratch solve of Messenger full to below 2.0 km/s by code a skeptic reruns from the stated seed, reproducing the vector, where the code reads no record vector and is initialised only from random samples within the bounds.

targets.verification_method: Download gtopx.cpp, main.cpp and the makefile from the GTOPX page, compile, and evaluate the record vector: the posted solutions/ < instance > .txt vector (for example 1.957873051874192 for Messenger full) or, for Rosetta, the GTOPX paper Table 13 local-search vector (1.34334419). Then evaluate the claimed vector, check the bounds from main.cpp and the constraint signs, and compute the relative improvement. Seconds.
angles: Monotonic basin hopping with problem-aware perturbations (resonance-aware time-of-flight jumps for the Mercury legs of Messenger full).
Pruning by sequential leg decomposition: grid the departure epoch and first legs, then prune with partial Delta-v bounds before full optimisation.
Massively parallel island-model differential evolution or CMA-ES with restarts (the MXHPC recipe), then a local SQP polish.
pitfalls: pykep and pygmo 'gym' versions of these missions use different ephemerides or models. Values from them are not comparable: evaluate only with gtopx.cpp.
The GTOP pages round values (1.959 vs 1.9579 for Messenger full). Compare against the GTOPX solution files.
Cassini1 and Sagas are considered easy and very likely at their global optima. A 0.1% improvement there almost surely means a bug or a bound violation.
The TandEM instances are not in GTOPX and their record vectors are mostly not posted (N/A), so they are out of scope here.

targets.name: Totally symmetric alternating sign matrices: a rigorous count A005164(25) (order 51), and an exact-enumeration check of the terms that rest on a conjectured formula
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (transfer matrix on the 1/8 fundamental domain, modular arithmetic plus CRT)
targets.statement: A005164 counts (2n+1) x (2n+1) alternating sign matrices invariant under all eight symmetries of the square (TSASMs). Besides DSASM and even-order DASASM, it is the only ASM symmetry class with no product formula. Robbins (Symmetry classes of ASMs, 2000) and Stanley (A baker's dozen of conjectures, 1986) list it, and Bousquet-Melou and Habsieger computed early terms. OEIS DATA runs to a(24) (order 49). Jean Lienardy added a(14)-a(19) in Aug 2020 and a(20)-a(24) in Sep 2022, next to his note that Hagendorf and Lienardy (arXiv:2008.03220) give a CONJECTURED multiple-contour-integral formula. That paper's abstract presents the TSASM link as a conjecture, so the terms from a(14) on may rest on it. Keyword 'more'; unchanged since 2022, re-fetched 2026-10-30. In October 2026 James Guillochon pushed the neighbouring class A005162 (ASMs symmetric about both diagonals) to n = 62 with a transfer matrix on the fundamental triangle (github guillochon/oeis-results). That suggests a direct enumeration of TSASMs to order 51 and beyond is a laptop computation.
targets.success_criterion: The exact integer A005164(25) (TSASMs of order 51), obtained by an exact enumeration (a transfer matrix, a DP or an equivalent count of the matrices themselves), not by evaluating the Hagendorf-Lienardy conjectured formula. The same program must reproduce a(0)..a(13) exactly. It must also either reproduce a(14)..a(24) or report each disagreement, and a second independent program must confirm every disagreement. Two independent runs must agree on a(25), using different prime sets or exact big integers and a different sweep order or state encoding. It counts only if a(25) is not in the DATA or a b-file of A005164 when re-fetched immediately before claiming.

partial_wins.statement: An exact enumeration (not the conjectured formula) that reproduces every term a(14)..a(24) of A005164, with code and per-term residues published, so the existing terms no longer depend on a conjecture.
An exact enumeration that reproduces a(0)..a(19) and finds a disagreement with a published term, confirmed by a brute-force count for that order or by a second independent program.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic (under an hour): brute-force the TSASMs of orders 1..9 (a(0)..a(4) = 1,1,1,2,4) and compare with the program. Rerun the claimant's code modulo one fresh 62-bit prime for a(25) and check that the program also reproduces a(24). A second independent implementation can follow.
angles: Six-vertex (square ice) encoding with reflecting boundaries along the symmetry axes: sweep the 1/8 wedge row by row, as Guillochon did for DASASM on the fundamental triangle.

Count modulo several 62-bit primes and recombine by CRT. a(25) is about 3 x 10^34 (a(24) = 5.3e31 and the ratio of consecutive terms is about 420 and rising), so two primes suffice and a third serves as a check.
pitfalls: Offset 0 and odd order: a(n) is order 2n+1, so a(24) is order 49 and the target a(25) is order 51.
A value computed from the conjectured contour-integral formula is not a win under this entry.
Guillochon is actively extending ASM symmetry classes in 2026; re-fetch A005164 and its history right before claiming.

targets.name: Ways to divide an n x n square into integer-sided rectangles: the next term A182275(13) (known to n = 12 since Butler 2014)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (column transfer matrix with Fibonacci-many states)
targets.statement: A182275(n) is the number of ways to divide an n x n square into rectangles with integer sides. It is the main diagonal of the array A116694 (Helena Verrill 2006; b-file of antidiagonals 1..20 by Alois P. Heinz) and of the triangle A333476 (Peter Kagey; Heinz's b-file gives rows 0..12, i.e. every rectangle up to 12 x 12). Klarner and Magliveras (1988) and Smith and Verrill (2006) treated fixed widths. Blanco, Dougherty-Bliss, Ter-Saakov and Zeilberger (arXiv:2606.05439, June 2026) revisited fixed-width counts but did not extend the diagonal. Matthew C. Russell entered the sequence in 2012 and Steve Butler added a(11)-a(12) in Mar 2014. a(12) = 5.96e49 is the last term (re-fetched 2026-10-30; entry unchanged since 2023). A column transfer matrix works here. Along the current grid line, its state records which unit segments are crossed by a still-open rectangle (with that rectangle's exact extent) and which are edges (merged into runs). That gives Fibonacci-many states, F(2n+1). An unoptimised Python version reproduces a(1)..a(9) in about 15 seconds (rerun by the skeptic), so a(13), and probably a(14), are laptop computations with a cell-by-cell sweep.
targets.success_criterion: The exact integer A182275(13) (dissections of the 13 x 13 square), not in the DATA when re-fetched immediately before claiming. It must come from two independent runs that agree exactly, using different decompositions (for example a column sweep vs a cell-by-cell broken profile, or a different state encoding). The same code must reproduce every published term a(0)..a(12) and every entry of the A116694 b-file.

partial_wins.statement: The exact number of dissections of the 13 x 12 rectangle into integer-sided rectangles (A116694(13,12), not in the A116694 or A333476 b-files), under the same two-run rule, with the code reproducing A182275(0..12).
A182275(14), after a(13) has been established, under the same two-run rule.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic (minutes to an hour): write an independent transfer-matrix program (the state description above is enough) and check it against the b-file for n <= 10. Then rerun the claimant's code for n = 13 with exact big integers or a fresh prime set.
angles: Processing cell by cell removes the exponential fan-out of whole-column transitions; exact Python integers are fine at this size (a(13) has about 60 digits).
pitfalls: Offset 0 (a(0) = 1); a(12) is the 12 x 12 square.
Dissections are counted as distinct, not up to symmetry. Do not confuse this with A045846 (squares only), which is a separate bank entry.

targets.name: Partitions of the n x n grid into connected pieces (polyomino tilings of the square): the next term A145835(13), or the symmetric count A291807(13) as a partial win
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (frontier DP with connectivity states, modular arithmetic)
targets.statement: A145835(n) counts compositions of the n x n grid graph, i.e. partitions of an n x n square into orthogonally connected regions; these are all tilings of the square by polyominoes of any shape. Brian Kell defined it in 2008, after Knopfmacher and Mays (Graph compositions I, 2001). Frank Simon computed a(7)-a(10) (2011 and his 2012 TU Dresden thesis) and John F. Rudge a(11)-a(12) in Apr 2026 with a Python program (github johnrudge/oeis); a(12) = 4.12e66. Rudge also took two related sequences to n = 12: the free count up to rotation and reflection, A291806 (John Mason's sequence; a(5) by Christian Sievers 2026), and the symmetric count A291807. The rectangular table A110476 has a b-file of 220 terms (Walter Trump; the first 40 by Hugo van der Sanden). All re-fetched 2026-10-30: there is no term for n = 13.
targets.success_criterion: The exact integer A145835(13), not in the DATA when re-fetched immediately before claiming. It must come from two independent runs that agree exactly, using different primes or exact integers and a different sweep order or state encoding. The same code must reproduce a(1)..a(12) and the A110476 b-file entries with m, n <= 12.

partial_wins.statement: A291807(13) (symmetric polyomino tilings of the 13 x 13 square), together with the counts of tilings fixed by each symmetry of the square, with the code reproducing A291807(1..12), under the same two-run rule.

The exact number of partitions of the 12 x 13 rectangle into orthogonally connected regions (A110476(12,13), not in Trump's b-file), under the same two-run rule, with the code reproducing A145835(1..12).

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: run Rudge's published program or an independent frontier DP for n <= 9 and compare with the b-files, then rerun the claimant's code for n = 13 modulo one fresh prime. A291806(13) follows from A145835(13) and the symmetric counts by Burnside's lemma, which the skeptic recomputes.
angles: Frontier state: give each of the n boundary cells a block label (a non-crossing set partition of frontier cells into regions) and record which regions may still be closed. Canonical relabelling keeps the state count near the Motzkin-like count.
pitfalls: Rudge extended the sequence six months ago; check the history page and his repository before claiming.
Do not mix up A145835 (all partitions), A291806 (up to symmetry) and A291807 (symmetric ones).

targets.name: Rhombic tilings of the 2n-gon (primitive sorting networks, A006245): the count for n = 17, or the next term of a higher-dimensional zonotopal-tiling column A060595-A060601
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (n = 17 rhombic tilings); laptop-hours to laptop-days for several zonotope cells
targets.statement: A006245(n) counts rhombic tilings of a 2n-gon. The same number counts primitive sorting networks on n elements, commutation classes of reduced words of the longest permutation, simple Euclidean arrangements of n pseudolines and rank-3 signotopes. No formula is known, only asymptotic bounds: Felsner-Valtr, with lower bounds improved by Dumitrescu-Mandal and Cortés Kühnast, Dallant, Felsner and Scheucher (arXiv:2402.13107, 2024). Terms: a(10) Felsner 1996, a(11) Yamanaka 2009, a(12) Samuel 2011, a(13) Toshiki Saitoh 2011 (PiDDs), a(14)-a(15) Yuma Tanaka 2013, and a(16) = 76413073725772593230461936736 by Gunter Rote (Dec 2021). a(17) is open: re-fetched 2026-10-30, and the 2024 table of Cortés Kühnast et al. also stops at n = 16. The higher-dimensional analogues count tilings of the zonotope Z(D,d) (higher Bruhat orders, signotopes of rank d+1); they are the columns of A060637. Known ranges: A060595 (d=3) D <= 10, A060596 (d=4) D <= 10, A060599 (d=5) D <= 11, A060597 (d=6) D <= 11, A060598 (d=7) D <= 12, A060600 (d=8) D <= 13, A060601 (d=9) D <= 13. Manfred Scheucher computed the recent terms (2021-2023), and his C++ program for enumeration is linked from A006245.
targets.success_criterion: The exact integer A006245(17), not in the DATA when re-fetched immediately before claiming. It must come from two independent runs that agree exactly: two different algorithms, or one algorithm under two different state encodings with exact or multi-prime arithmetic. The same code must reproduce a(1)..a(16).

partial_wins.statement: The next term of A060595 (D = 11) or A060596 (D = 11), with the code reproducing all published terms of that column, under the same two-run rule.

The next term of A060599 (D = 12), A060597 (D = 12), A060598 (D = 13), A060600 (D = 14) or A060601 (D = 14). The code must reproduce all published terms of that column and the D = d+3 values of A060602, under the same two-run rule.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: run Scheucher's published C programs or the claimant's code for small n and D and compare with the OEIS terms. Then rerun the claimed value modulo a fresh prime, or with a second algorithm (for A006245, a sweep-line DP over wiring-diagram cuts vs a signotope DP).
angles: Count, do not list: a(16) is 7.6e28, so a(17) needs a DP over sweep states (cuts of the wiring diagram) or signotope prefixes, never one-by-one enumeration.
For higher signotopes, a DP that adds one element at a time over the extension structure (Bergold-Felsner-Scheucher) is a natural route.
pitfalls: A006245 is the Euclidean (labelled) count; A006246 and A006248 are projective or up-to-symmetry order-type counts and are not this target.
Offsets differ by column (A060595 starts at D = 3, A060601 at D = 9).

targets.name: Solid and higher-dimensional partitions: the next term of A000293 (solid, n = 73) or A000334 (4D, n = 41), or of the 5- to 8-dimensional counts
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster for A000293(73); laptop-hours to laptop-days for the 6- to 8-dimensional partials
targets.statement: The number of d-dimensional partitions of n has no known generating function for d >= 3: MacMahon's guess A000294 fails for solid partitions (Atkin, Bratley, McDonald and McKay 1967; Knuth 1970). Solid partitions A000293 are known to n = 72. The Solid Partitions Project at IIT Madras (Suresh Govindarajan and Srivatsan Balakrishnan, with Intel India support) finished p3(72) = 3464274974065172792 on 3 Jan 2013 and has been paused since; the b-file 0..72 is Govindarajan's. Other OEIS ranges: 4D A000334 to n = 40 (Govindarajan), 5D A000390 to n = 30, 6D A000416 to n = 21, 7D A000427 to n = 20 and 8D A179855 to n = 17. These OEIS ranges for 6D-8D are stale. Govindarajan's 'Notes on higher-dimensional partitions' (JCTA 2013, arXiv:1203.4419) lists d <= 10 up to n = 23 (Table 1), and its F-matrix (Table 4) determines partitions of every n <= 25 in every dimension. His b-file for A119271, the triangle of partitions of n whose Ferrers diagram spans exactly m axes, now gives full rows n = 1..26. The sum p_d(n) = sum_m C(d+1,m) A119271(n,m) reproduces A000293, A000334 and A000390 at n = 26 (auditor check, 2026-10-30). So every dimension is determined for n <= 26, and in dimensions 6 and up the first unpublished value is n = 27. Balakrishnan-Govindarajan-Prabhakar (2011) and Destainville-Govindarajan (2015) studied the asymptotics, and Mondal (arXiv:2609.03034, Sep 2026) estimated them for d = 3..6 by Monte Carlo without adding exact terms. All re-fetched 2026-10-30.
targets.success_criterion: The exact next term A000293(73) or A000334(41), not in the DATA or b-file when re-fetched immediately before claiming. It must come from two independent runs that agree, using different algorithms or branch decompositions. The same code must reproduce every published term of that sequence and of at least one other dimension.

partial_wins.statement: A new exact count in a lower-cost dimension: A000390(31) (5D), or p_d(27) for some d in 6..8 (6D, 7D or 8D partitions of 27; every n <= 26 is already determined by row 26 of the A119271 b-file). The code must reproduce all published terms of that dimension, Govindarajan's Table 1 values for n <= 23 and the values for n = 24..26 derived from A119271, under the same two-run rule.

The full row n = 27 of A119271: the partitions of 27 whose Ferrers diagram spans exactly m axes, for every m. Then p_d(27) = sum_m C(d+1,m) A119271(27,m) gives partitions of 27 in every dimension. The values derived for d = 3, 4, 5 must equal the published A000293(27), A000334(27) and A000390(27), under the same two-run rule.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: check the code against the b-files for small n in two dimensions. Rerun the claimed term with an independent generator, for example a Bratley-McKay or Knuth-style generator vs the proper-partition binomial transform. For a cluster run, recompute a random sample of branches.
angles: The binomial relation over A119271 turns one enumeration into terms for every dimension at once. Govindarajan's 2013 triangles (A, C, F matrices) already halve the data needed; extending them from row 26 to row 27 is the natural route for the higher dimensions.

Since p_3 is known to 72, p_4 to 40 and p_5 to 30, A119271(n,m) for m <= 6 is already determined well beyond n = 27. Only the m >= 7 entries are new: p_6(27) needs just A119271(27,7), p_7(27) adds m = 8 and p_8(27) adds m = 9.
pitfalls: Offsets: A000293 starts at n = 0, the others at n = 1.
A Monte Carlo estimate is never a term; only exact counts count.

OEIS sequence entries lag for d >= 6: a value missing from A000416, A000427 or A179855 may already follow from the A119271 b-file (full rows to n = 26) or Govindarajan's 2013 tables. Check those before claiming.

Index convention: column m of A119271 counts Ferrers diagrams spanning exactly m axes (exactly (m-1)-dimensional partitions), and d-dimensional partitions use C(d+1,m), not C(d,m). Check the transform against A000293(26) = 120256653 before trusting it.

targets.name: Alternating sign hypermatrices: the number of 7 x 7 x 7 ASHMs, A144017(7) (a(6) found in Feb 2026)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (compiled meet-in-the-middle DP over 6.9e7 partial-sum states per middle layer; each step adds one of the 218,348 ASMs of order 7 compatible with the state, generated row by row rather than looped over; modular arithmetic)
targets.statement: An alternating sign hypermatrix (ASHM) of order n is an n x n x n array over {0,1,-1} whose nonzero entries alternate in sign, starting and ending with +1, along every line in all three directions (Brualdi and Dahl, Adv. Appl. Math. 2018). Those with no -1 entries correspond to the n x n Latin squares. A144017 was entered by Samuel Zbarsky (2008). Cian O'Brien corrected a(4) and added a(5) = 852960 (2023), and Ludovic Schwob reached a(6) = 27729279360 on 11 Feb 2026. a(7) is open (keyword 'hard,more', re-fetched 2026-10-30). Schwob also entered A389236 (ASHM Latin-like squares, after O'Brien 2020), known to a(5) = 848320. Each horizontal slice of an ASHM is an ASM, and the partial sums of the slices along the vertical lines must stay in {0,1}. A DP over these 0/1 partial-sum matrices, whose row and column sums equal the layer index, reproduces a(1)..a(5) exactly (written independently by the drafter, the skeptic and the auditor). For n = 7 the two middle layers each have 68,938,800 states (7 x 7 binary matrices with all line sums 3, or 4; A001501). There are 218,348 ASMs of order 7 (A005130; 7436 is the order-6 count), so the ASMs compatible with each state should be generated row by row, not by looping over all of them. Meet in the middle at layer 3 or 4 therefore makes a(7) a workstation computation in compiled code.
targets.success_criterion: The exact integer A144017(7), not in the DATA when re-fetched immediately before claiming. It must come from two independent runs that agree exactly, using different methods (for example the partial-sum DP vs a corner-sum or meet-in-the-middle count, or the same DP under a different layer order). The same code must reproduce a(0)..a(6).

partial_wins.statement: A389236(6), the number of ASHM Latin-like squares of order 6, with code reproducing A389236(1..5), under the same two-run rule.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: run an independent brute force for n <= 5 and the claimant's DP for n = 6 (minutes). Recompute a(7) modulo a fresh prime, or recompute the forward and backward counts of a random sample of middle-layer states and check the meet-in-the-middle sum.
angles: Meet in the middle: a(7) = sum over 0/1 matrices S with all line sums 3 of f3(S) * f4(J - S), where f_k counts k-slice prefixes reaching that partial sum (reversing the vertical axis turns suffixes into prefixes of J - S). Both layers have 68,938,800 states. The dihedral symmetry of the square acting on all slices at once cuts work and memory by up to 8x.
pitfalls: Lines in all three directions must alternate. Checking only the vertical lines over arbitrary slices overcounts, so each slice must itself be an ASM.
a(n) grows much faster than the Latin square count; use exact or multi-prime arithmetic.

targets.name: Tribone (T_2 stone) tilings of the triangle T_n (Conway-Lagarias, Propp's Problem 20): the next nonzero term A334875(45), unknown since 2020
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (row transfer matrix on the hexagonal triangle, 128-bit or modular counts)
targets.statement: Here a tribone, in OEIS A334875's sense, is three mutually adjacent hexagonal cells (the triangle T_2, a 'stone' in Propp's terminology), placed in either orientation. Conway and Lagarias (JCTA 1990) and Thurston proved that T_2 tiles the triangle T_n of hexagons (n cells per side) exactly when n = 12k + 0, 2, 9 or 11. A334875 counts these tilings. It came from a Code Golf challenge by Bubbler (2020); Jonathan Oswald entered it in May 2020 with data to a(44). The nonzero terms are known through a(38) = 3177501183165726091520, and the first unknown term is a(45), followed by a(47) and a(48). James Propp's 'Trimer covers in the triangular grid: twenty mostly open problems' (arXiv:2206.06472, v4 Jan 2024) asks about these numbers as Problem 20, including the observed growth of the power of 2 dividing them. His Benzel Tilings Site lists Problem 20 as open (status of June 2025). Re-fetched 2026-10-30: the DATA ends at a(44) = 0. The Code Golf page itself shows a bot check (BLOCKED), so the OEIS entry is the status source.
targets.success_criterion: The exact integer A334875(45), not in the DATA when re-fetched immediately before claiming. It must come from two independent runs that agree exactly, using a different sweep direction or state encoding with exact or multi-prime arithmetic. The same code must reproduce every published term a(0)..a(44), zeros included.

partial_wins.statement: A334875(47) or a(48) after a(45), under the same two-run rule.

Exact tribone tiling counts for every n <= 44 reproduced by a second, independently written program using a different algorithm (for example a transfer matrix vs the published recursive Python), with run times reported.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: run the short Python program in the OEIS entry for n <= 15 and compare with the claimant's code. Then rerun the claimant's code for n = 45 modulo a fresh prime or with exact integers.
angles: Sweep the triangle row by row. Each cell of the profile records whether it is covered and, for a tribone sticking out, how many more cells it needs along its direction.
pitfalls: Offset 0. Most terms are 0 by Conway-Lagarias, so 'the next term' means the next n = 12k + 0, 2, 9 or 11, i.e. 45.
The tile is the 3-cell triangle (both orientations), not three collinear hexagons: straight trimers never tile T_n. Reproduce a(9) = 2 and a(11) = 8 first.
A377309 (stones-and-bones tilings of T_n, Propp 2024) is a different sequence.
a(45) may exceed 2^64; use 128-bit, modular or exact arithmetic.

targets.name: Stones-and-bones tilings of benzels (Propp's Problems 15-18): the next terms of A364416 and A364417, or of the weighted A364418 and A364438
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours (transfer matrix on the triangular grid)
targets.statement: Benzels are hexagon-like regions of hexagonal cells, introduced by James Propp. A stones-and-bones tiling covers one with stones (three mutually adjacent hexagons, Conway-Lagarias T_2) and bones (three collinear hexagons, L_3). Propp's 'Trimer covers in the triangular grid: twenty mostly open problems' (arXiv:2206.06472, v4 Jan 2024) poses enumeration problems, and he entered the sequences in OEIS. A364416 counts all stones-and-bones tilings of the (n,2n-4)-benzel (Problem 15), known to n = 20 (a(20) = 87817595880192684). A364417 does the same for the (n,2n-3)-benzel (Problem 16), known to n = 19. Propp extended both in Apr 2024. No formulas are known; Propp conjectures 2-adic continuity. Weighting each stone by 3 gives A364418 and A364438 (Problems 17-18), with b-files to n = 17. Propp's Benzel Tilings Site lists Problems 14-20 as open but Problems 9 and 11 as solved (Byun, Ciucu and Lee). So A364481 and A364483 follow from proven formulas and are not part of this target. All re-fetched 2026-10-30.
targets.success_criterion: The exact next term A364416(21) or A364417(20), not in the DATA when re-fetched immediately before claiming. It must come from two independent runs that agree exactly, and the same code must reproduce every published term of A364416 and A364417.

partial_wins.statement: The next term of A364418 (n = 18) or A364438 (n = 18), the stone-weight-3 sums, with the code reproducing all published terms of both, under the same two-run rule.
Five or more new consecutive terms of A364416 or A364417 beyond the published range, under the same two-run rule.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: check the claimant's code against all published terms of A364416-A364418 and A364438 (small benzels can also be checked by an independent exact-cover count). Then rerun the new term modulo a fresh prime or with exact integers.
pitfalls: The (a,b)-benzel coordinates must follow Propp's paper exactly (cells whose barycentric centres satisfy -(a-1) <= j-i, k-j, i-k <= b-1); reproduce every published term before trusting new ones.
Offsets: all four sequences start at n = 3.
A364481 and A364483 (one bone orientation forbidden) are solved by formula and do not count here.

targets.name: Ways to quarter an n x n chessboard into four congruent connected pieces: the next term A006067(29) or A006067(30), open since Howroyd's n = 28 in 2016
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (transfer matrix over rotationally symmetric partitions)
targets.statement: A006067(n) counts the ways to dissect an n x n board (central square removed for odd n) into four congruent polyominoes. The problem comes from Popular Computing (Problem 15, 1973, edited by Audrey Gruenberger) and was analysed by Thomas R. Parkin in 1974 (his letters are linked from A257952). For even n the dissections fall into Parkin's two classes: four pieces with 90-degree rotational symmetry, or the board halved into two rectangles and each half cut in two. Both are counted up to rotation and reflection. For odd n every solution has 90-degree symmetry. M. F. Hasler clarified the definition for odd n and the connectivity of the pieces in Jun 2025. Even n is A257952 and odd n is A272070. Andrew Howroyd corrected a(8), computed a(9)-a(22) in Apr 2016 and supplied the b-file to n = 28 (a(28) = 1.12e42); Giovanni Resta illustrated a(8) = 766. Re-fetched 2026-10-30: the A006067 b-file ends at n = 28, and the DATA of A257952 and A272070 ends at n = 14 and n = 13.
targets.success_criterion: The exact integer A006067(29) (equivalently A272070(14)) or A006067(30) (A257952(15)), not in the b-file when re-fetched immediately before claiming. It must come from two independent runs that agree exactly, and the same code must reproduce every term of the A006067 b-file for n <= 28.

partial_wins.statement: An independent program (not Howroyd's) that reproduces every b-file term of A006067 for n <= 28, with code published.
Both A006067(29) and A006067(30), under the same two-run rule.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: compare the code with the b-file for n <= 16 (minutes) and with Parkin's hand counts for small n, then rerun the claimed term modulo a fresh prime.
pitfalls: The definition counts both of Parkin's classes and identifies dissections up to symmetry in a specific way; reproduce the small terms (1,1,1,5,7,37,104,766) before scaling up.
For odd n the central square is removed.

targets.name: Fault-free domino tilings of the 2n x 2n square: the next term A124997(13) (the 26 x 26 board), open since 2016
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours to laptop-days (transfer matrices with inclusion-exclusion over fault lines)
targets.statement: A domino tiling is fault-free if every grid line through the interior of the rectangle cuts some domino (Graham's fault-free tilings). A124997(n), entered by Don Knuth in 2008, counts fault-free domino tilings of the 2n x 2n square, starting 0,0,0,25506 (the 8 x 8 board). Alois P. Heinz added a(7) in 2015, and Xu Mingkuan added a(8)-a(11) and a b-file to n = 12 (24 x 24) in Dec 2016. All domino tilings of the square are given by Kasteleyn's product formula (A004003), but the fault-free subclass has no formula. Re-fetched 2026-10-30: the b-file ends at a(12).
targets.success_criterion: The exact integer A124997(13) (fault-free domino tilings of the 26 x 26 square), not in the b-file when re-fetched immediately before claiming. It must come from two independent runs that agree exactly, for example inclusion-exclusion over fault sets vs a direct transfer matrix tracking unbroken lines. The same code must reproduce a(1)..a(12).

partial_wins.statement: A124997(14) after a(13), under the same two-run rule.
The exact number of fault-free domino tilings of the 24 x 26 rectangle, from two independent runs that agree, with the code reproducing a(1)..a(12).

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: brute-force the 8 x 8 and 10 x 10 boards (25506 and 1759280998), rerun the claimant's code for n = 13 modulo a fresh prime, and check that a(13) < A004003(13).
angles: In a column transfer matrix, track which horizontal lines are still unbroken, and handle vertical faults by inclusion-exclusion over the columns where every row ends.
pitfalls: Offset 1 with board side 2n: a(12) is 24 x 24, and the target is 26 x 26.
Both horizontal and vertical faults must be excluded.

targets.name: Polyomino number theory: the next count of free polyominoes tiled by n copies of a tetromino (I: A397019, T: A397020, L: A397021, S: A397022)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (hash-sharded canonical enumeration on disk: about 2-3e10 shapes for I, T or S and about 2e11 for L, so hundreds of GB of disk)
targets.statement: An n-fold multiple of a polyomino P is a polyomino that n copies of P can tile (Cibulis, Liu and Wainwright, Polyomino Number Theory I, Crux Math. 2002; Golomb 1981). In June 2026 Haoyang Xu entered four sequences counting the free n-fold multiples of the tetrominoes, up to rotation and reflection: A397019 (I-tetromino) to n = 8, A397020 (T) to n = 7 (a(7) = 733980532), A397021 (L) to n = 6 and A397022 (S) to n = 7. He computed them with a parallel hash-sharded on-disk method. All four carry 'more' and were re-fetched 2026-10-30. At the last published step the counts grew by about 27x (I), 40x (T and S) and 87x (L). The next terms are therefore about 2-3e10 free shapes for I, T and S and about 2e11 for L, each to be enumerated and deduplicated. The sibling tromino sequences A397720 and A397723 (Jul 2026) are not part of this target.
targets.success_criterion: One new exact term: A397019(9), A397020(8), A397021(7) or A397022(8), not in the DATA when re-fetched immediately before claiming. It must come from two independent runs that agree exactly and differ in canonical form or enumeration order. For example, one run can use lexicographically minimal sorted cells and the other a different canonical encoding with a different shard key. Or one run can grow shapes by adding a piece to every (n-1)-fold multiple and the other by removing a piece from candidate shapes. The same code must reproduce every published term of that sequence.

partial_wins.statement: An independent program that reproduces every published term of all four sequences, with code and run times published.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: run the Python program in A397020 (it works to n = 5) against the claimant's code, check that the claimant's shape counts at each step reproduce the published terms, and rerun the new term with a different sharding.
pitfalls: A shape counts once however many tilings it has; deduplicate by free canonical form.
These are brand-new sequences and the author may extend them soon; re-fetch right before claiming.

targets.name: Linear trimer (I-tromino) tilings of the 3n x 3n square: the next term A139772(8), the 24 x 24 board
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (a 3^24 broken-profile state space, about 2.8e11 states) unless a better method is found
targets.statement: A139772(n) counts tilings of the 3n x 3n square by 1 x 3 and 3 x 1 trominoes, i.e. rigid linear trimers at close packing, whose residual entropy Van Craen studied (J. Chem. Phys. 1975). Steven Finch entered it in 2008, and Andrew Howroyd added a(6)-a(7) in Feb 2022: a(7) = 11281654633785546173131745084 for the 21 x 21 board. In Apr 2026 Nicolas Belohoubek added the bound a(n) <= 162^(n^2) and a conjectured asymptotic. Re-fetched 2026-10-30: 7 terms, keyword 'more'. The natural column transfer matrix has 3^(3n) profile states: about 1e10 at width 21 and 2.8e11 at width 24.
targets.success_criterion: The exact integer A139772(8) (linear trimer tilings of the 24 x 24 square), not in the DATA when re-fetched immediately before claiming. It must come from two independent runs that agree exactly, using different primes and a different decomposition. The same code must reproduce a(1)..a(7).

partial_wins.statement: The exact count of linear trimer tilings of the 21 x 24 rectangle (width 21, the largest width already handled), with the code reproducing A139772(1..7), under the same two-run rule.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: check the code against a(1)..a(5) (minutes), then recompute one residue of a(8) modulo a fresh prime with the claimant's code, or recompute a sample of transfer-matrix columns.
angles: Meeting in the middle across the central column (sum over profiles of left count times right count) halves the sweep but not the state space; the reflection symmetry of the profile halves memory.
pitfalls: A Monte Carlo or asymptotic estimate is not a term.
Index n gives the 3n x 3n board: a(7) is 21 x 21.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Domino tilings of the 8 x 8 x 8 cube: the exact count A028446(4) (6 x 6 x 6 solved in March 2026)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (a frontier DP of width 56 is out of reach without a new idea)
targets.statement: A028446(n) is the number of perfect matchings (domino tilings) of the 2n x 2n x 2n grid P_2n x P_2n x P_2n; three dimensions have no Kasteleyn-type formula. Per Hakan Lundow computed a(1) = 9 and a(2) = 5051532105 (1996-1998). On 29 Mar 2026 Steven Kotlarz found a(3) = 417898687046465734392674187695263185 for the 6 x 6 x 6 cube with a broken-profile DP in Rust. He used a diagonal vertex order, a peak of C(30,14) frontier states, three primes, a reverse ordering and a GF(2) parity check, all documented in the entry. Re-fetched 2026-10-30: a(4) is open. The neighbouring sequence A049507 (P_6 x P_6 x P_n, Lundow) lists only n <= 5. The 8 x 8 x 8 cube has 512 vertices and roughly 10^88 tilings (a bulk-plus-surface fit to a(1)..a(3)). Its diagonal frontier has about 56 vertices (C(56,28) ~ 7.6e15 states). The next term therefore needs a new idea: symmetry reduction, tensor-network contraction or a cleverer decomposition. The dimer constant of Z^3 is a separate bank entry; this one asks for the exact count.
targets.success_criterion: The exact integer A028446(4) (perfect matchings of P_8 x P_8 x P_8), not in the DATA when re-fetched immediately before claiming. It must come from two independent computations that agree exactly, using different decompositions and at least three primes or exact integers. The same code must reproduce a(1)..a(3) and the A028454 (P_4 x P_4 x P_n) terms.

partial_wins.statement: A049507(7) or A049507(8), the exact number of perfect matchings of P_6 x P_6 x P_7 or P_6 x P_6 x P_8, not in the A049507 DATA when re-fetched. It must come from two runs with different vertex orders that agree, with the code reproducing A049507(0..5) and A028446(1..3) (A028446(3) = A049507(6)).
The exact number of perfect matchings of P_6 x P_8 x P_8, under the same rules.

targets.verification_method: Skeptic: rerun the claimant's code on the 4 x 4 x 4 and 6 x 6 x 6 cubes. Check the parity of the claim against the determinant of the biadjacency matrix over GF(2), and its residue modulo a fresh prime with the claimant's code. For a(4), a cluster rerun of one prime is the minimum.
pitfalls: Index n gives side 2n: a(3) is the 6 x 6 x 6 cube.
Parity and small-case checks are necessary but nowhere near sufficient; insist on independent residues.

targets.name: Erdős #21 small cases (Erdős-Lovász): an intersecting 6-uniform family with cover number 6 and at most 17 edges (best known 18, lower bound 14)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days
targets.statement: Erdős Problem #21 (Erdős-Lovász 1975) asks about q(r), the fewest edges in an r-uniform intersecting hypergraph whose cover number is r (OEIS A391599): no set of r-1 vertices meets every edge. Kahn (1994) proved q(r) = O(r). The Erdős-Lovász lower bound 8r/3 - 3 stood until Sivashankar (arXiv:2606.24878, v1 23 Jun 2026, v2 29 Jul 2026). He proved q(r) >= 3r - 4 for every r by an elementary argument, and q(r) >= ((41 - sqrt 19)/12 - o(1))r, about 3.053r. Exact values: q(3) = 6 and q(4) = 9 (Tripathi 2014), and q(5) = 13. That last value is due to János Barát (J. Combin. Des. 29 (2021) 193-209, arXiv:2011.04444, three examples on 17 vertices). erdosproblems.com and OEIS credit 'Barát and Wanless', but the paper has Barát as its sole author. Barát also showed the q(4) example is unique. For r = 6 the best construction is Barát's 18-line subset of PG(2,5) with cover number 6, the unique optimum among line sets of PG(2,5) (his Corollary 7.5). So 14 <= q(6) <= 18. The erdosproblems page (edited 2025-12-03) still says 13 <= q(6) <= 18, and OEIS A391599 (edited 2026-06-24) lists terms only through q(5). For r = 8 the oval construction ((r^2+r)/2 lines; Aharoni-Barát-Wanless 2016, Lemma 7.1 in Barát's paper) is the set of 36 secant and tangent lines of a conic in PG(2,7). On 2026-10-30 its cover number 8 was re-checked by SAT and again by an exact branch-and-bound search, and no single line can be removed. Barát's exhaustive deletion search in PG(2,7) ran out of storage. His remark that the oval construction suggests m(8) < 28 computes (7^2+7)/2 = 28, which is not the size of the r = 8 oval construction (36), so 28 is not a known value. Sivashankar's bound gives q(8) >= 20.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit list of at most 17 distinct 6-element sets (direction: min, strictly below 18) that pairwise intersect and have cover number exactly 6, so that no set of 5 points meets every member. The skeptic checks pairwise intersection directly. The cover number is checked by brute force over all 5-subsets of the vertex set (at most C(102,5), and in practice the vertex count is small), or by SAT with an LRAT-checked UNSAT proof that no 5-cover exists. The skeptic also confirms on https://oeis.org/A391599, https://www.erdosproblems.com/21 and a fresh arXiv check that no value at or below the claimed one is already published. Fewer than 14 edges contradicts Sivashankar's proven bound q(r) >= 3r - 4 and means a bug.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit 8-uniform intersecting family with cover number 8 and at most 35 edges (lines of PG(2,7) or any other construction), verified as in the success criterion. This beats the 36-line conic (oval) construction and counts only if the skeptic finds no published family of that size or smaller.

A certified lower bound q(6) >= 15 (or the exact value q(6) = 18): a complete proof with the case reductions written out as checkable lemmas, whose computational part ends in LRAT-checked UNSAT certificates or a Lean proof, on CNFs the skeptic regenerates from the published encoding.

targets.verification_method: Check that all sets have size r and are distinct, and that every pair meets. Compute the cover number by exhaustive search over (r-1)-subsets with bitmasks and, independently, by a SAT/ILP minimum hitting set; for UNSAT claims check LRAT proofs with cake_lpr. Re-fetch A391599 and erdosproblems.com/21 and search arXiv for newer small values.
angles: Start from Barát's three q(5) = 13 examples and his 18-line PG(2,5) example; look for non-geometric 6-uniform families on 18-25 vertices with a cyclic or affine symmetry.

CEGAR search: choose candidate edges as orbit unions, ask a SAT/ILP for a 5-cover, add the cover as a forbidden pattern (some edge must avoid it), and repeat; keep pairwise intersection as hard constraints.
Use counting constraints from Erdős-Lovász and Sivashankar's proof (degree bounds forced by cover number r) to prune vertex degrees and vertex counts before searching.

For p1, search subsets of the 57 lines of PG(2,7) under its collineation group, as Barát did for PG(2,5), but with symmetry reduction or SAT instead of storing every intermediate subhypergraph; the 36-line conic set is edge-critical, so start from larger sets.
pitfalls: Do not confuse q(r) (cover number r) with q*(r), the smallest maximal intersecting family (no blocking set of size at most r; Dow-Drake-Füredi-Larson, q*(4) = 12); they differ.
The erdosproblems page still shows the old lower bound 13 for r = 6; the current lower bound is 14 (Sivashankar 2026).
Barát's 'm(6) = 18' is the optimum within PG(2,5) only, not the global q(6).
arXiv:2011.04444 / J. Combin. Des. 29 (2021) 193-209 has János Barát as sole author; erdosproblems.com and OEIS A391599 say 'Barát and Wanless'. Cite the paper, not the attribution.
A family can be pairwise intersecting with cover number r - 1 if some r - 1 points block every edge; always run the full cover-number check.

targets.name: Erdős #703 small cases: T(9,2) and T(9,3), the largest family of subsets of a 9-set with no two members meeting in exactly 2 (or 3) elements (OEIS A390645 row 9)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (exact maximum independent set on 512 vertices per cell, with S_9 symmetry)
targets.statement: Erdős Problem #703 ($250) concerns T(n,r), the largest family of subsets of {1..n} in which no two distinct members meet in exactly r elements; its asymptotic question was answered by Frankl-Rödl (1987). OEIS A390645 (Elijah Beregovsky, Dec 2025, keyword more; last edited 2025-12-29) tabulates rows n <= 8 by exact maximum-clique search. Row 8 is 128, 94, 67, 93, 163, 219, 247, 255, 256 for r = 0..8. The entry also gives formulas: T(n,0) = 2^(n-1); T(n,1) = A045621(n+1) + 1 (Frankl 1977), so T(9,1) = 187; T(n,n) = 2^n; T(n,n-1) = 2^n - 1; and T(n,n-2) = 2^n - n - 1, so T(9,7) = 502. The b-file stops at T(9,1). Splitting a family by whether it contains the element 9 gives T(9,r) <= T(8,r) + T(8,r-1). The family of all sets of size at most r gives T(n,r) >= C(n,0) + ... + C(n,r). For r = 4, 5, 6 the two bounds meet, so T(9,4) = 256, T(9,5) = 382 and T(9,6) = 466 follow at once from row 8, though they are not yet in the entry. The same argument gives T(10,5) = 638, T(10,6) = 848 and T(10,7) = 968 (checked 2026-10-30). So only T(9,2) and T(9,3) are genuinely open at n = 9. Frankl-Füredi (1984) determined the extremal family for fixed r and large n: all sets of size < r, plus the members A with |A| > (n+r)/2 when n+r is odd, or with |A \ {1}| >= (n+r)/2 when n+r is even. At n = 9 that family has 140 members for r = 2 and 120 for r = 3, while all sets of size at most 3 give 130. So 140 <= T(9,2) <= 161 and 130 <= T(9,3) <= 160. On 2026-10-30, local search on the conflict graph reproduced row 8 but found nothing above 140 and 130. Each cell is a maximum independent set problem on the 512 subsets (conflict when |A ∩ B| = r) with an S_9 symmetry.
targets.success_criterion: Success means the exact values of both open cells, T(9,2) and T(9,3), each with two parts. (a) An explicit family of that size (a list of 9-bit masks), checked so that no two distinct members meet in exactly r elements. (b) An optimality certificate the verifier checks independently: either an LRAT/DRAT proof (cake_lpr or drat-trim) of UNSAT for 'a family of size T+1 exists', on a CNF the verifier regenerates from the published encoding, or a VIPR-verified exact ILP certificate. Any symmetry-breaking constraints must be standard lex-leader constraints for S_9 that the verifier regenerates and checks for soundness. The values must not already be in the live https://oeis.org/A390645 entry, its b-file or its history, re-fetched immediately before claiming. T(9,2) must lie in [140, 161] and T(9,3) in [130, 160]; a value outside its range means a bug. The forced values T(9,4) = 256, T(9,5) = 382 and T(9,6) = 466 do not count.

partial_wins.statement: The exact value of T(9,2) or T(9,3), with a family and an optimality certificate as in the success criterion; each cell counts separately.

The exact value, with the same certificate standard, of T(10,2), T(10,3) or T(10,4). Their bounds are [271, 348], [232, 321] and [386, 416]. The other cells of row 10 follow from the A390645 formulas or from the size-at-most-r bound (T(10,5..7) = 638, 848, 968), so they do not count.

targets.verification_method: Check family sizes and all pairwise intersection sizes with popcount on 9-bit masks (at most 512^2/2 pairs). Rebuild the CNF or ILP from the published encoding, rerun it, and check the LRAT proof or VIPR certificate with an independent checker. Reproduce row 8 of A390645 with the same pipeline as a sanity test. Re-fetch the OEIS entry and history before confirming.
angles: Reproduce row 8 first with an exact max-clique solver (MoMC, CliSAT) on the complement graph, then inspect the n = 8 optima for structure (unions of size layers, stars at a point) to seed n = 9.
Use the decomposition F = F0 ∪ (F1 + {9}) with F0 avoiding r and F1 avoiding r-1 on [8], plus cross constraints between F0 and F1; branch over the size profile of F0 and F1.

Orbit-ILP: aggregate subsets by size and by intersection with a fixed small set, solve the symmetric relaxation for an upper bound, then close the gap with symmetry-broken SAT and cardinality constraints.
Lower bounds: tabu or simulated annealing on the 512-vertex conflict graph, seeded with the Frankl-Füredi family and with doublings of the n = 8 optima.
pitfalls: Convention: OEIS forbids |A ∩ B| = r only for distinct A, B (so T(n,n) = 2^n); the erdosproblems wording 'for all A, B' would also forbid r-sets. Use the OEIS convention.
Triangle indexing: row n has n+1 entries, and b-file index 45 is T(9,0) = 256, so the open b-file indices are 47 = T(9,2) and 48 = T(9,3).

T(9,4), T(9,5) and T(9,6) (256, 382, 466) and T(10,5..7) (638, 848, 968) follow from the rows above them: the split bound T(n,r) <= T(n-1,r) + T(n-1,r-1) is met by the family of all sets of size <= r. Computing them is not a win.
Complementation does not preserve intersection sizes, so it is not a symmetry of the problem; only S_9 acts.
Unsound symmetry breaking gives a wrong 'optimum'; the verifier must be able to regenerate and justify every symmetry-breaking clause.

targets.name: Erdős #1023 small cases: 80 subsets of an 8-set with no member a union of others (OEIS A347025; best known 79, upper bound 89)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: F(n) is the largest family of nonempty subsets of {1..n} in which no member is the union of other members (OEIS A347025, Jukka Kohonen 2021, keyword more). Equivalently, it is the maximum number of meet-irreducible elements in a lattice with n join-irreducibles (Süskind, Sep 2026). Erdős Problem #1023 asks for its asymptotics; they follow from Kleitman's solution of #447: F(n) ~ C(n, n/2). Known values for n = 0..7 are 0, 1, 2, 4, 7, 13, 24, 44. a(6) = 24 is due to Jinyuan Wang (2022). a(7) = 44 is due to William Blair (6 Jun 2026), who closed Wang's 44 <= a(7) <= 45 with an exhaustive OR-Tools CP-SAT search under two independent encodings and published a 44-set witness and verifier. For n = 8 the best lower bound is 79, from Jon E. Schoenfield's 2022 construction family, which gives 79, 144 and 270 for n = 8, 9, 10 (against C(n, ceil(n/2)) = 70, 126, 252). Andy Loo's recursive bound a(n) <= min_h a(h) + 2^h·a(n-h) (arXiv:1511.00170) with a(7) = 44 gives a(8) <= 1 + 2·44 = 89. So 79 <= a(8) <= 89 on 2026-10-30, with the entry last edited 2026-09-27.
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit list of at least 80 distinct nonempty subsets of {1..8} (direction: max, strictly above 79) such that no member S equals the union of the other members contained in S. The verifier checks this for every S, which covers unions of any number of other members. The size must exceed every value in the live https://oeis.org/A347025 entry, its comments, links and history, re-fetched immediately before claiming, and any value found in a fresh literature check. More than 89 sets contradicts Loo's bound and means a bug.

partial_wins.statement: An explicit union-free family (same check) of at least 145 subsets of {1..9} or at least 271 subsets of {1..10}, beating Schoenfield's construction values 144 and 270.

A certified upper bound a(8) <= 88 or lower, i.e. an LRAT-checked UNSAT proof (or VIPR certificate) that no union-free family of size 89 on {1..8} exists, on a CNF/ILP the skeptic regenerates from the published encoding.
The exact value of a(8) (including the case a(8) = 79): an explicit family of that size plus an optimality certificate of the p2 standard.

targets.verification_method: For each member S, OR together all other members T with T ⊂ S and assert the result is not S. Check distinctness and non-emptiness. For upper bounds, regenerate the encoding (x_S selects S; S selected implies some element of S is covered by no selected proper subset of S) and check the proof with cake_lpr or a VIPR checker. Reproduce a(4..7) with the same code first.
angles: Reuse Blair's published CP-SAT model and verifier (linked from A347025): it reproduces a(4..7), so add S_8 symmetry breaking and a solution hint from Schoenfield's 79-set family, and run with many workers.

Build structured families: a near-middle layer plus extra sets in adjacent layers chosen so that no added set is covered by its subsets in the family; Schoenfield's formula is one such scheme, so try other layer profiles by ILP over orbit counts.
Local search with incremental checks: maintain for every set the union of its family subsets; add/remove moves update only supersets and subsets, so tabu search on 255 candidates is fast.
pitfalls: 'Union of other members' includes unions of any number of members, not only of two (two is Erdős #447, a different problem).
The empty set is excluded in A347025's convention (it would be the empty union).
Loo's table predates a(6) and a(7); recompute the recursive upper bound with the current values rather than copying the published table.

targets.name: Erdős #20 small cases (Erdős-Rado sunflower numbers): beat Abbott et al.'s 38 three-sets with no 4-sunflower, 54 four-sets with no 3-sunflower, or 88 three-sets with no 5-sunflower (OEIS A332077)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-hours
targets.statement: Erdős Problem #20 concerns f(m,k), the largest family of m-element sets with no k-sunflower: no k members whose pairwise intersections all equal one common core, which may be empty. Erdős's $1000 prize is for the open asymptotic conjecture f(m,k) < c_k^m, not for these small cases. OEIS A332077 (M. F. Hasler, keyword more) tabulates Sun(m,n) = f + 1 for sets of size at most m. Padding each set with its own new points shows the uniform and 'at most m' versions agree. Known exactly: Sun(1,k) = k, Sun(m,2) = 2, Sun(2,k) by the Abbott-Hanson-Sauer formula (1972), and Sun(3,3) = 21. Three small cells are open, and their lower bounds have stood for decades. Sun(3,4) >= 39: a 38-set 3-uniform family with no 4-sunflower (Abbott-Exoo 1992). Sun(4,3) >= 55: 54 four-sets with no 3-sunflower (Abbott-Hanson-Sauer 1972). Sun(3,5) >= 89: 88 three-sets with no 5-sunflower (Abbott-Hanson 1974). Kyle Wood posted explicit example files for all three in Oct-Nov 2025, and the entry was last edited 2025-11-11. On 2026-10-30 the files were re-checked with an independent SAT-based checker: 38, 54 and 88 distinct sets, with no sunflower of the stated size. The next unknown term of A332077 is Sun(3,4). This is the uniform Erdős-Rado problem, not the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower-free capacity of subsets of [n] (a separate bank entry).
targets.success_criterion: Success means an explicit family F of distinct sets, all of the same size m, containing no k members with pairwise equal intersections (direction: max). It must have |F| >= 39 for (m,k) = (3,4), |F| >= 55 for (4,3), or |F| >= 89 for (3,5). The size must be strictly above the live lower bound Sun(m,k) - 1 shown in https://oeis.org/A332077 and its example files, re-fetched immediately before claiming, and above any value found in a fresh literature check. The verifier checks every possible core C (every proper subset of a member, including the empty set) and confirms that the petals {S \ C : S in F, C ⊆ S} contain no k pairwise disjoint sets. It uses two independent implementations: exhaustive search, and SAT with a cardinality constraint.

partial_wins.statement: The exact value of one of the three cells, e.g. Sun(3,4) = 39. This needs a complete proof that no larger family exists, with the ground-set reduction written out as checkable lemmas and the computational part ending in LRAT-checked UNSAT certificates or a Lean proof.

An explicit 5-uniform family with no 3-sunflower and more than 160 members, or a 4-uniform family with no 4-sunflower and more than 114 members. These beat the lower bounds f(5,3) >= 160 and f(4,4) >= 114 in the small-values table of the Wikipedia Sunflower article (from Abbott-Hanson-Sauer 1972 and Abbott-Exoo 1992). It counts only if the skeptic finds no larger published value for that cell.

targets.verification_method: For each core C (enumerate all subsets of members), collect the petals of the members containing C and test with two independent methods (backtracking and SAT) whether k pairwise disjoint petals exist. Check uniformity and distinctness. Re-run the checker on Kyle Wood's OEIS files (38, 54, 88 sets) as a positive control, and on a family with an added sunflower as a negative control.
angles: Inspect Wood's example files: the 54-set family is a union of two isomorphic 27-set blocks on disjoint 9-point sets, and the 38 and 88 families have visible structure; search for one-set extensions or two-out-three-in swaps with SAT.
Restrict to families invariant under a group on v points (cyclic, affine AGL(1,p), PSL(2,q)) and solve the orbit-selection problem exactly with SAT, adding sunflower constraints only between orbits.

Product lemma: if F1 and F2 on disjoint ground sets have no k-sunflower, neither does {A ∪ B}; it gives baselines such as 3·38 = 114 for the 4-uniform 4-petal cell, but beating the p2 bars needs better blocks or non-product constructions.
Tabu search with incremental conflict counts: for each core C keep the petals and a disjointness structure so a move updates only the cores inside the changed set.
pitfalls: Three pairwise disjoint sets form a 3-sunflower (empty core); forgetting empty cores inflates families.
OEIS uses Sun = (largest sunflower-free family) + 1 and 'at least n petals'; some papers use f(k,r) for 'more than r'; off-by-one errors are common.
The $1000 Erdős prize is for the asymptotic conjecture; no small-case record claims it.
Do not mix this up with sunflower-free capacity on a fixed ground set [n] (non-uniform, a separate bank entry).

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Chvátal's conjecture (Erdős #701): a downset whose largest intersecting subfamily beats every star, or a certified verification for ground sets of 8 elements
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (for a certified ground-set-8 verification); a counterexample search is laptop-days
targets.statement: Chvátal's conjecture (1974; Erdős Problem #701, open on erdosproblems.com on 2026-10-30) says: if F is a finite family closed under taking subsets (a downset), then some maximum-size intersecting subfamily of F is a star {A in F : x in A}. Several special cases are proved: Chvátal's own (families compressed with respect to an order), Sterboul (1974), Kleitman-Magnanti (1972) and Frankl-Kupavskii (2023) for intersecting subfamilies with covering number 2, and Borg (2011) for weighted versions. The computational frontier is the ground-set size. Eifler, Gleixner and Pulaj ('Chvátal's Conjecture Holds for Ground Sets of Seven Elements', Zuse Institute Berlin report, 2018) verified every downset on at most 7 elements with exact-arithmetic integer programming. The erdosproblems forum thread (comments up to 22 May 2026) cites no larger verification, and the problem page lists none. There are D(8) ≈ 5.6e22 downsets on 8 points (the Dedekind number), so any ground-set-8 approach needs symmetry and IP/SAT reasoning rather than enumeration. The formal-conjectures repository has a Lean statement (ErdosProblems/701.lean).
targets.success_criterion: Success means a counterexample: an explicit downset F, given by its maximal members on a finite ground set, and an explicit intersecting subfamily G of F with |G| strictly greater than max over x of |{A in F : x in A}| (direction: exceed every star). The verifier generates F as the down-closure of the maximal members and checks that G ⊆ F with distinct members. It checks that members of G pairwise intersect, so the empty set cannot be in G, computes every star size exactly, and compares. By the 2018 verification, any counterexample has at least 8 ground elements.

partial_wins.statement: A certified verification that the conjecture holds for all downsets on 8 elements. Every computational step must carry a certificate an independent checker accepts (VIPR for exact IP, or LRAT for SAT), and the code must regenerate every subproblem. It counts only if the skeptic finds no earlier published verification for 8 elements.

A Lean 4 proof, with no sorry and only standard axioms, of the covering-number-2 case (Kleitman-Magnanti 1972, Frankl-Kupavskii 2023), in the setting of the formal-conjectures definitions for Erdős #701. The statement: for every finite nonempty type X, every lower set F of Set X and every intersecting F' ⊆ F such that some set of at most 2 elements meets every member of F', there is x with #F' <= #{A ∈ F : x ∈ A}. It counts only if no formal proof of this case is already public.

targets.verification_method: For a counterexample: compute the down-closure by bitmask enumeration over subsets of each maximal member, verify G's membership and pairwise intersection, and compute all star sizes with two independent scripts. For p1: replay the IP/SAT certificates with VIPR or cake_lpr and audit the symmetry reduction. For p2: lake build against the pinned toolchain and #print axioms.
angles: Follow Eifler-Gleixner-Pulaj: for a fixed downset, the largest intersecting subfamily is a maximum-weight independent set problem; reformulate 'all downsets on 8 points' as one IP over downset indicator variables with symmetry breaking, solved by an exact solver that emits VIPR certificates.

Search for counterexamples among downsets generated by few maximal sets with large symmetry groups (designs, Kneser-like layers), where both the star sizes and the intersecting optimum can be computed exactly and fast.
Known proved cases (compressed families, covering number 2) rule out large regions; encode them as cuts to shrink the ground-set-8 search.
pitfalls: The conjecture compares with the largest star inside F, not the star in the full power set.
The empty set lies in every non-empty downset but in no intersecting subfamily of size >= 2; handle it consistently in both counts.
Infinite ground sets are discussed on the forum but are not the target; the criterion is finite.

targets.name: MOONSHOT - Eternity II: the full 480-edge solution, or a board beating the 470/480 record (or the 465 five-clue record)
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (the 470 boards took about a month on a 32-core home Threadripper with Blackwood's solver; scoring a board takes laptop-minutes)
targets.statement: Eternity II (designed by Christopher Monckton, sold by Tomy from 28 July 2007) is a 16 x 16 edge-matching puzzle: 256 square pieces, 22 colours, a grey frame, and a mandatory starter piece (id 138 counting from 0, piece 139 counting from 1) fixed at I8, which is cell 135 in row-major order counting from 0, rotation 0. A full solve matches all 2 x 15 x 16 = 480 internal edges. The $2M prize expired unclaimed at noon on 31 December 2010, and no 480 board on the official set has ever been published. Record history on the official set, starter clue only: 467 by Louis Verhaard (2008, won the $10,000 partial prize); 468 and then 470 by Joshua Blackwood (2020; 470 on 2021-03-30, eternity2 groups.io #10117); 469 by Peter McGavin (2020); Jef Bucas tied 470 on 2024-12-02. All five optional clue placements respected: 460 by Bruno Gauthier (2023), 464 by Benjamin Riotte (July 2026), then 465 from Riotte's shared five-clue fleet (August 2026). The community record page (Raphael Anjou's eternity2.dev, updated 2026-07-22) lists 470 and 465 as standing. This lane re-scored Blackwood's 470 board from the eternity2.dev viewer link with its own checker: the 256 cells are exactly the official piece multiset (after a colour relabelling), the frame is all grey, the starter piece sits at cell 135, rotation 0, and 470 internal edges match.
targets.success_criterion: A 16 x 16 placement of the official 256 Eternity II pieces (each piece used exactly once, any rotation) in which every frame edge is grey, the starter piece (id 138 from 0) sits at cell 135 (I8) at its official rotation, and all 480 internal edges match. Use the piece set in raphael-anjou/eternity2 research/starter-kit/data/official.json, which is identical to the community e2pieces/CSV set. Boards on other piece sets do not count: Brendan Owen's Clue-1/Clue-2 sets, the unframed TopCoder variant, and mixed expansion sets.

partial_wins.statement: A starter-only board on the official set (same rules as the success criterion) with 471 to 479 matching internal edges, strictly above the open record of 470 (Blackwood 2021, tied by Bucas 2024), provided the record on eternity2.dev/research/records is still 470 at verification time.

A board that respects all five official clue placements listed in official.json (cell 135 with piece 138 at rotation 0, cell 210 with piece 180 at rotation 1, cell 34 with piece 207 at rotation 1, cell 221 with piece 248 at rotation 2, cell 45 with piece 254 at rotation 1; cells counted row-major from 0, rotation convention as in that file) and has at least 466 matching internal edges, strictly above the 465 five-clue record (Riotte and the five-clue fleet, August 2026), provided that record still stands at verification time.

targets.verification_method: Write an independent checker that does not reuse a solver's code. (1) Load official.json: 256 pieces as URDL edge integers, with 0 for grey. (2) Parse the claimed board as 256 cells of URDL colours. If the colour labels differ (the eternity2.dev viewer uses letters a..w), find the colour bijection that makes the multiset of rotation-canonical cells equal to the official multiset. This also proves each piece is used exactly once. (3) Check that every frame-facing edge is grey. (4) Check that the starter cell equals piece 138 at its official rotation, plus the other four clues for p2. (5) Count matching horizontal and vertical internal edges out of 480. Cross-check the score in Jef Bucas's viewer at e2.bucas.name or the eternity2.dev viewer, both of which re-score a board from its own edges.
angles: Blackwood's solver (heuristic placement schedule with break-index limits) and Bucas's C rewrite libblackwood are the methods behind every 468-470 board. Retuning the break schedule took Blackwood from 469 to 470.

Treat the last ten broken edges as an exact sub-problem: free a region around the breaks and re-solve it exactly by SAT, CP or DLX with all remaining pieces, as on eternity2.dev's 'tail as its own exact problem' page.
Verhaard's 2008 approach annealed the composition of piece sets between regions, not only positions.
pitfalls: Many '480/480' boards online use other piece sets (Clue-1/Clue-2, TopCoder unframed, mixed sets). They are not solutions of Eternity II.
Starter-only and five-clue scores are different records. Do not compare a five-clue board with 470, or a starter-only board with 465.
Record announcements sit on the eternity2 groups.io list, which needs an account to read. Agents never sign up for anything: use eternity2.dev's records page and board viewer instead.
Piece files in different tools label colours differently. Always map colours back to official.json before claiming a score.

targets.name: Langford's problem: the number of Langford pairings L(2,31) or L(2,32), or the next Nickerson-Skolem (V(2,32), V(2,33)) or planar (P(43), P(44)) counts
targets.compute_profile: needs cluster (Godfrey-type inclusion-exclusion over about 2^62 sign vectors for n = 31; pruned planar searches may be laptop-days)
targets.statement: Langford's problem (C. Dudley Langford, 1958): arrange 1,1,2,2,...,n,n so that the two copies of k have exactly k numbers between them. L(2,n) counts solutions up to reversal (OEIS A014552). It is nonzero iff n = 0 or 3 mod 4. Known values: L(2,15), L(2,16) in the 1980s; L(2,19) 1999; L(2,20) 2002 (Godfrey's algebraic method); L(2,23) = 3,799,455,942,515,488 (Krajecki, Jaillet and Bui, 2004); L(2,24) 2005; L(2,27) = 111,683,611,098,764,903,232 and L(2,28) = 1,607,383,260,609,382,393,152 (Assarpour, Bar-Noy and Liu, arXiv:1507.00315, 2015). John E. Miller's Langford page (dialectrix.com) says that all n >= 31 are unknown. Zan Pan (2021) gave asymptotic estimates. Related tables: Nickerson's variant, where the two k's have k-1 numbers between them (Skolem-type, OEIS A059106, nonzero for n = 0, 1 mod 4), is listed through n = 31. The last nonzero terms, n = 28 and 29, come from Assarpour et al. (added in 2023), and a(30) = a(31) = 0, so V(2,32) and V(2,33) are next. Planar Langford sequences, where arcs joining equal numbers can be drawn without crossing (OEIS A125762), are known through n = 42. Knuth computed them through n = 28 (2007), Rory Molinari added n = 31 to 35 in 2018, and Edward Moody added n = 36 to 42 in April 2019. a(41) = a(42) = 0, so P(43) and P(44) are next. All three OEIS entries were re-fetched on 2026-10-30 and show these ranges.
targets.success_criterion: The exact value of L(2,31) or L(2,32), the first unknown terms of OEIS A014552 at verification time. It must come with complete source code and a run log, and be confirmed by a second independent computation (different code, or a different method such as direct enumeration on a subrange plus the algebraic formula), with agreement on every digit. Any claimed value must also pass consistency checks: the method must reproduce L(2,n) exactly for all n <= 28, and the value must be of the size predicted by Zan Pan's asymptotic formula.

partial_wins.statement: The exact Nickerson-variant count V(2,32) or V(2,33) (the next nonzero terms of OEIS A059106, which is listed through n = 31), verified as in the success criterion, with the method reproducing all known terms.
The exact planar Langford count P(43) or P(44) (the next terms of OEIS A125762 beyond n = 42), verified as in the success criterion, with the method reproducing all known planar terms.

An independent recomputation of L(2,27) and L(2,28), with code independent of Assarpour-Bar-Noy-Liu, that matches the OEIS values exactly, together with measured timings that project the cost of n = 31.

targets.verification_method: Rerun the released code on small n and check every known term of A014552, A059106 or A125762. For a new term, require two independent computations to agree. Where the Godfrey formula is used (a signed sum over plus-or-minus-one vectors of products of polynomial sums), recompute modulo several large primes in a separate implementation and check against the exact big-integer value.
pitfalls: A014552 counts up to reversal. A176127 counts ordered arrangements, which is twice as many. Do not mix the two conventions.
n = 29 and 30 are zero for L(2,n), since n must be 0 or 3 mod 4. The first unknown nonzero terms are n = 31 and 32.

targets.name: Longest uncrossed knight's path: settle the open 10 x 10 value (OEIS A003192, best known 61) or the closed 11 x 11 value (A157416, best known 70)
targets.compute_profile: laptop-days (heuristic search for longer paths is laptop-hours; an exhaustive optimality proof for 10 x 10 is laptop-days or more)
targets.statement: L. D. Yarbrough (1968-69) asked for the longest knight's path on an n x n board whose move segments, drawn as straight lines between square centres, never cross. The open-path maximum (OEIS A003192) is known for n <= 9: 0,0,2,5,10,17,24,35,47. Donald Knuth confirmed a(9) = 47 with ZDDs in 2010. The closed-cycle maximum (OEIS A157416) is known for n <= 10, ending in 54 on 10 x 10. Wikipedia (edited April 2026) states that open paths are known only for n <= 9 and closed ones only for n <= 10. Derek Kisman (2018, written up by Tanya Khovanova in 2023) computed exact closed values for all 3 x N to 10 x N strips and open values for 3 x N to 9 x N, using a periodicity argument. The best-known table for m x n boards up to 31 x 31 is Alex Chernov's, from his own and Kisman's searches. His site ukt.alex-black.ru no longer answers, but the Wayback Machine copy of 2021-04-16 lists 61 for the open 10 x 10 path and 70 for the closed 11 x 11 cycle. An older table by Jean-Charles Meyrignac (euler.free.fr/knight) also gives 61 for open 10 x 10, credited mainly to Robin Merson and George Jelliss.
targets.success_criterion: Either (a) an uncrossed open knight's path on the 10 x 10 board with at least 62 moves, strictly above the best known 61, or a reproducible exhaustive proof that 61 is the maximum, which settles A003192(10); or (b) an uncrossed closed knight's cycle on the 11 x 11 board with at least 72 moves (cycles have even length), strictly above 70, or a reproducible exhaustive proof that 70 is the maximum, which settles A157416(11). Proofs must be independently re-run and should reproduce the known values a(n) for n <= 9 (open) and n <= 10 (closed).

partial_wins.statement: An uncrossed open knight's path on an m x n board with 10 <= m <= n <= 31, or an uncrossed closed cycle on an m x n board with 11 <= m <= n <= 31, strictly longer than the corresponding entry in Chernov's archived table (web.archive.org copy of 2021-04-16). Rows with smaller m are proven optimal by Kisman and cannot be beaten.

targets.verification_method: Check that the claimed sequence of squares consists of legal knight moves, visits no square twice (except the closing return for a cycle), and stays on the board. Then test every pair of non-adjacent move segments for intersection, including touching and collinear overlap, using exact integer orientation tests. Count the moves. For optimality proofs, rerun the search code and confirm that it reproduces the known smaller values.
pitfalls: Length means the number of moves, not the number of squares visited.
Chernov's live site is gone, and the best-known table is only available as a 2021 Wayback copy. Check OEIS and Wikipedia for newer values before claiming.

targets.name: Smallest multimagic squares and cubes: a tetramagic square below order 243, a pentamagic below 729, a hexamagic below 4096, a trimagic of order 13 or 15, or a bimagic cube below order 16
targets.compute_profile: pure thought (algebraic or product constructions) with laptop-hours of search and checking
targets.statement: A normal k-multimagic square of order n uses 1..n^2 once each, and the sums of the entries' j-th powers are equal along every row, column and both main diagonals, for each j = 1..k. Christian Boyer's multimagie.com keeps the records. Bimagic: smallest order 8 (G. Pfeffermann, 1890; orders below 8 are impossible). Trimagic: smallest 12 (Walter Trump, 2002; below 12 is impossible, as is 14). Orders 13 and 15 are open: none is known, and none has been proven impossible.
